The Name — ỉmn and the Hidden One Amun's Egyptian name is ỉmn [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35] [𓇋𓅓𓈖] — three consonants, i-m-n , written with the reed i [Gardiner: M17] [𓇋], the owl m [Gardiner: G17] [𓅓], and the water ripple n [Gardiner: N35] [𓈖]. Egyptian writing does not record vowels, so the familiar spellings — Amun, Amon, Amen, Ammon — are all modern attempts at a sound the script itself never wrote down. Egyptologists reconstruct an early pronunciation close to Yamānu , later Amānu ; Coptic preserved the name as Amoun , and Greek writers rendered it Ammōn , identifying the god outright with Zeus. The spelling used in the archive's Amarna article is the same three-sign spelling given here: [𓇋𓅓𓈖]. What the name means is the god's whole theology in miniature. ỉmn [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35] is also a verb: "to hide, to be hidden, to conceal." The god's name is therefore conventionally translated "the Hidden One" — not as a nickname added later, but as the plain sense of the word itself. A fuller spelling found in the scholarly literature writes the name with the game-board sign mn [Gardiner: Y5] [𓏠], giving ỉmn [Gardiner: M17-Y5-N35] [𓇋𓏠𓈖], and temple spellings add the seated-god determinative nṯr [Gardiner: A40] [𓀭]. This article uses the simple phonetic spelling throughout, because it is the spelling a reader can decode sign by sign, and decoding is the archive's standard. Hiddenness was predicated of Amun from the beginning. In the Pyramid Texts of the Old Kingdom, Amun first appears in writing beside his female counterpart Amaunet (§446c, Utterance 301); a separate passage (§276c), whose unnamed addressee is conventionally read as Ra, has the dead king addressing a great god whose name is unknown — Wim van den Dungen's published translation of the early texts renders it: "O You, the Great God, whose name is unknown" (Pyramid Texts §276c, reign of Unis, c. 2350 BCE, as cited in Section XX). The epithet that grows from this root is exact: ỉmn-rn.f [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35-D21-N35-I9] [𓇋𓅓𓈖𓂋𓈖𓆑], "hidden of his name" — rn [Gardiner: D21-N35] [𓂋𓈖], "name," with the suffix .f , "his." In a culture where the name — the rn [Gardiner: D21-N35] — was a constituent part of the person, a god whose name is hidden is a god whose innermost self cannot be seized, spoken against, or worked upon by anyone else's heka . // READING THE SIGNS IN THIS ARTICLE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used and flagged: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . The name's hiddenness cuts in two directions, and both matter for everything that follows. Negatively, it is a doctrine of unknowability : Amun cannot be defined, depicted truly, or exhausted by any list of forms — Section IV follows the Ramesside hymns that state this with startling completeness. Positively, hiddenness is a doctrine of presence everywhere : the hidden god is the air and the wind, felt on the skin and in the sail but never seen — ṯꜣw [Gardiner: V13-G1-G43] [𓍿𓄿𓅱], "wind, breath," is the word the hymns reach for. A god who is wind can be in Thebes and in Nubia and in a workman's courtyard at the same moment, because no wall and no distance excludes air. The smallest fact about Amun — three consonants meaning "hidden" — already contains the largest claims ever made for him. One caution governs the etymology. That ỉmn [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35] "hidden" and the god's name are the same word is not in doubt; what scholars debate is the direction of derivation — whether the god was named from the quality, or the quality's theological weight was read back into an older proper name. The archive states the position plainly: the Egyptians themselves understood the name as "the Hidden One," exploited that sense in hymns, epithets, and wordplay for two thousand years, and it is their understanding, not a modern reconstruction of origins, that an article on the god must report. II. Amun in the Ogdoad — Hermopolis and the Eight Before Amun was king of gods he was one of eight. At Hermopolis — Egyptian ḫmnw [Gardiner: Aa1-Y5-G43] [𓐍𓏠𓅱], "the Eight (Town)," the city whose very name is the number — the priests taught that before creation there existed four pairs of primordial powers, male and female, frog-headed and snake-headed, swimming in the darkness before the first dawn. The system is the Ogdoad , and the archive treats it in full in Ennead and Ogdoad . Amun's place in it is the last and strangest of the four pairs. NUN AND NAUNET — THE WATERS nwn [Gardiner: N35-G43-N35] [𓈖𓅱𓈖] and his counterpart: the primeval water, the inert ocean out of which the first mound would rise. The Ogdoad begins in a flood that has not yet receded because land has not yet been invented. HEH AND HAUHET — INFINITY ḥḥ [Gardiner: V28-V28] [𓎛𓎛] and ḥḥt [Gardiner: V28-V28-X1] [𓎛𓎛𓏏]: endlessness of space and of time, the pair whose name is also the word for "millions" — the scale on which creation would be laid out. KEK AND KAUKET — DARKNESS kk [Gardiner: V31-V31] [𓎡𓎡] and kkt [Gardiner: V31-V31-X1] [𓎡𓎡𓏏]; their fuller form kkw [Gardiner: V31-V31-G43] [𓎡𓎡𓅱] is the ordinary word for darkness itself — the condition of a world with no sun in it yet. AMUN AND AMAUNET — HIDDENNESS ỉmn [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35] [𓇋𓅓𓈖] and ỉmnt [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35-X1] [𓇋𓅓𓈖𓏏], the feminine ending -t [Gardiner: X1] [𓏏] making Amaunet grammatically what she is theologically: Amun's own hiddenness doubled back on itself as a pair. The Ogdoad are not creator gods in the ordinary sense. They are pre-conditions : water, infinity, darkness, and hiddenness are what must already be true before a first thing can happen. The creation, in Hermopolitan telling, is what these eight do together — their commotion in the waters raises the primeval mound, and on the mound the first light is born, whether as an egg, a lotus, or a child. Thoth — ḏḥwty [Gardiner: G26] [𓅝] — is Hermopolis's own god and the Ogdoad's overseer in later telling, but the Eight themselves belong to no city and no dynasty. They are older than the world they make possible. Amun's membership matters for his later career in a way the other seven never shared. Nun stayed a cosmic abstraction; Heh became a supporting figure at the edge of scenes; Kek faded. Amun alone walked out of the primordial group, acquired a city, a wife, a son, a temple-state, and an empire — and then, in New Kingdom theology, turned around and claimed to have been the Ogdoad's secret all along: the one who was hidden within the eight, their innermost member and finally their source. The Leiden Hymns (Section IV) say in paraphrase that the Eight were Amun's first form, the shape he wore before he had finished becoming single. That is a Theban claim, made by Theban priests about a Hermopolitan system, and the archive reports it as such — a claim, not a neutral fact of Hermopolitan doctrine. The older city kept its own counsel; its god was Thoth, and its eight stayed eight. Amaunet's trajectory is the mirror image. She is fully Amun's equal in the Pyramid Texts and the Ogdoad — arguably the older attested form of the pair's idea, hiddenness itself wearing a feminine ending. At Thebes she was gradually displaced in the god's household by Mut (Section VIII), and survives there in a smaller, older precinct role and in the Ogdoadic chapels, while at Hermopolis she kept her primordial place. Her story is a useful corrective to any account of Egyptian religion as a finished system: even the king of gods began as half of a pair, and the half he began with was not the consort history kept. III. Iconography — Two Plumes, the Ram and the Hidden Form Amun is, paradoxically, one of the most recognisable gods in Egypt — recognisable precisely as the god whose true form cannot be shown. His standard image is a man: seated on a throne or striding, wearing a close-fitting flat cap from which rise two tall parallel plumes , the šwty [Gardiner: S9] [𓋛]. The plumes are divided vertically and banded horizontally; their name is a dual — "the Two Feathers" — built on šwt [Gardiner: H6] [𓆄], "feather." The Metropolitan Museum's records use exactly this diagnostic: its post-Amarna heads of Amun (07.228.34; 07.228.35) are identified by the braided divine beard and the flat cap with the remnants of the double plumes, and its Third Intermediate Period seated figures by the same flat crown "to which tall feathers were once attached." When the plumes are lost, the cap and beard still name the god. In his hands Amun carries the ordinary furniture of divine rule: the ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] [𓋹], "life," the wꜣs -sceptre [Gardiner: S40] [𓌀] of dominion, and often the ḫpš [Gardiner: Aa1-Q3-N37] [𓐍𓊪𓈙], the curved scimitar. The Met's solid-gold statuette of Amun (26.7.1412, c. 945–721 BCE) — an extremely rare survival of the precious-metal cult images that ancient descriptions place in the sanctuaries — shows the complete kit at under eighteen centimetres: flat crown with its suspension loop, braided beard, ankh in the left hand, scimitar across the chest. The British Museum's bronze Amun (EA64505, Late Period) adds a telling detail: a small squatting figure of mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: G17-G1-D36-X1] [𓅓𓄿𓂝𓏏] at the end of the god's base — the king of gods presented, even in miniature, standing upon right order. His flesh in painting is frequently blue — the blue of lapis lazuli and of the sky through which the hidden air moves. The colour is a theological statement in pigment: Amun's body is made of the same invisible element he is. The van den Dungen study of the hymns makes the connection explicitly, reading the blue flesh together with the twin plumes as signs of a god of air — as the wind, Amun can be felt but not seen, except in his effects, as blowing air moves through feathers. What the image shows, therefore, is never the god himself. It is the god's effects made visible : plume, colour, crown, and sceptre are a diagram of hiddenness, not a portrait. The Ram, the Goose and Kamutef Amun's sacred animal is the ram — specifically a breed with horizontally curving horns, kept in image along the processional avenues of Karnak as ram-headed sphinxes under whose chins the king's small figure stands protected. The ram is also the sign of the bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝] — the word for the mobile, manifesting power of a god or soul in the composite soul , written with the ram sign in the corrected post-audit value used in this archive. The pun is the doctrine: the ram is Amun's bꜣ [Gardiner: E10], the form in which the hidden god puts himself forth. In Nubia the balance tips further, and Amun is shown ram-headed outright (Section XVI); the British Museum's granite statue from Kawa, in which a recumbent ram shelters the standing figure of King Taharqa between its forelegs, is the type at its most monumental. A second animal belongs to Amun's primeval register: the goose, whose honking cry, in one Hermopolitan-Theban telling, was the first sound to break the silence of the waters — the hidden god announcing creation before there was light to see it by. And a third form fuses Amun with the fertility god Min: as Amun Kamutef , kꜣ-mwt.f [Gardiner: E1-G14-I9] [𓃒𓅐𓆑] — "Bull of His Mother," kꜣ [Gardiner: E1], "bull," upon mwt [Gardiner: G14] [𓅐], "mother" — he is the self-begetting god, ithyphallic, one arm raised bearing a flail, the father of his own mother and therefore his own ancestor. The British Museum holds hollow- and solid-cast figures of exactly this ithyphallic Amun-or-Min type, double-plumed and flail-bearing (EA69528; EA60046). Kamutef is not an eccentricity at the edge of the cult. He is the answer to the question every creator theology must answer — who made the maker? — given in a single name: his mother did, and he is his mother's bull. Finally, the images must be read with the archive's standing caution about all divine iconography: the cult statue in the sanctuary was not believed to be the god in the way a stone is a stone. It was a body the god's bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] could choose to inhabit for the purposes of the cult — fed, washed, dressed, and carried in procession under the daily temple ritual — while the god himself remained what his name says. Egyptian image-theology and Amun's hiddenness are not in tension. They are the same idea stated in wood, gold, and doctrine respectively: presence is real, and it is never exhausted by the thing present. IV. The Hiddenness Theology — the Leiden Hymns to Amun The fullest statement of what Amun's hiddenness means is a Ramesside papyrus: the Hymns to Amun of Papyrus Leiden I 350 , written in the Nineteenth Dynasty, in or near the reign of Ramesses II. The manuscript is a collection of hymns arranged in numbered chapters — the Egyptians' own chapter numbers run in hundreds — and its modern editions, above all Jan Zandee's great commentary and the translations that descend from it, made it the central text of what scholars call the New Kingdom theology of Amun. Jan Assmann built much of his account of Ramesside religion on it. It is quoted in this article under the archive's rule: verbatim only where a published translation has actually been read for this article, and as labelled paraphrase everywhere else. The one passage quoted verbatim is the hymn's statement of unknowability, from chapter 200, in Wim van den Dungen's translation ( Ancient Egyptian Readings , 2016, published on his study site and read in full for this article): "None of the gods knows His true form, His image is not unfolded in the papyrus rolls, nothing certain is testified about Him." — Hymns to Amun, Papyrus Leiden I 350, ch. 200, trans. van den Dungen Three denials, each precise. His form is not known — not even by the other gods, the beings best placed to know it. His image is not unfolded in the rolls — the temple libraries, which contained drawings and descriptions of everything else in heaven and earth, contain no true depiction; the statues of Section III are therefore acknowledged, by the cult itself, to be conventional. And nothing certain is testified — no report about his nature carries certainty. The hymn is not modest about this. Unknowability is not a failure of Egyptian theology in front of Amun. It is the theology. The same hymn-cycle, in paraphrase, extends the denial to all three registers in which a god might be grasped. His name is hidden: he is ỉmn-rn.f [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35-D21-N35-I9] [𓇋𓅓𓈖𓂋𓈖𓆑], hidden of name, and the hymns play on the fact that the name everyone uses — ỉmn [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35] [𓇋𓅓𓈖] — is itself the word for the concealment, so that to name him is to state that he cannot be named. His form is hidden: he is, in paraphrase, too great to be circumscribed, manifest in millions of forms while being confined to none. And his nature is hidden: the hymns describe a god who made himself, who began in the first time before any witness existed to report the event, and whose inner being therefore has no testimony behind it at all. Name, form, and nature — the three handles by which Egyptian thought gripped a person, the three things the composite soul is made of — are each, in Amun's case, declared ungraspable in turn. And yet the Leiden theologians were not agnostics, and the paraphrase must keep the hymn's second movement in view. The hidden god is simultaneously the manifest god, and the hymn-cycle's most famous chapter — chapter 300, given here in paraphrase, not quotation — resolves the whole pantheon into him: all gods, it says, are three — Amun, Ra , and Ptah — and these three are one god under three aspects: hidden as Amun in his name, Ra in his face, Ptah in his body. The archive's Ennead and Ogdoad article quotes the passage in the form in which it circulates in the literature; here it is paraphrased, because the translation read word-for-word for this article was a different chapter of the same papyrus. The doctrine itself is not in doubt: it is the high-water mark of Egyptian inclusive theology, in which other gods are neither denied nor demoted but contained — faces and bodies of the one hidden god. Two consequences follow, and both shape the rest of this article. First, a god who contains the other gods can absorb any of them by syncretism without loss — Amun-Ra (Section VII) is the Leiden doctrine wearing an older form. Second, a god who cannot be known by form or name can still be known by act : by the wind on the face, by the answered prayer, by the movement of his barque at the oracle. Ramesside religion's famous turn toward direct personal experience of the god (Section XIII) is not a contradiction of the hiddenness theology. It is its necessary complement. What cannot be known by description must be known by encounter — or not at all. V. Theban Beginnings — a Local God Becomes Patron of Thebes Amun's rise begins not with theology but with politics. Thebes — Egyptian wꜣst [Gardiner: R19] [𓋆], a name written with the wꜣs -sceptre [Gardiner: S40] itself — was an unimportant Upper Egyptian town through most of the Old Kingdom, its local war god the falcon-headed Montu, mnṯw [Gardiner: Y5-V13-G43] [𓏠𓍿𓅱]. Amun appears in the town's record as the Old Kingdom ends and the First Intermediate Period fragments the country. When the Theban Intef family fought its way north to reunify Egypt and founded the Middle Kingdom, it carried its gods with it — and by then the god it carried first was Amun. The hard evidence is unusually well fixed, thanks to Elaine Sullivan's survey for the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology, read in full for this article. The first incontrovertible evidence for a temple of Amun at Karnak comes from the reign of Intef II in the First Intermediate Period: a sandstone column of his, reused at Karnak, bears the name of Amun-Ra and records that the king made it as his monument for the god. Sullivan is equally clear about what the evidence does not show: Old Kingdom statuary found at Karnak does not prove an Old Kingdom temple there, and current excavation suggests no temple to Amun stood at Karnak before the First Intermediate Period. The archive follows Sullivan: Amun's Theban temple begins with the Theban kings who needed him, at the end of the third millennium BCE — not in a misty antiquity the stones cannot support. Why Amun, and why then? The sources give a political answer and a theological one, and both are probably true. Politically, a reunifying dynasty from a provincial town needed a god of its own stature: the old solar establishment of Heliopolis belonged to the north the Thebans were conquering, and Montu, the local falcon of war, was a fighter's god, too narrow for a kingdom. Amun — primordial, one of the Eight, older than creation in his own mythology — gave the upstart city a god as ancient as any in Egypt with no rival city attached to him. Theologically, the hidden god fitted a dynasty that had come from nowhere: his power, like theirs, had been present all along, unseen. By the Twelfth Dynasty the promotion was complete in stone. Senusret I rebuilt the Karnak temple greatly enlarged in limestone, with a portico of pillars bearing the king in the pose of Osiris — wsir [Gardiner: Q1-D4-A40] [𓊨𓁹𓀭] — and set along its processional routes the famous White Chapel, the calcite barque shrine whose reliefs of the king before Amun-Ra remain a high point of Middle Kingdom art (Section VI). The reunification kings also wrote Amun into their own names, and the names became the dynasty's signature. Amenemhat — "Amun is at the Head" — is borne by four kings of the Twelfth Dynasty; Ameny and Senusret alternate with it; and when the cycle repeated after the Hyksos period, the New Kingdom's founders did the same again on a larger scale: Amenhotep, "Amun is Satisfied," four times over. A god whose name sits inside the king's name is not a court fashion. He is the dynasty's charter, read aloud every time the king is announced. Compare Horus , whose name the king is : Amun's relation to kingship is different — not identity but sponsorship — and Section IX examines what that sponsorship cost and what it bought. Montu did not vanish. He kept his precinct at north Karnak and his towns at Armant, Tod, and Medamud, and remained a god of war to the end of Egyptian religion. But the patronage of Thebes had changed hands, and everyone in Egypt knew it: the town that would matter most in the second millennium BCE now belonged to the hidden god. The sacred geography of the archive maps Thebes as the imperial city whose temples made it a storehouse of divine power; the storehouse's owner, from the Middle Kingdom onward, is Amun. VI. Karnak — Ipet-isut and Fifteen Centuries of Building Karnak is not a temple. It is a city of temples that happens to have one landlord. The ancient name of Amun's precinct states its rank: ipt-swt [Gardiner: O15-S29-G43-X1] [𓉩𓋴𓅱𓏏], "the Most Select of Places" — ipt [Gardiner: O15] [𓉩], the private, chosen, innermost place. Sullivan's UCLA survey, the documentary spine of this section, traces more than 1,500 years of construction, destruction, renovation, and expansion in the precinct of Amun-Ra alone: four great sectors — Amun's central domain, Mut's precinct to the south, Montu's to the north, and the eastern quarter — bound together by processional avenues and a sacred lake, on the east bank of the Nile at Thebes, wꜣst [Gardiner: R19]. The growth pattern is the theology of Section IX rendered in architecture. Egyptian temples normally face a founding moment; Karnak faces an accumulation . Each king was expected to add — a pylon in front of his father's pylon, a hall behind it, obelisks in the court, a bark shrine on the processional route — and almost none was permitted to subtract. The result, read from the centre outward, is a stratigraphy of the Egyptian state itself. At the core: the Middle Kingdom court of Senusret I's limestone temple, its holy of holies lying, in Sullivan's reconstruction, off the main axis, reached by a turn — the hidden god's first stone house already arranged so that you could not walk straight at him. Around it, the early Eighteenth Dynasty wrapped courts, screen walls, and bark chapels, Amenhotep I adding the alabaster shrine on which Amun's processional barque first survives in representation. Then the empire built. Thutmose I drove the axis westward with pylons; Hatshepsut raised her twin obelisks and built the red quartzite bark shrine, the Chapelle Rouge; Thutmose III, the empire's great conqueror, enclosed the older shrine in his own, added the festival hall called the Akhmenu with its carved botanical garden of foreign plants brought home from campaign, and set up the annals of his wars on the temple walls — the god who had given the victories receiving their permanent record in his own house, a ḥwt-nṯr [Gardiner: O10-R8] [𓉡𓊹], "mansion of the god," that doubled as the empire's archive. Amenhotep III extended the southern axis toward Luxor with the tenth pylon and colossal works. The Ramessides roofed the space between pylons into the Great Hypostyle Hall — 134 columns, a stone forest through which the processional barque moved as through a petrified papyrus marsh at creation. Later ages did not stop: Kushite, Saite, and Ptolemaic rulers all built at Karnak, and the precinct's final great gesture, the massive first pylon and enclosure walls, belongs to Nectanebo I in the fourth century BCE — the last native dynasty still adding to a Middle Kingdom shrine. THE CENTRAL AXIS East–west, from the sanctuary through the hypostyle hall and the succession of pylons to the Nile quay: the route of the barque in procession, and the line along which fifteen centuries of kings queued to build. At its heart the barque shrine, where Amun's portable boat rested between festivals. THE SOUTHERN AXIS South from the Amun precinct through further pylons to Mut's temple and onward, by the avenue of ram-headed sphinxes, to Luxor Temple — the processional road of the Opet Festival (Section IX), walked by the god each year to renew the kingship. THE SACRED LAKE AND THE PRECINCTS The great lake south of the central temple served the priests' purifications and the god's ritual voyages; around the whole, the temples of Mut and Montu, the eastern temple of "Amun Who Hears Petitions" (Section XIII), treasuries, workshops, granaries, and priestly housing — a working city inside a wall. THE FOUNDATION RITE Every addition began with "stretching the cord": the king, with the goddess sšꜣt [Gardiner: R21] [𓋈] — Seshat, mistress of writing and measure, her name given in its corrected post-audit value — laid out the new building's plan on the ground, fixing the temple in the cosmos before a stone was cut. Two features of Karnak deserve emphasis because visitors, ancient and modern, consistently misread them. First, the darkness: the sanctuary at the axis's end was a small, nearly lightless room, entered through a sequence of ever-narrower, ever-darker halls, its great ꜥꜣ [Gardiner: O31] [𓉿] door-leaves — the word is given in its corrected value — opened only by the king and the highest priests. The architecture performs the name. You approach the Hidden One through graded concealment, and almost nobody, in three thousand years, was ever admitted to the last room. Second, the openness: the same precinct whose centre was sealed staged Egypt's most public religion at its edges — festival crowds in the outer courts, petitioners at the hearing-ear shrine on the eastern wall, litigants before the travelling barque. Karnak is not a compromise between a secret cult and a popular one. It is both, deliberately, in a single plan: hidden at the centre, heard at the walls. The temple the visitor walks today is the same argument in ruin. The archive's article on temple architecture gives the general grammar of such buildings; Karnak is that grammar's longest sentence. Nothing else in Egypt was built by so many hands for so long for one god — and the god in question is the one whose image, his own hymns insist, is not unfolded in any roll. The stones are not his portrait. They are his household. VII. Amun-Ra — Syncretism and the King of Gods Egyptian gods fuse. When two gods' spheres overlap, theology does not hold an election; it writes a double name, and the double name is a new god who is both of his parents and more than either. Amun's fusion is the most consequential in Egyptian history: ỉmn-rꜥ [Gardiner: M17-G17-N35-N5] [𓇋𓅓𓈖𓇳] — Amun-Ra — the hidden god joined to rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳], Ra, the sun god of Heliopolis, the oldest state god of Egypt. The fusion is already present on Intef II's column at the dawn of the Theban rise, and Sullivan notes the direction of travel precisely: existing texts refer to Amun-Ra only after the Old Kingdom, and the earliest Karnak cult was of Amun alone. The double god is a Theban creation of the reunification age, not an immemorial inheritance. What each partner contributed is legible in the compound. From Ra: visibility, antiquity, and the daily cosmic order — the sun's circuit as the guarantee that the world of ma'at , mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: G17-G1-D36-X1], continues; the royal genealogy, every king a "Son of Ra," sꜣ-rꜥ [Gardiner: G38-N5] [𓅬𓇳]; and the solar barque in which the god crosses the sky and the underworld. From Amun: hiddenness, primordiality, and wind — the power behind the visible order rather than the order itself. Amun-Ra is therefore not Ra with a Theban hat. He is a claim about the sun: that the most visible thing in the world is the face of something invisible. The Leiden paraphrase of Section IV states the finished doctrine exactly — as Amun he hides his name; he is Ra in face. The political yield was total. Heliopolis could not object: its god was not displaced but enthroned, given the empire's capital-temple as his house. Thebes could not object: its god's name came first. And the king inherited both legitimacies at once, son of Ra by titulary and sponsored son of Amun by oracle and divine birth (Section IX). By the early New Kingdom, after Ahmose I's expulsion of the Hyksos — a Theban victory credited to Thebes's god — Amun-Ra's supremacy was state doctrine: King of the Gods is not a courtesy title in the inscriptions but his standard style, and "Lord of the Thrones of the Two Lands," the epithet carried in this article's header, is how the Met's Ramesside barque stela (21.2.6) names the god whose portable shrine the hymn below it praises. Syncretism did not stop at Ra. The Leiden synthesis absorbs Ptah as Amun's body — Memphite theology, treated in the archive's Memphite Theology article, folded into the Theban one by containment rather than conquest. At the empire's edges the same operation runs outward: Amun of Napata in Nubia (Section XVI), Amun of Siwa in the western desert (Section XII), each a local face the Theban god could wear without ceasing to be himself. This absorptive capacity is the institutional form of the hiddenness doctrine. A god defined by a boundary can be contradicted by what lies outside it. A god defined by hiddenness cannot: whatever is found outside can always be declared to have been inside, unseen, all along. The archive registers one discipline about the phrase "King of the Gods" before moving on. It describes a rank , not a monopoly. Egypt under Amun-Ra's supremacy remained irreducibly polytheistic: temples to hundreds of gods were built by the same kings who hymned Amun's kingship, Ptah's priests at Memphis and Ra's at Heliopolis kept their estates and festivals, and nobody proposed closing them. The New Kingdom state god is better understood as a chairman of the pantheon than as its replacement — a point the Amarna episode proves by counterexample, since what Akhenaten attempted, the actual replacement, was experienced by his contemporaries as a rupture of a wholly different order (Section X). VIII. The Theban Triad — Mut and Khonsu Egyptian gods live in families, and a state god requires a household. At Thebes, Amun's household is the Theban Triad : Amun, his consort Mut, and their son Khonsu — the family whose three barques travelled together at the great festivals, whose temples stand as neighbouring precincts at Karnak, and whose small joint image, the British Museum's glazed-composition amulet EA11172, carries all three figures in procession on a plaque less than four centimetres high. The triad is the domestic form of the doctrine of Sections V–VII: the empire's god, presented as a father. MUT — THE MOTHER mwt [Gardiner: G14] [𓅐] — her name is simply the word "mother," written with the vulture. Consort of Amun from the New Kingdom's height, lady of the Isheru lake in her precinct south of Amun's at Karnak, where hundreds of statues of her lioness aspect Sekhmet stood. She wears the vulture headdress of queenship and the double crown: at Thebes she is the royal mother as Amun is the royal sponsor — the place once held by Amaunet (Section II), refilled by a goddess whose name is the relationship itself. KHONSU — THE TRAVELLER ḫnsw [Gardiner: Aa1-N35-S29-G43] [𓐍𓈖𓋴𓅱] — his name is built on a verb of travelling and crossing: Khonsu is the moon, iꜥḥ [Gardiner: N11] [𓇹], in its movement across the night sky. Shown as a youth with the sidelock of childhood, a crescent-and-disk crown, or falcon-headed with the lunar disk, he is the triad's child and its healer: Khonsu the Plan-Maker, whose statue was lent abroad in a famous Late Period narrative to expel a possessing spirit from a foreign princess. His temple within the Karnak enclosure is among the best preserved of the precinct. The triad did theological work for the state beyond modelling a family. In the divine-birth narratives (Section IX), Mut's place in the household is the one the queen mother ritually occupies; in the Opet procession, the three barques travelled as a court, and the renewal of kingship was staged as a family visit — Amun journeying south to Luxor Temple, ipt-rsyt [Gardiner: O15-T13-X1-Z4] [𓉩𓌘𓏏𓏭], "the Southern Private Place," with his household, to re-beget the royal kꜣ [Gardiner: D28] [𓂓]. And at the level of the individual worshipper, the triad gave the unapproachable state god a mother and a child: forms in which the hidden god could be prayed to by people who thought, as Egyptians did, in households. The archive's Pantheon survey places the triad among Egypt's local families — Memphis with Ptah, Sekhmet, and Nefertem; Heliopolis with its Ennead — and the pattern holds: every great cult centre thinks with a family, because a family is how power is made imaginable. A final precision, owed to Section II: Mut is not Amaunet renamed. The two goddesses coexist at Karnak, Amaunet in her older, Ogdoadic dignity — she receives a chapel and cult of her own in the precinct — and Mut in the triad. Egyptian theology preferred addition to replacement, again: the hidden god simply had, by the New Kingdom, both a primordial counterpart, with whom he precedes creation, and a royal consort, with whom he governs it. The household, like the god, is layered in time. IX. Kingship and Amun — Divine Birth, Coronation and the Opet Festival Horus 's relation to the king is identity: the living king is Horus. The Jackal God — Pre-Osirian Supremacy and the Colour of Transformation // PHILOLOGICAL ORIGINS // The name Inpu ( jnpw ) [𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱𓃣] has been subject to intense etymological debate. One prevalent theory links the root inp to the word for "decay" or "putrefaction," identifying the god directly with the biological reality he was tasked with managing. A competing theory suggests a connection to the word for "royal child" ( inpw ), perhaps indicating his original status as a son of the creator god Re. In the Old Kingdom, his name was often written simply with the couchant jackal [𓃢] or the jackal on a standard shrine [𓃤], stressing his immediate, physical presence in the necropolis landscape. Anubis — Ancient Egyptian Inpu or Anpu [𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱𓃣] — is among the oldest continuously venerated deities in the Kemetic pantheon, his image appearing in the earliest known funerary contexts of the Predynastic and Early Dynastic periods (c. 3100 BCE and before). Long before Osiris rose to prominence as the supreme Lord of the Dead — a process substantially complete by the Middle Kingdom — Anubis held that title alone. His Old Kingdom epithet Khenty-Imentiu ḫntj-jmntjw ("Foremost of the Westerners") [𓐍𓈖𓏏𓇋𓅓𓈖𓏏𓅱𓈉] identified him as the presiding authority over all who had journeyed to the West — the direction of the setting sun and of death — and over the necropoleis that lined the desert edges of the Nile valley. The identification of the animal associated with Anubis has undergone a scientific revolution in recent years. Traditionally identified as a jackal (specifically the golden jackal, Canis aureus ), DNA analysis and morphological studies have recently reclassified the Egyptian canid as the African Golden Wolf ( Canis lupaster ). This shift is not merely taxonomic; it alters our understanding of the god's symbolic "weight." The wolf, a larger and more formidable predator than the jackal, brings a different quality of protection and power to the deity. Jackals were conspicuous inhabitants of the boundary between the cultivated Black Land ( Kemet ) and the Red Land ( Deshret ) of the desert — scavengers who haunted the margins of burial grounds, digging at the edges of shallow graves. Rather than responding to this association with aversion, the Egyptians with characteristic theological sophistication recruited the canid's power into protective service: Anubis, depicted as the wolf/jackal or wolf/jackal-headed man who watched over the dead, conscripted the very animal that would otherwise desecrate the grave into its fiercest protector. The creature that scavenged became the guardian that prevented scavenging. His canonical black colouration requires specific attention. The African Golden Wolf's actual fur ranges from reddish-gold to grey-brown — never black. The choice of black was deliberate and theologically loaded. In the Kemetic colour-essence system ( iwn ), black held a dual significance simultaneously opposed to Western interpretations: it was the colour of the fertile Nile silt, the kemet itself, the rich dark earth that yielded all life. It was also the colour of the decomposing body — the Nigredo state — from which the resurrection would emerge. Black in the Egyptian system was not death as termination but death as the fertile void from which new life always emerges. To depict Anubis in black was to identify him with the deepest transformative potential of the death-state: the darkness that is full of generative power, the compost from which the next cycle grows. Evolution of Iconography — From Predator to Priest In the earliest depictions (Protodynastic labels and First Dynasty seals), Anubis is represented almost exclusively in his full animal form, often lying atop a chest or a shrine (the seshta -shrine). This "couchant jackal" pose emphasizes his role as the watchful sentinel. By the Second and Third Dynasties, the anthropomorphic "jackal-headed man" begins to appear, representing the god's increasing integration into the complex social and ritual hierarchies of the developing state. In this form, he often holds the Was Scepter ( wAs ) [𓌀], symbol of power and dominion, and the Ankh ( ꜥnḫ ) [𓋹], signifying his governance over the transition to eternal life. A critical but often overlooked iconographic element is the Shed-shed standard ( šdšd ). Frequently appearing in conjunction with Anubis (and Wepwawet), this enigmatic object consists of a standard topped by a curved protuberance, possibly representing the royal placenta or a sacred bundle. It was carried before the king in processions and at the head of funerary corteges, signifying the opening of the ways between the earthly and divine realms. Its presence links Anubis not just to the static protection of the tomb, but to the dynamic movement of the soul through the cosmos. // THE ANCIENT SUPREMACY — WHAT ANUBIS WAS BEFORE OSIRIS // The shift of the supreme funerary role from Anubis to Osiris — which occurred gradually from the Old Kingdom through the Middle Kingdom as the Osirian theological complex expanded — is one of the most significant transformations in Egyptian religious history. In the earliest Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE), Anubis is the primary funerary deity; Osiris appears but does not yet dominate. By the time of the Coffin Texts (c. 2000 BCE), the roles have begun to reverse. By the New Kingdom Book of the Dead, Osiris presides over the Hall of Judgment and Anubis has been repositioned as the master technician within the broader Osirian system. This repositioning was not a demotion but a functional refinement. Anubis retained and deepened his specific domain — the precise management of the threshold between death and afterlife — while Osiris absorbed the monarchical, judicial, and agricultural dimensions of the lord-of-the-dead role. The result was a more sophisticated system: Anubis as the expert practitioner of transition technology, Osiris as the ultimate judge and sovereign. Their functions are complementary, not competitive, in the mature theology. The older title Khenty-Imentiu was eventually adopted by Osiris, but it remains, philologically and historically, the original property of the Jackal. II. Divine Parentage and the Shadow Family — The Contested Origin The question of Anubis's parentage was genuinely contested in the Egyptian textual tradition, with different sources proposing different genealogies — a reflection of his extreme antiquity and the integration of originally distinct regional traditions into a unified theological system. OSIRIS AND NEPHTHYS — THE PLUTARCHAN VERSION One well-known genealogy makes Anubis the son of Osiris and Nephthys — conceived when Nephthys (Set's wife) disguised herself as Isis and lay with Osiris. This specific narrative is Plutarch's account ( De Iside et Osiride §14), a Greek text of c. 100 CE; it is Plutarchan tradition, not the canonical Egyptian version — Egyptian sources are varied and earlier, variously making Anubis the son of Ra, or of Hesat or Bastet, or of Ra and Nephthys, or of Osiris and Isis. This parentage places Anubis in the second generation of the Ennead and explains his presence at Osiris's mummification: he assists his father-figure's transition while also being, cosmologically, the product of a transgression that prefigures the broader disruption Set introduces. Isis, discovering the infant, adopted and raised him — reinforcing the Osirian family network while adding an adoptive-maternal dimension to Anubis's connection to Isis's powerful magical legacy. RE AS FATHER — THE OLDER TRADITION Earlier Pyramid Text sources assign Anubis a solar rather than an Osirian parentage — identifying him as the son of Re himself, placing him among the first generation of divine offspring and giving him a more cosmologically senior status. This tradition reflects his pre-Osirian supremacy; a deity who presided over all the dead before Osiris existed logically required a genealogy that predated the Osirian family structure. The tension between these two genealogies was never fully resolved — Plutarch's Nephthys-born version is the one most often retold for narrative coherence, while Egyptian tradition implicitly acknowledged the older solar connection through Anubis's continued association with the cyclic solar journey through the Duat. HESAT AS MOTHER Some sources identify Hesat [𓎛𓊃𓄿𓏏𓃒] — a cow goddess associated with nourishment and the milk of divine sustenance — as Anubis's mother, with Re as father. Hesat is a relatively obscure deity whose primary mythological role was as the divine cow who suckled sacred animals and humans with her life-giving milk. The mother-as-nurturer dimension this adds to Anubis is interesting theologically: it positions the god of death as himself having been tenderly nourished into existence, conferring on him a quality of genuine care for the souls he manages through their vulnerable transition. ANPUT — THE FEMALE COUNTERPART Anubis has a rarely-depicted female counterpart, Anput ( jnpwt ) [𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱𓏏𓃣]. She is his feminine aspect and his consort in his role as Lord of the Necropolis. Depicted as a woman wearing a standard topped with a jackal, she was particularly venerated in the 17th Nome of Upper Egypt (the Cynopolite Nome). Her existence emphasizes the Kemetic principle of gender duality ( complementarity ) — every potent force in the cosmos, even death itself, has both masculine and feminine expressions to maintain balance ( Ma'at ). KEBECHET — THE DAUGHTER OF THE EMBALMER Kebechet ( qbḥwt [𓈎𓃀𓎛𓏏𓆙]) is the daughter of Anubis and Anput. Her name means "Cooling Water" or "Purifying Water." Her role is critical in the mummification process: she is the goddess of purification through water, the one who brings libations to refresh the deceased. She is often depicted as a serpent or a woman with a serpent's head, representing the revitalizing power of the libation poured for the Ka . In the Pyramid Texts, she is called the "child of the great one" who refreshes the king on his journey to the sky. Her presence adds a dimension of literal and ritual "cooling" to the dry alchemy of mummification. THEOLOGICAL IMPLICATION OF THE AMBIGUITY The contested parentage and the expansion of the "canid family" is not a confusion or an error — it is a theological statement in the form of preserved plurality. Egyptian religion was not a monolithic creed but a living tradition that absorbed regional variants. Anubis's multiple genealogies reflect his genuine antiquity (predating any fixed mythological system), his functional importance across different theological frameworks, and the characteristic Egyptian willingness to hold multiple truths simultaneously without demanding a single authoritative resolution. He is both older than Osiris and of Osiris's family. Both are true at different levels of the myth. III. The Inventor of Embalming — Sacred Alchemy of the Weryt // THE WERYT // Weryt — "The Place of Pure Embalming" — was the designated sacred space where the embalming operation was performed. It was structurally separate from the tomb itself, often a tent or temporary pavilion of pure white linen. The chief embalmer wore an Anubis mask during the most sacred phases of the operation, literally becoming the god. In the Osiris myth , the first act of mummification was performed by Anubis — working alongside Isis, Nephthys, and Thoth — when he reassembled the scattered body of the slain king, wrapped it in linen, and prepared it for its passage into the Duat. This mythological prototype established the template for all subsequent funerary practice. Every Egyptian embalming was a re-enactment of Anubis's original operation on Osiris; every embalmed corpse was, ritually, Osiris's body; every embalmer was, in the moments of most sacred operation, Anubis himself. The Kemetic understanding of mummification was not primarily about body preservation as an end in itself. It was an operative alchemical transformation of the highest order — the conversion of the decaying Khat (physical body) into an eternal, transfigured vessel, the Sahu (glorified body), capable of serving as an anchor point for the returning Ka and Ba across the cycles of the afterlife. The physical chemistry of decay was the raw material; Anubis's technical mastery was the catalyst; the Sahu was the gold. The 70-Day Process — Astronomical and Alchemical Dimensions The embalming process lasted exactly 70 days — a number that was not arbitrary but astronomically precise. 70 days is the period during which the star Sirius ( Sopdet , identified with Isis) disappears below the Egyptian horizon before its annual heliacal rising, which marked the beginning of the Nile flood and the Egyptian New Year. The 70-day embalming thus synchronised the preparation of the body with the cosmic rhythm of Sirius's own death and rebirth — the deceased's transformation occurring in parallel with the star of Isis's annual passage through the Duat. NATRON — THE PURIFYING SALT The body was packed in dry natron — a naturally occurring sodium carbonate compound from Wadi Natrun — for approximately 40 days. Natron achieved desiccation (the removal of moisture that bacteria require for decomposition) while simultaneously performing a ritual function: natron was the supreme purification substance of the Egyptian system, used in priestly purification baths, in temple cleansing, and in the preparation of ritual implements. The body was being simultaneously preserved and purified — rendered chemically stable and ritually clean for its transformation. The chemical action of the sodium carbonate ( nṯrj ) [𓊹𓏭] was understood as a literal "divinization" of the flesh, turning the mortal remains into a substance of the gods. SACRED OILS AND RESINS — THE SCENT OF ETERNITY After desiccation, the body was anointed with a complex array of sacred oils and resins, including Antiu ( ꜥntjw ) [𓂝𓈖𓏏𓇋𓅱𓆭] — long translated "myrrh," but residue analysis of labelled vessels from the 26th-Dynasty embalming workshop at Saqqara (Rageot et al., Nature , 2023) shows antiu was a manufactured preparation, conifer oil/tar (cedar and/or juniper/cypress type) blended in an animal-fat base, not the Commiphora resin — Cedar oil , and Frankincense . These were not merely used for their fragrance; they were operative substances intended to seal the body and prevent the intrusion of "Isfet" (chaos/decay). The "Seven Sacred Oils" — Seti-heb , Hekenu , Sefet , Nesnem , Tuat , Ash (Best Cedar), and Tchenu (Best Libyan) — were applied in a precise sequence, each accompanied by a specific Heka invocation. These oils served as the "fluid of the god," replacing the lost biological fluids with a divine, non-corruptible essence. ORGAN REMOVAL AND THE CANOPIC SYSTEM The visceral organs — liver, lungs, stomach, intestines — were removed through an incision in the left flank. Diodorus Siculus (1.91) describes the rite's transgressive charge: the paraschistes who made the incision with a sharp Ethiopian stone immediately fled, pursued and pelted with stones by those present, as if the guilt of cutting the body fell on him. The organs were treated separately, wrapped, and placed in four canopic jars presided over by the Four Sons of Horus (Imsety, Hapy, Duamutef, Qebehsenuef). The heart — the seat of the Ib and the organ of judgment — was the single exception: it was left in place within the body, not removed, as it would be needed for the Weighing. The brain was removed via the nostrils using a hooked instrument and discarded — the Egyptians located thought, emotion, and moral discernment in the heart ( Ib ), not the head. WRAPPING, AMULETS, AND ANIMATION After desiccation and anointing, the body was wrapped in fine linen bandages in a specific sequence. As each layer was applied, amulets were placed at anatomically precise locations — the Udjat eye over the embalming incision, the Tyet at the throat, the Djed at the spine, the Heart Scarab over the heart. The wrapping itself was a Heka operation, each layer adding protection and reinforcing the identification of the body with the transfigured Osirian form. The quantities of linen consumed were very large. The British Museum's guide to its Egyptian galleries (1904) records bandages three to four inches wide and reports that "as many as 400 yards are said to have been employed for one mummy" — over 350 metres — with the coarsest linen nearest the body and the finest outside. Totals well beyond 100 metres are therefore documented for elaborate burials, though no standard total existed: the amount varied with the grade of embalming purchased and the means of the family. The result was a dense, protective shell that mirrored the cocoon of a transforming insect. THE IMIUT FETISH A distinctive sacred object found in royal tombs — consisting of a stuffed, headless animal skin (possibly feline or bovine) attached to a pole and inserted into a jar — the Imiut ( jmjwt , "that which is in its wrappings") was specifically sacred to Anubis. It is attested in royal funerary contexts — two Imiut fetishes were placed in the tomb of Tutankhamun — and in depictions of funerary rites from the earliest dynasties onward (Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses , 2003, pp. 280–81). No source warrants the stronger claim sometimes made for it, that it was present at every royal embalming; the honest statement is that where the full royal rite was staged, the fetish belonged to its furniture. Its exact operative function is debated, but it appears to represent the boundary between the animal body and the transfigured form — the skin left behind when the essence departs — and to concentrate Anubis's presence and protective power in the embalming space. It is the "skin of the god," a symbol of rebirth and the shedding of the mortal coil. THE EMBALMER AS ANUBIS The chief embalmer — titled the Hery-seshta ("Master of Secrets") — wore a full Anubis mask during the most sacred phases of the preparation, particularly during the removal of the organs and the final wrapping. This was not theatrical costume but operative identification: by wearing the god's face, the practitioner literally became the vessel through which Anubis operated. The mask collapsed the distinction between human technician and divine patron, ensuring that the most critical operations were performed by the god himself, channelled through a trained human instrument. The mask was often made of gilded wood or cartonnage, its black surface glistening like the fertile mud of the Nile. // THE OPENING OF THE MOUTH — ANUBIS AS ACTIVATOR // At the conclusion of the 70-day process, the completed mummy was brought to the tomb for the Opening of the Mouth ceremony — the final step that transformed the prepared Khat into a fully animated Sahu. While Anubis is not the primary officiant of this ritual (that role belongs to the Sem-Priest in the guise of Horus), his preparation of the body made the ceremony possible. The Opening of the Mouth animated what Anubis had prepared. Without Anubis's 70-day alchemy, there would be nothing for the wp-r to animate. The two rituals are complementary operations: Anubis creates the vessel; the Opening of the Mouth fills it. IV. Psychopomp and the Hall of Judgment Anubis's role as psychopomp — the divine conductor of souls between the living world and the afterlife — is one of his most ancient and continuously attested functions. In the Pyramid Texts, he leads the deceased king through the gates of the horizon; in the Middle Kingdom Coffin Texts, he guides any person of sufficient ritual preparation; in the New Kingdom Book of the Dead and the illustrated Papyri of Ani and Hunefer, he is the visible hand that escorts the soul into the Hall of Two Truths. The iconic psychopomp image from the Papyrus of Hunefer (British Museum, c. 1275 BCE) shows Anubis with his left hand on the wrist of Hunefer — not grasping, not pulling, but accompanying with a gentle precision that communicates both authority and care. This gesture is the definitive image of the Anubis relationship: he knows exactly where the soul needs to go; he ensures it gets there; but the accompaniment is not coercive. He is the guide who cannot be refused but who does not need to use force. The Weighing of the Heart — Anubis as Keeper of the Balance Within the Hall of Two Truths , Anubis performs the most technically exacting operation of the entire judgment process: he places the deceased's heart in one pan of the balance scale and the feather of Ma'at in the other, then reads the indicator needle with absolute precision. Thoth records the result; Osiris presides as judge; Ammit waits. But the actual measurement is Anubis's. The fitness of Anubis for this role is theologically elegant. The god who spent 70 days managing the most delicate physical transformation of mortal matter — weighing the precise amounts of natron, timing the removal of organs, judging the correct degree of desiccation — is exactly the being whose precision you want operating the cosmic scales at the moment of final accountability. His capacity for exact measurement is not a new skill acquired for the Hall; it is the same skill he has always exercised, applied at the highest possible stakes. Anubis — who is upon his mountain, who is in the place of embalming, lord of the Sacred Land — attends the balance as the heart of the justified one is weighed against the feather of Maat and found true. — Paraphrase of the judgment scene in Book of the Dead Spell 125 Keeper of the Duat's Gates Beyond the Hall itself, Anubis is described in the Netherworld Books tradition as a master of the threshold — associated with the gates of the Duat, the seven gates and twenty-one portals whose guardians and passwords the deceased must know in Book of the Dead Spells 145 and 146. (The forty-two of the judgment belong to a different series: the forty-two Assessors of Maat of Spell 125.) Anubis's connection to the gates is that of the guide who has escorted souls through them and the embalmer who prepared the traveller to pass; specific claims that in the Book of Gates his personal permission is required at each threshold go beyond what that text states, and are not made here. His knowledge of the Duat is presented in the sources as total — not merely its dangerous passages but its geometry, its guardians, its logic. This comprehensive knowledge of death's landscape is inseparable from his other roles: a deity who invented mummification necessarily understands where the mummy's soul will travel; a psychopomp who escorts every soul to the Hall has traversed every path of the Duat countless times. Anubis's mastery of the threshold is not theoretical but experiential — he has walked every route, spoken every password, negotiated every gate, in service of the souls he has guided. V. Divine Epithets and Titles Egyptian divine epithets are not merely honorific titles — they are operative descriptions of specific functional aspects of the deity's power. Each epithet of Anubis encodes a precise theological statement about one dimension of his role in the cosmic system. The full roster of his attested epithets reveals the extraordinary breadth of the Anubis principle. EGYPTIAN TRANSLATION THEOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE Khenty-Imentiu (ḫntj-jmntjw) [𓐍𓈖𓏏𓇋𓅓𓈖𓏏𓅱𓈉] "Foremost of the Westerners" His oldest known title — pre-Osirian supremacy over all who have died and journeyed to the West (the direction of the setting sun and of the dead). The Westerners are all the deceased; Anubis is their foremost leader and protector. Neb-ta-djeser (nb-tA-ḏsr) [𓎟𓇾𓂦𓋴𓂋] "Lord of the Sacred Land" The necropolis is the ta-djeser — the holy, set-apart land of the dead at the desert's edge. Anubis is its lord and sovereign. This title emphasises his governance of sacred funerary space itself. Imy-ut (jmj-wt) [𓇋𓅓𓇋𓅱𓏏𓍱] "He who is in the place of embalming" / "He who is in his wrappings" Associated directly with the Imiut fetish and with the embalming tent ( Weryt ). Marks Anubis as the presiding intelligence of the embalming operation, present in the sacred space where transformation occurs. Hery-seshta (ḥrj-sštA) [𓁷𓏤𓇋𓋴𓈙𓏏𓄿𓏛] "Master of Secrets" / "He who is over the mysteries" The title also given to the human chief embalmer who wore Anubis's mask. Refers both to the secrets of mummification technology and to the mysteries of the Duat — the hidden knowledge of death's geography and the techniques of successful navigation. Tepy-dju-ef (tpj-ḏw=f) [𓁶𓇋𓈋𓏤𓆑] "He who is upon his mountain" Depicts Anubis as the watchful guardian stationed on the desert cliffs above the necropolis — looking down over the burial ground like a sentinel, alert to any threat. The mountain-dwelling aspect aligns with the actual behaviour of canids in Egyptian desert terrain. SAb-šmw [𓄛𓄿𓈙𓅓𓅱] "Jackal of Upper Egypt" Refers to his primary cult associations in Middle and Upper Egypt, particularly at Asyut. Marks him as a regional power that became a national theological standard. Nb-r-ḏr [𓎟𓂋𓂧] "Lord to the Limit" An unusual but powerful title found in some later texts, suggesting Anubis's authority extends to the very edges of the cosmos — the limit of the Duat and the border of non-existence. VI. Archaeological Landscape — The Anubieion and Cult Centers The physical presence of Anubis in the Egyptian landscape was not confined to the individual tomb or the temporary embalming tent. His cult was supported by massive temple complexes and designated "Cynopolite" (canid-governed) districts, where the god's terrestrial representatives — dogs and wolves — were bred, maintained, and eventually ritually processed. The Anubieion at Saqqara Located on the plateau of Saqqara, near the Step Pyramid of Djoser, the Anubieion was a sprawling temple complex dedicated to Anubis. During the Late and Ptolemaic periods, it served as a major center for the ritual mummification of dogs. Archaeological excavations in the "Dog Catacombs" associated with the temple revealed a staggering 8 million canid mummies . These were not beloved pets but votive offerings — bred in temple kennels and sacrificed at a young age to serve as eternal messengers between the living world and the god. The Anubieion was more than a necropolis; it was a functioning economic and spiritual hub. It included administrative offices, priest quarters, and workshops for the production of the very amulets and bandages used in the funerary rites. The sheer scale of the Dog Catacombs testifies to the intensity of Anubis's popular veneration; for millions of ordinary Egyptians, the jackal god was the most accessible and reliable mediator of the afterlife's mysteries. HARDAI (CYNOPOLIS) — THE CITY OF THE DOG The 17th Nome of Upper Egypt was the heartland of Anubis's cult, with its capital at Hardai (Greek: Cynopolis , "City of the Dog"). This city was the administrative center of canid veneration. According to Strabo, the inhabitants of Cynopolis held dogs in such high esteem that they would go to war with neighboring nomes if a dog was killed or mistreated. The city served as a primary pilgrimage site and a center for the breeding of the specific canid strains associated with the god's physical manifestation. ASYUT (LYCOPOLIS) — THE WOLF CITY Further south, Asyut (Greek: Lycopolis , "City of the Wolf") was sacred to both Anubis and Wepwawet. The "wolf" of Lycopolis is now identified with the African Golden Wolf ( Canis lupaster ). The local theology at Asyut emphasized the "opener of ways" aspect of the canid deities, particularly in the context of the pharaoh's military and ritual successes. The rock-cut tombs of the local governors (nomarchs) at Asyut contain some of the most significant Middle Kingdom references to the Anubis/Wepwawet complex. THE SHRINE OF ANUBIS AT DEIR EL-BAHARI One of the most beautifully preserved cult sites is the Anubis Shrine within the mortuary temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari . The wall reliefs show the queen making offerings to Anubis, who is depicted with extraordinary artistic refinement. The presence of a major Anubis shrine within a royal mortuary temple underscores his role as the essential guarantor of the royal transition — even for a pharaoh as powerful as Hatshepsut, the Jackal's permission and protection were non-negotiable. VII. Anubis and Wepwawet — The Two Openers of Ways Wepwawet ( Wp-wAwt , "Opener of Ways") is a deity so closely associated with Anubis that ancient and modern interpreters have repeatedly confused or conflated them. Both are depicted as black or grey canids — Wepwawet as a wolf or wolf-headed man, Anubis as a jackal or jackal-headed man — both preside over the transition of souls, and both appear together in funerary processions and at the heads of royal expeditions. Understanding their distinction is essential to understanding both. WEPWAWET — THE WAY-OPENER Wepwawet's name is his function: he opens the way. His role is specifically the dissolution of obstacles — the clearing of the path before the main party arrives. In funerary processions, the Wepwawet standard was carried at the front, preceding the coffin. In royal military expeditions, Wepwawet led the way before the king's army. He is the advance scout, the pathfinder, the being who goes ahead to clear, test, and mark the route. His origin is at Asyut (ancient Lycopolis — "City of the Wolf") in Upper Egypt. ANUBIS — THE GUARDIAN AND GUIDE Where Wepwawet opens the way, Anubis ensures the traveller completes it correctly. Anubis accompanies the soul, manages its transition at each threshold, performs the weighing at the Hall, and monitors the soul's integrity throughout the journey. His role is not to clear the path but to shepherd the person through a path already laid out — ensuring it is navigated with the precision the system demands. Together, they constitute a complete transition technology: Wepwawet prepares the road; Anubis guides the soul along it. THE SED FESTIVAL CONNECTION In the royal Sed Festival — the pharaoh's 30-year ritual renewal — it was specifically the Wepwawet standard that led the processional, opening the way for the king's passage between the two thrones of Upper and Lower Egypt. This positioning confirms Wepwawet's role as the herald and path-opener in royal ceremonial contexts, while Anubis presided over the more intimate, interior dimension of the king's spiritual renewal. THE CANID CONFUSION The persistent confusion between the two deities in popular sources often reflects the genuine ambiguity that existed even in ancient Egypt. Some texts show their functions bleeding into each other; some images could be identified as either deity depending on context. The ambiguity is not error but theological depth: both express aspects of the same fundamental principle of threshold management, differentiated by emphasis (way-opening vs. way-guiding). They are two resonances of the same divine frequency, not two entirely separate entities. VIII. Anubis in the Greek Magical Papyri — Hermanubis The veneration of Anubis not only survived the Greek and Roman conquest of Egypt but flourished in new forms, acquiring a rich second life in the Greco-Roman religious and magical world. By the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, Anubis had become one of the most widely recognised Egyptian deities in the Mediterranean world — depicted on coins, worshipped in Isiac temples throughout the empire, and extensively invoked in the operative magical literature that became the Greek Magical Papyri (PGM). Hermanubis — The Syncretic Synthesis The syncretic fusion of Anubis with Hermes — forming Hermanubis ( Ἑρμανοῦβις ) — was one of the most theologically coherent syncretisms of the Hellenistic period. Both deities served as psychopomps — guides of souls between the living world and the realm of the dead. Both were associated with wisdom, with hidden knowledge, and with the communication between divine and human realms. Both were depicted with caduceus-adjacent symbols in syncretic imagery. The merger was not imposed but emerged naturally from the genuine resonance between two traditions' approaches to the same divine function. Hermanubis was depicted as a youthful figure combining the jackal head of Anubis with the caduceus and winged sandals of Hermes — or as a fully human figure with simply the addition of a small jackal head as a crown element. His worship spread throughout the Roman Empire alongside the Isiac religious complex, with which Anubis had always been intimately associated. The Emperor Commodus (reigned 177–192 CE) reportedly participated in Isiac processional rites wearing an Anubis mask — evidence of how deeply the god had penetrated Roman religious practice. PGM Invocations — Anubis as Operative Ally In the PGM corpus (c. 2nd century BCE to 5th century CE), Anubis appears as a primary paredros — a divine magical assistant who can be ritually engaged for specific operative purposes. The PGM invocations of Anubis draw on his traditional attributes while extending them into new applications consistent with the Greco-Roman magical framework: PGM Application Operative Mechanism Source Reference Spirit Communication Invoking Anubis to fetch the Ba of a specific deceased person for consultation — drawing on his role as psychopomp and master of the Duat's geography to locate and summon a specific soul from the afterlife.
