The Serpent's Names — Apep, Apophis, The Enemy // PHILOLOGICAL ORIGINS // The name Apep ( ꜥꜣpp ) or ( ꜥpp ) [𓉻𓊪𓊪𓆙] has been linked to the root ꜥp meaning "to slither" or "to glide," but also carries a resonance with the word for "giant" or "great one" in a distorted, monstrous sense. In the Late Period, his name was often written with the determinative of the fallen enemy [𓏱] or the decapitated serpent [𓆙], emphasizing his ritual defeat even in the act of naming. The Greeks rendered this as Apophis ( Ἀποφις ), a name that would eventually become synonymous with the "Destroyer" in Hellenistic magic. The name Apep carries precise theological significance. Beyond the "slithering" root, some scholars suggest a connection to the concept of "being hidden" ( jnp ), though this is more commonly associated with Anubis . Apep is the "un-nameable" in many contexts, referred to simply as The Enemy ( ḫftj ) [𓐍𓆑𓏏𓏭] or The Rebel ( sbj ) [𓋴𓃀𓇋𓏭𓀐]. The Greek rendering Apophis entered Western consciousness through Plutarch's treatment of the Typhon myth and other later writers; Herodotus, often cited in this connection, nowhere names Apophis in his surviving text. Many of his epithets reveal his essential nature: the Great Rebel (emphasizing his opposition to cosmic order), the Evil-Sting (emphasizing toxicity and sudden attack), the Roaring One (suggesting the sound of undifferentiated chaos), and "He Who Swallows the Sun" (his most distinctive act). A critical aspect of Apep's nomenclature is the Evil Eye ( jr-t-bjn-t ) [𓁹𓏏𓃀𓇋𓈖𓏏𓁻]. Apep's power is concentrated in his gaze, which is the "Bad Eye" that seeks to fascinate and paralyze the sun god Ra ( rꜥ ) [𓂋𓂝𓁚]. The evil eye is a genuine category of Egyptian magical thought, but no Egyptian source consulted for this article makes Apep its origin or its primordial source. What the sources give Apep is a stare of his own, the fascinating gaze treated in Section XIV; the wider doctrine of the evil eye belongs to the general magic of the gaze and is not sourced to the serpent here. In Egyptian texts, saying Apep's name aloud was considered dangerous — he could hear it and respond. Temple rituals deliberately pronounced his names when protected by ritual, specifically to enact symbolic victory over him. The principle being tested: that to name something is to have power over it, but only if you possess the strength to back the claim. To name Apep without the protection of Heka was to invite the gaze of the void. II. The Ontology of Chaos — Apep vs. Set vs. Isfet In Kemetic theology, it is critical to distinguish between three related but distinct principles: Set , Apep , and Isfet . Set ( stẖ ) [𓋴𓏏𓎛𓃩] represents contained chaos — the storm, the desert, the foreign lands, and the aggressive force required to defend the sun. Set is fierce, unpredictable, dangerous, but ultimately subject to Ma'at's authority. Set serves a function within the cosmic order: he defends Ra's boat against Apep each night. He is necessary, if dangerous. Isfet ( jzft ) [𓇋𓋴𓆑𓏏𓅪] is the abstract principle of chaos, disorder, non-order. It is the default state if Ma'at is not continuously maintained. Isfet is not inherently evil—it is simply the absence of order. Apep is something else entirely: he represents intentional, volitional chaos — the active principle of destruction and dissolution. Apep was never worshipped; he had no cult centers, only centers of execration. He was the only deity in the Egyptian pantheon who was considered entirely malevolent and beyond the reach of Ma'at's authority. He does not participate in the cycle of life and death; he seeks only the termination of the cycle itself. SET: CONTAINED CHAOS Necessary destructive force, subject to cosmic order. The storm god who burns and sweeps away, but within limits. Essential to Ra's defense and the solar principle's continuation. He is the "Strong One of the Barque." ISFET: ABSTRACT DISORDER The natural entropy that requires continuous ordering by Ma'at. The default state of non-organization. Not evil, but the necessary lack of form that must be organized into being. APEP: INTENTIONAL DESTRUCTION Volitional chaos seeking absolute termination. The one enemy that cannot be turned to service. The principle that seeks to unmake existence itself, to reduce all-being back to the void of Nun. III. Dissolution and the Void — The Anti-Creation Principle Apep represents an inversion of the creation principle. Where Atum generates himself from Nun ( nnw ) [𓈖𓈖𓏌𓇯] and brings forth differentiation, Apep seeks to collapse all differentiation back into undifferentiated void. Where Ptah ( ptḥ [𓊪𓏏𓎛𓁰]) speaks the world into existence, Apep silences the divine utterance. Where Isis ( ꜣst [𓊨𓋴𓏏𓅇]) gathers scattered pieces into wholeness, Apep scatters wholeness into fragments and then atomizes those fragments. In alchemical terminology, Apep represents the ultimate Calcination — the reduction to ash where no recovery is possible. He is not the Nigredo (productive darkness) but the nihil (absolute nothingness). The difference is critical: the Nigredo is darkness from which regeneration emerges; the nihil is the void from which nothing returns. Yet Apep is eternal. He is killed every night, defeated, pushed into the abyss, and yet he is eternally present to attack again. This suggests that dissolution, destruction, and the void principle are not temporary but fundamental and continuous. The cosmos must continually re-assert its existence against the principle of undoing. // THE PRINCIPLE OF UNDOING // Where creation is the process of differentiation from unity, Apep represents the process of collapse from differentiation back to void. Every force in the universe has this tendency toward dissolution — entropy, decay, heat death. Apep is the personification of this universal tendency. He is not external to the cosmos but its fundamental gravitational center: the pull toward nothingness that must be continuously resisted. IV. Apep in Cosmogony — The Primordial Enemy Apep was present before the creation of the world. In the Heliopolitan cosmology, before Atum ( jtm ) [𓇋𓏏𓅓] generated himself from Nun, there existed only the undifferentiated ocean of potential and within it, already, the principle of destruction: Apep, coiled in the depths. However, more nuanced traditions in the Coffin Texts (Middle Kingdom, c. 2000 BCE) provide a more complex origin story. The few accounts of Apep's origin usually place his birth after Ra: he was born from Ra's umbilical cord . A much later tradition has him spring from the saliva of the goddess Neith while she was still in the primeval waters, her spit becoming a snake 120 yards long. He was also commonly believed to have existed from the beginning in the waters of Nu. No source makes him from Ra's sweat or tears. The umbilical cord belongs to Apep's own birth, not to a tether he attacks: in the tradition above, it is Ra's cord, discarded at the sun's emergence, from which Apep himself came to be — darkness born at the same moment as light, from the very act that brought the creator forth. The creation of Ma'at and the establishment of cosmic order were understood partly as the containing of Apep. Every night, when Ra descends into the Duat and the cosmic order temporarily collapses into the undifferentiated darkness of sleep, Apep gathers his strength and attacks. Each dawn, Ra defeats him anew, and the world is restored. This suggests a profound theological truth: cosmic order is not permanent but perpetually renewed. Existence is not self-sustaining but requires continuous defense against the principle of dissolution. // THE VOID BEFORE THE WORD // Apep is the silence that Ra's word ( Hu ) must overcome. In the Bremner-Rhind tradition Apep stands as the unmade one, a direct contrast to the created gods ( neterw ) [𓊹𓏥]. He is the unmade, the un-become ( n-wnnt ), the eternal non-entity that persists alongside being. V. The Serpent's Anatomy — Form, Size, and Venom Apep is consistently described as a serpent ( ḥfꜣw ) [𓆙], and ancient sources emphasize his truly vast scale. In some texts, his coils fill entire waters of the Duat. His mouth is described as capable of swallowing the sun itself—the boat of Ra would fit entirely within his pharynx. His venom ( mtwt ) [𓂸𓅱𓏏𓈓] is a standing threat in the spell literature, whose litanies threaten him in return with the spilling of his poison and the softening of his teeth; the texts prefer threats to measurements. The measures they do give are surveyed in Section XII of this article: thirty cubits at the western mountain in Book of the Dead Spell 108, against the 120 yards of the late birth-tradition in Section IV. The serpent form is significant. Unlike most chaotic forces, which are depicted as formless, Apep has form—but it is a form that moves, undulates, flows. He is not crystallized chaos (which would be manageable) but living, responsive, adaptive chaos. The serpent represents intelligence and awareness combined with predatory hunger and the capacity to transform and strike from concealment. His venom specifically suggests a principle of infection—not merely destruction but corruption. Where an axe blow destroys a target physically, venom destroys it from within, corrupting its essential nature. This aligns with Apep as a principle of internal dissolution rather than external annihilation. THE SCALES In the rite's imagination the serpent's defence defeats ordinary attack, and the texts answer it not with stronger weapons but with Horus's iron spear and the flint knives of the executioners (Section IX). In this archive's reading, the impermeability figures the resistance of the dissolution principle to ordinary operative methods. ( nbwt ) [𓎟𓅱𓏏𓁐]. THE COILS Capable of encircling entire waters and the solar boat itself. Represent the entrapping, suffocating nature of chaos—the binding and constriction of form until dissolution occurs. ( qꜣꜣ ) [𓈎𓄿𓄿]. THE VENOM More poisonous than any natural serpent. Represents the corrosive principle that works from within to undermine stability and coherence. ( mtwt ) [𓂸𓅱𓏏𓈓]. VI. The Nightly Battle — Ra's Barque in the Duat Each night, as the solar barque (the Mesektet ) travels through the twelve hours of the Duat, it is intercepted by Apep. The serpent attempts to swallow the sun, using his massive coils to choke the celestial river and his hypnotic gaze to paralyze the crew. This battle is not just a fight; it is a Ritual Combat where every movement of the participants is fixed and meaningful. The Great Cat and the Persea Tree One of the most iconic images of Apep's defeat is found at the Persea Tree ( jšd ) [𓆭𓏤] in Heliopolis. In this myth, Ra takes the form of the Great Cat of Heliopolis ( mjw-ꜥꜣ ) [𓅓𓇋𓏲𓃠𓉻𓂝𓄿] to confront the serpent. The cat is shown pinning the snake to the ground with one paw and decapitating it with a large knife held in the other. The Persea Tree represents the Tree of Life and the repository of names (in a separate tradition, the names of the kings were inscribed on its leaves by Thoth ( ḏḥwtj ) [𓅝] and Seshat ( sšꜣt ) [𓋇]). By decapitating Apep at the foot of the tree, Ra protects the very record of existence and the principle of continuity. The Great Cat episode itself is Book of the Dead Spell 17, set at Heliopolis — not the Amduat's seventh hour. The cat's sharp senses and agility are the natural antidote to the serpent's slithering, hidden nature. The "Great Cat" resonance is a form of Mau (the cat's name also meaning "to see") — the eye that can see the serpent in the darkness. SET AT THE PROW Paradoxically, it is the god Set who stands at the prow of Ra's boat. Only Set possesses the strength and the immunity to Apep's hypnosis required to spear the serpent and allow the sun to pass. This highlights the Kemetic view that "contained chaos" (Set) is the only weapon against "absolute chaos" (Apep). Set is the only deity who can meet the serpent's gaze without blinking, as he is of a similar, though ordered, nature. THE SAND-BANK OF APEP In the seventh hour of the night, Ra encounters Apep at a place called the 'Sand-bank of Apep' ( šꜥ-n-ꜥꜣpp ) [𓈙𓂝𓈖𓄿𓊪𓊪𓆙]. Here, the serpent's body is so large that it fills the river and grounds the barque; he is subdued by Isis's magic and Set's strength, assisted by Serqet. This is a separate episode from the Great Cat at Heliopolis (Book of the Dead Spell 17, above). This is the moment where the river "fails" and the boat must be moved by magical words (Heka) rather than by rowing. VII. The Twelve Hours of Combat — Apep in Each Hour The Duat was organized into twelve hours of night, and Apep's attack occurred at different times with different intensities. The combat was most severe in the Seventh Hour — called the "difficult hour" or the "hour of the enemy" — where the solar river dries up and the boat must be towed by the gods and by the spirits of the deceased using Heka . In the First Hour , the serpent is already waiting at the "Gates of the West." In the Fourth and Fifth Hours , the terrain becomes the "Desert of Sokar" ( zkr ) [𓋴𓎡𓂋], a dry, sandy region where the boat is transformed into a serpent-form itself to navigate. Apep's presence here is a constant, suffocating heat and the sound of a "roaring that fills the sky." The Seventh Hour is the point of maximal entropy. Apep's coils encircle the boat completely. (No ancient source gives the coils a count; the number 77 sometimes attached to them in modern writing is examined, and set aside as unattested, in Section XXII.) It is here that Isis ( ꜣst ) [𓊨𓏏𓆇] uses her most powerful spells to distract and blind the serpent, while Set pierces his head with the spear. Without this precise intervention of the "Words of Power" ( ḥw ) [𓎛𓅱], the sun would be extinguished and the world would end. The Tenth and Eleventh Hours represent the final "disposal" of the serpent's remains, as he is cut into pieces and burned in the fire of the dawn-star. VIII. The Book of Overthrowing Apep — Defensive Heka The struggle against Apep was not considered a purely mythological event; it was a real-time crisis that required the active participation of humanity. The Book of Overthrowing Apep (contained in the Bremner-Rhind Papyrus , British Museum EA 10188) details the systematic magical operations performed daily at the Temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak. These rituals were designed to support Ra's celestial battle through terrestrial sympathetic magic. The Book of Overthrowing Apep prescribes spitting on, trampling, stabbing and burning the figure of Apep. That prescription is paraphrased here, not quoted: no single verbatim execration formula in those words occurs in the text. — On the Book of Overthrowing Apep, Papyrus Bremner-Rhind The Mechanics of Execration The rituals utilized sympathetic magic on a grand scale. Every morning, noon, and evening, priests would gather in the temple to perform the following: The Figure Drawn: A figure of Apep drawn on a new sheet of papyrus in green ink, the colour the rubric itself prescribes. ( rn ) [𓂋𓏤𓈖]. The Wax Image: An image of Apep made with a waxen body ( mnḥ ) [𓏠𓈖𓐍], his name inscribed on it in green ink. The King's Foes: Wax images of all the foes of Pharaoh, dead or alive, made and named in the same way and bound within a box. The Sequence of Acts: Spitting (four times), trampling with the left foot, the spear, binding, the knife ( ds ) [𓂧𓋴], and fire, in the spell order set out in Section IX. The Bryony Fire: The figures burnt in a fire of bryony; the remains placed in a pot of urine and pounded into one mass. The names also written on the ground and trampled with the left foot. The timing is the rubric's own, and it is more demanding than a daily office: the burning is prescribed for the morning, at noontide, and in the evening when Re sets in the West, at the sixth hour of the night and the eighth hour of the day, at every hour of the day and night, and on the new-moon, monthly, sixth-day, and fifteenth-day festivals, and likewise every day. Section IX gives the full schedule and the storm-weather use the same rubric prescribes. By performing these acts, the priests understood themselves to be weakening Apep's manifestations in the Duat in real time, providing Ra with terrestrial support in his journey. // THE SERPENT AND THE KING'S FOES // The same papyrus that prescribes the serpent's destruction extends it, in a single rubric, to all the foes of Pharaoh, dead or alive, whose wax images are bound in a box and destroyed with his (Section IX). The king's earthly enemies, foreign invaders and internal rebels among them, are thus felled in the same fire as the cosmic enemy. The preservation of Ma'at in the cosmos was inseparable, in the rite's own construction, from the preservation of order in the land of Egypt. IX. The Rite in Sequence — Spells and Rubrics of the Bremner-Rhind Book Section VIII named the book; this section performs it on the page, in the order its own rubrics prescribe. The account follows R. O. Faulkner's translation of the Book of Overthrowing Apep, Papyrus Bremner-Rhind (British Museum EA 10188), columns 22–32, published in the Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 22–24 (1936–1938), the edition on which all modern discussion rests. The book's opening line fixes its setting and its frequency: it is the book of the felling of Apep, foe of Re and foe of the king, performed daily in the temple of Amun-Re at Karnak. Nothing in what follows is this archive's invention; where the text is paraphrased, it is paraphrased closely, and the sequence is the text's own. The Six Opening Spells The rite opens with six named spells, each titled for the act it performs, and the acts escalate in a deliberate order. First, the spell of spitting on Apep , its refrain spoken four times, done, the text insists, for Re and his ka and equally for Pharaoh and his ka: every act against the serpent is simultaneously an act for the king, and the doubling runs through the whole book. Second, the spell of trampling on Apep with the left foot , in which Pharaoh crushes Re's foes and Re is called to crush Pharaoh's, dead or alive. Third, the spell of taking the spear : Horus has taken his spear of iron and battered the heads of the foes of Re, and the officiant's spear-work is Horus's, re-performed. Fourth, the spell of binding Apep , the bound ones warned that they are fettered by Horus and condemned by Re and shall not rise. Fifth, the spell of taking the knife , in which the warrior priest, the butcher of the rite, is called to seize and fell, and the flame of Sothis is invoked to cut the rebels up. Sixth, the spell of setting fire to Apep , and the spell to be uttered when putting Apep on the fire, after which the officiant tramples the figure four times more with the left foot, arms bent before the rising Re. The Rubric — Figure, Ink, Fire, and Hours The rubric that follows is the most quoted instruction in the book, and it is a manufacturing specification. The spell is to be spoken over a figure of Apep drawn on a new sheet of papyrus in green ink, and an image of Apep is to be made with a waxen body and his name inscribed on it in green ink, to be put on the fire so that he burns before Re at every manifestation: in the morning, at noontide, in the evening when Re sets in the West, at the sixth hour of the night and the eighth hour of the day, at the end of the evening, at every hour of the day and night, and on the festivals of the new moon, the monthly festival, the sixth-day and the fifteenth-day festivals, and likewise every day. He is to be burnt in a fire of bryony, and his remains placed in a pot of urine and pounded up into one mass. The same rubric extends the treatment to storm weather: the rite is to be performed when a storm brews in the east of the sky and when Re sets in the west, to prevent the storm-red from growing and thunder-storms from gathering, so that the sun may shine and Apep be felled in very truth. A second rubric widens the target list from the serpent to the state. An image of Apep is made in wax with his name written on it in green ink, and the images of all the foes of Pharaoh, dead or alive, are made in wax likewise, their names written in green ink, and they are bound within a box; they are then spat upon, trampled with the left foot, slaughtered with a knife, put on a fire of bryony, and quenched with urine. The names of Apep and of all the foes are also to be written on the ground and trampled with the left foot in the correct manner. The rubric closes with the book's own testimonial, paraphrased here: it will be well with whoever does this on earth, and well with him in the realm of the dead, and strength will be given him; the writer testifies that he has seen it come to pass in his own case. Another rubric is stricter about the operator than about the materials: one spell, it says, is to be recited by a man who is pure and clean. The books that follow the opening spells widen the assault before the volume closes. A second chapter fells not Apep alone but his whole confederacy, the foes, rebels, and children of revolt, who are to fall on their faces at the moment of Re. The litanies assign the serpent, piece by piece and god by god, to every power that can destroy him: to the Eye of Horus and the Eye of Re, to Isis who fells him with her magic and closes his mouth, to Nephthys who cuts him up, to Seth who breaks his vertebrae and severs his neck, to Sekhmet's executioners, to Thoth who cuts him to pieces with his magic and whose fingers are in his eyes, to fire in the south commanded by Sothis and Anukis, in the north by Wadjet, in the west by Ha lord of the West, in the east by Sopd lord of the East. The geography is the theology: there is no direction from which destruction cannot reach him, and no part of him, as Section XI shows, that the rite does not name in order to unmake. X. The Book of Knowing the Creations — A Cosmogony inside an Execration The Bremner-Rhind Papyrus is stranger than its title suggests. Between the felling spells, at columns 26–29, the manuscript sets two accounts of the creation of the world, and the second of them carries its own heading: the Book of Knowing the Creations of Re and of Felling Apep. The pairing is the doctrine. To fell the serpent you must know how things were made, because the felling is an unmaking, and an unmaking can only be aimed by someone who holds the original specification. Faulkner, in his introduction to the translation, singled these creation passages out as the parts of the papyrus that have most interested modern readers, and they repay the interest. In the account's paraphrase, the Lord of All speaks in the first person. When he came into being, Being itself came into being; he came into being in the form of Khepri on the First Occasion, alone, before Shu was spat out or Tefnut expectorated, and, in the text's most startling self-naming, his name was Magic: Heka is not a tool the creator later picks up but the name he bore while still alone in the Nun. He planned in his heart and surveyed with his sight, created beings in the Nun while as yet an Inert One with no place to stand, spat out Shu and expectorated Tefnut, was found by his wandering Eye and replaced it with the Glorious One, and wept, and from the tears of the Eye mankind came into being. Shu and Tefnut then begat Geb and Nut, and Geb and Nut begat Osiris, Horus, Seth, Isis, and Nephthys, and they begat and created many beings in the land. Then the cosmogony turns, in the same breath, into the execration it was copied to serve. The created beings, the text says, made conjuration in the creator's name so that they might fell their foes; they created the magic spells for felling Apep. Apep is imprisoned in the arms of Aker, the earth god, having neither arms nor legs, confined in one place as Re obstructs him. Children fell him and sunder his soul from his body and his shade; those in the south, north, west, and east fell him; and the creator charges the sages of the land and the Ennead who came into being from his flesh to be vigilant in felling Apep, to exorcise him and destroy his name, not to permit his name to be spread abroad, so that his children shall not exist and his seat shall not exist and he shall have neither soul nor body nor spirit. The creation account ends, uniquely among cosmogonies, with a standing order. The placement explains a feature of the rite that Section IX records without comment: its texts keep calling Apep armless and legless, a serpent who can neither rise nor copulate nor come forth from his place. In the cosmogony's logic this is not abuse but sentence. The unmade one is defined by the privations the created order imposes on him, listed in advance, and the daily rite at Karnak is the serving of that sentence one more time. Cosmogony and execration are one document because, in this theology, they are one act seen from its two ends: the world is the thing that was made, and Apep is the name of its being unmade, and the same words govern both. XI. The Names of Apep — Annihilation by Enumeration The papyrus closes its Apep material with the weapon this archive's Ren — Power of Names article treats as fundamental: the name, attacked by enumeration. The final columns give the Names of Apep (columns 32–33 in the manuscript's arrangement), and the litanies before them perfect a single grammatical machine for unmaking a being. Its pattern, in Faulkner's translation, is a drumbeat of negation: thou shalt not exist, and thy soul shall not exist; thou shalt not exist, and thy body shall not exist; and so on, item by item, through everything a being can be said to have. The enumeration deserves to be followed, because its order is a dissection. The litany proceeds through the components a person or god is made of, soul, body, shade, magic, and name, and then through the extensions of a self in the world: children, household, seed, and substance; seat, grave, cavern, and tomb; arms, flesh, bones, and mouth; form and shape and being and skin; and finally through the verbs, the pure capacities: utterance, entering, going, treading, sailing, sitting, growing. Nothing is too abstract to be revoked. A being, in this analysis, is a list, and the rite reads the list aloud with a negative before every line, forty and more times, until the list is empty. It is the Negative Confession of the Ma'at judgment run in reverse: there, a soul survives by the wrongs it can deny; here, a serpent is destroyed by the properties he is denied. The litanies also name his confederates and his aspects, because an unnamed ally is an unfelled one. The roarer Nehaher, whose name the rubric of Section IX commands the priest to drive off at the eighth hour of the day, is Apep in his acoustic form, the serpent as sound. Wenty is cut up in the knife spell. Neki, the Ill-disposed One, is bound by the god who created his own strength. The executioners of Sekhmet fill their mouths with his flesh; the Children of Horus break him up and set their spears in him; the wardens of the mysterious portals breathe their fiery blast against him. Even the insults are systematic: the litany can call him, in Faulkner's rendering, the bowel of Re and the intestine of the viscera, the creator's own waste addressed as a person the better to expel him. Naming, in the Bremner-Rhind Book, is not description. It is targeting. XII. Apep for the Dead — Book of the Dead Spells 7, 39, and 108 The temple rite of Sections IX to XI was state practice, performed by priests for Re and the king. The Book of the Dead puts the same enemy into private hands. Three spells in the standard numbering arm the individual dead against him, and together they map the three places a private traveller meets the serpent: on the road, in combat, and at the geography of the world's edge. Spell 7 is the travelling spell, for passing by Apep on the way through the realm of the dead: the serpent as an obstruction in the road, to be passed with the right words rather than fought at length. Spell 39 , for repelling the serpent Rerek in the underworld, is the combat spell, and the longest of the three: the deceased, gathering the gods' powers into his own voice, orders the serpent back, rehearses the destruction prepared for him, and speaks with the authority the temple litanies lend their officiant. Rerek is a serpent name of the underworld tradition, and the spell's tradition identifies its enemy with Apep himself; the private speaker borrows the state's war for his own journey. Spell 108 , for knowing the souls of the West, gives the serpent his surveyed dimensions: at the western mountain, Bakhu, where the sun goes down, lies a serpent thirty cubits long, the front part of him flint, and the spell's knowledge of him, his mountain, his measure, and his flint head, is itself the traveller's protection at the gate of the night. The thirty cubits of Spell 108 are worth pausing on, because they are the kind of number this article insists on sourcing. Thirty Egyptian cubits are roughly sixteen yards, and it is this description, a serpent of sixteen yards with a head of flint, that the reference tradition preserves beside the very different figure of Section IV, the newborn serpent of 120 yards from Neith's saliva. The two numbers do not agree, because they come from different texts with different purposes, a spell that surveys a guardian and a late myth that magnifies a birth. What they agree on is the method: the serpent is knowable, measurable, and named, and therefore, in the logic of Section XI, fellable. The dead person who carried Spell 108 in his papyrus carried a survey report on the monster at the world's edge, and the report was the weapon. XIII. Seth at the Prow — The Image of the Spearing The most durable picture of the whole war is a single figure at a boat's bow. From the New Kingdom, the god Seth stands at the prow of the solar barque with his spear levelled down at the water, the one god strong enough and strange enough to meet the serpent at the moment of attack. Section VI set out the paradox in doctrine; this section follows it in images, because the images are where most Egyptians, and most museum visitors since, have met it. The Book of Gates supplies the complementary picture, the war after the battle: Apep in chains, bound and held by a file of gods, the serpent processed like a prisoner through the hours he failed to stop. The vignette tradition made the chained Apep one of the standard sights of the royal tombs, chaos not as a force of nature but as a convict in a line, and the image travelled: in the late mythological papyri, among them the Papyrus Jumilhac, Seth's spear at the prow hardens into a fixed emblem of the defended sun, and at the temple of Hibis in the Kharga Oasis, in the Persian period, Seth spearing the serpent before him becomes monumental temple art, the desert god of the oases doing at the desert's edge what he does nightly at the sky's. The iconography corrects a modern misreading more efficiently than any argument. Seth is not Apep's colleague in these pictures, nor his brother in arms, nor a darker half of one chaos. He is the gaoler. The Egyptians who carved the prow scenes had a word for the difference, and this article has used it throughout: Seth's disorder is contained, sworn, and posted to a duty; Apep's is the refusal of all posts. The spear is the visible form of the distinction, and it is held, nightly and at Hibis alike, by the god the later tradition would blame for everything, doing the one job no other god could do. XIV. The Hypnotic Gaze — Paralysis and Fascination One of Apep's most dangerous weapon was his stare — described as having the power to paralyze all who witness it. Those who met his gaze directly would become frozen, unable to move or think, their will completely suppressed. In the ritual traditions, this was understood as a real danger: the sight of Apep was to be avoided at all costs. This is the Fascination of the Abyss , the seductive pull of the void that calls to the shadow-elements within the human soul. The hypnotic gaze represents the principle of fascination — the state in which consciousness becomes so absorbed in the object of attention that all other awareness ceases. Apep's gaze is the ultimate regression into non-consciousness: the state of absolute fixation where the self dissolves entirely. It is a "psychic paralysis" that mirrors the physical paralysis of a prey animal before a predator. The Concept of the Empty Heart In Kemetic psychology, the Ib (heart) [𓄣𓏤] must be "filled" with Ma'at to be stable. A heart that is "empty" ( wš-jb ) [𓅱𓈙𓄣] is vulnerable to Apep's gaze. The "empty heart" is a state of spiritual depletion, lack of purpose, or fragmentation. Apep does not create this state so much as he exploits it; he fills the vacuum of the empty heart with his own chaotic vibration, leading the individual toward self-destruction. The Name — Tm, Itm and the Complete One Atum's name is written itm [Gardiner: M17-X1-G17-A40] [𓇋𓏏𓅓𓀭]: the reed i [Gardiner: M17] [𓇋], the loaf t [Gardiner: X1] [𓏏], the owl m [Gardiner: G17] [𓅓], and the seated-god determinative [Gardiner: A40] [𓀭] that marks the word as a god's name and is not pronounced. Older Egyptological literature renders the name Tem , Temu , Tum or Atem ; modern transliteration gives itm , conventionally vocalised Atum . The initial vowel is a scholarly convenience — Egyptian writing records consonants, not vowels — but the consonantal skeleton t-m is secure, and everything the Egyptians made of this god begins from it. That skeleton is the root tm [Gardiner: X1-G17] [𓏏𓅓], and it must be handled carefully, because the root carries two opposite senses at once . James P. Allen, in Genesis in Egypt: The Philosophy of Ancient Egyptian Creation Accounts (1988), the standard philosophical study of the creation texts, sets the position out plainly: the name Atum is a form of the verb tm , and tm means both "to be complete, to finish" and "not to be." The name is built like an agent noun — the same formation as "builder" from "to build" — so that Atum is, in the first sense, "the Complete One" or "the Finisher," and, in the second sense, something close to "the one who is not (yet)." Both connotations, Allen argues, belong to the god, and the texts exploit both. The first sense is the one handbooks usually give, and it is genuinely Egyptian. Atum is called "lord of totality" in the Coffin Texts tradition Allen cites, and the Pyramid Texts can wish the king to be "complete in Atum" — complete in him, as in a whole that lacks nothing. Atum is complete because, alone before creation, he contains both sexes and all subsequent gods in potential: father and mother in one body, the totality from which the Ennead will unfold and to which, in the end, it will return (Section XII). Nothing is outside him because, at the beginning, there is nothing else. The second sense is stranger and just as important. Before creation there is, in Egyptian terms, a state the texts describe with negatives: no sky, no earth, no gods, no death. Atum exists in that state without yet being part of a world. A god named from tm "not to be" is therefore the god of pre-existence : the one who was , in the waters, before being was a property anything else could have. The same doubleness will reappear at the end of time, when Atum the Finisher unmakes the world and subsists again in Nun as what he was at the start. His name is, in miniature, his whole career: complete at the beginning because nothing has been subtracted from him, and complete at the end because everything has been gathered back. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: wp [Gardiner: F13] [𓄋], spd [Gardiner: M44] [𓇮], ꜥꜣ [Gardiner: O31] [𓉿], srḫ [Gardiner: O33] [𓊁], ḳꜣb [Gardiner: I14] [𓆙], sšꜣt [Gardiner: R20] [𓋇] and [Gardiner: R21] [𓋈], msḏr [Gardiner: F21] [𓄔], mḫꜣt [Gardiner: U38] [𓍝], bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝], and ꞽb [Gardiner: E8a] [𓃚]. Spellings of divine names follow James P. Allen, Middle Egyptian , and Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar , cross-checked against the archive's audited articles on the Ennead and Ogdoad and the cosmological deities , whose account of Atum this article expands and does not contradict. Two near-neighbours of the name deserve a caution. The negative verb tm [Gardiner: X1-G17] is sometimes written with the same determinative as Atum's name — a graphic overlap Allen notes in the Coffin Texts — which suggests the scribes themselves heard the pun. And the evening word-field around the god — he is the sun finishing its course — is a genuine association the tradition made when it placed Atum at sunset (Section VIII), not a modern etymological invention. What the archive will not do is collapse the two senses into one slogan. "Complete One" alone makes Atum sound like a finished product; "the one who is not" alone makes him sound like nothing at all. The texts hold both, and so does this article. Atum's name also travels as an element in other names. Kings bore throne names compounded with Ra rather than Atum, but ordinary Egyptians bore names invoking him, temples bore his name in their foundations (Section XV), and the syncretic forms Re-Atum and Atum-Re (Section XVII) put his name beside the sun god's from the Old Kingdom onward. The power of the name — the rn [Gardiner: D21-N35] [𓂋𓈖], a constituent of the person alongside the kꜣ [Gardiner: D28] [𓂓] and the bꜣ [Gardiner: G29] [𓅡] in the composite soul — applies to gods with particular force: to know that tm means both completion and non-being is to know something true about what kind of god this is. II. Before Creation — Nun and the Undifferentiated Before Atum there is Nun : nwn [Gardiner: N35-W24-N35] [𓈖𓏌𓈖], the primeval waters — dark, inert, boundless, and, crucially, not empty . The archive's survey of the cosmological deities states the position this article follows: Nun is undifferentiated potential, the state in which nothing has yet been distinguished from anything else. There is no sky, pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯], because nothing has been lifted up; no earth, because nothing has been set down; no death, because nothing has yet lived. The Hermopolitan Ogdoad gives that state eight names — Nun and Naunet, Heh and Hauhet, Kek and Kauket, Amun and Amaunet — but the Heliopolitan account is sparer: waters, darkness, and, latent within them, Atum. Atum's relation to Nun is stated two ways in the sources, and the difference is theological, not accidental. In most accounts Atum is self-created : he comes into being by himself, without a maker, the first act of differentiation inside the undifferentiated. In some texts, however, Nun is called his father — the Global Egyptian Museum's glossary entry on Atum records the variant plainly — as if the waters themselves were the nearest thing to a parent a self-made god can have. Egyptian theology tolerated both formulations in the same corpus because they answer different questions: who made Atum? (no one) and out of what did Atum emerge? (the waters that were already there). Creation, in the Heliopolitan telling, is not manufacture from nothing. It is the emergence of distinction within a potential that precedes it. That is why Nun never disappears. The ordered world, once made, remains an island inside the waters: Nun surrounds the sky, wells up in the Nile flood, fills the temple lakes, and waits beyond the horizon of the solar barque's nightly journey. Every sunrise is therefore a local repetition of the first emergence, and every threat to order — above all the serpent ꜥpp [Gardiner: D36-Q3-Q3] [𓂝𓊪𓊪], Apep — is Nun's undifferentiation pressing back against the distinctions Atum made. The full treatment of the waters is in the archive's article on Nun and the primordial waters ; what matters for Atum is that he is defined against them twice — at the beginning, as the one who rises out of them, and at the end, as the one who returns to them (Section XII). NUN — THE WATERS BEFORE DISTINCTION nwn [Gardiner: N35-W24-N35] [𓈖𓏌𓈖]. Dark, inert, and full of potential. Not a god who acts so much as the condition in which action first becomes possible — and the condition to which, in Spell 175 of the Book of the Dead, the world will one day return. ATUM IN NUN — THE LATENT ONE Atum before his emergence is the tm [Gardiner: X1-G17] paradox in person: complete, because he lacks nothing; not-yet, because nothing — including, in a sense, himself as a distinct god — has come into being. The Coffin Texts give him speech from inside this state (Section X). A useful discipline for the reader: whenever this article says "before creation," it means before differentiation , not before existence . The Egyptian texts are consistent on this point in their different idioms, and confusing the two produces the common modern error of describing Nun as "nothing." Nun is not nothing. Nun is everything, unseparated — which is precisely what Atum, the separator, is not. III. Self-Creation — How Atum Came Into Being The Heliopolitan account's central verb is ḫpr [Gardiner: L1-D21-Z1] [𓆣𓂋𓏤], "to come into being, to become, to evolve into a form." Atum does not get made; he ḫpr s — he comes into being by himself. The scarab god Khepri , whose very name is built from this root, is Atum's becoming given a separate face (Section VIII), and the archive's Khepri article treats the root's full word-field. For Atum the point is austere: the first event in the history of the world is an event with no external cause. A distinct being appears inside the indistinct waters, aware of himself, alone. The texts linger on the aloneness. In the long first-person creation account preserved in the Coffin Texts (Section X) and retold, centuries later, in the Papyrus Bremner-Rhind (British Museum EA10188), the creator surveys a world that does not yet contain a place to stand, a companion, or a second voice. Everything that will make existence bearable — ground, air, a paired order of things — has to be produced out of the one body that exists. Heliopolitan creation is therefore, from first to last, an art of self-division without self-loss : Atum will become many gods and remain, as head of the Ennead , the one they all came from. His completeness (Section I) is not threatened by creation; it is distributed by it. Egypt had other creation theologies, and this article keeps them in their own lanes, as the archive's cosmological survey does. At Memphis, Ptah creates by heart and tongue — conceiving in thought and commanding in speech — and the Memphite text preserved on the Shabaka Stone subordinates Atum to that process, presenting the Ennead as proceeding through Ptah's word; see Memphite theology . At Hermopolis the Ogdoad precedes the first sunrise, and Thoth presides over the emergence. At Thebes, Amun is the hidden source behind all of them. These are rival answers offered by rival priesthoods, later harmonised by theologians who preferred accumulation to exclusion. The Heliopolitan answer is the oldest attested in continuous form, and it is Atum's: I was alone; I came into being; I made the gods from myself. That sentence is a labelled paraphrase of the creator's speeches in the Coffin Texts and Bremner-Rhind, not a quotation. One more form of the emergence deserves record because the Book of the Dead preserves it: Atum as a serpent . The Global Egyptian Museum's Atum entry notes that in the Book of the Dead the sun god is said to have ascended from the chaos-waters with the appearance of a snake, the animal that renews itself by shedding its skin. The serpent is not a fall or a disguise; it is the appropriate body for a being who precedes limbs, sex, and species — long, legless, self-renewing, at home in water and earth at once. Section XII returns to the serpent, because it is also the body Atum resumes at the end of the world. IV. The Primordial Mound and the Benben A god emerging from water needs somewhere to be. The Heliopolitan answer is the primeval hill : the first mound of solid ground to rise out of Nun, the first dry place, the stage on which creation happens. In the Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts the mound and the god are so close that Atum himself can be addressed as the mound — he does not merely stand on the first ground, he is the first ground, distinction made solid. Every later Egyptian temple re-founded that mound in its own sanctuary, which is why the archive's article on temple architecture treats the sanctuary floor's rise toward the holy of holies as cosmology in stone: to walk into a temple is to walk back toward the First Time. The mound's cult object at Heliopolis was the benben : bnbn [Gardiner: D58-N35-D58-N35-O24] [𓃀𓈖𓃀𓈖𓉴], written with b [Gardiner: D58] [𓃀], n [Gardiner: N35] [𓈖] doubled, and the pyramid determinative mr [Gardiner: O24] [𓉴]. The Global Egyptian Museum's benben entry — the source followed here — derives the name from the verb wbn , "to rise, to shine forth," and records the two Pyramid Text interpretations side by side: the benben stone was a manifestation of Atum when he rose out of the primeval waters, or the primeval hill on which Atum first landed. The stone, conical in shape, was kept in the innermost sanctuary of the temple of Re at Heliopolis, in the shrine called the House of the Benben . It was, in the most literal sense Egyptian religion allowed, the first place in the world, preserved as an object. The one verbatim ancient sentence this article quotes comes from this context, and it is quoted in a named, public-domain translation. Pyramid Texts Utterance 600, in Samuel A. B. Mercer's translation (1952), addresses the god: "O Atum-Khepri, when thou didst mount as a hill, and didst shine as bnw of the ben (or, benben) in the temple of the bennu in Heliopolis" — and continues, in the same utterance, with the spitting out of Shu and the spitting out of Tefnut (Section V). The sentence compresses the whole Heliopolitan sequence into one breath: the god mounts as the hill, shines as the sacred stone, and creates. The bnw [Gardiner: D58-N35-G43] [𓃀𓈖𓅱], the Benu bird — the heron-like "phoenix" of Heliopolis, the soul of the sun god — belongs to the same word-family of rising and shining, and its perch was the benben itself. THE MOUND — FIRST GROUND The primeval hill is creation's first distinction between wet and dry, below and above. Atum identified with it, temples re-founded it, and the inundation re-enacted it every year: as the Nile flood fell, the first mounds to emerge were the world being made again. THE BENBEN — FIRST OBJECT The conical stone in the House of the Benben at Heliopolis. The Global Egyptian Museum notes that by the early reign of Amenhotep IV the word could denote an obelisk as cult image, and that the tops of obelisks — and of pyramids, the pyramidia — are themselves called benben: the first stone, multiplied across the sacred landscape. THE BENU — FIRST VOICE bnw [Gardiner: D58-N35-G43] [𓃀𓈖𓅱]. The bird whose cry, in the Hermopolitan telling preserved in this archive's Ennead and Ogdoad article, broke the silence of the waters from its perch on the mound. Heliopolis kept both bird and stone in one sanctuary complex. The mound also explains a feature of Atum's cult geography that Section XIV develops: Heliopolis claimed to be the place of emergence. A city that houses the first stone does not need to argue for its seniority. Whatever political capital Egypt's kings chose — Memphis, Thebes, Pi-Ramesse — the theological capital of creation remained Iunu, because the benben was there and nowhere else. V. The Creation of Shu and Tefnut — Sneeze, Spit and Wordplay Alone and complete, Atum produces the first pair: Shu and Tefnut . Shu — šw [Gardiner: H6-G43-A40] [𓆄𓅱𓀭], written with the feather šwt [Gardiner: H6] [𓆄] and w [Gardiner: G43] [𓅱] under the god determinative — is air, light, dryness, and the space between things. Tefnut — tfnt [Gardiner: U33-I9-N35-X1] [𓍘𓆑𓈖𓏏] — is moisture and cohesion, the wetness without which Shu's dry space would be a desert of separated dust. Together they are the first environment : a volume, and the medium that fills it. Their full profiles are given in their own articles; here the question is the manner of their making, because the texts give not one manner but several, and the several are the doctrine. The Variants, as the Texts Present Them Spitting and expectoration. In Pyramid Texts Utterance 600 — the utterance quoted in Section IV — Atum spews out Shu and spits out Tefnut, in Mercer's rendering. The Coffin Texts develop the mouth-account at length: Shu himself, in the speech preserved in Coffin Texts Spell 80 and the Shu spells around it, declares (in paraphrase) that Atum did not form him in a womb or shape him in an egg, but spat him forth with the spittle of his mouth, his sister Tefnut emerging behind him, enveloped in the breath of life. The account Robert Armour's Gods and Myths of Ancient Egypt reproduces from the Coffin Texts has Shu say exactly this in the first person. Creation by mouth is creation by breath and fluid together — the two things a living body can project into the world without tools — and it keeps the children of Atum's substance while making them distinct persons. The sneeze. In the Bremner-Rhind creation account — the late papyrus (British Museum EA10188, copied in 305 BCE) preserving much older material, published by E. A. Wallis Budge as the Legend of the Creation — the creator tells the story in the first person, and the sequence runs, in paraphrase: he was alone; no sky or earth existed; his fist became his spouse; and then he sneezed out Shu and spat out Tefnut . Budge's 1912 translation, a public-domain rendering, is the source the archive follows for this account's shape. The pairing is not random decoration. It is wordplay , and the Egyptian audience was expected to hear it. // THE WORDPLAY — IŠŠ AND TFN // The sneeze-verb in the account is išš , "to sneeze," and it sounds like šw [Gardiner: H6-G43-A40], Shu. The spit-verb is tfn , "to spit," and it is the consonantal core of tfnt [Gardiner: U33-I9-N35-X1], Tefnut. Egyptian theological wordplay works exactly this way across the corpus: the act that produces a god is chosen so that its sound contains the god's name . The name is not a label stuck on afterwards; in the logic of the name and of phonology and voice , the name is the being's nature made audible, and the pun is the proof that the act and the being belong together. Shu is what a sneeze projects — invisible air, suddenly expelled, carrying life outward. Tefnut is what spitting projects — moisture, the body's water made separate. The archive presents the wordplay as the texts present it: as theology conducted by sound. Masturbation and the Hand. The oldest stratum, the Pyramid Texts, is also the most physical. Utterance 527 states, in the standard scholarly paraphrase followed by Allen and by the Global Egyptian Museum alike, that Atum created by his masturbation in Heliopolis: he took his phallus in his fist to excite desire, and the twins Shu and Tefnut were born. Section VI is devoted to this variant and to the goddess who personifies the Hand, because it became a theology of its own. Here it is enough to note the consistency underneath the variants: in every version the children come out of Atum's own body — mouth, nose, hand, seed — and in no version does Atum take a partner, find material, or receive help. The variants differ in organ, not in doctrine. The lost children and the Eye. A further episode, developed in the Coffin Texts and later retellings, has Shu and Tefnut wander off into the darkness of Nun and become lost to their father. Atum sends his single Eye — irt [Gardiner: D4-X1] [𓁹𓏏] — to search for them; on their return he weeps, in some accounts, and from his tears humankind is born. The archive records this as the tradition presents it: a widespread Egyptian association of humanity with the tears of a god, attached here to Atum and elsewhere to Ra, rather than a single canonical scene. What is stable across the tellings is the naming: the returned Shu is named Life and Tefnut Order — mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U5-X1] [𓌷𓏏], Ma'at herself — as if the first pair, once recovered, received their functions as titles. Air is what lives breathe; moisture-in-measure is what order feels like. The punning theology of the sneeze becomes, here, a naming theology. From Shu and Tefnut the genealogy proceeds by ordinary — if divine — generation: their children are Geb and Nut , earth and sky, and theirs are the four who carry the story into history. Section VII sets out the whole tree. The point of the variants, taken together, is that Heliopolitan theology never reduced creation to a mechanism. Mouth, nose, hand, tears — the texts keep every door of the body open, because the doctrine is not how a body makes gods but that one complete body did. VI. The Hand of Atum and Iusaaset The masturbation variant of Section V generated a person. If Atum's hand performed the act by which the first gods were born, then the hand was, functionally, his spouse — the female principle inside the complete one, made visible as an organ. Egyptian theology, which personifies everything it takes seriously, duly made her a goddess: the Hand of Atum , worshipped at Heliopolis in the form of Iusaaset , "the Great One Who Comes Forth," a goddess whose very title describes emergence. In later Heliopolitan theology Iusaaset is honoured as a grandmother of the gods, and she could be identified with the goddess Hathor-Nebethetepet in the same cult centre. The archive records the identification as the later tradition presents it; the underlying figure is Heliopolitan and old. The Hand matters beyond its one scene. It is the Egyptian solution, in bodily form, to the problem Section I posed: how a god who is tm — complete, lacking nothing, including a partner — can nevertheless generate. The answer is that completeness is not sameness. Within the one body, hand and phallus, female and male, are already distinguished enough to act upon each other, while remaining one god. The cosmological survey's treatment of primordial androgyny makes the same point in general terms: gender in this system is a manifestation of duality, and duality first appears inside the One, not between two pre-existing beings. Iusaaset is that interior duality with a name and a cult. Hathor's recurring title "Hand of Atum" in other cult centres shows how far the figure travelled once coined. The archive notes the title without annexing Hathor's whole theology to this section: at Heliopolis the Hand is Iusaaset; elsewhere the title attaches to the great goddess locally present. Egyptian divine identity works by such attachments, and precision consists in saying which attachment, at which place, in which period — not in forcing a single answer on all of them. IUSAASET — THE GREAT ONE WHO COMES FORTH Consort-shadow of Atum at Heliopolis, personification of his creative Hand, ancestress — "grandmother" — of the gods in the later Heliopolitan tradition. Her cult is the institutional proof that the priests of Iunu took the Hand episode as theology, not embarrassment. THE HAND AS INSTRUMENT The hand is also the craftsman's organ. A creator who works with his hand stands closer to Ptah the fashioner than the mouth-account alone would suggest — one of the several bridges by which the Heliopolitan and Memphite theologies were later joined (Section XVII). VII. Head of the Ennead — the Heliopolitan Genealogy The Ennead — psḏt [Gardiner: N9-X1] [𓇷𓏏], "the Nine" — is Atum's family organised as a cosmos. The archive's dedicated article on the Ennead and Ogdoad gives the system's full analysis, including its numerical logic; this section gives Atum's place in it, which is the first place, in every sense. He is the one from whom the count begins: Atum, then Shu and Tefnut (two), then Geb and Nut (two), then the four children of Geb and Nut — one, two, two, four: nine. GENERATION ONE — ATUM ALONE itm [Gardiner: M17-X1-G17-A40] [𓇋𓏏𓅓𓀭]. The complete one on the mound in Nun. Source, father, and — through the serpent form and the end of the world (Section XII) — survivor of the whole genealogy. GENERATION TWO — AIR AND MOISTURE Shu , šw [Gardiner: H6-G43-A40] [𓆄𓅱𓀭], and Tefnut , tfnt [Gardiner: U33-I9-N35-X1] [𓍘𓆑𓈖𓏏]: space and its medium, dryness and wetness, the first environment (Section V). GENERATION THREE — EARTH AND SKY Geb , gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] [𓅬𓃀𓀭], and Nut , nwt [Gardiner: N35-W24-X1-N1] [𓈖𓏌𓏏𓇯]: the floor and the ceiling of the world, separated by their father Shu so that life can happen between them. GENERATION FOUR — THE OSIRIAN QUARTET Osiris , wsir [Gardiner: Q1-D4-A40] [𓊨𓁹𓀭]; Isis , ꜣst [Gardiner: G1-S29-X1] [𓄿𓋴𓏏]; Seth, stš [Gardiner: E20] [𓃩]; and Nephthys, nb.t-ḥwt [Gardiner: V30-X1-O6] [𓎟𓏏𓉗]. With them the cosmos acquires death, magic, violence, and mourning — history begins. See the Osiris myth . Two features of Atum's headship are easy to miss. First, the Ennead is not a council of equals with a chairman; it is a body unfolded from one body . Egyptian texts can speak of the gods as Atum's limbs, of the Ennead as his "members," and of creation as his own substance externalised — the doctrine Allen's Genesis in Egypt traces through the Coffin Texts, where the creator's speech moves between "I" and the gods he has made without a hard boundary. Second, headship persists after delegation. Atum does not retire. He remains the court of final appeal among the gods — the tribunal of the Horus and Seth contendings acknowledges his line's authority, the dead king is received by him (Section IX), and at the end of the world it is Atum, not any younger god, who speaks the last word (Section XII). The Ennead's number is also, as the archive's Ennead article notes, a number of completeness — nine as plural-of-plurals, three times three. That a god named tm [Gardiner: X1-G17], "the Complete One," should head the complete number of gods is the sort of fit Egyptian theology noticed and prized. This article records the fit as the tradition's own pattern-making, not as a claim about the system's historical origin, which was gradual and priestly rather than designed in a day. VIII. The Solar Triad — Khepri, Ra and Atum From the Old Kingdom onward Atum is also a sun god , and Egyptian theology organised the sun's day as a sequence of forms. The formula the whole tradition eventually settled on — stated as an identity by the justified dead in Book of the Dead Spell 17's orbit and assumed everywhere in the netherworld books — is a triad: Khepri in the morning, Ra at noon, Atum in the evening. One sun, three names, three bodies: the scarab who comes into being, the falcon-headed lord of the day's height, and the man who finishes the course and descends. Atum's share is the evening . The Global Egyptian Museum's entry gives the reason from the Egyptians' own word-field: the form itmw behind his name is glossed there as "to complete oneself," and Atum is accordingly "Re on the top of the western mountain" — the sun arriving at the western horizon, ꜣḫt [Gardiner: N27] [𓈌], its work done, its light reddening and withdrawing into the dwꜣt [Gardiner: N15] [𓇽], the Duat. Evening is not decline in this system; it is completion . The day, like the world, is a thing Atum finishes — the tm [Gardiner: X1-G17] root doing its work again, now on the scale of hours instead of aeons. Morning belongs to becoming ( ḫpr [Gardiner: L1-D21-Z1]); evening belongs to the finisher. The triad is a theological instrument, not a timetable, and the archive uses it as such. The three forms appear together, address each other, and merge: Pyramid Texts already combine Atum with Ra as Re-Atum (Section XVII), and the netherworld books show the night sun travelling in forms that accumulate Khepri's becoming and Atum's age in a single barque journey — see the solar barque . What the triad gives the worshipper is a grammar for the day: every dawn is the First Time rehearsed small, every dusk a rehearsal for the greater finishing of Section XII, and Atum presides over the dusk the way he presides over the end — not as an enemy of the light, but as the form the light takes when its course is complete. KHEPRI — MORNING ḫpr [Gardiner: L1-D21-Z1] [𓆣𓂋𓏤]. The scarab, self-creation at dawn. Full profile: Khepri . RA — MIDDAY rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳]. The sun at height, lord of the visible order. Full profile: Ra . ATUM — EVENING itm [Gardiner: M17-X1-G17-A40] [𓇋𓏏𓅓𓀭]. The finisher at the western horizon, descending into the Duat to be reborn. This article. IX. Atum in the Pyramid Texts The Pyramid Texts — the inscribed utterances of the late Old Kingdom royal pyramids, from Unas onward (Fifth and Sixth Dynasties) — are Atum's oldest surviving stage, and he is already fully himself there: creator, father of the gods, and father of the king. The archive's article on funerary texts gives the corpus its context; this section gives Atum's roles inside it. Creator. Utterance 527 gives the masturbation creation (Sections V–VI); Utterance 600 gives the mounting as the hill, the shining as the benben, and the spewing and spitting out of Shu and Tefnut, and then names the whole Ennead in sequence — Atum, Shu, Tefnut, Geb, Nut, Osiris, Isis, Seth, Nephthys, in Mercer's rendering of the passage fetched for this article — as the company under Atum's protection, a protection the utterance then extends to the dead king named in the text. Creation and kingship are not separate topics in these utterances; the same breath that makes the gods makes the king's safety. Father of the king. Across the corpus the dead king is addressed as Atum's son, is embraced by Atum, and is lifted by him toward the sky. The theology is exact: the living king was Horus ; the dead king becomes Osiris; but beneath both offices stands the older claim that the king is Atum's offspring, issued from the creator's own body as Shu and Tefnut were. Atum's embrace in the Pyramid Texts is therefore a homecoming — the separated thing gathered back into the complete one, without ceasing to be itself. Section XVI develops the kingship doctrine; here the textual root of it is enough. The paired Atum. The Pyramid Texts also know Atum in company — above all as Re-Atum , the fusion discussed in Section XVII, and in a remarkable dual conception in which the king's two aspects are figured as Atum's own double nature, the god who is both the one who was alone and the company he became. Scholars have long noted the corpus's interest in Atum as a totality that includes duality; the archive records the interest without building a system on it. What the texts warrant is this: from our earliest evidence, Atum is never merely a lonely monad. He is a one that contains a two. X. Atum in the Coffin Texts The Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom — spells painted on the coffins of non-royal as well as royal dead — give Atum what the allusive Pyramid Texts never do: a voice . The great creation speeches of the corpus, above all the Shu spells (Spells 75–83 in the standard numbering), let the first generations speak in the first person about how they were made, and let Atum speak about being alone. Allen's Genesis in Egypt builds its philosophy of Egyptian creation largely on these texts, and this section follows his reading. In the Shu spells, Shu narrates his own origin (Section V): not formed in a womb, not shaped in an egg — the egg, swḥt [Gardiner: H8] [𓆇], is named precisely to be denied — but spat from Atum's mouth and enveloped in the breath of life, on the day Atum appeared "in the infinity, the nothing, the darkness and shapelessness," in the Coffin Text phrasing as reproduced in Armour's standard handbook. The negations do philosophical work: they define creation against every ordinary mode of generation. What Atum does is not birth, not manufacture, not conception. It is a fourth thing, for which the texts use the mouth, the hand, and the verb ḫpr [Gardiner: L1-D21-Z1] [𓆣𓂋𓏤] — becoming — and leave the mechanism deliberately at the level of image. The Coffin Texts also give Atum the doctrine of the millions : the creator declares himself the maker of the gods and the one from whom the multitudes proceed, and the texts play on his titles of totality — "lord of totality" among them, from the root tm [Gardiner: X1-G17] itself (Section I). A second Coffin Text theme matters for Section XII: Atum in dialogue with Osiris. The germ of the Book of the Dead's last conversation — the dead god asking about duration, the creator answering with millions of years and with the final return to the waters — is already present in the Middle Kingdom corpus. Egyptian eschatology, like Egyptian cosmogony, was composed early and elaborated long. Finally, the Coffin Texts democratise Atum. A spell that identifies the deceased with the creator — "I am Atum" in the corpus's characteristic first person — puts the oldest god's name in a private person's mouth. The claim is not blasphemy in this system; it is the funerary programme itself, by which the dead person assimilates to the gods whose stories guarantee renewal. To be able to say "I am Atum when I was alone in Nun" is to claim a share in the one being whom non-being could not prevent and dissolution will not end. XI. Atum in the Book of the Dead In the Book of the Dead — the New Kingdom and later "Spells of Coming Forth by Day," surveyed in this archive's Book of the Dead passages — Atum appears in three registers: as an object of the deceased's identification, as a presence in the vignettes , and as a speaker at the end of the world. Spell 17 is the great glossed spell, a text that asks "who is he?" after its own statements and answers with identifications, and its answers repeatedly land on Atum and Ra-Atum: the self-created great god, the one in his sun-disk, the maker of his own names and members, whose arising the spell expounds line by line. Through Spell 17's glosses Atum became, for every owner of a Book of the Dead, a study-text: not only a god to meet but a doctrine to recite correctly. Spell 15's hymns to the setting sun address the god in his evening majesty; other spells invoke Atum among the Ennead who witness the deceased's vindication at the weighing of the heart .
