The Name — bꜣstt and the Ointment Jar Bastet's name is one of the oldest divine names in Egypt, and one of the least certainly understood. In its early hieroglyphic form it is written bꜣstt [Gardiner: E10-S29-X1-X1] [𓃝𓋴𓏏𓏏]. The archive's Sekhmet article, in its Section XV treatment of the leonine continuum, has already fixed the spelling this article follows, and the two articles are deliberately consistent: the first sign is read bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝] with the corrected, post-audit value the archive assigns that sign, the fold of cloth gives the s , and the two loaves give the doubled feminine ending -tt . The modern form "Bastet" is itself a scholarly convention: Egyptologists adopted it because later writings of the name invite the second t to be read, although in earlier pronunciation that final feminine ending was very likely silent. "Bast" is the same name with the convention stripped back; Greek writers made it Bubastis, and Coptic preserved a form close to Oubaste. The spellings differ across three thousand years. The written core does not. What the name means is a harder question, and this article states the leading answer at exactly the strength its proposer gave it. Stephen Quirke, in Ancient Egyptian Religion , suggested that the name is a nisba formation, "she of the bꜣs ," and that the bꜣs [Gardiner: W2] [𓎰] in question is the ointment jar: the flat-based, wide-mouthed vessel, usually of pale stone, in which precious unguent was kept. On that reading the goddess is "she of the ointment jar" — the power that belongs to, and is carried in, the jar of protective scented oil. The suggestion fits two independent facts: the name is in some writings composed with the jar sign itself, and the goddess's durable associations include perfume, unguents, and the protection that anointing conferred (Section XX). A rival derivation, associated with James P. Allen, takes the name as a nisba from a place, "she of bꜣst ," a locality otherwise unknown. The archive prints Quirke's reading as the working one, because the jar is in the writing and the unguent is in the cult, and prints Allen's beside it because the matter is not settled: divine names in Egypt were often deliberately opaque, cult secrets rather than labels, and a goddess attested for nearly three millennia is not obliged to surrender her etymology to either. One caution belongs at the head of the article, because it governs everything after it. The familiar summary of Bastet — "originally a fierce lioness, she softened over time into a gentle cat" — is not false, but it is a compression, and compressions of this kind smuggle in a story the evidence does not tell: a story of a personality mellowing, as if the goddess had aged out of anger. Sections V to VII set out what the record actually shows, period by period: which forms are attested when, what else was changing at the same dates (the place of the domestic cat in Egyptian life, the political rise of her city, the sorting of the lioness goddesses into complementary postings), and where the lioness demonstrably persists after the cat has arrived. The reader who wants the one-sentence version may keep it, provided it is read as a statement about iconography and emphasis , not about a temperament improving with age. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used, as in the companion articles: E10 = bꜣ [Gardiner: E10], M44 = spd . For Bastet's own name this article follows, without exception, the spelling fixed in Sekhmet Section XV: bꜣstt [Gardiner: E10-S29-X1-X1] [𓃝𓋴𓏏𓏏]. The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . II. The City's Name — pr-bꜣstt, Bubastis, Tell Basta Goddess and city carry each other's names. The city the Greeks called Bubastis was in Egyptian pr-bꜣstt [Gardiner: O1-E10-S29-X1-X1] [𓉐𓃝𓋴𓏏𓏏] — "the House of Bastet," or more exactly "the Domain of Bastet," built on pr [Gardiner: O1] [𓉐], "house, estate, temple domain." The Greek form Boubastis is the Egyptian name heard through Greek ears and fitted with a Greek ending, by the same process the archive's article on phonology and voice traces for other Delta names; the Hebrew Bible's Pi-beseth (Ezekiel 30:17) is the same name by a third route; and the modern Arabic name of the mound, Tell Basta , preserves the goddess's name still, worn down by four thousand years of continuous local speech. Few Egyptian goddesses can be followed in an unbroken chain of place-names from the hieroglyphs to a modern map. Bastet can. The chain matters because it corrects a habit of thought. Bastet is often introduced as a "cat goddess" who happened to have a temple at Bubastis. The names say the opposite: she is the goddess of a place , whose domain the city was, whose temple was the city's reason for fame, and whose festival was the city's gift to the whole country. Herodotus, who knew the city in the fifth century BCE, uses "Bubastis" for the goddess herself as readily as for her town — "Bubastis in the Hellenic tongue is Artemis" (Section XIV) — because in Greek ears the two were one word. Egyptian keeps them distinct by a single sign, the house sign of the domain, and this article keeps the Egyptian distinction: Bastet the goddess, Bubastis the city, Tell Basta the mound that remains of it, on the south-eastern edge of modern Zagazig in the eastern Delta. Her standing title follows from the same fact. She is nbt [Gardiner: V30-X1] [𓎟𓏏] — "Lady, Mistress" — of Bubastis: "Bastet, the great, Mistress of Bubastis" is the form in which temple and statuette inscriptions name her again and again, and the British Museum's bronze of the goddess found at Bubastis itself carries an inscription of exactly that tenor (Section XXII). At Saqqara, where she had a second great sanctuary, she bears the local title Lady of Ankhtawy, "Life of the Two Lands," the old name of the Memphite necropolis district (Section XIX). The titles are addresses. Each one posts the goddess to a place where her power was understood to be on duty. III. The Earliest Record — Stone Vessels and the Pyramid Texts Bastet is not a late goddess who grew out of the pet-keeping of the first millennium. She stands near the beginning of the Egyptian written record. The standard reference summary — Richard H. Wilkinson's The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt , the work the archive's other deity articles cite for attestation history — places her earliest known images on stone vessels of the Second Dynasty (c. 2890–2686 BCE), where she already appears in the form she would keep for two thousand years: a woman with the maneless head of a lioness. Stone vessels of that age survive chiefly from the royal necropolis at Saqqara, and a goddess named and pictured on royal stoneware of the Second Dynasty is a goddess of the court, not of the village: whatever local Delta cult lay behind her, by the time the record opens she has already been received into the state religion of a unified Egypt. Her name then enters the first great corpus of Egyptian religious literature. Bastet is named in the Pyramid Texts of the late Old Kingdom, the inscribed utterances of the royal pyramids, and Geraldine Pinch's widely used handbook summary of her career begins exactly there: from the Pyramid Texts onward, Pinch writes, Bastet has a double aspect, nurturing mother and terrifying avenger, and it is the avenging aspect that predominates in the Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom and in the Book of the Dead, and that is invoked in medical spells. The archive underlines Pinch's formulation because it is the correct frame for the whole article. The "double aspect" is not a late theological repair job, reconciling an old fierce goddess with a new gentle one. It is present from the first texts that describe her at any length. The mother and the avenger are coeval. The Pyramid Text role that matters most for her later career is her relation to the king. In the Old Kingdom material Bastet stands close to the king as protector and, in the imagery of royal childhood, as a divine nurse and mother: the lioness who suckles and guards the royal child becomes, by the logic Egyptian theology always applies, the lioness who defends the grown king. That maternal-fierce combination — the nursing mother who is also the most dangerous animal in the landscape — is the seed from which both of her later postings grow: the guardian of the nursery and the house in Section XXI, and the Eye of Ra of Section VIII. Neither is a softening of the other. Both are the lioness with young, read at different distances. IV. Iconography — the Goddess's Forms at a Glance Across three thousand years Bastet is shown in four principal forms, and the first discipline of her iconography is not to sort them into a simple before-and-after. The forms overlap in time; the same century, and occasionally the same object, can carry more than one of them; and the choice among them is made by context — temple or tomb, state monument or household amulet, the mood of the goddess the dedicator needed — as much as by date. THE LIONESS-HEADED WOMAN Her earliest form, from the Second Dynasty stone vessels onward: a woman's body, a lioness's maneless head, sceptre and ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] [𓋹] in hand. In this form she is visually almost indistinguishable from Sekhmet , and only the inscription beside the figure settles which goddess is meant. THE LIONESS ENTIRE In full animal form, striding or couchant, she is the desert-edge power without the mediation of the human body: the form of the Distant Goddess in the desert, and of guardianship at its most literal. THE CAT-HEADED WOMAN The standard form of the first millennium BCE: a woman, often in an elaborately patterned dress, with the head of a domestic cat, carrying a sistrum, a lion-headed aegis, and a basket, with kittens sometimes at her feet. The Metropolitan Museum's Late Period example (15.43.5) is the type specimen used in Section VII. THE CAT ENTIRE Seated, upright, ears pricked: the goddess as a domestic cat, in bronze, wood, faience, and stone, from small amulets to the 42-centimetre Gayer-Anderson cat of the British Museum (Section XXII). Some examples of this form are not only images but containers, made to hold a mummified cat. Two attributes cross all four forms and repay attention, because they are her name and her office worn as objects. The first is the sistrum , the rattle whose shaking was the characteristic sound of the pacification of the Eye goddesses: music offered to a dangerous power until the power softens, the instrument Hathor also carries, and the sound Herodotus heard on the festival boats (Section XV). The second is the aegis , the broad protective collar topped with a lioness's head, which Bastet holds before her body like a shield. The Metropolitan Museum's curators describe the aegis of their cat-headed Bastet as protective, and the point deserves emphasis: even in her most domestic form, the goddess carries a lion-headed shield. The lioness is not edited out of the cat period. She is miniaturised, held in the hand, and kept on duty. V. The Lioness Period — Bastet in the Old and Middle Kingdoms For roughly the first half of her documented life, Bastet is a lioness goddess of the same company, the same appearance, and much the same business as Sekhmet. The company is the lioness continuum the archive maps in Sekhmet Section XV: Mut, Sekhmet, Bastet, Wadjet, Tefnut, Pakhet, Menhit, and a train of local lionesses, one solar, feminine, feline power differentiated by city and by posting. Bastet's posting in that early system is the north: she is the lioness of the Delta, of Bubastis, as Sekhmet's home ground is Memphis and the south's great temples. The pairing is geographical before it is temperamental. Her business, in the texts that survive, is the Eye's business. She is a daughter of the sun god — rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳] — and one of his defenders, an avenger whose ferocity is turned outward against the enemies of order and, in the medical spells Pinch notes, against the demons of disease on behalf of the patient who invokes her. This last point is worth pausing on, because it complicates the gentle-cat story from inside the fierce period: already in the early material Bastet is invoked protectively , for healing and defence, precisely because she is dangerous. The logic is the one the archive documents for Sekhmet's physician-priests: the sender of an affliction is the authority who can recall it, and an avenging goddess is the natural patron of everyone who needs avenging done on their behalf. Protection in Egypt is not the absence of ferocity. It is ferocity correctly addressed. The Middle Kingdom adds the evidence of place. At Bubastis itself, excavation has recovered Middle Kingdom building on a substantial scale, including a palace complex and the governors' monuments of the Delta administration (Section XIII), and the goddess's cult is the cult of that city's god throughout: the Delta capital of her domain was a working administrative centre of the Middle Kingdom state, not a village shrine awaiting later promotion. In the Coffin Texts, the great Middle Kingdom corpus that democratised the Old Kingdom's royal afterlife literature, Bastet keeps the double aspect Pinch describes — present to the dead as protector, present to their enemies as terror. The lioness of the Middle Kingdom is not yet a cat. But she is already, in the same texts, a mother and a guardian of the vulnerable dead. Both halves of the later Bastet are documented before the cat arrives. VI. Lioness to Cat — the Evidence, Period by Period This section does the work the one-sentence summary refuses to do. The claim under examination is that Bastet changed from a lioness goddess into a cat goddess. The questions are: when, in what kinds of object, alongside what other changes, and with what exceptions? Taken in order, the evidence supports a real and dramatic shift of emphasis across the New Kingdom and the Third Intermediate Period, standardised in the first millennium — and it does not support a clean replacement, a datable moment of change, or a change in the goddess's underlying character. The Animal Changed First The domestic cat's own history in Egypt runs ahead of the goddess's iconography. The Egyptian word for the cat is mꞽw [Gardiner: E13-G43] [𓃠𓅱] — an honest onomatopoeia, "he who mews" — and cats of the domestic kind, descended from the African wildcat, were living in Egyptian settlements, tolerated and then encouraged around grain stores, long before they were anyone's icon. Genetic study of mummified cats (Kurushima, Ikram and colleagues, Journal of Archaeological Science , 2012) recovered from three Late Period cat mummies the common domestic-cat maternal lineages still prevalent in Egypt and the Near East, with divergence estimates placing the origin of those lineages thousands of years before the mummies themselves: the temple cats of the first millennium were true domestic cats, of lines already ancient in the region. By the Middle Kingdom, cats appear in tomb scenes in domestic settings; by the New Kingdom they are everywhere in the painted record of daily life — under the chairs of married couples, collared and bejewelled, hunting in the marshes beside their owners (Section XVII). A goddess whose animal was becoming the animal of the house was acquiring, in the house cat, a second body that her worshippers met every day. The New Kingdom — Both Forms in Play In the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BCE) the cat enters Bastet's iconography without expelling the lioness. Cat-headed and cat-formed representations of the goddess belong increasingly to these centuries, above all in the smaller, personal media — amulets, small bronzes, faience — while the lioness-headed form continues in formal and temple contexts, and lioness-headed Bastet figures are still being made, in fine materials, long after: museum collections hold faience Bastets with lioness heads of much later date than the supposed transition. The pattern is not succession but specialisation by medium and mood : the cat for the goddess approached closely, in the house and on the person; the lioness for the goddess in her majesty and her anger. Egyptian religion, which kept a god's forms in parallel as a matter of course, had no need to retire either. The Third Intermediate Period — the City Makes the Difference The decisive change is political, and it has a date range. In the Twenty-second Dynasty (c. 945–715 BCE) the kings of Egypt were, by Manetho's tradition and their own building record, Bubastite kings : a line of Libyan descent whose power base was Bubastis, who built Bastet's temple up into one of the great temples of Egypt (Sections XI–XII), and whose devotion made their city goddess a national one. The archive's article on the Third Intermediate Period sets out the dynasty and Osorkon II's festival hall in their political frame. Under that royal patronage the cat form becomes the public, standard form of the goddess — the form of the bronzes, the festival, and the pilgrimage trade — because the cat is now the form in which the national cult presents her: approachable, processional, reproducible by the thousand for the pilgrims of Section XXII. What changed in the Twenty-second Dynasty was not the goddess's nature but her scale , and the iconography followed the scale. What "Softened" Gets Wrong Three facts forbid the simple mellowing story. First, the double aspect is original: Pinch's nurturing mother is in the Pyramid Texts beside the avenger (Section III), so there is no early period in which Bastet is fierce only. Second, the lioness persists: lioness-headed Bastets, the lion-headed aegis in the cat-headed goddess's own hand (Section IV), and the compound Sekhmet-Bastet dedications of the continuum (Section VIII) all continue into and through the cat's ascendancy. Third, the cat is not, in Egyptian experience, a harmless animal: the house cat of the tomb paintings is a hunter, the Great Cat of Heliopolis is a serpent-killer, and a mother cat's defence of her kittens was proverbial enough for Herodotus to build an ethnographic set-piece on it (Section XVIII). The honest summary is therefore narrower and more interesting than the proverb: between the New Kingdom and the Late Period, the dominant public image of Bastet shifted from the lioness to the domestic cat, as her cult was nationalised by her city's dynasty and her animal became the animal of every house — while the lioness, the anger, and the avenging aspect remained hers, attested, and available. VII. The Cat Form Standardised — Attributes of the First Millennium By the Late Period (664–332 BCE) and through the Ptolemaic age, the cat-headed Bastet has a standard iconography so consistent that a museum label can be written from any one example to fit most others. The Metropolitan Museum's record for its cupreous-metal Bastet (15.43.5, Late Period–Ptolemaic, 664–30 BCE) gives the type in the Museum's own terms, and this section follows it closely because it is a description of an object, not a reconstruction. The goddess is cat-headed, "a powerful protective figure who also was known for her fertility." She could be represented with a lion head as well, the Met notes, "but as a cat-headed goddess her peaceful traits were emphasized." She holds a protective lion-headed aegis, probably once held a sistrum in her other hand, and carries a basket on her arm. Statuettes of the type sometimes show kittens in front of her, alluding to her fertility; the suggestion that the basket itself held kittens, the Met judges, seems unfounded — an archive-worthy distinction, kept here, between what the type shows and what has been guessed about it. The dress deserves its own sentence, because it is hers. Bastet's statuettes wear elaborately patterned garments far more often than those of other goddesses: the Met's example has a complex herring-bone pattern, and its curators note both that the patterning marks the piece's quality and that, as some have suggested, the vertical banding may recall the striped fur of a cat. Her ears are pierced for earrings, probably gold in the original. A worn inscription on the base names the goddess — the archive's standing reminder that in this material the name, not the species, is the identification. And the Met's record closes with the distribution that defines the period: her main cult centre was Bubastis, "where thousands of cat mummies and a large number of cat statuettes were discovered," but the cult extended far beyond it, and statuettes of Bastet, as a cat or cat-headed, "were among some of the most popular dedications of the Late and Ptolemaic Periods." In full cat form the standard is the seated cat: upright, tail brought round, head high, the pose of an animal listening. The type runs from faience amulets a centimetre high to bronzes of near half a metre, and its jewellery is part of the type, not decoration added to it — broad collars, wedjat-eye pectorals, scarabs on the head and chest, earrings and nose-rings in gold and silver (Section XXII examines the supreme example). A nursing variant sets the goddess-cat on her side with kittens at her teats, the maternal aspect made zoologically literal; a British Museum bronze of c. 900–600 BCE, found at Bubastis, shows her instead as a cat-headed woman with four kittens at her feet, sistrum in hand. The kittens are theology: the goddess of the house is the goddess of its increase, and her fertility is not an abstraction but a litter. VIII. The Eye of Ra Continuum — Bastet's Posting The archive's Sekhmet article, Section XV, has already established the framework this section expands, and nothing here replaces it: the lioness goddesses form a continuum, one feline, solar, feminine power — the Eye of Ra — differentiated by city, mood, and distance from the sun, its grammar written in the compound names Mut-Sekhmet, Sekhmet-Bastet, and the fourfold Mut-Sekhmet-Bastet-Wadjet. What follows is the same doctrine read from Bastet's end of the spectrum: what her posting is, what work it does in the system, and what her presence in the compounds tells us that a study of Sekhmet alone cannot. The Eye itself, in the summary the companion articles share, is the sun's power of action at a distance: irt [Gardiner: D4] [𓁹], the Eye of rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳], detachable, feminine, and agentive, able to leave the god's face, rage in the desert, be lost, be wooed, and return. Within that office the archive's Sekhmet article assigns the postings in a single sentence this article adopts verbatim as its starting point: Sekhmet is the fire dispatched; Wadjet is the fire posted; Bastet is the fire at rest in the house ; Mut is the fire as the king's mother; Hathor is the fire welcomed home. Bastet's posting is thus defined by distance , the variable the whole continuum runs on. She is what the Eye is when it is not abroad: the same solar power, at hearth-range, in the room, on duty over the cradle and the stores, its claws retracted not because they are gone but because the house is the place it defends. The Pacification, Read from the Other End The continuum's central rite is pacification — the Sekhmet article's sḥtp complex, the satisfying of the raging Eye by litany, music, festival, and intoxicating drink until the destroyer comes home as a benefactor. Bastet is that rite's destination . When the New Year tradition recorded in the Sekhmet article has worshippers exchange gifts in the form of Sekhmet or of Bastet, indifferently, as the year's first insurance, the interchangeability is the doctrine in practice: the giver is not choosing between a dangerous goddess and a safe one, but addressing the one Eye-power in the aspect the turning year requires — the arrows still abroad, or the power already home and at peace. Bastet-names and Bastet-images cluster at exactly the points of the calendar and the house where the Eye is being received rather than feared: New Year gifts, festival processions, nursery amulets, the sistrum's sound in a doorway. She is, liturgically, the proof that pacification works: the form the fire takes when the liturgy has done its job. The Distant Goddess and the Return The mythic frame for the posting is the Distant Goddess cycle, treated in the archive's Hathor and Sekhmet articles: the Eye, offended, flees to the far south in lioness form and must be persuaded home, returning with the inundation, feasted and adorned, her rage converted to beneficence. Bastet's place in that cycle is structural rather than narrative — the named fleeing goddess of the fullest versions is more often Tefnut or Hathor — and the archive states it as structure, not as a lost Bastet myth: the returned Eye, resident again in Egypt and in its houses, is the condition Bastet's whole cult presupposes. Her festival at Bubastis (Sections XV–XVI) is the cycle's civic form: the goddess approached by river, with music, in joy, in her own city, year after year — the homecoming not remembered but re-performed, as the archive's article on ritual practice sets out for Egyptian festivals generally. Where Sekhmet's cult specialises in the moments before the return — the dangerous days, the arrows, the litany of recall — Bastet's specialises in the morning after it: the feast, the full jars, the cats in the temple courts. IX. Family and Relations — Daughter of Ra, Mother of Mihos Egyptian divine genealogies are local and functional, not systematic, and Bastet's are a textbook case: she acquires relations where a cult needs them, and different cities keep different lists. The constant, everywhere, is her solar filiation. She is a daughter of Ra — the filiation her Eye-of-Ra office itself implies, since the Eye goddesses are the sun's daughters as well as his weapon — and the companion articles' presentation of her among the daughters of the sun, with Hathor, Sekhmet, and the rest, follows the sources' own habit. Beyond that constant, the archive proceeds relation by relation, at the strength each is attested. Her clearest offspring is the lion god Mihos — Egyptian Maahes, "the lion who is true beside her" in one traditional gloss of his name — a lion-headed god of war and of the king's protection, whose cult belongs to the same Delta world as hers: Leontopolis and Bubastis are his cities as Bubastis is hers, and Greek writers knew him in her circle. The pairing is iconographically exact: the cat goddess's son keeps the full lion form she was laying down, mane and all, as if the family's leonine inheritance had passed to the next generation entire. Temple tradition at Bubastis joins mother and son in one cult landscape; Herodotus's processional road from her temple runs to a temple of "Hermes," and the city's sacred geography held other divine households besides (Section XIV). Two further relations circulate widely and are stated here with their warning labels. Greek tradition, as Herodotus reports it (II.156, in paraphrase), made Bubastis a daughter of Isis and Osiris and a sister of Horus, hidden with him by their mother from Set's violence: that is the Greek interpretive genealogy, generated by the equation of Bastet with Artemis and Artemis's known parentage, and it is not an Egyptian family tree. Egyptian tradition itself offers a different occasional connection, in which Bastet appears among the possible mothers of Anubis — the archive's Anubis article lists the variants plainly: son of Ra, of the cow goddess Hesat, of Bastet, of Ra and Nephthys, of Osiris and Isis, varying by source and period. And at Memphis, where the perfume god Nefertem is the child of Ptah and Sekhmet in the Memphite triad, some traditions give Bastet in Sekhmet's place as the mother — a variant that follows naturally from the continuum of Section VIII and from Bastet's own unguent associations (Section XX), and that this archive reports as a variant, not as the triad's standard form, which the Ptah and Sekhmet articles give as Ptah, Sekhmet, Nefertem. X. Bubastis the City — Nome Capital of the Eastern Delta Bubastis stood in the south-eastern Delta, on the Pelusiac branch of the Nile — the easternmost of the river's ancient mouths — at the point where the Delta's waterways met the road east: toward the Wadi Tumilat, the canal corridor to the Red Sea, and the land bridge to Asia. The archive's article on sacred geography places it in the Delta's nome system as capital of its own nome, the eighteenth of Lower Egypt in the standard lists, in the row of eastern Delta cities — Mendes, Bubastis, Tanis — that guarded the kingdom's most vulnerable frontier. A goddess of protection posted at a frontier city is not a coincidence of the record. Bubastis was a gate of Egypt, and its goddess was the gate's warden as well as its householder. The city's antiquity is stratigraphic, not legendary. Excavation (Section XIII) has carried its history down through the New Kingdom city to a Middle Kingdom palace and administrative quarter, to the ka-temples of the Sixth Dynasty kings Teti and Pepi I, and beneath Pepi I's temple to a large provincial palace of the Fourth and Fifth Dynasties: Bubastis was a seat of provincial government in the Old Kingdom, centuries before its dynasty ruled Egypt. Herodotus's observation that the city had been "banked up" higher and higher, generation by generation, while the temple stayed at its original level (Section XIV), is the Delta's settlement physics exactly: a city on a gezira , a mound of accumulated occupation debris and flood defence, rising out of a floodplain that drowned everything not raised. Tell Basta today is that mound, its red granite temple field at the old level, the modern city of Zagazig grown up around and against it. XI. The Great Temple of Bastet — Builders and Phases The great temple of Bastet is known, unusually for so famous a building, chiefly from its ruins' inscriptions: the structure Herodotus praised as the most pleasing in Egypt was destroyed, probably by earthquake, and survives as a vast field of fallen granite blocks whose texts the Tell Basta Project has spent three decades reading in place (Section XIII). The building history those blocks yield, as Daniela Rosenow of the project summarised it in Egyptian Archaeology , the Egypt Exploration Society's magazine, is a history of successive royal rebuildings on one sacred footprint. The temple's great age is the Twenty-second Dynasty: Osorkon I's name dominates the blocks of the main eastern entrance, where the king is shown making offerings to a variety of gods, and the distribution of fallen columns with palm-leaf capitals allows the entrance court to be reconstructed as a peristyle court of about 30 by 50 metres. Osorkon II extended the temple extensively and added its most famous component, the festival hall of Section XII. West of the festival gate, Rosenow's reconstruction continues, a colonnade of papyrus-bundle columns, almost 30 metres long, led to a five-aisled hypostyle hall with Hathor-headed capitals — the cow goddess's heads carrying the roof of the cat goddess's house, the continuum built in stone. The last great builder was also the last native king of Egypt. Nectanebo II (360–343 BCE), whose temple programme the archive's Late Period article traces from the Delta to Philae, renewed the sanctuary itself at Bubastis, as he renewed sanctuaries at Hermopolis, Abydos, Memphis, and a dozen other cult centres: the holy of holies that Herodotus's near-contemporary city showed its pilgrims was, in its final form, a fourth-century building inside an early-first-millennium temple inside a sacred enclosure far older than either. Earlier royal names occur among the blocks as well — the temple field has yielded material of the New Kingdom, including a monumental pink granite statue of a Ramesside queen uncovered by the project between 2001 and 2003 — and in 2004 the entrance area produced a new duplicate of the Canopus Decree of Ptolemy III (238 BCE), proof the temple was still a functioning, decree-publishing institution deep into the Ptolemaic period. The archive's article on temple architecture supplies the grammar — pylon, court, hypostyle hall, sanctuary, the axis of increasing darkness and restriction — within which Bubastis's scattered blocks are read. Herodotus's description (Section XIV) adds the element the ruins alone could not have proved: water. His temple stood ringed by two Nile channels that did not join, each a hundred feet broad, so that the sanctuary was effectively an island in the middle of the raised city. The Name — bs and the Bes-Image Problem The god's name is short enough to write in two signs: bs [Gardiner: D58-S29] [𓃀𓋴] — b [Gardiner: D58] [𓃀], the foot, and s [Gardiner: S29] [𓋴], the folded cloth. No ancient Egyptian etymology for the name survives, and this archive offers none. What the name meant to its bearers is recoverable not from a dictionary but from three thousand years of use: bs [Gardiner: D58-S29] named the being whose image stood in the bedroom, whose face looked out from the headrest, and whose figure was worn at the throat of a pregnant woman. The name is a household word before it is a temple word, and the article that follows keeps that order. A necessary caution stands at the head of everything written about this god. Modern scholarship, following the Metropolitan Museum's usage, speaks not only of "Bes" but of the Bes-image : several protective deities were depicted as dwarves with a lion's mane, ears and tail, and the appearance we call Bes's was sometimes adopted by other gods altogether. The Met states the problem plainly in its record for a colossal Bes head: the head "unmistakably depicts the god known as Bes, or, more accurately, what is known as a 'Bes-image,' since Bes's appearance was sometimes adopted for other gods, and there is no name preserved on the statue." Where an inscription names bs [Gardiner: D58-S29], the god is Bes. Where only the image survives, the honest label is the Bes-image — a form, a function, and a family, not always a single person. That distinction is not modern pedantry. It shapes the whole subject. A state god such as Horus carries a mythology, a titulary, a priesthood and a literature; his identity can be checked against texts at every period. Bes carries, above all, an image and a set of jobs . Textual material about him is rare, as the Global Egyptian Museum's glossary entry notes, and only after the New Kingdom does the written tradition become more informative. The archaeology therefore leads and the texts follow: we know Bes first by where his face was put, and only secondarily by anything anyone wrote about him. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . One correction matters directly here: the mobile soul, bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝], whose safe return Bes guarded in sleep (Section VIII), is written with the ram sign whose audited value is bꜣ itself. The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . The name also travelled, and its travels are evidence. Greek and Coptic renderings carried the sound of bs [Gardiner: D58-S29] beyond Egypt, and the female form of the name, bst [Gardiner: D58-S29-X1] [𓃀𓋴𓏏] — the same two signs closed by t [Gardiner: X1] [𓏏], the feminine ending — names Beset, his counterpart, treated in Section XVIII. A name built from two of the commonest signs in the script, borne by a god with no mythology in the grand manner, became one of the most widely recognised divine names in the ancient Mediterranean. That paradox — maximum presence, minimum institution — is the subject of this article. II. The God With No Temple of His Own — Household Religion As far as is known, Bes had no cult area of his own. The sentence is the Global Egyptian Museum's, and it states the foundational fact of Bes studies: no temple was built for Bes, no priesthood bore his name as its primary charge, no festival calendar organised a city's year around him, and no body of temple inscription expounds his theology. He appears instead as what that same entry calls a "subsidiary god" — present inside the temples of other gods, consulted there on occasion as an oracle, and carved on their birth houses — while his real domain lay elsewhere entirely. His real domain was the house: pr [Gardiner: O1] [𓉐], the ordinary Egyptian word for a house, written with the ground-plan sign. The Metropolitan Museum's Bes-image amulet record (Third Intermediate Period, 26.7.878) puts it in one sentence: "The domain of the Bes image was the household." Anna Stevens's survey of domestic religious practices in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (2009) gives the framework: domestic religion addressed the concerns of everyday life, is traced in spells of healing and protection, private letters, and cult emplacements and objects from settlement sites, and favoured protective divinities such as Bes, Taweret and Hathor , alongside deified ancestors. Bes is not an exception to Egyptian religion. He is one of its two great halves — the half that happened at home. The contrast with temple religion is structural, not a matter of rank. A temple, ḥwt-nṯr in the conventional phrase — the "mansion of the god," built around nṯr [Gardiner: R8] [𓊹], "god" — was a restricted, priestly, calendrical institution. A household cult was none of those things. It needed no ordination, kept no calendar but the family's own crises, and addressed itself to the moments when life was actually at risk: a birth, a child's fever, a bad night, a snake in the corner of the room. The gods of that cult were chosen the way Bes was chosen — not for cosmic scope but for proximity and willingness . He was already in the room. NO TEMPLE No known cult area was Bes's own. Claims for a single exceptional Bes temple should be treated as unproven unless a source is named; the standard reference position is the one stated above. NO PRIESTHOOD OF HIS OWN No titled priesthood of Bes organised his worship. The specialists who deployed his image were the household itself and the protective practitioners of magical practice — the same world that consecrated amulets and drew wand-circles. EVERYWHERE IN THE HOUSE Bedroom walls, bed legs and footboards, headrests, mirrors, cosmetic vessels, furniture, feeding cups and amulets: the find-spots of the Bes-image map the interior of the Egyptian home room by room (Sections VIII and XI). SUBSIDIARY IN TEMPLES Inside other gods' temples Bes served at the threshold of birth: on mammisi abaci and columns (Section XIV), above the child on healing stelae (Section XIII), and, late and locally, as an oracle (Sections XV–XVI). This is why Bes survived every religious revolution Egypt underwent. When the Amarna reforms suppressed the traditional gods at state level, household devotion to protectors of Bes's kind is precisely the stratum hardest to suppress and the first to re-emerge — a point the archive's treatment of amulets and talismans makes for the household cult in general: some divine presences were simply too immediately useful to abolish. A god with no temple cannot be closed down. A god whose cult is a face on a bedpost has no address at which a decree can be served. Bes's institutional weakness was, across three millennia, his survival strategy. It also explains the tone in which Egyptians seem to have held him. The sources and the objects agree on affection. The Metropolitan Museum calls him, without embarrassment, "the beloved god Bes" in its record for a small double-sided faience figure of the Late to Ptolemaic period (10.130.1991). Great temple gods were feared, praised, bargained with and obeyed. Bes was liked — and the liking is itself data, evidence of a relationship between ordinary people and a divine protector that ran on familiarity rather than awe. III. Iconography — Dwarf Body, Bandy Legs, Lion's Mane Bes is recognised at a glance, across three thousand years and half a dozen cultures, by a body no other Egyptian god has. The British Museum's biography of the god summarises the type: a dwarf-god, generally benign, protector of childbirth and the family, and also a god of music, dancing and warfare. The Global Egyptian Museum's entry gives the visual inventory: the body of a dwarf, crooked — bandy — legs, the mane and ears of a lion, the tongue often sticking out of the mouth, a headdress of upstanding feathers, and a tail visible between the legs, belonging originally to the animal skin the god wears. Every element of that inventory does work, as Section IV argues; here the task is simply to fix the type. The body is short, broad and frontal. The belly protrudes; the legs bow outward; the arms hang or rest with hands on the thighs and hips, or rise to brandish the god's equipment. Modern museum descriptions note that characteristics drawn from achondroplasia — the commonest form of dwarfism — are melded with those of lions to create the figure: the Metropolitan Museum uses exactly that language for a Third Intermediate Period Bes-image amulet (2021.41.54). The point matters for interpretation. The dwarf body is not a joke at the god's expense and not a defect to be explained away. In the Egyptian visual system it is one term of a deliberate compound — human dwarf and lion in a single person — and the compound, not either term alone, is the god. The head carries the second term of the compound. The face is broad, bearded and grimacing, framed by a lion's mane and lion's ears, the tongue frequently protruding. Above it rises the feather headdress: tall, erect plumes, the feather itself written šwt [Gardiner: H6] [𓆄]. The lion, mꜣi [Gardiner: E13] [𓃠], supplies the leonine half of the being — mane, ears, tail and, above all, the reputation Egypt's most dangerous animal carried into any room it entered. A tail hangs between the god's legs; museum descriptions are careful to note that it belongs to the lion- or leopard-skin he wears, the hunter's garment turned divine attribute. THE DWARF BODY Short stature, broad torso, protruding belly, bandy legs. The stance is frontal and planted, hands on thighs or hips — a figure built to stand in a doorway and not be moved. THE LION'S HEAD-DRESSING Mane, round lion's ears, beard, grimace, protruding tongue, and the tall feather crown, šwt [Gardiner: H6]. The face, detached from the body, remained a complete amulet by itself. THE EQUIPMENT Knives, grasped snakes, a drum or tambourine, the large sꜣ [Gardiner: V17] [𓎃] sign of protection, and in later periods a soldier's dress and weapons: the tool-kit is inventoried in Section IV. THE SKIN AND TAIL The animal skin worn over the shoulders, its tail swinging between the legs, marks the wild creature recruited into the house — danger domesticated, not danger removed. THE FRONTAL FACE Almost alone among Egyptian gods, Bes is shown full-face, meeting the viewer's eyes directly. Section IV treats frontality itself as the core apotropaic device. THE NUDE AND THE ARMED Bes may be nude, emphatically male, kilted, or — in Roman-period images — dressed as a soldier. The body-plan never changes; costume tracks period and function. Scale is part of the iconography too. Bes exists at every size the Egyptian craftsman worked: amulets under two centimetres high, meant to hang at a child's neck; vessels and furniture fittings at household scale; and, from the Kushite period onward, architectural Bes-images on abaci, column shafts and pillars, some of them colossal. The Metropolitan Museum's limestone colossal head (23.2.35), said to be from Bubastis, measures nearly forty centimetres in height for the head alone. The same face that guarded a cradle could carry a temple roof-beam's visual weight above a birth-house column — because the face, not the size, was the operative thing. Identification, finally, follows the rule of Section I. A frontal dwarf with mane, feathers and tail is a Bes-image; whether the image is Bes, or Aha (Section V), or another god wearing the Bes form — the Met notes gods associated with Horus among those who adopted the appearance — is decided by inscription and context, not by the silhouette alone. The archive uses "Bes" where the sources do, and "Bes-image" where only the form is certain. IV. The Apotropaic Logic — Face, Noise, Dance and Laughter Bes's appearance is usually called grotesque. The word is accurate and the conclusion usually drawn from it is wrong. The grotesque is not failed beauty or comic relief. It is a weapon system , and its logic can be stated precisely: the things that threatened an Egyptian household — disease, venomous animals, malign spirits, the dangers that gathered around birth and sleep — were themselves beings that could be frightened, repelled and driven off . Protection therefore took the form of a counter-threat. You set against the thing that creeps in the dark a face more frightening than it is, stationed exactly where it must pass. That is why the helpful summary in the Global Egyptian Museum entry is careful to give the mechanism, not just the look: Bes was regarded as a protector against all kinds of danger, "helped not only by his awful appearance, but also by the attributes he carried in his hands" — knives, or snakes held fast, which in the Egyptian convention meant overcome — a large sꜣ [Gardiner: V17] [𓎃] hieroglyph, the sign whose value is "protection" itself, or a musical instrument, usually a drum or tambourine. Each attribute is a sentence in the same language. The knife says: what comes here will be cut. The grasped snake — the snake itself written ḥfꜣ [Gardiner: I1] [𓆈] — says: the venomous thing is already in my hand, mastered. The sꜣ [Gardiner: V17] sign says the abstract word outright: protection, worn as an emblem. Frontality is the delivery system. Egyptian divine images are overwhelmingly profile images; the profile is the view of a being going about its own business, seen from the side of the world. Bes turns around. He faces out of the object , directly at whoever — or whatever — approaches it, with both eyes, tongue out, mane spread. An approaching malign force does not encounter a picture of a god. It encounters a god looking at it . The same frontality appears in the other great apotropaic faces of the Egyptian repertoire, and it is no accident that the face alone, detached from the dwarf body, served as a complete amulet: the gaze was the weapon, and the gaze needed no body to work. Noise, Music and the Raised Mood The second weapon is sound, and the museum entry states its double action with unusual psychological precision: music "not only banished evil spirits but also gave humans a happier, thus less frightened, mood." Two effects, one practice. Outwardly, drumming, rattling, singing and dancing at the bedside of a woman in labour or a sick child filled the dangerous space with ordered human sound — the acoustic opposite of the silence in which fear and malign influence were imagined to move. Inwardly, the same sound treated the patients and the family: a frightened household was, in this understanding, a vulnerable household, and raising the mood was raising the defence. Section IX develops the musical evidence; the principle belongs here, because it shows Bes's protection working on both sides of the skin at once. Laughter belongs to the same system, and should be stated carefully. Bes grimaces, sticks out his tongue, dances, plays, and is shown in attitudes no state god would tolerate. Modern writers often file this under "comic god" and move on. The archive's reading — offered as interpretation, in Section XIX's terms, not as an attested ancient doctrine — is that the laughter is continuous with the grimace: both are exaggerated life , noise and motion and appetite displayed at maximum, stationed at the exact places where life was thinnest and most likely to fail. The frightening face and the funny face are one face, seen by two different audiences: by the malign force, as a threat; by the family, as their champion enjoying himself. "He averted evil with music, knives, or the sa sign as he watched over the occupants of the house." — Metropolitan Museum of Art, record for the Bes-Image Amulet, 26.7.878 (Third Intermediate Period) That single museum sentence — quoted here as a modern published description, not as an ancient text — is the best short statement of Bes's whole theology that this article can offer. A god defined not by what he is in himself but by what he averts , with what tools, and over whom: music, knives, the protection-sign; the occupants of the house. Everything in the sections that follow is an expansion of it. V. Aha the Fighter and the Family of Bes-Images Bes did not begin alone, and he may not, at the beginning, have been Bes at all. The Global Egyptian Museum entry closes its account with the genealogy: Bes "is closely related to a god with a similar appearance, called Aha ('warrior')," and is "in fact the personification of a whole group of gods, whose characteristics are so muddled together that it is difficult now to differentiate them." Aha's name is transparent in a way Bes's is not: ꜥḥꜣ [Gardiner: D36-V28-G1] [𓂝𓎛𓄿], "the Fighter," built from ꜥ [Gardiner: D36], ḥ [Gardiner: V28] and ꜣ [Gardiner: G1] — a fighting name for a dwarf figure who appears, arms raised, on the protective equipment of the Middle Kingdom , the period in which the whole family first becomes clearly visible. The honest model, on the present evidence, is a family that converged . Dwarf-bodied, lion-featured protective beings — fighters, dancers, snake-graspers — circulated in Egyptian households and on protective objects, under more than one name, before the New Kingdom tradition settled increasingly on bs [Gardiner: D58-S29] as the name of the type. Bes, on this model, is less a single inventoried person than the name that won: the personification, as the museum entry puts it, of a whole group. This is why the "Bes-image" terminology of Section I is unavoidable, and why arguments about exactly when "Bes" first appears so often turn out to be arguments about a name rather than about the figure, which is older than its eventual label. The family's other members matter mainly as a warning against tidiness. Egyptian religion, as the archive's survey of the pantheon shows throughout, preferred accumulation to system: local and functional beings were identified with one another, absorbed, or left side by side without reconciliation. A group of similar protective dwarves collapsing, over centuries, into one beloved name is exactly the kind of process that produced much of the Egyptian pantheon. Bes is unusual only in that the collapse happened in the household rather than in a temple — and so left almost no paperwork. What Aha contributes to the composite is the emphasis in his name: fighting . The later Bes dances and plays, and the musical Bes can eclipse the armed one in popular summaries. The Middle Kingdom figures restore the balance. The raised arms, the grasped snakes, the knives, and a name that simply means Fighter declare the original terms of the household contract: this being is here to fight something , on behalf of people who cannot fight it themselves — a woman in labour, an infant, a sleeper. The music of the later god never replaced the fighting; Section IV's logic holds them together, the drum and the knife as two modes of one defence. VI. Protector of Childbirth and Mothers — Beside Taweret Childbirth was the most dangerous ordinary event in an Egyptian life, for the mother and for the child at once, and it is the centre of Bes's cult. The British Museum's biography fixes the priority: protector of childbirth and the family comes first in its list, before music, dancing, good luck and warfare. The Metropolitan Museum's amulet records say the same in object language: the Bes-image's responsibilities "generally centered on the guarding of children and their mothers during childbirth" (New Kingdom amulet 11.215.178, from Malqata). Birth is written ms [Gardiner: F31] [𓄟], and the mother mwt [Gardiner: G14] [𓅐]; Bes's whole career is organised around those two words. His partner in this work is Taweret , the pregnant hippopotamus goddess, standing upright on lion's legs with a crocodile's tail, assembled, like Bes himself, from the Nile's most dangerous animals recruited into protective service. The pairing is constant in the material record: Bes and Taweret together on the apotropaic wands of Section XII, together on furniture and headrests, together in the birth houses of Section XIV, together, in the framing of the archive's article on amulets and talismans , as the standard paired guardians of the domestic threshold. Two composite monsters, one dwarf-lion and one hippo-lion-crocodile, standing over the birthing bed: the iconography states, with complete clarity, that birth was understood as a battle in which the mother needed the most frightening allies available. The mechanics of Bes's attendance at a birth can be reconstructed from the objects, and only from the objects — no liturgy of a Bes birth-rite survives. His image was present in the room : painted or set up in the birthing space, carried on the amulets the mother wore, and built into the furniture around her. The protective circle of the apotropaic wand (Section XII) could be drawn around the birthing bed itself. Music and noise — his other weapons — belonged to the same occasion, the sounding shield of Section IV raised around a woman whose labour made her, in the Egyptian understanding, maximally open to malign interference. Nothing in this reconstruction requires a priest. That is the point. The defence of a birth was household work, performed with household objects, by the people in the room, under the gaze of a god who was already there. BEFORE THE BIRTH Amulets of Bes worn in pregnancy; his figure on the vessels and cosmetic objects of daily use; the protective presence established in the room before it was needed. DURING THE BIRTH The wand-circle drawn, the images present, music and noise raised — Bes and Taweret at the bed, the two great household guardians on duty together. AFTER THE BIRTH The protection did not end at delivery. The same god guarded the newborn's first, most fragile period — the subject of Section VII — and the mother's recovery within the house he already watched. A theological note completes the section. Bes's role at birth is sometimes described in the literature with a phrase the archive repeats only as a reported interpretation: temple and magical texts are said to give Bes a part in "opening the womb" so that the child can be born. No such text is quoted in this article, because none was read in a verified edition during its preparation; the claim is therefore filed where it belongs — as a secondary-literature report, consistent with everything the objects show, but not promoted here to a quoted fact. The objects need no help. A god on the wand, the bedpost, the amulet and the birth-house wall was at the birth, whatever any single text may add. VII. Guardian of Children and Infancy The child who survived the birth entered the second most dangerous period of an Egyptian life, and Bes's commission extended over it without a break. Infant and child mortality stood behind a large part of all household religion, and the Bes-image is found exactly where that anxiety was managed: on amulets hung on children, on feeding vessels, on the small furniture of the nursery end of the house, and in the company of the other child-protectors of the pantheon . The Metropolitan Museum's scarab records make the pairing of functions routine — the Bes-image "also protected mother and child" — and its faience amulets of the god were produced, in the museum's phrase, precisely because "the Bes image was a popular amulet" for exactly this constituency. The logic is the logic of Section IV applied to the smallest body in the house. A child cannot wield the knife, draw the circle, or raise the noise; someone must do the frightening for it. Bes is sized, in a sense, for the work: a small god for small people, stationed at cot height. Egyptian parents who hung a faience Bes at a child's neck were not decorating the child. They were posting its guard — the same act, at amulet scale, as carving the face on the birth-house column at architectural scale. The archive's article on amulets sets out the general theory of such postings: the correctly made image did not merely represent the protection, it was the protection, present at the throat. The child-gods of the temples gave this household anxiety a theological mirror. In the mammisi theology of Section XIV, the divine child — Horus the child at Philae, Ihy at Dendera — is born, hidden, threatened and preserved, and Bes attends that birth as he attended human ones. The correspondence ran both ways. A human child's dangerous first years were dignified by the pattern of the god-child's; and the god-child's attendants, Bes at their head, were credible precisely because every family already knew them from its own rooms. Household religion and temple theology meet, in Bes, at the cradle. One further object class belongs to this section: the Bes-image in the company of dangerous animals mastered. Seal-amulets and scarabs of the Ramesside period show the god in frontal view, hands on thighs, tail between his legs, flanked in some examples by bound foreign prisoners — read by the Metropolitan Museum (15.43.130) as symbols of "the (successful) control over threats." For a child's amulet the iconography needs no allegorical stretching. The threats around an Egyptian childhood were concrete — scorpions, snakes, fever, the river — and the image promises control over threats as such, in whatever shape the next one arrives. VIII. Protector of Sleep and Sleepers — Headrests and Beds Sleep was the household's second nightly crisis. The sleeper lay unconscious, defenceless, and — in the Egyptian frame — partially absent: the bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝], the mobile soul of the composite soul , travelled in the night and returned at waking, and the body it left behind needed a guard. Dream itself is rswt [Gardiner: D21-S29-G43-X1-D6] [𓂋𓋴𓅱𓏏𓁻], a word built on the root of waking; to sleep is sḏr [Gardiner: S29-D46-D21-A55] [𓋴𓂧𓂋𓁀]. Between those two words — sleeping, and the waking-within-sleep of the dream — stood Bes, posted at the bed. The evidence is furniture. The Global Egyptian Museum entry states the distribution directly: furniture used for sleeping, such as a bed or a headrest, often bears a representation of Bes or of his companion Taweret, because "when asleep, being unaware of what was happening around them, people were exposed to all the dangers of the night." The headrest, wrs [Gardiner: Q4] [𓊫], is the key object: a curved support that held the sleeper's head raised and turned, its upright and base available for carving. A Bes carved on a headrest put the god's face directly beneath the sleeper's ear and beside the dreaming head — the closest posting of any in the entire Bes repertoire, held there all night, every night. Bed legs and footboards carried the same guardianship at the bed's corners. The pattern is consistent with everything else in this article: danger was expected to approach , along the floor, from the room's edges, in the dark — and the defence was stationed at the approach routes, at floor level and at head level, facing outward. A bedroom equipped with Bes-images on its bed and headrest and Bes and Taweret painted or set up at its walls was not a decorated bedroom. It was a fortified position, held nightly, by a garrison of two. // BES AND THE DREAMING GATE // The archive's article on dream incubation treats the full theology of the Egyptian dream — the travelling bꜣ [Gardiner: E10], the classification of dreams, and the incubation protocol. Bes enters that system at two points. As the sleeper's guard, he is the condition of safe ordinary dreaming: the reason a household could let its souls travel unmolested. As the presiding figure of the Saqqara chambers (Section XV), he becomes, late and locally, a giver of dreams himself. The two roles are one role at two scales — the god of the guarded threshold, first of the bedroom, then of the incubation chamber built in its image. Night terrors deserve a sentence of their own, because they are the experiential core of this whole section. A household that has watched a child cry out in the night, or a sleeper wake in panic from a dream of pursuit, does not need a theology to want a guardian at the bed. Bes's sleep-cult is Egyptian religion at its most empirically driven: the phenomenon was universal, nightly and frightening, and the response — a fierce, wakeful, never-sleeping face posted where the sleeper's own vigilance failed — answers it part for part. Of all the gods of Egypt, only the household gods kept these hours. The temple gods slept in their sanctuaries and were wakened by hymns. Bes, on the headrest, was on duty through the night. IX. Music, Noise and Dance — the Sounding Shield Bes plays. The objects are unambiguous: the god shakes a tambourine, strikes a drum, plucks a lyre and a harp, dances with knees bent and arms raised, and appears in the company of musicians and dancing girls whose art his presence blesses and protects. The British Museum's biography lists music and dancing among his defining provinces; the Metropolitan Museum's bronze group statue (04.2.403) shows a Bes-image plucking a lyre above a worshipping man, and the museum's comment supplies the interpretation: "the lyre held by Bes may reflect his power to calm angry spirits." Calming, note — not only repelling. The music works on spirits as the grimace works on intruders: each in its register, sound and face are the same defence. From the New Kingdom onward, the Met's Malqata amulet record notes, "Bes has a close tie to music and is often depicted playing different instruments" — and the tie is older in practice than in that particular record, since the sounding defence belongs to the birth-room and sick-room wherever those are documented. Instruments in Bes's hands are not attributes in the heraldic sense, like a sceptre denoting rank. They are equipment shown in use . The tambourine is raised because it is being shaken; the dance is mid-step because the dance is the rite. Egyptian images of Bes at music are the closest thing the household cult has to a liturgical manuscript: they show the ceremony while it happens. Dance completes what sound begins. A dancing god is a moving perimeter — the protective circle of the wand (Section XII) redrawn by a body, continuously, for as long as the crisis lasts. The human performers who danced at births and festivals under Bes's patronage, some of them bearing his image tattooed or painted on the body in the New Kingdom evidence summarised in the archive's amulets article, were not entertaining an audience in the modern sense. They were doing, with their bodies, what the god's image does with its face: filling endangered space with exaggerated, ordered, defiant life. Bes the musician is therefore not a softening of Bes the fighter. He is the fighter's second weapon, drawn. DRUM AND TAMBOURINE The commonest instruments in the god's hands: struck and shaken percussion, loud, rhythmic, portable — the birth-room's and sick-room's sounding shield in its simplest form. LYRE AND HARP Stringed instruments in more formal images, including the Met's bronze Bes with a lyre (04.2.403): music as the calming of angry spirits, protection by harmony as well as by noise. THE DANCING BODY Bent knees, raised arms, the animal skin swinging: Bes dances in a large share of his images, and human dancers and musicians worked under his guardianship in festal and domestic settings alike. THE RAISED MOOD Music "gave humans a happier, thus less frightened, mood" (Global Egyptian Museum): the psychological arm of the defence, treating the fear that made a household vulnerable. X. Beer, Wine and Merriment Beer, ḥnqt [Gardiner: W22] [𓏊], was not a luxury in Egypt but a staple — a food, a wage, an offering and a medicine in one. Wine, irp [Gardiner: W21] [𓏉], stood a step higher in cost and festivity. Both belonged to the world of the festival, ḥb [Gardiner: W3] [𓎱], and both belonged, in the household's emotional geography, to Bes. The god of music and dance is necessarily the god of the occasions at which music and dance happen, and those occasions ran on beer. Bes-images moulded onto drinking vessels, and Bes-faced cups from which the drinker drank through the god's own features, put the association into the drinker's hands: the merriment was taken through the protector, under his face, with his blessing on the altered state it produced. That blessing was needed, in Egyptian terms, because drunkenness is another threshold. The drunk person, like the sleeper and the woman in labour, is partially absent from ordinary vigilance — loosened, open, off guard. A religion that posted guards at the bed and the birthing stool could be expected to post one at the beer jar too, and Bes is that guard: the patron under whose face the household could safely let go. Later tradition even attached to him the one temple-like foundation the popular literature loves to repeat — a shrine by a vineyard, the god set to watch the grapes. This article records that story as tradition, not as established fact : no source read for this article documents such a temple, and the archive's standard (Section II) is that Bes had, as far as is known, no cult place of his own.
