The Names — Beer, Bread and the Staple Pair Beer and bread were not two items on an Egyptian menu. They were the menu's foundation, the wage, the offering, and the unit in which the state reckoned obligation. To understand Egyptian food is therefore to begin with two words. Beer is ḥnqt [Gardiner: W22] [𓏊] — the sign itself is a beer jar, a vessel with a pointed or rounded base made to stand in a ring or in sand. Bread, in its generic sense, is t [Gardiner: X1] [𓏏], written with the small flat loaf sign; a single baked loaf can also be written t [Gardiner: X2] [𓏐]. Between them, these two words head almost every offering list, ration account, and funerary formula in the language. The pairing is grammatical as well as dietary. The standard offering formula asks the gods to give bread and beer before it asks for anything else — ox, fowl, alabaster, linen, and "everything good and pure" follow after. Temple accounts, workmen's pay lists, and mathematical school exercises all treat loaves and jars as the first quantities to be settled. Hana Vymazalová's survey of the ration system in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology puts the position plainly, in paraphrase: bread, beer, and grain represented the basic components of rations in all periods; bread and beer were often allocated daily, while grain might be provided as a monthly payment, and meat was an extra. That hierarchy — daily bread and beer, periodic grain, occasional meat — is the skeleton of the Egyptian diet at every social level for which records survive. Wine stands apart from the pair. Wine is irp [Gardiner: W21] [𓏉], again written with its own vessel sign. Where beer was the drink of everyone, wine was, for most of Egyptian history, the drink of kings, temples, and the wealthy: vineyard land was limited, production was labour-intensive, and the finished product travelled in sealed, labelled amphorae as a prestige commodity. Sections XV and XVI treat it in its own right. The present article's centre of gravity, however, is where Egypt's own centre of gravity lay: with the grain processes — brewing first and fullest, then baking — because those are the processes Egypt ran every day, at household scale and at industrial scale, for more than three thousand years. // READING THE TERMS IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every technical Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes in the form [Gardiner: <codes-hyphenated>], and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . None of those corrected signs is needed for the core food vocabulary of this article, which is built from the stable vessel, grain, and loaf signs listed above. The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . A note on the title word. Beer is sometimes loosely transliterated in popular writing in ways that confuse it with other ḥ -initial words. The archive uses ḥnqt [Gardiner: W22] [𓏊] throughout: the jar sign is the word's own determinative and logogram, the spelling is the one the ration accounts use, and the V2 map gives W22 the whole-word value ḥnḳ.t directly. Likewise emmer is bdt [Gardiner: U9] [𓌽] and barley, in the ration accounts, is it [Gardiner: M33] [𓇠] — two words the reader will meet constantly below, because the entire staple economy is, at bottom, an argument about what to do with these two grains. That argument was settled differently for the two processes, and the difference is one of the article's main findings. Bread, on the surviving physical evidence, is overwhelmingly an emmer food. Beer is a mixed and flexible food, brewed from emmer, from barley, and from the two together. Why that should be so — what each grain does well, and what each costs in labour — is a technical question with technical answers, and Sections IV and XII give them. First, however, the archive must explain how any of this is known at all, because the best evidence for Egyptian brewing is not a text or a picture. It is a crust inside a jar, read under a microscope. II. Evidence and Method — Residues Under the Microscope Four kinds of evidence bear on Egyptian food processes, and they do not all deserve equal trust. There are texts: ration lists, offering lists, jar labels, mathematical exercises, and a small number of literary passages. There are pictures: tomb scenes and three-dimensional tomb models showing bakers and brewers at work. There are installations: excavated breweries, bakeries, ovens, vats, and moulds. And there are the foods themselves: desiccated loaves from tombs, and dried residues still adhering to the insides of vessels, preserved by Egypt's dry climate in a way that has no parallel in wetter archaeologies. The modern reconstruction of Egyptian brewing rests on the fourth kind of evidence correcting the second — on the foods themselves overruling what scholars thought the pictures showed. The decisive work is Delwen Samuel's. In her 1996 paper in Science , "Investigation of Ancient Egyptian Baking and Brewing Methods by Correlative Microscopy," Samuel examined desiccated bread loaves and beer residues by optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The abstract, quoted here in the journal's own words in paraphrase-tight summary, states the programme: ancient Egyptian baking and brewing were investigated by microscopy of desiccated loaves and beer remains; bread was made not only with flour from raw grain but sometimes also with malt and with yeast; and brewing blended cooked and uncooked malt with water, the mixture being strained free of husk before inoculation with yeast. Every clause of that summary matters, and Sections III to VII unpack them one by one. The method deserves explanation, because it is the reason the conclusions carry weight. A starch granule is not an inert speck. Under the electron microscope, a granule records what has happened to it. Heated in water, granules swell, fold, and eventually merge into one another as the starch gelatinises. Enzymes released in a sprouting grain attack granules from within, producing characteristic surface pitting and internal channelling. Dry heat blisters a granule's surface without merging it. Samuel's correlative microscopy compared the granules in ancient residues, form by form, with granules in modern cereal foods whose processing was known — and read the ancient process off the match. The samples were substantial: nearly seventy loaves and more than two hundred vessel contents were first examined optically, and fourteen loaves and forty vessel residues went forward to scanning electron microscopy. The bread spanned roughly 2000 to 1200 BCE; the beer residues came from two workmen's settlements, Deir el-Medina (c. 1550–1070 BCE) and the Workmen's Village at Amarna (c. 1350 BCE). Two consequences follow for how this article writes. First, where microscopy and tomb pictures conflict, the article follows the microscopy, and says so. Tomb scenes are compressed, conventional, and made to provision the dead, not to instruct the living; a residue is the process itself, fossilised mid-course. Second, where the evidence runs out, the article stops. Samuel herself is careful about flavourings — none had been detected in the beer residues she examined — and about the yeast question, where the inoculation route remains an inference rather than an observation. The archive preserves those cautions exactly where she placed them. A reconstruction that knows its own edges is worth more than a seamless one. The other evidence classes are used for what they are good at. Texts give quantities, names, and social distribution: who got how much of what, and what a jar claimed to contain. Pictures and models give the choreography of the workshop: the order of workstations, the division of labour, the shapes of vessels and ovens. Installations give scale: how much beer a predynastic town could make in a day, and how much bread a pyramid workforce required. Put together — residue for process, text for quantity, image for choreography, installation for scale — the four classes produce the fullest procedural account the archive can honestly offer. That account begins with a correction, because for most of the twentieth century the standard account of Egyptian beer was simply wrong. III. The Refuted Model — Beer Was Not Made from Bread The older model can be stated in one sentence, because it was repeated, with minor variations, for decades: Egyptian beer was made by crumbling lightly baked, well-leavened loaves — "beer bread" — into water, straining the mixture, and letting the yeast from the bread ferment it. The model had obvious attractions. It explained why bakeries and breweries appear together in tomb models. It explained the straining figures in tomb scenes: they were straining out bread. And it required no malting industry, because the bread did the grain-processing work. Generations of handbooks presented it as settled, and some popular accounts present it still. Samuel's microscopy refutes it. The point is precise and should be stated precisely. If beer had been made from bread, the residues would carry the starch signature of bread: granules exposed to dry oven heat, surface-blistered, partially merged in the pattern of a baked crumb, and — if the loaves had been only lightly baked, as the model required — a large population of undistorted granules alongside them. What the residues actually carry is a different and wider range of forms, extending, in Samuel's description, from undistorted but pitted granules to thoroughly fused starch. Pitting is the signature of enzymatic attack in germinating grain. Thorough fusion is the signature of starch cooked in abundant water. No single baked loaf, lightly or fully baked, produces both ends of that range in the proportions the residues show. Her conclusion, in the paper's own reasoning paraphrased closely, is that the microstructural data do not match the use of lightly baked bread for brewing, and that the process the data describe does not resemble modern brewing from bread at all. What the data describe instead is a two-part process conducted on malt, not on bread. One portion of ground malt — or of malted grain — was well heated in water, cooking its starch to the point of fusion. The other portion was left uncooked, its starch granules pitted and channelled by germination but otherwise undistorted. The two portions were then combined. That is the whole of the positive model at the level of the granules; Sections V and VI expand it into a working procedure. The important thing here is the negative: the beer-bread model is refuted by the residue evidence , and this archive no longer presents it as a live option. Where older archive material or older scholarship describes beer as fermented bread-water, it is describing a superseded reconstruction. // A NECESSARY NUANCE — BREAD IN THE BREWHOUSE // Refuting beer-from-bread does not mean bread and brewing never touched. Samuel found that some Egyptian bread was itself made with malt — germinated grain dried and milled into the flour, which would have sweetened the loaf — and the two crafts shared buildings, grain stores, sieves, and staff. The Metropolitan Museum's description of the Meketre model says the making of bread and beer was closely related, both using basically the same kind of ingredients, and places them in one workshop complex with separate rooms. Shared ingredients, shared premises, shared workforce: all true. The refuted claim is narrower and specific — that finished or half-finished loaves were the brewing material. They were not, on the New Kingdom residue evidence. The straining in the tomb scenes is the removal of husk from a malt mash, as Section VII explains. IV. The Brewing Grains — Emmer against Barley Egypt grew two staple cereals. Emmer, bdt [Gardiner: U9] [𓌽], is a hulled wheat: each grain stays locked inside a tough chaff envelope, and the harvested unit is the spikelet, not the free grain. Barley, it [Gardiner: M33] [𓇠] in the ration accounts, was grown in two-row and six-row forms and threshes far more easily. Both grains were brewed, and Samuel's optical survey is explicit on the point: both emmer and barley were used for brewing, sometimes separately and sometimes mixed together. Barley is often described in older literature as the preferred brewing cereal; the residues counsel against hardening that preference into a rule. Egyptian brewers used what the store held, and the store held both. Bread tells the opposite story. Almost all of the loaves Samuel examined were made from emmer, identified by the chaff fragments and the whole or broken grain embedded in the crumb; barley loaves are the exception, and inclusions such as coriander and fig occur occasionally. Emmer's dominance in the loaf is plausibly a matter of dough behaviour and tradition together: emmer flour makes the dense, moist dough whose starch signature — granules partially fused, boundaries still visible, air pockets lined by distorted but distinct granules — Samuel found again and again in the ancient crumb. The archive therefore states the distribution as the samples give it: emmer for bread, emmer and barley for beer , with the mixture varying by place, period, and supply. The grains also divided the pay packet. At Deir el-Medina , the New Kingdom village of the royal tomb-builders, the monthly grain payment to an ordinary workman was four sacks ( ḫꜣr [Gardiner: Aa1-G1-D21], the sack measure) of emmer and one and a half sacks of barley. The proportions are instructive: the emmer, the larger share, is the bread grain, issued for the household's baking; the barley, the smaller share, is identified in the scholarship of the site as the brewing grain. A workman's family did not receive finished beer as its whole entitlement; it received grain, and the household converted it. State and temple institutions, by contrast, also issued finished bread and finished beer directly, and the great installations of Sections VIII and IX existed to do that conversion at scale. EMMER — bdt [Gardiner: U9] [𓌽] Hulled wheat. Harvested and stored as spikelets; needs pounding to free the grain (Section XII). The bread grain of the examined loaves, and a brewing grain in its own right, alone and mixed with barley. BARLEY — it [Gardiner: M33] [𓇠] Two-row and six-row forms. Threshes free of its husk far more readily than emmer. A brewing grain throughout, and the smaller, brewing-designated share of the Deir el-Medina monthly payment. THE SHARED STORE Granary models, including Meketre's, show scribes measuring and recording grain as it enters the store. Bread and beer drew on one accounted stock; the ration system (Section X) is that stock, distributed. Processing cost is the hidden variable in every choice above. Barley's relative ease made it the economical brewing grain where it was available; emmer's labour cost — the pounding chain of Section XII — was paid anyway for bread, so emmer was always in the building, cleaned and ready, and brewers used it. Neither grain was malted by accident. Malting is a decision, taken days before the brew, and it is the subject of the next section: the first true step of the Egyptian beer process, and the step the beer-bread model allowed scholars to overlook for half a century. V. Malting — Germination, Kilning and the Malt Store Malting is controlled germination. The brewer wets sound grain and lets it sprout, just far enough for the grain to mobilise its own enzymes — the amylases that will later convert starch to sugar — and then stops the growth by drying. It is the oldest piece of applied biochemistry in this article, and the residues prove the Egyptians practised it deliberately. Samuel's case rests on two independent observations. In the residues, starch granules show the pitting and channelling that sprouting enzymes produce; pre-harvest or storage sprouting is precluded, as she notes, by Egypt's dry climate, so the germination must have been induced after harvest, on purpose. And in a grain sample from Amarna, individual grains retaining their rootlets show a vitreous texture demonstrating that germination was followed by controlled heating — that is, by kilning. Germination plus kilning is malting, by definition. The Malting Sequence, as Reconstructed 1. Select and clean the grain. Sound, whole grain is required: emmer must first be freed from its spikelets by the pounding chain of Section XII, or malted in spikelet and cleaned after, a point on which the evidence does not adjudicate; barley needs only winnowing and sieving. Broken and chaffy material malts unevenly and was, on the household evidence, more likely to go to the quern than to the malting floor. 2. Steep. The cleaned grain is soaked in water until it has taken up enough moisture to wake. No Egyptian text gives a steeping time, and the archive invents none; ethnographic and experimental brewing with hulled grains works in hours to a day of steeping, with the water changed if it sours. The step is a reconstruction from the requirements of germination itself, labelled as such. 3. Germinate. The steeped grain is spread in a heap or a shallow layer and kept moist while the rootlets emerge and the grain's internal enzymes develop. Samuel's granule evidence — pitting and channelling without distortion in the uncooked fraction — is this stage, fossilised. Germination must be stopped before the shoot consumes the starch the brewer intends to ferment; a few days, judged by rootlet length and by the grain's mealy texture, is the working window in every traditional malting culture, and the rootlet-bearing Amarna grains show Egyptian maltsters making exactly that judgment. 4. Kiln. The green malt is dried with gentle heat to halt growth and make the malt storable. The Amarna grain's vitreous texture is the receipt for this step: germination followed by controlled heating. Kilning temperature is a flavour and enzyme decision in modern malting — hotter kilning darkens the malt and destroys more enzyme — and the two-part mash of Section VI depends on the malt retaining living enzymes, so the Egyptian kilning of at least the uncooked portion must have been gentle. That, too, is an inference from the process's requirements, and the article labels it one. 5. Store and mill. Dried malt keeps. It could be held in the granary beside raw grain and drawn on brew day, when it was ground — coarsely, by the standards of bread flour, since the husks had a job to do in the straining bed (Section VII). The Meketre brewery's first workstations, a man crushing grain with a pestle and women grinding at querns, are this preparation caught in wood and paint, whatever the model-maker believed the material was. Why malt at all? Because raw grain will not ferment usefully. Its starch is locked in granules that yeast cannot eat, and its enzymes are dormant. Malting wakes the enzymes; cooking, the next stage, opens the starch to them. The Egyptian process, as Samuel reconstructed it, is a rational division of labour between heat and enzyme — and it is, in its essentials, the same division every malt brewer on earth still uses. The difference lies in how the two are brought together, and there the Egyptian method has a character of its own. VI. The Two-Part Mash — Cooked Grain and Raw Malt Combined Mashing is the conversion step: malt enzymes meet gelatinised starch in warm water and cut it into sugars that yeast can ferment. The Egyptian mash, as the residues describe it, was made in two parts. One portion — malt, or unsprouted grain; Samuel's reconstruction leaves the cooked portion open — was cooked in water — cooked thoroughly enough that its starch granules swelled, folded, and fused, the fully merged starch that dominates parts of every residue Samuel sectioned. The other portion was not cooked at all: its granules entered the mixture pitted and channelled by germination but undistorted by heat, and its enzymes entered alive. Combined, the cooked portion supplied accessible starch and the raw portion supplied the enzymes to convert it. In modern terms, the cooked fraction is a gelatinisation step and the raw fraction is the enzyme charge, and the Egyptian brewer achieved with two pots what a modern mash tun achieves with a temperature programme. The elegance of the method is that it solves the central problem of primitive mashing without any instrument. Starch gelatinises only at temperatures that destroy malt enzymes; enzymes work only well below those temperatures. A single vessel of malt and water, heated directly, either undercooks the starch or kills the enzymes, and usually does some of both. The Egyptian answer was separation in time and vessel: boil one part without mercy, keep the other part cool, then marry them at a temperature the enzymes can survive. The residue's extreme range of granule forms — from undistorted-but-pitted to thoroughly fused, coexisting in one sample — is precisely the fingerprint of that marriage, and no simpler process produces it. Temperatures — What Can and Cannot Be Said No Egyptian source states a mashing temperature, and the archive will not fabricate one. What can be said is bounded by the physics the residues imply. The cooked portion must have reached the gelatinisation range of cereal starch in abundant water — sustained heat at or near a simmer, held long enough for the granules to fuse as completely as the samples show. The combined mash must have settled below the temperature at which amylases are rapidly destroyed, or no conversion could have occurred and no beer would have resulted; the existence of the beer is the proof that the combined temperature was survivable. Modern reconstructions that brew Samuel's model, including the Tutankhamun Ale project discussed in Section XX, work the combined mash in the familiar warm range of traditional mashing, roughly the warmth of a hot bath to just above it. The archive presents that range as a modern brewer's working equivalent, not as an attested Egyptian figure. Egyptian control was tacit: by proportion (how much boiling mash to how much cool), by vessel, by hand and experience — the same way the potters of the same towns judged kiln heat without a pyrometer. Conversion, once the parts were combined, took time: the mash stood warm while the enzymes worked, sweetening as the starch cut down to sugars. Samuel notes, with a scientist's honesty, that large quantities of starch remain in the residues — evidence, as she puts it, of the relative inefficiency of the process beside modern brewing. Some starch never gelatinised, some sugar never converted, and the finished beer carried body, cloud, and nourishment that a fully attenuated modern beer does not. That inefficiency is not a failure to be apologised for. It is why Egyptian beer was food: a cloudy, grain-rich drink whose calories and protein survived into the jar, closer in spirit to a fermented gruel than to a filtered lager, and exactly suited to its role as half of the national wage. Ratios are the other unrecorded variable. How much malt went to how much water — the strength of the brew — was not left to taste, however: it was an administrative quantity, reckoned by the pesu system of Section X, which expressed the grain-to-product conversion of bread and beer alike. A weak beer and a strong beer were different quantities of grain wearing the same jar, and the accounts knew the difference even where the drinker is not told. With the mash converted, the process turns physical again: the liquid must be separated from the husks that carried it, and given to the yeast. VII. Straining, Fermentation and Yeast The converted mash is a porridge of liquid, husk, and grain debris. Before fermentation it was strained. Samuel's abstract states the sequence without ornament: the mixture was strained free of husk before inoculation with yeast. This single sentence re-reads a hundred tomb scenes. The brewers shown straining mash through sieves into vats — figures the beer-bread model cast as men squeezing crumbled loaves — are doing exactly what the residues require: separating sweet wort from spent husk. Husk fragments nevertheless travelled onward in quantity: coarsely shredded chaff is a common feature of the residues, and large jars held substantial amounts of embedded husk and bran, while thin residue coatings in small cups, husk slivers and all, show that the drinker met some of it in the cup. Egyptian straining was a practical separation, not a filtration to brilliance. Vessels and the Fermenting Room The strained wort went into large pottery vessels to ferment. The Meketre model again supplies the choreography the residues imply: mash treaded or stirred in a tall vat, the liquid set aside in four tall crocks to ferment, and after fermentation poured off into round jugs closed with black clay stoppers. The sequence in the model — vat, crock, jug, stopper — is the vessel chain of a working brewery: open or loosely covered vessels for the active ferment, closed jugs for storage and issue. Beer jars are among the commonest vessels on Egyptian sites, and their forms — pointed bases for standing in sand or rings, necks suited to mud sealing — are production equipment, not tableware. Beer was also a short-lived product by modern standards: brewed, fermented, issued, and drunk young, in a continuous cycle geared to the ration calendar rather than to cellaring. Yeast — Observed Cells, Inferred Inoculation Yeast is present in the evidence as a body, not only as an effect. Samuel's paper figures yeast cells from an ancient brewing residue in a tomb vessel from Deir el-Medina: cells with bud scars visible, some caught in the act of budding — active growth, frozen at the moment the residue dried. At least some Egyptian beer, then, was fermented by yeast populations growing in the wort, not merely soured by accident. How the yeast got there is the question the evidence does not directly answer, and the archive keeps the candidates distinct. A portion of a previous brew, or its lees, carried forward as inoculum is the route ethnography supports for traditional breweries and the route the dossier of processes assembled for this archive adopts as most likely. Ambient inoculation — yeast resident in vessels, sieves, and the brewhouse itself, seeding each new wort from the room — is compatible with the same evidence and in practice overlaps with carry-over: a brewery used daily is a yeast culture with a building around it. What is not supported is the old model's specific claim that the yeast arrived inside baked bread; the bread route falls with the bread model itself. Samuel's bread evidence shows yeast in some loaves — a few yeast cells were observed in particular loaves, making it likely those loaves were leavened — but a leavened loaf is a baker's tool, not, on the residue evidence, a brewer's one. Fermentation itself was warm and, by modern standards, quick: an Egyptian brewhouse at ambient Nile-valley temperatures, a wort rich in sugar and nutrients, and a house yeast population at full strength would have worked vigorously and finished in days. The product was then issued — into the ration system, onto the offering table, and into the small cups whose thin residues Samuel sampled. Alcohol content is nowhere recorded and estimates in popular literature vary widely; the archive notes only that a partially converted, body-rich beer of this kind is a foodstuff first and an intoxicant second, and that Egyptian texts, which celebrate beer at festivals without embarrassment, treat drunkenness as a feast-day excess rather than the drink's daily purpose. Scale is another matter: the daily purpose, multiplied by a town or a workforce, becomes an industry, and the industry's remains are the subject of the next two sections. VIII. The First Breweries — Hierakonpolis and Abydos Brewing at industrial scale is older than the Egyptian state. At Hierakonpolis — Nekhen, the predynastic city of the falcon god, treated in the archive's survey of the Predynastic period — the excavators of the Hierakonpolis Expedition uncovered, at locality HK24A, the so-called Vat Site: a brewery of c. 3500–3400 BCE, centuries before the First Dynasty. Six conical ceramic vats stood in a domed heating platform, set in two rows, their interiors encrusted with the shiny black residue that the expedition identifies as the signature of brewing. The vats are coarse work — clay tempered with straw and small stones, walls up to three centimetres thick — and they were heated from around and below, in a structure roofed, on the excavators' reading of the mud-coated sherd debris, with an improvised superstructure of the most abundant material on site: broken pottery. Scale is the point. Each HK24A vat held, on the expedition's estimates, roughly sixty-five litres, giving the six-vat installation a batch capacity near 390 litres; a second, larger installation nearby preserved emplacements for sixteen vats. The expedition's published estimates for the complex run to several hundred gallons of beer a day for the smaller installations and up to roughly a thousand litres per operation for the larger ones — figures the archive reports as excavators' estimates, with the vat counts and per-vat capacities, which are measured, kept distinct from the daily totals, which are modelled. Even at the measured minimum, this is not household brewing. It is production for a community: for feasts, for offerings, and for the concentrated ceremonial consumption of one of Egypt's first cities. Residue from the site, as Section XI discusses, included emmer and barley debris with date skins and grape pips — the earliest hint that a predynastic brewer might enrich a batch with fruit, kept here in its place as a local attestation, not a national recipe. Five centuries later the scale jumps by an order of magnitude. At North Abydos, the American-Egyptian mission led by Matthew Adams of New York University and Deborah Vischak of Princeton rediscovered in 2018–2020 a brewery first noted by T. Eric Peet's excavators a century earlier and then lost. It dates to about 3100–3000 BCE, the age of Narmer and the dawn of the First Dynasty, and it consists of at least eight separate semi-subterranean production units. Each unit is about twenty metres long by two and a half metres wide and holds some forty large ceramic vats in two rows, the vats — roughly sixty-five to seventy centimetres across and seventy deep, up to about seventy litres each — held in place by rings of vertically set mud struts, the "fire legs," so that the mash of grain and water could be heated in them. Eight units at forty vats give a total capacity the mission estimates at approximately 22,400 litres per batch. Adams's interpretation, reported by the mission, is that the Abydos brewery was built to supply the funerary cults of Egypt's first kings at their Abydos cemeteries — beer for royal ritual, brewed beside the royal tombs, at a volume with no known equal in the early Egyptian record. The archive adopts that interpretation as the excavators' own, while noting what it implies either way: by 3000 BCE, brewing was already a state technology. The slow cooking in the Abydos vats — mashing, in the mission's terminology — is the two-part Egyptian process of Section VI organised as a production line: the same granules Samuel read at Deir el-Medina and Amarna, manufactured here by the tens of thousands of litres, fifteen centuries earlier. IX. State Bakeries and Breweries — Giza and the Workers' Towns The Old Kingdom state fed its workforces from purpose-built food factories, and the best excavated example stands at Giza. South of the Sphinx, at Heit el-Ghurab — the "Lost City of the Pyramid Builders," excavated since 1988 by Ancient Egypt Research Associates under Mark Lehner — lay a planned settlement of more than seven hectares that served as the base of operations for building the pyramid complexes of Khafre and Menkaure, and probably Khufu before them. Its streets included bakeries, kitchens, and commissaries on an industrial footing, a royal administrative building with great grain silos, and the galleries that housed the rotating workforce. The pottery tells the provisioning story in bulk: bread moulds and beer jars in quantity, everywhere. The Giza bakeries worked in a distinctive vessel, the heavy bell-shaped mould the Egyptologists call, from its Egyptian name, the bedja mould — thousands of fragments of which litter the site. The method, reconstructed by Lehner's team and tested in a replica bakery built for the purpose, runs as follows: the empty moulds are heated in an open fire; dough is filled into the hot moulds; the filled moulds are set in hot ashes, with a second heated pot inverted over the top as a lid; the loaf bakes in the stored heat of the clay. The largest moulds exceed thirty centimetres across and turn out tall conical loaves. Names & Categories — The Corpus Overview The ancient Egyptians had no single term for what modern scholars call the "funerary corpus." Different categories existed at different historical periods: Pyramid Texts (Old Kingdom, c. 2350-2181 BCE), Coffin Texts (Middle Kingdom, c. 2055-1650 BCE), Book of the Dead (New Kingdom onward, c. 1550 BCE-Ptolemaic era), and Books of Breathing (earliest copies c. 350 BCE; bulk Ptolemaic and Roman). These categories overlap chronologically—texts from earlier periods continued to be copied and used in later periods. A New Kingdom tomb might contain both Pyramid Texts (for their ancient power) and the latest Book of the Dead spells. The funerary corpus thus represents a cumulative knowledge base, with each era contributing new technology without entirely abandoning the old. The Egyptian term Pert em Hru ("Going Forth by Day"), commonly associated with the Book of the Dead, actually represents the fundamental principle underlying all these texts: the deceased's ability to move through the underworld realm and emerge transformed into an Akh (radiant spirit). II. Ontology of the Funerary Text — Software for the Soul The funerary texts were not merely literary compositions, prayers, or commemorative records. They were functional technologies of consciousness —encoded instructions for navigating a specific realm of awareness and achieving a specific transformation. In this research framework, these texts can be understood as navigational software . The soul of the deceased faces a complex passage through the Duat—a non-physical realm with its own geography, inhabitants, obstacles, and opportunities. Without proper knowledge (the spells), the soul becomes lost. With correct knowledge deployed properly (the correct utterance of spells with proper intention), the soul arrives safely at its destination. The texts function on multiple levels: literal (providing actual directions and protective formulae), symbolic (encoding cosmic principles), and transformative (reshaping the consciousness of the reader). A living person reading the funerary texts could experience death and transfiguration while still in the body—a form of initiatic mysticism. A deceased person would use the same texts as an actual map through the underworld. // HEKA AS FUNCTIONAL MAGIC // Heka (Egyptian magic) is not supernatural—it is the fundamental principle of how consciousness shapes reality. The funerary texts deploy Heka by combining precise linguistic formulae (the correct utterance of divine names and sacred words), intentional consciousness (the proper mental focus and emotional state), and knowledge of cosmic principles (understanding the laws that govern the realm being entered). The effectiveness depended not on faith but on correct knowledge and correct application. III. Pyramid Texts — The Oldest Magic The Pyramid Texts are humanity's oldest known religious literature, inscribed on the interior walls of 5th and 6th Dynasty pyramids (c. 2350-2181 BCE). The corpus in Sethe's and Faulkner's numbering runs to 759 utterances; Unas, the first king to bear them, holds 228 of them in that numbering (Allen's edition divides the Unas material differently, into 283). Over 700 distinct spells survive, carved in hieroglyphs and, in the classic first corpus of Unas, filled with blue pigment. The primary goal of the Pyramid Texts was the celestial ascent of the pharaoh . Unlike later conceptions of the afterlife (which emphasized underworld passage), the Pyramid Texts focused on the deceased king joining the immortal stars, particularly the circumpolar stars that never set. The king was to become one of the "Imperishable Stars" — the circumpolar stars (not the decans, which are a different set of stars: they rise and set, and their successive risings mark the hours) — achieving eternal visibility and eternal motion with the cosmos. The texts address the king directly: "O Pharaoh, you shall not die, you shall live forever." They provide assistance from various gods, particularly Horus (who guides the king to the sky). Spells ensure the king's body is preserved, his name is remembered, and his ascent is achieved. Many spells are very brief (one or two sentences), designed to be recited as magical invocations rather than read as texts. PYRAMID TEXT CHARACTERISTICS Inscribed on tomb walls, forming a complete funerary apparatus through written magic. Addressed the king directly. Focused on celestial ascent rather than underworld journey. Royally exclusive (not used for non-royalty). Represent the oldest stratum of Egyptian funerary knowledge. IV. Coffin Texts — Democratization of Immortality The Coffin Texts (Middle Kingdom, c. 2055-1650 BCE) were once described as a "democratization" of afterlife knowledge, as if royal funerary privileges had been extended to non-royals as central authority weakened. That older model has been formally abandoned (Mark Smith, "Democratization of the Afterlife," UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology, 2009; Hays, 2015): the evidence shows no such one-time transfer from royal to non-royal use. What the Coffin Texts do show is funerary texts in wider, non-royal use on Middle Kingdom coffins. Written on the interior surfaces of wooden coffins, these texts presented a more complex model of the afterlife than the Pyramid Texts. The journey was no longer purely celestial but included passage through an underworld realm (the Duat) with multiple hazards and opportunities. The Book of Two Ways , the first illustrated map of the underworld, appears in the Coffin Texts—showing two routes, by land and by water, separated by a lake of fire — the fire is the divider between the routes, not itself one of the paths. The Coffin Texts also introduce a more personalized afterlife. The deceased is not merely identified as the king but as an individual named person. Spells are adapted to allow the deceased to become any form they desired, to visit the living world, and to achieve resurrection within the Duat rather than purely celestial ascent. COFFIN TEXT CHARACTERISTICS Written on coffin interiors, surrounding the deceased with protective and transformative knowledge. Non-royal access. Introduced underworld geography and multiple pathways. Personalized to individual deceased. More diverse transformation possibilities. THE BOOK OF TWO WAYS The first illustrated map of the Duat, showing celestial and terrestrial paths. Multiple routes to desired destinations. Guardians and obstacles at strategic points. Still used in modern initiatic work as a model of consciousness journey. V. The Book of the Dead — Prt em Hru (Going Forth by Day) The Book of the Dead (known to the Egyptians as Pert em Hru , "The Spells for Coming Forth by Day") represents the New Kingdom standardization of funerary knowledge (c. 1550 BCE onward). Rather than inscriptions on tomb walls or coffins, these were typically written on papyrus scrolls placed in the tomb with the deceased. The total known corpus runs to about 192 spells (roughly 200 formulae), but no single manuscript contains anything like the whole corpus: each surviving Book of the Dead is a selection, and the number of spells in circulation at any one time did not exceed about 150. The Saite Recension's standard sequence, numbered 1–165, derives from Lepsius's 1842 edition of the Turin papyrus of Iufankh. To the spells are added rubrics (instructions in red ink) and vignettes (illustrations). The spells are organized thematically rather than narratively: transformation spells, protection spells, navigation spells, opening of the mouth spells, and journey spells. The text is highly modular—different versions for different deceased individuals could draw from the standard spell library. The Book of the Dead introduces the concept of the "Negative Confession" (Spell 125), where the deceased declares innocence of 42 transgressions before a tribunal of 42 divine judges. The successful outcome of this judgment determines the soul's ability to achieve transfiguration (Akh state) and eternal existence. THE CORPUS AT A GLANCE Pyramid Texts: 759 utterances (Sethe/Faulkner numbering); first inscribed for Unas, 228 utterances. Coffin Texts: 1,185 spells (de Buck's edition, 1935–61). Book of the Dead: c. 192 spells in the total corpus; Saite sequence numbered 1–165 (Lepsius, 1842). Litany of Ra: the sun god invoked in 75 forms. Amduat and Book of Gates: the night in 12 hours; Book of Caverns: six sections, not hours. BOOK OF THE DEAD CHARACTERISTICS Written on papyrus, customizable to individual needs. A corpus of c. 192 spells, of which each manuscript is a selection, forming a modular knowledge system. Includes illustrations (vignettes) for visual magical resonance. Standardized yet flexible framework. Widely produced and available. The most extensive afterlife technology we possess. VI. Spell 125 — The Negative Confession Spell 125 is the climax of the Book of the Dead journey and the most psychologically complex spell in the funerary corpus. It details the soul's arrival in the Hall of Two Truths (wsḫt mꜣꜥty), where the Weighing of the Heart ritual takes place. Aaru — the Field of Reeds — is not the hall: it is the paradisiacal destination the justified dead reach after judgment. The deceased faces a tribunal of 42 divine assessors (representing 42 cosmic principles or nomes of Egypt, accounts vary). To prove worthiness for eternal existence, the deceased must make the Negative Confession —declaring innocence of 42 specific transgressions: "I have not killed," "I have not stolen," "I have not told lies," "I have not caused pain," and so forth. Simultaneously, the Weighing of the Heart occurs: the heart (Ib), representing all memories and moral consequence of the life lived, is weighed against the feather of Ma'at (Truth/Order). A heart light with truth skips the scale; a heart burdened with isfet (violence, dishonesty, selfishness) sinks. If deemed worthy (achieving "Ma'at Kheru," "True of Voice" status), the soul achieves transfiguration (Akh state). If judged unworthy, the soul is consumed by Ammit, the "Devourer," resulting in the "Second Death," the complete annihilation of individual consciousness. In Spell 125 the deceased declares his purity four times, and his purity is the purity of that one great bennu — the great phoenix — which is in Heracleopolis (Henenesut). The genuine line concerns that single bennu; it mentions no scales. — Paraphrase of Spell 125A, the Negative Confession VII. The Amduat — That Which Is in the Underworld The Amduat ("That Which Is in the Underworld") is not, strictly speaking, a funerary text like the others but rather a cosmological map inscribed on tomb and temple walls throughout the New Kingdom. It details the 12-hour night journey of the sun god Ra through the underworld, encountering various deities, demons, and transformations at each hour. The Amduat functions as a literal map and as a metaphor for internal consciousness transformation. Each hour represents a stage of consciousness the initiate passes through. At Hour 7, Ra is in maximum danger (directly confronting Apep). At Hour 12, he is reborn, emerging from the womb of Nut. The deceased is understood to traverse the same journey each night through the Duat, paralleling Ra's nightly voyage. Modern practitioners use the Amduat as a meditation map—visualizing passage through the twelve hours as a form of inner alchemy, dying to the old consciousness and being reborn to new understanding. The text thus functions from multiple perspectives: literal (cosmology), metaphorical (psychological journey), and practical (meditation guide). // THE TWELVE HOURS OF THE NIGHT — THE TEXT'S OWN CONTENTS // The hour-by-hour contents below follow Erik Hornung, The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Afterlife (1999), the standard modern account of the Amduat . Hour 1: the sun god enters the western horizon (akhet), the transition between day and night. Hours 2 and 3: he passes through an abundant watery world — Wernes in Hour 2 and the Waters of Osiris in Hour 3. Hour 4: he reaches Imhet, the difficult sandy realm of Sokar, crossing dark zigzag pathways, dragged on a serpent-boat. Hour 5: the tomb of Osiris, an enclosure beneath which lies a lake of fire, covered by a pyramid-like mound on which Isis and Nephthys have alighted as two kites. Hour 6: the theological climax — the ba of Ra unites with the body of Osiris within the circle formed by the Mehen serpent, and regeneration begins. Hour 7: Apep lies in wait and is subdued in chains by the magic of Isis and the strength of Serqet. Hour 8: the sun god opens the doors of the tomb, and Horus calls on a fire-breathing serpent to destroy the enemies of Osiris, burning their corpses and cooking their souls. Hour 9: the crew leave the sandy island of Sokar, rowing vigorously back into the waters. Hour 10: regeneration continues through immersion in the waters. Hour 11: the god's eyes — the emblem of his health and wholeness — are fully regenerated. Hour 12: he enters the eastern horizon, ready to rise as the new day's sun. // THE TWELVE HOURS — THIS ARCHIVE'S INTERPRETIVE READING // The following glosses are modern interpretive readings offered by this archive for meditative use; they are not summaries of the ancient text's contents, and where they differ from the Hornung summary above, the Hornung summary governs. Hour 1: entry and encounter with the guardians. Hour 2: confrontation with shadow-forms. Hour 3: an initial assessment before divine judges. Hour 8: reformation begins. Hour 9: encounter with advanced consciousness-forms. Hour 10: integration of transformed knowledge. Hour 11: preparation for emergence. Read in this spirit — as a contemporary meditation map laid over the ancient itinerary — the glosses have their use; read as a table of contents of the Amduat , they mislead, and this archive no longer presents them that way. VIII. The Litany of Ra — Re's Night Journey The Litany of Ra is a complementary text to the Amduat, focusing specifically on Ra invoked in his 75 forms — the number that defines the Litany's structure (the twelvefold count belongs to the Amduat's hours, not to the Litany). While the Amduat provides the map, the Litany provides the magical formulae and the invocation sequence. Ra is invoked in 75 forms in the Litany: at dusk, he is Atum-Ka (the evening form); through the underworld hours, he takes various sacred names, culminating in the Khepri (scarab) form at the moment of rebirth. Each form represents both a specific stage of the journey and a specific frequency of consciousness. The deceased who reads or understands the Litany gains knowledge of these sacred names and the power to invoke them. To speak the name of a deity with proper intention is to activate that deity's presence and protective power. A traveler in the Duat armed with these names can call upon Ra's own power to navigate the underworld successfully. IX. Structure of the Duat — Twelve Hours & Multiple Layers The Duat is not a single unified realm but a complex landscape with multiple layers, each with distinct characteristics. The upper Duat is more accessible, resembling the living world but inverted or transformed. The middle Duat becomes increasingly alien and dangerous. The lower Duat contains the absolute depths—realms of dissolution and primordial potential. Horizontally, the Duat is divided into regions or "nomes," each governed by specific deities. The eastern Duat (where the sun rises) is associated with rebirth. The western Duat (where the sun sets) is associated with death and dissolution. The southern Duat is associated with chaos and testing. The northern Duat is associated with the eternal stars. Temporally, the Duat follows the 12-hour cycle of the night, but within each hour are numerous sub-cycles and timeless zones where normal time does not flow. A soul could potentially spend an infinite time in a particular chamber of the Duat, though the goal is to progress through all 12 hours before dawn. THE TWELVE REALMS Each hour/region of the 12-hour night journey has specific guardians, obstacles, opportunities, and transformation possibilities. The books name a great many distinct places, gates, and regions; no ancient or modern source fixes a total count of them. THE GUARDIANS Each region is guarded by specific deities or demons who challenge the traveler. Knowing their names and the proper passwords allows safe passage. Ignorance leads to obstruction or predation. THE TRANSFORMATIONS As one progresses through the Duat, the soul undergoes progressive transformation, shedding lower consciousness forms and acquiring higher capacities. By the 12th hour, complete transfiguration has been achieved. X. Guardians & Demons — Entities of the Underworld The Duat is not empty but inhabited by numerous beings, some helpful and some dangerous. These entities are not demons in the Christian sense (evil beings to be destroyed) but rather cosmic principles manifested as personified beings. Some test the traveler's knowledge; others offer assistance; still others represent natural obstacles within the realm. Key guardian figures include: Anubis (guardian of tombs and the entrance to the Duat), Thoth (keeper of knowledge and the scales of justice), Ammit (the Devourer of the unworthy heart), Sekhmet (the fierce lioness who tests worthiness). The underworld books name hundreds of beings, many by descriptive epithets that state their function — devourers, burners, slaughterers, guardians of gates and bends of the river. Those names are catalogued hour by hour in the Amduat and the Book of Gates, and they are the traveller's real syllabus: advanced knowledge of their names and functions allows the soul to understand them not as random threats but as parts of the system to be navigated. NAMES AS KEYS In the funerary texts, knowing an entity's true name is knowing how to control or work with it. To call a guardian by their true name creates a relationship; to know their weakness is to know how to pass safely. This principle of "secret names" permeates all Egyptian magical knowledge. XI. Names & Passwords — The Secret Word A major component of the funerary texts consists of spells that provide secret words and names of power . Many Book of the Dead spells bear titles like "The Name of the Ferry-Boat" or "The Secret Name of the Eastern Gate," indicating that the spell contains a specific piece of knowledge needed to pass a specific obstacle. These "passwords" function at multiple levels. Literally, they allow the soul to negotiate with guardians. Symbolically, they represent knowledge of cosmic principles. Internally, they activate specific frequencies within consciousness. To speak the secret name of a deity is to activate that deity's presence and power within oneself. The most powerful spells deal with the "true names" of the gods—names considered so potent that to speak them fully was dangerous, hence their restricted access. The living initiates who learned these names gained a degree of power over the realms of consciousness those names represented. // ACTIVATION OF DIVINE NAMES // To work with a divine name, one must first understand what principle it represents. The name Aker (the underworld guardian) represents the boundary between waking and sleeping consciousness. Through meditation on this name, one learns to consciously cross that threshold. The name Asar (Osiris) represents the principle of death and resurrection. Through contemplation of this name, one participates in that transformation. Modern practitioners can work with divine names through repeated utterance (like a mantra), visualization of hieroglyphic forms, and deep meditation on the principle represented. The name itself becomes a doorway to the principle it names. XII. Transformation Spells — Becoming Divine A major category of Book of the Dead spells — the transformation series, Spells 76–88 — allows the deceased to assume various divine or animal forms: becoming a falcon of gold (Spell 77), a divine falcon (78), a lotus (81), Ptah (82), a bennu bird (83 — the same spell also translated "becoming a phoenix"; it is one spell, not two), a heron (84), a living soul (85), a swallow (86), a snake (87), or a crocodile (88). The series contains no spell "for becoming Osiris" or "for becoming Thoth." These are not mere fantasies but represent acquiring specific capabilities and frequencies of consciousness. To "become the Bennu Bird" (Spell 83) is to acquire the freedom of flight through multiple realms, the ability to see from transcendent perspective. To "become Ptah" (Spell 82) is to identify with the creator god of Memphis. The transformation follows a specific process: the deceased first affirms their identity as a specific divine form, then performs specific actions (walking in a particular way, making specific gestures, speaking specific formulae). Through series of transformations, the soul gradually sheds its earthly form and acquires its transfigured Akh-form, which integrates all the capacities of the individual divine forms encountered. XIII. Books of Breathing — Late Period Evolution From the late 4th century BCE onward — the earliest known copy dates to about 350 BCE, and copies continue into the 2nd century CE — the Books of Breathing emerged as an evolution of the Book of the Dead. These texts represented an attempt to preserve and update funerary knowledge as Egyptian civilization was losing its independence and as the initiatic schools migrated from temples to more private settings. The Books of Breathing focused particularly on breath and life-force (hence the name). They understood the soul's journey as increasingly interiorized—less dependent on external ritual and more on the internal transformation of consciousness. The texts were often shorter than the Book of the Dead, designed for practical use in non-temple settings. These texts represent the bridge between the ancient Egyptian funerary tradition and the Hermetic schools of Alexandria. As the temples closed and the priesthood was dispersed, the knowledge migrated from institutional temples to mystery schools and individual practitioners. The Books of Breathing are essentially the "portable" version of Egyptian funerary knowledge—no longer requiring elaborate tomb preparations but achievable through meditation and internal practice. XIV. Mechanics of Transfiguration — Components & Process The funerary texts describe transfiguration (achieving Akh status) as a multi-part process involving several components. The process begins with death of the physical body but continues through multiple stages of consciousness transformation: Stage 1: Preservation of the Body — The mummification process preserves the physical form, providing a stable anchor for the soul throughout its underworld journey. Without this anchor, the soul risks dissolution. Stage 2: Activation of Knowledge — The funerary texts are read aloud during the burial ritual and placed in the tomb. The soul, upon awakening to its new condition, finds these texts available to guide it. The texts awaken the soul's knowledge of safe passage. Stage 3: Underworld Journey — Equipped with knowledge and protected by funerary magic, the soul navigates the Duat, encountering and overcoming obstacles. Each successful encounter strengthens the soul's capacities. Stage 4: Judgment — At the climax of the journey, the soul faces judgment (both by divine councils and by its own heart). Successful judgment results in "Ma'at Kheru" (True of Voice) status. Stage 5: Transfiguration — Upon achieving Ma'at Kheru, the soul undergoes final transformation into the Akh state—a radiant, immortal spirit that can move freely through both spiritual and material realms, can embody physical form when desired, and participates eternally in cosmic cycles. // THE COMPONENTS OF THE SOUL // Egyptian psychology understood the soul not as a single unified entity but as a complex of multiple bodies and capacities: The Khat (physical body), the Ka (the vital life-force double), the Ba (personality, mobility, desire), the Khaibit (shadow, the subtle body), the Ib (the heart — the organ of thought, memory, and moral record, and the very thing weighed in Spell 125), the Sah (the spiritualised body), the Sekhem (power, the effective form), the Akh (the transfigured spirit), and the Ren (the name, the principle of identity). See The Composite Soul . The transfiguration process involved all these components achieving final integration and elevation. XV. Historical Development — From Pyramid to Papyrus The funerary corpus represents a continuous evolution spanning roughly 2,000 years (c. 2350-332 BCE) and reflecting changes in Egyptian theology, social structures, and institutional knowledge preservation. The Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts (c. 2350-2181 BCE) represent the oldest, most archaic version of the knowledge. They are brief, cryptic, and focused on the pharaoh's celestial ascent. They were inscribed on tomb walls as permanent magical technology. The Middle Kingdom Coffin Texts (c. 2055-1650 BCE) represent an elaboration of cosmological understanding — the older description of them as a "democratization" of royal knowledge is no longer accepted (see §IV). Longer, more complex, more individualized. They introduced the concept of multiple pathways through the underworld. The New Kingdom Book of the Dead (c. 1550 BCE onward) represents the stabilization and comprehensive documentation of the knowledge. More accessible, more systematically organized, more widely distributed. The texts shifted to papyrus rolls, making them more portable and affordable. The Books of Breathing (from c. 350 BCE, chiefly Ptolemaic and Roman) represent the transition toward internal, meditation-based practice. Shorter, more portable, designed for non-institutional transmission. They represent the preservation of essential knowledge as institutional temples were declining. XVI. Contemporary Practice — Navigating Consciousness Thresholds Modern practitioners can work with the funerary texts not as ancient history or quaint beliefs, but as practical navigational maps of consciousness. The Duat journey, whether undertaken as an ancient Egyptian or a contemporary practitioner, follows certain universal principles: Preparation — Before encountering underworld realms, the practitioner should establish a solid foundation of spiritual practice, understanding of cosmic principles, and conscious connection to higher guidance. Without preparation, the encounter with dissolution-realms (which the Duat represents) can be destabilizing. Knowledge Acquisition — Study the texts, understand their terminology, internalize the maps. The funerary texts function best when the traveler has pre-loaded the knowledge into consciousness. Reading the myths and understanding the cosmology creates mental structures that the consciousness can navigate by. The Underworld Journey — Through meditation, dream-work, or visionary practice, undertake an intentional journey through underworld realms. The journey follows the 12-hour cycle of dissolution and reformation, each stage corresponding to a specific process of consciousness transformation: // THE TWELVE-HOUR MEDITATION // Hour 1-2: Enter darkness. Journey inward. Encounter shadow-forms. Practice: Meditation in dim light, acknowledging inner darkness without fear. Hour 3-4: Judgment begins. Face your own choices and their consequences. Practice: Honest self-assessment, journaling on key decisions and their effects. Hour 5-6: Sokar's realm, then the union of Ra with Osiris — the climax of the Amduat, not a dissolution. Practice: Meditation on that union of solar and Osirian principles. Hour 7: Confront chaos (Apep). Meet your deepest fear directly. Practice: Deliberately visualizing what you most fear, responding with wisdom rather than reaction. Hour 8-9: Reformation begins. Gradually reintegrate consciousness. Practice: Slow return to body consciousness, gentle reintegration of selfhood. Hour 10-11: Approach rebirth. Achieve clarity and wholeness. Practice: Meditation on divine wisdom, integration of insights gained. Hour 12: Rebirth. Emerge as transfigured consciousness. Practice: Affirmation of new understanding, commitment to embodying new integrated self. Over multiple moon cycles, repeat the journey, gradually deepening the experience and integration. The living person who completes this process regularly develops the same consciousness transformation that the ancient Egyptians expected their deceased to achieve. XVII. The Book of Two Ways — The First Map of the Duat The Book of Two Ways is the closing section of the Coffin Texts in the el-Bersha version, painted on the floor of the coffin itself, beneath the body of the deceased. It is the earliest surviving illustrated map of the afterlife in Egyptian history, and it belongs to the Middle Kingdom necropolis of el-Bersha, where the great cedar coffins of nomarchs such as Djehutynakht preserved it. The map shows two routes through the realm of the dead: an upper route by land and a lower route by water, drawn as winding bands across the coffin floor and separated by a lake of fire . Gates, guardians, and demonic keepers stand along both routes, each to be named and passed. The destination of both ways is the realm of Osiris and the Field of Offerings, where the justified dead are sustained. The text that accompanies the map (Coffin Texts spells 1029–1185 in de Buck's edition, The Egyptian Coffin Texts I–VII, 1935–61) is part itinerary, part liturgy: it names what the traveller will meet, supplies the words to say, and identifies the traveller successively with the gods whose road this is. The total Coffin Texts corpus in de Buck's edition runs to 1,185 spells , against the Pyramid Texts' 759 utterances — the measure of how far the funerary literature grew between the Old and Middle Kingdoms. In this research framework, the Two Ways matter because they are the corpus's first admission that there is no single road. From this point onward, Egyptian funerary literature is a literature of routes : chosen, named, gated, and reversible only at a price. The Book of the Dead's ferry spells and the Book of Gates' gated hours both descend from this coffin-floor map. XVIII. The Litany of Ra in Detail — Seventy-Five Forms Section VIII stated the Litany's defining number; this section sets out its setting. The Litany of Ra , also called the Great Litany, is first known from the burial chamber of Thutmose III (KV34) and from the tomb of his vizier Useramun — the same generation that produced the first complete Amduat . It later spread widely through New Kingdom royal tombs. Its structure is an invocation, not a narrative. The sun god is praised in seventy-five forms , each named and figured: forms that run from the primeval and creator aspects of the god through his manifestations in the gods of the Ennead and the beings of the underworld. The king who recites the Litany does not merely praise Ra; he identifies himself, form by form, with the god in all his forms, so that the recitation is also a programme of union. Hornung's edition and discussion ( The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Afterlife , 1999) remain the standard orientation. The Litany's seventy-five is not a round ritual number but the count of the forms as the text itself enumerates them, which is why the twelvefold scheme of the Amduat 's hours must never be imported into it: the two compositions were used together in the same tombs precisely because they do different work — one maps the journey, the other names the traveller-god in his fullness. For the practitioner, the Litany is the corpus's clearest statement that a god, in this system, is not one figure but a field of forms , and that to know the god is to be able to call the forms in order. The deceased equipped with the seventy-five names carries the whole solar theology as a single recitable instrument. XIX. Manuscripts, Editions, and How the Corpus Survives The funerary corpus survives by three different material routes, and the differences govern what we can know. The Pyramid Texts survive as architecture: carved in the subterranean chambers of late Old Kingdom pyramids, beginning with Unas at Saqqara, and recovered as inscriptions, edited first by Kurt Sethe and translated in full by R. O. Faulkner (1969) and, in a newer edition, by James P. Allen. The Coffin Texts survive as furniture: painted and inked on the interior surfaces of Middle Kingdom wooden coffins, above all from el-Bersha, Asyut, and Thebes. Adriaan de Buck's seven-volume edition (1935–61) is still the corpus's backbone. Because coffins were private commissions, the Coffin Texts vary from coffin to coffin far more than the royal Pyramid Texts do: each coffin is an edition. The Book of the Dead survives as a book trade. New Kingdom and later workshops produced papyrus rolls to order — the scribe left blanks for the purchaser's name, and vignettes were painted to standard patterns with varying skill. The great museum copies — the Papyrus of Ani and the Papyrus of Hunefer in the British Museum among them — are luxury products of that trade; thousands of plainer copies, excerpts on coffins, shrouds, and tomb walls, and the amuletic use of single spells, carried the same texts far beyond the luxury market.
