Sources and Primary Evidence I. Play as Evidence — Why Games Belong in a History of Daily Life A history of Egypt written only from temples, tombs and tax accounts would miss something the Egyptians themselves clearly valued: the hours that were not work, not ritual and not sleep. Games fill part of that gap, and they fill it with objects. A senet board is not a text about leisure. It is leisure, surviving in wood, faience and ivory, handled until its squares wore smooth. When the Metropolitan Museum of Art surveyed the board games of Egypt and the Near East, it made the social point directly, in paraphrase: games are found in every sort of context, from a graffito scratched on a brick to an ornate box of exotic material, and they were popular across all social classes. That spread, from brick to ebony, is the first fact of this article. Play is unusually good evidence for daily life for three reasons. First, it is voluntary. A ration list tells us what the state issued; a game board tells us what somebody chose to do when no one was issuing anything. Second, it is social. Almost every Egyptian board game in this article is a two-player race game, which means almost every board implies a partner, an opponent, a watcher, a wager of time if of nothing else. Third, it is conservative. The Met's survey notes that senet stayed in favour from the Predynastic Period to at least the Late Period, a run of well over two thousand years, with its board's basic form, three rows of ten squares, remaining recognisably the same. Customs that stable are not decoration on a culture. They are part of its furniture, mental as well as wooden. Sport does the same work for the body that games do for the table. The wrestling walls of Beni Hasan, the stick-fighters performing before a king, the royal inscriptions boasting of arrows driven through copper targets: none of these is a military manual, and none is a work record. They show Egyptians training, competing, showing off and watching other people show off. Wolfgang Decker, whose Sports and Games of Ancient Egypt (German edition 1987; English translation by Allen Guttmann, Yale University Press, 1992) remains the standard survey, treated kings and commoners in one frame for exactly this reason: the same civilisation that staged wrestling before Pharaoh also scratched game boards into temple roofs where workmen and priests could reach them in an idle hour. This article therefore reads play in both directions at once. Read forward, a board is a thing to be played: squares, pieces, a randomiser, a finish. Read backward, it is a document: of who had leisure, of who played whom, of what a culture thought a race, a trap, a safe house and a second chance looked like. Senet's second, funerary life, in which the board became a map of the soul's passage through the afterlife, is only possible because its first life was so ordinary. Nobody builds a theology on an object nobody recognises. The deceased in the Book of the Dead plays senet in the next world because the living played it in this one, constantly, for millennia. // THE SHAPE OF THIS ARTICLE // Sections IV to XIII treat senet, the best documented and the most misreported of the games, and they do so under a strict rule, set out in Section III: what is attested is stated as attested, what is reconstructed is named as a modern reconstruction and credited to its reconstructor, and what is unknown is called unknown. Sections XIV to XVI treat mehen, the game of fifty-eight holes, and the wider shelf of boards. Sections XVII and XVIII treat manufacture and children's play. Sections XIX to XXI treat sport: wrestling, stick-fighting, archery, the water sports and the hunt. Section XXII places music and dance by cross-reference rather than duplication, and asks who, in Egypt, actually got to rest. II. The Names — Senet, Mehen and the Words for Play The game the world calls senet was called, in Egyptian, znt : a word whose root sense is "passing." The British Museum, the Metropolitan Museum and Peter Piccione's scholarship all give the name in that sense, and the Met adds the interpretive step the Egyptians themselves later took: in the New Kingdom the game of "passing" became associated with the journey to the afterlife, the soul passing through the netherworld as the pieces pass along the board. Two cautions belong with the name. The first is philological: the older transliteration writes the first consonant as z , where later convention writes s , so the game appears in the literature as both znt and snt . The second is archival: this archive's V2 sign map merges the two sibilants in a single value, so no bracketed Gardiner spelling in this article is offered for the game's name. The name is given in transliteration only, by the rule this archive applies everywhere: where a spelling cannot be composed confidently from the map, the bracket is omitted rather than guessed. Mehen's name is in better shape. The game is mḥn [Gardiner: V22-N35] [𓎔𓈖], "the coiled one," and the Met's survey gives the name in exactly that sense: the board depicts a coiled snake, and the name belongs first to the protective serpent deity who wrapped around the sun god Re during his journey through the night. The game, the god and the coil share one word because they share one shape. The archive treats the serpent Mehen as a divine figure in its own right in the account of the solar barque's nightly crew; here the emphasis is on the board that borrowed his body for a racetrack. The third game in this article has no ancient name at all, and that absence is itself a datum. "Hounds and Jackals" is a modern nickname, given because one famous set's pins are topped with hounds' heads and jackals' heads. The Met is explicit, in paraphrase: despite their popularity, the names and rules of some ancient games remain unknown, and the game of Fifty-eight Holes bears many modern names, Hounds and Jackals among them. Every use of the name in Section XV should therefore be read in invisible quotation marks. Egyptians played the game for centuries, across half the Near East, and did not leave us, or did not leave us surviving, the word they played it by. A handful of further terms recur through the article and are glossed here once. A safe or fortunate square on the senet board is marked, on many boards, with the sign for nfr [Gardiner: F35] [𓄤], "good, beautiful, perfect": the word is the marking, and Section VI follows the consequences. The ring sign that crowns the fifty-eight-holes track is the šn ring, the sign of encircling and of eternity, named here in transliteration without a bracketed spelling. The lion pieces of mehen are lions in the plain sense, rw [Gardiner: E23] [𓃭]. And the principle that orders the whole funerary reading of senet is mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: Aa11-X1] [𓐙𓏏], truth and right order, against which, in the judgement scenes, the heart was weighed. The archive's full treatment of that weighing is separate; here it matters only that a game could be imagined as a small, playable rehearsal for it. III. Evidence and Its Limits — The Honesty Rule for This Article Begin with the sentence every popular account of senet avoids: the rules of senet are not fully recoverable, and no complete ancient rulebook exists. The British Museum states the position in its own summary of the game, in paraphrase: two players race their pieces to the end of a thirty-square board using casting sticks or bones rather than dice, and some boards carry hieroglyphs on their squares that represent additional game rules. That is the shape of the whole problem in one sentence. The boards survive. The pieces survive. The randomisers survive. Pictures of play survive, in quantity, across three thousand years. What does not survive is a single ancient text that says, in order, how a turn works. Contrast makes the loss precise. For the Royal Game of Ur, senet's Mesopotamian contemporary, the British Museum can point to an actual rule text: the game's rules were written on a cuneiform tablet by a Babylonian astronomer in 177 BCE, and Irving Finkel deciphered them from it. Ur has a rulebook, late and partial as it is. Senet has none, at any date. What senet has instead is a body of religious texts, above all the composition modern scholarship calls the Great Game Text, which speaks of the board's squares in the language of the soul's journey, and a set of marked boards whose signs cluster, tellingly, at the end of the track. Reconstructions are built from those two things, plus the pictures, plus analogy with other race games. They are intelligent, informed, playable, and modern. Section VII and Section VIII keep them labelled as such throughout. // THE RULE APPLIED IN EVERY SECTION THAT FOLLOWS // Three grades of claim appear in this article, and they are not interchangeable. Attested : a board, piece, picture or text that survives, cited to its museum or publication. Reconstructed : a rule or procedure proposed by a named modern scholar, chiefly Timothy Kendall (1978) and Peter A. Piccione (doctoral dissertation, University of Chicago, 1990), presented as that scholar's proposal, never as an ancient rule. Unknown : everything else, stated as unknown. Where a reconstruction is summarised, the summarising is this article's paraphrase of published accounts of it, not a quotation, and no ancient wording is invented anywhere in these pages. A reader who finishes this article unable to play an historically guaranteed game of senet has understood the evidence correctly. The same discipline applies, with even more force, to mehen and to fifty-eight holes. For mehen, the Fitzwilliam Museum states the position without softening, in paraphrase: it is not known how the game was played, although certain aspects have been deduced. For fifty-eight holes, the Met likewise presents the race to the final hole as probable, not documented. And for sport, the evidence is pictorial and inscriptional rather than regulatory: Egypt left no rulebook for wrestling either, only walls covered in holds and throws and royal texts whose boasts are ideology before they are reportage. Sections XIX to XXI read those walls for what they can bear, technique, training, occasion, and refuse the extra step of inventing scoring systems, weight classes or league tables for which no evidence exists. IV. Senet I — The Board of Thirty Squares The senet board is the most recognisable gaming object to survive from the ancient world: thirty squares in three parallel rows of ten. The British Museum gives the layout in those terms, and the Met adds the two details that turn a grid into a track. The players moved their pieces in a boustrophedon, an S-shaped, direction, turning at each row's end like an ox ploughing a field, and the last five squares of the track are consistently decorated. Both details matter. The S-path means the thirty squares are one road, not three: a piece travels along the first row, back along the second, and forward again along the third, in the numbering modern scholarship, following Piccione, assigns from 1 to 30. The decorated ending means the road changes character as it nears its finish, which is where every reconstruction concentrates its special rules. The board's antiquity is not in doubt, even where its earliest history is debated. The British Museum dates senet to around 3100 BCE, among the earliest known board games. The Met places it in favour from the Predynastic Period onward, and Walter Crist, Anne-Elizabeth Dunn-Vaturi and Alex de Voogt, in Ancient Egyptians at Play: Board Games across Borders (Bloomsbury, 2016), trace fragmentary boards to the First Dynasty and follow the game, in their chapter structure, through Old Kingdom ritual use and graffiti, Middle Kingdom change and consistency, and New Kingdom religious meaning. A famous early witness is pictorial rather than physical: the Third Dynasty tomb of Hesy-Re at Saqqara, dated by the Met to about 2700 BCE for its mehen equipment and by the Fitzwilliam to about 2650 BCE for its painting, shows the equipment of three board games, senet among them, laid out with a draughtsman's precision. Form followed setting. At one end of the range stands the full gaming box: a hollow wooden case, its top gridded for senet, its underside very often gridded for the game of twenty squares, and a drawer in its body holding the pieces and casting sticks, the whole object a portable games cupboard. The Met illustrates the type with an ivory and copper-alloy gaming box of about 1580 to 1458 BCE and with faience gameboards of the reign of Thutmose III. At the other end stand the graffiti boards: grids scratched on bricks, pavements and temple roofs, which the Met counts among the game's contexts and which Crist and his co-authors have recorded at previously excavated sites. Between box and graffito lies every intermediate: boards painted, boards woven or drawn on perishable material and now lost, boards a workman could make in an evening and a king could commission in ebony and ivory. One structural fact deserves emphasis because reconstructions quietly depend on it: not all boards mark the same squares. The British Museum notes that some boards have completely blank squares, while others include squares decorated with hieroglyphs. The Met's "last five consistently decorated" describes a strong tendency, not a law without exception, and the marked squares beyond the final five, notably square 15 on some boards, vary by period and by set. Any rule that rests on a marking therefore rests on the boards that carry that marking. A reconstruction that universalises one board's decoration into every Egyptian's rules has already gone one step further than the objects, and Sections VII and VIII flag the places where that step is taken. V. Senet II — Pieces, Casting Sticks and Knucklebones Two players faced each other across the board, each moving a set of pieces distinct in form from the other's. The Met describes the vocabulary of shapes: game pieces for senet and twenty squares were given geometrically simple forms such as cones or spools, as well as more elaborate articulations, with some pieces shaped as archers, bound prisoners of war, or animals. The cone and the spool, one player's cones against the other's spools, are the classic pairing, surviving in faience, wood, ivory and stone. How many pieces each player fielded is a question the sets answer inconsistently: published accounts of the reconstructions and of the surviving sets give five pieces a side in many sets and seven in others, with the number varying across the game's long history. This article states the range, five to seven, because the evidence states the range. A single fixed number, presented as the ancient rule, would be a reconstruction wearing an attested costume. Movement was governed not by dice but by lots. The Met's survey is the clearest short account, in paraphrase: throw sticks functioned as the principal randomising agent in Egypt from the Predynastic Period onward; knuckle bones, typically the astragalus bone of a sheep or goat, have four unique faces and could be thrown to give different results; and a great variety of dice existed in the wider region, with the origin of the cubic die probably to be sought in the Indus Valley. Egyptian senet equipment, in the sets that survive complete enough to judge, centres on the casting sticks: flat or half-round sticks, dark on one face and light on the other, thrown together and read by how many fall light-side up. Four sticks give throws in the range modern reconstructions score as one to five, the throw of none-light counting as five, but the scoring is part of the reconstructions, not a surviving Egyptian table, and Section IX presents it under that label. The British Museum's senet entry makes the same point from the player's side, in paraphrase: two players compete to race all their pieces to the end of the board, using casting sticks or bones, rather than dice, to determine the number of squares moved with each throw. "Race all their pieces to the end" is as much of the object of the game as any ancient or museum source states, and it is worth noticing how much it does not say. It does not say how a piece enters the board, whether pieces begin on the board or off it, what happens when a piece lands on an opponent, whether adjacent pieces protect each other, or how a piece leaves the final square. Every one of those questions is answered by the modern reconstructions, differently, and none is answered by a surviving rule text. The equipment is eloquent. The procedure is silent. CONES AND SPOOLS The standard opposed sets: conical pieces against reel- or spool-shaped pieces, distinguished at a glance and by touch. The Met's collection holds individual faience examples of both forms from the fifteenth century BCE. Elaborated sets replace the plain forms with figures, including archers, bound prisoners and animals, without changing the underlying need: two visibly different armies on one track. CASTING STICKS Two-sided sticks, thrown as a set, are Egypt's characteristic randomiser from the Predynastic Period onward, on the Met's account. Tutankhamun's tomb, Section XIII, contained casting sticks with the boards. A stick has no numbers. The number is produced by the fall, by counting faces, which is why the scoring of a throw belongs to reconstruction, however natural any particular scoring feels. KNUCKLEBONES Astragali, the ankle bones of sheep or goats, have four unlike faces and land in four unlike positions. The Met illustrates knucklebone gaming pieces of about 1550 to 1458 BCE and treats the bones as a genuine alternative randomiser. Their presence beside a board proves a throw was made. It does not prove how the throw was converted into movement. THE DRAWER Gaming boxes commonly store their own equipment: pieces and sticks in a drawer within the box body. A complete box is therefore a self-contained social occasion, board, armies and lots in one carried object. It is also an archaeological trap: a drawer found empty proves nothing about what its game required. VI. Senet III — The Marked Squares and What Their Signs Say The strongest evidence for how senet worked is written on the board itself, in the signs carved, painted or inlaid on particular squares. The signs are not evenly spread. They cluster at the end of the track, squares 26 to 30 in the modern numbering, with a further marking frequently reported at square 15. Published summaries of Piccione's work, and the museum accounts that follow the scholarship, agree on the core inventory, and this section gives it at exactly that strength: as the usual markings of the late squares on the boards that mark them, with the conventional modern names that scholarship gives those squares, each name a rendering of a sign, not a quotation from a rulebook. Square Usual marking Conventional name What the sign itself says 15 Marked on some boards, including, in published accounts, Tutankhamun's House of Rebirth The name is a modern rendering. The square's role as a place of return is a reconstruction, Section VII. 26 The sign nfr [Gardiner: F35] [𓄤] House of Happiness; also rendered House of Goodness or Beauty nfr means good, beautiful, perfect. The sign attests fortune or favour at this square, not a procedure. 27 Water: wavy lines, or a cross-like mark on some boards House of Water Water, at the end of a journey through the netherworld, is danger: the drowning square of the reconstructions. 28 Three: three strokes, or three figures House of the Three Truths The marking is numerical or triple. The name "Three Truths" is a scholarly rendering, not a board inscription translated word for word here. 29 Two: two strokes, or two figures House of Re-Atum; also rendered of the Two Truths or Two Gods As with 28, the board gives a count. The theological name varies between published accounts, and this article does not pretend otherwise. 30 Varies: a god, a feather, or other closing signs occur House of Horus; also rendered of Re-Horakhty The last square is the least consistently marked of the five. Its name is the least secure, and is given here as convention only. Read strictly, the table proves three things. First, the end of the track was special: Egyptians spent carving and inlay on the last squares and left the first twenty-odd plain, which no one does for squares that behave like all the others. Second, fortune and danger stand adjacent: the good square, 26, immediately precedes the water, 27, so that a piece that has nearly finished its passing stands one throw from disaster, a shape any race-game designer, and any theologian of the judgement, would recognise. Third, the counts on 28 and 29, three and two, look like instructions of some kind. What kind is the question on which the reconstructions divide, and the division is instructive. A count can be a throw required to leave the board, a number of truths or gods to be faced, or a label with no mechanical force at all. The board does not say which. The scholars choose. Behind the marked boards stands the one substantial body of ancient writing about senet's meaning: the religious texts, including the Great Game Text known from later copies, one of them a Turin papyrus that pairs the text with drawings of the board, which speak of the squares in the first person of the deceased passing through them. Peter Piccione's 1990 Chicago dissertation, The Historical Development of the Game of Senet and Its Significance for Egyptian Religion , listed by the Met among its further reading for the game, is the modern study that built most fully on that material. Its evidence is theological before it is ludic: it tells us what the squares meant to a New Kingdom and later religious imagination. Converting meaning into mechanics, this square sends you back, that square protects you, is the reconstructors' work, and it is to that work, honestly labelled, that the next two sections turn. VII. Senet IV — The Piccione Reconstruction Peter A. Piccione's reconstruction, developed in his 1990 University of Chicago dissertation and in the work that followed it, approaches senet from the religious texts outward. Its starting point is the game's New Kingdom transformation: by that period, on the Met's summary as on Piccione's argument, senet had become a playable image of the soul's journey, its squares corresponding to stations, deities and hazards of the passing through the netherworld toward judgement and rebirth. The reconstruction therefore treats the board's markings and the texts' theology as the primary evidence, and builds a playable game in which the late squares carry the weight the texts give them. In paraphrase of the published summaries of Piccione's reading: the deceased-player's passage is the game's real subject; the good square at 26, marked nfr [Gardiner: F35] [𓄤], is a fortunate and protected station; the water at 27 is the passage's mortal hazard, from which a piece is returned toward the square of rebirth at 15; and the counted squares at the track's end govern the final exit from the board, the soul's release, by exact throws corresponding to their numbers. Piccione also gave the field its standard square numbering, the 1-to-30 S-path numbering that museum labels, commercial sets and later reconstructions, including Kendall-derived ones, now share. That numbering is so familiar that it is easy to forget it, too, is a scholarly convention laid over boards that carry no numbers at all. The strength of Piccione's approach is its fidelity to what Egyptians wrote about the game when they wrote about it theologically. Its limit is the mirror image of that strength. A text describing the soul's passage is not describing a Tuesday-evening game between two workmen, and rules inferred from theology may describe the game as priests imagined it rather than as families played it. Piccione's senet is also, in the published summaries, a game whose religious development he traced historically: the secular race of the early periods acquiring, by the New Kingdom, the funerary meaning that the Book of the Dead vignette, Section XII, displays. A reconstruction keyed to the late, religious form of the game should not be projected backward, unmarked, onto the First Dynasty boards with which the game's history begins. VIII. Senet V — The Kendall Reconstruction, and Where the Two Differ Timothy Kendall's reconstruction, published in 1978 as Passing Through the Netherworld and since then the basis of most museum demonstration sets and commercial editions, approaches the same evidence from the board outward. Where Piccione begins from the texts, Kendall begins from playability: given thirty squares, two opposed sets of pieces, casting sticks, marked late squares and the pictures of play, what complete, coherent race game best fits all of them at once? The answer he built is a genuine game, tactically rich, and it is the version most modern players who have "played senet" have in fact played. It remains, in every particular that goes beyond Section VI's table, a 1978 proposal. In paraphrase of Kendall's rules as published and as summarised in the museum and games literature: pieces begin arranged on the first row, alternating between the two players; a throw of the sticks moves one piece forward along the S-path; a piece landing on an opponent's piece exchanges places with it, the attacked piece moving backward to the square the attacker came from; two friendly pieces side by side form a block that cannot be attacked, and three in a row a barrier that cannot be passed; throws of one, four or five earn a further throw; every piece must land exactly on the good square, 26, before proceeding; a piece falling on the water, 27, returns to the square of rebirth, 15, or the nearest free square before it; and pieces leave the board from the final squares by exact throws, three from 28, two from 29, one from 30, the first player to bear off all his pieces winning the race. Question Piccione, in summary Kendall, in summary Ancient evidence Primary evidence Religious texts and the board's theology The boards, pieces, pictures and playability Both bodies of evidence survive; neither is a rulebook Square numbering Supplied the standard 1 to 30 numbering Adopts the standard numbering Boards are unnumbered; numbering is modern convention Starting arrangement Treated within a historically developing game Pieces alternate along the first row; first throw decides details of entry Pictures show games in progress, not a rules diagram of the start Attack Subordinate to the passage theology Landing on an opponent exchanges the two pieces' positions No ancient text states an exchange rule Blocks and barriers Not the centre of the reading Pairs are protected; triples cannot be passed Inferred from playability, not attested in words The water, 27 Return toward rebirth, within the soul's passage Return to square 15, or the nearest free square before it The water marking is attested; the destination is reconstructed Leaving the board Exact throws keyed to the counted final squares Exact throws: 3 from 28, 2 from 29, 1 from 30 The counts 3 and 2 are attested as markings; their use as exit throws is inference The table is this article's central exhibit, and it should be read column by column. The first two columns are modern scholarship, serious and divergent. The fourth column is all that antiquity left. Where the first two columns agree, as on the water's danger and the exact-throw ending, the agreement raises confidence that something of the kind stood behind the markings, but agreement between two reconstructions built from the same marks is not the same as an ancient statement. Where they differ, in emphasis, in the start, in the tactical machinery of blocks and exchanges, the honest conclusion is not that one scholar is right. It is that the evidence underdetermines the game, and both men filled the same silence with different, defensible plaster. IX. Senet VI — How a Game Probably Ran, Step by Step What follows is a composite procedure: the most defensible modern picture of a game of senet, assembled from the attested equipment and the two reconstructions above. Every step carries its confidence with it. A reader who wants only the attested skeleton should read the steps marked ATTESTED and skip the rest; the skeleton is short, and that shortness is the truth about senet. // A GAME OF SENET, AS FAR AS IT CAN BE RECONSTRUCTED // Step 1 — Set out the board. ATTESTED in form. A thirty-square board, three rows of ten, very often the top of a box whose reverse carries twenty squares and whose drawer holds the equipment. Step 2 — Set out the pieces. PARTLY ATTESTED. Two opposed sets, cones against spools or their figured equivalents. Their count, five or seven a side, varies in the surviving sets. RECONSTRUCTED: their starting squares. Kendall's alternating first row is a proposal, not a photograph. Step 3 — Throw for the move. ATTESTED in equipment, RECONSTRUCTED in scoring. Casting sticks, or knucklebones, are thrown. That sticks and bones were the randomisers is museum-secure. That four sticks score one to five by light faces, with none-light counting five, is the reconstructions' shared convention, not a surviving table. Step 4 — Move one piece along the road. ATTESTED in outline. The Met states the boustrophedon, S-shaped, direction of travel. Which piece a player chose, and whether a player who could not move forward moved backward or lost the turn, is RECONSTRUCTED, and the reconstructions are not unanimous. Step 5 — Meet the opponent. RECONSTRUCTED. Kendall's exchange, the attacked piece sent back to the attacker's starting square, and his protected pairs and impassable triples, make the game's tactics. They are consistent with a race game of this family. No ancient sentence states them. Step 6 — Reach the good square. MARKING ATTESTED, RULE RECONSTRUCTED. Square 26 carries the sign for nfr [Gardiner: F35] [𓄤], good. That every piece must land on it exactly, and may not pass it by, is Kendall's rule, widely adopted, plausibly grounded, and unproven. Step 7 — Risk the water. MARKING ATTESTED, CONSEQUENCE RECONSTRUCTED. Square 27 carries water. That a piece landing there returns to 15, the rebirth square, is the reconstructions' common reading of the two markings together. The pairing is elegant. Elegance is not evidence, and the article records the rule as inference, however good. Step 8 — Leave the board. COUNTS ATTESTED, PROCEDURE RECONSTRUCTED. Squares 28 and 29 carry three and two. That a piece bears off from them, and from 30, only on the exact matching throw is the standard modern reading. That the game was won by bearing off all one's pieces first is the race-game frame the British Museum states in summary, and is the least doubtful of the reconstructions' shared claims. Step 9 — Play again. ATTESTED as a social fact. Boards worn by use, boards buried with their owners, boards scratched where idle hands could reach them: whatever the precise rules were, the game was replayed for three thousand years. The procedure above is a modern script for an ancient habit. Two features of that script deserve a final word. The extra throw on high or low casts, one, four and five in Kendall's version, is the kind of rule every race game needs to keep its pace, and the kind no board can prove. And the backward move, imposed in some versions when no forward move is possible, shows reconstruction at its most exposed: a gap in the evidence, a design problem, a plausible patch. Modern editions differ on both points because antiquity is silent on both points. A museum set that prints its rules without the word "reconstruction" on the box has misled its buyer, kindly and completely. X. Senet VII — What No Source Tells Us This section is deliberately the plainest in the article. No surviving source tells us who moved first, or how the first player was chosen. No source tells us whether pieces started on the board, entered it by a throw, or were placed by agreement. No source states the scoring of the casting sticks as a table of values, the consequence of a throw for which no legal move exists, or whether a player could choose not to use a throw. No source states the exchange rule, the block, the barrier, the protection of the good square, or the exact destination of a piece that fell in the water, in so many words. No source tells us whether the game was played for stakes, and if so in what, although a much later Egyptian tale, the Roman-period story of Setne Khamwas, imagines a board game played against a dead prince for the prize of a magical book, which proves that Egyptians could imagine gaming stakes raised to the highest possible level without proving what changed hands over an ordinary board. No source, either, resolves the game's own history at the points where a player would most want certainty. Epithets and Principal Forms XVII. Esoteric Analysis — the Ground That Judges XVIII. Sources and Primary Texts I. The Name — gb and the Goose Sign Geb is the earth. Not a god who rules the earth from elsewhere, not a spirit who inhabits it, but the earth itself given a face, a genealogy, and a voice in the councils of the gods. His Egyptian name is written gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] [𓅬𓃀𓀭]: the goose sign g in its fuller value here, [Gardiner: G38], followed by the foot b [Gardiner: D58] [𓃀], and closed by the seated-god determinative nṯr [Gardiner: A40] [𓀭], which marks the word as the name of a divinity and is itself never pronounced. Egyptologists also cite a fuller form gbb , with the second b written out; older handbooks, working from the Greek-period pronunciation and from early misreadings of the goose sign, printed the name as Seb or Keb. Those forms survive in older literature and are retained in this archive only as cross-references. The standard modern reading, used throughout this article, is Geb. The goose at the head of the name is the single most consequential sign in this article, and Section VI is devoted to it. For now, the philological point must be fixed firmly, because a whole popular mythology has been built on blurring it. In the writing of Geb's name the goose functions as a phonogram : a picture-sign used for its sound, to spell the consonants of the god's name. Herman te Velde, in the standard Lexikon der Ägyptologie entry on Geb, states the position plainly, in paraphrase: the bird-sign serves to write the name and is not, by itself, evidence that the goose was Geb's cult animal. The goose that actually belongs to the creation-by-cackling complex is a different bird of a different species, with a different Egyptian name (Section VI). Scribes chose signs for their sounds as readily as for their pictures, and the discipline of reading them — set out in the archive's hieroglyph reference — is to ask of every sign first what it says , and only then what it shows. What the name means , beyond naming the god, is less certain than popular accounts suggest. gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] is the god's proper name; the ordinary Egyptian word for the earth as ground and land is a different word, tꜣ [Gardiner: N16] [𓇾], the flat land-sign, which gives the set phrase sꜣ-tꜣ [Gardiner: G38-N16] [𓅬𓇾], "son of the earth," used of snakes (Section IX). Egyptians could therefore speak of the land without speaking of Geb, and of Geb without meaning a field. The god is the earth personified and ensouled : the same ground that tꜣ [Gardiner: N16] names as terrain, gb names as a father, a judge, and a former king. That distinction — land as place, earth as person — organises everything that follows. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The spelling of Geb's own name follows the form used consistently across this archive's cosmological articles: gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] [𓅬𓃀𓀭] — goose, foot, and the seated-god determinative. Geb's maleness deserves emphasis at the outset, because it reverses the expectation most readers bring from other mythologies. In the Greek tradition the earth, Gaia, is a goddess and the sky a god; in Egypt the earth is a god and the sky, Nut , is a goddess. The archive's survey of the cosmological deities notes the same inversion. It is not a curiosity but a clue to how Egyptian cosmology was built: from observed pairs — dry and moist, above and below, sown field and overarching heaven — assigned genders by the logic of each local system rather than by any universal rule. Geb fathers; Nut bears; and their children are the gods of the Osirian generation around whom Egyptian religion, in its historical form, principally turns. A final preliminary: Geb has no major myth of his own in the sense that Osiris or Horus has one. No single surviving narrative is "the story of Geb" from beginning to end. He appears instead at the load- bearing joints of other stories — at creation, where he is separated from the sky; at the succession, where his inheritance passes to Osiris and Horus; at the tribunal, where the dispute of his grandsons is settled under his authority; and at the grave, where the dead are given into his body. To write about Geb is therefore to write about the structure of the Egyptian cosmos itself, with the earth as its narrator. The sections that follow take the joints in order. II. Son of Shu and Tefnut — Geb in the Ennead Geb belongs to the third generation of the Heliopolitan Ennead, the ninefold family — psḏt [Gardiner: N9-X1] [𓇷𓏏], "the Nine" — through which the priests of Heliopolis organised creation into a genealogy. The sequence, given in its classic form in Pyramid Text Utterance 600 (§1655 in Sethe's numbering), runs: Atum, the self-created source; Shu and Tefnut, the first pair; Geb and Nut, the second pair; and Osiris, Isis, Seth, and Nephthys, the children of Geb and Nut. The archive's article on the Ennead and Ogdoad treats the system as a whole; what matters here is Geb's exact place in it, because his place is his function. His father is Shu — šw [Gardiner: H6a] [𓆅], written with the feather — the god of air, light, and the space between things. His mother is Tefnut — tfnt [Gardiner: X1-I9-N35-X1] [𓏏𓆑𓈖𓏏] — the goddess of moisture, Shu's twin sister and consort. Air and moisture, acting together, produce the two great surfaces of the experienced world: the solid ground below and the vault above. Geb is the ground; his sister Nut — nwt [Gardiner: N35-W24-X1-B1] [𓈖𓏌𓏏𓁐] — is the vault. Brother and sister are also husband and wife: their union is not an embarrassment the system tolerates but the engine of the next generation, for from Geb and Nut together come the four gods whose drama defines Egyptian myth. OSIRIS — THE ELDEST INHERITANCE wsir [Gardiner: Q1-D4-A40] [𓊨𓁹𓀭]. Geb's son and heir, to whom the kingship of the earth passes (Sections XI–XII); murdered by his brother Seth, father of Horus, and king of the dead. See Osiris and the Osiris myth . ISIS — GREAT OF MAGIC ꜣst [Gardiner: G1-S29-X1] [𓄿𓋴𓏏]. Geb's daughter; wife and reviver of Osiris, mother and advocate of Horus, mistress of heka . See Isis . SETH — THE DISRUPTER stš [Gardiner: E20] [𓃩]. Geb's son; the storm, the desert, and the violent claimant whose contest with Horus is judged under Geb's authority (Section XIII). NEPHTHYS — THE MOURNER Geb's youngest daughter in the standard genealogy; wife of Seth who nevertheless mourns Osiris and guards the dead beside her sister Isis. HORUS THE ELDER — THE FIFTH CHILD Ḥr-wr [Gardiner: G5-G36] [𓅃𓅨], "Horus the Great." Several lists, including the tradition Plutarch preserves, count five children of Geb and Nut; the fifth is the elder, cosmic Horus, distinguished from Horus son of Isis in the archive's article on Horus . Genealogy in Egypt is never mere family romance; it is physics and law stated in the idiom of birth. That Geb is the grandson of the creator and the son of air and moisture tells the theologian that the earth is neither eternal in its present form nor self-explanatory: it was produced, at a definite stage of creation, out of prior and subtler principles, and it stands in definite relations of descent and obligation to everything else. That Geb is the father of Osiris tells the jurist something equally precise: kingship on earth descends through Geb's line, and every later claim to the throne — Osiris's, Horus's, and each human king's after them — is, in form, a claim upon Geb's estate. Sections X to XIII unpack that legal theology, which is Geb's most distinctive contribution to Egyptian religion. Geb and Nut together also mark the boundary of the ordered world. Between his upper surface and her lower surface lies everything that lives; above her is the primeval water, Nun, from which creation emerged and by which it is still surrounded; within and below him lies the realm of the dead, the dwꜣt [Gardiner: N15] [𓇽]. The pair are, in the phrase of modern summaries, the permanent boundary between the waters and the created world — floor and ceiling of the house of life, which the Egyptians could accordingly call, in a phrase preserved in the handbook tradition, the house of Geb. Section VIII returns to that image. III. The Separation — Shu Between Earth and Sky The most famous image in Egyptian cosmology is a separation. Geb lies below, Nut arches above, and between them stands Shu with arms raised, holding the sky off the earth and making the space in which life is possible. The scene is known from coffins, tomb ceilings, and above all from the mythological and funerary papyri of the Third Intermediate Period; its classic exemplar is sheet 87 of the Greenfield Papyrus, the Book of the Dead of Nestanebetisheru, now in the British Museum (EA10554,87; late 21st to early 22nd Dynasty, c. 950–930 BCE). The British Museum's collection record describes the vignette exactly: a full-page vignette of Geb, Nut, and Shu, in which Geb is shown as a semi-recumbent figure stretching out his limbs while the body of Nut arches over him and Shu supports her, aided in the fuller versions by ram-headed gods. Every figure carries its hieroglyphic label; the image is a diagram as much as a picture. The narrative the diagram presupposes is told in later texts and summaries rather than in any single early canonical version, and the archive states it with that caution. Geb and Nut, in the beginning, lay locked in a permanent embrace — earth and sky in contact, with no room between them for air, light, or living things. Their father Shu, acting in some tellings on the command of the high god, forced them apart: standing upon Geb, he lifted Nut high above him, and the space his own body occupies between them became the atmosphere, the breathable interval of the world. Nut, already pregnant, then bore her children. Plutarch's Greek account ( De Iside et Osiride , c. 100 CE) adds the famous machinery of the curse and the five epagomenal days won at draughts by Thoth, on which the five children were born — a late, Greek-framed telling that this archive uses, as elsewhere, only with its date kept in view. The scene's meaning is architectural. Before the separation there is no world in the Egyptian sense — no up and down, no east and west, no path for the sun. After it, the cosmos has the form the archive's cosmological survey describes as nested order: the waters outside, the sky as container, the air as interval, the earth as floor. The sun, rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳], can now travel: swallowed by Nut at the western horizon, ꜣḫt [Gardiner: N27] [𓈌], carried through the night, and born from her again in the east. The sky itself is pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯]. Geb's part in the founding scene is passive in posture and absolute in importance: he is what the world stands on. Every later Egyptian statement about stability — every throne, every temple foundation, every claim that order, mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: C10] [𓁦], holds against disorder — presupposes that the floor is still there, still Geb, still in his place. Artists took the diagram personally. On coffins of the period, Nut is painted inside the lid and Geb is associated with the base and the earth beneath, so that the justified dead lie literally between sky and earth, enclosed by the separated pair. In some vignettes Geb is drawn prostrate with one knee raised and his body twisted, the unevenness of his limbs read by interpreters as the hills and valleys of the land itself; in others — including the Greenfield sheet — one arm and leg stretch toward Nut, the gesture of a union remembered and permanently deferred. The archive presents those readings as interpretations of the images, not as captions the Egyptians supplied: what the images themselves state, with their labels, is only and exactly the separation — father between, daughter above, son below. // THE SEPARATION IN ONE GLANCE // Below = Geb, gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] [𓅬𓃀𓀭], the floor of the world. Above = Nut, nwt [Gardiner: N35-W24-X1-B1] [𓈖𓏌𓏏𓁐], the vault. Between = Shu, šw [Gardiner: H6a] [𓆅], the air that holds them apart. The space made = the world of the living, beneath pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯] and upon tꜣ [Gardiner: N16] [𓇾]. Principal witness: the Greenfield Papyrus, British Museum EA10554,87. IV. Iconography — the Reclining God Beneath Nut Geb is usually a man. Encyclopaedia Britannica's summary, which the archive follows here, makes the point that surprises visitors: Geb "was usually portrayed as a man without any distinguishing characteristics" — bearded, of divine but unremarkable form — "but at times he was represented with his head surmounted by a goose, the hieroglyph of his name." His identity in a scene is therefore carried less by a unique body than by position, company, and inscription: the man reclining at Shu's feet beneath the arched body of Nut, labelled gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] [𓅬𓃀𓀭], is Geb; the same figure standing in a divine procession is Geb because the text beside him says so. Egyptian iconography works this way throughout the pantheon : the caption is part of the image, and an unlabelled god is an unfinished statement. In his reclining form — the form the separation scene fixed for all later periods — Geb lies on his side or back along the bottom of the composition, sometimes propped on one elbow, his body forming the baseline of the cosmos. Later vignettes, especially in the mythological papyri of the 21st Dynasty and in Book of the Dead manuscripts such as the Greenfield Papyrus, develop the body into landscape: plants spring from his torso and limbs, his skin is coloured green or patterned with vegetation, and grain grows along his ribs. The image states Section VIII's doctrine directly — the earth's fertility is not something Geb causes at a distance; the crops are his body, growing out of the god the way hair grows out of skin. Where the painter gives Geb a green body, the colour is doing theological work of the kind surveyed in the archive's article on colour in Egyptian art and thought: green is the colour of wꜣḏ [Gardiner: M13] [𓇅], freshness, growth, and regeneration. In standing and enthroned forms Geb carries the ordinary furniture of divine authority: the wꜣs -sceptre [Gardiner: S40] [𓌀] of dominion, the ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] [𓋹], "life," and on occasion the crook ḥqꜣ [Gardiner: S38] [𓋾] that marks rulership — appropriate to a god whom the texts remember as a king (Section XII). In a small number of later depictions he takes animal or hybrid forms: the handbook tradition records representations as a ram, a bull, and — in a Book of the Dead vignette of the lady Heryweben — a crocodile. The archive lists these as attested exceptions, not as Geb's standard repertoire: the ram and the bull belong far more characteristically to other gods, and the bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝] — the ram-form in which a god's power could manifest, the value of the sign being the post-audit correction bꜣ — is a general Egyptian category, not a Geb specialty. The god's oldest surviving representation sets the human norm early: a fragmentary relief from Heliopolis, dated to the reign of Djoser in the 3rd Dynasty, already shows Geb as an anthropomorphic bearded figure accompanied by his name. Geb also appears where a modern reader does not expect an earth god: presiding in state. In temple and tomb scenes he sits enthroned among the Ennead, receives offerings, and takes part in the presentation and legitimation of kings. The contrast between the two registers — the god sprawled as landscape at the bottom of the cosmos, and the same god seated in judgment at the head of the gods — is not an inconsistency to be explained away. It is the subject of Sections X to XIII: in Egyptian thought the earth is simultaneously the passive floor of the world and the active source of all legitimate rule over it. V. The Crown of Geb and the Earth-God's Regalia When Geb wears a crown, he wears the crowns of the land he is. The handbook tradition most often shows him with the Red Crown, dšrt [Gardiner: S4] [𓋕], the crown of Lower Egypt, sometimes combined with the tall plumed Atef crown associated with Osiris, his heir; other images set the goose of his name upon his head in place of a crown altogether, the hieroglyph worn as regalia. Each choice is a statement. The Red Crown binds Geb to the Delta half of the Two Lands; the Atef binds him forward, to the son who inherits from him; the goose binds him to his own written name, gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40], in the visual pun Egyptian art never tired of. The White Crown, ḥḏt [Gardiner: S1] [𓋑], of Upper Egypt and the combined Double Crown, sḫmty [Gardiner: S5] [𓋖], the "Two Powerful Ones," belong in the strictest usage to the king and to Horus rather than to Geb himself — but the boundary is porous in the images, precisely because Geb is the former king from whom the crowns descend. The plumed headdress šwty [Gardiner: S9] [𓋛], two tall feathers, also appears on Geb in some representations, linking him visually to his father Shu, whose feather — šw [Gardiner: H6a] [𓆅] — is the sign of air and of mꜣꜥt -order alike. Iconographic borrowing of this kind is the normal grammar of Egyptian divine portraiture: a shared element declares a shared nature or a family relation, and the viewer who knows the system reads a genealogy off a silhouette. The archive's treatment of Horus sets out the same grammar for the falcon's crowns; Geb's versions are quieter, as befits a god whose majesty is that of ground rather than sky, but they are exactly as deliberate. One further item of regalia is easy to overlook because it is a piece of architecture: the throne. Geb's throne is the earth itself, and Egyptian royal language preserves the equation. The Pyramid Texts place the justified king "upon the throne of Geb" (Section X), and the king's literal throne furniture could carry the serekh — srḫ [Gardiner: O33] [𓊁], the post-audit value of the palace-façade sign — binding the seat of rule to the palace and the falcon. To sit, in Egypt, is to sit on Geb: there is no other ground to sit on. The crown of Geb is therefore best understood not as one headdress among others but as the whole apparatus of landed kingship — crown, throne, palace, and soil — gathered onto the body of the god who is all four. VI. The Goose — Geb's Animal and the Great Cackler Question No part of Geb's dossier has generated more confident error than the goose, and this section exists to separate three things that popular accounts habitually fuse: the goose sign in Geb's name, the goose as a supposed cult animal of Geb, and the primordial creator-goose called the Great Cackler. They are three different subjects, and the evidence treats them differently. The Sign First, the sign. The bird that writes gb [Gardiner: G38-D58-A40] [𓅬𓃀𓀭] is identified in the specialist discussion, following te Velde's Lexikon entry, with the white-fronted goose. Its role in the name is phonetic: it spells the god. The same sign, [𓅬], in other words carries the value sꜣ , "son" — Egyptian signs are polyvalent, and context, not the picture alone, decides the reading. A sign's picture is therefore not a portrait of the god's sacred animal. The falcon on the perch [Gardiner: G5] [𓅃] happens to be both sign and animal for Horus; for Geb, the corresponding inference — goose sign, therefore goose god — is precisely the inference the specialists warn against. The Great Cackler Second, the creator-goose. Egyptian creation traditions know a primordial goose whose cackle broke the silence of the uncreated world and who guarded or laid the cosmic egg — swḥt [Gardiner: H8] [𓆇], "egg" — from which the sun and the ordered world emerged. This bird's name is Ngg-wr [Gardiner: N35-W11-W11-G36] — "Great Honker," conventionally rendered "Great Cackler": ngg , the onomatopoeic honking, built from n [Gardiner: N35] [𓈖] and g [Gardiner: W11] [𓎼], plus wr [Gardiner: G36] [𓅨], "great." Richard H. Wilkinson's Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt treats this goose — Gengen Wer — as a distinct minor creator god in his own right (p. 213), the guardian of the celestial egg and a figure of creative energy, with a small role in Book of the Dead Spell 59 tradition. Ornithologically the Cackler is the Nile or Egyptian goose, called in Egyptian smn [Gardiner: S29-G17-N35] [𓋴𓅓𓈖] — a different species from the white-fronted goose of Geb's name-sign, and a different word. Third, the association with Amun. The Nile goose smn [Gardiner: S29-G17-N35] is a sacred bird of Amun of Thebes: New Kingdom stelae can call Amun himself the beautiful smn -goose, and the goose's association with the first act of creation — the honk that broke the primeval silence — attached in Theban theology to Amun as hidden creator. A coloured vignette on a 21st-Dynasty mythological papyrus depicts the Nile Goose with opened beak in an unmistakably solar-creation context, captioned for the Great Honker. When a handbook tells you that "the Great Cackler" laid the world-egg, the god most securely in the background is therefore this primeval goose itself, Gengen Wer, and in Theban dress, Amun — not Geb. What, then, is Geb's real goose connection? It is genuine but narrower than the legend. The goose sign stands at the head of his name and could be worn on his head as an identifying emblem (Sections IV–V); late and popular tradition, ancient as well as modern, played on the resulting association, and some Egyptologists — Jan Bergman, Terence DuQuesne, and at points Wilkinson himself among them — have argued for a real association between Geb and a creator-goose who laid the world-egg. The counter-position, stated by te Velde and now widely followed, is that this association rests on a confusion between the gb(b) white-fronted goose of the name-sign and the smn Nile goose of creation. The archive's verdict follows the evidence as it stands: the Geb–goose link is graphic and phonetic first , emblematic second, and cultic only weakly if at all; the Great Cackler is primarily Gengen Wer , secondarily a form or animal of Amun, and only by later conflation a title of Geb. The conflation itself is an Egyptian habit — gods absorb each other's animals and epithets constantly — but an archive's duty is to date and label the layers, not to melt them back together. The cosmological articles of this archive, which in places call Geb "the Great Cackler" directly, are to be read with this section's correction in hand. VII. The Laughter of Geb — Earthquakes in Later Tradition It is often said that earthquakes are Geb's laughter. The statement is everywhere in modern handbooks — Geraldine Pinch's Handbook of Egyptian Mythology (2002, p. 135) and Wilkinson's Complete Gods and Goddesses (pp. 105–106) both transmit it, and from them it has passed into virtually every popular account of the god — and it is exactly the kind of statement this archive is required to source carefully. No surviving Pharaonic text has been produced, in the standard literature, that says in so many words "the earthquake is the laughter of Geb." What the handbooks transmit is a piece of later tradition and interpretive inference : the earth-god's body shakes; a body that shakes with sound is laughing; the cackling association of Section VI supplies the voice. The archive therefore presents the laughter of Geb as it presents the wedjat-fraction story in the article on Horus : as a famous, attractive, and only lightly anchored tradition — believed and repeated in later retellings of Geb, consistent with his nature as the living earth, but not to be quoted as a doctrine of the Pyramid Texts. What is anchored in the early texts is the trembling. The Pyramid Texts know the bones of Geb shaking at a theophany: in the sequence Samuel A. B. Mercer translated as Utterances 273–274 (the so- called Cannibal Hymn), the heavens darken and — in Mercer's rendering, paraphrased here — the bows shake and the bones of Geb tremble at the appearance of the king as a god. The image is precise and physical: when overwhelming power manifests, the earth's frame quakes in its joints. Geb has bones because Geb is a body; the quake is what that body does under stress. Between Mercer's trembling bones and Pinch's laughter there lies a long history of retelling in which the earth's shaking acquired an emotion and a sound. The archive keeps both ends of that history visible: the early image, which is attested, and the later interpretation, which is labelled. The inference was, in any case, an easy one for Egyptians and their successors to make, because Geb's earth was never inert. The ground that grows barley from its ribs, imprisons or releases the dead, and supplies the snake with its name (Section IX) is a ground that acts . Egypt is not a highly seismic land, but it is not aseismic either: tremors are recorded across its history, and a culture that personified the ground as a great recumbent man had a ready grammar for them. If the god shifts, the land moves; if the god laughs, the land shakes. The archive's esoteric reading of the motif is reserved for Section XVII and is offered there as reading, not as fact. VIII. The Body of the Earth — Crops, Plants and the House of Geb Geb's generosity is agricultural before it is anything else. The black land of the Nile valley — the flood-renewed soil on which Egyptian civilisation materially rested — is his body in its fertile aspect, and the handbook tradition states the equation in his own anatomy: barley grows from his ribs; trees, plants, herbs, and grain spring from his surface; the earth that feeds everyone is called the house of Geb. The vignettes of Section IV draw the same doctrine: shoots rising from the reclining god's torso, his body patterned with the plant sign ḥn [Gardiner: M2] [𓆰] and with growing things. In a country where a failed inundation meant famine within the year, the personification of soil as a father who gives the crop was not ornament. It was the theological form of the food supply. The two faces of the land are both his. Geb is personified fertile earth and barren desert together: the cultivated valley and the red waste that borders it, the field and the necropolis that was always dug at the field's desert edge. Egyptian geography made the duality daily experience — walk an hour from any riverside town and you are in Geb's other aspect, where nothing grows and the dead are buried. The god's body thus includes the tomb as naturally as the furrow, a point Section XV develops: what is sown in Geb rises again, and what is buried in Geb is in his keeping. The seed and the corpse are entrusted to the same god, and Egyptian funerary hope is built on the resemblance between them. Geb also dispenses what the earth contains rather than what grows on it: minerals, stones, and the wealth of mines and quarries fall within his jurisdiction in the handbook summaries, as the produce of his interior. The point is systematic rather than picturesque. Everything a human being can stand on, eat, build with, bury in, or dig out belongs to the one god whose body is the ground and all that is in it. When the Pyramid Texts call Geb "lord of the entire earth" (Section X), the totality is meant literally and in depth: surface, soil, and underworld are one estate, and its lord is the father of the kings who administer its topmost layer. THE FIELD Geb fertile: barley from his ribs, grain and herbs from his body, the inundation's gift made personal. The god of the harvest because he is the harvested ground. THE DESERT EDGE Geb barren: the red land that borders the cultivation, holds the quarries and mines, and receives the necropoleis. The same body, in its aspect of withholding. THE INTERIOR Geb below: stones, minerals, caves, tombs, and the dwꜣt [Gardiner: N15] [𓇽] itself. Death is a return into the god, as the seed's burial is. A theological refinement completes the picture. The earth in Egypt is not the bottom of everything: beneath and around the ordered world lie the waters of Nun, and Geb himself rests upon — or within — that older deep. Creation did not abolish the waters; it built a floor over them, and the floor is a person who can be addressed, thanked, feared, and inherited from. The archive's article on the cosmological deities places Geb in that nested scheme; the Memphite theology gives the complementary picture, in which Ptah fashions the world by heart and tongue. Egypt kept both systems, and several more, in simultaneous use. Geb's claim needs no reconciling with Ptah's: the earth can be a god in his own right at Heliopolis and the handiwork of another god at Memphis, and the same priest could serve both accounts without strain. IX. Father of Snakes — Nehebkau, Mines and What Lies Below The earth has a dangerous population, and it too belongs to Geb. Snakes live in the ground, emerge from the ground, and return to the ground; Egyptian accordingly named the snake, in one of its common designations, sꜣ-tꜣ [Gardiner: G38-N16] [𓅬𓇾] — "son of the earth" — and counted Geb as the father of snakes. The paternity is not affectionate. Geb was feared in this aspect: the handbook tradition is explicit that the fatherhood made him a power to be placated, and the late Brooklyn papyrus devoted to snake identification and snakebite remedies works within a world where the creatures of the earth answer, ultimately, to the earth. The archive's material on Egyptian healing and heka meets the same world from the patient's side. The mythic summit of the snake-line is Nehebkau, a primeval serpent of great power, whom a Coffin Texts spell names as Geb's offspring — Geb described, in the spell's terms as the handbooks paraphrase them, as father of the snake Nehebkau of primeval times. Nehebkau himself is a double-natured figure of the netherworld books: a serpent who can threaten the gods and who also, in the judgment tradition, announces and serves the justified dead. That the earth's most ancient serpent should be Geb's son fits the system's logic exactly. What crawls out of the ground in the first days is the ground's own child, older than the kingship, and not entirely tamed by it — a reminder, built into the genealogy, that the floor of the world has depths its rulers do not govern. See the archive's survey of the netherworld books for Nehebkau's later career. One further late episode shows Geb's earth-power in a regal register. In the Book of the Heavenly Cow tradition and its echoes, the ageing sun god Ra complains of the snakes of the earth troubling him, and Geb is summoned into the council of the gods in the matter — the earth called to account for its creatures by the heaven. The scene is minor beside the succession material of the next sections, but it completes Geb's portfolio: plants above, stones within, snakes below, and a seat in council when any of them becomes a matter of state. X. Geb in the Pyramid Texts — Hereditary Prince of the Gods Geb is already, in the oldest religious texts Egypt has left — the Pyramid Texts carved in the royal pyramids of the late Old Kingdom, from the reign of Unas onward — a god of the first rank, and the rank is stated in a title that never leaves him: hereditary prince of the gods . The great utterance devoted to him, Utterance 592 in Sethe's numbering (§§1615–1626), addresses Geb directly, and Mercer's published translation (1952) — the version quoted and paraphrased throughout this section, from the text as published — gives the titles in sequence: Atum has given Geb his heritage; Geb is the eldest son of Shu, his primogeniture; he is, in Mercer's words, "Hereditary prince of the gods." The dead king, Osiris N., is placed under Geb's protection as Geb's own son, for the text's purpose is to gather the king into the family that owns the earth. The same utterance states Geb's judicial supremacy in the sentence from which this article's epithet is taken. In Mercer's translation: "Thou art standing on the earth; thou judgest at the head of the Ennead" (§1619a), followed at once by "thou art lord of the entire earth" and "thou art powerful over the Ennead and even over every god" (§§1621a–b). Read those lines against the reclining figure of Section IV and the whole Geb paradox stands in two sentences: the god who is the ground also stands on it as its judge; the floor of the council chamber is also its president. The Ennead itself — psḏt [Gardiner: N9-X1] [𓇷𓏏] — is in this conception Geb's own court and kindred: the family he heads because he is its eldest earth-born prince, heir of Atum through Shu. The opening utterances of the corpus make the same point from the king's side. In Utterance 2, Geb himself speaks the adoption formula over the dead king — in Mercer's rendering: "To say by Geb: This is my son, N., of my body." Utterance 3, spoken by Nut, places the king "upon the throne of Geb, with whom he has been satisfied," and adds the legally decisive clause, again in Mercer's words: Geb gave the king "his inheritance in the presence of the Great Ennead." Every element of the later kingship theology is already present in these three utterances of the Old Kingdom: the king is Geb's son; his seat is Geb's throne; his title is an inheritance; and the inheritance is valid because it was transferred before witnesses — the assembled gods.
