Key Determinatives — The Classifiers of Reality Determinatives are perhaps the most overlooked and most philosophically rich element of the hieroglyphic system. They are the system's ontological sorters — silent signs that tell the reader what category of reality the word belongs to. They do not add pronunciation; they add meaning-context. A word that ends with 𓂡 (throwing stick) involves foreigners or enemy forces. A word ending with 𓏛 (papyrus roll) involves abstract concepts, books, or knowledge. A word ending with 𓀭 (seated god) belongs to the divine realm. This determinative system encodes the entire Kemetic worldview: the categories into which the Egyptians sorted all reality. By studying which determinatives attach to which words, a researcher can reconstruct an implicit Egyptian ontology — a map of how they believed reality was organized at the deepest level. GLYPH GARDINER CATEGORY IT MARKS ESOTERIC SIGNIFICANCE 𓀭 A40 Divine beings, deities Marks the boundary between human and divine reality 𓁐 B1 Female person, woman Feminine principle, receptive, generative 𓌙 T14 Foreigners, enemy The external, the unincorporated, chaotic forces 𓂻 D54 Motion, movement Dynamic force, change of state, journey 𓆑 I9 Serpents Liminal power, protection and danger simultaneously 𓊵 R4 Offerings, sacred bread The sacrificial axis between human and divine levels 𓈖 N35A Water, liquids The Nun, primordial potential, the unconscious 𓊖 O49 Towns, cities, place names Points of cosmic anchoring in the terrestrial plane 𓋴 S29 Cloth, fabric Linen wrapping, the material envelope of the soul 𓏛 Y1 Abstract concepts, books Knowledge, the written reality, the akashic register 𓏤 Z1 Singular determinative stroke Individuation; the marking of unique identity 𓏥 Z2 Plural determinative Multiplicity; the collective principle 𓂝 D36 Actions of the arm Willed action, the extension of magical agency 𓀢 A30 Prayer, adoration, praise The posture of reception; alignment with the divine XIII. Special Signs — Cartouche, Serekh, and Royal Glyphs Beyond the standard Gardiner categories, several signs of supreme theological importance operate as structural elements of royal and divine naming rather than phonetic or determinative elements within words. These are the architectural elements of royal identity. 𓍶 / 𓍷 THE CARTOUCHE (Šnw / Shenu) — V9/V10 The cartouche (from the French for "gun cartridge" — an entirely inappropriate modern name) is the oval ring formed by a doubled loop of rope, closed at the base with a horizontal bar. In Egyptian it is called šnw — from the verb "to encircle" — and it represents an infinite loop, a ring that contains and protects the divine name within. Royal names (from the 4th Dynasty onward) were invariably written inside the cartouche. The cartouche declares: this name is encircled by the sun's circuit; it endures for as long as the sun revolves; it is protected by the infinite circumference of Re's path . To write a name in a cartouche is to bind it to solar time — to make it as durable as the sun's daily journey. 𓍶 Shen Ring → [ NAME ] → 𓍷 Cartouche enclosure 𓊁 THE SEREKH — The Palace Façade Predating the cartouche, the serekh is a rectangular enclosure depicting the façade of the royal palace (the "palace façade" pattern), topped by a falcon (Horus). The pharaoh's Horus-name — their oldest and most theologically fundamental royal title — was written inside the serekh. The serekh makes the identity statement that the king is not merely a person in a palace; the king is the Horus-principle, housed in the material structure of the palace as the divine soul is housed in the body. The falcon on top is not decorative — it is the statement of what inhabits the structure below. 𓋹 THE ANKH (ꜥnḫ) — S34 The most recognizable Egyptian sign and one of the most discussed. Gardiner S34. Phonetically: ꜥnḫ = "life." Its graphic origin remains debated — proposed derivations include a sandal strap, a knot, a mirror, a tjet knot, or a looped cross of foreign origin. What is not debated is its semantic weight: the ankh is ꜥnḫ , life itself, life force, the animating principle that distinguishes the living from the dead. It was held by deities as a gift of life; it was placed at the nostrils of the dead in resurrection spells to restore the breath of life. In practical esoteric work, it functions as the primary symbol of the vital force — analogous to Prana , Qi , Pneuma , and Orgone in other traditions. 𓊽 THE DJED PILLAR (Ḏd) — R11 Ḏd = "stability." The djed is one of the most ancient Egyptian symbols, predating the dynastic period. It appears as a stylized object of debated origin (possibly a bundle of grain stalks, a tree with branches lopped off, or a spinal column). Its primary meaning is stability, endurance, continuity . As the backbone of Osiris, it represents the restoration of order after dissolution — the spine of Osiris reassembled by Isis, standing upright as proof that death has been defeated and structure restored. The "Raising of the Djed" was a central rite in the Sed festival and Osirian ceremonies. It encodes the alchemical truth that the Great Work is not complete until stability is achieved — until the volatile is fixed and the structure can stand without support. 𓌀 THE WAS SCEPTER (Wꜣs) — S40 Wꜣs = "dominion, power." The was scepter — a long staff with a distinctive forked base and an animal head (possibly the Set animal) at the top — is carried by deities and pharaohs as the sign of divine power and authority. Unlike the crook and flail (symbols of royal pastoral and agricultural authority), the was scepter represents direct divine force. It is what the gods hold; the power that is theirs by nature rather than by function. In esoteric practice, it corresponds to the channeled will of the operator — the capacity to direct Heka through a consecrated instrument. XIV. Extended Sign List — Ptolemaic Additions The classical Gardiner list of ~750 signs represents the Middle Kingdom standard — the corpus used by professional scribes of the 12th Dynasty (c. 1991–1802 BCE), which became the canonical literary register. But the hieroglyphic system did not freeze there. In the Ptolemaic period (332–30 BCE), the priestly tradition underwent a remarkable expansion of the sign repertoire, ultimately producing walls at temples like Esna, Edfu, and Dendera that employed over 6,000 distinct signs . This expansion was not graphical inflation or scribal showing-off (though it was sometimes that too). It served a primarily cryptographic and theological function : by multiplying signs, the priestly class created a layer of encoded knowledge accessible only to the initiated. Words could be written in multiple ways; signs could be substituted based on phonetic or visual resemblance; new signs encoding theological concepts could be invented for particular texts. The outer walls of temples displayed accessible material; the inner sanctuaries encoded material that required initiation to decode. See Enigmatic Writing for full treatment of this dimension. SIGN MULTIPLICATION Ptolemaic scribes invented signs for specific theological concepts — abstract principles that did not correspond to any single object. They also repurposed existing signs by reassigning their phonetic values based on visual resemblance or pun relationships. A sign depicting a heron might be assigned to a word beginning with the sound "bꜣ" because the heron's beak shape resembled the letter Ba in another script. THE ESNA SIGN LIST The Ptolemaic temple of Esna (Khnum's temple, Upper Egypt) contains the most extensive preserved collection of Ptolemaic cryptographic signs. Its hymns to Khnum were written in signs where virtually every hieroglyph depicts a ram or a crocodile — the two sacred animals of the temple — making the entire text simultaneously a devotional hymn and a zoological catalogue of the divine. This is not wordplay; it is a fully operational theological statement inscribed in visual form. XV. The Esoteric Dimension — Signs as Living Frequencies Modern Egyptology treats hieroglyphs as a writing system: notation for language, decoded via phonology and grammar. This is correct as far as it goes. But the Kemetic tradition understood the signs as something more. They were — and in active practice, remain — living configurations of Heka . The sign is not a representation of a reality; it is a reality operating at a different level. This understanding has parallels in every major esoteric tradition: the Hebrew letters of the Qabalah are understood as the building blocks of creation, each encoding a divine force. The Sanskrit mantric system holds that the phoneme OM is not a symbol for the Absolute but the Absolute sounding itself. The Germanic runes were not alphabetic signs but cosmic principles in visual form. In each case, the writing system is simultaneously a cosmological map and a set of operational tools. The Kemetic system is no different — and in some respects deeper than the others, because it survived for 3,500 years of continuous priestly development, accumulating layers of operational experience that most other traditions did not have time to develop. // OPERATIONAL NOTE — WORKING WITH THE SIGNS // Those engaged in practical work with Medu Netjer should treat each sign as a distinct frequency-pattern that can be activated, contemplated, or invoked depending on the working. The uniliteral alphabet provides 24 primary frequencies corresponding to the 24 consonants. These align, with varying correspondence, to Hebrew letters, planetary forces, and elemental attributions in Western esoteric systems. The determinatives are not neutral classifiers — they are the signs' declarations of which domain of reality the operation addresses. When constructing a Heka-working using hieroglyphic inscription, the choice of determinative is the specification of which plane the operation targets. Choose accordingly and consciously. The esoteric significance of individual signs has been preserved in multiple streams: directly in the Egyptian magical papyri (see Greek Magical Papyri ), in the Hermetic tradition's doctrine of signs and signatures (see Hermeticism ), and in Coptic-era magical texts that continued to use hieroglyphic signs in amulets and ritual objects long after the script had ceased to be used for ordinary writing. The scribal knowledge did not disappear when the temples closed — it went underground, where it has remained operational through the long dark of the medieval period into the modern revival. The last dated hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in 394 CE — the graffito of the priest Esmet-Akhom. After that, the signs fell silent until their decipherment in the nineteenth century. — Paraphrase of Jan Assmann, The Search for God in Ancient Egypt , 2001 XVI. Practical Reference — Reading Direction and Orientation Hieroglyphs can be written in three directions: right to left (most common in classic inscriptions), left to right , and vertically in columns (reading top to bottom, columns arranged right to left). The determining rule is: the living creatures in the signs face the beginning of the text . If the falcons, men, and animals face right, read from right to left. If they face left, read from left to right. This orientation rule is not arbitrary. In classical texts, living beings face toward the source of speech — toward the deity, the king, or the ritual officiant. The orientation is a form of reverential alignment. The entire inscription is organized around the principle that the written word moves toward the sacred, not away from it. HIERATIC — THE CURSIVE FORM For administrative and literary texts, scribes used Hieratic — a simplified, cursive version of the hieroglyphs developed from very early in the dynastic period. Hieratic always reads right to left. It is to hieroglyphs what a simplified handwritten script is to printed block letters: the same system, expressed in a more fluid and rapid form. Most of the major literary and magical papyri are written in Hieratic, not Hieroglyphs. ENCODING SOFTWARE Modern scholars and practitioners use JSesh (free, open source) for composing hieroglyphic texts with Gardiner codes. The system accepts standard Gardiner notation (e.g., G17-N35-R8 ) and renders the corresponding signs. Unicode now supports hieroglyphs directly (U+13000–U+1342F) though rendering quality varies by font. Recommended fonts: Noto Sans Egyptian Hieroglyphs, Segoe UI Historic. // CAUTION — ON PRONUNCIATION // Reconstructed Middle Egyptian pronunciation (as used in Egyptological convention) is a scholarly approximation, not a precise recovery of the ancien

The Name — Ḥr and the Distant One Horus is among the oldest gods of Egypt whose name can still be read. His Egyptian name is ḥr [Gardiner: G5], written with a single sign: the falcon on its perch, [𓅃]. The sign is a logogram — the picture is the word — and the V2 transliterator of this archive accordingly gives G5 the whole-word value Ḥr . In fuller writings the name appears as ḥr.w , the final w marking an old ending that later fell silent. Egyptologists reconstruct an early pronunciation close to Ḥāru ; by Coptic times the name had become Hōr , and Greek writers rendered it Hōros — the form that survives in English as Horus. The god is therefore, before anything else, simply the Falcon . What the name means beyond "falcon" is debated, and the debate matters because each proposed meaning describes a different god. The most widely repeated derivation connects ḥr [Gardiner: G5] with the root ḥr in the sense of distance and height: Horus is "the Distant One" or "the One Who Is Above" — the falcon seen from below, a speck circling at the limit of vision, untouchable and overseeing everything. On this reading the name is a description of the sky itself as experienced from the ground: remote, elevated, and all-seeing. A second line of interpretation treats the name as primary and unanalysable — the falcon god's proper name, no more to be translated than the name of any person. The archive presents the "Distant One" derivation as the leading scholarly proposal, not as a settled fact: the Egyptians themselves left no etymological dictionary, and their own scribes were happy to exploit the name's sounds rather than explain them. Those sounds were productive. Egyptian is rich in ḥr -words, and temple theology played on them deliberately. The word for "face" and the preposition "upon" are both written ḥr [Gardiner: D2] [𓁷] — a different sign, the human face in profile, with the same consonants. The falcon god is thus, by a pun no Egyptian scribe would have missed, the one who is upon all things and whose face is the sky. The word for "day," hrw [Gardiner: N7] [𓇵], belongs to the same sound-world: the day is the period of Horus's visible rule. Such wordplay — the raw material of the archive's study of phonology and voice and of the power of names — is not decoration in Egyptian theology. It is one of the ways theology was done. // READING THE NAME IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used and flagged: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , R21 = sšꜣt , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . Horus was also known by place. As the falcon of Nekhen (Hierakonpolis), the predynastic capital of Upper Egypt whose Greek name literally means "Falcon City," he was the patron of the earliest kings — a local Horus who became, as Nekhen's rulers became kings of all Egypt, a national one. Other towns kept their own falcon gods, many of them gradually identified with Horus or distinguished from him only by a local epithet: Horus of Mesen the harpooner at Edfu, Horus of Letopolis, Horus of Hebenu. The pattern is characteristic of the Egyptian pantheon : one great name, many local faces, and no central authority ever insisting that the faces be reconciled. The name outlived the temples. It survives compounded in personal names borne by ordinary Egyptians for three thousand years — Harsiese, "Horus, son of Isis," is only the most transparent — and in the Greek form Hōros it passed into the vocabularies of Hermeticism and Gnosticism , where "Horos" could even detach from the falcon entirely and name a boundary or limit. Section XIV returns to that strange afterlife. The falcon on the perch, however, never changed: from the labels of Dynasty 0 to the last Ptolemaic temple walls, [𓅃] means Horus. II. Two Horuses — the Elder and the Son of Isis The single most important fact for understanding Horus is that Egyptian theology itself distinguishes two of him. Modern handbooks sometimes present this as a scholarly tidying-up of a confused tradition. It is not: the distinction is ancient, explicit, and load-bearing, because the two Horuses have different parents, different myths, and different jobs. Horus the Elder — Ḥr-wr Ḥr-wr [Gardiner: G5-G36] [𓅃𓅨] — "Horus the Great," conventionally "Horus the Elder," Greek Haroeris — is the original sky falcon. In the Heliopolitan genealogy of the Ennead , he belongs to the generation of the children of Geb and Nut: brother of Osiris , Isis , Seth, and Nephthys. The Ennead itself is written psḏt [Gardiner: N9-X1] [𓇷𓏏], "the Nine," and Horus the Elder stands inside it as a cosmic power in his own right, not as anyone's heir. His consort in several local theologies is Hathor ; his great cult centre in later periods is Kom Ombo, where he is worshipped as Haroeris alongside the crocodile god Sobek (Section XII). The Elder is the Horus of the sky : his face is the heavens, his eyes the sun and moon (Section IV), and his wings the span of the firmament written pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯]. Crucially, the Elder is also the elder brother in the first version of the conflict with Seth. Before the Osiris myth fully crystallised, the rivalry of Horus and Seth appears to have been a duel of near-equals — sky against storm, north against south — rather than an avenger's quest. Traces of that older, more balanced conflict survive in the dual kingship symbolism discussed in Section VII, where one early king could place Horus and Seth together above his name. Horus, Son of Isis — Ḥr-sꜣ-ꜣst The second Horus is Ḥr-sꜣ-ꜣst [Gardiner: G5-G38-G1-S29-X1] [𓅃𓅬𓄿𓋴𓏏] — "Horus, son of Isis," Greek Harsiesis (from the Egyptian name itself: Ḥr + sꜣ [Gardiner: G38] [𓅬], "son," + ꜣst [Gardiner: G1-S29-X1] [𓄿𓋴𓏏], "Isis"). He is the child of the Osiris myth : conceived by Isis from the revived body of the murdered Osiris — in Egyptian terms, wsir [Gardiner: Q1-D4-A40] [𓊨𓁹𓀭] — hidden by his mother in the Delta marshes at Khemmis, stung and healed in infancy, and raised in secret until he was old enough to claim his father's throne. His defining epithet states his mission in four signs: Ḥr-nḏ-it.f [Gardiner: G5-Aa27-U10-I9] [𓅃𓐩𓌾𓆑], "Horus, Avenger of His Father" — nḏ [Gardiner: Aa27], "to protect, to avenge," upon it [Gardiner: U10] [𓌾], "father." Where the Elder is the sky, the Son acts in the world: he sues, fights, is wounded, is healed, and finally reigns. He is the Horus of narrative. The two were never kept in watertight compartments. Egyptian theology preferred accumulation to system: a hymn could praise the cosmic falcon whose eyes are the luminaries and in the next breath call him Isis's child, and no priest experienced this as a contradiction to be solved. At Edfu the temple's god is simultaneously Horus of Behdet, an Elder-type solar falcon, and the son who triumphs over his father's murderer. The honest way to state the position — and the position this archive takes — is that "Horus" names a cluster : a sky-falcon god of great antiquity, an Osirian son generated by the funerary myth, and a royal office into which every living king stepped. The sections that follow keep the strands distinct where the sources do, and say so where they merge. HORUS THE ELDER (HAROERIS) Ḥr-wr [Gardiner: G5-G36]. Son of Geb and Nut; brother of Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys within the Ennead. Primordial sky god; his eyes are the sun and moon. Consort of Hathor in local theologies; lord of Kom Ombo with Sobek. The Horus of cosmic order rather than of story. HORUS, SON OF ISIS (HARSIESIS) Ḥr-sꜣ-ꜣst [Gardiner: G5-G38-G1-S29-X1]. Posthumous son of Osiris and Isis, hidden at Khemmis, healed of the scorpion's sting, plaintiff and combatant against Seth, and finally king. The Horus of the Osiris myth, of the judgment hall, and of every royal succession. THE CHILD (HARPOCRATES) Ḥr-pꜣ-ẖrd [Gardiner: G5-Q3-G1-A18], "Horus the Child," is the young Son of Isis before his vindication: finger to mouth, sidelock of youth, standing on the crocodiles of the healing cippi. Section VIII is devoted to him. A third axis of distinction is generational mathematics . Egyptian lists of gods could speak of Horus as the last of the divine kings — the god-king who succeeded Osiris on earth and then handed kingship to human rulers, each of whom was Horus in turn. This is why the same god can be older than Osiris's myth and younger than Osiris himself: as office, Horus is the eternal successor; as Elder, he precedes the succession; as Son, he enacts it. Kingship theology (Section VII) runs on exactly this productive ambiguity. III. The Falcon — Iconography and the God's Forms Horus is a falcon, a falcon-headed man, a child, a winged disk, and — in one of his most majestic forms — a falcon standing protectively behind or above a king who is himself Horus. The falcon is not a costume. Egyptian artists, as the Metropolitan Museum's educators put it, composed the image of Horus from the properties of the peregrine falcon and the lanner falcon and other falcon species, rather than portraiture of a single species: the lanner, still nesting in the limestone cliffs at the desert margin, supplied much of the bird's familiar profile — the bold dark malar stripe running down from the eye, the sleek head, the long wings — while the peregrine contributed the aura of the fastest creature on earth, stooping from the height of heaven onto its prey. What mattered theologically was the falcon's behaviour as seen from Egypt : it lives in the sky, it sees farther than any other creature, it strikes without warning, and it returns to a perch above the world. Every one of those traits becomes a doctrine somewhere in this article. In his full animal form Horus stands on a perch or standard, often wearing a crown. The double crown — sḫmty [Gardiner: S5] [𓋖], the "Two Powerful Ones," combining the White Crown ḥḏt [Gardiner: S1] [𓋑] of Upper Egypt with the Red Crown dšrt [Gardiner: S4] [𓋕] of Lower Egypt — identifies the falcon as king of the united land. A small faience amulet in the Metropolitan Museum (Third Intermediate Period, c. 1080–664 BCE) shows exactly this: a brilliant blue falcon wearing the double crown, a suspension loop behind its head, the scalloped feather-pattern engraved on its breast. The god could be carried on the body, at a scale of under four centimetres, without losing any of his kingship. For the broader culture of such objects, see Amulets and Talismans . As a falcon-headed man, Horus wears the same crowns or the double-plumed headdress šwty [Gardiner: S9] [𓋛], and carries the standard furniture of divine kingship: the crook ḥqꜣ [Gardiner: S38] [𓋾], the wꜣs -sceptre [Gardiner: S40] [𓌀] of dominion, and the ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] [𓋹], "life." In this form he walks in processions, receives offerings, presents kings to other gods, and leads the justified dead by the hand (Section XIII). The hybrid body is the Egyptian solution to a theological problem: the god must be recognisably the sky-bird and yet able to act in the human world of hands, doors, boats, and thrones. The colour symbolism of his images — gold flesh for divinity, the black-and-white precision of the falcon's facial markings — follows the same double logic. THE FALCON The god entire: perched, standard-borne, or swooping. Cult statues in this form received the daily temple ritual; the living sacred falcon kept at Edfu was crowned annually as the god's embodiment (Section XII). THE FALCON-HEADED MAN The god in society: crowned, sceptred, striding among gods and kings. The default form for mythological narrative in relief and papyrus, and for the Horus who conducts the dead to Osiris. THE CHILD Nude, sidelocked, finger to mouth: Horus before his vindication, and therefore the form under which he protects other children and heals the stung and bitten (Section VIII). THE WINGED DISK Horus of Behdet as pure emblem: sun disk, falcon wings, twin uraei, set over every temple doorway in Egypt (Section X). THE FALCON BEHIND THE KING From the Old Kingdom statue of Khafre — the falcon spreading its wings around the king's head from behind the throne — to the Late Period statue of Horus protecting the small standing figure of Nectanebo II between his legs (Metropolitan Museum), the god literally enfolds his human embodiment. THE SPHINX-BODIED KING-GOD At Giza the New Kingdom worshipped the Great Sphinx itself as Horus-in-the-Horizon, Ḥr-m-ꜣḫt [Gardiner: G5-G17-N27] (Section XI): the falcon's kingship translated into lion-bodied stone. Not every falcon in Egyptian art is Horus. Montu, the war god of Thebes, and Sokar, the necropolis god of Memphis, are also falcon-headed, and Ra himself travels with a falcon's head in his solar forms. Identification rests on context, crown, accompanying inscription, and company kept — a discipline the archive applies throughout, and a useful warning against reading any single attribute as a label. What is unique to Horus is the combination : falcon plus kingship plus the Osirian story. Where a falcon wears the double crown, stands on the srḫ [Gardiner: O33] palace-façade (Section VII), or confronts the Seth-animal, the falcon is Horus. Real falcons were kept, mummified, and buried by the thousand in the animal cults of the Late Period . A hollow bronze falcon in the Metropolitan Museum, X-rayed in modern times, was found to contain the bones of an actual falcon inserted beneath its tail — votive statue and sarcophagus in one. The bird in the cliffs, the god in the temple, and the sign on the page are three registers of a single presence, and Egyptian religion moved between them without friction. IV. Lord of the Sky — His Eyes as Sun and Moon The oldest layer of Horus is the sky itself. In the conception attached above all to Horus the Elder, the god's body is the firmament: his face is the heaven, pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯]; his outspread wings cross it from horizon to horizon; the stars are the patterning of his speckled plumage; and his two eyes are the two great lights. His right eye is the sun , rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳]; his left eye is the moon , iꜥḥ [Gardiner: N11] [𓇹]. The generic word for "eye," irt [Gardiner: D4-X1] [𓁹𓏏], thus becomes a cosmological term: to speak of the Eye of Horus is to speak of a luminary moving in the sky, liable — in the case of the moon — to injury, waning, and restoration. Section V follows that liability into myth. This is a theology you can watch. The falcon circles at a height where it seems to hang motionless in the blue; the sun and moon cross the same blue on their fixed paths; the identification requires no argument, only looking up. Egyptian cosmology in the archive's survey of the cosmic gods is full of such observed equations, and Horus's is among the most durable: hymns of every period address him as the one whose eyes illumine the Two Lands, and the phrase "Lord of the Sky" — the title this article bears — translates his commonest great epithet, lord of pt [Gardiner: N1]. The horizon is where the sky-god's two eyes do their most important work. The Egyptians wrote "horizon" ꜣḫt [Gardiner: N27] [𓈌] — the place of becoming radiant, from the same root as ꜣḫ [Gardiner: G25] [𓅜], the "transfigured, effective spirit" of the composite soul . The sign itself shows the sun cradled between two hills. Scribes distinguished it carefully from the near-homophone ꜣḥt [Gardiner: G1-V28-X1-N23] [𓄿𓎛𓏏𓈇], "field, arable land": one letter's difference separates the farmer's plot from the doorway of the sun. Horus is pre-eminently a god of the first word. As Ḥr-ꜣḫty [Gardiner: G5-N27-Z4] [𓅃𓈌𓏭], "Horus of the Horizon" — more exactly, of the two horizons, east and west, the dual ending -ty written with y [Gardiner: Z4] [𓏭] — he is the sun at its rising and setting, the falcon at the two gates of the day. Section XI traces his solar forms from this root. The moon-eye deserves its own paragraph, because it explains the god's healing aspect. The moon visibly changes : it is bitten away night by night and made whole again across the month. A sky-god whose left eye is the moon is therefore a god whose eye is periodically damaged and periodically restored — and the myth of the Eye torn out by Seth and healed by Thoth (Sections V–VI) is, among other things, the narrative form of the lunar cycle, just as the offering of the healed Eye to Osiris is its ritual form. Egyptian mathematics and astronomy tracked the same cycle in tables; the myth and the table are two notations for one observation. // THE SKY IN ONE GLANCE // Face = the sky, pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯]. Right eye = the sun, rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳]. Left eye = the moon, iꜥḥ [Gardiner: N11] [𓇹]. Wings = the span of heaven from ꜣḫt [Gardiner: N27] to ꜣḫt . Day itself, hrw [Gardiner: N7] [𓇵], bears his consonants. The brightest star of the southern sky, Sopdet, spdt [Gardiner: M44-X1] [𓇮𓏏] — written with the "sharp, pointed" sign spd [Gardiner: M44] (post-audit value) — belonged not to Horus but to Isis; the sky, like the family, was shared. A falcon god also governs height as rank . The Egyptian idiom for a god's or king's glorious manifestation is ḫꜥ [Gardiner: N28] [𓈍], "to appear in glory, to be crowned" — the sign shows the sun rising over a hill, and coronation vocabulary is built from it. When the king "appeared" as Horus on the throne, the language said that the sun had risen. The Distant One of Section I is distant the way the sun is distant: not absent, but too high and too bright to approach — and precisely therefore able to see, judge, and give life to everything below. V. The Wedjat Eye — the Wounded and Healed Eye If Horus has a single emblem known beyond Egyptology, it is the Wedjat Eye : wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀]. The sign is itself a small work of art — a human eye with a falcon's markings: the brow line above, the spiral curl and the descending tear-line below, borrowed from the facial plumage of the lanner falcon. The word derives from the verb wḏꜣ [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀], "to be sound, whole, uninjured, prosperous." The wedjat is therefore not "the eye" in general — irt [Gardiner: D4-X1] is the ordinary word — but the Eye in its restored condition : the Sound One, the Whole One. Its name is its biography. The biography, told across the Pyramid Texts, the Coffin Texts, the Osiris cycle , and the late mythological papyri, runs as follows. In the combat between Horus and Seth — the subject of Section VI — Seth tore out Horus's eye (in some tellings, both eyes; in Plutarch's Greek retelling the injury is one episode among many) and, in the fullest versions, tore it into pieces. Thoth — ḏḥwty [Gardiner: G26] [𓅝], the ibis god of writing, reckoning, and heka — gathered the pieces, spat upon and reassembled them, and returned the eye to Horus whole. Horus then did the act that fixes the wedjat at the centre of Egyptian funerary religion: he gave the healed eye to his dead father . Osiris received it, and was revived by it. The Eye offered to Osiris becomes, in the offering liturgy of every temple and tomb, the prototype of every offering: each gift of bread, beer, incense, or wine presented to a god or a dead person could be called, and depicted as, the Eye of Horus — the thing once broken, now whole, handed over to restore the one who receives it. Hence the wedjat's career as Egypt's most ubiquitous protective device. Wedjat amulets in blue-green faience, gold, silver, carnelian, and glass were worn by the living and placed in their thousands among mummy wrappings; the British Museum's quadruple wedjat amulet (Third Intermediate Period, EA13430) multiplies the eye fourfold to multiply its strength. Wedjat eyes were painted on coffins — so that the deceased could see out — on the bows of boats, so that the vessel itself could see its way, and on stelae and temple walls as a standing apotropaic guard. The logic is exact: the eye that was destroyed and made whole is the one power in the cosmos that knows injury from inside and has overcome it. Protection by the wedjat is not the protection of the untouched; it is the protection of the healed. The archive's article on amulets and talismans treats the object's typology; the medical papyri show its clinical neighbours, for the wedjat also presided over prescriptions and the restoration of bodily wholeness. The Eye and the Fractions — a Necessary Caution A famous tradition, repeated in many older handbooks, holds that the six parts of the wedjat were used as fraction signs for parts of the heqat grain measure — 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, 1/64 — summing to 63/64, with the missing 1/64 supplied by Thoth's magic. The fractions themselves are real, and capacity-measure signs resembling parts of an eye are genuinely attested. But the neat equation of the two systems is now largely abandoned by specialists : T. Eric Peet already objected in 1923 that the supposed eye-part signs appear too late to be the origin of the measure signs, and Jim Ritter's palaeographic study (2002) showed that the measure signs developed separately and only later converged in appearance with the eye. The story is best filed where this archive files all such material: as a later scribal reinterpretation — probably a New Kingdom flourish — rather than as the origin of Egyptian fractions. It is quoted here because it is famous, and flagged here because the archive's standard is that famous is not the same as true. The genuine mathematical culture behind the question is treated in Mathematics and Astronomy . Distinguish, finally, the Eye of Horus from the Eye of Ra . The two are related — both are wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] eyes, both protective — but they are not the same organ. The Eye of Ra is the sun god's own fiery daughter-power, sent out as Hathor or Sekhmet to punish and protect; the Eye of Horus is the moon-eye , the injured and restored left eye of the falcon. Popular usage conflates them constantly; Egyptian usage kept a distinction that this article preserves: Ra's Eye burns ; Horus's Eye heals . VI. Horus and Seth — the Contendings and the Triumph Every succession in Egypt rehearsed one story: the rightful heir against the violent usurper, order against disorder, ma'at against isfet . The heir is Horus; the usurper is his uncle Seth — written in his older form stš [Gardiner: E20] [𓃩], with the enigmatic Seth-animal as his sign. Seth had murdered Osiris, his own brother, and seized the throne. Horus, raised in hiding, came of age with a single claim, stated in his epithet Ḥr-nḏ-it.f [Gardiner: G5-Aa27-U10-I9]: the son must avenge the father and take the father's office. Egyptian sources tell the ensuing struggle in two very different registers — a legalistic, often comic narrative, and a temple drama of cosmic war — and the archive treats them separately, because they are separate works with separate dates and purposes. The Contendings of Horus and Seth — Papyrus Chester Beatty I The Contendings of Horus and Seth survives in a single manuscript: Papyrus Chester Beatty I, written in hieratic in the Twentieth Dynasty, in the reign of Ramesses V (c. 1149–1145 BCE), probably at Thebes, and now in the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin. A. H. Gardiner published the editio princeps in 1931; Miriam Lichtheim's translation in Ancient Egyptian Literature (vol. II) is the standard English version. The story opens with the case already ancient: Horus and Seth have been litigating before the Ennead for eighty years . The Ennead is deadlocked and irritable. Most of the gods favour Horus — Shu and Thoth argue that the office belongs to the son of Osiris by right — but Ra, presiding, favours the stronger and older Seth and resents the young claimant. The tribunal writes for an outside opinion to Neith of Sais, who answers for Horus and proposes compensation for Seth; Ra refuses to accept the letter's verdict. Isis, barred from one session of the court on an island because Seth fears her advocacy, crosses in disguise, and traps Seth into condemning himself out of his own mouth with a parable about a widow's son and a stranger seizing his father's cattle — the gods laugh, and Seth, realising he has ruled against his own case, is furious. Argument gives way to ordeal. The rivals dive as hippopotamuses to see who can stay submerged longest; Isis, harpoon in hand, wounds her own son by mistake, heals him, then harpoons Seth — who pleads kinship so effectively that she lets him go, whereupon Horus, in rage at her mercy, strikes off his mother's head; Thoth replaces it with a cow's head, an episode the text itself uses to explain an iconography of Isis. Seth later finds Horus resting, tears out his eyes and buries them on a mountain, where they become lotus plants; Hathor heals Horus with gazelle's milk. Seth's attempt to disgrace Horus by a sexual assault is inverted by Isis's counter-trick with a pot of lettuce, so that before the tribunal it is Seth's own claim that collapses when Thoth calls the seed to account. In the final contest the rivals race in boats of stone; Seth's boat is genuinely stone and sinks, while Horus's is pinewood plastered to look like stone — a cheat the text reports without embarrassment, since trickery in a just cause is Isis's own method. At last the gods write to Osiris in the realm of the dead, and Osiris's answering letter — reminding the Ennead that he created the grain that feeds gods and men, and that his messengers can fetch any heart that does evil — settles what eighty years of advocacy could not. Horus is awarded the office of his father and crowned; Seth, in a settlement characteristic of Egyptian rather than modern justice, is not annihilated but placed : given to Ra to thunder in the sky at the prow of the solar barque, a bound and useful power. On the solar barque Seth's violence is exactly what the voyage needs against the serpent Apep . Two cautions govern the archive's use of this text. First, its tone is genuinely literary — satirical, bawdy, and self-aware; it is a scribal entertainment built on sacred material, not a liturgy, and it should not be quoted as if it were temple doctrine. Second, it is one telling among many. The Pyramid Texts, a thousand years older, know the eye-wounding and the tribunal in allusive fragments; Plutarch, a thousand years later, retells the conflict with Greek moralising and omissions he himself acknowledges. The Contendings is the fullest narrative, not the canonical one — Egypt never canonised a single version of anything. The Triumph of Horus — the Edfu Drama The second register is carved on the inner face of the western enclosure wall of the temple of Edfu: the text H. W. Fairman published as The Triumph of Horus (1974, from the studies of Blackman and Fairman in the Journal of Egyptian Archaeology , 1942–44). The inscription is Ptolemaic, of the second century BCE, but its language preserves Late Egyptian features suggesting it was compiled from much older papyrus exemplars kept in the temple library. It was not merely read: it was performed , annually, at Edfu's Festival of Victory — a sacred drama in which Horus of Behdet, played in procession and rite, harpoons Seth in the form of a red hippopotamus. Scene by scene the reliefs show the ten harpoons striking — head, neck, ribs, limbs — the chorus urging the god to hold fast, and finally the dismemberment and distribution of the hippopotamus's body among the gods, a ritual butchery that converts the enemy into offerings. The king played Horus's part in the rite's theology: each performance re-founded his kingship on the victory it re-enacted. Read together, the two works show the conflict's full range. The Contendings insists that Horus wins by right — by birth, by law, by his mother's advocacy and his father's posthumous authority — and that even the gods must submit to the verdict. The Triumph insists that he wins by force , harpoon by harpoon, and that the force must be renewed every year. Egyptian kingship needed both claims, and made both, in different rooms of the same civilisation, for three thousand years. The wider pattern of such performances is surveyed in the archive's article on ritual practice . VII. Horus and Kingship — Serekh and the Fivefold Titulary The living king of Egypt was Horus. This was not a metaphor the court poets reached for on feast days; it was the constitutional theory of the state, written into the king's name, his monuments, his coronation, and his funeral. The dead king became Osiris; the reigning king was Horus; the king's mother occupied the place of Isis. Every accession therefore re-enacted Section VI: the son of the dead king took the office against whatever Seth-forces — rivals, rebels, disorder — the moment supplied, and the gods' tribunal was understood to have ruled, again, for the heir. The Serekh and the Horus Name The king's oldest name is his Horus name , and its frame is the serekh : srḫ [Gardiner: O33] [𓊁] — the post-audit value of the sign, which depicts the niched palace façade that the serekh frame itself represents. The name is written inside the rectangle of the palace; above it perches the Horus falcon. The composition says everything at once: the falcon is upon the palace; the god is in residence in the king . Serekhs appear from Dynasty 0 — the falcon above the names of Narmer and Aha, among the very first written artefacts of the Egyptian state — and the Horus name remained the first element of the royal titulary into the Roman period. Early Horus names are programmes in miniature: Aha is "Horus the Fighter," and Khasekhemwy's name proclaims that "the Two Powers are at peace." That last name carries the great exception that proves the theology's flexibility. The Second Dynasty also produced King Peribsen, who set the Seth -animal, not the falcon, above his serekh — and Khasekhemwy, in whose serekh Horus and Seth stand together , reconciled. Egyptologists still debate the politics behind these monuments — a religious schism, a reunification after civil conflict — but their mere existence shows that the Horus–Seth opposition could be balanced as well as fought, and that the serekh was the surface on which the balance was declared. The Early Dynastic evidence is treated in its own article; the principle matters here: kingship was Horus's, but the wise king, like the Ennead's verdict, found a place for Seth too. The Fivefold Titulary By the Middle Kingdom the king's full style comprised five names, and three of the five bind him to Horus and to the falcon's family: 1 · THE HORUS NAME Written in the srḫ [Gardiner: O33] serekh beneath the falcon Ḥr [Gardiner: G5] [𓅃]. The king as Horus incarnate; the oldest name, and the name by which the earliest kings are still known to history. 2 · THE NEBTY NAME Introduced by nbty [Gardiner: G16] [𓅒], "the Two Ladies" — Nekhbet the vulture of Upper Egypt and Wadjet the cobra of Lower Egypt on their baskets. The king under the protection of the two tutelary goddesses of the Two Lands. 3 · THE GOLDEN HORUS NAME Introduced by the falcon upon the gold sign: Ḥr-nbw [Gardiner: G5-S12] [𓅃𓋞], "Horus of Gold" — gold, nbw [Gardiner: S12], being the flesh of the gods and the sign of the imperishable. The reading and sense of this name were already debated by the Egyptians' successors; its falcon is unmistakably Horus again. 4 · THE THRONE NAME (PRENOMEN) In a cartouche, preceded by nswt-bity [Gardiner: A43-X1-A45] [𓀲𓏏𓀵] — "King of Upper and Lower Egypt," written with the sedge nswt [Gardiner: A43-X1] [𓀲𓏏] and the bee bity [Gardiner: A45] [𓀵]. Assumed at accession; usually compounded with Ra. 5 · THE SON OF RA NAME (NOMEN) The king's birth name in a cartouche, preceded by sꜣ-rꜥ [Gardiner: G38-N5] [𓅬𓇳], "Son of Ra." The title inserts the king into the solar genealogy: Horus by office, Ra's son by proclamation — the two claims run in parallel, exactly as the two Horuses run in parallel in Section II. The coronation made the theory flesh. The king's "appearance in glory," ḫꜥ [Gardiner: N28] [𓈍], was staged with the release of falcons to the four points of the sky — Horus's birds carrying the news of Horus's accession to the ends of the world — and the great renewal festival of the reign, the Sed festival , ḥb-sd [Gardiner: W3-F33] [𓎱𓄢], re-proved the ageing king's fitness to remain Horus, typically after thirty years and at intervals thereafter. Even the palace vocabulary is falconine: the throne itself, in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology's study of the institution, carries serekh-decoration "probably inspired by the Horus-name of the royal titulary," alluding to the king as "living Horus" and lord of the palace. Horus is not the king's patron. He is the king's job description . The succession's other half was funerary. When the king died, his son — the new Horus — performed for him the rites the myth prescribes, above all the Opening of the Mouth , wp-r [Gardiner: F13-D21] [𓄋𓂋], written with the corrected value wp [Gardiner: F13], "to open," upon r [Gardiner: D21], "mouth." In the ritual's own words the officiating son speaks as Horus to the father become Osiris: the myth is the script, the funeral its performance, and the new reign its outcome. No other Egyptian god is so completely the grammar of political time — the form in which Egypt said before , now , and next about its own government. VIII. Horus the Child — Harpocrates, Mammisi and Healing Cippi Between the hidden birth and the tribunal stands the childhood, and Egyptian religion gave the child his own name and cult: Ḥr-pꜣ-ẖrd [Gardiner: G5-Q3-G1-A18] [𓅃𓊪𓄿𓀖]
