The Ontology of Modern Practice — Systematic Re-activation Modern Alchemy is not a nostalgic revival of a dead pseudo-science, but the Systematic Re-activation of the Unbroken Chain connecting Ancient Kemet to the present. The work of the House of Life continues through dedicated circles of practitioners who utilize traditional laboratory methods alongside modern consciousness studies. In this research framework, modern alchemy is viewed as High-Fidelity Frequency Management . The practitioner seeks to refine their own Composite Soul (Ba, Ka, Ib) while simultaneously working with material substances to manifest higher-dimensional data into the physical plane. Alchemy is the Science of Transmutation —the technology used to bridge the gap between the "Lead" of habitual, low-frequency existence and the "Gold" of transfigured, high-frequency awareness ( Akh ). A note on evidence, because this article surveys a living practice and liveliness invites credulity in both directions. Where the article states a checkable fact — a date, an institution, a publication, a pharmacopoeial monograph — it follows the standard of the rest of the archive: documented, and checkable by the reader. Where it reports what practitioners believe, claim or experience, it says so, in those words, at the point of report (§XXII). And where the tradition's own account of itself is the only source — a lineage, a master's biography, an institution's inner history — the article attributes it to that account, as it does for Bartlett's Paralab years (§XII), rather than laundering testimony into fact. Modern alchemy deserves the same courtesy the archive extends to ancient Egypt: its real history, which is interesting enough, without invented antiquity or invented results. II. Defining the Art — The Raising of Vibrations Within the modern tradition's own vocabulary, to practise alchemy is to raise the vibration of a substance — and, by correspondence, of the practitioner. The phrase is the tradition's self-description, recorded here as such: a prepared medicine is said to carry a finer, more coherent pattern than the crude material it was made from, and the operator's task across the operations of §III is to refine matter and awareness together, each serving as the measure of the other. The term belongs to the modern revival rather than to the older literature, whose authors spoke instead of purification, exaltation, and the separation of the subtle from the gross. It is not a quantity in physics, and this archive does not present it as one; it names how contemporary practitioners understand what they are doing, in the same way that Ma'at alignment (§X) names the ethical condition they hold the work to require. III. The Wet Path — Laboratory Operativity The Wet Path ( Via Humida ) operates through the physical laboratory. It utilizes glassware, heat, and solvents (menstrua) to perform operations on plants, minerals, and metals. In the modern context, the laboratory acts as a Microcosmic Map of the practitioner’s internal process. Every distillation, calcination, and conjunction performed in the vessel is a physical demonstration of the practitioner’s ability to direct Heka . The Wet Path provides an Objective Feedback Loop : the physical changes in the substance (the color stages of Black, White, and Red) are indicators of the successfully applied theurgical intention. See Alchemy — The Sacred Art . The Wet Path's humblest instrument carries its longest pedigree. The water bath — the bain-marie — descends from the balneum Mariae attributed to Maria Hebraea and transmitted by Zosimos: a vessel within a vessel of boiling water, capping its charge at the bath's temperature, for digestions and evaporations that direct fire would scorch. It is the one ancient alchemical technology that never left the laboratory or the kitchen; every double boiler and laboratory water bath in current use is Maria's device, uninterrupted. A modern spagyrist digesting a tincture in a water bath is therefore doing something more literal than 'following tradition': she is using the founding apparatus of her art, in its original form, for its original purpose — gentle, capped, patient heat. IV. The Dry Path — Internalized Theurgy Alongside the Wet Path of §III, the literature of the Work distinguishes a Dry Path ( Via Secca , also called the short or royal way): work carried out in the crucible at high temperature, without the prolonged solvent circulations of the humid way, and correspondingly faster and harder to control. In the accounts transmitted by Fulcanelli and set out most openly by his pupil Eugène Canseliet, the dry way is bound up with the antimony work — stibnite and its regulus — and is treated as the more dangerous of the two routes precisely because its fires are literal and its stages compressed. The contrast the texts draw is one of tempo and risk rather than of goal: the Wet Path works over months at gentle heats in glass, the Dry Path in days at furnace heat in the crucible, and both are presented as roads to the same Stone. This archive records the distinction as the literature states it; the internalised reading of the Dry Path as work within the practitioner's own vessel is taken up at §XVIII. Canseliet is the dry way's chief witness, and his testimony should be characterised exactly. Eugène Canseliet (1899–1982) presented himself, from the prefaces to Fulcanelli's books onward, as the master's pupil and the tradition's continuator; his own works — on alchemy, on the two alchemical dwellings, on the work's stages — describe the dry way's antimony path with a fullness Fulcanelli never permitted himself, while withholding, by his own declaration, the one operative secret on which, he held, everything turned. Scholars of the revival treat Canseliet as a primary source for 20th-century French practice and as an interested one: the pupil who controls the master's posthumous meaning controls the lineage. The archive cites him in that double capacity — witness and gatekeeper — which is also, §XII suggests, the structural position of every modern lineage-holder, Bartlett included. V. The Operations — Calcination, Distillation and the Rest of the Grammar Modern laboratory alchemy speaks a grammar of named operations, inherited from the medieval and early modern laboratory and still used, in the same senses, in the schools of §XVI. The list below gives the core vocabulary as the tradition itself defines it — the verbs of the Wet Path (§III) — because a reader who cannot parse the operations cannot grade any claim made with them. Calcination. Reduction of a body to ash or calx by strong heat — the fate of the plant marc in §VII, and of metals and salts in the mineral work of §VIII. Distillation. Separation by vapour and condensation in the alembic line that descends, name and form, from Maria's apparatus (§III): the drawing-off of a plant's spirit, the rectification of solvents. Fermentation and digestion. The slow work of warmth and time — a material sealed and held at gentle heat, in the bain-marie or the dung-bed of the older books, until it changes its nature: putrefaction as the gateway operation of the plant work. Solution and filtration. Dissolving a calx or ash in water or spirit, and clearing it — the leaching step by which the Salt of a plant is drawn from its ashes. Coagulation and cohobation. The fixing of the volatile: cohobation pours a distillate back over its residue and distils again, concentrating by repetition; coagulation is the general name for bringing a dissolved or volatilised body back to fixity. Circulation. A sealed, self-returning digestion in a pelican or circulator vessel, vapour rising and condensate falling in a closed loop for weeks — the maturation stage to which practitioners attribute the 'exaltation' of a finished tincture. Sublimation. The rising of a solid directly to vapour and its collection above — the operation of the volatile salts, and, with mercury, sulfur and arsenic compounds in the old books, among the most dangerous in the grammar (see §XX). Two things about the list are worth noticing. Every operation in it is also an operation of classical chemistry — the continuity is the Albertus school's founding claim (§XIII). And none of them is exotic equipment: furnace, still, water bath, sealed vessel and balance exhaust the traditional bench. What the tradition adds to chemistry is not apparatus but interpretation and sequence — which operations, in which order, on which day (§XI), toward which of the three principles (§VI). The operations also mark the boundary between the article's two modern alchemies. Every operation in the list above is performed, with the same names, by the laboratory schools; the internal school of §XVIII performs them in imagination, mapping calcination onto the burning-off of habit, distillation onto the refinement of attention, cohobation onto the return of insight to its residue. The shared grammar is why the two schools can talk to each other — and why their talk so easily confuses outsiders, for whom a 'calcination' may be a crucible or a crisis. This article disambiguates by context wherever the term does work: operations are laboratory operations unless the section says otherwise, and the internal senses are introduced, each time, as the internal school's reading. VI. Plant Spagyrics — The Extraction of Essences Spagyric medicine is the most accessible point of entry for modern laboratory work. It involves the separation and recombination of a plant's three principles: SULFUR (SOUL) The essential oils and active volatile principles. Represents the plant's unique Vibrational Signature . Corresponds to the Ba . MERCURY (SPIRIT) The alcohol produced through fermentation. Represents the Carrier Wave of the life-force. Corresponds to the Ka . SALT (BODY) The mineral salts extracted from the plant's calcined ash. Represents the Grounding Matrix . Corresponds to the Khat . Recombining these purified principles creates an Integrated Medicine . Unlike standard herbal extracts, a spagyric preparation addresses the patient's entire composite being, restoring balance through "Vibrational Realignment." The three principles should be read as the tradition reads them — as principles, not chemicals. Sulfur is not brimstone, Mercury is not quicksilver, and Salt is not table salt, though each principle borrows its name from the substance that best displays it: the combustible and oily, the volatile and spirituous, the fixed and earthy. Paracelsus's demonstration, repeated in every primer since, is a burning piece of wood: the flame is its Sulfur, the smoke and vapour its Mercury, the ash its Salt. The spagyric procedure of §VII is that bonfire slowed down and put in glass — fermentation and distillation for the volatile, calcination and leaching for the fixed — which is why the schools insist the method is the philosophy enacted, and not a metaphor laid over a tincture. VII. Spagyric Procedure in Full — Separation, Purification, Recombination The spagyric method of §VI, set out as a bench procedure, is the best-documented process in modern alchemy — described in the same terms by Paracelsian tradition, by Manfred Junius's Practical Handbook of Plant Alchemy , and by Robert Allen Bartlett in Real Alchemy (2007), from which the staging below is drawn in paraphrase. The word itself states the method: spao , to separate, and ageiro , to gather together — the coinage tradition assigns to Paracelsus. THE STAGES, AS THE SCHOOLS TEACH THEM 1. Preparation and fermentation. The plant — harvested, in the full traditional form, at its planetary election (§XI) — is crushed and set to ferment in water and its own juices. Fermentation generates the plant's own alcohol: its Mercury, the spirit, made by the plant itself rather than added to it, in the strict form of the method. 2. Distillation of the Mercury. The fermented mass is distilled, and the spirit redistilled to purity and set aside. What the alcohol has carried with it — the plant's volatile oils and aromatics — constitutes its Sulfur, the soul; in procedures that separate them, the oil is drawn off as the Sulfur in its own right. 3. Calcination of the body. The spent plant matter — the marc, the caput mortuum — is dried and burned in a crucible to ash, then heated on until the ash is white or grey-white: the blackening and whitening of the old colour-stages enacted on the plant's body. 4. Extraction of the Salt. The white ash is leached with distilled water; the solution is filtered and the water evaporated, yielding the plant's mineral salts — chiefly potassium carbonate with the species' trace minerals. Dissolving, filtering and evaporating are repeated, in careful work several times, until the salt is clean and white. 5. Cohobation — the reunion. The purified Salt is returned to the reserved Mercury and Sulfur — ground in, dissolved, and allowed to marry the tincture. This is the step an ordinary herbal tincture never takes, and the tradition's whole claim rests on it: body restored to spirit and soul, each purified in the interval. 6. Circulation and maturation. The recombined preparation is sealed and circulated at gentle heat — traditionally for a philosophical month of forty days — and then aged, in the Albertus line's practice, with samples retained for later analysis (§XIII). Safety, stated as procedure rather than decoration: the method works with flammable spirit over heat, with glass under thermal stress, and with crucible temperatures that take ash to whiteness. Its hazards at plant level are the ordinary serious hazards of a chemistry bench — fire, burns, fumes — and they are managed by the ordinary disciplines: no open flame near spirit, ventilation, eye protection, and the laboratory training the schools require before the mineral work (§XX) is opened at all. VIII. Mineral Alchemy — The Purified Earth Beyond the plant work of §VI, the modern curriculum takes up the mineral kingdom : salts, and then the metals and their ores, worked through the acetate route and kindred preparations transmitted in the Paracelsian literature. In the teaching sequence documented for the Albertus school (§XIII), mineral and metallic work forms the third and final stage of instruction, after plant and animal work, and its preparations — the oils and tinctures of the metals among them — are correspondingly the longest-aged and most closely held of the laboratory's products. It is also the stage at which the tradition's safety discipline bites hardest. The ores in question include antimony and mercury compounds, and practitioners in the Albertus line insist on dried solvents and analytical checking for metallic work, since even the small water fraction in ordinary rectified spirit can dissolve a potentially toxic amount of a mineral salt into a preparation (see §XXI). Mineral work is therefore presented in the literature as advanced work, undertaken only after the plant operations are routine. The acetate route, named in this section's introduction, deserves its sentence of explanation. In the Paracelsian mineral literature transmitted to the Albertus school, metals and their calces are opened with vinegar and its distilled and radical forms — the acetates being soluble, workable salts from which the tradition prepares its metallic tinctures and oils. The route is long (digestions and distillations counted in weeks), and its intermediates include the toxic compounds catalogued at §XX, which is why the curriculum places it last, behind years of plant work, and why this archive describes its existence and its place in the sequence without describing its bench detail. Description has a stopping point, and mineral alchemy is where this article observes it. IX. Monatomic Elements — The White Powder Mystery One of the most controversial and high-priority areas of modern alchemical research is the investigation of Monatomic Elements (also known as ORMUS or High-Spin state matter). Modern promoters present these substances as the material correlates of an ancient Potable Gold . The Egyptian identification does not hold: mfkꜣt means turquoise , the product of the Sinai mining expeditions under Hathor, Lady of Turquoise; no Egyptological source attests it as a powder used by any priesthood (see Potable Gold & White Powder ). Promoters claim that in this state metals like gold and iridium lose their metallic bonds and exhibit Superconductive Properties ; those claims have never been confirmed in peer-reviewed literature and remain scientifically unverified. From a theurgical perspective within the modern tradition, monatomic elements are treated as High-Bandwidth Intermediaries for the soul — a belief of that tradition, recorded here as such. The commercial form of the monatomic claim belongs in this survey, since for most contemporaries it is modern alchemy's public face. Powders and liquids sold as ORMUS — precipitated, by vendor-specific methods, from seawater, salt solutions or metal salts — are marketed in the vocabulary of Hudson's lectures (see the physics section of Potable Gold ), with meditation, healing and perception claims attached. The archive's grading, applied there and repeated here, is threefold: the Egyptian identification is false ( mfkꜣt is turquoise); the physical claims are unverified and unreplicated; and the products are uncharacterised in any published independent analysis. Within the laboratory tradition proper, the monatomic episode is generally regarded as a cautionary tale — the Albertus school's insistence on analysis (§XXII) exists, in part, so that its preparations can be told apart from exactly this. A survey that omitted the episode would flatter the field; a survey that adopted its claims would betray the archive. X. Ma'at Alignment in Practical Work Modern alchemy emphasizes that laboratory results are directly dependent on the Ethical Integrity of the operator. A practitioner who works with a heart heavy with Isfet (greed, anger, or dishonesty) will find their experiments fail or produce unstable results. This is the Law of Resonance . In the Hall of Judgment , the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at ; in the laboratory, the success of the transmutation is the weight. The "Integrated Alchemist" must maintain a state of ritual purity and ethical alignment to successfully "Command" ( Hu ) the spirits of the matter. XI. Astrological Calibration — The Timing of the Stone Modern laboratory practice in this tradition is electional : operations are begun at astrologically chosen times. The documented pattern is planetary — work on a plant or metal is commenced in the day and hour of the planet that tradition assigns to it, harvests are timed to the relevant planetary and lunar conditions, and long circulations are counted against the calendar of the heavens as the older texts prescribe. The scheme descends from the electional astrology of the medieval and Renaissance art, in which the timing of an operation was held to be part of its recipe rather than a decoration upon it. Practitioners record the elections they used alongside the operations themselves, so that a preparation carries its timing as part of its laboratory record. Whether the heavens act on the vessel is the tradition's claim, held as such; that contemporary spagyric practice is in fact organised around planetary timing is a matter of its own documented routine, visible in the curricula and workbooks of the schools surveyed at §XVI. The mechanics of election, for readers who have not met them, are determinate and computable — whatever one thinks of their efficacy. A planet's day runs from sunrise: Sunday to the Sun, Monday to the Moon, and so through the week in the Chaldean order. The daylight and the night are each divided by twelve into planetary hours of unequal, seasonal length, ruled in sequence from the day's ruler. To begin a solar work 'in the day and hour of the Sun' is therefore an instruction as precise as a temperature: Sunday, first hour after sunrise, or the eighth hour, and so on. Practitioners compute elections from ephemerides and record them in the laboratory notebook beside weights and durations (§V) — a survival, inside a working laboratory, of the Hellenistic electional astrology that the medieval art inherited entire. The archive records the system as the tradition's documented routine; the heavens' action on the vessel remains, as this section's main text says, the tradition's claim. XII. Robert Allen Bartlett — The Paralab Years in His Own Account The modern Albertus line has a primary source, and it is Bartlett's own. In the introduction to Real Alchemy: A Primer of Practical Alchemy (2007), Bartlett sets out his formation in the first person, and the dates in this section are his, as the task of this archive requires: precision about institutions begins with not confusing them. 1974. Bartlett begins intensive study at the Paracelsus Research Society (PRS) in Salt Lake City — later Paracelsus College — under Albert Riedel, Frater Albertus. His first class, the Prima, opens the graded curriculum of §XIII: the classes ran, in his account, Monday to Saturday, nine to five, with homework and continuous laboratory work, for two weeks each year across seven years of returning study. 1976. At Albertus's prompting he returns to university to finish the chemistry degree he had suspended — Albertus's condition, in Bartlett's telling, for the work he hoped to do: the laboratory of the Art staffed by a trained chemist. 1979. On graduating, he is appointed Chief Chemist at Paralab — and the institution must be named exactly. Paralab was the commercial arm of the enterprise, its producing laboratory for herbal and mineral preparations made on alchemical principles for research and alternative-healthcare use. Bartlett was chief chemist of Paralab, not 'of the PRS': the Society taught; Paralab manufactured and analysed. The distinction is his own, and accounts that blur it misplace both the man and the institutions. Late 1983. Paralab closes, and the college with it in the same unwinding; Albertus dies in 1984. Bartlett had been selected, he records, as a Director of Research for the projected Tristar complex — college, laboratory and healing-arts centre united — which Albertus's death left unbuilt. 2003. Bartlett founds the Spagyricus Institute to teach the work in the PRS succession (§XVI), and publishes the graded method in Real Alchemy (2007) and The Way of the Crucible (2009). Bartlett's account is a practitioner's testimony and is cited here as such — for institutional facts (dates, roles, the PRS/Paralab distinction) it is the best source there is, being the recollection of the office-holder, corroborated by the conference and publication record of the revival. His claims for the preparations themselves are a different category, and §XXII grades them accordingly. Bartlett's later teaching completes the account his introduction begins. At the Spagyricus Institute (founded 2003) he taught the graded work in the PRS sequence — plant spagyrics first, in courses built around the bench operations of §V and §VII — and his conference workshops of the 2000s carried the same curriculum to the wider revival (§XVI). His published stance toward evidence is the one §XXII grades the field by: preparations described with their analyses, claims for his best-known work stated with its analytical limits attached, and the chemistry degree Albertus made him finish standing behind the whole enterprise as its entry condition. In a field whose public face is the ORMUS marketplace (§IX), that stance is the Albertus line's distinguishing mark, and this article has treated it as such throughout. XIII. The Legacy of Frater Albertus — PRS and Beyond Frater Albertus — Albert Richard Riedel (1911–1984) — is the pivotal figure of the 20th-century laboratory revival in the English-speaking world. Trained in the Rosicrucian milieu of the 1930s and 1940s, he founded the Paracelsus Research Society (PRS) in Salt Lake City in 1960 and taught alchemy there as a graded laboratory curriculum — Prima, Secunda, and Tertia classes moving from plant work through the animal kingdom to the mineral and metallic work of §VIII. Paralab , the Society's laboratory, was its commercial and analytical arm, producing spagyric preparations and cell salts and employing trained chemists; Robert Allen Bartlett, who took his first PRS class in 1974, served as its chief chemist from 1979 until the Society's closure in late 1983. Albertus's Alchemist's Handbook (1960) carried the graded, hands-on method to readers the Salt Lake classes could not reach, and his insistence that students complete ordinary scientific training — he sent Bartlett back to finish the chemistry degree he had suspended — set the line's characteristic posture: laboratory alchemy practised with, not against, analytical chemistry. The schools and teachers of §XVI descend from PRS directly or by reaction to it. The Tristar project, mentioned in Bartlett's account (§XII), is the school's might-have-been and belongs in the record: Albertus's plan to unite college, producing laboratory and healing-arts centre on one site — teaching, manufacture and clinic under one roof, the House of Life re-founded as a Utah campus. It died with him in 1984, unbuilt. The revival that actually happened was diasporic instead: students carrying the curriculum to their own benches and institutes (§XVI), the books carrying it further (§XV). The archive notes the pattern because it recurs in the tradition's history — Fulcanelli's master likewise vanished, leaving books and pupils — and because a lineage that survives by teaching and text, rather than by institution, is exactly the kind whose documents must be kept with the care §XVII describes. XIV. Fulcanelli and the 20th Century Transition Fulcanelli is the pen name on the two books that re-set the terms of French alchemy: Le Mystère des cathédrales ( The Mystery of the Cathedrals ), published in Paris in 1926, which reads the sculpture of the Gothic cathedrals as an alchemical programme in stone, and Les Demeures philosophales (1930). Both appeared with prefaces by the author's declared pupil, Eugène Canseliet, who maintained for the rest of his life that his master was a single, accomplished adept who had withdrawn from public view. Who Fulcanelli was remains an open question . Candidates proposed in print include the artist Julien Champagne, who illustrated the books; René Schwaller de Lubicz; the bookseller Pierre Dujols; Canseliet himself; and a small committee of these men — and Canseliet rejected each of these identifications in turn. No identification has been established, and the archive records the question as unresolved: what is certain is the books' effect, which was to hand the 20th-century revival a textual authority for the dry way (§IV) and for the cathedral symbolism taken up across the modern literature. The Fulcanelli literature's afterlife in English began with translation — The Mystery of the Cathedrals in Mary Sworder's rendering (1971) — and continued through the century's occult revival, in which the cathedral-reading became a genre of its own. Its scholarly assessment has since caught up with its popular one: historians of alchemy treat the two books as major documents of the 20th-century French revival — learned, serious in their command of the older literature, and evidentially worthless about the medieval cathedrals, whose sculptors left no sign of the programme Fulcanelli reads in them. That double verdict is the archive's: Fulcanelli is a primary source for modern alchemy (§IV, §XVII) and a secondary fantasy about the Middle Ages, and the sections that cite him cite him in the first capacity only. XV. The Books of the Revival — Handbook, Primer and Curriculum A laboratory tradition that teaches bench-side (§XVI) still lives by its books, and the revival's shelf is short enough to survey whole. Frater Albertus's The Alchemist's Handbook (1960) is the founding text of the Salt Lake school: a manual of graded laboratory practice — plant work first, with its tinctures, ens preparations and salt extractions in the manner of §VII — addressed to students Albertus expected to work, not merely to read. Its authority in the line is curricular: it is the book the Prima class put into hands. Manfred M. Junius, an Ayurvedic physician and spagyrist working in India and Australia, published The Practical Handbook of Plant Alchemy in 1979 — the most systematic spagyric manual of the century, setting out the three-principles method, the operations of §V, and the preparation of plant quintessences with a pharmacist's completeness. Junius matters to this archive for a structural reason: his book demonstrates that by the 1970s the spagyric method was a documented, teachable procedure with a literature , independently of any single school's lineage claims — the same conclusion the German pharmacopoeial tradition (§XIX) supports from inside regulated pharmacy. Bartlett's two books (§XII) complete the shelf: Real Alchemy (2007) as the primer — history, principles, and the plant work set out for a beginner's bench — and The Way of the Crucible (2009) carrying the method toward the mineral kingdom under the safety discipline of §XXI. Read together, the four books are the revival's canon: two generations, two continents, one method, argued over in detail and agreed in structure. What they do not contain, anywhere, is controlled clinical evidence for their preparations — the gap §XXII addresses. XVI. Initiatic Orders and the Modern Chain The modern work is carried by a loose ecology rather than a single church: teaching schools in the PRS succession, of which Bartlett's Spagyricus Institute (founded 2003) is the direct continuation of the Albertus line; practitioner associations such as the International Alchemy Guild, which archive the lineages' documents and conference record; and independent study circles and orders that combine laboratory instruction with the graded, initiatic framing their members inherit from the Rosicrucian and Hermetic orders of the previous century (see Esoteric Orders ). What these bodies share is transmission by instruction rather than by book alone: the operations of §§III–VIII are taught bench-side, in sequence, with the student's preparations examined before the next grade is opened. The chain they claim is therefore a chain of teachers — Albertus to his students, Canseliet to his — and it is as a documented succession of teaching, not as an unbroken antiquity, that this archive records it (see The Unbroken Chain ). The ecology has a documentary infrastructure worth naming. The International Alchemy Guild, founded in the revival's conference era, maintains archives of the lineages' papers and a journal; the Alchemy Conference circuit — at which Bartlett taught spagyrics workshops, in programmes that survive — gave the schools a common room in which PRS-descended, European and independent practitioners could compare preparations and pedigrees. University collections have begun to acquire the revival's papers, as they acquired Newton's (§XVII): the historian and the archivist now stand inside the tradition's transmission chain, preserving a movement that once preserved itself by secrecy. Whether that preservation is the chain's continuation or its museumification is a question practitioners debate among themselves; the archive records the debate as the field's own, unresolved. XVII. The Scholars Arrive — Historians, Replication and the Making and Knowing Project Modern alchemy has acquired, in the last half-century, a second literature besides its own: academic history of science, which arrived at the laboratory door with different questions. Lawrence Principe's The Secrets of Alchemy (2013) and William Newman's work — on Newton (§XVII's sibling case in the Newton article) and on the wider chymical tradition — established the scholarly frame this archive uses throughout: early modern chymistry as a real experimental culture, its cover-names decodable, its processes replicable, its transmutation claims unfulfilled. Principe replicates period processes at the bench as a historical method; the Leyden sulfur-water replication cited in Potable Gold is his. The Making and Knowing Project at Columbia, under Pamela Smith, generalised the method: a 16th-century French practitioner's manuscript (BnF Ms. Fr. 640) reconstructed process by process — casting, pigment-making, imitation gems among them — on the principle that a recipe's silences are data, visible only to hands that have tried to follow it. The project's relevance to the modern schools is direct: it supplies the evidential standard — reconstruction, analysis, published failure — against which a living tradition's claims can be tested without caricature, and it is the standard Bartlett's own analytical instincts (§XIX) reach toward from inside the tradition. The encounter cuts both ways, and the archive records it neutrally. Sources and Primary Texts I. The Words for the Work — Mummy, Embalmer, and Workshop The English word "mummy" is not Egyptian. It descends, through medieval Latin and Arabic mūmiyā — a word for bitumen and for a bituminous medicinal substance — from the dark appearance of many excavated bodies, whose resinous coatings were mistaken for bitumen long before chemical analysis showed how rarely true bitumen was used at all. The Egyptians had no single word that means exactly what "mummification" means in English, because for them the process was not one act but a sequence of distinct crafts — washing, opening, drying, anointing, wrapping — each with its own vocabulary, its own personnel, and its own place. This article follows their vocabulary, because their vocabulary is the process map. The finished product — the preserved, wrapped, ritually completed body — is the sꜥḥ [Gardiner: S29-D36-V28] [𓋴𓂝𓎛]. The word carries a double sense that English cannot reproduce: sꜥḥ is both the mummy as an object and a title of dignity, "the noble, the august one." The wrapped dead person is not refuse awaiting disposal; the word itself promotes them. The body as mere physical frame, by contrast, is the ẖt [Gardiner: F51] [𓄹] — the belly, the trunk, the material substrate on which the work is done. Egyptian funerary language keeps the two registers apart with complete consistency: the ẖt [Gardiner: F51] is what decays; the sꜥḥ [Gardiner: S29-D36-V28] is what the craft makes of it. The craftsman is the wt [Gardiner: G43-X1] [𓅱𓏏] — literally "the wrapper," from the verb wt [Gardiner: G43-X1], "to wrap, to bandage." The choice of defining act is telling. Greek and modern accounts fixate on the dramatic opening of the body; the Egyptian professional title names the patient, repetitive, textile work of the second half of the process, the work the Ritual of Embalming (Section XIII) actually describes in detail. The place of the opening and drying work is the wꜥbt [Gardiner: G43-D36-D58-X1] [𓅱𓂝𓃀𓏏] — the "pure place," conventionally rendered "embalming workshop" — and the place of preliminary washing is the ibw [Gardiner: M17-D58-G43] [𓇋𓃀𓅱], the purification tent. A further name, pr-nfr [Gardiner: O1-F35] [𓉐𓄤], "the House of Beauty" (or "House of Perfection"), attaches to the embalming establishment in several periods: the place where the dead are made nfr — beautiful, complete, good — again. // READING THE TERMS IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20/R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . Above the whole establishment stands a god. Anubis — jnpw [Gardiner: M17-N35-Q3-G43-E16] [𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱𓃣] — is the divine embalmer: in the Osiris myth it is Anubis who first performs the work, on the body of Osiris himself, and every human chief embalmer thereafter works in his person. His epithets are job descriptions. He is ḥry-sštꜣ [Gardiner: V28-D21-Z4-S29-N37-X1-G1] [𓎛𓂋𓏭𓋴𓈙𓏏𓄿], "Master of Secrets" — the secrets are the workshop's. He is Imy-wt, "He Who Is in the wt [Gardiner: G43-X1]," in the place of wrapping. The archive's article on Anubis treats the god in full; this article treats his craft. The two cannot finally be separated, and Section IV returns to the moment in each working day when the chief embalmer put on the god's mask and the distinction formally dissolved. A last preliminary distinction. "Embalming" and "mummification" are used interchangeably in popular writing. In this article embalming names the active treatments — excerebration, evisceration, desiccation, anointing — and mummification names the whole transformation, treatments plus wrapping plus ritual completion, that turns a corpse into a sꜥḥ [Gardiner: S29-D36-V28]. The distinction matters because the surviving Egyptian manual literature divides along exactly that line: the Greek historians describe the embalming bench, while the Egyptian Ritual describes the mummification liturgy, and neither source alone gives the whole (Section III). II. Why Preserve the Body — Soul, Recognition, and the Transfigured Dead Egyptian anthropology did not locate the person in a single immortal soul that could simply vacate a disposable body. The person was a composite — the archive's full treatment is the composite soul — and several of its components remained bound to the preserved body. The kꜣ [Gardiner: D28] [𓂓], the vital double and sustaining presence, needed a recognisable home to return to and a mouth that could receive offerings. The bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝] — written here with the post-audit value of the saddle-billed stork sign — the mobile, individual manifestation of the dead person, travelled out into the world by day and returned to the body in the tomb by night. If the body was destroyed, the circuit was broken. Preservation was therefore not sentimentality about remains; it was infrastructure for a continuing existence that was understood to be, in part, located . The heart makes the point most sharply. The ib [Gardiner: F34] [𓄣] was the seat of thought, memory, emotion, and moral record — the organ with which an Egyptian, in his own idiom, thought. It was therefore the one major organ the embalmers normally left exactly where it lay (Section VIII), because the dead person would need it at the judgment, where it was weighed against the feather of mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U1-D36-X1] [𓌳𓂝𓏏] — truth, order, rightness — in the rite the archive treats as the Weighing of the Heart . The brain, by the same anthropology, had no such role, and its routine removal (Section VII) shocked Greek observers precisely because Greek assumptions ran the other way. Neither culture was being careless. Each was preserving what its own model of the person said mattered. The goal state has a name too. The dead person who has been correctly embalmed, wrapped, furnished, and judged becomes an ꜣḫ — a transfigured, effective spirit — and the wrapped body is the anchor of that state. This is why the process closes not at the workshop door but with the Opening of the Mouth — wp-r [Gardiner: F13-D21] [𓄋𓂋], written with the corrected value wp [Gardiner: F13], "to open," upon r [Gardiner: D21], "mouth" — the rite that restored breath, sight, speech, and eating to the completed sꜥḥ [Gardiner: S29-D36-V28] before the tomb was sealed. Embalming preserved the instrument; the Opening reactivated it. The funerary texts buried with the dead are the script for what the reactivated person then does. It is equally important to say what mummification was not . It was not universal. Across three thousand years, the full process described in this article was always a purchased service, graded by price (Sections V–VI), and the great majority of Egyptians were buried simply — in sand, in a mat, in a plain coffin — relying on the desert's own desiccation, which had suggested the artificial process in the first place: predynastic bodies buried in hot, dry sand above the flood line are frequently preserved to this day, skin, hair, and nails intact, with no embalmer ever having touched them. The craft began as an imitation of the desert and became, for those who could pay, an improvement on it. Nor was the full process static: the techniques of the Old Kingdom , the classical perfection of the New Kingdom , and the elaborate surface artistry of the Ptolemaic and Roman periods differ in detail at almost every step, and this article flags period difference wherever the evidence requires it. // THE OSIRIAN PATTERN // Every mummification rehearsed one precedent. In the myth, Osiris — wsir [Gardiner: Q1-D4-A40] [𓊨𓁹𓀭] — is murdered and dismembered; Isis gathers the body; Anubis embalms it; and Osiris rises, not back into earthly life, but into kingship of the dead. The embalmers' client was therefore not merely being preserved but being Osirified : the first grade of Herodotus's price list (Section V) was said by the embalmers themselves to belong to the god whose name Herodotus declines, on grounds of piety, to speak in that context — and every reader in antiquity understood the unspoken name. The workshop procedure in Sections V–XV is, in the Egyptians' own framing, a technology for repeating that first, divine embalming on human material. III. How We Know — Texts, Workshops, and the Mummies Themselves No single source describes the whole process, and the first duty of a craft article is to say plainly what each kind of evidence can and cannot establish. Five kinds survive. Greek and Roman literary accounts — above all Herodotus, Histories 2.86–89 (c. 450 BCE), and Diodorus Siculus, Library 1.91 (1st century BCE) — describe the embalming bench from outside: the grades, the incision, the natron. They are outsiders' reports of a closed, hereditary craft, generally accurate on sequence and sometimes wrong or garbled on mechanism, and they are used in this article as reports to be checked against the bodies, not as bench manuals. Egyptian ritual manuals — the Ritual of Embalming and the older Papyrus Louvre-Carlsberg manual — describe the work from inside, but only its second, liturgical half (Sections XII–XIII). Labelled workshop material — pre-eminently the inscribed vessels of the Saqqara workshop (Section XVI) — names substances and the body parts they were for. The mummies themselves , examined by imaging and chemistry rather than by the destructive unwrappings of earlier centuries, are the final court of appeal for every claim in the other four. And modern replication (Section XVIII) tests whether a described procedure, performed as described, actually does what the texts say it does. The UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology's treatments of funerary ritual — notably the entries on funerary rituals for the Pharaonic and for the Ptolemaic and Roman periods — supply the frame within which the archive reads these sources: embalming as one stage in a longer funerary sequence that begins at death and ends at the sealed tomb, with the workshop phase itself subdivided by the Egyptians into purification, treatment, and wrapping. The British Museum's synthesis of the process for its collections makes the same structural point in museum terms: roughly forty days of the seventy belong to drying in natron, and the balance to washing, anointing, and wrapping — a division this article adopts as its working reconciliation in Section XII, while presenting each source's own numbers separately rather than flattening them into one. Two cautions govern everything that follows. First, period . Herodotus watched (or heard described) the craft of the 26th Dynasty and later; the Louvre-Carlsberg manual was written around 1450 BCE; the Saqqara workshop is 26th Dynasty; the Ritual of Embalming survives in Roman-period copies of an older composition. A detail true of one is not automatically true of another, and the popular composite "Egyptian mummification" — brain hook plus canopic jars plus seventy days, all at once, for three thousand years — is a museum-label fiction that this article avoids by dating its claims. Second, grade . The sources overwhelmingly describe the best work money could buy. The third grade of Herodotus — a purge and a natron bed, nothing more (Section VI) — was probably the experience of far more bodies, and the archaeological record of modest burials confirms it. Where a claim in this article rests on a single famous retelling, it is flagged as such in place. Where the evidence genuinely divides — dry natron against natron solution is the standing example (Section XI) — both positions are presented with their best evidence and neither is declared the winner. That is the archive's standard, and embalming, of all subjects, needs it: the subject's literature is unusually rich in confident sentences that dissolve on contact with a CT scan. IV. The Workshop and Its People — Roles at the Embalming Table Embalming was a hereditary, temple-adjacent profession, practised in a purpose-built establishment set apart — for reasons at once ritual and practical — near the necropolis. Diodorus, in paraphrase, stresses the embalmers' honour: they were admitted to temples, ate with priests, and were treated as pure men whose work, however it touched the dead, did not pollute them. The single exception in his account proves the rule by inversion, and Section VI gives it in full: the one worker who made the flank incision was ritually driven off with stones and curses, the community's horror at the cutting of a human body discharged onto the one pair of hands that performed it, so that the rest of the team could proceed with clean status. The Ritual of Embalming names the senior staff of the second half of the process, and its hierarchy is exact. At the head stands the ḥry-sštꜣ [Gardiner: V28-D21-Z4-S29-N37-X1-G1] [𓎛𓂋𓏭𓋴𓈙𓏏𓄿], the Master of Secrets, who supervises the whole. Under him for the most delicate work — the head, inside and out — serves the ḫtmw-nṯr [Gardiner: Aa1-X1-G17-G43-R8] [𓐍𓏏𓅓𓅱𓊹], the god's sealer or divine seal-bearer. The ḫry-ḥbt [Gardiner: Aa1-D21-Z4-V28-D58-X1] [𓐍𓂋𓏭𓎛𓃀𓏏], the lector — literally "he who carries the ritual book" — speaks the glorifications that pair with each manual act. And the wt [Gardiner: G43-X1] [𓅱𓏏] proper, the wrappers, do the bandaging itself. The division of labour is a division of kinds of knowledge: hand, seal, and voice. The manual chapters of the Ritual read, as Töpfer notes, almost like medical prescriptions in their dry, unemotional phrasing; the glorification spells paired with them do the theological work. Both were necessary. Neither was decoration for the other. The chief embalmer's identification with Anubis was performed, not merely asserted: workshop scenes and later tradition show the presiding figure masked as the jackal god at the bier, and the god's own title — ḥry-sštꜣ [Gardiner: V28-D21-Z4-S29-N37-X1-G1], Master of Secrets — is the human chief's title too. The body, meanwhile, arrived by a fixed route. It was first carried to the ibw [Gardiner: M17-D58-G43] [𓇋𓃀𓅱], the purification tent, where it was washed — Herodotus's sequence presupposes this washing, and the Louvre-Carlsberg manual places purification first, before excerebration and evisceration — and only then taken into the wꜥbt [Gardiner: G43-D36-D58-X1] [𓅱𓂝𓃀𓏏] for the opening work. One practical detail the replication literature recovered (Section XVIII) explains a feature of the archaeology: embalming tables are strikingly wide, because the natron bed that covered the body had to be accommodated beside and beneath it. The table was sized for the salt, not for the corpse. Herodotus adds the commercial front office, and it deserves quoting as procedure rather than colour: the embalmers kept wooden models of corpses, painted to show the finished result of each grade, and showed them to the family, agreed a price, and only then began. Diodorus, again in paraphrase, adds an itemised price-list laid before the relatives. Embalming was a craft, a priesthood-adjacent office, and a retail business at the same time, and the sources that forget any one of the three misdescribe it. V. Herodotus, Grade One — the Most Perfect Way, Step by Step Herodotus, Histories 2.86, in A. D. Godley's Loeb translation as read on the Perseus Digital Library, gives the fullest surviving bench sequence for the most expensive grade. What follows is his sequence, step by step, in his order, with each step checked against the other evidence in its own paragraph. Short quotations are Godley's; everything else is labelled paraphrase. Herodotus prefaces the sequence with the models and the price agreement (Section IV) and with the remark that the most perfect manner "belongs, they say, to One whose name it would be impious for me to mention in treating such a matter" — the unspoken Osiris of Section II. STEP 1 — THE BRAIN, THROUGH THE NOSTRILS In Godley's rendering, the embalmers "first draw out part of the brain through the nostrils with an iron hook, and inject certain drugs into the rest." The iron hook, the nostril route, and the two-part method — mechanical extraction for what the hook can reach, chemical treatment for the residue — are all Herodotus's. Section VII takes up the anatomy (the route passes through the ethmoid region into the cranial cavity), the wide variation the mummies themselves display, and the modern replication finding that liquefying and draining worked where scooping failed. STEP 2 — THE FLANK INCISION, WITH THE ETHIOPIAN STONE Next, in paraphrase of Godley's text: making a cut near the flank with a sharp knife of "Ethiopian stone," they take out all the contents of the abdomen. The stone is conventionally understood as obsidian or a fine flint — a lithic blade retained, in a bronze- and iron-using culture, for this one cut, which is itself a datum about the rite's conservatism. Diodorus adds that a scribe first marked on the left flank how much was to be cut, and that the cutter — the paraschistes — fled at once under ritual pelting (Section VI). The left-flank position is confirmed by the incisions preserved on innumerable mummies, frequently covered afterward by an embalming plate. STEP 3 — CLEANSING: PALM WINE AND POUNDED SPICES The emptied cavity is then cleansed — in Godley's words, "rinsing it with palm wine and bruised spices." Palm wine is mildly alcoholic and acidic; the pounded aromatics are antiseptic in effect whatever their intended rationale. The viscera themselves received parallel treatment — washed, dried, anointed, and wrapped — detailed in Section VIII. Nothing in this step is symbolic excess: a rinsed, spiced, emptied cavity is precisely what a body about to spend weeks in a desiccant bed requires if the desiccation is to start from a clean field. STEP 4 — FILLING AND SEWING Then, in Godley's rendering of the sequence, they fill the belly with pure ground myrrh and casia (cassia) and other spices — "save only frankincense" — and sew up the incision. The exclusion of frankincense is one of those details no outsider invents: it is a workshop rule, reported without explanation, and the article preserves it without inventing one. The filling served mechanically as well as aromatically, giving the shrunken cavity a pack that supported the body wall through drying; later practice filled with linen, sawdust-like materials, resin-soaked cloth, and the treated organs themselves returned as packages (Sections VIII and XIII). STEP 5 — THE NATRON BED The body is then concealed in natron for the appointed period. Herodotus's own figure belongs to the total: his text, in Godley's version, speaks of the body kept in the natron ("saltpetre" in the older rendering of the Greek litron ) for the seventy days of the whole process, "no longer time being allowed." The reconciliation of that figure with the roughly forty days of drying given by museum synthesis and the 35 + 35 structure of the Egyptian manual is the subject of Section XII; the natron itself, of Section X. What Herodotus establishes beyond dispute is the principle: a full bed of the desiccant, inside and out, for a fixed, ritually bounded term. STEP 6 — WASHING, WRAPPING IN GUMMED LINEN, RETURN When the term ends, in Godley's sequence, they wash the body and wrap the whole of it in bandages of fine linen cloth smeared with gum — "which the Egyptians mostly use instead of glue" — and return it to the family, who enclose it in a hollow wooden figure in human form and stand it upright in the burial chamber. The wrapping Herodotus compresses into one sentence is, in Egyptian practice, the whole second half of the seventy days (Sections XIII and XV); his compression is the clearest sign that he is reporting the bench work he could learn about, not the liturgy he could not. Read as a whole, Herodotus's grade one is a sound industrial process: remove the two great putrefactive reservoirs (brain and gut contents), sterilise the cavity, pack it with aromatics, desiccate the whole under controlled conditions, then seal the result in resinous, gummed textile. Every step has a material function a modern preservation scientist can state, and every step also has the ritual framing the Egyptian sources supply. The article holds both readings together throughout, because the workshop did. VI. Grades Two and Three — Cedar Oil and the Purge; Diodorus and the Price List Herodotus's second grade (2.87), in paraphrase of Godley's translation, abolishes the knife entirely. Syringes are filled with oil of cedar — the Greek kedria , most plausibly a cedar or juniper tar-oil of the kind the Saqqara residue programme later found saturating that workshop's vessels (Section XVI) — and the oil is injected into the belly through the anus, the passage then being stopped so it cannot run back. The body lies in natron for the appointed days. On the last day the oil is allowed to escape, and Herodotus claims for it a remarkable power: that it brings the stomach and intestines out dissolved with it, and that the natron meanwhile has so worked on the flesh that nothing remains but hide and bones. That dissolution claim is presented here exactly as what it is — Herodotus's report, not a demonstrated chemical result . No modern replication has reproduced the dissolution of the viscera by retained cedar oil, and the archive does not upgrade his report into a mechanism. The third grade (2.88) is the economy service entire: in Godley's rendering, "they cleanse the belly with a purge, embalm the body for the seventy days and then give it back to be taken away." No incision, no evisceration, no spices, no fine wrapping — a clyster, a natron bed, and return. Herodotus adds at 2.89, here paraphrased, the workshop's handling rule that the wives of notable men and women of great beauty were not handed to the embalmers until three or four days after death, and at 2.90 the special rule for the drowned and those taken by crocodiles, who were embalmed by the priests of the Nile town where the body came ashore and buried in sacred ground, untouchable by lay hands. Diodorus (1.91), writing four centuries later and used in this article in paraphrase throughout, supplies what Herodotus omits: figures and theatre. The first-class preparation, he says, cost a talent of silver; the second, twenty minae — a third of a talent; the third, very little. The scribe marked the incision line on the left flank. The slitter cut with the Ethiopian stone and fled instantly, pelted with stones and cursed by those standing by — the rite's way of expelling the sacrilege of the cut from the community onto its necessary performer. The evisceration itself was done by hand through the opening, sparing, in Diodorus's account, the heart and the kidneys — a detail Herodotus does not give. Another worker washed each viscus in palm wine and spices. And Diodorus describes the finished body dressed for over thirty days, first with cedar oil and other preparations, then with myrrh, cinnamon, and such spices as both sweeten the smell and preserve — a thirty-plus-day anointing phase that aligns strikingly with the 35-day wrapping half of the Egyptian manual (Section XII). He describes neither excerebration nor a natron heap in this passage; his silence is a reminder that each literary source is a window, not a wall. Every grade, including the cheapest, received the natron bed and its term, because desiccation is what makes a mummy at all. What money bought was everything around it — the surgery, the aromatics, the oils, the linen, the liturgy, and the case. The Saqqara vessels (Section XVI) and the Ritual (Section XIII) both describe the expensive end of that market; the archaeology of ordinary cemeteries describes the other, and a complete craft history has to hold the price list and the purge in the same field of vision. VII. Excerebration — the Brain, the Ethmoid Route, and What the Evidence Actually Shows Excerebration — the removal of the brain — is the step modern readers find most startling, and the step on which the evidence most punishes generalisation. Herodotus's first-grade method (Section V) enters through the nostrils with an iron hook: part extracted mechanically, the rest treated with drugs. Anatomically, the route runs up the nasal cavity and through the thin bone of the ethmoid region — the cribriform area at the roof of the nose — into the cranial cavity; CT studies of mummies routinely show the breach exactly there. Once inside, the hook could be worked to break up the tissue, which was then extracted piecemeal, drained, or rinsed out. Resin or linen was sometimes introduced into the emptied skull, and in a number of mummies a resinous mass fills part of the cranial cavity, poured or settled in after treatment. But the mummies refuse to make excerebration a rule. Imaging surveys find the full range: skulls emptied through the nose; skulls emptied through a breach elsewhere; skulls in which the brain was never removed at all and survives inside, shrunken and desiccated, where the natron reached it through the body's general drying. The 2011 replication team (Section XVIII) left the brain in place deliberately, noting that X-ray evidence shows about half of 18th-Dynasty royal mummies retaining theirs. The honest statement is therefore period- and grade-sensitive: transnasal excerebration is real, well attested, and characteristic of fine work in several periods — and it was never universal, even for kings. Popular accounts that present the hook as the invariable first act of every mummification overstate the record by exactly the margin the scanners measure. Why remove it at all, if the heart was the thinking organ? For a bench reason, not a theological one: the brain is a soft, fatty, water-rich mass sealed in a bone box, and left untreated inside a drying body it liquefies and putrefies on its own schedule, staining and compromising the head — the most recognisable, portrait-bearing part of the sꜥḥ [Gardiner: S29-D36-V28]. Where it was left, the embalmers relied on the body's general desiccation reaching it; where the grade paid for certainty, they took it out. The replication evidence supports the practical reading: Brier and Wade's trials on donated heads found that patient scooping with a hook was slow and incomplete, whereas whisking the tissue to a slurry with a rod and irrigating with water, then draining the liquid through the nose with the head positioned for it, cleared the cavity effectively — twenty minutes of whisking and about an hour and a half of draining, in one published retrospective account of their trials. The Egyptian toolkits that survive, and the clean ethmoid breaches in the scans, are consistent with a mature version of exactly that combined technique. The eye — irt [Gardiner: D4] [𓁹] — belongs to this section's anatomy. The Louvre-Carlsberg manual lists the collapsing of the eyes among the operations completed by day four, before the natron begins: the globes, unsupported once their fluids are gone, sink, and the lids close over them. Later fine work sometimes restored the face's fullness with packing, with painted or inlaid eyes on the mask or coffin, or — in the Roman period's famous portrait mummies — with a painted panel likeness set over the face of the wrapped body. The wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀], the sound, restored Eye that the archive treats under amulets and talismans , was among the forms placed with the dead: the organ that had collapsed in the workshop returned, in amuletic form, whole. VIII. Evisceration and the Treatment of the Organs — and the Heart Left in Place Through the left-flank incision — in fine modern replication, an opening of roughly three to three and a half inches sufficed, worked with patience — the embalmer's hand removed, in the order the anatomy presents them, the intestines, the stomach, the liver, and the lungs. These four are the wettest, most bacteria-laden tissues in the body, the engines of putrefaction; their removal is the single most consequential act of the whole process after desiccation itself. Each organ was then treated as a small mummy in its own right: washed — Diodorus says in palm wine and spices — dried in natron, anointed, and wrapped in linen into a compact package. The Ritual of Embalming catches the packages mid-process (Section XIII): placed in a faience vessel, covered with the ointment called fdt-nṯrw [Gardiner: I9-D46-X1-R8-Z3] [𓆑𓂧𓏏𓊹𓏪], "perspiration of the gods," and stored temporarily in a box, awaiting their final disposition. That disposition changed over time, and the change is one of the clearest period markers in the whole craft. In the classical canopic arrangement (Section IX), the four packages went into four jars under the protection of the Four Sons of Horus, and the jars went into the tomb in a chest beside the coffin. In later practice — already characteristic of many Third Intermediate Period burials and standard in the world the Ritual describes — the treated packages were returned to the body cavity before the final wrapping: chapter x+VI of the Ritual is precisely this act, the anointed organs placed back into the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the body then filled with substances called pḫrt [Gardiner: Q3-Aa1-D21-X1] [𓊪𓐍𓂋𓏏], "remedy" or "medicament." Dummy canopic jars — solid, symbolic, containing nothing — often continued to be buried alongside, the form outliving the function. Neither arrangement is a decline from the other; they are two theologies of completeness, one keeping the parts guarded beside the whole, the other restoring the whole before sealing it. The heart — ib [Gardiner: F34] [𓄣] — was left in place. The Metropolitan Museum's note on the heart scarab of the queen Manhata states the doctrine in one sentence: the Egyptians regarded the heart as the seat of the spirit, and it was not removed during mummification. It had a future engagement: the weighing against mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U1-D36-X1] [𓌳𓂝𓏏] in the hall of judgment, treated in the Weighing of the Heart . Over it, in the wrappings, the embalmers placed the heart scarab, inscribed with Book of the Dead Spell 30B, which asks the heart not to stand against its owner at the judgment; the Met's Third Intermediate Period example, found within the wrappings of the mummy of Henettawy over her chest, shows the placement exactly. Diodorus's additional detail — that the kidneys too were spared — is reported here as his account; the heart's exemption is the one the bodies themselves confirm as doctrine. Where a heart is occasionally absent or displaced in a scanned mummy, the record shows accident or period variation, not a counter-doctrine. The emptied body was then packed for drying: the cavity filled with bags of natron (the replication count is given in Section XVIII), with temporary aromatic packing, or with linen, according to period and grade, and the incision left open, covered, or sewn at different stages — the Ritual is explicit that during the back treatment of chapter x+V the incision was still being kept open, because the organs had not yet been returned. Sequence, in this craft, is not pedantry. A sewn incision before the return of the organs would be a workshop error, and the manual legislates against it by the order of its chapters. IX. Canopic Jars and the Four Sons of Horus The four treated organ packages belonged, in the classical arrangement, to four guardians: the Four Sons of Horus — Ḥr [Gardiner: G5] [𓅃] — each son protecting one organ, each himself protected by a goddess, each assigned a cardinal direction.
