IV. Wepwawet — The Opener of Ways at the Threshold The festival was led by the standard of the wolf-god Wepwawet ( wp-wꜣwt [Gardiner: F13-Z1-G43-G43-X1-Z2], "The Opener of Ways"). Wepwawet acted as the Navigational Anchor for the jubilee. His role was to magically dissolve the barriers between the Pharaoh's aging state and his rejuvenated, transfigured self. In the ritual procession, the wolf-standard "cleared the path" through the invisible static of Isfet, ensuring that the King’s Ba could move freely between the terrestrial and divine courts of the festival complex. See Anubis & Wepwawet . Wepwawet's place in the sequence is fixed by the Bubastis cycle (§V): midway through the festival the procession halts at his chapel, and the king performs two acts in his presence — he anoints the god's standard with ointment, an offering made to the festival's guide in person, and he changes his cloak before the run, exchanging the enthronement dress for the runner's. The run that follows is made with the standard: the Opener does not merely precede the king's circuit of the field; he is carried around it. When later summaries say the run "symbolised the whole festival" (§V), it is this image they compress — the wolf standard and the running king, the way opened and the land reclaimed in a single moving figure. His standard's form is worth a sentence, because the reliefs insist on it: the wolf or jackal stands atop a tall pole, accompanied by the uraeus and the distinctive shedshed element, carried by a standard-bearer at the procession's head. Where Anubis (see Anubis ) guards the necropolis and the embalming, Wepwawet's domain is the road — processions, campaigns, and this festival's course — and the Sed opens under the sign of the road-god because its central act is a journey in miniature: out, around the markers, and back to the throne. V. The Sed Court — Microcosmic Architecture of Kemet The festival required its own architecture: a Sed court with a pavilion housing the double throne (§VII), a running track marked by boundary markers for the ritual run (§VI), and rows of shrines for the visiting gods (§IX). The fullest surviving plan is Djoser's court at Saqqara (§X), where the chapels lining the court reproduce, in stone, the two archaic shrine forms of Egypt — the vaulted shrine of Upper Egypt and the pitched-roof shrine of Lower Egypt — so that the architecture itself assembles the Two Lands around the king. Later kings built jubilee halls rather than whole courts: Thutmose III's festival hall at Karnak, Amenhotep III's installations at Malqata (§XI), and Osorkon II's great granite jubilee gateway and hall at Bubastis, whose reliefs are a principal source for the festival's episodes. Because no single text gives the festival's running order, these courts and their relief cycles — Niuserre's at Abu Ghurab among the earliest detailed — are how the sequence is reconstructed. In the archive's terms the court is a Microcosm : a scale model of Kemet in which the king could re-enact possession of the whole country in a single enclosed field. How the Sequence Is Known — Niuserre, Karnak, Bubastis No festival book of the Sed survives; the running order is reconstructed from relief cycles, and three cycles carry most of the weight. Niuserre's sun temple at Abu Ghurab preserves the Old Kingdom's fullest sequence in its relief rooms. Thutmose III's festival hall at Karnak (the Akhmenu, "most splendid of monuments") housed his jubilee programme. And the granite gateway of Osorkon II at Bubastis, carved for his Sed in the 22nd Dynasty, gives the latest complete cycle — it is Osorkon's reliefs that underlie the standard modern summary of the festival's acts used in Ritual Practice , §VII. That summary, in UCL's presentation, runs: foundation rites; the king's inspection of building works and the cattle census; the procession in which the king first appears in the Sed cloak, his children beside him; the procession of the lion-bed furniture, for the king's rebirth; the presentation of the people of the whole country before the king, twice over; a procession of Min; the king's halt before Wepwawet's chapel, where he anoints the standard, changes his cloak, and performs the run with the standard — "the running seems to be the most important part of the festival; it often symbolised the whole festival"; the presentation of cattle to the gods; and finally the bringing of the carrying chair, the king enthroned in it, and the procession of the chair to the chapels. Foundation, census, rebirth furniture, the peoples, the run, the chair: the festival in twelve acts, recovered from carved walls because its book is lost. VI. The Ritual Run — Reclaiming the Territorial Field The most athletic component of the Heb-Sed was the Ritual Run . The King, wearing the short Sed cloak or the short kilt with the bull's tail, ran a series of laps between two semicircular boundary markers — the paired stones, still standing in Djoser's South Court, that delimited the course. (An earlier draft called the markers "B-shaped"; the surviving stones and the depictions show semicircular markers, and the text is corrected.) What the king carries varies by depiction — in different scenes he holds the flail, the mekes -case, or the ḥpt -oar; these are alternatives across the relief tradition, not a single kit carried at once. Britannica's summary of the reliefs gives the run's developed form: the course run four times, before the king is carried in procession to visit the chapels of the gods. This was a Sympathetic Circuit . The markers represented the southern and northern boundaries of Egypt. By physically moving his body between these points, the King "reattached" his spirit to the entire geography of the kingdom. He was "measuring the field" with his own feet, declaring that every square cubit of the "Black Land" was still under his authoritative Hu (Command). The run was a physical demonstration of Vitality-Integration . The pavilion furniture tells the same story in wood and stone. The double throne sits on the raised platform of §X, its two seats served by the two staircases — the king ascends as King of Upper Egypt and as King of Lower Egypt in turn, and the architecture makes him climb twice. In the Bubastis sequence the enthronement is prepared by the procession of the lion-bed furniture (§V), the ceremonial bed carried in for the king's rebirth: before the king can sit renewed on the thrones, the furniture of his regeneration is processed before him, as a coffin-shaped bed might be carried for a god who is about to rise. Enthronement, furniture, and run are one argument in three media — the king laid down, raised, seated, and sent running — and the relief cycles never tire of making it. VII. The Double Enthronement — Sema-Tawy Realization The climax of the festival involved the King sitting on Two Thrones located within a specialized pavilion. He would wear the White Crown ( ḥḏt [Gardiner: S1]) for Upper Egypt and then the Red Crown ( dšrt [Gardiner: D46-N37-D21-X1-S3]) for Lower Egypt. This was the ritual enactment of Sema-Tawy (The Union of the Two Lands). It confirmed that the King remained the singular point of integration for the dualities of existence. By occupying both thrones in sequence, the Pharaoh proved he could hold the "High-Frequency" energy of the South and the "Materializing" energy of the North in a single, unified consciousness without decoherence. This is the ultimate "System Sync" of the Pharaonic OS. VIII. Sacrificial Data — Feeding the Renewed Monarch A Sed was, among other things, an enormous offering event . Relief cycles show processions of offering-bearers, cattle, fowl, bread, beer, and wine presented to the enthroned king and to the assembled gods, and the king in turn presenting offerings to the gods whose standards filled the court. The literary frame is reciprocity: the gods grant the king renewed life, dominion, and "millions of years," and the king answers with the produce of the whole land laid out in ordered rows. The quantities were also accounts. Jar labels from Malqata (§XI) record wine and provisions by regnal year and estate, giving an unusually concrete picture of the logistics behind Amenhotep III's jubilees. In this framework the offerings are the festival's Sacrificial Data : the measurable input — food, drink, livestock, labour — that the state converted into the renewed authority of the monarch, and then redistributed as feasting (see §XVII). The offering processions of the relief cycles are itemised enough to name their traffic: cattle led by their horns, cranes and antelope among the desert game, geese and fowl in crates, and bearer after bearer of bread, beer jars, wine, fruit, and flowers, marshalled by nome and estate. Niuserre's Abu Ghurab cycle is the connoisseur's source — its relief rooms move from the festival's rites to the produce of the seasons themselves, as if the whole agricultural year were being carried into the court behind the king. That is the economic theology of §XVII stated in pictures three thousand years early: the land's yield, assembled in order, is what a renewed kingship is made of , and the Sed is the occasion on which the kingdom inspects its own substance. IX. Provincial Participation — Bringing the Gods to the King The Sed was not staged by the capital alone. The gods of the provinces travelled to the festival: their standards and cult images were brought to the Sed court and set up in its shrines, and delegations from the nomes attended on the king. The "visiting of the gods" is a standard episode of the relief cycles — the deities of Upper and Lower Egypt arrive, are received, and take their places around the throne — so that, for the festival's duration, the entire pantheon was physically gathered in one court. The political meaning is the same act seen from the other side: every district's god witnessing and endorsing the renewal made the jubilee a ratification by the whole country, not a private rite of the palace. Djoser's stone chapels (§X) freeze exactly this assembly — one shrine for each participating cult — into permanent form. In the archive's language this is Provincial Participation : the periphery brought to the centre so that the centre's renewal binds the whole field. The visiting gods arrived as standards and images, and the cycles name the company by their shrines: the gods of the Upper Egyptian nomes and the gods of the Lower, Wadjet of Buto and Nekhbet of el-Kab at their head as the Two Ladies of the royal titulary, with Wepwawet opening the way (§IV) and Min processing in his own act of the festival (§V). Each visiting god received offerings from the king and returned the festival's currency — life, stability, dominion, and years — in the reliefs' speech-scrolls of grant and counter-grant. A Sed is thus also a parliament: the only occasion in the ritual year when the entire divine population of Egypt was, by design, in one enclosure, and the king's renewal was transacted in their full assembly rather than before a single patron god. X. Saqqara Hardware — The Eternal Sed Festival Site The most complete architectural record of the jubilee is found in the Step Pyramid complex of Djoser at Saqqara. Imhotep designed a massive Sed Festival Court lined with "Dummy Chapels"—stone representations of the provincial shrines. These chapels were built solid, with no internal rooms. In our research framework, this is Hardware Hardening . Djoser wanted a site where he could celebrate the Heb-Sed eternally in the afterlife. By building the ritual landscape in limestone, he created a permanent "Virtual Environment" where his Ka could continue to reset its power for millions of years. The Court Described — Platform, Chapels, and the South Court Djoser's Heb-Sed court is a rectangular court within the Step Pyramid enclosure, and its furniture can still be walked through. At its southern end rises the festival platform : a broad dais reached by two staircases, Upper and Lower Egypt's ascents, bearing the double throne of §VII. Along the court's sides stand the dummy chapels in two architectural dialects — the arched, vaulted shrine form of Upper Egypt and the pitched, reed-built shrine form of Lower Egypt, translated into limestone — each solid, each with a false door and a niche for a divine image that was never meant to be entered. South of the pyramid lies the separate South Court , the running ground: a long open field with the two semicircular boundary markers (§VI) still standing in it, and in the galleries beneath, reliefs of Djoser himself performing the run in Sed dress (§XVIII). The complex is usually described as a "stage set," and the archive accepts the phrase with one correction of emphasis: a stage set is struck after the run of the play. Djoser's court was built to outlast performance — dummy chapels precisely because no living congregation would ever need their interiors, in a material chosen because eternity was the brief. It is less a theatre than a machine for celebrating, left running. The White Chapel — A Jubilee Building Taken Apart and Rebuilt Senusret I's White Chapel deserves its footnote in any account of the festival's architecture, because its survival is a parable of the evidence. Built of fine white limestone for the king's Year 31 jubilee (§III), carved on every face with the festival's own imagery — the king before the gods of the nomes, the standards, the grants of years — it was dismantled in the New Kingdom and its blocks used as fill inside Karnak's Third Pylon. There it slept, protected by the pylon's core, until excavators recovered the blocks in the twentieth century and reassembled the chapel in Karnak's Open Air Museum, where it stands today: the most complete Middle Kingdom Sed monument, preserved by being destroyed carefully. The reliefs' programme is the festival's guest list (§IX) in stone — the gods of the provinces in procession, each presenting the king with the emblems of renewed rule — and its texts are among the sources from which the thirty-year rule's Middle Kingdom observance is known at all. XI. The Three Jubilees of Amenhotep III — High-Bandwidth Renewal Amenhotep III (r. c. 1390–1352 BCE, Shaw's chronology) celebrated three Sed festivals, in his Years 30, 34, and 37 — the best-documented jubilees of the New Kingdom. Their stage was Malqata (ancient Per-Hay, "House of Rejoicing"), the palace-city he built on the Theban west bank: the court moved there in Year 29, and the complex included a festival hall, a temple of Amun, and the Birket Habu, a vast artificial harbour basin some two kilometres long excavated for the celebrations. The official Amenhotep, son of Hapu, was charged with organising the first jubilee, researching precedents from earlier reigns. The scale was programmatic. The king's mortuary temple at Kom el-Hetan — fronted by the Colossi of Memnon and, in its day, the largest mortuary temple in Egypt — was populated with hundreds of statues, including the famous series of Sekhmet figures and dyads showing the king with the gods, presenting the rejuvenated monarch as divine in his own lifetime. Tomb paintings of officials such as Kheruef (TT192) and Khaemhat (TT57), the Soleb temple reliefs, and thousands of inscribed jar labels from Malqata together make these three festivals the archive's fullest case of the Sed as state spectacle. Organising a Jubilee — Amenhotep, Son of Hapu, and the Steward Kheruef Amenhotep III's first jubilee is the one Sed whose production we can watch. The king charged Amenhotep, son of Hapu — his chief of works and the age's most favoured official — with researching how the festival had been done before: the jubilee was prepared, in part, as an work of archival scholarship, its precedents compiled from earlier reigns' records before a single course was run. The steward Kheruef (tomb TT192) had his chapel walls carved with the festival itself — the king enthroned under the jubilee canopy, the offerings, the officials in attendance — and Khaemhat (TT57) shows the harvest-and-offering side of the same machine. Between the Malqata jar labels (wine and provisions dated by regnal year and supplying estate), the Soleb reliefs, and these officials' tombs, Amenhotep III's three festivals give the archive its one complete cross-section of a Sed: text, image, accounts, and architecture all surviving at once. The detail that matters most is the precedent research. A rite supposedly immemorial was, in its best-documented performance, reconstructed — by the king's own antiquarian, from records, on purpose. The Egyptians knew their festival had a history and treated that history as a specification to be recovered, which is the most scholarly act this whole article records. The Birket Habu repays a closer look as the festival's largest single artefact. The basin — roughly two kilometres long, excavated on the desert edge south of the palace — was dug so that the jubilee could include a water procession: the royal and divine barques launched on a lake that had not existed the year before, before the court assembled on its banks. Its spoil heaps still ridge the site. A festival that digs its own harbour has passed beyond ceremony into landscape architecture, and the labour figures implied — a basin of that volume moved by corvée in the years around Year 30 — belong in §XVII's ledger beside the wine and the cattle: the Sed consumed earthworks as readily as offerings. XII. The Ramesside Scale — 14 Festivals of Ramesses II Ramesses II (r. 1279–1213 BCE) reigned sixty-six years, and his jubilee count outran every other king's: after his first Sed in Year 30 he repeated the festival, usually every three years and sometimes after only two, reaching thirteen, or by the usual maximum count fourteen, Sed festivals in total. Two details often attached to the later jubilees are flagged here as unverified , following the archive's accuracy pass, which searched for their sources and did not find them. The first is that the later festivals were proclaimed by announcement stelae surviving "from as far apart as the Delta and Nubia": that the jubilees were announced to the temples is the natural reading of a state festival, but the specific stela distribution is not documented in the sources consulted, and this article no longer asserts it. The second is that the ageing king "remained at Pi-Ramesses" for the later jubilees: the capital was indeed his Delta residence, but where the king physically celebrated each later Sed is not recorded, and the picturesque picture of the old king staying home while heralds carried his jubilee to the provinces is a modern reconstruction, presented here as such and no more. Repetition changed the rite's weight. What for most kings was a single, once-in-a-reign renewal became, under Ramesses II, a recurring rhythm of the state's later decades — less a test passed once than a standing claim, renewed on schedule, that the king's vitality was undiminished. In this framework the Ramesside Sed is the protocol at Maximum Scale : the same re-initialization, run more times than the system was designed for, by the one reign long enough to do it. XIII. Osirian Integration — Death and Resurrection Themes The Sed's renewal was never only about a living king growing strong again; its imagery borders on Osirian territory. The king wrapped in the tight Sed cloak (§XIV) visually resembles a mummiform, Osiris-like figure, and a standard episode of the festival was the raising of the djed pillar — the emblem of stability associated with Osiris — in which the king himself hauled on the ropes. A rite that re-erects the djed is handling the central Osirian object: the god who died and was reconstituted, raised upright again. The overlap should not be overstated: the Sed remained a festival of the living king, distinct from the mortuary cult, and its texts promise years on the throne of Horus, not resurrection from the tomb. But the two systems shared a grammar — envelopment, raising, re-emergence — and in the afterlife the boundary dissolved entirely, when the dead king hoped to celebrate Sed festivals forever (§XVIII). The archive reads this as Osirian Integration : the renewal protocol borrowing the resurrection pattern without surrendering its living subject. Raising the Djed — The Festival's Osirian Act in Detail The djed-raising deserves its choreography stated. The pillar — a column with four crossbars, Osiris's emblem of stability and, in the usual reading, his backbone — begins the episode lying down. Ropes are passed around it; the king, with priests and officials, hauls on the ropes; and the pillar is raised upright amid the festival, to stand as the visible proof that what was prone is erect again. The act belongs equally to the Khoiak mysteries of Osiris's own reconstitution, and its presence inside a festival of the living king is the precise point at which the two systems touch (§XIII): the king does with his own hands, to Osiris's sign, what the festival claims the gods are doing to him. XIV. Ritual Regalia — The Short Cloak and the Flail The king's Sed dress is one of the most recognisable costumes in Egyptian art: a short, close-wrapped cloak that reaches only to the knees and binds the arms to the body, leaving the hands free at the chest to hold the insignia — typically the flail , often paired with the crook or the mekes -case and hepet -oar carried in the ritual run (§VI). The cloak's tight wrapping gives the enthroned king the still, mummiform silhouette noted in §XIII; the same figure, in the run, wears the short kilt and the bull's tail — the "Feast of the Tail" — that gave the festival its name, ḥb-sd [Gardiner: V28-D58-S29-D46]. Regalia marked the festival's stages. For the double enthronement (§VII) the king appeared in turn with the White Crown of Upper Egypt and the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, enthroned under each aspect; statues of kings in Sed dress — Djoser from his serdab is the earliest famous example — were themselves cult objects, fixing the renewed form in stone. In the archive's terms the garments are the Ritual Interface : the visible, standardised surface through which an invisible renewal was displayed to the court. Theurgy of Movement — The King as Solar Motor In the Alchemical interpretation of the rite, the King’s run corresponds to the Circulation of the Spirits within the Athanor. The Pharaoh acts as the Solar Motor , his movement generating the heat required to "cook" the volatile energies of the state into a stable, renewed form. The "short cloak" he wears represents the Prima Materia being tightened and refined. The "Double Enthronement" is the Coagulation —the moment when the refined power is successfully "fixed" into the two poles of the royal identity. XVI. The Priesthood of the Jubilee — Managing the Flow No king staged a Sed alone. The festival ran on priestly and official labour : lector priests reciting the ritual texts, sem-priests attending the king's person and costume, standard-bearers carrying the gods (§IX), and the great officers of state — viziers, treasurers, and stewards — organising provisioning, construction, and the reception of delegations. Under Amenhotep III the organiser of record was Amenhotep, son of Hapu, whose own posthumous cult began with the favour the jubilees won him. The relief cycles are careful to show this hierarchy in action — officials presenting the king, priests censing the barques, heralds proclaiming the festival — because the support structure was part of the claim: a kingship renewed in proper form, by the properly qualified hands. In this framework the priesthood is the festival's Flow Management : the trained personnel who kept text, timing, offerings, and crowd in their appointed channels so the central act could proceed without disorder. XVII. Economic Redistribution — The Bounty of the King A Sed festival moved goods on a national scale. Estates and temples delivered wine, grain, cattle, and cloth to the festival city — the Malqata jar labels (§VIII, §XI) name the supplying domains and vintages — while craftsmen produced regalia, statues, and festival architecture for years in advance, and the Birket Habu at Malqata shows the state reshaping landscape itself for a jubilee. Preparation for a Year 30 festival was a building programme of the reign's second half, not an afterthought. Much of that input flowed back out. Festival feasting fed the court, the priesthoods, the workforces, and the crowds who attended the processions, and royal largesse — gifts, bonuses, and remissions proclaimed with the jubilee — redistributed stored wealth downward at the moment the king's renewed bounty most needed displaying. In the archive's terms the Sed is an act of Economic Redistribution : the treasury's accumulation, converted in public into the visible generosity of a king whose resources, like his strength, were declared inexhaustible. The provisioning had a paper trail unusual in festival studies. Because Malqata was a purpose-built jubilee city occupied for a handful of years, its rubbish is a closed archive of the festivals themselves: jar dockets in hieratic give the regnal year, the commodity, the estate of origin, and often the responsible official, so that the wine of Year 30 can be distinguished from the wine of Year 34 in the ground. The Name — Sḫmt, the Powerful One Sekhmet's name is a job description. The goddess is sḫmt [Gardiner: S42-X1] [𓌂𓏏] — the feminine form of the word sḫm [Gardiner: S42] [𓌂], "power, might, mastery," with the feminine ending -t [Gardiner: X1] [𓏏] written after it. The sign for sḫm itself is not a weapon but an instrument: the sḫm -sceptre, the forked staff with an animal head that gods and kings carry as the badge of exercised power. Her name therefore does not mean "the violent one" or "the angry one," however violent and angry she can be. It means the Powerful One — power itself, in feminine form, before any decision about what the power will be used for. Everything in this article follows from that precision: Sekhmet is not a goddess of a mood. She is a goddess of a capacity , and the whole of her cult is the management of that capacity. The root runs through the language of Egyptian rule. The double crown of the united kingdom is the sḫmty [Gardiner: S5] [𓋖], "the Two Powerful Ones" — the White Crown and the Red Crown named, together, as a pair of powers. When a temple hymn calls Sekhmet by her name, it is using the same word a coronation uses for the crown. This is why she belongs simultaneously to war, to plague, and to the person of the king: all three are theatres in which sḫm [Gardiner: S42] operates, and Egyptian theology, which preferred a single charged word to a tidy system, let one goddess hold all three. The archive's study of the power of names treats the wider doctrine; Sekhmet is its sharpest case, because her name and her function are the same word. Greek and later writers rendered the name variously — Sachmet, Sakhmet, Sekhet — and modern museum labels still alternate between "Sekhmet" and "Sakhmet." The British Museum's catalogue, following the transliteration sḫmt [Gardiner: S42-X1], gives the sense plainly: her name means "she who is powerful." The Metropolitan Museum, which spells her "Sakhmet," describes the same goddess whose lioness head, in its words, "bespeaks her potential for violence" and who "elicited great efforts of appeasement." The spellings differ; the being does not. This archive uses Sekhmet , the spelling preferred in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology's list of preferred forms. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . One further name-fact must be fixed at the outset, because retellings blur it constantly. Sekhmet is not a separate species of being from Hathor . In the myth at the centre of this article (Section IV), the goddess who is sent out is the Eye of Ra in the form of Hathor, and it is in the course of the slaughter that, in the standard scholarly paraphrase of the text, Sekhmet "came into being." The two names mark two states of one power: Hathor at rest and welcomed, Sekhmet unleashed and wading in blood. Egyptian sources themselves move between the names without embarrassment, and the compound form Sekhmet-Hathor is also attested. This article keeps the distinction the texts keep — it speaks of Sekhmet where the sources speak of the unleashed, plague-bearing, war-making power, and of Hathor where they speak of the pacified and returning goddess — and Section V examines the boundary in detail. II. The Lioness — Iconography and the Goddess's Forms Sekhmet is a lioness, or a woman with a lioness's head, and the choice of animal is observed natural history before it is symbolism. The lioness — mꜣi [Gardiner: E24] [𓃮] names the lion-kind in Egyptian — is the hunter of the pride: the animal that actually kills, at speed, in the heat of the day, at the desert margin where cultivation ends. Egypt's other great predators are ambushers or scavengers; the lioness is an open, solar killer, and she defends her young with a ferocity every herdsman on the desert edge knew personally. A goddess of war, plague, and the scorching sun could have no other body. Where Horus takes the falcon for sight and height, Sekhmet takes the lioness for impact: the moment of the strike. In her standard form she stands or sits enthroned as a woman in a close-fitting dress — often described in the sources as red linen, the colour of blood and of the Red Land — with the head of a lioness: rounded ears, a ruff of mane framing the face, and the long muzzle whose "small intense eyes and prominent sinewy jaws" the Metropolitan Museum notes on its great granodiorite example. Above the head rides the sun disk, rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳], fronted by the uraeus — the rearing cobra that is itself a form of the fiery Eye (Section XV). The disk is a genealogy worn as a crown: she is the sun's daughter and the sun's weapon, and the image says both at once. In her hands she characteristically holds the ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] [𓋹], "life," and the wꜣs -sceptre [Gardiner: S40] [𓌀] of dominion, or a papyrus sceptre built on wꜣḏ [Gardiner: M13] [𓇅], "green, flourishing." The attributes are the doctrine in miniature: the destroyer carries life in her fist. The Met's curators make exactly this point of the seated statues — that in withholding her power, Sakhmet bestowed life, symbolised by the ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] she holds. THE STANDING LIONESS Striding, sceptre in hand: Sekhmet on campaign and on patrol. The standing statues of Amenhotep III's programme (Section XIV) pair with the seated ones, one of each, in the leading reconstruction of the original installation. THE ENTHRONED LIONESS Seated on a throne, ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] on her lap: the power at rest but not disarmed. This is the form of the hundreds of granodiorite statues now in the Mut precinct and in museums worldwide — the most reproduced divine image of the New Kingdom. THE LIONESS ENTIRE In full animal form, couchant or striding, she is the desert power itself, without the mediation of the human body — the form in which the Distant Goddess flees to Nubia (Section V) and in which temple guardianship is most literal. THE URAEUS As the fiery cobra on the brow of Ra and of the king, the Eye's power is worn rather than embodied: the same fire, miniaturised into a guardian that spits flame at whatever approaches from the wrong direction. Scale matters in her iconography. The Amenhotep III statues are over life-size — the Met's seated example (15.8.2) stands 210 centimetres in its restored height — carved in granodiorite, the dark, hard stone whose speckle reads at a distance as a starfield and at close range as unyielding weight. Granodiorite is not the material of a decorative goddess. It is the material of permanence under pressure, chosen for a programme meant to hold its position for every day of the year, forever (Section XIV). Smaller Sekhmets — bronzes, faience amulets, the New Year gifts exchanged in her and Bastet's forms (Section VIII) — carried the same charge at personal scale: the archive's article on amulets and talismans treats the type. A caution on identification, parallel to the one the archive applies to falcons: not every lioness-headed figure is Sekhmet. Mut, Bastet in her early form, Wadjet, Pakhet, and a crowd of local lioness goddesses share the body. Identification rests on inscription, crown, company, and context — on the name written beside the figure, not on the mane alone. Section XV is devoted to the family resemblance and to what, within it, is distinctively Sekhmet's. III. The Eye of Ra — the Sun's Detachable Fire Sekhmet's cosmic office is stated in two words: she is the Eye of Ra . The sun god — rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳] — possesses an Eye, irt [Gardiner: D4] [𓁹], that is not a passive organ of sight. The Eye of Ra is detachable, feminine, and agentive: it can leave the god's face, travel, act, rage, be lost, be sought, and return. Egyptologists use "the Eye of Ra" for a whole class of goddesses who fill this role — Hathor, Sekhmet, Tefnut, Bastet, Wadjet, Mut, and others — because the role is older and larger than any single occupant of it. The Eye is the sun's power of action at a distance: its heat, its glare, its capacity to find and burn an enemy wherever the enemy hides. When the Eye is pleased, it is the sun's beneficent warmth and the uraeus on the brow; when it is enraged or absent, it is drought, plague, and slaughter. Sekhmet is the Eye in the second condition, and pre-eminently so: of all the Eye goddesses, she is the one whose name the texts reach for when the Eye kills. Distinguish the Eye of Ra from the Eye of Horus, as the archive's Horus article insists. The wedjat — wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀] — is the moon-eye of the falcon, injured by Seth and restored by Thoth : an eye whose story is wounding and healing. The Eye of Ra is the sun's own fire sent outward: an eye whose story is dispatch and recall. The two eyes meet in Sekhmet's cult from opposite directions — she is Ra's Eye as destroyer, and, because the sender of an affliction is the one authority who can recall it, she becomes a healer whose priests treat the wounded and the plague-struck (Sections IX–XI). But the conflation of the two Eyes in popular writing, as if "the Eye" were one symbol with one meaning, erases precisely the distinction that makes Sekhmet intelligible. Ra's Eye burns ; Horus's Eye heals ; Sekhmet, uniquely, is asked to do the first so completely that she alone can be trusted to stop it and do the second. The Eye's fire has a weather. Egyptian experience of the sun was not of a friendly lamp but of a power that ripens grain and kills travellers, that dries the inundation into cracked earth and sends the hot desert wind — the breath the texts attribute to Sekhmet herself — across the cultivation. Plague, in the Egyptian aetiology examined in Section VII, travels on that wind and in that heat. The Eye theology is thus an observed cosmology: the same solar force, at different distances and in different humours, is life and death. The king understood himself to live under the same dispensation. Crowned with the uraeus, he wore the Eye's fire on his own brow, and the srḫ [Gardiner: O33] [𓊁] — the palace-façade frame of his Horus name, its sign read with the post-audit value srḫ [Gardiner: O33] — set that fire inside the architecture of rule. Sekhmet's protection of the king, and her threat to him, are two faces of his own crown. // THE EYE IN ONE GLANCE // The sender : Ra, rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳]. The organ : the Eye, irt [Gardiner: D4] [𓁹]. The Eye at peace : Hathor — welcomed, feasted, given drink. The Eye unleashed : Sekhmet, sḫmt [Gardiner: S42-X1] [𓌂𓏏]. The Eye worn : the uraeus, Wadjet, on the brow of god and king. Not this Eye : the wedjat, wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀], the healed moon-eye of Horus. Because the Eye is a daughter as well as a weapon — the texts call the Eye goddesses daughters of Ra — the relationship carries a family's emotional grammar. The Eye can sulk, flee, take offence, and require wooing; the Distant Goddess cycle of Section V is unintelligible without that grammar. Ra does not repair his Eye as one repairs a tool. He sends for it, argues with it, feasts it, and gets it drunk. Sekhmet's mythology is what happens when the most powerful weapon in the cosmos also has a will, a memory, and a taste for blood once tasted. The cult's entire liturgical technology — litany, hymn, festival, statue programme — is built to manage a person, not a force of nature in the abstract. IV. The Book of the Heavenly Cow — the Destruction of Mankind Sekhmet's one great narrative is the opening movement of the Book of the Heavenly Cow , the composition Egyptologists also call the Destruction of Mankind . The text survives only in New Kingdom copies, inscribed in the royal tombs of Tutankhamun (on a gilded shrine), Seti I, Ramesses II, Ramesses III, and Ramesses VI — no single copy is complete, and the work is reconstructed by combining them — though its language and theology are generally held to be older than its surviving manuscripts. It is a royal funerary text, not a folktale: it explains why the sun god no longer walks the earth among men, why death and distance entered the world, and why certain festivals, drinks, and priestly duties exist. Sekhmet's rampage is its engine, and the archive tells it here strictly as the text tells it, because the episode is misreported in popular retelling — including, in an earlier form, elsewhere in this archive — with a strategist inserted whom the text never mentions. The Rebellion and the Council The story opens in the world's first age, when Ra ruled gods and mankind together and had grown old in the kingship: his bones, the text says in Erik Hornung's translation (in William Kelly Simpson's edition, The Literature of Ancient Egypt ), were of silver, his flesh of gold, his hair of genuine lapis lazuli. Mankind, seeing the god aged, contrived a plot against him. Ra, learning of it, summoned a secret council — his Eye, Shu, Tefnut, Geb, Nut, and the primordial god Nun with his courtiers — and laid the matter before the eldest god, declaring that he would not slay mankind until he had heard counsel. Nun's answer, again in Hornung's translation, is to hold the throne and let the Eye act: "Send out your Eye that it may smite them for you, those who have conspired so wickedly." The council adds the specification on which everything turns: the Eye is to descend in the form of Hathor . Note who decides, because Section IV's correction depends on it. The counsel is Nun's and the council's; the order is Ra's; the agent is Ra's Eye. Thoth — ḏḥwty [Gardiner: G26] [𓅝] — plays no part in this stratagem, neither in the council scene nor in the beer device that follows. Thoth has real and important roles elsewhere in Egyptian myth — healing the wedjat, arguing Horus's case, recording the judgment, and, in the separate Distant Goddess cycle, coaxing the fleeing Eye home with stories (Section V) — and the archive's Thoth article documents the Heavenly Cow point explicitly: the episode "is resolved not by Thoth — who plays no role in the episode — but by Ra himself." Retellings that hand Thoth the red beer confuse two different myths and two different divine functions. In this text, the mercy, like the wrath, is the sun god's own. The Slaughter, and Sekhmet Comes Into Being The goddess went out and slew mankind in the desert, where the rebels had fled. She returned to Ra's welcome and reported, in the translation's paraphrase of her triumph, that she had overpowered mankind and that it was agreeable to her heart. Ra then attempted to limit the killing — he would gain power over mankind as king, he said, without decimating them — and it is at precisely this hinge that the text, as Hornung's editorial summary puts it, marks the change: at this point Sekhmet came into being, whose bloodlust was unquenchable. The goddess sent out had gone as Hathor; the goddess who could no longer be called off is Sekhmet. The common scholarly reading — the goddess goes out as Hathor and returns as Sekhmet — is a reading of this hinge, not a second myth pasted onto the first, and the archive's Hathor article frames the same relation from the other side: the Eye, enraged, manifests as the fierce lioness Sekhmet to annihilate the enemies of order. For three nights, in the fuller retelling tradition, the goddess waded in the blood of men, the slaughter beginning at Herakleopolis. Ra, who had ordered a punishment, now faced an extermination he had not ordered and could not revoke by command. The weapon had acquired momentum. That is the theological problem the rest of the text exists to solve, and it is Sekhmet's defining problem in all her cult: sḫm [Gardiner: S42], once released, does not obey the hand that released it. Ra's Stratagem — the Seven Thousand Jars Ra solved it himself, by substitution. In Hornung's translation, he summoned "speedy emissaries whose pace is as swift as a body's shadow" and ordered them: "Run up to Elephantine and fetch me red ocher in quantity." The ochre was brought. Ra assigned the Side-locked One of Heliopolis — the high priest of Ra, identified by his sidelock — to pulverise it, while maidservants ground barley for beer, ḥnqt [Gardiner: W22] [𓏊]. The red ochre was added to the beer-mash until it was, in the translation's words, "just like human blood." Then the famous count: "Seven thousand jars of beer were thus produced." Ra inspected the beer with the gods on the eve of the day the goddess was to resume the slaughter on her journey south, approved it — "How good it is! I shall preserve mankind from her" — and rose in the deep of the night to have it poured out on the fields where she had said she would kill. The fields filled with the liquid, the text says, to a height of three palms (in older translations, four fingers' breadth over the inundated meadows; the measure varies by version, the device does not). Every agent in the device is named by the text, and the archive lists them because the correction of the record is a listing: Ra conceives and orders; the emissaries fetch; the Side-locked One grinds; the maidservants brew — an aetiology the text itself draws, making the brewing of intoxicating draughts the maidservants' charge at the seasonal feasts from that first day forward. No god of wisdom whispers the plan. No mandrake is involved in Hornung's reading: the colouring and soporific agent is the beer itself, reddened with ochre. (E. A. Wallis Budge's older translation, working from a different reading of the Elephantine commodity, rendered it doubtfully as "mandrakes (?)" mixed with the blood of the slain; the archive notes the variant because Budge's version still circulates, and follows Hornung, whose "red ocher" is the reading current scholarship prints.) The stratagem is a king's, executed by a court's ordinary machinery, in one night, against a goddess. The Drinking, the Sleep, and the Welcome The goddess set out in the morning to kill and found the fields inundated with what her delighted face took for the blood she had been promised. She drank. In Hornung's translation, she "proceeded to drink and it was just fine in her estimation," and she "returned so drunk that she had been unable to recognize mankind." The slaughter did not resume. Ra greeted the returning goddess — "Welcome, darling!" in Hornung's rendering, the greeting from which the text derives the beautiful women of Imau, a Hathor cult centre — and ordained that intoxicating draughts be prepared for her at the seasonal feasts of the year, forever: the pacification was to be repeated calendrically, not remembered once. Then, weary of mankind, Ra withdrew: Nut, transformed into the heavenly cow who gives the book its name, bore him up into the sky, the gods reordered the world beneath him, and the age of the sun's earthly kingship ended. Sekhmet's episode is the first act of that larger departure — the moment after which gods and men no longer share a country, and the management of divine wrath becomes a permanent institution rather than an improvisation. // THE CORRECTION, STATED ONCE // An earlier article in this archive credited Thoth with tricking the goddess into drinking red-dyed beer. That attribution is wrong for the Book of the Heavenly Cow and is not repeated here: in the text, Ra orders the beer, Ra's emissaries fetch the ochre, Ra's priest grinds it, and Ra has it poured out. Thoth's genuine role as the Eye's persuader belongs to the Distant Goddess cycle (Section V), a different composition with a different plot — flight, not rampage; persuasion over a journey, not a flooded field in a single night. Keeping the two apart is not pedantry. It is the difference between a sun god who takes responsibility for his own weapon and a committee that lets him off the hook, and the Egyptians wrote the first of those. V. The Distant Goddess and the Festival of Drunkenness The Heavenly Cow is one member of a family. Egyptologists group a cluster of narratives under the modern label the Distant Goddess : the Eye of Ra, offended or enraged, flees from Egypt into the Nubian desert or the far south in lioness form, and must be persuaded, feasted, and escorted home, returning transformed — pacified, adorned, and reinstalled as a beneficent power whose return coincides with the coming inundation. In the fullest versions, preserved in demotic and temple texts of the later periods, it is Thoth , and in some tellings Shu as well, whom Ra sends after her: Thoth wins the lioness home with fables, flattery, music, and argument across a long journey — there is Thoth's genuine, documented role as the Eye's persuader, and it needs no borrowed beer to be interesting. The goddess of that cycle is most often named Tefnut or Hathor; Sekhmet overlaps with her because all of them are the one Eye in different weathers, but the archive keeps the compositions distinct, as Section IV's caution requires: flight-and-return is not dispatch-and-rampage, even when the same goddess stars in both. What the two cycles share is the ending, and the ending is a festival. The Heavenly Cow itself ordains intoxicating draughts at the seasonal feasts in memory of the night of the jars; the historical cult celebrated a Festival of Drunkenness — attached above all to Hathor at Dendera and to the Mut precinct at Thebes — at which the community drank, made music, and danced the goddess from wrath to joy in public. The sistrum and the menat necklace, Hathor's instruments treated in the archive's Hathor article, are pacification technology in this setting: sound offered to the Eye until the Eye softens. Drunkenness in the rite is not licence for its own sake. It is a re-enactment with a precise theological object — the worshippers take the goddess's own medicine, in company, under ritual control, on the date appointed, so that the uncontrolled intoxication of blood need never happen again. The archive's article on ritual practice sets such re-enactment within the wider Egyptian festival system. The return of the Eye was timed to the year itself. The goddess comes back from the far south as the inundation comes from the far south; her pacification and the flood's arrival are one rhythm in two registers. The heliacal rising of Sopdet — spdt [Gardiner: M44-X1] [𓇮𓏏], written with the "sharp, pointed" sign spd [Gardiner: M44] in its post-audit value — heralded both the New Year and the flood, and the Eye's homecoming festivals cluster at that hinge of the calendar. It is at the same hinge that Sekhmet is most dangerous as well as most welcome: Section VIII takes up the year's turning, when the pacified goddess of the festival and the plague-sender of the epagomenal days are separated by five days and no wall at all. VI. War and Kingship — the Lioness at the King's Side In war, Sekhmet is the king's battle-power externalised. Royal inscriptions reach for her name at the moment of contact: a stela text of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel, cited in the scholarly literature on divine wrath, describes the king trampling the land of Hatti and heaping corpses "like Sekhmet raging during a plague" — the simile works because her two theatres, battlefield and pestilence, were understood as one theatre: the sudden, mass, divinely-sent destruction of human bodies. The British Museum's seated statues carry the same charge in dedicatory form: one throne-front inscription, noted in the Museum's catalogue tradition, dedicates the image to "Sekhmet, who smites the Nubians." She smites the south in that text; other texts send her against Asiatics, Libyans, and rebels generally. The enemy varies. The smiter does not. Her war function is protective before it is aggressive, which is why the king courts her rather than merely invoking her. The sḫm -power [Gardiner: S42] that annihilates an army is the same power that stands between the king's body and every arrow, spear, and sickness aimed at it; the uraeus on his brow is her fire in garrison. Temple reliefs across the New Kingdom and later show lioness goddesses nursing, crowning, and embracing kings — the destroyer as nurse is no paradox in a system where the fiercest mother in nature is the lioness with cubs. The archive's survey of the pantheon places her among the national gods on exactly this ground: she is one of the powers of which the Egyptian state is made, not a foreign import of violence into an otherwise gentle system. There is also a limit built into the war theology, and the Heavenly Cow states it. The king who unleashes destruction he cannot recall re-enacts Ra's error, not Ra's Majesty. Egyptian royal ideology praised the king as Sekhmet against enemies and as the pacifier of Sekhmet at home — the two roles alternate in the festival calendar (Section VIII) and in the statue programme of a king who filled his mortuary temple with her images not in triumph but in appeasement (Section XIV). A purely celebratory war-goddess would need no litany. Sekhmet has hundreds of statues and a liturgy of apology: the cult's own evidence that her violence, even in a just war, is a danger to be managed after the battle as much as a weapon to be aimed during it. VII. Plague — Arrows, Messengers and Slaughterers Sekhmet's ordinary jurisdiction — the one that touched peasants oftener than kings — is epidemic disease. Egyptian aetiology pictured plague, iꜣdt [Gardiner: M17-G1-D46-X1] [𓇋𓄿𓂧𓏏], not as a miasma in the abstract but as an attack by agents: the goddess shoots, and her emissaries carry the shot home. The texts name the machinery with administrative precision. Her messengers — wpwtyw [Gardiner: F13-G43-X1-Z4] [𓄋𓅱𓏏𓏭], built on wp [Gardiner: F13] in its post-audit value — go out over the land. Her slaughterers , the butcher-demons who do the killing at close quarters, roam with them. And her arrows — the missiles of the attack, loosed, as some of the demonological sources picture them, on pestilential winds — strike the individual victim, who falls sick as a man falls shot. Modern scholarship on Egyptian demons, including recent work on the Calendars of Lucky and Unlucky Days discussed in Archaeology magazine's survey of the demon archers, stresses the wind: winds are invisible, travel everywhere, enter every house, and carry sickness seasonally, exactly as the demons were said to do. The metaphor had an epidemiology inside it. Tradition numbered the arrows at seven — the Seven Arrows of Sekhmet, matched by seven emissary powers in the developed demonology — and the number organises the protective liturgy of Section VIII, in which the king is defended arrow by arrow, first to seventh, in a single invocation cycle (the form preserved in Philippe Germond's study of Sekhmet and the protection of the world, Sekhmet et la protection du monde , as adapted in the secondary literature). The archive states the sevenfold scheme as what it is: the form the New Year defence took in the texts Germond published, not a universal Egyptian doctrine that every plague in every period had exactly seven components. Egyptian demonology was local, cumulative, and happy to multiply agents; what is constant is the structure — a sender, a missile, a messenger, a victim — and the identity of the sender. That structure explains the phrase the sources use for a bad year: a "year of Sekhmet" is a plague year, a year in which the arrows flew thick. It also explains why the defence against plague was never purely medical in the modern sense and never purely magical either. If disease is an emissary of a goddess, then treatment has two fronts — the body the arrow struck, and the court from which the arrow came — and the same practitioner must work both. Section X introduces the practitioners: the physician-magicians whose title names this goddess, and whose existence is the institutional form of the double front. // THE PLAGUE MACHINERY, PRECISELY // The power : sḫm [Gardiner: S42] [𓌂], exercised by the goddess sḫmt [Gardiner: S42-X1] [𓌂𓏏]. The affliction : iꜣdt [Gardiner: M17-G1-D46-X1] [𓇋𓄿𓂧𓏏], plague, pestilence. The carriers : her messengers, wpwtyw [Gardiner: F13-G43-X1-Z4] [𓄋𓅱𓏏𓏭], and her slaughterer-demons. The strike : her arrows, seven in the New Year liturgy. The counter-rite : sḥtp sḫmt [Gardiner: S29-V28-X1-Q3-S42-X1], "pacifying Sekhmet" (Section VIII). Popular writing that calls the plague-demons "the wadjet" confuses the healed Eye of Horus, wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀], with the plague machinery of Ra's Eye; the archive does not use the term for them. VIII. The Dangerous Year — Pacifying Sekhmet at the New Year The Egyptian civil year — rnpt [Gardiner: D21-N35-Q3-X1] [𓂋𓈖𓊪𓏏] — ran to 365 days: twelve months of thirty and five extra days, the epagomenal days, "the days upon the year," which belonged to no month and stood outside the year's ordinary protection. Myth gave those five days to the births of Osiris, Horus the Elder, Seth, Isis , and Nephthys; experience gave them to fear. At the year's hinge the order of things was thinnest, the old year's defences were discharged and the new year's not yet installed, and Sekhmet's messengers were understood to walk abroad. The end of the year was therefore the cult's busiest season, and its characteristic rite gives this section its title: sḥtp sḫmt [Gardiner: S29-V28-X1-Q3-S42-X1] [𓋴𓎛𓏏𓊪𓌂𓏏], "pacifying Sekhmet" — sḥtp [Gardiner: S29-V28-X1-Q3], "to pacify, to satisfy, to make content," the causative of the word for peace, applied to the goddess as a standing operation. The rite's textual monument is the composition modern scholarship calls the Book of the Last Day of the Year , preserved among the Sekhmet rituals published by Germond: a litany of invocations in which the goddess is called upon, name by name and arrow by arrow, to come toward the king and to save, protect, and preserve him from each of the year's arrows in turn — first arrow through seventh — while the community's corresponding practice, as the secondary literature summarising Germond describes it, was humbler and more portable: the book's words recited over a piece of cloth worn about the neck through the dangerous days, an amuletic text for people who had no temple liturgy of their own. On the first day of the New Year itself, the same tradition records, people exchanged gifts in the form of Sekhmet or of Bastet — the fierce goddess and her gentle counterpart, given and received as the year's first insurance. The archive presents this complex as Germond's published material presents it: a named rite, a named book, and a folk practice gathered around both, at the turn of the year. Pacification was not confined to the year's end. The verb sḥtp [Gardiner: S29-V28-X1-Q3] names what the daily temple liturgy did in miniature, what the Festival of Drunkenness did in public, what the Litany of Sekhmet at Edfu did in hymnic form (Section XVI), and what Amenhotep III's statue programme did in stone (Section XIV) — a single operation at four scales. Egyptian religion, which had watched the sun cross the sky and the flood rise and fall on schedule for three thousand years, did not believe that a power like Sekhmet could be pacified once. It believed in maintenance. The goddess is satisfied the way a fire is banked: daily, by professionals, with the fuel laid in advance — and the year's end is simply the night the banked fire is most likely to blow open, and therefore the night the whole establishment turns out to tend it. IX. The Healer — Why the Plague-Bringer Cures Sekhmet heals for the same reason she sickens, and the Egyptian sources state the logic without embarrassment: an affliction that is sent can be recalled , and only the sender can recall it. A plague that arrived as the goddess's arrow is not fully treated until the goddess has been addressed; a fever that is her breath in the room is not fully treated until her breath is turned aside. The British Museum's reassessment of its Amenhotep III statues ( The Antiquaries Journal 98, 2018) puts the duality in one sentence of its introduction: she "was regarded as the bringer of destruction, but also as a healer who could protect against illness and plague." The Metropolitan Museum's statue texts make the same point from the patient's side: Egyptian physicians saw the treatment of illness in part as a way to appease Sakhmet, and in withholding her power she bestowed life. Healing, in this system, is not the opposite of the goddess's activity. It is her activity, persuaded into its other direction. This is why the archive resists the modern framing of Sekhmet as a paradox — "goddess of plague and yet , surprisingly, of healing" — as if two portfolios had been stapled together by accident. In the Egyptian frame there is one portfolio: sḫm [Gardiner: S42] over the body's integrity. The power that can shatter that integrity is, by definition, the power whose favour constitutes it, and the physician who serves the power serves both ends of the transaction. The pattern is general in Egyptian religion — the archive's article on heka treats the operative force that harms and heals by the same grammar — but Sekhmet is its most institutionalised case, because in her case the logic grew a profession, a literature, and, under one king, a forest of statues. Sections X and XI follow the profession and the literature in turn. H
