The Name — stẖ, stš and Sutekh No Egyptian god is harder to introduce honestly than Set, because no Egyptian god carries two reputations so completely opposed. The scribes who wrote his name wrote it in several forms, and the variation itself is part of the evidence. The commonest later spelling is stẖ , with an older and very durable alternative stš [Gardiner: E20] [𓃩], in which the whole name is carried by a single sign: the Set animal itself, seated, ears squared, tail erect. The sign is a logogram — the picture is the word — and the archive's V2 transliterator accordingly gives E20 the whole-word value stš . A fuller writing, swtẖ , preserves an initial sw element, sw [Gardiner: M23] [𓇓], that later fell away, and it is from this fuller form that Egyptologists derive the conventional vocalisation Sutekh . Greek writers rendered the name Sēth — the form that survives in English as Seth — and in Coptic the name became Sēt . This article uses Set , the spelling now standard in most museum and university publication, and gives Seth where a cited source or a king's conventional name (Seti, Sethnakhte) requires it. What the name means is not known, and the archive says so plainly rather than repeating the confident guesses of older handbooks. Proposals have connected stẖ [Gardiner: E20] with roots of separation, of desertion, and of turning aside; none commands a consensus, and the Egyptians left no etymological statement of their own. What can be documented is the name's company . The Set-animal sign does duty in Egyptian writing far beyond the god's name: words for turmoil, confusion, illness, storm and rage are written with Sethian determinatives, so that the sign itself came to mark a semantic field — the field of things disordered, violent, and out of place. The god's name and the vocabulary of disorder grew up together, each reinforcing the other, for three thousand years. A god whose sign means disturbance in ordinary words is a god the language itself has already judged — and yet the same sign stands, unashamed, in the names of kings (Section XIV). The tension is not a modern invention. It is in the writing system. // READING THE NAME IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used and flagged: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20/R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . One word must be kept distinct from the name from the outset, because confusing them has distorted Set's reputation for two millennia. isft [Gardiner: M17-S29-I9-X1] [𓇋𓋴𓆑𓏏] — "disorder, wrong, chaos" — is the abstract opposite of mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U1-D36-X1] [𓌳𓂝𓏏], the order-truth the archive treats in Ma'at and Isfet . Set is a god : a person, with a family, temples, priests, and a seat among the Ennead . Isfet is not a person and has no cult. Apep , the serpent of absolute chaos, stands outside the ordered cosmos altogether and is never worshipped. Set stands inside it — dangerously, disruptively, but inside. Holding that distinction is the single most important discipline in everything that follows: Egyptian religion did not confuse its storm god with its devil, because Egyptian religion had no devil, and it is the later conflation of Set with Apep — and then with the Greek Typhon, and then with Satan — that produced the one-dimensional villain of popular retelling. The Egyptian record is stranger and more interesting than that. II. The Family — Son of Geb and Nut, Brother of Osiris In the Heliopolitan genealogy of the Ennead — psḏt [Gardiner: N9-X1] [𓇷𓏏], "the Nine" — Set is no intruder from outside creation. He is family at the deepest level the system recognises. The earth god Geb and the sky goddess Nut — nwt [Gardiner: N35-G43-X1] [𓈖𓅱𓏏] — bore five children in the intercalary days of the year: Osiris , wsir [Gardiner: Q1-D4-A40] [𓊨𓁹𓀭]; Horus the Elder, Ḥr-wr [Gardiner: G5-G36] [𓅃𓅨]; Set; Isis , ꜣst [Gardiner: G1-S29-X1] [𓄿𓋴𓏏]; and Nephthys , nbt-ḥwt [Gardiner: V30-X1-O10] [𓎟𓏏𓉡], "Mistress of the House," who became Set's wife. The murder at the centre of the Osiris myth is therefore not an invasion. It is a fratricide inside the ruling house of the cosmos, and Egyptian theology never lets the reader forget it: the plaintiff's uncle, the defendant's brother, the judge's son. Every party to the great litigation of Sections VIII–IX is related to every other. The pairing of Set and Nephthys repays attention. Nephthys is, by every account, one of the kindest powers in the pantheon: mourner of Osiris, protector of the dead, guardian — with Isis, Neith and Serqet — of the canopic shrine. Her marriage to Set is the systematic counterweight Egyptian theology loves: the barren desert wedded to the faithful mourner, and the union is, in most tellings, childless in the way the desert is childless. A later tradition made Anubis , inpw [Gardiner: C6] [𓁢], the son of Nephthys — by Osiris in the dominant version, by Set in a minority one. Herman te Velde, whose 1967 monograph Seth, God of Confusion remains the standard study of this god, doubted that Set was ever regarded as Anubis's father in genuine Egyptian religion, and the archive follows that caution: where the parentage matters in this article, Osiris is the father named by the sources. Set's recognised consorts in the New Kingdom are instead the foreign goddesses Anat and Astarte (Section XIV) — a theological statement in itself about where Set's affinities were felt to lie. Set's position among the five siblings is structural. Osiris rules the fertile land and then the dead; Isis rules by heka , ḥkꜣ [Gardiner: V28-D28-G1] [𓎛𓂓𓄿]; Horus the Elder is the sky, pt [Gardiner: N1] [𓇯], whose eyes are the sun, rꜥ [Gardiner: N5] [𓇳], and the moon, iꜥḥ [Gardiner: N11] [𓇹]. Set's portion is everything the others are not: the desert margin, the storm, the foreign country, the night wind, violence itself. The Ennead did not exile him to that portion after the murder; in the oldest strata the portion is simply his, as the sky is Horus's. The myth of the murder (Section VII) explains the enmity , not the office . Confusing those two things — supposing that because Set killed Osiris his whole domain is a punishment — is the second great error in popular accounts, and this article will return to it at the settlement (Section IX), where the gods themselves are shown distinguishing between the crime, which is judged, and the power, which is retained and posted. THE FIVE CHILDREN OF GEB AND NUT Osiris , the murdered king; Horus the Elder, the sky falcon; Set, the storm; Isis , great of magic; Nephthys , the mourner. Set is the middle term of the five: neither the firstborn king nor the youngest sister, but the strong brother in between — a position the litigation will exploit, since his claim to succeed Osiris rests on seniority and strength against the son's claim by birth. SET AND NEPHTHYS nbt-ḥwt [Gardiner: V30-X1-O10] [𓎟𓏏𓉡]. Husband and wife in the Ennead's pairing, yet Nephthys mourns Osiris, helps Isis recover the body, and guards the dead — her loyalty in the myth runs consistently against her husband's crime and with his victims. Egyptian theology tolerated the contradiction without dissolving it: a marriage is a cosmic pairing, not a political alliance. SET AND THE FOREIGN GODDESSES In New Kingdom accounts Set is joined with Anat and Astarte, warrior goddesses of the Levant received into the Egyptian pantheon . The marriages are syncretism written as genealogy: the god of foreign lands takes foreign wives, exactly as the god of foreign lands had already been identified with the foreign storm god Baal (Section XIII). III. The Paradox — Disorder Within the Cosmic Order The whole of this article is contained in one sentence of Christiane Zivie-Coche's study of foreign deities in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology, here paraphrased because it states the matter exactly: the border-crosser par excellence was Seth, who embodies that role in all his ambiguity — protector of the sun god in the solar barque, murderer of his brother Osiris, and god of the deserts, disturbing and threatening — a trickster. Three portraits in one breath, and all three are documented Egyptian positions, held simultaneously by the same civilisation, often in the same temple. Set is the Osiris cycle's antagonist and murderer. Set is also Ra's indispensable defender, the only god stationed at the prow of the solar barque with the spear against Apep . And Set is the god of the desert, of storms, of foreign lands and foreigners — of everything outside the Nile's green order that nevertheless presses on that order daily and cannot simply be wished away. The archive's framing, following the analysis in the Apep article , is a threefold distinction. Apep is absolute chaos: uncreated, unpersonlike, outside the cosmos, seeking only its dissolution, never worshipped, never reconciled. Isfet , isft [Gardiner: M17-S29-I9-X1], is disorder as an abstract condition — the sum of wrong, decay and falsehood that mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U1-D36-X1] perpetually holds down. Set is contained disorder: a created god, a member of the Ennead, whose violence is real, culpable, and punishable — and also usable , because the cosmos itself contains storms, deserts and enemies, and needs a power that is native to them. Only a being of Set's nature can meet Apep's gaze at the prow; the archive's Apep article makes the point in its own terms, that contained chaos is the only weapon against absolute chaos. Set is therefore not order's opposite number in a dualism. He is order's most dangerous employee . That is why the familiar modern summary — "Set, Egyptian god of evil" — fails on the evidence at every period before the very latest, and fails even then in the ways Section XVI documents. Evil, in the Egyptian frame, is not a person. Persons can be judged, and Set is judged: the tribunal of the gods tries his crime at length and rules against him (Sections VIII–IX). But the same tribunal does not — cannot — vote the storm out of the weather. What Egyptian theology does with Set, across three thousand years, is more subtle than either worship or condemnation alone: it litigates him, binds him, posts him, marries him abroad, names kings for him, and finally, in a changed political world, erases him — and even the erasure is never total. Each of those verbs gets a section. The paradox is not a puzzle to be solved before the article can proceed; it is the article. // THREE KINDS OF DISORDER // Apep — ꜥꜣpp [Gardiner: E7-Q3-Q3] [𓃘𓊪𓊪]: the serpent outside creation; absolute chaos; destroyed nightly, returning nightly; no cult, no temple, no reconciliation. Isfet — isft [Gardiner: M17-S29-I9-X1]: disorder as a condition, the abstract contrary of mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U1-D36-X1]. Set — stš [Gardiner: E20] [𓃩]: disorder as a person — created, related, culpable, indispensable. The first must be annihilated daily; the second must be held down perpetually; the third must be governed . Egypt's whole theology of Set is the technology of that government. IV. The Set Animal — an Iconography Without a Species Every other great god of Egypt can be introduced by an animal that exists. Horus is a falcon; Anubis is a jackal; Hathor is a cow. Set's animal does not exist — or, if it once did, no one has identified it — and Egyptologists therefore call it, with deliberate neutrality, the Set animal : the creature written stš [Gardiner: E20] [𓃩] and, in a second common form, [Gardiner: E21] [𓃫]. Its diagnostic features are consistent across three thousand years of representation: a slender, dog-like body; a long head ending in an elongated, downward-curving snout; two tall ears whose ends are cut off square — the feature found in no living animal and therefore the creature's signature; and a stiff, erect tail, in the full form forked at its tip or tipped with a tuft. From its oldest undoubted representations, in the protodynastic period (Naqada IIIA/B), the animal already has exactly this form: dog-like, square-eared, long-snouted, tail erect. The type was fixed before the pyramids and never fundamentally changed. The candidates proposed for its natural original make a small history of Egyptology in themselves: the aardvark, the African wild dog, the saluki hound, the fennec, the jackal, the donkey, the pig, the oryx and other antelopes, the okapi, and the giraffe — whose flat-topped ossicones were once held to explain the square ears, though the Egyptians depicted giraffes distinctly and knew the difference. A recent re-examination of the iconography (in the journal Egyptological Hypotheses , 2024) restates the difficulty precisely: the body is undoubtedly that of a canid, while the face is anything but dog-like when set beside Anubis or the dogs of the hunting scenes. The honest conclusion, and the one this archive adopts, is that the Set animal is best understood as a composite or conventional creature — an artificial animal for an artificial category, assembled, like the griffin or the sphinx, to be recognisable precisely by being unnatural. A god of the unclassifiable gets an unclassifiable beast. Whether an extinct or locally known animal lies somewhere behind the type cannot now be recovered, and claims to have "solved" the Set animal should be read with the same suspicion this archive applies to the wedjat-fraction story in the Horus article : famous is not the same as demonstrated. The animal's career in art begins at the summit of the state. On the ceremonial macehead of the predynastic King Scorpion (Naqada III) the Set animal stands on a standard among the standards of the powers of the land. Cylinder-seal impressions from the tombs of Second Dynasty kings show the Set animal standing on top of the king's serekh — the position the Horus falcon usually occupies — in the reign of Peribsen, who set the Seth-animal, not the falcon, above his palace-façade name (Section XI). From the Old Kingdom onward the god also appears in the mixed form that becomes his standard portrait: a man's body with the Set animal's head, wearing the tripartite wig, with or without the Double Crown, and the royal kilt. One of the few preserved full statues of this type, from Medinet Habu, is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo (JE 31628). The two forms — beast entire, and beast-headed man — are the same statement at two registers: the beast entire for the god's raw nature, the hybrid for the god in society, striding among gods and kings with sceptre in hand. Around the central animal clustered a whole Sethian bestiary — the real animals Egyptians associated with Set's domain and temper: the donkey, ꜥꜣ [Gardiner: E7] [𓃘], beast of the desert tracks; the pig, šꜣ [Gardiner: E12] [𓃟]; the jackal, sꜣb [Gardiner: E17] [𓃥]; the oryx of the desert margin; the hippopotamus of the river's violence; the crocodile; and, in the hostile texts of the Late Period , the turtle and the serpent. In the mythic combat Set himself takes hippopotamus form against Horus (Section VIII), and in the Edfu temple drama treated in the Horus article he is harpooned as a red hippopotamus. The bestiary matters for the demonisation (Section XV): as Set's reputation darkened, his animal associations darkened with it, until in Late Period representation he is increasingly shown simply as a donkey or a donkey-headed man — the composite mystery-creature traded in for an animal of stubbornness and lust in the ancient stereotype — and in the Book of the Faiyum he appears, most strangely, with a flamingo's head. The iconography is a graph of the theology, and it can be read in either direction. SQUARE-TIPPED EARS The diagnostic feature. No natural animal has them; every Set animal does. Whatever the type's origin, the squared ear became the god's trademark — visible at a glance across a relief, and sufficient by itself to identify a damaged figure as Set's. THE CURVED SNOUT Long, thin, and downturned at the end — aardvark-like to some eyes, greyhound-like to others. Combined with the ears it produces a head that is elegant, alert, and slightly wrong: the visual equivalent of the god's character. THE ERECT, FORKED TAIL Carried stiffly upright, often forked or tufted at the tip like an inverted arrow. In the hieroglyph the tail is as diagnostic as the head: [𓃩] cannot be mistaken for any natural canid sign in the list. THE CANID BODY Slender, deep-chested, long-legged — the body of a desert hunting dog. The composite is therefore not random: desert body, impossible head. Set's animal is built the way his domain is built, out of the margin's real materials recombined past nature. V. Iconography — the Was Sceptre and the God's Forms In his anthropomorphic form Set is a man with the Set animal's head, and his furniture is the standard furniture of divine power, each piece of it legible. He carries the ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] [𓋹], "life," and the crook ḥqꜣ [Gardiner: S38] [𓋾] in royal contexts; he wears the White Crown ḥḏt [Gardiner: S1] [𓋑] of Upper Egypt or the Double Crown sḫmty [Gardiner: S5] [𓋖], the "Two Powerful Ones," when his kingship is the point; and above all he carries — and in a real sense is — the was-sceptre : wꜣs [Gardiner: S40] [𓌀]. The was is a tall staff whose top is an animal head with long ears and a curved snout, and whose bottom ends in a fork. Its very name is the word for dominion and well-being: to hold the was is to hold power in its settled, effective form. The connection between the was and Set is old, close, and — characteristically for this god — debated in its direction. The Metropolitan Museum's record for a Middle Kingdom was-sceptre head (25.3.284h, reign of Amenemhat III) summarises the scholarship with proper care: various interpretations exist of the staff's origins and its relationship to Seth; the staff appears already in Predynastic rock art; some scholars link it to the Seth animal, pointing to its symbolic use in the nome sign of Oxyrhynchus, a city where Seth was celebrated, and to the discovery of a gigantic was-sceptre in the god's temple at Ombos; others propose, conversely, that the god's iconography derived from the staff itself. Gardiner held that the sceptre's head is probably the head of the Seth-animal. The archive states the position as the Met states it: Set is strongly associated with the was, the was-head and the Set-animal's head are at minimum close cousins, and the direction of borrowing is unresolved. What is not debated is the sceptre's cosmic use: was-sceptres stand at the corners of the world holding up the sky , pt [Gardiner: N1] — the dominion of Set's sceptre is, quite literally, load-bearing. A Ramesside prayer could accordingly appeal to Seth himself as a supporter of the sky. The murderer's staff props up heaven. That is the paradox of Section III rendered as furniture. Set's colour is red . He is the red god as the fertile land's gods are black-earth gods: red hair and ruddy skin are Sethian marks in the texts, red animals are his, and the red hippopotamus of the Edfu drama is his ritual form. The colour belongs to his domain term: the desert is the dšrt [Gardiner: S4] [𓋕], the "Red Land," against the kmt [Gardiner: V31-Aa15-X1] [𓎡𓐝𓏏], the "Black Land" of the flood silt — the same sign dšrt [Gardiner: S4] that writes the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, a coincidence of writing the Egyptians exploited and the modern reader must keep untangled by context. Section VI follows the red into geography. Here it is enough to note the iconographic consequence: where Horus's images run to gold, lapis and the falcon's precise black-and-white, Set's run to red ochre, red stone, and the desert palette — the colour symbolism of the two gods is the map of Egypt in two pigments. Finally, Set is the god Egyptian art shows acting with his hands more than almost any other: brandishing the great sceptre he boasts of in the Contendings , grasping the spear at the prow, presenting the king, smiting the king's enemies in the company of Horus (Section XI), and — in the Ramesside images of Section XIV — standing in foreign dress as Seth-Baal with spear and shield. Even his erased figures (Section XV) are usually erased mid-action . The iconography never permits him the stillness of a purely contemplative god. He is the god of the verb. VI. Lord of the Red Land — Desert, Storms and Foreign Lands Egypt is two lands in more ways than the political one. The kmt [Gardiner: V31-Aa15-X1], the Black Land, is the ribbon of flood silt, in places only a few hundred metres wide, where everything Egyptians ate grew. The dšrt [Gardiner: S4], the Red Land, is everything else: the sandstone and gravel deserts rising on both sides of the valley to the horizons — beautiful, waterless, and lethal. Horus, in the standard theological geography, is lord of the Black Land; Set is lord of the Red. This is not a consolation prize. The Red Land is where Egypt's gold came from, where its desert roads ran, where its weather was made, and where its enemies lived. To be lord of the Red Land is to be lord of the conditions of Egyptian life rather than of its comforts. Storms are Set's weather. In a land of almost no rain, the storm is not a commonplace but an event: the sudden black wind off the desert, the rare violent rain over the valley, thunder — which the texts hear as Set's voice, and which the settlement of Section IX will make his eternal employment, thundering in the sky in Ra's service. Unseasonal and violent natural events belong to his register generally: eclipses, earthquakes, and the disordering of the luminaries are Sethian disturbances in the sources that catalogue them. The star lore belongs here too: the northern constellation the Egyptians saw as a bull's foreleg was bound, in the astronomical texts, in Set's keeping — the imperishable stars chained so that the Sethian power among them could not run loose. Even in the sky, the technology is the same: not annihilation, but binding and posting. Foreign lands are Set's country in the political sense. The Egyptian word is ḫꜣst [Gardiner: N25] [𓈉], "foreign land, hill country" — the sign shows the desert hills themselves — and its plural ḫꜣswt [Gardiner: N25-Z2] [𓈉𓏥] names the foreign countries collectively. Set is lord of the ḫꜣswt [Gardiner: N25-Z2] as Horus is lord of the Two Lands: the peoples beyond the frontier — Libyans to the west, the Asiatics of Retjenu and Canaan to the northeast, Nubians to the south — live in his element and, in Egyptian theological logic, under his patronage. This is precisely why he, alone of the great gods, could be identified with foreign gods rather than merely compared to them (Section XIII): Baal of Ugarit and Canaan, Teshub of the Hittites — storm gods of the foreign hills — were recognised by Egyptian theologians as Set wearing foreign dress, and by foreigners in Egypt as their own god wearing Egyptian. Zivie-Coche's border-crosser is a border-crosser because his domain is the border: the desert edge where Egypt ends and the world begins, and where everything dangerous and necessary — gold, incense roads, storms, invaders, and new gods — comes from. The desert also made Set a god of the oases and of travellers, a fact Section XVI will need when the demonisation comes. The western oases — Kharga, Dakhla, Siwa, Bahariya — are islands in Set's sea of sand, reached only by his roads and watered at his sufferance; their inhabitants had a permanent, practical reason to keep the desert god's goodwill that Nile-valley theology, rewritten by later politics, could not talk them out of. Set as lord of the oasis is attested as a cult title in its own right. Keep the fact in reserve: it is one of the hinges on which the last sections turn. // THE TWO LANDS OF THE TWO GODS // The Black Land — kmt [Gardiner: V31-Aa15-X1] [𓎡𓐝𓏏]: silt, crops, cities, the ordered valley; the portion of Horus and of Osiris . The Red Land — dšrt [Gardiner: S4] [𓋕]: desert, storm, gold roads, foreign peoples; the portion of Set. The geography is moral without being dualist: Egypt needed both lands, feared one of them, and assigned the feared one a god of its own rather than pretending it was godless. What a civilisation does with the country it fears is give it a lord and negotiate. VII. The Murder of Osiris — Set as Antagonist Against all of the above stands the crime, and this article does not soften it. In the Osiris cycle — the most important myth Egypt produced, treated in full in its own article and in the archive's Osiris article — Set murders his brother. The Egyptian sources, which are allusive for a thousand years before they are narrative, know the core facts early: Osiris is killed by Set's agency, drowned and/or enclosed and cast away, his body recovered by Isis and Nephthys, in the developed tradition dismembered and scattered, and revived — not to earthly life, but to kingship of the dead — through Isis's heka and the offering of the healed Eye of Horus, the wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] [𓂀]. Plutarch's Greek retelling ( De Iside et Osiride , c. 100 CE) supplies the famous furniture — the measured coffin at the banquet, the seventy-two conspirators, the body cut into fourteen pieces — and this article, following the archive's standing caution, uses Plutarch only as a late Greek witness to a story whose Egyptian core is far older, never as the story's source. The Pyramid Texts of the late Old Kingdom — the oldest religious corpus in the world — already hold the two halves of Set side by side, and the archive insists on the point because it disproves the tidy modern narrative in which a once-benign god was later slandered. In the Pyramid Texts Set is already the one who struck Osiris down, already Horus's opponent in the struggle for the Eye and the office — and already, in the same corpus, a power whose strength the dead king needs, a god who can be addressed, propitiated, and enlisted. Enmity and utility are coeval in the sources. There is no recoverable stratum in which Set is simply good, and none, until the very end, in which he is simply evil. Te Velde's study makes the complementary warning against the opposite simplification: later scholars who begin from the demonised Set of the Late Period and read him backward across three thousand years are reading the verdict of one political age as the character of the god. Motive, in the Egyptian tellings, is constitutional before it is personal. Set claims the throne of Osiris as the elder surviving brother and the strongest of the gods — a claim by seniority and by capability, of a kind Egyptian succession practice itself recognised as arguable; Horus claims it as the son and heir — a claim by birth. The myth is therefore not a morality play about a villain's envy, though envy and violence are in it; it is a succession dispute between two principles of legitimacy that Egypt's own kingship held in permanent tension, prosecuted first by murder and then — and this is Egypt's distinctive turn — by lawsuit . The murder puts Set in the wrong. It does not put his claim outside the court's jurisdiction. Section VIII is the lawsuit. One more datum belongs to the crime's dossier, because the demonisation will lean on it: the wound Set gives and the wound he receives. In the combat traditions around the litigation, Horus loses his eye — the injury behind the wḏꜣt [Gardiner: D10] and the whole healing theology of the Horus article — and Set loses, in the blunt symmetry of the sources, his testicles: the storm's generative power damaged as the falcon's sight is damaged, each god carrying the other's mark out of the fight. Egyptian myth thinks in such exchanges. Neither party emerges whole; that is why the ending cannot be a simple execution and must be a settlement. VIII. The Contendings of Horus and Set — Eighty Years in Court The fullest surviving telling of the succession struggle is a lawsuit. The Contendings of Horus and Seth survives in a single manuscript, Papyrus Chester Beatty I, written in hieratic in the Twentieth Dynasty, in the reign of Ramesses V (c. 1149–1145 BCE), probably at Thebes, and now in the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin. A. H. Gardiner published the editio princeps in 1931; Miriam Lichtheim's translation in Ancient Egyptian Literature , vol. II (1976), is the standard English version. The account of the text given here follows the archive's treatment in the Horus article , with the emphasis reversed: this is the one great Egyptian narrative in which Set is not a walk-on menace but a litigant — present on every page, arguing, boasting, cheating, sulking, and, scene by scene, losing a case he is never simply thrown out of court for bringing. The story opens with the case already ancient: Horus and Set have been litigating before the Ennead for eighty years . Set's position in court is stronger than a modern reader expects. He is the elder; he is, by common consent, the strongest of the gods — his own argument, pressed repeatedly, is his service: he alone stands at the prow of Ra's barque and slays Apep daily, and he brandishes a sceptre of fantastic weight as the exhibit of his strength. Ra, presiding, favours him and resents the young claimant. Against him, Shu and Thoth — ḏḥwty [Gardiner: G26] [𓅝] — argue the son's right: the office belongs to the son of Osiris by birth. The Ennead is deadlocked, irritable, and — the text is unembarrassed about this — faintly comic: the tribunal consults the ram god of Mendes, writes for an outside opinion to Neith of Sais, receives her verdict for Horus with a proposal of compensation for Set, and watches Ra refuse to accept it and retire in a sulk to be coaxed back by Hathor. Set's conduct of his own case is a study in the trickster's strengths and limits, the aspect of the god te Velde analysed in his 1968 study of Seth as trickster. He will not plead while Isis is in court, fearing her advocacy, so the tribunal removes to an island and forbids the ferryman to carry any woman resembling her across; Isis crosses anyway, in disguise, and traps Set into condemning himself out of his own mouth with a parable of a widow's son and a stranger seizing his father's cattle — Set, judging the parable, awards the cattle to the son, and the court laughs as he realises he has ruled against his own claim. Argument gives way to ordeal, and Set is formidable in every ordeal: the rivals dive as hippopotamuses to outlast each other submerged; Isis's harpoon wounds her own son, heals him, then strikes Set — who pleads kinship so effectively that she releases him, whereupon Horus, raging at her mercy, strikes off his mother's head, and Thoth replaces it with a cow's head, an episode the text uses to explain an iconography of Isis. Set finds Horus resting and tears out his eyes, burying them on a mountain where they grow as lotuses; Hathor heals Horus with gazelle's milk. Set's attempt to disgrace Horus by a sexual assault is inverted by Isis's counter-trick with a pot of lettuce, so that when Thoth calls the seed to account before the tribunal, it is Set's claim that collapses in the court's laughter. Read Set's part whole, and a pattern emerges that neither the demonised nor the rehabilitated caricature captures. Set loses every legal test and wins or nearly wins every physical one; he is beaten by advocacy, by parable, by maternal cunning and by documentary evidence — never by superior force. That is not an accident of plotting. It is the theological thesis of the work: strength is a fact, but office is a judgment , and a cosmos ruled by mꜣꜥt [Gardiner: U1-D36-X1] is one in which the strongest god alive can still lose his case. Set's tragedy in the Contendings — the text permits the word — is that his one unanswerable argument, his service at the prow, is an argument for employment and not for kingship, as the settlement is about to show. // SET'S CASE, AS HE MAKES IT // Seniority — he is the elder brother, surviving heir of the previous generation. Strength — the strongest of the gods, with the great sceptre as his exhibit. Service — he alone spears Apep at the prow of the solar barque , daily. The presiding judge's favour — Ra backs him for most of the eighty years. It is not a frivolous case. That the court finally rules against it anyway is the point of the eighty years: Egyptian legitimacy is not seniority, muscle, or even service, but succession rightly judged. Set's counsel loses; Set's service is retained. Hold both halves. IX. Judgment and Settlement — the Divided Land and the Placed God The Contendings ends, after the stone-boat race — Set's boat genuinely stone, and sunk; Horus's pinewood plastered to look like stone, a cheat the text reports without embarrassment, since trickery in a just cause is Isis's own method — with the gods writing to the one authority not yet heard: Osiris in the realm of the dead. Osiris's answering letter reminds the Ennead that he created the grain that feeds gods and men, and that his messengers can fetch any heart that does evil. What eighty years of advocacy could not settle, the dead king's letter settles. Horus is awarded the office of his father and crowned. The standard treatment of the verdict's royal dimension — the srḫ [Gardiner: O33] [𓊁] serekh, the fivefold titulary, the son performing the Opening of the Mouth

Ethics of Substitution — Responsibility for the Delegated Act I. The Ontology of the Shabti — Functional Surrogacy A Shabti (also shawabti or ushabti ; wšbtj [Gardiner: G43-N37-D58-X1-Z4-A40]) is a small anthropoid figurine found in Kemetic tombs. Only the later form ushabti , prevalent after Dynasty 21, is derived from wšb "to answer" — hence "The Answerer." The earlier shabti/shawabti has a debated derivation; a leading explanation is from šwꜣb , the persea wood of the earliest figures. Their function was to perform manual labor on behalf of the deceased in the afterlife, specifically the agricultural maintenance of the Field of Reeds ( sḫt-jꜣrw [Gardiner: S29-Aa1-X1-M17-G1-D21-G43-M20]). In this research framework, shabtis are viewed as Delegated Sub-Processes . They are functional magical surrogates designed to handle the "Low-Frequency" material maintenance of the afterlife, freeing the transfigured Akh to focus on high-bandwidth divine navigation and solar resonance. The shabti is an Autonomous Informational Agent —a piece of "Ritual Hardware" programmed with a specific "Activation Script" ( Spell 6 ). Form of the word Period of prevalence Derivation šꜣbtj / šꜣwꜣbtj (shabti, shawabti) Middle Kingdom to Dynasty 21 Debated; a leading explanation derives it from šwꜣb , persea wood, the material of early figures wšbtj (ushabti) After Dynasty 21, through the Ptolemaic period From wšb , "to answer" — the figure that answers "Here I am" (Section IV) The corpus against which every general claim in this article is checked is Schneider's Shabtis (National Museum of Antiquities, Leiden, 1977): three volumes cataloguing the Leiden collection by period, material, iconography, and inscription, and still the typological backbone of shabti studies, supplemented by the Auberts' Paris corpus (Section VI). Shabtis are, with scarabs, among the most numerous of all Egyptian antiquities — which is why the type can be studied statistically, as a production history, and not only as a gallery of masterpieces. II. Origins — Retainer Burials and the Later Appearance of Shabtis The concept of the shabti represents a profound ethical and technical advancement in the Kemetic awareness field. In the 1st Dynasty (under kings like Aha and Djer), the burial of the Pharaoh was accompanied by Subsidiary Burials —hundreds of retainers and craftsmen who were ritually executed to serve the King in the afterlife. Shabtis themselves do not appear in the 2nd Dynasty, and no source links them to the end of retainer sacrifice. They first appear in the Middle Kingdom , and the shabti spell first occurs as Coffin Texts Spell 472 (mid-12th Dynasty, c. 1850 BCE), later becoming Book of the Dead Spell 6. The retainer burials themselves deserve a precise sentence, since they are the article's point of departure. Around the tomb and funerary enclosure of Djer at Umm el-Qaab, Abydos, the subsidiary graves number in the hundreds — courtiers, craftsmen, and women of the court, buried with the king in the early 1st Dynasty. The practice fades within the dynasty and is gone by the 2nd; human sacrifice is not a standing institution of pharaonic Egypt but an episode of its first century. Between that episode and the first shabti lies more than a thousand years with no connecting evidence — model servants in Middle Kingdom tomb equipment (Section XVI) belong to the shabti's own era, not to a survival from Djer's. Older literature sometimes proposed the Old Kingdom reserve heads — limestone heads placed in 4th-Dynasty mastaba burials — as the shabti's ancestors, as substitute bodies for the dead. The Art Institute of Chicago's standard summary (Emily Teeter) repeats the suggestion only to anchor the chronology against it: the first shabtis proper are Middle Kingdom, and no developmental line from the Giza reserve heads to the Deir el-Bersha figures has been demonstrated. This article follows the demonstrated chronology: substitute body first (Middle Kingdom, Section XVII), labour spell attached in the 12th Dynasty, workforce thereafter. The Amarna episode supplies the institution's strangest royal variant, and it belongs to the origin story's end rather than to §XI's survey. Akhenaten, whose funerary beliefs broke with Osiris and the Duat, was nonetheless buried with shabtis — figures of the king in the traditional mummiform shape, many now fragmentary from the Royal Tomb at Amarna — inscribed not with Spell 6 (§XI) but with an offering formula to the Aten. The institution was older than the theology that explained it, and at Amarna it outlasted its own explanation for the length of one reign: the answerers answered a sun-disc instead. III. The Evolution of the Set — From Solitary to Industrial The earliest burials held a single figure : one shabti in the Middle Kingdom, occasionally a pair. Through the 18th Dynasty the number grew slowly — a handful in an elite burial, still conceived as the deceased's own substitute rather than a workforce. In the 19th Dynasty sets of several figures become normal, and by the late New Kingdom a wealthy burial might hold ten or more. The decisive change came in the Third Intermediate Period . The set was reorganised on the calendar: 365 worker shabtis , one for each day of the Egyptian year, supervised by 36 overseers , one for each gang of ten — 401 figures in total (see Section VIII). Hans Schneider's three-volume corpus Shabtis (1977), the standard typology of the figures and their spells, documents this standardisation across the Leiden collection and beyond. In practice the full complement was an ideal more often approached than reached, and many sets fall short of it. In the Late Period the numbers stayed in the hundreds but the overseer type was dropped; the workers once again carried the whole duty alone. In this framework the arc is a scaling history: from a solitary Surrogate to a calendrical Array — the same function, industrialised. The crystallised Third Intermediate Period set can be audited in a museum drawer. The burial of the chantress Nauny (Dynasty 21, reign of Psusennes I), found in TT 358 at Deir el-Bahri by the Metropolitan Museum's excavations of 1928–29, contained 393 shabtis — the Met's object records count 355 workers and 37 overseers among them — divided between seven shabti boxes (Section XIV). Nauny was not royalty; she was a temple singer of Amun's household. That a private burial of c. 1050 BCE fields a near-complete calendar array is the single best exhibit for this section's claim: by Dynasty 21 the industrial set was an elite norm, not a royal extravagance. The set was also a purchase , and one receipt survives: the papyrus now British Museum EA 10800 records the production of a full complement of 401 shabtis for one Padikhonsu — documentary proof, from the period itself, that the 365 + 36 array was a standard commercial specification a customer could order and a workshop could be held to. The priestly dynasties of Thebes show the array at work inside a ruling house. The High Priests of Amun of Dynasty 21 — Herihor, Pinudjem I, and their families — were buried with shabti sets in the hundreds, in faience of the period's characteristic blue, and their women with sets to match (Nauny, §III, was of this world). The royal cache (DB 320) and the Bab el-Gasus cache (§V) between them held the shabtis of an entire governing class, which is why the Third Intermediate Period, poor in monuments beside the New Kingdom, is the richest of all periods in shabtis: the institution had become the dynasty's principal funerary investment. Spell 6 of the Book of the Dead — The Activation Code The shabti was brought to life through the recitation of Spell 6 from the Book of the Dead . This text was usually inscribed directly on the figurine's body in horizontal bands of hieroglyphs. THE ACTIVATION SCRIPT "O shabti, if the Osiris [Name] is counted off for any work that is to be done there in the realm of the dead... to cultivate the fields, to water the banks, to transport sand of the east to the west; 'Here am I' you shall say." This formula is a Theurgical Binding . It utilizes the name ( Ren ) of the deceased to link the figurine to the individual's Ka-field . When the celestial "Call to Labor" is issued by the guardians of the Duat, the shabti's programming intercepts the signal and "answers" in place of the owner. It is an act of Identity Masking for the purpose of labor-evasion. The spell has a textual history as articulated as the figures'. Its first form, Coffin Texts Spell 472 (mid-12th Dynasty, c. 1850 BCE, on coffins from Deir el-Bersha), already addresses the figure and assigns it the field labour; the Book of the Dead Spell 6 recension expands the commission — the fullest versions add the transport of sand "of the east to the west" and the formula of self-announcement quoted in this page's header (Faulkner's translation, which this archive prints as its epigraph and preserves verbatim). Shorter and longer recensions circulated side by side for a millennium, and Schneider's corpus edits the spell from the figures themselves — hundreds of inscribed copies, no two workshops' texts quite alike (Section XV). Placement carried meaning too. On the classic mummiform figure the spell runs in horizontal registers down the body, or in a single vertical column on the front; on Third Intermediate Period faience workers it is often reduced to the owner's name preceded by the formula's opening words — the whole spell present, as Section XV puts it, by implication. The inscription is not a label about the figure. Within the spell's own logic it is the figure's commission, worn where a worker wears his orders. The spell also circulated off the figures. Book of the Dead papyri carry Spell 6 among their chapters — in the great illustrated papyri the chapter stands with its vignette of the mummiform figure — and the text was copied onto coffins and, in the Middle Kingdom, exists only in its coffin-text form (§IV, second part). The figure in the tomb and the chapter in the book are two deliveries of one instruction; a fully equipped burial had both, as it had both a body and a name. When the papyrus tradition ends, the figures continue alone for another thousand years — the spell's longest-lived carrier turned out to be the statuette it was written for. The Bersha provenance of the spell's first form matters to its reading. Coffin Texts Spell 472 stands on coffins of the nomarchal court of the Hare nome — the great painted cedar coffins of el-Bersha — where the shabti spell keeps company with the object friezes and the Book of Two Ways: the figure's commission was composed in the same scribal world that mapped the netherworld's roads. From the beginning, the answerer is a creature of texts — commissioned by a spell, in a book, on a coffin — before it is a product of workshops. V. Heka and the Binding of the Ka — Theurgy of the Figurine A shabti left the workshop as an object; it entered the tomb as an agent. What made the difference, in Egyptian terms, was Heka — the operative force by which a spoken and written word takes effect — applied through three linked acts: naming, inscription, and deposition . First, the figure was given the owner's name and titles, very often in the form "the Osiris N": the deceased, already identified with Osiris, is the one the figure stands for. Second, Spell 6 (Section IV) was inscribed on the body or spoken over it, binding the figure to answer when its owner was called. Third, the figure was placed with the burial equipment, in its box or miniature coffin (Section XIV), where the call was expected to reach it. The spell's own wording is a speech act: the owner addresses the figure directly and instructs it to say "Here I am." No separate consecration rite for shabtis is preserved as a standalone liturgy; the activation is the formula, the name, and the tomb context working together. In this framework, inscription is programming and naming is addressing: the Ren (name) routes the summons, and Heka is the power that makes the route live. Deposition had its own archaeology, and it shows the figures treated as a workforce in store. Sets were found packed upright in their boxes (Nauny's seven boxes, Section III), ranged around the coffin, placed in wall niches, or — in the great Theban priestly caches of Dynasty 21, above all the Bab el-Gasus cache of 1891, which held the burials of 153 priests and priestesses of Amun — present in such quantity that shabtis and their boxes form a major share of the cache's entire contents. A summons-based system (§IV) needs its answerers findable : the box by the coffin is the muster point, and the cache evidence shows the institution operating at the scale of a whole priestly community at once. A comparison object sharpens the mechanism. The heart scarab , inscribed with Book of the Dead Spell 30B's plea to the heart, is the shabti's cousin in activation: a manufactured object, given a text that instructs it how to behave at a future moment of crisis, and placed on the body to speak when its owner cannot (see Weighing of the Heart ). Egyptian funerary technology repeatedly takes this form — object plus inscribed instruction plus deposition — and the shabti is its most elaborated instance, the only one that grew a workforce, a management layer, and a housing industry (§§VIII, XIV) around the basic device. VI. Materials and Frequencies — Faience, Wood, and Stone What the sources support about shabti materials is a distribution by period and production scale , with status correlations that are real but loose — not the tidy social ladder (stone for kings, terracotta for commoners) that older versions of this section printed. The standard references are Hans D. Schneider, Shabtis (1977), whose typology organises the figures by material, form, and text together, and Jean-François and Liliane Aubert, Statuettes funéraires égyptiennes du département des monnaies, médailles et antiques (1974) and their subsequent corpus work. On their evidence: Faience: the most common shabti material overall, and overwhelmingly the material of the large sets — because it could be moulded in quantity (Emily Teeter, Art Institute of Chicago: the 401-figure sets were "commonly molded from faience or pottery"). Blue and green glazes dominate; see Section VII for the technology. Wood: prominent from the beginning — the earliest figures are wood and wax (Section XVII), and the word shawabti itself is plausibly tied to šwꜣb , persea wood (Section I) — and standard for well-made private figures of the New Kingdom, often painted in fine detail. No source supports the claim that wooden shabtis were "animated by being painted," and the specific association of wood with Osiris's regenerative power, printed in an earlier version of this section, could not be verified in Schneider or the Auberts and has been removed. Stone: used for royal shabtis and for high-elite private ones — hard-stone figures of senior officials are a recognised class in Schneider's corpus — so stone marks expense and ambition, not royalty exclusively. The claim that stone was "reserved for" royal shabtis is not supported and has been removed. Taharqa's hard-stone array (Section XII) is exceptional in scale, not in kind. Terracotta and pottery: cheap moulded figures occur in quantity in the mass sets of the Third Intermediate Period and later, and unfired clay is among the materials of the earliest experiments (Section XVII). That made pottery the accessible option for modest burials, but "the version used by the common population" overstates a correlation as a rule, and has been softened accordingly. Wax, glass, bronze: wax belongs to the earliest phase (Section XVII); a small number of figures in glass and in bronze are known, chiefly royal or high-elite — curiosities at the edge of the corpus, not classes of their own. In this research framework the material still reads as a durability choice — faience's gleam, stone's permanence, clay's economy — but the framework now follows the catalogues: material tracks date, workshop, and budget first, and cosmic symbolism second. Section VII treats the dominant material's manufacture in full. Colour follows material. The faience palette is dominated by the blues and blue-greens of Section VII, but the catalogues record white, yellow, and red-glazed figures occasionally, and the Third Intermediate Period Theban sets are often a paler, greener blue than the saturated glaze of the New Kingdom. Wooden figures take their colour from paint over gesso; stone figures from the stone itself, serpentine's dark green and calcite's honey-white doing the work paint does elsewhere. "Frequency," in this section's retained title, is therefore read in the archive's voice as a spectrum of finishes — with the distribution above, drawn from Schneider and the Auberts, as the factual ground on which that reading stands. VII. Egyptian Blue — The Tjehnet Resonance Most shabtis that survive in quantity are blue faience . Faience — Egyptian tjehenet , "the gleaming, dazzling one" — is not a clay ceramic but a sintered quartz body with an alkali glaze, and its manufacture is one of the best-reconstructed processes in Egyptian technology. Egyptian blue, the related synthetic pigment and frit (the mineral cuprorivaite, CaCuSi 4 O 10 ), is a different material made from similar ingredients; the two are kept distinct here. Faience — the shabti body (after Tite, Freestone and Bimson's analyses of ancient pieces): Grind white quartz pebbles to powder. Mix the quartz with a little lime, an alkali flux (natron or plant ash), and a copper colourant — metal filings or crushed malachite — with water to a paste. The paste is non-plastic and slumps; it is shaped by hand or pressed into fired-clay open moulds, the standard route for shabtis. Glaze by one of three attested routes: efflorescence (soluble alkali mixed into the body migrates to the surface as it dries), cementation (the dried body is buried in glazing powder and fired), or direct application of a glaze slurry. Fire once at c. 870–1000 °C ; above c. 1000 °C the glaze bubbles and runs. Cool, and paint the details — wig, collar, inscription — in black manganese-based pigment (the black that analysis of surviving shabtis identifies: a manganese compound). Egyptian blue — the related frit: the one surviving ancient recipe is Vitruvius, De architectura 7.11.1 (paraphrase): sand and natron are ground together, copper is filed over the mixture, and the paste is rolled into balls, dried, and fired in jars until it turns blue. Modern reconstruction (Tite and Hatton) runs in two stages: a first firing at c. 950–1000 °C , grinding of the resulting frit, then a second firing at c. 850–950 °C to give a fine, even colour. For blue, copper must exceed lime; invert the ratio and the product is green frit. The colour was the meaning: a saturated turquoise-blue, the colour of the Nile, of lapis, and of rebirth, produced not by mining a rare stone but by manufacturing gleam itself — which is why this archive reads tjehenet as a resonance technology as much as a glaze. VIII. The Rais — Management of the Magical Labor Array In the Third Intermediate Period , the shabti array became complex enough to require its own management layer. New Kingdom sets were far smaller; the full calendar array described below is the Third Intermediate Period standard, not a New Kingdom one. The Overseer Shabti ( rꜣ-is [Gardiner: D21-A1-M17-S29]) was depicted wearing a triangular kilt and holding a whip rather than agricultural tools. Their function was Supervisory Heka . Just as a modern computer requires an "Operating System" to manage sub-routines, the Third Intermediate Period standard set — 401 in total — set 36 overseers over the 365 worker shabtis, one overseer for each gang of ten. The overseer shabti is the personification of the Administrative Intelligence of the soul. The overseer's dress is the detail that proves the type's realism. Where the worker is mummiform — a corpse's shape, with tools — the overseer wears the daily dress of a living foreman : a long kilt, sometimes a shirt, one arm free, a whip or flail in hand. Egyptologists call the type the rais , from the Arabic ra'īs , "chief" — the word modern Egyptian work-gangs still use for their foreman, borrowed back onto the ancient figures by the excavators who employed those gangs. Tutankhamun's exceptional set adds a second management tier the standard array lacks: twelve monthly overseers above the thirty-six of the ten-day gangs — 413 figures in all (365 + 36 + 12), a king's establishment chart drawn in faience, wood, and stone. The overseers' inscriptions mark the hierarchy in text as their dress marks it in form. Workers carry the spell or its opening; overseers very often carry only the owner's name and title , or a short offering formula — they are not themselves spell-bound to labour, and their texts accordingly do not commission work but identify command. In the Nauny set (§III) the ratio in the drawers matches the doctrine in the texts: 37 overseers among 393 figures, each kilted figure legible at a glance among the mummiform ranks. Management, in the shabti array, is a visible caste — which is how the Egyptians ran every other workforce they had. IX. Tools and Iconography — Mapping the Celestial Tasks From the New Kingdom onward the shabti was supplied with the kit of its work, modelled in the round, incised, or simply painted on the body. The standard equipment maps one-to-one onto the tasks named in Spell 6: Hoes , one in each hand or crossed on the chest — for cultivating the fields. A pick or mattock — for breaking ground and working the irrigation banks. A seed basket , slung over the left shoulder and shown hanging down the back, its netted or cross-hatched pattern incised — for carrying grain to the sowing, and on some readings for the sand-carrying task of the spell. Water pots on a yoke, on some New Kingdom figures — for watering the banks. A brick mould , on a minority of figures — for the building work the dead might also be assessed for. The rest of the iconography is the mummy's: tripartite wig, broad collar, crossed arms, and — on figures with a daily-life form rather than a mummiform one — the dress of a living worker. Overseers (Section VIII) break the pattern deliberately: kilt, no tools, a whip instead. Iconography here is a job description worn on the body : read the hands and the back, and you know which clause of the spell the figure was built to fulfil. Two cautions govern the reading of the kit. First, period : modelled tools belong to the developed New Kingdom figure; Middle Kingdom figures carry none, and on the mass faience of the Third Intermediate Period the tools shrink to painted or lightly moulded tokens — the basket on the back reduced to a hatched patch. Second, medium : the finest royal sets were supplied with real miniature equipment kept separately — Tutankhamun's burial contained model hoes, baskets, and yokes in wood and metal alongside the figures, tools at a scale no moulded hand could hold. Iconography and equipment are two deliveries of the same job description, one worn, one issued. The Late Period figure adds one structural feature that belongs to this section's reading of the body: the back pillar , a dorsal slab against which the figure stands, its surface carrying the spell in vertical columns, and the integral base on which the figure stands like a statue (§XVIII). The worker has become monumental — a small upright stela in human form, text-bearing on its back — at exactly the period when the overseers vanish and the single canonical figure must carry the whole institution alone. Form follows reorganisation, here as everywhere in the corpus. Two implements complete the standard reading. The flail , carried by some overseers and a few grand worker figures, is borrowed from the regalia of Osiris himself — authority's emblem, miniaturised to a foreman's badge. And the brick mould (§IX, first part) deserves its clause: brick-making for the tombs and temples of the necropolis was itself assessed labour in the Egyptian economy, and its presence in the kit — rare, and mostly New Kingdom — shows the spell's commission being read expansively by the workshops, beyond the letter of its three named tasks. X. The Field of Reeds (Sekhet-Aaru) — The Site of Labor The workplace named in the spell is the Field of Reeds ( Sekhet-Aaru ), the cultivated paradise of the afterlife pictured most fully in Book of the Dead Spell 110. It is not an escape from agriculture; it is agriculture perfected — a well-watered estate of canals, banks, and grain fields, modelled on the Nile valley itself, where the justified dead plough, reap, eat, and drink. Spell 6 lists the corvée exactly: to cultivate the fields, to irrigate the banks (riverbanks), and to transport sand from the east to the west (Faulkner translation, quoted in Section IV). These were the real levied labours of Egyptian life — field work, canal and dyke maintenance, and hauling — transferred to the next world and assessed there, in the spell's wording, "as a man is assessed for his dues." The shabti system is unintelligible without this premise: the afterlife ran on the same labour tax as Egypt, and the figure is the receipt that pays it. Hence the logic of the whole array (Sections III and VIII): a year of days requires a year of workers, and the Field's harvest — figured in Spell 110 with grain of fabulous height — feeds the dead forever. Labour, delegated, becomes abundance. The Field's most famous portrait is also its most instructive complication. In the tomb of the craftsman Sennedjem (TT 1, Deir el-Medina), the Spell 110 vignette shows Sennedjem and his wife themselves ploughing, sowing, and reaping in the Field of Reeds — the owners at work, in paradise, with their own hands. The shabti was therefore never a simple refusal of labour: the same culture that bought 401 answerers pictured its blessed dead happily farming. The spell's own wording resolves the paradox — the dead are assessed for labour "as a man is assessed for his dues," a corvée owed to the order of things — and the shabti answers the assessment , the levy, not the blessed work of one's own estate. Delegation, here as in §XX, has a defined and limited jurisdiction. Spell 110's geography repays a closer look, because it is a map . The vignette tradition divides the Field into registers of canals and islands, names its waters and its guardian, and gives the blessed dead a working estate with a harbour, a ferry, and neighbouring plots held by the gods themselves — the Field of Offerings ( Sekhet-Hetep ) adjoining the Field of Reeds in the fuller descriptions. The grain of its fields is of fabulous measure in the texts that quantify it. A workplace this thoroughly surveyed is not a metaphor for rest: it is Egypt improved and made permanent, and the shabti's commission (§IV) is written against its survey — fields to cultivate, banks to water, sand to carry from its east to its west. Spell 6 task Season of the earthly original The levy it answers Cultivate the fields Peret — sowing and tending after the flood recedes The agricultural corvée of the estate system Irrigate / water the banks Akhet into Peret — dyke and channel work as waters are managed The hydraulic maintenance every landholder owed Transport sand, east to west Year-round hauling labour Clearing sand from canals and fields — the spell's most purely servile clause XI. Royal Shabtis — High-Bandwidth Sovereignty Proxies Royal shabtis (such as those of Amenhotep III or Seti I) were produced with extraordinary artistic and technical precision. These figurines were often made of precious materials like blue glass or carved from hard stones like serpentine. They functioned as High-Fidelity Proxies for the Pharaoh's Sekhem (Power). Royal shabtis characteristically bear Book of the Dead Spell 6, like other shabtis — Tutankhamun's set, for example, carries the full spell on 29 of his 413 figures, with name and title only on the rest. The well-known royal exception is Akhenaten's, whose shabtis bear an Aten offering formula instead of the shabti speech. No source supports royal shabtis inscribed with "royal decrees" for administrative functions in the Duat. The royal corpus has its own benchmarks. The non-royal tomb of Yuya and Tjuyu (KV 46) — the parents of Queen Tiye — held shabtis of a quality indistinguishable from royal work, one more proof (with Section VI) that the top of the shabti market served rank and wealth, not kingship alone. From the tomb of Seti I (KV 17) come large wooden shabtis now dispersed among the world's museums, carved with a sculptural finish no mould ever produced; from Tutankhamun's , the 413 figures of Section VIII in wood, faience, quartzite, and calcite, the finest wearing the king's own face and the nemes headdress. Royal shabtis differ from private ones in budget and finish. In text, dress, and duty they are the same institution — the king, too, is assessed for his dues (§X). At the institution's social summit stand the shabtis of the God's Wives of Amun of the Third Intermediate Period — the celibate princess-priestesses who ruled Thebes in Amun's name. The stone shabtis of the God's Wife Amenirdis I are among the best-known figures of the period: royal in material and finish, private in scale of set, and a precise marker of where sovereignty actually sat in the Thebes of her century. The class confirms this section's rule from §VI — material and workmanship track power and wealth as they were, not a constitutional diagram of who was allowed what. XII. The Taharqa Array — The 25th Dynasty Hardening The largest royal shabti provision known belongs to Taharqa (reigned 690–664 BCE), the Kushite king of the 25th Dynasty, buried in pyramid Nu 1 at Nuri in Nubia. Excavated by George Reisner's Harvard University–Museum of Fine Arts expedition in 1916–1918, the burial held shabtis on a scale beyond any Egyptian royal set: Dows Dunham's publication of the royal cemeteries of Kush and the Auberts' catalogue estimated about 1,070 figures, and Joyce Haynes's study of the Boston holdings puts the total at at least 1,122 , counting the hundreds of fragments preserved there. The material is the message. Where contemporary Egyptian sets were faience, Taharqa's figures were carved in hard stones — serpentine and other coloured stones among them — making him, on Haynes's assessment, the first king since the New Kingdom to commission hard-stone shabtis, and the figures are correspondingly large, the finest series standing over 40 cm tall. They carry versions of Book of the Dead Spell 6 and are now dispersed among museums worldwide, the largest group in Boston. Later Napatan kings followed the precedent — Senkamanisken's Nuri set is the direct heir. Whether his set was smaller than Taharqa's is not settled : published counts for Senkamanisken vary, and at least one catalogue estimate exceeds 1,200 figures, which would rival or exceed the Taharqa totals above; the "reduced scale" wording of an earlier version of this section is therefore not repeated here. In this framework the Taharqa array is a hardening : the calendar workforce of Section III re-executed in the most durable medium available, by a dynasty asserting pharaonic legitimacy in stone. The dispersal is part of the record. Taharqa's figures reached museums in Khartoum, Boston, London, Paris, Berlin, Copenhagen, and beyond — largely through the partage of the Reisner excavations and the antiquities market that followed earlier, unrecorded digging at Nuri — so the "array" of this section's title is today a scholarly reconstruction from dozens of catalogues, Schneider's and the Auberts' among them, rather than a set any single visitor can see. The two headline counts (§XII, first paragraph) differ because the populations they count differ — whole figures in Dunham's publication against the Boston fragments in Haynes's — and the archive prints both attributions rather than averaging them into a false precision. XIII. Craftsmen of the Surrogates — The Artisans of Deir el-Medina Who made the shabtis? For the Theban necropolis the best evidence comes from Deir el-Medina , the village of the royal tomb crew — the "Servants in the Place of Truth" — whose members were themselves the most prolific private buyers and makers of funerary equipment in the New Kingdom. The same carpenters, sculptors, and painters who cut the kings' tombs produced coffins, stelae, and shabtis for their own families and for each other, in private
