Ethics of Navigation — Maintaining the Solar Frequency I. The Ontology of the Barque — The Celestial Circuit The Solar Barque (Ancient Egyptian: wiꜣ [Gardiner: P1]) is the primary divine vehicle utilized by the sun god Re to traverse the sky and the underworld. The journey is a continuous, twenty-four-hour cycle that ensures the maintenance of Ma'at and the perpetual rebirth of the universe. In this research framework, the Barque is viewed as a Coherent Energy-Envelope . It is the functional shield that protects the divine essence (the solar frequency) as it passes through the diverse densities, dimensional thresholds, and entropic dangers of the awareness field. The Barque is not merely a "boat" in the physical sense, but a localized zone of Stabilized Ma'at that permits the creator to navigate the chaotic potential of the Nun . II. The Sky as River — The Watery Field of Nut The Egyptians viewed the sky not as a void, but as a celestial river (the Mehet-Weret [Gardiner: G17-V28-X1-G43-D21-X1], "The Great Flood"). This river is the manifest form of the goddess Nut. Because the sky is a watery medium, navigation requires a vessel. The Solar Barque is the Terrestrial Prototype for all Egyptian rivercraft, but on a cosmic scale. This watery ontology implies that reality is fundamentally Fluid and Informational . The sun god does not "fly" through space; he "sails" through the data-currents of the divine mind. The celestial river has a name of its own in the oldest texts: the Winding Waterway, the channel of the northern sky across which the ferryman of Section XIX plies. Its winding is the point. The sky-river is not the straight canal of the irrigation surveyor but a meandering stream with sandbanks, shallows, and a far bank that must be reached by skill, which is why the sun's vessel needs a crew of faculties rather than a single ferryman, and why Apep's chosen weapon, in Section XIV, is a sandbank. Geography is destiny in the Duat: whoever controls the water controls the journey, and the whole nightly war is fought over draught, depth, and the few metres of water under the hull. III. The Mandjet — The Day Barque of Manifestation The Mandjet ( mꜥnḏt [Gardiner: G17-D36-N35-I10-X1-P1]) is the vessel of the rising and midday sun. It sails across the celestial river from dawn to dusk. This phase represents the Diurnal Bandwidth —the time of manifest light, growth, and the established order of the Pharaonic state. The Mandjet is the "Barque of Becoming," where the solar potential is fully actualized in the material field. It is characterized by High-Frequency Visibility . During this phase, the sun god is at his most accessible and authoritative, presiding over the "Land of the Living." The day vessel's passenger is the god in his public forms. At dawn he is Khepri, the scarab, the becoming one, pushing himself into the sky as the beetle pushes its ball; at noon he is Re in his strength, the falcon-headed lord of the horizon; toward evening he ages into Atum, the complete one, whose name carries the sense of a finished sum. The Books of the Sky (Section XVIII) chart these hours across the body of Nut, and the temple day was built to rhyme with them: the dawn service of the daily ritual, whose sequence the archive sets out in Ma'at & Isfet , opened the god's shrine at the hour the Mandjet cleared the eastern horizon, so that the cult image in its dark room and the sun in the brightening sky began their day in the same gesture. The Mandjet is therefore also a timetable for human worship; to know which vessel the god is in is to know what the temples are doing. IV. The Mesektet — The Night Barque of Regeneration The Mesektet ( msktet [Gardiner: G17-S29-V31-X1-X1-P1]) is the vessel of the setting and nocturnal sun. As the sun enters the western horizon ( Akhet ), it transitions from the Mandjet to the Mesektet. This phase represents the Nocturnal Bandwidth —the time of hidden transformation, the processing of data from the day, and the perilous work of regeneration. The Mesektet is the "Barque of Dissolution," where the solar essence must descend into the Duat to be "recharged" by the chthonic power of Osiris . This is the Nigredo phase of the solar cycle, where the light is hidden and the system is most vulnerable to the entropic noise of Apep . The night vessel's passenger is the god in his hidden form: ram-headed, a form the texts call Afu-Ra, the flesh of Re, the sun as body rather than blaze. The change of form is a change of physics. The day form radiates; the night form is carried. In the first hours the Mesektet is rowed and towed through watered country; in the Sokar hours it is hauled over sand; at the sandbank of Apep it is stuck fast and must be freed by magic; and in the last hour it is drawn through the body of the great serpent Life of the Gods and comes out of the serpent's mouth renewed. The vessel that enters the west is a ship; the vessel that leaves the east is a birth. The Mesektet's twelve hours, charted in Section XII, are the record of how the one is turned into the other without ever ceasing, in the texts' own presentation, to be the same boat with the same god in the shrine. V. The Names of the Vessels — wjꜣ, mꜥnḏt, msktt The barque has a vocabulary before it has a mythology, and the vocabulary is worth setting out exactly, because the names carry the theology. The generic word for a sacred or freight boat in the texts is wjꜣ [Gardiner: P1], written with the boat sign itself. The day vessel of Section III is the mꜥnḏt [Gardiner: G17-D36-N35-I10-X1-P1], the Mandjet; the night vessel of Section IV is the msktt [Gardiner: G17-S29-V31-X1-X1-P1], the Mesektet. Neither name has a secure etymology, and the archive does not invent one; what the names do in the texts is mark the two watches of a single duty. The sun does not own two boats in the way a king owns two chariots. He owns one office with a day shift and a night shift, and the names are the shift titles. The day vessel also carries the grandest title in the whole complex: the Boat of Millions of Years, wjꜣ-n-ḥḥw , the vessel whose passengers and crew are reckoned not in dozens but in the ḥḥw , the millions, the uncountable company of the gods and the justified dead who travel with the sun. The title appears already in the spell literature the dead used to claim their own passage (Section XIX), and it states the social fact about the barque that the royal books sometimes obscure: the barque is crowded. Re sails as a king sails, with a court, and Egypt's hope, from the Coffin Texts onward, was to be mustered into that court rather than left standing on the bank. A third name completes the set, and it belongs to the earth. When the god's image travelled on land or water in procession, it travelled in a portable barque carried on poles, and the greatest of these, the river barque of Amun at Karnak, bore its own name, Userhat. Section XXIII treats the processional barques as the solar vessel's terrestrial counterparts. The names matter because Egyptian theology trusts names: to call the boat Mandjet at dawn and Mesektet at dusk is to say that the change of name is itself part of the machinery, the moment the office changes watch and the god takes his night form, ram-headed Afu-Ra, for the passage through the body of the underworld. VI. The Divine Crew — The Crew of the Solar Mind The Solar Barque is not navigated by Re alone. It is steered, defended, and powered by a crew of deities representing the creator's Essential Faculties . This crew constitutes the "Operating Team" of the universe. The crew includes Sia, Hu and Heka, who are grouped in New Kingdom theology with Irer and Sedjem as creative powers of Amun-Ra (see Sia Wiki ). No authoritative source identifies the crew as a numbered list of fourteen Kas of Re. Each god on the boat manages a specific "Bandwidth" of the operation, ensuring that the solar frequency does not decohere during the passage. VII. Sia — The Lookout of Perception Sia (Perception) stands at the prow of the barque. He is the Divine Scout . His role is to "witness" the path. Because the Duat is a non-linear, illusory environment, Re requires a faculty of Perfect Pattern-Recognition to identify the gates and the "Hidden Forms" of the entities encountered. Sia provides the "Input Data" required for navigation. Without Sia, the Barque would be blind and would surely crash against the shoals of chaos. See Sia — Divine Perception . VIII. Hu — The Pilot of Authoritative Utterance Hu (Utterance) also stands at the prow, often paired with Sia. He is the Divine Pilot . His role is to "speak" the Barque through the thresholds. In the Kemetic afterlife, every gate-guardian must be addressed by their "True Name." Hu provides the Vibrational Password that forces the gates to open. He is the "Output Command" that materializes the path perceived by Sia. See Hu — Authoritative Utterance . IX. Heka — The Energy of the Defense Heka (Magic) is the primary defender of the Barque. He provides the Active Shielding . Heka represents the underlying energy that allows the thoughts of Sia and the words of Hu to affect the fabric of the Duat. He is the "Current" that powers the Barque’s magical weaponry. When the serpent Apep attempts to "paralyze" the boat through his hypnotic gaze, Heka provides the counter-frequency that keeps the crew focused and the boat moving. See Heka — The Primordial Force . X. Set — The Martial Protector against Apep In the New Kingdom versions of the journey, Set ( stẖ [Gardiner: E20]) occupies a crucial role. He stands at the prow, spear in hand, as the only god capable of looking directly at Apep without fear. This is the Rehabilitated Set (see Hyksos Exchange ). His "low-frequency" martial power is the only force capable of physically repelling the "extreme low-frequency" chaos of the serpent. Set acts as the Kinetic Firewall of the Barque, physically spearing the entropic monster every night to ensure the sun's passage. XI. The Wider Crew — Variation, Towing Gods, and the Company of the Barque Sections VII to X describe the crew by function: perception, utterance, power, and the spear. A necessary caution belongs over the whole arrangement, and the sources themselves impose it. The crew's stations vary by text and by tableau. One standard arrangement, repeated across New Kingdom representations, sets the ram-headed night form of the god, Afu-Ra, in the shrine amidships, flanked by Sia ahead of him and Heka behind, with the coils of Mehen (Section XV) wrapped around the shrine itself. Other scenes redistribute the company, add gods for a single hour, or show the barque hauled by teams of towing gods on the banks where the water fails. No single station plan is universal, and this article's functional reading should be taken as a reading of roles, not as the deck plan of one historical vessel. Beyond the core faculties, the wider tradition staffs the boat from the whole pantheon as the journey requires. Thoth attends as reckoner and scribe of the voyage, the moon-god whose own light keeps the count of the night hours. Ma'at herself may stand at the prow, order personified riding at the front of the vessel whose whole journey is her maintenance. In the hours of the Amduat the company changes with the country: unnamed gods of each region join the tow-ropes or fall back as their hour passes, the justified dead take oars, and in the twelfth hour the barque is drawn through the body of the great serpent by gods stationed at either end of the passage. The crew, in other words, is not a fixed complement but a muster, renewed hour by hour from whatever ordered beings the night provides. The theological weight of the variation is easy to miss. A boat with a single eternal crew would make the journey a private affair of the sun. A boat whose crew is recruited from gods, dead kings, and the justified dead of every region makes the journey the constitution of the cosmos: everything that exists in order takes its turn at the ropes. That is why the spell literature of Section XIX can promise an ordinary dead person a place in the vessel. The promise is not flattery. It is a job posting, and the night has twelve hours of shifts to fill. XII. The 12 Hours of the Night — The Topography of the Duat The night journey is charted, hour by hour, in the Amduat , "That Which Is in the Netherworld," the earliest of the royal Netherworld Books (§XVI), whose earliest complete version covers the walls of the tomb of Thutmose III (KV34). The Duat is divided into twelve hours, each a named region with its own gate, inhabitants and conditions, drawn in three registers with the barque travelling the middle register. In the first hour Re enters through the western horizon, the transitional zone between day and night. In the second and third hours the barque sails a well-watered country, the region called Wernes and then the Waters of Osiris, distributing provision to the gods and the dead who dwell there. In the fourth hour the water fails: the barque enters the sandy realm of Sokar, Imhet, where it is hauled along zigzag paths in darkness, transformed for the passage into a fire-breathing serpent. In the fifth hour it passes over the hidden cavern of Sokar, beneath the mound that covers the tomb of Osiris, with the Lake of Fire beside it. The sixth hour is the midnight depth, the union of Re and Osiris treated in §XIII. In the seventh hour Apep attacks and is bound, the crisis of §XIV. In the eighth hour Re opens the doors of the tomb and calls the gods of the caverns to life with his voice. In the ninth hour the barque is rowed vigorously back onto open water. In the tenth hour the regeneration begun at midnight proceeds in the depths of the waters. In the eleventh hour Re's eyes are made whole again, the damned are punished in pits of fire, and the barque is made ready at the Mouth of the Cavern. In the twelfth hour the barque is towed through the body of the great serpent called Life of the Gods, entering at its tail and emerging from its mouth, and Re comes out into the eastern horizon renewed, in the form of Khepri, the scarab of the morning. The twelve hours are thus a single itinerary with a fixed topography: descent, water, desert, union, crisis, and ascent, in that order, every night. The Twelve Hours at a Glance — The Amduat Register Hour 1: entry through the western horizon; the barque and its crew are mustered for the night. Hour 2: the watered country of Wernes; provisions are distributed to the gods and the dead. Hour 3: the Waters of Osiris; the distribution continues along the banks. Hour 4: the water fails; the sandy realm of Sokar, Imhet, where the barque is hauled and takes serpent form. Hour 5: the hidden cavern of Sokar beneath the mound of Osiris's tomb, the Lake of Fire beside the road. Hour 6: the midnight depth; the union of Re and Osiris (Section XIII). Hour 7: Apep's sandbank; the serpent bound and cut (Section XIV). Hour 8: the doors of the tombs opened; the gods of the caverns called to life by the god's voice. Hour 9: open water again; the crew rows with renewed strength. Hour 10: regeneration proceeds in the depths of the waters. Hour 11: the god's eyes made whole; the damned punished in pits of fire; the barque readied at the Mouth of the Cavern. Hour 12: passage through the body of the serpent Life of the Gods; emergence in the east as Khepri. XIII. The Sixth Hour — The Midnight Union of Re and Osiris The deepest point of the nocturnal journey occurs in the Sixth Hour . This is the moment of the Midnight Union . RA IN OSIRIS, OSIRIS IN RA: In the tomb of Seti I, this hour is described as the moment when the "Corpse of Re" and the "Soul of Osiris" merge. This is the Alchemical Marriage of the solar (active/spirit) and chthonic (receptive/body) principles. The union triggers a massive theurgical "Flash"—the spark of life that will eventually lead to the sun's rebirth at dawn. It is the moment when "Potential" and "Actuality" become one, proving that the solar order cannot exist without the depth of the underworld. The Amduat's own account of the hour is sparer and stranger than the allegory built on it. The barque reaches the deepest region of the Duat, where the corpse of the sun god lies, and the god's ba, his mobile soul, unites with his own corpse: the traveller and the destination are the same being at two ends of his life. The hour also holds the ordered dead, kings and gods of the deep, who receive the god's address and their provisions in the darkness, so that the union is not private ecstasy but administration conducted at the bottom of the world. An inscriptional formula associated with this mystery in the New Kingdom sums the reciprocity in one line of paraphrase: Re rests in Osiris, and Osiris rests in Re. What the formula claims is that neither god completes the circuit alone. The sun needs the corpse's stillness to be remade; the corpse needs the sun's visit to be more than a corpse. The barque is the appointment between them, and it is kept nightly, at the hour when nothing else in the Duat is awake to witness it. XIV. The Seventh Hour — The Crisis of the Serpent Apep Immediately following the union, the Barque faces its greatest crisis in the Seventh Hour . The serpent Apep drinks the water of the celestial river, attempting to ground the boat and terminate the solar cycle forever. This is the Entropic Crisis . The Barque must navigate through a "dry" landscape, relying entirely on the Heka of Isis and the spear of Set to overcome the monster. This hour represents the moment in any creative or spiritual work where the "Fuel" (the water) seems to vanish, and the operator must rely on pure Will and Magic to maintain the trajectory. The hour's mechanics are given in the Amduat with unusual precision. Apep has swallowed the water of the stretch before the barque, and his sandbank, the shoal his own body makes, grounds the vessel; the crew cannot row a river that is inside the serpent. The counter-attack is magical before it is martial. Isis works her spells from the prow, Serqet assists in the binding, and the serpent is lassoed, chained, and cut by the knife-bearing gods of the hour, his head held down while the barque is worked free across his back. Set's spear-work of Section X belongs to the same complex of images, the prow as the place where the fight is joined. The sequence matters for the whole article: the barque is saved not by sailing faster but by being correctly defended in place, word, chain, and knife, until the river is given back. Every anti-Apep rite performed on earth, the whole of the archive's Apep article, is this hour re-enacted by human crews in temples, at the hours the text prescribes. XV. Mehen the Enveloper — Protective Theurgical Geometry The naos (shrine) containing Re on the Barque is protected by the coiled serpent Mehen ( mḥn [Gardiner: V22-N35]). Mehen envelops the solar essence in its massive coils, acting as a Faraday Cage for the spirit. In the "Game of Mehen" (a Predynastic board game), the player navigates a coiled path to reach the center—a mirror of the soul's journey. Mehen represents the Protective Geometry required to shield high-frequency information from the background radiation of the Duat. It is the "Hardened Shell" of the solar consciousness. The game deserves its evidence stated plainly, because it is among the oldest board games in the world. Mehen boards, a coiled serpent whose body is divided into squares, are known from the Predynastic period and the early dynasties, played with gaming pieces in the form of lions and lionesses and with small spheres, the whole set travelling a spiral path toward the serpent's head at the centre. The game's religious charge is visible in its name: the board is the god. To play Mehen was to move pieces along the coils of the protector who wraps the shrine of Re, a domestic rehearsal of the night journey at the scale of a table, in which reaching the centre alive is the whole object. The boards disappear from the record after the Old Kingdom, but the god does not: Mehen keeps his post around the shrine in the netherworld books for two thousand years after his game is forgotten, the coils outlasting the counters. XVI. The Netherworld Books — Navigation Manuals The barque's journey is documented in a connected corpus of New Kingdom royal compositions, the Netherworld Books , treated in full in The Netherworld Books . The Amduat (§XII) gives the twelve-hour itinerary itself. The Book of Gates , first attested in the late Eighteenth Dynasty, retells the same passage with the emphasis on the gates between the hours, their guardians and the judgment of the dead set within the journey. The Book of Caverns divides the night into six caverns and follows the barque's light into the deepest places of punishment and renewal, while the Book of the Earth gathers the chthonic scenes of the sun's passage through the body of the earth. Around these stand the solar litanies and the Books of the Sky, which chart the sun's course across the body of Nut by day as the books of the night chart it below. These were working documents of the royal tomb, inscribed on burial-chamber walls so that the dead king, identified with Re and with Osiris, possessed the names, the order of the regions and the words required at each gate. In the framework of this article they are the barque's Navigation Manuals : not illustrations of a journey imagined once, but the retained charts of a route sailed nightly, kept where the one traveller who most needed them would find them. The detailed topography, hour by hour and book by book, is given in The Netherworld Books . XVII. The Litany of Ra — Seventy-Five Forms of the One God The barque's god is one, but the texts insist on counting him. The composition modern scholarship calls the Litany of Ra, whose full title runs "Book of Praying to Re in the West, Praying to the United One in the West," opens with a Great Litany invoking the sun in seventy-five forms , each named and, in the illustrated versions, each pictured as a distinct figure: the god as flame, as serpent, as cat, as corpse, as child, form after form of a single power that the night keeps dividing and the litany keeps reuniting. A second part follows in which the king, praying, assumes the forms of gods and of nature in turn, until the identification the whole night journey works toward is stated outright: the king and the sun are one traveller. The Litany's first home is the tomb of Thutmose III (KV34), the same burial that holds the first complete Amduat of Section XII: the seventy-five forms cover the faces of the two pillars of the burial chamber, standing at the room's centre exactly where the Amduat on the walls reaches its midnight depth, so that text, image, and architecture make one argument about the union of Re and Osiris. The composition is also early attested in the tomb of Thutmose's vizier Useramun, a rare favouring of a non-royal tomb, and a complete early copy survives on the linen burial shroud that Amenhotep II dedicated to his father. From the reign of Seti I the Litany moves to the entrances of royal tombs, a threshold text: the visitor meets the god's seventy-five names before meeting his journey. Erik Hornung's edition of 1975 remains the standard presentation of all the New Kingdom versions. For this article the Litany matters as the barque's manifest. The Amduat tells where the vessel goes; the Litany tells who, in full, is aboard: not one form of the sun but seventy-five, gathered by name at the start of the night so that none of them can be lost in it. The count is the archive's fixed point wherever it appears in these pages: seventy-five forms, neither seventy-four nor seventy-six, the number Hornung's edition establishes and the number the archive's consistency checks enforce across every article that cites it. XVIII. The Books of the Sky — Nut's Body and the Day Journey Section XVI followed the books of the night. The day has books too, and they are drawn on a body. In the Books of the Sky, the goddess Nut arches over the world, and the sun's day journey is a journey across her: swallowed by her in the evening, carried through her body in the night, and born from her in the morning, red with the birth. The Book of the Day and the Book of the Night , preserved most fully in the tombs of the later Ramesside kings, divide the same circuit at the horizon line, the day book following the barque across the sky from hour to hour of daylight, the night book following it through the hours of darkness that the Amduat maps from below. The two perspectives are complementary instruments: the netherworld books chart the river; the sky books chart the body the river runs through. Behind both stands the older composition scholars call the Book of Nut, or, from its content, the Fundamentals of the Course of the Stars. Its earliest surviving setting is the cenotaph of Seti I at Abydos, the Osireion, and it pairs its picture of the goddess with a working astronomy: the decanal stars, the thirty-six star-groups whose risings marked the hours and the ten-day weeks of the Egyptian calendar, are shown transiting the body of Nut, entering and leaving her as the sun does. The barque's journey is therefore also a clock. To sail with Re is to be carried through a measured night by a vessel whose timetable the stars on the goddess's body publish to anyone who can read them. The day journey has its own stations in these books: the hours of the morning when the god is a child, the blaze of noon when the barque rides highest and the shadow shrinks to nothing, the afternoon decline in which the god ages toward the western horizon and the form of Atum, the evening form, the complete one who ends the day as Khepri began it. The archive's Ra article treats the forms of the day in full. Here the point is the vessel's continuity through them: Mandjet and Mesektet are one barque under two names (Section V) because the body it sails is one body, and the sky books are the proof drawn at full scale on tomb ceilings, where the king sleeps inside the diagram. XIX. Boarding the Barque — The Ferryman's Questions and Spells 99–100 The royal books reserve the barque to the king and the gods. The spell literature gives it to anyone who can pass an examination. Its classic form is Book of the Dead Spell 99, "for bringing a ferryboat," whose ancestry runs back through Coffin Texts Spells 404–405 to the early Middle Kingdom coffins, and whose procedure UCL's Digital Egypt presentation, following the Papyrus of Nu (British Museum EA 10477), sets out in detail. The dead traveller must first summon the ferry across a difficult sandbank, addressing its crew, the bringer of the ferry, the lord of the tempest, the keeper of the secret ferry, in terms that already name the danger of the crossing: the sandbank is called the sandbank of Apep. Then the boat itself interrogates him. The examination is a naming test, part by part, and every part answers with a mythological name that the traveller must supply. The mooring-post is Lord of the Two Lands in the shrine. The mallet is the haunch of the Apis. The prow-rope is the tress of Anubis from the embalmers' labour. The rudder is Aker, the earth god. The mast is the bringer of the great goddess after her distance. The sail is Nut. The oars are the fingers of Horus the Elder. The bailer is the hand of Isis staunching the blood from the eye of Horus. The steering-oar is named, with a ferryman's professional pride, "Accurate, shining in water." Even the wind and the river are examined: the wind is the north wind that comes from Atum to the nose of Khentimentiu, and the river's name is "Whom They See." A traveller who can name the whole boat, fitting by fitting, has demonstrated the only passport the Duat honours, exact knowledge of the world he is moving through. Behind Spell 99 stands the older ferryman tradition of the Pyramid Texts, where the ferryman of the Winding Waterway, Mahaf, "He Who Looks Behind Him," must be woken and persuaded, and where the terror that drives the whole literature is stated in a single word: to be boatless . Spell 100 and its companions then do the final work, rowing Re and boarding the barque itself, while the group of spells 130–136 carries the justified dead along the whole solar circuit, and Spell 136B promises sailing in the great barque of Re and passage over the circle of fire. The democratisation is real but it is not free: the price of a place in the Boat of Millions of Years is the whole of Sections XII to XVIII of this article, learned by heart. XX. The Barque before the New Kingdom — Pyramid and Coffin Texts The New Kingdom books of Sections XII to XVIII are a systematisation, not an invention. The barque is already fully at work in the oldest religious corpus Egypt left, the Pyramid Texts of the late Old Kingdom, where the dead king's whole ambition is nautical: to cross the Winding Waterway, the celestial river of the northern sky, to board the vessel of Re, and to take his seat in it as a god among gods. The ferryman material of Section XIX belongs to this stratum, and so does the pairing of the vessels themselves: the sun's two barques, of the day and of the night, are already a pair in the early tradition, long before the Amduat assigns each hour of the dark its painted register. What the Pyramid Texts add, and the later books never lose, is the barque's use as an instrument of rank. To be refused passage is the afterlife's definition of failure; to be ferried is to be recognised. The ferryman must be summoned, the boatless state escaped, the great crossing made, in spell after spell whose imagery Dilwyn Jones's Egyptian Boats (British Museum Press, 1995) collects: the sounding-poles of Horus and the wings of Thoth are invoked as ferries, the king declares that he will not be boatless and will not be turned away from the horizon, for he is Re. The barque in these texts is less a vehicle than a verdict, the visible form of the judgment that the traveller belongs in the sky. The Coffin Texts of the Middle Kingdom widen the passenger list, as they widen everything. The ferry spells that become Book of the Dead Spell 99 are already here (Spells 404–405, with their companions for knowing the boat's parts), and the Book of Two Ways, painted on the coffin floors of el-Bersha, draws the afterlife as a map of routes by land and by water, with the barque of Re sailing its circuit at the map's heart and a lake of fire on the road the unwary might take. By the time the New Kingdom royal tombs take up the journey, every element of this article is present in embryo: the two vessels, the crew of faculties, the serpent in the water, the examination at the ferry, and the promise that a person who knows the names can ride. The royal books give the embryo its anatomy. They do not give it its life; it already had one. XXI. Sun Temples — Terrestrial Docking Stations In the 5th Dynasty, the Kings built Sun Temples at Abu Ghurab. These complexes often included a massive brick-built barque located outside the temple proper. These were Terrestrial Docking Stations . By building a physical model of the Barque on the earth, the King "anchored" the solar frequency into the material field of Egypt. The temple was the site where the "Above" and "Below" were synchronized, ensuring that the energy of the cosmic Barque was available to power the state bureaucracy and the agricultural cycle. The brick barque is not a metaphor, and it is not lost. South of the sun temple of Nyuserre at Abu Ghurab, excavators found a boat built of mudbrick, about thirty metres long and ten wide, its hull once plastered and whitewashed, buried within a mudbrick chamber beside the temple whose name, Shesep-ib-Re, "Delight of Ra," states its purpose. The temple was excavated in 1898–1901 by Ludwig Borchardt and Friedrich Wilhelm von Bissing for the Berlin Museum; Userkaf's earlier sun temple, Nekhen-Re, stands some 650 metres away in the same precinct, and only these two of the six or more Fifth-Dynasty sun temples have been found. The buried brick vessel is the day barque rendered at full scale in the cheapest monumental material Egypt had, brick instead of cedar, because its voyage was to be made in place, forever, at the temple's south side. XXII. The Khufu Barque — A Full-Scale Material Model One solar barque survives at full scale. In 1954 the Egyptian archaeologist Kamal el-Mallakh, supervising clearing work beside the Great Pyramid of Giza, uncovered a sealed pit cut into the bedrock on the pyramid's southern side. Inside it, undisturbed since the Fourth Dynasty, lay a complete vessel of Lebanon cedar, dismantled into 1,224 pieces and stacked in ordered layers with its ropes, matting and oars. The ship had been buried beside the pyramid of Khufu (reigned c. 2589–2566 BCE, Shaw's chronology), and its reconstruction, directed by the restorer Ahmed Youssef Moustafa, reassembled it as it had been laid down: a vessel 43.4 metres long and 5.9 metres wide, built shell-first, its planks lashed together with rope rather than fixed with nails or a keel, among the oldest and largest wooden ships to survive from antiquity

The Name — tꜣwrt, "The Great One," Taurt and Thueris Her name is a description before it is a name: tꜣwrt [Gardiner: X1-G1-G43-D21-X1-B1] [𓏏𓄿𓅱𓂋𓏏𓁐] — "the Great One," in the feminine. Read sign by sign, it is tꜣ [Gardiner: X1-G1] [𓏏𓄿], the feminine definite article "the," followed by wrt [Gardiner: G43-D21-X1] [𓅱𓂋𓏏], "great," itself feminine, and closed in the full spelling by the seated-woman determinative [Gardiner: B1] [𓁐], which classifies the word as a female person and is not pronounced. No mythology is packed into this name, no birthplace, no genealogy. She is simply the Great One — great in body, great in the room, the largest presence at the bedside — and the name's plainness is itself evidence for the kind of goddess she was: a being known first by her size and her nearness, and only secondarily by anything a temple might have written about her. The name travelled through more spellings than almost any other in the household pantheon, and the variants are worth fixing at the head of the article, because the reader will meet all of them in the literature. Egyptological writing gives Taweret (the form this archive uses), Tawaret , Taueret , Twert and Taurt — all attempts at the same tꜣwrt [Gardiner: X1-G1-G43-D21-X1-B1]. The Greek world, which received her late and warmly, rendered the name as Thueris , also written Thoeris , Taouris and Toeris : Greek spellings of an Egyptian sound, carrying no Gardiner spelling of their own, and given here without brackets for exactly that reason. Section XIX treats the Greek career of the name. What matters at this end of the article is that every one of these forms, Egyptian and Greek alike, names the same upright hippopotamus — the name is one of the most stable identifiers in Egyptian religion, attached to one of its most stable images. A caution parallel to the one that opens the archive's article on Bes stands here too, and Section VI develops it. Several hippopotamus goddesses — Ipet, Reret, Hedjet — share Taweret's body, her jobs and sometimes her objects, and where an inscription does not name tꜣwrt [Gardiner: X1-G1-G43-D21-X1-B1], the honest label for an unnamed upright hippo goddess is "hippopotamus goddess," with Taweret named where the sources name her. The Metropolitan Museum observes exactly this discipline in its record for a glazed steatite magical container of the late Thirteenth to early Eighteenth Dynasty (ca. 1640–1500 BCE): "The hybrid hippopotamus goddess that is known as Taweret or Ipet functions here as magical jar." Taweret or Ipet. The archive follows that example throughout: the image is certain; the personal name is claimed only where it is earned. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . One correction matters directly here: the mobile soul, bꜣ [Gardiner: E10] [𓃝], whose safe lying-down and rising the birth chamber's guardians also watched over (Section XIV), is written with the ram sign whose audited value is bꜣ itself. The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . One more feature of the name deserves emphasis, because it organises the whole article. State gods tend to carry names of cosmic scope — sky, sun, hiddenness, order. Taweret carries a name of scale within a room . "The Great One" is what you call the biggest thing present. In the birth chamber, amid a labouring woman, her attendants, the bricks, the wand and the amulets, Taweret's image — on the wall, on the furniture, at the mother's throat — was exactly that: the great one of the chamber, present at a size no other protector matched. Her name is her posting order. II. No Great State Temple — Household Religion as Her Sphere Taweret had no great state temple. No precinct bore her name as its primary dedication, no city organised its festival year around her, no priestly college expounded a Taweret theology in carved inscription, and no body of temple literature survives in her honour. This is not a gap in her importance. It is the definition of her sphere, and it is shared, point for point, with her partner Bes , whose article in this archive establishes the framework this section applies to her: the two great halves of Egyptian religion were the temple and the house, and Taweret belongs wholly, deliberately and successfully to the house. The house is pr [Gardiner: O1] [𓉐], the ordinary word written with the ground-plan sign. Anna Stevens's survey of domestic religious practices in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (2009) — the framework source for this archive's household-religion articles — describes a religion that addressed the concerns of everyday life, traced in spells of healing and protection, private letters, and cult emplacements and objects from settlement sites, and that favoured protective divinities such as Bes , Taweret and Hathor , alongside deified ancestors. Taweret stands in that list at the head of the female protectors. Her cult needed no ordination and kept no calendar. It was activated by the events of a woman's life: a pregnancy recognised, a labour beginning, a child feverish in the night. What this means for the evidence must be stated plainly, because it governs everything the rest of this article can and cannot say. A temple god leaves texts: hymns, rituals, offering lists, theological commentary, carved on stone built to last. A household goddess leaves objects : amulets worn against skin until they broke, faience figures set up in room corners, images on bed legs and headrests, on feeding cups and cosmetic vessels, on the ivory wands of Section XI and the bricks of Section X — most of them in perishable or fragile materials, most of them from settlements rather than tombs, and settlements are precisely the contexts Egyptian archaeology preserves worst. The record of Taweret is therefore enormous in aggregate and thin in any single place: thousands of small witnesses, almost no long ones. When this article reconstructs a procedure — how a wand was made and used, how a birth chamber was staffed and equipped — it is building, transparently, from object distributions, wear patterns, inscriptions on the objects themselves, and the spells that name the practice. No liturgy of a Taweret birth-rite survives, and none is invented here. NO GREAT TEMPLE No known state temple was Taweret's own. She appears inside other gods' temples as a guardian — on birth houses (Section XVI) and on outer walls, where her frightening body did threshold work — never as the resident deity of a great precinct. NO PRIESTHOOD OF HER OWN The specialists who deployed her image were the household itself, the midwives and attendants of the birth chamber (Section IX), and the protective practitioners of magical practice . EVERYWHERE IN THE HOUSE Amulets, figurines, beds and headrests, feeding cups, cosmetic objects, wands and bricks: her find-spots map the rooms where women and children lived, laboured and slept — the subject of the archive's treatment of women, family and childhood . BELOVED ACROSS RANK Her objects run from a princess's residence at South Abydos (Section X) to workmen's houses at Deir el-Medina and Amarna (Section XV). Household religion was not a poverty cult, and Taweret was not a poor woman's goddess. The institutional weakness was, as with Bes, a survival strategy. A goddess with no temple cannot be closed down; a cult carried on amulets and bedposts has no address at which a decree can be served. When the Amarna reforms suppressed the traditional gods at state level, Taweret images continued in the houses of the workmen who built the heretic capital itself (Section XV) — the clearest possible demonstration that her sphere answered to needs no royal theology addressed. Childbirth did not pause for a revolution, and neither did she. It also explains her tone in the record. The great temple gods were praised in hymns of cosmic scope. Taweret is addressed, where she is addressed at all, in the short functional texts of working objects — the wand inscriptions of Section XI speak of protection for named mothers and their children, in the room, tonight. Her religion is measured in outcomes: a birth survived, a child still breathing at dawn. The archive's article on amulets and talismans sets out the general theory of such religion; this article follows one goddess through it, from the amulet at a pregnant woman's throat to the relief on a birth-house wall. III. The Composite Body — Iconography Read Element by Element Taweret is recognised at a glance, across three thousand years, by a body no other Egyptian goddess has: a pregnant hippopotamus standing upright on lion's legs, a crocodile's back and tail running down her spine, human breasts on a hippo's chest, and forepaws that rest on the sign of protection or grip a knife. The Metropolitan Museum's summary of the type, in the magical-container record quoted in Section I, calls her "a fusion of a hippopotamus, lion, crocodile, and human." The fusion is the meaning. Each element is read in turn below, because in this goddess — more completely than in any other Egyptian composite — the iconography is the theology: there is no myth-cycle to consult, only the body and what it was built to do. THE HIPPOPOTAMUS BODY The trunk, head and massively swollen belly are a hippopotamus's — and specifically a pregnant hippopotamus's. The hippo was among the most dangerous animals in Egypt (Section V), and the female hippo was famous for the ferocity with which she defended her calf. The body therefore states two things at once: this is the river's most dangerous mother, and she is carrying young, as you are. THE SWOLLEN BELLY The belly is not the hippo's ordinary bulk. It is drawn gravid — rounded, forward, unmistakably a pregnancy. Taweret does not merely protect pregnant women from outside their condition; she is shown inside it, sharing the body's state she guards. Identification, in this iconography, is a protective device in itself. THE LION LIMBS Her legs and paws are a lion's — in many images all four limbs, planted, clawed and muscled. The lion supplies the fighting equipment: the paw that strikes, the stance that does not yield. A hippo defends in the water and by mass; a lion defends on land, at the threshold of a room. The composite posts both defences at one door. THE CROCODILE BACK AND TAIL Down her back runs the ridged spine of a Nile crocodile, ending in a crocodile's tail. The crocodile is the river's ambush predator, the danger that arrives without warning from below the surface — precisely the shape that danger took, in Egyptian understanding, around a birth: sudden, unseen, at the moment of greatest exposure. She wears that danger on her back, mastered and turned outward. THE HUMAN BREASTS On the hippo's chest hang pendulous human breasts. They are the composite's nursing term: the goddess who fights with hippo, lion and crocodile feeds with a human mother's body. The breasts also drive the function of the vessels of Section XII, in which liquid issues from the goddess's own breast — the iconography made hydraulic. THE HUMAN ARMS Her forelegs end, in the developed type, in paws that do human work: they rest upon the sꜣ [Gardiner: V17] [𓎃] sign, they grip knives, they hold a torch or a small crocodile upright like a weapon (Section IV). Arms that can hold tools make her an agent , not merely a presence — she does not only stand over the bed; she works at it. The stance completes the reading. Taweret stands upright , bipedal, facing outward toward whoever approaches — a posture no real hippopotamus holds and no merely animal figure in Egyptian art is given. Uprightness is personhood: she is a being who has taken the animals' powers into a person's stance, at a person's post, doing a person's job. Set her beside the other great composite of the birth sphere, the dwarf-lion Bes , and the design logic of the whole household pantheon becomes visible at once: in both cases the body is an arsenal, assembled from the most dangerous creatures available and stationed, full-face, between a vulnerable human body and everything that might approach it. Variation exists within the type, and it is informative rather than accidental. In some images the crocodile is reduced to the tail alone; in others a full small crocodile rides her back. Her head may wear a modius or a horned sun-disc headdress in later periods, borrowing the crowns of Hathor and Isis as those goddesses' maternal prestige grew. On the wands of Section XI she is one figure in a procession and may be drawn at small scale with her knife in paw. Through every variation the identifying core never changes: upright, gravid, hippo-bodied, lion-limbed. A figure missing that core is not Taweret, whatever a label may claim; a figure with it is a hippopotamus goddess, and Taweret unless an inscription says otherwise (Section VI). Scale, finally, is part of her iconography as it is of Bes's. She exists as amulets under two centimetres high, worn at a pregnant woman's throat; as faience figures at household-shrine scale; as the working figure of wands and bricks; and, in the temple contexts of Section XVI, at relief and architectural scale on birth-house walls, where the same body that guarded a workman's bedroom guards the birth of a god. The body-plan never changes. Only the size of the room does. IV. The Sa-Sign, the Knife and the Torch — Her Equipment Taweret's commonest attribute is not a weapon but a word. In the standard image her forepaws rest upon, or grip, the large sꜣ [Gardiner: V17] [𓎃] hieroglyph — the sign whose value is "protection" itself. The device is worth pausing over, because it is almost a caption worn as equipment: where a state god carries a sceptre denoting rank, Taweret leans on the abstract noun for what she does. The sign declares the function to anyone who could read a single hieroglyph, and its shape — a looped, folded form, explained in the sign lists as a rolled or folded protection — made it one of the most reproduced signs in the whole amuletic repertoire. A Taweret resting on the sꜣ [Gardiner: V17] is a complete sentence: the Great One: protection . Beside the sign stands the blade. On the apotropaic wands (Section XI) Taweret and her fellow guardians carry knives, and in independent images she may grip a knife herself — the same statement the wand makes at instrument scale: what approaches the bed will be cut. Some images give her a torch, whose logic is the night watch's logic (Section XIV): fire carried into the dark corners where danger was imagined to gather, light as a weapon in the hours when the household slept and the mother laboured. A further, startling attribute appears in a minority of images: a small crocodile held upright in her paw, brandished like a club — the river's predator picked up by the tail and swung. Whether read as mastery displayed or as a weapon improvised from the enemy's own kind, it belongs to the same grammar as the grasped snakes of Bes : the dangerous thing, held fast, is the proof of protection. The equipment should be read as a kit, not a wardrobe. Sign, knife, torch and mastered crocodile correspond to the four modes of her guard: declaration (the word protection , posted), force (the blade), vigilance (the light), and domination (the enemy's creature in her grip). No single image need carry all four. Any one of them identifies the register in which a given figure is working, and the wands — where the whole guardian troop marches with knives drawn — show the kit at its most complete. V. The Hippopotamus — Danger Recruited, and the Male Hippo She Is Not Everything in Taweret's body begins from a zoological fact every Egyptian knew at first hand: the hippopotamus was one of the most dangerous animals in the Nile valley. Bulls charged boats, wrecked riverside fields and killed people; a female with a calf was dangerous in a second way, attacking anything that came between her and her young with a speed and mass no other river animal matched. Egyptian religion processed the animal in both registers at once. The male hippopotamus, chaos in animal form, was hunted by kings in ritual hunts and assimilated to the disorder of Set . The female hippopotamus, the defending mother, was recruited — as Taweret, and as her kindred of Section VI — into the defence of human mothers. Same animal, opposite valence, divided by sex and by behaviour: destruction in the bull, protection in the cow. That division is the key to her celebrated ambivalence, and Section XVII returns to it at the scale of the inundation. Here the point is iconographic honesty: Taweret is not a sanitised animal. Her body keeps the open jaws, the mass and the threat of the real creature, because the protection was understood to work by the threat. A guardian who could not kill could not guard. The Egyptians who set her image at a birthing bed were not asking for comfort in the modern sense; they were posting the river's most dangerous mother at the door and relying on everything else in the dark to make the same calculation a crocodile makes at a hippo cow's stare — and go elsewhere. The material of her cult carries the same recruitment one step further. The apotropaic wands of Section XI are cut from hippopotamus ivory: her own animal's substance, split from the tusk, incised with her image, and dragged around the bed. Substance, image and animal are one continuous argument — the hippo's power, taken into the hand, in the hippo's own material, under the hippo goddess's own figure. No other Egyptian deity is so completely present in the physical stuff of her instruments. VI. Ipet, Reret and Hedjet — the Kindred Hippopotamus Goddesses Taweret did not hold the hippopotamus body alone. Three kindred goddesses share it, and the archive states their relations as the scholarship leaves them — grouped, overlapping, and at the edges genuinely indistinguishable. Ipet (also written Ipy, and in older literature Apet) is the eldest of the family: a hippopotamus goddess already named in the Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts in a maternal, nursing role, and the form under which the Met's magical container of Section I may equally be read. Reret , "the Sow," carries the same upright gravid body with a pig's name — another fierce mother of the farmyard and the marsh edge translated into the type. Hedjet , "the White One," completes the usual trio of named sisters. All four guard pregnancy, birth and early childhood; all four wear the composite body of Section III. The honest model, as with the Bes-image family treated in the Bes article, is a family that converged . Local and functional hippo goddesses, arising wherever women gave birth along the river, were identified with one another over centuries, their names kept or dropped by place and period, until tꜣwrt [Gardiner: X1-G1-G43-D21-X1-B1] — the Great One — became the name that won: the generic title that absorbed the sisters, exactly as a title meaning simply "the great (female) one" would be expected to do. Some scholars accordingly treat Ipet, Reret and Hedjet as aspects of a single hippopotamus-goddess complex rather than as separate persons; the objects, which so often carry the body without the name, cannot settle the question, and this article does not pretend they do. Two practical consequences follow for the reader of the wider literature. First, a museum label reading "Taweret" on an uninscribed figure is a classification, not a transcription — it may mean no more than "the hippopotamus goddess, in her usual form." Second, the family's plurality is itself evidence about the cult's social location: a religion administered by temples produces one goddess with one name and a managed mythology; a religion carried by households produces a body everyone recognises under whatever name the village used. The kindred goddesses are what household religion looks like before anyone tidies it. VII. Beside Bes — the Partnership of the Birth Chamber Taweret's constant partner is bs [Gardiner: D58-S29] [𓃀𓋴] — Bes , the dwarf-lion of the bedroom, whose full treatment stands in his own article and is not duplicated here. What belongs to her article is the partnership seen from her side: what she brings to the pair that he does not, and how the division of labour between them maps the birth chamber itself. The pairing is constant in the material record: together on the apotropaic wands, together on headrests and bed fittings, together in household shrines and birth-house reliefs, together — in the framing of the archive's article on amulets and talismans — as the standard paired guardians of the domestic threshold. But the two figures are not interchangeable halves. Bes is the chamber's noise and motion : frontal face, drum and dance, the sounding shield raised around the bed, the guard of sleep and of the festive thresholds. Taweret is its mass and maternity : the great body stationed at the bed, herself pregnant, the guard whose protection runs through identification with the mother's own state. He frightens danger off. She outweighs it, out-mothers it, and is still standing there, gravid and armed, when the noise stops. The gendered complementarity is real but should not be over-systematised. Later tradition sometimes pairs them almost as a couple, and the female Bes-figure Beset — treated in the Bes article — complicates any tidy scheme of one male and one female guardian. What the objects actually show is simpler and stronger: two composite monsters, built from the same design logic out of different animals, posted together so often that the pairing itself became the conventional sign for "this place is guarded." A wand, a bed or a birth-house wall carrying both figures is making a claim about the space, not narrating a marriage. Her seniority in the pair deserves one sentence of its own. The hippopotamus goddess stands on the protective objects of the Middle Kingdom at the head of the wand processions, in the period when the Bes-figure was still crystallising out of the dwarf-fighter family of Aha. If either partner can be called the elder guardian of the birth chamber, on the surviving evidence it is she. VIII. Pregnancy — the Long Vigil Before the Birth Taweret's commission began months before the birth chamber was prepared. Pregnancy, in a world without any means of seeing inside the womb, was a long uncertainty carried in one body: the child's life and the mother's were both at hazard throughout, and the hazards were understood to include agencies — malign spirits, the envious dead, the attention of powers that preyed on thresholds — against which the household's defences were precisely designed. Her image therefore entered the pregnant woman's daily equipment early and stayed there: faience amulets of the goddess worn on the body, figures set up in the rooms she used, her form on the cosmetic vessels and small objects of the toilet, where the body was washed, oiled and dressed each day under the guardian's face. The practice can be reconstructed, in outline, as a procedure with stages, and this article presents it in that form — labelled as reconstruction from the objects, since no pregnancy manual survives. First, posting : the image established on the woman's person and in her rooms, so that protection was continuous rather than summoned in crisis. Second, wearing : the amulet against the skin, the form of the goddess carried through every errand and every night's sleep of the pregnancy — the amuletic theory of the archive's amulets article, in which the correctly made image did not merely represent the protection but was the protection, present at the throat. Third, preparation : as the term approached, the chamber was furnished — bricks, wand, figures, vessels — the subject of Sections IX to XII. The stages are the household's own logic made visible: guard the mother, then guard the room, then guard the hour. // THE VIGIL, AS THE OBJECTS GIVE IT // On the body: Taweret amulets, among the commonest faience amulets at every social level. In the room: figures and images at the bed and the shrine-corner (Section XV). At the toilet: her form on vessels for the oils and cosmetics of daily care. In the hand, at need: the wand and its circle (Section XI), drawn not only at the birth but around the sleeping places of pregnancy and early childhood. At the breast, after: the vessels of Section XII and the feeding cups of Section XIII, carrying the same guard from pregnancy through nursing. No text prescribes this sequence. The objects, found together again and again, are the prescription. One feature of the pregnancy evidence deserves emphasis against a common modern misreading. Taweret is often filed in popular works as a "fertility goddess," a label that suggests women invoked her chiefly to conceive. The objects say otherwise. Her densest presence is not at conception but at carrying and delivering : the gravid body of the goddess guards gravid bodies, the amulets cluster on the equipment of pregnancy, birth and nursing, and her great instruments — wand and brick — belong to the delivery itself. She is not primarily a goddess of becoming pregnant. She is the goddess of surviving it. IX. The Birth Chamber — Personnel and Equipment No Egyptian text describes a birth chamber the way a medical treatise might, and this section is explicit about its method: the chamber is reconstructed from the birth brick's painted scenes, the wand inscriptions, the object distributions of Sections VIII and XI, the birth-house reliefs of Section XVI, and the spells for mother and child preserved in the magical papyri as treated in the archive's articles on magical practice and the medical papyri . What emerges is not a temple rite transposed indoors. It is a staffed, equipped, defended room, organised around a squatting woman — and Taweret presides over it not as a visiting deity but as its resident guardian, already present in image before the first contraction. The Personnel At the centre, the labouring woman herself — mwt [Gardiner: G14] [𓅐], "mother," is the word the occasion makes of her. Around her, the painted scene on the South Abydos brick (Section X) shows the essential staff: two women attendants flanking the seated mother and her newborn, figures Wegner's publication reads in the orbit of Hathor's priestesses and of midwives — the experienced women, kin or professionals, whose hands did the physical work of the delivery. Birth, ms [Gardiner: F31] [𓄟], was women's work, conducted by women, in a room from which the household's men are conspicuously absent in every representation the archive can cite. A protective practitioner — the wand's user, in some households a specialist of ḥkꜣ [Gardiner: V28-D28-G1] [𓎛𓂓𓄿], the operative power of Heka — might attend where means allowed, but the chamber's defence did not depend on one: the wand, the bricks and the images were household equipment, usable by the household, and the attendants themselves are shown within the protected space they maintained. The Equipment THE BRICKS The birthing bricks under the mother's feet as she squatted — painted, in the surviving example, with the guardian troop itself (Section X). Furniture and amulet in one object. THE WAND The hippopotamus-ivory apotropaic wand, its circle drawn around the bed or the bricks before the crisis peaked (Section XI) — the chamber's perimeter, renewed as needed. THE IMAGES Taweret and Bes figures present in the room — on furniture, set up at the walls, worn by the mother — the resident guard in visible form. THE VESSELS Taweret-form vessels for the liquids of the occasion — water, oil, milk or prepared substances, their exact contents the debate of Section XII — and the ordinary vessels of washing and first feeding. THE AMULETS The mother's worn amulets, and a new set waiting for the child: the guard transferred, at the moment of birth, from one body to two (Section XIII). SOUND Bes's department (Section VII): music, rattling and raised voices at the bed — the sounding shield of the Bes article, part of this chamber's equipment as surely as the bricks. Read whole, the chamber is a small fortress organised by a single idea: every approach to the two vulnerable bodies is covered — the floor by the drawn circle, the feet by the painted bricks, the air by noise, the room by the images, the mother's skin by the amulets, and the liquids that will touch either body by the goddess-shaped vessels. Nothing in the arrangement requires a temple, a priesthood or a text. Everything in it requires Taweret, present in more media, at more scales, than any other being in the room except the mother herself. X. Birthing Bricks — Meskhenet and the South Abydos Brick Egyptian women gave birth squatting, supported on bricks. The practice is attested in texts long before any brick survived, and it was theologised in a goddess: Meskhenet , the birthing brick personified, shown as a brick with a woman's head, who attended every birth and pronounced the newborn's destiny at the moment of delivery. The brick was therefore never merely furniture. It was a divine presence built into the posture of birth itself — the thing under the mother's feet was a goddess, and what stood on goddesses was, by the chamber's logic, already inside the protection. In 2001 the type acquired its surviving specimen. Excavating the mayoral residence at South Abydos — the Middle Kingdom town of Wah-Sut, founded for the mortuary cult of Senwosret III — Josef Wegner of the University of Pennsylvania found a polychrome painted birth brick of unfired mud, dated to about 1750–1700 BCE, the first actual birth brick ever recovered. The Penn Museum's account gives the essentials: the brick measures about 36 cm in length; it was one of a pair that would have supported a woman's feet as she squatted in delivery; its upper surface is crumbled away, damage Wegner suggested may itself be the wear of long use across many deliveries; and the residence's female quarters produced seal impressions naming a noblewoman and king's daughter, Reniseneb, who may have been its owner. A princess's brick, in a mayor's house, worn down by use: the whole social argument of Section II in a single object. Its decoration is the point for this article. The brick's sides carry the same guardian troop as the apotropaic wands — the protective gods and demons of the birth sphere, Taweret's company — rendered in paint on mud; and one face carries the chamber's only self-portrait: a mother enthroned with her newborn, attended by two women and flanked by standards of Hathor , an image Wegner reads as a two-dimensional visual spell transfiguring the mother, at the moment of birth, into Hathor herself. Wegner further relates the brick's protective imagery to the myth of the infant sun god defended at his daily rebirth on the eastern horizon: every human birth re-enacted, under guard, the sun's own dangerous dawn. The brick under a labouring woman's feet thus carried the wand's procession, the birth's ideal image, and a cosmic precedent — three layers of protection in unbaked mud, a material chosen, as Wegner notes, perhaps precisely because such bricks were made, painted and renewed within the life of the town, an industry of care rather than a monument. // THE BRICKS IN USE — THE PROCEDURE AS RECONSTRUCTED // 1. A pair (in some reconstructions, two stacked pairs) of bricks is set parallel on the chamber floor, spaced to the mother's stance. 2. The bricks in the surviving example are painted on their sides with the guardian procession — the protection faces outward, toward the room. 3. The mother mounts the bricks and squats between or upon them, supported by her attendants, so that gravity assists the delivery and the child is received below. 4. The wand's circle (Section XI) encloses the whole arrangement — bricks, mother, attendants, child. 5. After the birth, mother and newborn are shown, in the brick's own painted scene, enthroned together: the posture of danger exchanged for the posture of arrival. The steps are reconstruction from the brick, its scene and the textual tradition of the bricks of birth (Roth and Roehrig's study, cited in Section XX), and are labelled as such. Taweret's place in this section is the place she holds everywhere in the chamber: not the brick's personification — that is Meskhenet — but the head of the troop painted on its sides, the great guardian in whose company the brick-goddess works. The division is characteristic of the birth sphere's crowded, cooperative pantheon: Meskhenet under the feet and speaking the destiny, Hathor in the transfiguring image, Bes raising the noise, and Taweret — largest of them — at the perimeter, where the danger comes from. XI. Apotropaic Wands — Manufacture, Inscription and Use The apotropaic wand — also called the birth tusk or magic knife — is the best-documented instrument of Taweret's cult and the archive's fullest window into household protective procedure.
