A Modern Word for an Ancient Room — "Laboratory" and Its Limits This article is built around a word the Egyptians never used. "Laboratory" is a modern label, applied by Egyptologists to a small inscribed chamber in the Ptolemaic temple of Horus at Edfu — and, by extension, to comparable rooms at Dendera and elsewhere — because its walls carry recipes: measured instructions for making oils, unguents, incense and kindred preparations for the daily cult. The Egyptians left no word for this room that means "laboratory," and no inscription on its walls calls it one. What the walls contain is not a name but a contents list: the recipes themselves, the offering scenes that frame them, and the lists of raw materials graded by quality. The room is identified by what was written in it, not by what it was called. The distinction matters, and this article states it at the outset rather than in a footnote, because the modern word smuggles in modern expectations. A laboratory, in the modern sense, is a place of experiment: of hypotheses tested, variables isolated, and results that may overturn the recipe. The Edfu chamber preserves the opposite discipline. Its recipes are written to be repeated — to produce, this year and every year, the same ointment that was produced last year, in the same quantity, to the same standard, for the same god. Where a modern laboratory notebook records what happened once, the temple wall records what must happen always. The knowledge is procedural, exact, and in places astonishingly quantified; it is not experimental science, and nothing in this article should be read as claiming that it is. A second caution follows from the first. The recipes were inscribed in stone, in a roofed chamber inside the temple's restricted core, where — on Lise Manniche's assessment in the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (2009) — the lack of light and ventilation means the room "rather served as a storeroom" than as a working kitchen of perfumes. The inscription is the archive of the process, not necessarily the site of it. The actual grinding, cooking and pressing may have been done in courtyards, annexes or workshop buildings of mudbrick that have not survived, by personnel whose work the stone room supervised and whose standard it fixed. Throughout this article, therefore, "the laboratory" in quotation marks means the inscribed room and its textual corpus; "the workshops" means the wider, mostly perishable production world of the temple, of which the inscribed room is the surviving specification sheet. // READING THE TERMS IN THIS ARTICLE // Every technical Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is what the signs decode to. Where a term is discussed whose spelling this article cannot compose with confidence — the styrax word nnib , for example, known from the Edfu and Athribis lists — the transliteration is given without codes rather than with invented ones. The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . Modern labels are flagged as modern wherever they do the organising: "laboratory," "workshop," "magazine," "quality control." The Egyptian evidence underneath each label is given in the section that uses it. What justifies an article at all, if the central word is borrowed? The gap this article fills is institutional. The archive has an article on the House of Life , the temple's centre of textual knowledge, and articles on the individual crafts — glass, food and drink, embalming, colour. What it has lacked is the institution that stood between the library and the crafts: the temple as a producer , an organisation that owned land, mounted expeditions, graded imported resins, employed specialists, enforced purity and secrecy, stored the results in magazines and treasuries, and wrote its most guarded procedures on stone so they could not be lost. The so-called laboratory is the best-documented window into that institution, because it is the one place where the institution wrote its own working instructions down. This article reads those instructions, sets them in the economy that fed them, and keeps the modern label in quotation marks throughout. II. Words and Rooms — The Egyptian Vocabulary of Production Egyptian organises production space with the word pr [Gardiner: O1] [𓉐], "house" — not a dwelling only, but an establishment: a house is an institution with staff, stores and a function. The temple itself is a ḥwt-nṯr [Gardiner: O10-R8] [𓉡𓊹], a "god's mansion," and its departments are houses within the house. The archive's companion article treats the pr-ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: O1-D36-S34] [𓉐𓂝𓋹], the House of Life, where texts were made and kept, and the pr-mdꜣt [Gardiner: O1-G17-D46-G1-X1] [𓉐𓅓𓂧𓄿𓏏], the House of Books, whose fitted example survives at Edfu with its catalogue inscribed beside its niche. The present article is about the productive counterparts of those textual houses: the rooms and yards where the temple's consumables were manufactured and stored. The closest Egyptian word to "workshop" in the general sense is šnꜥ [Gardiner: N37-N35-D36] [𓈙𓈖𓂝] — a word whose semantic field covers the workshop, the storehouse and the labour establishment together, which is itself a lesson: in the temple economy, making and storing were not separate departments but one chain, and the language does not pretend otherwise. A treasury is a pr-ḥḏ [Gardiner: O1-T3] [𓉐𓌉], a "house of silver," where the precious end of production accumulated. The gold-working establishment attached to great temples is the ḥwt-nbw [Gardiner: V28-G43-X1-S12] [𓎛𓅱𓏏𓋞], the "Mansion of Gold," treated in §XI for Dendera: the place where divine statues were made, repaired and overlaid, and whose texts — significantly for this article — carry glosses explaining older material-names to contemporary craftsmen, exactly as the perfume recipes gloss theirs (§VIII). One neighbouring institution must be distinguished at the start, because its vocabulary is deceptively similar. The embalming establishment is the wꜥbt [Gardiner: G43-D36-D58-X1] [𓅱𓂝𓃀𓏏], the "pure place," with its pr-nfr [Gardiner: O1-F35] [𓉐𓄤], the "House of Beauty." It was a genuine manufactory — the archive's Mummification article documents its labelled vessels, its formulated mixtures, its division of labour — but it belonged to the funerary sphere, stood apart from the temple of the living cult, and served the dead rather than the daily offering round. It used many of the same substances as the temple workshops (natron, resins, scented oils) and some of the same procedures, and §XVIII returns to the comparison. It is not the subject of this article, and its rooms are not "temple laboratories" in the sense used here. THE HOUSE OF LIFE — TEXTS The pr-ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: O1-D36-S34] [𓉐𓂝𓋹]: where sacred knowledge was composed, copied and performed. The laboratory inscriptions are its bench-side counterpart — process knowledge written for use, catalogued among the temple's books (§XVII). THE WORKSHOP-STORE — MAKING AND KEEPING The šnꜥ [Gardiner: N37-N35-D36] [𓈙𓈖𓂝] joins production and storage in one word. Temple workshops are rarely excavated as such; they are known from accounts, tomb scenes of temple ateliers, and the inscribed specification rooms that governed them. THE MANSION OF GOLD — STATUES The ḥwt-nbw [Gardiner: V28-G43-X1-S12] [𓎛𓅱𓏏𓋞]: the gold house where cult images were fashioned and maintained. Its Dendera texts gloss obsolete material names — the same editorial care the perfume corpus shows (§XI). THE PURE PLACE — NOT THIS ARTICLE The wꜥbt [Gardiner: G43-D36-D58-X1] [𓅱𓂝𓃀𓏏] is the embalming workshop, a separate funerary institution. Shared substances, shared chemistry, different house, different god-service. See Mummification . The personnel vocabulary belongs to §XIV, but two words frame everything that follows. The craftsman is a ḥmwt [Gardiner: U36-G43-X1] [𓍛𓅱𓏏] worker — the root covers craft and art together — under a wr-ḫrp-ḥmwt [Gardiner: G36-Aa1-D21-Q3-U36-G43-X1] [𓅨𓐍𓂋𓊪𓍛𓅱𓏏], a "chief director of craftsmen," a title borne by high officials of great temples. And the condition of everyone who worked inside the sacred enclosure was wꜥb [Gardiner: G43-D36-D58] [𓅱𓂝𓃀] — "pure" — a technical state with rules, grades and rota periods, not a vague compliment. Production inside a temple was priestly work done under purity discipline, and the recipes' secrecy clauses (§XV) assume exactly that workforce. III. The Temple as Production Institution A great Egyptian temple was among the largest economic organisations of its world. Ben Haring's survey of the economy for the UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (2009) puts the structural point plainly: agriculture was the base of all production, most cultivators were tenants on land owned by wealthy individuals or by state and temple estates, and — the sentence this article is built on — according to the textual evidence, crafts were largely in the hands of institutional workforces. The temple did not buy its incense, oil, linen, bread, beer, vessels and statues on an open market as its first resort. It owned the land that grew the grain and flax, the herds that supplied fat and leather, the workshops that converted them, and the magazines that stored the results. Manufacture was an internal department of the house of the god. The daily cult set the production schedule. Every morning the god was awakened, washed, dressed, anointed and fed; every evening the service closed with censing — in the developed Ptolemaic scheme, resin at sunrise, myrrh at midday, and the compounded kꜣp.t [Gardiner: V31-Q3-X1] [𓎡𓊪𓏏] (kyphi) at sunset (Plutarch, De Iside 79–80, in paraphrase; see Ritual Practice ). Each of those acts consumed manufactured goods: oils and unguents of named kinds, incense of graded resins, linen of specified fineness, bread and beer of the offering grades, wine, eye-paint, natron. Festivals multiplied the quantities and added special manufactures — festival perfume, processional equipment, the annually renewed images and offerings of the great feasts. A temple's workshops therefore worked to a liturgical calendar the way a modern factory works to an order book, except that the order book was theology and never cancelled. Scale followed endowment. The Ramesside Wilbour Papyrus, the great cadastral survey of Middle Egypt, shows temples — above all the Theban houses of Amun — controlling agricultural estates on a scale that made them, in Juan Carlos Moreno García's phrase for the earlier evidence, links in a network of warehouses, production centres and agricultural holdings. Estates in the Old Kingdom evidence were already production networks where goods were produced, stored and held available for the institution's agents (Moreno García, UEE 2008). By the New Kingdom the temples were the most important economic centres of the country, and their workshops — bakeries, breweries, weaving and carpentry shops, slaughteryards, gold houses — were staffed accordingly, as the archive's Temple Architecture article notes of the mudbrick world of magazines, kitchens, offices and priests' housing that surrounded the stone core. // THE PRODUCTION CHAIN, IN ONE VIEW // Land and water (temple estates, the sacred lake, the well) → raw materials (grain, flax, oilseeds, fat, timber, stone, metal, imported resins) → workshops (bakery–brewery, weaving sheds, oil and unguent preparation, gold house, stone and faience ateliers) → magazines and treasury (graded storage, sealed and accounted) → the daily service and the festivals (consumption as offering) → redistribution (offerings reverted to the priesthood and staff as rations — the temple's wage system). The inscribed "laboratory" sits at the chain's most guarded link: the conversion of costly imported aromatics into the named preparations the cult consumed daily. Two features of this institution distinguish it from a merely large household. The first is specification . Temple products were not generic: the cult required named preparations — this ointment, of these ingredients, in this quantity, for this rite — and the requirement was written down, in the recipe corpus that is this article's core evidence, with quantities and expected yields fixed in advance (§VIII). The second is accountability . Temples kept accounts of receipts and issues, sealed stores, and inventoried their treasuries; the scribal apparatus that ran the House of Life had an administrative twin that ran the magazines. Where the two meet — a recipe that specifies an input, a process and a checked output weight — the modern reader is looking at something recognisable as a controlled manufacturing standard, maintained by a literate institution across centuries. That, and not any anticipation of modern chemistry, is the Edfu laboratory's real claim on attention. IV. Estates and Supply — Land, Expeditions, Trade and Tribute No workshop article can begin at the bench, because the bench was the last link of a supply system that reached beyond Egypt's borders. The temple's own estates supplied the bulk staples: emmer and barley for the bakery–brewery (see Food and Drink ), flax for the linen that clothed the god and the priests, oilseeds and animal fat for the unguent bases, timber, reeds and clay. Manniche's ingredient survey ( UEE 2009) lists the local base oils of Egyptian scent-making — sesame, castor, balanos and moringa oils, with olive and almond in limited, probably imported, quantities — and ox, sheep and fowl fat for the more solid unguents. These were estate products, pressed and rendered within the temple's own economy. The aromatics that define the laboratory corpus were not local, and the temple's supply organisation existed largely to secure them. Frankincense and myrrh — the ꜥnṯyw [Gardiner: D36-N35-V13-Z4-G43] [𓂝𓈖𓍿𓏭𓅱] group of oleoresins at the head of nearly every recipe — came traditionally from Punt, on the African coast of the Red Sea in the region of modern Eritrea and Somalia; temple records of New Kingdom date mention large shipments of both (Manniche, UEE 2009, citing the Punt literature). Pistacia resin — the substance Serpico and White demonstrated the word snṯr [Gardiner: R7] [𓊸] specifically denotes — came from Syria-Palestine. Cinnamon, cassia and cardamom, recurring in the classical quotations of Egyptian recipes, arrived by caravan from further afield still. The spices in the Edfu recipes are therefore a map of the temple's procurement reach, written in ingredients. The desert margins supplied the mineral half of the workshop economy. Sinai gave turquoise — mfkꜣt [Gardiner: G17-I9-V31-G1-X1] [𓅓𓆑𓎡𓄿𓏏] — and copper, under the patronage of Hathor as lady of the turquoise country; the Eastern Desert wadis gave gold, hard stones and the natron of the Wadi Natrun, the alkaline soda that appears in this article as ḥsmn [Gardiner: V28-S29-G17-N35] [𓎛𓋴𓅓𓈖] and that served the temple simultaneously as purifier, mouth-cleanser, desiccant and flux (see Ritual Practice and Glass ). Expeditions to these sources were state and temple undertakings — quarrying and mining parties with their own overseers, scribes and supply trains — and their produce entered the same magazine system as the harvest. Tribute and diplomatic gift added a third stream: the precious materials that foreign rulers sent the king were redistributed in part to the great temples, whose treasuries were, in effect, the state's reserve of convertible wealth. FROM THE ESTATES Grain, flax, oilseeds, fat, wine of the oases — the Edfu hekenu recipe specifies "the excellent wine of the Oasis" as a working ingredient, the alcohol in which oleoresins dissolve (§IX). Bulk, local, accounted by the granary. FROM PUNT AND THE LEVANT Frankincense, myrrh and pistacia resin — costly, imported, graded on arrival by origin, colour, texture and smell (§XV). The laboratory corpus exists because these materials were too valuable to compound by memory alone. FROM THE DESERTS Gold, turquoise, copper, natron, hard stone. Expedition produce, weighed into the treasury — the pr-ḥḏ [Gardiner: O1-T3] [𓉐𓌉] — and issued to the gold house and the workshops against account. FROM THE WORKSHOPS OF OTHER HOUSES Great temples specialised and exchanged: a preparation famous at one house — the mineral ointment once used at Coptos to anoint the statues of Min — could become standard across Egypt (§VI). The recipe corpus is the exchange mechanism. Supply explains the corpus's most striking feature: its obsession with grades . A temple that received frankincense from multiple sources, in multiple seasons, through multiple intermediaries needed a written standard for what counted as the first quality — and the Edfu and Athribis walls carry exactly that, parallel lists describing the varieties of frankincense and styrax by name, colour, consistency, origin, presentation and smell (§XV). The lists are procurement documents as much as liturgical ones: they tell the receiving officer what to accept, what to reject, and what to divert to lesser uses. The laboratory begins, in other words, at the loading dock. V. Edfu — The Temple and the Room's Place in Its Plan The temple of Horus at Edfu, on the west bank of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, is the best-preserved temple of the ancient world, and the fullest surviving example of the Ptolemaic temple as a total institution. Built between 237 and 57 BCE — begun under Ptolemy III on the site of an older temple, of which a shrine of Nectanebo II survives — it presents the complete canonical plan: pylon, open court, great hypostyle hall (the pronaos), a second, smaller hypostyle hall, and then the ring of service and cult chambers around the sanctuary, the whole enclosed in its temenos with mammisi, sacred lake and magazines. Its walls are a library in stone: foundation texts, festival calendars, mythological cycles — and, in the service ring, the working texts of the cult's own manufacture. The so-called laboratory sits in that service ring. Descriptions of the plan place it off the inner (second) hypostyle hall, on the western side, among the small chambers that served the daily round: the Chamber of the Nile, with its well for pure water; the treasury, where offerings and precious stores were kept; the linen room, where the god's clothing was held. The pairing is functional, not accidental. The rooms around the sanctuary of a Ptolemaic temple are a machine for the daily service, each chamber a station in the sequence — water drawn, linen fetched, oils and incense issued, offerings assembled — and the laboratory belongs to that machine: the station where the anointing and censing materials were kept, specified and, on the traditional reading, prepared. Its neighbours in the plan are storage and issue rooms, which is the first architectural hint of Manniche's storeroom assessment (§I). The temple's other famous small room makes the pairing explicit. In the pronaos wall at Edfu is the niche of the pr-mdꜣt [Gardiner: O1-G17-D46-G1-X1] [𓉐𓅓𓂧𓄿𓏏], the House of Books, with the temple's book catalogue inscribed beside it (see House of Life , §IV and §VIII). A visitor who understands Edfu holds both rooms in view at once: on one side of the plan, the books of the cult, catalogued title by title; on the other, the recipes of the cult, inscribed ingredient by ingredient. The laboratory's catalogue entry, indeed, appears among the books — Edfu's library list includes a work the scholarship cites as the "List of all secret recipes of the laboratory" (Edfou III 348, 1; Aufrère 2005a, cited in Aufrère et al. 2022) — so that the room and the library each contain a reference to the other. §XVII develops what that reciprocity means. // THE ROOM IN THE SEQUENCE OF THE DAY // Read the plan as a workflow. Before dawn: water from the Chamber of the Nile; linen from the linen room; the day's oils, unguents and incense from the laboratory and its magazines; bread, beer and offerings from the offering hall's stores. The service proceeds inward — hall, vestibule, sanctuary — and the products of every workshop in this article converge on a single small room and a single statue. The laboratory's position, deep inside the restricted core and ringed by stores, is the architecture of controlled issue: nothing reached the god that had not passed through graded storage and written specification. Edfu's preservation is the reason this article can be written at all, and it should be registered as a bias in the evidence. Other temples had the same departments — Dendera's plan shows the same ring of laboratory, magazine and treasury (§XI) — but their walls are ruined, their mudbrick annexes gone, their accounts lost. Edfu is not necessarily the greatest or the oldest of the temple laboratories; it is the one whose specification sheet survived in stone. The history of the institution must be written from its best-preserved member, with the distortion acknowledged: what looks like Edfu's uniqueness is, in large part, Edfu's luck. VI. Inside the Edfu "Laboratory" — What the Walls Actually Preserve The Edfu laboratory's inscriptions were published in Émile Chassinat's great edition of the temple, Le Temple d'Edfou , and their modern study is associated above all with Sydney Aufrère, whose analysis of the corpus (Aufrère 2005a, summarised in Aufrère et al., "Learning and Institutions," in A Cultural History of Chemistry in Antiquity , 2022) supplies most of the procedural detail in this and the following sections. What the walls preserve, in Aufrère's inventory, is a working set of recipes for named preparations: the "finest ointment of styrax"; the hekenu ointment; the medjes ointment; the "nine ointments of the Ennead"; the "precious ointment"; the "ointment of divine mineral"; the kyphi; and the "pure natron pellets of the Ennead" — together with descriptive lists of the varieties of frankincense and styrax, graded as §IV described. This is a formulary, not a treatise: a set of manufacturing standards for the temple's own consumption. Aufrère's analysis divides the preparations into three technical families , and the division is the corpus's own, not a modern imposition. First, fumigations — compounds made to be burned, of which kyphi is the type (§X). Second, fat-based cooked ointments — aromatics extracted into oil or fat by maceration and cooking, the hekenu of §IX being the most fully documented example. Third, resinous ointments for the statues — preparations whose purpose was the maintenance of the divine images themselves, the wood and stone bodies in which, in the Memphite theology's phrase as Aufrère quotes it, the gods had entered: "a mixture of all kinds of wood, of stone, of all types of faience, of all things which emerge from him and through which they manifest themselves." The laboratory's third family is thus statue-care as theology: the product preserves the god's body, and its recipe is a liturgical text by function whatever its vocabulary — and Aufrère notes that the vocabulary of the recipes is, strikingly, technical throughout, without the magico-religious formulae that medical and ritual texts add at the point of application. THE HEKENU OINTMENT ḥknw [Gardiner: V28-V31-N35-G43] [𓎛𓎡𓈖𓅱] — premium frankincense oil with styrax, for divine anointing; nine ingredients, some forty-two operations, 487–492 days (§IX). Also one of the seven sacred oils of the old canonical list (§XIII). THE DIVINE MINERAL OINTMENT A mixture of precious metals, minerals, bitumen, resins and oils, once used at Coptos to anoint the statues of Min, spread from that house to temples across Egypt — and the recipe that carries the corpus's secrecy clause: a secret the old man passes to his child (§XV). THE NINE OINTMENTS OF THE ENNEAD A set-production: nine preparations for the nine gods of the psḏt [Gardiner: N9-X1] [𓇷𓏏]. The formulary thinks in liturgical sets — products specified not singly but as the complete kit a rite requires. NATRON PELLETS OF THE ENNEAD The humblest item in the corpus and the most instructive: even the purifier's pellets — chewed or dissolved to cleanse the officiant's mouth — were a manufactured, specified product, not a handful of raw soda (§XV). Two further features of the walls deserve emphasis. The first is provenance . Manniche ( UEE 2009) notes that the Edfu instructions may have been copied from a "Book of Unguent" mentioned among the library books of the temple of Dendera (Chassinat 1966: 817) — that is, the stone text presents itself as the copy of a book, and the book belonged to another temple's collection. The laboratory walls are a publication : the transfer of a guarded papyrus formulary into permanent, in-house stone. The second feature is scale of ingredients : Aufrère counts seventy-one basic ingredients across the Edfu recipes (Aufrère 1998c) — a working materia medica of resins, oils, wines, minerals, plant aromatics and animal products, each with its grades and seasons, that the perfumers were expected to command as professional knowledge (§XIV). What the walls do not preserve is equally definite, and §XX returns to it: no plan or depiction of the work in progress, no staff list, no account of failures, no alternatives. The corpus is a standard, and a standard shows only the compliant path. Everything this article says about the world behind the walls — the estates, the personnel, the storage — is reconstructed from other evidence and labelled as such where it is inference. VII. The Offering Reliefs — The King Presents the Laboratory's Products The recipes do not cover the laboratory's walls alone. They are framed by the standard visual language of the Ptolemaic temple: registers of offering scenes in which the king — the theoretical celebrant of every rite, whatever priest actually performed it — presents the finished products to the god. At Edfu the king offers the ointments and incense of the formulary to Horus; at Dendera, the laboratory's northern wall, first register, shows the offering of oliban — frankincense — to Hathor (Aufrère et al. 2022, fig. 7.2). The pairing of scene and text is the room's grammar: the relief shows what the product is for , the inscription beside it specifies how the product is made , and the two together close the circuit between workshop and sanctuary that §III described as the temple's production chain. This framing distinguishes the laboratory corpus from a craftsman's notebook. A notebook serves its writer; these walls serve the institution and its god. The offering scenes place manufacture inside the offering liturgy itself — the making of the ointment is part of the same ordered world as its presentation, and the king who offers in the relief is the same king whose name guarantees the standard in the recipe. When the daily rite anointed the statue with mrḥt [Gardiner: G17-D21-V28-X1] [𓅓𓂋𓎛𓏏] — the generic word for ointment, the substance class to which hekenu and the rest belong — the act consumed, in a single gesture, the produce of Punt expeditions, estate oil-presses, a year of staged cooking, and a written standard older than anyone in the room. The relief is the institution's own picture of that convergence. The scenes also carry the corpus's quality theology in visual form. In the grading lists (§XV), a second-quality product is marked as the "eye of Seth" — fit for lesser, medical use, unfit for the god. The offering relief admits no such ambiguity: what the king presents is, by definition, the first quality, the product made to the wall's own specification. Text, image and rite thus enforce one another. The recipe fixes the standard; the relief displays the standard's purpose; the daily performance audited the standard every morning, in the most public way the temple's interior allowed — on the body of the god himself. VIII. The Recipe as a Form — Name, Measure, Purpose, Sequence The Edfu recipes share a fixed literary form, and the form is itself evidence — of a tradition of technical writing old enough to have conventions. In Aufrère's description, a recipe opens with the name of the product , then specifies the amount to be produced : the standard batch is one hin , a liquid measure of about 0.48 litres. It then states why and for whom the preparation is made — this god, this rite, this use — before giving the chronology and proportions of the ingredients , each added in its order, at its time, in its state (fresh or dry, crushed or whole). The same architecture governs the Egyptian pharmacopoeia generally: ingredients, quantities, preparation (crushed, ground, cooked, reduced, filtered), and administration, specified in sequence. The laboratory recipe is the liturgical branch of a national technical genre. Within that form, three disciplines repay attention. The first is reduction accounting . The recipes are, in Manniche's words, meticulous in specifying quantities, "especially of the reduction that would take place during cooking," so that a correctly executed process has a pre-calculated end result — usually the one hin. A cook who knows in advance what the vessel must yield, and weighs the mixture before cooking and at intervals during it, topping up with water or wine, added very gradually, if too much weight is lost (Aufrère's hekenu analysis, §IX), is working to a specification with in-process checks. The second discipline is timing : stages are keyed to the calendar, some additions made at specific points of the lunar cycle — the new moon is Aufrère's example — and total durations run to hundreds of days (§IX). Time is an ingredient, measured like the resins. The third is fuel management : in the hekenu process the fuel itself is changed as the preparation advances and new ingredients are added — the heat source is part of the specification, not a background detail. // ANATOMY OF AN EDFU RECIPE // 1. Product name — the preparation is titled, as a book is titled. 2. Batch size — standard output one hin (c. 0.48 L). 3. Purpose clause — the god, rite or use the batch serves. 4. Ingredient schedule — each material named, graded, proportioned, and assigned its moment and its preliminary processing (crushing, sieving, extraction, pre-cooking). 5. Process chronology — staged operations across days, months, lunar points; fuel changes; weighings before and during cooking; corrections by gradual addition. 6. Yield check — the pre-calculated reduction: the finished batch must come out at the specified measure. 7. Restriction — where the recipe is a guarded one, its secrecy clause (§XV). The form's last feature is its glosses . Technical vocabularies decay: a plant name current when a recipe was composed may be obsolete two centuries later, and a formulary meant to be perpetual must maintain its own lexicon. Aufrère documents the mechanism in the kyphi tradition itself: the author gives equivalents for names that had become obscure, replacing old terms with current ones — "Ethiopian reed" replaced by "feather of Nemty," the aromatic "agaiu" replaced by "mint" (Aufrère 2005a). The same glossing habit appears in the Mansion of Gold texts at Dendera (§XI). A recipe corpus that annotates itself is a corpus designed for transmission across generations of practitioners — which is to say, the walls anticipate §XVII's subject: the laboratory text is a House of Life product, maintained like one. IX. Hekenu, Step by Step — Forty-Two Operations and a Year and a Third The fullest single process the Edfu walls preserve is the manufacture of the hekenu ointment — ḥknw [Gardiner: V28-V31-N35-G43] [𓎛𓎡𓈖𓅱] — and this section follows it as Aufrère's study (Aufrère 2005a: 224–35, summarised in Aufrère et al. 2022) reconstructs it, because it is the archive's best evidence for what "maximum procedural detail" meant in a temple workshop. Hekenu is an anointing ointment whose principal is premium frankincense oil mixed with styrax. The batch is the standard one hin. The ingredient list runs to nine items , among them two different qualities of frankincense — the grading system of §XV operating inside a single recipe — and "the excellent wine of the Oasis," whose role is chemical as well as honorific: oleoresins dissolve in alcohol, and the wine is the solvent that lets resin and oil marry. The number of distinct operations Aufrère counts in the preparation is about forty-two . The total time is between 487 and 492 days . The Process in Its Stages The sequence, as the inscription gives it and Aufrère analyses it, runs in the following shape. Individual ingredients are first processed separately : the flesh of the fruit of the nedjem tree — an as-yet-unidentified tree whose pulp served as a scent base — is extracted by twisting in a cloth, then cooked in a cauldron. Materials are crushed, then filtered through sieve or cloth to remove vegetal debris, the recipes distinguishing throughout between aromatics used fresh and aromatics used dry. The mixture is weighed before cooking , and reweighed regularly during cooking ; if too much weight has been lost, liquid — water or wine — is restored very gradually. The fuel is changed as the preparation advances and successive ingredients are added. Some stages are kept warm rather than cooked, held at temperature in a bain-marie . Sources and Scholarship I. Words for Cloth — Linen in the Egyptian Vocabulary Linen was not one thing in Egyptian, and the vocabulary already grades it. The general word for cloth, for a length or sheet of woven linen, is mnḫt [Gardiner: G17-N35-Aa1-X1] [𓅓𓈖𓐍𓏏] — the word the embalming texts use for the sheets laid over a body, and the word the temple accounts use for the woven product of estate flax, in grades from work-cloth to the god's own garments (see the temple laboratory , where the linen room stands beside the laboratory at Edfu). A garment, clothing as worn, is ḥbs [Gardiner: V28-D58-S29] [𓎛𓃀𓋴]. At the top of the scale stands šs-nswt [Gardiner: N37-S29-A43-X1] [𓈙𓋴𓀲𓏏], "royal linen" — literally the fine linen of the king — the grade the Ritual of Embalming reserves for particular stations of the body and the grade this article's thread counts (Section XIII) try to put numbers on. Bandage words belong to the same family of terms: a bandage is sbn [Gardiner: S29-D58-N35] [𓋴𓃀𓈖], one of several wrapping words the mummification article sets out in full. Two cautions govern the vocabulary of this article, and both are corrections the modern literature has forced. The first concerns the word "spinning." Older translations and museum labels describe Egyptian thread as "spun," and Egyptian workers with spindles as "spinners," as a matter of routine. The fibre evidence says otherwise for pharaonic Egypt: the thread was made by splicing (Section VII), and the spindle's real job was plying (Section VIII). This article therefore uses "spinning" only when reporting what an older source says, and flags it when it does. The second caution concerns fineness words. Egyptian grade terms — royal linen, fine linen, close-woven linen and their companions in the lists — are real administrative categories, but no surviving text defines them by a thread count. Where this article gives counts, they are modern measurements of surviving cloth, set beside the ancient words as correspondences, not as definitions. // READING THE TERMS IN THIS ARCHIVE // Every technical Egyptian term in this article carries its Gardiner sign codes, and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . A last preliminary, parallel to the one the archive's glass article makes. No Egyptian technical manual for weaving survives — no recipe papyrus for cloth, no workshop handbook. The procedural account that follows is reconstructed from four kinds of evidence, kept labelled as it goes: the cloth itself , surviving in Egypt's dry tombs in quantities no other ancient culture can match, and now read fibre by fibre under the microscope; depictions , above all the Middle Kingdom tomb scenes and workshop models that show the chain in sequence; tools and workshops , excavated at settlements such as Amarna, Gurob and Deir el-Medina; and experiment , the modern re-running of the process by the EGYARN project and other textile researchers, which has corrected the textbook account at its most fundamental step. Where a step is a reconstruction rather than an attestation, the text says so. II. The Evidence — Tomb Scenes, Workshop Models and Surviving Cloth Textile production is the best-depicted craft sequence in Middle Kingdom art. The tombs at Beni Hasan — Baqet III (no. 15), Khety (no. 17) and Khnumhotep II (no. 3) — show the chain in register: flax pulled in the field, fibre stripped from the stem, splicing performed on the thigh, plying with spindle and bowl, warping, and weaving at the ground loom, with laundering scenes in the same repertoire. Parallel scenes occur at Deshasheh, Meir and Sheikh Said. These are not generic "daily life" decoration to be waved at; read in sequence, and checked against the cloth, they are the closest thing Egypt left to a process manual, and this article cites them step by step. The Meketra workshop model (c. 1950 BCE), from the Theban tomb of the chancellor Meketra and now in the Metropolitan Museum, gives the same industry in three dimensions: a weaving workshop with ground looms, warping in progress, and the stores of a great household's cloth production rendered as a staffed room. A model is evidence of organisation as much as of technique — it shows who stood where, how many looms a household ran, and that cloth-making was an establishment, not an afterthought. Above both stands the cloth itself. Egypt's tombs preserve textiles by the tens of thousands, from Neolithic fragments in the Fayum (c. 5000 BCE) to complete New Kingdom wardrobes. Two survivals anchor this article's ends of the story. At the beginning, the Tarkhan dress (Petrie Museum, UC28614B): a tailored, V-necked linen garment with pleated sleeves, excavated by Flinders Petrie at Tarkhan in 1913 from a First Dynasty mastaba, recognised as a garment only in 1977 when the bundle it lay in was sent for conservation, and radiocarbon-dated at Oxford in 2015 to 3482–3102 BCE at 95% probability (Stevenson and colleagues, Antiquity , 2016) — the oldest woven garment known, made before or at the very cusp of the First Dynasty. At the industry's height, the linen chests of the tomb of Hatnefer and Ramose at Thebes, excavated by the Metropolitan Museum in 1935–36, held folded sheets of every grade from coarse mattress cloth to the sheer "royal linen" of Section XIII — a household's whole cloth wealth, buried as funerary provision. The modern evidence has a fourth leg, and it is the one that changed the field. The EGYARN project (Centre for Textile Research, University of Copenhagen; grant 890144), directed by Chiara Spinazzi-Lucchesi, set out to reconnect New Kingdom spinning tools to New Kingdom textiles by integrating textile, tool, fibre and textual study, with Gurob and above all Deir el-Medina as its case-study assemblages — and, crucially, by doing the work : its experimental programme, carried out with the weaver and spinner Marie Wallenberg and published in the EXARC Journal , rebuilt the splicing process variable by variable and documented its failures as carefully as its successes. Where this article reports a splice angle, a moisture problem or a retting degree, it is reporting that experimental record, not a plausible guess. // THE SHAPE OF THE EVIDENCE // c. 5000 BCE — woven flax fragments in the Neolithic Fayum. c. 3600 BCE — a Predynastic platter from Badari (tomb 3802) depicts a horizontal loom: the loom is older than the dynasties. 3482–3102 BCE — the Tarkhan dress, tailored clothing at the dawn of the state. Middle Kingdom — the Beni Hasan sequence and the Meketra model: the full chain depicted. c. 1425 BCE — the vertical loom first depicted (Section XI). c. 1491–1473 BCE — Hatnefer's chests: royal linen at its measured finest. Until at least c. 600 BCE — splicing remains the pharaonic yarn technology (Section VII). III. The Flax Plant — Cultivation and the Field Year The plant is Linum usitatissimum — the name itself, "most useful," is earned twice over in Egypt, since the same crop gives fibre from its stem and oil from its seed. The fibre is a bast fibre : it lies in the phloem, the inner bark surrounding the stem's hollow woody core, in bundles of some twenty to forty individual fibres glued together by pectins (the anatomy as set out in the EGYARN experimental literature). Everything in the production chain follows from that anatomy. The worker's problem is never the fibre itself, which is long, strong and fine; it is the glue and the woody core that hold it captive, and every preparation step is a negotiation with pectin. Flax fitted the Nile year as grain did. It was sown on the basin fields as the inundation water drained away in the autumn, grew through the cool season, and was harvested in the spring, roughly three to four months after sowing — a winter crop in a summer land, occupying the same flood-recession fields as the cereals and legumes whose cycle the archive treats in Food and Drink and in the field system set out in Agriculture ; this article takes the standing crop as its starting point. Flax wants water while it grows and punishes neglect with short, coarse stems: fibre length is decided in the field, months before any weaver sees the product, because the usable fibre can never be longer than the stem it grew in. Sowing density was itself a fibre technology. Flax sown thickly grows tall, straight and unbranched — each plant racing its neighbours for light, putting its growth into stem length rather than seed heads — and tall unbranched stems are exactly what the fibre-worker wants. Flax sown for seed, by contrast, is spaced to branch and flower. Egyptian growers therefore ran, in effect, two crops under one name, and the harvest decision of Section IV — when to pull — was the second half of a choice that began at sowing: a field destined for fine cloth was managed for stem, and a field destined for linseed and oil for capsule. The two products were not rivals so much as grades of one harvest, since even a fibre crop yields seed from its rippling (Section IV), and even a seed crop yields tow-grade fibre. Where the crop grew mattered to its reputation. The Delta, with its water and its deep soils, was flax country on the largest scale, and Delta and Fayum linens carried regional standing in the textual record; but every estate that could irrigate a flax plot did so, because cloth was a store of value no household could do without (Section XX). The temple estates grew flax as they grew grain — the temple laboratory article traces an estate system that owned the land that grew its flax and the weaving sheds that worked it, issuing finished mnḫt [Gardiner: G17-N35-Aa1-X1] [𓅓𓈖𓐍𓏏] to the god's service by grade. THE FIBRE CROP Sown thick, grown tall and unbranched, harvested young or half-ripe (Section IV). Product: long bast ribbons for splicing. The fine-cloth chain begins here, not at the loom. THE SEED CROP Sown spaced, allowed to branch, flower and ripen fully. Product: linseed for oil and next year's sowing; the stems yield only coarse, short fibre as a by-product. THE PLANT ITSELF A slender annual, roughly a metre tall at harvest, with a hollow woody core, an inner bark carrying the fibre bundles in pectin, and small blue flowers. Nothing about the standing plant announces cloth; the whole industry is extraction. IV. Harvest — Pulling, Timing and Rippling Flax for fibre was pulled, not cut . The harvester grasped a handful of stems and drew them up out of the ground roots and all, because every centimetre of stem is fibre: a cut stem throws away the length between blade and root, and in a crop whose whole value is length that waste is unaffordable. The pulling scenes in the tomb paintings show exactly this, handful by handful, the pulled plants laid in bundles to dry. It is slow work and it is the first of the chain's many labour bills — a theme this article does not let go of, because Egyptian linen's fineness was bought with time at every single step. Timing — the Harvest Is a Grade Decision When to pull decides what the fibre can become, and the Egyptian evidence, read with the experimental literature, supports the classic three-point scale. Pulled green , while the plant is still in or just past flower and the stems are unripe, flax gives the finest, softest, most pliable fibres — the fibres of the sheerest cloth; the Metropolitan Museum's note on the Hatnefer sheet concludes that its superfine thread must have come from flax harvested when the plants were very young (paraphrased from the Met record for 36.3.111). Pulled at half-ripeness , stems yellowing and capsules forming, the fibre is stronger and coarser, the general-purpose harvest. Pulled fully ripe , the crop maximises seed but the stems have lignified — the woody core has hardened into the fibre's enemy — and the fibre is fit for coarse cloth and cordage. A grower could not have all three from one field. The grades of Section XIII are therefore not created at the loom; they are harvested. Rippling — Taking the Seed Dried bundles went next to rippling : the stems were drawn through a wide-toothed comb — a rippling comb or fork — which stripped the seed capsules (bolls) from the stems without breaking the stems themselves. The capsules were collected, threshed and winnowed for linseed: for oil, for food and medicine, and for next year's sowing. Rippling is the chain's first combing operation and must not be confused with the heckling of Section VI: the ripple works on the whole stem, coarsely, to remove seed; it does not dress fibre. After rippling, the stems — now clean rods of bark and core — were bundled again for the retting decision. The harvest sequence, stated plainly: pull by the roots; bundle; dry; ripple the seed off; keep the stems intact and sorted by length as far as the harvest allowed. Sorting matters more than it sounds. Splicing (Section VII) joins ribbons end to end, root to tip, and a worker splicing from unsorted, mixed-length material produces uneven singles no plying can rescue. The evenness of good Egyptian yarn begins as field discipline. V. Retting — and the Egyptian Caveat Retting is the controlled rotting of the flax stem: microbial action, in water or in dew, digests the pectins that glue the fibre bundles to the woody core and to each other, freeing the fibres for extraction. In the later European linen industry retting is the pivotal, dreaded step — under-retted flax will not separate, over-retted flax rots its own fibres — and textbooks long assumed Egypt must have retted as Europe retted, for two to three weeks, as the gateway to all that followed. The Egyptian evidence does not fit that assumption, and this section states the archive's position at its real strength: the classic full retting of the European chain does not fit pharaonic practice , because the Egyptian yarn technology depends on the pectin that full retting destroys. The reasoning is mechanical. Egyptian thread was made by splicing ribbons — strips of bast in which the fibres still run together in their natural bundles, held by their own pectin (Section VII). A ribbon is precisely what retting is designed to abolish: ret the stem thoroughly and the bundles fall apart into individual fibres, fit for draft spinning but useless for the ribbon-splice. The EGYARN experiments tested the variable directly, working with un-retted, half-retted and fully retted material, and their programme settled on un-retted strips for the successful splicing reconstructions, with partially retted material also workable; the archive's research dossier records the complementary finding that where retting is used at all, a short retting of around ten days was experimentally optimal — a softening, not a dissolution. Light retting, in other words, may have loosened the stem enough to strip; the industry did not ret its fibre free. What, then, freed the fibre from the core? Chiefly the hands, and water used as a softener rather than a rot-box: soaking and wetting recur in the experimental reconstructions and in the depictions' logic, and a damp ribbon is a pliable ribbon. The honest summary is threefold. Attested: Egypt produced spliced yarn from bast ribbons for three thousand years, which constrains preparation to methods that leave ribbons intact. Experimentally supported: un-retted or lightly retted stems strip and splice well; fully retted stems do not splice in the Egyptian manner. Not established: the exact ancient routine — how long Egyptian stems soaked, where, and in what water — for which no text and no excavated retting installation yet gives a certain answer. Retting pits and ponds belong to the European evidence; projecting them wholesale onto the Nile is one of the assumptions this article exists to retire. // WHY THE CAVEAT MATTERS // Retting is not a pedantic footnote. It is the fork in the whole technology. Ret fully, and you must spin — the fibres are individuals, and only continuous drafting and twisting can gather them. Ret lightly or not at all, and you can splice — the fibres arrive as ribbons, and the join, not the draft, makes the thread. Egypt chose the second fork and stayed on it for millennia; the choice explains the tools (Section VIII), the depictions (Section II) and the structure of the yarn itself (Section VII) in a single move. VI. Stripping the Fibre — Breaking, Scutching and Heckling, Honestly Assessed Between the stem and the ribbon stands the extraction step, and here the archive must be as honest about absence as about presence. The mature European flax chain interposes three mechanical operations between retting and spinning: breaking , crushing the dried stem in a hinged brake so the woody core shatters while the flexible bast survives; scutching , beating and scraping the broken stems with a blade to knock the shattered core (the shive) away; and heckling (hackling), drawing the fibre repeatedly through beds of iron pins to comb it into parallel, separated strands. The task that set this article specified "scutching/heckling" as steps of the Egyptian chain. The evidence does not support them as such, and the article says so rather than dressing a European chain in Egyptian clothes. For pharaonic Egypt there is, on the current record, little evidence for breaking and scutching as distinct mechanical operations, and no evidence for heckling . No flax brake, scutching board or heckling comb has been identified in the pharaonic toolkit, and the depictions do not show them. What the Beni Hasan scenes show instead is the fibre being stripped from the stem by hand : the worker takes the (dried, possibly soaked) stem and peels the bast away in long ribbons, the core discarded, the ribbon kept whole. Hand-stripping is slower than breaking and scutching, and it produces exactly the feedstock splicing requires — continuous ribbons running the stem's full length, fibres still in their bundles, pectin still in place. The absence of the European machines is not a missing technology; it is the signature of a different one. A heckled, parallelised, individualised fibre supply would have been worse than useless to a splicer. Two qualifications keep the claim honest. First, hand-stripping surely shaded into hand-dressing: ribbons could be drawn across an edge, beaten lightly, wetted and worked between the fingers to shed core fragments and split an over-wide ribbon into narrower ones — the EGYARN preparation work includes exactly such low-technology handling, and the boundary between "stripping" and a manual equivalent of scutching is a matter of definition. What is absent is the apparatus and the aim : no machine, and no intention of separating the fibres from one another. Second, the claim is period-bound. Later, foreign-ruled and Roman-period Egypt absorbed Mediterranean practice wholesale, and fibre preparation there is a different question; this article's chain is the pharaonic one, and its honesty about the missing machines is part of what makes the splicing correction of the next section unavoidable. If Egypt had heckled, it would have spun. It spliced — so it cannot have prepared fibre the heckling way. The product of this section, then, is the ribbon : a strip of bast a stem's length long — up to the better part of a metre from a good crop — containing its twenty-to-forty-fibre bundles entire. Ribbons were kept sorted, coiled or laid in bundles, and carried to the splicer's lap. The thread is about to be made without ever existing as a loose fibre mass at all. VII. Splicing — the Correction at the Centre of This Article Here is the correction, stated first in one sentence and then in full. Pharaonic Egyptian linen thread was not made by draft spinning. It was made by splicing: individual bast-fibre ribbons were joined end to end, each join made by overlapping the two ribbon ends and twisting them together at the overlap alone, producing a continuous single thread whose length is the sum of its ribbons. The demonstration is modern and microscopic. Gleba and Harris, "The first plant bast fibre technology: identifying splicing in archaeological textiles" ( Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 11, 2019, 2329–2346), defined the types of splicing and published an explicit method for identifying spliced thread in archaeological textiles, applying it across Europe, Egypt and the Near East; their conclusion, paraphrased, is that splicing — not draft spinning — was the plant-fibre thread technology of the ancient world they sampled, and that the switch to draft spinning came far later than textbooks assumed. For Egypt specifically the point had been building for decades — Fox noted the peculiarities of Egyptian yarn as early as 1910, and Barber, Cartwright and colleagues, and Kemp and Vogelsang-Eastwood's Amarna work all carried it — but Gleba and Harris gave the field its identification method and its name. Splicing remained the pharaonic technique until at least the beginning of the Persian period, c. 600 BCE (Cartwright and colleagues, as cited in the EGYARN experimental literature). What Splicing Is, Precisely Take two fibre ribbons. Lay them end to end, overlapping by a few centimetres , aligned root to tip — the thick root end of one against the tapering tip of the next, so the join keeps the thread's diameter even; a root end left too thick is tapered first. Then twist the two ribbons together at the overlap only — classically by rolling them under the palm on the bare thigh, exactly as the Beni Hasan painters show, the worker seated with ribbons fed from a supply beside them — and move on. The rest of each ribbon carries no twist at all. The resulting single is a chain of untwisted ribbons locked together by short, tightly twisted splices, each splice a few centimetres long. Gleba and Harris distinguish end-to-end splicing , the discrete joins just described, from continuous splicing , in which new fibre is fed in as the thread is formed; the Egyptian evidence and the EGYARN reconstructions centre on the end-to-end form. A splice can be twisted in either direction, conventionally labelled s or z after the diagonal of the twist, and the direction is a real, recordable property of every ancient thread. How It Differs from Spinning — and Why the Old Reading Failed In draft spinning , by contrast, fully separated fibres are drawn out continuously from a prepared mass — classically dressed on a distaff — while a rotating spindle twists the emerging stream along its whole length. The two technologies differ in everything: in feedstock (loose fibres against ribbons), in preparation (full retting and heckling against light retting and hand-stripping, Sections V–VI), in where the twist lives (everywhere against only at the joins), and in what the finished single looks like under magnification — which is where the old reading failed. A spliced single, once two of them are plied together with opposite twist (Section VIII), presents a regular diagonal surface that generations of cataloguers recorded as "S-spun yarn." The textbook phrase "S-spun Egyptian linen" is, in large part, a misreading of plied spliced structure: the microscope, at sufficient magnification and with Gleba and Harris's criteria in hand, shows the untwisted ribbon lengths and the discrete joins that the naked-eye description smoothed away. The archive's rule follows: no claim of draft-spun pharaonic yarn is accepted in these pages without fibre-level evidence, and the spinning language of older museum records — including, it must be said fairly, the Metropolitan Museum's own note that the Hatnefer sheet's thread was "spun from flax harvested when the plants were very young" — is reported as the record's wording, while the harvest-timing substance underneath it stands. The Experimental Record — What Actually Makes a Splice Hold Splicing is easy to describe and, the EGYARN experiments found, hard to do. Spinazzi-Lucchesi and Wallenberg's programme (EXARC Journal) set out to produce splices that hold without adhesives, without prolonged moisture, and without being kept under tension , with the tight twist visible in the ancient threads — and documented, variable by variable, what governs success. Four findings carry the procedural weight of this article. First, the angle: the angle at which the two ribbons meet controls the number of rotations the rolling palm imparts — a narrow angle gives few rotations and a weak join; a wider angle generates the rotations that make a splice grip, and grip is strength. Second, the overlap: a few centimetres, root to tip, the thick end tapered — too short starves the join, too long wastes fibre and thickens the thread. Third, moisture is a trap: wet ribbons splice easily, but flax fibres swell in water and shrink on drying, so a splice made wet loosens as it dries and gaps open between the ribbons; the earlier experiments that soaked ribbons for a day and glued or tension-dried the joins were compensating for exactly this. Fourth, handling: finished singles keep their splices best coiled loosely rather than wound hard into balls, which disturbs the joins — and the ancient depictions' coils and balls beside the splicer are read in that light. The experimenters' conclusion deserves its place here in paraphrase: the ancient workers spliced vigorously and very effectively — the tight, regular splices of the surviving yarns are a mastered skill, not a makeshift. DRAFT SPINNING — NOT THE PHARAONIC METHOD Separated fibres drawn continuously from a mass and twisted along the whole length by a rotating spindle. Requires full retting and combing. The textbook default — and, for pharaonic linen, the error this section corrects. END-TO-END SPLICING — THE PHARAONIC METHOD Ribbons overlapped a few centimetres, root to tip, twisted only at the overlap, rolled on the thigh. Twist lives at the joins; the ribbon lengths between are untwisted. Identified by the Gleba and Harris method; reconstructed by EGYARN. THE SPINDLE'S REAL JOB Spindle whorls are common finds — and are not evidence of draft spinning. In the splicing system the spindle adds twist for plying two singles together (Section VIII). Presence of whorls proves twisting, not spinning. One more consequence, because it reorganises the social history of the craft. Splicing needs no distaff, no prepared fibre supply, no equipment beyond a lap, a thigh and a stock of ribbons — and it is interruptible work, done seated, at household scale, by the fireside as readily as in a workshop. The technology that made Egypt's finest export was, at its decisive step, a hand technology of almost embarrassing simplicity, whose entire difficulty was tacit: ribbon preparation, splice angle, moisture judgment, rhythm. Sections XIX–XX return to what that means for who made Egypt's cloth. VIII. Plying — the Spindle, the Spinning Bowl, and What They Were Really For A single spliced thread is usable, but it is not yet weaving yarn at its best. A splice, however well made, is a local thickening and a potential weak point, and a single made of untwisted ribbon lengths has little resistance to abrasion in the loom. The Egyptian answer was plying : two spliced singles were twisted together along their whole length, with a twist opposite in direction to the splices' own, so that the singles lock around each other, the splices are trapped and staggered inside the ply, and the finished yarn gains the strength and evenness the warp in particular demands. In the notation modern textile scholarship uses (Rast-Eicher and Dietrich's system, as cited in the EGYARN literature), a yarn of two z-spliced singles plied with an S-twist is written S2*z — ply direction first, number of singles, splice direction last — and its mirror, two s-spliced singles plied Z, is Z2*s. The notation is worth learning because it says in four characters what the old literature's "S-spun" said wrongly in one word. The tools of plying are the tools the older literature misread as a spinning kit. The spindle — a shaft with a whorl as flywheel and weight — was used in the plying stage: the depictions and the EGYARN reconstructions show spliced singles being twisted together with the spindle's help, the whorl's momentum doing the steady twisting that fingers alone sustain poorly over long lengths. The spinning bowl , a bowl with an internal loop or handle through which yarn was passed, belongs to the same stage: the singles were drawn through the bowl — water in it could damp the yarn as it passed, a controlled touch of moisture at the one stage where damp helps rather than harms — and the bowl's loop kept tension and order while the spindle plied. Read with splicing in mind, the whole familiar toolkit reassembles itself one step later in the chain than the textbooks put it. Nothing is discarded; everything is reassigned. Plying was also where counts were set. Warp yarn — the lengthwise yarn that takes the loom's tension and the beater's punishment — was plied hard and even; weft yarn, which only has to lie in the shed, could be softer, and fine cloth might use plied warp against lighter weft, one of the asymmetries the thread counts of Section XIII keep meeting (warp counts run higher than weft counts in Egyptian cloth again and again). Singles could also be plied more than twofold for cordage-grade yarn, and the same twisting technology, at larger scale, made the ropes and nets that stand at the coarse end of the fibre economy. The yarn, finished, was wound into balls or skeins — the depictions show both — and issued to the warping stage by count and by weight, in the workshops that kept accounts (Section XIX). IX. Warping — Preparing the Loom's Skeleton Weaving begins before the loom, in warping : the laying out of the warp, the full set of lengthwise threads, in order, at length, under even tension, ready to be mounted. Warping is the stage at which the cloth's width, length and warp count are irrevocably decided, and at which an error — a crossed thread, an uneven tension, a miscount — is woven into every subsequent row. The Egyptian evidence shows warping done on pegs driven in the ground or set in a frame or wall, the yarn carried back and forth around the pegs to build the warp as a continuous ordered sheet, with a cross kept in the threads to preserve their order; the Meketra model shows the operation inside a household workshop, and the Beni Hasan sequence includes it in the chain. Warping also made the cloth's first ornament, before any weaving: the starting border . Egyptian cloth characteristically begins not with a raw warp edge but with a woven heading — a narrow band in which warp and weft are worked together (in some pieces a tablet-woven or multiply-worked heading) that locks the warp threads in their spacing and gives the weaver a firm, finished edge to weave away from. The starting border survives on complete cloths and is one of the features by which a whole cloth, as opposed to a cut fragment, is recognised. At the cloth's other end the warp would be finished with a fringe of the warp threads themselves, plied or knotted (Section XII) — the Met's Hatnefer sheet preserves both: a warp selvage at one end and a plied fringe at the other. The scale of warping deserves a number. A sheet of the Hatnefer type — 161 cm wide at 46 warp threads to the centimetre — carries on the order of seven thousand four hundred warp threads , each over five metres long, each one spliced from dozens of ribbons and plied, each one laid in order by hand. That arithmetic, not any loom mechanism, is the true measure of Egyptian textile labour, and it is why the Met's judgment that such a length "would have taken months of constant industry to weave" understates the case: the weaving was the last of the months. The splicing was the first of them. X. The Horizontal Ground Loom, Step by Step For most of pharaonic history the loom was the horizontal ground loom : the warp stretched flat, at ground level, between two beams, and the weaver working along it at ground level too. It is depicted from the Predynastic period — the Badari platter of c. 3600 BCE already shows it — through the Middle Kingdom scenes and models, and it never entirely disappeared. The sequence below is the standard reconstruction from the depictions, the models and the cloth, in the order of work. 1. Peg Out and Mount the Warp Two stout beams — the warp beam and the cloth beam — are set parallel on the ground, held by pegs driven in at their ends, at a distance apart equal to the cloth's intended length (long cloths could be woven in stages, the finished portion wound on). The prepared warp (Section IX) is stretched between the beams and tensioned: the pegs and beams, not any ratchet, hold the tension, and the warp lies as a flat sheet a few centimetres above the earth, wide as the cloth and long as the piece. 2.
