Sources and Modern Scholarship I. The Name — Zōsimos the Panopolitan Every other article in this archive that treats a person begins with a god, a king, or a text. This one begins with something rarer in the alchemical literature: an author. The Greek alchemical corpus is crowded with famous names — Hermes, Democritus, Moses, Maria, Agathodaimon — and modern scholarship regards nearly all of them as pseudepigrapha, honorific masks under which anonymous recipe-writers and commentators published their work. Zosimos is the great exception. As Olivier Dufault puts it in his study of early Greek alchemy (University of California, 2019), in contrast to the majority of names in the corpus, "Zosimus of Panopolis" does not appear to be pseudepigraphic: behind the name stands a real writer, working at a real date, in a real city, for a real patroness whose household, rivals, and questions can still be traced in his pages. He is, in the phrase this archive uses throughout, the earliest alchemical author whose works survive substantially — not the first person to practise the art, and not the inventor of its recipes, but the first practitioner-theorist whose own voice reaches us in bulk. His name in Greek is Zōsimos — a common late-antique name built on the root of the verb "to live," with a sense close to "the living one" or "he who will live." His ethnic, the word that does the identifying work, is ho Panopolitēs , "the Panopolitan," the man from Panopolis. The manuscripts of the alchemical corpus style him regularly with that ethnic, and later alchemists often cite him by the ethnic alone, as "the Panopolitan," the way a modern field might cite "the Leiden professor." Two external witnesses agree with the manuscripts: the Byzantine chronicler Georgius Syncellus calls him a Panopolitan, and Photius, the ninth-century patriarch and bibliographer, calls him a Theban from Panopolis. Against this consensus stands a single dissenting voice, and it is an important one because it comes from the source that preserves the largest claims about his output: the Suda , the tenth-century Byzantine lexicon, calls him an Alexandrian . Michèle Mertens, in the introduction to her standard edition of the Authentic Memoirs (1995) and in her study of alchemy, Hermetism and Gnosticism at Panopolis (2002), works through the discrepancy with characteristic care. The eighteenth-century scholar Fabricius proposed the comfortable reconciliation — born at Panopolis, resident at Alexandria — and most historians of alchemy adopted it. Mertens is less comfortable: the Suda 's compiler, she notes, knew how to say "adopted city" when he meant it, as he does for other figures; the likelier explanation is that his sources were silent or incomplete on Zosimos's origin and that Alexandria, the default city of Greek learning in Egypt, filled the gap. This article follows Mertens: Panopolis is the origin the evidence supports; Alexandria is a possibility about his working life, not a fact about his birth , and the distinction is flagged wherever it matters. A second naming caution concerns the language of this article itself. Zosimos wrote in Greek . His technical vocabulary — the words for his apparatus, his operations, his spirits and tinctures — is Greek, and this article transliterates it as Greek, without Gardiner sign codes, because Gardiner codes belong to the Egyptian hieroglyphic script and forcing them onto Greek words would be a category error. Gardiner codes appear here only where genuinely Egyptian words are in play: the names of his city in its older Egyptian form, the name of the land itself, and the Egyptian gods and institutions that form his background. Those Egyptian terms follow the archive's usual protocol, set out in the reading note below. // READING THE NAMES IN THIS ARCHIVE // Greek terms are given in transliteration with their Greek forms where the form itself matters: chēmeia (χημεία), the art; Cheirokmēta (χειρόκμητα), "things made by hand," his title for the work; baphē (βαφή), a dyeing or tincture. Egyptian terms carry Gardiner sign codes in the form [Gardiner: <codes>], and every bracketed glyph string has been composed sign by sign from the archive's V2 Gardiner map, so that the printed transliteration is exactly what the signs decode to. Where a post-audit correction supersedes the map's draft value, the corrected value is used and flagged: F13 = wp , M44 = spd , O31 = ꜥꜣ , O33 = srḫ , I14 = ḳꜣb , R20 and R21 = sšꜣt , F21 = msḏr , U38 = mḫꜣt , E10 = bꜣ , E8a = ꞽb . The full sign list is given in the hieroglyph reference . One more name belongs in this opening section, because Zosimos himself insists on it: the name of the art. In the treatise transmitted as the Book of Sophe , Zosimos retails an origin story in which the first book of the art was called Chema , after the fallen angels who, in his telling, revealed it — and from that book, he says, the science took its name. The story is myth, and Section XVII treats it as myth. But the etymological instinct behind it is the same one the archive examines in the alchemy article : the Greek chēmeia or khymeia has repeatedly been derived from the Egyptian name of Egypt itself, kmt [Gardiner: I6-G17-X1-O49] [𓆎𓅓𓏏𓊖] — "the Black Land," written with the crocodile-skin sign km [Gardiner: I6], "black," the reed m [Gardiner: G17], the loaf t [Gardiner: X1], and the town determinative niwt [Gardiner: O49]. Whether or not the derivation is linguistically sound — scholars remain divided, and a competing derivation from Greek khymos , "juice," has its defenders — Zosimos's own framing is unambiguous about the geography of his art: it is Egyptian knowledge, revealed in Egypt, guarded by Egyptian adepts, and written down, in his case, by an Egyptian from the upper Nile valley who happened to write in Greek. The bilingual, bicultural character of the work is not an accident of transmission. It is the work's native condition, and it is why a profile of Zosimos belongs in an Egyptology archive at all. II. Panopolis — Ipu, Khent-Min, City of Min Panopolis is modern Akhmim , on the east bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, a few kilometres north-east of modern Sohag. To understand what Zosimos's ethnic meant to his first readers, the city's layers of name have to be unfolded in order, because each layer is a different civilisation's reading of the same place. In ancient Egyptian the town was ipw [Gardiner: M17-Q3-G43] [𓇋𓊪𓅱] — i [Gardiner: M17], p [Gardiner: Q3], w [Gardiner: G43] — rendered in older literature as Ipu or Apu. Its cult name was ḫnt-mnw , "Foremost of Min," written here in a transparent phonetic spelling [Gardiner: Aa1-N35-X1-G17-N35-G43] [𓐍𓈖𓏏𓅓𓈖𓅱]: ḫ [Gardiner: Aa1], n [Gardiner: N35], t [Gardiner: X1], then mnw [Gardiner: G17-N35-G43], the god Min. The town was the capital of the ninth nome of Upper Egypt and the great cult centre of Min, the ithyphallic fertility god whose raised arm and flail made him one of the oldest continuously worshipped gods in Egypt. Greek speakers heard ḫnt-mnw and compressed it into Khemmis or Chemmis ; and because they identified Min with their own Pan — the identification resting on the god's generative, wild-country character — they also called the city Panopolis , "Pan's city." Herodotus, who visited in the fifth century BCE, already knows it as Chemmis, with a temple and a curious local cult of Perseus. Strabo, five centuries later, describes a population of linen-weavers and stone-cutters — a craftsman's city, which is exactly the kind of city Zosimos's work presupposes. The weaving matters. Panopolis was famous in the Roman period for its textiles — for fine linen and, increasingly, for the tapestry-woven wool that would make Akhmim's late-antique and Coptic fabrics famous across the Mediterranean. A city of weavers is a city of dyers , and dyeing is one of the four great crafts around which the whole early alchemical recipe tradition is organised (Section IX). When the Stockholm Papyrus, copied in the same broad period and region, devotes some seventy recipes to mordanting wool and imitating Tyrian purple, it is describing the daily economy of towns like Panopolis. Zosimos's own central technical metaphor — the baphē , the dyeing or tincture that fixes a new colour permanently into a prepared body — is a weaver-dyer's metaphor before it is a philosopher's. The archive does not claim that Zosimos personally stood at a dye-vat; nothing in the evidence places a vat in his hands. It claims the weaker and more defensible thing: the conceptual furniture of his art — preparation, mordanting, immersion, fixation, the colour that goes all the way through and cannot be washed out — is the furniture of the industries his city lived by. Panopolis was also, by Zosimos's lifetime, a place where the old Egyptian religion, Greek learning, and the newer currents of Hermetism and Gnosticism met in unusual concentration. Mertens's Panopolis study takes its title from exactly this conjunction — alchemy, Hermetism and Gnosticism at Panopolis around 300 CE — and assembles the hints in Zosimos's work for the place those currents held in his town. The pattern outlasted him: a century and a half later the same city produced Nonnus, author of the Dionysiaca , the most extravagantly learned pagan epic of late antiquity, and the region's monasteries and copyists would preserve texts — Hermetic, Gnostic, and Christian alike — that were lost everywhere else. The archive's articles on Hermeticism , Gnosticism and the Corpus Hermeticum treat that wider world; Zosimos is its earliest Panopolitan voice, and the only one who speaks from inside a workshop tradition. His city also stood within reach of the older institutional Egypt: the temple House of Life , pr-ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: O1-D36-S34] [𓉐𓂝𓋹] — "house" written pr [Gardiner: O1], "life" written ꜥnḫ [Gardiner: S34] with its phonetic complement ꜥ [Gardiner: D36] — was the kind of priestly library and scriptorium in which the older Egyptian technical and ritual literature had been kept for millennia. Zosimos never claims membership of such an institution, and this article does not claim it for him. But the guarded, book-centred, initiation-flavoured character of his teaching, examined in Section XVII, is continuous with the culture of those houses in a way his Greek philosophical vocabulary alone cannot explain. Finally, the city's gods frame his imagination. Min's city was a city of generation — of the god who makes things grow, beget, and come forth. Up and down the valley the same theology was stated in the language of heka , ḥkꜣ [Gardiner: V28-D28-G1] [𓎛𓂓𓄿] — written with ḥ [Gardiner: V28], the ka-sign kꜣ [Gardiner: D28], and the reed ꜣ [Gardiner: G1] — the operative power by which words and rites take effect in matter. Zosimos does not use the Egyptian word; he writes Greek, and his operative power is the pneuma , the spirit that can be drawn out of bodies and fixed into them. But a historian reading him against his hometown notices the family resemblance without needing to force it: in both vocabularies, correctly prepared matter, correctly handled by a correctly prepared operator, at the correct time, undergoes a change that is real, permanent, and charged with more than chemistry. Section XIX returns to that resemblance, labelled as interpretation rather than descent. III. The Life — What Is Known, What Is Inferred The honest biography of Zosimos can be written in one short paragraph, and this section will write it — then spend the rest of its length showing the working, because in Zosimos's case the working is the scholarship. What is known: a Greek-writing Egyptian named Zosimos, from Panopolis in Upper Egypt, composed a substantial body of alchemical treatises in the form of letters, commentaries, and technical memoirs, addressed principally to a woman named Theosebeia; he treated the earlier alchemical authorities — above all the Democritus tradition and Maria — as classics to be expounded; he described and had drawn a range of furnaces and stills; and his work was already authoritative enough, within a few generations, to be excerpted, translated, and fought over. What is not known: his birth date, his death date, his family, his occupation in any civic sense, his religion in any confessional sense, and whether he ever set foot in Alexandria. No inscription names him. No contemporary outside the alchemical tradition mentions him. Everything else in the standard biographies — the priest, the Gnostic initiate, the temple chemist — is inference from his texts, of varying quality, and this article marks it as such wherever it appears. Even his date is a bracket, not a point. Mertens establishes that he must have been active about 300 CE , and Dufault, reviewing the whole evidentiary base, gives the outer limits as roughly 240 to 391 CE : he must postdate the authorities he comments on and the recipe culture of the third century, and he must predate the late-fourth-century writers who already treat the alchemical commentary tradition as established. Within that bracket, "late third to early fourth century, flourishing around 300" is the consensus formulation, and it is the one this article's header uses. The bracket matters for more than pedantry. A Zosimos of about 300 writes after the great age of the Greek Magical Papyri , in the same Theban-Upper Egyptian world that produced those papyri and the recipe books of Section IX; he writes before the Christian empire's suppression of the temples, in the last generations in which a pagan-Hermetic teacher could operate openly from a patroness's household; and he writes at exactly the moment when the older Egyptian temple economy that had sustained practical chēmeia for centuries was beginning its long contraction. His encyclopaedic urgency — the sense, everywhere in his work, that the tradition must be collected, ordered, and explained now , or lost — reads differently once that date is felt. His social position can be recovered a little more concretely, thanks to Dufault's central argument. Reading the letters to Theosebeia against the sociology of late-antique scholarship, Dufault presents Zosimos as a client scholar : a learned man informally retained by a wealthy patroness to teach, to expound difficult texts, and to produce new work — the alchemical counterpart of the grammarians, physicians, and philosophers who staffed great households across the Roman world. The evidence is circumstantial but mutually reinforcing. Theosebeia's household, as glimpsed in the correspondence, has a library and servants of some standing, including a table-server whose duties imply formal dining; Zosimos is invited to dinner in a household that is hers and others'; treatises are written at her request and in answer to her questions; and his tone to her moves between deference, professorial command, and open polemic against rival teachers competing for her ear — precisely the register of a retained expert whose position depends on remaining the indispensable interpreter. None of this makes him a hired hand in the modern sense. The client-scholar of late antiquity was a friend, a dependent, and an authority at once, and Zosimos's self-presentation — the visionary of Section XVI, the guardian of the ancients' secrets — is the self-presentation of a man whose claim on his patroness's attention rested on being more than a technician. Section IV follows the relationship in detail; here it is enough to fix the category, because the category explains the corpus. Letters, commentaries, encyclopaedic collection, and polemic are what a client scholar produces. A temple's internal manual or a guild's notebook would look quite different — and, in the Leyden and Stockholm papyri, we can see exactly how different (Section IX). KNOWN Panopolitan origin (manuscripts, Syncellus, Photius); Greek authorship of an extensive alchemical corpus; Theosebeia as principal addressee; commentary on Democritus-tradition and Maria; apparatus descriptions with drawings; activity around 300 CE. INFERRED — WITH GROUNDS Client-scholar relationship to Theosebeia's household (Dufault, from the letters' internal evidence); Hermetic and Gnostic colouring of his religious thought (from his own texts); first-hand familiarity with workshop practice (from the precision of the apparatus treatises). NOT KNOWN Dates of birth and death; family and civic occupation; confessional identity (pagan, Hermetic, Gnostic, and Christian colourings all appear in or have been claimed for the corpus); residence at Alexandria (the Suda alone, against the consensus); any event of his life outside the correspondence. A last biographical trap deserves naming, because the older literature falls into it constantly: there were other Zosimoi. The name was common, late antiquity produced several literary men who bore it — a historian, rhetoricians, a Zosimos of Gaza, a Zosimos of Ascalon — and Byzantine compilers were not always careful to keep them apart. Mertens's edition exists in large part to perform that separation for the alchemical corpus: of the mass of material travelling under Zosimos's name in the Greek manuscripts, she distinguishes the groups that may be attributed to him with certainty from extracts, summaries, and outright false attributions inherited from Berthelot's more inclusive edition. When this article says "Zosimos," it means the Panopolitan alchemist as delimited by that critical work. Where a striking doctrine rests on a text of contested attribution — the Book of Sophe material of Section XVII is the chief case — the article says so at the point of use. IV. Theosebeia — Patroness, Sister, Addressee Almost everything Zosimos wrote, he wrote to somebody, and the somebody is overwhelmingly one person: Theosebeia . Her name is Greek and transparent — "god-revering," "pious toward the gods" — and the Suda calls her Zosimos's adelphē , his "sister." No modern scholar takes the word as a statement about parentage. In the religious associations of late antiquity, "brother" and "sister" are the ordinary courtesies between fellow-initiates, and the salutation is evidence — of the kind this archive handles carefully — that teacher and pupil understood themselves as members of a shared circle with a shared commitment. What that circle was has been argued over for a century: Reitzenstein proposed an initiatory group on the strength of the word alone; more recent work, including Christian Bull's and Peter Fraser's, pictures Zosimos and Theosebeia at the centre of a small Hermetic ritual community ; and a salutation preserved from the end of one of his letters, quoted by a later Christian author, greets its recipients in explicitly Christian terms, which has fed a parallel line of argument about the circle's Christian colouring. Dufault's review of the whole dossier is judicious: a Syriac translation of a lost work of Zosimos partly supports the circle theory while also suggesting that Zosimos himself stood somewhat apart from Theosebeia's group — its adviser and teacher rather than simply its member. This article presents the "sister" as a religious courtesy inside a real teaching relationship, and the competing reconstructions as reconstructions. Theosebeia herself emerges from the letters with unusual clarity for an ancient addressee, because Zosimos is constantly reacting to her: to her questions, her other teachers, her impatience, and her requests for the parts of the doctrine he would rather not write down. She was, on Dufault's reading of the household evidence, an aristocratic woman who led a group of like-minded students of alchemy and who commissioned Zosimos's advice on the questions the group was working through. She was not a passive pupil. A Syriac-preserved text confirms that she taught others herself; the treatise On the Letter Omega records, in Zosimos's own defensive formulation, that she had asked for "things that ought not" to be mentioned — the final doctrines, the teleia — and his answer is a small masterpiece of the client-scholar's art: he pleads his predecessors. He had, he says, found no such final doctrines in the ancients; allegory he had interpreted; he had done what was appropriate for a commentary. Reverence for the tradition becomes, in the same gesture, an honourable refusal, a boundary on what patronage can buy, and an advertisement that there is a further teaching which his commentary faithfully serves. The whole letter-corpus runs on that tension: the teacher who must satisfy the patroness's demand for the art's secrets, and the guardian who must not surrender them to writing, to rivals, or to the unprepared. The rivals are named, and they give the correspondence its polemical heat. Chief among them is Neilos , whom Zosimos calls, with audible irony, Theosebeia's priest — "your priest," ho sos hiereus — a religious expert attached to her circle rather than, so far as the phrasing suggests, to any temple, god, or city. In the treatise On the Treatment of the Body of Magnesia , Zosimos's most explicit attack, Neilos appears marvelling with his disciples before divine statues, and Zosimos's counter-argument is bibliographic as much as theological: Neilos's failure, like Theosebeia's own moments of "imperfection," is diagnosed as insufficient acquaintance with the Democritean corpus — he has not read the ancients properly. Other figures flicker at the edges of the polemic: a certain Taphnouti, against whose company Theosebeia is warned, and unnamed "uneducated men" and women practitioners whose readings Zosimos labours to discredit before he will expound a recipe, warning her against any interpretation that contradicts his own. Read sociologically, this is a retained expert defending his retainer. Read as the history of alchemy, it is something more valuable: the first surviving record of alchemical controversy — competing teachers, competing readings of the same ancient texts, and a patroness whose favour was worth competing for. The art, in Zosimos's pages, is already a tradition with insiders, outsiders, and an orthodoxy under construction. The doctrinal content of the teaching she received can be sampled from the work Dufault analyses most closely, the Final Count (also rendered Final Quittance ). There Zosimos lays out a history of the tinctures and then turns the history into an exhortation: Theosebeia is to stop wandering in search of God from place to place, to cease sacrificing to the local overseer-spirits, to stay home and rectify herself — the Greek verb is dieuthynein , to make straight, to set right — and so avert the daimones and perfect her soul. Doing so, he promises, she will find the "genuine, natural and propitious tinctures." The passage is the whole Zosimian synthesis in miniature, and Section XV unpacks it: laboratory success and spiritual condition are not two topics but one, because the tincture that takes permanently in metal and the rectification that takes permanently in the soul are, for Zosimos, the same operation described in two registers. It is also, read plainly, pastoral counsel from a teacher to a patroness he believed was being led astray by competitors — theology doing the work of a professional boundary. Both readings are true to the text, and the archive keeps both. The letter form itself deserves a closing word. Zosimos did not write a systematic treatise and then excerpt it into letters; the letters are the work, each one occasional — answering a question, correcting an error, expounding a passage of Democritus or Maria, prefacing a technical memoir — and the system, such as it is, must be reconstructed across them, which is what Mertens's edition and the scholarship of Section XX collectively do. The Arabic tradition understood the form perfectly and preserved it: the Book of Pictures (Section VIII) is cast as a dialogue between Zosimos and Theosebeia in which she complains, with some justice, about the ambiguity of his explanations, and he answers with images. A teacher whose pupil talks back in the text is a teacher being read closely by a real person. Of all the evidence for the historical Zosimos, that may be the most humanly convincing. V. The Corpus — the Cheirokmēta and the Twenty-Eight Books Zosimos called his subject-matter by a word that states his whole conception of it: Cheirokmēta (χειρόκμητα), "things made by hand" — hand-wrought products, artefacts, the output of skilled manual work raised to a science. The word is rare and deliberate. Alchemy, in its author's own title for it, is not a speculation about matter but a making , and the treatises that expound it are commentaries on makings: recipes, apparatus, and the authorities who handed both down. The Latin tradition would later garble the word in the most instructive possible way. The early medieval recipe collection known as the Mappae Clavicula — "the little key [and] the cloth," a nonsense title — is now generally identified, following Halleux and Meyvaert, as a Latin translation of a lost Greek recipe corpus whose title joined kleidion , "little key," to cheirokmētōn , "of the hand-made things": a translator who misread the rare Greek word as cheiromaktron , "hand-towel," produced mappa , "cloth," and nonsense with a pedigree. The episode, treated in the archive's research dossier on repeatable processes, is a parable of the transmission this whole article traces: Zosimos's world survived into the Latin West even where its vocabulary was no longer understood. Against that background, the largest claim in the tradition can be stated and weighed. The Suda credits Zosimos with a great alchemical work in twenty-eight books , organised — in the usual account of the entry — under the letters of the Greek alphabet and addressed to Theosebeia. This article presents that figure exactly as the task of honest scholarship requires: as tradition and attribution, not as a surviving table of contents . No twenty-eight-book work exists. What exists is roughly a hundred pages of Greek under his name, a substantial Syriac corpus, and an Arabic tradition of unexpected richness (Sections VI–VIII) — fragments, extracts, and reworkings from which the shape of a much larger œuvre can be glimpsed but not recovered. Two considerations nevertheless keep the Suda 's number from being mere legend. First, the letter-organisation it implies is independently attested in the Syriac transmission, where a surviving treatise on the making of tin is headed as the work of the Letter Ḥet — the eighth letter of the Syriac alphabet — and greets "the queen Theosebeia": a book numbered by its letter, exactly as the encyclopaedia tradition describes. Second, the scale is credible for the genre and the man. Zosimos's surviving excerpts refer backward and forward to other treatises of his own, preface lost works, and summarise lost works; the Final Count presupposes a history of the art in many parts; the commentator's posture itself — expounding a canon — implies an author who thought in corpora. The archive's verdict, following Mertens's caution, is that Zosimos very probably did compose an encyclopaedic lettered collection of which the Suda 's twenty-eight is the tradition's count, and that reconstructing its contents book by book is not possible on present evidence. Both halves of that sentence are load-bearing. What the encyclopaedic ambition consisted in can still be described, because its habits survive even where its volumes do not. Zosimos collects: authorities, recipes, apparatus designs, etymologies, origin-myths, and dream-visions all enter the same corpus and are made to comment on one another. He cross-refers: a tincture expounded in a letter is the same tincture whose preparation the apparatus memoir makes possible and whose meaning the vision dramatises. He argues from precedent like a jurist and from canon like a theologian, citing Democritus against Neilos (Section IV) as a church father cites scripture. And he writes, in the Authentic Memoirs , what amount to the first textbooks of the art's hardware — descriptions meant to be built from. Earlier alchemy, so far as it survives, is recipes and revelation-frames (Section IX; the pseudo-Democritus article of the tradition is treated in the dossier and in the alchemy article ). Zosimos adds the third genre that turns a recipe tradition into a literature: the commentary , in which an identified author takes responsibility for what the ancients meant. Dufault's formulation is the sharpest available: Zosimos is the first known commentator of alchemy. The twenty-eight books, whatever their exact contents, were the library that commentary served. // THE CORPUS AT A GLANCE // Greek: c. 100–109 pages under Zosimos's name in the Byzantine compendia, delimited by Mertens into four attributable groups (Section VI). Syriac: some 64 pages in three late manuscripts (15th–16th c.), preserving material lost or abbreviated in Greek, including treatises organised by letter. Arabic: the Book of Pictures and the Book of the Keys of the Work , extensive quotation in later authors, and manuscripts catalogued by Sezgin in six libraries (Section VIII). Tradition's frame: the Suda 's 28 lettered books, the Cheirokmēta , addressed to Theosebeia. Nothing like the whole survives in any one language; the corpus is a triangulation, and every modern account of Zosimos is an exercise in reading three damaged witnesses against each other. VI. The Authentic Memoirs — Mertens and the Four Groups The Greek Zosimos reaches us inside a collective artefact: the Greek alchemical corpus , a compendium of some forty authors probably first assembled at Constantinople in the seventh or eighth century and preserved in codices copied between about 1000 and 1500. The chief witnesses are conventionally cited by letter. M is Marcianus graecus 299, of the tenth or eleventh century, now in the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice — the oldest and most important alchemical codex, and the same manuscript that preserves, on a single famous leaf, the diagrams of Cleopatra the Alchemist (Section XIV). B is Parisinus graecus 2325, thirteenth century; A is Parisinus graecus 2327, fifteenth century; a Laurentian manuscript ( L ) completes the usual sigla. These are copies of copies, seven hundred to twelve hundred years younger than their author, made by scribes who did not always understand the apparatus they were drawing — a fact with consequences Section XIV states plainly. The first printed edition of the corpus, Marcellin Berthelot and Charles-Émile Ruelle's Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (1887–88), made the texts generally available and remains, in Dufault's assessment, dated and incomplete yet still the best edition for many works. For Zosimos it has been superseded. The supersession is Michèle Mertens's life work on the corpus, published as Les alchimistes grecs , Tome IV.1: Zosime de Panopolis: Mémoires authentiques (Les Belles Lettres, 1995), with a long introduction — over a hundred pages of it — that remains the foundation of all modern Zosimos biography and bibliography. Mertens sorted the jumble of the Greek manuscripts into four groups of works attributable to Zosimos with certainty : 1 · THE AUTHENTIC MEMOIRS Thirteen short treatises, also transmitted under the title On Apparatus and Furnaces . They open with the programmatic On the Letter Omega and contain the apparatus descriptions with their drawings, the discussions of divine water, and the three dream-vision texts known as the Visions or On Excellence ( Peri aretēs ). The technical heart of the corpus, and the subject of Mertens's edition. 2 · CHAPTERS TO EUSEBIA A second letter-group, addressed to an Eusebia — whether a second patroness, a variant of Theosebeia's name in transmission, or a distinct circle is debated; the archive notes the group and the debate without resolving either. 3 · CHAPTERS TO THEODORUS A third letter-group, to a male addressee — evidence that Theosebeia, for all her centrality, was not Zosimos's only correspondent, and that his teaching circulated in more than one household. 4 · THE BOOK OF SOPHE AND THE FINAL COUNT The most myth-laden group: the Book of Sophe material, with its account of the art's revelation by fallen angels, and the Final Count (or Final Quittance ), the summation addressed to Theosebeia analysed in Section IV. Attribution within this group is the most delicate in the corpus, and individual doctrines drawn from it are flagged accordingly in this article. Two features of Mertens's work deserve emphasis for any reader who will go on to the texts themselves. The first is her apparatus dossier : the edition prints some fifty apparatus diagrams preserved across the manuscripts, making visible at a glance both the richness of the tradition and its instability — the same device drawn recognisably in one codex and decoratively in another. The second is her exclusion list : works Berthelot and Ruelle had printed as Zosimos's are shown to be later exegetes' compositions, and one memoir in the received sequence is argued out of the authentic set altogether. What This Article Is — And What It Is Not This is a Tier B article: Ancient Tradition . That label governs everything that follows. Tier B does not mean "attested fact," and it does not mean "modern invention." It means that the material here survives in ancient texts, written by ancient scribes, in ancient languages, and that this article treats those texts as texts — what they say, how they are built, who copied them, and what later readers have made of them. The central text is the composition modern scholars call the Sumerian King List : a Sumerian-language list of cities, kings, and reign lengths, running — in its fullest surviving form — from the first kings before a great flood down to the kings of Isin in the early second millennium BCE. Alongside it stand the Mesopotamian flood narratives: the Sumerian flood story centred on Ziusudra, the Akkadian poem of Atrahasis, and the flood account embedded in Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, where the hero is called Utanapishtim. Tier discipline, in practice, means this: when the King List assigns a reign of 28,800 years to Alulim, this article reports that the list assigns 28,800 years to Alulim. It does not narrate Alulim as a historical person who reigned for 28,800 years. It does not narrate him as a historical person at all. The reign lengths are the texts' claims. They are presented here as claims — remarkable, patterned, and historically revealing claims about how Mesopotamian scribes imagined their own deep past — but claims nonetheless. // A NOTE ON LANGUAGE THROUGHOUT // Verbs matter in this article. "The list says," "the poem tells," "Berossus reports," and "the scribes assigned" are the normal forms here. Where a scholar's interpretation is given, the scholar is named. Where a number comes from a specific manuscript, the manuscript is named. No reign length, flood date, or antediluvian lifespan in this article should be read as the Archive's statement of historical fact. That restraint is not scepticism for its own sake. It is what makes the texts interesting in the first place. A list that opens before the flood, totals 241,200 years for eight kings, and then — after a single line about water — resumes with reigns that shrink, dynasty by dynasty, toward ordinary human spans is doing deliberate literary and political work. Reading it as a failed attempt at modern chronology misses the work entirely. Reading it as a scribal composition, with a structure, a mathematics, and a purpose, recovers it. II. The King List as a Text The Sumerian King List is not a chronicle in the modern sense. It does not narrate events, describe battles in detail, or record omens, treaties, and building works year by year. It is, at its core, a list — and the list form is the point. City, king, reign length. City, king, reign length. Subtotal. Transition. Next city. The composition is written in Sumerian, the older literary and administrative language of southern Mesopotamia, even in copies made long after Akkadian had become the spoken language of the region. That choice of language is itself traditional: Sumerian was the language of the scribal schools, of hymns, proverbs, and learned compositions, and a king list in Sumerian carried the authority of that learned world. No single "original" of the King List survives, and scholars do not treat any one manuscript as the text. What survives is a family of copies — tablets and prisms, complete and fragmentary, from several cities — that agree in structure and in much of their content while differing in names, figures, and whole sections. The modern text that readers encounter, in Thorkild Jacobsen's 1939 edition or in the Oxford Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (ETCSL), is a composite: an editorial reconstruction built by comparing the witnesses, not a transcription of any one object. Section X below takes up those differences in detail, because they are essential to honest reading. Dating the Composition The earliest known witness to the list belongs to the period of the Third Dynasty of Ur (Ur III, c. 2112–2004 BCE). Piotr Steinkeller published an Ur III manuscript of the list in 2003, confirming that the composition's basic structure predates its earliest previously known copies. Jacobsen, working earlier, placed the original composition around the time of Utu-hegal of Uruk, the king credited in tradition with driving out the Gutians — that is, at the threshold of the Ur III age. The fullest copies, including the Weld-Blundell Prism discussed below, are Old Babylonian, from the early second millennium BCE. Two cautions follow from those dates, and both are regularly dropped in popular retellings. First, the copies are separated from the reigns they describe — even the historical reigns — by centuries. Second, the antediluvian section, the part of the list this article is chiefly about, is not present in the same form in every witness, and Jacobsen argued on grammatical and structural grounds that it is a later addition to the composition. That argument is presented in Section VI. It does not make the section unimportant. It makes it a datable act of scribal composition in its own right: at some point, learned scribes decided the list needed a beginning before the flood, and they built one. III. How the List Is Built — One Kingship, Moving City to City The list's governing idea can be stated in one sentence, and the Ashmolean Museum's summary of its prism states it plainly in paraphrase: dominion over the land, determined by the gods, could be exercised by only one city at a given time, and only for a limited period. Kingship — in Sumerian, nam-lugal — is a single office. It descends from heaven. It resides in one city. That city falls, or is defeated, and kingship is carried to the next city. There is never a vacancy in principle, and never a rival: the list admits no simultaneous kingships. Each dynastic block follows the same formula. Kingship comes to a city. Its kings are named, each with his reign length, sometimes with a filiation ("son of") or a short epithet. The block closes with a subtotal: so many kings, so many years. Then comes the transition formula — in the post-flood sections, the city was defeated (in some manuscripts, "smitten with weapons") and the kingship was taken to the next city. The ETCSL composite translation renders the antediluvian transitions more simply, with the city "falling" and kingship being "taken" onward, and marks some of those readings with a query, a small sign that the underlying text is not everywhere certain. THE UNIT OF THE LIST The list's true subject is not any individual king. It is kingship itself — one office, heaven-sent, moving through history city by city. Individual kings matter as holders of the office and as entries in its unbroken succession. THE FORMULA City receives kingship. Kings are listed with reign lengths. A subtotal is given. The city falls. Kingship is carried to the next city. The repetition is the argument: the same pattern, from Eridu to Isin, across the flood itself. WHAT THE FORMULA EXCLUDES Historically, the cities of early Mesopotamia often held power at the same time. Kish, Uruk, Ur, and Lagash overlapped. The list irons that simultaneity into a single sequence. That is not an error to be corrected; it is the composition's thesis, and Section XVII examines what the thesis was for. THE FLOOD AS HINGE The flood is the list's great dividing line. Kingship descends from heaven, runs through five cities, is interrupted by the flood, descends from heaven again, and resumes at Kish. One office, two descents, one history. Because the alternative modern title for the composition — Chronicle of the One Monarchy — captures exactly this doctrine, it is worth keeping in mind while reading the tables below. The numbers are spectacular, but the structure is the argument. IV. The Witnesses — Manuscripts, Prisms, and Fragments The King List survives in more than a dozen manuscripts — counts vary with how fragments are grouped, and figures of sixteen or more witnesses are commonly cited — written in Sumerian cuneiform on clay tablets and on prisms, principally from Nippur, with others associated with Kish, Larsa, Isin, and Susa, among other provenances. Most of the surviving copies are Old Babylonian school or library products: the list was a learned text, copied and recopied in the scribal tradition. The first fragment was published in 1906 by Hermann Volrath Hilprecht, and a second in 1911 by Jean-Vincent Scheil. Stephen Langdon published the great Weld-Blundell Prism in 1923. It was Jacobsen, in 1939, who first collated the witnesses then known into a critical edition — comparing their variants line by line rather than printing any one copy as definitive. The ETCSL composite translation follows that comparative method: its notes name the manuscripts (by the sigla of Vincente 1995) wherever witnesses differ, and state that, unless otherwise noted, the numerical data follow manuscript WB — the Weld-Blundell Prism. // READING A COMPOSITE // When a translation prints a reign length without comment, that does not mean every manuscript agrees. The ETCSL text is full of bracketed variants — one manuscript's 960 against another's 900, and so on. The antediluvian figures happen to be comparatively stable in the WB tradition, but stability in one tradition is not unanimity across all of them. The Ur III manuscript published by Steinkeller deserves separate emphasis. It is roughly three centuries older than the Weld-Blundell Prism, it was associated with the court of Shulgi of Ur, and — crucially — in its form of the list, kingship descends and lands at Kish, after the flood's position in the later copies, without the developed antediluvian opening. Several of the copies Jacobsen worked from — three from Nippur and one from Susa, in his account — likewise began with Kish. The pre-flood kings, the most quoted part of the entire composition, are absent from its oldest stratum. Section X returns to what that means. V. WB 444 — The Weld-Blundell Prism The best-known witness, and the one from which the familiar antediluvian figures are drawn, is the Weld-Blundell Prism , museum number AN1923.444 in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford — cited by Assyriologists as WB 444 . It is a four-sided baked-clay prism, a little under 20 cm tall and about 9 cm across, inscribed with two columns of Sumerian cuneiform on each face, with a hole running through it from end to end. The Ashmolean describes it as the most extensive and most complete surviving version of the list. It was presented to the museum by Herbert Weld-Blundell in 1923 and published the same year by Stephen Langdon in the Oxford Editions of Cuneiform Texts . Its provenance is given carefully by the museum as "probably Larsa," in southern Iraq; Weld-Blundell assembled his collection largely by purchase, and the prism's exact findspot is not securely documented. Popular accounts that state a firm excavation provenance go beyond the record. The prism's text runs from the antediluvian kings through the dynasties of Kish, Uruk, Ur, Akkad, and Ur III, and ends with the kings of Isin — its last named king is Sin-magir of Isin, who reigned around 1827–1817 BCE. Because Sin-magir is given an eleven-year reign in the text, the prism is usually dated to about 1800 BCE, in or near the final year it records. A closing line beneath a double ruling at the foot of the last face names the scribe: Langdon read it as "by the hand of Nur-Ninsubur"; Jacobsen read the name slightly differently, as a possession line. Even the colophon, in other words, is a reading, not a certainty — a fitting emblem for the whole object. Feature WB 444 — As Reported by the Ashmolean and Its Editors Object Four-sided clay prism, c. 20 × 9 cm, two cuneiform columns per face Collection Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, AN1923.444; presented by Herbert Weld-Blundell, 1923 Date c. 1800 BCE (Old Babylonian), inferred from its last king, Sin-magir of Isin Provenance Probably Larsa, southern Iraq — the museum's own careful wording First edition Stephen Langdon, Oxford Editions of Cuneiform Texts II, 1923 Contents The fullest surviving King List: antediluvian kings to the Isin dynasty The Ashmolean's own characterisation of the prism is worth quoting in paraphrase because it sets the scholarly tone for this whole article: the list, the museum states, is not history as we would understand it, but a combination of myth, legend, and historical information — and its gallery presentation has described it, memorably, as ancient political spin. Section XVII examines that judgement and the scholarship behind it. VI. Jacobsen and the Standard Edition Thorkild Jacobsen (1904–1993), the Danish-American Assyriologist, published The Sumerian King List in 1939 as Assyriological Studies 11 (University of Chicago Press). It remains the standard critical edition and the starting point for all subsequent work: a collation of the witnesses, a reconstructed text, a translation, and a sustained argument about how the composition was assembled. Jacobsen's most consequential argument for this article concerns the antediluvian section itself. Comparing the manuscripts, he observed that several copies — including witnesses from Nippur and Susa — begin with Kish and have no kings before the flood at all. He further argued from the text's grammar and formulas: the pre-flood section moves between cities with a different transition formula from the post-flood sections, and its subtotals use plural verb forms even for cities with a single king, a habit the older sections do not share. His conclusion, as it is usually summarised from the 1939 edition, was that the role of the antediluvian section in the tradition could no longer be in doubt: it is a later addition. That conclusion should be reported precisely. Jacobsen did not argue that the antediluvian kings were invented from nothing in the Old Babylonian period, still less that the flood tradition itself was late. Flood stories, king lists, and traditions of primeval kings circulated in Mesopotamia in several forms, and other compositions — the Sumerian flood story, the Instructions of Shuruppak tradition, the later Berossus — preserve related material independently. Jacobsen's argument is about this composition : the pre-flood opening, as an opening to the King List, was attached to a list that had originally begun after the flood, at Kish. Later scholarship, including Steinkeller's publication of the Ur III manuscript, has broadly confirmed the picture of a list that grew at both ends — extended forward to reach each new ruling dynasty, and eventually backward, across the flood. // WHY THE ADDITION MATTERS // An addition is not a footnote. Whoever attached the antediluvian section gave the list a new beginning: kingship no longer merely resumed after a catastrophe, it originated before one, in the same five cities the flood story names as the first cities. The list and the flood narrative were drawn together deliberately. That editorial act — datable, motivated, and visible in the manuscripts — is itself a piece of history, even though the reigns it records are not. VII. The Opening — Kingship Lowered from Heaven The list does not begin with a creation account, a genealogy, or a date. It begins with an event: kingship descends. In the ETCSL composite translation (t.2.1.1), verified against the Oxford text for this article, the opening runs — in paraphrase of its structure, with the verified wording given in the pull-quote below — as follows: after the kingship descended from heaven, the kingship was in Eridug; in Eridug, Alulim became king. The phrasing often quoted in popular works as "when kingship was lowered from heaven" renders the same Sumerian opening; translations differ in wording, and this article uses the ETCSL rendering, which it actually consulted, rather than mixing renderings from different editions. "After the kingship descended from heaven, the kingship was in Eridug. In Eridug, Alulim became king; he ruled for 28800 years." — The Sumerian King List, lines 1–39, ETCSL translation t.2.1.1 (Oxford) Three features of the opening deserve attention. First, kingship is a thing that can descend, reside, fall, and be carried — an institution with a location, not an abstraction. Second, its first earthly seat is Eridug (Eridu), the ancient southern city associated with the god Enki and, in the flood story's own account of the first cities, the first city founded. The list and the flood story share a geography of origins. Third, there is no king before Alulim and no time before the descent: the list's history begins when the office arrives. Whatever the scribes imagined before that moment, the list does not say. After the flood, the formula repeats. In the ETCSL translation, the post-flood section opens by saying that after the flood had swept over, and the kingship had descended from heaven, the kingship was in Kish. The second descent is structurally necessary: the flood has emptied the office's earthly seat, so the office must be given again. The symmetry — descent, succession, flood, descent, succession — is the composition's frame, and every dynasty that follows, down to historical kings with reigns of a decade or two, is placed inside it. VIII. The Eight Kings Before the Flood In the WB tradition as printed by the ETCSL, eight kings rule in five cities before the flood. The table below gives the text's claims exactly as that translation presents them: name, city, and assigned reign. Spellings follow the ETCSL (Alulim, Alalĝar, En-men-lu-ana, and so on); other editions transliterate slightly differently — Alalngar for Alalĝar, Larak for Larag, Sippar for Zimbir, Shuruppak for Šuruppag — without referring to different figures. # King — As the List Names Him City Reign Assigned by the List In Sar / Ner 1 Alulim Eridug (Eridu) 28,800 years 8 sar 2 Alalĝar (Alalngar) Eridug (Eridu) 36,000 years 10 sar 3 En-men-lu-ana Bad-tibira 43,200 years 12 sar 4 En-men-gal-ana Bad-tibira 28,800 years 8 sar 5 Dumuzid, the shepherd Bad-tibira 36,000 years 10 sar 6 En-sipad-zid-ana Larag (Larak) 28,800 years 8 sar 7 En-men-dur-ana Zimbir (Sippar) 21,000 years 5 sar, 5 ner 8 Ubara-Tutu Šuruppag (Shuruppak) 18,600 years 5 sar, 1 ner Total — the list's own subtotal 241,200 years 67 sar The subtotals are the list's own. Eridu's two kings are totalled at 64,800 years; Bad-tibira's three at 108,000 years; Larak, Sippar, and Shuruppak have one king each. The section then closes, in the ETCSL translation, with the summary that in five cities eight kings ruled for 241,200 years — and then the flood line, quoted in full in Section XI. Notes on Individual Figures Alulim is, in the list's presentation, the first king ever: the first holder of the descended office, at Eridu. He is not attested as a historical ruler in Early Dynastic inscriptions, and Assyriologists treat him as a figure of the list tradition. A separate composition, the Ballad of Early Rulers, also names him — and assigns him a different reign (36,000 years), an early reminder that even ancient witnesses did not agree on the figures. Dumuzid, the shepherd , carries the list's only occupational epithet in this section. The name Dumuzid (Tammuz) belongs elsewhere in Mesopotamian tradition to a shepherd god associated with fertility and the cycle of the seasons; the list also knows a different Dumuzid, "the fisherman," among the post-flood kings of Uruk. Whether the antediluvian shepherd and the god are to be identified is a question the list itself does not answer, and this article does not settle it. En-men-dur-ana of Sippar has attracted particular comparative attention, because Sippar was the city of the sun god, and later Mesopotamian tradition remembered Enmeduranki — a form of the same name — as a primeval king taken into the gods' confidence and shown heavenly knowledge. That association has often been compared with the biblical Enoch, seventh in the Genesis list, who is credited with 365 years — the number of days in a solar year — and is said to have walked with God. The comparison is presented, with its proper cautions, in Section XVIII. Ubara-Tutu of Shuruppak is the last king before the flood, and his position matters beyond the list. In Gilgamesh Tablet XI, the flood hero Utanapishtim is introduced as the son of Ubar-Tutu (in Akkadian form, Ubara-Tutu). The list and the epic thus lock together at exactly the flood's edge: the last antediluvian king is the flood hero's father. Shuruppak, his city, is the flood hero's city in every major version. IX. The Numbers — Sar, Ner, and Sexagesimal Reckoning The antediluvian reigns look arbitrary until they are read in the number system in which they were written. Mesopotamian scribal mathematics was sexagesimal — base-60 — and its named units for large numbers included the soss (60), the ner (600, ten sosses), and the sar (3,600, ten ners, or sixty sosses). Read in those units, every antediluvian reign resolves into whole numbers of sar and ner, as the table in Section VIII shows: 28,800 is 8 sar; 36,000 is 10 sar; 43,200 is 12 sar; 21,000 is 5 sar and 5 ner; 18,600 is 5 sar and 1 ner; and the grand total, 241,200, is exactly 67 sar. Scholars draw two conclusions from that pattern, and both should be attributed rather than asserted as this article's own discovery. First, the figures are constructed : they are round numbers in the scribes' own system, built from its largest familiar units — the numerical equivalent of writing a reign in round thousands. Numbers of this shape are what one expects from scribes composing an impressive, ordered past, not from records of observed reigns. Second, the pattern is meaningful within the system : the sar was a unit of grandeur, and assigning a primeval king eight, ten, or twelve sar is a statement about the scale of the age, made in the mathematical language the scribal schools themselves used. The numbers are, in that sense, scribal mathematics doing literary work. Unit Value Relation Soss 60 60 units Ner 600 10 sosses Sar 3,600 10 ners; 60 sosses Sar-u (greater sar) 36,000 10 sar — the unit of Berossus's largest reigns, see Section XVI A persistent popular literature attempts to rescue literal chronology from these figures by dividing them — by 12, to turn "years" into months, by 360, to turn them into days, or by other factors — until plausible reign lengths emerge. Such schemes should be reported for what they are: modern reinterpretations, not readings found in the texts. The texts present the figures as years of reign, in round sexagesimal units, and the scholarly discussion — from Jacobsen onward — treats them as schematic and ideological numbers, not as garbled records awaiting a conversion key. Where individual scholars have proposed specific numerological readings, those proposals are theirs, and are labelled as such in the literature. This article follows the mainstream presentation: the pattern of the numbers is the evidence, and the evidence points to composition, not transcription. // 67 SAR // 241,200 = 67 × 3,600. The total is as constructed as its parts. A scribe totalling observed reigns does not arrive, reign after reign and total after total, at whole numbers of his largest unit by accident. It is also worth noting what changes after the flood. Post-flood reigns in the earliest Kish dynasty are still large — 1,200 years, 960, 900 — but they are no longer uniformly round sar figures, and they include odd, specific-looking numbers and even fractions of months and days in the dynastic totals. The mathematics itself narrates the transition: from the pure, large units of the primeval age toward the messy specificity of remembered history. Whether that gradient was designed or accumulated, it is one of the list's most effective literary devices. X. Variants — The Lists Do Not Agree With Each Other Any honest account of the antediluvian kings must reckon with the fact that "the" list is a modern editorial convenience. The witnesses differ, and their differences are not confined to spelling. They include which sections exist at all. THE UR III WITNESS The oldest known manuscript, of the Ur III period and published by Piotr Steinkeller in 2003, presents the list beginning at Kish — the first post-flood city in the later copies — without the developed antediluvian opening. The pre-flood section is missing from the list's oldest stratum. THE NIPPUR AND SUSA COPIES Of the copies Jacobsen collated in 1939, several — three from Nippur and one from Susa, in his account — likewise began with Kish and had no kings before the flood. Jacobsen's argument for the section as a later addition rested in part on exactly this distribution. DIFFERING TOTALS Where antediluvian sections do survive in variant forms, their kings, cities, and totals are not everywhere identical; totals substantially larger than WB's 241,200 years are reported in the variant tradition. The 241,200-year figure is WB's figure — the most complete witness's, and the one the ETCSL prints — not a universal figure of "the" list. DIFFERING REIGNS Individual reigns vary between witnesses throughout the list, as the ETCSL's bracketed variants show on nearly every line of the post-flood sections, and independent compositions such as the Ballad of Early Rulers assign Alulim a different reign from the list's. Ancient scribes transmitted a tradition, not a fixed table. None of this diminishes the texts. It locates them. The King List was a living scribal composition across at least three centuries of copying, extended forward as dynasties changed and backward as its frame was completed. The antediluvian section, on the mainstream scholarly account following Jacobsen, belongs to that growth: it is the moment the list acquired a beginning worthy of its structure — kingship descending before the flood, in the flood story's own first cities, in numbers built from the scribal system's grandest units. XI. After the Flood — The Reigns Shrink The flood occupies exactly one line of the King List. In the ETCSL translation, the antediluvian section closes with its subtotal and then, without narrative, description, cause, or hero, the text says the flood swept over — and the next line begins the second descent of kingship, at Kish. The list does not tell the flood story. It assumes it. The story itself lives in other compositions, taken up in Sections XII to XV. Within the list, the flood is a hinge, not an episode: the boundary between the age of sar-long reigns and everything after. "In 5 cities 8 kings; they ruled for 241200 years. Then the flood swept over." — The Sumerian King List, close of the antediluvian section, ETCSL translation t.2.1.1 After the hinge, the numbers descend by stages. The first post-flood dynasty, at Kish, is credited in the WB tradition with 23 kings ruling 24,510 years, 3 months, and 3½ days — its first king, Gushur, is assigned 1,200 years, and individual reigns remain in the hundreds for much of the dynasty. Among its later kings stands En-me-barage-si, assigned 900 years — a figure of particular interest because, unlike the antediluvian kings, Enmebaragesi of Kish is also attested in contemporary inscriptions and is generally treated by historians as a real ruler of roughly the 27th–26th century BCE. The list, that is, does not switch from fiction to fact at a single line. It shades: legendary scale, then exaggerated scale around figures some of whom existed, then — by the dynasties of Akkad, Ur III, and Isin — reign lengths that match the historical record closely enough to be checked against it. Uruk's dynasty illustrates the middle of the gradient. Its kings include Lugalbanda, assigned 1,200 years, and Gilgamesh — "whose father was a phantom," in the ETCSL rendering of his epithet, lord of Kulaba — assigned 126 years. A reign of 126 years is still beyond a human span, but it is an order of magnitude below the antediluvian figures and two orders below his own dynasty's founder figures. By the time the list reaches Ur-Namma of Ur, founder of Ur III, it assigns him 18 years — his historical reign. The long diminuendo from 43,200 to 18 is the list's quietest and most persuasive piece of composition. XII. Ziusudra — The Sumerian Flood Hero The earliest surviving Mesopotamian flood narrative is Sumerian. The composition modern scholars call the Sumerian Flood Story — ETCSL 1.7.4, also widely known by Jacobsen's title for it, the Eridu Genesis — is preserved principally on a tablet from Nippur, excavated by the University of Pennsylvania expedition and recognised by Arno Poebel in the early twentieth century, with further fragments from Ur and a later bilingual fragment from the library of Ashurbanipal. The main Nippur tablet is dated to around 1600 BCE. Roughly a third to two-thirds of the text is lost, in varying estimates, and the surviving portions are heavily broken — a fact every summary of the story should carry with it. What survives, in the ETCSL translation, has a clear shape. After the creation of humankind and animals, kingship descends, the divine rites are perfected, and the first five cities are founded and assigned to their gods: Eridu to Nudimmud (Enki), Bad-tibira to the Mistress (Inana), Larak to Pabilsag, Sippar to Utu, and Shuruppak to Sud. These are the King List's five antediluvian cities, in the same order. The two compositions share the tradition's map of the first age. Then, after a break, the gods resolve on destruction. The hero is Zi-ud-sura — Ziusudra, a name understood as "life of long days" — presented as a king and a gudug priest, humble and reverent, standing day by day at his devotions. The god Enki, bound by an oath the gods have sworn, does not address Ziusudra directly. In the ETCSL translation's paraphrasable sense, he speaks to a wall, with Ziusudra standing at its side listening: a flood will sweep over the land; the decision that the seed of mankind is to be destroyed has been made; Ziusudra is to heed the instructions that follow. The boat-building instructions themselves fall in a lacuna. The flood, when the text resumes, lasts seven days and seven nights. Afterward Ziusudra opens the boat to the sun god Utu's light, prostrates himself, and sacrifices oxen and sheep in abundance. In the closing preserved movement, An and Enlil grant him life like a god's — the tradition's explanation, within its own terms, for the hero's unending lifespan. // ON RECONSTRUCTION // Because so much of the Sumerian flood tablet is lost, popular retellings silently fill its gaps from the later, fuller Akkadian versions — Atrahasis and Gilgamesh XI — and present the composite as "the Sumerian story." Bendt Alster's work on the Sumerian flood tradition, and the ETCSL's own presentation with its gaps and queries marked, model the honest alternative: what survives is remarkable enough, and its missing third is part of the evidence, not an embarrassment to be papered over. Ziusudra's city is Shuruppak — Ubara-Tutu's city, the last city of the King List's antediluvian section. The Sumerian tradition thus places its flood hero exactly where the list leaves off: in the final reign before the waters. Later tradition, including the Instructions of Shuruppak, remembered Shuruppak as a seat of primeval wisdom, and the flood hero as its king. XIII. Atrahasis — The Akkadian Flood Poem The fullest early telling of the flood is the Akkadian poem modern scholars call Atrahasis , after its hero, whose name means "exceedingly wise." Composed in the Old Babylonian period — the best-preserved early copy is dated to the reign of Ammi-saduqa in the 17th century BCE — the poem runs to three tablets and roughly 1,245 lines in the standard edition of W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard (1969), and is most widely read today in Stephanie Dalley's translation in Myths from Mesopotamia (Oxford University Press, 1989). Atrahasis is not only a flood story. It is a complete account of why human beings exist, why they multiply, why the gods turn against them, and why — after the flood — human life is permanently restructured. Its opening movement, in paraphrase, begins among the gods themselves: the lesser gods labour, rebel at their workload, and humankind is created to carry the labour in their place. Humanity multiplies. And then the poem gives its famous, unglamorous motive for catastrophe: noise. In Dalley's translation's sense, the land bellows like a bull; the god Enlil is kept from sleep by the uproar of humankind; and Enlil moves, step by step, to reduce the noise — first plague, then drought and famine, each attempt frustrated by Enki's quiet countermeasures on humanity's behalf, delivered through his servant Atrahasis. The flood is Enlil's final measure, undertaken after the lesser measures fail, and bound by an oath imposed on Enki himself. Enki circumvents the oath as in the Sumerian version — speaking not to the man but to his house's wall — and Atrahasis builds the vessel, loads it, and rides out a flood that the poem, in its third tablet, sets at seven days and seven nights of storm. Afterward, Atrahasis sacrifices; the hungry gods gather to the offering; Enlil rages at the survival — and is answered, by Enki and by the mother goddess, with the poem's settlement: humanity will continue, but under new limits — mortality, barrenness for some, and celibate priestly classes are presented as the permanent checks that replace annihilation. The flood, in Atrahasis, is the event that explains why human life has the shape it has. Two scholarly

What Babylonian Sky Science Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: its subject is a documented practice — observations written on clay, in dated tablets, by named professions, in excavated archives — and every load-bearing claim in it can be walked back to a published tablet, a standard edition, or a named scholar's argument. One element of the material does not belong to Tier A, and this article flags it wherever it appears: the Babylonians' own account of where their knowledge came from . The series present their contents as wisdom shown by the gods to the sages of old. That is the texts' claim about themselves — a Tier B framing, of exactly the kind this hub records in Antediluvian King Lists — and it is labelled as such in §II. The watching, the recording, and the computing are attested. The revelation is reported. The two are never allowed to borrow each other's strength. The scale of the practice is the first fact. Between the middle of the eighth century BCE and the first century BCE, scholars in Babylon and its sister cities kept a nightly record of the sky — the Moon's place among the stars, the planets' appearances and disappearances, eclipses expected and eclipses seen, the weather, the height of the river, the price of barley — that runs, with gaps in survival but not in intent, for some seven hundred years. It is the longest continuous observational programme of the ancient world, and very probably the longest deliberate scientific record-keeping enterprise anywhere before the modern era. Out of that archive, and only out of it, Babylonian scholars extracted the periods of the Moon and planets, learned to predict eclipses, invented the zodiac of twelve equal signs, cast the first horoscopes, and built a mathematical astronomy — arithmetic without geometry, tables without a physical model — accurate enough that Greek astronomers took its numbers over wholesale, and precise enough that its eclipse records are still used today to measure the slowing rotation of the Earth. This article follows the practice in the order the practice itself developed: first the watch (§I) and the omen library that gave the watch its purpose (§II); then the great compendium that ordered the visible sky (§III) and the oldest datable observations it absorbed (§IV); then the Diaries, the archive itself (§V), and the two predictive methods built directly on the archive — goal-year reckoning (§VI) and the Saros (§VII); then the zodiac (§VIII) and the horoscopes it made possible (§IX); then the full mathematical astronomy of Systems A and B (§§X–XI), with the computation of a lunar ephemeris walked through step by step; and finally the transmission of the whole apparatus to Greece (§XII). The cities of the story are Babylon above all, with Nineveh, Uruk, Borsippa, Sippar, and Nippur in supporting roles; its deep background — the urban world of temple households and scribal schools from which the watchers came — is set out in this hub's Ubaid and Uruk article. I. The Observational Programme — Scribes, Temples, and the Nightly Watch Babylonian sky science was not the hobby of gifted amateurs. It was a profession , with a title, a training, an employer, and a duty roster. The title was ṭupšar Enūma Anu Enlil — "scribe of (the series) Enuma Anu Enlil " — naming the man by the omen library he had mastered. The ṭupšarru (the word is plural in sense: a corps, not a person) were scholars attached to temples and to royal courts, heirs to a scribal education that ran from sign lists through the great canonical series to the commentaries that explained them. Francesca Rochberg's The Heavenly Writing (2004) remains the standard account of this world: a closed, hereditary-leaning guild of experts whose authority rested on demonstrable mastery of a written tradition, and whose daily work joined observation, textual scholarship, and counsel to power in a single job description. The employer's interest was not curiosity. In the world the ṭupšarru served, celestial phenomena were signs addressed to the king and the land — the premise examined in §II — and a sign missed was a warning unheard. Hence the watch. The Akkadian term behind the later Diaries is naṣāru ša ginê , "the regular watching," and regularity is the operative word: the sky was observed not when something interesting was expected but every night , in the three watches into which the Babylonian night was divided, because the sign might be a halo, a conjunction, a planet's first appearance in the dawn, or an eclipse that no one had predicted. Observation was a standing duty of the state, maintained the way a garrison is maintained — continuously, at public expense, whether or not anything happened. // THE PROFESSION // Ṭupšar Enūma Anu Enlil "Scribe of Enuma Anu Enlil": the court and temple scholar whose title names him by the celestial omen series he had mastered. // THE DUTY // Naṣāru ša ginê — "the regular watching" The standing nightly observation of the sky, kept in three watches of the night, whether or not any phenomenon was due. // THE ARCHIVE // c. 747 BCE – 61 BCE The span of the Astronomical Diaries tradition: the longest continuous observational record of the ancient world (§V). // THE INSTRUMENTS // Eye, water clock, and gnomon Positions were estimated against reference stars in cubits and fingers; times were measured by water clock and shadow (§III). Watching, in Practice What did a watcher actually do ? The Diaries (§V) let the procedure be reconstructed in detail, because they are its product. Working from a temple precinct — in Babylon, the great temple complex of Esagila, Marduk's house, is the institutional home the later texts presuppose — the observer tracked a fixed checklist of phenomena. The Moon was the primary object: its position each night was recorded by its distance, in cubits (KUŠ, roughly two and a half degrees) and fingers (one thirtieth of a cubit), from one of a standard set of some thirty reference stars near the ecliptic — the Normal Stars , as modern scholarship calls them — with the direction specified: so many cubits "in front of," "behind," "above," or "below" the star. The planets were logged by the same star-relative method, and by their characteristic events: first appearance after invisibility, the two stationary points, acronychal (evening) rising, and last appearance. Around new and full moon the watchers measured, with the water clock, the six standard time intervals between the risings and settings of Sun and Moon that scholarship calls the Lunar Six (§V) — the raw material from which the Moon's behaviour would eventually be computed rather than watched. Two features of this procedure deserve emphasis, because they are what make the archive science rather than mere chronicle. The first is standardisation : the same reference stars, the same units, the same formulaic phrasing, night after night, city after city, century after century — so that an observation made in 700 BCE and one made in 100 BCE are directly comparable numbers, not two men's impressions. The second is the honest negative . The Diaries record, in their set phrase, NU PAP — "not watched" — and DIR NU PAP, "cloudy, not watched," when the sky failed or the watch did. A predicted eclipse that cloud hid is entered as predicted, not as seen; an observed eclipse is marked with a different word order from a merely expected one. The distinction between observed , predicted , and not observed is maintained inside the record itself. That discipline — not any instrument — is the Babylonians' first invention, and everything else in this article is built on it. Reporting to the King The watch had a second product besides the archive: the report . From the Neo-Assyrian court of the eighth and seventh centuries BCE — the reigns above all of Esarhaddon (680–669 BCE) and Ashurbanipal (668–c. 627 BCE) — there survive more than five hundred astrological reports and a large correspondence of scholars' letters, preserved in the royal archives at Nineveh and published in the State Archives of Assyria series (the reports edited by Hermann Hunger as volume 8, the letters by Simo Parpola as volume 10). Scholars stationed in Nineveh itself and in Babylon, Borsippa, Uruk, and other cities wrote to the palace, sometimes daily, in a set form: the phenomenon observed; the omen or omens from Enuma Anu Enlil that it matched, quoted verbatim; and, where needed, a brief comment on what the omen did and did not portend for the king. The letters show the system working under pressure, and they are the best evidence for how observation and interpretation actually interacted. Scholars argue with the evidence and with each other: a report is corrected because the observation was made through cloud; a colleague's reading is disputed on textual grounds; the king is reassured that a threatening configuration "does not concern" him, or advised that a ritual response is required. The gravest case was the lunar eclipse whose omen pointed at the king's death. The court's answer — documented step by step in the letters — was the substitute king ritual: a man of no account was enthroned, robed, anointed, and fed as king, the written omens were recited over him and bound into the hem of his garment, and the real king withdrew under the title "the farmer" until the danger period passed — whereupon the substitute, having absorbed the fate, was put to death. The ritual belongs to the history of religion; but its paperwork belongs here, because it shows what the observational programme was for in its own time: not the advancement of knowledge in the abstract, but the timely protection of the king and the state. That the same records later yielded mathematical astronomy is the great irony — and the great fact — of Babylonian sky science. The institutional setting shifted with the empires — Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, Seleucid — and the watch shifted with it, from a service of the Assyrian court at Nineveh to a function of the temples of Babylon and Uruk under foreign kings who had no personal stake in Babylonian omens at all. That the programme survived every conquest, and outlasted the belief system that had created it by centuries, is a datum to hold in mind through what follows: by the Hellenistic period the watchers were keeping the record because keeping the record was what their profession did , and the computations of §§X–XI, which need no omens at all, grew directly out of the archive the omen service had accumulated. The library that housed the series at Nineveh — Ashurbanipal's — is also the library that preserved the flood tablet of Gilgamesh ; the archive habit was one habit, applied to every kind of text the scribes valued. II. The Omen Series — Enuma Anu Enlil and the Framing Claim The ṭupšarru took their title from a book. Enūma Anu Enlil — "When (the gods) Anu and Enlil…," from its opening words — is the great canonical series of celestial omens: some seventy tablets (sixty-eight to seventy, depending on the recension) holding an estimated 6,500 to 7,000 omens . Its materials reach back to the Old Babylonian period; its canonical form was assembled by the later second millennium BCE; its surviving copies, from Nineveh, Babylon, Uruk, and elsewhere, run from the eighth century BCE into the second century BCE. For more than a thousand years it was the reference work of Mesopotamian sky-watching: the text the watchers quoted to the king, commented on in an extensive commentary literature, and organised their observations around. Hunger and Pingree's Astral Sciences in Mesopotamia and Egypt (1999) is the standard modern survey of the series and its world. Every omen has the same grammatical skeleton: a protasis , "If X is seen…," describing a celestial or atmospheric configuration, and an apodosis , "…then Y will happen," naming a consequence for the king, the army, the harvest, the land, or its neighbours. The series is organised by subject in four great blocks. Tablets 1–14 treat the Moon: its first appearance in the month, its shape, haloes, and conjunctions — closing with Tablet 14, which is not omens at all but a mathematical scheme for the Moon's visibility, the series' own acknowledgement that some of its subject is computable. Tablets 15–22 treat lunar eclipses, encoding date, watch of the night, and the eclipsed quadrant of the Moon's disc — each quadrant standing for a land — into predictions for regions and kings. Tablets 23–39 treat the Sun: its appearance, colour, and markings, and solar eclipses. Tablets 40–49 treat weather — thunder above all — and earthquakes. The final block, Tablets 50–70, treats the stars and planets, Venus first among them: it is in this block, as Tablet 63, that the Venus observations of §IV are preserved.
