The question matters to this hub, because the answer is a claim of exactly the kind its tier system exists to label. The Mesopotamian scholarly tradition understood the sky as a text: the stars were šiṭir šamê , "the writing of heaven," a phrase Rochberg takes as the title and organising metaphor of her study — the gods wrote their intentions in celestial configurations, and the ṭupšarru's art was literacy in that script. The series themselves were presented, in colophons and in the scholarly tradition that surrounded them, as revealed knowledge : the lore of the apkallu , the antediluvian sages, transmitted from the gods through the sages to the scribal families who guarded it as a "secret of the great gods," not to be shown to the uninitiated. Learned catalogues assign series to divine or semi-divine authorship; the knowledge is old because it was given old. // THE TIER DISCIPLINE, APPLIED TO THIS ARTICLE'S OWN SUBJECT // The claim that Babylonian sky knowledge was shown by the gods is the texts' claim about themselves. In this hub's terms it is Tier B framing inside a Tier A practice : the practice — the watching, recording, and computing — is attested by the tablets themselves; the revelation is what the tablets say , and it is reported here as their saying, never endorsed as this archive's finding. The same discipline governs the parallel material wherever it occurs in this archive: the medical series likewise present their lore as handed down from the gods and the sages, and are treated under the same rule in Omens and Medicine . A reader who keeps the two apart loses nothing of the Babylonian achievement. The achievement is greater, not smaller, when it is credited to the watchers rather than to the revelation they believed in: men, not gods, kept the seven-hundred-year record. Two consequences of the framing are historical facts in their own right, whatever one makes of the claim itself. First, the omen form shaped the observations: because the series asked whether the Moon appeared on the expected day, whether an eclipse began in a given watch and quadrant, whether Venus was present or absent for a stated interval, the watchers recorded dates, times, positions, and durations — precisely the quantities from which periods and predictions can later be extracted. Divination's checklist became astronomy's dataset. Second, the framing made the knowledge conservative and cumulative : a revealed corpus is copied exactly, collated against old exemplars, and commented on rather than discarded — which is why observations made in the seventeenth century BCE (§IV) were still being copied, accurately enough to argue over, in the seventh. The archive exists because the tradition believed the texts must not be lost. The historian may give the credit to the belief's effects without sharing the belief. III. MUL.APIN — The Compendium That Ordered the Sky If Enuma Anu Enlil is the watchers' omen library, MUL.APIN is their handbook of the sky itself. The title is the work's first word: mulAPIN , "the Plough," the constellation with which its star list opens. The compendium runs to two tablets (a third, auxiliary tablet of commentary is sometimes attached in the manuscripts), and it survives in dozens of copies and fragments from Assyrian and Babylonian libraries — the earliest dated copy was written in 687 BCE , and copies were still being made around 300 BCE. The standard edition is Hunger and Pingree's MUL.APIN: An Astronomical Compendium in Cuneiform (1989), superseded in presentation by Hunger and John Steele's Routledge edition, The Babylonian Astronomical Compendium MUL.APIN (2019). When was it compiled? The task of this article states the conventional answer, and the literature supports it with a nuance that must be kept visible. The compilation is generally placed around c. 1100 BCE , assembled from older materials — the so-called "Three Stars Each" lists (the astrolabe texts, assigning three stars to each month) are its direct ancestors — and Hunger and Pingree argue for a date around 1000 BCE for the compendium in something like its final form. Independent checks on the data point older: computations by Bradley Schaefer and by Teije de Jong of the heliacal rising dates embedded in the text find them fitting the latitude of Assur best for an epoch somewhere in the range c. 1400–1100 BCE. The honest summary is the one this article uses throughout: MUL.APIN was compiled around 1100 BCE, give or take a century, from observational material some of which is older still — a handbook whose contents, like the Venus Tablet's (§IV), are a stratified deposit, not a single season's work. Tablet I — The Static Sky The first tablet is an inventory and a map. Its opening list catalogues the stars and constellations — seventy-one entries in the usual counting of the opening list — and assigns every one of them to one of three great bands across the sky, the paths of three gods, defined by celestial latitude: the northern path of Enlil , with thirty-three stars and constellations; the equatorial path of Anu , a belt roughly seventeen degrees to either side of the celestial equator, with twenty-three; and the southern path of Ea , with fifteen. The scheme is the first known attempt to organise the entire visible sky under a single geographical system: to know a star's path is to know, at once, roughly where it rises, how high it climbs, and in what company it travels. Many of the Babylonian constellation figures in these lists — the Bull of Heaven, the Great Twins, the Crab, the Lion, the Scorpion, the Goat-Fish — are the direct ancestors, name and figure alike, of the zodiacal constellations the Greek world would inherit (§XII). The lists that follow turn the inventory into a clock and a calendar. One list gives the heliacal rising dates of thirty-four stars and constellations — the date of each one's first visible rising in the dawn after its period of invisibility in the Sun's glare — plotted against an ideal year of twelve thirty-day months, 360 days, in which the equinoxes fall on the 15th of the first and seventh months and the solstices on the 15th of the fourth and tenth. Further lists give the stars that rise and set simultaneously, the numbers of days between successive heliacal risings, and the ziqpu stars — stars whose culmination (passage across the meridian) at nightfall or through the night served as the watcher's clock, marking the hours against which the water clock was checked. The tablet closes with the constellations that stand in the path of the Moon : the band of sky along the ecliptic through which the Moon, and with it the Sun and planets, actually travel — the working sky of all later Babylonian astronomy, and the raw material from which the zodiac of §VIII would be cut. Tablet II — The Moving Sky, the Calendar, and Time The second tablet treats everything that changes . It names the Sun and the five planets and states that they travel the Moon's path; it gives schematic periods of visibility and invisibility for each planet — how many days, in the idealised scheme, each is a morning star, absent, an evening star, absent again; it fixes the cardinal points of the year by observation — which stars rise, and where the full moon stands, at solstice and equinox; and it preserves the compendium's most practically consequential material, its intercalation rules . The problem those rules solve is the calendar's permanent defect. Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, eleven days short of the solar year; left uncorrected, the first month, Nisanu, would drift through the seasons, and the spring festivals and the barley harvest with it. The correction is intercalation : in some years a thirteenth month — a second Addaru, or a second Ululu — is inserted. MUL.APIN's rules decide the question by observation . The best known is the Pleiades rule : observe the Moon's position against the Pleiades at the opening of Nisanu — in the formulation preserved in the compendium and its tradition, if the Moon stands in the prescribed relation to the Pleiades on the evening appointed at the month's head, the year is normal; if the conjunction falls late (on the third day rather than the first), the year is intercalary. Companion rules use the heliacal risings of the Pleiades, of Sirius (the Arrow), and of ŠU.PA (the stars around Arcturus), and the Moon's relation to them. The procedure, step by step, is: (1) watch at the appointed dawns and evenings; (2) compare the observed configuration with the rule's stated norm; (3) if the sky is behind its schedule, proclaim the extra month. For centuries the proclamation was the king's, made on scholarly advice — the letters of §I include calendar business — and only in the fifth century BCE was the decision itself reduced to arithmetic, when the fixed nineteen-year cycle (235 lunar months ≈ 19 solar years; seven intercalary months in nineteen years, in a set order) passed from near-regular practice to official rule, fully standardised by 380 BCE on the evidence assembled by Parker and Dubberstein and summarised by Rochberg. MUL.APIN stands at the head of that development: its rules are the observational form of a problem its successors would solve by computation. Tablet II also carries the compendium's timekeeping schemes : a table of the gnomon's shadow lengths at stated hours on the solstices and equinoxes, and a water-clock scheme in which the length of day and night through the year is given by the weight of water — in minas — to be measured out: at the summer solstice, four minas for the day against two for the night in the schematic version, three and three at the equinoxes, the values varying month by month in a simple arithmetic progression. The day:night ratio of 2:1 built into that scheme is schematically wrong for Babylon's latitude (the true extreme ratio is nearer 3:2, which later texts adopt), and the error is itself instructive: MUL.APIN's numbers are a model of the year — tidy, computable, and only approximately true — set down beside the observations it was the watchers' duty to keep making. Babylonian sky science would live in that tension, between the scheme and the sky, for the rest of its history; its greatest achievements (§§X–XI) are what happened when the schemes were forced, column by column, to fit the archive. The compendium ends, characteristically, with omens. The placement is the document's own statement of purpose: the star lists, the rising dates, the intercalation rules, and the clocks exist so that the signs of Enuma Anu Enlil can be caught, timed, and named correctly. MUL.APIN is not a rival to the omen series but its instrument panel — the ordered sky against which every sign must be located before it can be read. // READING MUL.APIN'S DATES // The dates in MUL.APIN are dates in the ideal 360-day year, not entries from a diary. "ŠU.PA rises on the 15th of Ululu" states a position in the scheme — a norm against which a given year's actual rising, early or late by days, could be judged and the calendar corrected. Confusing the scheme with a record is the commonest beginner's error with this text, and the editions of Hunger and Pingree and of Hunger and Steele both warn against it explicitly. IV. The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa — Old Observations, Open Chronology The oldest body of planetary observations to survive from anywhere is preserved as the sixty-third tablet of the omen series itself. The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa — Enuma Anu Enlil Tablet 63, edited in the standard modern treatment by Erica Reiner and David Pingree, Babylonian Planetary Omens, Part One: The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa (1975) — records, for twenty-one years , the first and last visibilities of Venus: the dates on which the planet appeared and disappeared as morning and evening star, and the lengths of its intervals of invisibility between disappearance and reappearance. The observations are attributed to the reign of Ammisaduqa , the fourth king after Hammurabi in the First Dynasty of Babylon — that is, on the conventional Middle Chronology, to 1646–1626 BCE . No tablet of the seventeenth century BCE survives: the text reaches us in some twenty copies and fragments, all of the first millennium BCE, the Nineveh copies of the seventh century BCE prominent among them — a transmission of a thousand years, through the copying discipline described in §II, between the observation and the oldest manuscript we can hold. The form of the entries shows the double nature of the whole tradition in miniature. Each observation is stated in the calendar — month, day, direction of appearance or disappearance, days of absence — and each is followed by its omen : the apodosis for the land, of the type "the harvest of the land will prosper" or rain, flood, or the king's fortune, attached to that configuration of Venus. To the scribe who copied it, the tablet was a chapter of the omen series that happened to be built from real dated observations. To the modern historian, it is the reverse: a chapter of observational astronomy that happens to carry its omens with it. Both readings are correct about the same object, and the tablet is the cleanest single proof that in Babylonia the two were one enterprise. As observation, the data are good enough to argue with — which is precisely the problem. Venus's appearances repeat on a near-exact cycle: five synodic periods of the planet equal eight years, less about four days, so that the pattern of visibilities in any twenty-one-year run closely resembles the pattern eight, sixteen, and twenty-four years earlier or later, and resembles it again, with accumulating drift, at intervals governed by that near period — the candidate absolute datings for the same tablet fall in families separated by fifty-six or sixty-four years . The relative chronology of the First Dynasty is secure: king lists and year names fix who reigned, in what order, for how long, and Ammisaduqa's distance from Hammurabi and from the sack of Babylon that ended the dynasty is not in dispute. What the Venus data are asked to supply is the absolute placement of that whole floating sequence — and the tablet, because of Venus's obliging periodicity, supplies not one answer but a ladder of them. The Middle Chronology (Hammurabi 1792–1750 BCE) remains the conventional default of textbooks and museum labels, and dates quoted from the literature in this article — including Ammisaduqa's reign above — are given on it and labelled as such. But the contest is live and the positions are held on evidence: Peter Huber's statistical studies of the tablet's month-lengths and Venus data have repeatedly favoured the High chronology; Teije de Jong and collaborators, modelling the atmospheric visibility of Venus at Babylon, found the fits for the rival chronologies statistically indistinguishable — and argued that a cluster of anomalously poor visibilities in Ammisaduqa's twelfth and thirteenth years might register the atmospheric effects of the Thera (Santorini) eruption, which would tie the choice to the radiocarbon dating of that event; dendrochronological and radiocarbon arguments have been deployed against the Low chronology in particular; and a minority of scholars question whether the transmitted Venus data, copied for a millennium and partly schematic in places, can bear the weight placed on them at all. The spread between the extreme candidates exceeds a century and a half. Where this hub's other articles need second-millennium dates — the king-list material of Antediluvian King Lists among them — the same rule applies: the chronology in use is named, and the debate is not silently resolved. What the tablet establishes beyond the chronological quarrel is worth stating plainly, because it is the foundation fact of this whole article. By the seventeenth century BCE — on any of the rival chronologies — Babylonian observers were already recording a planet's first and last visibilities to the day, in a standard calendar format, as part of a state scholarly enterprise; and their successors valued the record enough to copy it, with its omens, for a thousand years. The observational programme of §I did not begin with the Diaries. The Diaries are what happened when a habit already a millennium old was intensified into a system. V. The Astronomical Diaries — From Nabonassar to the Last Tablet The Astronomical Diaries are the archive the watch produced: cuneiform tablets, each normally covering six months of a Babylonian year (occasionally seven), in which the phenomena of every night were entered in a fixed order and a fixed phraseology. The edition of record is Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia , begun by Abraham Sachs and completed by Hermann Hunger (volumes I–III, the Diaries proper, 1988–1996, with the related text genres — goal-year texts, almanacs — in the volumes that followed). More than a thousand diary tablets and fragments survive, the great majority in the British Museum; most come from Babylon itself, with a smaller body from Uruk. When do they begin? The tradition of the discipline, ancient and modern, gives the same answer, and the manuscripts give a more complicated one — both must be stated. The systematic keeping of the record is associated with the reign of Nabonassar (Nabû-nāṣir, 747–734 BCE), the Babylonian king whose accession the Greek astronomer Ptolemy, nine centuries later, took as the epoch of his own chronological system — the Era of Nabonassar , beginning 26 February 747 BCE in proleptic Julian reckoning — precisely because, as Ptolemy says in the Almagest , ancient observations were preserved complete from that reign onward. The oldest Babylonian eclipse records Ptolemy actually cites belong to 721 and 720 BCE, within a generation of the era's start. The surviving diary tablets , however, begin later: the oldest preserved diary fragment is dated to 652 BCE , the oldest preserved diary in the full standard form to 568 BCE , and the record grows dense and near-continuous only from the fifth century BCE. John Steele's study of the Diaries' early history (in Keeping Watch in Babylon , 2019) adds the necessary caution that the "Era of Nabonassar" as a deliberate foundation — a king ordering systematic astronomy into being — is a modern construction laid over a real change: what the evidence shows is a marked increase in the quality, frequency, and preservation of observations from the mid-eighth century onward, from which the later compilations demonstrably drew. The last known diary is dated to 61 BCE . Between those bounds the programme ran for some seven centuries — through the Neo-Assyrian, Neo- Babylonian, Persian, and Seleucid empires and into the Parthian period — and the related almanac tradition carried Babylonian astronomical publication a further century and more beyond it. What a Diary Contains A diary's month is a dossier. Its astronomical core is the nightly log: the Moon's passage by the Normal Stars, entered in the form Rochberg's Heavenly Writing quotes from the diary for 331 BCE — the Moon so many cubits below one reference star, having passed a fraction of a cubit behind another — with the laconic honesty of the working record preserved in the same lines: an equinox entered, and against another night, "I did not watch"; against another, "clouds were in the sky." Around that core the month assembles, in fixed categories: Category What Is Recorded Why It Matters The Lunar Six Six timed intervals between the risings and settings of Sun and Moon around new and full moon (below) The Moon's motion made measurable; the data from which month length and syzygy times were later computed The Moon nightly Distances in cubits and fingers from the Normal Stars, with direction A continuous positional record of the Moon against a fixed star frame The planets First and last visibilities, stations, acronychal risings, passages by Normal Stars and by the Moon The dataset from which every planetary period of §VI

How This Bibliography Is Organised This page is a hub utility page, and it carries no tier badge of its own : it spans all three of the hub's tiers at once, and a single badge would mislabel two-thirds of what it lists. Instead, the tier discipline is applied at the level of the sections. Every work consulted for any article in this hub appears exactly once below, in the section of the tier of the article (or articles) it grounds, with the article or articles named in a tag line under each entry. The entries are harvested from the articles themselves — from the Sources section of each of the hub's thirty-four articles, and from §VII, "Sources and Further Reading," of the hub's index page . Nothing is listed here that no article's Sources section (or the hub's §VII) names. Where several articles rest on the same work — the hub's chronology anchor, Shaw's Oxford History of Ancient Egypt , is the standing example — the work is consolidated into a single entry and every article that uses it is tagged. Within each tier the entries run alphabetically by author or, for anonymous and institutional works, by title. Each entry gives the citation as the article's Sources section gives it — author, title, year, and journal or publisher where the article supplies them — followed by one line on what the work grounds in this hub: the claim, date, reading, or account for which it is the cited authority. Where an article's Sources section cites a work in a deliberately limited way — "as cited in" another work, "via the discussions in" a synthesis, or as reference orientation only — this bibliography preserves that limitation rather than upgrading the citation. A reader who wants to check any claim in this hub should therefore be able to walk from the claim, to the article's Sources section, to this page, and out to the work itself without a gap. // A NOTE ON WHAT A CITATION MEANS HERE // A Tier A citation means the work is evidence: excavated, dated, and published material a reader can re-examine. A Tier B citation means the work is a witness: an edition or translation through which an ancient text's own claims reach us. A Tier C citation means the work is a document: a primary publication of a modern tradition, cited as the record of what that tradition teaches, or the modern scholarship that studies it. The same physical book can in principle serve in more than one of these ways; in this hub it is listed where the article that cites it stands, and the grounds line says which way it is being used. These are works whose claims can in principle be re-tested — a stratigraphy re-excavated, a date re-run, a residue re-analysed — and the articles treat them that way: where two Tier A works disagree, the disagreement is reported, not resolved by editorial preference. Dating methods, calibration, and stated uncertainty are part of the evidence, and the grounds lines below note where a work's contribution is precisely a revision — a re-dating, a re-reading of fauna, a withdrawal of an earlier interpretation — because in Tier A the corrections are as load-bearing as the discoveries. The tier is stated here, in words, because it governs every sentence that follows. Tier B material survives in ancient texts, in ancient languages, copied and recopied by ancient scribes. This article treats those texts as texts : it seats each part of the Enochic corpus at the date scholarship assigns to its composition, names the languages and manuscripts by which it reaches us, names the edition or translation actually consulted, and attributes every claim to the text that makes it. When the Book of the Watchers says that angels descended before the Flood and taught men metalwork, this article reports that the book says it — a composition of the third century BCE, set in a claimed antediluvian age. The antiquity of the events described is the tradition's claim, and it is labelled as such throughout. The antiquity of the text is a separate, documented matter, and it is the text that this article is about. The discipline matters here because few ancient books have been asked to carry so much modern weight. The Book of Enoch has been read as suppressed scripture, as a key to the pyramids, as a log of extraterrestrial contact, and as a charter for half the occult systems of the last two centuries. Almost all of that reading skips the first question a Tier B article must ask: what is this object, in what language was it written, when, and by what road did it survive? The answers are stranger than most of the uses made of them. "1 Enoch" is not one book but a small library of five, assembled over some three centuries. It was written mostly in Aramaic, translated into Greek, lost to the Greek and Latin worlds that had once quoted it as scripture, and preserved complete only in Ethiopia, in the classical language Ge'ez, inside the canon of the Ethiopian church. Its most famous narrative — the descent of the Watchers and the arts they taught — occupies barely a dozen chapters of its hundred and eight. This article sits, deliberately, on the archive's alchemy spine. The Antiquity hub follows, across its articles, a single long question: how did the ancient world believe its crafts and sciences began, and what did it think that beginning cost? The Book of the Watchers gives the sharpest answer in any ancient text. In its telling, the arts of civilisation — the working of metals and the making of weapons, cosmetics and adornment, the reading of the stars, enchantment and the cutting of roots — did not rise slowly from human hands. They arrived as a package, delivered from above by beings who had no right to deliver them, and the price of the delivery was the corruption of the earth and a judgement by water. Section X gives that catalogue exactly as the text gives it, from a named translation, without embellishment. Section XIII then states, and labels as this hub's own reading, why the catalogue matters to a history of transmitted craft-knowledge. Everything between is the book itself: its parts, its dates, its survival, its story, and its long afterlife in and out of canons. I. What "1 Enoch" Is — A Library in One Binding The work modern scholarship calls 1 Enoch — also the Ethiopic Enoch, to distinguish it from the Slavonic 2 Enoch and the Hebrew 3 Enoch treated in §XVII — presents itself as the revelation of Enoch, the seventh from Adam, the patriarch of Genesis 5 who "walked with God" and was taken without an ordinary death. In its received form it runs to 108 chapters. It is not, and on the scholarly consensus never was, the product of a single author or a single generation. It is a composite: five originally separate works, written in Aramaic (and, in one case, still debated) across roughly the third century BCE to the turn of the era, gathered at some point into one corpus, translated as a corpus into Greek and from Greek into Ge'ez, and transmitted thereafter as a single book with a single name. The five parts are conventionally distinguished as follows. The Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36) tells of the angels who descended, took human wives, fathered giants, and taught forbidden arts, and of Enoch's journeys through the cosmos as their unwilling messenger. The Parables , also called the Similitudes (chapters 37–71), present three parables of judgement centred on a figure called the Son of Man, the Elect One, the Head of Days presiding. The Astronomical Book , also called the Book of the Courses of the Heavenly Luminaries (chapters 72–82), sets out a solar calendar of 364 days revealed by the angel Uriel. The Book of Dreams , or Dream Visions (chapters 83–90), recounts two visions, the second of them — the so-called Animal Apocalypse — a retelling of history from Adam to the Maccabean age in animal allegory. The Epistle of Enoch (chapters 91–108) is a letter of exhortation and woe, containing the Apocalypse of Weeks, a periodised history of the world in ten "weeks," and closing with material on the righteous and the fate of sinners. // RECEIVED FORM // 108 chapters, five books The Book of the Watchers (1–36), the Parables (37–71), the Astronomical Book (72–82), the Book of Dreams (83–90), and the Epistle (91–108) — separate works, gathered into one corpus. // ORIGINAL LANGUAGE // Aramaic (the Parables debated) Aramaic fragments of four of the five books survive from Qumran. No Aramaic of the Parables has ever been found — the problem of §III. // COMPLETE SURVIVAL // Ge'ez only The whole corpus survives complete only in the classical Ethiopic language, in the canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. // THE SPEAKER // Enoch, seventh from Adam The corpus is pseudepigraphal: written in the name of the antediluvian patriarch of Genesis 5, to whom Genesis gives 365 years and a departure without death. Three terms used throughout this article should be fixed at the outset. Pseudepigrapha — "writings under a false name" — is the standard scholarly label for the large body of Jewish and Christian works of this era attributed to ancient worthies: Enoch, Moses, Ezra, Baruch, the twelve patriarchs. The label describes the attribution, not a moral verdict; in the world that produced these books, writing in the name of the ancient seer who was held to have received the revelation was a recognised way of presenting teaching, and the Enochic corpus is the largest single monument of the practice. Apocalypse , as John J. Collins's standard genre study defines it, is a narrative revelation mediated by an otherworldly being to a human recipient, disclosing a transcendent reality both temporal and spatial — the world above and the judgement to come. Much of 1 Enoch fits the definition exactly, which is why Enoch, more than any other figure, became the patron of the genre. Watchers renders the Aramaic word for the angels of the story: the "wakeful ones," those who do not sleep — in the Book of Daniel, the same word names a class of heavenly beings, and in the Enochic books it becomes the name of the ones who woke, watched, desired, and fell. A word, finally, on the numbering. "1 Enoch" is a modern scholarly convenience, coined to order a family of Enoch books that no ancient canon ever numbered. The Ethiopian church, which kept the book, knows it simply as the Book of Enoch — Henok — one book among the eighty-one of its broader canon. The numeral matters because the family is real and the members are distinct: the Slavonic and Hebrew Enoch books of §XVII are later, separate compositions that share a hero and almost nothing else. Conflating them — a routine error in popular literature — scrambles three different centuries, three different languages, and three different theologies into one imaginary tome. This article treats 1 Enoch alone, and names the others only to keep them apart. II. The Five Books and Their Dates Because the corpus is composite, it has no single date, and any account that gives it one has already gone wrong. Each of the five books is dated by the scholarship on its own evidence: the historical events its allegories reach, the manuscripts that attest it, the language and ideas it shares with datable neighbours. The datings below are those of the standard critical literature — George W. E. Nickelsburg's Hermeneia commentary on chapters 1–36 and 81–108 (2001), Nickelsburg and James C. VanderKam's companion volume on chapters 37–82 (2012), and VanderKam's study of the growth of the Enochic tradition — stated at the precision that literature itself claims, which is the precision of centuries and half-centuries, not of years. Part Chapters Scholarly Dating Principal Grounds Book of the Watchers 1–36 Core 3rd c. BCE; older strands within Aramaic fragments at Qumran among the oldest Enochic manuscripts; the work presupposed by the other books; chapters 6–11 widely held to weave still older Watcher traditions Parables (Similitudes) 37–71 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (debated; see §III) Absent from Qumran; no Aramaic witness; dating argued from content — the Son of Man figure, possible allusions to events of the late Second Temple period Astronomical Book 72–82 3rd c. BCE, possibly reaching into the late 4th c. The Qumran Aramaic manuscripts of the Astronomical Book are among the earliest of all Enochic copies, copied c. 200 BCE or before on palaeographic grounds; the work itself is older than its copies Book of Dreams 83–90 Mid-2nd c. BCE The Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90) retells history in animal code down to the Maccabean revolt, whose leader it greets as a horned ram — a terminus the allegory itself supplies Epistle of Enoch 91–108 2nd c. BCE, with later framing The Apocalypse of Weeks and the woes against the rich fit the world of the other 2nd-century Enochic works; chapters 91–105 form the letter proper, 106–108 an appendix on Noah's birth and the last things The Watchers Core — Third Century BCE The Book of the Watchers is the corpus's foundation and its oldest narrative stratum. Its core — the descent story of chapters 6–11, Enoch's commission and journeys in chapters 12–36, framed by the oracle of judgement in chapters 1–5 — is placed by the consensus of the critical literature in the third century BCE, earlier than Daniel, earlier than most of the literature with which it is usually shelved. Within that core, chapters 6–11 are themselves composite (§VIII): two tellings of the fall, centred on two different chiefs, woven into one narrative by an editor whose seams remain visible. The traditions behind those tellings may be older still; how much older is not something the surviving evidence lets anyone measure, and this article does not pretend otherwise. What can be said on evidence is that by the time the Qumran community copied the book in the second century BCE, it was already an old work, copied alongside — and in more copies than — most of the books that would become the Hebrew Bible. The Astronomical Book — As Old, and Stranger The Astronomical Book stands with the Watchers at the head of the corpus. Its Aramaic manuscripts from Qumran Cave 4 (4Q208–4Q211) include copies written, on the palaeography, around 200 BCE or earlier — among the very oldest manuscripts of any Enochic work — and a composition must precede its copies. Henryk Drawnel's edition and study of the Aramaic Astronomical Book (2011) presents the Qumran text as a learned, technical composition: a synchronistic calendar coordinating sun and moon, built with the scribal tools of the Babylonian astronomical tradition it adapts. The Ethiopic version of chapters 72–82 is, by comparison, an abbreviation — the full Aramaic work was longer and more detailed than the form in which the corpus transmitted it. The calendar itself is treated in §XIV; what matters here is the date. The Enochic library begins, in the third century BCE, with two works at once: a myth of fallen angels and a treatise on the motions of the luminaries. The pairing is not accidental, and §XIII returns to it. Dreams and Epistle — The Second Century The Book of Dreams and the Epistle belong to the corpus's second age, the second century BCE — the century of the Maccabean crisis, which left its mark on both. The Animal Apocalypse of the Dreams retells the whole of biblical history as a pageant of clean and unclean animals, sheep and beasts of prey, and its code is transparent at exactly one point: the great horned ram who leads the sheep against the ravens and eagles of the 160s BCE is Judas Maccabeus, and the vision expects the judgement to follow his wars. The Epistle, cast as Enoch's letter to his children, divides history into ten weeks and places its own generation in the seventh — the age of an apostate generation, just before the week of judgement. Both works therefore date themselves, in the only way apocalypses do: by the point at which their coded history stops being past and starts being prophecy. For the Dreams that point is the 160s BCE; for the Epistle's sources, the same broad Maccabean horizon. These are works of a community reading its own persecution into a cosmic script whose first act was the fall of the Watchers. III. The Parables Problem — The Book Qumran Does Not Have One of the five books breaks the pattern of the other four, and the break is the most instructive dating problem in the whole corpus. The Parables (chapters 37–71) — the section that speaks of the Son of Man, the Elect One, the Head of Days, the judgement of kings and the mighty — is attested by no Aramaic manuscript from Qumran, although Qumran preserved multiple Aramaic copies of every other Enochic book, and by no early Greek witness either. It reaches us, in full, only in the Ge'ez transmission, as the second panel of the five-book corpus. Everything about its date must therefore be argued from its contents, and the argument has run for a century. The poles of the debate are these. Józef T. Milik, the editor of the Qumran Aramaic fragments, concluded from the silence of the caves that the Parables did not yet exist in the Qumran period, and proposed a late date — the late third century CE — with Christian composition or heavy Christian reworking. That proposal has not carried the field. The critical consensus represented by Nickelsburg and VanderKam's Hermeneia volume on chapters 37–82 treats the Parables as a Jewish work of the late Second Temple period, dated across the first century BCE and the first century CE: its world is the world of Herodian and Roman Palestine, its Son of Man is built from Daniel 7 and the older Enochic material, its judgement falls on "the kings of the earth and the strong" in a register that fits the age of Herod and his successors, and nothing in it requires a Christian hand. Within that consensus, proposals distribute themselves across the range — some anchoring the work near the Parthian invasion of 40 BCE, which chapter 56 has been read as reflecting; others in the reign of Herod; others still after 70 CE. This article reports the range as the scholarship gives it — first century BCE to first century CE — and the debate as a debate. It does not pick a decade the evidence will not bear. // AN ARGUMENT FROM SILENCE, LABELLED AS ONE // The Parables' absence from Qumran is a fact about surviving manuscripts, not a fact about the second century BCE. Qumran's caves preserved what one community owned, copied, and finally stored; whole works known to have existed in the period are missing or nearly missing from them. The absence is evidence — it is the reason the Parables cannot be dated by manuscript, and it rightly disciplines every claim made for their age — but it is evidence of the weaker kind, and the field's movement away from Milik's late dating is precisely a judgement about how much weight silence can bear. Tier B practice states the silence, states the weight given it, and moves on. Why does the problem matter beyond the specialists? Because the Parables are the part of 1 Enoch that stands closest to the New Testament's language about the Son of Man — and the direction and date of any influence between them turns on exactly the dating that cannot be fixed by manuscript. A Parables of the first century BCE is part of the Jewish world into which the Gospels' Son of Man sayings were spoken; a Parables of the third century CE would be their echo. The scholarly consensus for the early dating is strong, and this article follows it — while recording, as the tier requires, that it rests on internal evidence and scholarly judgement, not on a dated copy. The contrast with the other four books, whose Aramaic copies can be held in the hand, is the point: within one corpus, the evidence itself changes tier-like in strength from book to book, and honest treatment changes with it. IV. The Survival Chain — Aramaic, Greek, Ge'ez No ancient book in this hub has a stranger transmission than 1 Enoch, and none repays the telling of it more. The corpus was composed in Aramaic in the land of Israel. It was translated into Greek in the Hellenistic world. It was quoted as scripture by early Christian writers, then set aside by the churches of the Greek and Latin worlds and by rabbinic Judaism alike, until the complete work ceased to circulate in them at all. And it survived — whole, canonical, copied and recopied for well over a thousand years — in the highlands of Ethiopia, in Ge'ez, the classical language of the Ethiopian church, which had received it in late antiquity and never let it go. Every modern edition is a negotiation among those three languages and the very different witnesses each preserves. The Aramaic Witnesses — Qumran The oldest witnesses are the Aramaic fragments recovered from Cave 4 at Qumran, by the Dead Sea, and published by Milik in 1976. Eleven manuscripts (4Q201–4Q212) preserve portions of the Enochic books in their original language: copies of the Book of the Watchers, of the Astronomical Book, of the Book of Dreams, and of the Epistle — several works in more than one copy. They are fragments, often exasperatingly small, and the corpus they attest is not quite the corpus we have: the Qumran Enochic manuscripts include, alongside the five-book materials, fragments of a related Book of Giants, telling of the dreams and doom of the Watchers' monstrous sons, which the Ethiopic corpus did not retain. Palaeography dates the oldest of the copies — an Astronomical Book manuscript among them — to about 200 BCE or the decades around it. The Qumran evidence therefore does double work in this article: it dates the books (§II), and it proves that the library was Aramaic before it was anything else. The Greek Witnesses — Fragments of a Lost Whole The Greek translation, made from the Aramaic in the centuries around the turn of the era, was once complete and widely read; what survives of it is a ruin. The chief witness is the Akhmim codex, a parchment manuscript of the fifth or sixth century CE found at Akhmim in Egypt — ancient Panopolis — preserving chapters 1–32 of the Book of the Watchers, the text on which all study of the Greek Enoch rested for a generation. A fourth-century papyrus (the Chester Beatty– Michigan papyrus) preserves much of the Epistle, chapters 97–107, together with related material. Beyond the manuscripts stand the excerpts: the Byzantine chronographer George Syncellus, in the early ninth century, copied out substantial passages of the Watchers story from earlier chronographic sources, preserving Greek wording for parts of the narrative the Akhmim codex gives differently — a reminder that even the Greek text circulated in more than one form. Scattered quotations in the church fathers and a short Latin fragment of chapter 106 complete the western dossier. It is a dossier of pieces. No Greek manuscript of the whole book exists, or is known ever to have survived antiquity's end. The Ge'ez Witnesses — The Whole Book The complete text exists in Ge'ez alone. The Ethiopic version was translated from the Greek, most plausibly in the Aksumite period — the fourth to sixth centuries CE, when the kingdom of Aksum received its Christian literature in translation and fixed the unusually broad canon within which Enoch, alone among the pseudepigrapha of its age, stands to this day as canonical scripture in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church (and in the tradition of the Beta Israel). The surviving Ethiopic manuscripts are medieval and later — the oldest complete copies date to the fifteenth century and after — and they are numerous: modern editors have collated dozens. The interval matters for method. Between the Aramaic autographs and the oldest Ge'ez copies lie some seventeen centuries and two translations; the wonder is not that the text bears marks of the journey, but that the journey can be checked at all — which it can, wherever the Qumran Aramaic or the Greek fragments overlap the Ethiopic, and at those points the Ethiopic version proves, on the editors' showing, a faithful if sometimes literal-minded witness to its Greek parent. // THREE LANGUAGES, THREE EVIDENCES // The practical rule of Enochic scholarship follows from the chain. Where Aramaic survives, it controls: it is the language of composition. Where only Greek and Ge'ez survive, the two are read against each other, the Greek closer to the source, the Ge'ez often preserving the fuller text. Where Ge'ez stands alone — as it does for most of the Parables and much else — the reader is reading a translation of a translation, and the critical editions say so at every doubtful line. Quotations in this article are taken from the modern translations named in the Sources, which are built on exactly this hierarchy of witnesses. The chain has one more link, and it is the one that explains the book's modern fame: for roughly a thousand years, between the fading of the Greek copies and the eighteenth century, the complete Book of Enoch existed, so far as the record shows, only in Ethiopia. The western world knew the Watchers story from Genesis 6's four cryptic verses, from Jude's quotation, from the fathers' allusions — a title, a reputation, a rumour of a book. The book itself was elsewhere. Its return is the subject of the next section. V. The Recovery — Bruce, Laurence, Charles, and the Critical Editions The modern history of 1 Enoch begins with a Scotsman coming down from the Ethiopian highlands with three manuscripts in his baggage. James Bruce of Kinnaird, who had travelled in Ethiopia in 1769–1772 in search of the sources of the Nile, returned to Europe in 1773 carrying, among his other prizes, three copies of the Book of Enoch in Ge'ez — a book Europe had not possessed entire for a millennium. One copy went to the Bodleian Library at Oxford. There the matter largely rested for two generations: the manuscripts were famous, the language was read by few, and the book's contents were known in Europe chiefly by report until an Oxford Hebraist took the Bodleian copy in hand. That Hebraist was Richard Laurence, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Oxford and later Archbishop of Cashel. In 1821 he published The Book of Enoch the Prophet — the first English translation of the complete work, made from the Ethiopic — and with it, the Watchers, the journeys, and the calendar entered modern European reading. Laurence's volume is a landmark of the recovery, and it is also a period piece: he presented the book, as his age was inclined to, as a genuine relic of antediluvian revelation, a framing the subsequent scholarship would dismantle even as it built on his text. The recovery's second act belongs to R. H. Charles, the Irish scholar who made the pseudepigrapha his life's work. Charles published an English translation in 1893, an edition of the Ethiopic text in 1906 — the first built on a wide collation of manuscripts — and in 1917 the revised translation by which two generations of English readers knew the book: The Book of Enoch or 1 Enoch , translated from the editor's Ethiopic text. Charles's datings of the parts, his division of the corpus into its five books, and his text remained the standard into the age of Qumran. Qumran changed the ground under the book, and the editions changed with it. Milik's 1976 edition of the Aramaic fragments, The Books of Enoch , gave the corpus its original-language foundation for the first time — and attached to it Milik's controversial redating of the Parables (§III). Michael A. Knibb's two-volume Ethiopic edition and translation (1978) re-founded the Ge'ez text on a fresh collation. The translation through which most English readers now meet the book in scholarly dress is E. Isaac's, in James H. Charlesworth's The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha , volume 1 (1983) — the translation quoted and paraphrased in this article wherever the Ethiopic text is rendered. The commentary standard is the Hermeneia series: Nickelsburg's 1 Enoch 1 (2001) on chapters 1–36 and 81–108, and Nickelsburg and VanderKam's 1 Enoch 2 (2012) on chapters 37–82, with the same scholars' 1 Enoch: The Hermeneia Translation (2012) presenting the whole in a single English text built from all three language traditions. When this article says "the text says," it is those editions — Isaac's rendering, checked against the Hermeneia commentary — that stand behind the verb. // ON QUOTING THIS BOOK // This article quotes 1 Enoch sparingly, and only in the named modern translations listed in the Sources. The reason is the transmission itself: a sentence quoted in English from the Ge'ez stands at two removes from the Aramaic its author wrote, and quotation marks promise a precision the chain cannot always deliver. Where the wording matters — above all in the catalogue of the gifts in §X — the translation is named at the quotation, and the catalogue's items are given with the translator's own terms. Everything else is paraphrase, and is presented as paraphrase. VI. The Seed in Genesis — Enoch and the Sons of God The Book of the Watchers is, among other things, the longest ancient commentary on the shortest strange passage in Genesis. The passage is Genesis 6:1–4: the "sons of God" see the daughters of men, take wives from them, and father the Nephilim, the giants, "the mighty men that were of old, the men of renown" — four verses, unexplained, standing at the threshold of the Flood narrative like a door left ajar. Behind it stands Genesis 5: the genealogy of Adam's line, in which Enoch, seventh from Adam, is given 365 years — a solar number, the years of the calendar his Astronomical Book will reveal — and the notice, unique in the list, that he walked with God and was not, for God took him. Two riddles: a patriarch taken alive into heaven, and a race of angels who came down out of it. The Enochic books are what ancient Judaism built in the space those riddles opened. The building is systematic. Genesis says Enoch was taken; the Enochic corpus makes him heaven's scribe and tour-guide of the cosmos, shown the storehouses of the stars, the prison of the fallen, the tree of life, the ends of the earth — because a man who entered heaven alive is the one witness who can report on it. Genesis says the sons of God took wives; the Book of the Watchers expands the four verses into a full narrative with names, numbers, a place, a motive, and a judgement (§§VII–XII). And Genesis says almost nothing of what the giants' age was like; the Watchers book fills the silence with its catalogue of taught arts and shed blood, and makes the Flood — which in Genesis follows immediately — into the judgement on that teaching. The relationship runs one way: the Enochic writers are reading Genesis, not the reverse. That is why the corpus can be dated by its exegesis: it is a library of expansions on a text already fixed and revered. It is worth pausing on the Flood connection, because it seats this article in the hub. In the telling of Flood Traditions , Genesis sends the deluge as a moral judgement on human wickedness and violence. The Book of the Watchers agrees on the judgement and reassigns the guilt: the corruption that fills the earth with blood begins not in human hearts but in heaven's defection — the arts and appetites the Watchers brought down. The Flood, in the Enochic frame, is the cleansing of a contamination that came from above. The same hinge appears in the chronology of The Antediluvian King Lists , where the flood divides the impossible reigns from the human ones: in Mesopotamia the water closes an age of kings, in Genesis an age of patriarchs, in Enoch an age of angels. Three literatures, one hinge — and, as the flood article argues, no warrant for melting them into a single event. VII. The Descent — Two Hundred on Mount Hermon The story proper opens at chapter 6, and it opens with a number. In the days of Jared — Enoch's father, in the Genesis genealogy; the narrative's own wordplay links Jared's name with descent — the sons of heaven, the Watchers, saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, and desired them. Their leader, Semyaza (also written Shemihazah), voices the story's first scruple: he fears he alone will bear the guilt of the great sin, and will not act unless all act together. So they swear. The whole company — two hundred in number, the text says — binds itself by mutual oath and curse, and descends on the summit of Mount Hermon , the great mountain at the head of the Jordan valley, on the border of the promised land. The text itself glosses the mountain's name from the oath: Hermon, it says, because on it they swore and bound one another with curses — the Hebrew root for a devoted, banned thing standing behind the pun. The fall, in this telling, begins not with lust but with a contract: a conspiracy formalised in advance, each angel's guilt underwritten by all. Chapter 6 also gives the company's officers: the chiefs of tens, some twenty names in the lists as the manuscripts give them — Semyaza first, then, in Isaac's rendering of the Ethiopic text, names including Urakiba, Ramiel, Kokabiel, Tamiel, Daniel, Ezeqeel, Baraqiel, Azazel, Armaros, Batarel, Ananel, Zaqiel, Samsapeel, Satarel, Turel, Jomjael, and Sariel. The lists are not perfectly stable across the Aramaic, Greek, and Ethiopic witnesses — names shift in spelling and a few in identity — and the critical editions print the variants rather than ironing them out. This article follows their practice: the names above are the list as Isaac's translation gives it, and where a name carries a story of its own — Azazel above all — the story is told in §VIII and §X. Several of the names are transparently functional: Kokabiel is the star-angel, Baraqiel the lightning-angel, Ezeqeel the cloud-watcher, Sariel the moon's prince. The company that falls is, in its naming, a faculty: each chief a department of the heaven he is about to betray — which is precisely how the catalogue of teachings in chapter 8 will be organised. They took wives, the text continues, each choosing for himself, and began to go in to them. The wives conceived and bore the giants. With that sentence the narrative's second engine starts: the offspring are not angels and not men, and the earth, made for neither appetite, cannot feed them. But before the giants' story runs its course (§IX), the text turns aside to the teaching — chapter 8's catalogue, the heart of this article, held for §X. First, the matter of the two chiefs, because the text the reader meets is not one telling but two, and the difference explains the catalogue's shape. VIII. Two Chiefs — Semyaza and Azazel Read closely, chapters 6–11 of the Book of the Watchers tell the fall twice. In one telling, the chief is Semyaza: the sin is the descent itself — the oath, the wives, the giants — and the guilt is corporate, sealed on Hermon. In the other, the chief is Azazel : the sin is the teaching — the revelation of heaven's secrets to men, the metals and the weapons and the cosmetics of chapter 8 — and the guilt is personal, laid by the judgement of chapter 10 on Azazel by name: to him, the text says in God's commission to Raphael, ascribe all sin. The critical literature, from Charles through Nickelsburg's Hermeneia commentary, reads these as two originally separate traditions — a Semyaza cycle and an Azazel (or Asael) cycle — combined by the editor who gave the Book of the Watchers its present form. The seams show in the narrative's doublings: two leaders, two emphases, two punishments (§XII). The distinction is worth the reader's attention, because it locates the catalogue of gifts inside the story's own architecture. In the Semyaza telling, the catastrophe is biological: forbidden union, monstrous offspring, blood. In the Azazel telling, the catastrophe is epistemological: forbidden knowledge , legitimately heaven's, illegitimately handed down. The Azazel strand is the one that makes this book matter to a history of craft. Its Azazel is not merely a rebel; he is a corrupt instructor, and his curriculum — swords and shields, bracelets and eye-paint, enchantments and the signs of the stars — is the first syllabus in the archive's whole alchemy spine: the arts of men listed entire, and listed as contraband. The name itself carried older freight: Azazel is the wilderness power of Leviticus 16, to whom the scapegoat bearing Israel's sins is sent on the Day of Atonement. The Enochic writers did not invent the name; they promoted its bearer from a desert cipher to the teacher of the world's corruption — and the judgement of chapter 10 will send him back to the desert, bound under rough stones, to wait for the fire (§XII). // WHY THE SEAMS ARE PRINTED, NOT HIDDEN // Popular retellings of the Watchers story
