What Çatalhöyük Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do, sharply, about the size of the population, the meaning of the famous "volcano" painting, and the reality of the town's celebrated equality — the disagreement itself is reported, with its positions attributed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. One discipline needs stating at the outset, because Çatalhöyük attracts mythology the way few sites do: the readings of its first excavator, James Mellaart — the "shrines", the mother goddess, the matriarchal town — are treated throughout as historiography , a layer in the site's modern history, and not as current consensus. Where this article reports what the ground shows, it follows the re-excavation of the site by the Çatalhöyük Research Project under Ian Hodder (1993–2017) and the specialist literature that project produced. Çatalhöyük is a double settlement mound on the Konya plain of central Anatolia, in modern Turkey, built up on the alluvial fan of the Çarşamba river. Its East mound carries one of the longest and most densely built Neolithic sequences in the world: house upon house, for well over a thousand years, in a fabric so tight that there were no streets at all. People crossed the town on its roofs, climbed down ladders through holes in those roofs into their homes, cooked, slept, painted their walls, set the horned skulls of wild bulls into their benches, and buried their dead — hundreds of them, across the excavated sample — in pits cut through the floors they lived on. Then they filled each dead house in, and built its successor on the same footprint, on the stumps of the same walls. The hub's index states the claim this article exists to test: that Çatalhöyük is "the standing proof that early urban life did not require kings." The excavated record does show something remarkable — a community of town-like scale and density with no palace, no temple precinct, no central storehouse, no chiefly burials, and no monumental architecture that anyone has identified in more than half a century of digging. But a proof is a strong thing, and §VIII of this article weighs the claim at its real strength: the positive evidence for an egalitarian organisation, the counter-evidence of the "history houses" and of change over time, and the standing weakness of all arguments built on absence — that authority which leaves no monument is authority the spade cannot see. The reader will find the claim largely sustained, and carefully qualified. That is the only form in which this tier prints it. I. Two Mounds on the Konya Plain — The Place and the Sequence Çatalhöyük — the name is modern Turkish, çatal , a fork, and höyük , a mound — lies on the southern Konya plain at roughly 1,000 metres above sea level, some 40–50 km southeast of the modern city of Konya, near the present-day village of Küçükköy in Çumra district. The settlement stood on the alluvial fan of the Çarşamba river , which in the Neolithic ran between what are now the site's two mounds and spread seasonally across the plain in a mosaic of channels, marshes, and dry ground. That mosaic was the town's larder and its building yard at once: river clay and marl for mudbrick and plaster, reeds and grasses for mats and baskets, wetland grazing and wildfowl at the door, and drier rises for fields within reach of the houses. The plain is ringed by hills that supplied timber, stone, and game; far to the northeast, on a clear day, the twin peaks of the volcano Hasan Dağı stand on the horizon — a landmark that matters to §VI of this article. // LOCATION // Konya plain, central Anatolia On the alluvial fan of the Çarşamba river, c. 40–50 km southeast of Konya, Turkey, at c. 1,000 m above sea level. // THE EAST MOUND // c. 13.5 hectares, c. 21 m high The Neolithic town: 18 occupation levels of densely packed mudbrick houses, the sequence on which this article concentrates. // THE WEST MOUND // c. 8.5 hectares, lower The Early Chalcolithic successor settlement, across the old river channel; occupied as the East mound was given up (§IX). // OCCUPATION // East c. 7100–5950 BCE (Bayesian) See the dating discussion below: older literature and the UNESCO listing give the East mound as c. 7400–6200 BCE; the two mounds together span roughly two millennia. The East mound is the famous one. It rises some 20 metres above the plain and covers about 13.5 hectares, and excavation has distinguished eighteen levels of Neolithic building within it — level upon level of the same dense house fabric, each generation's town founded on the levelled remains of the last. The West mound, a few hundred metres away across the former river channel, is lower and smaller, and carries the settlement's Early Chalcolithic continuation: painted pottery, changed house forms, and a materially different, though related, community (§IX). The site as a whole was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012, under criteria that cite, in the listing's own framing, its streetless neighbourhoods, its roof-access houses, and a social organisation read as largely egalitarian — a judgement §VIII examines rather than assumes. The Dates — A Necessary Correction of the Round Numbers Çatalhöyük's chronology comes in two generations, and this article keeps them apart because the difference is instructive. The conventional dates , established in the Mellaart era and still carried by the UNESCO listing, give the East mound as c. 7400–6200 BCE and the West as c. 6200–5200 BCE — the figures behind the round span, c. 7500–5700 BCE for the settlement as a whole, that this hub's timeline prints. The revised dates come from the Hodder project's programme of Bayesian radiocarbon modelling, in which hundreds of AMS determinations are ordered by the stratigraphy they came from, so that each date constrains its neighbours. Bayliss and colleagues (2015), modelling the start of the South Area sequence, placed the beginning of occupation on the East mound at 7165–7085 cal BCE (95% probability) — some three centuries later than the older estimate. Work on the mound's summit levels (Marciniak and colleagues, 2015) dates the abandonment of the last East mound houses to around 5950 BCE . New AMS dating of the West mound (Orton and colleagues, 2018) then dissolved the old picture of a clean succession: the two mounds were occupied together for a time, the focus shifting gradually, probably over a century or two around 6000 BCE, and the West mound occupation ran on to roughly 5600–5500 BCE . The working chronology of this article is therefore: East mound, c. 7100–5950 BCE ; West mound, beginning in the late seventh millennium and running to c. 5600–5500 BCE ; a total settlement history of some fifteen to sixteen centuries on the East mound alone. Where the older round figures appear below, they are flagged as the older figures. The correction matters beyond pedantry: a town founded around 7100 BCE is not a pioneer outpost of the first farming spread but a mature, late foundation, established by people whose ancestors had farmed Anatolia for well over a millennium — at Aşıklı Höyük and Boncuklu, a short distance away, the region's earlier experiments in settled life can still be read. Çatalhöyük's achievement was not priority. It was scale, and duration. How Many People? — The Population Problem No number in this article is softer than the population, and the honest treatment is to show the machinery that produces the figures rather than to pick one. The classic estimate, built up in the Mellaart tradition and formalised by Craig Cessford for the Hodder project, runs as follows: measure the roofed area of a well-excavated level; count its houses; multiply by an assumed household — five to ten persons, on ethnographic analogy — and scale up to the whole mound. On those assumptions the peak population of the East mound comes out at 3,500 to 8,000 people , the range this hub's sources and most syntheses quote. Every step of the machinery, however, carries an assumption that can be challenged, and in 2024 Kuijt and Marciniak challenged nearly all of them at once. Their critique, published in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology , works from building biographies: houses were not all standing at once, not all roofed space was residential at any given moment, buildings spent part of their lives as ruins, stores, or animal pens, and the roofed fraction of the mound at any one time was perhaps only half to two-thirds of the whole. Rebuilding the estimate on those terms, they arrive at 600 to 800 people in an average year of the town's Middle phase (c. 6700–6500 BCE) — an order of magnitude below the classic peak. Other recent syntheses split the difference, quoting working ranges of roughly 500 to 5,000. The disagreement is not noise; it is the measurement. What survives every version of the arithmetic is the density : whether the town held eight hundred people or eight thousand, it held them in a continuous fabric of shared-wall houses with no streets, no plots, and no open public ground inside the built area — a crowding that has no parallel among ordinary farming villages of its millennium, and that frames every social question the site poses. Estimate Figure Method Standing Classic (Mellaart tradition; Cessford) 3,500–8,000 at peak Roofed area of excavated levels × houses × 5–10 persons per household, scaled to the full mound Long the standard figure; assumes most roofed space simultaneously residential Recent syntheses c. 500–5,000 Compromise ranges allowing for non-residential and unoccupied buildings Quoted, with the spread itself flagged, in current bioarchaeological literature Kuijt & Marciniak (2024) 600–800 in an average Middle-phase year Building-biography approach: house lifespans, abandonment phases, and ethnographic occupancy, house by house The standing challenge; reframes Çatalhöyük as a very large village rather than a proto-city This article therefore speaks of "hundreds to thousands" where the argument does not depend on the count, gives the classic 3,500–8,000 where it reports the classic literature, and names the 2024 revision where the scale of the community is itself the point at issue. One comparison orients the range. The walled town of Jericho , a millennium older, held its thousands behind a wall and under a great tower; Çatalhöyük, at any point in its population range, held a comparable crowd with no wall, no tower, and no centre. How it held together at all is the subject of §§IV, V, and VIII. II. Mellaart, 1961–65 — The Discovery and Its First Reading The East mound was identified in November 1958, during a survey of the Konya plain by James Mellaart of the British Institute of Archaeology at Ankara, with David French and Alan Hall. Mellaart excavated for four seasons, 1961 to 1965 (the 1964 season was lost to the political fallout of the Dorak affair, an unrelated controversy over Bronze Age finds that ended his Turkish career). Working at a speed and on a scale that no modern project would attempt, his teams cleared more than 160 buildings in the southwest of the East mound and cut two trenches into the West mound, establishing the level sequence — his Levels XII to I, earliest to latest — on which all later work still builds. His synthesis, Çatal Hüyük: A Neolithic Town in Anatolia (1967), presented the site to the world, and its photographs of painted walls, horned benches, and corpulent figurines made Çatalhöyük famous within the decade. The excavation itself was a genuine achievement, and the Hodder project's re-excavation has confirmed its stratigraphic skeleton: the agglutinative houses, the roof entry, the underfloor burials, the paintings, and the installations are all real, and all where Mellaart said they were. What has not survived is the interpretive superstructure he built on them, and the distinction between the two — the digging and the reading — is the single most important thing a modern account can preserve. Mellaart's reading ran as follows, and it is given here in his terms because its afterlife has been so long. The "Shrines" Mellaart divided the buildings he cleared into ordinary houses and "shrines" — by his count some forty rooms whose richer decoration, paintings, reliefs, and bull-horn installations marked them, in his view, as cult buildings served by priests. The shrines anchored his whole reconstruction: a town of temples, in which religion was housed in dedicated architecture and mediated by specialists. The Hodder project's verdict, after excavating comparable buildings stone by stone and sample by sample, is that the category does not hold. Every "shrine" so far re-examined is a house : it has the full domestic kit — oven, hearth, storage bins, platforms, food-processing debris, burials — and its elaboration differs from its neighbours' in degree, not in kind. Buildings at Çatalhöyük form a continuum from the plain to the spectacularly decorated; the line Mellaart drew across that continuum, with temples on one side and homes on the other, is not in the ground. The consequences run through this whole article: the town's ritual life was not concentrated in a temple quarter. It was distributed, house by house, through the same rooms in which people cooked and slept — a finding that matters as much to the equality question (§VIII) as to the history of religion. The Mother Goddess Mellaart's second great construction was theological. The figurines of women — above all a seated figure flanked by two felines, found in a grain bin in a late level — he read as images of a Great Goddess , a mother deity of fertility and the harvest, heading the pantheon of what he presented as an essentially matriarchal society; the many sexless figurines he took as further symptoms of a culture in which, in his framing, the female principle dominated. Marija Gimbutas built the Çatalhöyük goddess into her wider vision of a goddess-worshipping "Old Europe", and through her the site became a place of modern pilgrimage for the Goddess movement. All of this is historiography now. The systematic re-study of the figurine corpus by Lynn Meskell, Carolyn Nakamura, and their colleagues (§VI) found that clearly female figures are a small minority of the whole — under three per cent of the diagnostic corpus — that most figurines are animals or unsexed abbreviated forms, and that they come overwhelmingly not from shrines or altars but from middens and fills, discarded with the rubbish. A goddess cult may have existed at Çatalhöyük; the figurines, counted rather than cherry-picked, do not evidence one. This article therefore uses "goddess figurines" only as the name of a debate, never as a description of a find. // READING MELLAART TODAY // Mellaart's 1967 volume remains the primary publication of the 1960s excavation and the source of its plans, photographs, and find records; it is cited in this article's Sources in exactly that capacity. Its interpretations — shrines, goddess, matriarchy, and the town-plan reading of the "volcano" painting (§VI) — are reported as his, attributed at every occurrence, and weighed against the re-excavation. That double treatment is not a courtesy. It is the archive's standing rule for any excavator whose synthesis outran his evidence: keep the record, retire the reading, and say plainly which is which. After 1965 the mound slept for a generation. The site was protected, the finds went to the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara — where the seated figure, the paintings' originals, and the great aurochs-hunt mural still anchor the Neolithic galleries — and Çatalhöyük entered the textbooks in Mellaart's version: the earliest city, the goddess town, the peaceful matriarchy. When excavation resumed in 1993, it resumed under a director, Ian Hodder, who had been Mellaart's student, and who came to the site with the explicit intention of testing the inheritance — including, as it turned out, most of his teacher's conclusions. The methods he brought with him are the subject of the next section, because at Çatalhöyük the method is part of the evidence: several of the findings this article relies on — the plaster micro-sequences, the burial biographies, the figurine statistics — exist only because the second excavation dug at a fineness the first never attempted. III. The Hodder Project, 1993–2017 — Reflexive Archaeology The Çatalhöyük Research Project , directed by Ian Hodder from 1993 to 2017 — twenty-five years of fieldwork, with the permit concluding in 2018 and Turkish-led work continuing since — is among the largest and longest archaeological projects ever run on a single Neolithic site. Its excavation areas re-opened and extended Mellaart's ground in the South Area of the East mound, opened new ground in the North Area, and returned in later seasons to the summit levels and to the West mound. Under the field direction of Shahina Farid , the project's excavation summaries established the fine stratigraphic framework — a re-lettered sequence of levels, South G to T and their northern equivalents — within which the Bayesian dating of §I and every building biography in this article are set. The project's publication output is correspondingly vast: the multi-volume Çatalhöyük Excavations monographs, specialist studies in every material from plaster chemistry to human ancient DNA, and Hodder's own synthesis, The Leopard's Tale (2006), the single most readable account of the site and the source this article leans on most. The project's scale, however, is less distinctive than its method. Hodder came to Çatalhöyük as a founder of post-processual archaeology — the movement arguing that the past is not simply recovered but interpreted, and that the interpretation should therefore be documented as part of the record. The project practised what it called reflexive archaeology , briefly and factually: interpretation was pushed down to the trowel's edge, so that excavators recorded their readings of a deposit as they dug it, in diaries kept alongside the formal context records; specialists — bone, plant, pottery, plaster — worked on site, in daily "priority tours" of the trenches, rather than receiving finds in distant laboratories months later; the project's databases and diaries were opened to outside comment from early on; and multiple, sometimes conflicting, interpretations were published side by side rather than resolved into a single directorial voice — the "multivocality" the project made its watchword. One may or may not find the philosophy congenial. Its practical yield is not in doubt: a record of unusual depth and unusual auditability, in which the reasoning behind a claim can be traced back through diary, context sheet, and sample. The method also changed what could be seen. Mellaart's teams had dug building by building; the Hodder teams dug within buildings at the scale of the single rake-out, the single replastering, the single dumped basket of ash. Micromorphology — the microscopic study of undisturbed sediment blocks — resolved floor and wall plasters into sequences of individual coats and sweepings (§V). Flotation recovered plant remains by the tens of thousands of samples (§VII). Every burial was excavated as a biography: position, wrapping, sequence of interment, later disturbance. It is not too much to say that the Çatalhöyük of this article — a town known through the life histories of individual houses — is a product of that fineness of digging, and that the older Çatalhöyük, of shrines and goddesses, was in part a product of digging too fast to see the houses for the rooms. // TWO EXCAVATIONS, ONE MOUND // The contrast is worth holding in mind throughout. Mellaart: four seasons, 160+ buildings, broad exposures, interpretation published as a single confident synthesis. Hodder: twenty-five seasons, fewer buildings, each excavated at micro-stratigraphic resolution with an army of on-site specialists, interpretation published as an open, multi-author archive. Where the two agree — the plan, the burials, the art — the evidence is as solid as Neolithic archaeology gets. Where they disagree, this article follows the slower dig, and says why. A final fact of method belongs here because it disciplines everything that follows: only a minority of the East mound has been excavated at all . Mellaart's exposures and the Hodder project's areas together open a few hectares of the 13.5 — the rest is known from surface survey, geophysics, and coring, not from the spade. The town plan of §IV is real but partial; the absence of public buildings in §VIII is an absence within the excavated sample, extrapolated, reasonably but not certainly, to the whole. Tier A practice is to carry that caveat in the open, and this article does so at each point where the argument leans on it. IV. The Agglutinative Town — Houses Without Streets The plan of Çatalhöyük is the plan of no city planner. Houses stand wall to wall in a continuous fabric — agglutinative building, in the literature's term — each rectangular mudbrick house abutting its neighbours on every side, with its own set of walls even where a neighbour's wall already stood, so that party walls are doubled. Between the houses there are, in the classic levels, no streets, no lanes, and no courtyards at ground level: the only open spaces inside the settlement are the midden areas — patches of accumulated refuse, ash, and dung, used also for penning animals and for work too dirty for the house — which punctuate the fabric where a building has been abandoned or not yet rebuilt. The town's public surface was its roofscape : the flat roofs, at roughly common height within a neighbourhood, formed the streets, squares, and work yards of Çatalhöyük, and the excavated plan is best read as a map of cellars beneath a town that was actually lived one storey up, in the sun and the smoke, on surfaces that have not survived. Movement followed from the plan. To visit a neighbour, one crossed roofs. To enter one's own house, one climbed a ladder to the roof and descended a second ladder through the roof opening — the house's only door, and also its chimney and its principal window. The opening stood, in the standard plan, over the southern part of the main room, directly above the oven and hearth, so that smoke rose past the ladder and out; the arrangement made every house defensible in a small way — draw up the ladder and the house is shut — though whether defence explains it, rather than the simple absence of any ground-level access in a streetless fabric, the evidence does not decide. Goods moved as people moved: grain, fuel, dung, carcasses, and building clay all came and went over the roofs and down the ladders, and the middens below the roofscape's edge received what the houses threw out. In the upper levels, after c. 6500 BCE, the fabric loosens — houses stand in clusters with gaps between, and something closer to lanes appears — a change that §VIII and §IX take up, since it tracks a loosening of the social fabric as well. Anatomy of a House Within the fabric, the individual house is one of the most standardised dwellings of the Neolithic world — a template repeated, with variations, in house after house and level after level, and set out here because §V and §VIII both argue from it. A typical house is a single storey of mudbrick on a footing of the levelled house beneath, its main room commonly around 25 square metres, with one or two small side rooms. The main room is zoned with a consistency that amounts to a grammar: the southern zone , beneath the roof hole, is the dirty working end — domed clay oven set against the south wall, a hearth on the floor beside it, ash, food debris, and the wear of daily traffic; the northern and eastern zones are the clean end — raised platforms of plastered mudbrick, kept swept and white, for sitting, working, and sleeping, and it is beneath these platforms that the dead are buried. The side rooms are for storage: clay bins built against their walls held grain, lentils, and peas; baskets, mats, tools, and stores filled the rest. Timber roof beams and posts, reed and clay roofing, wall niches, and — in the elaborate houses — benches and installations complete the inventory. Every house has its own oven, its own storage, its own platforms: the unit is functionally complete, a fact on which the equality argument of §VIII substantially rests. Element Form Function and Evidence Walls Mudbrick, each house with its own set, even against a neighbour Agglutinative fabric; doubled party walls; walls founded on the stumps of the house below Entry Opening in the flat roof, reached and descended by ladders The only door; also chimney and light source; set over the oven end of the main room Oven and hearth Domed clay oven against the south wall; open hearth nearby Cooking and heating in the "dirty" southern zone; smoke exits by the roof hole Platforms Raised plastered platforms along the north and east walls The "clean" zone: sitting, sleeping, display; burials cut beneath them Side rooms One or two small rooms off the main room Storage: built clay bins for cereals and pulses; baskets, tools, and stores Installations Benches, niches, wall reliefs, bucrania in the elaborate houses The symbolic furniture of §VI; present in degree, absent as a separate building type Above the single house stands the neighbourhood . Bleda Düring's analysis of the Central Anatolian settlements ( Constructing Communities , 2006) showed that the Çatalhöyük fabric is not uniform porridge: houses cluster in groups — his "clustered neighbourhoods", of the order of a few dozen households — separated by midden areas and slight breaks in the building line, and these clusters, he argued, were the town's operative social units above the household: the people whose roofs formed one continuous walking surface, whose dead and whose stores were near, and whose cooperation the daily logistics of a streetless town required. More recent spatial work by the project complicates any rigid version of the scheme — groupings overlap, shift between levels, and cross-cut one another — but the nested picture it supports is the one this article uses: household within house-cluster, cluster within sector, sector within town, with no level of the nesting marked by a building bigger or grander than the rest. The contrast the hub invites is with Göbekli Tepe , three millennia earlier and a day's journey east in its day: there, a community without farming built monuments and no town; here, a farming community built a town and no monuments. The Neolithic contained both experiments. NO STREETS In the classic levels the built fabric is continuous: no lanes, alleys, or plazas at ground level. Circulation, visiting, and much outdoor work happened on the roofs. ONE DOOR, IN THE ROOF Every house is entered from above, by ladder through the roof opening — simultaneously its door, chimney, and window, set over the oven end of the main room. A GRAMMAR OF ZONES South is dirty (oven, hearth, ash, traffic); north and east are clean (white platforms, display, sleep). The same grammar recurs in house after house, level after level. MIDDENS BETWEEN The only ground-level open spaces are middens — refuse, ash, and dung accumulations used for penning and dirty work, in the gaps of the house fabric. V. The House as History — Rebuilding, Plaster, and the Dead Beneath the Floors A Çatalhöyük house had a life, and the town's deepest habit was to make that life legible. Houses stood for roughly a human lifetime — estimates from the building biographies run to some fifty to eighty years — and at the end of a life, a house was not simply abandoned. It was closed : cleaned out, its roof timbers salvaged, its installations sometimes carefully removed or buried, its upper walls pushed in, and its shell filled with clean material to form a level platform. On that platform, on the stumps of the old walls and to the old alignments, the successor house was built — same footprint, same orientation, same internal grammar, often with its platforms and oven in the same relative places. Repeat the cycle for a millennium and the mound explains itself: 21 metres of houses, each generation standing quite literally on its predecessors. Continuity of place was not an accident of a crowded town; the care taken in closure and rebuilding, and the retrieval and re-deposition of objects and remains between houses, show it being maintained , house by house, as a practice. Replastering — The Calendar on the Wall Within a house's life, the maintenance rhythm was plaster. Floors and walls were coated in a fine white marl plaster, and the coating was renewed again and again: micromorphological study of wall sections counts the coats one by one, and the numbers are startling — dozens of replasterings in an ordinary house, and in extreme cases several hundred micro-layers within 20 cm of accumulated wall plaster , with counts up to around 450 coats reported for the most-renewed surfaces. Not every coat was a full re-whitening; many are hair-thin skim coats, and the rhythm they record — seasonal, perhaps in part annual, punctuated by heavier re-plasterings at life events — made the wall a calendar of the household's care. Platforms were kept the whitest: swept, clean, and renewed most often, the visible centre of the room. Paintings (§VI) belong to this cycle: a painting was made on fresh plaster, lived with, and in time plastered over, sometimes to be succeeded by another on the same wall. The imagery of Çatalhöyük was not permanent public art. It was domestic, renewable, and repeatedly buried by the household's own hand — which is why so much of it survives. The Dead Beneath the Floors The dead stayed in the house. The standard burial at Çatalhöyük is a primary inhumation beneath the floor : a narrow oval pit cut through the plaster — most often beneath the northern or eastern platforms of the main room — the body laid tightly flexed, frequently wrapped in matting or textile and sometimes set in a basket, the pit filled and the floor replastered over it, so that the household continued to sit and sleep above its dead. Infants and the very young were more often buried near the oven or in side rooms; the platform burials are disproportionately adults. The scale of the practice is best given in the project's own counts: the skeletal remains of at least 741 individuals were excavated from Neolithic contexts in the Hodder seasons of 1993–2017 alone (Larsen and colleagues, 2019), of whom sub-floor primary burials account for 471; with the Mellaart-era dead added, the excavated total runs to around 800 individuals . Burial was not a single event but a continuing relationship: floors were reopened for successive interments in the same house, some burials were later disturbed or partly removed, and a minority of the dead — about thirteen per cent of the assemblage — are secondary burials, loose or partly articulated remains re-deposited, sometimes with a primary burial. Skulls, in a small number of cases, were retrieved and kept: a few were plastered and painted, in the wider Anatolian and Levantine tradition this hub meets at Jericho , and one famous burial held a plastered skull cradled in its arms. Two findings discipline the romance of the ancestor house. First, burial in a house was selective and uneven : some houses accumulated burials by the dozen — the most laden hold thirty, forty, in the extreme over sixty individuals across a building sequence — while many houses hold few or none. The dead of Çatalhöyük were not distributed one family to one house; they were gathered, disproportionately, into particular houses. Second, the gathered dead were not necessarily kin. Dental and ancient-DNA studies of co-buried individuals have repeatedly found that people buried together in a house were often not close biological relatives — membership of a house, and burial beneath its floor, appear to have been social facts, made by residence, affiliation, and practice, as much as genealogical ones. The house, in the project's phrase, made its people; it did not merely descend from them. "History Houses" The houses at the laden end of that distribution are the ones Hodder named "history houses" . A history house is a building sequence that stands out on every axis of elaboration at once: rebuilt on its footprint more times than its neighbours, more thickly plastered, more richly installed and painted, and the repository of far more burials than the town's average — a house that accumulated, in Hodder's reading, the memories, remains, and prestige of a wider group, something like a lineage or sodality headquarters embedded in an ordinary street of roofs. The type specimen of the project's accounts, Building 1 in the North Area, held dozens of burials through its sequence; other sequences show the same signature of repeated rebuilding plus dense burial plus heavy installation. History houses matter to this article out of proportion to their number, because they are the strongest internal evidence against a flat reading of the town's equality: here, visibly, some houses were more equal than others — in symbolic capital, in ancestors, in the labour their upkeep absorbed. What they did not accumulate, on the project's analyses, is the subject of §VIII: no larger stores, no richer burials, no control of production has been shown for them. They were first in memory. Whether "first in memory" is a kind of power that leaves the equality claim intact, or the crack through which hierarchy eventually entered, is the sharpest question the site poses, and it is argued, not assumed, below. // A HOUSEHOLD YEAR, RECONSTRUCTED FROM THE DEPOSITS //

How to Read This Article — Tier C, and the Two Columns This article is classified Tier C — Modern Construction , and the classification is stated in words here, at the outset, because everything that follows depends on it. Tier C, in the scheme of this hub, means that the subject is a body of ideas built in modern times — in this case, in the first half of the twentieth century — whatever ancient materials those ideas claim as their sources. The subject here is the Atlantis and Egypt material in the trance readings of Edgar Cayce (1877–1945). The companion article Mu and Atlantis Reborn treats Cayce briefly, as one figure in the longer modern Atlantis tradition; this article is the full treatment of Cayce himself, and it does not repeat that article's wider story. Cayce's material demands a discipline the other Tier C subjects do not, because it comes in two columns that are constantly confused. In the first column stands what is documented : a real man, real sessions, on real dates, in real rooms, taken down in shorthand by a named stenographer, typed, filed, indexed, and preserved to this day by an organisation he founded. That column is unusually solid — few bodies of claimed revelation in history are as well attested as documents . In the second column stands what the readings assert : that Atlantis existed and fell in stages ending around 10,500 BCE; that its refugees carried civilisation to Egypt; that the Giza monuments were built under a priest named Ra-Ta at that remote date; and that a Hall of Records lies sealed between the Sphinx and the Nile. Nothing in the second column is established by the solidity of the first. A transcript proves that words were spoken. It does not prove that what the words describe ever happened. This article will keep the two columns visibly separate in every section: documented frame first, assertion labelled as assertion, and — where an assertion has been tested against independent evidence — the result of the test stated plainly. // A NOTE ON QUOTATIONS // The readings are a copyrighted, archived corpus, and this article quotes them only once, briefly, from a published scholarly summary in which the wording was verified (Joscelyn Godwin, Atlantis and the Cycles of Time , as presented on the publisher's page). Everywhere else, the readings' content is paraphrased and attributed, with reading numbers given so that any reader with access to the A.R.E. archive can check the paraphrase against the transcript. That checkability is the corpus's genuine strength, and this article uses it rather than decorating itself with unverified quotation. A last word of register. The readings are not a dead curiosity. The Association for Research and Enlightenment, founded by Cayce in 1931, is active today; its members study the readings as a living spiritual tradition, and the archive at Virginia Beach is their scripture's manuscript room. This article treats that tradition with the respect due to any living faith — and treats its historical assertions with the scrutiny due to any historical claim. Those two duties do not conflict. They are, in fact, the same duty performed twice: to say exactly what a thing is. II. The Documented Man — Edgar Cayce, 1877–1945 The biographical frame is not in dispute, and it can be stated briefly. Edgar Cayce was born on 18 March 1877 near Hopkinsville, in Christian County, Kentucky, and raised in the Disciples of Christ tradition — a devout, Bible-reading churchgoer and Sunday-school teacher for most of his life. His formal schooling ended early, and he worked in bookshops and then as a photographer, the trade he followed for much of his adult life. In 1901, in the standard account preserved by his organisation and his biographers, he gave the first of his trance discourses: having lost his voice to a persistent laryngeal condition, he was hypnotised and, in that state, spoke a diagnosis and treatment for his own ailment — after which, the account holds, his voice returned. Whether the episode is read as the opening of a psychic career or as a striking case of suggestion and psychosomatic illness is a question this article leaves to the reader; that the episode was reported, and that Cayce thereafter gave readings for others, belongs to the documented column. For two decades the readings were occasional and mostly unrecorded. The career became an institution in stages that are likewise documented: the move to Virginia Beach, Virginia, in the 1920s; a hospital venture there at the end of that decade; the founding in 1931 of the Association for Research and Enlightenment (A.R.E.) , the membership organisation that promoted, published, and organised the work; and a final period of extraordinary demand during the Second World War, when the waiting list for readings stretched for years and Cayce, against the advice his own readings gave him, increased his daily sessions to a pace his health could not sustain. He died on 3 January 1945 in Virginia Beach. His sons — Hugh Lynn Cayce, who led the A.R.E. for decades, and Edgar Evans Cayce, who compiled the Atlantis readings — carried the organisation and the archive forward. The popular biography There Is a River by Thomas Sugrue, published in Cayce's lifetime, and Jess Stearn's later bestseller The Sleeping Prophet — "sleeping" because Cayce reclined and closed his eyes to give a reading — made him, posthumously, the most famous American psychic of the twentieth century. 1877 Born 18 March, near Hopkinsville, Kentucky. Devout Disciples of Christ upbringing; later a photographer by trade. 1901 The first trance discourse, in the standard account: a self-diagnosis for the laryngeal condition that had taken his voice. 1923 Gladys Davis becomes his stenographer; from September of this year the readings are recorded systematically. Reincarnation enters the readings. 1931 The Association for Research and Enlightenment is founded at Virginia Beach to carry the work. 1945 Dies 3 January at Virginia Beach, after a final period in which demand had driven him far beyond the two readings a day his own readings advised. THE NICKNAME "The Sleeping Prophet" — from the posture of the performance: recumbent, eyes closed, hands folded, speaking in his own voice in answer to questions put by a conductor. III. The Reading as Performance — Couch, Conductor, Stenographer A Cayce reading was not a manuscript, a vision written up afterwards, or a book dictated over months. It was a performance with a fixed liturgy , and the fixity matters to the historian, because it is what makes the corpus a corpus. Cayce would loosen his collar and belt, lie down on a couch, fold his hands, and enter — by his own account and that of every witness — a sleep-like trance. His wife, Gertrude Evans Cayce , ordinarily served as conductor : she read aloud a formulaic suggestion naming the subject — often a person far away, identified by name and location — and posed the questions the subject or the sitters had submitted. Cayce then spoke, in a normal voice, in discourse that ranged from medical prescription to cosmology. At the end, the conductor gave the formula for waking, and Cayce woke, ordinarily remembering nothing of what he had said. The third figure in the room is the one to whom the archive owes its existence. From September 1923, the readings were taken down in shorthand by Gladys Davis (later Gladys Davis Turner), Cayce's stenographer, who recorded her first reading for him on 30 August 1923 and began full-time work on 10 September 1923. Davis transcribed her shorthand into typewritten copies — one for the subject, one for the file — and over the following decades she built the subject index and cross-referencing system by which the corpus can be searched, work she continued with the Edgar Cayce Foundation long after Cayce's death. Readings given before 1923 survive only patchily, which is why the systematic corpus is effectively a 1923–1945 corpus. The point cannot be overstated: the readings exist as evidence because a stenographer was in the room . What the historian possesses is not Cayce's inner experience, about which the record can say nothing, but a dated, witnessed, transcribed text of what was said in that room — and that is already, for a claimed revelation, a great deal. // WHAT THE PERFORMANCE ESTABLISHES — AND WHAT IT DOES NOT // The stenographic record establishes, to a standard few comparable corpora meet, that specific words were spoken by Edgar Cayce, in trance, on specific dates, in response to specific questions, for specific named or numbered subjects. It does not establish the source of those words — Cayce's own account invoked a universal record and a higher self; sceptical accounts invoke the subconscious, prior reading, and the expectations of sitters — and it does not establish the truth of any historical statement the words contain. Both halves of that sentence are the archive's real value. IV. The Archive — A.R.E., the Foundation, and the Numbering of the Readings The counts in this section are the A.R.E.'s own published figures, checked against the organisation's current statements. The A.R.E. puts the complete corpus at 14,306 readings — the figure given on its own site for the entire set, held in its library at Virginia Beach and made available to members in a searchable database. (Counts of 14,307 or 14,308 circulate in secondary literature, reflecting small differences in how fragments and duplicates are tallied; the figure used here is the organisation's own headline number.) Of these, the A.R.E.'s health materials state that nearly 70 percent concern the diagnosis of disease and the outlining of treatment — the medical readings were always the bulk of the work, and the Atlantis and Egypt material treated in this article is a minority strand within the whole. The readings in their entirety address, by the organisation's count, some 10,000 different topics. Two institutions divide the custody. The A.R.E. , founded 1931, is the membership and publishing body. The Edgar Cayce Foundation , chartered in 1948 after Cayce's death, is the legal custodian of the readings themselves — the transcripts, reports, and correspondence — preserving the originals and governing research access. The readings are cited by a numbering system devised under Gladys Davis : each recipient or subject was assigned a number, and that person's readings are numbered in sequence after it. Thus 294 is Edgar Cayce himself, and 294-8 is the eighth reading in his own file; 378-16 is the sixteenth reading for subject 378; 958-3 the third for subject 958. Names were replaced by numbers in the public set to protect recipients' privacy — approximately 5,750 people received readings — and the numbering, reorganised under an indexing plan in 1959, is the citation system every scholarly and A.R.E. publication uses. When this article gives a reading number, it is giving the reader an address: the claim can be found, dated, and read in full in the archive. That is how a trance corpus ought to be cited, and it is to the Foundation's credit that it can be. Figure Count Source of the Count Total readings in the corpus 14,306 The A.R.E.'s own published figure for the entire set Share concerned with health Nearly 70% The A.R.E.'s published description of the corpus Life readings given, 1923–1944 Around 2,500 Joscelyn Godwin's tabulation in Atlantis and the Cycles of Time Readings mentioning Atlantis No fewer than 700 Tabulated by Edgar Evans Cayce; reported by Godwin and in A.R.E.-derived summaries People told of a life in Egypt c. 10,500 BCE More than 1,100 Commentary in the A.R.E. Circulating File, Archaeology: Egypt & Gobi Reading recipients c. 5,750 people Edgar Cayce Foundation archival accounts of the numbering system One caution belongs with the numbers. A count of readings mentioning Atlantis is a count of a theme in a corpus, assembled over twenty years of individual sessions for individual clients — not the chapters of a single composed history. The composite Atlantis and the composite Egypt that later books present were assembled from these scattered statements, principally by Edgar Evans Cayce in Edgar Cayce on Atlantis (1968) and by the A.R.E.'s own research files. The assembly is legitimate work, and the A.R.E. does it openly. But the reader should know that the seamless narrative is an editorial product laid over a fragmentary record — as, to be fair, is much of ancient history. The difference is that ancient history's fragments are then tested against independent evidence. Sections XIV–XVII trace what happened when Cayce's were. V. Life Readings — How Atlantis and Egypt Entered the Corpus Reincarnation was not in Cayce's teaching from the start, and its entry is datable. Cayce began as a fundamentalist Christian who wrestled, by his own account, with doubts about what was speaking through him. In 1923 — the year the stenographic record begins — the readings took up the idea of past lives, and a new genre, the life reading , was born: instead of diagnosing the subject's body, the reading narrated the subject's previous incarnations and drew lessons for the present life from them. The first life reading's subject, in the tabulation reported by Godwin, was Cayce's own son Edgar Evans. Over the following twenty years, on Godwin's count, Cayce gave around 2,500 life readings — and no fewer than 700 of them placed a former life of the subject in Atlantis . In 1932 Cayce also consented to a deliberate series of readings on the deep past itself — the 364 series — which supplies much of the systematic Atlantis material: its geography, its factions, its destructions. The mechanism by which a lost continent entered so many biographies deserves a plain statement, because it explains the corpus's shape. A life reading answered the client in front of it. When hundreds of clients, over two decades, were each told of an Atlantean incarnation, the readings accumulated a shared world — consistent in its furniture, its factions, and its chronology to a degree that believers read as corroboration and sceptics read as the natural product of one mind, one room, one set of expectations, and an organisation that indexed and cross-referenced every statement, allowing later readings to be given in a context already saturated with earlier ones. Both readings of the consistency are available; the archive itself cannot decide between them. What the archive can do — and what this article does — is report the composite faithfully, attributed to the readings, and then ask the only question evidence can answer: whether anything outside the corpus matches it. // THE COMPOSITE, AS ASSEMBLED — A STANDING LABEL // Sections VI–XII present "Atlantis as asserted" and "Egypt as asserted." Every statement in them is a statement of the readings , drawn from the tabulations and summaries named in the Sources — principally Edgar Evans Cayce's Edgar Cayce on Atlantis (1968), Godwin's scholarly summary, and the A.R.E.'s own published research files. None of it is presented as established history, and the verdict of independent evidence is reserved for Sections IX and XIV–XVII, where it belongs. VI. Atlantis as Asserted — Poseidia, the Law of One, and the Sons of Belial Atlantis, in the readings, began — as the composite presents it — as a continent-sized land in the Atlantic, which successive catastrophes broke into islands. The readings name the principal remnants: Poseidia , the northern and last-surviving island, in the region of the Bahamas; Aryan , in the central Atlantic; and Og , in the west. Humanity in Atlantis, in the readings' telling, was immensely old — the story reaches back hundreds of thousands of years — and divided, across all its later history, into two enduring factions whose conflict is the moral engine of the whole narrative. The Children of the Law of One held to a single God, spiritual discipline, and the protection of the vulnerable. The Sons of Belial sought material power and self-gratification, and exploited a class of beings the readings call the "things" — in the composite, hybrid, part-animal creatures kept as labourers and worse, whose treatment is the readings' central Atlantean sin. The debt of this picture to its predecessors should be noted here and developed in Section XIII: staged destructions and a final island called Poseidonis are Theosophical furniture (see Lemuria ), and the single-source civilisation diffusing its gifts worldwide is Donnelly's architecture of 1882 (see Mu and Atlantis Reborn ). What Cayce adds is not the frame but the interior : named regions, a priesthood, a theology of the Law of One, and thousands of individual biographies staged inside the frame, one per client. It is also worth recording what the readings' Atlantis is for , in its own terms. A life reading was a pastoral instrument: the Atlantean past life explained a present aptitude, a present fear, a present relationship, and carried a moral — most often, a warning against repeating, in this life, the misuse of power that had drowned the last one. Atlantis in the readings is less a place than a diagnosis. That does not make it history; but it does explain why, for the people who received these readings, its truth was felt in the present tense. VII. The Firestone — Atlantean Technology as the Readings Describe It The readings describe an Atlantis whose technology, in its high periods, resembled and in places exceeded that of the twentieth century: aircraft and submarines, electrical devices, forms of communication and transport at a distance, and — at the centre of the system — a great crystal the readings call the Tuaoi stone and, in later readings, the firestone . As the composite presents it, the firestone was housed in a special building, gathered and focused the energy of the sun, and supplied power for transport, industry, and healing. Its misuse is woven through the destructions: in Godwin's summary of the readings, the first catastrophe followed the turning of advanced technology to destructive purposes — against the great animals the readings say then overran the earth — and the second was precipitated when the firestone's power was turned too high. By the final period, in the readings' telling, crystal power was being used for coercion, and Poseidia had become, morally, what Plato's Atlantis was in miniature: a rich, armed, corrupted sea power awaiting its day and night of misfortune. The historian's note on this section is short and is the same note sounded in the companion article: none of this technology is Plato's. Plato's Atlantis has canals, triremes, and orichalcum; the crystal power station, the aircraft, and the death-dealing rays enter the tradition with the twentieth century, in a country electrifying itself and learning to fly. That a trance discourse of the 1920s and 1930s should furnish its lost continent with the wonders of its own decade is exactly what the through-line of this hub would predict — each era adds what it wants (see Mu and Atlantis Reborn , §XVI). The readings' defenders reply, fairly, that Cayce disclaimed any reading of the Atlantis literature — his son Hugh Lynn stated that Cayce had not read Plato on Atlantis or the books about it — and that the question of influence is therefore open. It is open as a question about Cayce's reading habits. It is not open as a question about evidence: no artefact, site, or deposit corresponding to the readings' technological Atlantis has ever been identified, anywhere, and the ocean floors where it would have to lie have been mapped and sampled for half a century. VIII. The Three Destructions — The Readings' Chronology The readings do not sink Atlantis once. They break it in three destructions , and the tabulation of those destructions — made by Edgar Evans Cayce from his father's files — is the chronological spine of the whole Cayce Atlantis. In the standard summary, represented here by Godwin's: a first destruction around 50,000 BCE (some tabulations give 50,700 BCE), in which part of the continent went down and the land began its fragmentation; a second destruction around 28,000 BCE , preceded by the emigration of the Law of One's followers to refuges that the readings name across the world — Peru, the Yucatán, the Pyrenees, Egypt, and places in what is now the American West among them; and a final destruction of the last island, Poseidia, which the readings place at the horizon this article will meet repeatedly: Cayce cited 10,014 BCE in one tabulation for the final sinking, the process being complete, in Godwin's summary, by about 9500 BCE . The round figure the tradition carries — c. 10,500 BCE — is the horizon of the final catastrophe and of the Egyptian events of Sections X–XII, and it is the date around which the entire later controversy orbits. First, the readings were given across twenty years, in answer to thousands of different questions, and their internal dates are not perfectly uniform; the tabulations smooth them, and different A.R.E.-derived summaries smooth them slightly differently — which is why this article gives ranges and names its summariser rather than pretending to a precision the corpus does not possess. Second, the resemblance of the final horizon to Plato's chronology — Atlantis sinking some 9,000 years before Solon, which lands in the same millennium — is real, and cuts both ways in the literature: for believers, independent convergence; for sceptics, the clearest fingerprint of the tradition Cayce inherited. The archive records the resemblance. It does not adjudicate it. IX. Bimini — The 1968–69 Expectation and the Stones Themselves Cayce's connection with the Bahamian island of Bimini began in his own lifetime: he travelled there in 1927 in connection with a treasure venture, and readings of that period identified the island, in the composite, as the site of a temple of the Poseidians and as the highest ground of the sunken land still above water. The famous statement came in a reading given on 28 June 1940 (reading 958-3) : that Poseidia would be among the first portions of Atlantis to rise again, and that this was to be expected in 1968 and 1969 . This article's single verified quotation from the readings is that statement, as quoted in Godwin's scholarly summary: Poseidia will be among the first portions of Atlantis to rise again — expect it in '68 and '69 — not so far away! READING 958-3, 28 JUNE 1940 — AS QUOTED IN JOSCELYN GODWIN, ATLANTIS AND THE CYCLES OF TIME On 2 September 1968 — the first of the two named years — divers off Paradise Point, North Bimini, among them J. Manson Valentine of the Miami Museum of Science, found the formation since known as the Bimini Road : a pavement-like alignment of large, flat, roughly rectangular limestone blocks, about 0.8 kilometres long, in some five and a half metres of water, with a hooked turn at its southwestern end. The coincidence of place and year made it the most celebrated underwater site in the Atlantis literature, and the full account — the discovery, the surveys, and the coring — is given in the companion article Mu and Atlantis Reborn (§XI) and is summarised, not repeated, here. The geological assessment, from the detailed examination by Gifford and Ball and the coring work of Eugene Shinn and others, is that the Road is natural beachrock : a limestone of carbonate-cemented shell debris that forms in the intertidal zone, lithifies as a continuous layer, and fractures along straight joints into apparently laid blocks. The decisive observations were that no second course of blocks exists anywhere on the features; that bedrock lies close beneath the whole area; that no tool marks were found; and that cores through adjacent blocks show the rock's internal bedding running continuously from block to block — one layer, broken in place. Radiocarbon results reported from the coring placed the shell material at roughly 3,500 years and its cement at roughly 2,800 years — thousands of years younger than any date proposed for Atlantis. // BIMINI — THE BALANCE SHEET, RESTATED FOR THIS CORPUS // The 1940 statement was real, dated, archived, and fulfilled in its year as a matter of timing : something was found off Bimini in 1968. What was found is, on cores, bedding, and dates, a natural formation. A prophecy can score on its calendar and fail on its geology, and this one did both. For the method of this hub, Bimini is the Cayce corpus in miniature: the documented column is impeccable — the reading exists, its date is 1940, its text says 1968–69 — and the asserted column, tested at last against the physical world, does not hold. X. Egypt as Asserted — The Migration and the Building on the Mounds If Atlantis is the readings' lost world, Egypt is its heir — and the Egypt material is, by the A.R.E.'s own research files, the richest store of prehistory in the whole corpus. The Circulating File Archaeology: Egypt & Gobi , the Foundation's compilation of the Egypt extracts, opens with the observation that of all the prehistoric periods in the readings, Egypt dominates: more than 1,100 people were told, in their life readings, that they had lived there around 10,500 BCE. Assembled, those hundreds of individual statements compose a single narrative, and it is that narrative — the readings' narrative, attributed throughout — that this section and the next two set out. As the readings present it, the story begins with the destructions. As Atlantis broke up, there came — in the paraphrase of reading 5748-6 as quoted in the A.R.E.'s own published research — an egress of peoples from the Atlantean land, who built a city near the edge of the Sahara. Egypt, in the readings, was not empty when they came: the same reading tradition holds that the land had known far older occupation — reading 341-9 is cited in the A.R.E. file for the statement that the country had been submerged for nearly a quarter of a million years since civilisation had last been in that portion of it — and that the newcomers conducted what the readings themselves describe as archaeological research, discovering ancient mounds and building upon them. The monuments, in reading 341-9's account as quoted by the A.R.E., were unearthed and added to from time to time, and many were buried again beneath shifting sands. The picture, in other words, is not of a civilisation founded from nothing in 10,500 BCE, but of one deliberately restored — by immigrants who understood themselves as heirs, excavating and rebuilding on foundations they believed immemorially old. It is a sophisticated piece of world-building, and it is worth noticing how much of the later alternative-Egyptology imagination — the monument repeatedly rebuilt, the knowledge older than the stones that carry it — is already present in it, in readings of the early 1930s. At the centre of the restoration stands one figure, and he is the subject of the next section: the priest under whose direction, the readings say, the works at Giza were planned — and who, the readings say, Edgar Cayce himself had been. XI. Ra-Ta — The Priest the Readings Say Cayce Had Been The Ra-Ta narrative is anchored in Cayce's own file. The 294 series comprises the readings given for Cayce himself, and reading 294-8 , given on 9 February 1924, is his own life reading — the document in which his incarnations, including an Egyptian high priest, were set out. Across the 294 series and the wider Egypt readings, that priest acquired a name, a biography, and a mission: Ra-Ta . As the A.R.E.'s published paraphrase, Egypt 10,500 B.C. , presents the story — paraphrased there from the readings, and paraphrased again here — Ra-Ta was born among the tribe of Zu, in the region of Ararat, a child set apart from his people, who grew into a prophet and priest. Foreseeing catastrophe, he counselled migration: a company, led in the narrative by the king's son Arart with Ra-Ta as its spiritual head, journeyed to Egypt, where Arart became king — succeeded in the readings' genealogy by Araaraart — and Ra-Ta became high priest of a restored civilisation. Under his direction, the readings say, the works at Giza were laid out: reading 294-151 is cited by A.R.E. researchers for the statement that Giza was formed according to a plan Ra-Ta had worked out in the mount, in relation to the positions of the stars and the constellation Libra. The temples of the period — the readings name a Temple of Sacrifice and a Temple Beautiful — served, in the narrative, the healing and purification of the hybrid "things" and the teaching of the Law of One : the one God, the one law, that the Atlantean faithful had carried out of the drowning world. // THE CLAIM, AS THE READINGS LEAVE IT // The readings assert that the Great Pyramid and the Sphinx at Giza were built in the period of Ra-Ta, around 10,500 BCE , under his direction — some eight thousand years before the date Egyptology assigns them. Individual readings fill in the scene: the reading for subject [993], for example, placed that subject's past life in Egypt during the Great Pyramid's construction, with Ra-Ta as priest, at circa 10,500 BCE — and the same file tradition holds that still earlier pyramids preceded Ra-Ta's, built in an Egypt more ancient still. The claim is precise, dated, and attributed. It is also, as Section XVII sets out, contradicted by the whole independent evidentiary record of the Giza plateau. Two scholarly cautions complete the section. The first is about the name: Ra-Ta is not an attested ancient Egyptian person . No inscription, king list, tomb, or text of any period knows a priest of this name directing works at Giza, and the name itself is not formed as Egyptian names of the Old Kingdom are formed. He exists in exactly one corpus — this one. The second caution is about the identification: that Cayce was Ra-Ta is itself a reading-internal claim, developed across the 294 series rather than delivered complete in 294-8, and later A.R.E. literature is frank that the whole Ra-Ta period was understood within the organisation as the pattern and precedent of Cayce's modern work — reading 294-197, quoted in the A.R.E.'s own booklet, states that Cayce's present period of activity is a replica of the Egyptian one. The narrative, in other words, does double duty in the tradition: it is offered as ancient history, and it functions as the founding charter of a twentieth-century organisation. A researcher can honour the second function while withholding assent from the first. That is what this hub does. XII. The Hall of Records — Three Repositories and a Sealed Chamber at Giza Of all the assertions in the corpus, one has driven more expeditions, more television, and more drilling permits than any other: the claim that the records of Atlantis survive, sealed, and can be found. The claim took its canonical form in a concentrated series of readings given from October to December 1933 . As the readings present it, the Atlanteans, foreseeing the end, preserved their records in three repositories : one in the Atlantean land itself, sunk with Poseidia — the Bimini repository of Section IX; one in the Yucatán, overshadowed, in reading 2012-1's paraphrased terms, by a temple there; and one in Egypt — the Hall of Records . Reading 2012-1 (25 September 1939), quoted in the A.R.E.'s published research, names the three together: the one in the sunken Atlantean land, which the reading says will rise and is rising again; the one in Egypt, reached by the place of the records that leads from the Sphinx to the hall of records; and the one in the Yucatán land. Reading 5750-1 adds the tradition's most quoted summary of the doctrine, given by the A.R.E. in paraphrase here: that the three places are one, and that when the time of changes draws near, the three may be opened together — the records are one.
