Nothing in it should be read as a statement that gods, demigods, or spirits of the dead historically ruled Egypt. What it documents is something else, and something genuinely attested: that Egyptian and classical sources claimed they did , in writing, repeatedly, and with numbers attached. The papyri, stone annals, temple inscriptions, and Greek histories discussed below are real objects and real texts. The reigns they assign to divine rulers are their claims, and this article attributes every one of them — "the Canon assigns…", "Manetho's transmitters report…", "the priests told Herodotus…" — rather than narrating them as fact. That distinction is not a dismissal. A civilisation's account of its own beginnings is primary evidence about that civilisation: about how its priests understood kingship, how its temples justified their authority, and how deep its sense of antiquity ran. When a Ramesside scribe, copying a king list on the back of a discarded tax register, chose to begin his list not with a man but with gods, he was making a theological and political statement that his culture took seriously for well over a thousand years. The claim is the data. The contrast is stated plainly where it belongs, in Section XV : the archaeologically attested record for the centuries before Dynasty 1 shows the gradual development of the Naqada culture in Upper Egypt and the farming communities of the Delta — chiefdoms, expanding trade, early writing, and eventual political unification around 3100 BCE. It shows no divine reigns, no millennia-long kings, and no break in continuity that would require them. The full attested account is given in the Egyptology division at Predynastic Egypt and the Egyptian Timeline . Both records are presented here fairly, and neither is mocked: the tradition is honoured as tradition, and the evidence is honoured as evidence. // HOW TO READ THE NUMBERS // Every large year-total in this article is a number a source gives, not a number this archive endorses. Where transmitters disagree — and they disagree constantly — the disagreement is shown, because the disagreement is itself part of the evidence for how these texts were copied, epitomised, and argued over in antiquity. A note on quotations. Following the archive's standard, a passage appears in quotation marks only where it has been verified in a named published translation actually consulted for this article — principally W. G. Waddell's Loeb edition of Manetho, G. C. Macaulay's translation of Herodotus, and C. H. Oldfather's Loeb translation of Diodorus Siculus. Everything else that renders an ancient author's wording is paraphrase, and is framed as such. II. The Shape of the Claim Across otherwise very different sources, the Egyptian account of the time before the human kings has a remarkably stable architecture. Kingship begins with the gods themselves, ruling in succession. It passes next to beings who stand between gods and men — demigods, heroes, and the transfigured dead, the akhu . Only then does it reach mortal kings, and the first of them, in the Egyptian tradition as the Greeks received it, is Menes — the king the Egyptian lists place at the head of Dynasty 1. 1 — THE GODS Named deities rule in sequence: in the Greek renderings, Hephaestus (Ptah), Helios (Ra), Sôsis (Shu), Cronos (Geb), Osiris, Typhon (Seth), and Horus, son of Osiris and Isis. Their reigns are measured in thousands of years. 2 — THE INTERMEDIARIES Demigods, heroes, and "Spirits of the Dead" — Manetho's Greek for categories the Turin Canon expresses in Egyptian as the akhu and the Shemsu-Hor, the Followers of Horus — hold kingship for further thousands of years. 3 — THE MORTAL KINGS Menes opens the human dynasties. From him, Manetho's system counts thirty dynasties of mortal kings down to the Persian period — the framework Egyptology still uses, in corrected form, today. Two features of this architecture deserve emphasis before any single source is examined. First, it is a succession , not a separate mythology bolted onto history: the same list, the same format, and often the same column of writing runs unbroken from Ra to a reigning pharaoh. Second, the boundary the sources draw is not between "myth" and "history" in the modern sense. The Turin Canon gives reign lengths in years, months, and days for human kings and applies the same list-form to the gods before them. The modern distinction between the two parts of the list is ours, imposed on a document that does not make it — which is precisely why the document is so instructive about Egyptian self-understanding. The sections that follow take the witnesses one at a time, in roughly the order of their own antiquity as objects: a Ramesside papyrus, an Old Kingdom stone annal, Ptolemaic temple theology, a Ptolemaic history surviving in late-antique Christian chronography, and two Greek visitors who reported what Egyptian priests told them. III. The Turin Royal Canon — The Papyrus Itself The single most important Egyptian witness is the papyrus now in the Museo Egizio in Turin, conventionally called the Turin Royal Canon or Turin King List. It is a hieratic papyrus, written on the back — the verso — of a discarded administrative document, a tax register of the reign of Ramesses II (1279–1213 BCE). The list itself is generally assigned to that reign or shortly after it; its compiler was therefore writing in the 19th Dynasty, some eighteen centuries after the unification he records at the head of his human dynasties. The papyrus reached Turin through the collection of Bernardino Drovetti, the Italian diplomat and collector, who acquired it at Thebes in 1822. It did not survive the journey well. A roll that appears to have been substantially intact when found arrived in fragments, and the history of the Canon ever since has been a history of reconstruction: Jean-François Champollion recognised its importance during his Turin work in the 1820s; Gustav Seyffarth attempted an early arrangement; Giulio Farina, director of the Turin museum, published a major restoration in 1938; and Alan H. Gardiner published the edition that remains the standard point of reference, The Royal Canon of Turin (Oxford: Griffith Institute, 1959), proposing a new placement of many fragments. Further fragments recovered from the museum's stores in 2009 prompted renewed study, and Kim Ryholt's work on the Canon — beginning with his 1997 study of the Second Intermediate Period and continuing in his 2004 reassessment of the King List — has revised the placement and reading of a number of passages. The papyrus today consists of some 160 fragments; both its beginning and its end are lost, so the list has neither its original introduction nor its conclusion. Why Egyptologists Trust the Human Half For the human dynasties, the Canon is the backbone of Egyptian chronology before Ramesses II, and it earns that status. Unlike the temple-wall king lists at Abydos or Saqqara — carved, ceremonial, and selective — the Canon includes ephemeral rulers, rulers of small territories, and even the Hyksos kings of the 15th Dynasty, whom the monumental lists omit and whom the Canon marks as foreigners. It gives reign lengths, in places to the month and day. Its groupings of kings correspond approximately, though not exactly, to the dynasties of Manetho. In short, for kings who can be checked against other evidence, the Canon behaves like a serious administrative-historical compilation, copied — somewhat carelessly, Gardiner noted — from an older and more detailed original. That seriousness is exactly what makes its opening columns so striking. The same document, in the same hand and format, does not begin with Menes. It begins with gods. // THE STATE OF THE TEXT // The divine section of the Canon is among its most damaged. Names are lost, numerals are partly restored, and the arrangement of the opening fragments has been disputed from Seyffarth to Ryholt. Every specific figure given in the next two sections should be read with that condition attached: these are the readings of damaged fragments as reconstructed by Gardiner and later scholars, not a clean inscription that can simply be transcribed. IV. Inside the Canon — Gods, Akhu, and the Followers of Horus As reconstructed, the Canon's opening columns list a succession of gods as kings of Egypt. The names that survive or can be restored with reasonable confidence belong to the familiar Heliopolitan sequence: Ptah stands at or near the head in some restorations; Ra is securely read; and Shu, Geb, Osiris, Seth, and Horus follow in the order Egyptian theology itself prescribes — the generations of the Ennead descending from the creator to Horus, the god whose earthly embodiment every living pharaoh claimed to be. Individual reign figures attached to the gods in the fragments run to hundreds of years; the reign of Horus, for example, is read as 300 years in the early publications of the fragments. Beyond Horus, a small number of further divine names survive, among them Thoth and Maat, before the text passes to its next category of ruler. That next category is the one that has attracted the most attention outside Egyptology, and it deserves to be described in the Canon's own terms. The papyrus speaks of the akhu — the transfigured, effective spirits of the dead, a central and entirely mainstream category of Egyptian religion, not an exotic import — and of the Shemsu-Hor , the "Followers of Horus" ( šmsw-Ḥr ). The Followers of Horus are not an invention of the Canon: they appear across Egyptian religious literature as the semi-divine entourage and predecessors associated with Horus, and in later periods the phrase could be used of the semi-legendary predynastic rulers of Egypt as a class. In the Canon they occupy the structural position Manetho's Greek would later render as demigods and Spirits of the Dead: after the gods, before the men. Then, at the head of the next section, comes Menes — in Egyptian, Meni — and with him the dynasties of human kings, reign by reign, down through the centuries toward the compiler's own time. The Canon does not mark the transition with any change of format or apology. Gods, akhu , Followers of Horus, Menes, and the kings of Dynasties 1 through 19 stand in one continuous register of rulers of Egypt. The Canon does not distinguish, in form, between the reign of a god and the reign of a man. The list is one list. The distinction between its theological prologue and its historical body is a modern reading of an ancient document that presents both in the same hand, the same format, and the same columns. What the Canon does not contain should be stated as clearly as what it does. It contains no narrative — no flood, no catastrophe, no description of the divine age, no account of what the gods or the Followers of Horus did. It is a list: names and numbers. Every story later attached to those names and numbers comes from somewhere else. V. The Canon's Sums — 13,420, 23,200, and the 36,620 That Is Not Written There Near the end of its second column, as Gardiner's reconstruction reads it, the Canon gives summation lines for the pre-Menite rulers. Two figures are read there. One line assigns to the akhu , the Followers of Horus, a total of 13,420 years — with a damaged remainder, conventionally written "13,420 + x," since the papyrus is broken where smaller units may have followed. A second line gives a cumulative total "up to the Followers of Horus" of 23,200 + x years . Menes follows immediately after. These are the Canon's own sums as modern editions read the fragments, and they are the figures any honest account of the document must start from: damaged, partly restored, but genuinely there in substance — the papyrus really does sum the reigns before Menes in tens of thousands of years. A third figure circulates far more widely than either, and it requires a correction. Popular literature on the Canon very often quotes a grand total of 36,620 years for the divine and semi-divine reigns. That number is not a total written on the papyrus. It is an addition — 13,420 + 23,200 — performed by the twentieth-century esoteric writer R. A. Schwaller de Lubicz in Sacred Science , on the assumption that the two summation lines are separate blocks to be added together. If the second line is instead what it appears to be — a cumulative total that already includes the first — then adding them double counts. Egyptological editions do not print 36,620 as the Canon's total, and this article follows them: the figure belongs to the modern reception of the Canon, not to the Canon. It is recorded here because a reader searching the subject will meet it immediately, and deserves to know where it comes from. Figure What It Is Status 13,420 + x years Summation for the akhu , Followers of Horus, in the Canon's second column Read on the papyrus as reconstructed by Gardiner; end of the numeral damaged 23,200 + x years Cumulative summation "up to the Followers of Horus," immediately before Menes Read on the papyrus as reconstructed; partly restored 36,620 years The sum of the two figures above Not written on the papyrus; Schwaller de Lubicz's addition, widely repeated in popular works Even taken at their most conservative reading, the Canon's sums make the document's own position unmistakable: its compiler, or the older original he copied, placed more than twenty thousand years of rule before the first human king. That is the claim. It is a claim made by a text written around 1250 BCE about a period its author placed before 3100 BCE — a gap of nearly two millennia across which the Canon offers no sources, no narrative, and no means of checking. Egyptology reads the pre-Menite columns as the theological frame of the list, the point at which the document passes from the order of creation into the order of recorded kingship — not as chronology. Section XV sets out the record against which that reading rests. VI. Manetho and the Aegyptiaca — A History That Survives Only in Fragments The second great witness is a book that no longer exists. Manetho , an Egyptian priest from Sebennytos in the Delta, writing in Greek under Ptolemy II Philadelphus in the third century BCE, composed the Aegyptiaca — a history of Egypt in three books, drawn, as he presented it, from Egyptian temple records. Its organisation of the human kings into thirty dynasties remains the skeleton of Egyptian chronology today. But the Aegyptiaca did not begin with the dynasties. Like the Turin Canon before it, it began with the gods. No copy of Manetho's work survives. What we have are fragments — quotations, epitomes, and king lists — preserved by later writers, each with his own agenda: the Jewish historian Josephus in the first century CE; the Christian chronographers Julius Africanus (early third century CE) and Eusebius of Caesarea (early fourth century CE), whose Chronica survives in part through an Armenian translation and through the excerpts of the Byzantine monk George Syncellus (around 800 CE); and a scattering of later sources including the Excerpta Latina Barbari and John Malalas. The standard modern edition is W. G. Waddell's Loeb Classical Library volume, Manetho (1940), which prints the fragments with English translation and is the edition consulted for this article. This transmission history matters for every number that follows. Africanus and Eusebius do not agree with each other — on reign lengths, on totals, sometimes on names — and Syncellus, who preserves both, preserves them partly in order to argue with them. The Christian chronographers who kept Manetho alive were trying to fit Egyptian antiquity inside a biblical timescale running from Adam through the Flood, and they said so openly. Their favourite tool, visible throughout the fragments, was reinterpretation: the Egyptians' immense "years," they argued, must really have been months, or seasons. A reader of the divine dynasties is therefore always reading at least three layers at once — an Egyptian priestly tradition, a Ptolemaic priest's Greek history of it, and late-antique Christian attempts to tame its chronology. The layers are distinguished below wherever the fragments allow it. VII. Manetho, Fragment 1 — The Eusebian Reckoning Waddell's Fragment 1, taken from the Armenian version of Eusebius's Chronica , is the fullest surviving statement of Manetho's divine dynasties, and it is worth following in its own sequence. In paraphrase of Waddell's translation: the history's three books treat the gods, the demigods, the Spirits of the Dead, and the mortal kings down to Darius. The first ruler in Egypt is Hephaestus — the Greek name under which Manetho presents Ptah — renowned as the discoverer of fire. His son Helios, the Sun (Ra), follows; then Sôsis (Shu); then Cronos (Geb), Osiris, Typhon (Seth), brother of Osiris, and lastly Horus, son of Osiris and Isis. From these first rulers, the fragment says, kingship passed in unbroken succession down to a figure named Bydis (or Bites) across 13,900 years . The fragment then gives the succeeding blocks, and these figures are the ones for which Manetho's divine dynasties are usually cited: Block (Fr. 1, via Eusebius) Duration Assigned The Gods, down to Bydis 13,900 "years" Demigods 1,255 years Another line of kings 1,817 years Thirty kings of Memphis 1,790 years Ten kings of This 350 years Spirits of the Dead and Demigods 5,813 years Subtotal of the five blocks after the Gods 11,000 years Whole rule of Gods, Demigods, and Spirits of the Dead 24,900 "lunar years" The quotation marks around "years" are the fragment's own doing. Already in this Eusebian version, the transmitter insists that the years of the gods are lunar years of thirty days — what we call a month, the Egyptians of that age supposedly called a year — so that the whole 24,900 lunar years are converted to 2,206 solar years . Whether that conversion stood in Manetho or was supplied by his Christian transmitters to shrink Egyptian antiquity toward the biblical frame cannot now be recovered; Waddell prints it as part of the fragment, and this article reports it as the fragment's claim, in the fragment's own layered voice. What is not in doubt is the structure, which matches the Turin Canon's exactly: gods, then intermediary beings, then — through the kings of Memphis and This, cities of the earliest dynasties — the mortal line. "These deal with the Gods, the Demigods, the Spirits of the Dead, and the mortal kings who ruled Egypt down to Darius, king of the Persians." — Manetho, Fr. 1, on the contents of the Aegyptiaca; Waddell, Loeb edition One further detail of Fragment 1 deserves notice, because it shows an ancient transmitter already reasoning like a modern sceptic. Faced with the excess of years, the fragment suggests that perhaps several Egyptian kings ruled at the same time in different regions — This, Memphis, Saïs, Ethiopia — so that the dynasties were parallel rather than successive, and the total is an artefact of adding them in series. The harmonising instinct, in other words, is not a modern invention imposed on innocent texts. It begins inside the transmission itself. VIII. Manetho Through Syncellus, Africanus, and the Old Chronicle The version of Manetho preserved by Syncellus (Waddell's Fragments 2 and 3) gives the divine dynasties a different total, and the difference is instructive. Here the six dynasties of gods are said to have reigned for 11,985 years — again immediately glossed as lunar years, which the Alexandrian chronographer Panodorus, quoted by Syncellus, converted to 969 solar years. The individual divine reigns in this version, once reduced by the same lunar reckoning, shrink to human scale in Syncellus's list: Hephaestus, whose unreduced reign is given as 9,000 years, becomes 727¾ years; Helios 80⅙; Agathodaemon 56½; Cronos 40½; Osiris and Isis 35; Typhon 29 — followed by nine demigods, Horus among them at 25 years, whose 858 seasonal "years" Panodorus reduced to 214½. Syncellus himself reports all of this with open contempt for the Egyptian material, calling the gods in question gods "who never existed." The hostility of the transmitter is part of the record, and a reason the fragments must be read as an argument in progress, not a neutral copy. Africanus, Eusebius, and the Threshold of Dynasty 1 For the mortal dynasties, Waddell prints Africanus and Eusebius side by side, and both mark the same threshold in the same words, in paraphrase: in succession to the Spirits of the Dead and the Demigods , the First Dynasty consists of eight kings, the first of whom is Menes of This. Africanus gives Menes 62 years and a memorable end — carried off by a hippopotamus — and a dynasty total of 253 years; Eusebius gives Menes 60 years and the same hippopotamus. The agreement on the threshold is the point: in every surviving recension, the divine and semi-divine rulers are not an appendix to Manetho's history but its opening books, and Menes succeeds them directly. For Dynasty 1, both lists reach us as Syncellus quotes them. Writing his Ekloge Chronographias around 800 CE, the Byzantine monk set the Africanus and Eusebius epitomes in parallel columns precisely so they could be compared; Eusebius also survives through Jerome's Latin version and an Armenian translation, but it is Syncellus's side-by-side setting that preserves the two recensions together. Africanus, about a century earlier, is generally treated as the fuller witness, yet neither man copied Manetho himself: each worked from the lost Epitome, in a version already differing from the other's. The divergence is sharpest in the first four reigns — Athothis at 57 years in Africanus against 27 in Eusebius, Ouenephes at 23 against 42 — while the last four reigns agree exactly (20, 26, 18, 26) and only their names vary slightly. Even the totals fail their own arithmetic: Africanus's reigns add to 263, not his stated 253; Eusebius's to 258, not his stated 252; and the Armenian Eusebius cuts Menes himself to 30 years. Modern editors do not repair this: Waddell prints both recensions with their stated totals intact, and Verbrugghe and Wickersham, in the second full English translation of the fragments, follow the same parallel presentation — keeping the discrepancy as evidence that each epitome was corrupted at different points, not harmonising it away. The Old Chronicle and the Sothic Total Syncellus also preserves a document he calls the Old Chronicle , an Egyptian king list in thirty dynasties whose total span he gives as 36,525 years . The number gives itself away: 36,525 is exactly 25 × 1,461, and 1,461 years is the length of the Sothic cycle — the period after which the Egyptian civil calendar and the heliacal rising of Sirius realign. A total built as a whole number of Sothic cycles is schematic arithmetic, not accumulated record: whoever framed it was constructing a theologically satisfying span, in which the gods (in the Old Chronicle's version, Helios alone is assigned 30,000 years, and Cronos with the other twelve gods 3,984, before eight demigods reign 217 years) fill out a number chosen in advance. Ancient chronography of this kind is best read the way its own construction invites: as sacred mathematics about the past, not as a measurement of it. THE TRANSMITTERS DISAGREE Gods' reigns: 13,900 years (Eusebian Fr. 1, before lunar conversion) against 11,985 (Syncellus's Manetho). A third fragment, the Excerpta Latina Barbari (Fr. 4 in Waddell), totals the gods at just 1,550 years and the Spirits of the Dead at 2,100. No two surviving recensions give the same divine chronology. WHAT SURVIVES THE DISAGREEMENT Every recension agrees on the order — gods, demigods, spirits of the dead, then Menes — and on the premise that the pre-human span was vastly longer than the human one. The tradition is unanimous about the shape and divided about the numbers, which is the signature of a theological schema transmitted for centuries, not of a record copied from registers. IX. The Palermo Stone — Crowned Kings Before Dynasty 1, Without the Gods The oldest witness in this article is also the most restrained, and the contrast is valuable. The Palermo Stone is the largest surviving fragment of a black basalt stele known as the Royal Annals of the Old Kingdom, carved probably in the Fifth Dynasty (c. 2500 BCE) and now in the archaeological museum at Palermo, with six smaller fragments of the same monument held in Cairo and London. The Annals recorded, year by year, the notable events of each king's reign — Nile flood heights, festivals, statue-making, expeditions — from Dynasty 1 into the Fifth Dynasty. They are, for the dynasties they cover, among the most sober historical documents to survive from ancient Egypt. Above the first register of dynastic annals, the Palermo fragment carries a preliminary row: a series of compartments, each containing the name of a king shown wearing the Red Crown of Lower Egypt. These are presented as kings of the north who reigned before the First Dynasty. The names that can be read — readings vary slightly between editions — include Seka, Khayu, Tiu, Thesh (Tjesh), Neheb, Wazner (Wadj-adj), and Mekh, with further names lost or illegible at the broken edge. Companion fragments and reconstructions suggest the complete row, and a corresponding row for the south, once held many more. Three things distinguish the Palermo evidence from everything else in this article. First, its pre-dynastic rulers are not gods, demigods, or spirits: they are kings, wearing a specific, historically real crown, in the same graphic format as the dynastic kings below them. Second, the stone assigns them no reign lengths at all — no years, no totals, no thousands. Third, the document is an attested archaeological object of the Old Kingdom itself: whatever one makes of its predynastic row, the row proves that by around 2500 BCE the Egyptian state itself officially remembered named kings before Dynasty 1. Some of the names may preserve genuine memory of late predynastic Delta rulers — the Delta's own archaeological record is badly eroded and waterlogged, and its chiefdoms are far less visible than those of the south — but none of the Palermo names has been confirmed by an independent contemporary inscription, and the stone gives no chronology by which they could be placed. The honest summary is that the Palermo Stone attests an official tradition of pre-dynastic kingship, human in form and unquantified in time: the modest end of the spectrum of claims this article surveys. X. Zep Tepi — The First Time Behind the king lists stands a concept that gives them their meaning: sp tpy , conventionally vocalised Zep Tepi , "the First Occasion" or "the First Time." In Egyptian theology, the First Time is the moment of creation itself — when the primeval mound rose from Nun, the inert waters of chaos; when light first appeared; when the gods established the order of the world, maat , in its perfect and undamaged form. Everything that happens afterward happens in derivative time. The First Time is not merely earlier than history; it is the template history is supposed to reproduce. This is why the concept saturates Egyptian religious practice rather than sitting in a mythological appendix. A temple was not simply built; it was founded on the primeval mound, re-enacting the First Time in its own ground plan. A coronation did not merely install a king; it renewed the accession of Horus at the beginning. Ritual, in the analysis of scholars such as Ragnhild Bjerre Finnestad ( Image of the World and Symbol of the Creator , 1985) and Paul John Frandsen's work on kingship, works precisely by collapsing the distance between the present act and the First Occasion: the first act and its ritual repetition are held as one sacred time. Kingship in the divine dynasties is therefore not, in Egyptian terms, a claim about the remote past alone. It is the standing charter of the present king, whose reign is legitimate because it continues, unbroken, a succession that began when the gods ruled in person. Read in this light, the Turin Canon's structure explains itself. A list that began with Menes would have been, theologically, a list that began in the middle. The gods and Followers of Horus stand at its head because Egyptian kingship was understood to be the institution the gods founded at the First Time and handed down — through the demigods and the transfigured dead — to the mortal line. The immense reigns are the numerical expression of that priority: the founding age is not a little older than the present, it is older by orders of magnitude, as befits the age when the world itself was made. // A MODERN MISREADING TO AVOID // In some modern popular literature, "Zep Tepi" is treated as the name of a datable historical era — a lost golden age located at a specific year. In the Egyptian sources it is nothing of the kind: it is a theological category, the First Occasion, standing outside ordinary chronology and renewed by ritual. The sources give it no date, because in their framework it is the thing dates are measured from. The concept is attested across the whole span of Egyptian religious literature, from the earliest temple texts to the great Ptolemaic inscriptions — which brings the argument to the temple where the First Time receives its fullest surviving exposition. XI. Edfu and the Book of the Temple — A Temple That Claims an Ancient Book The Temple of Horus at Edfu, built under the Ptolemies between 237 and 57 BCE, is the best-preserved temple in Egypt, and its walls carry the most extensive surviving exposition of the First Time: the so-called Building Texts or Edfu cosmogony. In the reading established by E. A. E. Reymond — first in her 1962 study "The Primeval Djeba" in the Journal of Egyptian Archaeology and then in her The Mythical Origin of the Egyptian Temple (1969) — these inscriptions describe the creation of the first sacred place: a primeval island or mound emerging from the waters, a falcon god alighting upon a reed perch, and a company of creator powers, the Shebtiu , who establish and secure the first temple precinct. The Edfu texts present the temple on its site as the direct successor and re-foundation of that first precinct: the ground the Ptolemaic priests served was, in their account, ground first consecrated at the beginning of the world. The texts make a further claim, and it is the claim that matters for this article's theme. The Edfu inscriptions, like temple foundation texts elsewhere in Ptolemaic Egypt, present their specifications as derived from an ancient book — a written archetype handed down from the time of the gods, in the wider tradition Egyptologists discuss under the name of the Book of the Temple : the notion that the plan, proportions, and ritual geography of a true temple were not invented by its builders but copied from a primordial written source, in some versions said to have descended from heaven in the age of the gods' own rule. Reymond argued that the Edfu cosmogony preserves genuinely old material — she traced its likely origin to a predynastic or early dynastic theological tradition, probably Memphite or Heliopolitan in background. Later scholarship, including Finnestad's study of the temple as an image of the created world and the ongoing Edfu Project editions under Dieter Kurth, reads the texts primarily as Ptolemaic temple theology: a sophisticated late composition in archaic dress, whose primeval island is the standard Egyptian image of the mound rising from Nun, not the memory of a specific place or event. Both readings agree on the fact that carries the weight here: the priests of Edfu, in the last centuries BCE, inscribed on their temple the claim that its order derived, through an ancient book, from the First Time and the company of divine founders. That claim — attested in stone, in a temple anyone may still walk through — is Tier B evidence of the purest kind: not evidence that the events occurred, but first-class evidence of what the temple's own custodians taught about their origins, at the very end of the three thousand years of tradition this article surveys. Popular retellings that add a sunken overseas homeland, refugee sages carrying advanced technology, or a date for the First Time go beyond anything Reymond read in the texts and beyond anything the inscriptions say; those additions belong to Tier C, and are treated in this hub's companion articles, not here. XII. Herodotus at Thebes and Memphis — 341 Generations and 345 Statues The Greek historian Herodotus, travelling in Egypt in the fifth century BCE, gives the earliest surviving outsider's report of the Egyptian priests' own chronology — and it is subtler than the king lists, because the priests he questioned drew a line the lists do not. In Book II of the Histories (2.142), in G. C. Macaulay's translation — the translation consulted for this article — Herodotus reports that the priests reckoned 341 generations from Egypt's first king down to the priest of Hephaestus (Ptah) who was reigning last in their sequence, with the same number of kings and of chief priests. His arithmetic follows theirs: three generations to a century, so 300 generations make 10,000 years and the remaining 41 make 1,340 — a total of 11,340 years . And across that whole span, the priests insisted, no god had appeared in human form: not in those years, not before them, and not after. What the Sea Holds — An Assessment Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on published geological, archaeological, and genetic evidence — sea-level curves built from dated corals, landscapes mapped from seismic data, artefacts with recorded findspots, and sites excavated by divers. Where scholars disagree, as they do sharply over the Storegga tsunami's human toll and more quietly over the flooding of the Bering Strait, the disagreement is reported with its positions attributed. Nothing here depends on legend, and nothing is borrowed from the hub's other tiers. One plain statement belongs at the front, because this article is the attested counterpart of a famous fantasy. Where popular writing reaches for Atlantis — a rich civilisation swallowed in a day, as this hub's Tier C treatment of Mu and Atlantis Reborn documents in detail — the geological record offers something both less theatrical and far larger: whole inhabited landscapes, the size of countries and small continents, drowned not in a day but across some twelve thousand years, as the melting of the last ice sheets raised the world's oceans by about 120 metres. There were no cities on those plains and no kings to lose. There were hunting camps and fishing villages, river valleys and grazing herds, and — in Beringia — arguably a homeland in which a people's distinctive ancestry was formed. The loss was not of a civilisation. It was of most of the stage on which the late Palaeolithic and Mesolithic world had lived. That loss is this article's real subject, and it is methodological before it is romantic. Human beings of the last glacial period were, like human beings now, disproportionately coastal and riverine: the richest hunting, fowling, fishing, and gathering grounds lay exactly where the rising sea struck first and deepest. The archaeological record on dry land is therefore not a fair sample of the human past. It is the upland residue of a mostly lowland world — a survival bias built into every map, every distribution plot, and every claim of "earliest" or "first" in this hub's Tier A timeline. Three drowned landscapes carry the argument. Doggerland , the Mesolithic plain beneath the North Sea, is the best mapped. Sundaland , the drowned half of Southeast Asia, is the largest. Beringia , the plain between Siberia and Alaska, is the most consequential, because a continent's peopling was staged there. Each is treated in turn; the working methods that recover them, and the famous claims that fail the same tests, close the article. I. The Low Ground Went First — The Scale of the Loss Begin with the arithmetic of exposure. At the Last Glacial Maximum, roughly 26,000 to 19,000 years ago, so much of the world's water stood on land as ice — in the Laurentide sheet over North America, the Fennoscandian sheet over northern Europe, and their fellows — that global sea level lay about 120 metres below its present stand (published estimates cluster between about 120 and 130 metres). Every continental shelf on Earth stood dry. The exposed land was not marginal fringe. For Europe alone, the SPLASHCOS synthesis (Bailey et al. 2020) puts the additional land at lowest sea level at about 2.5 million square kilometres — some 40 per cent added to the continent's present area — much of it, in the editors' assessment, well-watered and well-stocked lowland, often more attractive to hunter-gatherers than the colder, higher hinterland behind it. Comparable shelves ring every inhabited continent: the Sunda Shelf in Southeast Asia, the Sahul Shelf between Australia and New Guinea, the Bering and Chukchi shelves, the broad plains off eastern North and South America, the floor of the Persian Gulf. // THE LOWSTAND // c. 120 m below present Global sea level at the Last Glacial Maximum, on the coral and isotope records summarised in §II — the shelves of the world stood dry. // THE RISE // c. 19,000 – 6,000 BP Deglacial sea-level rise, uneven and punctuated by meltwater pulses, returning the ocean to near its modern level by the mid-Holocene. // EUROPE'S SHARE // c. 2.5 million km² Additional European land exposed at lowest sea level — about 40% of the present continent (Bailey et al. 2020). // THE SURVIVING RECORD // c. 2,600–3,000 find spots Recorded underwater find spots around Europe's coasts, from isolated artefacts to in-situ settlements (SPLASHCOS). Now run the water forward. Between about 19,000 and 6,000 years ago the ice sheets wasted and the sea took the shelves back, strip by strip, generation by generation. What drowned was not a random cross-section of the inhabited world. It was, systematically, its lowest and richest fraction : the coastal plains where marine and terrestrial foods meet, the lower river valleys, the estuaries and lagoons, the lakeshores of basins like the southern North Sea's. The record that survives on dry land is correspondingly skewed toward the places people used least — uplands, cave country, the interiors — and toward the periods after the flooding stopped. Archaeologists have a name for the resulting distortion in other contexts, and it applies here with unusual force: this is survival bias , and it is not a footnote to the deep past. It is a property of the evidence itself. Three consequences follow, and they structure everything below. First, absence is cheap : a missing site, a missing migration route, a missing millennium on the shelf is what the flooding predicts, and it cannot be argued from as though the shelf had been searched and found empty — for most of human prehistory it has barely been searched at all. Second, coastal routes are under-evidenced by design : any dispersal that hugged the shore — into Sahul, around Southeast Asia, down the Pacific coast of the Americas — will have left its earliest stations under tens of metres of water, which is one reason this hub's treatments of Sahul and of the peopling of the Americas lean so heavily on genetics and on the few surviving inland witnesses. Third, the bias is corrigible, slowly : the shelf is not destroyed, only submerged, and §XIII describes the young discipline — seismic mapping, targeted coring, diver excavation — that is learning to read it. The drowned landscapes are an archive, not a void. But they are an archive most of which remains unopened, and honesty about that proportion is the price of admission to everything this article claims. // WHY THESE THREE // Doggerland, Sundaland, and Beringia are not the only drowned landscapes — the Persian Gulf oasis, the Sahul Shelf, and the plains off the Americas matter too, and the Gulf and Sahul are treated where this hub treats their regions. These three are chosen because each is documented by a different strength of evidence: Doggerland by direct mapping, Sundaland by bathymetry and genetics, Beringia by genetics and palaeoecology against a near-total absence of sites — the full spectrum of how a drowned world can be known. A final preliminary, about words. None of the three names is ancient. Doggerland was coined in 1998 (§III). Beringia was coined in 1937 (§XI). Sundaland is a biogeographer's term for the shelf region, extended by geologists to its drowned Pleistocene extent. The peoples who lived on these plains left no names for them that we can recover. The modern names are tools, not traditions, and this article uses them as such — a small, exact instance of the hub's standing rule that the record, the tradition, and the telling be kept apart. II. The Curve — About 120 Metres of Water The sea-level curve is the single most load-bearing document in this article, and it deserves to be introduced as evidence rather than scenery. It is built principally from two archives. The first is coral : reef corals live within a narrow depth band below the surface, so a fossil reef terrace is a fossil sea level, and uranium-thorium dating of drilled coral cores — from Barbados in the Caribbean and from Tahiti in the Pacific, far from the former ice sheets — converts terraces into a dated curve. Richard Fairbanks's Barbados record (1989) first resolved the deglacial rise into its steps; the Tahiti cores of IODP Expedition 310, published by Deschamps and colleagues in Nature (2012), tightened the fastest step of all. The second archive is the oxygen-isotope record of deep-sea sediment cores, which tracks the total volume of ice on land and so corroborates the coral curve's broad shape. Where the two agree — and on the headline figure they do — the result is as robust as anything in Quaternary science: from the glacial lowstand, the ocean rose by roughly 120 metres to reach approximately its present level in the mid-Holocene. The rise was not smooth, and its unevenness is the human story. Long stretches of comparatively gradual rise — on the order of a metre a century, fast enough for a community to watch its fishing grounds migrate within a lifetime — were interrupted by meltwater pulses , episodes of ice-sheet collapse in which the sea rose by metres within a few centuries. Two pulses dominate the literature, and they recur throughout this article. Meltwater Pulse 1A — c. 14,600 BP The best-documented pulse began, on the Tahiti evidence, after 14,650 BP and ended before 14,310 BP — a window of at most about 340 years, coincident with the abrupt Bølling warming that ended the last glacial cold. Deschamps and colleagues constrain its amplitude at Tahiti to between 12 and 22 metres, with a most probable value of 14 to 18 metres : a rate of eustatic rise exceeding 40 millimetres a year, sustained for centuries. On a low-gradient shelf — and the Sunda and North Sea shelves are among the lowest-gradient coasts on Earth — a vertical rise of that speed translates into a shoreline retreating by kilometres within a human lifetime, river mouths drowning in place, and low islands planed away between one generation's memory and the next. Meltwater Pulse 1A is the event that did much of the work of drowning Sundaland (§VIII) and that cut deep into every shelf on Earth simultaneously. Its sources remain debated — the Tahiti team demonstrated a significant Southern Hemisphere (Antarctic) contribution against an older assumption of an almost wholly northern source — but its timing and scale are no longer seriously in question. Meltwater Pulse 1B — c. 11,500–11,000 BP, and a Standing Disagreement The second pulse is the curve's honest uncertainty, and this article reports it as one. Fairbanks's Barbados record showed a second rapid jump, of up to roughly 28 metres, in the centuries after the Younger Dryas cold interval, about 11,500–11,000 BP; he named it Meltwater Pulse 1B. Later records — including the Tahiti sequence — have not reproduced a jump of that size, and subsequent studies suggest the true figure may have been much smaller, or that the Barbados step partly reflects local effects. The pulse's existence in some form is supported by independent evidence at one critical locality: the flooding of the Bering Strait (§XII), where a well-dated core records the Pacific breaking through at about 11,000 BP in a shift its authors associate with Meltwater Pulse 1B. The balanced statement is this: a rapid phase of rise in the centuries around 11,500–11,000 BP is widely accepted; its global amplitude is disputed, with published estimates running from a few metres to Fairbanks's original figure; and any argument that needs the large number should be read as resting on the Barbados record specifically. Readers will meet this pattern again — a solid event, a contested magnitude — at the Storegga tsunami, and the hub's treatment is the same in both places. Two refinements complete the picture. The first is the difference between eustatic and relative sea level. The coral curve describes the ocean's global volume; what any given coast experienced also depended on the land's own motion — crust still rebounding upward where ice had pressed it down (as in Scotland and Scandinavia), or subsiding under the water load and the collapsing forebulge beyond the ice margin (as in the southern North Sea, which has been sinking gently throughout the Holocene). Doggerland therefore drowned faster than the global curve alone predicts, and parts of Scotland rose even as the sea did — which is why tsunami deposits of the same age sit at different heights on different coasts (§VI). The second refinement is the tail of the curve: after about 6,000 BP the rise slowed to a creep, and coastlines approached their modern positions. Every landscape treated below was gone, in its inhabited form, before that quietus — drowned not by the sea of the farming age but by the last convulsions of the ice age itself. Doggerland — A Country, Not a Bridge The southern North Sea is shallow — mostly less than 50 metres deep — and at the glacial lowstand it was not sea at all. From the east coast of Britain across to the present Netherlands, Germany, and Denmark stretched a continuous land: low hills, broad river valleys, marshes, lakes, and, as the climate warmed, spreading woodland. The great rivers of two modern countries ran together across it. The Thames, the Rhine, the Meuse, and the Scheldt were tributaries of one system that flowed south-west down the dry bed of the English Channel to an Atlantic shoreline far west of the present Strait of Dover. Britain was not an island but a peninsula of Europe — its north-western highlands the upland margin of a plain whose centre now lies under tens of metres of grey water and shipping lanes. The land had no agreed name until 1998 , when the archaeologist Bryony Coles published "Doggerland: A Speculative Survey" in the Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society (64: 45–81). Coles took the name from the Dogger Bank, the great shallow in the middle of the southern North Sea — itself named for the doggers , Dutch fishing boats of the seventeenth century — and she was explicit that the naming was an argument: the drowned plain should be studied as a place in its own right, with its own topography, ecology, and inhabitants, not treated as a corridor between two real countries or as a blank between Britain and the continent. Her survey was, by its title's own admission, speculative: in 1998 the evidence consisted of bathymetry, of finds trawled up over the preceding century (§V), and of inference from the onshore record. What has happened since — the seismic mapping of §IV — turned her speculation into a surveyed landscape, and the name stuck precisely because the argument was right. What kind of country was it? The reconstruction assembled by the Birmingham and Bradford teams (§IV) shows a landscape that changed character as the post-glacial warming proceeded. In the late glacial it was open tundra-steppe, grazed by reindeer, horse, and — earlier still — mammoth. Through the early Holocene it became the classic Mesolithic mosaic: oak, hazel, and alder woodland on the higher ground; reed swamp, salt marsh, and lagoons along a long, shifting coastline; rivers carrying fish runs; lakes in the hollows — among them the basin now charted as the Outer Silver Pit. Coles judged it, on its ecology, possibly the richest hunting, fowling, and fishing territory in Mesolithic Europe, and nothing in the subsequent mapping has overturned that judgement. Its inhabitants were Mesolithic hunter-gatherers whose material culture — microlithic flint industries, barbed points of antler and bone — matches the contemporary cultures of Britain, the Low Countries, Denmark, and northern Germany, for the sufficient reason that those cultures were, at the time, one world with Doggerland at its centre rather than at its edge. That inversion — centre, not edge — is Doggerland's first lesson, and it generalises. On a modern map the North Sea coasts of Britain and the continent look like margins, and their Mesolithic sites are conventionally described as peripheral settlements of peoples whose heartlands lay inland. On the map of 10,000 BCE the geometry reverses: the heartland is the drowned plain, and the surviving coastal sites of England, the Netherlands, and Denmark are its upland fringe — the camps that happened to stand high enough to survive. The same reversal awaits any region whose centre of gravity lay on the shelf, which is to say most regions of the late glacial world. Doggerland is simply the place where the reversal has been demonstrated in detail, river by river. THE RIVERS Thames, Rhine, Meuse, and Scheldt joined in one system flowing down the Channel river to the Atlantic; seismic mapping has traced individual channels — among them the Shotton River, draining the Dogger Bank hills to the Outer Silver Pit lake. THE ECOLOGY Tundra-steppe giving way to hazel and oak woodland, marsh, lagoon, and lake: on Coles's assessment, possibly the richest Mesolithic hunting, fowling, and fishing ground in Europe. THE PEOPLE Mesolithic hunter-gatherers culturally continuous with Britain, the Low Countries, Denmark, and north Germany — because all four were provinces of one plain-centred world. THE NAME Coined by Bryony Coles in 1998, from the Dogger Bank. The naming was programmatic: a country to be mapped, not a corridor to be crossed in a sentence. Doggerland's human story also runs far deeper than the Mesolithic. The plain was crossed and hunted through the Palaeolithic whenever climate allowed — the dredged handaxes and the Neanderthal fossil of §V are its witnesses — and its final, Mesolithic chapter is only the best-lit part of a much longer occupation. But it is the Mesolithic chapter that the drowning terminated, and its ending was a process with a chronology the literature states in round, debated figures: Britain's separation from the continent is commonly placed around c. 6500 BCE , as the Channel and the southern bight flooded through; the remaining land shrank thereafter to an archipelago, and then to the single low island of the Dogger Bank itself, whose final submergence is generally placed around c. 7000 BP (c. 5000 BCE) . Between those dates falls the one violent day in the story — the Storegga tsunami of §VI — and the question of how much of the ending was the wave's work is taken up in §VII. IV. Reading a Drowned Plain — Seismic Survey and Cores Doggerland could not be excavated in the ordinary way: it lies under 20 to 40 metres of water, much of it buried beneath marine sediments, in one of the busiest and roughest seaways in the world. Its reconstruction is instead a worked example of the method this article returns to in §XIII — remote sensing first, ground-truth by coring second, artefacts third — and the procedure deserves to be set out as procedure, because it is the template for submerged prehistory everywhere. Step One — Borrowed Seismic Data The oil and gas industry had, for its own purposes, already sounded the North Sea floor in three dimensions. Seismic reflection survey — firing acoustic pulses at the seabed and timing their echoes from buried surfaces — can image not only the modern seabed but the buried land surfaces beneath it: old ground surfaces, the channels of drowned rivers, lake basins, peat beds. Between 2003 and 2007 the North Sea Palaeolandscapes Project at the University of Birmingham, led by Vincent Gaffney with Kenneth Thomson and Simon Fitch, took seismic data provided for research by the survey company Petroleum Geo-Services and reinterpreted them archaeologically, mapping some 23,000 square kilometres of the early Holocene landscape of the southern North Sea. River systems invisible from any boat — the Shotton River among them — emerged as continuous mapped features, with banks, tributaries, and confluences. The results appeared as a technical monograph, Mapping Doggerland (2007), and as the synthesis Europe's Lost World: The Rediscovery of Doggerland (Gaffney, Fitch & Smith, 2009). Step Two — Cores as Test Pits A seismic map shows shapes, not dates or environments. The second step is therefore to core : to drill or drive tubes into the mapped features and recover columns of sediment whose contents — pollen, plant macrofossils, molluscs, peat, and, in the newest work, sedimentary ancient DNA — reconstruct the landscape's ecology and give radiocarbon dates for its drowning. The successor programme to the Birmingham project, the European Research Council–funded Europe's Lost Frontiers project (from 2015, led from the University of Bradford), industrialised this step: working from research vessels over a study area of some 190,000 square kilometres between Britain, Denmark, and the Dover Strait, it took long core transects across the mapped river valleys — notably the valley its team calls the Southern River — and built from them a dated environmental history of the plain's last millennia, including, in its cores, sedimentary evidence bearing on the Storegga wave (§VII). A core is a keyhole, not a trench; but a hundred cores along a mapped river amount to something no other drowned landscape yet possesses: a sampled, dated countryside. Step Three — The Finds, Put Back on the Map The third step reunites the map with the century of chance finds described in §V. A trawled antler point with no context is a curiosity; the same point plotted against a mapped coastline of its period becomes evidence of where people hunted. Dutch practice has gone furthest in systematising this: the great land-reclamation and port works at Rotterdam (the Maasvlakte extensions) dredged enormous volumes of North Sea sediment from known offshore localities and sieved the spoil, recovering Palaeolithic and Mesolithic assemblages whose offshore origins are recorded by dredging block — context at the scale of a landscape rather than a trench, but context nonetheless. The methodological moral is worth stating plainly, because popular accounts invert it: in submerged prehistory the map comes before the site. One does not find Doggerland by diving at random; one maps a buried countryside from a ship, dates it from cores, and only then knows where a diver, a dredger, or a development-led excavation could meaningfully look. // INDUSTRY AS INSTRUMENT // Doggerland science runs on borrowed infrastructure: oil-industry seismic surveys, aggregate dredging, shell extraction, and offshore wind-farm site investigation. The dependence is double- edged. The same dredging that recovers a Neanderthal fossil (§V) destroys its context in the recovering; the same wind-farm survey that maps a river valley precedes construction across it. The field's standing arrangement — archaeologists embedded in industrial survey, with protocols for finds — is described in §XIII. What the method has produced, to date, is a landscape, not a settlement pattern. No Mesolithic house floor has been excavated in the open North Sea; no Doggerland village plan exists to set beside Atlit-Yam's (§XIV). The mapped rivers are real, the dated cores are real, the trawled tools are real — but between them they establish where people could and did live , and only rarely where a named group of people did . That gap is not a failure of effort. It is the present resolution limit of the best-studied drowned landscape on Earth, and it calibrates what may responsibly be claimed for the less-studied ones: Sundaland's reconstruction (§VIII) rests on bathymetry and genetics without Doggerland's density of cores, and Beringia's (§XI–XII) on genetics and palaeoecology with, as yet, no confirmed site at all on the drowned plain itself. V. What the Nets Brought Up — Trawled and Dredged Finds Doggerland was known from its objects long before it was mapped. Through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, North Sea fishing vessels working the shallow banks hauled up, in their nets and dredges, the debris of a land fauna where no land should be: mammoth molars and bones by the tonne, woolly rhinoceros, horse, reindeer, bison — and, mixed with them, unmistakably human work. The find that fixed scientific attention came in 1931 , when a trawler working the Leman and Ower Banks, east of the Wash, brought up a barbed point of antler — a Mesolithic hunting weapon of a type known from dry-land sites, recovered from the seabed far off the English coast, in association with the peat beds fishermen called "moorlog" — drowned land, hauled up in lumps. The point did not prove a countryside; but it proved inhabitants, and it made the question Coles formalised in 1998 unavoidable. The trawled and dredged assemblage has grown ever since, and its character is worth describing exactly, because it defines both the strength and the weakness of this class of evidence. Its strength is range : handaxes of the Middle Palaeolithic, Levallois flakes, Mesolithic microliths and antler work, animal bone in industrial quantities, human bone occasionally — a cross-section of the plain's whole occupation, recovered across the whole of its area, at no excavation cost. Its weakness is context : a trawl integrates everything along its tow, a dredger everything in its cut, and a find's provenance may be no finer than a named bank. Individual objects can still carry remarkable information — in 2019 a flint flake dredged off the coast of The Hague was found to retain a lump of birch-bark tar , the Palaeolithic world's standard adhesive, still adhering to its surface: hafting technology, and the birch-processing behind it, attested from the open sea. But the assemblage as a whole testifies to presence and to industry, not to settlement, season, or society. Krijn — The Zeeland Ridges Neanderthal One dredged object stands apart, and it is the single most important human fossil ever recovered from the sea. In 2001 , in the sieving debris of a shell-extraction company working the Zeeland Ridges , some 15 kilometres off the Dutch coast, the collector Luc Anthonis recognised a fragment of human frontal bone — part of a brow ridge — among Late Pleistocene animal bones and Middle Palaeolithic artefacts, including small handaxes and Levallois flakes, dredged from the same sediments. The specimen, nicknamed "Krijn" and published by Hublin and colleagues in the Journal of Human Evolution (2009), was assigned unambiguously to Homo neanderthalensis on the morphology of the brow and on three-dimensional geometric morphometrics: a young adult male. Carbon and nitrogen isotopes in the bone show a diet of overwhelmingly terrestrial meat, matching other Neanderthals and showing no sign of aquatic foods. A lesion in the bone was diagnosed as an intradiploic epidermoid cyst — a benign tumour of a type identified here, the authors note, for the first time in Neanderthal remains. The bone cannot be dated directly; its age is inferred from its context and morphology, broadly Late Pleistocene, commonly quoted at roughly 50,000 years or more. Krijn's significance is triple. He is the first Pleistocene hominin fossil recovered from under seawater, and the first Neanderthal recorded from the Netherlands. He demonstrates — in a single, identified individual — that the drowned plain was Neanderthal country, part of the world treated in this hub's Neanderthals and Denisovans , and that its submerged sediments preserve fossil hominin material of the first quality. And he is a parable of the method: found not by an expedition but in industrial spoil, by a collector who knew what a brow ridge looked like, in a country whose heritage law had to reckon with a seabed archive it had barely begun to manage. The richest fossil ground in north-western Europe, the southern North Sea has been called on the strength of its mammal yields alone. Krijn is what that ground can hold. // A NOTE ON PROVENANCE // Everything in this section arrived without excavation context, and this article grades it accordingly. Trawled and dredged finds establish presence — of species, of industries, of a dated individual — at the scale of a bank or a dredging block. They do not establish association between objects found together in a net, and no argument in this article rests on treating them as though they did. The contrast case is §XIV: Atlit-Yam, where houses, burials, and a well were excavated in situ on the seabed by divers — the standard the North Sea material, for all its richness, has not yet met in the open sea. VI. The Storegga Wave — c. 6200 BCE Off the coast of western Norway, where the continental shelf breaks to the deep Norwegian Sea, lies the scar of one of the largest submarine landslides known anywhere: the Storegga Slide — Storegga is Norwegian for "the great edge." Around 6200 BCE (about 8150 calibrated years BP), a slab of shelf-edge sediment some 290 kilometres long failed and ran out across the ocean floor. Published estimates of the displaced volume run from about 2,400 to 3,500 cubic kilometres — a quantity of sediment comparable, in the comparison the literature itself uses, to Iceland buried tens of metres deep. The displaced water crossed the North Atlantic as a tsunami, striking Norway, the Faroe Islands, Shetland, Scotland, and the coasts of the northern North Sea — including, on the reconstructions debated in §VII, what was left of Doggerland. The Evidence for the Wave A prehistoric tsunami is not observed; it is read, from the sediment it leaves behind, and the Storegga deposits are the type example of the genre. Around the coasts of the Norwegian Sea and northern North Sea, fieldworkers — Stein Bondevik, Alastair and Sue Dawson, and their colleagues prominent among them — have documented a distinctive layer at the right stratigraphic horizon: a sheet of marine sand and gravel, containing ripped-up clasts of peat, redeposited lake mud, and marine microfossils, laid down on land , over peat and lake sediment, and subsequently buried by renewed peat growth. In Scotland the layer has been traced in the Montrose Basin and the Firth of Forth, running kilometres inland and standing metres above the tide levels of its day. In western Norway the deposits indicate runups of some 10–12 metres. In Shetland , closest to the slide on the wave's path, Bondevik and colleagues traced the sand up peaty hillsides to 9.2 metres above present high-tide level; because sea level there then stood at least 10–15 metres lower than today, the runup above the sea of that morning exceeded 20 metres — the finding announced in their 2003 Eos paper as a record-breaking height for an 8,000-year-old tsunami. Radiocarbon dates on plant material immediately above and below the deposits converge, in the most recent syntheses, on about 6225–6170 BCE for the event. Two cautions belong with the numbers, and the literature states both itself. The first is that runup is not wave height: a tsunami's inundation height at a given hillside depends on the shape of that coast, and Shetland's exceptional figures are local maxima, not a North-Atlantic-wide wall of water. The second is that sediment-based and model-based reconstructions do not perfectly agree — a 2020 discussion by Dawson and colleagues, from the Shetland evidence, sets sediment-traced inundation limits against numerical models that produce lower maxima, and leaves the discrepancy open as a problem in tsunami geoscience rather than resolving it by preference. Neither caution touches the event itself. That a very large tsunami crossed the northern North Sea in the centuries around 6200 BCE is established by deposits on four coasts, independently dated. What remains genuinely open — and it is the question that matters for this hub — is what the wave did to the people in its path. Around 8200 calBP, large parts of the now submerged North Sea continental shelf ('Doggerland') were catastrophically flooded by the Storegga Slide tsunami, one of the largest tsunamis known for the Holocene. — Weninger et al., Documenta Praehistorica 35 (2008) — the strong form of the claim, debated in §VII VII. Did the Wave End Doggerland? — The Debate The Storegga debate is this article's set-piece disagreement, and it is reported here the way this hub reports all of them: positions named, evidence distinguished from inference, and no verdict smuggled in by adjective. The Catastrophic Reading — Weninger and Colleagues The strong form of the claim is Weninger and colleagues' 2008 paper in Documenta Praehistorica , "The catastrophic final flooding of Doggerland by the Storegga Slide tsunami." Working from a refined radiocarbon chronology for the slide and from reconstructions of the contemporary coastline, they argued that by c. 6200 BCE the remnant of Doggerland was a low-lying archipelago whose Mesolithic population was already compressed by rising seas — and that the tsunami inundated large parts of that remnant at a stroke, with an unexpectedly high impact modelled for the western coasts of Jutland as well as for the North Sea coasts. On this reading the wave was the final flooding: not the cause of Doggerland's long decline, which the sea-level curve had been driving for millennia, but the coup de grâce that ended its habitability and severed, culturally as well as geographically, the British Mesolithic from the continent's.
