The Traditions Side by Side — A Comparative Table XVIII. What Comparison Can and Cannot Show Sources I. Tier B — The Deluge as Text, Not as Event This is a Tier B article: Ancient Tradition . The tier is stated here, in words, because it governs every sentence that follows. Tier B material survives in ancient texts, in ancient languages, copied and recopied by ancient scribes and poets. This article treats those texts as texts : it gives each one's composition date as scholarship establishes it, names the manuscripts or the transmission chain by which it reaches us, names the edition or translation actually consulted, and attributes every claim to the text that makes it. That discipline matters more for the flood than for almost any other subject in this division of the Archive, because the flood is the point at which four great literatures are most often melted down into one. Popular retelling speaks of "the Flood" as if there were a single story — a single vessel, a single hero, a single mountain — of which Ziusudra, Noah, and Deucalion were local names. The texts do not say that. The Sumerian story gives its hero seven days and seven nights of storm and no birds at all in its surviving lines. The Akkadian poem of Atrahasis sends the flood because human beings have become too loud . Genesis sends it as a moral judgement and ends it with a covenant no Mesopotamian text contains. The Greek story rescues exactly two people, in a chest, and repopulates the earth from stones. Egypt, as Sections XIII to XVI argue at length, has no such story at all. To harmonise those tellings into one "real flood" behind them all is to destroy the evidence in the act of presenting it. What comparison can legitimately show — literary transmission, shared motifs, deliberate theological reworking — is taken up in Sections IX and XVIII, with the scholarly positions stated fairly, including the positions this article does not adopt. What comparison cannot show, on the evidence of the texts themselves, is a single historical deluge of which all four traditions are garbled memories. No text in this article claims that status for itself, and this article claims it for none of them. // THE RULE OF THIS ARTICLE // Every flood in what follows belongs to a named text, in a named language, of a named date. "The poem says," "Genesis narrates," "Apollodorus reports," and "the Egyptian text does not say" are the normal forms here. Where a scholar's interpretation is given, the scholar is named. Quotations are confined to editions actually opened in the preparation of this article, and are named as such. Everything else is paraphrase, and is presented as paraphrase. A companion article in this division, The Antediluvian King Lists , treats the flood as a chronological hinge — the single line in the Sumerian King List at which 241,200 years of claimed reigns give way to history. This article is its counterpart: where the King List gives the flood one line, the narratives gathered here give it whole poems. Read together, the two articles show the same event functioning as a date in one genre and as a theology in another — which is precisely what it means to treat the deluge as text. II. A Map of the Traditions — Four Literatures, Four Floods Four literary worlds stand behind this article, and they should be kept distinct from the outset, because their flood traditions differ in age, in genre, and in purpose as much as in detail. MESOPOTAMIA — THE LONG LINE A Sumerian flood story centred on Ziusudra; an Old Babylonian Akkadian poem centred on Atrahasis; the same story retold as personal testimony in Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, centred on Utnapishtim; and a Hellenistic Greek retelling by the Babylonian priest Berossus, centred on Xisouthros. Four compositions, one evolving tradition, spanning roughly two thousand years of copying. Sections III to VII. GENESIS — THE WOVEN TEXT Genesis 6–9, the account of Noah, his ark, and the covenant, read by mainstream scholarship as two older strands — conventionally called J and P — interwoven by editors into a single narrative whose seams are still visible in its numbers, its animals, and its two endings. Sections VIII and IX. GREECE — THE LATE, BRIEF TELLING The flood of Deucalion and Pyrrha: alluded to by Pindar in the fifth century BCE, summarised by the mythographer Apollodorus, and given its fullest literary form by the Roman poet Ovid. Later than the Mesopotamian line in its surviving witnesses, briefer than any of them, and distinct in its vessel, its survivors, and its stone-born repopulation. Sections X to XII. EGYPT — THE ABSENCE No native Egyptian text tells of a universal deluge destroying mankind by water. Egypt's great destruction myth destroys by the fiery Eye of Ra, not by flood; its primeval waters, Nun, are the beginning of the world, not its catastrophe; and its annual inundation is the year's blessing, not its terror. The absence is itself the finding. Sections XIII to XVI. The order of the article is the order of the evidence. The Mesopotamian line comes first because its witnesses are oldest and fullest, and because every serious comparison in this field is a comparison with it. Genesis comes second because its relationship to the Mesopotamian material — close in motif, distant in theology — is the most studied and the most debated. Greece comes third because its telling is later, shorter, and shaped by Greek concerns that owe less to Mesopotamia than popular accounts assume. Egypt comes last, and at length, because the honest answer to "what is Egypt's flood myth?" is that there isn't one — and the reasons why are among the most instructive in all comparative mythology. III. The Sumerian Flood Story — Ziusudra and the Eridu Genesis The earliest surviving Mesopotamian flood narrative is Sumerian. The composition is cited in the Oxford Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature as ETCSL t.1.7.4 , under the title The Flood Story ; it is also widely known by the title Thorkild Jacobsen gave it, the Eridu Genesis . This article quotes the ETCSL translation, which it opened directly, and follows the ETCSL's own presentation of the text — gaps, queries, and missing lines included. The Manuscript and Its Date The story survives principally on a single tablet from Nippur, excavated by the University of Pennsylvania expedition and recognised by Arno Poebel in the early twentieth century, with further fragments from Ur and a later bilingual fragment associated with the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. The main Nippur tablet is dated to around 1600 BCE — that is, it is an Old Babylonian-period copy of a Sumerian composition whose own date of composition cannot be fixed more precisely than the early second millennium BCE tradition it belongs to. The distinction matters, and this article keeps it throughout: c. 1600 BCE is the date of the surviving clay, not a claim about when the story was first told. The tablet is badly broken. Estimates of the loss vary, but between a third and two-thirds of the composition is missing, and the ETCSL translation marks the losses openly: Segment A opens with approximately 36 lines missing, further gaps of some 32, 34, and 38 lines interrupt the narrative, and whole passages are marked too fragmentary for translation. Any summary of "the Sumerian flood story" that does not carry those gaps with it is silently filling them from later versions — a practice Bendt Alster's work on the Sumerian flood tradition warns against, and one this article avoids. In particular, the boat-building instructions, so detailed in the Akkadian versions, fall in a lacuna in the Sumerian text. We do not know what Ziusudra's vessel looked like. We know only that the text calls it, when the storm comes, a huge boat. What Survives The surviving shape, in the ETCSL translation, is this. After An, Enlil, Enki, and Ninhursaja fashion humankind and make the animals multiply, kingship descends from heaven and the first five cities are founded and assigned to their gods: Eridug (Eridu) to Nudimmud, that is Enki; Bad-tibira to the Mistress, Inana; Larag (Larak) to Pabilsag; Zimbir (Sippar) to the hero Utu; and Shuruppak to Sud. These are the five antediluvian cities of the King List, in the same order — the two compositions share a tradition's map of the first age, a point developed in the companion article, The Antediluvian King Lists . After a break, the gods resolve on destruction. The text, as the ETCSL presents it, shows the divine assembly swearing an oath, the goddess Nintud lamenting, and Enki taking counsel with himself. The hero is Zi-ud-sura — Ziusudra, a name understood as "life of long days" — presented as a king and a gudug priest, humble, committed, and reverent, standing day by day at his devotions. Enki, bound by the oath, does not address the man directly. He addresses a wall, with Ziusudra standing at its side listening. The verified wording of the warning, in the ETCSL translation opened for this article, is given in the pull-quote below. "A flood will sweep over the ...... A decision that the seed of mankind is to be destroyed has been made." — The Flood Story, Segment C, ETCSL translation t.1.7.4 (Oxford) The ellipses are the ETCSL's own: they mark broken clay, and they are part of the quotation, not an editorial embarrassment. A text that reaches us in this condition is evidence of a particular and valuable kind — it shows exactly how much of the earliest flood narrative we actually have, and how much of the familiar "Sumerian version" in popular books is Atrahasis and Gilgamesh wearing Sumerian dress. When the text resumes, the storm has come: all the windstorms and gales arise together, and the flood sweeps over the land. The huge boat is rocked by waves and windstorms for seven days and seven nights . Then Utu the sun god comes out, illuminating heaven and earth; Ziusudra drills an opening in the boat, prostrates himself before Utu, and sacrifices oxen and innumerable sheep. In the closing preserved movement, An and Enlil treat Ziusudra kindly: in the ETCSL's wording, they grant him life like a god and bring down to him eternal life, and they settle him in an overseas country, in the land of Dilmun, where the sun rises, because he has preserved the animals and the seed of mankind. // WHAT THE SUMERIAN TEXT DOES NOT CONTAIN // In its surviving lines the Sumerian story has no birds released to test the waters, no mountain on which the boat grounds, no dimensions for the vessel, and no stated motive for the gods' decision that survives the breaks. Those elements belong to the later Akkadian tellings. Reading them back into Ziusudra's story is the single most common error in popular flood comparison, and the easiest to avoid: read the gaps as gaps. IV. Atrahasis — Noise, Plague, and the Flood as Last Resort The fullest early telling of the flood is not Sumerian but Akkadian: the poem modern scholarship calls Atrahasis , after its hero, whose name means "exceedingly wise." The standard edition is W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard, Atra-ḫasīs: The Babylonian Story of the Flood (Oxford, 1969), and the poem is most widely read in Stephanie Dalley's translation in Myths from Mesopotamia (Oxford University Press, 1989). This article's summary follows the Lambert and Millard edition as reported in the scholarly literature consulted for it; renderings of the poem's wording are given as paraphrase. Date, Copy, and Transmission The poem was composed in the Old Babylonian period. Its best-preserved early copy is a three-tablet edition whose colophons name its scribe — read in earlier scholarship as Ku-Aya and now generally as Ipiq-Aya — and date the copying to the reign of Ammi-saduqa of Babylon, in the 17th century BCE (Ammi-saduqa's reign is conventionally placed c. 1646–1626 BCE). As with the Sumerian tablet, the date is the copy's date; the composition itself is older by an interval scholarship puts at no more than a century or two on Lambert and Millard's judgement. The poem runs to roughly 1,200–1,250 lines across its three tablets in the reconstructed edition. It did not stop being copied in the Old Babylonian period: later Assyrian recensions and fragments, including material from Ashurbanipal's library and a fragment from Ugarit, show the poem still being transmitted more than a thousand years after its best early copy was written. The Poem's Argument Atrahasis is not only a flood story, and reading it as one flattens it. It is a complete account of why human beings exist and why their lives have the shape they have. In paraphrase of the poem's opening movement: the lesser gods, the Igigi, labour at digging the rivers and canals, rebel at the workload, and burn their tools. Humankind is created — from clay mixed with the flesh and blood of a slain god, in the poem's striking account — to carry the labour in the gods' place. Humanity multiplies. And then the poem gives its famous and deliberately unglamorous motive for everything that follows: noise . The land, in the image the translators render with a bellowing bull, has grown loud with people; the god Enlil cannot sleep for the uproar — rigmu in Akkadian — and moves, step by step, to reduce it. The steps matter, because the flood is the last of them, not the first. Enlil sends plague; Enki, through Atrahasis, counsels the people to concentrate their worship on the plague god until the plague lifts. Enlil sends drought, and then famine; each measure is frustrated the same way, by Enki's quiet countermeasures delivered through his servant. Only then does Enlil bind the gods by oath and decree the flood. Enki circumvents the oath exactly as in the Sumerian telling — speaking not to the man but to the wall of his house — and Atrahasis builds the vessel, loads his family and the animals, and rides out a storm the poem sets at seven days and seven nights. Afterward he sacrifices; the gods, who have gone hungry without human offerings, gather to the sacrifice; Enlil rages at the survival and is answered by Enki and by the mother goddess with the poem's settlement: humanity will continue, but under permanent new limits — mortality as now experienced, barrenness for some women, and celibate classes of priestesses — presented as the checks that make another flood unnecessary. // NOISE, NOT WICKEDNESS // The distinction between Atrahasis and Genesis begins here. In Atrahasis, on the standard reading following Lambert and Millard, the flood's cause is demographic and acoustic: too many people, making too much noise, for one god's rest. There is no charge of human wickedness, violence, or corruption. A reader who imports Genesis's moral cause into the Akkadian poem — or the poem's noise into Genesis — has stopped reading either text. A later Old Babylonian witness deserves mention here because it shows the tradition still at work on practical detail. The tablet Irving Finkel published as The Ark Before Noah (2014) — an Old Babylonian Atrahasis-tradition tablet of roughly 1900–1700 BCE — gives boatbuilding instructions of unusual specificity: a great round vessel on a circular plan, a giant coracle of coiled palm-fibre rope, wooden ribs, and bitumen. The Mesopotamian ark, in its most detailed surviving specification, is round because Mesopotamian river boats were round. The long ship-shaped ark of later Western illustration belongs to a different tradition's imagination. V. Gilgamesh Tablet XI — Utnapishtim Tells His Own Story The most famous Mesopotamian flood account is a story inside a story. In Tablet XI of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh — the version traditionally associated with the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni — the hero Gilgamesh, grieving for Enkidu and terrified of his own death, crosses the waters of death to find the one man who was granted unending life, and asks him how he got it. The flood story is the answer. The standard modern edition is Andrew R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (Oxford University Press, 2003), with George's Penguin translation, The Epic of Gilgamesh (1999), as the usual point of entry; Dalley's Myths from Mesopotamia also translates the tablet. This article paraphrases the tablet following George's edition as reported in the scholarship consulted. Manuscripts and the 1872 Sensation The Standard Babylonian epic is known principally from seventh-century BCE copies from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, among other witnesses, including a fragment from Ugarit of around 1200 BCE that George published in 2007. The Nineveh flood tablet — British Museum K.3375 and its joins — is the object George Smith read when he announced a Babylonian flood account to the Society of Biblical Archaeology on 3 December 1872. The sensation that announcement caused — a flood narrative older than Genesis, in cuneiform — permanently changed the study of both corpora, and it is the historical reason the comparisons in Section IX carry the charge they do. The tablet Smith read is a copy roughly a thousand years younger than the Atrahasis copy of Ammi-saduqa's reign, retelling a story already ancient when its scribe wrote. Utnapishtim's Narration The hero is Utnapishtim — rendered Utanapishtim in some editions — "the Faraway," son of Ubar-Tutu, of Shuruppak on the Euphrates: the King List's last antediluvian city, and its last king's household. In paraphrase following George: the great gods resolve on the flood; Ea — Enki under his Akkadian name — betrays the secret to the wall of Utnapishtim's reed hut; the hero is told to tear down his house and build a boat whose length and breadth are to be equal, roofed over, and to load it with the seed of all living things, his family and kinsfolk, craftsmen, cattle and wild beasts, and his silver and gold. The vessel of Tablet XI is, in its stated proportions, a great cube of 120 cubits — a specification unlike both the Ark Tablet's coracle and Genesis's oblong ark, and a reminder that even within one tradition the boat would not stay the same shape. The storm, in the tablet's telling, lasts six days and seven nights — one day shorter than the Sumerian and Atrahasis storms, a small variant that honest comparison should note rather than smooth away. All humankind turns to clay. The boat grounds on Mount Nimush — Nisir in older translations — and holds fast. On the seventh day, in the sequence every reader of Genesis should meet first in its Babylonian form, Utnapishtim releases birds: a dove , which finds no perch and returns; a swallow , which likewise returns; and a raven , which sees the waters receding, eats, scratches the ground, and does not return. He releases the animals, sacrifices on the mountain, and the gods gather to the offering's savour. Enlil, furious that anyone has escaped, is rebuked — and in settlement blesses Utnapishtim and his wife, making them like the gods, to dwell far away at the mouth of the rivers. Scholarship is plain about the tablet's literary source: Lambert and Millard concluded, and George's edition confirms, that the flood story in Tablet XI is adapted from Atrahasis — at points nearly line for line — and reshaped as personal testimony. The reshaping has a purpose inside the epic, and the epic states it by what happens next. Utnapishtim's immortality, his narration insists, was a unique grant made in circumstances that will never recur. Challenged simply to stay awake for six days and seven nights, Gilgamesh falls asleep at once, and Utnapishtim's wife bakes a loaf for each day of his sleep so that the failure cannot be denied. The man who cannot conquer sleep will not conquer death. The flood, in Gilgamesh, is not told for its own sake: it is told to close a door. VI. Berossus — Xisouthros and the Books Buried at Sippar The Mesopotamian line's last great ancient retelling is not in cuneiform at all. Berossus (Berossos), a Babylonian priest of Bel writing in Greek under Antiochus I in the early third century BCE, composed the Babyloniaca , a history of Babylonia for a Hellenistic audience, published around 278 BCE on the usual dating. The work is lost as a whole. It survives in fragments and summaries transmitted through Alexander Polyhistor, Josephus, Eusebius, and the Byzantine chronographer George Syncellus, among others — the flood fragment principally through Syncellus, in the translation of G. P. Verbrugghe and J. M. Wickersham consulted for this article in paraphrase. Every statement about Berossus should carry that chain with it: we read a ninth-century CE chronographer's excerpts of a first-century BCE epitomator's excerpts of a third-century BCE priest's Greek history of traditions already two thousand years old. In Berossus's second book, as the fragments report it, ten kings reign before the flood for a total of 120 sar — 432,000 years — and the tenth and last is the flood hero himself: Xisouthros (Xisuthros), the Greek form of Ziusudra's name, son of the ninth king — Otiartes or Ardates in the fragments' variant spellings, corresponding to Ubara-Tutu. The promotion is the point: where the Sumerian story makes Ziusudra a king in Shuruppak and the King List makes him no king at all in its own list — Ubara-Tutu is its last antediluvian king — Berossus completes the identification and puts the hero on the throne. The tradition, fifteen centuries after the Weld-Blundell Prism, is still editing itself. The flood account the fragments preserve, in paraphrase, runs as follows. The god Cronus — Ea/Enki, under the Greek identification of gods that scholars call interpretatio graeca — appears to Xisouthros in a dream and reveals that on the fifteenth day of the month Daisios mankind will be destroyed by a great flood. Xisouthros is ordered first to bury all the writings — the first, the middle, and the last tablets, in the fragment's phrase — at Sippar, the city of the sun , and then to build a boat and board it with his family, his best friends, provisions, and animals of every kind. The flood comes and abates. Xisouthros releases birds, which return finding no food and no place to rest; releases them again after some days, and they return with mud on their feet; a third release does not return. The vessel grounds in Armenia, in the fragments' geography; Xisouthros disembarks with his wife, his daughter, and the pilot, sacrifices to the gods — and disappears, translated to live with the gods for his piety, with his wife, daughter, and pilot sharing the honour. A voice from the air instructs the remaining companions to return to Babylonia, dig up the buried tablets at Sippar, and hand them over to mankind. They do so, refound cities and temples, and restore Babylon. The fragments add that a piece of the vessel still remained in the Gordyenian mountains of Armenia in Berossus's telling, and that people scraped its bitumen for use as a protective charm. // THE PRIEST'S EMPHASIS // The buried books are Berossus's own emphasis, and they are a Babylonian priest's emphasis. What survives his flood is not only life but the written record — beginnings, middles, and ends, dug up and republished. For a priest explaining his tradition's antiquity to a Greek king, no detail could be more pointed: civilisation, in Berossus, is a text that a flood cannot drown. VII. The Mesopotamian Line — A Thousand Years of Retelling Before turning to Genesis, the Mesopotamian evidence should be allowed to state its own lesson, because it is the control case for every comparison that follows. Here is a flood tradition whose transmission we can actually watch, in dated copies, across roughly two thousand years — and what we watch is not preservation but continuous revision. Feature Sumerian Story Atrahasis Gilgamesh XI Berossus Hero Ziusudra Atrahasis Utnapishtim Xisouthros Warning Enki speaks to a wall Enki speaks to a wall Ea speaks to a reed hut's wall Cronus appears in a dream Cause, as the text states it Lost in the breaks Human noise; failed plague, drought, famine first The great gods' resolve; no cause argued Cronus announces the date; no cause argued Storm's length 7 days, 7 nights 7 days, 7 nights 6 days, 7 nights Not specified in the fragment Birds None in surviving lines Not a feature of the surviving flood tablet Dove, swallow, raven Unnamed birds, three releases Hero's end Eternal life in Dilmun Survival under a new settlement for mankind Made like the gods; dwells at the rivers' mouth Translated to live with the gods Three conclusions follow, and all three are conclusions about texts, not about weather. First, the stable core of the tradition is small: a divine decision, one warned man, a vessel, a storm, a sacrifice, an exceptional fate for the hero. Everything else — the cause, the boat's shape, the storm's length, the birds, the mountain, the hero's kingship — moves. Second, the movement is not random decay: each retelling reshapes the story toward its own work — Atrahasis toward an argument about population and labour, Gilgamesh XI toward an argument about the unrepeatability of immortality, Berossus toward an argument about the antiquity of Babylonian learning. Third, and most important for what follows: if this much change is what a tradition undergoes when we can watch it, in dated manuscripts from one civilisation, then the amount of change to expect across languages, centuries, and theologies — the Genesis case — should surprise no one. Similarity of motif is evidence of contact or shared inheritance. It is not evidence of transcription, and it is not, by itself, evidence of an event. VIII. Genesis 6–9 — Two Strands Woven Into One Narrative Genesis 6–9 tells of Noah: of human wickedness and violence, of God's decision to blot out life from the earth, of the ark built to exact dimensions, of the animals gathered, of rain and of the fountains of the great deep, of the ark resting on the mountains of Ararat, of a raven and a dove sent out over the waters, of Noah's sacrifice and God's resolve never again to curse the ground, and of the covenant sealed with the bow in the clouds. This section presents the account as mainstream biblical scholarship presents it — stated as the scholarly account, fairly, and attributed to that scholarship throughout. It is not the only way the text has been read: Jewish and Christian tradition read it for millennia as a single unified narrative, and many readers, including many scholars of faith, still do. The documentary account is given here because this article's subject is the text's composition and transmission, and on those questions it is the account a reader will meet in the standard literature — in Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (1878), in Richard Elliott Friedman's Who Wrote the Bible? (1987), and in the introductions to modern critical translations. Quotations from Genesis in this article follow the New Revised Standard Version (NRSV) , in the excerpts consulted for this article. The Documentary Account On the documentary hypothesis in its classical form, the Pentateuch was woven by editors from older written sources, conventionally labelled J (the Yahwist), E (the Elohist), D (the Deuteronomist), and P (the Priestly source), reaching its final form in the fifth century BCE or thereabouts. Modern scholarship debates the model's details vigorously — the sources' dates, their extent, and whether "documents" or successive layers of supplementation better describe the process — but the compositeness of the flood narrative itself is among the least contested results of the whole inquiry, because the seams are visible in the received text without any theory at all. Two tellings have been interwoven, verse by verse, and each can still be followed through the weave. The seams, as the standard analyses — Friedman prominent among them — lay them out, include these. The narrative opens twice: once with the LORD seeing human wickedness and grieving (Genesis 6:5–8, the J strand, in the conventional attribution), and again with the earth corrupt and filled with violence in God's sight (6:11–13, the P strand). The animals are commanded twice, differently: P's Noah is to bring two of every kind (6:19–20); J's Noah is to bring seven pairs of every clean animal and one pair of the unclean, with seven pairs of the birds (7:2–3) — the clean animals in surplus because J's Noah, unlike P's, will sacrifice some of them when the waters fall. The flood's mechanism and measure differ by strand: J's flood is rain, falling forty days and forty nights; P's flood is cosmic, the fountains of the great deep bursting forth and the windows of the heavens opening, with the waters swelling for 150 days within a dated chronology that stretches the whole event to about a year, from the six hundredth year of Noah's life, second month, seventeenth day, to dry ground in the six hundred and first year, second month, twenty-seventh day. And the narrative ends twice: first with Noah's altar, the pleasing odour, and God's resolve in his heart never again to curse the ground (8:20–22, J); then with the formal covenant, its sign the bow in the clouds, addressed to Noah, his descendants, and every living creature (9:8–17, P). "never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth" — Genesis 9:11, NRSV, as quoted in the J/P flood analysis consulted for this article Read as the documentary account proposes — two complete tellings, cut and interleaved by an editor who preserved both rather than choosing between them — the doublings stop being problems to be harmonised and become evidence to be read: evidence that Israel, like Mesopotamia, told its flood story more than once, in more than one theological dialect, and that its editors valued the inherited tellings too highly to discard either. The parallel with Section VII is exact, and it is a parallel about scribes, not about water. Dating Genesis as a Text On the conventional datings within the documentary model, the J strand is the earlier — placed by Friedman and others in the early monarchy, around the ninth or tenth century BCE in its classical form, though later datings have their advocates — and the P strand is exilic or post-exilic, of the sixth to fifth centuries BCE. The Babylonian exile (586–538 BCE) is the setting scholarship most often proposes for the intensive contact between Israelite scribes and Babylonian learning that the flood parallels, taken up in the next section, seem to require — though contact through earlier centuries of a shared ancient Near Eastern world cannot be excluded and is also argued. What can be said without controversy is the order of attestation: the Mesopotamian flood texts are attested in writing many centuries before any date proposed for any strand of Genesis. Priority of attestation is a fact about manuscripts. What it means is the subject of Section IX. IX. Genesis and Mesopotamia — Vessel, Birds, Mountain, Sacrifice The relationship between Genesis 6–9 and the Mesopotamian flood texts has been debated since George Smith's announcement in 1872, and the debate is best conducted, as this section conducts it, at the level of specific motifs — comparing what each text actually says, item by item, without harmonising the items into a single story neither text tells. THE WARNING AND THE VESSEL In every Mesopotamian version the hero is warned indirectly — a god speaking to a wall, a dream in Berossus — because the warning god is bound by an oath or acting against the divine council's resolve. In Genesis, God warns Noah directly, in speech, and gives the vessel's design in the same speech: an ark of cypress wood (gopher wood in older translations), 300 cubits long, 50 wide, and 30 high in P's specification, with rooms, a roof, a door, and pitch inside and out. The oblong, measured ark is Genesis's own; no Mesopotamian version gives those proportions — Gilgamesh's vessel is a cube, the Ark Tablet's a coracle. THE CAUSE Atrahasis: noise. Gilgamesh XI: the gods' unexplained resolve. Genesis: human wickedness, corruption, and violence, stated at length in both strands — the LORD's grief at the inclination of the human heart in J, the earth filled with violence in P. The moralisation of the flood's cause is Genesis's most consequential reworking of the inherited material, and it is a reworking: nothing in the Mesopotamian line charges humankind with sin as the flood's reason. THE BIRDS Gilgamesh XI: dove, swallow, raven — the first two return, the raven does not. Genesis 8: a raven first, which flies to and fro until the waters dry; then a dove, sent three times at seven-day intervals — returning, returning with an olive leaf, and finally not returning. The bird sequence is the closest single parallel between the two corpora, and even here the order, the species, and the olive leaf are Genesis's own. Berossus's three releases of unnamed birds, the last betrayed by muddy feet, stand between the two in structure — a reminder that motifs travel in more than one direction and more than one form. THE MOUNTAIN AND THE SACRIFICE Gilgamesh's boat grounds on Mount Nimush; Genesis's ark rests on the mountains of Ararat — a region, in the Hebrew text's geography, not a single named peak; Berossus grounds his vessel in Armenia, the same broad northern geography Ararat names. In all three, the survivor sacrifices on landing, and the divine response to the sacrifice is the story's hinge: the Mesopotamian gods gather hungrily to the savour and quarrel; Genesis's God smells the pleasing odour and resolves — in J, in his heart; in P, by covenant and sign — never to do it again. What the Epic Is and Is Not Evidence For Sources This is a Tier B article: Ancient Tradition . Everything in it rests on ancient texts — poems in Sumerian and Akkadian, written in cuneiform on clay tablets, copied and recopied by ancient scribes — and it treats those texts as texts : each version is seated at the date its composition or its manuscripts actually carry, each claim is attributed to the text that makes it, and every direct quotation is taken from a named, published modern translation and credited to its translator. No claim here depends on treating the poem as a report of events, and none is allowed to borrow the authority of archaeology it does not possess. That discipline matters for Gilgamesh more than for almost any other subject in this division, because the epic invites a confusion its own first lines encourage. The poem is about a king of Uruk whom the tradition places in the third millennium BCE — in the age this hub's Ubaid and Uruk article treats from the ground. But the poem itself is not a third-millennium document. It is a layered work: independent Sumerian poems of about 2100 BCE, a unified Akkadian epic of about 1800 BCE, and a standardised twelve-tablet edition credited by Babylonian tradition to a scholar named Sîn-lēqi-unninni and dated by modern scholarship to roughly 1300–1000 BCE. The antiquity the poem claims — a hero of the deep past, tidings from before the Flood — is the tradition's claim, and this article labels it as such wherever it appears. The antiquity the poem has is the stratigraphy of its manuscripts, and that is old enough, and strange enough, to need no inflation. This article also tells the story whole. The epic is famous in fragments of itself — the Flood of Tablet XI above all, which this hub's Flood Traditions article owns and treats at full length. Here the Flood takes its proper place as one movement among twelve: after the making of Enkidu, the journey to the Cedar Forest, the insult to Ishtar, and the death that sends a king walking to the edge of the world; and before the plant, the serpent, and the return to the walls of Uruk with which the poem deliberately closes. Read whole, Gilgamesh is not a flood story with adventures attached. It is a poem about mortality that contains a flood — and the difference is the subject of this article. I. Tier B — A Poem, Not a Chronicle Begin with what the object is. The Epic of Gilgamesh is a narrative poem — in its fullest ancient form, some three thousand lines of Akkadian verse distributed over twelve clay tablets — preserved not in any author's autograph but in dozens of fragmentary copies, made in scribal schools and palace libraries across more than a thousand years, and reassembled by modern scholarship from pieces held in museums from London to Baghdad. About two-thirds of the standard version's lines have been recovered; the rest are lacunae — gaps where the clay is broken — which editors mark and translators bridge, honestly or otherwise, according to their practice. When this article quotes the poem, it quotes A. R. George's Penguin translation, The Epic of Gilgamesh (1999; Penguin Classics edition 2003), the reading text companion to his two-volume critical edition of 2003, and it says so at the quotation. Stephanie Dalley's translation in Myths from Mesopotamia (Oxford, 1989; revised edition 2000) and Benjamin R. Foster's in The Epic of Gilgamesh (Norton, 2001; second edition 2019) are the other standard English doors into the poem, and the differences among the three — in how much broken text each restores, and how — are themselves part of the evidence a careful reader is handling. The poem's hero requires the same care. That a king named Gilgamesh — in Sumerian, Bilgames — was remembered at Uruk is the tradition's own testimony, repeated in the Sumerian King List, in offering lists, and in the poems themselves. Whether a historical king of that name reigned at Uruk in the early third millennium BCE is a question the surviving contemporary record does not answer: no inscription of his reign, no monument, no administrative tablet naming him has been recovered from his supposed lifetime, and scholars who accept a historical kernel behind the figure do so as an inference from the persistence and specificity of the tradition, not from a document. This hub treats the King List's Gilgamesh entry — his phantom father, his impossibly long reign — in The Antediluvian King Lists , under that article's own rules. Here it is enough to fix the posture: the epic is evidence for what Mesopotamians of the second and first millennia BCE told, taught, and copied — which is a great deal — and it is not a chronicle of a reign in the third. // THE RULE OF THIS ARTICLE // Dates in this article are dates of texts : of compositions, editions, and surviving copies. When the poem says its hero lived before the Flood, that is the poem speaking, and it is reported as the poem speaking. When a tablet is dated to the seventh century BCE, that is a manuscript, and it is reported as a manuscript. The two kinds of date are never allowed to stand in for each other. One more preliminary, because it shapes everything that follows. There is no single ancient object called "the Epic of Gilgamesh" in the way there is a single printed book of that name today. There is a tradition : Sumerian poems that are not yet an epic, an Old Babylonian epic that is not yet standard, a Standard Babylonian edition that later scribes copied with variants, and peripheral versions in other languages that paraphrase freely. Jeffrey H. Tigay's The Evolution of the Gilgamesh Epic (1982) — still the classic study of the poem's growth — made that layered growth its subject, comparing the surviving stages line by line to show what each age added, dropped, and re-thought. This article follows Tigay's and George's stratigraphy throughout: the next three sections walk the layers in order, before the story itself is told, so that the reader always knows which Gilgamesh is on the page. II. The Stratigraphy — A Poem in Layers The epic's history, as modern scholarship reconstructs it from the manuscripts, has four great strata. They are summarised here and treated one by one in §§III–VI. // STRATUM ONE // Sumerian poems, c. 2100 BCE Five independent poems about Bilgames of Uruk, composed in the age of the Third Dynasty of Ur or its aftermath; surviving mostly in Old Babylonian school copies. // STRATUM TWO // Old Babylonian epic, c. 1800 BCE The first unified Akkadian epic, known by its opening words, "Surpassing all other kings"; surviving in scattered tablets and fragments only. // STRATUM THREE // Standard Babylonian, c. 1300–1000 BCE The twelve-tablet edition credited to Sîn-lēqi-unninni, known by its opening words, "He who saw the Deep"; the form all later copies follow. // STRATUM FOUR // The copies, to the late 1st millennium First-millennium manuscripts from Assyria and Babylonia — above all the seventh-century BCE library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh — are the survival vehicle through which the poem reached the modern world (§XV). Two features of this stratigraphy deserve emphasis before the detail. The first is the gap between hero and poem . Even the earliest stratum — the Sumerian poems of about 2100 BCE — stands centuries after the era in which the tradition sets its king, in the Early Dynastic age of Uruk's first greatness. The poems were never contemporary reportage; from their first recoverable moment, Gilgamesh was already a figure of the remembered past, a hero of long ago around whom stories had gathered. The second is the direction of growth . The tradition does not decay from a perfect original; it builds. Episodes that begin as separate Sumerian tales are woven into a single Akkadian arc; a flood story belonging to another poem is drawn in and made the arc's climax; a frame is fitted around the whole that turns a hero's adventures into a meditation on what a mortal life can leave behind. Each stratum is an act of authorship, and the editors are, in Tigay's demonstration, as creative as the poets. Stratum Date Language & Form What Survives Sumerian poems Composed c. 2100 BCE Sumerian; five independent poems Old Babylonian school copies, chiefly from Nippur; no unified epic Old Babylonian epic c. 1800 BCE Akkadian; a single epic, incipit "Surpassing all other kings" A handful of tablets — the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets chief among them — and fragments Middle Babylonian witnesses c. 1500–1000 BCE Akkadian, with Hittite and Hurrian versions Peripheral fragments: Hattusa, Ugarit, Emar, Megiddo (§XV) Standard Babylonian epic Edition c. 1300–1000 BCE Akkadian; twelve tablets, incipit "He who saw the Deep" First-millennium copies, the Nineveh manuscripts fullest; about two-thirds of the lines recovered Tablet XII Appended to the standard edition Akkadian prose rendering of part of a Sumerian poem Complete in outline; contradicts the epic it is attached to (§VI) A note on the dates themselves. They are scholarly working dates, and their authority differs by stratum. The Sumerian poems are dated by the language and cultural setting of their composition and by the date of their surviving copies; the Old Babylonian epic by the script, language, and provenance of its tablets; the Standard Babylonian edition by Babylonian tradition's attribution and by comparison of its text against the older versions — Tigay's method — which shows the standard text reworking Old Babylonian material that must precede it. None of these dates comes from a colophon saying "written in this year," and the range given for Sîn-lēqi-unninni — some three centuries wide — is the honest measure of what the evidence fixes. This article prints the ranges, not false precision. III. The Sumerian Poems — Bilgames, King of Uruk The tradition begins in Sumerian, and it does not begin as an epic. Five poems about Bilgames — the Sumerian form of the hero's name, of which "Gilgamesh" is the later Akkadian form — survive as independent compositions: Gilgamesh and Aga , in which Aga of Kish besieges Uruk and is defeated; Gilgamesh and Huwawa , in two versions, telling the expedition to the Cedar Forest; Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven ; Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld , in which Enkidu descends to the land of the dead; and The Death of Gilgamesh , in which the hero, dying, is promised remembrance and a place among the judges of the dead rather than the life he wanted. The poems are generally dated to the age of the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2100 BCE, though they survive almost entirely in copies made by scribal students some three centuries later, in the Old Babylonian schools — chiefly at Nippur — where Sumerian, by then a learned language no longer spoken in the street, was taught through its classics. Three things about these poems matter for everything after. First, they are separate : no ancient manuscript joins them into one life of the hero, and their episodes do not agree in the way chapters of a single work agree — the Gilgamesh who defies Aga is a city king in a political tale, the Gilgamesh of the Netherworld poem a master whose servant Enkidu is still alive at a point where other tellings have buried him. Second, Enkidu's status differs from the later epic's: in the Sumerian poems he is Gilgamesh's servant and companion, not the wild man created as the king's equal and opposite; the friendship of equals, on which the Akkadian epic turns, is a later reimagining. Third, the poems already contain, in seed, the epic's two great preoccupations: the winning of a name that outlasts death — the Cedar Forest expedition is undertaken, in the Sumerian telling as in the Akkadian, to establish exactly that — and the confrontation with death itself, in the Netherworld poem's bleak inventory of how the dead fare and in the Death of Gilgamesh 's direct refusal of the hero's hope. The Akkadian poets did not invent their themes. They inherited them, and then they did something new with them: they made them one story. // WHY UR III? // The kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur claimed descent from Gilgamesh and honoured him as a divine forebear; the dynasty's founder's successors presented themselves as his kin and, in the case of Shulgi, as his brother. That royal investment is the usual explanation offered in the literature (George 2003) for why poems about a long-dead king of Uruk were composed, or at least collected and prized, at exactly this period: the hero had become dynastic ideology. The poems are, among other things, what a court wanted told about its ancestor. It is worth pausing on the evidentiary shape of this stratum, because it is the pattern of the whole article in miniature. We possess these poems because schoolboys copied them, on clay, as exercises — and because the copies were buried and the clay endured. What a tradition teaches its children is among the strongest evidence of what it values, and by 1800 BCE the schools of Mesopotamia were already teaching Bilgames. But school copies are not archives of fact about 2700 BCE. They are the literature of 1800 BCE looking backward, in a language already ancient to its copyists, at a king already ancient to its poets. IV. The Old Babylonian Epic — "Surpassing All Other Kings" Sometime around 1800 BCE — the early second millennium, the Old Babylonian period — an Akkadian poet, or a succession of them, did the decisive thing: the separate tales were drawn together into a single epic in the Semitic language of Babylon, organised as one life with one arc, from the king's tyranny and the making of his friend, through the Cedar Forest and the Bull of Heaven, to Enkidu's death and the hero's terrified wandering. The poem was known, as Mesopotamian works were known, by its first words: Šūtur eli šarrī , "Surpassing all other kings" — a title that announces a hero's boast where the later edition will announce a sufferer's wisdom. That difference of opening is the difference of the versions in miniature, and Tigay's comparison of the strata rests heavily on it. The Old Babylonian epic survives badly, and the manner of its survival should be stated plainly. No complete copy exists. What we have is a scatter: two substantial tablets known by their modern homes as the Pennsylvania tablet and the Yale tablet, which together carry much of the Cedar Forest journey; a tablet from Sippar preserving the ale-wife Siduri's famous counsel to the wandering hero (§XI); and a handful of smaller fragments and school excerpts. From these pieces — supplemented, cautiously, by what the later standard version demonstrably reworks — scholars reconstruct the Old Babylonian poem's outline. The reconstruction is good enough to show the epic's shape and its great scenes; it is not good enough to quote the version entire, and any modern "Old Babylonian Gilgamesh" a reader meets is a mosaic with the joins showing, in George's edition honestly marked. What the fragments do establish, beyond reasonable dispute, is the transformation itself. In the Old Babylonian telling, Enkidu is already the wild man: formed from clay, living with the beasts, humanised by the woman Shamhat, and set against the king as his match before he becomes his friend. The friendship is the poem's centre of gravity, and death is its engine: it is the Old Babylonian epic, on Tigay's analysis, that first binds the Cedar Forest expedition, the Bull of Heaven, and the death of Enkidu into a causal chain, and that sends its hero out beyond the known world to ask the one immortal man how death may be escaped. Whether the flood story already stood in the Old Babylonian epic as it stands in the standard version is not established — no Old Babylonian Gilgamesh tablet preserving Utnapishtim's tale has been recovered — and the positions are taken up in §V and §XII, where they belong. What is certain is that by about 1800 BCE, in Akkadian, the epic exists: Gilgamesh has become a poem. THE PENNSYLVANIA TABLET One of the two great Old Babylonian witnesses: the heroes' journey toward the Cedar Forest, Enkidu's foreboding, and the elders' counsel — the epic's road narrative in its earliest recoverable form. THE YALE TABLET The Pennsylvania tablet's companion: the arrival at the forest, the dreams on the way, and the confrontation with its guardian in a version older than, and different in detail from, the standard text. THE SIPPAR TABLET Preserves Siduri's speech to the wandering Gilgamesh — the counsel of food, clothing, family, and joy that the standard version will shorten and displace (§XI, §XIV). FRAGMENTS AND EXCERPTS Smaller pieces and school extracts fill gaps and confirm episodes. The Old Babylonian epic is a reconstruction from parts, and its modern editions print it as one. V. The Standard Babylonian Version — Sîn-lēqi-unninni The form in which the world reads Gilgamesh — twelve tablets, a prologue praising the hero's hard-won wisdom, the flood set into Tablet XI, the return to Uruk's walls closing the poem — is the work of a late second-millennium revision that Babylonian tradition itself credited to a named man. Later scholarly lists from Uruk preserve the name Sîn-lēqi-unninni : a scholar and exorcist-priest ( mašmaššu ) of Uruk, from whom learned families of the city later claimed descent, and to whom the tradition assigned the epic as its author or editor. Modern scholarship, following Tigay's demonstration of how deeply the standard text reworks its predecessors, generally accepts the attribution in substance while correcting its scale: Sîn-lēqi-unninni is best understood not as the poem's inventor but as its decisive editor — the man who gave the epic its final, fixed form — and he is accordingly, as George has observed, among the earliest editors in recorded history whose editorial work can still be examined. His date cannot be fixed from any document of his lifetime; the name's form and the textual evidence place him somewhere in the period c. 1300–1000 BCE , and this article uses that range throughout. What the revision did can be listed, because Tigay listed it — by comparing the standard text against the Old Babylonian fragments wherever both survive. The editor supplied a new prologue : where the old poem opened on the king surpassing all kings, the new one opens on the traveller who "saw the Deep," who "brought back a message from the antediluvian age" and set his labours on a stele — recasting the whole poem, before it begins, as the record of wisdom bought by suffering. He fitted the poem with its frame : the praise of Uruk's walls that stands in the prologue returns, nearly word for word, as the poem's last speech (§XIII), so that the epic ends where it began, at the city. He interpolated the Flood : Utnapishtim's tale in Tablet XI is adapted from the older Akkadian flood poem Atrahasis — the correspondences, of episode and at points of wording, are set out in this hub's Flood Traditions — and set into the epic as the answer to the hero's question, the one case of granted immortality, explained as unrepeatable. And he regularised the poem's texture: parallel passages were harmonised, repetitions lengthened and fixed, until the text acquired the formal, liturgical steadiness that first-millennium scribes then copied as standard. Whether Sîn-lēqi-unninni himself performed every one of these acts, or completed a revision already under way in the Middle Babylonian centuries — the peripheral fragments of §XV show the poem in motion in exactly those centuries — is a refinement the evidence leaves open; the attribution of the finished form to his hand is the tradition's, and the reworking itself is demonstrable from the tablets. He who saw the Deep, the country's foundation, who knew the proper ways, was wise in everything! — Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I, opening lines, in A. R. George's translation, The Epic of Gilgamesh (Penguin, 2003) The standard version was known by those opening words: Ša naqba īmuru , "He who saw the Deep." Its twelve tablets carry, in the usual numbering, roughly three thousand lines; the copies that preserve them are first-millennium manuscripts, Babylonian and Assyrian, of which the fullest come from Nineveh (§XV). George's critical edition of 2003 — The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic: Introduction, Critical Edition and Cuneiform Texts (Oxford University Press, two volumes) — is the modern foundation for all work on the poem: it collects every known fragment, including twenty-three published there for the first time, in transliteration, translation, and cuneiform copy, after its editor's personal examination of the surviving pieces. When this article gives a tablet's contents, it gives them as George's edition and the standard translations present them, and where the text is broken at a point that matters, it says so. VI. Tablet XII — The Appended Tablet The twelve-tablet form contains a known impostor, and honesty about it is part of telling the epic whole. Tablet XI ends the poem: the hero is home, the walls are praised, the frame is closed (§XIII). Tablet XII then begins again — with Enkidu alive. Its content is a close Akkadian rendering, in a prose-like translation, of the second half of the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld : the hero loses objects into the land of the dead, Enkidu — here still the servant of the Sumerian telling — descends to retrieve them against instruction, is trapped below, and is allowed up as a shade for one conversation, in which he describes, item by item, how the dead fare according to how they died and how they were buried. The tablet flatly contradicts the epic it is attached to: in Tablets VII and VIII Enkidu dies of a decreed illness and is mourned and buried; in Tablet XII he is alive, descends in body, and returns as a ghost. Both cannot be the same story, and ancient scribes, who copied the twelve tablets as a set, appear to have valued completeness of the Gilgamesh dossier over consistency of its plot. Why it was appended is debated, and the positions should be attributed. Tigay treated the tablet as an inorganic addition — a piece of the older Gilgamesh material preserved by attachment rather than integrated by revision, its presence explained by the scribal impulse to completeness and perhaps by the attraction of a twelve-tablet set. George prints and translates it with the Sumerian poem it renders, as the dossier's final document. Other readers, ancient and modern, have found in it a grim appropriateness as a last word: after all the hero's travelling, the one report from the dead themselves is the report the poem leaves ringing — that the dead do not return, and that their condition is not to be envied. That is a reading, not a compositional fact, and this article labels it as such. What is fact: the poem Sîn-lēqi-unninni's tradition built ends at Tablet XI, and most modern reading translations either print Tablet XII separately, as an appendix, or flag it in place. This article follows the story through Tablet XI and treats Tablet XII here, in the stratigraphy, where its evidence belongs. VII. The King and the Wild Man — Tablets I–II The story, in the standard version, opens with its ending already in view. The prologue (Tablet I) presents a Gilgamesh who has completed his journey: two-thirds divine and one-third human in the poem's reckoning, king of Uruk-the-Sheepfold, builder of its wall, and the man who travelled to the world's end and brought back tidings from before the Flood. The reader is invited up onto that wall in the poem's first movement — to survey the fired brickwork and the foundations the Seven Sages laid — and is shown the tablet-box of cedar in which the hero's own record is said to rest. Only then does the narrative step back to the beginning: to Uruk groaning under its king. Gilgamesh in his strength takes the city's sons for his works and its daughters for his pleasure — the text states the oppression through the people's cry rather than through a charge-sheet, and modern translators differ in how precisely they specify the abuses — until the complaints reach the gods. The gods' answer is not punishment but balance . The mother-goddess Aruru, who made mankind, is charged to make the king's match: she pinches off clay, casts it into the wilderness, and forms Enkidu — hairy, strong, knowing nothing of people or country, eating grass with the gazelles and drinking at the waterhole with the beasts. A trapper, whose pits and nets the wild man keeps spoiling, is advised to fetch Shamhat , a woman of the temple, and the poem's account of Enkidu's humanisation is one of its most deliberate pieces of construction: after his union with Shamhat the animals flee him — he has become, in the text's terms, like a god in understanding, and weaker in the body — and she clothes him, teaches him bread and beer, the food of the land, and leads him, anointed and dressed, toward Uruk. On the way the shepherds receive him; at the city's gate, in Tablet II, the two heroes meet. The meeting is a fight, and the fight is the friendship's foundation. Enkidu blocks the door with his foot against the king on an errand of his privilege; they grapple — in the poem's wrestling imagery, like bulls — the doorposts shake, the wall trembles, and Gilgamesh prevails, or is prevailed upon to stop: the versions and translations distribute the last moment differently, and the outcome that matters is not the fall but what follows it. The rage passes; the heroes embrace and make friendship. The king's mother, the goddess Ninsun , will in Tablet III formally adopt Enkidu as her son — a scene George's edition restored in full from a manuscript published in 2003 — making the wild man the king's brother in law as well as in affection. Uruk has its balance: the force that oppressed the city is now doubled and turned outward, and the poem's question becomes what two such men will do with a world too small for them. Gilgamesh's answer, proposed at the end of Tablet II, is the Cedar Forest. // TWO-THIRDS DIVINE // The poem's arithmetic of the hero — two-thirds of him god, one-third man — is its own theology, stated in the text and reported here as the text's claim, not as a doctrine about a historical person. It does exact narrative work: Gilgamesh is close enough to the gods to demand their privileges, and human enough, by the decisive third, to be refused them. The whole epic unfolds inside that fraction. VIII. The Cedar Forest — Tablets III–V The expedition to the Cedar Forest (Tablets III–V) is the epic's first great deed, and the poem is explicit about its motive, in both the Sumerian forerunner and the Akkadian telling: since a mortal cannot escape death, he can establish a name that death cannot take. The forest stands far away — in the Lebanon or Amanus ranges of the west, as the tradition locates it — and it is guarded by Humbaba (Sumerian Huwawa), a monstrous keeper appointed by the god Enlil, whose roar is a storm, whose mouth is fire, whose breath is death, and whose sevenfold radiance or terrors — the text's melammū , auras of divine dread — protect the cedars of the gods. To kill Humbaba is to do evil in Enlil's sight, and Enkidu, who knew the forest from his wild years, says so. The elders of Uruk say so too, in council, before blessing the venture and entrusting their king to Enkidu's guidance. Ninsun ascends her roof, offers incense to the sun-god Shamash — the expedition's divine patron — and adopts Enkidu. The smiths cast axes and swords of fabulous weight. The heroes set out. The journey is told as a rhythm of distance and dream: stages of travel compressed into days, halts at which Gilgamesh sleeps in a pit dug for the purpose and wakes with dreams that Enkidu interprets — each dream more violent than the last, each interpretation more determinedly favourable. The Old Babylonian Pennsylvania and Yale tablets preserve much of this movement in its earlier form, and Tigay's comparison shows the standard version heightening the pattern: dream, terror, interpretation, advance. At the forest's edge the poem pauses, unusually for Babylonian narrative, on landscape: the cedar mountain, the trees' shade and scent, the paths Humbaba's tread has worn. That descriptive passage is precisely where the text grew in our own century — the Sulaymaniyah tablet published in 2015 (§XVII) filled a gap in Tablet V with the forest alive around its guardian: cedars dripping resin, and monkeys, cicadas, and birds making the noise that entertained Humbaba in his solitude. The monster of the standard version is met, in the new lines, as a keeper in his own kingdom before he is met as an enemy. The fight itself (Tablet V) is swift against its long approach: Shamash raises thirteen winds to blind and bind Humbaba, the heroes close, and the guardian — suddenly a suppliant — pleads for his life, offering the forest and its timber. Gilgamesh wavers; Enkidu urges the kill, warning that a spared Humbaba means their own deaths and that Enlil's anger is a price to be faced after, not a reason to falter now. Humbaba curses them both — in the standard text the curse falls prophetically: may the two friends not grow old together; may Enkidu die first — and the heroes strike, felling the guardian and then the forest's greatest cedar, from which Enkidu fashions a door of fabulous size for Enlil's own temple at Nippur, as if the theft could be repaid as a gift. The raft of cedar timber floats the heroes home down the Euphrates. The deed is done, the name is made — and the poem has carefully shown the reader its cost being incurred: a god's appointed keeper killed, a god's forest felled, a curse spoken with a dying breath. Tablets VI and VII are the bill arriving. IX. Ishtar and the Bull of Heaven — Tablet VI Tablet VI is the epic's hinge, and its shortest road to catastrophe. Gilgamesh, home from the forest, washes off the journey, dresses in clean garments and his crown — and the goddess Ishtar , goddess of love and war, Uruk's own goddess, sees him and proposes marriage, offering the chariot, the tribute of kings, and the fertility of flocks and fields. The hero's refusal is the poem's most famous speech of insult: a catalogue, lover by lover, of what befell those who accepted her before him — Tammuz condemned to annual weeping, the bird whose wing she broke, the lion she trapped in pits, the horse given the whip, the shepherd turned wolf, the gardener turned frog or mole — each item a small myth in itself, several of them otherwise lost to us. The refusal is not modesty; it is a public reckoning that no mortal, and no former lover, could survive making. Ishtar ascends to her father Anu in tears and demands the Bull of Heaven to loose on Uruk, threatening, if refused, to raise the dead to eat the living. Anu yields. The Bull's descent is a disaster in three snorts: its first breath opens a pit that swallows a hundred men, its second two hundred, its third reaches Enkidu, who seizes it by horns and tail while Gilgamesh drives his sword into its neck. The heroes kill the Bull of Heaven together, tear out its heart for Shamash, and — in the episode's deliberate final outrage — Enkidu hurls a haunch of the Bull at the goddess herself as she wails on Uruk's wall, telling her he would do the same to her. Ishtar gathers her women to mourn the Bull over its remains; Gilgamesh gathers the craftsmen to admire its horns, has them worked with lapis lazuli, and hangs them in his father's shrine. Uruk feasts. And in the palace, that night, Enkidu dreams. Read as the poem constructs it, Tablet VI completes the pattern the Cedar Forest began. In the forest the heroes offended Enlil by killing his keeper; at Uruk they offend heaven itself by killing its Bull and insulting its goddess. The deeds are glorious, the fame is real, and the poem does not ask the reader to wish them undone — but it has arranged its theology as a ledger. The gods in council, in the dream that opens Tablet VII, state the account exactly: for the killing of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, one of the two must die. The only question the council debates is which. X. The Death of Enkidu — Tablets VII–VIII Enkidu's dream (Tablet VII) shows him the council of the great gods: Anu and Enlil decreeing that because the heroes killed Humbaba and the Bull, one must die; Enlil naming Enkidu, against Shamash's protest that the expedition was undertaken at the gods' own prompting. Enkidu wakes to a world already sentenced. He turns first on the cedar door he made — addressing it as if it could have warned him — and then, in the poem's most human sequence of curses, on the trapper who found him and on Shamhat who humanised him, wishing the wild's hardships on them both. Shamash speaks from heaven in mitigation: Shamhat gave him bread, beer, clothing, and Gilgamesh — a friend who will mourn him, lay him on a great bed, and make Uruk weep for him. The curse on Shamhat turns, in Enkidu's own mouth, to a blessing. The illness then takes its course, twelve days of decline that the text counts off day by day, and Enkidu dreams again — of a dark house of dust, the netherworld of the Sumerian poem's inventory, where kings and priests and the hero himself will eat clay. He dies, in the standard version's telling, not in battle but in bed: the death no deed can answer. Tablet VIII is the lament, and it is among the most celebrated movements in Akkadian poetry. Gilgamesh mourns over the body in set speeches that summon the whole world of the poem to witness: the elders of Uruk, the paths of the Cedar Forest, the beasts of the steppe, the rivers Ulaya and Euphrates, the shepherds, the ale-wives — all are called to weep for Enkidu as the kin
