Why It Matters for “Before Egypt” XXIII. Sources I. A Tier A Site: What Is Attested, and What Is Not This article is Tier A — Attested . Every substantive claim in it rests on excavated material, radiocarbon measurement, or peer-reviewed and project publication that the reader can check in the Sources section at the end. Where scholars disagree — and at Göbekli Tepe they disagree about a great deal — the disagreement itself is reported, with the positions named and attributed. Where a popular claim goes beyond the evidence, it is labelled as speculation in Section XX, plainly and without mockery. Nothing in this article is presented as a deciphered text, a recovered doctrine, or a lost teaching: the builders left no writing, and no one can quote them. The attested core is extraordinary enough without embellishment. On a limestone ridge north-east of modern Şanlıurfa, in what archaeologists call Upper Mesopotamia, communities who lived by hunting and gathering built large circular enclosures ringed with monolithic T-shaped pillars, many carved in low relief with wild animals. The earliest enclosures belong to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, conventionally placed around c. 9500–9000 BCE in the scheme used throughout this hub, with occupation continuing, in smaller and more rectangular forms, to around c. 8000 BCE . That is roughly six thousand years before the unification of Egypt and more than six millennia before the Great Pyramid. Three cautions belong at the front, because later sections return to them repeatedly. First, temple is an interpretation, not a find. The excavators themselves now generally prefer the neutral term special buildings for the great enclosures, and recent work has recovered domestic buildings alongside them. Second, the familiar three-layer chronology of the site's first director, Klaus Schmidt, has been revised: the round enclosures and the rectangular buildings overlap in time more than the original scheme allowed. Third, the famous claim that the enclosures were deliberately and ritually buried — a claim Schmidt's team itself made — is now questioned by his successors, who read much of the fill as the product of slope slides. A Tier A article does not hide those revisions. It treats them as the science working as it should. ATTESTED Monumental T-pillar enclosures built in the 10th–9th millennia BCE by people with no domesticated plants or animals; extensive wild-game and wild-cereal processing; a regional family of related sites; inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018. DEBATED AMONG SPECIALISTS Whether the enclosures were temples, communal houses, or buildings that were both at once; whether people lived on the hill year-round; how the enclosures filled up; and whether monument-building helped cause, resisted, or merely accompanied domestication. SPECULATION, LABELLED AS SUCH Readings of the carvings as a star map, a comet record, or a 365-day calendar; claims of precise stellar alignments as the enclosures' purpose; and appropriations of the site as evidence for a lost advanced civilisation. See Section XX for each claim and the published responses to it. NOT KNOWN What the builders called the place, what they believed, what any single carving “means”, and what was said or done inside an enclosure. The iconography plainly carried meaning for its makers; without texts, its specific content is beyond recovery, and honest scholarship says so. II. The Hill and Its Landscape Göbekli Tepe — the name is Turkish for “potbelly hill” — is an artificial mound, a tell, rising about 15 metres above a flat limestone plateau in the Germuş mountain range, some 15 kilometres north-east of Şanlıurfa and about 90 kilometres east of the Euphrates. The mound measures roughly 300 metres across and covers about 8–9 hectares. From its top the Harran plain opens to the south; on a clear day the view reaches toward the Syrian border. The plateau itself supplied both of the builders' essential raw materials on the spot: soft limestone bedrock for pillars and walls, and flint for the tools that worked it. The world of 9500 BCE was not the dry steppe of today. At the end of the last Ice Age and in the early Holocene the region was a more open, better-watered grassland. Pollen, charcoal, and faunal evidence assembled by the project indicate a landscape of wild cereals — wild einkorn, emmer, and barley among them — with pistachio and almond the dominant trees in the charcoal record, and grazing herds of gazelle, wild sheep and goat, aurochs, and equids on the plains below. That abundance matters for everything that follows: Göbekli Tepe was not built in a marginal desert by desperate people. It was built at a rich ecotone, where plant foods could be gathered in quantity and game — above all the seasonally migrating goitered gazelle — could be hunted at scale. Water was the site's one obvious problem, and for two decades it was used as an argument that nobody can have lived there: there is no spring on the hill. Work reported by Lee Clare and colleagues for 2015–2019 changed that picture. Channels cut in the bedrock, covered in places with limestone slabs, lead toward large rock-cut cisterns; one partially excavated pit in the north-west of the mound measures some 8 metres across and 2.8 metres deep. The project now reads the plateau as a rainwater-harvesting system capable of supporting occupation. The absence-of-water argument against settlement has not survived its own excavation. // READING THE MOUND // A tell is not a natural hill. It is the accumulated debris of occupation itself — collapsed walls, discarded tools, ash, bone, and fill, layer upon layer. Göbekli Tepe's mound is therefore part of the evidence: the hill the builders' successors stood on was, in large part, made by the building. The site also sits inside a named geography that the Sources use consistently. Upper Mesopotamia here means the upland arc between the middle and upper Euphrates and Tigris and the Taurus foothills — modern south-eastern Turkey, northern Syria, and northern Iraq. In the literature on early farming this same arc, where the wild ancestors of the founder crops overlap, has been called the “Golden Triangle” and, by Lev-Yadun and colleagues, a core area — sometimes rendered “cradle” — of agriculture. Göbekli Tepe stands near its centre, within reach of the Karacadağ mountains, where genetic work beginning with Heun and colleagues in 1997 located the wild einkorn population most closely related to domesticated einkorn. Monument and wheat share a landscape. Whether they share a causal story is the subject of Section XVII. III. Discovery: From a Survey Note to a Research Project Göbekli Tepe was not lost, exactly. It was recorded, filed, and misunderstood. In 1963 a joint survey by Istanbul University and the University of Chicago visited the hill; Peter Benedict's report described mounds of reddish soil, recognised Neolithic flint on the surface, and took the worked limestone slabs for parts of a much later cemetery. The significance of the flint carpet and the slabs was not grasped, and the site rested in the literature for thirty years. Popular retellings sometimes sharpen this into a story of blindness; the record is duller and more instructive. A survey sees surfaces, and on the surface the tops of T-pillars look like grave markers. What changed the reading was not a better guess but a comparison — with a site that had just been dug. That comparison came from Nevalı Çori , a Pre-Pottery Neolithic B settlement excavated under Harald Hauptmann between 1983 and 1991 in advance of the Atatürk Dam, which flooded it in 1991–92. Nevalı Çori produced a rectangular communal building unlike its houses: benches around the walls, monumental sculpture, and T-shaped pillars — including a central pair — set into its fabric. A member of that team was Klaus Schmidt (1953–2014). When Schmidt set out in 1994 to survey the Urfa region for further early sites, he carried Nevalı Çori's plan in his head. Guided to the flint-covered hill, he recognised a worked stone in a field-clearance heap as the head of a T-pillar of the Nevalı Çori type. Schmidt's own published account of that October 1994 visit, reproduced in the DAI team's Expedition article listed in the Sources, describes the moment the bare limestone plateau began, in his word, to glitter with worked flint. Excavation began in 1995 as a joint project of the Şanlıurfa Museum and the German Archaeological Institute (DAI), directed by Schmidt. The first test trench, at the base of the south-eastern slope, struck rectangular buildings of what Schmidt would call Layer II. In the same season a landowner clearing his field uncovered the heads of two huge T-pillars and had begun to break one up with a sledgehammer before he was persuaded to stop; work in that south-eastern depression from 1996 onward revealed the first of the great circular enclosures, and with them the site's fame. Schmidt directed the excavation for twenty seasons, published the synthesis Sie bauten die ersten Tempel (2006; English edition, Göbekli Tepe: A Stone Age Sanctuary in South-Eastern Anatolia , 2012), and died suddenly in July 2014. Work did not stop with him. The project continued under the Şanlıurfa Museum and the DAI, with Lee Clare of the DAI's Istanbul Department coordinating research, and with Turkish prehistorian Necmi Karul of Istanbul University taking a leading role in the region's archaeology — including, from 2019, the excavation of Karahan Tepe and, from 2021, the coordination of the Taş Tepeler programme (Section XVIII). Two large protective shelters now cover the main excavation areas, and the deep soundings dug for their supports in 2015–2019 produced, incidentally and importantly, some of the evidence that has revised Schmidt's own interpretation. Less than a tenth of the mound has been excavated; geophysical survey indicates at least twenty large enclosures in total, most still underground. c. 9500–9000 BCE LAYER III ENCLOSURES Construction and use of the great circular enclosures (PPNA, extending in revised chronologies into the very early PPNB), in the dating scheme used by this hub. c. 9000–8000 BCE LAYER II AND LATER OCCUPATION Smaller rectangular buildings with reduced T-pillars, alongside continuing domestic occupation; building activity declines and the Neolithic settlement is abandoned around c. 8000 BCE. 1963 SURVEY RECORD The Istanbul–Chicago survey records the site; its Neolithic flint is noted but the T-pillar slabs are read as a later cemetery. 1994–1995 RECOGNITION AND FIRST SEASON Klaus Schmidt recognises the T-pillar head in October 1994; excavation by the Şanlıurfa Museum and the DAI begins in 1995. 2014 SCHMIDT'S DEATH Schmidt dies in July 2014. The project continues under Turkish and DAI direction; building-archaeology and dating programmes intensify. 2018 WORLD HERITAGE INSCRIPTION UNESCO inscribes Göbekli Tepe on 1 July 2018 under criteria (i), (ii), and (iv). See Section XXI. 2021 TAŞ TEPELER LAUNCHED Turkey's Ministry of Culture and Tourism launches the Taş Tepeler programme, coordinating work at about a dozen related sites under Necmi Karul. IV. Chronology: Layers, Radiocarbon, and Revision Schmidt divided the mound into three layers. Layer III , the oldest, contained the great round enclosures and was assigned to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA). Layer II contained smaller rectangular buildings with much reduced T-pillars and was assigned to the early and middle Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB). Layer I was simply everything above — the plough horizon and later traces. In round numbers, and in the form this hub uses, Layer III belongs to c. 9500–9000 BCE and Layer II runs on to the site's abandonment around c. 8000 BCE . Those dates remain a fair summary of the span. What has changed is how sharply the layers are separated, and how the dates were obtained. Dating a stone building is indirect work. Radiocarbon measures organic material — charcoal, bone, the organic fraction in mud mortar and wall plaster — not the limestone itself, so every date constrains a context: a fill, a floor make-up, a mortar, a repair. Göbekli Tepe's first dates, published from 1998, came from enclosure fill and clustered in the late 10th and early 9th millennia, younger than a PPNA attribution predicted. Schmidt's team explained the discrepancy through their backfilling theory: the fill, they proposed, was material brought in at abandonment and so post-dated use. Dates on organic material in wall plaster seemed to restore the older chronology. Both props have since been kicked away by the project's own later work: the fill is no longer read as imported (Section XVI), and plaster dates are recognised as vulnerable to the “old wood effect”, in which long-lived or reused timber makes a sample older than its context. The current position, set out in Clare's 2020 summary of the 2015–2019 research and in the building-archaeology programme of Kinzel and Clare, rests on AMS dates from the mud mortar of the special buildings themselves. Those dates are more homogeneous than the fill dates and they tell a longer story: enclosures A–D were multi-phase buildings, maintained, remodelled, and repaired over centuries, with some final building phases around the middle of the 9th millennium BCE — more than five hundred years after their foundations. On Clare's calibration, the round-oval special buildings (Schmidt's Layer III) span roughly 9500–8700 BCE and the rectangular buildings (Layer II) roughly 8700–8200 BCE , with a clear overlap between them, and the site as a whole is now commonly cited as c. 9500–8000 BCE . Schmidt's neat three-part sequence has been abandoned by the project in favour of a finer, multi-phase history — eight phases in the most recent published synthesis. The enclosures were not a single generation's gesture. They were institutions with biographies. Unit Character Dates used in this article Period Layer III Large circular–oval enclosures; T-pillars to c. 5.5 m c. 9500–9000 BCE (foundations; use and remodelling into the mid-9th millennium in the revised chronology) PPNA, into earliest PPNB Layer II Smaller rectangular buildings; T-pillars reduced, sometimes absent c. 8800–8000 BCE Early–middle PPNB Layer I Post-Neolithic surface horizon After c. 8000 BCE — Karahan Tepe Rock-cut and built special buildings; T-pillars Broadly contemporary, c. 9400–8000 BCE for main building activity PPNA–early PPNB // A NOTE ON DATES IN THE POPULAR PRESS // Headline ages for Göbekli Tepe vary — 11,000, 11,600, or 12,000 years — mostly because writers convert differently from BCE or round from different phases. The disagreements that matter are smaller and more specific: which context a sample came from, and whether it dates a building's construction, use, repair, or filling. Any claim that hangs a precise year on a single pillar — including the astronomical claims in Section XX — should be asked which dated context it rests on. Usually, it rests on none. V. The Pre-Pottery Neolithic Framework The Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) is the early Neolithic of the Levant and Upper Mesopotamia before the adoption of ceramic vessels: a world of stone, bone, wood, basketry, plaster, and ground-stone technology. Kathleen Kenyon coined the subdivisions PPNA and PPNB from her excavations at Jericho, and the terms stuck for the whole region. In the calibrations used by the Göbekli Tepe project, the PPNA runs approximately 9600–8800 BCE and the PPNB approximately 8800–7000 BCE , with the early PPNB (EPPNB) covering roughly 8700–8200 BCE. Different textbooks shift these boundaries by a century or two; the sequence, not the exact hinge years, is what carries weight. Across those two millennia and more, the PPN saw, in uneven and locally variable order: the first permanent and semi-permanent villages of round, then increasingly rectangular, houses; the intensive management of wild cereals and pulses; the appearance of morphologically domesticated founder crops — einkorn and emmer wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch, flax; the domestication of goat, sheep, pig, and cattle, mostly a PPNB story; large communal buildings at many sites; plastered human skulls and other elaborate treatments of the dead; and long-distance movement of valued materials such as Anatolian obsidian. The older textbook image of a single “Neolithic Revolution” — V. Gordon Childe's coinage of 1936 — has given way to a long transition in which different elements arrive at different times in different valleys. Göbekli Tepe's importance inside that framework is precise: its monumental phase falls at the beginning of the sequence, when villages were new, farming did not yet exist, and pottery, metal, and writing were all millennia in the future. PPNA · c. 9600–8800 BCE Round houses; communal buildings including Jericho's tower phase and Göbekli Tepe's first enclosures; intensive wild-cereal use; no domesticated crops or herds yet in the Upper Mesopotamian record. PPNB · c. 8800–7000 BCE Rectangular, often two-storey houses; domesticated crops widespread and herded animals appearing; large planned villages such as Çayönü and 'Ain Ghazal; plastered skulls; Göbekli Tepe's later, smaller buildings belong to its first half. AFTER THE PPN Pottery Neolithic communities spread farming lifeways across Anatolia and into Europe and deepen them in Mesopotamia. Cities, states, and writing are still three to five thousand years away — a gap this hub's Egyptian articles take up from the other end. One more framework term recurs in the literature and is worth defining once, carefully: the excavators' phrase special buildings . Across the PPN, some buildings differ from houses in scale, in fittings — benches, pillars, terrazzo or plaster floors, niches — in the objects deposited in them, or in their position within a settlement. Archaeologists call these special or communal buildings and infer gatherings, ceremonies, and collective work from them. The term is deliberately non-committal about gods, priests, or doctrine. Göbekli Tepe's enclosures are the largest and earliest famous examples of the class, but they are members of a class — a fact that matters when the site is treated, in popular writing, as if it had no relatives. VI. Architecture: The Great Enclosures A Layer III enclosure is a ring, not a roofed hall in any simple sense. A wall of rough, unworked stone set in clay mortar, roughly circular or oval and between about 10 and 30 metres across, encloses a floor that is often the smoothed bedrock itself, sometimes laid with a terrazzo-like burnt-lime surface. Into the inner face of the ring wall stand T-shaped pillars, up to about 4 metres high in the ring, their broad faces turned inward. A low stone bench commonly runs along the wall between them. At the centre stand two much larger T-pillars, parallel to one another, set into pedestals cut from the bedrock — in Enclosure D the pedestals are only about 20 centimetres deep, a socket that has prompted much discussion of how the pillars were stabilised, braced, and possibly roofed. Whether the enclosures carried roofs is genuinely unresolved. Schmidt generally envisaged open or partly covered structures; Banning argued in 2011, from the span, the pillars' proportions, and ethnographic parallels, that roofing was feasible and likely; the DAI team's building archaeologists now discuss partial roofing, collapse, and repeated repair as parts of the buildings' long lives. The honest summary is that the ground plan is certain and the elevation is reconstruction. Drawings that show a single confident roofline are showing a hypothesis. The enclosures were also not built once and frozen. Building archaeology — the close reading of wall junctions, inserted pillars, blocked passages, added benches, and repaired damage — shows walls rebuilt inside earlier walls, ring pillars replaced or supplemented, floors renewed, and, in Enclosure C, a sequence of concentric rings. Enclosure C's central pillars were smashed in antiquity; their fragments, found in a pit dug for the purpose, were laser-scanned and virtually reassembled by the project to an original height of about 5 metres. Damage, repair, and remodelling are part of the record, and they are one reason the project's current language speaks of building biographies rather than a single construction event. Layer II: The Rectangular Turn The Layer II buildings are smaller, rectangular, and far less monumental: rooms and small complexes in which T-pillars, where present at all, stand under 2 metres and may number only a central pair — the so-called Lion Pillar Building, named for its pair of pillars carved with rearing lions, is the best known — or none. Under Schmidt's scheme this was a later, diminished phase. Under the revised chronology the rectangular form overlaps the enclosures' later lives and also belongs to the site's domestic architecture, which raises a possibility the older literature underplayed: the difference between Layer III and Layer II may be as much functional and social as chronological — great communal buildings and houses changing together — as it is a simple story of decline. The temptation to read shrinking pillars as fading faith should be resisted; it imports a narrative the stones do not supply. VII. Enclosures A–D, and Beyond The excavated enclosures are lettered in order of discovery. Four dominate the literature, and each has a distinct character — a fact worth dwelling on, because it suggests the enclosures were not copies of a single template but individual buildings, perhaps belonging to different groups, occasions, or generations. ENCLOSURE A Among the first excavated in the south-eastern depression. Its pillars carry snakes prominently, including a net-like relief of serpents on one pillar, and its plan includes a distinctive entrance arrangement. A is a reminder that each enclosure's imagery leans toward particular animals — a pattern whose meaning is debated but whose existence is not. ENCLOSURE B A smaller ring whose pillars are dominated by foxes. Its central area produced a floor of terrazzo-like material, and bone samples from B have figured in the site's radiocarbon discussions. B's modest scale, beside D's monumentality, is part of the evidence that the enclosures were built to different briefs. ENCLOSURE C The boar enclosure: wild boars dominate its sculpture, including free-standing boar statues and, on Pillar 27, a predator carved in high relief descending the shaft, cut from the same stone as the pillar itself. Its concentric rings and its smashed-and-reassembled central pillars make C the key building for the site's biography approach. ENCLOSURE D The largest and best preserved. Two central pillars (18 and 31), about 5.5 metres high and around 8–10 tonnes each, stand in bedrock pedestals inside a ring of eleven excavated wall pillars. Foxes, snakes, cranes and other birds, boar, aurochs, gazelle, and more crowd its reliefs — including Pillar 43, the so-called Vulture Stone, discussed in Sections IX and XX. Beyond A–D, enclosures E to H and further structures have been identified in the western and north-western parts of the mound. Enclosure E, the so-called rock temple, was largely cleared of its fittings in antiquity and survives as a bedrock-cut platform with pillar pedestals and a relief frieze; Enclosure H, excavated more recently, has added further large pillars and sculpture to the corpus. Geophysics — principally geomagnetic survey and ground-penetrating radar — indicates at least twenty enclosures across the mound. The excavated sample on which all generalisations rest is therefore small, selected by erosion, land use, and the accident of where trenches were opened. Every confident sentence about “Göbekli Tepe” in general should be read with that sampling warning attached. Two associated finds widen the architectural picture. First, the quarries: on the plateau beside the mound lie unfinished T-pillars still attached to the bedrock, the largest about 7 metres long and estimated at some 50 tonnes — abandoned workpieces that show both the method (a pillar was cut free as a single monolith) and the ambition (the largest pillar ever attempted at the site was never moved). Second, sculpture in the round: statues, animal figures, and a composite “totem pole” recovered in 2009, carved with stacked figures and found in a Layer II context, show that the pillars were one element of a broader sculptural practice, not the whole of it. VIII. The T-Pillars Are Figures The T-shape is an abstraction, and the site itself tells us of what. On the central pillars of Enclosure D the narrow side of the shaft carries, in low relief, two arms bent forward, long-fingered hands meeting above the belly, a decorated belt, and a loincloth formed like an animal skin hanging below it. Read with those details, the pillar resolves: the broad T-head is a head in profile — its narrow edge the face, featureless by design — the shaft is a body, and the pillar is not decorated with a person. It is a person, rendered at monumental scale in the most economical possible geometry. The DAI team's synthesis makes this reading explicitly, and the belted, loinclothed central pair of Enclosure D is its standard exhibit. The excavators have further noted the strongly masculine cast of the imagery: where the sex of a depicted animal can be determined it is male, and comparison with belted male figurines from Nevalı Çori led Schmidt's team to read the Enclosure D pair as male figures, while acknowledging that the loincloths cover the evidence and certainty is impossible. That observation is worth keeping in its exact, limited form. It describes a pattern in the carvings; it does not recover a theology of masculinity, and the literature's more expansive claims in that direction go beyond the reliefs. Two consequences follow from the anthropomorphic reading. The first is architectural: an enclosure is a gathering of stone persons around a central pair — a ring of presences facing inward — whatever else it also was. The second is comparative, and it has recently sharpened. At Karahan Tepe in 2025 the excavators announced a T-pillar bearing a carved human face — brows, eyes, nose — the first of its kind reported from the Taş Tepeler, found, notably, in a building with domestic equipment. If the T-pillars are stylised human figures, a faced example is the missing explicit instance. The announcement is recent and its full publication is awaited, so this article records it as reported by the excavation director rather than as a settled datum — but it points the same way as the arms, hands, belts, and loincloths have pointed since Enclosure D was cleared. How a Pillar Was Made A T-pillar began in the plateau quarries as a single block outlined in the bedrock, freed with flint tools, and shaped where it lay or after a short move; the unfinished 7-metre example shows the process interrupted. Finished pillars were transported — distances on site are short, but a 10-tonne monolith is a 10-tonne monolith — erected into wall or pedestal, and carved, at least in part, in place. No metal, no wheels, no draught animals, and no pulleys are attested anywhere in this world. Flint picks and hammerstones, levers, ropes of plant fibre, timber, water, abrasion, and organised human muscle are the entire available toolkit, and experimental and ethnographic reasoning about megalith transport elsewhere in prehistory shows that toolkit to be sufficient. The achievement is organisational, not technological — which is precisely why it is historically important. IX. Iconography: A World of Wild Animals The reliefs cover the broad faces and shafts of the pillars, usually in flat, carefully modelled low relief, occasionally in high relief or in the round. The repertoire is overwhelmingly animal and overwhelmingly wild: foxes, snakes in profusion, scorpions, spiders, wild boar, aurochs, gazelle, wild ass, cranes, storks, ibis, ducks and other birds, vultures, and large predators. Domesticated animals are absent because domesticated animals, in this place and century, did not yet exist. Alongside the fauna stand abstract signs — H-shaped and crescent-and-disc motifs among them — and, rarely, human figures, most famously the headless man on Pillar 43. Schmidt's team observed early that the animal emphasis differs by enclosure — boars in C, foxes prominent in B and D, snakes in A — and proposed that the enclosures may have belonged to different groups, each with its own emblematic animal, or that the imagery encodes narratives now unrecoverable. Both proposals remain proposals. What the reliefs establish beyond reasonable dispute is narrower and still remarkable: a shared, disciplined visual language, executed by skilled carvers to a consistent standard across multiple buildings and generations, depicting the dangerous and powerful wildlife of the builders' own landscape. Snakes, scorpions, predators, and carrion birds are not a random bestiary; the repertoire leans toward creatures that command caution and respect. Dietrich and Notroff's work on the imagery treats it as a communicative system embedded in the architecture — the pillars do not merely stand in the building, they populate it. Pillar 43, the “Vulture Stone” Pillar 43, a ring pillar in Enclosure D, carries the site's most discussed composition. Described neutrally, its broad face shows, in registers: rows of nested V-shaped marks along the top; three bag- or basket-like forms, each surmounted by an animal; a large vulture with one wing raised toward a disc or sphere; a scorpion; further birds and animals; and, at the lower right, a headless human figure. A separate head appears nearby in the composition. Every element in that description is visible on the stone. Every further statement — that the animals are constellations, that the disc is the sun at a particular solstice, that the scene dates a comet — is interpretation, and contested interpretation at that. The pillar gets its own full treatment in Section XX, because the gap between the carving and the claims made for it is the clearest case study this hub has in how Tier A evidence and modern construction come apart. // HOW TO READ A RELIEF CLAIM // Ask three questions of any proposed reading of Göbekli Tepe's imagery. Does it account for the whole corpus — more than sixty excavated pillars — or only for one photogenic example? Does it assume the builders saw the same constellations, symbols, or calendar as a much later culture, and if so, on what evidence? And could the same carvings be “read” to a different conclusion by the same method? The excavators' published response to the astronomical readings (Notroff, Dietrich, and colleagues, 2017) presses exactly these points. X. The Builders: Hunter-Gatherers, Not Farmers The single most consequential fact about Göbekli Tepe is a negative: in decades of excavation, no domesticated plant and no domesticated animal has been identified from its Neolithic occupation. The archaeobotanical record, though sparse in carbonised remains, yields wild einkorn, wild barley, and possibly wild wheat or rye, with almond and pistachio. The faunal record, by contrast, is enormous. Joris Peters and colleagues' archaeozoological work on more than a hundred thousand bone fragments shows a diet and a debris dominated by wild game: goitered gazelle above all — over 60 per cent in the assemblages Schmidt's team reported — with aurochs, wild boar, wild sheep and goat, red deer, hare, fox, and birds. Seasonal indicators point to large-scale gazelle hunting between midsummer and autumn, consistent with intercepting the herds' migrations past the hill. The builders were therefore hunter-gatherers — but the phrase misleads if it conjures small, fleeting bands. The PPN world of Upper Mesopotamia was already experimenting with permanence: semi-sedentary and sedentary hunter-gatherer villages precede and accompany Göbekli Tepe across the region, and the old opposition between mobile foragers and settled farmers has dissolved in the evidence. People could live in one place for much of the year, store wild grain, manage stands of wild cereals, build in stone, and still plant no domesticated crop and herd no domesticated animal. Göbekli Tepe's builders stood inside that in-between world, and the site's later fame rests on the demonstration that monumentality belongs to it. Did they live on the hill itself? Schmidt's answer was no: the early seasons found no houses, hearths, or middens where he expected them, and the site was interpreted as a sanctuary visited periodically by groups from a wide catchment. That answer has been reversed by the project's own later work. The 2015–2019 deep soundings found agglutinated round-oval houses with hearth sequences and bead-working debris in the north-west, further round houses on the western slope, and, for the early PPNB, dense rectangular domestic building — in one case with a sub-floor burial, a hallmark of PPN domestic sites. Lithic assemblages are, in Clare's summary, wholly characteristic of domestic contexts. The current picture is of a settlement that contained special buildings — or, in Banning's sharper formulation discussed in Section XVII, of very large, symbolically charged houses within a settlement. Either way, “a temple with nobody home” is no longer a description the excavation team itself defends. XI.

x: Before Kemet Antiquity · The World Before Dynastic Egypt // BEFORE 3100 BCE :: THE RECORD, THE TRADITION, AND THE TELLING KEPT APART // A research hub for everything that came before the unification of Egypt — what archaeology can attest, what ancient texts claimed, and what modern writers constructed, each labelled as what it is. TIER A — ATTESTED TIER B — ANCIENT TRADITION TIER C — MODERN CONSTRUCTION ANTIQUITY HOME // ARCHIVE CONTENTS // I. Introduction — Three Kinds of Evidence II. How to Read This Hub III. The Master Timeline — Tier A: The Attested Deep Past IV. The Master Timeline — Tier B: Ancient Traditions About the Deep Past V. The Master Timeline — Tier C: Modern Constructions VI. Article Index — The Mesopotamia Wing — Tier A — The Attested Record — Tier B — Ancient Traditions — Tier C — Modern Constructions VII. Sources and Further Reading I. Introduction — Three Kinds of Evidence This hub covers what came before dynastic Egypt — before the unification of the Two Lands around 3100 BCE that opens the Egyptology archive proper. Its subject is therefore enormous: the first pigment workshops of the African Middle Stone Age, the first bread, the first temples, the first metals and the first writing, and the long human story that made Kemet possible. But its subject is also double. Alongside the attested past stand the stories told about that past — by Sumerian scribes, Egyptian priests, Plato, and, much later, by Theosophists, antiquarians and modern esoteric orders. Popular writing habitually blurs those two subjects into one seamless "hidden history." This hub refuses the blur. It separates, plainly and prominently, three kinds of evidence : TIER A Attested deep past. Archaeology and the physical sciences: excavated sites, dated objects, laboratory chronologies. Tier A entries can be cited, checked and argued with on evidence. Where specialists debate a date or an interpretation, the debate is stated. TIER B Ancient traditions about the deep past. Real texts — king lists, flood epics, philosophical dialogues — studied seriously as texts . A Tier B entry sits on the timeline at its text's real date of composition, and what the text says about remoter ages is always labelled as the text's claim , never narrated as fact. TIER C Modern esoteric constructions. Nineteenth- to twenty-first-century creations — Lemuria, Mu, root races, clairvoyant chronologies — presented with their documented origins: who proposed them, when, and from what materials. They are treated respectfully, as a living tradition and a real chapter of intellectual history, and never passed off as attested fact. // THE HUB'S RULE // Every timeline entry and every article in this hub wears its tier. Speculation is studied seriously as tradition — and never passed off as attested fact. If you remember nothing else from this page, remember the badge. The rule cuts both ways. Tier A is not a certificate of final truth: radiocarbon calibrations shift, a "stone circle" may turn out to be a cattle kraal, and this hub says so where scholars say so. Tier B is not a wastebasket: the Sumerian King List is a sophisticated political-theological document, and the Egyptian idea of a First Time shaped three thousand years of temple building whether or not any golden age preceded it. Tier C is not a punchline: the modern lost-continent literature is the native mythology of the modern esoteric revival, and orders that still teach from it — the Inner Garden Foundation among them — are part of the record this hub exists to document fairly. A word about models and debts. The single chronological spine of this page owes a structural debt to traditional timelines of the kind maintained by modern orders — the Inner Garden Foundation's timeline is the example closest to hand — which set Lemuria, Atlantis, the patriarchs and the pharaohs on one continuous line. That format has a real virtue: it lets a reader see a tradition's whole shape at once. This hub keeps the single spine and changes one thing: every entry on it is tiered, so that a reader can also see, at a glance, which entries rest on excavation, which on ancient testimony, and which on modern construction. The tradition's shape is preserved; its epistemology is made visible. Nothing here copies the text of any order's timeline, and errors found in popular timelines — a Papyrus of Ani misdated by millennia, an Arab conquest of Egypt misdated by centuries — are not inherited: every date below was checked independently for this hub. The hub's endpoint is deliberate. At c. 3100 BCE the timeline crosses a threshold into the dynastic record, and the story continues in the Egyptology division: see the Predynastic article and the Egyptology timeline . Everything after that threshold on this page — the Tier B texts and the whole of Tier C — is here not because it predates Kemet, but because it talks about what predates Kemet. // DELIBERATE EXCLUSIONS // Two absences in this hub are decisions, not oversights. The civilisations of the pre-Columbian Americas are out of scope: the Americas enter this archive's story through the peopling of the continents, not through their later states, which belong to no hub here. And Iron Age Europe — Celts, druids, the Norse world — is likewise excluded; Europe's Neolithic megaliths are in scope as part of the attested deep past, but its Iron Age peoples feed no line this archive follows. Future audits should not re-flag either as a gap. II. How to Read This Hub Dates before the historic era are given as BP (years before present, the archaeologist's convention) where the literature uses BP, and as BCE thereafter; "c." marks an approximate date throughout. Tier A dates are calibrated scholarly estimates, not anniversaries — treat the last two digits of any Pleistocene date as weather, not clockwork. Tier B entries are dated by composition or by the date of the surviving copies, and the antiquity the text claims is stated inside the entry, in the entry's own words, as a claim. Tier C entries are dated by publication or by the documented life of the tradition that produced them. READING TIER A Ask: what was found, where, and how was it dated? The entries name the site and the method — radiocarbon, uranium-series, stratigraphy — wherever the claim depends on them. READING TIER B Ask: who wrote this, when, and for whom? A king list is an argument about legitimacy before it is a chronicle; a dialogue is philosophy before it is reportage. Genre is evidence. READING TIER C Ask: what did the author actually have in hand? A zoological puzzle, a misread codex, a claimed clairvoyant record — the documented origin is always more interesting than the rumour of one. // A NOTE ON RESPECT // Tiering is a claim about evidence, not about worth, sincerity or spiritual value. Several Tier C chronologies are taught today within living traditions whose members hold them in good faith. This hub documents those teachings in their own terms, corrects only what the documentary record settles (publication dates, misattributed sources, demonstrable misdatings), and leaves questions of inner meaning to the traditions themselves. III. The Master Timeline — Tier A: The Attested Deep Past Fifty-six entries run from the first systematic use of pigment to the threshold of the pharaonic state, and a short coda of four later entries — flagged where they stand — follows the threshold marker: sixty in all. This is the spine of fact against which everything else in the hub is measured. c. 176,500 BP TIER A Bruniquel — building in the dark. 336 metres inside Bruniquel Cave in southwestern France, beyond all daylight, early Neanderthals broke more than 400 stalagmites to a standard length and laid them in two rings — the larger 6.7 by 4.5 metres — and four stacks, with traces of fire throughout the chamber. Uranium-series dating of regrowth on the structures and of burnt bone gives a replicated age of 176.5 ± 2.1 thousand years, making these the oldest well-dated constructions attributed to any human population. What the rings were for is unknown; that they required sustained light, several builders, and a shared plan is inference from the structure itself. See The Other Humans — Neanderthal and Denisovan Symbolic Worlds . c. 164,000 BP TIER A Ochre use at Pinnacle Point, South Africa. In cave PP13B on the southern Cape coast, Marean and colleagues documented systematic collection and use of red ochre alongside early exploitation of shellfish, dated to about 164,000 years ago (give or take some 12,000). It is among the earliest widely accepted evidence that early Homo sapiens treated a pigment as worth gathering, grading and keeping. The pigment sequence that begins here is traced in full in Ochre and Symbol . c. 142,000–100,000 BP TIER A Shell beads across Africa and the Levant. Perforated marine shells — at Bizmoune Cave in Morocco possibly as early as c. 142,000 years ago, and at Skhul and Taforalt in the c. 135,000–82,000 BP range — show that personal ornament, and with it a social, symbolic self, long predates any cave painting. The Moroccan dates remain debated; the pattern across sites does not. c. 130,000–115,000 BP TIER A Neanderthal ornament and pigment. In a single level at Krapina, Croatia, dated to about 130,000 years ago, Neanderthals accumulated eight white-tailed eagle talons from at least three birds — cut-marked, polished, and notched as if strung together as jewellery. Some fifteen millennia later, at Cueva de los Aviones in Spain, Neanderthals perforated and pigment-stained marine shells and mixed prepared pigment recipes in shell containers, in a deposit sealed under flowstone uranium-series dated to about 115,000–120,000 years ago. Both finds predate any modern human presence in Europe, closing the argument that such practices were copied from incoming neighbours. See The Other Humans — Neanderthal and Denisovan Symbolic Worlds . c. 100,000 BP TIER A The Blombos ochre-processing workshop. At Blombos Cave, South Africa, Henshilwood's team recovered two abalone shells holding a liquefied red pigment mixture — ochre, bone and charcoal, ground and stirred to a recipe — with the grindstones and hammerstones of the toolkit beside them ( Science , 2011). It is the earliest known paint-making kit: chemistry, storage and planning in one assemblage. See Ochre and Symbol . c. 77,000–75,000 BP TIER A Engraved ochre and Nassarius beads at Blombos. Pieces of ochre ground flat and incised with deliberate cross-hatched designs, and perforated Nassarius shell beads worn from stringing, come from the same cave's Still Bay layers. The engravings carry no practical function anyone has identified; they are pattern for pattern's sake, and therefore among the earliest material signs of symbolic thought. c. 73,000 BP TIER A The Blombos silcrete drawing. A flake of silcrete from Blombos bears nine red lines drawn with an ochre crayon — the oldest known drawing, published in Nature in 2018. Modest as it looks, it demonstrates the full chain — pigment prepared, point shaped, lines planned on a surface — tens of millennia before Lascaux. c. 65,000 BP TIER A Madjedbebe, Arnhem Land. At a sandstone shelter on the western edge of the Arnhem Land plateau, in Mirarr Country, excavators piece-plotted some 11,000 artefacts and dated the lowest dense occupation band — edge-ground hatchet fragments, grinding stones, and ground ochre — by single-grain optically stimulated luminescence to about 65,000 years ago (Clarkson et al., Nature 2017): if the association between artefacts and dated sand holds, the earliest occupation of Sahul yet published. The association is contested — O'Connell and colleagues argue that termite bioturbation could have carried younger artefacts into older sediment, and hold an age beyond 50,000 years unlikely; the excavators answer with refits, intact hearths, and trampling experiments, and the debate remains open. The uncontested floor for northern Australia is c. 50,000 BP. See Sahul — The First Crossing and the Long Occupation . c. 60,000 BP TIER A Engraved ostrich eggshell at Diepkloof. Fragments of ostrich eggshell containers from Diepkloof Rock Shelter, South Africa, carry repeated hatched and parallel-line motifs, made over generations to a shared convention. A motif repeated to a standard is a symbol system in embryo: the mark identifies the container, and perhaps its owner. c. 50,000 BP TIER A Denisova Cave — three populations, one sequence. Denisova Cave in Siberia's Altai Mountains is the only site where Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans are all attested in one sequence. Its Early Upper Palaeolithic levels, spanning the period around 50,000 years ago when all three populations used the cave, yielded ostrich-eggshell beads, ivory and tooth pendants, a marble ring, a drilled chloritolite bracelet, and an eyed bone needle among the oldest known. No Denisovan fossil was found in direct association with these objects, and their maker cannot yet be assigned with confidence — a caution the archive prints alongside the finds. See The Other Humans — Neanderthal and Denisovan Symbolic Worlds . at least c. 45,500 BP TIER A Figurative cave art in Sulawesi, Indonesia. A painting of a Sulawesi warty pig at Leang Tedongnge is at least 45,500 years old by uranium-series dating of the calcite over it, and a narrative scene at Leang Karampuang has since been dated to at least 51,200 BP. Figurative art was not a European invention; it was already old on the far side of the world while Europe's painted caves were still in the future. c. 43,000 BP TIER A The Ngwenya hematite mine, Eswatini. The Lion Cave at Ngwenya is the oldest known mine in the world: Middle Stone Age miners dug for hematite and specularite — red pigment ore — some 43,000 years ago. Industrial-scale desire for colour, organised and inherited, is itself a datum about the minds that wanted it. c. 36,000 BP TIER A The Chauvet Cave paintings, France. The Ardèche cave's lions, rhinoceroses and horses, drawn in charcoal and ochre in two main phases around 37,000–33,500 BP, display shading, wall preparation and composition of a maturity that overturned the idea of art evolving from crude to skilled. Chauvet is the European benchmark — and, after Sulawesi, no longer the world's oldest. c. 34,000 BP TIER A Early textiles — the Dzudzuana fibres, Georgia. In the clay deposits of Dzudzuana Cave, in the foothills of the Caucasus in Georgia, microscopic bast fibres survive from Upper Palaeolithic layers radiocarbon dated to 32,000–26,000 years BP, about 36,000–31,000 calendar years ago. Identified by Kvavadze and colleagues ( Science , 2009) as wild flax — an identification formally disputed since, in favour of bast fibre generally — the fibres number in the hundreds in the oldest unit alone. Some are spun, some twisted, one thread knotted, and dozens are dyed, in black, grey, turquoise, and other colours: worked thread and cordage in routine use more than thirty millennia before farming. The full treatment is given in Ochre and Symbol . c. 23,000–21,000 BP TIER A Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico. On the shore of palaeolake Otero in the Tularosa Basin, trackways of barefoot people — mostly adolescents and children, among mammoth and giant sloth tracks — survive on multiple buried surfaces at WHSA Locality 2. Bennett et al. ( Science , 2021) dated them by Ruppia seed layers to the Last Glacial Maximum; a reservoir-effect critique (Oviatt et al., 2022) was answered by independent pollen radiocarbon and quartz OSL ages (Pigati et al., Science , 2023) and lakebed-mud dates (Holliday et al., 2025) converging on the same span. If the age stands, people were south of the ice sheets during the glacial maximum itself. The full argument, both rounds, is set out in The Peopling of the Americas . c. 20,000 BP TIER A Pottery at Xianrendong Cave, China. Sherds from Xianrendong, Jiangxi, dated to about 20,000–19,000 BP ( Science , 2012), are the earliest known pottery vessels — made by Ice Age hunter-gatherers some ten thousand years before farming. Fired clay begins as a forager's technology, a fact that reorders the usual story in which pots follow ploughs. from c. 14,000 BCE TIER A The Jōmon period of Japan begins. Around 14,000 BCE, hunter-fisher-gatherers in Japan begin making some of the earliest pottery in the world — cord-marked vessels by people who would sustain a sedentary, pottery-using way of life for more than thirteen thousand years without staple agriculture. Pit-house villages, shell middens, storage pits, lacquer working, and clay dogū figurines elaborate across the sequence, reaching their greatest scale at settlements such as Sannai-Maruyama (c. 3900–2200 BCE), where hundreds of people lived in a planned village on fish, game, and managed chestnut forest. The Jōmon are the standing proof that sedentism and complexity do not require farming. The full treatment is at Neolithic East Asia — Jōmon, Yangshao, and Jiahu . c. 15,000–11,500 BP TIER A The Natufian culture of the Levant. The Natufians were the first broadly sedentary hunter-gatherers of the region: stone-built settlements, burials with ornaments, sickles and grinding stones for intensive wild-cereal use. They stand at the hinge between foraging and farming — settled life demonstrably came first, agriculture second. c. 14,800 BP TIER A The African Humid Period begins. Around 14,800 years ago, as the last ice age loosened, the strengthening monsoon began turning the Sahara green: lakes rose, rivers ran, and over the following millennia the largest desert on earth became savanna crossed by fishers, hunters, and then herders. The onset date rests on lake-core and dust records read together; the florescence it opened is entered below at c. 7500–5500 BCE. The green Sahara and its image-world are surveyed in The Green Sahara and Its Image-World . c. 14,600 BP TIER A Meltwater Pulse 1A and the drowning of Sundaland. As the Bølling warming began, global sea level rose 14–18 m in under 350 years (Tahiti coral record; Deschamps et al. 2012) — on the near-flat Sunda Shelf, a shoreline retreat of tens of kilometres within generations. Sundaland, the continent joining mainland Southeast Asia to Sumatra, Java, Borneo, and Bali, lost roughly half its area between the glacial maximum and the mid-Holocene; genetics (Hill et al. 2007; Kim et al. 2023) reads the modern map of the region's peoples as, in part, the signature of that displacement. See Drowned Landscapes . c. 14,500 BP TIER A Monte Verde, Chile — a settlement older than Clovis. On Chinchihuapi Creek in southern Chile, a peat bog preserved a community of some twenty to thirty people: a tent-like structure of about a dozen rooms, each with its own hearth, wooden tools, cordage, mastodon bone, dozens of food and medicinal plants, and nine species of seaweed carried from the Pacific coast (Dillehay excavations, 1977–1985). Its age — about 12,500 radiocarbon years, c. 14,500 calibrated years BP, a millennium before Clovis — was resisted for twenty years, then confirmed unanimously by a visiting panel of specialists in 1997, ending the Clovis-first consensus. Monte Verde remains the benchmark pre-Clovis site. See The Peopling of the Americas . c. 14,400 BP TIER A Bread at Shubayqa, Jordan. Charred remains of flatbread baked by Natufian hunter-gatherers at Shubayqa 1, from wild grains, tubers and mustard, predate the domestication of wheat by some four thousand years ( PNAS , 2018). Baking — and the labour chain behind it — was a forager invention that farming later inherited, not the other way round. c. 14,200 BP TIER A The Bonn-Oberkassel dog (Germany). In a double human burial at Oberkassel, near Bonn, a man and a woman were laid to rest with grave goods and two dogs — the oldest known joint burial of humans and a dog. Re-examination (Janssens et al., 2018) showed that the younger dog, dead at about 27–28 weeks, had survived repeated bouts of a distemper-like illness between 19 and 23 weeks of age, a survival the authors argue was possible only with weeks of intensive human care for an animal of no working use. The grave is the earliest durable evidence that the first domestication was also a companionship. The full treatment is in Göbekli Tepe . c. 13,000 BP TIER A Melian obsidian reaches Franchthi Cave. Pieces of obsidian in the Upper Palaeolithic levels of Franchthi Cave, on the shore of the Argolic Gulf, have been assigned by characterisation analysis to the quarries of Melos — an island never joined to the Greek mainland — and direct hydration dating of Melian exploitation spans the 13th to late 10th millennium BP. The glass crossed some 120 km of Aegean water in the hands of hunter-gatherers, millennia before farming: the earliest well-documented sea transport of a raw material anywhere. The full evidence, and the laboratory method that proves it, is set out in Early Seafaring and the Obsidian Trade . c. 9500 BCE TIER A Göbekli Tepe begun, southeastern Anatolia. On a hill above the Harran plain, communities still living largely by hunting and gathering raised circular enclosures of T-shaped limestone pillars, carved with animals and abstract signs, in the earliest phase dated to around 9500 BCE. Its excavator Klaus Schmidt argued the sanctuary came before the city; current research complicates that slogan — there is evidence of settlement too — but not the site's primacy among monumental ritual architecture. The site and its debates are examined in Göbekli Tepe . c. 11,000 BP TIER A The flooding of Beringia. The rising sea overtopped the c. 53 m sill of the Bering Strait and drowned the plain that had joined Siberia to Alaska for some twenty thousand years. A Herald Canyon core (Jakobsson et al. 2017) dates the Pacific's breakthrough to c. 11,000 cal BP; modelling (Pico et al. 2020) argues a two-phase flooding from c. 13,000 BP. Either way, the homeland in which the ancestors of the First Peoples had lived out the glacial maximum — the Beringian standstill — ceased to exist. See Drowned Landscapes and The Peopling of the Americas . c. 9000 BCE TIER A Karahan Tepe and the Taş Tepeler. Some 35 km from Göbekli Tepe, Karahan Tepe — occupied in the same Pre-Pottery Neolithic world, broadly c. 9400–8000 BCE — adds its own T-pillars, a bedrock-cut chamber and a hall of phallic pillars watched by a carved human head. Göbekli was not an anomaly but the best-known member of a whole ritual landscape, the "Stone Hills" now under excavation across the Şanlıurfa region. See Göbekli Tepe . c. 9000 BCE TIER A Jericho settled. Tell es-Sultan, Jericho, shows occupation by Natufian hunter-gatherers and then one of the earliest sustained farming settlements on earth, from around 9000 BCE. Its springs made it a place people returned to for eleven thousand years; its fame in later texts rests on this very real antiquity. The full sequence — Natufian camp, first farmers, tower and wall — is set out in Jericho — Eleven Thousand Years at the Spring . c. 8500 BCE TIER A Domestication of wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent. Across the arc from the Levant to the Zagros foothills, communities brought einkorn, emmer and barley under cultivation in a process spread over centuries around 8500 BCE and after. There was no single "invention of agriculture": the archaeobotanical record shows a long, regional mosaic of pre-domestication cultivation becoming dependence. c. 8500–8000 BCE TIER A Domestication of sheep, goat and cattle. Herd animals followed crops within the same broad horizon: goats and sheep under human management in the Zagros and Anatolia, cattle in the upper Euphrates region. The managed herd — wealth that walks, breeds and can be raided — remade economy, diet and social competition across the Near East and, in time, Africa. c. 8000 BCE TIER A The Tower of Jericho. Around 8000 BCE Jericho's inhabitants built a stone tower some 8.5 metres high with an internal stair of 22 steps, attached to a massive wall. Defence, flood control and ritual display have all been argued; what is not in doubt is the communal labour — among the earliest monumental building by a farming town anywhere. The tower, the wall, and the arguments over both are examined in Jericho — Eleven Thousand Years at the Spring . c. 7500–5700 BCE TIER A Çatalhöyük, Anatolia. For over a thousand years this dense town of mudbrick houses — entered through the roof, its dead buried beneath the floors, its walls painted and set with bulls' horns — housed thousands without streets, palaces or temples anyone can identify. Çatalhöyük is the standing proof that early urban life did not require kings. The town's houses, burials, paintings, and the argument over its supposed goddess are treated in Çatalhöyük — The Town Without Streets . c. 7500 BCE TIER A Native copper worked in Anatolia. At sites such as Çayönü, naturally occurring native copper was cold-hammered and annealed into beads, pins and awls by the mid-8th millennium BCE — metal treated as a rare, malleable stone. This is metallurgy's first chapter: working metal found as metal, long before anyone learned to win it from ore by fire. See First Metals . c. 7500–5500 BCE TIER A The African Humid Period — the Green Sahara florescence. Strengthened monsoons turned the Sahara into savanna and lake country. Pastoral peoples spread across what is now desert, leaving rock art of cattle, swimming figures and ceremony from the Tassili to the Ennedi. The "desert" of later Egyptian imagination was, within human memory of the region's peoples, a watered homeland — climate context no account of early Egypt can omit. The period's image-world — its periods, its dating problems, and its cattle — is surveyed in The Green Sahara and Its Image-World . c. 8000–6000 BCE TIER A Cattle pastoralism at Nabta Playa, Egypt's Western Desert. Cattle bones occur in Nabta's earliest levels, and the site's excavators read them as evidence of an independent African domestication — herders keeping cattle around the seasonal lake and digging wells deep enough to hold a settlement through the dry season. Metrical re-examination (Smith; Grigson) places the early animals within the range of wild aurochs, genetics favours a Near Eastern origin for African domestic cattle, and domestic herds reach the region shortly before 6000 BCE. The claim and its audit are both part of this entry's record, and Nabta's pastoral tradition fed directly into the prehistory of the Nile Valley. The pastoral world behind this entry is set out in Nabta Playa . from c. 7000 BCE TIER A Mehrgarh — farming begins at the Bolan Pass. At the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, a settlement sequence excavated by the French mission under Jean-François and Catherine Jarrige runs unbroken from an aceramic Neolithic (c. 7000 BCE) toward the Indus world. Its grains are the Near Eastern founder package; its zebu cattle, on Meadow's argument, were domesticated locally from the Indian aurochs — a farming hearth half borrowed, half its own. Its graveyards hold the earliest known drilled teeth (Coppa et al., Nature 2006), dentistry's first chapter, written by bead-drillers. The sequence is set out in Mehrgarh and the Road to the Indus . c. 7000–5700 BCE TIER A Jiahu — music, signs, and the first fermented drink. Jiahu, a sedentary village in the upper Huai valley of Henan, was occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BCE and packs an extraordinary record into its excavated fraction: early rice in use and very probably under cultivation at the plant's northern limit; crane-bone flutes that are the oldest complete, playable, dated musical instruments known, one of them acoustically tested and shown to carry a coherent scale; tortoise shells bearing eleven certainly incised signs — deliberate sign use, claimed by some as a first step toward writing and treated by critics, and by this hub, as not yet writing; and, in its earliest jars, the chemically attested mixed fermented beverage of rice, honey, and fruit, the earliest known anywhere. The site is treated in full at Neolithic East Asia — Jōmon, Yangshao, and Jiahu . c. 6500 BCE TIER A The Ubaid period begins in southern Mesopotamia. The Ubaid expansion carried a shared repertoire — painted pottery, tripartite houses, early temple platforms — from the southern alluvium across Mesopotamia. It laid the institutional groundwork, temple households included, on which the Uruk world and then the Sumerian cities would be built. The temple sequence that anchors the period — eighteen building levels on one footprint at Eridu, from a 2.8-metre shrine to a tripartite platform temple — and the interaction sphere that carried the Ubaid repertoire from the Gulf to north Syria are set out in Ubaid and Uruk — The First Cities . c. 6200 BCE TIER A The Storegga tsunami and the end of inhabited Doggerland. A submarine landslide off Norway — the Storegga Slide, displacing some 2,400–3,500 km³ of sediment — sent a tsunami across the northern North Sea: deposits in Shetland record runup above 20 m over the sea of that day, and the layer is dated to c. 6225–6170 BCE. What the wave did to the Mesolithic remnant of Doggerland is debated: catastrophic final flooding (Weninger et al. 2008), a lesser inundation within a retreat already driven by sea-level rise (Hill et al.), or a real but indecisive blow (Walker, Gaffney et al. 2020). The Dogger Bank island drowned later, c. 5000 BCE. See Drowned Landscapes . c. 5400 BCE TIER A The first shrine at Eridu. On virgin soil at the marsh-edge town of Eridu, a community raised the first building in the longest temple sequence known from Mesopotamia: a single mud-brick cella of about 2.8 × 2.8 metres, with a niche for a cult image and a pedestal for offerings (Temple Sounding, Level XVII, above the sleeper walls of Level XVIII). Rebuilt on the same footprint through eighteen levels — platformed by Level XI, tripartite by Level VIII, its final Ubaid form (Level VI) receiving offerings of fish — the shrine's ground became, by accumulation, the temple platform from which the ziggurat form descends. The sequence is walked level by level in Ubaid and Uruk — The First Cities . c. 4800 BCE TIER A The Nabta Playa stone circle and alignments. Nabta serves as a regional ceremonial centre from the Middle Neolithic (c. 6050–5550 BCE); the small stone circle belongs to its Late Neolithic phase, a hearth beside it dated to about 4800 BCE, and the alignments of slabs follow in the Final Neolithic, the main quarrying between about 4500 and 4200 BCE. Claims that the stones form a precise astronomical observatory are debated and are flagged as such in this hub's Nabta Playa article; the deliberate, ceremonial arrangement of stone by a pastoral society is not debated. c. 5400–4500 BCE TIER A The Vinča culture of the central Balkans. Across Serbia and neighbouring regions, farming communities built tell settlements — Vinča-Belo Brdo beside the Danube among them — occupied and rebuilt for centuries, producing dark burnished pottery, thousands of clay figurines, a shared repertoire of incised signs, and, at villages such as Belovode and Pločnik, the social setting of the world's earliest secure copper smelting. Bayesian radiocarbon modelling at the type site places the culture between about 5400/5300 and 4500 BCE, closing in a horizon of burned houses. Its tells, signs, figurines, and hoards are treated in full in Old Europe — Vinča and the Cucuteni-Trypillia World . c. 5000 BCE TIER A Copper smelting at Belovode, Serbia. Slag, furnace remains and finished metal from the Vinča-culture site of Belovode give the world's earliest securely dated evidence of high-temperature copper smelting, around 5000 BCE (Radivojević and colleagues). Smelting — ore, fire and air combined to birth metal — appears in the Balkans at least as early as anywhere in the Near East. See First Metals . c. 5000 BCE TIER A The Rudna Glava copper mine. In eastern Serbia, Vinča miners followed malachite veins down some twenty shafts with stone hammers and antler picks around 5000 BCE. Rudna Glava and Belovode together show a complete early industry — mine, smelter, smith — in Copper Age Europe. c. 5000 BCE TIER A The Fayum and Merimde Neolithic — farmers on the Nile. By about 5000 BCE, farming communities on the Fayum lake shore and at Merimde, on the western edge of the Delta, were growing emmer wheat and barley and herding sheep, goat and cattle — the first fully Neolithic horizon in Lower Egypt, and the bridge between the Mesolithic Nile and the predynastic cultures that followed. See The Nile Bridge . c. 5000–3000 BCE TIER A The Yangshao culture of the middle Yellow River. The Yangshao is the mature millet-farming Neolithic of north China. Its villages follow a shared plan — semi-subterranean houses around communal open space inside a ring ditch, with kilns and cemeteries outside — documented whole at Jiangzhai, where some 120 houses stood in five residential groups around a 4,000 m² plaza, and at the type site of Banpo near Xi'an. Its painted pottery, black mineral pigment on a red ground fired in updraft kilns, develops from the naturalistic fish of the Banpo phase to the pure geometry of Miaodigou and the swirling wares of Majiayao. The older textbook claim that these villages were matriarchal is now treated as historiography, not evidence. See Neolithic East Asia — Jōmon, Yangshao, and Jiahu . c. 4600–4200 BCE TIER A The Varna gold cemetery, Bulgaria. Graves at Varna, radiocarbon-dated to about 4569–4340 BCE, held more than 3,000 gold objects — among the oldest worked gold in the world — concentrated in a few burials, some of them cenotaphs with gold-mask faces. Varna is the earliest dramatic evidence that metal had already become a language of rank and inherited inequality. See First Metals . c. 4400–4000 BCE TIER A The Badarian culture of Upper Egypt. Around el-Badari, farming villages produced the finest pottery of predynastic Egypt — black-topped redware of eggshell thinness — together with early copper objects, glazed steatite and carved slate. The Badarians are the first Nile Valley culture whose cemeteries show craft specialisation and graded wealth: Egypt's long social story starts here, in the ground. c. 4000–3100 BCE TIER A The Uruk period in Mesopotamia. Uruk grew into the world's first true city, and the Uruk expansion carried its material signature — bevel-rim bowls, cylinder seals, temple precincts — across the Near East, with outposts and influence reaching Egypt's doorstep. Urbanism, bureaucracy and mass production enter the record together, and none of them ever leaves it again. Uruk's scale is an estimate with stated error bars — c. 250 hectares, 25,000–50,000 people by the area-and-density method — and its precincts, ration bowls, sealings, and northern outposts, with the debate between Algaze's world-system model and Stein's distance-parity alternative, are treated in Ubaid and Uruk — The First Cities
