What Jericho Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do, sharply, about the purpose of the Tower and the date of the Bronze Age destruction — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. One boundary is observed throughout. A famous later textual tradition, the conquest narrative of the Book of Joshua, attaches itself to this mound's Bronze Age walls. That tradition is a text, and its treatment belongs to Tier B elsewhere in this archive. What this article reports is what the excavation record shows, in the order the strata give it; where the record and the tradition are compared, the comparison is stated as a matter of dates and deposits, and nothing more is claimed in either direction. Jericho's mound — Tell es-Sultan, beside the spring of 'Ain es-Sultan in the Jordan Valley, some 258 metres below sea level — holds one of the longest settlement sequences on earth. Natufian hunter-gatherers camped by the spring before farming existed. By about 9000 BCE a permanent village stood there, and by about 8000 BCE that village — a community of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, without pottery, without metal, without writing — had built a stone wall more than three and a half metres high, dug a rock-cut ditch in front of it, and raised inside it a stone tower eight and a half metres tall with a staircase of twenty-two steps sealed within its solid core. A millennium later its Pre-Pottery Neolithic B successors were modelling the faces of their dead in lime plaster over the bone of the skull itself, inlaying the eye sockets with shells — the earliest portraiture, of a kind, that survives anywhere. Cities of the Early, Middle, and Late Bronze Ages followed on the same mound, and occupation of the oasis, in one form or another, has never wholly ceased since. Jericho is therefore two things at once, and this article keeps them separate. It is a type-site : the place where Kathleen Kenyon defined the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B for the southern Levant, and where the stratigraphic method she practised became a standard for the region. And it is a test case for the discipline of this hub: a site so loaded with later meaning that every generation of excavators has had to dig, visibly, against the expectations it brought with it. The stones, read at their own strength, need no help from the fame. A farming village that built monumentally in stone eleven thousand years ago is remarkable enough on the evidence alone. I. The Place — Tell es-Sultan and the Spring Tell es-Sultan is an oval mound of accumulated settlement debris, roughly four hectares in extent and rising some twenty metres above the plain, on the northwestern edge of the modern city of Jericho (Ariha) in the Jordan Valley. It stands about ten kilometres north of the Dead Sea and about ten kilometres west of the Jordan River, at approximately 31°52′ N, 35°26′ E. Its elevation — around 258 metres below sea level — makes the oasis the lowest permanently inhabited place on earth, a fact that is not a curiosity but a cause: the depth of the valley gives Jericho a long, warm growing season, frost-free winters, and a climate in which dates, bananas, and winter vegetables ripen while the hills above are cold. // LOCATION // c. 31°52′ N, 35°26′ E Northwestern edge of modern Jericho, southern Jordan Valley, c. 10 km north of the Dead Sea and c. 10 km west of the Jordan River. // ELEVATION // c. 258 m below sea level The lowest permanently inhabited place on earth: a deep, warm rift-valley oasis with a frost-free winter growing season. // THE MOUND // c. 4 hectares, c. 20 m of deposit An oval tell of stacked settlements — Neolithic village, Bronze Age cities, and later occupation — excavated in more than twenty successive strata. // THE SPRING // 'Ain es-Sultan A perennial spring at the mound's eastern foot, flowing at roughly 3.8 m³ per minute in modern measurement — the constant that explains the site. Everything at Jericho begins with the spring. 'Ain es-Sultan — the Sultan's Spring, known in later tradition as Elisha's Spring — rises at the eastern foot of the tell, where water collected in the limestone hills of the Judaean wilderness to the west emerges along the fault line of the valley floor. Its modern measured flow is on the order of a thousand gallons (about 3.8 cubic metres) a minute, enough to irrigate some ten square kilometres of the oasis through a network of channels. In a valley where rainfall is low and summer heat extreme, a flow of that size and reliability is not an amenity. It is the difference between a camping place visited in season and a settlement that can be held all year, every year, for millennia. The UNESCO inscription of 2023 puts the point in its formal language: the property consists of the tell "and the adjacent perennial spring of 'Ain es-Sultan, which for millennia has been an important source of water for the inhabitants of this area." The spring is not beside the site. In every functional sense, the spring is the site. The setting offered more than water. West of the tell the land rises steeply to Jebel Quruntul — the Mount of Temptation of later tradition — and the Judaean hills; the wadi that drains those hills past the site, the Wadi Qelt system, is also the site's recurring hazard, the source of the flood and silt problem examined in §IV and §V. Eastward the valley floor runs flat to the Jordan and the crossing places of the river, and beyond them to the hills of Moab. Jericho thus sits at a junction: water at its feet, a route westward up the wadi to the hill country and Jerusalem, a route eastward across the river, and the great north–south rift corridor running past it. Settlement persisted here for the same compound reason it persisted at this hub's other long-lived places — water, cultivable land, and a road — but at Jericho the combination is present in its most extreme form, and so, in the event, was the persistence. A caution about the famous superlative belongs at the front. Jericho is routinely called the oldest continuously inhabited city in the world, and the oasis does have an extraordinary claim: archaeological deposits at the tell reach back, in the UNESCO dossier's dating, to about 10,500 BCE, and habitation at the oasis has recurred in every period since. But "continuously inhabited" smooths over what the strata actually show, which is a sequence with real gaps and thinnings — the tell itself was at times reduced to a small settlement or effectively abandoned (the Late Bronze Age of §XIII is the contested case) while life continued around the spring and in the oasis at large. The accurate statement is stronger for being accurate: people have lived by this spring, in settlement after settlement on or beside this mound, for some eleven thousand years. No charter of unbroken urban continuity is needed, and none is claimed here. The comparison this hub invites is with the other great spring-and-route settlements of the early Neolithic world treated in this division. At Göbekli Tepe , hunter-gatherers built monumentally on a hilltop with no permanent water and no village at all; at Çatalhöyük , a large farming town grew on an Anatolian river plain without walls, streets, or public buildings anyone can identify. Jericho is the third pattern, and in some ways the most conventional: a watered place, farmed early, defended — or at least enclosed — early, and rebuilt on its own debris until the debris itself became a hill. Its fame is disproportionate to its size at almost every period. Its antiquity is not. II. First Camp, First Village — Natufian to PPNA The first people at the spring were not farmers. In the Epipalaeolithic levels at the base of the tell, Kenyon's excavations found the traces of Natufian hunter-gatherers — the culture, spread across the Levant in the closing millennia of the last Ice Age, that first experimented with sedentary life before domestication. The Jericho Natufian left a scattering of the culture's diagnostic crescent-shaped microliths and evidence of structures Kenyon termed proto-Neolithic. During the cold, dry interruption of the Younger Dryas (c. 10,900–9700 BCE), permanent habitation anywhere in the region was precarious; the spring, flowing when the hills were dry, made Jericho the kind of place a mobile group returns to — a fixed point of water in a seasonal round. The Italian-Palestinian expedition's periodisation pushes the first, Mesolithic presence at the site back to about 10,500 BCE (its Sultan Ia phase), a dating the UNESCO dossier adopts. With the warming that ended the Younger Dryas, the camp became a village. The first permanent settlement at Tell es-Sultan belongs to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA), conventionally c. 9600–8500 BCE in the southern Levant, with Jericho's own PPNA — the phase Kenyon's terminology called Pre-Sultan and Sultanian — running in her sequence from about 9000 BCE. The name states the period's defining absence: these are farming communities that do not yet make pottery. Their containers were baskets, skins, stone vessels, and unfired clay; their architecture, at Jericho, was the round house. The Round Houses and the Stored Harvest PPNA Jericho was a village of small circular dwellings built of plano-convex mud bricks — bricks moulded by hand, flat on one face and domed on the other, sometimes called hog-backed bricks — set in mud mortar, each house a single room a few metres across, its floor often sunk slightly below the contemporary ground surface. The dead were buried beneath house floors, a practice that runs through the whole Levantine Neolithic and that matters at Jericho for a specific reason: the treatment of the skull, separated from the body after burial and kept or reburied in groups, begins here, in the PPNA levels, long before the plastering of §VII elaborated it. Kenyon's excavations recovered concentrations of unplastered skulls from PPNA contexts — dozens of individuals in the anthropological counts — the plain first chapter of a mortuary tradition whose decorated second chapter made the site famous. The village's subsistence was transitional in the strict sense. Its people cultivated emmer wheat, barley, and pulses — the plant remains and the sickle-glossed flint blades attest harvesting — and they hunted, gazelle prominently, on a large scale. Whether the cereals of PPNA Jericho were fully domesticated forms or cultivated wild stands under intensive management is a question the surviving plant evidence answers only in part, and the literature states it with corresponding care: Jericho stands at the threshold of agriculture, with cultivation certain and the domestication status of its crops debated in detail. What is not debated is the sedentism. A community does not bury its dead under its floors, rebuild its houses on the same plots for centuries, and — as the next sections show — quarry, carry, and lay thousands of tons of stone, on the basis of a seasonal camp. By 9000 BCE, on the evidence of its own strata, Jericho was a place people lived. // HOW LARGE WAS PPNA JERICHO? // The walled PPNA settlement covered about four hectares (40,000 m²). Population estimates in the literature diverge by an order of magnitude — from as low as 200–300 to as high as 2,000–3,000 — depending on the assumed density and on how much of the enclosed area is taken to have been built up. The divergence is itself the finding: the archaeology fixes the area and the labour, but not the head-count, and this article uses the range rather than either end of it. By about 8500 BCE the village entered the phase on which its reputation rests. Within a few centuries, its inhabitants had enclosed the settlement in a stone perimeter, dug a ditch outside it, and raised the great Tower against its inner face — works dated by the radiocarbon series published from Kenyon's samples in 1981 and 1983 to construction around 8300 BCE and use until about 7800 BCE, conventionally rounded, in this article and in the hub's timeline, to c. 8000 BCE . Those works are so far out of scale with everything else known from the ninth millennium BCE that they require, and receive, three sections of their own: the Tower's construction (§III), the debate over its purpose (§IV), and the wall and ditch with which it is associated (§V). One framing point before the detail. The PPNA is, in the wider region, the age of the first communal architecture: the great enclosures of Göbekli Tepe in the north, the communal buildings of Jerf el Ahmar and Mureybet on the Euphrates, the tower-houses of Tell Qaramel in Syria — the last now known to rival or precede Jericho's Tower in date. Jericho's works belong to that world and are not a solitary miracle. They are, however, its most completely published southern example, and the only one raised by a settled farming village around its own houses — which is why the argument about what they were for has run for seventy years without closing. III. The Tower — Stone by Stone The Tower stands on the western side of the PPNA settlement, against the inner face of the perimeter wall, in the deep trench — Kenyon's Trench I — where it was uncovered in the 1950s seasons. It is, on the published measurements, a solid stone structure of slightly conical profile: about nine metres in diameter at the base, narrowing to about seven metres at the surviving top, and preserved to a height of about 8.5 metres. Kenyon's sections showed it was not a single build but a structure with a history — an initial tower, subsequent thickening and heightening, and phases in which parts of it were blocked or remodelled — and that its use-life, on the radiocarbon evidence, ran from about 8300 to about 7800 BCE. It remains among the oldest stone towers known anywhere, and the oldest monumental building in the southern Levant. The Fabric — Undressed Stone, Laid Dry The construction material is the local limestone, used as it came from the ground. The Tower is built of undressed stone — unshaped fieldstones and rough quarry blocks, laid in courses without dressed faces and without, in the main mass, any surviving evidence of a mortar technology comparable to the lime plaster the settlement used elsewhere; the stability of the structure comes from its mass, its battered (inward-sloping) profile, and the care of its laying. The walling is about 1.5 metres thick where it is measurable as a shell, but the Tower is not a hollow drum: it is a solid core of stone and rubble fill, through which a single passage — the staircase — is threaded. Bar-Yosef's published estimate put the mass of the structure at about 1,000 tons. There are no rooms inside it, no chambers, no burials: the Tower contains exactly one piece of interior architecture, and that piece is a way up. The Staircase — Twenty-Two Steps The staircase enters at the eastern side, from inside the settlement, at ground level, and climbs within the solid core to an outlet at the top — the original outlet, Kenyon's sections showed, before later phases blocked the stair and a new arrangement replaced it. It consists of twenty-two stone steps . Unlike the undressed mass around them, the steps are made of flat, cut slabs of limestone, hammer-dressed smooth — the only deliberately finished stonework in the structure, and among the earliest true staircases known. The passage is steep and narrow, about a metre wide, roofed as it rises by corbelling and slab lintels within the core; a single file of climbers is all it accommodates. At the top, the stair emerged onto the Tower's summit platform — what stood or was done there, no deposit survives to say directly, and every reconstruction of the summit (lookout, platform for display, roofed cap) is an inference from the stair, the mass, and the position, not a find. The labour accounting has been done more than once, and the figures are worth stating with their authors. Kenyon's own estimate, repeated through the literature, was that the wall and Tower together would have taken a hundred men more than a hundred days to build. Naveh, extending Bar-Yosef's estimates on the basis of half a cubic metre of construction per worker per day, calculated at least 10,400 working days for the complex; the figure of roughly 11,000 working days circulates widely for the Tower alone. The estimates differ in their assumptions, but they converge on the conclusion that matters: this was a communal work, requiring the organised labour of the whole settlement — plausibly of more than the settlement — sustained over a season or repeated seasons, by a community of at most a few thousand and perhaps only a few hundred people (§II). Whoever ordered it, persuaded it, or shamed it into being, the Tower is the material signature of a social fact: by 8000 BCE, Jericho could mobilise labour on a monumental scale, five and a half millennia before the pyramids. Feature The Tower of Jericho Date PPNA; radiocarbon series (published 1981, 1983) places construction c. 8300 BCE, use to c. 7800 BCE; conventionally c. 8000 BCE Dimensions c. 9 m diameter at base, c. 7 m at surviving top; preserved height c. 8.5 m; slightly conical profile Position Western side of the settlement, against the inner face of the perimeter wall, inside the enclosed area Fabric Undressed limestone fieldstone and rough blocks; solid rubble core; mass estimated by Bar-Yosef at c. 1,000 tons Interior No rooms or chambers; a single internal staircase of 22 cut and hammer-dressed stone slabs, c. 1 m wide, entered from the settlement side Phasing Built, thickened, and remodelled in successive stages; the staircase was blocked in a later phase (Bar-Yosef's Stages VI–VIA) as deposits rose around it Labour Estimates from c. 10,400 working days (Naveh, extending Bar-Yosef) to Kenyon's hundred men for over a hundred days for wall and Tower together Source Kenyon, Digging Up Jericho (1957) and Excavations at Jericho III (1981); Bar-Yosef, Current Anthropology 27 (1986) A final construction detail carries interpretive weight, and the excavators noticed it from the first: the Tower was built inside the perimeter. It does not project outward from the wall, as a fighting tower must if its defenders are to shoot or drop missiles along the wall's outer face; it rises behind the wall, within the town, and its staircase is entered from the town side. Whatever it was for, its architecture is not the architecture of a bastion. That single observation, developed by Bar-Yosef, is the hinge on which the whole interpretation debate of the next section turns. IV. What Was the Tower For? — The Interpretation Debate Four main readings of the Tower stand in the published literature. They are not equally supported, and this section states each with its author, its evidence, and its standing — because at Jericho the history of the interpretations is part of the evidence for how archaeology handles a monument whose builders left no text. Kenyon — A Fortress Tower Kenyon's reading was the first and, for a generation, the standard one: the Tower was part of a system of defences — wall, ditch, and tower together — with which the PPNA town protected itself and its stored wealth (Kenyon, Digging Up Jericho , 1957; Kenyon & Holland, Excavations at Jericho III, 1981). The reading had an obvious strength: the ensemble looks like fortification, and its scale implies something worth defending. It also fitted a mid-twentieth-century expectation that stored agricultural surplus and organised violence arrive together. Its weaknesses were visible in Kenyon's own plans, and it was left to Bar-Yosef to enumerate them. Bar-Yosef — Flood, Silt, and a Communal Centre Ofer Bar-Yosef's "The Walls of Jericho: An Alternative Interpretation" ( Current Anthropology 27, 1986: 157–162) remains the debate's pivot. His argument proceeds from the sections. The wall, he showed from Kenyon's drawings, was rebuilt and thickened repeatedly at short intervals; the ditch in front of it filled rapidly; and the deposits banked against the wall's western face were not occupation debris but natural alluviation — silt and gravel washed down from the hills. The enemy at Jericho's west wall, on this evidence, was not an army but the wadi flood : flash floods and mudflows descending from Jebel Quruntul after winter rain, in a climate the palaeoenvironmental indicators suggest was wetter than today's, repeatedly burying the settlement's edge in silt. The wall was a flood-defence and silt barrier, heightened as the deposits rose; the ditch was its catchment, cleaned and re-cut until the labour of maintaining it was abandoned and the staircase itself blocked by the rising ground. As for defence against people, Bar-Yosef stated the negative plainly: there is no archaeological evidence — no burned settlements, massacre deposits, or unambiguous fortifications — for organised social aggression in the Levant before the sixth millennium BCE; and a tower built inside its wall, from which defenders cannot cover the wall's outer face, is not a fighting platform in any case. His positive proposal for the Tower was accordingly social and ritual rather than military: a massive communal structure raised above the flood line, associated in his reconstruction with communal storage and serving as a centre of ritual activity — a monument of the community to itself, whose building was itself a social act. The Critics and the Cosmological Readings Bar-Yosef's flood hypothesis was itself challenged on hydrological grounds. Ronen and Adler (2001) argued that the water sources around Jericho could not have generated floods of the volume the silt-defence reading requires — the wadis are either too small or too distant — and proposed instead a symbolic defence: a wall and tower built massively toward the west, where the sun sets, as a bulwark against malign forces, shifting the ensemble's purpose from engineering to cosmology. That cosmological direction was then given a precise, testable form by Roy Liran and Ran Barkai of Tel Aviv University ("Midsummer Sunset at Neolithic Jericho," Time and Mind 1, 2008; developed in Antiquity , 2011). Using computer modelling of the ancient landscape, they showed that the axis of the Tower's staircase aligns with the setting sun at the summer solstice behind the highest peak of Jebel Quruntul, and that on solstice evening the mountain's shadow falls first on the Tower and then spreads across the whole town. The Tower's conical profile, they argued, echoes the conical peak it faces. Their reading of its function follows: the Tower was a cosmological marker and an instrument of social power — a monument that linked the town to the hills and the heavens, created awe at the turning of the year, and served those who organised its building as a warrant for the new disciplines of farming and hierarchy. Archaeoastronomers outside the team have counselled the usual caution — alignments can arise by chance in a complex landscape, and intentionality is hard to prove — but the alignment itself is a matter of measurement, and it stands in the literature as the most specific claim ever made for the Tower's design. Where does the debate rest? The defensive reading in Kenyon's original form — a fortress tower against human enemies — has lost the most ground, on the architectural objection (an internal tower cannot fight) and on the absence of any contemporary evidence for warfare in the region. The flood reading commands the stratigraphy of the wall and ditch, which it explains better than any rival, while its hydrology remains disputed. The astronomical reading accounts for the staircase axis and the Tower's siting in a way neither rival attempts. The readings are not, in fact, mutually exclusive in every part: a silt barrier can carry a communal monument, and a communal monument can be aligned on the solstice. What the literature no longer sustains is the simple picture with which the site entered the textbooks — the world's first fortress, built by the world's first farmers against the world's first army. The stones are older and stranger than that. // POSITIONS, ATTRIBUTED // Defence against enemies: Kenyon (1957, 1981). Weakened by the Tower's internal position and the absence of regional evidence for warfare at this date. Flood and silt defence, with the Tower as communal/ritual centre: Bar-Yosef (1986). Strongest on the wall's stratigraphy; hydrology contested by Ronen & Adler (2001). Symbolic/cosmological defence toward the sunset: Ronen & Adler (2001). Solstice alignment and social power: Liran & Barkai (2008, 2011) — alignment measured, intention inferred. This article reports the debate at this standing and adopts none of the four as settled. V. Wall, Ditch, and the Word "Fortification" The Tower did not stand alone. On the western side of the settlement, where Kenyon's trenches cut deepest, the PPNA perimeter consisted of three elements in sequence from inside out: the Tower, the wall , and the ditch . The first perimeter wall, as Bar-Yosef summarised Kenyon's sections, stood about 3.6 metres high, 1.8 metres thick at its base and about 1.1 metres at its preserved top — a massive stone construction by any Neolithic standard, of the same undressed limestone as the Tower. In front of it the inhabitants dug a ditch into the bedrock, on the order of eight metres wide and nearly three metres deep in the sections where it is best preserved. Around this first ensemble the ground then rose, inside and out, by the combined accumulation Bar-Yosef documented: natural alluviation against the outer face, occupational build-up within. The response, in successive stages, was a second wall — or a thickening of the first — then a third, each raising the barrier as the silt rose against it, until in the final stages the ditch had filled, the works were abandoned, and the Tower's own staircase was blocked by the deposits it had been built to overlook. Read as a sequence rather than a snapshot, the western perimeter is therefore not one fortification but a centuries-long negotiation with a rising ground surface . That sequence is the strongest single piece of evidence in the whole debate of §IV, and it is evidence of a particular kind: it is very hard to explain by human attack, since armies do not deposit laminated silt against a wall at a steady rate for centuries, and very easy to explain by water, slope-wash, and a settlement generating its own debris on the inside of its own barrier. Bar-Yosef's reading was built on exactly this asymmetry, and subsequent discussion has not displaced it from the wall and ditch, whatever is concluded about the Tower. What, then, does "fortification" mean at this date? The word smuggles in a garrison, a siege, and an enemy, and at 8000 BCE none of the three is attested at Jericho or anywhere in the contemporary Levant. The defensible vocabulary is the excavators' more careful one: a perimeter work — a wall, ditch, and tower ensemble that unquestionably enclosed the settlement, controlled its western approach, kept animals in or out, marked a boundary between the town and the world, and, on the stratigraphic evidence, held back water and silt. Enclosure is a fact; fortification, in the military sense, is an interpretation, and at Jericho it is currently the weaker one. This hub's usage follows the evidence: the ensemble is called a perimeter, a wall, a work — and the site is described, as UNESCO's listing describes it, as a permanent settlement with a wall, a ditch, and a tower by the ninth to eighth millennium BCE. The popular formula "the oldest fortified city in the world" compresses three contestable words — fortified, city, and the superlative itself — into a slogan the strata do not quite sign. What they sign is remarkable enough: the earliest known town wall, the earliest known town ditch, and the earliest known stone tower, built together by one small farming community at the dawn of settled life. THE WALL First phase c. 3.6 m high, 1.8 m thick at the base, of undressed stone; thickened and succeeded by further walls as deposits rose against it — a sequence of rebuildings, not a single build. THE DITCH Rock-cut, on the order of 8 m wide and nearly 3 m deep, in front of the wall on the west. It filled rapidly with silt and debris — the observation from which the flood reading of the whole ensemble begins. THE TOWER Inside the wall, not projecting from it; entered from the town; solid but for its stair. Architecturally a communal monument, whatever else it was — not a bastion. THE SEQUENCE Wall, ditch-filling, heightened wall, blocked stair: the western perimeter records centuries of rising silt and rising occupation, and was finally abandoned to both. VI. The PPNB Town — Houses, Floors, and Plaster Between the PPNA village and the town of the plastered skulls there is a break in the sequence — a hiatus in occupation after the PPNA, on which the excavators agree in outline if not in every detail — and then a refoundation. The Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB) settlement at Jericho, conventionally from the earlier seventh millennium BCE in the site's current periodisation (the Italian-Palestinian scheme runs its PPN broadly c. 8500–6000 BCE, with the classic PPNB town of the skulls in its middle phases, c. 7400–6500 BCE), is a different kind of place from its predecessor. Where the PPNA built round, the PPNB built rectangular : multi-roomed houses of mud brick on stone foundations, laid out room against room in the rectilinear manner that becomes the Levantine standard. The change of plan is one of the period's signatures across the region, and Jericho — where Kenyon first defined the PPNA/PPNB contrast — is its type-site. The PPNB town's defining material is neither stone nor brick but lime plaster . Its production was an industry: limestone burned at temperatures in the range of 600–900 °C to make quicklime, slaked, and worked into a plaster that could be laid in floors of remarkable quality — thick, burnished, sometimes coloured — spread over walls, and modelled in the round. PPNB Jericho's houses have plaster floors that were renewed again and again, layer upon layer, across a building's life. The same material, in the same centuries, coats the skulls of §VII and builds the statues of §IX: plaster is the medium in which this community expressed everything from domestic finish to the faces of its ancestors, and the fuel and labour its burning demanded — wood in quantity, in a landscape where wood was not free — are part of the period's economy, debated in the environmental literature of the wider PPNB world. Subsistence, meanwhile, had completed the transition the PPNA began. The PPNB town farmed emmer, barley, lentils, and other pulses intensively — the Italian-Palestinian expedition's work in the oasis has added evidence for the early management of the spring's water in channels for cultivation — and herded sheep and goats under domestication, while hunting, gazelle above all, continued to contribute. Burial practice kept the PPNA pattern and elaborated it: the dead under the floors of houses, in primary burials from which, after an interval, the skull was in selected cases retrieved. It is that retrieval, and what was done with the skull afterwards, that the next two sections follow in procedural detail — because at Jericho the procedure survives completely enough to be reconstructed step by step, and because it produced the most famous objects ever found in a Neolithic context. // A REGIONAL PHENOMENON // Jericho did not plaster its skulls alone. Modelled and painted skulls are known from 'Ain Ghazal, Beisamoun, Kfar HaHoresh, Yiftahel, Tell Ramad, Tell Aswad, and Köşk Höyük — some seventy examples across the Levant and Anatolia in the usual counts, about half of them badly deteriorated. Jericho's distinction is priority and preservation: the first found, the largest single-site group, and the best published. The scale of the PPNB town should be stated plainly, because the skulls' fame inflates it in the imagination. It was a large village or small town of the same few hectares as its PPNA predecessor — one of the substantial settlements of the southern Levantine PPNB, though smaller than the great Transjordanian "mega-sites" such as 'Ain Ghazal at their height. Its importance is not size. It is the completeness of what it preserved: houses, floors, burials, skulls, and statues in stratified association, excavated and published to a standard that still anchors the period's study — and a mortuary art that has no parallel, for naturalism attempted at full scale, anywhere else in the Neolithic world. VII. The Plastered Skulls — How a Face Was Made In 1953, in the closing days of the season, Kenyon's team noticed a skull protruding from the section of a trench. Her own rule forbade digging into a standing section; the find was too important, and the rule was broken — the excavators spent days burrowing into the section face to recover what proved to be a cache of seven plastered skulls (registered D110–D116), set in a pit beneath a PPNB house floor. Two more followed in 1956 (D117–D118) and a further example in 1958 (E22), with later counts from the full Kenyon archive bringing the modelled Jericho series to about a dozen specimens, plus two painted only. The seven of 1953 remain the core group: the first plastered skulls ever recognised, and still the most vivid. What the makers did to a skull can be reconstructed as a procedure, because the finished objects, the unfinished evidence, and — since 2009 — the CT imaging of §VIII preserve its stages. What Tier C Means Here — A Biography of an Idea This article is classified Tier C — Modern Construction . That classification is stated here in words, as this hub requires, and it governs everything that follows. Tier C does not mean “uninteresting,” and it does not mean “invented yesterday out of nothing.” It means that the subject as a lost, inhabited continent is a product of the modern period — in this case, of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries — whose history can be documented publication by publication, even though the continent itself is not attested in ancient sources and is not supported by modern geology. Lemuria is unusually well suited to that treatment, because unlike Atlantis — which begins, famously, in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias — Lemuria begins in print, on a known date, in a named scientific journal, for a stated scientific reason. We can watch it being proposed. We can watch other scientists adopt, extend, map, and debate it. We can watch an evolutionary biologist turn it into a hypothesis about human origins. We can watch Helena Petrovna Blavatsky take the name and the broad Indian Ocean geography and rebuild both inside a very different system — a system of Root Races, immense timescales, and claimed archaic records — in The Secret Doctrine in 1888. We can watch W. Scott-Elliot give that second Lemuria maps, chronologies, and physical descriptions in 1904. And we can watch twentieth-century geology dissolve the first Lemuria while the second continued, quite independently, in esoteric publishing, popular culture, and — by a separate route — in Tamil cultural revival, where it was merged with the distinct tradition of Kumari Kandam. That is the story told here: not “did Lemuria exist?” in the abstract, but “who proposed what, when, on what evidence, and what happened to the proposal next?” Where a claim belongs to Sclater, it is attributed to Sclater. Where a claim belongs to Haeckel, it is attributed to Haeckel. Where a claim belongs to Blavatsky — above all, her claim to be commenting on the “Book of Dzyan” — it is attributed to Blavatsky as her claim. Where modern geology contradicts a claim, that is said plainly, with the evidence, and, it is hoped, kindly: the people who first proposed Lemuria were not fools, and the reasons they found it plausible are part of the record. // HOW TO USE THIS ARTICLE // Sections II–VII treat the scientific Lemuria of 1864–c. 1900. Sections VIII–XII treat the Theosophical Lemuria of 1888 onward. Sections XIII–XIV explain why the scientific hypothesis ended. Section XV treats Kumari Kandam separately, on purpose. Section XVI treats real submerged continental fragments and explains why they are not Lemuria. A note on tone is warranted at the outset. The history of lost continents is often told in one of two unhelpful registers: credulous wonder, in which every later elaboration is treated as suppressed ancient knowledge; or contempt, in which everyone involved before the present is treated as gullible. Neither register is accurate. The first Lemuria was a falsifiable scientific hypothesis, proposed inside the best biogeographical framework available in 1864, and it was in due course falsified — which is what happens to a great many good hypotheses. The second Lemuria was a religious and esoteric construction, offered by its authors on different grounds altogether — claimed clairvoyant and initiatory access to archaic records — and it should be described accurately on those terms, neither confused with the science it borrowed its name from nor mocked for failing tests it never claimed to be taking in the same way. Holding those two histories apart, while showing exactly where and how they touched, is the whole work of this article. THE SCIENTIFIC LEMURIA (1864– ) A former land connection across the Indian Ocean, proposed by Philip Lutley Sclater to explain the distribution of lemurs and related mammals. Extended by Ernst Haeckel into a hypothesis about human origins. Mapped and debated by geologists and biogeographers. Superseded by continental drift and plate tectonics. THE THEOSOPHICAL LEMURIA (1888– ) A vast continent, chiefly in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, taught by H. P. Blavatsky in The Secret Doctrine (1888) as the homeland of the Third Root Race, and elaborated with maps by W. Scott-Elliot in The Lost Lemuria (1904). Presented by its authors as archaic record, not as zoogeography. The table below gives the spine of the chronology. Every entry in it is taken up in the sections that follow. Date Publication / Event What Changed 1864 Sclater, “The Mammals of Madagascar,” Quarterly Journal of Science The name “Lemuria” is proposed for a former continent / land bridge. 1868 / 1870 / 1876 Haeckel, Natürliche Schöpfungsgeschichte ; English The History of Creation (1876) Lemuria becomes a candidate “cradle of the human race.” 1887 Neumayr, Erdgeschichte First systematic mapping of hypothetical land bridges, including Lemuria / Indomadagassia. 1888 Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine , Vol. II, Anthropogenesis Lemuria rebuilt as the continent of the Third Root Race, sourced by Blavatsky to the “Book of Dzyan.” 1904 Scott-Elliot, The Lost Lemuria Theosophical Lemuria given two maps, a chronology, and descriptions of its inhabitants. 1912 / 1915 Wegener proposes continental drift; Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane An alternative mechanism — moving continents — is on the table, though not yet accepted. 1960s Seafloor spreading and plate tectonics accepted The scientific need for sunken land bridges disappears; Lemuria as science ends. 2013 / 2017 Torsvik et al. on Mauritia; Mortimer et al. on Zealandia Real submerged continental fragments are characterised — on timescales and by mechanisms wholly unlike Lemuria. II. 1864 — Sclater and “The Mammals of Madagascar” Philip Lutley Sclater (1829–1913) was an English lawyer turned zoologist and biogeographer, a leading authority on birds and mammals, and the man who had earlier divided the world’s land fauna into the zoogeographical regions that, in modified form, are still taught today. In 1864 he published a short paper, “The Mammals of Madagascar,” in The Quarterly Journal of Science , vol. 1. It is there — not in a myth, a romance, or a work of occultism — that the word Lemuria first appears in this sense. Sclater’s proposal, in his own words as quoted in the Scientific American history-of-geology account of the paper (Bressan, “A Geologist’s Dream: The Lost Continent of Lemuria,” 2013, quoting Sclater 1864), was as follows: “The anomalies of the Mammal fauna of Madagascar can best be explained by supposing that anterior to the existence of Africa in its present shape, a large continent occupied parts of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans stretching out towards (what is now) America to the west, and to India and its islands on the east; that this continent was broken up into islands, of which some have became amalgamated with the present continent of Africa, and some, possibly, with what is now Asia; and that in Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands we have existing relics of this great continent, for which as the original focus of the ‘Stirps Lemurum,’ I should propose the name Lemuria!” — Philip Lutley Sclater, “The Mammals of Madagascar,” Quarterly Journal of Science (1864), as quoted in Bressan (2013) Several features of that sentence deserve attention, because later retellings often lose them. What Sclater Actually Proposed First, Sclater proposed a former continent that had broken up , not, in the first instance, a continent that had dramatically “sunk” in a single catastrophe. Break-up into islands, amalgamation of some fragments with Africa and others with Asia, and survival of Madagascar and the Mascarenes as “existing relics” — that is the mechanism in the 1864 text. The language of wholesale foundering beneath the waves belongs more to the broader nineteenth-century land-bridge literature and to later popularisation than to Sclater’s careful sentence. Second, the continent is named for an animal group, not for a people. Stirps Lemurum — the stock, or lineage, of the lemurs — is given as the reason for the name. No human beings, no civilisation, no temples, no catastrophe witnessed by anyone, appear in Sclater’s proposal at all. Lemuria in 1864 is a piece of zoogeography. Third, Sclater’s continent was very large and very vague. In the sentence above it occupies parts of both the Atlantic and the Indian Oceans, reaching toward America in one direction and toward India in the other. That breadth reflects how little could then be known about the floors of those oceans. There were no echo-sounded bathymetric maps of the deep Indian Ocean, no seismic profiles, no radiometric dates, and no samples of oceanic crust. A biogeographer reasoning from the distribution of living and fossil mammals had coastlines, island faunas, and a handful of geological sections to work from — and a very large blank in the middle of the map. Lemuria was drawn, in part, into that blank. Sclater returned to the idea in later work, and there he was, if anything, more cautious and more specifically Indian Ocean in scope. In The Geography of Mammals (Sclater and Sclater, 1899), again as quoted by Bressan, he wrote that the ancient “Lemuria,” “as the hypothetical continent which was originally the home of the Lemurs has been termed, must have extended across the Indian Ocean and the Indian Peninsula to the further side of the Bay of Bengal and over the great islands of the Indian Archipelago.” The word “hypothetical” is his, and it matters: Sclater presented Lemuria as a hypothesis to explain a pattern, not as a discovered place. // A COMMON MISREADING, CORRECTED // Sclater did not claim to have found a lost civilisation, to have translated an ancient record of a sunken continent, or to have identified the homeland of humanity. Those claims enter the Lemuria story later, in other hands, and attributing them back to 1864 confuses the whole history. What Sclater claimed was narrower and, in its own terms, testable: that the mammal fauna of Madagascar is anomalous unless Madagascar was once connected, by land, to regions that are now separated from it by sea. III. The Puzzle Sclater Was Solving To understand why a competent zoologist proposed a continent, it helps to state the puzzle as he saw it, in the terms he used. Sclater’s “lemurs” were a broader grouping than the lemurs of modern taxonomy. As Bressan’s account summarises, Sclater’s Lemuridae / Lemuroid grouping included the true lemurs, the indri, and the aye-aye of Madagascar; the galagos (bushbabies) of Africa; the lorises of Asia; and, in some arrangements, the tarsiers of Indonesia. Modern systematics separates these groups differently, but the distributional pattern Sclater was looking at was real under any arrangement: close relatives were richly present in some places and strikingly absent from the places in between. The figures Sclater cited, as quoted by Bressan, make the asymmetry vivid: some thirty different species of lemurs in Madagascar alone, eleven or twelve in all of Africa, and only three in the Indian region. Madagascar — an island — held the diversity; the great continent next door held far less; and a second, distant centre of the group lay across an ocean, in India and Southeast Asia, with the intervening lands of Africa and the Middle East showing, in Sclater’s reading of the fossil and living record, no comparable presence to serve as a corridor. MADAGASCAR Extraordinary diversity of lemurs and their kin; a fauna with many endemic forms found nowhere else. For Sclater, the “original focus” of the group. AFRICA Galagos present, but far fewer forms than Madagascar, despite Africa’s size and proximity. The expected corridor did not look like the centre. INDIA & THE EAST Lorises and fossil relatives present across an ocean, with no continuous chain of the group through the lands between India and Madagascar. A pattern of that kind — related forms on two sides of a sea barrier, absent or sparse between them — is called a disjunct distribution , and it demands some historical explanation. Either the organisms crossed the barrier somehow, or the barrier was not always there, or the group was once widespread and has since vanished from the middle of its range. Nineteenth-century biogeographers used all three kinds of explanation, but for terrestrial mammals — poor swimmers, unlikely rafters over thousands of kilometres of open ocean as then understood — a former land connection was a natural first resort. Sclater chose it. It is worth adding that Sclater was not working in isolation from geology. Geologists and palaeontologists working in India and South Africa — notably the Blanford brothers and their colleagues in the Geological Survey of India — were independently struck by resemblances between Indian and African fossil floras and faunas, including the Permian–Triassic Glossopteris flora and the Karoo / Panchet fossil assemblages. H. F. Blandford’s paper on the former connection of Africa and India, quoted at length by Scott-Elliot in 1904 (see §XI), argued from fossils, from freshwater deposits implying large land areas, and from a chain of banks and atolls across the Indian Ocean, for a former Indo-Oceanic land. Zoogeography and palaeontology were pointing, by different routes, at the same blank on the map. That convergence is a large part of why Lemuria was taken seriously, and §VII returns to it. IV. Land Bridges as Respectable Science Lemuria looks strange only from the far side of plate tectonics. Inside the geological framework of the mid-nineteenth century, it was an ordinary move, made by ordinary means, in very distinguished company. The reigning assumption of that framework was permanence : the continents and the ocean basins were taken to be, in their broad positions, fixed features of the Earth, ancient and essentially immobile. Land could rise and sink vertically — elevation and subsidence were well attested, from raised beaches to drowned forests — but continents did not travel horizontally across the globe. Within that picture, a naturalist confronting a disjunct distribution had, in practice, two respectable options: long-distance dispersal across the water as it now stands, or a former land connection that had since subsided. For many terrestrial groups, the second option looked far more plausible than the first. Land bridges were therefore proposed freely, all over the map, by leading figures, throughout the second half of the century. Company Lemuria Kept Sclater was not the first to imagine a southern or Indian Ocean land, and he said nothing to suggest he thought otherwise. Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire had speculated about a connection between Madagascar and India some two decades earlier, around 1840, without giving it a name. The English geologist Searles V. Wood Jr. hypothesised a great southern continent in the “secondary era” (the Mesozoic). Alfred Russel Wallace proposed a sunken continent to explain the fauna of Celebes (Sulawesi) in 1859, though he later became one of the most eloquent critics of promiscuous land-bridge building — a useful reminder that the framework itself was being argued about, from inside, by its own practitioners. Thomas Henry Huxley inferred a Miocene land connection in the Indian Ocean region on palaeontological grounds. Andrew Murray, and others, proposed their own versions. Blandford proposed “Indo-Oceana” for essentially the land Sclater had named Lemuria, while noting, in the passage Scott-Elliot later quoted, that Sclater’s name was the one “most generally adopted.” In other words: the name was Sclater’s; the kind of idea was the period’s. To single out Lemuria, among dozens of contemporary hypothetical bridges and continents, as if it alone were a lapse of judgement is hindsight. What distinguishes Lemuria historically is not that it was proposed — many were — but what happened to it afterwards: it was taken up for human origins, and then for esoteric history, and so it outlived all its siblings. // THE FALSIFIABILITY POINT // Within its paradigm, Lemuria was a falsifiable hypothesis, and being falsifiable, it was eventually falsified. It made claims about what the Indian Ocean floor should be (continental, formerly above water, in the right places and of the right ages) and about how Madagascar’s fauna should relate to India’s and Africa’s. When oceanography, seismology, and palaeomagnetism finally described that floor directly, and when plate tectonics supplied a different history for Madagascar and India, the hypothesis had nowhere to stand. That is not a disgrace in the history of science. It is the normal fate of a hypothesis that reaches beyond the instruments of its time. V. Haeckel Makes Lemuria Human The second decisive step in Lemuria’s biography was taken not by a geologist but by Germany’s most forceful populariser of evolution: Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919). In 1868 Haeckel published Natürliche Schöpfungsgeschichte (“The Natural History of Creation”), a bestselling, richly illustrated presentation of evolutionary theory addressed to a general readership. The English translation by E. Ray Lankester appeared in 1876 as The History of Creation . It is in Haeckel’s hands that Lemuria stops being only about lemurs and becomes a hypothesis about us . Haeckel’s reasoning, in outline, was this. Humans are most closely related to the anthropoid apes of Africa and Asia. Between ape and fully human, he posited an intermediate, hypothetical stage — the “speechless man,” Pithecanthropus alalus — for which no fossil was then known. Where had that transition happened? Haeckel favoured Asia, and specifically the region of India and the Sunda Islands, as the likeliest theatre, while keeping Africa in play. Sclater’s sunken continent, lying conveniently between southern Asia and eastern Africa, offered him a third possibility that elegantly united the other two: a tropical homeland, now beneath the Indian Ocean, from which early humans could have radiated in every direction. The chronology of Haeckel’s adoption matters, and the sources are clear that it developed across editions. Bressan’s account, comparing the plates, notes that the German version of 1868 did not yet feature Lemuria in the famous map, while later editions and the English version of 1876 emphasise it — the continent labelled, in Haeckel’s hypothetical sketch of the origin and dispersal of the “twelve races of Man,” as the starting point of human migration, and in the text as “Paradise.” By 1870 Haeckel was stating the proposal in the form Scott-Elliot would later quote (via The History of Creation ) at the head of The Lost Lemuria : “The probable primeval home or ‘Paradise’ is here assumed to be Lemuria, a tropical continent at present lying below the level of the Indian Ocean, the former existence of which in the tertiary period seems very probable from numerous facts in animal and vegetable geography. But it is also very possible that the hypothetical ‘cradle of the human race’ lay further to the east (in Hindostan or Further India), or further to the west (in eastern Africa).” — Ernst Haeckel (1870), as quoted in Bressan (2013) and in Scott-Elliot (1904) Read that quotation carefully, because it shows Haeckel’s actual epistemic posture, which later retellings flatten. Lemuria is “assumed.” Its existence “seems very probable” on biogeographical grounds. And two alternatives — mainland India and eastern Africa — are explicitly kept open in the same sentence. Haeckel was advocating a hypothesis, forcefully, as was his manner, but he was advocating it as a hypothesis. The same caution appears in his treatment of particular peoples: the primeval home of the Malays, he wrote in the passage quoted by Bressan from the 1876 English edition, “must be looked for in the south-eastern part of the Asiatic continent, or possibly in the more extensive continent which existed at the time when further India was directly connected with the Sunda Archipelago and eastern Lemuria.” “Or possibly” is doing real work there. Why Haeckel’s Adoption Mattered So Much Three consequences followed from Haeckel’s prestige and reach. First, scale of audience. Sclater wrote for zoologists. Haeckel wrote for everyone. Natürliche Schöpfungsgeschichte went through edition after edition — eleven by 1909, with translations into some twenty-five languages, as standard biographical accounts record — and its striking plate showing human dispersal radiating from Lemuria fixed the continent in the visual imagination of a generation of educated readers who never opened the Quarterly Journal of Science . Second, a new question attached to the name. After Haeckel, “Lemuria” no longer answered only “why are lemurs distributed so strangely?” It also answered “where did humanity begin?” A continent that is the cradle of mankind is a very different cultural object from a continent that is a corridor for mammals, even if the map is the same. Origin and catastrophe — the place we came from, and the place that sank — are the two charges Lemuria would carry for the rest of its history, and Haeckel soldered the first of them on. Third, a bridge to readers Haeckel never intended. Among the readers who encountered Lemuria through Haeckel and through the wider evolutionary popular literature were readers looking for exactly what academic science could not supply: a deep, meaningful human past, narrated as a whole. H. G. Wells, as late as 1919 in his Outline of History (quoted by Bressan), could still write, in a work of serious popular history, that the region where certain early peoples developed was “probably … somewhere about south-western Asia, or in some region now submerged beneath the Mediterranean Sea or the Indian Ocean.” The submerged-homeland idea was, by then, simply in the air that educated readers breathed. Theosophy did not have to invent an audience for Lemuria. Haeckel had already assembled one. // HAECKEL AND DARWIN DISAGREED // Charles Darwin himself favoured Africa as the likeliest cradle of humanity, on the grounds of our closest living relatives, the gorilla and chimpanzee, being African. Haeckel favoured Asia / Lemuria. The disagreement is a reminder that “science said Lemuria” was never true in the singular: leading evolutionists argued the human-origins question both ways, with the fossil evidence then available far too thin to settle it. The African evidence that would eventually prevail — the australopithecines, beginning with the Taung Child in 1924 — still lay in the future. VI. Mapping a Continent That Was Not There — Neumayr, Blandford, Suess Between Haeckel’s adoption and Blavatsky’s, Lemuria had a continuing life inside geology and palaeogeography proper, and that life is worth recording in its own right, because it produced the maps, the neighbouring concepts, and the confusions that still surround the name. Melchior Neumayr and the First Systematic Bridges (1887) The Austrian palaeontologist Melchior Neumayr (1845–1890), in his Erdgeschichte (“Earth History,” 1887), made what standard histories describe as the first systematic attempt to map the hypothetical land bridges and former continents of the geological past as a coherent set. Following Sclater and Huxley, as Leviton and Aldrich’s study of the Geological Survey of India (2004) puts it, Neumayr argued in 1887 for the “peninsula” or land bridge Lemuria — his term for the configuration is also given as Indomadagassia — stretching from Madagascar to India and including a spur to the granitic Seychelles. In the same work Neumayr advanced a broad continental connection between Africa and South America on stratigraphic and palaeontological evidence. That second proposal is historically the more consequential, because it fed directly into the Gondwana synthesis described below. But for Lemuria’s biography the point is simpler: by 1887 the continent had a place in a systematic, textbook palaeogeography, drawn by a leading professional, alongside other connections that modern geology would, in transformed form, vindicate. Being on Neumayr’s map was, at the time, a mark of respectability. The Blanfords, the Geological Survey of India, and Gondwana Running alongside the bridge-building tradition was a second, partly independent line of evidence: the field geology of India. William Thomas Blanford and Henry Francis Blanford and their Survey colleagues had, from the 1850s onward, documented the Gondwana sequence of Indian coal-bearing rocks and its fossil flora, and had argued for a former southern landmass linking India with Africa (and, in their fuller versions, with Australia). Eduard Suess, synthesising this work in Das Antlitz der Erde (“The Face of the Earth,” 1885–1909), coined Gondwana-Land (initially, in 1885, for a more limited Indo-African continent) for that Palaeozoic–Mesozoic southern landmass. William Blanford, reviewing and expanding the concept in 1890 in light of Neumayr’s work, extended it to South America and suggested an Antarctic involvement — approaching the modern outline of Gondwana. This history matters for Lemuria for two reasons. First, it shows that the Indian Ocean evidence was genuinely two-sided and genuinely strong in places: the Glossopteris flora, the Karoo-type faunas, and the matching Gondwana sequences of India, Africa, Australia, South America, and eventually Antarctica are real, and they do record a former union of those lands. Sclater’s instinct that Madagascar and India had once been joined was, at that level of generality, correct . Second, it supplies the distinction that §XIV and §XVI insist on: Lemuria is not Gondwana. Gondwana, as reconstructed by modern geology, is a supercontinent assembled hundreds of millions of years ago and broken up, by drift, across the Mesozoic and Cenozoic. Sclater’s Lemuria was a specifically sunken Indian Ocean continent, invoked to bridge Madagascar and India for the distribution of mammals — including, in Haeckel’s version, in the Tertiary, close to human time. Conflating the two — “science has proved Lemuria, it is called Gondwana” — mistakes a correct general intuition (former union) for a specific mechanism and timescale (recent sinking) that geology has rejected. Concept Proposed By / When Mechanism Timescale Modern Verdict Lemuria Sclater, 1864 Former continent, broken up / subsided beneath the Indian Ocean Sufficiently recent to shape living mammal distribution; Tertiary in Haeckel’s human version Rejected as formulated; no such sunken continent exists Gondwana / Gondwana-Land GSI fieldwork; Suess names it, 1885 Former supercontinent, broken up by (in modern terms) plate drift Palaeozoic assembly; Mesozoic–Cenozoic break-up Accepted, in plate-tectonic form Indomadagassia Neumayr, 1887 Peninsular land bridge, Madagascar–India via the Seychelles Mesozoic–early Cenozoic palaeogeography Superseded; the India–Madagascar union is real, the bridge mechanism is not Other competent contemporaries filled out the picture. Alfred Russel Wallace, in The Geographical Distribution of Animals (1876) and Island Life (1880), discussed the ancient connection between the Ethiopian region and Madagascar needed to explain the Lemurine type and other affinities, and the former southern continent of which Ceylon and South India looked like remnants — passages Scott-Elliot would quote, approvingly and at length, in 1904, while noting that Wallace later denied the necessity of postulating such a continent. That pattern — early sympathy, later retraction as dispersal and better data did more work — recurs across the period, and it is the normal, healthy behaviour of a research programme testing a hypothesis to destruction. VII. Why Serious People Found Lemuria Plausible It is easy, a century and a half later, to ask how anyone believed in a sunken continent. The honest answer requires reconstructing what was not yet known in, say, 1880, and what positive evidence seemed to point Lemuria’s way. Five considerations did most of the work. 1. The Biogeographical Pattern Was Real Lemurs in Madagascar and relatives in Asia; Glossopteris in India, Africa, Australia, and South America; matching fossil faunas between the Karoo and India. The patterns demanding explanation were not illusions, misidentifications, or travellers’ tales. They were documented, in museums and survey memoirs, by the best field workers of the age. Any adequate theory had to explain them, and “they were once connected by land” explained them very directly. 2. There Was No Rival Mechanism for Moving Continents Permanence of continents and ocean basins was not a lazy assumption; it was supported, as then understood, by the physics of a cooling, contracting Earth and by the apparent impossibility of ploughing a continent through solid ocean floor. Wegener’s drift hypothesis, when it came in 1912, would be rejected by most geologists for decades precisely because it offered no adequate mechanism — a rejection that looks stubborn now but was, on the evidence then weighed, defensible. Without drift, vertical movement — up and down — was the only large motion available, and sunken lands were its natural product. 3. Vertical Movement Was Directly Observed Raised beaches, submerged forests, drowned river valleys, coral atolls implying slowly sinking volcanic foundations (Darwin’s subsidence theory of atolls, broadly vindicated), and coastlines visibly rising in Scandinavia: nineteenth-century geologists had abundant proof that land does sink beneath the sea and rise from it. Extrapolating from observed subsidence to a subsided continent was an extrapolation, but it was an extrapolation from something real, not an invention from nothing. Scott-Elliot’s 1904 geological chapter is essentially a catalogue of this evidence — Haeckel on perpetual elevation and depression, Wallace on former connections, Blandford on the atoll chain from the Laccadives through the Chagos to the Seychelles as the backbone of a drowned land — and as a catalogue of what the science of the day said , it is not a foolish document. 4. The Ocean Floor Was Unknown Before systematic echo-sounding, the deep Indian Ocean was, scientifically, a blank. A continent could be hypothesised there without contradicting any direct observation of the floor itself, because there were almost no direct observations to contradict. Hypotheses flourish in blanks on maps. Lemuria shrank, in scientific use, roughly as the blank filled in. 5. Human Origins Needed a Place, and the Fossil Record Was Nearly Empty In 1870 there were no australopithecines, no Homo erectus (Dubois’s Java Man came in 1891, explicitly inspired in part by Haeckel’s prediction of an Asian Pithecanthropus ), and no dated African sequence. A handful of Neanderthal bones and a great deal of comparative anatomy were all anyone had. In that evidential vacuum, a lost tropical homeland was no worse supported than any other location — and it had the narrative advantage of explaining why no fossils of the transition had been found: the workshop had sunk. That advantage should be recognised for what it is — an argument from absence that later evidence dissolved — but in 1870 the absence was total, and every theory faced it. Lemuria attracted serious people because, for several decades, it was a serious answer to serious questions — asked before the instruments existed that could show the answer was wrong. Sumathi Ramaswamy, in the standard modern study, The Lost Land of Lemuria: Fabulous Geographies, Catastrophic Histories (University of California Press, 2004), makes a complementary point that §XVII develops: Lemuria’s scientific origin was crucial to everything that followed. Because the continent came credentialed by science, occultists and Tamil revivalists alike could take it up as something more than a fable — as a place the learned world itself had posited and then, in their telling, abandoned or suppressed. The science gave the later Lemurias their distinctive authority, even as those later Lemurias left the science behind. VIII. The Theosophical Turn — Blavatsky and The Secret Doctrine (1888) Helena Petrovna Blavatsky (1831–1891), co-founder of the Theosophical Society (founded 1875, with Henry Steel Olcott and others), had mentioned Lemuria as early as Isis Unveiled (1877). Its full Theosophical form, however, comes in her major work, The Secret Doctrine: The Synthesis of Science, Religion, and Philosophy , published in two volumes in London in 1888 by the Theosophical Publishing Company: Volume I, Cosmogenesis , and Volume II, Anthropogenesis . Lemuria and its inhabitants belong to Volume II. In Blavatsky’s teaching, humanity develops through a succession of seven Root Races , each occupying its own continent and era, each in turn giving way to the next. In the usual Theosophical enumeration as Blavatsky presents it: the First Root Race is associated with an imperishable sacred land; the Second with Hyperborea; the Third with Lemuria ; the Fourth with Atlantis; the Fifth — in her scheme, our own — with the present world; and the Sixth and Seventh lie in the future. Lemuria, in this system, is therefore not primarily a piece of geography at all. It is a stage : the stage at which, in Blavatsky’s account, humanity first became fully physical. The continent is the theatre of that stage, and it shares the stage’s fate.
