What Megalithic Europe Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do about the single-origin model of §V and the dismantled Welsh circle of §X — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. Archaeoastronomy is audited throughout by the rule this hub applied at Nabta Playa : an alignment demonstrated by survey, or a light effect that can still be watched today, is attested; an elaborate stellar or computational programme reconstructed from the same stones is a claim, and is graded as one. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. Between about 4800 and 2000 BCE, the farming peoples of Atlantic and Mediterranean Europe built in large stone on a scale their world had never attempted: passage tombs under cairns the size of hills, temples among the oldest free-standing stone buildings on Earth, rows of standing stones running for kilometres, and stone circles whose lintels were jointed like carpentry. The phenomenon has a conventional inventory figure — some 35,000 megalithic monuments are known across Europe, the count used in Bettina Schulz Paulsson's 2019 synthesis — and a real geography: dense along the Atlantic façade from Iberia to Scandinavia, dense again on the Mediterranean islands, thinner inland. Its builders were Neolithic farmers and herders. They had stone tools, bone and antler, timber, rope, and draught animals late in the story. They had no states, no palaces, no writing, and — for most of the period — no metal. What they had was organisation, and the organisation is the subject of this article as much as the stones. The article moves as the evidence moves. It begins with scale and with method — how stone was quarried, moved, dressed, and raised, since every later claim about labour and society stands on those procedures — then takes the regions in the order the radiocarbon record presents them: Brittany first, where the earliest monuments stand; the Breton-origin model and its critics; Malta's temple culture; Stonehenge in its phases, with its two great sourcing results and its one great contested claim; Newgrange, where a solstice effect can still be witnessed; and Orkney, where the builders' houses survive with their furniture in place. It closes with the social question the whole phenomenon poses, and with an audit of what the stones do not show. I. A Continent of Stones — The Phenomenon and Its Scale "Megalith" is Greek for "large stone," and the word names a building habit, not a culture. Under it, European prehistory groups several distinct kinds of monument. There are tombs : chambers of upright slabs (orthostats) roofed with capstones and buried under mounds or cairns — the simple dolmens, the gallery graves, and the passage tombs whose chambers are reached down a stone corridor. There are standing stones : single menhirs, rows and alignments of them, and the stone circles of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany. There are the temples of Malta, free-standing roofed buildings of dressed megalithic masonry, a type found nowhere else. And there are the earth-and-stone enclosures — henges, cursus monuments, causewayed enclosures — that frame the stone monuments in landscapes like Salisbury Plain and the Boyne Valley. The types overlap in time and region, but they are not one blueprint copied everywhere: a Breton passage tomb, a Maltese temple, and an Orcadian circle are answers in a shared medium to questions each region posed itself. Whether the medium itself had one birthplace is the debate of §V. // THE INVENTORY // c. 35,000 monuments The conventional count of known megalithic sites in Europe used by Schulz Paulsson (2019) — tombs, menhirs, alignments, circles, and temples together. // THE SPAN // c. 4800 – 2000 BCE From the first Breton cairns of the fifth millennium to the last remodellings at Stonehenge and the final Orcadian buildings — nearly three thousand years. // THE MAP // Atlantic façade + Mediterranean islands Densest in Brittany, Iberia, Britain, Ireland, and Scandinavia, and on Malta, Sardinia, and Corsica; the distribution hugs coasts and navigable water. // THE BUILDERS // Farming societies, no states Neolithic and earliest Bronze Age communities of farmers and herders — no kings, palaces, writing, or (for most of the span) metal tools are attested for them. The chronology is the first discipline. When radiocarbon dating was young, European megaliths were routinely explained as copies of Near Eastern and Aegean prototypes carried west by missionaries or prospectors — the monuments of the Atlantic were assumed to be too accomplished to be native. Calibrated radiocarbon dating destroyed that scheme in the 1970s: the Breton tombs proved older than the Mycenaean tholos tombs they were supposed to copy, and the Maltese temples older than the pyramids beside which they had been dated by style. Colin Renfrew's generation drew the conclusion that the megaliths were independent regional inventions, and for forty years that was the working consensus. Schulz Paulsson's 2019 model (§V) has reopened the question in a new form — not an eastern origin, but a Breton one, diffused by sea. What no party to the debate disputes is the sequence itself: the earliest megalithic monuments in Europe stand in northwestern France in the middle centuries of the fifth millennium BCE, and the tradition's great regional florescences — Malta from c. 3600, the Boyne passage tombs and Stonehenge's first phase around c. 3300–3000, the Orcadian complex across the same centuries — follow over the next two thousand years. The second discipline is survival. The 35,000 are the residue. Stone was robbed for roads, walls, and churches for two thousand years; tombs were emptied, circles ploughed flat, menhirs toppled or Christianised with carved crosses. Some of the most famous landscapes are partly modern restorations — at Carnac, many stones were re-erected in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, not always with records of where they had fallen — and every distribution map is therefore a map of survival and recording as well as of building. The phenomenon was larger than its inventory, by an amount that cannot be recovered. One comparison fixes the hub's frame. At Göbekli Tepe , hunter-gatherers in Anatolia had raised monumental stone enclosures five thousand years before Barnenez — monumentality itself was not invented in Brittany, and this article claims no such thing. What begins in Neolithic Europe is something else: monument-building as the ordinary, repeated practice of farming communities across a whole continent, sustained for nearly three millennia. At Nabta Playa , Saharan herders had already shown that a society without farmers, kings, or cities could quarry, haul, and align large stones. Megalithic Europe is that same lesson written at continental scale, in the imperative mood, by the first farmers. II. How a Megalith Was Made — Quarry, Sledge, Hammer, Rope Every social inference in this article — about labour, feasting, and organisation — depends on the physical procedures being feasible with Neolithic means, and on their costs being roughly known. The procedures are reconstructed from three kinds of evidence: the monuments themselves (quarry faces, half-finished stones, stone holes, dressing debris); the tools and materials excavated at building sites; and full-scale experimental archaeology, in which modern teams using only period materials have quarried, moved, and raised multi-tonne stones. The experiments do not prove which method the builders used. They prove which methods work , and what each costs in people and days — which is what the social argument needs. Quarrying and Dressing Most megalithic stone was not cut from deep quarries but won from outcrops and surface boulders close to the building site — the sarsens of southern England are glacially scattered surface blocks of silcrete; the flagstones of Orkney split naturally along their bedding planes; the limestones of Malta were cut in shallow open quarries near the temples. Where bedrock was worked, the technique exploited natural joints: a line of the rock was freed by hammering, by wedges driven into cracks — wooden wedges swollen with water are the usual reconstruction, directly evidenced at the Welsh bluestone quarries of §X, where stone wedges and hammerstones were excavated in the working platforms — and by levering with timber. Dressing was done with stone on stone. At Stonehenge, hundreds of hammerstones and heavy mauls of sarsen and flint were found in and around the monument: large mauls for rough shaping, smaller hammerstones for finishing, the surfaces pecked and pounded smooth by hours of percussion. The finest dressing is concentrated where it would be seen — the inner faces of the trilithons and the north-eastern arc of the sarsen circle, the faces that frame the solstitial axis — a distribution that itself records a builder's priorities. Transport — Sledges, Rollers, Water On land, the demonstrated vehicle is the timber sledge. A stone lashed to a sledge, hauled by rope teams over a prepared track — of laid timbers, or of ground lubricated with water or fat — can be moved by human muscle at rates the experiments have measured: loads of a tonne by a score of people on the flat, and, by scaling the teams, loads of tens of tonnes. Full-scale trials have repeatedly moved concrete replicas of 10–40 tonnes with teams in the low hundreds. Log rollers are the traditional alternative of the textbooks and are possible under lighter stones, but rollers under the heaviest loads tend to sink, slew, and crush, and most modern reconstructions favour the sledge on a timber trackway, with rollers at most an auxiliary. Where water offered, it was used: the bluestones' journey from Wales (§X) is most plausibly reconstructed as part waterborne — rafts or boats along the coast and up the rivers — because the arithmetic of ton-miles overland for some eighty stones is so punishing, though no Neolithic craft from the journey survives and the route remains inference. The Breton diffusion model of §V is, at bottom, a claim about this same capability: that fifth-millennium communities could move not just stones but an architectural idea, reliably, by sea. The hub's Early Seafaring article weighs the boat evidence on its own terms. Erection — Pits, A-Frames, Cribs, and Levers An upright was raised into a dug stone hole. The excavated holes at Stonehenge and elsewhere show the standard geometry: one side vertical, the other sloped, so the stone could be slid or lowered base-first down the slope until its foot rested against the vertical face; timber stakes and packing protected the hole's edge; then rope teams, hauling over a timber A-frame or shear legs, pulled the stone upright while levers and counterweights controlled it, and the hole was rammed tight with packing stones and chalk rubble. Lintels and capstones were raised differently: the leading reconstruction, supported by experiment, is the timber crib — a platform of crossed logs built up course by course beside the uprights, the lintel levered up one end at a time, the crib growing under it, until the stone could be slid sideways into place. Earthen ramps are the older textbook suggestion; they leave no trace at Stonehenge and the crib needs none, but at tomb sites a capstone could simply be dragged up the growing mound or cairn itself, and several passage-tomb roofs were almost certainly placed that way, from the back of the monument as it rose. None of this requires any machine beyond rope, timber, lever, and organised muscle. All of it requires the muscle to be organised — fed, timed, directed, and kept safe around loads that kill the careless — which is why the procedures matter to §XVI. // WHAT EXPERIMENTS PROVE // An experiment that moves a 40-tonne block with 130 people proves feasibility and cost — that the thing can be done this way, by this many, in this long. It does not prove the builders did it this way. This article cites experimental results only at that strength: as the price list, in labour, against which the social claims of §XVI are checked. Corbelling — the roofing technique of Malta and the Boyne — is treated where it survives, in §VII and §XIII, because its finest evidence is in the buildings themselves. It belongs to the same procedural family: no arch, no mortar, no metal — only the controlled oversailing of one stone course beyond the one below, held by weight and friction, until the span is small enough to cap. With the methods in hand, the tour can begin where the dates begin. III. Brittany First — Barnenez and the Early Tombs The earliest megalithic monuments in Europe stand on the Atlantic coast of Brittany, in the present-day departments of Finistère and Morbihan. The type-site is the great cairn of Barnenez , on the Kernéléhen peninsula near Plouezoc'h, overlooking the bay of Morlaix. Barnenez is a terraced cairn of dry-stone construction about 72 m long, up to 25 m wide and some 8 m high, built in two main phases. Within it are eleven passage graves — stone chambers, some corbel-vaulted, each reached by its own corridor from the cairn's southern face. Radiocarbon dates place the first phase in the range c. 4850–4250 BCE, conventionally summarised as c. 4800 BCE: Barnenez was already old when the first stones of most of this article's monuments were quarried, and it predates the earliest Egyptian pyramid by roughly two thousand years. The cairn's mass has been estimated at some 13,000–14,000 tonnes of stone; the excavators' oft-cited labour figure — quarrying, moving, and building about four worker-days for each cubic metre — gives a sense of a community project measured in years of part-time work rather than in a pharaoh's corvée, a scale that will recur throughout this article. Barnenez was not an isolated flash. Across the fifth millennium, Brittany and the neighbouring Atlantic regions filled with megalithic tombs: the cairn of Bougon in Poitou, the long mounds and passage graves of the Morbihan, and — crucially for §V — a preceding Breton tradition of monumental earthen graves, large elaborate tombs without stone chambers, from around 5000 BCE. Brittany is the one region of Europe where a local developmental sequence can be walked: earthen long mound, then stone chamber under a cairn, then the great passage tombs of the fourth millennium, among them Gavrinis (c. 3500 BCE), whose passage orthostats carry some of the richest carved decoration of the European Neolithic — axes, arcs, and shield-like motifs pecked across nearly every stone, on slabs that include fragments of an earlier carved menhir reused in the tomb, a palimpsest that shows the tradition already old enough, by 3500 BCE, to be recycling its own monuments. At Locmariaquer, the Er Grah tumulus ran some 140 m long, and beside it stood the stone of §IV. The builders of these tombs were among Europe's first farmers — communities of the Atlantic Neolithic growing wheat and barley and herding cattle and sheep on the Breton coast — not, as older popular accounts sometimes had it, a mysterious pre-Celtic master race, and not hunter-gatherers: the "hunter-gatherer origin" phrase that attached itself to the 2019 headlines mislabels a farming population that retained strong maritime and hunting traditions, as coastal farmers do. Their tombs were collective: the chambers held the remains of many individuals, deposited over generations, and the grave goods — polished stone axes, callaïs (variscite) beads from Iberian sources, fine pottery — speak of exchange networks already reaching across the sea lanes the diffusion model will need. The tombs faced the sea because the communities lived by it. Whatever else spread from Brittany, it spread from working harbours. // BARNENEZ // c. 4800 BCE, first phase A terraced dry-stone cairn c. 72 m long at Plouezoc'h, Finistère, containing eleven passage graves; among the earliest megalithic monuments in Europe. // GAVRINIS // c. 3500 BCE An island passage tomb in the Gulf of Morbihan whose orthostats are carved over almost their whole surface — the Breton tradition's surviving masterpiece. // ER GRAH // Tumulus c. 140 m long The great mound at Locmariaquer, raised over a closed stone cist — among the largest Neolithic burial mounds in Europe. // BEFORE THE STONES // Earthen tombs, c. 5000 BCE Northwest France alone, in Schulz Paulsson's survey, has monumental graves without megalithic chambers that precede the stone tombs — a local ancestry for the idea. IV. Carnac — Alignments, Tumuli, and the Broken Menhir South of Barnenez, around the modern town of Carnac in the Morbihan, stands the densest concentration of megaliths on Earth. More than 3,000 standing stones survive there and in the neighbouring communes — the surviving fraction of a far larger Neolithic landscape of tombs, enclosures, and rows, inscribed with the wider Morbihan megalithic landscape on the World Heritage List in 2025. The famous monuments are the alignments : parallel rows of menhirs running across the countryside, in three great groups. At Ménec , 1,099 stones stand in eleven rows over about 1,167 m, the rows ending in stone enclosures at either extremity; at Kermario , some 1,029 stones in ten rows run for about a kilometre; at Kerlescan , 555 stones in thirteen rows form a shorter, squarer system. The stones are undressed local granite, graded in height — tallest at the western ends of the Ménec rows — and set in shallow stone holes packed with wedging stones, the same erection procedure as §II at its simplest: no dressing, no joinery, only selection, haulage, and setting. The alignments' date and purpose are the two honest difficulties of Carnac, and a Tier A account must state both plainly. Granite cannot be radiocarbon dated, the acid soils destroy bone, and many stones were re-erected during nineteenth- and twentieth-century restorations without complete records — so the rows carry no direct chronology of their own, and their assignment to the Neolithic, broadly the fifth-to-third millennia with the main building usually placed in the fifth and fourth, rests on association with the dated tombs and settlements around them. (A Bayesian programme led by Schulz Paulsson, published in Antiquity in 2025, has since modelled several Carnac-area alignments to c. 4600–4300 BCE on dates from associated contexts — a result that, if it holds, makes the rows nearly as old as Barnenez itself.) As to purpose: the rows have attracted every theory in the archaeoastronomical repertoire, including elaborate lunar observatory claims of the kind audited in §XII, none of which has won general acceptance. Alexander Thom, who surveyed the rows exhaustively with his son, concluded in print that they did not know what the alignments were for. Processional ways, territorial statements, arenas of assembly, and monuments to ancestors have all been proposed; the stones, undated and uninscribed, do not choose among them, and this article follows Thom's example in leaving the question open rather than filling it with astronomy the evidence cannot grade. The third Carnac monument is a single stone. The Grand Menhir Brisé at Locmariaquer — Er Grah, "the great stone" — now lies in four pieces where it fell or was felled, beside the Er Grah tumulus and the Table des Marchands tomb. Reassembled in the mind, it stood about 20.6 m high and weighed on the order of 280–330 tonnes: the largest stone known to have been transported and erected by Neolithic Europeans, of a granite whose nearest source lies several kilometres away. It appears to have stood at the head of a row of smaller menhirs, and to have fallen — or been pulled down — in later prehistory; earthquake and deliberate destruction have both been argued, and the question is open. Its carved fragments were reused in neighbouring tombs, as at Gavrinis: the Breton tradition, at its height, was already monumental enough to quarry its own past. The Grand Menhir is the calibration point for every transport claim in this article: a community of Breton farmers moved a stone heavier than any single block at Stonehenge or Malta, with stone tools, timber, and rope, in the fifth millennium BCE. The procedures of §II are not conjecture about what such people might manage. They are the minimum the record requires. V. One Origin by Sea? — The Breton Diffusion Model and Its Critics In February 2019, Bettina Schulz Paulsson of the University of Gothenburg published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences the most ambitious chronological study the megalithic debate has produced: "Radiocarbon dates and Bayesian modeling support maritime diffusion model for megaliths in Europe" ( PNAS 116/9: 3460–3465). She assembled 2,410 radiocarbon dates from megalithic sites, from the "pre-megalithic" monumental graves that precede them, and from contemporary non-megalithic contexts across Europe, filtered them for quality, and modelled the appearance of megalithic architecture region by region. Her conclusions were threefold. First, the earliest megaliths occur in northwest France , in the second half of the fifth millennium BCE — and northwest France is the only region that also has the preceding earthen monumental graves, giving the stone tombs a visible local ancestry there and nowhere else. Second, the subsequent spread falls into three successive phases along the coasts: a first expansion, within some two to three centuries, to southern France, Catalonia, Corsica, Sardinia, and Atlantic Iberia; a second to Britain, Ireland, and the rest of Iberia; a third, in the third millennium, to Scandinavia and northern Europe. Third, the geography of that spread — new tomb types appearing abruptly at coastal sites, specific architectural forms travelling long distances by water while inland regions lag — identifies the vector: the megalithic idea diffused by sea , which in turn implies a level of fifth-millennium seafaring well beyond what the boat evidence alone had established. The model's reception defines its current standing, and both halves of it belong in this article. The support was immediate and senior: Michael Parker Pearson, the leading Stonehenge archaeologist, told Science 's news service that the study demonstrated that Brittany was the origin of the European megalithic phenomenon, and Gail Higginbottom, a specialist in megalithic landscapes, judged the maritime reading plausible. But the qualifications were published alongside the praise, and they are not minor. Parker Pearson himself added that the study did a good job of establishing the Breton priority but did not quite rule out that some later cultures developed megalithic building independently. Karl-Göran Sjögren of Gothenburg — the author's own institution — accepted northwest France as among the first building regions but withheld assent from the single origin: earlier megaliths may yet be uncovered elsewhere, and future redating may push known monuments in other regions earlier. The standing objections, as the debate has settled, are these: the model is only as strong as its date list, and radiocarbon dates date burials and charcoal in and around tombs, not the stones — a region's "first megalith" is a sampling statement as much as a historical one; the three-phase pattern depends on which monument types are counted as megalithic, a classification on which specialists differ; and similarity of tomb form across the sea lanes, while real, does not by itself distinguish an idea carried by voyagers from forms converged upon by similar farming societies facing similar needs — the objection on which Renfrew's independent-invention model had rested for forty years. // THE MODEL, AT ITS EXACT STRENGTH // Established by the study: on the largest quality-filtered radiocarbon dataset yet assembled, the earliest megalithic tombs are Breton, the Breton tombs have a local earthen ancestry found nowhere else, and later appearances pattern along the coasts in a sequence consistent with maritime diffusion. Not established: that every regional tradition descends from Brittany — the model cannot exclude independent invention in later phases, and its critics, including sympathetic ones, have said so in print. The Breton origin of the earliest megaliths is now the reference position of the debate; the single origin of all megaliths remains a live claim, reported here as such. Two further bodies of evidence have entered the debate since 2019, and both cut in instructive directions. Ancient DNA — notably Sánchez-Quinto and colleagues' 2019 sequencing of individuals buried in megalithic tombs in Ireland, Scotland, and Sweden — shows the tomb-builders to have been farming populations of ultimately Anatolian descent mixed with local hunter-gatherers, with kinship structured burials (one Irish tomb held an extended family across generations): the megaliths were built by the ordinary Neolithic population of each region, not by a single wandering master people, which fits diffusion of an idea among related farming communities better than migration of a megalithic tribe. And the sea lanes themselves are independently attested for the period — obsidian, callaïs, and polished axes crossed these waters in quantity — so the model's vector is not an ad hoc invention; what remains unproven is that the architectural idea travelled it as a single package, once. Readers weighing the seafaring claim itself should continue to Early Seafaring , where the direct boat and island-colonisation evidence is audited on its own. Malta, to which the article now turns, is the test case both sides cite: an island temple culture of unmistakably local genius, which any diffusion model must reach by sea — and which resembles nothing in Brittany at all. VI. Malta — An Island Temple Culture The Maltese archipelago — Malta, Gozo, and Comino, some 316 km² of limestone in the central Mediterranean, 90 km south of Sicily — holds the most concentrated monumental landscape of the Neolithic world. Farmers reached the islands from Sicily by about 5400–5200 BCE, bringing the full Neolithic package across open water. After two millennia of village life, the islanders entered what Maltese prehistory calls the Temple Period : from the Ġgantija phase (c. 3600–3200 BCE) through the Saflieni phase (c. 3300–3000) to the Tarxien phase (c. 3000–2500 BCE), they built more than thirty stone temples — free-standing, roofed, multi-roomed buildings of megalithic masonry, each organised as a series of semicircular chambers (apses) opening off a central court behind a concave façade and an oval forecourt. UNESCO's inscription of the six principal complexes states their rank without embroidery: the temples "rank amongst the earliest free-standing stone buildings in the world." They are older than Stonehenge's stones and older than the Great Pyramid, and they were built by an island farming population that had no metal, no wheel, no draught animals larger than cattle, and no contact-driven need to impress anyone but themselves. The oldest and largest complex is Ġgantija on Gozo — the name, "the giantess's tower," preserves the local folklore that a giant built it, the standard folk verdict on megalithic masonry everywhere. Two temples stand side by side inside a single massive boundary wall of coralline limestone: the South Temple (c. 3600–3200 BCE), with five great apses, walls surviving in places to over 6 m, and traces of the wall plaster that once smoothed its interior; and the smaller, later North Temple of four apses. The enclosing wall is itself among the largest megalithic constructions of the islands, built of alternating upright blocks set face-out and edge-out (§VII). On Malta's southern coast, 500 m apart on a ridge above the sea, stand Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra . Ħaġar Qim, of the softer globigerina limestone, is the most inventive plan of the group — a central passage threading a cluster of apses and independent chambers, with carved altar tables, mushroom-shaped offering tables, and one of the largest single blocks in any Maltese temple in its outer wall. Mnajdra, below it, preserves three temples, of which the Lower Temple carries the alignment evidence audited in §VII's closing paragraphs. Inland, the Tarxien complex (c. 3000–2500 BCE) is the culture's late masterpiece: four linked temples with relief carvings of spirals and of domestic animals — bulls, goats, a sow with piglets — cut into altar blocks, and the remains of its colossal statue (§VIII). Between them, these buildings served their communities for over a thousand years. // ĠGANTIJA, GOZO // c. 3600–3200 BCE Two temples within one great coralline boundary wall; the South Temple's five apses and 6 m walls make it among the world's oldest free-standing stone buildings. // ĦAĠAR QIM // Globigerina limestone The most complex temple plan on Malta, with carved altars and offering tables — and the soft stone now weathering under a protective shelter. // MNAJDRA // The solar temple Three temples on the slope below Ħaġar Qim; the Lower Temple's equinox and solstice light effects are still observable today (§VII). // TARXIEN // c. 3000–2500 BCE The late florescence: animal reliefs, spiral altars, and the lower half of a statue that once stood some 2.5–3 m tall. What the temples were must be stated at the evidence's strength. They were not houses — no domestic assemblage belongs to them — and not tombs: the culture buried its dead elsewhere, in rock-cut tombs and the Hypogeum of §VIII. Their finds are consistent and strange: animal bones in quantity, including deposits of skulls and horn cores; stone and clay figurines; carved altars and libation holes; evidence of fire; and, at several temples, arrangements of rooms that grade access from the public forecourt through the central court to small inner apses reachable only through porthole slabs — architecture that stages a progression from the many to the few. The conventional label "temple" is an interpretation, but it is the interpretation the buildings' own plan argues: communal ritual buildings, used for ceremonies involving animals, fire, and restricted inner rites, maintained and enlarged over centuries. Who officiated, and what was believed, no evidence says. The Maltese temples are the purest case in this article of monumental architecture as a society's central institution — built by a population of, on most estimates, only some thousands of people, on islands with no stone to spare and no neighbours to overawe. VII. Malta in Stone — Walling, Corbelling, and the Roofing Problem Maltese temple building is a complete technology, and it can be described stepwise because its elements survive in combination. The islands offer two limestones, and the builders used each where its properties belonged — the material knowledge UNESCO's assessment singles out. Coralline limestone , hard, grey, and weather-resistant, forms the outer walls and the Ġgantija boundary. Globigerina limestone , soft, pale, and easily cut when fresh, forms the sheltered interiors, the doorways, and every carved element. A temple wall is not a single skin but a built sandwich: an outer face of large coralline blocks, set alternately face-out and edge-out so that headers tie deep into the wall's core; an inner face of upright slabs (orthostats); and between them a packing of earth and rubble that binds the whole into one mass. Façades rise from a bench-like plinth of orthostats; doorways are trilithons — two uprights and a lintel — or porthole slabs pierced with a rectangular opening, dressed with stone hammers, chisels of flint and imported obsidian, and abrasion. Floors are flagstone, or torba — crushed globigerina laid on rubble, wetted and pounded to a hard, polishable surface, a recipe closer to concrete-making than to paving. Interiors were plastered and, in places, painted with red ochre, traces of which survive at Ġgantija and elsewhere. Above the orthostats, the walls continue in horizontal courses of smaller blocks that step progressively inward — the beginnings of a corbelled vault . The mechanics are those of §XIII's Irish vault in miniature: each course oversails the one below by a few centimetres; the load of the courses above and behind counterweights the overhang; the span narrows course by course until it can be closed. The surviving horizontal masonry at several temples demonstrates that the apses were carried up in this way to a considerable height. Whether any apse was ever closed entirely in stone is the roofing problem , and it is genuinely open. No collapsed stone roof has been excavated in any temple; the spans of the largest apses (over 6 m at Ġgantija) strain what corbelling in this limestone can do; and two pieces of the culture's own evidence point the other way — a small stone temple model from Ta' Ħaġrat, which appears to show a slab roof, and a carved graffito at Mnajdra showing a façade with a pitched or slabbed top. The reconstruction most specialists now work with is mixed: corbelled stone carried as high as the span allowed, closed by timber beams, brushwood, and clay or hide above — UNESCO's summary, "corbelled roofs, probably capped by horizontal beams," states the consensus at its proper tentativeness. What Mehrgarh Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do about the domestication of the zebu and the purpose of the drilled teeth — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. Mehrgarh is a cluster of settlement mounds on the Kachi plain of Balochistan, in modern Pakistan, at the foot of the Bolan Pass — the great corridor between the Iranian plateau and the Indus plain. Excavated by the French Archaeological Mission from 1974 into the 2000s, it preserves something no other South Asian site of its age can match: a continuous, stratified sequence of occupation running from an aceramic farming village of about 7000 BCE through five thousand years of development to the threshold of the Indus civilisation. In that sequence, excavators found compartmented mud-brick granaries before pottery existed; burials furnished, from the very beginning, with lapis lazuli, turquoise, and marine shell carried over hundreds of kilometres; the earliest cotton fibres known anywhere in the Old World, preserved inside the corrosion of a copper bead; and eleven human teeth, drilled in life with flint-tipped bow drills — the earliest dentistry-like practice known to archaeology. Mehrgarh also poses, in its sharpest form, the question this hub asks of every farming hearth: how much was imported, and how much was made at home? Its grains are the wheats and barleys of the Near Eastern founder package, and they tie the village westward, to the Zagros and the Fertile Crescent. Its cattle tell the opposite story. On the argument first made by the mission's faunal analyst, Richard Meadow, and broadly supported by later genetic work, the humped zebu of South Asia was domesticated here, or in this region, from the local Indian aurochs — an independent act of animal domestication standing beside the imported seeds. Mehrgarh is therefore not a colony of the western Neolithic and not an isolated invention either. It is a meeting ground, and its five-thousand-year sequence is the deep foundation on which the Indus tradition was built. I. A Village at the Foot of the Pass — The Place Mehrgarh lies on the western bank of the Bolan River, near the modern town of Dhadar, in the northern Kachi plain of Balochistan — the broad alluvial apron where the mountains of the plateau's edge give way, eastward, to the Indus floodplain. The site sits at approximately 29°23′ N, 67°37′ E, between the present-day cities of Quetta, Kalat, and Sibi, and a short distance from the mouth of the Bolan Pass. Geography is the first fact of the site's history, and the excavators have never tired of stating it: the Bolan is one of the two classic routes — the other is the Khyber, far to the north — between the Iranian plateau and Central Asia on one side and the Indus valley on the other. Whoever settled at Mehrgarh settled on a road. // LOCATION // c. 29°23′ N, 67°37′ E On the Bolan River, northern Kachi plain, Balochistan, Pakistan — at the foot of the Bolan Pass, west of the Indus valley. // THE SITE // 200+ hectares of mounds A cluster of successive settlements (sectors MR.1–MR.6 and companions), not one town: each generation's village partly abandoned and rebuilt nearby. // OCCUPATION // c. 7000 – 2000 BCE A continuous stratified sequence from aceramic Neolithic village to the age of the mature Indus cities — the longest in South Asia. // THE CORRIDOR // Plateau ⇄ Indus plain The Bolan Pass links the Balochistan highlands and, beyond them, eastern Iran and southern Afghanistan with the Indus lowlands. The Kachi plain is a demanding but workable farming landscape: hot, dry, and dependent on the seasonal water of the Bolan River and on the runoff from the hills — conditions suited to the winter-sown cereals, wheat and barley, that the first settlers grew, and to grazing on the plain and in the foothills for their herds. The hills behind the site offered stone, including the cherts and flints of the tool industry; the river offered a permanent line of water and a route down to the Indus. The plain also offered neighbours in every direction: eastward, the Indus valley itself; westward and northward, the highland valleys of Balochistan, where a scatter of contemporary and later settlements — Kili Gul Mohammad, Rana Ghundai, and others — forms the regional context in which Mehrgarh must be read. One caution about scale belongs at the front, because popular accounts inflate it. The archaeological area of Mehrgarh covers more than 200 hectares, but that figure measures five thousand years of accumulated settlement debris spread across a cluster of mounds — the mission's sectors are numbered MR.1 through MR.6 and beyond — not the footprint of any single community. At any one moment, Mehrgarh was a village, later a large village and then a small town. Its importance is not urban size. It is duration : nowhere else in the Greater Indus region can the whole arc from first farming to civilisation be walked, layer by layer, in a single place. The comparison this hub invites is with the parallel hearths treated elsewhere in this division. At Nabta Playa , Saharan herders built a ceremonial world around cattle without ever farming; at Göbekli Tepe , Anatolian hunter-gatherers raised monumental enclosures on the eve of domestication. Mehrgarh is the third pattern: a settled farming village from its earliest excavated level, growing crops whose ancestors are western and herding cattle whose ancestors, on the prevailing argument, are its own. The three sites are contemporary witnesses that the Neolithic was not one event with one birthplace, but a set of regional experiments that exchanged materials, animals, and ideas along routes like the Bolan. II. The French Mission — Excavation, 1974–2000 Mehrgarh was identified in 1974 by the French Archaeological Mission to Pakistan, working in collaboration with the Department of Archaeology of Pakistan, and excavation began in December of that year under the direction of Jean-François Jarrige , with Catherine Jarrige as co-director of the mission's work in the region. The first seasons explored mounds of the third and fourth millennia BCE near the river; the discovery, in the mission's third season (1976–1977), of an aceramic Neolithic occupation in the northern sector — sector MR.3 — transformed the project. What had been a Chalcolithic and Bronze Age site became the type-site for the entire early prehistory of northwestern South Asia. The mission worked at Mehrgarh continuously from 1974 to 1986, then — after a decade given largely to the excavation of nearby Nausharo (§XIV) — returned to the Neolithic sector from 1997 to 2000. Those final seasons mattered out of proportion to their length: excavation of the Period I settlement was extended to some 1,700 m² of exposed buildings, the deepest levels were reached over a smaller area, and the internal stratigraphy of the aceramic sequence was re-established on a footing secure enough that the mission renumbered the Neolithic levels from the bottom up. The site's publication record matches its excavation: the synthetic volume Mehrgarh: Field Reports 1974–1985 — From Neolithic Times to the Indus Civilization (Jarrige, Jarrige, Meadow & Quivron, eds., 1995) remains the standard point of entry, supplemented by a long series of specialist studies — Lorenzo Costantini on the plant remains, Richard Meadow on the fauna, and many others on the beads, the burials, the pottery, and the teeth. Two consequences follow for the reader. First, Mehrgarh is a specialist-rich site: its famous claims — early cotton, local zebu domestication, drilled teeth — each rest on a dedicated laboratory study published in a peer-reviewed venue, not on field impressions. Second, the interpretation of Mehrgarh has been shaped by a single long-running mission, and its director's framing — Jean-François Jarrige argued, against an older diffusionism, that Mehrgarh had an earlier local background and an originality of its own within a wider cultural continuum stretching to eastern Mesopotamia — is itself a position in a debate, reported as such in §VI and §XV. The strata are the mission's gift; the readings of the strata are scholarship, and scholarship argues. // THE SECTOR MAP // The mission's grid divides the mound cluster into sectors cited throughout the literature: MR.3 is the Neolithic sector, with its cemetery of more than 300 graves; MR.4 carries much of the Period II occupation; MR.2 is the great Chalcolithic mound of Period III, with its own cemetery; MR.1 and its neighbours carry the later periods toward the Bronze Age. When a find in this article is tied to a sector — the drilled teeth to MR.3, the Period III potters' ovens to MR.2 — the sector is part of the evidence, because it fixes the find in the sequence. A note on dates. The chronology used here is the mission's periodisation in its conventional calibrated form, as summarised in the standard syntheses (Jarrige et al. 1995; Possehl 2002). Individual radiocarbon determinations exist for many contexts, but the period boundaries — c. 7000, 5500, 4800, 3500 BCE and so on — are rounded working figures, and different publications round them differently or subdivide periods differently (a Period VIII, at the Sibri cemetery some kilometres away, is sometimes added). Where a specific find carries its own date — the cotton burial to the first half of the sixth millennium BCE, the drilled teeth to a graveyard dated 9,000–7,500 years ago — this article gives the find's date in the form its publishers gave it, and says so. III. The Sequence — Periods I to VII The mission divided Mehrgarh's occupation into seven principal periods, defined by stratigraphy, architecture, and material culture, and correlated across the mound cluster. The scheme is the site's backbone: every claim in this article hangs on it. Dates are the conventional calibrated approximations used in the mission's syntheses and in Possehl's The Indus Civilization (2002); they are rounded, and the transitions between periods were processes, not events. Period Approx. Dates (BCE) Character Signature Evidence I c. 7000–5500 Aceramic Neolithic Compartmented mud-brick storage buildings; burials with lapis, turquoise, carnelian, marine shell; wheat and barley farming; cattle, sheep, and goat management; no pottery II c. 5500–4800 Ceramic Neolithic First pottery, handmade, later wheel-finished and wheel-made toward the period's end; growing craft production; the MR.3 cemetery ground continues in use III c. 4800–3500 Chalcolithic Mass wheel-made painted pottery and potters' quarters; steatite micro-bead production; copper crucibles; compartmented (button) seals; figurines; the MR.2 cemetery IV c. 3500–3250 Later Chalcolithic Continued settlement growth; regional styles of the Balochistan highlands and the Indus borderlands draw closer together V c. 3250–3000 Transitional Developments anticipating the Early Harappan; settlement focus begins to shift within the mound cluster VI c. 3000–2700 Early Harappan horizon Occupation contemporary with the first period at neighbouring Nausharo; the regional tradition now feeds directly into the Indus sequence VII c. 2700–2000 Indus age Mehrgarh largely yields primacy to Nausharo, 6 km away, as the mature Indus civilisation develops; occupation continues at reduced scale Three features of the sequence deserve emphasis before the detail begins. The first is its continuity : the mission found no sterile break, no destruction layer marking a replacement of one world by another, between the first farmers and the Indus age. Buildings were rebuilt, cemeteries succeeded cemeteries, crafts intensified — but the sequence reads as development in place, which is precisely what makes Mehrgarh the foundation document of the Indus tradition rather than a mere predecessor of it. The second is its shape : the centre of settlement migrates across the mound cluster over time, from the northern Neolithic sector toward the southern mounds, so that "Mehrgarh" names a landscape of successive villages rather than a single tell that simply grew. The third is a warning: continuity of culture is not automatically continuity of population . Dental anthropologists John Lukacs and Brian Hemphill, studying the skeletal series, argued that the Chalcolithic population of Mehrgarh was not simply descended from its Neolithic population — a finding that complicates any straight-line story and is taken up again in §XV. The periods that follow in this article are weighted as the evidence is weighted. Periods I to III — the Neolithic and the earlier Chalcolithic, c. 7000–3500 BCE — carry the site's most distinctive and most debated evidence, and they receive the fullest treatment. Periods IV to VII are treated more briefly, in §XIV and §XV, because their story is increasingly the story of the whole Greater Indus region, and its proper home is the Indus treatment this hub points toward (§XVI). IV. Period I — The Aceramic Village: Buildings and Burials Period I (c. 7000–5500 BCE) is the aceramic Neolithic: a farming village that made no pottery at all. Its absence of ceramics is not a mark of poverty — the same levels yield worked copper ornaments, beads of stones carried from Afghanistan and Iran, and buildings of a distinctive and purposeful plan — but of a technological choice-set in which containers were baskets, skins, stone, and unfired clay. The flint industry produced blades with the gloss of sickle-use; grinding stones processed grain; bone tools, polished stone axes and adzes, and bitumen — used to line baskets and to haft blades — complete the toolkit of a community that was, from its first excavated level, sedentary and agricultural. The Compartmented Buildings The signature architecture of Period I is the mud-brick building divided into small square compartments. Excavation in sector MR.3 cleared dozens of structures — forty-six buildings in the area exposed by the 1997–2000 seasons alone — built of hand-formed mud bricks, their interiors subdivided into two, four, or more small cells. Many of the compartmented buildings have no doorways at workable height: they were entered, the excavators argue, from the roof, and their cells were filled and emptied from above. The standard reading, from the mission's first reports onward, is that these are storage buildings — granaries in which the community's harvested grain was kept in bulk, cell by cell. Beside them stood smaller rectangular houses, likewise of mud brick, and open spaces between the buildings that served, as the next paragraphs show, as burial ground. The granaries matter beyond their function. Bulk storage of a harvest is a social fact as much as an architectural one: it implies a surplus worth guarding, a calendar organised around sowing and reaping, and arrangements — household or communal, the plans alone cannot say — for holding food across the year. The same storage-first pattern appears at the very beginning of the farming story told in this hub's Nile Bridge article for the contemporary Nile margin, and it is one of the quiet continuities of the early Neolithic world: before pottery, before metal in any quantity, before seals or writing, there is the granary. Mehrgarh's version is simply among the earliest and clearest anywhere. The Burials — Wealth from the Start The dead of Period I were buried in the open spaces among the buildings, in simple pits and in graves lined or capped with mud brick, the body typically flexed. More than 300 graves were excavated in the MR.3 cemetery ground, which spans the Neolithic occupation. What transformed the site's reputation was the furnishing of these early graves. Burial goods include stone and bone tools, baskets, beads and pendants — and the materials of those ornaments are the point: lapis lazuli , whose nearest ancient source is Badakhshan in northeastern Afghanistan; turquoise , attributed to sources in Iran; carnelian and other hard stones; and marine shell , which can only have come from the Arabian Sea coast, hundreds of kilometres to the south. Some graves contained the remains of young goats, placed with the dead. Unfired clay figurines of women and animals, among the earliest from South Asia, accompany the settlement levels. Read plainly, the burials say two things at once. First, the aceramic villagers of Mehrgarh were already nodes in exchange networks of continental reach — lapis, turquoise, and shell do not walk to the Bolan Pass by themselves — and those networks are as old as the village itself, present in its earliest levels rather than grafted on later. Second, the community chose to deposit that far-travelled wealth with its dead, in the ground between its granaries. Whatever social distinctions the graves express — and the mission's analysts have noted variation in the richness of furnishing — they express them through ornament : through the same bead-making materials and skills that later produced the drilled teeth of §IX and the lapidary industry of §XI. Mehrgarh's craft tradition and its exchange tradition are one tradition, and both begin in Period I. STORAGE FIRST Compartmented, doorless mud-brick buildings, entered from above and read by the excavators as granaries, stand among the Period I houses from the earliest levels — bulk grain storage precedes pottery at Mehrgarh by the whole length of Period I. GRAVES BETWEEN THE HOUSES The MR.3 burial ground, with more than 300 excavated graves, lies in the open spaces of the settlement itself. The dead remained inside the village's plan, furnished with tools, baskets, ornaments — and sometimes a young goat. DISTANCE IN THE GRAVE GOODS Lapis lazuli from the direction of Badakhshan, turquoise from the direction of Iran, shell from the Arabian Sea coast: the Period I ornament assemblage maps exchange routes radiating from the Bolan in every direction, from the village's first centuries. NO POTTERY — BY ABSENCE, NOT POVERTY Period I is aceramic, yet its levels yield copper ornaments, bitumen-lined baskets, sickle-glossed blades, and figurines. The container gap was filled by basketry, skins, stone, and unfired clay. V. The Plant Package — Wheats and Barleys from the West The evidence for Mehrgarh's crops comes by an elegant accident of preservation: the mud bricks themselves. Grain and chaff mixed into the mud as temper left impressions in the fired and unfired brick of the Period I buildings, and the mission's archaeobotanist, Lorenzo Costantini, built the site's plant record substantially on those impressions, supplemented by charred remains. The assemblage he identified is unambiguous in its affinities. The cereals are barleys — two-row hulled barley and six-row forms, including naked (free-threshing) barley — and wheats : emmer, einkorn, and free-threshing bread-type wheats. Wild and gathered plants supplement the package, among them jujube and other fruits of the plain and foothills, but the staple core is cereal farming of a fully developed kind. That package has a passport, and the passport is western. Emmer and einkorn are two of the founder crops of the Near Eastern Neolithic, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent; the barleys likewise belong to the western founder set. No wild progenitors of emmer or einkorn grow in Balochistan, and the current archaeobotanical consensus — stated, for South Asia, in Dorian Fuller's syntheses of the region's domestication history — is that the wheat-and-barley complex arrived in the Indus borderlands from the west, whether carried by migrating farmers, passed community to community across the Iranian plateau, or some braided combination of the two; the archaeology of a seed cannot distinguish a migrant's sack from a neighbour's gift. What the Mehrgarh sequence shows is the package in place and diversifying by c. 7000 BCE: multiple wheat and barley forms grown together, in a winter-cropping regime fitted to the Kachi plain's seasons, and stored in bulk in the granaries of §IV. Two qualifications keep the picture honest. The first is that "arrived" does not mean "arrived finished and never changed": the prominence of free-threshing forms and naked barley at Mehrgarh has been read as local selection under local conditions, the package adapting to its new ground within the sequence itself. The second is that the western package was never the whole diet. Hunting remained important in Period I — the earliest faunal assemblages are dominated by wild species, gazelle prominent among them — and gathered wild plants continued alongside the cereals. Mehrgarh's first farmers were also herders and hunters; the Neolithic, here as almost everywhere, was a broadening of the economy, not a switch thrown in a generation. // A FOUNDER PACKAGE, ADOPTED // The contrast that structures this whole article is set in the plant record. For the grains, Mehrgarh is a recipient: the founder wheats and barleys are western domesticates, and no local domestication of wheat or barley is claimed for the site in the current literature. For the cattle of the next section, the claim runs the other way. A hearth can be secondary for one domesticate and primary for another — Mehrgarh is the textbook case, which is why the hub calls it a third farming hearth in its own right rather than an outpost of the first. Cotton belongs to the plant story too, but its evidence is so singular — a few threads inside a bead — that it receives its own section (§VIII). It is enough to register here that if the wheats tie Mehrgarh to the west, the cotton, whatever its domestication status, ties it to its own region: Gossypium is a plant of the South Asian world, and its presence in a sixth-millennium grave at Mehrgarh is the earliest sign anywhere of the fibre that would one day define Indus textiles. VI. The Zebu Question — Cattle Domesticated on Home Ground The animal bones of Period I tell a story in two movements. In the earliest levels, wild species dominate: gazelle above all, with wild sheep, wild goat, wild cattle, onager, and pig among the hunted fauna, and domestic or managed stock a minority presence. Through the Period I sequence the balance shifts — sheep, goats, and above all cattle increase steadily as a proportion of the assemblage, until by the later Neolithic the domesticates dominate. The mission's faunal analyst, Richard H. Meadow , devoted his Mehrgarh studies to reading that shift, and from it he drew the site's most consequential argument: that the cattle being brought under management at Mehrgarh were not imported Near Eastern taurines, but the local humped cattle — the zebu , Bos indicus — domesticated here from the Indian aurochs, Bos primigenius namadicus . Meadow's Argument The argument is morphometric — built on measurement. Meadow documented, across the Period I stratigraphy, a progressive decrease in the size of the cattle represented in the bone assemblage, together with their rising frequency. Size reduction under human management is the classic osteological signature of domestication in progress: animals bred in herds, culled selectively, and kept from the full growth of their wild kin grow smaller than the wild population from which they are drawn. At Mehrgarh, Meadow argued, the sequence catches that signature in the act — large wild cattle in the early levels giving way, within the site's own strata, to smaller managed animals — and the managed animals are of the zebu kind: figurines of humped bulls and the morphology of the later material mark the herd as Bos indicus , not the humpless Bos taurus of the Near East. The wild progenitor was at hand: the Indian aurochs ranged the subcontinent's plains into historical times. On Meadow's reading, Mehrgarh is therefore a centre of independent animal domestication — for cattle, the most important domesticate in South Asian history — even though its grains came from the west. Sheep and Goats — The Supporting Herd The zebu does not stand alone in the faunal record, and the supporting cast complicates the picture usefully. Sheep and goats are present from early in the sequence and grow in importance alongside the cattle; Meadow argued for management of goats at an early date, and the precise geography of caprine domestication — western introduction, local domestication of the region's wild goats, or both braided together — remains debated in the literature, with the wild progenitors of both species native to the Balochistan highlands themselves. The honest summary is that Mehrgarh's herding economy was assembled from more than one source: the village stood where the western domesticates and the subcontinent's own wild herds met, and it drew on both. That mixed origin is not a weakness in the site's claim to importance. It is the claim: the Bolan corridor was a place of combination , and the Indus tradition was born of combination from its first village onward. The Genetic Verdict — Broad Support, Open Detail Genetics entered the zebu question a generation after Meadow, and its broad verdict has favoured him. Mitochondrial studies from Loftus and colleagues (1994) onward established that zebu and taurine cattle descend from aurochs populations that had diverged long before domestication — the signature of two separate domestications , not of one herd carried east and humped by later crossing. Chen and colleagues, surveying 844 zebu mitochondrial sequences across Asia in Molecular Biology and Evolution (2010), concluded that domestic zebu are, in their title's words, "an exclusive legacy of the South Asia Neolithic": two maternal haplogroups (I1 and I2), with diversity for the I1 lineage highest in the Indus valley — supporting the Indus region as a primary centre of zebu domestication. Later modelling of autosomal data has added texture rather than reversal: a domestication process in South Asia, probably diffuse, with substantial later interbreeding between managed herds and local wild aurochs. What genetics cannot do is point at a mound. The genes locate zebu domestication in South Asia, and for one lineage most plausibly in the greater Indus region; they do not and cannot certify that the process happened at Mehrgarh itself rather than across a Balochistan-and-Indus world of which Mehrgarh is simply the best-excavated witness. Nor is the chronology closed: proposals for the span over which zebu domestication unfolded at and around Mehrgarh run broadly across c. 7000–4500 BCE, and the contribution of additional centres elsewhere in the subcontinent remains argued. This article therefore states the standing of the argument exactly: a separate zebu domestication in the Indus region is the prevailing position, supported independently by osteology and genetics; Mehrgarh is its earliest and fullest archaeological witness; the precise locus, tempo, and unity of the process remain open questions in the published literature. That is a strong claim. It is also, at that strength, a defensible one — which is the only kind this tier prints. // THE MIRROR OF NABTA // Readers of this hub will recognise the shape of the argument — and should note that its fortunes are the reverse of Nabta Playa's. At Nabta (§VII of that article), an independent African cattle domestication was proposed on ecological grounds and has lost ground to metrical and genetic criticism. At Mehrgarh, an independent zebu domestication was proposed on metrical grounds and has gained ground from genetics. The difference is not the boldness of the excavators; it is the evidence. Independent domestication is a claim that stands or falls site by site, bone by bone, genome by genome — and this archive reports each site at the strength its own evidence has reached. VII. Period II — The Ceramic Neolithic Period II (c. 5500–4800 BCE) is defined by a single innovation: pottery. The first ceramics at Mehrgarh — found principally in sector MR.4 — are handmade vessels, coarse at first, some bearing the impressions of the baskets in which or against which they were formed. Through the period the ware improves: finer pastes, better firing, and, toward the period's end, the first wheel-finished and wheel-made pottery — the rotary technology that would come to dominate Period III production. The appearance of pottery in a community that had farmed without it for fifteen centuries is a reminder that the Neolithic package was assembled piece by piece, at different times in different places: Mehrgarh took the grains early and the pots late, exactly reversing the order seen at Nabta, where pottery precedes farming altogether. The rest of Period II is intensification. Settlement expands; craft production grows in volume and variety; the burial ground at MR.3 continues in use, its graves now accompanied by pottery as well as by the older ornament repertoire. Copper appears in small but telling quantities — a ring, beads, a small ingot are reported from Period II contexts — worked metal still an ornament material, not yet an industry. Figurines continue, in unfired and now fired clay. And two of the site's most famous bodies of evidence belong to this broad horizon and the centuries on either side of it: the cotton threads of the next section, preserved in a burial of the sixth millennium BCE, and the drilled teeth of §IX, from the MR.3 graveyard whose use spans the later Neolithic. Period II is also when Mehrgarh's regional setting thickens. The mission's syntheses place the period within an expansion of settled farming communities across the Balochistan borderlands — contemporary occupations at Kili Gul Mohammad and a scatter of sites in the highlands and toward the Indus plain — so that by 5000 BCE the Bolan village was one node, albeit the largest and longest-lived, in a settled Neolithic landscape. The farming hearth had become a farming region . That regionalisation, more than any single artefact, is what made the later developments of Period III possible: crafts specialise where there are neighbours to exchange with, and by Period II Mehrgarh had neighbours in every direction. VIII. Cotton — Threads Preserved in Copper The earliest cotton known anywhere in the Old World survived by a chemical accident, inside a bead. The context is a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh dated to the first half of the sixth millennium BCE: beside the left wrist of an adult skeleton lay a set of eight copper beads — small annular beads, 2.2 to 4.8 mm in diameter, each formed by rolling a narrow strip of copper sheet around a rod. The beads had presumably been strung as a bracelet. When the bead set was subjected to metallurgical analysis in Paris, one bead (catalogued MR.84.03.158.01b) was found to be heavily corroded — and within its corrosion, preserved as mineralised casts, were several threads : organic fibres that the corroding copper had impregnated with metallic salts, fossilising their microscopic form as the fibre itself decayed. Identifying a fibre from its mineralised ghost required a method built for the purpose. Christophe Moulherat and colleagues combined reflected-light microscopy with scanning electron microscopy to read the fibres' diagnostic morphology — the flattened, twisted, ribbon-like convolutions characteristic of cotton — and identified them as cotton, Gossypium sp. The threads, they concluded, were the remains of the string on which the beads had been threaded. The paper — Moulherat, Tengberg, Haquet & Mille, Journal of Archaeological Science 29 (2002): 1393–1401 — states its conclusion in its abstract's own measured terms: the Mehrgarh fibres are the earliest known example of cotton in the Old World, putting the first attested use of the fibre back by more than a millennium. // THE EVIDENCE, AT ITS EXACT STRENGTH // What was found: several mineralised threads, preserved within the corrosion of one copper bead from a set of eight, in a burial of the first half of the sixth millennium BCE. What the analysis shows: the fibres are cotton ( Gossypium sp.), of varying ripeness, identified by microscopic morphology against modern reference material. What it does not show: the species — the method cannot distinguish the Old World cottons at species level — and therefore the domestication status. The authors state plainly that it cannot be ascertained whether the fibres came from an already domesticated plant. Wild cotton gathered and spun, and cultivated cotton, are both consistent with the threads. What is certain is use: cotton fibre was known, prepared, and spun into thread at Mehrgarh by c. 6000–5500 BCE. The find's significance is best seen against the later record. Cotton becomes, in the mature Indus civilisation, a signature material — the fibre of Indus textiles traded as far as Mesopotamia — and South Asia is one of the Old World cotton's homelands, with the tree cotton Gossypium arboreum generally treated as a subcontinental domesticate. Moulherat and colleagues, noting the accumulation of early cotton evidence in Pakistani Balochistan and the Indus valley (a fourth-millennium cotton string preserved inside a carnelian bead at Shahi Tump, in the Makran, among it), proposed a South Asian origin, probably in the greater Indus area, for one of the Old World cottons. The Mehrgarh threads do not prove that domestication happened here — the authors are careful, and this article follows them — but they place the exploitation of cotton at the Bolan Pass at the very beginning of the region's farming sequence, millennia before the looms of the Indus cities.
