What the Other Humans Do and Do Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, sequenced, and published evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do, sharply, about cave art, about flowers in a grave, and about what counts as a burial at all — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. In this field that discipline matters more than usual, because the central question is not only what Neanderthals and Denisovans did. It is what standard of proof we require before we say they did it. For most of the twentieth century the answer, in practice, was asymmetric. A perforated shell in a modern human context was an ornament and evidence of symbolism; a perforated shell in a Neanderthal context was, first, a problem to be explained away — by intrusion, by misdating, by a carnivore, by a rodent. That asymmetry is now itself an object of study (§X), and the last two decades of work have made it harder to sustain: stalagmite constructions built 336 metres inside a French cave at about 176,500 years ago; eagle talons cut, polished, and apparently strung in Croatia at about 130,000 years ago; perforated and pigmented shells in Spain at about 115,000 years ago; and, from Siberia, an entire population — the Denisovans — recognised from DNA in 2010 before any diagnostic skeleton for it existed. None of those findings, on its own, settles what these humans thought. Together they settle something narrower and firmer: the old picture of two populations without ornament, without construction, and without care for their dead cannot be held in its simple form any longer. This article is the full treatment promised by the single Neanderthal paragraph in this hub's Ochre and Symbol article. It proceeds from the strongest evidence to the most contested, in that order on purpose: the dated construction first, the dated ornaments next, the cave-art claim and its published audit after that, and the burials — where the evidence is oldest, most famous, and most argued over — with the criteria debate stated in full. The Denisovan half of the story is shorter, because the Denisovan record is shorter: a handful of bones and teeth, one mandible from a high cave on the Tibetan Plateau, one first-generation hybrid, and a genetic legacy out of all proportion to the fossils. That disproportion is itself one of the findings. A population can be almost invisible in stone and unmistakable in genomes. I. The Cast — Two Populations, Two Kinds of Evidence The Neanderthals are the archaeologically visible population of the two. Named for the Neander Valley in Germany, where the type specimen was recognised in 1856, they are known from hundreds of individuals and thousands of sites across Europe and western Asia — from Iberia and Wales in the west to the Altai Mountains of Siberia in the east, and south into the Levant, where at caves such as Kebara and Amud they lived, at times, within the same landscape as early modern humans. Their classic range of dates runs, in round terms, from about 400,000 years ago for their antecedents to about 40,000 years ago for their last well-dated populations, though both ends of that range are argued over site by site. Their material signature for most of that span is the Mousterian: prepared-core stone technology, hearths, hunted large game, and — the subject of this article — a sparse, scattered, and fiercely debated trail of pigment, ornament, construction, and burial. The Denisovans are the opposite case: a population known first, and still primarily, from molecules. In 2008 Russian excavators working in Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of southern Siberia, recovered a small distal finger bone — the tip of a juvenile's fifth finger — from a layer dated broadly to 50,000–30,000 years ago. The bone looked like nothing in particular. Its mitochondrial DNA, published by Johannes Krause and colleagues in 2010, looked like nothing known: it diverged from the lineage leading to both modern human and Neanderthal mitochondrial genomes roughly twice as deeply as those two diverge from each other. The nuclear genome, published the same year by David Reich and colleagues in Nature , resolved the relationship differently and more precisely: the finger-bone individual belonged to a group that shared a common origin with Neanderthals — a sister group, not a distant outlier — which had not taken part in the gene flow from Neanderthals into Eurasians, but which had contributed some 4–6 per cent of its genetic material to the genomes of present-day Melanesians. Reich and colleagues gave the group its name in that paper: Denisovans, after the cave, exactly as Neanderthals were named after their valley. // NEANDERTHALS // Europe to the Altai; Levant Antecedents from c. 400,000 BP; last well-dated populations c. 40,000 BP. Hundreds of individuals; Mousterian material culture throughout. // DENISOVANS // Identified from DNA, 2010 Named from a finger bone in Denisova Cave, Siberia. Sister group to Neanderthals. No diagnostic skeleton existed when the population was recognised. // THE SHARED ANCESTRY // Divergence >390,000 years ago Neanderthals and Denisovans separated from each other more than 390,000 years ago (Slon et al. 2018); both separated earlier from the modern human lineage. // THE EVIDENCE ASYMMETRY // Stone and bone vs. genomes Neanderthals: a dense archaeological record, genomes later. Denisovans: genomes first, a sparse fossil record still being assembled around them. The sequence of discovery deserves emphasis, because it reversed the normal order of palaeoanthropology. Every other named human population began as a skeleton that was measured, compared, and classified; its genome, if one was ever recovered, came a century later. The Denisovans began as a genome in search of a skeleton. A large molar from the same cave carried a closely similar mitochondrial genome and shared no derived features with either Neanderthals or modern humans, but teeth and a finger tip do not make an anatomy. For nearly a decade after 2010, researchers could say what Denisovans were related to, roughly where their genes survived (§IX), and almost nothing about what they looked like. The Xiahe mandible of §VIII — identified as Denisovan-related by ancient protein, not DNA, in 2019 — was the first substantial piece of Denisovan anatomy found outside Denisova Cave itself, and it came from 3,280 metres up on the Tibetan Plateau. The cast, in short, is still being assembled, and this article marks, at each step, whether a Denisovan claim rests on a bone, a protein, a genome, or an inference from living people's DNA. Those are four different kinds of evidence, and they do not carry the same weight. Species, Subspecies, Populations — A Note on Names This article calls Neanderthals and Denisovans populations and groups , and the choice is deliberate. Whether Neanderthals are a separate species, Homo neanderthalensis , or a subspecies of our own, Homo sapiens neanderthalensis , remains unsettled in the literature, and the Denisovans have never received a formal Linnaean name at all — a genome is not a type specimen in the traditional sense. Chris Stringer and Julia Galway-Witham, reviewing the species questions for the Natural History Museum, London, have set out the difficulty plainly in their recent syntheses: the fossil record of the Middle Pleistocene does not sort itself into clean species boxes, interbreeding between the groups is now a documented fact (§§VIII–IX), and any taxonomy has to accommodate populations that were distinct for hundreds of thousands of years and yet not reproductively isolated. Readers should therefore take every species label in the sources cited here as a working label, not a verdict. What is not in dispute is the underlying pattern: by the later Middle Pleistocene, Eurasia held several distinguishable human populations, of which ours was one, and they met, and at least sometimes they had children together. One further caution governs everything that follows. To show that a population made ornaments is not to show what the ornaments meant ; to show that a body was deliberately buried is not to show that it was buried with ritual, belief, or grief as we would recognise them. The sources in this article are at their best when they keep those steps apart, and at their weakest — on both sides of every debate — when they run them together. This article follows the sources at their best. Where a claim of symbolism is made, it says on what object, at what date, by what method, and who has answered it. II. Bruniquel — Building in the Dark, c. 176,500 BP Bruniquel Cave, in southwestern France near Montauban, was sealed by a natural collapse during the Pleistocene and re-entered only in 1990, when cavers dug through the blocked entrance. Deep inside it — 336 metres from the entrance, well beyond any daylight — they found something no one had a category for: structures built from broken stalagmites. The archaeologist François Rouzaud recognised their importance, but his early death and the cave's restricted access stalled study for two decades. In 2013 Jacques Jaubert and colleagues returned to date and record the structures, and published the results in Nature in 2016 (Jaubert et al., Nature 534: 111–114). The structures are six in number, all in the cave's largest chamber, and all made exclusively of stalagmites and stalagmite fragments — pieces the paper calls speleofacts. Two are annular, ring-shaped. The larger is an ellipse of about 6.7 by 4.5 metres; the smaller, about 2.2 by 2.1 metres. Each ring is built of one to four aligned layers of stalagmite pieces, with smaller fragments wedged in as supports. The other four structures are accumulations — stacks and piles — two of them inside the large ring. In total the builders used more than 400 pieces. The pieces are strikingly standardised: an average length of about 34.4 cm in the large ring and about 29.5 cm in the small one. Stalagmites were broken at a consistent size, carried to the chamber, and laid in courses. Several traces of fire accompany the structures, including reddened and cracked stalagmite and a fragment of burnt bone, and heated zones on and near the rings. Feature Bruniquel Cave Location 336 m from the entrance, in the largest chamber; total darkness without artificial light Structures 6 in total: 2 annular rings (c. 6.7 × 4.5 m and c. 2.2 × 2.1 m) and 4 accumulation structures Material 400+ broken stalagmite pieces (speleofacts), standardised to mean lengths of c. 34.4 cm and c. 29.5 cm Fire Multiple traces: heated and reddened stalagmite, burnt bone, localised heated zones Date 176.5 ± 2.1 thousand years, by uranium-series dating of stalagmite regrowth on the structures and of burnt bone, replicated across samples Attribution Early Neanderthals: the only humans present in the region at that date Source Jaubert et al., Nature 534 (2016): 111–114 The date is the finding's foundation, and the paper builds it carefully. Uranium-series dating was applied not to one sample but to a system: to the tips of stalagmites built into the structures, which must predate their breaking; to the calcite regrowth that formed over the broken pieces after they were laid, which must postdate construction; and to the burnt bone. The results converge on a replicated age of 176.5 thousand years, plus or minus 2.1 thousand years . At that date, in that place, the attribution is not really in question: early Neanderthals were the only humans in western Europe. No modern human presence anywhere near the region is claimed for another 130,000 years. If the structures are human-made — and their geometry, standardisation, layering, and fire traces are the paper's argument that they are — then Neanderthals made them. Chris Stringer, commenting at publication, accepted the attribution on those grounds. What Building Them Required — Inference, Labelled as Such The paper itself is restrained about purpose, and this article follows it: what the rings were for is unknown. No occupation debris, no tool assemblage, and no further trace of activity in the chamber has been found to explain them. What can be stated is not purpose but requirement — the minimum capacities the construction itself demonstrates, as inference from the structure. The builders worked 336 metres from daylight, so they carried a reliable, sustained source of light — the fire traces are consistent with torches or hearths maintained in the chamber, not a single brief visit. They selected, broke, and standardised hundreds of heavy calcite pieces, which is work for several people over an extended period, not an individual's afternoon. They laid the pieces in a shared plan — two rings and four stacks in one chamber — which requires that the plan existed before and during the building, was communicated, and was followed. Jaubert and colleagues summarise the implication in general terms: the constructions show that humans of this period had mastered the underground environment, a step they describe as major. Beyond that summary, every richer reading — shelter, storage, ritual enclosure, social space — is speculation, and is labelled as such wherever it appears in the secondary literature. One alternative was aired at publication and should be recorded, because this hub records alternatives: could cave bears, which hibernate in such chambers and shift material as they dig their sleeping hollows, have made the structures by accident? The paper's answer, which has carried the field, is that bear hollows are smaller than the large ring, that bears push material aside rather than stacking it in aligned courses of standardised pieces, and that bears do not account for the fire traces or the burnt bone. The bear suggestion survives in popular retellings more than in the specialist literature. The standing position, stated at its proper strength, is this: the Bruniquel structures are the oldest well-dated constructions attributed to humans anywhere, they are Neanderthal work, and their function is unknown. That combination — certainty about the building, honesty about the purpose — is the model this article asks the reader to hold for every claim that follows. // WHY 176,500 YEARS MATTERS // The date falls in Marine Isotope Stage 6, a glacial period — yet calcite was actively depositing on the rings at the time, indicating a locally warm, humid interval within the cold stage. More importantly, the date is roughly three times older than any Neanderthal evidence in §§III–VI. Whatever Neanderthals were doing with shells and pigment at 130,000–115,000 years ago, their ancestors had already organised collective construction in total darkness some fifty millennia earlier. Bruniquel does not prove symbolism. It removes the premise that organised, planned, cooperative work was beyond them. Bruniquel also reframes the geography of the Neanderthal world. Cave use by early humans is usually a story of entrances and rock shelters — the lit, sheltered margin where daylight, hearths, and debris accumulate. The deep cave, beyond the twilight zone, was long treated as a modern human territory, entered for art and ritual in the Upper Palaeolithic. Bruniquel puts Neanderthals in the deep cave, building, at a date earlier than any dated modern human cave art anywhere. It does not follow that they entered for the same reasons. It does follow that darkness itself was not a barrier they failed to cross. III. Pigment and Ornament — Shells, Talons, and Colour If Bruniquel is a single extraordinary site, pigment and ornament are a pattern — thinner, wider, and individually weaker, but repeated across the Neanderthal range and across tens of thousands of years. The pattern has three strands: mineral pigments collected, ground, and sometimes mixed; shells perforated and stained; and raptor talons and feathers selected and modified. Each strand has a functional reading as well as a symbolic one, and this section gives both. What it will not do is what the weaker literature does on both sides: call every lump of ochre a crayon of ritual, or every perforated shell a accident of the sea. Cueva de los Aviones — Shells and Pigment Mixtures, c. 115,000 BP Cueva de los Aviones is a sea cave near Cartagena, in southeastern Spain. Excavated in the 1980s and re-studied by João Zilhão and colleagues, its Neanderthal-associated Middle Palaeolithic deposit yielded a small, dense assemblage unlike ordinary food debris: marine shells of cockle and mussel-like bivalves, several of them perforated; shells stained with red pigment; and, most tellingly, shells used as containers, holding residues of prepared pigment mixtures. One Spondylus shell held a compound of red lepidocrocite with ground inclusions of haematite and pyrite. Another context produced a lump of natrojarosite, a yellow mineral pigment, and red and yellow colourants more generally. The perforations and the haematite residue on the inner face of one shell were read by the excavators as the traces of suspension and wear: shells hung, probably as ornaments, and pigment mixed and kept in shells, as paint or cosmetic is mixed and kept in a pot. The assemblage was first published in 2010 with a radiocarbon age of roughly 45,000–50,000 years on associated food shells — already early, already before any secure modern human presence in the region, but close enough to the contact period to invite the objection that Neanderthals might have learned the practice from incoming modern humans. In 2018 Dirk Hoffmann and colleagues closed that door with a different clock. Uranium-series dating of the flowstone that caps the Aviones deposit — carbonate laid down over the archaeological layer, so that everything beneath it must be older — gave an age of about 115,000 to 120,000 years for the capping flowstone, and therefore a minimum age in that range for the shells and pigments beneath it (Hoffmann et al., Science Advances 4 (2018): eaar5255). At 115,000 years ago there were no modern humans in Europe to learn from. The authors' conclusion, stated at its exact strength, is that the Aviones finds predate the earliest comparable evidence associated with modern humans — the shell beads and pigment work of the African Middle Stone Age — by some 20,000 to 40,000 years, and that the roots of symbolic material culture may therefore lie in the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans, more than half a million years ago. The second half of that sentence is an inference, and a large one. The first half is a date, a context, and an assemblage, and it has not been overturned. Krapina — Eight Eagle Talons, c. 130,000 BP The Krapina rock shelter in northwestern Croatia was excavated between 1899 and 1905 under Dragutin Gorjanović-Kramberger, and produced one of the largest Neanderthal fossil collections in Europe. More than a century later, Davorka Radovčić and colleagues re-examined the site's faunal collection and identified, from a single level dated by ESR and uranium-series to about 130,000 years ago — the last interglacial, MIS 5e — eight white-tailed eagle talons, mostly complete, together with an associated foot bone (Radovčić et al., PLoS ONE 10 (2015): e0119802). Eight talons from one level is more than the entire rest of the European Mousterian has produced. Duplication of one talon position shows the eight come from at least three different eagles: they were accumulated, not taken from a single carcass. The modifications are the argument. Four talons bear multiple cut marks, their edges smoothed — the signature of cuts made in life-fresh tissue and then worn. All eight show polishing facets or abrasion. Three of the largest bear small notches at roughly the same position on the underside, interrupting the margin of the talon in a way the authors read as the wear of a cord. Taken together — cutting to remove the talons, smoothing, polishing where adjacent hard objects rub, notching where a binding would sit — the pattern matches what happens to talons mounted together in a strung assemblage, a necklace or bracelet, and matches nothing in ordinary butchery, where a raptor foot has no meat worth this attention. A later surface study of one talon (Radovčić et al., Scientific Reports 2020) added a fibre preserved within a wide cut mark, identified as degraded collagen consistent with a leather or sinew binding, and spots of two ochres and charcoal on the same surface. That study is supportive, not decisive — a single fibre on a museum specimen handled for a century must be read with care — and this article rests the Krapina case where its authors rested it in 2015: on the number, the selection, and the modifications of the talons themselves. White-tailed eagles are large, uncommon, and dangerous birds. Acquiring the talons of three of them, and keeping eight together, was a project. The Pigment Record Generally — and Its Functional Shadow Beyond Aviones, ochre and other mineral pigments — red haematite, yellow goethite and natrojarosite, black manganese oxides — occur at Neanderthal sites across Europe and the Levant, in some cases from well before 100,000 years ago, occasionally ground, faceted from use, or scored. Shell beads and perforated shells are reported from a small number of other Middle Palaeolithic contexts; cut-marked raptor wing bones and talons, suggesting the deliberate removal of feathers and claws, recur at several French and Italian sites in the later Mousterian. The full inventory is maintained in the specialist literature and in this hub's Ochre and Symbol article, which treats the pigment record from its earliest African occurrences onward. The functional shadow must be stated, because the critics state it well. Ochre has uses that are not symbolic: it is an ingredient in hafting mastics, a hide-processing agent, an insect repellent, and a sunscreen, and each of those uses is experimentally supported. A lump of ochre, alone, therefore proves collection and use, not symbolism. The symbolic reading gains strength only where the context excludes or outruns the functional ones: pigment mixed to a recipe and stored in a shell container, as at Aviones; pigment applied to an object with no practical surface to protect, as on the Krapina talon; a perforation placed and worn in the way ornaments are worn. That is the standard this article applies throughout, and it is the standard the strongest papers on both sides now claim to apply as well. Where the two readings remain genuinely open — as they do for much of the plain ochre record — §XI will say so, and say that pigment use is attested while pigment symbolism, at those sites, is not proven. AVIONES, c. 115,000 BP Perforated, pigment-stained marine shells and shell containers holding mixed pigment recipes, sealed under flowstone dated by U-series to c. 115,000–120,000 years. No modern humans in Europe at that date. KRAPINA, c. 130,000 BP Eight white-tailed eagle talons from at least three birds, in one level: cut-marked, polished, and notched as if strung together. Excavated 1899–1905; recognised in a museum collection in 2015. PIGMENT, WIDELY Red, yellow, and black mineral pigments collected and ground at Neanderthal sites across two continents. Collection is attested everywhere; symbolism is proven only where context excludes the functional uses. FEATHERS AND TALONS, REPEATEDLY Cut-marked raptor bones at multiple later Mousterian sites extend the Krapina pattern: birds of prey were selected for their flight feathers and claws, parts with display value and no food value. IV. The Cave-Art Claim and Its Audit — c. 65,000 BP On 22 February 2018, Science published the most consequential — and most contested — claim in this article. Dirk Hoffmann and colleagues reported uranium-thorium dates on carbonate crusts overlying pigment in three Spanish caves (Hoffmann et al., Science 359 (2018): 912–915). At La Pasiega, in Cantabria, a red ladder-like sign — horizontal and vertical bars, a scalariform — lay beneath carbonate dated to more than 64,800 years ago. At Maltravieso, in Extremadura, a hand stencil lay beneath carbonate of comparable antiquity. At Ardales, in Andalusia, red pigment on stalagmite formations was bracketed by carbonate dates reaching back beyond 65,000 years. The logic is the logic of Aviones, applied to walls: carbonate that formed over pigment must be younger than the pigment, so its date is a minimum age for the painting beneath it. A minimum age of 65,000 years, for art in Iberia, precedes the earliest secure modern human presence in the region by roughly twenty millennia. The paper's conclusion followed directly: the paintings were made by Neanderthals, and Iberian cave art — the first parietal art in Europe, on these dates — is a Neanderthal creation. This section gives the claim, then its audit, at full strength on both sides, and ends where the literature ends: unresolved. Readers who meet this claim elsewhere stated as settled fact, in either direction, are meeting advocacy, not the published record. The Case for the Dates The Hoffmann team's case rests on method as much as on numbers. Uranium-thorium dating of cave carbonate is an established technique with a range reaching back some 500,000 years; the team analysed more than sixty samples, each of a few milligrams, taken with surgical care from crusts directly overlying the pigment. Crucially, they sampled sequentially through the crusts: a series of subsamples from the outer surface inward, toward the pigment, should grow older in stratigraphic order if the carbonate has behaved as a closed system since it formed. The team published multiple such sequences, from all three caves, in the expected order, and presented that ordering as the test for the disturbance their critics fear. They also dated crusts at the same sites that returned very young ages — around a thousand years — which they argue is incompatible with the idea that the cave drip waters carry enough inherited thorium to fake great antiquity: water loaded with old thorium could not produce a thousand-year date. Finally, the team points to pattern: the oldest minimum ages come from three caves, hundreds of kilometres apart, for three different motifs. A single aberrant sample can be an accident. A regional pattern of minimum ages beyond 64,000 years, they argue, is a phenomenon that requires an explanation, and Neanderthal authorship is the explanation that fits the chronology of human presence in Iberia. The Audit — Slimak, White, and the Open System The responses came in the same journals, within the year, and they attack the method at its foundation. Ludovic Slimak and colleagues, in a Technical Comment in Science (2018), raised three objections. First, open-system behaviour: cave carbonates are not sealed clocks — uranium can be leached by percolating water, and loss of uranium makes a sample calculate older than it is; the critics argue that ordered subsample sequences do not exclude every form of that disturbance. Second, the corrections applied for detrital thorium — thorium that was in the carbonate from the start, not produced by decay within it — depend on assumed initial values, and different defensible assumptions move the oldest dates substantially. Third, an archaeological objection: if Neanderthals were painting caves at 65,000 years ago, the near-absence of comparable dated art for the following twenty-odd millennia, until the modern human Upper Palaeolithic, is a strange silence that the claim does not explain. Randall White and colleagues then extended the critique in a full-length paper whose title states its verdict — "Still no archaeological evidence that Neanderthals created Iberian cave art" ( Journal of Human Evolution 144 (2020): 102640). White's team argued that uranium leaching in thin calcite crusts can account for the anomalous ages; that the association between some dated crusts and the pigment beneath them is less direct than the claim requires — at Ardales, in particular, whether the red colouration of the stalagmites is human-applied pigment at all, rather than natural iron staining, has been questioned; and that a claim overturning a century of archaeological context should be carried by archaeological evidence — tools, occupation, a Neanderthal presence demonstrated at those caves at those dates — and not by physicochemical measurements alone. Maxime Aubert, and David Pearce and Adelphine Bonneau, published parallel methodological cautions in the same period. The Hoffmann team answered in kind, in a formal Response in Science (2018). On the supposed hiatus: a minimum age cannot create a gap — the same caves carry younger minimum ages and bracketing date pairs that place painting episodes squarely inside the alleged silent interval, so the silence is an artefact of reading minimum ages as exact ages. On open-system behaviour: the sequential sequences stand, and the critics, they argue, propose no mechanism that disturbs the system while preserving perfect stratigraphic order across multiple sequences in three caves. On the Ardales pigment: its anthropogenic character, they reply, is supported by more than a century of study of the cave, including technical features of its application. On the isochron re-analysis offered by the critics for one key sample: three points cannot define an isochron, and the exercise assumes, without evidence, that the crust formed in a single short episode. The exchange, at the time of writing, rests there: claim, comment, response, and a long-form critique unanswered in equally long form. // THE VERDICT THIS ARTICLE PRINTS // Unresolved. The U-Th minimum ages are real measurements, published with their methods, and no critic has shown a specific sample to be wrong by a specific amount. The critics' central point is also real: uranium leaching biases this clock in one direction only — toward ages that are too old — and the burden on a claim of this size is to exclude that bias sample by sample, not in general. Neanderthal authorship of the La Pasiega, Maltravieso, and Ardales marks is therefore a live, well-supported, and genuinely contested hypothesis. It is not an attested fact, and it does not appear in this article's assessment (§XI) as one. Note what does not depend on it: Aviones and Krapina (§III) rest on different materials, different contexts, and — in the Aviones case — a capping flowstone, not a thin crust over pigment. There is a wider lesson in the exchange, and the hub's readers will recognise it from the zebu argument at Mehrgarh and the cattle argument at Nabta Playa: a dating method is not a verdict. It is an instrument with known failure modes, and its readings become history only where the failure modes have been tested in the specific material at hand. Hoffmann's team tested them one way; Slimak's and White's teams argue the tests are insufficient; both positions are in the peer-reviewed record, attributed, and open. This article's tier discipline requires exactly that presentation — and it requires the same discipline in reverse: the critics have not disproven the dates either. "Not yet proven" and "proven false" are different findings, and only the first is available here. V. Burials I — Shanidar and the Flowers Shanidar Cave, in the Zagros Mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, at about 750 metres in the foothills of the Baradost range, is where the Neanderthal burial debate acquired its most famous exhibit and its most famous cautionary tale. Ralph Solecki, of Columbia University, excavated the cave from 1951 to 1960 and recovered the remains of ten Neanderthals — seven adults and three infants, in the usual count — from its Mousterian levels. Solecki argued that some of the dead had been killed by rockfalls from the cave roof, and that others had been deliberately buried. One burial carried the argument into the culture at large. Shanidar IV, an adult male, was found with soil samples around the body that contained, on analysis by the palynologist Arlette Leroi-Gourhan, strikingly concentrated pollen — in a cave whose sediments were otherwise pollen-poor. The pollen occurred in clumps, which Leroi-Gourhan read as the signature of whole flowers deposited at once, and the species identified included yarrow, groundsel, grape hyacinth, St Barnaby's thistle, and hollyhock-type pollen, among twenty-eight taxa in total. Solecki's conclusion, published in his 1971 book Shanidar: The First Flower People and in the journal literature in 1975, was that the dead man had been laid on, or covered with, flowering plants gathered in their late-spring blooming season — a flower burial, and with it, evidence of ritual, care, and something like mourning among Neanderthals. The Taphonomic Critique — Jirds, Bees, and Wind The flower burial was doubted early and dismantled in stages. Robert Gargett, in a wide-ranging critique of Middle Palaeolithic burial claims (1989; extended 1999), argued that natural agencies — wind, animals, sediment movement — had not been excluded at Shanidar or anywhere else, and that wishful reading had done the rest. Jeffrey Sommer then supplied the specific mechanism the critique had lacked ( Cambridge Archaeological Journal 9 (1999): 127–129). The Persian jird, Meriones persicus , is a burrowing rodent native to the Shanidar region, living in colonies, digging burrow systems metres deep in soft cave-front soils — and storing large quantities of seeds and flower heads in its burrows. Excavated jird burrows contained many of the same flower species as the Shanidar IV samples. A jird colony working the sediments around a skeleton after its burial could introduce concentrated, clumped flower pollen exactly where Solecki found it, without any Neanderthal ever gathering a flower. Assessment — Three Independent Proofs Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do about the domestication status of Jiahu's rice, the meaning of its incised signs, the early dates claimed for millet at Cishan, and the social order of the Yangshao villages — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. Two disciplines govern the whole article and are worth naming at the outset. First, cultivation is not domestication : tending a wild plant, planting it, and harvesting it are behaviours; domestication is the measurable, heritable change in the plant that those behaviours eventually produce, and the two can be separated by millennia. Second, sign use is not writing : an incised mark can be real, deliberate, and meaningful without recording speech, and this article holds the Jiahu signs to exactly that standard — the same standard this hub applies to the Vinča marks in Origins of Writing . The Neolithic, as the older textbooks told it, was a single invention with a single address: farming began in the Fertile Crescent, pottery and settled villages followed from it, and the rest of the world received the package, later and derivatively, by migration or imitation. East Asia refutes that story three times over, and this article is organised around the three refutations. Its pottery is the oldest in the world — fired clay vessels at Xianrendong Cave in Jiangxi are dated to about 20,000 years ago, made by Ice Age foragers some ten thousand years before anyone in the region farmed. Its most famous forager culture, the Jōmon of Japan, built sedentary villages, shell middens, lacquer workshops, and settlements of hundreds of people across more than ten thousand years without staple agriculture. And its farming, when it came, grew from its own plants: broomcorn and foxtail millet in the dry north, rice in the wet centre and south — domestications with no western progenitor, worked out on East Asian ground from East Asian wild grasses. Three bodies of evidence carry the argument. The Jōmon sequence of the Japanese archipelago (from c. 14,000 BCE) supplies the forager proof: among the world's earliest pottery, pit-house villages, and at Sannai-Maruyama (c. 3900–2200 BCE) a settlement of a scale that forced archaeology to separate the idea of complexity from the fact of farming. The early village of Jiahu in Henan (c. 7000–5700 BCE) supplies the densest single site: early rice, the oldest playable musical instruments known anywhere, tortoise shells bearing incised signs whose status this article examines at length, and — named here in its site setting, and treated comparatively elsewhere in this hub — the earliest chemically attested fermented beverage in the world. The Yangshao culture of the Yellow River (c. 5000–3000 BCE) supplies the mature farming village: the ditch-enclosed, plaza-centred settlements of Banpo and Jiangzhai and the painted pottery whose manufacture this article follows step by step. Read together, they are not the Far Eastern chapter of a Near Eastern book. They are a second book. I. An Independent Trajectory — Not an Echo Independence, in archaeology, is a claim about evidence, not a sentiment about regions, and it has to be earned trait by trait — the same discipline this hub applied at Mehrgarh , where the grains proved western and the cattle proved local, and the site's originality turned out to be the originality of combination. East Asia's case is stronger and cleaner, because for its defining traits the western connection is not merely unproven but impossible on the chronology. Pottery in China and Japan predates the earliest Near Eastern pottery by several thousand years; there was no western pottery tradition in existence to copy. Millet and rice have no wild progenitors in western Asia at all: the plants themselves are East Asian, and their domestication could only have happened where they grew. Whatever moved along the long routes across Central Asia in later millennia — and much did, in both directions — the foundations were laid separately. // POTTERY FIRST // c. 20,000 BP, Xianrendong The world's earliest dated pottery, made by foragers at the Last Glacial Maximum — some 10,000 years before farming in the region (§II). // FORAGER SEDENTISM // Jōmon, from c. 14,000 BCE Sedentary pit-house villages, middens, lacquer, and large settlements sustained for millennia without staple agriculture (§§III–V). // OWN DOMESTICATIONS // Millets north, rice centre-south Broomcorn and foxtail millet and East Asian rice: domestications from local wild grasses, independent of the western founder package (§§VII, XI). // THE MATURE VILLAGE // Yangshao, c. 5000–3000 BCE Ditch-enclosed, plaza-centred farming villages — Banpo, Jiangzhai — and a painted-pottery tradition of the first rank (§§XII–XIV). The sequence also runs in an order the old model did not predict. In the textbook Near Eastern progression, farming comes first and pottery follows — the earliest farming villages of the Levant and Anatolia are famously aceramic , making no pottery for their first millennia, exactly as at Mehrgarh's Period I. In East Asia the order is reversed: pottery precedes farming by a span longer than the whole of recorded history. The reversal is not a curiosity. It tells us what pottery was for in its first home — not a farmer's storage technology but a forager's cooking technology, a way of boiling, simmering, and extracting more from wild foods — and it breaks, at the root, the idea of a single Neolithic "package" whose parts must travel together. Sedentism, too, comes loose from farming in the East Asian record: the Jōmon sat still for ten thousand years on fish, nuts, and game. Village life, fired clay, plant management, and eventually plant domestication were assembled in East Asia piece by piece, in an order of East Asia's own — which is what an independent trajectory means. One boundary should be drawn before the detail begins. "East Asia" in this article means the Japanese archipelago and the river systems of what is now China — the Yellow River and its tributaries in the dry loess north, the Huai and Yangtze systems in the wetter centre and south. The Korean peninsula's contemporary Jeulmun sequence, with its own early comb-pattern pottery, belongs to the same broad world and is noted where the comparison matters, but its full treatment belongs with a Korea the hub has not yet built. Within the stated ground, the article follows the evidence in chronological order: the pottery prologue, the forager achievement, the first farming villages, and the threshold — deliberately not crossed — where the Neolithic gives way to the ranked, walled world that leads toward early China. II. The Pottery Prologue — Xianrendong and the Order Reversed Xianrendong Cave — the name means "Cave of the Immortals" — is a limestone cave in Wannian County, Jiangxi Province, some 100 kilometres south of the Yangtze River, with the companion rockshelter of Diaotonghuan nearby. Excavated in campaigns from the 1960s onward, the cave preserves a long Late Palaeolithic sequence: stone, bone, and shell tools, the debris of hunting and gathering at the end of the Ice Age — and, in its lower layers, fragments of fired clay vessels. Claims for very early pottery at the cave were made for decades, but the dating was contested, because a sherd cannot be radiocarbon dated directly and the age of the layer around it is only as secure as the stratigraphy. The question was settled, as far as current evidence settles anything, by a targeted re-excavation: in 2009 an international team led by Wu Xiaohong of Peking University reopened trenches into the intact pottery-bearing deposits and dated the contexts themselves, sample by sample. The result was published in Science in 2012 (Wu et al., "Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China," Science 336: 1696–1700). Radiocarbon ages for the contexts of the earliest sherds fall between 20,000 and 19,000 calendar years before present — two to three thousand years older than any other pottery then known, and squarely within the Last Glacial Maximum, the coldest phase of the Ice Age. The sherds themselves are fragments of large, bag-shaped vessels; many bear scorch marks, the blackening of use over fire. The makers were mobile hunter-gatherers. No plant or animal domestication of any kind is associated with these layers, and none would appear in the region for roughly ten thousand years. The entry already stands on this hub's timeline; this article gives it its context. What Pottery-Before-Farming Means The Xianrendong date rearranges the logic of invention. Pottery is heavy, fragile, and useless to people who move constantly and carry everything — or so the older reasoning ran, tying ceramics to the sedentary farmer's need to store a harvest. The East Asian evidence shows the reasoning was backwards. The first potters were foragers who returned to favoured places — caves, river terraces, shell-rich coasts — often enough, and stayed long enough, for a breakable cooking vessel to pay its way. What a pot offers a forager is not storage but transformation : prolonged boiling renders foods that cannot be eaten raw or merely roasted — extracting grease and marrow from crushed bone, detoxifying bitter nuts, simmering shellfish, small fish, and wild grains into digestible form. Wu and colleagues propose exactly such uses for the Xianrendong vessels, and the scorch marks on the sherds are the use-wear of cooking, not of a granary. Fired clay, on this evidence, begins as kitchen equipment for people who had no fields. Nor is Xianrendong an isolated flash. At Yuchanyan Cave in Hunan, pottery-bearing contexts are dated to about 18,000 years ago (Boaretto et al., PNAS 2009); early pottery follows across the region in the millennia after the glacial maximum — in south China, in the Russian Far East, and in the Japanese archipelago, where the Incipient Jōmon sherds of §III reach back toward 16,000 years ago. The pattern is regional and sustained: a broad East Asian world of late-glacial and early post-glacial foragers took up pottery thousands of years before the Near East did, and used it, for most of that span, without farming at all. When farming did arrive in East Asia, it arrived in communities that had been potters for longer than civilisation has yet lasted. The pot came first. Everything else in this article happens in a world where that was already true. // A DATE FOR A CONTEXT, NOT FOR A SHERD // The Xianrendong chronology dates the sediments and associated charcoal and bone of the sherd-bearing layers, established by micromorphological study of the stratigraphy — not the sherds themselves, which contain no datable carbon of their own. That is the strongest method available for early ceramics anywhere, and the Science team's stratigraphic controls are the reason the date commands assent; but the form of the claim should be kept exact: pottery occurs at Xianrendong in contexts dated to 20,000–19,000 cal BP. Claims for still earlier pottery elsewhere in the region, resting on looser associations, are not made in this article. III. Jōmon Japan — The Long Sequence The Jōmon period of Japan is conventionally dated from about 14,000 BCE to the first millennium BCE — a span of more than thirteen thousand years, longer than the distance from the first Egyptian pyramids to the present day twice over. The name means "cord-marked": it derives from the rope-impressed decoration of the pottery, noted in 1877 by the American zoologist Edward S. Morse at the Ōmori shell mounds in Tokyo, and it names the period after its most durable artefact. Archaeologists divide the span into six phases — Incipient, Initial, Early, Middle, Late, and Final — defined largely by pottery typology and anchored by radiocarbon. The phases are a filing system, not a story: across thirteen millennia and an archipelago running from Hokkaidō to the Ryūkyū Islands, Jōmon communities were always regional, always various, and never a single people marching in step. What unifies them is a way of life: pottery-using, increasingly sedentary hunter-fisher-gatherers, exploiting the forests and seas of the islands with a sophistication that grew, over the millennia, into one of the most durable forager adaptations on earth. The setting explains the durability. As the Ice Age ended, sea level rose and cut the archipelago off from the continent; broadleaf deciduous forest — beech, oak, chestnut, walnut — spread over the hills of northeastern Honshū and southern Hokkaidō, producing reliable autumn harvests of nuts, while the meeting of cold and warm currents offshore made the coasts rich in fish and shellfish, and the rivers ran with salmon. It was, by forager standards, a generous landscape: storable plant staples from the forest, protein from the sea, game in between. Jōmon communities built their whole long history on the management of that generosity — on storage pits for nuts, on processing technology for bitter and toxic plant foods (acorns and horse chestnuts require leaching before they can be eaten), on fishing gear, boats, and weirs — and on staying put. Junko Habu's Ancient Jomon of Japan (Cambridge, 2004), the standard English synthesis, frames the period's central fact precisely: sedentism and cultural complexity developed here within a hunting-gathering economy, sustained not by domesticated staples but by the intensive, knowledgeable use of wild ones. Phase Approx. Dates (BCE) Character Signature Evidence Incipient c. 14,000–10,000 First pottery Small sherd assemblages (e.g. Ōdai Yamamoto I) among late-glacial forager camps; pottery appears while life remains mobile Initial c. 10,000–6000 Settling in First pit-houses and shell middens; lacquered ornaments at Kakinoshima B, Hokkaidō, c. 7000 BCE horizon Early c. 6000–3500 Village formation Larger pit-house settlements; storage pits; growing regional pottery styles; early dogū Middle c. 3500–2500 The demographic peak Largest settlements (Sannai-Maruyama at full extent); elaborate "flame-style" vessels in the Chūbu highlands; dense occupation of central and northern Honshū Late c. 2500–1000 Contraction and ritual elaboration Population falls from the Middle Jōmon peak in many regions; stone circles and ritual deposits prominent in the north Final c. 1000–300 (regional) The long ending Jōmon lifeways persist latest in the north; wet-rice farming of continental origin transforms the west from c. 1000–300 BCE — beyond this hub's remit The earliest pottery deserves its own sentence of care. Sherds from Ōdai Yamamoto I in Aomori, at the northern tip of Honshū, have been dated by association to roughly 16,000 years ago — among the oldest ceramics known anywhere, though younger than Xianrendong's (§II). Habu notes that most Japanese scholars long assumed pottery must have been introduced from the mainland; the accumulating dates reversed the presumption, and the current picture is of an early pottery horizon shared across East Asia — south China, the Amur basin, and the archipelago — within which the precise geography of first invention cannot presently be resolved and need not be: the Tier A claim is the horizon itself, forager-made and pre-agricultural, not a single birthplace. What Japan adds to that horizon is continuity : nowhere else was the forager-pottery adaptation sustained, elaborated, and documented for so long. IV. Sedentary Foragers — Villages, Middens, Lacquer, and Dogū The Jōmon settlement form is the pit-house village : dwellings dug partly into the ground — a circular or rectangular pit, roofed on posts with thatch — clustered, in the larger settlements, around open spaces, and accompanied by storage pits, burials, and working areas. Villages of a handful of houses are the norm through much of the sequence; villages of dozens, occupied and rebuilt across centuries, become common in the Early and Middle phases. The sedentism was real but should be stated exactly: many settlements were occupied year-round or near it, some were seasonal stations within a settled territory, and mobility never vanished from the system. What the record will not support is the old picture of Jōmon bands wandering at random. A community that digs hundreds of storage pits, buries its dead in formal cemeteries beside its houses, and rebuilds on the same terrace for a thousand years is sedentary in every sense that matters to archaeology — and it did so, for most of the sequence, without a single domesticated staple crop. Shell Middens — Archives of the Diet Along the coasts, Jōmon life left its most visible monument: the shell midden , an accumulated mound of discarded shell — clam, oyster, and other shellfish — mixed with fish bone, animal bone, broken tools, and pottery. Middens such as Ōmori, where Morse's 1877 excavation effectively founded Japanese archaeology, are not rubbish heaps in the dismissive sense; they are stratified archives of diet, season, and craft, and their alkaline shell matrix preserves bone that Japan's acid soils elsewhere destroy — including, at some sites, human burials and the remains of the Jōmon's domestic dogs, buried with a care that marks them as companions and hunting partners rather than food. The middens also chart the economy's reach: inland sites received marine shell and dried fish, coastal sites received inland stone, and obsidian from sources such as Kōzushima island and the Shinshū highlands, jade from Itoigawa, and asphalt and lacquer moved across the archipelago in exchange networks hundreds of kilometres long. The Jōmon world was connected, and its connections ran on forager logistics. Lacquer — A Chemistry of Patience Of all Jōmon crafts, lacquer is the most technically demanding, and among the earliest attested anywhere. Lacquer is the sap of the lacquer tree ( Toxicodendron vernicifluum ), tapped by scoring the bark, collected, filtered, and homogenised, then applied in thin coats that cure not by drying but by enzymatic polymerisation in warm, humid air — a process requiring controlled conditions, repeated coats, and weeks of work for a finished object, with a raw material that is itself a potent skin irritant. At Kakinoshima B in Hokkaidō, ornaments coated in red lacquer were recovered from a pit grave dated to about 9,000 years ago (c. 7000 BCE) — the oldest lacquered objects known in the world, reported as such in the site literature. The attribution carries a noted caveat, recorded in the analytical literature: the Kakinoshima pieces were identified as lacquer without the full chemical confirmation that later pyrolysis studies have applied to other early pieces, and this article reports them at that strength. The broader Jōmon lacquer tradition — combs, vessels, bows, and ornaments from waterlogged sites across the following millennia, chemically confirmed in multiple cases — is not in doubt. A forager society mastered one of the most unforgiving coating chemistries of the pre-industrial world, and used it for beauty. Dogū — Described Plainly The dogū are clay figurines — hand-modelled, fired, ranging from a few centimetres to some 40 cm tall — produced from the Early Jōmon onward and most numerous and elaborate in the Middle, Late, and Final phases of northern and eastern Japan. Most represent a human-like figure, conventionally read as female on the evidence of breasts and emphasised hips on many examples; the best-known Late and Final Jōmon forms have large, protruding eyes that modern viewers compare to goggles, heart-shaped or triangular faces, and bodies covered in cord-marked and incised patterning. They are very frequently found broken, and often in refuse or midden contexts rather than in graves or shrines. That is the description. What dogū were — the literature offers healing or childbirth figures, dolls, ritual objects deliberately broken in use, representations of spirits or ancestors — the evidence does not decide, and the confident modern readings, whether "fertility goddess" or anything stranger, go beyond it. This article records the figurines as a major, long-lived Jōmon art form whose function is unresolved, and notes the one hard pattern in the data: a sedentary forager society sustained figurine-making, as it sustained lacquer and fine pottery, for thousands of years. Symbolic elaboration did not wait for farming either. PIT-HOUSE VILLAGES Semi-subterranean houses, storage pits, cemeteries, and working areas on favoured terraces, rebuilt across centuries — sedentary settlement without staple agriculture. SHELL MIDDENS Stratified shell mounds preserving diet, craft, burials, and dogs; the Ōmori midden's 1877 excavation by Edward Morse founded Japanese archaeology. LACQUER AT 9,000 YEARS Red-lacquered ornaments from a Kakinoshima B grave, c. 7000 BCE — the world's oldest reported lacquer, its identification noted as resting on less than full chemical confirmation. DOGŪ, PLAINLY Clay figurines, often found broken, made for millennia across northern Japan. Their function is unresolved in the literature; no cult is asserted here. V. Sannai-Maruyama — The Large-Settlement Case Sannai-Maruyama, in Aomori Prefecture near the northern end of Honshū, was found in 1992 when construction of a baseball stadium cut into the site; the prefecture cancelled the stadium, excavated on a large scale, and preserved the ground — an outcome Japanese archaeology is entitled to be proud of. The settlement was occupied for roughly seventeen centuries, c. 3900–2200 BCE , spanning the Early and Middle Jōmon, on a terrace between river and bay. Its excavated remains are the fullest picture of a large Jōmon community anywhere: hundreds of pit-house foundations, large pillar-supported buildings including a long structure over 30 metres in length, raised-floor storehouses, storage pits in quantity, roads — a packed-earth thoroughfare some 12 metres wide in places — formal burial areas with adult graves ranged along the roads and a separate zone of child burials in pottery jars, and great mounds of accumulated refuse rich in pottery, stone, bone, and plant remains. Population estimates for the settlement at its height commonly run to several hundred people. In 2021 the site was inscribed, with the other Jōmon sites of northern Japan, on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The building that made the site famous is its six-pillar structure : six enormous postholes, evenly spaced in two rows, each holding a chestnut post about a metre in diameter. The posts' regularity — the spacing is uniform enough to have prompted speculation about standardised measurement — implies a large roofed or tower-like building of communal scale, raised by coordinated labour with stone tools. Its function is unknown: watchtower, assembly hall, and ritual structure have all been proposed, and this article asserts none of them. What the postholes prove without interpretation is organisation — timber felled, transported, shaped, and erected at a scale beyond any household, in a community with no chiefs anyone can identify in its burials, no metal, and no crops. Beside the structure, the exchange evidence widens the picture: jade and obsidian from distant sources, lacquerware, and amber show Sannai-Maruyama plugged into the archipelago-wide networks of §IV at their northern end. The Chestnut Question — Management or Cultivation? The settlement stood in chestnut country, and chestnut dominates its plant remains — as food, in storage pits full of nuts, and as timber, in posts like the six pillars. The debate is whether that dominance is an accident of local forest or a human product. Pollen evidence around the site shows chestnut rising to unusual prominence during the occupation, and archaeobotanical study has argued that the inhabitants managed the surrounding forest — protecting, encouraging, and selectively using chestnut (and other useful trees) so systematically that the groves around the village amount to a tended landscape: arboriculture without fields. Genetic study of chestnut remains has been brought to bear on both sides, and the strong claim — deliberate planting and selection amounting to cultivation — remains argued rather than settled. The careful statement, and the one this article makes, distinguishes the levels: that Jōmon communities used chestnut intensively is certain; that they managed the forest to favour it is the prevailing reading of the pollen and assemblage evidence; that they domesticated it, in the genetic sense claimed for cereals, is not demonstrated. Sannai-Maruyama's people also used a few genuinely cultivated plants in small quantities — bottle gourd and others attested in the assemblage — as supplements at the margin of a forager economy, which is exactly the point: cultivation at the margin, sedentism and complexity at the centre. Sannai-Maruyama's lesson for this hub is the Jōmon's lesson at full scale: complexity without agriculture . A settlement of hundreds, maintained for seventeen centuries, with monumental communal building, formal roads and cemeteries, craft production in lacquer and jade, and exchange reaching hundreds of kilometres, rested on fish, game, and managed forest. The same theme is sounded, in a farming key, at Çatalhöyük , where a town of thousands likewise shows no palace, no temple quarter, and no ruling house anyone can find: in both places the equation of social scale with hierarchy and of settlement with farming fails, and fails on excavated ground. The Jōmon simply fail it for longer, and without the crops. // WHY THE NORTH KEEPS ITS SECRETS POORLY — AND WELL // Japan's acid volcanic soils destroy bone and wood at most sites, which is why the Jōmon skeletal record is thin and why middens and waterlogged deposits carry so much of the evidence. Sannai-Maruyama's waterlogged lower layers preserved wooden artefacts, plant remains, and lacquer that would have vanished on a dry terrace. The record's unevenness cuts both ways: absence of a material at a Jōmon site is weak evidence, and the richest sites are rich partly because they preserved. Population and complexity estimates in this section are read with that caution. VI. Jiahu — The Village on the Huai Jiahu lies near Wuyang in Henan Province, in the upper Huai River valley — the border country between China's dry millet-growing north and its wet rice-growing centre — east of the Funiu Mountains, between the floodplains of the Ni River to the south and the Sha River to the north. The settlement is an irregular oval roughly 275 by 260 metres, some 55,000 m² in extent, occupied, on the radiocarbon evidence published with the flute study (twenty determinations, calibrated), from 7000 to 5700 BCE in three sub-periods (c. 7000–6600, 6600–6200, and 6200–5700 BCE). It was identified in 1962 and excavated in campaigns from the 1980s onward under the Henan Provincial Institute, with Juzhong Zhang as its leading excavator. Only a small fraction — about 4–5 per cent — of the site has been excavated, and that fraction has yielded an inventory out of all proportion to its size: 45 house foundations, 370 storage or cellar pits, 9 pottery kilns, more than 300 graves, and thousands of artefacts in bone, pottery, and stone (Zhang et al., Nature 1999). // LOCATION // Upper Huai valley, Henan Near Wuyang, between the Ni and Sha rivers — the ecological border between millet north and rice centre (§VII). // OCCUPATION // c. 7000–5700 BCE Three sub-periods across some 1,300 years; earlier at its inception than the Peiligang culture it was once folded into. // EXCAVATED // c. 2,400 m² of 55,000 m² 45 houses, 370 pits, 9 kilns, 300+ graves from under 5 per cent of the site — the sample behind every Jiahu claim. // ECONOMY // Rice, game, fish, gathered plants Early rice use within a broad-spectrum economy of deer, fish, turtles, nuts, and wild plants — farming at the margin (§VII). The village was, from its first phase, sedentary and organised: semi-subterranean and surface houses, dedicated pottery kilns, storage pits, and cemeteries in which the dead were buried with goods — tools, pottery, ornaments, and, in a number of graves, the tortoise shells and bone flutes of §§VIII–IX. Its material culture is correspondingly rich: polished stone tools including harvesting implements, bone tools of many kinds, pottery in a developing repertoire of jars and basins (the vessels whose residues §X examines), and evidence of animals managed as well as hunted, with pig and dog among the domesticates present in the assemblage as the sequence proceeds. The subsistence base remained broad — deer, fish, freshwater shellfish, turtles, water chestnut, acorns, and other wild plants bulk large in the remains — with rice present from the early phases as one resource among many. Jiahu, in the excavators' phrase as reported in the Nature paper, was an organised, well-established sedentary village of long duration in the very early Chinese Neolithic: not a camp on the way to farming, but a settled community experimenting, over thirteen centuries, with the plants and animals around it. That border-country setting is the key to everything that follows. Jiahu sits near the northern climatic limit of wild rice and at the southern edge of the zone where the northern millets would be domesticated; it is the kind of ecotone where two of the world's great grain traditions could meet in a single village's stores. The four bodies of evidence that made Jiahu famous — its rice, its flutes, its signs, and its fermented beverage — are treated in the next four sections in ascending order of contention: the flutes, whose evidence is the soundest and strangest; the rice, whose domestication status is genuinely open; the beverage, chemically attested and briefly handled here; and the signs, where this article's discipline is tested hardest. VII. Jiahu — Early Rice and Its State of Evidence Rice at Jiahu is attested by three independent kinds of remain. Carbonised grains occur in the site's deposits — one such grain supplied one of the twenty radiocarbon dates of the flute paper — and rice husks were used as temper in pottery. Phytoliths — the microscopic silica bodies that form in plant tissues and survive where the plant itself decays — were recovered from Jiahu sediments in a 1995 study (published in Chinese Science Bulletin ) that identified fan-shaped and other phytolith forms diagnostic of rice, including forms from the grain husks, in the site's early levels, and assigned the cultivated material to the japonica type of Oryza sativa . And the residues of §X identify rice as an ingredient of the village's fermented beverage, which presupposes rice available in quantity worth brewing. Taken together, the three lines establish beyond reasonable dispute that Jiahu's people used rice, from the site's early centuries, as a significant resource . They do not, by themselves, establish what kind of rice it was. The open question is domestication status, and it is open for a principled reason: the traits that distinguish domesticated rice from wild rice — above all the non-shattering rachis, the mutation that stops the ripe grain falling from the stalk and so makes the plant dependent on human harvest and sowing — are read from spikelet bases and grain metrics in large, well-preserved assemblages, and Jiahu's rice assemblage, recovered largely before systematic flotation became standard in Chinese archaeology, is not of that character. The site's excavators, notably Zhang Juzhong with Wang Xiangqun, argued from the grains and phytoliths that Jiahu's rice was already a cultivated, early domesticated japonica , and proposed the upper Huai as a centre of rice cultivation in its own right, north of the Yangtze heartland. The wider archaeobotanical synthesis — Dorian Fuller and colleagues' work on the protracted, millennia-long domestication of rice in the Yangtze valley, where the shift to non-shattering forms can be tracked grain by grain and was not complete until roughly 4000 BCE — counsels a different framing: at 7000–5700 BCE, rice anywhere was at most in the early stages of a long domestication process, and Jiahu's material is best described as rice under cultivation or intensive use while domestication was still under way. Reviews of the 10,000–7000 BP rice evidence (e.g. Pan 2023) likewise treat Jiahu as an early and important node in the rice story whose precise status — wild-collected, cultivated wild, or incipiently domesticated — the surviving samples cannot finally resolve. This article therefore states the Jiahu rice claim at its defensible strength: rice was used and, on the phytolith and grain evidence, very probably cultivated at Jiahu from the seventh millennium BCE — among the earliest such evidence anywhere; whether that rice was morphologically domesticated, and whether the upper Huai was an independent centre of domestication or the northern reach of the Yangtze process, remain open questions in the published literature. The caution is not a diminishment. A village brewing with rice (§X) at the plant's northern limit, a thousand years before the Yangtze sequence shows domestication completed, is evidence enough that the rice story was wide, early, and regional — and Jiahu's place in it is secure at exactly that strength. // HOW A PHYTOLITH IS RE
