What the Bridge Carries — A Summary in Dates Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence. Where scholars disagree — about the age of a ware, the wild or domestic status of an animal, or the direction from which an idea travelled — the disagreement is reported with its positions attributed, and no winner is declared that the evidence has not declared. Pharaonic Egypt did not begin with farmers who had always farmed, on a river that had always been farmed. For thousands of years before the first Egyptian village, the middle Nile in what is now Sudan was home to hunter-fisher-gatherers who made pottery — some of the earliest pottery in Africa — ground wild grain, buried their dead in formal cemeteries, and lived well off fish, game, and gathered plants without a single domesticated animal or sown field. West of the river, across a Sahara that was then green, cattle herders built the world documented in this archive's Nabta Playa article. East and north, in the Levant, a different Neolithic — wheat, barley, sheep, goats — had been assembled earlier still. Egyptian farming, when it finally appears in the Fayum and on the Delta's edge in the sixth and fifth millennia BCE, appears at the meeting point of those three worlds. This article walks the bridge between them, from south to north and from older to younger: the Khartoum Mesolithic and Neolithic of the Sudanese Nile; the Saharan pastoralists driven east as their grasslands dried; the Fayum Neolithic; Merimde-Benisalame; El-Omari; and Maadi, where the sequence runs into the predynastic cultures proper. It ends with the question the whole route poses — how much of predynastic Egypt is Saharan, how much Levantine, and how much the Nile's own invention — stated as the open scholarly problem it remains. I. A Bridge, Not a Birthplace — The Argument of This Article The metaphor in the title is chosen carefully. A bridge is not a birthplace: it does not explain where the traffic on it was born, only that the traffic crossed. The claim defended here is the modest, well-evidenced one — that between about 8000 and 3500 BCE the Nile corridor and its desert margins formed a connected landscape along which pottery, livestock, grain, techniques, and people demonstrably moved, and that the farming cultures of early Egypt cannot be understood from the valley alone. The stronger claims sometimes built on that connection — that Egypt was "founded" by Saharan refugees, or "given" farming by Levantine colonists — are examined in §XVII and found, in their strong forms, unproven. // THE SOUTHERN ANCHOR // Khartoum, Sudan Early Khartoum (Khartoum Mesolithic) is currently dated overall to c. 8800/8500–5000 BCE; pottery-using hunter-fisher-gatherers, no domesticates. // THE NORTHERN ANCHOR // Merimde & the Fayum Egypt's earliest well-evidenced mixed farming: Merimde c. 5000 BCE (earliest radiocarbon c. 5300 BCE); Fayum domesticates from c. 5400 BCE, abundant in the 5th millennium. // THE CLIMATE FRAME // Desiccation from c. 5300 BCE Kuper & Kröpelin's Eastern Sahara synthesis: gradual drying from c. 5300 BCE, with the desert effectively emptying toward the Nile and the south by c. 3500 BCE. // THE FAR BANK // Badarian c. 4400–4000 BCE The established hub chronology (per Shaw): the Badarian of Upper Egypt, then Naqada, then unification c. 3100 BCE. This article ends where that sequence begins. A note on names and dates. "Mesolithic" and "Epipalaeolithic" are both used in the literature for the early Holocene hunter-gatherer cultures of the Nile; Sudanese archaeology conventionally says Khartoum Mesolithic , Egyptian archaeology conventionally says Epipalaeolithic (hence "Qarunian" in the Fayum). The labels describe toolkits and economies, not peoples, and the same human world can appear under either. All dates are calibrated calendar dates (BCE) unless a radiocarbon age (bp) is explicitly flagged. II. The River Before Farming — The Late Palaeolithic Inheritance The bridge's foundations are older than the Holocene. In the Late Palaeolithic, roughly 20,000–12,000 years ago, communities along the Upper Egyptian and Nubian Nile — the Kubbaniyan of Wadi Kubbaniya, north of Aswan, is the best studied — already practised the riverine specialisation that would define the Mesolithic Nile: intensive fishing (above all Clarias catfish, taken at the flood-season spawn and, the excavators argued, smoked and stored), hunting of large game, and systematic grinding of wetland tubers and wild seeds on stone implements. Charred plant remains at Wadi Kubbaniya include wild barley and other grasses; early claims that these represented cultivation have not held up, and the current reading is intensive gathering, not farming. The point matters for everything that follows: the Nile's people were processing plants with grinding stones, and storing fish, millennia before anyone in the valley kept an animal or sowed a seed. In Lower Nubia the Qadan culture (c. 15,000–11,000 years ago in broad terms) carried the same pattern — grinding stones, early sickle-like tools, heavy use of wild grasses — and left cemeteries, most famously at Jebel Sahaba, whose burials with embedded projectile points are among the earliest widely accepted evidence of organised violence anywhere. The lesson the Late Palaeolithic leaves for this article is double. Economically, the "Neolithic" toolkit of the Nile — grinding, storage, scheduled exploitation of the flood — was assembled by hunter-gatherers long before domestication. Socially, those hunter-gatherers were already capable of formal burial grounds and collective conflict. Neither farming nor complexity arrived in the valley as an import; both had local rehearsals. // WHY THE DEEP BACKGROUND MATTERS // When pottery, domestic sheep, and emmer wheat later appear in the valley, they land in a landscape whose inhabitants already knew how to grind grain, store food, fish a flood cycle, and bury their dead together. The debate in §XVII is therefore never "invention versus nothing." It is always about what was added to a capable local base, by whom, and how fast the addition was transformed. III. Early Khartoum — Arkell Defines the Khartoum Mesolithic The southern end of the bridge was defined in the 1940s by one excavator. A. J. Arkell, working for the Sudan Antiquities Service, excavated in 1944 a Mesolithic occupation near Khartoum Hospital and published it in 1949 as Early Khartoum . The assemblage he recovered set the type for what is now called the Khartoum Mesolithic : a microlithic stone industry worked largely from quartz pebbles; bone working, including some 270 harpoon and spearhead fragments, a few incised with decoration; grinders probably used on wild grain; broken stone rings of still-uncertain function; and — the find that made the site famous — pottery, in a settlement with no trace of houses, no domesticated animals, and a fauna of hunted and fished wild species. The UCL Petrie Museum's summary of the site states the economy plainly: these people lived by hunting and fishing, and no domesticated animals were found. Arkell himself saw the paradox and, as later reviewers have noted, remarked on the contrast with the Levantine Natufian, which had sickles but (in the understanding of the time) no pottery, while Early Khartoum had pottery but no farming. The sequence he built from Khartoum — a pottery-bearing Mesolithic followed, at Shaheinab (§VII), by a Neolithic with domesticates — became the framework into which seventy years of Sudanese finds have been fitted, criticised, and refined. Modern dating places the Early Khartoum phenomenon overall between about 8800/8500 and 5000 BCE, a span of more than three millennia: not a moment of transition, but a durable, successful way of life. That durability is the first fact to hold onto. The Khartoum Mesolithic was not a waiting room for the Neolithic. Its communities occupied favoured riverine and lacustrine settings along the White and Blue Niles and their tributary wadis for longer than the whole of pharaonic history, adjusting pottery styles, toolkits, and settlement patterns as the early Holocene climate shifted around them. When domestic animals finally appear in central Sudan, they appear inside this world — adopted by it, on its terms — rather than replacing it. IV. Wavy Lines — Among the Earliest Pottery in Africa The diagnostic artefact of the Khartoum Mesolithic is a pot that no longer survives whole. No complete vessel was found at the Khartoum Hospital site; the ware is known from sherds, reconstructable as simple-rimmed bowls. Its characteristic decoration — the wavy line — was incised into the wet clay with a combing tool, possibly, as the UCL summary suggests, the spine of a catfish ( Synodontis schall ), examples of which were found on the site. A second motif, the dotted wavy line , was impressed rather than incised. Arkell treated the incised wavy line as characteristic of the earlier Mesolithic and the dotted wavy line as characteristic of its later phase; later work across Sudan and the Sahara-Sahel belt has complicated that tidy evolution — the two techniques overlap in time and vary by region — but the horizon itself is real: wavy-line and dotted wavy-line wares mark a broad early Holocene ceramic world stretching along the central Nile and across the southern Sahara. The dates are what give the ware its continental significance. Ceramic production in Africa begins, on the current evidence reviewed in the seventy-year retrospective of Sudanese pottery studies ( African Archaeological Review , 2021), between the tenth and the mid-ninth millennium BCE, made by early Holocene hunter-gatherers. On the Nile itself, dated Mesolithic contexts include Abu Darbein, el-Damer, and Aneibis on the Atbara reach, with radiocarbon series running from about 8640 ± 120 bp down to about 7700 ± 140 bp at Abu Darbein, and a wavy-line assemblage at Shabona on the White Nile dated in the eighth millennium bp. A shell date of 10,060 ± 150 bp from Saggai (§V) has been reported for a Mesolithic assemblage but is treated in the literature as suspect — shell dates are vulnerable to reservoir effects — and this article does not build on it. // "EARLIEST" — A CLAIM TO HANDLE WITH CARE // Sudanese and Saharan pottery is routinely described as "among the earliest in Africa," and that qualified form is the correct one. Comparably early ceramics are claimed elsewhere in the Sahara-Sahel (Niger sites among them), absolute priority depends on a handful of dates of varying quality, and East Asia's hunter-gatherer pottery is earlier still. What is not in dispute is the point that matters here: on the middle Nile, pottery was invented or adopted by fisher-hunter-gatherers thousands of years before farming — independently of the Near Eastern sequence, in which pottery follows farming villages. In Sudan, the pot precedes the plough by an entire era. What were the pots for? Residue analysis at al-Khiday (§V) gives an unusually direct answer for the Mesolithic: the vessels processed plants — wild grasses, leafy plants, sedges, and underground storage organs such as tubers — and some low-fat animal products, while fish, paradoxically, left no trace of having been cooked in them despite dominating the bone assemblage. The Mesolithic pot, on this evidence, was a plant-processing technology: a way to boil, soak, and detoxify gathered foods. Pottery on the Nile begins as cookware for a gathering economy, and only much later becomes the storage and serving ware of farmers. V. Fisher-Hunters of the Middle Nile — Saggai, al-Khiday, and the Mesolithic World Khartoum Hospital is the type-site, but the Mesolithic is now known from dozens of sites along the middle Nile, and three of them carry much of this article's evidence. Saggai 1 , about 40 km north of Khartoum on the east bank, was excavated from 1979 by the University of Rome mission under Isabella Caneva; its surface scatter covered some 3.6 hectares with a cultural deposit up to about 1.35 m deep — a substantial, repeatedly occupied settlement, not a camp — and Caneva's monograph on it bore the programmatic title Pottery Using Gatherers and Hunters at Saggai . Umm Marrahi , west of the Nile north of Khartoum, produced radiocarbon dates of 8920 ± 180 bp and 8240 ± 120 bp (calibrating broadly to the ninth–eighth millennia BCE), confirming an early Mesolithic presence away from the main river. Sites such as Sarurab, Kabbashi Haitah, Shaqadud, and el-Barga near Kerma extend the same world north and into the desert hinterland. The richest recent window is al-Khiday , a cluster of sites on the west bank of the White Nile some 35 km south of Omdurman, excavated by Donatella Usai, Sandro Salvatori, and colleagues. Its stratified sequence runs from about 7000 to 4000 cal BCE across Mesolithic and early Neolithic occupations. The Mesolithic settlement phase is well dated to about 6580–6440 cal BC, set on a ridge that then stood among seasonal flood-fed swamps. The faunal assemblage is dominated — around 90 per cent in the Mesolithic deposits — by fish, above all the shallow-water Clarias catfish of the floodplain swamps, alongside warthog, Nile monitor, and mud turtle; dental and starch evidence adds gathered plants to the menu. Recent syntheses of the Khartoum Mesolithic stress what al-Khiday exemplifies: a phase lasting at least 3,000 years, with real regional variability in pottery production and settlement — a complex of communities, not a single static "culture." Picture the economy whole. At flood season, fish crowded into the shallows and could be taken in quantity with harpoons, traps, and nets; catfish could be dried or smoked against lean months, as at Wadi Kubbaniya ten millennia earlier. On the savanna margins, hunters took antelope and other game. Gatherers worked the wild grasses, fruits — Celtis seeds are a recurring find — and tubers, grinding and cooking them in the wavy-line pots. Settlement followed the water: substantial base settlements on ridges and terraces, thinner scatters at seasonal stations. Nothing in this system required improvement, and for three thousand years it received none that archaeology can see — until, gradually, herded animals were folded into it (§VIII). VI. The Dead Before the Farmers — Mesolithic Cemeteries and Social Complexity Hunter-gatherers are not supposed, in the textbook version, to maintain formal cemeteries. The Sudanese Mesolithic did. At al-Khiday 2, beneath the later settlement and cemeteries, the excavators found a pre-Mesolithic cemetery — some 120 individuals in the excavated sample overall at the mound — whose burials are stratigraphically older than the Mesolithic pits that cut them, and therefore earlier than about 6600 cal BC on the associated radiocarbon evidence; the skeletons themselves, depleted of collagen, cannot be dated directly. The excavators' Antiquity report presented the cemetery as evidence of a distinctive funerary outlook among these early Holocene foragers, generations before any domestication in the region. A Neolithic community later reused the same mound as a burial ground (c. 4360–4250 cal BC), and a Meroitic one did so again two thousand years after that — a single low ridge gathering the dead of three unrelated eras. Al-Khiday is not alone. The Mesolithic cemetery at el-Barga near Kerma, and the long Sudanese tradition of riverine burial grounds running back to Jebel Sahaba, make the same point at regional scale: attachment to place, expressed through the dead, precedes farming on the Nile by millennia. Recent reviews of the Khartoum Mesolithic explicitly frame the new stratified data as a challenge to the old static picture, opening the question of social complexity among hunter-gatherer-fishers — ranked or corporate groups, territorial cemeteries, specialised pottery production — as a live research problem rather than a contradiction in terms. For the argument of this article the implication is direct: when farming later spreads along the Nile, it spreads among peoples who already had places, ancestors, and institutions. Adoption was a decision made by societies, not a vacuum being filled. VII. Shaheinab — The Khartoum Neolithic Arkell's second type-site stands about 50 km north of Omdurman, on the west bank of the Nile. Excavated in 1949–50 and published in 1953 as Shaheinab , it gave its name to the Khartoum Neolithic (also "Shaheinab Neolithic," and in Arkell's terminology the "Gouge Culture," after its characteristic polished stone gouges). The site is a gravel ridge some 200 m long beside a small wadi; beneath and beside its Neolithic settlement lay an earlier Early Khartoum (Mesolithic) occupation and, later, Late Neolithic and Meroitic graves. The modern restudy of its ceramics (D'Ercole, Dunne, Eramo, Evershed & Garcea, 2024) confirms the broad framework: the Shaheinab Neolithic in central Sudan spans about 5000–3800 BCE , with the type-site's own Neolithic occupation dated by radiocarbon to the mid-fifth millennium, roughly 4700–4200 cal BCE. The material signature is continuity with a difference. The pottery continues the Mesolithic repertoire — dotted wavy-line ware (rows of four to six dotted wavy lines in Arkell's description) and impressed wares — rather than replacing it. Lip plugs, beads, and other personal ornaments appear. And in the fauna, for the first time in the Khartoum sequence, domestic animals are present. Arkell's original identifications — a dwarf domestic goat, a twisted-horn goat or sheep, and possibly a further sheep — made Shaheinab, in his assessment, the earliest record of domestication and of sheep and goat in Sudan. Later reanalysis (Peters, 1986, and subsequent work) revised the details: the "two goat breeds" do not hold up osteologically, and bones Arkell had classed as wild buffalo were reidentified as domestic cattle. The corrected picture is more interesting than the original: domesticates make up roughly 16 per cent of the reanalysed fauna, against 84 per cent wild — hippopotamus and giraffe the most plentiful wild species, fish still common — with caprines (sheep/goats) forming about three-quarters of the domestic fraction and cattle about a quarter. No domesticated plants were found at all; gathered Celtis fruit stands for the plant economy. // ONE SITE, TWO BANKS // The 2024 restudy adds a landscape point worth keeping: Shaheinab's west-bank setting — a narrower alluvial plain, hilly slopes, restricted grazing — differs from the east bank opposite, and the team reads the site's strong emphasis on wild meat and its particular ceramic recipes as a local adaptation to that narrower niche. The Khartoum Neolithic was not a uniform blanket laid over Sudan; it was the same broad transition, negotiated bank by bank. Shaheinab does not stand alone either. Kadero, Geili, Zakiab, Umm Direiwa, and the upper Shaqadud midden show the same pattern — Mesolithic ceramic and lithic continuity plus domestic livestock — with the livestock share varying wildly by site: around 88 per cent of the fauna at Kadero (mostly cattle, per Gautier's analysis), about half at Shaheinab on the older counts, and over 90 per cent at Zakiab. The variation is itself the finding: neighbouring communities adopted herding at different intensities, some becoming committed pastoralists, others — like Shaheinab — keeping one foot in the old hunting-fishing economy for centuries. VIII. Herds Without Harvests — How Domesticates Entered Sudan The Sudanese Neolithic, as the Shaheinab evidence defines it, is a Neolithic of animals without crops. Sheep and goats are Southwest Asian domesticates — neither has a wild African progenitor of the domestic form — and domestic cattle, on the current genetic and metrical evidence summarised in this archive's Nabta Playa article, likewise descend from the Near Eastern domestication, whatever local aurochs introgression may later have added. All three therefore arrived in Sudan: down the Nile, across the Red Sea hills, or through the drying Sahara with the pastoralists of §IX — the routes are debated, the arrival is not. Syntheses of the central Sudanese transition place the Khartoum Neolithic proper at about 6000–5000 bp in radiocarbon terms (broadly the fifth millennium BCE), with livestock herding spreading across the Sahel over the following thousand years as its central feature. Domesticated plants , by contrast, are absent from the Khartoum Neolithic record. No emmer, no barley, no domesticated sorghum occurs at Shaheinab or its peers; cereal agriculture reaches central Sudan late and patchily, long after herding, despite a local plant-processing tradition (grinding stones, cooking pots, wild sorghum use) that was thousands of years old. Firm morphological evidence for domesticated sorghum in Africa comes only in the fourth millennium BCE, in eastern Sudan. The order of events in Sudan is thus the reverse of the classic Levantine package, in which crops and livestock arrive together: here, pottery came first (by millennia), livestock second, and crops a distant third. Any model of "the Neolithic" as a single imported bundle fails on the Sudanese evidence alone. The Pastoral Sahara Moves East West of the Sudanese Nile lay the other half of the bridge: the cattle-pastoral world of the green Sahara, whose Egyptian capital was Nabta Playa. That world — its wells, villages, cattle tumuli, cemeteries at Gebel Ramlah, and its debated early cattle — is treated in full in Nabta Playa and the Green Sahara and is not repeated here. What belongs to this article is the connection. The pastoralists of the Eastern Sahara and the fisher-hunters of the middle Nile were not strangers: the wavy-line ceramic horizon spans both; Saharan sites and Nile sites share impressed-ware traditions; and the livestock that appears in fifth-millennium Sudan had to cross, or round, the same desert the Nabta herders inhabited. Andrew B. Smith's classic summary of the Sudanese transition states the direction plainly: the domestic animals of the Khartoum Neolithic sites had to have been introduced from the Sahara or from the north. The traffic was not only animal. Cattle-centred ritual — the burial of whole cattle, the feasting deposits, the treatment of herds as wealth seldom eaten — is the Sahara's signature contribution to the wider region, and it has a Nile afterlife: cattle burial occurs in the predynastic valley, and the fifth-millennium "primary pastoral community" identified by Wengrow and colleagues (2014) — a horizon of shared funerary practice linking the Egyptian and Sudanese Nile — suggests the valley's own Neolithic formed inside this African pastoral world rather than apart from it. The bridge, in other words, carried meaning as well as meat: a way of valuing cattle, and of burying the dead among kin, that both banks of the desert shared. X. The Drying — The End of the African Humid Period The pastoral world had an expiry date, set by the sky. The African Humid Period — the long early-Holocene interval when strengthened monsoons greened the Sahara — ended as Earth's orbital precession weakened northern summer insolation and the rain belt retreated south. For the Eastern Sahara, Kuper and Kröpelin's synthesis of radiocarbon dates from some 150 excavations ( Science , 2006) remains the standard frame: humid conditions and settlement begin abruptly around 8500 BCE; gradual desiccation sets in from about 5300 BCE ; settlement then breaks up in stages, surviving in refuges such as the Gilf Kebir and the oases, with dated sites growing younger southward as populations track the retreating desert margin toward the Sahel — and concentrating, eastward, in the Nile Valley. By about 3500 BCE, the date this hub uses for the effective end of the process, the Eastern Sahara outside the Nile and the oases was essentially empty. Two cautions keep the frame honest. First, tempo: marine and lake records disagree on whether the humid period ended abruptly (around 5,500 years ago in the deMenocal cores) or gradually (the Lake Yoa record), and the archaeology — repeated abandonment and return at Nabta, staged retreat in Kuper and Kröpelin's phases — fits a stepped, regionally uneven drying better than a single catastrophe. Second, agency: desiccation explains pressure , not outcomes. The same drying that pushed some herders east to the Nile pushed others south to the Sahel, where Saharan pastoralism seeded traditions of its own, and left others in the oases. The Nile received a stream of desert people; it was not flooded by the whole Sahara. What that stream contributed on arrival is the subject of §XVII — and it is a question about culture, not just climate. c. 8500 BCE Humid onset. Monsoon rains return to the Eastern Sahara; settlement spreads across what is now hyperarid desert (Kuper & Kröpelin 2006). c. 5300 BCE Desiccation begins. The long retreat starts; Egyptian Sahara settlement breaks up, surviving in refuges. c. 5000–3800 BCE The bridge in use. Khartoum Neolithic herding in Sudan; Merimde founded; Fayum domesticates appear — desert, river, and Delta in one connected system. c. 3500 BCE The desert empties. Final Neolithic occupation fades at Nabta (abandoned by c. 3400 BCE); population concentrated in the Nile Valley, the oases, and the Sahel. XI. The Fayum Before the Farmers — The Qarunian North now, to the Fayum: a great natural depression west of the Nile, holding Lake Qarun — in the early Holocene a much larger, fresher lake, fed by a Nile channel and fluctuating with the flood. The Fayum's pre-farming occupation is the Qarunian , the Epipalaeolithic culture Gertrude Caton-Thompson and Elinor Wight Gardner originally labelled "Fayum B." Their lettering implied that B followed A; later stratigraphy and radiocarbon reversed the order — B is older — and the neutral name Qarunian is now standard. Securely dated contexts run from about 8220 ± 105 bp to 7140 ± 120 bp; in calibrated terms the Qarunian is generally placed at roughly 7100–6000 cal BC (Hassan's chronology), with some syntheses giving c. 7530–6090 BC. The Qarunian toolkit is microlithic — small blades and bladelets — and its economy was the lake's: fishing first, with hunting of gazelle and other game, and little or no use of cereal grains on the plant evidence. There is no pottery, no ground stone to speak of, and no domesticates. Between the Qarunian and the Neolithic that follows, the Fayum sequence shows an apparent occupational gap associated with low lake levels — a reminder that even the "permanent" water of the Fayum was a fluctuating resource, and that the depression's human history is a history of returns. The Qarunian matters to this article as the Fayum's version of the Khartoum Mesolithic lesson: a capable, lake-tuned forager world already in place when domesticates arrived — and, as §XIII will show, the boundary between its people and the first "farmers" may be blurrier than the culture labels suggest. XII. Fayum A — Kom K, Kom W, and the First Stored Grain in Egypt The Fayum Neolithic — Caton-Thompson and Gardner's Fayum A , also called the Fayumian — was defined in their three seasons of 1924–28 on the lake's north shore and published in The Desert Fayum (1934). Its type-sites are two occupation mounds, Kom K (about 6,568 m²) and Kom W (about 7,196 m²), each within about a kilometre of the contemporary lakeshore: dense scatters of hearths, pits, and settlement debris, with hundreds of shallow depressions (248 recorded at Kom W, 60 at Kom K) but — a fact whose significance §XIII takes up — no convincing house plans. The assemblage that made the culture "Neolithic" is a package: handmade pottery (whole pots at Kom W settled the attribution), polished stone axes, finely made bifacial tools and hollow-based arrowheads, sickle blades — and domesticates. The domesticates are Southwest Asian, as in Sudan: emmer wheat and hulled barley; sheep, goats, cattle, and probably pigs. Their most eloquent context is not the koms themselves but the granaries Gardner found by chance away from them: two groups of storage pits — the Upper and Lower K Pits, 183 pits in all on Caton-Thompson's count — lined with basketry, some still holding grain, with a complete composite sickle among the finds. Wheat and barley from the Upper K Pits have been radiocarbon dated to about 4450 BCE. Storage on this scale is a social fact as much as an economic one: grain was harvested in quantity, carried to a dedicated place, sealed in lined pits, and kept — the earliest well-preserved domesticated cereals in Egypt, and the clearest early Egyptian evidence of a harvest worth storing. Yet the Fayum Neolithic diet, measured in bones, was still mostly the lake's. The large new faunal assemblages from Kom K and Kom W published by Linseele and colleagues (2014) are dominated by fish, in direct continuity with the Qarunian and earlier Holocene pattern; the excavators' dates for the two mounds run about 4850–4250 BC. The Fayum A people were farmer-herders who fished — or, with equal justice, fishers who had added herds and fields. That doubleness is not a defect in the evidence; it is the character of the Egyptian Neolithic everywhere on this bridge, from Shaheinab to Merimde. XIII. How Old, How Settled? — The Fayum Dating and Mobility Debate Two debates run through the modern Fayum literature, and the spec of this archive requires both to be stated fairly. The Dating Debate The older frame (Caton-Thompson & Gardner, refined by Hassan and Hendrickx) places the Fayum Neolithic at roughly 5200/5400–4400 cal BC: a sixth-to-fifth millennium phenomenon, contemporary with or slightly earlier than Merimde. The newer frame , from the URU Fayum Project's re-excavation since 2004, splits the evidence: the stratified hearth mounds of Kom K and Kom W themselves date to the mid-fifth millennium , about 4650–4350 BCE, while charcoal and botanical samples from beyond the mounds give older, scattered dates reaching well into the sixth millennium. Linseele and colleagues' synthesis (2014) generalises the pattern into two phases for Egypt as a whole: domesticates appear from about 5400 BC but in very small numbers, with only caprines present; from the fifth millennium BCE the sites, species, and bone counts all increase dramatically. On this reading the sixth-millennium dates are real but represent a thin, perhaps episodic first presence — not yet a farming economy — and the substantial Fayum Neolithic is a fifth-millennium affair. Neither frame requires the other to be fraudulent; they differ in what a handful of early dates is allowed to mean. The Mobility Debate Were the Fayum A people sedentary villagers at all? The classic reading said yes, taking the basket-lined granaries as proof of settled life. The URU project's reconsideration (Wendrich & Holdaway, 2017) points out that the pits were sealed in a way suited to long-term caching — storage by people who intended to leave and return — and that storage does not equal sedentism; combined with the absence of substantial dwellings, they leave the Fayum Neolithic's mobility an open question, with sites read as short-term fishing and hunting stops plus larger seasonal base camps. Norio Shirai's lithic studies argue a middle position: not nomadic, but tethered to the lakeshore , with residential moves reduced and logistical trips increased as farming and herding were adopted — and Shirai further challenges the assumption of a centuries-long gap, and two separate peoples, between the Qarunian and the Neolithic, proposing instead a reorganisation of mobility within a continuing population as the climate dried in the sixth millennium and people aggregated around permanent water. The fair summary: the Fayum's first farmer-herders were, at minimum, far more mobile than the word "village" implies, and the transition there looks increasingly like adaptation in place, assisted by imported livestock and seed, rather than colonisation. // LAKE LEVELS — A SECOND MOVING PART // Both debates are entangled with Lake Qarun's level, which governed where settlement was possible. Phillipps and colleagues (2016), re-modelling the north shore's topography from satellite data, cast doubt on previously published lake-level curves and on the basin-by-basin shoreline reconstructions built on them since Caton-Thompson's day. Fayum chronology is thus being revised at both ends at once — the dates and the water — and current literature should be read with that double revision in mind. XIV. Merimde-Benisalame — A Village of Farmers on the Delta's Edge If the Fayum gives Egypt's Neolithic in its most mobile form, Merimde gives it in its most settled. Tier A — What This Article Is, and How to Read It This article is Tier A — Attested . Every substantive claim in it rests on the published archaeological record: peer-reviewed excavation reports, laboratory analyses, and dated stratigraphic sequences that any reader can check against the sources listed at the end. Where scholars disagree — and on the meaning of ochre they disagree vigorously — the disagreement itself is reported, with positions attributed to the researchers who hold them. Nothing here depends on a later tradition, a revealed text, or a modern reconstruction. Those kinds of material have their own articles in this hub, under their own tier badges, and they are never blended into this one. The subject is the deep root of everything else this archive covers. Long before there were temples, scripts, furnaces, or pharmacopoeias, there were people collecting coloured earth, grinding it to powder, mixing it with fat and gum, wearing it, marking objects with it, and — in at least one place — digging into a mountainside to get more of it. The Egyptian pigment tradition, the alchemical laboratory, and the painted tomb all stand downstream of that first decision: that a particular red rock was worth carrying home. Three cautions govern everything that follows. First, dates are approximate and method-dependent : ages for the Middle Stone Age rest on luminescence and uranium-series techniques with error ranges of thousands of years, and this article gives those ranges where the literature supplies them. Second, presence is not purpose : a piece of ochre in a cave proves collection and transport, not what it was used for. Third, the word "symbolic" is a conclusion, not a description — it is the most contested term in this field, and Section XVII is devoted to the contest. // A NOTE ON "BP" // Ages in this article are given in BP ("before present," conventionally before 1950) or as "ka" (thousands of years ago), following the usage of the papers cited. For the deep record the two are effectively interchangeable at the precision available. Egyptian material in Section XVIII is dated in BCE, following Egyptological convention. II. What Ochre Is — Iron, Earth, and Colour Ochre is not a single mineral. As the archaeological literature uses the term, it is an informal label for a family of iron-rich rocks and earths that can be ground to a coloured powder and used as pigment. The colour comes from iron oxides and oxyhydroxides held in a matrix of clay and silica. Two minerals do most of the work: HAEMATITE — RED Haematite (hematite, α-Fe 2 O 3 ) is the principal red pigment mineral. Earthy, fine-grained haematite is red ochre. In its coarsely crystalline, metallic form it is called specularite or specular haematite — a glittering, micaceous ore that was specifically sought at several early sites, including the Ngwenya mine discussed in Section XI. GOETHITE — YELLOW Goethite (α-FeOOH), a hydrated iron oxyhydroxide, gives yellow ochre its colour; the looser field term "limonite" covers mixed yellow-brown hydrated iron oxides. Yellow ochres are common and widespread, yet in assemblage after assemblage the red material is disproportionately selected — a preference examined in Sections VI and XV. THE WIDER PALETTE The early pigment repertoire was not red alone. Manganese oxides give black; charcoal and burnt bone give black by another route; white clays and calcite give white. At Twin Rivers in Zambia (Section IV) the collected pigments included specularite, haematite, limonite, ochreous sandstone, and manganese dioxide side by side — a palette, not a single colour. FIRE CHANGES THE COLOUR Heating yellow ochre drives off its water and converts goethite to haematite: yellow becomes red. The transformation begins at temperatures an ordinary hearth easily reaches. Whether Middle Stone Age people deliberately heat-treated ochre to redden it is debated site by site, but the chemistry was available to anyone who left a yellow lump at the edge of a fire — and controlled use of that chemistry is one of the behaviours the Blombos workshop (Section VII) is argued to display. Why should coloured dirt matter so much? Because ochre is, archaeologically, unusually legible. It is inorganic, so it survives where skin, hide, wood, and fibre decay. It is visually unmistakable, so excavators notice and record it. It stains the tools it was processed with and the objects it was applied to, leaving a chain of evidence from outcrop to cave floor. And it had to be chosen : nobody trips over five kilograms of red rock inside a shelter by accident. Every ochre assemblage is therefore a record of decisions — which outcrop, which colour, how much, carried how far, ground how fine, mixed with what. The argument in this field is never really about whether those decisions happened. It is about what they meant. A Material That Works Ochre is also genuinely useful stuff, and any honest account has to hold that fact in view from the start. Iron oxide powder is mildly antiseptic. Mixed into plant gum it makes a better adhesive. Rubbed into hide it assists tanning and preservation. Smeared on skin it measurably blocks ultraviolet light and appears to discourage biting insects. Section VI sets out the experimental evidence for each of these functions. The point to carry forward is that "functional" and "symbolic" are not rival boxes into which each lump of ochre must be sorted: in living cultures that still use ochre daily, the same red paste is simultaneously sunscreen, cosmetic, medicine, and a statement of identity. The archaeological question is when that layered significance began — not whether the earliest users were engineers or artists. III. How Archaeologists Know — Wear, Residue, Sourcing, Dating Four kinds of laboratory work turn a red lump in a cave deposit into evidence. Understanding them matters, because the strength of every claim in this article depends on which of them stands behind it. Use-Wear and Modification A piece of ochre that has been used looks different from one that has merely been collected. Grinding produces flat, striated facets; rubbing produces smoothed, rounded surfaces; scoring and engraving produce deliberate incisions. Tammy Hodgskiss and Lyn Wadley's study of the Rose Cottage Cave assemblage — ochre spanning roughly 96,000 to 30,000 years ago — classified pieces by exactly these traces and showed that the techniques changed through time: rubbing, which transfers powder directly onto a soft surface such as skin or hide, dominates some phases, while grinding, which produces powder for mixing into paint, cosmetics, or adhesive, dominates others. The processing trace is a proxy for the use, and the use is a proxy for the intention. The traces are read against an experimental reference collection, and that step is what makes the classification more than impressionistic. In Hodgskiss's experimental programme, geological ochre pieces were ground, scored, and rubbed under controlled conditions and the resulting wear recorded at macro- and microscopic scale: grinding against coarse or fine slabs leaves parallel striations and faceted edges; scoring leaves grooves whose frayed terminations betray repeated strokes, with microstriations inside the grooves; rubbing on soft materials leaves smoothing, edge rounding, and polish, occasionally with a metallic lustre. Only then were the archaeological pieces assessed against those signatures. At Rose Cottage, 11.2 per cent of the assemblage bore identifiable use-wear — a figure that is itself a floor, since a piece ground entirely to powder, or a crayon used up in the hand, leaves nothing behind to classify. Residue Analysis Ochre rarely travels alone. On stone tools from Sibudu Cave, Marlize Lombard's residue and use-trace analyses found ochre concentrated on the bases of points and segments — the parts once inserted into hafts — in close association with plant resin and gum. That distribution cannot be explained by tools resting on stained ground; it is the signature of ochre mixed into the adhesive itself. Residue work of this kind is what converted "ochre as glue ingredient" from a plausible guess into a demonstrated practice (Section VI). The Sibudu case rests on counting, not on impression. In Lombard's 2007 extension of the study, stone segments from Sibudu and a second KwaZulu-Natal site were examined microscopically and every ochre and resin occurrence plotted: on 53 tools she documented 502 ochre occurrences and 585 resin occurrences, with about 80 per cent of the ochre and 87 per cent of the resin falling on the backed portions — the parts once seated in the haft. The comparison set matters as much as the counts: replicated tools hafted with ochre-loaded adhesives, blind-tested experimental pieces, and tools used to process plant and animal products supplied the reference patterns against which the archaeological distributions were judged, and ochre found in engraved grooves on top of a resin deposit could be recognised, by its position, as later handling contamination rather than recipe. A chemical frontier has since opened behind the microscopy: gas chromatography–mass spectrometry has identified Podocarpus resin in a hafting adhesive from Diepkloof and conifer resin on a segment from Sibudu — naming the glue's ingredients where microscopy could only map them. Geochemical Sourcing Ochre from different outcrops carries subtly different trace-element chemistry — a fingerprint. Neutron activation analysis, X-ray fluorescence, and related techniques can match an artefact to its geological source, sometimes over distances of a hundred kilometres. The landmark application is Brandi MacDonald and colleagues' 2024 study of Stone Age Eswatini, which fingerprinted ochres from ten archaeological sites against nine geological source localities and traced material from the Ngwenya mine across the region (Section XII). Sourcing turns "they used red pigment" into "they went there for it, generation after generation, even when nearer material would have served" — and that is a claim about tradition, not just technology. The Eswatini workflow shows what a fingerprint costs in practice. Artefacts and source samples were first screened by portable X-ray fluorescence, chiefly to flag manganese-rich material — above about 5 per cent manganese — which distorts bulk analysis. Characterisation then ran on two complementary tracks: neutron activation analysis, applied to 388 artefacts and source samples of suitable mass and low manganese content; and laser-ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, reserved for pieces too small, too manganese-rich, or bearing use-wear that destructive sampling would erase. X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy supplied the mineralogy. The grouping is statistical — principal-component analysis of the trace-element data — and it is governed by the provenance postulate : a source can only be claimed where the chemical variation between sources exceeds the variation within each source. Where sources overlap, the honest result is a shortlist, not an address; a sourcing claim is only ever as strong as the geological sampling behind it. Dating the Undateable Ochre itself cannot be radiocarbon dated; it contains no carbon. Its age comes from its context. The methods that built the chronology in this article are: Method What It Dates Where It Matters Here Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) Last exposure of quartz sand grains to sunlight Blombos Cave phases; Pinnacle Point; Diepkloof sequence Thermoluminescence (TL) Last heating of burnt stone Blombos engraved ochre layers (mean age c. 77 ka); Diepkloof Uranium-series (U–Th) Calcite crusts grown over or under cave paintings Sulawesi and Borneo cave art; Pinnacle Point speleothem checks Radiocarbon (¹⁴C) Charcoal and other organics; reliable only to c. 50 ka Ngwenya charcoal dates; Chauvet charcoal drawings Stratigraphic bracketing Age between dated layers above and below Twin Rivers pigments, bracketed between c. 270 ka and c. 170 ka Two consequences follow. Ages near the radiocarbon limit — Ngwenya is the case in point — should be read as minimum ages with wide uncertainty, not as birthdays. And a date is only as good as the association between the dated material and the artefact: the long-running care taken at Blombos to confirm, by independent methods, that the engraved ochres really sat in layers of the age claimed is a model of how the field handles its most important finds. IV. The Deep Record — Kapthurin and Twin Rivers The ochre story does not begin with anatomically modern humans, and it does not begin at 100,000 years ago. Its earliest chapters are older, sparser, and harder to interpret — but they establish that pigment collection is a behaviour with roots in the Middle Pleistocene, practised before our species had finished becoming itself. KAPTHURIN FORMATION, KENYA — >285,000 YEARS At site GnJh-15 in the Kapthurin Formation, west of Lake Baringo, Sally McBrearty's excavations recovered more than seventy pieces of red ochre with a combined weight of over five kilograms, from deposits dated to more than 285,000 years ago. The same formation produced early blades and points of comparable age. Five kilograms is not an accidental inclusion: it is a collected stock of pigment, assembled by hominins of the late Middle Pleistocene — the population among which, on current evidence, Homo sapiens was emerging. TWIN RIVERS, ZAMBIA — c. 270,000–170,000 YEARS Lawrence Barham's re-excavation and analysis of Twin Rivers, near Lusaka, documented at least 306 pieces of pigment — specularite, haematite, limonite, ochreous sandstone, and manganese dioxide — associated with the Lupemban industry and bracketed between roughly 270,000 and 170,000 years ago. A small proportion of pieces show grinding or rubbing. Barham estimated that the 1950s excavations alone had removed on the order of 60 kilograms of colouring material. Notably, the assemblage includes glittering specularite — material whose most obvious property is that it sparkles. What were these earliest pigment collectors doing? The honest answer is that the record cannot yet say. Neither Kapthurin nor Twin Rivers preserves engraved pieces, beads, or burials that would anchor a symbolic reading; what they preserve is selection and accumulation — coloured material, including visually striking material, gathered in quantities beyond any single act of use. Barham drew the implication carefully: if the Twin Rivers pigments and the backed tools of the Lupemban do belong to a symbolic system, then symbolism is not the exclusive property of anatomically modern humans, since the Lupemban is plausibly associated with archaic populations related to the Kabwe ( Homo heidelbergensis / rhodesiensis ) lineage. That conditional — if — is where the matter still rests. Nor was pigment use confined to Africa or to our own lineage. Hematite at Maastricht-Belvédère in the Netherlands has been reported from contexts around 200,000–250,000 years old, associated with Neanderthal ancestors, and manganese oxides at Pech-de-l'Azé in France, around 50,000 years old, bear wear consistent with rubbing on a soft material — probably skin. The Neanderthal pigment record is thinner and later than the African one, but it is real, and it warns against treating ochre as a badge that only one species could earn. // READING THE DEEP RECORD HONESTLY // Early pigment finds are vulnerable to two opposite misreadings. The first inflates them: every red lump becomes "art," every accumulation a "ritual." The second deflates them: because a function can be imagined, no significance is allowed. The literature's own position is narrower and stronger than either. Collection, transport, colour selection, and processing are demonstrated for the Middle Pleistocene record. Meaning is inferred , with confidence growing as the associated evidence — engraving, ornament, burial, sourcing over distance — accumulates in the later record described below. V. Pinnacle Point, c. 164,000 BP — Pigment at the Shore Pinnacle Point is a headland of caves on South Africa's southern coast, near Mossel Bay, overlooking the Indian Ocean. In 2007 Curtis Marean and an international team reported, in Nature , the results from cave PP13B: a small occupation dated to about 164,000 years ago (with an uncertainty of roughly ±12,000 years), from a glacial interval — Marine Isotope Stage 6 — when much of Africa was cold, dry, and difficult, and the coast offered a dependable larder. Three finds arrived together, and their conjunction is the point. First, the earliest secure evidence then known for systematic exploitation of marine foods: shellfish remains, dominated by brown mussels, together with a whale barnacle suggesting scavenging from beached whales — pushing coastal foraging back some 40,000 years beyond previous evidence. Second, small bladelet stone tools, a technology previously thought far younger. Third, pigment: fifty-seven pieces of haematite, several with flattened, grooved facets showing they had been scraped or ground to produce red powder. Marean and colleagues interpreted the pigment as evidence of symbolic behaviour — the inhabitants marking bodies or objects in ways that communicated socially. That interpretation was, and remains, an interpretation: Alison Brooks and others noted at the time that pigment at a living site could equally have served in adhesive manufacture, and no engraved or ornamented object was found at PP13B to settle the question. What Pinnacle Point established beyond dispute was the antiquity and the company pigment kept : by 164,000 years ago, in a population sheltering through a glacial bottleneck on the Cape coast, red ochre was being worked alongside the coastal diet and bladelet technology that would characterise later Middle Stone Age life. The symbolic toolkit, whatever its first use, was assembled early — in Africa, not in Ice Age Europe. // WHY THE DATE MATTERED // Before Pinnacle Point, the standard model held that recognisably "modern" behaviour — symbolism included — appeared late, perhaps 50,000–40,000 years ago, and possibly first in Europe. A securely dated pigment assemblage at 164 ka did not by itself refute that model, but it moved the burden of proof. Every subsequent early find in this article — Blombos, Diepkloof, Ngwenya — has been excavated in the space Pinnacle Point opened. VI. The Functional Repertoire — Hide, Glue, Sun, and Skin Before turning to the finds most often called symbolic, the functional evidence deserves its full weight. Experimental archaeology — actually making and using ochre preparations with period-appropriate materials — has tested each proposed use. Several pass the test decisively. A material can be useful and meaningful; but the uses must be known before the meanings can be argued. Adhesive — The Demonstrated Case Lyn Wadley's replication studies, begun in 2005 and extended with Tom Hodgskiss and Michael Grant in 2009, addressed a concrete observation: Middle Stone Age tools from Rose Cottage and Sibudu Caves carry red ochre on their hafted portions. Wadley's team made adhesives as Middle Stone Age artisans could have — plant gum or resin, with and without ochre loading — and hafted replica tools with them. Unloaded gum is brittle and hard to work; ochre-loaded gum is less brittle, resists re-dissolving in damp conditions, and can be tuned: a brittle recipe lets a projectile point detach and stay in the prey, a robust recipe keeps a spearhead seated. The 2009 study pressed the point further, arguing that compound adhesive manufacture — sourcing, combining, heat-managing materials whose properties change with acidity, drying, and working — is itself evidence of complex, multi-stage cognition, whether or not any symbolism is invoked. Lombard's residue work at Sibudu (Section III) supplies the archaeological half of the argument: traces of compound adhesives, ochre included, occur on tools from around 70,000 years ago. Hide Processing Ethnographic and experimental work supports ochre as a hide-working agent: iron oxides assist in preserving and softening skins and may inhibit bacterial decay. Rubbing traces on ochre pieces — powder transferred directly onto a soft substrate — are consistent with application to hide as well as to skin, and the Rose Cottage sequence shows rubbing as a persistent, deliberate technique across tens of thousands of years. A hunter-gatherer group that dressed hides with ochre would leave exactly the kind of assemblage many Middle Stone Age sites contain, without any recourse to symbolism at all. That is precisely why ochre alone, in bulk, is weak evidence for symbolism — and why the engraved, perforated, and sourced finds in the following sections carry the argumentative weight. Sun and Insect Protection — The Tested Case Riaan Rifkin, Francesco d'Errico, and colleagues tested the sunscreen hypothesis directly. Ochre samples — including preparations made by Ovahimba women in Namibia's Kunene Region, whose red otjize paste of ochre and butterfat remains in daily use — were assessed for sun protection factor, first in vitro and then, in a 2015 PLoS ONE study, in vivo on human skin. Red ochres provided measurable ultraviolet protection, with in vitro SPF values ranging from about 2 to about 13 depending on the sample, the reddest ochres performing best; the authors argue that protection on skin, in a fat-based preparation, would exceed the powder-only laboratory figures. Rifkin's related experimental work also found ochre effective as an insect repellent — an effect Ovahimba consultants themselves reported for protection against mosquito bites. For lightly pigmented or sun-exposed foragers moving through the high-UV environments of Pleistocene Africa — and later, for populations dispersing into new latitudes and altitudes — a habitual red coating would have been a genuine adaptive technology. Medicine and Preservation Iron oxides are astringent and mildly antibacterial, and ochre preparations appear in documented traditional pharmacopoeias as wound dressings and skin treatments. Claims of this kind for the Middle Stone Age are necessarily indirect — no residue study can yet diagnose a poultice — but the Egyptian endpoint of this article is instructive: the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) prescribes ochre clays among its remedies (Section XVIII), showing that by the time written records begin, ochre's medical use was already established practice rather than innovation. Food preservation and insect deterrence in stored goods have also been proposed and have ethnographic parallels, though the archaeological evidence is thinner. // THE HIMBA MIRROR // The Ovahimba of northern Namibia prepare otjize by grinding red ochre between stones, mixing the powder with clarified butterfat (and, in some preparations, aromatic resin), and applying it to skin and hair. Documented functions of the single preparation include sun protection, insect repellence, skin cleansing and care, hair treatment — and beauty, identity, and the marking of life-stage and status. Ethnography cannot prove what a Middle Stone Age preparation meant. It can and does prove that "it protected their skin" and "it said who they were" are not alternatives. In the one living tradition where the full context can be observed, both are true of the same red paste, applied in the same act. VII. Blombos Cave I — The 100,000-Year-Old Ochre Workshop Blombos Cave sits in a cliff above the Indian Ocean near Still Bay, on South Africa's southern Cape coast, some 300 kilometres east of Cape Town. Excavated by Christopher Henshilwood and colleagues since the 1990s, it has produced the densest cluster of early symbolic-culture evidence anywhere in the world. Its oldest headline find is not an artwork. It is a workshop. In 2008 excavators recovered, in a layer dated by optically stimulated luminescence to about 100,000 years ago, two complete toolkits preserved where they had been left. Each centred on an abalone shell — Haliotis midae — used as a container. Inside and around the shells lay the components of a production process: ochre, crushed bone (some of it heated, plausibly to extract marrow fat as a binder), charcoal, quartzite grindstones and hammerstones, and a bone implement suited to stirring and transferring the mixture. Residue on one shell's rim and the bright red deposit preserved inside it showed what the kit had made: a liquefied, ochre-rich compound — in plain terms, paint — produced in the shell and stored in it, one shell found with a stone still covering its opening. "The conceptual ability to source, combine, and store substances that enhance technology or social practices represents a benchmark in the evolution of complex human cognition." — Henshilwood, d'Errico, van Niekerk et al., "A 100,000-Year-Old Ochre-Processing Workshop at Blombos Cave, South Africa," Science 334 (2011) The paper's argument, quoted above, is deliberately cognitive rather than artistic. To make the Blombos compound, someone had to obtain ochre (the nearest known sources lie at a remove from the cave), grind it fine, heat bone and crush it, produce charcoal, combine the ingredients in workable proportions, and store the result in a container adapted for the purpose — its respiratory holes apparently plugged so it would not leak. That is a chaîne opératoire , a planned production sequence held in the mind before it was performed with the hands, and it predates the previous oldest known pigment workshop by some 40,000 years. What was the paint for ? The authors state the position exactly: the application of the mixture is unknown, with decoration and skin protection the leading possibilities, and the absence of resin or wax in the recipe telling against an adhesive use for this particular compound. A workshop that manufactures a coloured coating, in quantity, in a container made to keep it, is not yet proof of symbolism. It is proof of something arguably prior to it: a material culture in which coloured surfaces were worth organised, repeated, knowledgeable labour. The two finds from Blombos that follow — engraved ochre and shell beads — come from the same cave, tens of thousands of years later, and they carry the argument the workshop begins. VIII. Blombos Cave II — Engraved Ochre, c. 77,000–75,000 BP In 2002 Henshilwood, d'Errico, and colleagues reported in Science two pieces of red ochre from the Middle Stone Age layers of Blombos that had been deliberately engraved. Each piece had first been ground to produce a flat surface; onto that prepared surface a geometric design — cross-hatching bounded by parallel lines — had been incised with a stone point. Thermoluminescence dating of burnt lithics from the containing layers gave a mean age of about 77,000 years, and an OSL age of about 70,000 years on the overlying dune confirmed that the deposits had not been disturbed from above. The significance lies in the combination of traits. The surfaces were prepared ; the marks are patterned , not random scoring; the same cross-hatched motif recurs on both pieces; and the marks serve no conceivable role in producing powder — grinding a lump does not require drawing on it first. An expanded study (Henshilwood, d'Errico, and Ian Watts, Journal of Human Evolution , 2009) described thirteen further engraved pieces from Blombos, some from levels around 100,000 years old, with designs including cross-hatching, fan-like and wavy line arrangements. Reviewing the enlarged sample, archaeologists who had been publicly sceptical of the original two pieces — Paul Pettitt among them — were reported as considering the doubt removed: the engraving was intentional and patterned, not an accident of processing. What the designs mean is unrecoverable, and the literature does not pretend otherwise. Henshilwood's claim is the measured one: the plaques are abstract representations — external marks, made to a shared pattern, on a durable medium — and as such they are evidence that the cognitive equipment for symbol use was present and exercised in Africa at least 35,000 years before the Upper Palaeolithic of Europe. Whether a given plaque was a tally, a ownership mark, a teaching piece, a decoration, or something for which we have no category, it was a sign before it was anything else. That is the threshold this article's title names. // BLOMBOS IN ONE SEQUENCE // The cave's Middle Stone Age sequence, read as a whole, is the strongest single-site argument for gradual assembly rather than sudden invention: a paint-production workshop at c. 100 ka; engraved ochre pieces spanning c. 100–75 ka; a cross-hatched drawing on a silcrete flake at c. 73 ka; finely made bifacial points and formal bone tools; shellfish exploitation and fishing; and, at c. 75 ka, the shell beads of the next section. No single find carries the case. The stratigraphy does. The Silcrete Drawing, c. 73,000 BP The Blombos sequence has one more first. From levels dated to about 73,000 years ago comes a flake of silcrete bearing nine red lines drawn with an ochre crayon — a cross-hatched design laid on the flake's surface (Henshilwood and colleagues, Nature , 2018). It is the oldest known drawing: not pigment ground for some further use, and not an engraving cut into a plaque, but pigment applied to a surface as a design, and as nothing else. The distinction matters to this article's argument. The workshop of §VII shows ochre made ; the plaques of this section show ochre marked ; the flake shows the full chain the hub's timeline names for it — pigment prepared, a point shaped, lines planned on a surface — present at Blombos tens of millennia before the painted caves of Europe. IX. Beads — Perforated Shells and Worn Meaning If engraved ochre is a sign on a surface, a bead is a sign on a body — and personal ornaments are the least ambiguous symbolic artefacts in the early record, because a perforated shell has no plausible function except to be strung, worn, and seen. From the M1 phase of Blombos Cave, dated by OSL to 75.6 ± 3.4 thousand years ago (with a thermoluminescence mean of 77 ± 6 ka for the same phase), Henshilwood, d'Errico, Marian Vanhaeren, and colleagues reported forty-one perforated shells of the small estuarine gastropod Nassarius kraussianus , the tick shell. The case that they are beads rests on a chain of exclusions and observations published in Science (2004) and in full in the Journal of Human Evolution (2005): SELECTION The shells are all adults of a species living in estuaries some 20 kilometres from the cave. They are too small to be food refuse, cannot derive from the cave walls, and their age profile rules out accidental arrival in seaweed gathered for bedding — natural death assemblages contain all age classes; the Blombos shells do not. PERFORATION Eighty-eight per cent are pierced dorsally near the lip — a perforation type absent in living populations and rare in natural assemblages, but readily reproduced experimentally by piercing through the aperture with a sharp bone point. USE-WEAR Microscopic facets flatten the outer lip and polish the perforation edges in a pattern absent on natural shells and consistent with friction against thread, skin, and neighbouring beads — the wear of objects strung and worn. GROUPING The beads were recovered in clusters of up to seventeen, each cluster sharing shade, wear pattern, and perforation size — consistent with single beadwork items, lost or discarded together, rather than with shells accumulated one by one. Blombos is not alone. Perforated Nassarius shells from Taforalt (Grotte des Pigeons) in Morocco have been dated to about 82,000 years ago (Bouzouggar, Vanhaeren, d'Errico, and colleagues, PNAS , 2007), and shell beads from Skhul and Qafzeh in the Levant have been placed between roughly 100,000 and 135,000 years ago (Vanhaeren and colleagues, Science , 2006) — ornaments made by the early Homo sapiens populations who first moved out of Africa into the Levant. Ostrich eggshell beads join the record later, by around 50,000 years ago in East Africa. The pattern across all of these is the one d'Errico and Vanhaeren emphasise: bead-making appears in widely separated places, in the same broad period, using locally available shells — the signature of a shared behavioural capacity expressed through regional traditions, not of a single invention diffusing from one cave. A bead, it should be said plainly, communicates. It is visible at conversational distance; it is durable beyond a single wearing; its materials, colours, and arrangement can be standardised or varied. Henshilwood described the Blombos beads as evidence for the storage of information outside the human brain — meaning carried by an object, legible to others, surviving its maker. Whatever else was true of the people who wore them, that much is a description of the artefact, not a speculation about it. X. Diepkloof — An Engraving Tradition on Ostrich Eggshell, c. 60,000 BP Blombos shows that individuals engraved. Diepkloof Rock Shelter shows that a community did, repeatedly, to a shared standard, for thousands of years. That difference — from act to tradition — is why Pierre-Jean Texier and colleagues' 2010 report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences is one of the load-bearing papers of this field.
