What Old Europe Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological evidence — tells dug in stratigraphic layers, houses recovered by magnetometry, signs catalogued object by object, and slags analysed in laboratories. Where scholars disagree, as they do about the Vinča signs, the burning of the houses, and the population of the mega-sites, the disagreement itself is reported, with its positions attributed. One large interpretive construction is treated in this article at length — Marija Gimbutas's vision of a goddess-centred “Old Europe” — and it is treated as what it is: historiography, the history of an idea about the past, not the voice of this article and not Tier A evidence. It receives its own section (§XIV), fenced off from the excavated record it was built on, so that the reader can see exactly where the record ends and the construction begins. “Old Europe” itself needs the same discipline, and it gets it here at the start. The phrase is Gimbutas's term for the Neolithic and Copper Age cultures of southeastern Europe before the steppe migrations of the later fourth and third millennia BCE. This article uses it in one sense only: as a geographic-chronological label for a place and a span of time — roughly, the Danube basin, the Balkans, and the forest-steppe between the Carpathians and the Dnieper, from about 5700 to about 3500 BCE. Used that way, the label is convenient and harmless. It carries, in this article, no claim about goddesses, matriarchy, or a lost peaceful civilisation. Those claims are Gimbutas's, they are contested, and §XIV says so in detail. What the excavated record does show is remarkable enough without them. In the sixth millennium BCE, farming communities of the middle Danube built tell settlements that grew, layer on layer, for eight centuries; they fired some of the finest dark burnished pottery of the Neolithic world, modelled thousands of clay figurines, and incised a repertoire of signs on pots, spindle whorls, and figurines — a sign system that has been claimed as Europe's first writing and that the mainstream of scholarship, for reasons this article sets out in full, does not accept as writing at all. In the fifth millennium, villages of this same world became the setting for the earliest copper smelting yet securely evidenced anywhere — a metallurgical story told in this hub's First Metals article, and treated here only in its social setting. And in the early fourth millennium, far to the northeast, the related Cucuteni-Trypillia communities built planned settlements of up to some 400 hectares, with thousands of houses arranged in concentric rings — among the largest settlements anywhere on earth at that date — without palaces, without royal tombs, and without any writing at all. This article is the hub's account of that world, and its demonstration case for a question the whole division depends on: where, exactly, does a system of marks become writing? The Vinča signs are where the line is drawn, and drawn in public. I. The Danube World — A Name and a Map The world of this article is defined by two river systems and the land between them. In the west and centre stand the Balkans and the middle Danube: the plains of modern Serbia, the Banat, southern Hungary, western Romania, and northern Bulgaria, where the Danube and its tributaries — the Sava, the Tisza, the Morava — cut corridors of loess soil through hill country rich in copper ore, salt, and obsidian-bearing volcanic glass. In the east stands the forest-steppe of modern Moldova and Ukraine, between the Carpathian arc and the Dnieper River, where the Prut, Dniester, and Southern Bug run south to the Black Sea across some of the deepest black-earth soils in Europe. The two zones are distinct, and the archaeology keeps their names distinct — Vinča for the Danubian world, Cucuteni-Trypillia for the eastern one — but they were in contact throughout, shared crops, animals, pottery technologies, sign repertoires, and the habit of burning houses, and they rose and transformed on roughly the same clock. Treating them in one article is not a merger. It is a recognition that the questions they pose — about scale without hierarchy, signs without writing, and fire as a way of ending a house — are the same questions. // THE SPAN // c. 5700–3500 BCE From the mature Danubian Neolithic through the mega-site centuries. Individual cultures begin and end inside this span; the span itself is the article's frame, not a single culture's dates. // VINČA // c. 5400/5300–4500 BCE The Danubian tell culture of the central Balkans, named for Vinča-Belo Brdo near Belgrade; dated by a Bayesian-modelled radiocarbon programme at the type site itself (§III). // CUCUTENI-TRYPILLIA // c. 5050–2950 BCE The painted-pottery world of Romania, Moldova, and Ukraine. Its mega-sites belong to the centuries around 4100–3400 BCE, at their height c. 4000–3600 BCE. // THE LABEL // “Old Europe” Gimbutas's term, used in this article as a geographic-chronological label only. Her interpretation of the world it names is historiography, treated in §XIV and nowhere else as this article's voice. The chronological frame matters because this world is contemporary with — not derivative of — the early civilisations treated elsewhere in this hub. While Vinča's tells were rising beside the Danube, the Ubaid world of southern Mesopotamia was building its temple platforms and, in the centuries that followed, Uruk was becoming the first great city (see Ubaid and Uruk ). The comparison is instructive precisely because the two worlds diverge. Uruk's growth produced administrators, seals, numerical tablets, and finally writing. The Danube world's growth produced — at its Trypillia extreme — settlements as large as early Uruk, and produced no writing, no sealing bureaucracy, and no visible ruling stratum at all. Scale, it turns out, does not compel hierarchy; and marks, it turns out, do not compel writing. Both halves of that lesson are documented in the ground, and both are central to what this hub exists to record. A word on names and spellings. The eastern culture carries a double name because it was discovered twice: at Cucuteni in Romania, excavated from 1884, and at Trypillia (Tripolye) near Kyiv, excavated by Vikentiy Khvoyka from the 1890s. Romanian and Moldovan scholarship says Cucuteni; Ukrainian scholarship says Trypillia; the hyphenated form is the standard compromise and is used here. Vinča, with its caron, is the Serbian village beside the type site; the culture's Romanian extension is sometimes called Vinča-Turdaș after the Transylvanian site of Turdaș, where Zsófia Torma excavated inscribed pottery in the 1870s — the first Vinča signs ever recovered, decades before the culture had a name (§VI). II. Farming Comes Up the Danube — The Package in Its Danubian Form Farming reached the Danube from the south. The Near Eastern founder package — emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, chickpeas, bitter vetch, and flax, with sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs — had entered Greece and the southern Balkans by the seventh millennium BCE, and in the centuries around 6200–5700 BCE communities of the Starčevo culture (and its Körös and Criș relatives) carried it into the middle Danube basin and the Carpathian foothills. The Danubian form of the package, as it stabilised in this cooler, wetter, more continental climate, is the economic foundation of everything in this article, and its local adjustments are as informative as its imports. Cereals remained the staple core, grown on the loess terraces above the floodplains; pulses and flax accompanied them; and the animal economy leaned harder on cattle than the Aegean south had done — cattle for meat and, increasingly as the millennia pass, for milk and traction, alongside pig in the riverine woods and sheep and goat on the drier ground. Hunting — red deer, wild boar, aurochs — and Danube fishing continued beside the herds, as they did at Mehrgarh , where the same western grains met a different local world at the other end of the farming expansion. Longhouses West, Tells East The package travelled in two architectural forms, and the contrast between them structures the settlement geography of Neolithic Europe. Northwest of the Danube world, up the river and across the loess belt of central Europe, the Linearbandkeramik (LBK) farmers built the famous longhouses : massive timber halls, commonly 20 to 30 metres long and sometimes more, housing an extended household, its stores, and often its byred animals under one roof, grouped in loose villages that shifted within their territories as houses aged. The longhouse village was a settlement of a generation or two, not of centuries. In the Balkans and the Danube basin itself, by contrast, the dominant trajectory ran the other way: toward the tell . Where a community rebuilt on the same plot for centuries — levelling the remains of burned or decayed houses and building on the platform of debris — the settlement rose into an artificial mound. Tells concentrate everything this article studies: deep stratigraphy, dense rebuilding, long local memory, and assemblages rich enough to argue from. The Vinča world is a tell world at its core, ringed by flat, shorter-lived settlements of longhouse scale and plan; the Cucuteni-Trypillia world, which began with smaller villages of the same Danubian stock, would later take settlement aggregation to its extreme in open, planned, unfortified mega-sites (§XI). Both forms grew from the same farming package. What differed was how long a community stayed, and how it chose to gather. Two further features of the Danubian economy deserve note before the tells themselves, because they explain the tells' wealth. The first is exchange over distance . Obsidian from the Tokaj mountains of the Carpathians, marine shell — above all Spondylus — from the Aegean, salt from Transylvanian and Carpathian sources, high-quality flint, and copper minerals and metal (§IX) all moved along the river corridors, and tell communities sat on the junctions. The second is craft investment in the household : the Danubian Neolithic put extraordinary labour into objects that farming does not require — polished stone axes, burnished and graphite-painted pottery, carved bone and antler, woven textiles attested by loom weights and spindle whorls, and the figurines of §V. This was a world with surplus, skill, and time, organised — so far as the record shows — without anyone visibly in charge of it. Hold that observation; §XIII returns to it with the whole evidence in hand. // THE PACKAGE, COMPARED // This hub has now met the western founder package three times: on the Nile margin, where it arrived late and mixed with Saharan pastoralism; at Mehrgarh, where its grains met locally domesticated zebu; and here, in the Danube basin, where it met cattle-rich river plains and copper-bearing hills. In each place the package changed in the meeting. The Danubian changes — cattle emphasis, tell settlement, pyrotechnology — are the ones that matter for this article, because the road from Danubian kilns to Danubian furnaces (§IX) is one of the shortest in prehistory. III. Vinča-Belo Brdo — The Tell and Its Times The type site stands on the right bank of the Danube some 14 kilometres southeast of central Belgrade, where a high loess terrace — Belo Brdo, “White Hill” — rises above the river near the mouth of the small Bolečica stream. Miloje Vasić, Serbia's first professional archaeologist, began excavating there in 1908 and returned across three decades; his four-volume Prehistoric Vinča (1932–1936) made the site, and the culture named from it, foundational for Balkan prehistory. The tell's cultural deposits run to roughly nine to ten and a half metres in depth — an accumulation without parallel in the northern Balkans — and the greater part of that depth is Neolithic: beneath later Copper Age, Bronze Age, and medieval traces lies the stacked record of the Vinča settlement itself, founded on a terrace that had already seen a Starčevo occupation. Stratigraphy — How a Tell Keeps Time A tell is a clock made of houses. At Vinča-Belo Brdo the excavators distinguished successive building horizons: floors of packed clay, the collapsed and levelled debris of the houses that stood on them — much of it burned daub, fired hard in the fires that ended so many Danubian houses (§XII) — and the floors of the next generation laid over the top. Vasić's deep sounding divided the Neolithic sequence by depth below datum, and the culture's internal phasing still carries his framework, refined by later excavators into the four phases used throughout the literature: Vinča A (c. 5400/5300–5200 BCE), B (c. 5200–5000/4950), C (c. 5000/4950–4850/4800), and D (c. 4850/4800–4600/4500) , the first two forming the early, the last two the late Vinča period. Pottery style is the phase-marker in practice: the dark burnished wares, vessel forms, and decorative habits change horizon by horizon in a seriation anchored at this site and recognised, with local variation, at tells across the culture's range — Selevac, Pločnik, Gomolava, Divostin, and dozens more. The framework was placed on an absolute footing by the Bayesian radiocarbon programme published by Tasić and colleagues in 2015–2016 (“Vinča-Belo Brdo, Serbia: the times of a tell”), which modelled some six hundred radiocarbon determinations from the site and its culture. Its conclusion, now the standard citation, is that the Vinča culture at the type site runs from the first decades of the fifty-third century BCE to the later forty-sixth century — in round terms c. 5300 to c. 4600 BCE for the tell's main occupation, within a culture span of c. 5400/5300–4500 BCE . The same modelling sharpened a second fact: the culture's end, around 4600/4500 BCE, is marked at many sites by a horizon of burned buildings — the tell habit, and much of the world that sustained it, closes in fire (§XII). // THE TELL // c. 9–10.5 m of deposits An artificial mound of levelled houses, floors, and refuse on a loess terrace above the Danube — the deepest Neolithic stratigraphy in the northern Balkans. // THE FOOTPRINT // c. 10 ha built core Estimates of the settlement's settled extent vary with the phase and the survey method; the tell core is about ten hectares, with occupation traces beyond it. Population estimates reach c. 2,500 at the maximum — and are estimates, not counts. // EXCAVATION // From 1908, Vasić Begun by Miloje Vasić and continued, with long interruptions, through the twentieth century; renewed systematic excavation and dating programmes run to the present. // THE PHASES // Vinča A–D Four phases seriated on pottery and stratigraphy at the type site, c. 5400/5300 to c. 4600/4500 BCE — the chronological skeleton for the whole culture. John Chapman's syntheses — from The Vinča Culture of South-East Europe (1981) onward — established the reading of the culture that this article follows: Vinča is best understood not as a uniform state-like entity but as a network of tell and flat settlements sharing pottery styles, figurine traditions, exchange goods, and sign repertoires across the central and northern Balkans — an interaction sphere of farming communities, some of them large and long-lived, none of them, on present evidence, capitals. The culture's settlements range from hamlets under a hectare to tells of ten hectares and more; a few flat sites spread far wider. What they share is a material style so consistent that the “culture” label has survived a century of scrutiny — and a social organisation so undemonstrative that the same century has failed to find its rulers. IV. Houses, Rows, and Daily Life at the Tells The Vinča house, as recovered at Belo Brdo and its sister tells, is a rectangular, timber-framed building: walls of wattle — woven hazel or willow withies — daubed inside and out with clay, a pitched roof, and a floor of packed clay that was resurfaced as it wore. Houses divide internally into one to three rooms; many contain a built clay oven or hearth, clay benches and bins, and storage vessels set into or standing on the floor. At Belo Brdo the later houses stand in rows , aligned on common axes with narrow lanes between them — a planned regularity, renewed rebuilding by rebuilding, that excavators have reasonably called street-like. Some walls were plastered and painted. The houses were substantial, maintained, and — the point that will matter in §XII — very often burned at the end of their lives, their daub fired to a durable orange-red mass that preserved floor plans, fallen roof timbers as voids and impressions, and the contents of rooms as they were left or placed. Inside and around those houses, the assemblage of daily life is rich and, by Neolithic standards, remarkably complete. The pottery is the culture's signature: dark burnished wares, black-topped and graphite-painted vessels, carinated bowls, amphorae, and lids, fired in kilns whose control of atmosphere produced the deep black and grey surfaces that no open firing achieves reliably. Ground stone axes and adzes, chipped stone of flint and Carpathian obsidian, bone awls and antler tools, spindle whorls and loom weights for textiles, clay stamps, and — from the later phases — copper ornaments and tools (§IX) fill out the inventory. Food remains track the economy of §II: cereal grains and pulse seeds from storage contexts, animal bone dominated by cattle, pig, sheep, and goat with a persistent wild component, and fish bone and shell from the Danube itself. Burial, by contrast, is the record's conspicuous gap, here and across most of the Danube world. Vinča tells yield few formal cemeteries; the dead appear sparsely — occasional burials within settlements, scattered human bone — and the great majority of the Vinča dead are archaeologically missing, disposed of in ways that left no recoverable trace. The Cucuteni-Trypillia world shares the pattern almost completely (§XIII). The gap matters methodologically: a civilisation whose graves cannot be read cannot have its hierarchy read from graves either, and claims about its social order — egalitarian or otherwise — must rest on houses, goods, and settlement plans instead. It also matters for §XIV: where the dead are invisible, imagination has room to move in, and it did. THE HOUSE AS ARCHIVE Because so many Vinča houses burned, their plans, ovens, bins, and floor assemblages survive as fired-clay snapshots. The tell's stratigraphy is built of these snapshots, stacked eight centuries deep at Belo Brdo. ROWS, NOT CLUSTERS Later Vinča houses at Belo Brdo stand in aligned rows with lanes between — order imposed at the scale of the neighbourhood, maintained across rebuildings, without any central monument for the order to radiate from. THE MISSING DEAD Formal burials are rare across the Vinča world. Most of its dead left no recoverable trace — a fact that limits every social argument built on graves, in both directions. KILN-FIRED BLACK WARE The culture's dark burnished pottery required controlled, reducing kiln atmospheres — the same pyrotechnological mastery that, turned on copper ore, produced the first smelting (§IX). V. The Figurine Corpus — Described Plainly No class of object has carried more interpretive weight in this field — or buckled under it more visibly — than the clay figurines. The corpus first, in plain terms. Vinča sites yield anthropomorphic figurines in the thousands when fragments are counted: standing or seated human figures, typically a few centimetres to perhaps twenty centimetres tall, modelled in clay and fired. Many wear the culture's most recognisable face — a triangular or pentagonal “mask-like” visage with incised or applied eyes, a prominent nose, and incised detail marking hair, clothing, belts, and ornaments on the body. Zoomorphic figurines — cattle above all — accompany them, as do clay models of furniture, altars or tables, and houses. The figures are found in houses, in pits, and in settlement debris; most are broken, and complete examples are the minority. Female figures, identified by breasts and other modelled features, predominate among the sexed examples; male and unsexed figures also occur. That is the corpus. Everything beyond it — goddess, ancestress, doll, votive, teaching device, self-representation — is interpretation, and the history of the interpretations is a warning this article intends the reader to receive. Fragmentation — Chapman's Wager The most influential modern reading of the corpus is not about what the figurines depict but about what was done to them. In Fragmentation in Archaeology (2000), John Chapman argued that the breakage pattern of Neolithic objects in southeastern Europe — figurines, vessels, and other things — is too patterned to be accident alone: objects were, in many cases, deliberately broken , and their fragments circulated, deposited in different places and contexts. Drawing on anthropological accounts of personhood, Chapman proposed that fragments acted as tokens of relationships — his term is enchained relations: a broken figurine's parts, kept by different people or placed in different houses and pits, materially bound those people and places together, and carried something of the object's and its maker's identity with them. Later work with Bisserka Gaydarska refined the argument object-class by object-class, and contextual studies — for example at Selevac, where complete figurines associate significantly with houses and transversely broken ones with pits — have found patterning of the kind the hypothesis predicts. The argument is reported here at exactly its standing: it is a serious, evidence-engaged interpretation, widely discussed and not a consensus . Critics have pressed two points that remain live. First, deliberateness is hard to prove object by object: figurines break at their weak points — necks, waists, leg junctions — under trampling and soil pressure as readily as under a deliberate hand, and some re-analyses find breakage patterns compatible with ordinary taphonomy. Second, the step from patterned breakage to enchained personhood is an analogy, borrowed from Melanesian ethnography, and analogies illuminate without demonstrating. What is not in dispute is the underlying observation that made the debate worth having: the figurines were made in quantity, used in domestic space, and broken — somehow — as a normal part of their lives. A Tier A account describes the corpus, reports the wager and its critics, and declines to tell the reader what a Vinča figurine “was.” Nobody knows. The next two sections show the same discipline applied to a harder case, where a wrong answer has been printed in a hundred popular books. // THE GODDESS SHORTCUT // The fastest way to misread this corpus is to call every female figurine a goddess and stop thinking. The label forecloses the questions the objects actually raise — who made them, where they were kept, why they broke, what the masks and incised clothing meant — and it imports a theology no Vinča text exists to confirm. Gimbutas's goddess reading is treated as historiography in §XIV. In this section the figurines are clay, context, and breakage: what can be shown. VI. The Vinča Signs — The Corpus The signs were found before the culture was. In the 1870s, Zsófia Torma excavated the Transylvanian site of Turdaș and recovered pottery fragments incised with marks she could not read; in 1908 Vasić's first season at Vinča produced more, and as excavation spread across the culture's range, the marks accumulated into a corpus. Its present shape, after a century of collection, is this. Inscribed objects number in the hundreds — the later Danube-wide databases, which extend the net beyond the Vinča culture proper to related sign-using groups, catalogue over nine hundred inscribed artefacts and several thousand individual sign occurrences, but the strictly Vinča corpus is the smaller, hundreds-strong set on which the argument turns. The objects are overwhelmingly pottery: vessel bases, walls, and rims incised or painted with marks. The remainder are ceramic spindle whorls, figurines, and a small scatter of other things — clay tablets, stamps, and weights among them. The signs themselves form a repertoire of a few hundred distinct types in the broadest catalogues, fewer when variants are grouped: straight and crossed lines, chevrons, triangles, circles and spirals, comb- and brush-like clusters, ladder and net patterns, and a minority of pictorial forms — schematic animals and human-like figures among them. The decisive facts about the corpus, however, are distributional, and they are not in serious dispute. More than 85 percent of all inscriptions consist of a single sign. Groups of two or more signs are the exception; long sequences are vanishingly rare; and where signs do group, their order and reading direction are usually indeterminate — there is no demonstrable syntax, no line structure, no recurring formula of the kind that even the most pictographic true scripts display. Sign use is also partitioned by object: single signs sit almost exclusively on pots, while grouped signs cluster on spindle whorls — a division that already suggests different jobs being done by the same repertoire. Winn's Catalogue — Care as a Method The corpus received its scholarly foundation in Shan M. Winn's Pre-Writing in Southeastern Europe: The Sign System of the Vinča Culture ca. 4000 B.C. (1981) — a work whose title is itself the most important sentence ever written about these signs. Winn, a linguist, catalogued the inscribed objects site by site (the catalogue designations, such as the Jela spindle whorls, still anchor discussion), classified the sign forms, and examined their combinations. His conclusion was deliberately modest: the material demonstrated a sign system — conventional, shared, meaningful marks, some of them plausibly functioning as pictograms or ideograms — but the evidence did not warrant calling it writing. He called it pre-writing , and the care of that choice deserves emphasis, because the literature since has split precisely on it: scholars who begin from Winn's catalogue and keep his discipline reach his conclusion; claims that go beyond it characteristically go beyond his evidence as well. Later quantitative work has broadly sustained the catalogue's picture. One much-cited linguistic-statistical analysis sorts the sign occurrences into roughly 59 percent sharing the properties of potters' marks , some 11.5 percent belonging to the asymmetric ornament typical of spindle whorls, and some 29.5 percent that may represent a symbolic — semasiographic — notation: signs that convey meaning without encoding speech. Those proportions are one study's model, not a census of intentions; but every serious analysis of the corpus lands in the same neighbourhood. Most of the signs, most of the time, were doing the ordinary work of marks. Feature The Vinča Corpus Early True Writing (Uruk, for contrast) Typical inscription length One sign (over 85% of cases) Multi-sign tablets; accounts with many entries Longest sequences A handful of signs; order indeterminate Hundreds of signs in ruled registers Syntax None demonstrable Fixed formats: commodity, quantity, name Numerals No agreed numerical system Multiple explicit metrological systems Media Pots, whorls, figurines — signs ride on objects Dedicated medium: the tablet exists for the text Function (best evidence) Ownership / maker marks, tallies, ritual and identity signs Administration: grain, livestock, labour, rations The contrast column is not a rhetorical device; it is the argument. Writing, as this hub defines it in The Origins of Writing , is a system that encodes language — or, at its proto-cuneiform threshold, a system of accounts with fixed sign order, numerical systems, and standardised formats administered by specialists. The Vinča corpus displays none of those diagnostics. It displays something else, interesting in its own right and diminished by being miscalled: a durable, widely shared repertoire of conventional marks, maintained across a culture area for centuries, doing work — marking, counting perhaps, invoking, identifying — that human societies very often do without writing. Before that verdict is sealed in §VIII, however, one group of objects must be faced on its own, because it is the exhibit on which the entire script claim has been made to rest. VII. Tărtăria — Three Tablets and a Disputed Context In 1961, at the Neolithic site of Tărtăria in Transylvania, Romania, a team directed by Nicolae Vlassa excavated a pit containing, on the excavators' account, the burned and disarticulated remains of an adult human, a group of some twenty-six clay figurines and other objects, and three small clay tablets — two rectangular, one round, two of them pierced — incised with pictorial and abstract signs. One rectangular tablet carries a horned animal, a schematic figure, and a vegetal motif; the others bear rows of abstract signs. Vlassa interpreted the signs as a kind of primitive writing comparable to early Sumerian pictography, and the find became, at a stroke, the most famous — and the most contested — in Balkan prehistory. The Dating Problem, Stated Exactly The tablets' date cannot be read off the tablets, and the reason is a conservation accident with permanent consequences: after excavation, the originally unbaked tablets were baked by museum conservators to preserve them , destroying the possibility of directly radiocarbon-dating their clay. Every date ever offered for them is therefore by association. The famous early date — around c. 5300 BCE , which would make the tablets older than Sumerian proto-writing by well over a millennium — rests on radiocarbon determinations from other materials attributed to the site's relevant layers, extended to the tablets through the excavators' account of the pit's stratigraphy. Both links of that chain are disputed. The stratigraphic circumstances of the discovery were never published to the standard the claim requires, and Vlassa's account has been questioned in detail; scholars have argued that the tablets could be an intrusion from higher, later levels of the site, which would bring them down toward the fourth millennium or later. Gheorghe Lazarovici, the leading Romanian specialist on the Tărtăria material and a defender of the tablets' Neolithic context, has argued the case for the early association at length; other specialists, including contributors to the same debates, regard the context as unproven. The forgery claims that circulate at the debate's fringe — that the signs copy Sumerian forms from popular publications — are themselves unproven, and this article gives them no more than this sentence. The correct Tier A statement is therefore narrow, and it is worth watching how much of the popular edifice it supports: three incised clay tablets were excavated at Tărtăria in 1961 in a pit assemblage whose exact stratigraphic position is disputed; the tablets cannot be dated directly; dates proposed for them range, on the published arguments, from the later sixth millennium to the fourth millennium BCE and beyond. Even at their earliest proposed date, moreover, the tablets would prove only that someone incised sign-rows on clay — the question of whether those rows are writing is separate, and it is answered by the corpus as a whole, not by three objects. A date is not a decipherment, and an early date for a mark is not evidence that the mark encodes a language. The Tărtăria tablets are genuine objects of Neolithic southeastern Europe, most plausibly of the Vinča-Turdaș world; they are the corpus's most evocative members; and they are, evidentially, its weakest foundation — a claim about the world's first writing built on the one context in the corpus that cannot be checked. // HANDLE WITH BOTH HANDS // Popular accounts typically report the c. 5300 BCE date as the tablets' date and the script claim as their meaning. Both steps exceed the evidence: the date is an association through a disputed context, and the meaning is an inference the corpus as a whole does not support (§VIII). The tablets deserve their fame — as the clearest lesson in this hub that an artefact's importance and an artefact's evidentiary strength are different things. VIII. Script or Sign System? — Where the Line Falls The claim, in its strongest published form, is Marija Gimbutas's: that the signs constitute an “Old European script” — a sacred writing system of the sixth and fifth millennia BCE, used for some two thousand years, predating Sumerian cuneiform, and readable, in her presentations, as the script of a goddess-centred civilisation. The claim has been carried further by others under names such as the “Danube script,” with proposed decipherments and sign-lists running to several hundred characters. It is an attractive claim. It would give Europe the world's first writing, give the Danube world a literate civilisation to set beside Uruk, and give the figurines of §V a text to be read by. It must nonetheless be reported plainly: the claim is not accepted by the mainstream of archaeology or of linguistics, and the reasons are evidential, not territorial. The Mainstream Verdict, and Its Grounds The verdict rests on the corpus facts of §VI, and they can be stated as a short chain. Writing encodes utterances, and utterances are long: a system of writing generates texts, and texts have length, order, and internal structure. The Vinča corpus has, overwhelmingly, single signs; its rare groups show no fixed order, no direction, no recurring formulae, no numerals that anyone has demon

What This Corpus Is and Is Not Sources This is a Tier B article: Ancient Tradition . Its objects are ancient textual systems — omen compendia, a diagnostic handbook, therapeutic recipe collections, and incantation series — preserved on cuneiform tablets and studied here as texts and as documented practices . That double description is the article's discipline, and it needs stating plainly at the outset, because the material invites confusion in both directions. On one side stands what can be reported as documented practice: that scholars copied, catalogued, and consulted these series; that a diviner slaughtered a sheep, inspected its liver in a fixed order, and delivered a written report; that a healer visited a sick man's house, worked through his symptoms from head to foot, and pronounced whether he would live or die; that drugs were pounded, sifted, boiled in beer or oil, and applied as drinks, salves, bandages, fumigations, and enemas. All of this is attested in the tablets, letters, reports, colophons, and catalogues, and it is reported here as practice, with its sources named. On the other side stands what the systems themselves claimed. The omen series claim that the gods write signs into the sky, the liver, and the newborn child, and that the trained reader can recover their verdicts. The medical series claim that sickness is sent — by a god, a ghost, a demon, a witch, a broken oath — and that the right incantation, spoken over the right preparation at the right hour, can lift it. The scholarly tradition claims, further, that the whole body of knowledge descends from the gods themselves, delivered before the Flood by the antediluvian sages, the apkallu . Those are the tradition's claims. This article reports them, in the tradition's own terms, and labels them as claims wherever they appear. It does not endorse the efficacy of a single prescription, and it does not narrate a single omen's prediction as an event that happened. What remains, held apart in that way, is not diminished. It is, on the contrary, one of the most remarkable intellectual constructions of the ancient world: a literate, systematising culture that spent well over a thousand years turning observation into lists, lists into series, and series into libraries — and that left the working manuals behind, in clay, for us to read. Mesopotamia's scribal sciences are the subject. Their procedures, given here in the fullest detail the sources allow, are the evidence. I. What This Article Is — Tier B and Two Kinds of Truth Every hub in this archive badges its articles, and the badge is a promise about how the sentences inside may be read. A Tier A article promises excavated, dated, published evidence. A Tier C article promises a modern construction, documented at its real date and in its makers' own terms. This article is Tier B, and its promise is narrower and stranger than either: the things it describes are neither dug out of the ground as objects nor invented in modern times. They are systems written down by ancient scholars — and a written system makes two kinds of statement at once, which the reader must never allow to merge. The first kind is procedural and institutional, and it is as checkable as anything in Tier A. A series has a number of tablets, an order, an incipit, a catalogue entry, a colophon naming its copyist or its royal owner. A profession has titles, a training, a place at court or in a temple household. A rite has a sequence: these words, these materials, this hour of the night. Statements of this kind — the Diagnostic Handbook runs to forty tablets; the Maqlû ceremony occupied a single night; the extispicy report was written and could be checked against a second sheep — rest on the tablets and on the modern editions named in the Sources, and this article makes them at full strength. The second kind is the system's own claim about the world, and it is reported, never adopted. When a tablet says that a lunar eclipse portends the death of a king, the article's sentence is that the series assigns that apodosis to that protasis . When a diagnostic entry names the "hand of a ghost" as the cause of a seizure, the article reports the entry's aetiology in the entry's own language, attributed. When the tradition traces its learning to Ea, god of wisdom, speaking through the seven antediluvian apkallu , the article presents that descent as what it is in the sources: the scholars' own account of where their knowledge came from — a claim about origins, made by the tradition, preserved in its catalogues and lists of sages. The companion article on the Antediluvian King Lists reads the kingly side of that same deep past under the same rule. // A NOTE ON VERBS THROUGHOUT // "The series says," "the entry assigns," "the handbook pronounces," and "the tradition claims" are the normal forms in this article wherever a prediction, a cause, or a cure is at issue. "The diviner slaughtered," "the scribe copied," and "the healer bandaged" are the normal forms wherever a documented human action is at issue. The distinction is not pedantry. It is the whole tier system in miniature, applied sentence by sentence. One further boundary belongs here. Modern readers meet this material under modern words — "astrology," "magic," "medicine," "science" — and every one of those words cuts the corpus at a joint the corpus itself does not have. The Mesopotamian scholars organised their learning not by our disciplines but by series and by crafts : the craft of the āšipu , the craft of the bārû , the scribal art itself, ṭupšarrūtu . Francesca Rochberg's The Heavenly Writing (2004), a foundation of this article, argues the point at length for the celestial sciences: omen-reading, observation, and mathematical astronomy were one scribal culture, practised by the same men, copied onto the same library shelves. Jean Bottéro, in Mesopotamia: Writing, Reasoning, and the Gods , makes the complementary argument for the list itself: the Mesopotamian list — of signs, of words, of omens, of symptoms, of drugs — is not a primitive failure to reach theory. It is the characteristic instrument of a reasoning that worked by exhaustive arrangement. This article follows both guides. It will speak of "medicine" and "divination" because English must, but it will keep returning to the units the sources themselves use: the scholar, the series, the tablet, the entry, the procedure. The corpus, finally, in outline. Three great omen compendia organise the readable world: Enūma Anu Enlil , the celestial omens; Šumma ālu , the terrestrial omens of city and house; and Šumma izbu , the omens of anomalous births (§§V–VII). One solicited oracle stands apart from the unsought signs: extispicy, the inspection of the sacrificed sheep's entrails, practised by the bārû (§VIII). Two medical corpora organise the sick body: the Diagnostic Handbook, Sakikkû , which reads symptoms and pronounces outcomes (§IX), and the therapeutic texts, which prescribe (§§XI–XII). Between and around them stand the incantation series — Maqlû , Šurpu , and their companions — where diagnosis, ritual, and drug meet (§XIV). Behind them all stands the institution that trained the men, kept the tablets, and copied them for a millennium and more (§§XVI–XVII). The article takes the scholars first, because in this world the knowledge and the knowers cannot be separated. II. The Two Scholars — The Āšipu and the Asû A sick Mesopotamian of means did not send for "a doctor." He sent, in the developed practice of the second and first millennia BCE, for one or both of two differently trained experts, whose titles the tablets keep distinct even where their work overlapped. The āšipu — the word is also written with its older or more vernacular doublet mašmaššu — was the incantation and ritual expert: the scholar who diagnosed, pronounced the prognosis, identified the supernatural sender of the illness, and deployed the spoken and enacted remedies — incantations, rituals, amulets, purifications — that his craft commanded. The asû was the practitioner of the drug-lore: the expert in medicinal substances and their preparation, who compounded and applied the potions, salves, bandages, and other physical treatments that the therapeutic texts prescribe. Older English scholarship rendered the pair, too neatly, as "exorcist" and "physician," and then, more neatly still, as "magic" and "medicine." The tablets support the titles. They do not support the neatness. // THE ĀŠIPU // Incantation & ritual expert Also called mašmaššu. Diagnosed from the Diagnostic Handbook, pronounced prognosis, identified the divine or demonic sender, and treated by incantation, ritual, amulet, and purification — his craft is āšipūtu. // THE ASÛ // Expert in drugs & preparations The practitioner of the materia medica: compounding, preparing, and applying potions, salves, bandages, suppositories, and enemas. His craft is asûtu. The Code of Hammurabi already regulates his fees and liabilities for operations. // THE BĀRÛ // The diviner of the entrails The third scholar of this article: the haruspex who put questions to Šamaš and Adad and read the answer in the sacrificed sheep's liver and lungs (§VIII). His craft is bārûtu. // THE ṬUPŠARRU // The scribe-scholar Underlying all three crafts: the literate scholar, trained in the scribal art (ṭupšarrūtu), without whose copying, cataloguing, and commentary none of the series would exist at all. The Old Picture — Two Professions, Two Worlds The classic modern account descends from Edith Ritter's influential 1965 study of the two healing professions, and it drew a bright line. On one side, the āšipu : a temple-linked scholar-priest whose world was supernatural aetiology — gods angered, demons seizing, ghosts afflicting, witches working — and whose instruments were the word and the rite. On the other, the asû : a more secular craftsman whose recipe texts, strikingly bare of gods and demons, treat symptoms with substances, and whose world was the pharmacy. On this reading, Mesopotamia had two medicines — a magical one and an empirical one — running in parallel, and the recipe texts' silence about the supernatural was the signature of the second. The reading had real evidence behind it. The therapeutic prescriptions, in their thousands, do indeed proceed with barely a glance at aetiology: if a man suffers such-and-such, pound these drugs, he drinks them in beer, he will recover. And the Diagnostic Handbook, the āšipu 's book, does indeed name a god, ghost, or demon in entry after entry. The division of the texts is genuine. The question is what it divides. Geller's Revision — One Corpus, Overlapping Crafts Markham J. Geller's Ancient Babylonian Medicine: Theory and Practice (2010), the anchor study for this section, works through the evidence for both professions — the titles in the lexical lists, the colophons that name copyists and owners, the catalogues of what each craft must master, the letters that show practitioners at work — and arrives at a deliberately less tidy picture, which subsequent scholarship has broadly worked within even where it argues the details. Its main points, as Geller states them, are these. First, the two titles for the ritual expert are not two jobs. Āšipu and mašmaššu are, in Geller's analysis, registers of one profession: āšipu the learned, prestigious term of scholarship and literature, mašmaššu the term of more general use — and the English "exorcist," applied to either, is far too narrow for a craft whose curriculum, set out in the so-called Exorcist's Manual (the catalogue KAR 44), runs from temple ritual and the purification of divine statues through diagnostics to the whole incantation corpus. Exorcism, in the modern sense of expelling a possessing spirit, was one procedure among many in a much larger ritual technology. Second, the crafts overlap in the texts themselves. The āšipu did not merely pray over patients: the diagnostic craft was his, the prognosis was his, and therapeutic prescriptions — drugs included — circulated within his lore as well as the asû 's; colophons and catalogues refuse to sort the medical corpus into two sealed libraries. JoAnn Scurlock's Sourcebook for Ancient Mesopotamian Medicine (2014), which translates the corpus whole, accordingly reverses the old English labels altogether, rendering āšipu as "physician" — the scholar-diagnostician whose role-set comprised diagnostician, prognostician, exorcist, and healer — and asû as "pharmacist," the compounder of the drugs the diagnosis called for. The reversal is itself the lesson: the Akkadian titles name competences and trainings , not the modern boundary between a doctor and a priest. Third — and here Geller both keeps and qualifies the old picture — the two crafts did maintain distinguishable profiles, and could stand as alternative, even competing, systems of explanation at the bedside. The āšipu 's characteristic question was who sent this, and what will happen ; the asû 's characteristic act was preparing what would treat it . A patient, or a family, could consult both, in sequence or together, and the letters from the Assyrian court — where kings kept both kinds of expert on staff and played their opinions against each other — show exactly that consultation pattern at the highest level. What the evidence will not bear is the inference from the recipe texts' silence to a secular worldview: a prescription is a workshop document, written to be used, and its omission of aetiology shows its genre, not its author's theology. Geller's own summary position — that Babylonian "magic" and "medicine" are best treated as complementary and inseparable aspects of one healing culture, distinguishable as crafts but not separable as worldviews — is the position this article adopts, attributed to him. // THE SURGEON IN THE LAW CODE // The asû of the early second millennium could also be a cutter. The Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE) fixes the fees for operations performed with the bronze lancet — on an eye, a wound, a bone — and the penalties when the patient dies or loses the eye, graded by the patient's status. No surgical treatise survives from Mesopotamia, and the therapeutic corpus is overwhelmingly conservative — bandages, oils, drugs — but the law code's clauses are documentary proof that operative intervention belonged, at least at that date, to the asû's regulated craft. A third scholar completes the cast, though his patient was usually the king rather than the sick man: the bārû , the diviner, master of extispicy (§VIII) and interpreter of the unsought signs as well. At the Neo-Assyrian court of the eighth and seventh centuries BCE — the best-documented scholarly court of the ancient world, thanks to the letters and reports preserved from Nineveh — the king's experts included āšipu s, asû s, bārû s, astrologer-scribes, and lamentation priests, corresponding with the throne in a steady traffic of reports, quotations from the series, and recommendations. The king did not experience these as separate magics and medicines. He experienced them as his ummânu — his master scholars (§XVI) — each reading the same written world with a different instrument. To understand the instruments, the article turns first to the claim that underwrote them all: that the writing being read was, in the end, the gods' own. III. The Claim of Descent — Ea, the Gods, and the Apkallu Mesopotamian scholarship did not present itself as invention. It presented itself as inheritance — and the inheritance had a named source, a named channel, and a named moment after which, in Berossus's later Greek summary of the tradition, nothing fundamentally new was discovered. The source was Ea — Sumerian Enki — god of the sweet waters of the Apsû, of wisdom, of craft, and of effective ritual knowledge, patron of Eridu, the city the King List names first. The channel was the seven apkallu , the antediluvian sages: semi- divine culture-bringers, in the iconography often fish-cloaked or bird-headed, whom the tradition placed beside the first kings before the Flood as the teachers of humankind. The moment was the Flood itself, after which the semi-divine sages were succeeded, in the lists that pair sages with kings, by human scholars — the ummânu — who stood to the apkallu as heirs to founders. The claim is not a vague piety; the scholarly corpus states it in its own documentary forms. The Catalogue of Texts and Authors — a library catalogue that assigns the great series to their authors — credits bodies of learning to divine and antediluvian authorship: diagnostic knowledge is there presented as coming "from the mouth of Ea," written down, in the catalogue's phrase, at his dictation by Adapa, the first and greatest of the sages. Colophons and catalogues mark certain series as niṣirtu — secret, restricted knowledge, "the secret of the gods" — to be shown by the knowing to the knowing, and withheld from the uninitiated. Esagil-kīn-apli, the very human editor of the Diagnostic Handbook (§IX), frames his own editorial work within the same architecture: the forty tablets of his series answer, in the tradition's reckoning, to the number of Ea, the god who gave mankind diagnostic knowledge. The editor edits; the knowledge descends. Tier discipline requires the next sentence, and the article makes it without flinching: this descent is the tradition's claim about itself, and it is reported here as such. No tablet excavated at Eridu was dictated by a god; no fish-cloaked sage has been dug out of a pre-Flood stratum, for there is no such stratum to dig. What archaeology and philology can document is the claim's career : that first-millennium scholars believed their series descended from divine and antediluvian sources, wrote that belief into their catalogues, used it to authorise their editions and to restrict their circulation, and carved the apkallu on palace walls and buried their figurines under floors as protectors of the houses the knowledge served. A claim believed, institutionalised, and acted on for a thousand years is a historical fact of the first order — about the believers. About the Flood-age sages themselves, it is evidence of nothing but the claim. The Antediluvian King Lists article treats the paired lists of kings and sages, and Berossus's fish-man Oannes — the Greek dress of Uanna, the first apkallu — in full. The claim also did practical work. If the series are transcripts of a divine writing-system — Rochberg's "heavenly writing," the gods' script across sky, liver, and body — then the scholar's task is not to test the system but to read it correctly : to copy it exactly, arrange it exhaustively, comment on its difficulties, and guard it. That is precisely the behaviour the tablets display. And if sickness is a message as well as an affliction, diagnosis is a branch of reading too — the āšipu at the sick man's door doing with symptoms what the astrologer does with eclipses. The corpus's unity is the claim, at work. THE SOURCE — EA / ENKI God of the Apsû, of wisdom and of ritual efficacy. In the tradition's own catalogues, diagnostic and incantatory knowledge issues from Ea; the Diagnostic Handbook's forty tablets answer to his sacred number. THE CHANNEL — THE SEVEN APKALLU The antediluvian sages, Adapa first among them, placed beside the pre-Flood kings as teachers of humankind. Their figurines were buried apotropaically in houses; their images guarded palace walls. THE HEIRS — THE UMMÂNU After the Flood, in the lists' scheme, human master scholars succeed the sages. Historical ummânu — court scholars, series editors — are the claim's institutional reality (§XVI). THE SEAL — NIṢIRTU, "SECRET" Colophons restrict the great series as the secret knowledge of the gods, to be transmitted from the knowing to the knowing. Esotericism here is not a modern overlay; it is in the tablets' own paratext. IV. The Omen as a Sentence — Protasis and Apodosis Before the individual compendia, their shared grammar. Nearly every entry in every series in this article — celestial, terrestrial, teratological, extispicy, diagnostic — is built as a single conditional sentence of two clauses, for which modern scholarship uses the Greek-derived terms protasis and apodosis . The protasis, introduced by šumma , "if," states the sign: an observed, observable, or — the point matters — merely conceivable state of the world. The apodosis states what the sign, in the system, portends or pronounces: for the king, the land, the army, the harvest, the householder, or the patient. "If X, then Y" is the atom of Mesopotamian divination, and the compendia are its molecules, built by the tens of thousands. The building method is systematic variation, and it explains both the compendia's size and their strangest entries. Take a sign-bearing object — the moon, a liver lobe, a newborn's ear — and vary its parameters one by one: month by month, day by day; right against left; above against below; white, black, red, green-yellow, variegated; present, absent, doubled, displaced. Each combination receives its entry, and its apodosis is assigned by the system's internal logic: by analogy (the lion's ear to the strong king), by wordplay between the Akkadian or Sumerian terms of protasis and apodosis, by the great polarities of right (favourable) against left (unfavourable) and light against dark, and by precedent — the remembered association of a sign with a famous king's fate, the so-called historical omens embedded especially in the extispicy tradition. The method guarantees completeness, and completeness guarantees impossibilities: eclipses on days of the month when eclipses cannot occur, births no midwife ever saw, liver configurations no sheep ever grew. The compendia contain them anyway, because the list, as Bottéro saw, aims at the exhaustive ordering of the possible , not at a register of the observed. A modern reader who asks of every entry "did this really happen?" is asking the list a question it was never built to answer. The entries were made to be used , and their physical form serves the lookup. Within a tablet, entries are grouped by protasis, similar signs together; each entry is marked off by the single vertical wedge (the sign DIŠ) at its head; tablets are numbered within their series and identified by incipit — the first words of the first entry — and catalogues listing the incipits in order served as the system's finding device. When a sign occurred — an eclipse, a malformed lamb, a pig crossing the āšipu 's path to a patient's house — the scholar turned to the series, found the protasis, and read off the apodosis. The surviving reports of the Assyrian court scholars show the practice in action: a phenomenon is reported to the king with its series entry quoted verbatim , the quotation doing the argumentative work. The compendium was not a book to be read through. It was an instrument to be consulted, and its authority in consultation was the authority of the written tradition itself. // HOW TO READ AN OMEN ENTRY IN THIS ARTICLE // Where this article quotes an entry, the quotation is short, confined to a named published translation, and identified as that translator's rendering. Where it paraphrases, it says the series "assigns," "pairs," or "pronounces" — never that the predicted event occurred. Apodoses concerning kings and lands belong to the state divination of a court culture; apodoses concerning householders and patients belong to the private consultation. The two scales coexist in the same series and are distinguished, where it matters, in the text. One more distinction organises what follows: signs unsought against signs solicited . The omens of §§V–VII are unsought — the world offers them, and the art is recognition and lookup. Extispicy (§VIII) is solicited: a framed question, a provided sheep, an answer written for that question into that animal. Diagnosis (§IX) stands between: the symptoms are unsought, but the visit is a consultation, and the handbook opens not with a symptom but with a journey — the scholar already reading signs on his way to the sick man's house. The compendia follow, from the sky downward. V. Enūma Anu Enlil — The Heavens in Some Seventy Tablets The celestial omen series takes its title, in the Mesopotamian manner, from its opening words: Enūma Anu Enlil — "When Anu and Enlil…," the great gods who, in its prologue's framing, ordained the signs of heaven and earth. In its received first-millennium form it runs to some seventy tablets and roughly seven thousand omens — the figures are conventional because the series is reconstructed from many incomplete copies, Nineveh's above all, and because tablet divisions vary between recensions. Its materials are older than its form: celestial omens are attested already in the Old Babylonian period, in the early second millennium BCE, and the series grew by the same accretion, arrangement, and late-second-millennium editing that the other great series underwent. What the first-millennium scholar held was not a composition but a canon : the sky, edited. The Four Sections The series is organised by the divine owners of the phenomena, in four great sections. The first, Tablets 1–22 in the usual reconstruction, belongs to Sîn, the moon : the moon's appearances, its horns, its halo, its light and darkening — and, as a coherent sub-series within it, the lunar eclipses, the most dreaded of all celestial signs, whose apodoses run to the death of kings and the fall of lands. The second, Tablets 23–39, belongs to Šamaš, the sun : the sun's appearance at rising, its colour and marks, and again a block of eclipse omens. The third, Tablets 40–49, belongs to Adad, the storm god : thunder, lightning, rain, wind, cloud, and earthquake — weather admitted to the celestial series because it, too, is written in the sky. The fourth, Tablets 50–70, belongs to Ištar : the planets — Venus first and most fully — and the fixed stars, their risings, settings, conjunctions, and colours. Within each section the variation machine of §IV runs at full power: the same eclipse worked through every month, every day, every watch of the night, every quadrant of the moon's disc, each with its assigned land and its assigned fate. Embedded in the lunar section is the series' most famous single document: the so-called Venus Tablet of Ammi-ṣaduqa (Tablet 63 in the received numbering), which pairs observations of Venus's appearances and disappearances, attributed to the reign of a king of the First Dynasty of Babylon in the seventeenth century BCE, with their omens. Modern scholarship has mined it for chronology; the ancient scholars who copied it for a thousand years valued it as the series in miniature — observation and apodosis bound together under a king's name. It is treated, with the rest of the Babylonian sky tradition, in the companion article Babylonian Sky Science , to which this article defers for the astronomy proper: the diaries, the goal-year texts, and the mathematical schemes that grew, in Rochberg's demonstration, from the same scribal culture as the omens and were never, in that culture, a separate "science" set against them. Whom the Omens Concern — and What Was Done About Them The apodoses of Enūma Anu Enlil are overwhelmingly public. They concern the king, the land, the army, the harvest, the neighbouring lands and their kings — the celestial series is state divination, and its natural home is the court. That home is documented in unusual fullness: the letters and reports of the astrologer-scholars of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal (seventh century BCE) quote the series constantly, report observed phenomena against its entries, and advise the king on what the entries require. What they could require was drastic. For the most dangerous lunar-eclipse apodoses — the death of the king — the system provided an institutional answer in the substitute king ritual: a stand-in was enthroned, dressed, and treated as king for the danger period (in the sources, up to about a hundred days), to draw the apodosis onto himself, while the true king withdrew under the title of "farmer." The substitute was afterwards put to death and buried with royal honours — the apodosis, in the system's logic, honourably discharged. More routinely, unfavourable signs of every class could be met with namburbi rituals — "undoing" rites, studied in Erica Reiner's Astral Magic in Babylonia (1995) — whose whole purpose was to avert an announced evil before it landed: the omen stated a verdict, and the ritual appealed it to the gods who had issued it, Šamaš and Ea above all. The system, that is, was never fatalistic in practice. A verdict written by the gods could be petitioned, by the gods' own procedures, for reversal — and the petition, too, was a written series, copied and catalogued like the omens it answered. // THE HEAVENLY WRITING // Rochberg's governing image, from the series' own idiom: the gods write the signs — the sky is a tablet, the phenomena are its script, and celestial divination is a branch of literacy. The image is the tradition's, not the modern scholar's decoration: Akkadian calls the starry sky šiṭir šamê , "writing of the heavens," and the same verb of writing serves for the marks in a liver and the symptoms on a body. One script, three surfaces — that is the intellectual unity of this article's whole corpus. A worked example, paraphrased, fixes the form. Across the lunar-eclipse tablets, the series works an eclipse through its variables — date, watch of the night, quadrant first darkened, the shadow's direction, the disc's colour — and distributes the threatened fates among the four great lands, Akkad, Subartu, Elam, Amurru, quadrant answering to land. The king received the report with its recommended response, a namburbi or, at the extreme, the substitute: in form, a legal consultation — a code consulted, a case stated, a remedy prescribed from the same shelves. VI. Šumma Ālu — The City, the House, and Everyday Signs If Enūma Anu Enlil is the sky edited, Šumma ālu ina mēlê šakin — "If a city is set on a height," from its first entry — is the lived world edited. It is the largest of the omen series: in its fullest reconstruction, more than a hundred tablets — the catalogue tradition counts up to about 120 — carrying, by the modern editors' reckoning, well over ten thousand omens (some estimates run toward thirteen thousand). Terrestrial omen collections are attested from the Old Babylonian period; the series in something like its received shape is documented from the eleventh century BCE onward, and its fullest copies, once again, are Nineveh's. Its first entry sets its scale and its tone at once, in Sally Freedman's edition of Tablets 1–21: If a city is set on a height, living in that city will not be good. — Šumma ālu, Tablet 1, opening entry, in the edition of S. M. Freedman, If a City Is Set on a Height (1998) From the city, the series descends through the whole fabric of ordinary life, and its table of contents is a map of what could carry meaning. Houses: their foundations, doors, walls, and beams; the creatures that enter them and the sounds heard in them. Animals in their dozens of tablets: snakes, scorpions, lizards, ants and other insects; dogs, pigs, cattle, sheep, donkeys, horses; the wild animals that stray into settled space; fish, frogs, and birds — the animal omens of Tablets 22–40 and 63–79 are among the series' largest blocks, now the object of the Vienna Bestiarium Mesopotamicum project. Fire, water, and weather at ground level. Human behaviour: dreams' daytime counterparts, sexual acts and their occasions, speech, laughter, stumbling, the body's involuntary signs. Nothing is too small. A moth in a man's house, a crow calling before an army on campaign, a snake seen at a particular hour of a particular day — each has, or is given, its entry and its apodosis, and the apodoses here are characteristically private where the celestial series' were public: they concern the householder, his family, his property, his health, his standing — the fortunes of the bēl bīti , the head of the house, in whose name the consultation was made. Two features of Šumma ālu deserve emphasis against caricature. The first is that the series is not a chaos of superstitions but an arrangement , thematic tablet by thematic tablet, worked by the same variation method as the sky: the snake varied by place, hour, colour, direction of movement, and behaviour, entry by entry, until the permutations are spent. Whatever else it is, it is scholarship — the exhaustive cartography of a meaningful world, executed with the list as its instrument. The second is that the series already contains, inside itself, the germ of its own mitigation: a strand of entries appends to the dire apodosis the counter-rite — if a man sees such-and-such and wishes not to suffer its announced outcome, let him do such-and-such — the namburbi logic of §V operating at household scale. The terrestrial world announced more evils than the celestial one, because it was closer; and it is in Šumma ālu 's world — the house, the street, the road to a patient's door — that the medical practice of §§IX–X will be found already reading signs before it ever reaches the patient. The series also marks the omen culture's social breadth: the terrestrial signs occurred to everyone, and consulting a scholar about a snake or a household prodigy was an ordinary transaction of urban life.
