What the Origins of Writing Do and Do Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published evidence — clay tablets, clay envelopes, seals, and inscribed labels recovered from named sites and edited in the scholarly literature. Where scholars disagree, as they do sharply over the token theory of writing's origin and over whether Egypt invented its script independently, the disagreement itself is reported, with each position attributed to the scholar who holds it and stated at the strength its holder gives it. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction. The one ancient story this article retells — the Sumerian tale of Enmerkar, in §XI — is labelled for what it is: a composition written down more than a thousand years after the events it imagines, evidence for what later scribes believed about their craft, not for how the craft began. Writing was invented at least twice in the ancient world this hub covers, and the two inventions happened within a few centuries — perhaps within a few decades — of each other. In southern Iraq, in the great city of Uruk, administrators of the late fourth millennium BCE pressed and drew signs on clay tablets to record grain, livestock, beer, land, and labour: the script now called proto-cuneiform . In Upper Egypt, in a royal tomb at Abydos, officials of a predynastic kingdom incised signs on small labels of bone and ivory and painted them in ink on wine jars, to record goods and the places they came from: the first hieroglyphs . A third system, proto- Elamite , arose in Iran in the same centuries, borrowed the idea and some of the machinery, built a script of its own — and died undeciphered, as it remains today. Behind the Mesopotamian invention lies a still longer prehistory. For some five thousand years before the first tablet, farming communities across the Near East had kept accounts with small clay counters — tokens — shaped as cones, spheres, discs, and cylinders. Whether those tokens are the direct ancestors of writing, as Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued in Before Writing (1992), or only the ancestors of its numbers, as her critics Robert Englund and Paul Zimansky reply, is the central scholarly argument of this article, and it is given in full on both sides (§§IV–V). What is not in dispute is the destination. By about 3400–3200 BCE the counters, envelopes, seals, and numerical tablets of the old accounting world had been joined — at Uruk, and at first only there — by something new under the sun: a repertoire of more than seven hundred signs that could record not only how many, but what, whose, and from whom. Within a few more centuries those signs would learn to record sounds, then grammar, then — slowly, and last of all — stories. This article follows that sequence at the level of the objects themselves: how an account was physically made, sealed, totalled, and filed, before it asks what the accounts mean. I. What Counts as Writing — And What Does Not The argument of this article turns on a definition, and the definition must be fixed before the evidence is weighed. Scholars of early scripts — the usage followed in Stephen Houston's The First Writing (2004) and in Christopher Woods's Visible Language (2010), the two syntheses on which this article most relies — reserve the word writing for a system of visible marks that records language : marks whose values are tied to the words and sounds of a particular tongue, so that a text can, in principle, be read aloud as an utterance. Systems of marks that convey information without tying it to a specific language — tallies, property marks, heraldic emblems, the picture-signs a traveller can read in any country — are classed as proto-writing or notation. The distinction is not a value judgement. A tally can run an economy; an emblem can carry a theology. But only writing can record a name exactly, distinguish "the sheep were delivered" from "the sheep will be delivered," and preserve a sentence its author never spoke in the reader's presence. The definition matters because the ancient world is full of sign systems that are not writing under it, and two of them stand close to this article's subject. The first is the token system itself (§II): a cone could mean a small measure of grain to anyone who had learned the code, whatever language they spoke, precisely because the cone did not stand for a word . The second is the case this hub treats in Old Europe : the Vinča signs of the Neolithic Balkans (c. 5300–3500 BCE), a repertoire of incised marks — crosses, chevrons, combs, spirals, and abstract forms — found chiefly on pottery, spindle whorls, and figurines across the Vinča culture and its neighbours. The Vinča signs are older than cuneiform by well over a millennium, and they are sometimes popularly called "the first writing." On the excavated evidence they are not, and the reasons are instructive. More than 85 per cent of Vinča inscriptions consist of a single sign . The longest groups run to only a handful of signs, with no fixed reading order that analysis has established. The signs do not accumulate into archives: there are no Vinča accounts, no lists, no labelled stores, no sign of the administrative machinery that everywhere else accompanies early script. Shan Winn's great catalogue of the signs (1981) — some 210 sign types in his analysis — was published under the deliberately chosen title Pre-Writing in Southeastern Europe : Winn himself concluded that the signs were not texts. Later quantitative analysis has sorted most of the repertoire into potters' marks, ornament, and a residue of perhaps a third that may be symbolic notation of some kind — ownership, identity, cult — without demonstrating any tie to a spoken language. The famous Tărtăria tablets of Romania, three small clay tablets whose signs are the strongest Vinča candidates for a "text," carry their own unresolved problems of find context and dating by association, and no reading of them has won scholarly assent. The Vinča case is therefore this article's control experiment: a farming society, centuries deep, with a rich and long-lived sign repertoire — and no writing. Signs alone do not make a script. What was missing at Vinča, and present at Uruk, was not ingenuity. It was an institution that needed to record, exactly and at volume, who owed what to whom. // THE TEST // Does it record language? Writing, in the scholarly usage followed here, ties marks to the words and sounds of a particular language. Notation that any reader can decode without knowing a language — tallies, tokens, emblems — is proto-writing, however sophisticated. // THE NEAR MISS // The Vinča signs, c. 5300–3500 BCE Some 210 sign types in Winn's catalogue, but over 85% of inscriptions are a single sign, with no archives, no lists, and no demonstrated tie to speech. A sign system that is not writing. // THE FIRST PASS // Proto-cuneiform, c. 3400–3200 BCE More than 700 signs plus multiple numerical systems, organised in ruled cases on tablets, totalling accounts — a system already recording what, how many, and whose, though not yet grammar. // THE MEASURE // Names, then sentences A system becomes full writing as it acquires phonetic signs — able to write a personal name exactly — and then grammatical elements. In Mesopotamia that turn takes the centuries c. 2900–2600 BCE (§XI). One more preliminary belongs here, because it disciplines everything that follows: the earliest scripts sit at the boundary of the definition themselves. Proto-cuneiform, as Woods emphasises, records very little grammar; its sign order does not yet follow spoken word order, and its texts must in a real sense be interpreted from their format rather than read as transcribed speech. Whether the language behind the earliest tablets was even Sumerian is, as §XI shows, a question the specialists themselves leave open — Englund finds no definitive evidence for it, and Woods calls the direct evidence "quite slim" while noting that most scholars assume it. This article therefore uses the field's own careful vocabulary: proto-cuneiform for the Uruk script in its first phases, writing for the achievement toward which it was travelling, and exact dates and corpora wherever the argument depends on them. The boundary is not an embarrassment to the story. It is the story: writing was not found complete, like a stone on a road. It was assembled, device by device, over millennia — and the assembly can be excavated. II. Before Writing — The Token Systems of the Neolithic Near East The tokens appear with farming. From about 8000 BCE — the early Neolithic, when wheat, barley, sheep, and goats were first brought under cultivation and herding — small objects of clay begin to occur on sites across the whole arc of the Fertile Crescent and beyond: in Anatolia, Syria, the Levant, Iraq, and Iran. They are among the humblest artefacts in any museum drawer. A typical token is one to three centimetres across, pinched or rolled from a pellet of clay, sun-dried or lightly baked. Schmandt-Besserat's catalogue, assembled over two decades and published in Before Writing (1992), counted more than eight thousand tokens from over a hundred sites, spanning some five thousand years. Whatever else they were, they were not rare, local, or brief: the token is the most widely distributed accounting artefact of the prehistoric world. Plain Tokens — The First Repertoire The earliest and commonest forms — Schmandt-Besserat's plain tokens — are geometric solids: cones, spheres, discs, cylinders, ovoids (egg-shapes), tetrahedra (triangular pyramids), and a few other regular shapes, in larger and smaller sizes. They carry no decoration. Their power lay in convention: within a community that shared the code, a shape stood for a commodity in a standard quantity. In Schmandt-Besserat's reconstruction — the readings are hers, argued from the later evidence of §§III–IV, and the reader should hold them at that attribution — the cone, the sphere, and the flat disc stood for small, larger, and largest standard measures of grain; the ovoid for a jar of oil; the cylinder for an animal of the flock; the tetrahedron for a unit of labour, a person-day of work. A storekeeper holding three cones and a cylinder held, in his palm, a record: three small measures of grain and one animal, owed, delivered, or in store. The tokens could be counted, bundled, handed over, and recounted — a ledger that could be audited by touch, by parties who shared no language, because the code was in the shapes and not in any tongue. The procedure, reconstructed from find contexts, was physical and exact. Tokens representing a delivery were counted out in the presence of the parties; tokens representing a debt were set aside and held by the creditor or the store; tokens were strung, in some cases, on cords through perforations, or kept in groups in bowls, jars, and rooms of the buildings they served. Assemblages of tokens are found in precisely the contexts an accounting reading predicts: in storerooms, in administrative buildings, with seals, and — in the fourth millennium — inside the sealed envelopes of §III. It is equally important to state what the record does not give us. No Neolithic text explains the tokens; their meanings are inferred, backwards, from their shapes, their contexts, and their resemblance to later signs. Some small clay objects catalogued as tokens may have served other purposes entirely — gaming pieces, counters in other games of number, or things whose use is lost. That uncertainty is the seed of the controversy of §V, and it is present from the first drawer of cones. Complex Tokens — The Repertoire Grows Teeth For some four thousand years the plain repertoire changed little. Then, in the mid-fourth millennium BCE — the age of the first cities, of Uruk's explosive growth and of the Uruk expansion treated in this hub's Ubaid and Uruk article — a second repertoire appears beside it: Schmandt-Besserat's complex tokens . These keep the old solids but add new shapes modelled on artefacts and animals — vessels, tools, heads of stock — and, above all, they are marked : incised with lines and crosses, punched with dots, built up with applied pellets and coils of clay. Where a plain cone said "a measure of grain," a marked token could in principle say which grain, which product, which grade: the incisions multiply the code's distinctions just as the urban economy multiplied the goods to be distinguished — types of oil, of textile, of beer, of processed food, of animal by age and kind. On Schmandt-Besserat's count the complex repertoire runs to some hundreds of distinguishable types, against the plain repertoire's handful. The timing is her argument's foundation: the token system elaborated itself, suddenly and dramatically, in exactly the generations in which the cities' administrations outgrew what a handful of cones and spheres could say — and in exactly the place where writing then appears. // ONE-TO-ONE CORRESPONDENCE // The token system's logic is what Schmandt-Besserat calls concrete counting: there is no token for "three." Three measures of grain are three cone-tokens; three animals are three cylinder-tokens; the number exists only as the pile. Quantity and commodity are fused in the object itself. The long history that follows — envelopes, impressed signs, abstract numerals — is the history of those two ideas, how many and of what , being prised apart until each could be written separately. Whether that history shows a people incapable of abstract number before writing, as the strong form of the token thesis holds, is contested: later critics, Peter Damerow's work among them, treat number as abstract in use long before it is abstract in notation. The piles, at least, are fact. Tokens did not vanish when writing came. They continued in use alongside tablets for centuries, and sporadically for far longer — a famous envelope from Nuzi, in northern Iraq, of the second millennium BCE, held forty-nine pebbles and bore a cuneiform inscription listing forty-nine animals, a token account still doing its work some two thousand years after the first tablets. The old technology persisted because it was good at what it did: it was cheap, portable, language-blind, and self-verifying. What it could not do was grow. A token account cannot name the debtor, date the debt, qualify it, or total a hundred deliveries on a single surface. The devices of the next section are best understood as attempts — ingenious, and ultimately insufficient — to make the token system do those things. III. Envelopes, Seals, and Numerical Tablets — The Bridge Devices The bridge from tokens to tablets was built, in the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, out of three devices, each of which survives in the ground. They are best taken in the order of the problem each one solved. The Envelope — An Account That Cannot Be Altered A loose pile of tokens can be added to or raided; a debt recorded in tokens is only as honest as its keeper. The clay envelope — the bulla — solved this. The procedure can be reconstructed object by object. The accountant counted out the tokens for a transaction — a delivery of grain, a consignment of animals — in the presence of the parties. He then took a lump of wet clay, hollowed it into a ball around the tokens, and closed it with the tokens sealed inside. Before the clay dried, he rolled a cylinder seal across the surface: a small stone cylinder, engraved in reverse, whose rolling left a continuous frieze of figures — the signature of the responsible official or institution, pressed into the very skin of the account. The envelope now was the record. It could travel with the goods as a bill of lading. It could be stored. And it could be verified in only one way: by breaking it open and counting the tokens against the delivery. An envelope that arrived intact, seal unbroken, guaranteed that its contents had not been touched since the sealing. Accountability had acquired a tamper- evident seal — in the literal, physical sense. Envelopes of this kind are known from sites across the Uruk world, with the key stratified sequence at Susa, in Khuzestan (southwestern Iran), where envelopes come principally from level 18 of the Acropole excavations, immediately before the numerical tablets of level 17. Some 130–150 envelopes and fragments have been excavated in total. Most remain unopened to this day — only a handful have been broken in modern times — though computed tomography (CT) scanning of intact examples, including envelopes from Chogha Mish now in Chicago, has begun to read their contents without destroying them, and has confirmed tokens inside where the accounting reading predicts them. It was Pierre Amiet who, in the 1960s, first pointed to the decisive detail on which the next step turns: the surfaces of some envelopes bear impressions that match the tokens sealed inside. The Impression — The Account Moves to the Surface An envelope that must be broken to be read is secure but blind. The remedy was obvious once seen: before sealing, press each token into the wet surface of the envelope, so that its shape is recorded on the outside. The surface then declares the contents — three cone-impressions, a cylinder- impression — while the tokens inside remain as the sealed guarantee. Envelopes bearing such token impressions are excavated fact. But the device contains its own abolition: once the surface carries the whole account, the tokens inside are redundant. Drop them, flatten the ball into a slab, keep the impressions and the seal — and the envelope has become a numerical tablet : a solid lump of clay bearing impressed signs for quantities, rolled with the seal of the responsible party, and nothing else. Numerical tablets — quantities without commodities, or with at most the seal to say whose account it was — are found across the Uruk world in the generations immediately before proto-cuneiform: at Uruk itself, at Susa, at Habuba Kabira and Jebel Aruda on the Syrian Euphrates, at Godin Tepe in Iran, and elsewhere in the contact zone. Englund's term for the next and last bridge form is the numero-ideographic tablet : a numerical tablet to which one or two drawn signs have been added naming the commodity itself — butter oil, textiles, small cattle, in the Susa examples he cites. With that addition, every element of the later account tablet exists. What remained was to systematise it. // THE DEVICES, IN SEQUENCE // Tokens (from c. 8000 BCE): shaped counters, one per unit of goods; the pile is the number. Envelopes / bullae (mid-4th millennium BCE): tokens sealed inside a hollow clay ball, the surface rolled with a cylinder seal; verified by breaking. Impressed envelopes : tokens pressed into the surface before sealing, so the outside declares the contents. Numerical tablets : the tokens dropped, the impressions kept, on a solid slab — quantities only. Numero-ideographic tablets (Englund's term): quantities plus one or two drawn signs naming the commodity. Proto-cuneiform tablets (§VII): quantities, commodities, persons, and institutions, in ruled cases, with totals. The sequence is Englund's reconstruction of the Susa–Uruk evidence; its first steps are the least contested part of the whole token debate. The Seal — The Second Technology Running through every device in this section is an object that deserves its own sentence of credit: the cylinder seal. Developed in the Uruk period world — Mesopotamia first, with Egypt adopting the form soon after, itself a datum for §XIII — the cylinder seal turned identity into a mechanism. Rolled across wet clay, it marked a tablet, an envelope, a jar sealing, or the clay lump on a storeroom door as the act of a particular office. Sealing is not writing: a seal image identifies without recording language, and seals were used by administrations for three thousand years alongside script. But sealing taught the accounting world the two habits writing would inherit: that a clay surface could carry authority, and that a standardised repertoire of images, learned and recognised across a whole society, could be trusted at a distance. The first tablets are unthinkable without the sealed envelope that preceded them — and the envelope is unthinkable without the seal. IV. The Token Thesis — Schmandt-Besserat's Argument at Full Strength Denise Schmandt-Besserat, an archaeologist at the University of Texas at Austin, built the token theory across a series of publications from the 1970s to its full statement in Before Writing (1992, two volumes: the argument, and the site-by-site catalogue of tokens), with a condensed version in How Writing Came About (1996). The theory is the most influential account of writing's origin ever offered, and this article states it first at its full strength, as its author states it, before the critics are heard in §V. A theory that reorganised a field deserves to be met in its best form. The argument has four movements. First , the tokens were a system: not casual counters but a shared code, stable in its plain forms across five millennia and the whole Near East, in which shape signified commodity and standard quantity — the earliest code, in her phrase, for processing data. Second , the system elaborated under urban pressure: the complex tokens of the mid-fourth millennium, with their incised and applied marks, multiplied the code's distinctions as the redistributive economy of the first cities multiplied the goods to be tracked. Third , the envelope episode converted the three-dimensional code into two-dimensional signs: tokens impressed on envelope surfaces left marks that are , shape for shape, the earliest impressed numerical signs of the tablets — and the marks of complex tokens, drawn rather than impressed, became the drawn, pictographic signs for commodities. Fourth , the solid tablet inherited both families of signs at once, and writing was born as the union of the two: impressed signs for quantities, drawn signs for goods. On this account, specific correspondences can be exhibited token by token and sign by sign: the cone's impression becomes the sign for the small grain measure; the sphere's, the larger; the disc bearing a cross — her token for a sheep — becomes the cross-in-circle sign by which proto-cuneiform writes sheep and goats, a sign whose pictographic origin in any actual sheep is impossible and whose token origin is, she argues, written on its face. The theory's explanatory reach is its glory. It explains why writing appears where and when it does — in the accounting departments of the first cities, at the climax of a five-thousand-year development of accounting, not in temples as hymn or on walls as royal display. It explains why the earliest tablets are accounts and nothing else. It explains the otherwise baffling duality of the earliest script, in which numbers are impressed with the stylus's ends while commodity signs are drawn with its point — two techniques, two ancestries, fused on one surface. It explains why the numerical signs are the most conservative element of the system, keeping the shapes of counters long after the word-signs stylised beyond recognition. And it grounds a larger claim about cognition that Schmandt- Besserat presses throughout her work: that the token system was an external extension of memory which, by handling ever more data in ever more abstract form — from the thing itself, to a token for the thing, to a mark for the token, to a sign that could at last stand for a sound — trained the abstraction that writing then embodied. On her chronology the phases run: tokens, 8000–3500 BCE; envelopes and impressions, c. 3500 BCE; tablets with impressed and drawn signs, c. 3300–3100 BCE; phonetic signs, introduced to write the names of persons, c. 3100–3000 BCE. Writing, in the famous summary, began as counting — and humanity learned to write because it first needed to keep accounts. // THE CREDIT WHERE IT IS DUE // Two elements of the theory were not Schmandt-Besserat's inventions, and she credited them herself: A. Leo Oppenheim had drawn scholarly attention to the tokens as a class of object, and Pierre Amiet had noticed, in the 1960s, that envelope surfaces bear impressions matching the tokens inside. Her achievement was the synthesis: to assemble the Near-East-wide catalogue, to propose the commodity readings of the shapes, and to carry the argument the whole way from the Neolithic cone to the cuneiform sign list. Criticism of the synthesis, in §V, should not be mistaken for a denial that the catalogue itself transformed the evidence available to everyone who argues about it. V. The Critics — Englund, Zimansky, and the Objections The token theory has been under expert fire for as long as it has existed, and the fire has burned away parts of it. This section gives the objections at the strength their authors give them. They fall into three groups: objections to the chronology and unity of the token system, objections to the matches between tokens and signs, and an alternative account of what the solid core of the theory actually proves. Chronology and Unity — Zimansky's Objection Paul Zimansky's review of Before Writing (1993) remains the most quoted statement of the sceptical case, and Woods's synthesis adopts its central points. The tokens, Zimansky observed, span the ninth millennium to the end of the fourth and a geographical arc from Anatolia to Iran — yet the theory treats them as one system , a single code persisting essentially unchanged for five thousand years across dozens of cultures that shared no state, no priesthood, and no school to maintain it. No other human institution is credited with such stability, and the catalogue's own method manufactures part of the appearance of unity: objects gathered from a hundred sites and fifty centuries are sorted into types by a modern scholar, and the types are then read as the code's signs. The frequency evidence, he argued, cuts against the commodity readings themselves. The token Schmandt-Besserat reads as "sheep" — the disc with an incised cross — occurs, on her own catalogue's figures as Zimansky cited them, only some fifteen times in seven thousand years, while the commonest tokens in the record are forms she reads as "nails" and "work days." A Near East that accounted for nails and labour far more often than for sheep — the foundation animal of its economy, the very commodity the first tablets count obsessively — is, on the critics' reading, a reductio of the identifications: the commonest shapes are probably not commodity tokens at all, and the code dissolves, at its centre, into a miscellany of small clay objects whose uses we do not know. The Matches — Englund's Objection Robert K. Englund — of the Berlin Archaische Texte aus Uruk project and the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative, the editor of more proto-cuneiform material than anyone living — has faulted Schmandt-Besserat, in his own phrase as Woods reports it, for over-interpreting both the systematisation and the iconic differentiation of the tokens. The specific objections are epigraphic. Most of the tokens claimed as forerunners of particular word-signs were never found inside envelopes — the one context that would tie them to the accounting chain. Many of the proposed correspondences between complex tokens and proto-cuneiform signs are, in Woods's summary of the critical consensus, simply not plausible: two systems can share a shape — a cross, a jar outline, a head — without sharing a meaning, and resemblance asserted across five thousand years and a thousand kilometres is not descent demonstrated. Englund's own test case is instructive: a token form that Schmandt- Besserat and others equated with the sign for "precious metal" is, on his analysis of the numerical contexts, more likely to have stood for the fraction one-half. Where the theory needs a picture of a thing, the contexts deliver an arithmetical value. The word-signs, the critics conclude, were in their great majority invented with the script itself — drawn fresh by the Uruk administrators who needed them, from the world of vessels, plants, animals, and body parts around them — not inherited from a Neolithic code. Jean-Jacques Glassner, in The Invention of Cuneiform (2003), presses the point into a counter- thesis: writing was not a slow evolution out of counters at all, but a deliberate, comparatively sudden invention — a system conceived as a whole, by identifiable intellectual effort, to render the Sumerian language; the genuinely pictographic fraction of the earliest sign repertoire is, he argues, far too small to carry an evolution from pictures, and the accounting-first model mistakes the script's first employers for its inventors . What Survives — The Agreed Core And yet the critics are not demolitionists, and the present state of the question — the position a Tier A article must report — is a partitioned one. Englund himself calls the role of the simple tokens as forerunners of the impressed numerical signs "core knowledge" among cuneiformists: the chain from plain tokens, through envelope impressions, to the numerical tablets and the numerical signs of proto-cuneiform is accepted by essentially all parties, Englund and Woods included. Woods's formulation is the sharpest: tokens and envelope impressions relate to the numerals — "and these two systems, and only these two, appear to be related" — with the numerical tablets bridging the gap; the word-signs are another matter. A handful of individual signs may indeed descend from tokens — the cross-in-circle for sheep and goats is the standing candidate, accepted even by cautious accounts as apparently borrowed from the older accounting. The dispute is over the systematic claim: that the complex tokens, as a repertoire, became the word-signs, as a repertoire. That claim has not carried the field. // THE VERDICT, AT ITS EXACT STRENGTH // Accepted: plain tokens were accounting counters; their impressions on envelopes and numerical tablets are the ancestors of proto-cuneiform's numerical signs; cuneiform therefore began, in one of its two components, with numbers. Rejected or unproven: that the tokens formed one unchanging pan–Near Eastern code for five thousand years; that the complex tokens' commodity readings are secure; that the word-signs as a body descend from complex tokens. Open: a small number of individual sign derivations (sheep-and-goats the chief), and the degree of system in the Neolithic material itself. The first writing was thus born as accounting — that much of the famous thesis the evidence sustains — but it was not born only as accounting's child: its vocabulary of things was, on the prevailing critical view, a fresh invention of the Uruk age itself. VI. Uruk — The City That Needed Accounts Writing appears in a city, and the city must be pictured before the tablets can be understood. Uruk — modern Warka, in southern Iraq, east of the Euphrates — grew in the later fourth millennium BCE into something the world had not previously contained: a settlement of some 200 hectares or more, with a population Englund estimates as approaching 40,000, organised around great institutional households and crowned by the monumental temple precinct of Eanna , sacred to the goddess Inana, whose terraced and niched buildings were raised, levelled, and rebuilt in continuous succession. Around it, the alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia was being settled and irrigated at scale, and the Uruk world reached outward — colonies, outposts, and contact stations up the Euphrates into Syria and across to Iran — in the expansion this hub treats in Ubaid and Uruk . It is not a coincidence that the bridge devices of §III cluster in that contact zone: the accounting technology travelled with the trade and the colonists. The administrative problem of such a city is easily stated and was, before writing, insoluble. The great households — temple and palace establishments whose exact constitutional form is still debated — received grain, oil, beer, textiles, livestock, and labour from a countryside of farms, estates, and dependent settlements; stored them in bulk; processed them in breweries, bakeries, weaving sheds, and byres; and disbursed them again as rations to hundreds or thousands of dependent workers, as offerings, as seed, as fodder, and as the materials of craft. Every movement was an obligation: a delivery owed, a ration due, a flock entrusted, a field assigned. Human memory, witnessed delivery, tokens, and seals could carry such a system to village scale. At Uruk's scale — thousands of transactions, hundreds of personnel, obligations running across seasons and years — the record itself had to become an institution: standardised, totalled, archivable, and readable by an official who had not been present at the transaction. That requirement, and not any literary ambition, is the documented cradle of the script. Nearly all the earliest tablets come from the Eanna precinct itself — though, as the next section insists, they come from its rubbish, not from its shelves. // THE CITY // Uruk (Warka), southern Iraq Some 200 hectares and perhaps 40,000 people at its Late Uruk height (Englund's estimate) — the largest settlement yet built, and the findspot of nearly all the earliest tablets. // THE PRECINCT // Eanna, temple of Inana The monumental central precinct from whose building levels — and from the fill beneath their floors — the archaic tablets were excavated by the German Archaeological

Assessment — What Is Settled, What Remains Open Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published evidence — archaeological sites, radiocarbon and luminescence chronologies, and ancient and modern DNA — and where scholars disagree, as they do, sharply, over the footprints at White Sands, the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed and its evidence weighed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. That discipline needs stating plainly in this case, because the peopling of the Americas is also the subject of this hub's Tier C counterpart, Mu and Atlantis Reborn , where modern traditions have populated the Ice Age Americas with sunken motherlands and lost civilisations. This article is the attested counterpart to those claims: the same continents, the same deep past, reconstructed only from what has been dug, dated, and sequenced. The two accounts are kept apart by design, and the reader should keep them apart too. A note on dates and terms. Ages are given as cal BP — calibrated years before present, "present" being 1950 by radiocarbon convention — unless a source is quoted in its own terms. The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), the coldest phase of the last Ice Age, when the great ice sheets stood at their greatest extent, is placed by the White Sands literature at roughly 26,500 to 19,000 years ago . "Clovis" names an archaeological complex of fluted stone points and associated tools, not a tribe; "Beringia" names the now partly drowned landmass that joined Siberia to Alaska. Many Native nations hold their own accounts of their origins, placing their ancestors in their homelands from the beginning; this article addresses only the archaeological and genetic question of when and how the hemisphere's first populations arrived, and it does not adjudicate traditions that answer a different question. I. The Question — The Last Continents By about 45,000 years ago, modern humans had reached nearly every habitable corner of the Old World and had crossed open water to Australia. One double continent remained empty. North and South America — a quarter of the Earth's land surface, running from the Arctic to within a thousand kilometres of Antarctica — held no human beings at all until, at some point in the late Pleistocene, people crossed from northeastern Asia and spread through both continents with a speed that, on any chronology, counts as rapid. When that crossing happened, how many people made it, and which of two possible roads they took south past the ice sheets, are the three questions this article follows. They sound simple. They have occupied archaeology for a century, overturned one consensus already, and are being fought over again today at a dry lakebed in New Mexico. // THE HOMELAND // Northeast Asia Ancient and modern DNA agree: the first Americans descend from East Asian and Ancient North Eurasian ancestors who met and mixed in the far northeast of Siberia. // THE GATEWAY // Beringia The landmass exposed between Siberia and Alaska when Ice Age sea levels fell by more than 100 metres — a country up to 1,000 km wide, not a narrow bridge. // THE OLD ANSWER // c. 13,000 BP Clovis-first: big-game hunters walk through an ice-free corridor about 13,000 years ago and become the first Americans. The 20th-century consensus, now abandoned. // THE NEW FLOOR // c. 23,000–21,000 BP? The White Sands footprints, if their dates stand — and §VIII weighs whether they do — put people in New Mexico during the Last Glacial Maximum itself. The shape of the problem is set by geography and ice. Between Asia and the American interior stood two barriers in series. The first was water: the Bering Strait, which disappears whenever global sea level falls far enough, as it did for long stretches of the Ice Age. The second was ice itself: at the glacial maximum, the Laurentide Ice Sheet over Canada and the Cordilleran Ice Sheet over the western mountains merged into a near-continuous wall from the Atlantic to the Pacific, sealing Beringia and Alaska off from the rest of the continent. A population could therefore be in the Americas — on Alaskan soil, say — for thousands of years without being able to go anywhere. Much of the modern debate is really about that seal: when it formed, when it broke, and whether people found a way around its western edge, along the Pacific coast, before it broke at all. The evidence comes in three kinds, and the history of the question is the history of their changing balance. The oldest kind is the artefact in its layer : a stone point among mammoth bones, a hearth, a butchered bone — dated by the radiocarbon in associated charcoal or bone, and believed exactly as far as its context is secure. The second kind is the trace without an artefact : a footprint, a coprolite, cut marks on bone — human presence attested by what a body did rather than what it made. The third kind, and the one that has transformed the field since about 2010, is the genome : DNA from living Indigenous peoples and from ancient skeletons, which records splits, mixtures, and isolations in a population's past whether or not that population left a single datable object. The strongest conclusions in this article are those where all three kinds agree. The sharpest fights — White Sands above all — occur where one kind of evidence runs far ahead of the others. One more framing point, because it disciplines everything that follows. An archaeological "first" is a floor, not a date of arrival: the oldest found site can only show that people were present by that time, never that they were absent before it. Every generation of this debate has mistaken its current floor for the ceiling of the possible — Clovis-first did exactly that for fifty years — and the honest way to read the record assembled below is as a sequence of floors, each one excavated, dated, and argued over, with the true arrival somewhere at or before the oldest of them. II. Clovis First — The Consensus and How It Was Built The Clovis-first model was not a prejudice that happened to capture a field; it was built, find by find, on evidence that was genuinely strong — and understanding why reasonable scholars defended it for so long is necessary to understanding what it took to move them. Its foundation was laid in 1927 near Folsom, New Mexico , where excavators from the Colorado Museum of Natural History, working under Jesse Figgins, found a slender stone point lodged among the ribs of an extinct bison, Bison antiquus — and, crucially, left it in place until a visiting panel of senior scholars could see it there, undisturbed, with their own eyes. Folsom settled a question that had been bitterly contested for decades: human beings had indeed lived in North America alongside Ice Age animals. It also set the field's evidentiary standard — association demonstrated in situ , before witnesses — that every later claimant, Monte Verde and White Sands included, would be held to. The second foundation stone fell a few years later at Blackwater Draw , near Clovis, New Mexico, where excavations in the early 1930s under Edgar B. Howard of the University of Pennsylvania found larger fluted points with mammoth remains in layers below the Folsom material. The Clovis point — lanceolate, bifacially flaked, with a channel-like flute struck from its base — became the signature of the earliest recognised culture in the hemisphere. Over the following decades, Clovis points and Clovis kill and camp sites turned up across North America, from coast to coast, and radiocarbon dating eventually compressed them into a strikingly brief window. No comparably convincing older site appeared. The conclusion drew itself: the makers of Clovis points were the first Americans. The Model, Whole In its mature form, Clovis-first was a complete and elegant story. The ancestors of Native Americans crossed Beringia from Siberia late in the Ice Age. They waited north of the ice, or passed as soon as they could, and then — sometime around 13,500 to 13,000 years ago — moved south through the ice-free corridor , the strip of deglaciated land opening between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets along the eastern flank of the Rockies. Emerging onto the northern Plains as specialised hunters of mammoth and other great game, they spread with extraordinary speed — Clovis points appear from Alberta to Mexico within a few centuries — reached South America, and, in the model's boldest extension (associated with the archaeologist Paul Martin's "overkill" hypothesis), hunted the continent's megafauna into the extinction that coincides with their arrival. One migration, one corridor, one technology, one wave: the model explained the apparent simultaneity of Clovis, the absence of anything older, and the extinctions, in a single gesture. It also acquired, as long-lived consensuses do, a gatekeeping function. Claims of older occupation were announced regularly through the twentieth century — from the "American palaeoliths" of the 1870s onward — and nearly all collapsed on inspection: artefacts that proved to be naturally fractured stone ("geofacts"), bones broken by carnivores or trampling rather than butchers, charcoal from natural fires, or genuinely old layers contaminated by younger material worked down into them. Each collapse raised the bar for the next claim, and the bar was enforced, sometimes abrasively, by the field's senior figures. The result was a paradox that the next section resolves: the standard of proof that protected the field from a hundred false dawns also delayed its recognition of the one site that could meet it. That site was not in North America at all. It was in Chile, some 13,000 kilometres from the Bering Strait — which was precisely the problem. // WHY DISTANCE WAS THE OBJECTION // A site in southern Chile older than Clovis does not merely add a few centuries to a timeline. It requires people to have crossed Beringia, traversed the whole of North America, passed the ice sheets by some route, crossed the equator and the Andes' flank, and settled at the far end of South America — all before the date at which the model said the journey began. Monte Verde's age and its address were a single claim, and both halves had to be swallowed together. A note on what Clovis-first got right, because the correction of an error should not erase the evidence that made it plausible. Clovis is remarkably widespread and remarkably brief — the best modern redating (Waters, Stafford & Carlson, 2020) confines it to about 13,050–12,750 cal BP , a span of some three centuries — and a technology that appears across a continent within three hundred years is a real phenomenon demanding explanation, whether its makers were firstcomers or, as §XIII argues, a later horizon spreading through a hemisphere already peopled. The model's error was not invention. It was inference: from "nothing older has been proved" to "nothing older exists." The proof, when it came, came from a peat bog. III. Monte Verde — The Site That Broke the Barrier Monte Verde lies on the banks of Chinchihuapi Creek in the Los Lagos region of southern Chile, some 50 km inland from the modern Pacific coast near Puerto Montt — and farther from the coast still in the late Pleistocene, when lower sea level pushed the shoreline some 90 km west. The site was found in the mid-1970s, when erosion and logging exposed bones and worked wood along the creek, and from 1977 it was excavated by Tom D. Dillehay , then of the Universidad Austral de Chile, with an interdisciplinary Chilean and international team. What the creek had preserved, under a cap of peat that sealed it in waterlogged, oxygen-free sediment, was something North American archaeology had never produced for so early a date: a settlement whose perishable half had survived. Monte Verde II — The Occupation The principal layer, designated Monte Verde II (MV-II) , held the remains of a small community of perhaps twenty to thirty people. Its centrepiece was a tent-like residential structure some 20 metres long: a foundation of logs and planks, divided into about a dozen small rooms or cubicles, each with its own clay-lined hearth or brazier, its food remains, its tools. A short distance away stood a second, wishbone-shaped structure associated with mastodon bone and a concentration of medicinal plants — read by the excavators as a specialised workshop and healing place. Around and within the structures lay wooden lances and digging sticks, mortars, knotted cords and rope of twisted plant fibre, animal hides, stone tools, hearths, food debris of dozens of plant species from forest, coast, and distant inland zones — and a small human footprint preserved in the creek-side sediment. Radiocarbon dates on the layer's wood, charcoal, and bone clustered at about 12,500 radiocarbon years BP , which calibrates to roughly 14,500 cal BP — a full millennium and more before Clovis, at the wrong end of the hemisphere. Two features of the assemblage carried weight out of proportion to their size. The first was seaweed : remains of nine species of marine algae, recovered from hearths and living floors and directly dated in a later study (Dillehay et al., Science , 2008) to between about 14,220 and 13,980 cal BP. The seaweed had been carried to the site from beaches and estuaries tens of kilometres away, and chewed cuds of it, mixed with other plants, were found in the wishbone structure. Seaweed is not a curiosity in this argument: it is short-lived, unmistakably marine, and directly datable, and it ties an inland settlement to the Pacific coast — the first material hint, from the far south, of the coastal orientation that §X would place at the centre of the peopling story. The second feature was the sheer ordinariness of the whole. Monte Verde II is not a kill site or a quarry stop; it is a settled camp of foragers with a broad diet — mastodon and other game, yes, but also wild potatoes, seeds, nuts, berries, and shoreline foods — practising plant medicine and living in built housing. Whatever the first South Americans were, by 14,500 years ago at Monte Verde they were not a blitzkrieg of mammoth hunters racing south. They were residents. Twenty Years of Resistance Dillehay reported the site's antiquity from the late 1970s, and the field's response, for roughly twenty years, was refusal. The objections were not frivolous, and they are worth listing at their real strength, because the Monte Verde fight defined the standard that every pre-Clovis claim — White Sands included — is still judged by. The stone tools were said to be too simple, some of them possibly natural. The association between artefacts and dated material was questioned: could younger objects have sunk, or older charcoal have been redeposited, in a creek-side bog? The radiocarbon dates themselves were audited for contamination. And beneath the technical objections sat the structural one from §II: a settlement older than Clovis at the far end of South America implied an entry into the hemisphere so much earlier, by a route so different, that the conservative reading of any single ambiguous object was always "not proven." Dillehay's team answered with volume — the site's final publication ran to two large monograph volumes (1989 and 1997) documenting stratigraphy, dating, and every class of find in exhaustive detail — and with patience. The end came in January 1997, in the manner Folsom had pioneered seventy years earlier: by inspection, before witnesses. A delegation of twelve senior specialists — including prominent defenders of Clovis-first — travelled first to examine the artefacts and records, then to the site itself, much of which had by then been damaged by bulldozing, to inspect what remained of the stratigraphy. Their published conclusion, carried in American Antiquity later that year (Meltzer et al., 1997), was unanimous on the central question: MV-II is genuinely archaeological, and there is no reasonable ground to doubt its age of about 12,500 radiocarbon years BP. Later challenges — most extensively a 1999 critique by Stuart Fiedel, answered point by point by Dillehay — did not dislodge the consensus the visit had created. Monte Verde II is today the benchmark pre-Clovis site: the proof, accepted across the field, that people were living in South America at least a millennium before Clovis. // MONTE VERDE I — THE LAYER THAT DID NOT CARRY // Beneath and beyond MV-II, Dillehay reported a sparser, older component, Monte Verde I, for which dates around 18,500 cal BP have been proposed, and still older burned material from the vicinity has occasionally been cited. These claims have never won the acceptance MV-II won: the assemblage is thin, the association of the dated material with human activity is disputed, and Dillehay himself has treated the early material cautiously. This article therefore uses Monte Verde at its accepted strength — c. 14,500 cal BP — and lists MV-I among the open questions of §XIV. The distinction matters: it is the same discipline, applied by the same excavator, that makes MV-II's acceptance meaningful. What Monte Verde changed, once accepted, was not only a date but a method. After 1997, the question was no longer whether anyone preceded Clovis, but by how much, and by which road — and claims that would once have been dismissed unread began to receive the full audit instead: excavation, redating, replication. Paisley Caves, Page-Ladson, and Cooper's Ferry (§XI) all entered the literature through the door Monte Verde opened, and the genetic standstill model of §V was developed in a field that now needed an earlier entry to explain. The Clovis barrier had functioned, in effect, as a dam on interpretation. Monte Verde broke it — not with a point in a ribcage, but with huts, hearths, seaweed, and twenty years of documentation. IV. Beringia — A Country, Not a Bridge Every version of the peopling story begins in the same place, and the place is persistently misdrawn. "Land bridge" suggests a narrow causeway, crossed in a journey. Beringia was a subcontinent: the broad plain — up to about 1,000 km from north to south at its greatest extent — exposed when Ice Age sea levels fell more than 100 metres below today's, joining Chukotka in Siberia to Alaska and the Yukon in a single landmass that also includes the now-drowned shelves of the Bering and Chukchi seas. The term covers, by convention, the whole unglaciated region from the Lena River in Siberia to the Mackenzie River in Canada. For most of the last 60,000 years some version of this country existed, dry, cold, and largely ice-free, while the continents to its south lay under ice sheets kilometres thick. Its story — its climate, its vegetation, its long human occupation, and its drowning — is told at full length in this hub's Drowned Landscapes ; what matters here is the part Beringia plays in the peopling argument. The first point is that Beringia was inhabitable — not a wasteland to be hurried across, but a homeland that could hold a population for millennia. The older picture of the land bridge as barren steppe-tundra, too poor in fuel and game to support people through the glacial maximum, has been revised by palaeoecology: sediment cores from the Bering Sea floor and from lakes on the now-emerged margins preserve pollen, plant macrofossils, and insect remains showing that central Beringia carried mesic shrub tundra — birch, willow, and alder scrub, with spruce in favoured refuges — through the LGM. Shrubs mean firewood; firewood, in a treeless world, means the difference between a place people can winter and a place they cannot. Hoffecker, Elias, and O'Rourke, in the synthesis that anchors this section ( Science , 2014), drew the conclusion explicitly: a shrub-tundra refugium in central Beringia is precisely the kind of place where the genetic isolation described in §V could have happened — a population settled, not stranded, for the duration of the cold. The second point is archaeological, and it is an absence with a reason. If people lived in central Beringia for ten thousand years, where are their camps? Mostly, under water. The heartland of the refugium — the low plain between modern Siberia and Alaska — was flooded as the ice sheets melted and sea level rose after about 13,000 years ago, and now lies beneath the Bering Sea. What survives on dry land is Beringia's eastern and western edges: in Siberia, the Yana Rhinoceros Horn Site and its successors show people hunting in the Arctic by about 32,000 years ago, well before the LGM; in Alaska and the Yukon, the oldest firmly dated occupations — Swan Point, and later Upward Sun River (§XII) — cluster around and after 14,000 years ago. Between those edges lies a gap in the site record exactly where the standstill model puts its population, and exactly where the sea now is. Absence of evidence, in a drowned landscape, is the weakest form of evidence of absence — a principle this hub applies again, in §X, to the drowned Pacific coast. WESTERN BERINGIA Siberian side. Arctic occupation by c. 32,000 BP at Yana; mammoth-steppe hunting cultures persist toward the LGM. The source region of the founding population's Asian ancestry. CENTRAL BERINGIA The now-drowned plain. Shrub-tundra refugium on the core and insect evidence; the proposed home of the standstill population — and, being submerged, archaeologically almost silent. EASTERN BERINGIA Alaska and the Yukon. Ice-free throughout the LGM, but sealed from the south by the merged ice sheets; dated sites from c. 14,000 BP, including Upward Sun River at c. 11,500 BP. THE EXIT PROBLEM To peopling the continents, it was not enough to reach Beringia. The way south — corridor or coast — was blocked by ice and sea at the LGM. The routes are the subject of §X. Beringia also frames the question of who the first Americans were, genetically. The genomes of §V and §XII show a founding population formed from two sources: an East Asian lineage and the so-called Ancient North Eurasians, a Siberian population known from the 24,000-year-old Mal'ta child in south-central Siberia, whose ancestry contributes roughly a third of the Native American genomic inheritance. The mixture happened somewhere in northeastern Asia or Beringia itself, in the millennia before the glacial maximum. Beringia, in other words, is not only where the first Americans waited. It is, in part, where they became a distinct people — the place their genomes diverged from every Asian relative and began the separate history that the next section reads out of the DNA. V. The Standstill — Ten Thousand Years in the Refugium The genetic evidence for a long Beringian pause arrived before the palaeoecology that made it plausible. Through the 1990s, studies of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) — the small genome inherited only from the mother — had established that Native Americans carry a handful of founding maternal lineages (the haplogroups A2, B2, C1, D1, D4h3, and X2a) derived from Asian ancestors. In 1997 two Latin American geneticists, Sandro Bonatto and Francisco Salzano, proposed that these lineages had diversified in Beringia before dispersing. A decade later the proposal was formalised by Erika Tamm and colleagues ( PLoS ONE , 2007), working with 623 complete mitochondrial genomes from the Americas and Asia. Their finding was a pattern of private mutations : changes present in the American founding lineages but in no Asian population — the signature of a population that had been genetically isolated, accumulating its own mutations, for thousands of years between leaving Asia and spreading through the Americas. Applying a molecular clock, they estimated that the American lineages had diverged from their Asian sisters more than 25,000 years ago , but had dispersed through the New World less than 15,000 years ago . Between those two bounds lay the standstill: on the order of ten thousand years, spent — the geography left only one candidate — in Beringia. Whole-genome studies have since filled in the pause with people and dates. The founding population's ancestors split from East Asians around 36,000 years ago (the modelling of §XII gives 36 ± 1.5 ka), with gene flow between the diverging populations continuing until about 25,000 years ago . Between about 25,000 and 20,000 years ago the founding population received its Ancient North Eurasian component. Thereafter it was isolated — through the whole of the LGM — until its descendants began moving south of the ice sheets, on the genetic modelling, sometime between about 17,500 and 14,600 years ago , when the northern and southern branches of Native American ancestry diverged, probably already south of the ice (Waters, Science , 2019, summarising the genomic literature). The effective size of the isolated population was small — mtDNA modelling has suggested on the order of a few thousand breeding women, implying a total community in the low tens of thousands at most — and palaeoecological carrying- capacity estimates for shrub-tundra Beringia land in the same range. A small people, then, in a cold refugium, for longer than the whole of recorded history several times over. // WHAT A "STANDSTILL" IS — AND IS NOT // What the model claims: that between divergence from Asian ancestors (complete by c. 25,000 BP) and dispersal south of the ice sheets (c. 17,500–14,600 BP on the genomic modelling), the ancestral Native American population was genetically isolated, most plausibly in Beringia, and accumulated the private mutations its descendants still carry. What it does not claim: that the population was static, unchanging, or camped in one place — "standstill" describes gene flow, not culture or movement within Beringia. Its standing: the isolation itself is supported by every major genomic study since 2007; its duration and its precise location (central Beringia versus a Siberian refuge) are modelled quantities, and different models return different spans. This article uses the conventional c. 25,000–15,000 BP framing of the task the evidence is usually summarised by, and flags the genomic southward window separately where it matters (§X). The standstill matters to this article for two reasons beyond its own elegance. The first is that it independently requires an early presence : a population cannot have been isolated in Beringia from 25,000 years ago unless its ancestors had already crossed northeastern Asia and reached the refugium before the LGM sealed the region — which makes the genetics, from 2007 onward, a standing argument that the hemisphere's peopling began well before Clovis, whatever the site record then showed. The second is that it sets the trap into which the White Sands dates would fall, and from which they would have to escape. If people were in New Mexico by 23,000–21,000 years ago — south of the ice, during the LGM — then either the standstill population leaked south far earlier than the genomic dispersal window allows, or a separate, earlier movement reached the interior Southwest and left the footprints, while the ancestors of all sampled Native American genomes came later. Neither option is impossible; ancient DNA has repeatedly revealed populations that left no descendants. But the tension is real, and §VIII returns to it, because it is the strongest external argument in the White Sands debate — stronger, in the end, than any argument about seeds. First, though, the footprints themselves. VI. White Sands — Footprints at the Glacial Maximum White Sands National Park, in the Tularosa Basin of south-central New Mexico, is a gypsum dune field of unearthly whiteness — and, beneath and beside the dunes, the floor of a vanished Ice Age lake. Palaeolake Otero filled much of the basin during the late Pleistocene; as it shrank and dried toward the end of the Ice Age it left the broad playa called Alkali Flat, a mosaic of mudflats, shallow pools, and stream margins. Around that lake walked the Pleistocene megafauna — mammoths, giant ground sloths, camels, dire wolves, sabre-toothed cats — and their tracks, pressed into wet gypsum-rich mud and then buried, are preserved there in the tens of thousands. Park resource manager David Bustos first recognised the significance of the human tracks among them in 2009, and the years since have made White Sands the richest tracksite of its kind in the Americas: whole trackways recording behaviour — a human carrying a child, setting the child down, picking it up again; a giant sloth rearing and wheeling, apparently at a human approach — at a resolution no artefact scatter can match. Many of the surface tracks are "ghost tracks," visible only in particular conditions of moisture and light, and the survey methods developed for them are part of §IX. The dated evidence comes from one intensively studied section: WHSA Locality 2 , on the eastern margin of Alkali Flat, where an erosional scarp exposes the lake-margin sediments. There, in 2019–2020, a team led by geologist and ichnologist Matthew R. Bennett of Bournemouth University, with the U.S. Geological Survey's Kathleen Springer and Jeffrey Pigati , the National Park Service, Cornell University, and the University of Arizona, excavated a trench through the footprint-bearing sequence. The results were published in Science in September 2021 (Bennett et al., 2021). The Claim The excavated sequence is a stack of fine-grained lake-margin deposits, and within it the team documented 61 human footprints distributed across multiple distinct stratigraphic horizons — surfaces on which people had walked, separated by layers of sediment, and therefore by time. The prints are unmistakably human: bare feet, of modern anatomy, in trackways that include adults and, predominantly, adolescents and small children, judging by foot size. Interbedded with the footprint horizons — below them, above them, and in layers between them — lay dense bands of seeds of the aquatic plant Ruppia cirrhosa (spiral ditch grass), which the team radiocarbon-dated by accelerator mass spectrometry. Eleven aliquots of seeds, in correct stratigraphic order from the base of the sequence to the top, returned calibrated ages running from 22,860 ± 320 years BP at the bottom to 21,130 ± 250 years BP at the top. The footprints, bracketed by those seed layers, were therefore made between about 23,000 and 21,000 years ago — squarely within the Last Glacial Maximum, roughly eight thousand years before the oldest then-accepted site in the hemisphere, and at a time when the ice sheets to the north stood at or near their maximum extent and the ice-free corridor did not exist. // THE SITE // WHSA Locality 2, Alkali Flat Eastern margin of palaeolake Otero, Tularosa Basin, New Mexico. Fine-grained gypsum-rich lake-margin sediments exposed in an erosional scarp. // THE TRACKS // 61 human footprints excavated On multiple superimposed horizons, with mammoth, sloth, canid and other megafaunal trackways; thousands more tracks unexcavated across the playa. // THE TRACKMAKERS // Mostly the young Foot-size analysis: the majority of the dated trackways were made by adolescents and children, with adults present — a lakeshore population, not a passing war-band. // THE 2021 DATES // c. 23,000–21,000 cal BP Radiocarbon ages on in situ Ruppia cirrhosa seed layers bracketing the footprint horizons, in stratigraphic order (Bennett et al., Science 2021). The paper's importance was not only its date. A footprint is the one class of evidence that cannot be redeposited, curated, traded, or dropped by a burrowing animal into an older layer: a trackway exists only where and when a foot pressed the ground. If the White Sands tracks are as old as their bracketing sediments, then human beings were present in the interior Southwest of North America — south of the ice sheets, a thousand kilometres from any coast — during the LGM, and every model of the peopling built on a post-glacial entry is wrong not in detail but in kind. The authors said so, in measured terms, and the paper landed accordingly. It was immediately clear, however, that the entire claim rested on a single load-bearing element: not the footprints, whose human origin no one disputed, but the dates of the seeds . And the seeds were of an aquatic plant. Within months, the critique arrived — aimed, precisely, at the water the plant had grown in. VII. The Dating Fight, Round One — The Seed Critique The critique of the White Sands chronology is the methodological centrepiece of this article, and it deserves to be stated the way this hub states every contested claim: at full strength, in its authors' own terms of argument, before any reply. It came in two connected publications — a formal Comment in Science (Madsen, Davis, Rhode & Oviatt, 2022) and a full assessment in Quaternary Research (Oviatt, Madsen, Rhode & Davis, 2022; journal issue 2023) — from a team combining a Quaternary geologist of the Great Basin (Charles G. Oviatt), archaeologists David B. Madsen and Loren G. Davis, and palaeoecologist David Rhode. Davis's presence is worth noting: the lead excavator of Cooper's Ferry (§XI), no defender of Clovis-first. The critique was not a rearguard action by the old consensus. It was a dating argument, and it was a good one. The Reservoir Effect — The Core Objection Radiocarbon dating measures the carbon-14 a once-living thing took from its environment. For a land plant, that carbon comes from the air, and the air's carbon-14 content at any past date is known from the calibration curve — the date is sound. But Ruppia cirrhosa is not a land plant. It grows submerged, in lake and wetland water, and it builds its tissues substantially from carbon dissolved in that water . Lake water in a limestone and gypsum basin like the Tularos
