Tier B — What This Article Is, and Is Not This is a Tier B article: ancient tradition . That label has a precise meaning in this hub. Tier B does not mean that the events described are attested fact. It means that an ancient text makes a claim, that the claim can be read, checked, and quoted in named translations, and that ancient and later readers argued about it — and all of that can be documented. Nothing in this article attests a real Atlantis. No Egyptian inscription naming Atlantis has been found. No source older than Plato mentions Atlantis at all. No archaeological site has been shown to be Plato's island on Plato's own terms — its place, its date, and its scale at once. The article's job is narrower and, for that reason, stronger: to set out what Plato actually wrote, how he framed the story's transmission, what work the story does inside his philosophy, and how the ancient world itself received it. That discipline matters because almost all later Atlantis lore — the lost-continent literature of the nineteenth century, the occult Atlantean root-races, the modern hunt for a drowned city in every ocean — claims descent from this one text. The modern telling is treated in its own Tier C article, Mu and Atlantis Reborn . This article is the text that telling must answer to. Where the modern version adds aircraft, explosives, energy crystals, or a global mother-civilisation, the reader can return here and check: Plato says none of that. // TIER DISCIPLINE — A NOTE ON VERBS // Throughout this article, Atlantis claims are attributed, never narrated as fact: the priest in Plato's dialogue says… , the Critias describes… , Proclus reports that Crantor held… When a sentence states something without attribution — that Plato wrote two dialogues, that the Critias breaks off unfinished, that Strabo reports a view of Posidonius — that is a claim about a text or a documented scholarly position, and it is sourced as such. Quotations from Plato in this article are taken only from named, published translations actually consulted for it, principally Benjamin Jowett's translation of the Timaeus and the Critias , with the Loeb translations of Strabo and Plutarch and Thomas Taylor's translation of Proclus used for the reception material. Each quotation is cited to its translator. Everything else that renders an ancient author's wording is paraphrase, and is presented as paraphrase. II. Two Dialogues, One Source Atlantis appears in exactly two works by the Athenian philosopher Plato (c. 429–347 BCE): the Timaeus and its unfinished sequel, the Critias , both generally placed among his late dialogues and dated to around 360 BCE. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's article on the Timaeus (Donald Zeyl) notes that the orthodox view places the dialogue in Plato's late period, while recording that this dating has been debated — G. E. L. Owen famously argued for a middle-period date. The exact year of composition is not settled, and this article does not pretend otherwise. The two dialogues divide the story between them. The Timaeus gives the frame, the transmission claim, and a compressed summary of the whole tale: the island, the empire, the war, and the destruction, all within a few pages ( Timaeus 24e–25d). The Critias was to give the tale in full — the two cities described at length, then the war itself — but it breaks off before the war is narrated, in the middle of a speech by Zeus. A third dialogue, the Hermocrates , was projected as the conclusion of the sequence and was never written. The sequence as planned ran from the creation of the cosmos (the main business of the Timaeus , in a long speech by Timaeus of Locri on the making of the world and of humankind), through the earliest human history (the Critias ), to the present age (the unwritten Hermocrates ). Atlantis, in other words, sits inside a much larger design: a history of everything, from the origin of the universe to Plato's own day. THE TIMAEUS A dialogue whose main subject is cosmology — the creation and structure of the universe. Atlantis enters in the introductory conversation (20d–27b) as a story Critias offers in answer to Socrates' request, and is summarised by the Egyptian priest's speech at 24e–25d. The Atlantis material is a preface to the cosmology, not its subject. THE CRITIAS The sequel in which Critias retells the story at full length: primeval Athens first (109b–112e), then Atlantis (113c–121c) — its god, its kings, its city, its plain, its laws, and its moral decline. The text stops at 121c, mid-sentence, as Zeus rises to pronounce judgement. The speakers matter. In both dialogues the Atlantis story is told not by Socrates, and not by Plato in his own voice — Plato never speaks in his own voice anywhere in the dialogues — but by Critias : an Athenian aristocrat, a relative of Plato's, and, in history, a figure Plato's readers knew as one of the Thirty Tyrants who ruled Athens brutally in 404–403 BCE. Plato puts his "true story" in the mouth of a man his audience associated with a violent, failed regime. Scholars have long noted the oddity; at minimum, it is a reason not to read the dialogue's truth-claims as Plato's own affidavit. Jowett, in his introduction to the Critias , states the conclusion he draws from the whole construction in plain terms: in his judgement the entire narrative is due to the imagination of Plato, who used the name of Solon and introduced the Egyptian priests to give verisimilitude to his story. That is a translator's scholarly judgement, offered here as such — Section XIII below sets out how far modern scholarship agrees with it, and where it dissents. III. The Chain of Transmission, As Plato Frames It Plato does not present the Atlantis story as his own research, and he does not present it as a myth in the ordinary sense either. He presents it as a tradition with a pedigree — a chain of named tellers, each link of which the reader is invited to inspect. Understanding that chain is essential, because the chain itself, not any external evidence, is the story's entire claim to authority. The Occasion: Socrates Asks for the Ideal City in Action At the opening of the Timaeus , Socrates recalls a conversation of the previous day about the best city — a discussion closely resembling the argument of Plato's Republic — and says, in paraphrase, that a description of a city at rest does not satisfy him: he wants to see that city in motion, engaged in a war worthy of it, negotiating, fighting, and showing in action the character its constitution gave it in theory ( Timaeus 19b–c). Critias answers that he knows just such a story. It is, he insists, a true one — and its truth is the point, because only a real deed, he argues, can show the ideal city really at work. The Atlantis tale is thus introduced, from its first lines, as the answer to a philosophical commission: show us the city of the Republic, alive and at war. Section XII returns to what that commission implies. The Chain, Link by Link As Critias tells it in the Timaeus (20d–21b), the chain runs: LINK 1 An Egyptian Priest at Sais An unnamed, very aged priest of the goddess Neith at Sais in the Nile Delta tells the visiting Athenian Solon what, he says, the temple's written records preserve: the deeds of Athens 9,000 years earlier, forgotten by the Greeks themselves. LINK 2 Solon of Athens Solon (c. 640–c. 560 BCE), the Athenian lawgiver and poet, counted among the Seven Sages, hears the account in Egypt. In the dialogue's telling he intended to work it into a poem, but was prevented by the political troubles he found on his return home. LINK 3 Dropides Solon, a relative and friend of Critias' great-grandfather Dropides, tells the story to him. In the Critias (113a–b), Critias adds that Solon's own written version — his notes for the projected poem — passed to Dropides and remained in the family's possession, and that he himself studied it as a boy. LINK 4 Critias the Elder Dropides' son, Critias' grandfather — nearly ninety years old at the time of telling, in the dialogue's frame — repeats the story to his grandson, then about ten years old, during the festival of the Apaturia, when children recited poetry and Solon's poems were sung. LINK 5 Critias the Narrator — and Plato The younger Critias, now a grown man, retells the story to Socrates, Timaeus, and Hermocrates — and Plato writes the retelling down, some two centuries after Solon's lifetime. Every word of Atlantis that survives reaches us through this final link alone. Two features of the chain deserve emphasis. First, it is entirely internal to Plato's text . No writing of Solon's about Atlantis survives — indeed, no fragment of Solon's surviving poetry mentions it — and no source independent of Plato records the conversation at Sais. Later writers who name the priest or repeat the story (Section XVI) are working from Plato, not from a second archive. Second, Plato builds verisimilitude into the chain with unusual care. The Critias even pauses (113a–b) to explain, in paraphrase, why the foreign names in the tale sound Greek: Solon, preparing his poem, asked what the Egyptian renderings of the names meant, and translated the meanings back into Greek — so the names the reader hears are, within the fiction of the transmission, translations of translations. A storyteller inventing a pedigree could hardly do more to make it feel documented; a historian reporting a genuine archive would not need to. Readers from Jowett onward have drawn opposite morals from the same detail, and both responses are recorded in Section XIII. // THE FESTIVAL FRAME // Critias dates his hearing of the tale to the Apaturia, the Athenian festival of phratries (kinship groups), on the day called Koureotis, when boys were enrolled and recited poems. The detail roots the transmission in family and festival — memory carried by a household, not by a state archive. That is exactly the kind of memory Plato's own priest will say Greece cannot rely on. Critias also stresses, at the start of the Critias (108e–110a in paraphrase), that he has reconstructed the story by a night's effort of memory, turning over in his mind what he heard as a child and comparing it with Socrates' account of the ideal city. The dialogue itself, read closely, flags the tale as something recalled, reconstructed, and fitted to a philosophical brief — a point Christopher Gill's study of the Atlantis story presses with care, as Section XII notes. IV. Why Egypt? Sais, Neith, and Athena The story could have been set anywhere old. Plato sets it in Egypt, and the choice is load-bearing. Egypt does three kinds of work in the framing: it supplies antiquity (records older than any Greek memory), it supplies kinship (a goddess shared between the two cities), and it supplies authority (a priesthood that kept written archives while Greece, in the priest's telling, repeatedly lost its own past). Sais and Its Goddess At Timaeus 21e, in the translation by R. G. Bury for the Loeb Classical Library as reproduced on Perseus, Critias locates the scene: in the Delta of Egypt, where the Nile's stream parts, lies the Saitic district, whose chief city is Sais — the home of King Amasis — whose founding goddess, the text says, bears the Egyptian name Neith and is asserted to be the same as the Greek Athena . Jowett's rendering makes the same identification in the same place. Neith was a real and ancient Egyptian goddess, attested from the earliest periods of Egyptian history, whose chief cult centre was indeed Sais in the western Nile Delta; her emblems were the bow, crossed arrows, and shield, and she was a goddess of war, of hunting, and in later theology a creator. Her cult rose to particular prominence in the Twenty-sixth Dynasty (664–525 BCE), when Sais was the capital of Egypt — the very period in which Solon is placed in Egypt, and the reign of Amasis (570–526 BCE), the philhellene king the text names, overlaps Solon's later years. The framing, that is, is historically well-dressed: the city, the goddess, and the king all belong to Solon's world as a Greek of Plato's day could have known it, not least from Herodotus, whose Histories (Book II) describe Sais, Neith's festival of lamps, and Amasis at length. The citizens of Sais are, in the dialogue's words, great lovers of the Athenians, and claim a kinship with them — because the same goddess founded both cities. PARAPHRASE OF TIMAEUS 21E, AFTER JOWETT AND BURY What the Identification Does The Neith–Athena identification is the hinge of the whole story. Because Athena founded Athens — in the priest's account, a thousand years before she founded Sais itself — the Egyptian archive is not a foreign curiosity but, within the tale, a family record : the younger sister-city's temple has preserved the elder city's forgotten deeds. The priest can therefore tell Solon, an Athenian, the history of Athens itself, and the Athenian has no standing to dismiss it as alien fable. Plato's construction makes Egypt the memory of Greece. There is also a real Greek habit behind the device. Greek writers of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE routinely identified foreign gods with their own — Herodotus does it throughout his Egyptian book — and routinely treated Egypt as the source of great antiquity: of geometry, of astronomy, of religious rites, of laws. Solon's Egyptian journey was itself a Greek tradition older than Plato: Herodotus (1.29–30) already sends Solon travelling, and to Egypt and Amasis among other destinations, though Herodotus says nothing of Atlantis. Plato's frame, in short, uses materials his audience already believed — Egypt is old, Egypt keeps records, Solon went there — to carry a story no one had heard before. For this hub's purposes, one caution is essential. The dialogue's Egypt is a Greek literary Egypt : a Sais of the Greek imagination, staffed by a priest who speaks like a Platonic character and whose "records" contain a war between a Greek ideal city and a western sea-empire. Nothing in the Egyptian record — no temple inscription, king list, or papyrus from any period — contains Atlantis, primeval Athens, or this war. The Egyptian colouring is Plato's framing device, and Tier discipline requires it to be described as exactly that. The companion Tier B article on the antediluvian king lists shows, by contrast, what genuine ancient Near Eastern records of the deep past look like when they survive independently. V. The Priest's Rebuke — Memory, Floods, and Forgetting Before the priest tells Solon anything about Atlantis, he tells him something about the Greeks — and it is the most famous sentence in the whole Atlantis corpus. In Jowett's translation ( Timaeus 22b), the aged priest says: “O Solon, Solon, you Hellenes are never anything but children, and there is not an old man among you.” PLATO, TIMAEUS 22B — TRANS. BENJAMIN JOWETT The priest explains the rebuke, in paraphrase of 22b–23c: the Greeks are children in soul because they keep no old opinion handed down from antiquity and no knowledge hoary with age. The reason is catastrophe. Many destructions of humankind have occurred and will occur — the greatest by fire and water, lesser ones by countless other agents. The priest retells, as an example, the Greek story of Phaethon, who drove the sun's chariot and burned the earth: the story, he says, has the form of a myth, but its truth is a periodic deviation of the heavenly bodies that brings long cycles of destruction by fire upon the earth. Egypt, by contrast, is protected: the Nile preserves it from both fire and the deluges that drown other lands, and so in Egypt all notable deeds — Greek deeds included — are written down in the temples and preserved. Whenever a flood wipes out a Greek civilisation, the survivors are, in the priest's account, unlettered mountain herdsmen who keep only the names of their ancestors and none of their deeds; civilisation, literacy, and memory must begin again from nothing. That, the priest says, is why Solon can recite Greek genealogies yet knows nothing of the Athens of 9,000 years before: his city has forgotten itself many times over. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR READING THE TEXT The priest's speech is Plato's theory of why the story has no corroboration. The absence of any Greek record of Atlantis is not, within the dialogue, an embarrassment to be explained away later — it is predicted by the frame itself: of course the Greeks forgot; forgetting is what floods do. A modern reader should see the device for what it is, a self-sealing structure: the story explains in advance why no evidence for it can be produced. That does not make the device dishonest — Plato is writing philosophy, not filing a report — but it does mean the frame cannot be used as evidence. The speech also does philosophical work beyond the frame. Its doctrine of recurrent cosmic catastrophe — destructions by fire and water at long intervals, civilisations rising and perishing in cycles — belongs to the cosmology of the Timaeus as a whole, and Plato returns to it in the Laws (Book III), where the Athenian Stranger reconstructs the rebirth of society after a flood. Atlantis is one episode in a universe where such episodes are the rule. Primeval Athens and Atlantis are both, in the priest's telling, civilisations of a previous cycle — which is precisely why their story can instruct the present one. VI. The 9,000 Years — The Text's Own Figure The single most consequential number in the Atlantis story is given twice, once in each dialogue. In the Timaeus (23e), the priest dates the founding of Athens to 9,000 years before Solon's visit — and the founding of Sais to 8,000 years before, a thousand years later. In the Critias (108e), the narrator repeats the figure as the elapsed time since the war: nine thousand years, in Jowett's rendering of the passage, was the sum of years since the war between those who dwelt outside the Pillars of Heracles and all who dwelt within them. Three precisions are required, because popular retellings routinely blur all three. ANCHORED TO SOLON The figure is 9,000 years before Solon — before the priest's conversation with him in Egypt, conventionally placed in the 590s–570s BCE — not 9,000 years before Plato, and not 9,000 years before the present. Plato's text never converts the figure into any other era. “c. 9600 BCE” IS ARITHMETIC, NOT TEXT The familiar date of about 9600 BCE is a modern sum: Solon's floruit plus 9,000. It appears nowhere in Plato. It is a fair gloss of the text's claim, provided it is labelled as a computation from the text, not a quotation of it. A CLAIM, NOT A DATE The figure is something a character in a dialogue attributes to temple records that no one else ever saw. It belongs to Tier B: it is what the tradition says. At c. 9600 BCE, the Aegean held Mesolithic hunter-gatherers; there was no Athens, no writing, no state, and no war of empires for a record to record. The scale of the figure should also be felt. Nine thousand years before Solon is roughly as far before Solon as Solon is before the present day — and then half as far again. Plato, whose historical horizon reached back a few centuries to the Trojan War as a dimly remembered event of perhaps 700 years before his time, is deliberately placing his tale in a depth of time no Greek tradition could fill with content. The number functions in the dialogue the way the Egyptian frame does: it puts the story beyond checking, in a past accessible only through the one archive the story itself supplies. Later attempts to rescue the story's historicity have almost all had to begin by altering this number — most famously the proposal, discussed in Section XVII, that the figures were inflated tenfold somewhere in transmission, so that 9,000 years "should" be 900. The reader should note what that manoeuvre concedes: on the text's own figure, no known civilisation fits, so the text must be corrected before it can be matched to history at all. L. Sprague de Camp's much-quoted maxim in the Atlantis literature applies with force here, in paraphrase: one cannot change all the details of Plato's story and still claim to have Plato's story. VII. Primeval Athens — The Other City in the Story Half of the Atlantis story is not about Atlantis. The priest's tale, and still more the Critias , describe two cities, and the first of them — given precedence, as Critias says, in the telling — is an Athens of 9,000 years before, utterly unlike the Athens of Plato's day. In the Critias account (109b–112e, paraphrased from Jowett's translation), Attica fell by lot to Athena and Hephaestus together — deities of wisdom and craft — who settled in it a race of good men, native to the soil, and taught them the order of a state. The land itself was richer then: deeper soil, abundant springs, forests on the mountains, pasture where Plato's contemporaries saw bare rock. The dialogue lingers, remarkably, over the erosion of Attica — the soil washed to the sea over the millennia, leaving what Jowett's summary calls the mere skeleton of the land — a passage often noted as one of the earliest surviving observations of landscape degradation in Greek literature. The city on the Acropolis — a larger Acropolis than the classical one, in the account, extending to the rivers Eridanus and Ilissus and taking in the Pnyx and Lycabettus — was ordered by classes: craftsmen and farmers below, and apart from them a warrior class, the guardians, who lived in common dwellings around the temples of Athena and Hephaestus, held their possessions in common, took their meals together, kept their numbers steady at about twenty thousand men and women fit for war, and neither hoarded gold and silver nor lacked what was needful. Men and women of the guardian class trained and fought in common — Critias points, in the account, to the armed statue of Athena as surviving evidence of that ancient custom. Primeval Athens is the Republic's city with an address and a date: guardians in common, property held in common, women sharing the work of war — set down in Attica, 9,000 years before Solon. EDITORIAL SUMMARY OF CRITIAS 110C–112E, AFTER JOWETT No reader of Plato can miss the resemblance, and none is meant to. The primeval Athenians are the guardian class of the Republic made historical: the same communism of property and family life, the same separation of the warrior order, the same indifference to wealth. Socrates asked at the Timaeus ' opening to see the city of the previous day's conversation in action; Critias' Athens is that city, wearing the dress of antiquity. Atlantis, when it comes, will be everything this city is not. The priest's summary in the Timaeus gives primeval Athens its deed: when the Atlantic power attacked, Athens led the Greeks; when her allies deserted her, she stood alone, defeated the invader at the extremity of danger, freed those already enslaved within the Pillars, and preserved the rest from enslavement (24e–25c, after Jowett). The pattern — Athens alone against a vast invading empire from across the sea, Athens as liberator of Greece — is the pattern of the Persian Wars of 490 and 480–479 BCE as Athenian memory cherished it, transposed nine thousand years into the past. Section XII takes up that transposition directly. VIII. Atlantis in the Timaeus — Geography, Empire, War, and End Everything the Timaeus says about Atlantis itself is contained in the priest's speech at 24e–25d. It is short — a few hundred words in Greek — and it is the only Atlantis the earliest readers ever had. In Jowett's translation, the priest relates that the records tell of a mighty power that advanced from the Atlantic Ocean against the whole of Europe and Asia, and that Athens put an end to it. The passage, in Jowett's wording, runs in part: “In those days the Atlantic was navigable; and there was an island situated in front of the straits which are by you called the Pillars of Heracles; the island was larger than Libya and Asia put together, and was the way to other islands, and from these you might pass to the whole of the opposite continent which surrounded the true ocean.” PLATO, TIMAEUS 24E–25A — TRANS. BENJAMIN JOWETT (PARAPHRASED LINE BREAKS) The geography deserves slow reading, because it is the geography of a Greek mental map, not of a surveyed place. The Pillars of Heracles are the Strait of Gibraltar. Beyond them lies the outer ocean — the "true ocean," of which the Mediterranean, in the priest's image, is merely a harbour with a narrow entrance. In front of the straits lies the island, larger than Libya (North Africa as the Greeks knew it) and Asia (Asia Minor and the Persian world) combined. Beyond the island, other islands; beyond them, a continent enclosing the ocean on the far side. Plato's cosmos here is a ring: the known world around its harbour-sea, the ocean around that, the opposite continent around the ocean. Atlantis is the stepping-stone power of the outer ring. The Empire and the War On this island, the priest says (25a–b, after Jowett), arose a great and wonderful empire: its kings ruled the whole island, many other islands, and parts of the opposite continent; and on the near side of the straits they had conquered Libya as far as Egypt and Europe as far as Tyrrhenia (Etruria, in modern Italy). This assembled power then attempted, in a single campaign, to enslave all the lands within the straits — Egypt and Greece included. Athens resisted, first as leader of the Greeks, then alone, and won. Element What the Timaeus Says (24e–25d) Stephanus Location In the Atlantic, in front of the Pillars of Heracles 24e Size Larger than Libya and Asia put together 24e–25a Reach Other islands and parts of the opposite continent; within the straits, Libya to Egypt and Europe to Tyrrhenia 25a–b The attack A single bid to enslave all peoples within the straits 25b The resistance Athens leads the Greeks, then stands alone and liberates the enslaved 25b–c The end Violent earthquakes and floods; both armies destroyed; the island sinks; mud shoals remain 25c–d The Destruction The end comes, in the priest's account, not as a consequence of the war but after it — a catastrophe that falls on victor and vanquished alike. In Jowett's translation (25c–d): “But afterwards there occurred violent earthquakes and floods; and in a single day and night of misfortune all your warlike men in a body sank into the earth, and the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea.” PLATO, TIMAEUS 25C–D — TRANS. BENJAMIN JOWETT The priest adds the aetiological tail of the story: the sea in those parts is, in his day, impassable because of the shoal of mud left by the subsided island. Note the completeness of the erasure. The Athenian army perishes with its enemy; no veterans return to tell the tale; no wreck, ruin, or colony survives to be visited; even the sea-route to the site is blocked by mud. As with the forgetting of Section V, the story furnishes, inside itself, a reason for every absence of evidence outside itself. That is either the mark of a tradition that has thought hard about its own survival — or the mark of a construction built to be uncheckable. The scholarly argument of Section XIII is, at bottom, an argument about which of those two readings the construction deserves. IX. Atlantis in the Critias — Poseidon, Cleito, and the Ten Kings Where the Timaeus summarises, the Critias builds. Critias' full account (113c onward) begins in the age when the gods divided the earth among themselves by lot — peaceably, the dialogue insists, without the strife of the old myths — and each god settled and tended his own portion as a shepherd tends his flock. Atlantis fell to Poseidon , god of the sea and of earthquakes: the two powers whose combination will, in the end, destroy it. In the centre of the island, the account continues (113c–d, after Jowett), lay a plain said to be the fairest of all plains, and near its centre a low hill, where dwelt one of the earth-born men of that country, Evenor, with his wife Leucippe and their only daughter, Cleito . Her parents died; Poseidon desired her; and to enclose and secure the hill he broke the ground around it into concentric zones — the origin of the ringed city that every later image of Atlantis reproduces. “…breaking the ground, he inclosed the hill in which she dwelt all round, making alternate zones of sea and land, larger and smaller, encircling one another; there were two of land and three of water…” PLATO, CRITIAS 113D–E — TRANS. BENJAMIN JOWETT Poseidon also brought up two springs within the enclosure, one of hot water and one of cold — a detail later readers have connected with volcanic islands, though the text itself connects it with nothing but the god's provision for the place. By Cleito, Poseidon fathered five pairs of twin sons. The eldest of the first pair was Atlas , whom Poseidon made king over the whole island; from Atlas, the account says, the island took its name — Atlantis, the island of Atlas — and the surrounding sea its name, Atlantic. Atlas's twin, called Gadeirus in the local tongue (Eumelus in Greek, the dialogue explains), received the extremity of the island toward the Pillars of Heracles, the district of Gades — modern Cádiz. The other eight brothers were made rulers over the island's other regions, and the kingship in each line passed to the eldest son, generation after generation (114a–c, after Jowett). A CONFEDERACY OF TEN KINGS Atlantis, in the Critias, is not a single monarchy but a confederacy: ten royal houses, descended from ten brothers, each absolute in his own territory, bound to one another by the laws of Poseidon inscribed on a pillar of orichalcum, and forbidden to make war on each other. The eldest line, Atlas's, holds a primacy the others acknowledge. NAMES THAT POINT AT THE MAP Gadeirus–Gades anchors one end of the island at the straits themselves. Atlas carries a second charge: in Greek myth Atlas is the Titan who holds up the sky at the world's western edge, and the Atlas Mountains of north-west Africa bore his name. Plato's naming is cartography by mythology — the far west, where the sun sets and the known world ends. The descent from a god through a mortal woman gives the Atlantean kings a literally divine portion in their nature — and the whole moral machinery of the Critias depends on it. As long as the divine portion predominates, the kings are just; as generation dilutes it with mortal admixture, they corrupt. Atlantis's fall, when Plato finally narrates its cause in Section XI, is written into its founding genealogy from the start. X. The Ringed City, the Plain, and Orichalcum The central books of the Critias (115c–118e) contain the most circumstantial description of an imaginary place in all of Plato's work: dimensions, materials, hydraulics, agriculture, and military establishment, given in numbers. The precision is part of the text's effect — and part of its problem, since precision invites measurement, and measurement, as Section XVII shows, is where every proposed identification eventually fails. The Rings and the Canal Later kings, the account says (115d–116a, after Jowett), bridged Poseidon's rings, built the royal palace on the central island, and cut a canal from the sea through the rings to the centre: three plethra (about 300 feet) wide, a hundred feet deep, and fifty stades long. The rings themselves are measured: the central island five stades in diameter; the innermost water ring one stade wide; the next land and water rings two stades each; the outermost water and land rings three stades each. Ships could pass through the rings by passages cut in the land zones, roofed over in places where the rock allowed the docks to be hollowed beneath the ring's edge. The whole ringed citadel, rings included, measures some twenty-seven stades across — roughly five kilometres. Walls, Metals, and the Temple of Poseidon The walls around the rings were built, in the account (116a–b), of stone quarried from the island itself in three colours — white, black, and red — and were coated in metals: the outermost wall with brass, the next with tin, and the wall of the citadel itself with orichalcum , which, in Jowett's rendering, flashed with a red light. Orichalcum — "mountain copper" — was, the text says (114e), mined in many parts of the island, and was then the most precious metal known after gold, though by Plato's day it had become, in his phrase, only a name. Modern writers have variously identified it with brass, with a gold–copper alloy, and with other materials; Plato's text identifies it with nothing but its value, its colour, and its loss. Within the citadel stood the temple of Poseidon and Cleito, enclosed by a golden wall and never entered, and within it Poseidon's own temple, a stade in length, its exterior covered with silver and its pinnacles with gold, its interior roof of ivory worked with gold, silver, and orichalcum, and at its centre a statue of the god standing in a chariot drawn by six winged horses, his head touching the roof, ringed by a hundred Nereids on dolphins (116c–e, after Jowett). Around it stood golden statues of the ten kings and their wives, the altars, the palaces, the hot and cold baths, the grove of Poseidon, and — in the larger land ring — a racecourse for horses a stade wide running the ring's whole circuit. What the Image-World Does and Does Not Show Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on published archaeological, palaeoclimatic, and rock-art research, and where scholars disagree — as they do, fundamentally, about the chronology of Saharan rock art — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction. One famous modern construction does appear, in §VI, because it attached itself to these paintings in the twentieth century and cannot be honestly omitted from their history; it is labelled there for what it is, given one paragraph and no more, and its home in this archive is the Tier C division. The subject is the rock art of the central Sahara: the paintings in the sandstone shelters of the Tassili n'Ajjer in southeastern Algeria, the engravings cut into the black-varnished plateau of the Messak in southwestern Libya, the painted canyons of the Ennedi in northeastern Chad, and the shelters of the Gilf Kebir and Jebel Uweinat in Egypt's far southwest. Together these massifs hold tens of thousands of images — cattle by the thousand, elephants and giraffes and hippopotami, masked and floating human figures, hunters, herders, dancers, horsemen, camel riders, hand stencils, and beasts that match no living animal. They were made, in the main, while the Sahara was green: during the long wet interval climatologists call the African Humid Period, when monsoon rain reached hundreds of kilometres north of its modern limit, lakes filled basins that are now dust sources, and pastoral peoples spread across country that today supports almost no life at all. Dating honesty is this article's spine, and it is stated here so that nothing later needs to be taken back. Almost no Saharan panel is directly dated. The pigments are mostly mineral — iron oxides and manganese — and carry no radiocarbon clock of their own; the engravings are cuts in rock, and a cut has no date stamped in it. What the chronology of this art actually rests on, panel by panel and scheme by scheme, is indirect: one image lying over another (superimposition), the darkening of a surface with age (patina and desert varnish), the animals depicted and the periods when those animals are independently known to have lived in the region, and — rarely, and therefore precious — excavated deposits physically associated with a decorated stone. Every date offered in this article should be read with that scaffolding in mind. Where a scheme's dates are contested, the contest is printed beside them. This article is also the home, in this hub, of material that two companion articles invoke in passing. Nabta Playa and the Green Sahara treats the pastoral world of Egypt's Western Desert and gestures at the rock art of the wet Sahara as that world's picture of itself; The Nile Bridge weighs the Saharan contribution to predynastic Egypt. Both gestures land here. What follows is the image-world itself: its climate stage, its corpus, its great sites, its contested chronology, its methods, and — in §XII — an assessment of what it does and does not show, kept at exactly the strength the evidence has reached. I. The Climate Stage — The African Humid Period Every image in this article was made on a stage that no longer exists. The modern Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth, some nine million square kilometres in which the centre receives, in the Eastern Sahara synthesis discussed below, under 2 mm of rain a year against potential evaporation measured in thousands of millimetres. For most of the last glacial period the desert was, if anything, larger and harsher, and the central massifs stood empty or nearly so. Then the rains came back — not as a local accident, but as the regional expression of a planetary mechanism — and for roughly nine thousand years northern Africa carried grass, trees, rivers, and lakes where it now carries sand. The rock art is the human record of that interval. The interval itself must be understood first, on the climate evidence, before a single painting is allowed to testify. The Orbital Mechanism, Stated Plainly The driver is precession : the slow wobble of Earth's axis that moves the seasons around the planet's elliptical orbit on a cycle of roughly twenty-one thousand years. In the early Holocene, that geometry placed the Northern Hemisphere's summer close to perihelion — Earth's nearest approach to the Sun — and northern summer insolation rose to peak values on the order of eight percent above today's, as Peter deMenocal and colleagues set out in the marine-core study that still anchors the period's dating ( Quaternary Science Reviews 19, 2000). More summer heat over the North African landmass means a stronger contrast between hot land and cooler ocean, and a stronger contrast pulls the West African monsoon — the seasonal rain system that today waters the Sahel — far to the north of its modern limit. Rain that now falls on Mali and Niger fell, in the humid period's height, on the Hoggar, the Tassili, and the Fezzan. The mechanism is gradual; the climate's response, the records suggest, was not — vegetation and ocean feedbacks amplified the slow orbital push into comparatively abrupt transitions, a non-linearity that matters again at the period's end. DeMenocal's core — Ocean Drilling Program Site 658C, off Cap Blanc, Mauritania — works as a dust gauge: wind-blown sediment from the Sahara settles offshore, so the flux of land-derived material in the core tracks how much bare, eroding ground the desert presented to the wind. That flux is low from about 14,800 to 5,500 years ago , and those two numbers bracket what is now called the African Humid Period . Both transitions, in the core, are abrupt — accomplished within decades to centuries — and both occurred, on the authors' calculation, as summer insolation crossed a threshold about 4.2 percent above its present value. A dry interruption corresponding to the Younger Dryas punctuates the humid interval in the same record. These are the dates this article uses for the period as a whole: c. 14,800–5,500 BP — while noting at once that a bracket drawn from a marine core off Mauritania is a continental frame, not a local timetable, and that individual basins filled and emptied on their own schedules within it. // THE PERIOD // c. 14,800 – 5,500 BP The African Humid Period as bracketed by the ODP 658C dust record off Mauritania (deMenocal et al. 2000); onset and termination both abrupt in that record. // THE DRIVER // Precession + monsoon Northern summer near perihelion raised summer insolation c. 8% above present at peak; the West African monsoon was drawn hundreds of kilometres north. // LAKE MEGA-CHAD // c. 361,000 km² Reconstructed area of the great pluvial lake in the Chad Basin (Armitage et al. 2015) — for scale, larger than the modern Caspian's African rivals and among the largest lakes on Earth at the time. // OCCUPATION ONSET, EAST // c. 8500 BCE Sudden onset of humid conditions and settlement across the Eastern Sahara in the Kuper & Kröpelin radiocarbon synthesis of 150 excavations. A Watered Continent — Lakes, Rivers, Fauna The scale of the wet Sahara is easiest to grasp at its largest single feature. In the Chad Basin, south of the central massifs, shorelines and lake deposits record a water body the literature calls Lake Mega-Chad . Simon Armitage and colleagues, dating its shorelines and sediments by luminescence methods ( Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , 2015), reconstructed it at highstand at about 361,000 square kilometres in area and up to some 160 metres deep — very probably the largest lake on Earth at the time — against the few thousand square kilometres of the modern Lake Chad that is its shrunken remnant. Humid conditions appear in its basin by about 15,000 years ago; the lake reached its highstand by about 11,500 years ago and held it until about 5,000 years ago, when its level fell rapidly. Its northern basin, dry for roughly the last thousand years, is today the Bodélé Depression — one of the most productive dust sources on the planet, a neat emblem of the reversal. Mega-Chad was the giant, not the exception. Across the modern desert, the humid period filled playa basins like the one at Nabta Playa , sustained groundwater-fed lakes such as Lake Yoa in northern Chad — whose annually layered sediments give the eastern Sahara its finest continuous climate archive — and set rivers running down wadis that are now dry valleys: the Wadi Irawan system draining the Messak, the watercourses of the Tassili whose plateau name itself, in the usual rendering, means a plateau of rivers. The fauna followed the water. The lake and river deposits, the faunal assemblages from excavated camps, and — with the cautions of §X — the rock art itself agree on the cast: elephant, rhinoceros, giraffe, hippopotamus, crocodile, buffalo including the great extinct Pelorovis (the Bubalus of the older literature), warthog, antelopes and gazelles in variety, and the large predators behind them. This was savanna country of varying wetness — lush along the lakes and rivers, dry grassland between, always seasonal and always capable of failing — and not, anywhere in the central Sahara, a jungle. The qualification matters, because the art is sometimes recruited to prove a paradise. It proves a savanna, which is remarkable enough. People on the Stage — The Climate-Controlled Model The human timetable for the eastern half of this world was set by Rudolph Kuper and Stefan Kröpelin, synthesising radiocarbon dates from some 150 excavated sites across the Eastern Sahara of Egypt, Sudan, Libya, and Chad ( Science 313, 2006: 803–807). Their finding is stated in their title: occupation was climate-controlled . Settlement appears across the region with the sudden onset of humid conditions at about 8500 BCE ; it flourishes through the early and middle Holocene; and from about 5300 BCE a gradual desiccation drives a staged retreat — populations shifting southward toward the Sahel and eastward toward the Nile as the desert margin moves over their former ground. The authors drew the large conclusion plainly: that southward-shifting desert margin helped trigger the emergence of pharaonic civilisation along the Nile and influenced the spread of pastoralism across the continent — the argument this hub's Nile Bridge article examines from the Nile side. Two cautions keep the model at its real strength. The first is geographical: Kuper and Kröpelin's synthesis is an Eastern Sahara synthesis, built on excavated and dated occupation sites; the central massifs of this article lie at and beyond its western edge, and their occupation history — read mostly from the art and from sparser excavation — need not march in step with the eastern transect in every detail. The second is about the ending. Whether desiccation was abrupt, as the Mauritanian dust core and the Mega-Chad shorelines suggest, or gradual, as the Lake Yoa pollen succession suggests — humid ecosystems there giving way progressively between roughly 5,000 and 3,000 years ago (Kröpelin et al., Science , 2008) — remains a live question in the climate literature, and the honest answer is that both patterns may be true at different places: a system can cross a threshold quickly in one basin and unwind slowly in a groundwater-buffered lake a few hundred kilometres away. For the art, what matters is the direction, which no record disputes: after about 5,500 BP the wet world contracted, century by century, toward the desert of today, and the later imagery — horse, then camel — was made inside that contraction. // BP, BCE, AND THIS ARTICLE // The climate literature dates in BP (years before present, present conventionally 1950); the archaeological literature mixes BP and BCE. This article keeps each source's own scale when reporting it — deMenocal's bracket in BP, Kuper & Kröpelin's onset in BCE — and converts only where it says so. 5,500 BP is, roughly, 3550 BCE; the reader should treat all such conversions as approximations, because the sources themselves round. II. The Corpus — What Survives and What Does Not No complete inventory of Saharan rock art exists, and none is close. The counts that can be responsibly given are local: more than 15,000 drawings and engravings identified on the Tassili n'Ajjer alone, in UNESCO's figure; thousands of figures in the single shelter of Wadi Sura II; more than five hundred sites recorded by Gérard Bailloud in one-sixth of the Ennedi in a single pioneering survey. Summed across the central massifs — Tassili, Tadrart Acacus, Messak, Ennedi, Tibesti, Gilf Kebir, Uweinat, the Hoggar, the Aïr — the corpus runs to the tens of thousands of images the brief for this article describes, and every surveyor who has worked a new wadi has added to it. Digital enhancement is still adding to it without moving a stone: when photographs from one famous Tassili site were processed with the DStretch software that accentuates faint pigment, an inventory of 51 subjects recorded by Lhote's team expanded to 165, with figures appearing on walls previously thought blank (reported in Le Quellec's synthesis of the field). The corpus is not a closed canon. It is a sample, still growing, of an original production whose total size is unknowable. Two Media, Two Survivals The corpus divides by technique, and the division is a preservation filter before it is an artistic one. Engravings — images pecked, incised, or abraded into exposed rock surfaces: boulders, plateau pavements, the walls of wadis — are cut into the stone itself and survive as long as the surface does. The great engraved bestiaries of the Messak and of the Oued Djerat belong to this medium, their lines darkened or lightened against the surrounding varnish according to age and exposure. Paintings — pigment laid on the rock, in red and yellow ochres, white clays, black manganese and charcoal — survive only where the rock shelters them: under overhangs, in shallow caves, on walls protected from direct sun, rain-wash, and wind-blown sand. The Tassili's painted shelters, the Ennedi's painted canyons, and the Wadi Sura shelters are all, in this sense, accidents of geology — sandstone that happened to weather into roofs. The consequence is a double bias that every interpretation of this art must carry. First, the painted record is a shelter record: whatever was painted on open faces — and there is no reason to think nothing was — is gone, so the balance between painting and engraving in the surviving corpus says little about their balance in the living culture. Second, the surviving record is a stone record: images on wood, hide, bark, basketry, or skin — the portable art that ethnographic pastoralists produce in quantity — have perished entirely, along with any painting on mud, plaster, or tent leather. What the massifs preserve is the fraction of a visual culture that happened to be executed on durable rock in protected places. It is an enormous fraction, and it is still a fraction. Claims that begin "the Saharans depicted…" should silently continue "…on the rock that survives, in the places that sheltered it." ENGRAVINGS Pecked and incised images on exposed rock — wadi walls, boulders, plateau stone. Survival is a function of the surface: where desert varnish reforms over a cut line, the line can be read; where the surface spalls, the image goes with it. PAINTINGS Mineral pigments on sheltered walls — red and yellow ochre, white clay, black manganese and charcoal. Survival requires a roof. The painted corpus is therefore a map of sandstone shelters as much as of painters. STENCILS Hands — and, at Wadi Sura II, apparently not only hands (§VIII) — outlined by blowing pigment around them. A stencil preserves a body's outline at life size: the most indexical image in the corpus, and among the hardest to date. THE MISSING MEDIA Wood, hide, fibre, skin, and plaster leave no Saharan record. The rock corpus, however vast, is the durable residue of a visual culture whose portable majority is lost — a bias stated here and assumed throughout. Who Made It — The Standing Answer The makers were the hunter-gatherer and then pastoral populations of the humid Sahara: communities known independently from their camps, their burials, their pottery, their stone tools, and their herds, whose sequence the companion articles in this hub trace for the eastern desert. Nothing in the corpus requires any other authorship, and §VI will deal, in its place, with the one modern attempt to supply some. Within that plain answer, almost everything specific is inference. A painted cattle scene shows that its maker knew cattle intimately; it does not name the maker's language, ethnicity, or polity, and the older literature's habit of assigning each style to a distinct incoming "people" — a Bubalus people, a Round Head people — is one of the habits the critics of §V dismantled. Styles are evidence of communities of practice. They are not passports. The massifs treated in this article are a selection, made on the strength of their documentation. The Tassili (§III–VI) is the type-site of the whole field and the source of its classic chronology. The Ennedi (§VII) is its eastern-central giant, least excavated and most continuous into living tradition. The Gilf Kebir and Uweinat (§VIII) anchor the east and hold the corpus's most-discussed shelters. The Messak (§IX) holds its most important dated monuments. The neighbouring Tadrart Acacus in Libya — Fabrizio Mori's ground, and the Tassili's twin across an unnatural modern border — is treated here as part of the Tassili-Acacus world rather than given a section of its own; its evidence enters wherever the chronology debate requires it, which is often. III. Tassili n'Ajjer — The Plateau and Its Imagery The Tassili n'Ajjer is a sandstone plateau in southeastern Algeria, at the borders of Libya, Niger, and Mali, covering — in the boundaries of its World Heritage inscription — some 72,000 square kilometres. Tassili n Ajjer is a Tamahaq name, conventionally rendered "plateau of the Ajjer," for the Kel Ajjer Tuareg whose country this is. Erosion has cut the plateau into a landscape early visitors described in architectural metaphor and never improved on: "forests of stone," "rock cities" — freestanding towers and blocks of sandstone, deep gorges, natural arches by the hundred, and, in the sheltered hollows between the towers, the shallow rock shelters whose walls carry the paintings. Relict life survives in the gorges on a scale that itself testifies to the wetter past: permanent pools, a flora of hundreds of species, and the Saharan cypress, the tarout , among the rarest trees on Earth, growing nowhere else. The plateau was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 and as a Biosphere Reserve in 1986. UNESCO's summary remains the cleanest statement of the corpus: more than 15,000 drawings and engravings identified, recording — in the inscription's own framing — climatic changes, animal migrations, and the evolution of human life on the edge of the Sahara from about 6000 BCE to the first centuries of the present era. Two features of that framing deserve the reader's care. The start date is the conservative one the inscription adopted; claims for earlier beginnings are part of the chronology debate of §V, not a settled extension of it. And the phrase "drawings and engravings" conceals the plateau's true range: naturalistic animal studies of the first quality, vast multi-figure compositions, tiny schematic signs, masked figures, domestic scenes of camps and herds, chariots, inscriptions in Libyc and Tifinagh scripts running into the recent past — ten thousand years of image-making, by the longest schemes, stacked in the same shelters, often on the same walls. // THE PLATEAU // 72,000 km² inscribed Sandstone plateau in southeastern Algeria at the Libyan, Nigerien, and Malian borders; administrative centre for visitors at Djanet, on its southeastern edge. // THE COUNT // 15,000+ images Drawings and engravings identified to date (UNESCO) — a floor, not a total, as DStretch re-survey keeps demonstrating (§II). // KEY LOCALITIES // Sefar · Jabbaren · Tin Tazarift The great painted localities of the plateau's southeast, with the engraved gorge of the Oued Djerat — some 30 km of engravings — in the north. // PROTECTION // World Heritage 1982 National park from 1972; UNESCO World Heritage inscription 1982 (cultural and natural criteria); Biosphere Reserve 1986. The Imagery, Walked in Order of the Walls A reader meeting the Tassili corpus for the first time should begin where its makers' world is most legible: the animals. The engraved gorge of the Oued Djerat , in the plateau's north, carries along some thirty kilometres of wadi wall a bestiary in cut stone — elephants, rhinoceroses, giraffes, hippopotami where the wadi once held water, and the great buffalo Pelorovis antiquus with its sweeping horns, one famous panel showing the buffalo ringed by small dog-headed human figures, a composition to which §IX returns in its Messak context. The paintings add the herds: cattle in their hundreds in the pastoral scenes, shown horned and lyre-horned, piebald and solid, in camps, on the move, being milked, tethered at night lines — the most complete visual ethnography of early African pastoralism that exists anywhere, painted by the pastoralists themselves. The human imagery divides, even to an untrained eye, into two worlds. The later world is narrative and grounded: hunters with bows, herders with staffs, women and children in camps, warriors with shields, horsemen, camel riders — people with feet on an implied earth, doing recognisable things. The earlier world — the paintings classed, in the classic scheme, as Round Head — is stranger, and §V and §VI are devoted to it: large figures with smooth, featureless, globular heads, bodies that float or swim in empty space, arms raised, figures wearing what read as masks or elaborate coverings, beings of more than human scale attended by tiny humans, animals that match no species. Compositions in this manner lack the ground lines, landscapes, and backgrounds of the later scenes; figures hang in the rock's own field. It is the most distinctive painted manner in the whole Saharan corpus, and the least understood — a combination that has made it, as §VI records, a screen for other people's theories ever since it was first published. Between and around these worlds lie the plateau's quieter records: the Running Horned Woman of Aouanrhet — a graceful running female figure with horn-like projections, dots streaming from her body, found by Lhote's team in a secluded massif they took for a sanctuary — geometric signs, hand stencils, and the long tail of the tradition running through horse and camel imagery to Tifinagh inscriptions of the historic Tuareg world. The Tassili's claim on the world's attention is not any single panel. It is density sustained over millennia in one walkable landscape: no other place on Earth lets a visitor read so much of a prehistoric image-world in so few days' travel — which is precisely why the fight over how to order that world in time, taken up in §V, has been so long and so consequential. IV. Lhote and the Copying Enterprise — Historiography The Tassili's art was never lost. The Kel Ajjer knew the shelters; what happened in the twentieth century was not discovery but publication — the transfer of the paintings from local knowledge into the European archive — and the manner of that transfer shaped everything the world has since thought about them. This section tells it as historiography: who copied what, by what methods, with what consequences, because in this field the copies are themselves primary documents, and some of the most famous "Tassili paintings" in circulation are, in part, documents of 1956 rather than of the Holocene. From Brenans to the 1956–57 Expedition The first systematic European recording was military. Between 1933 and 1940, Lieutenant Charles Brenans , a French camel-corps officer, sketched and noted dozens of sites in the plateau's canyons and deposited his records with the Bardo Museum in Algiers, whence they reached the great prehistorian Henri Breuil in Paris. Brenans also guided the young Henri Lhote — explorer, ethnographer, and Breuil's protégé — to the plateau, travelling with Kel Ajjer guides whose knowledge located the art. Lhote returned repeatedly — in 1956–57, 1959, 1962, and 1970 — but it is the first great expedition that fixed the Tassili in the world's imagination: sixteen months in 1956–57, a team of artists and copyists working shelter by shelter, producing hundreds of full-size copies of painted walls. Exhibited in Paris at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in 1957–58, the copies caused a sensation among artists and scientists alike; Lhote's book, À la découverte des fresques du Tassili (1958; in English, The Search for the Tassili Frescoes , 1959), became the field's founding popular text and remains the source from which most general readers, and most later writers, have taken their Tassili. The achievement was real, and this article records it at full strength before the audit: the expeditions inventoried a corpus of world importance that might otherwise have faded unrecorded, established the plateau's protection trajectory — national park, World Heritage, biosphere reserve — and gave scholarship a first corpus to argue about. Without the copies, there is no debate in §V, because there is no shared body of images to debate. Every later worker in the central Sahara, including Lhote's sharpest critics, has worked downstream of the enterprise of 1956–57. The Copies as Documents — and the Damage Debate The audit, stated factually and without relish, has three heads. First, the recording method damaged originals. To make faint paintings legible for tracing and photography, the team routinely wetted the walls — Lhote's own narrative describes setting out with a can of water and a sponge — and in places traced or heightened lines directly. Wetting raises pigment colour dramatically for a few minutes and accelerates its flaking and fading thereafter; repeated wetting by later visitors, following the pioneers' example, compounded the loss. Modern assessments, including Jeremy Keenan's severe retrospective in Antiquity (2002), describe the practice in the vocabulary of vandalism; the factual core beneath the vocabulary — walls washed, colours brightened for the copy at the original's expense, archaeological material collected and removed in quantity from the shelters — is not seriously disputed, and its worst cost is scientific: surface material that might one day have carried datable organic traces was, in places, washed or handled away before the questions that needed it had been formulated (§XI). Second, the copies are interpretations. A full-size hand copy is a reading: the copyist decides where a faded line runs, what counts as figure and what as stain, and — in documented instances in this corpus — completes or sharpens what the wall only suggests. Some of the most widely reproduced Tassili images owe part of their crispness and drama to the copy rather than the original, and at least a few figures published from the expeditions have been alleged, by named critics from the 1960s onward, to be modern additions or jokes worked into the record. The allegations attach to specific figures, not to the corpus; they have never been shown to touch its great majority; and the correct scholarly response — the one the field has in fact adopted — is neither to discard the copies nor to trust them blindly, but to treat each as a document requiring verification against the wall, exactly as §XI describes modern re-recording doing, with photography and DStretch where the pioneers used sponge and tracing paper. Third, the naming did interpretive work. Lhote was a romantic writer of genuine gifts, and his names — the "Great God," the "Horned Goddess," the joking "Martians" for the Round Head figures — taught the public how to see the paintings before scholars had agreed on what they were. §VI follows one of those names into its long afterlife. The point here is archival: in the Tassili literature, the layer of 1950s mediation — copies, names, and narrative — lies between every modern reader and the walls, and honest work in the field consists largely of keeping that layer visible. That is the spirit in which Lhote is cited in this article's Sources: as historiography — the indispensable, compromised record of how this corpus entered the world's knowledge — and not as a dating authority. // THE TUAREG ERASURE // One further count in the modern audit belongs in the text, not the margin. The expeditions' published narratives centred the European "discoverer" and treated the Kel Ajjer guides — without whom the shelters would not have been found, reached, or survived in — as auxiliaries, in language Keenan's critique quotes to the record's discredit; the Swiss ethnologist Yolande Tschudi, whose Tassili work preceded Lhote's, went unacknowledged in his discovery claims. The paintings' first custodians were the plateau's own people. This article's phrasing throughout — the art was published, not discovered — is deliberate. V. The Classic Periodisation and Its Critics Every account of Saharan rock art, this one included, must organise tens of thousands of undated images into some order, and the order the world inherited is the classic periodisation : a succession of five great manners, each named for its signature subject, marching from wild fauna to the modern desert's animal. The scheme grew from the work of the pioneers — Breuil, Lhote, and Fabrizio Mori in the Acacus — and was consolidated in the grand synthesis of Paul Huard and Jean Leclant in the 1970s. It is presented here in full, because it remains the field's shared vocabulary; and it is presented, as the brief for this article requires, as a scheme — a scholarly instrument with named critics and a revised successor — and never as settled chronology. Classic Period Signature Imagery Dates in the Huard–Leclant Form Standing Bubalus / Wild Fauna Large naturalistic engravings of wild animals, above all the extinct buffalo Pelorovis antiquus ; hunters c. 10,000–8,000 BCE Recast by Muzzolini as a style rather than a period, overlapping later manners; its great antiquity unproven Round Head Painted figures with large, featureless globular heads; floating bodies; masked and superhuman-scale beings c. 6,500–4,000 BCE The scheme's problem child: unity, date, and even coherence as a single manner all contested (§V, below) Pastoral / Bovidian Cattle herds, camps, milking, domestic life; sheep and goats join the repertoire c. 4,000–1,500 BCE Subdivided by Muzzolini into multiple regional nuclei; the pastoral florescence itself undisputed, its internal order debated Horse / Caballine Horses, chariots, mounted warriors; giraffe and cattle persist in a drying land c. 1,500 BCE – 0 Broadly accepted as a horizon: the horse is a datable introduction, though its first Saharan appearances are argued site by site Camel / Cameline Dromedary caravans and riders, increasingly schematic figures, Tifinagh inscriptions from c. 0 onward Accepted as the final horizon; its beginning is placed anywhere from the early centuries CE to, in Le Quellec's central-Saharan revision, c. the 5th century CE Dates as summarised in Le Quellec's review of the classic scheme. Other presentations of the same scheme — the British Museum's African Rock Art chronology among them — assign the periods different spans (Wild Fauna 12,000–8,000 BP, Round Head 10,000–8,000 BP, Pastoral 7,500–4,000 BP, Horse 3,000–2,000 BP, Camel 2,000 BP–present). The variation between presentations of a single scheme is itself part of the evidence for how soft its absolute dates are. What the Scheme Got Right The periodisation endures because its relative order is anchored in observation. Where images overlap on a wall, the pastoral manner does overlie the wilder manners, and horse and camel imagery does sit latest in the superimposition sequences; the faunal succession the scheme encodes — wild megafauna, then cattle, then horse, then camel — matches the independently known ecological succession of the drying Sahara (§X). As a first map of a vast corpus, drawn by scholars who had walked the massifs when no map existed, it was a formidable achievement, and its terms remain the only ones in which specialists from different schools can reliably understand one another. What failed, under audit, was not the map's outline but its legend: the absolute dates hung on each period, the assumption that each manner was one period, and the peoples marched in behind each style. Muzzolini's Revision — The Short Chronology The audit began in earnest with Alfred Muzzolini , whose L'art rupestre préhistorique des massifs centraux sahariens (1986) subjected the classic scheme to the archaeological record it had largely floated free of. His principal findings, as Le Quellec's later synthesis fairly summarises them: there was no consistent archaeological basis for the single vast hunting culture the Huard–Leclant narrative had imagined behind the early art; the Bubaline was more a style than a period , one that could still have been in use when pastoralists were already working in other manners — which dissolves the neat succession of the table above into overlapping regional practices; and the Bovidian was not one manner but several stylistic and cultural nuclei, whose separate delineation offered the only credible route to a finer chronology. The systematic result was a short (or recent) chronology : central Saharan rock art, on Muzzolini's argument, emerges around 5000 BCE — not in the terminal Pleistocene, not twelve thousand
