What Sahul Shows — An Assessment Sources This is a Tier A article: everything in it rests on excavated, dated, and published archaeological, palaeoecological, and genetic evidence, and where scholars disagree — as they do, sharply, about the age of Madjedbebe and the cause of the megafaunal extinctions — the disagreement itself is reported with its positions attributed. No claim here depends on ancient legend or modern construction, and none is allowed to borrow strength from either. One date in this article, the c. 65,000 BP occupation of Madjedbebe, is presented throughout as what it is in the literature: a published claim with published critics and published replies, not a settled fact. Sahul is the name archaeologists give to the Pleistocene continent formed, at low sea level, by Australia, New Guinea, and Tasmania joined in a single landmass. It was never joined to Asia. Between Sahul and the Asian mainland shelf of Sunda lay Wallacea, an archipelago of deep-water islands separated by straits that no fall in sea level ever closed. Whoever first reached Sahul therefore crossed open sea — repeatedly, over legs measured in tens of kilometres — and did so earlier than any other securely evidenced sea crossing anywhere in the world. That single geographical fact makes the peopling of Sahul a founding event in the history of seafaring, and its date a founding question in the history of our species. What followed the crossing was not a visit but an occupation without interruption. Within a few thousand years of the earliest dates, people were living in the highlands of New Guinea, on the continent's southwestern and southeastern coasts, in its arid interior, and across the cold plain that is now Bass Strait, in Tasmania. They ground seed and ochre, hafted edge-ground axes, painted rock walls, cremated and ochre-buried their dead in ceremonies among the earliest ritual burials known anywhere, and lived alongside — and, on one contested body of evidence, preyed upon — the giant marsupials and birds of the Pleistocene continent. This article walks that record in order: the continent, the crossing, the contested first date, the spread, the art, the burials, the extinctions, and the fire — and it closes where the archaeology itself closes, with continuity: the deep past documented here is the deep past of the world's oldest continuous living culture, and it is written about in that knowledge throughout. I. A Continent Joined — Sahul, Sunda, and the Sea Between Begin with the map as it was, not as it is. Through most of the last hundred thousand years, global sea level stood far below its present stand — by roughly 120 metres or more at the Last Glacial Maximum, and by several tens of metres at the time of the first crossing, around 65,000–50,000 years ago. Land now drowned stood dry. In the west, the Malay Peninsula ran unbroken into Sumatra, Java, and Borneo: that exposed shelf continent is Sunda , and a traveller from mainland Asia could walk its whole length. In the east and south, Australia, New Guinea, and Tasmania stood as one: New Guinea joined to the Australian mainland across the plain now drowned by the Torres Strait and the Gulf of Carpentaria — where a great enclosed lake, Lake Carpentaria, occupied the gulf's basin at low stands — and Tasmania joined to Victoria across the broad, cold Bassian Plain now beneath Bass Strait. That joined continent is Sahul , roughly a third again as large as modern Australia alone, much of the addition being the now-submerged shelves off its northern and northwestern coasts — the first country the voyagers landed on, and country no archaeologist can excavate, a loss this hub treats in Drowned Landscapes . // THE CONTINENT // Sahul Australia, New Guinea, and Tasmania joined at low sea level, with the northern and northwestern shelves dry land. // THE WESTERN SHELF // Sunda Mainland Southeast Asia joined to Sumatra, Java, and Borneo — walkable from Asia to its eastern shore. // BETWEEN THEM // Wallacea Sulawesi, the Lesser Sundas, the Moluccas, Timor: deep-water islands never joined to either continent. // THE CROSSING // Always by sea Even at the lowest sea levels, reaching Sahul required multiple open-water legs, the longest modelled at c. 90–100 km. Between Sunda and Sahul lay the islands that belong to neither: Wallacea , named for Alfred Russel Wallace, whose line — running between Bali and Lombok and between Borneo and Sulawesi — marks the great faunal boundary between the animals of Asia and the animals of Australasia. Wallacea's islands are separated from each other and from both shelves by straits cut through deep water. That depth is the decisive fact of this entire article. The shelves of Sunda and Sahul are shallow, and a fall of a hundred metres joins them to their continents; the Wallacean straits are hundreds of metres deep, and no Pleistocene sea-level fall — not even the maximum of the last glaciation — ever drained them. There was never a land bridge to Sahul. Not at 65,000 years ago, not at 20,000, not ever, in the whole span of human existence. The first Australians did not walk in, and they did not drift in on a shoreline that later sank beneath them as a causeway. They crossed water. How much water is a question of route and of date, because the legs shorten as sea level falls and the exposed shelves widen. The modelling literature (§V) converges on the shape of the answer even where it argues about the route: a voyage to Sahul meant a chain of crossings through Wallacea — a series of island hops, most of them in the range of roughly 20–30 km, with at least one long final leg to the Sahul shore. For the southern route, from Timor or Roti to the then-emergent islands of the Sahul Banks off the northwest coast, that final leg is modelled at about 87–100 km even with the shelf exposed. For the northern route, through Sulawesi and the northern Moluccas to the Bird's Head of New Guinea, the individual legs are generally shorter but more numerous. Either way, the minimum statement is the one the geography forces: at the lowest sea levels of the age, the shortest single crossings between Wallacean islands and the Sahul coast ran to several tens of kilometres of open sea, and the full passage required making such a crossing not once but repeatedly, island after island, and then doing it with enough people, arriving alive together, to found a population. A single castaway does not colonise a continent. The genetics and the demographic modelling (§V) both say the founding was plural. Two consequences follow, and they organise everything after this section. First, the peopling of Sahul is the earliest well-evidenced episode of deliberate open-water voyaging in the world — earlier, on any dating, than the settlement of the Mediterranean islands or the crossing to the Americas' offshore worlds — and the hub treats its technology and seamanship in the companion article Early Seafaring , to which this article defers on watercraft and defers gladly: no Pleistocene boat from Wallacea survives, and what can be said rests on the modelling and the geography, not on a hull. Second, because the landing coasts themselves are now under the sea, the archaeological record of the occupation begins inland , at the oldest surviving sites on the raised ground — and the oldest and most argued-over of those sites is a sandstone shelter on the western edge of the Arnhem Land plateau, in Mirarr Country in what is now the Northern Territory: Madjedbebe. II. Madjedbebe — The Shelter on the Arnhem Land Escarpment Madjedbebe — spelled Malakunanja II in the earlier literature, a name the reader will meet in every paper before 2017 — is a rock shelter at the foot of the Arnhem Land escarpment, at approximately 12°30′ S, 132°53′ E, some twenty metres above sea level, near the modern town of Jabiru and the edge of Kakadu National Park. The shelter sits in Mirarr Country , and the modern excavations were conducted in formal partnership with the Gundjeihmi Aboriginal Corporation, the Mirarr traditional owners exercising, in the excavators' own reporting, significant operational control over the research on their land. That partnership is not a courtesy detail. It is part of the site's modern history, and it stands in deliberate contrast to the older history of Australian archaeology — including the removal of the Mungo ancestors told in §IX — in which excavation proceeded without the consent of the people whose past was being excavated. The shelter's deposits are sands: a basal unit of culturally sterile orange sand, overlain by the occupation deposits — a pink sand unit carrying the lowest artefacts, grading upward into brown sands and, at the top, a Holocene midden rich in shell and bone. The site was excavated first in 1973, and then in 1989 by a team associated with Rhys Jones, whose excavation recovered more than 1,500 stone artefacts from the lowest levels, together with silcrete flakes, ground ochre, and a grindstone. The sediments around those lowest artefacts were dated by thermoluminescence to around 60,000–50,000 years ago — but with total uncertainties of 16,000–20,000 years, and the claim that Madjedbebe was Australia's oldest site, at perhaps 60,000 years, was contested from the moment it was made: critics questioned whether the artefacts had stayed where they were dropped, in loose sand subject to disturbance, and whether they truly belonged with the dated grains around them. Two of the 1989 sediment samples were later re-dated by the then-new single-grain OSL method, and those ages supported the early chronology — but the argument did not close. It waited, for more than twenty years, on a better excavation. The better excavation came in 2012 and 2015, when a team led by Chris Clarkson of the University of Queensland — with dating specialists Zenobia Jacobs and Richard Roberts, lithics specialist Richard Fullagar, and a large interdisciplinary team — opened twenty 1 × 1 m squares adjacent to and enclosing the earlier trenches, digging to a maximum depth of 3.4 m. The scale of recording is the first thing to grasp, because the whole later debate turns on it: the three-dimensional coordinates of approximately 11,000 artefacts and other features — hearths, burials, pits — were recorded individually, and samples were collected throughout for dating, geoarchaeology, and plant-remains analysis. The artefacts were not spread evenly through the sand. They were concentrated in three dense bands , separated by sparser deposits, and each band carried its own raw-material and technological character — the stratigraphic pattern of repeated occupation episodes, not of a churned deposit in which everything has slid together. The lowest dense band, designated phase 2, lay at 2.60–2.15 m depth and contained an in situ hearth. It is the contents of that band, and the age of the sand that holds it, on which the claim of §III stands. The Lowest Assemblage — What Was in the Sand The phase 2 assemblage is made mostly from quartzite, silcrete, mudstone, and dolerite, and its inventory matters as much as its age, because it is not the toolkit of a shipwrecked handful but a full occupation assemblage. It includes flakes and cores of several forms, among them faceted discoidal cores and thinning flakes; whole and fragmentary edge-ground hatchets — axes whose cutting edge had been shaped by grinding, a technology then unknown anywhere in the world at anything like this age; grinding stones , including stones used for grinding seed; ground ochre , including a ground ochre "crayon" and pieces of ground yellow ochre found with fragments of sheet mica wrapped around them — mica being a reflective additive, ground ochre mixed or accompanied by a substance whose only evident purpose is to make the pigment glitter; and residue and macrofossil evidence for the use of fuel wood and a range of plant foods — seeds, tubers, and Pandanus nuts — from the eucalyptus and monsoon vine-thicket country around the shelter. Later specialist study of the grinding stones (Hayes and colleagues, 2022) traced grinding-stone use at the site continuously through the sequence, and archaeobotanical work (Florin and colleagues, 2021) documented changing plant-food use across the full span the excavators claim for the site. Read at face value, then, the lowest band at Madjedbebe contains, together: the world's oldest known edge-ground axe technology; seed-grinding; and pigment prepared with a reflective additive — grinding, hafting, and ochre, the three threads this article follows through Warratyi (§VI), the painted Kimberley (§VIII), and the ochre burials of Lake Mungo (§IX) — present, together, in the first occupation layer of the continent's most discussed site. Everything depends, therefore, on the age of the sand. The next section gives the dating programme the space it needs, because at Madjedbebe the method is the argument. // WHY THIS SHELTER, OF ALL SHELTERS // Madjedbebe's claim does not rest on its being uniquely old in kind — other northern sites, Nauwalabila among them, have carried early claims of their own — but on the conjunction of depth, density, and dating effort: a thick sand deposit at the escarpment foot, occupied repeatedly, in which the lowest artefact band could be excavated afresh, piece-plotted artefact by artefact, and dated by dozens of OSL samples through the profile. Sites that might be older exist on the drowned shelves and cannot be dug. Madjedbebe is the oldest claim that can be tested — which is precisely why it, and not a quieter site, carries the argument. III. Dating Madjedbebe — OSL as Procedure, and the 65,000-Year Claim Radiocarbon cannot reach Madjedbebe's lowest levels: beyond roughly 50,000 years, too little carbon-14 survives in any sample for the method to return a finite age, and the basal deposits in any case hold little dateable charcoal. The 2017 chronology therefore rests on optically stimulated luminescence — OSL — and the method must be understood as a procedure, not invoked as a label, because every later criticism of the site is a criticism of what OSL does and does not date. OSL, Step by Step Quartz sand grains are natural dosimeters. Ionising radiation from the surrounding sediment — from the decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the deposit, and from cosmic rays — steadily knocks electrons in the quartz crystal into trapped states, where they accumulate for as long as the grain lies buried in darkness. Sunlight empties the traps: a grain exposed to daylight on a surface is, in the jargon, bleached — its clock reset to zero. The procedure follows from the physics. Sediment samples are collected in the field in opaque tubes, so that no light reaches them after collection. In the laboratory, under controlled low light, individual quartz grains are stimulated with light and the luminescence they emit is measured: the brightness records the burial dose , the total radiation the grain absorbed since it was last bleached — that is, since it was last on a sunlit surface and was then buried. Separately, the dose rate of the surrounding sediment is measured — how much radiation the deposit delivers per thousand years. Age is the quotient: burial dose divided by dose rate gives the time since the grain was last exposed to sunlight. At Madjedbebe, the team dated the sediments by single-grain OSL : thousands of grains measured one by one, so that grains whose doses betray disturbance, incomplete bleaching, or intrusion can be identified statistically rather than averaged invisibly into a bulk age — the refinement that had already, in its early form, supported the 1989 chronology, and that the 2017 programme applied at a scale of dozens of samples through the profile, with ages combined in a Bayesian stratigraphic model that uses the known order of the layers to constrain the age of each. What OSL dates, stated exactly, is the sand : the last sunlight exposure of the grains among which the artefacts lie. It does not date the artefacts themselves. The inference from sediment age to occupation age therefore carries a load-bearing assumption — that the artefacts and the dated grains entered the deposit together and have stayed together. If artefacts sank, were trampled down, or were carried down by burrowing creatures into older sand, OSL would faithfully return the age of the older sand and the association would be false. The Clarkson team's paper is best read as two arguments bolted together: a dating argument, that the phase 2 sands were last bleached around 65,000 years ago; and an integrity argument, that the phase 2 artefacts belong in those sands. The first argument has attracted little direct attack. The second is where the fight of §IV takes place. The Integrity Argument — Refits, Hearths, and Trampling The integrity argument, as published, has three main timbers. First, refitting : broken silcrete artefacts whose pieces could be fitted back together were found within the dense bands — fourteen refits in the lower band and three in the middle band — and none between bands ; the median vertical distance between refitted pieces was 10.6 cm. If the deposit had been churned over metres, conjoining pieces would be scattered across bands; they are not. Second, patterning : there is no size-sorting of artefacts with depth — small pieces are not systematically deeper than large ones, as gravity-driven sinking through loose sand would tend to produce — burnt artefacts concentrate in the dense bands rather than between them, and an intact hearth survived in phase 2, a feature that wholesale disturbance would be expected to disperse. Third, experiment : the team ran modern trampling experiments at the site, walking over artefacts laid on the surface, and measured how far trampling actually moves pieces in this sand — movement of the order of centimetres to about ten centimetres, consistent with the refit distances and far short of the distances required to carry a younger assemblage down into 65,000-year-old sand. On these three timbers the team concluded that post-depositional vertical movement at Madjedbebe is restricted to roughly ten centimetres, that the three dense bands are genuine occupation horizons, and that the phase 2 band lies in sand dated to about 65,000 years ago. The published conclusion, in the paper's own abstract (Clarkson et al., Nature 547 (2017): 306–310), is that human occupation at Madjedbebe "began around 65,000 years ago," with the distinctive assemblage of §II, and that the evidence sets a new minimum age for the arrival of humans in Australia and for the dispersal of modern humans out of Africa. The claim landed with corresponding force. It pushed the peopling of Sahul some fifteen thousand years earlier than the previously secure floor of about 50,000 years; it placed people in Australia while Neanderthals and Denisovans still lived across Asia (§VII); it lengthened the overlap between people and megafauna (§X); and it implied a dispersal out of Africa early enough to sit awkwardly with the then-standard genetic chronologies of that dispersal. A claim that rearranges four debates at once invites examination in all four. The examination arrived the following year, and §IV gives it in full — because a Tier A article does not protect its most interesting claim from its critics. Element The Madjedbebe Programme, as Published Excavation 2012 and 2015 seasons; twenty 1 × 1 m squares enclosing the 1973 and 1989 trenches; maximum depth 3.4 m Recording Three-dimensional coordinates for c. 11,000 artefacts and features (hearths, burials, pits) Structure Artefacts concentrated in three dense bands; lowest band (phase 2) at 2.60–2.15 m, with an in situ hearth Dating Single-grain OSL on the sediments through the profile, with radiocarbon in the upper levels; ages combined in a Bayesian stratigraphic model Integrity tests Refits within bands only (median vertical separation 10.6 cm); no size-sorting with depth; intact hearth; modern trampling experiments Claim Occupation began c. 65,000 years ago (Clarkson et al. 2017) Challenge An age over 50,000 years judged unlikely (O'Connell et al. 2018) — see §IV IV. The Challenge — O'Connell et al. 2018, and the Replies The critique appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in August 2018: James O'Connell, Jim Allen, and seven colleagues, "When did Homo sapiens first reach Southeast Asia and Sahul?" ( PNAS 115 (2018): 8482–8490). Its frame is the whole arc from South China to Sahul, and its conclusion about Madjedbebe is stated without softening: reviewing the regional evidence, the authors find that an age estimate of more than 50,000 years for the site "is unlikely to be valid," and that the data offered in support of a pre-55,000-year dispersal of modern humans through the region are not compelling. The paper's positive position is that anatomically modern humans spread from Africa in the main at about 50,000–55,000 years ago, and that Sahul was reached within that movement — the chronology the genetic evidence, on their reading, independently favours. The Site-Formation Argument The heart of the critique is not the OSL physics but the sand. Madjedbebe sits in a regionally extensive sand sheet in a tropical environment of pronounced wet and dry seasons, and O'Connell and colleagues catalogue the post-depositional processes such substrates undergo: rain-splash erosion, subsurface washing (eluviation), creep — and, most notably, bioturbation by termites . Termites move sediment on a vast scale in northern Australia; their abandoned galleries collapse and vanish, leaving little visible trace in a sand profile, while the processes as a whole, on the extensive geomorphological literature the authors cite, facilitate the downward movement of stones — including artefacts — into deeper, older deposits. An artefact that has sunk a metre through bioturbated sand will sit among grains OSL dates to 65,000 years, and no measurement of the grains can expose the substitution. The authors press the precedent of Nauwalabila , another Arnhem Land sand site where early claims beyond 50,000 years were abandoned once the effects of such disturbance were demonstrated — a site, they argue, whose fate Madjedbebe's may repeat. They further dispute particulars: the purported occupation "pit" in phase 2 is read as a dripline gutter worn by water falling from the shelter's edge; and they note what they present as an inconsistency in the excavators' handling of the deposits below phase 2 — the phase 1 artefacts, which the Clarkson team itself attributed to post-depositional settling from above. If settling explains the artefacts beneath the claimed horizon, the critics ask, why may it not explain the horizon itself? The Replies The excavators' defence, in their responses and in the team's subsequent work, returns to the three timbers of §III and adds a fourth: specificity. Refits do not cross bands; there is no size-sorting; hearths survive intact; trampling experiments bound the movement that feet can cause. Against the termite mechanism specifically, the reply is that a mechanism possible in tropical sands generally must still be shown at this site, in this profile — and that the Madjedbebe profile lacks the diagnostic products the mechanism leaves where it has operated at scale. That point was later examined independently: a geoarchaeological assessment of how termite stone lines can be distinguished from genuine artefact horizons (Ward and colleagues), taking Madjedbebe and Nauwalabila as its case studies, concluded that neither site contains a termite stone line — while cautioning that both sites have complex formation histories and that bioturbation must be treated as part of every tropical site's sedimentary history, not waved away. The team's positive programme continued in parallel: residue and use-wear studies of the Madjedbebe grinding stones reported continuous grinding-stone use across the claimed 65,000-year span (Hayes et al. 2022), and the archaeobotanical sequence was published as a record of plant-food use running from the earliest levels (Florin et al. 2021) — work that presupposes the chronology and so cannot independently prove it, but that deepens the assemblage the chronology carries. Later syntheses by participants on both sides (Allen and O'Connell's subsequent reviews among them) have continued to argue the matter at the level of the whole regional dataset — how many sites, dated how well, must exceed 50,000 years before the floor itself moves. // THE VERDICT THIS ARTICLE PRINTS // This archive does not declare a winner, because the literature has not. The position stated here is the one the evidence, as published, supports: Madjedbebe's c. 65,000 BP occupation is the earliest widely discussed date for the peopling of Sahul, advanced by a large, well-published dating and integrity programme, and contested at its edges — the contest turning not on the OSL ages of the sand, which few dispute, but on whether the lowest artefacts belong with the sand that dates them. The uncontested floor, accepted by the critics themselves, is an occupation of northern Australia by about 50,000 years ago. Between that floor and the 65,000-year claim lies fifteen thousand years of live scientific argument, reported here as argument — with the excavators' tests, the critics' mechanisms, and the independent geoarchaeological assessment all on the record. Readers who meet the 65,000-year figure elsewhere stated as simple fact, or dismissed as simple error, are meeting advocacy, not the literature. V. The Crossing — Routes Through Wallacea However the Madjedbebe argument settles, the crossing itself is not in doubt — only its date within a range and its route within a pair. The framework was set in 1977 by Joseph Birdsell, who mapped the possible passages from Sunda to Sahul as two families of routes. The northern route runs from Borneo across to Sulawesi, then east through the northern Moluccas — the islands of the Sula and Banggai chains, Buru, Seram and their neighbours in the various reconstructions — to a landfall on the western end of New Guinea, around the Bird's Head and the island of Misool. The southern route runs along the Lesser Sunda chain — Bali, Lombok, Flores, Alor — to Timor or Roti, and then across the long final leg to the exposed Sahul shelf off what is now the Kimberley coast of northwestern Australia. Every later model is a refinement, a re-costing, or a re-dating of Birdsell's pair. The debate is not whether people island-hopped through Wallacea; it is which chain they hopped, and the two chains make different predictions — a northern entry peopling New Guinea first and Australia from the north-east, a southern entry landing directly on the Australian northwest — that the distribution and dating of the earliest sites might, in principle, decide. Least-Cost Modelling — Kealy, Louys, and O'Connor The most cited modern treatment is the least-cost pathway modelling of Shimona Kealy, Julien Louys, and Sue O'Connor ( Journal of Human Evolution 125 (2018): 59–70). Extending earlier out-of-Africa least-cost models through Wallacea, the authors digitised Birdsell's routes and costed movement across reconstructed landscapes at 65,000 and 70,000 years ago — costing slope, visibility between islands, access to fresh water, and the difficulty of each sea leg. Their result was emphatic: the models recover overwhelming support for the northern route , with a landing on present-day Misool Island at the western end of New Guinea, and only minimal support for a southern crossing — recovered in the 70,000-year models as a possible passage from eastern Timor. Two riders in the paper deserve the emphasis the authors gave them. The northern Wallacean islands crossed by the favoured route are, archaeologically, among the least explored in the region: the model points at a map gap, not at a confirmed chain of camps. And the better-studied southern islands, Timor included, have produced no occupation dates comparable in age to the earliest dates claimed for Sunda and Sahul — an absence that cuts against the southern route as the first passage, though absence on islands whose Pleistocene coasts are drowned is, as always in this region, weaker evidence than it looks. Voyage Modelling — Timor, Drift, and Intent The southern route has its own modelling defence. Bird and colleagues ( Quaternary Science Reviews 191 (2018): 431–439), working from new bathymetry and drift modelling, showed that from about 70,000 to 10,000 years ago a chain of habitable, resource-rich islands stood emergent off the northwest Sahul coast — now mostly submerged — visible from high points near the Timor–Roti coast and as close as about 87 km. Accidental drift arrival from Timor–Roti was improbable at any period, they found; but purposeful voyages in the summer monsoon were very likely to succeed, over four to seven days. The demographic evidence points the same way: genomic estimates of the founding population — put by the modelling literature at figures of the order of a thousand or more founders for long-term viability, and in the Timor study's citation at more than 72–100 individuals at minimum — are taken to indicate deliberate, repeated colonisation rather than a single accidental rafting. Bird, Bradshaw, and colleagues ( Scientific Reports 9 (2019): 8220), combining coastal viewshed analysis — which islands can be seen from which, building on the intervisibility work associated with Kasih Norman and colleagues on both route families — with ocean drift modelling and population projection, put a number on the accident hypothesis: the probability of reaching Sahul by random drift is below five per cent unless at least forty adults are washed off an island at least once every twenty years, whereas choosing a departure time and making even minimal headway — half a knot — toward a destination transforms the odds. Their conclusion, that the settlement of Sahul was not an accident and that its people could plan and make open-sea voyages lasting several days by at least 50,000 years ago, is now the modelling mainstream — with arrival via New Guinea judged more likely than via northwestern Australia in their runs, and later continental-scale simulations (Bradshaw and colleagues, 2021) finding the southern entry through Timor potentially dominant in the peopling of the continent's interior. The models, in short, agree on intent and disagree on the door. What kind of craft made the crossings, this article does not speculate beyond the literature: no Wallacean watercraft survives from the Pleistocene, and the candidates canvassed in the seafaring literature — bamboo rafts, bark and bundled-reed craft, dugouts — are assessed in Early Seafaring . Two fixed points may be stated here. The crossings were made by people whose descendants, within the span of the earliest sites, were grinding seed, hafting axes, and working ochre (§II): the voyagers were not a marginal population but a fully equipped one. And the route passed the painted caves of Sulawesi — whose art, dated to at least 51,200 years for a narrative scene at Leang Karampuang, is treated in this hub's Ochre and Symbol and is not re-treated here: it is enough to register that the corridor to Sahul was itself inhabited and painted by the people, or the close kin of the people, who made the crossing. Sahul was not reached from an artless world. It was reached from a world already making images — which is the world §VIII finds waiting, in paint, on the far shore. VI. The Spread — Interior, South Coast, and the Plain to Tasmania A landing is not a continent. The second fact of Sahul's occupation — after the crossing itself — is the speed and completeness with which the whole landmass was taken up. By about 50,000 years ago, on dates accepted across the Madjedbebe argument by both sides, occupation is attested in the highlands of New Guinea, where the Ivane Valley sites (Kosipe and its neighbours) place people in mountain country at roughly 49,000–44,000 years ago; on the far southwestern coast, at Boodie Cave on Barrow Island and at Devil's Lair near the Leeuwin coast, both carrying occupation around 50,000–48,000 years ago; in the southeast, where the Willandra Lakes record (§IX) begins around 50,000–46,000 years ago; and across the north, where Madjedbebe's contested claim stands at the head of a cluster of Arnhem Land and Kimberley sites. Continental-scale modelling of the spread (Bradshaw and colleagues, 2021) finds the peopling of every corner of Sahul achievable within a few thousand years of entry — an establishment rate of the order of a kilometre a year — and consistent with entry at either door, or both. The pattern the dates describe is not a slow seep from a beachhead. It is the rapid occupation, by people who already knew how to live from coasts, rivers, and ranges, of a continent whose every environment was new and none of whose animals had ever seen a human being. The Arid Interior — Warratyi, c. 49,000 BP The interior was long assumed to be the last country taken up — the desert heart imagined as a barrier crossed late, when climate allowed. Warratyi rock shelter, in the northern Flinders Ranges of South Australia, in Adnyamathanha Country some 550 km north of modern Adelaide and 200 km inland, overturned the assumption. Excavated after its chance discovery in 2011 by Adnyamathanha elder Clifford Coulthard, working with archaeologist Giles Hamm, the shelter yielded more than 4,300 artefacts and a bone assemblage spanning occupation from about 49,000 to 10,000 years ago (Hamm et al., Nature 539 (2016): 280–283). Assessment — Why This Hub Tiers the System as It Does Sources This is a Tier C article: its subject is a modern construction — a system of ancient history published between 1976 and 2007 by one named author, Zecharia Sitchin — and it is treated here the way this hub treats every Tier C subject. The system is first stated whole and fairly, in its author's own terms, from his own books, because a construction that millions of readers have found persuasive cannot be understood from a caricature of it. The evidence position is then given plainly, from the standard cuneiform dictionaries, the museum literature, and the published scholarly responses, because the system's claims are claims about checkable things — the meanings of Akkadian and Sumerian words, the iconography of a catalogued seal in Berlin, the arithmetic of the Sumerian King List — and checkable claims can be checked. Neither half of the article is allowed to borrow the other's voice. Where Sitchin speaks, the text says so. Where the dictionaries speak, it says that instead. The construction, in one paragraph, is this. Sitchin held that the solar system has a twelfth member — a planet he called Nibiru , travelling a vast elliptical orbit of about 3,600 years — and that its people, the Anunnaki of the Mesopotamian texts, came to Earth some 450,000 years ago in search of gold, mined it first in the waters of the Persian Gulf and then in south-eastern Africa, and, when their own labour force rebelled, created humanity by genetic intervention: a worker species, the lulu , made by mixing Anunnaki genes with the stock of Homo erectus . The great texts of the ancient world — the Babylonian creation epic Enūma Eliš , the flood epic of Atrahasis, the opening chapters of Genesis, the Book of Enoch — were, on his reading, not myths at all but garbled technical and historical records of these events, misread as religion by scholars who had decided in advance what the texts were allowed to say. His Exhibit A was an object: an Akkadian cylinder seal in Berlin, VA 243, which he read as a map of the twelve-body solar system, drawn by people who had been told what was out there. Every load-bearing element of that paragraph is examined below at the strength its evidence has reached. The words are checked against the Chicago Assyrian Dictionary (CAD) and the Pennsylvania Sumerian Dictionary in its electronic form (ePSD) — the two lexical controls of the field, both compiled from the whole published cuneiform corpus. The seal is checked against the Vorderasiatisches Museum's own description of it. The arithmetic is checked against the King List figures this hub has already set out in Tier B, in The Antediluvian King Lists . And the most sustained scholarly engagement with Sitchin — the published critiques of the Semiticist Michael S. Heiser, who spent years answering the system claim by claim — is presented with its author's own background stated as fairly as Sitchin's is. The reader who finishes this article will know what Sitchin taught, what the texts say, and exactly where the two diverge. That divergence, and not the modernity of the books, is what the tier badge records. I. How to Read This Article — What Tier C Means Here Tier C, in the scheme of this hub, is not a synonym for "worthless," and it is not a synonym for "false because recent." This hub's Tier C shelf holds the Inner Garden Foundation's traditional timeline, the Theosophical chronology, and the Cayce readings, and it holds them for one reason only: they are bodies of teaching about the ancient world that were composed in modern times , by identifiable modern authors, whatever ancient materials they claim as their sources. Sitchin's Earth Chronicles belong on that shelf by the same test, and by a second test that matters more. The system's central assertions are assertions about ancient texts — that a Sumerian word means one thing rather than another, that a Babylonian poem describes one event rather than another — and those assertions have been examined by the people whose profession is those texts, and have not survived the examination. Section XX states the hub's reasoning in full. Sections V to IX simply present the system. Sections X to XVIII present the examination. The method throughout is attribution, as it is in this hub's companion Tier C treatment, Mu and Atlantis Reborn . When Sitchin gives Nibiru an orbital period, that figure is presented as Sitchin's, from a named book, at a real date. When the CAD gives nēberu a meaning, that meaning is presented as the dictionary's, from a named volume. Quotations are kept to the minimum the subject allows — a handful of short, famous, verifiable phrases, each attributed — and everything else is paraphrase, because a paraphrase can be checked against the book on the reader's shelf while an invented quotation cannot be checked against anything. The system's defenders and its critics are held to the same rule: Michael Heiser's arguments are summarised from his published papers, not ventriloquised, and Sitchin's are summarised from his published books, not sharpened into absurdity. One further distinction should be fixed before the system is stated, because the whole article turns on it. There are two questions here, and they have different answers. The first is: what do the ancient texts say? That question has professional answers, reached by grammar, lexicon, and context, and on the points that matter to Sitchin's system those answers are not in serious dispute among Assyriologists. The second is: why did a system built on other answers persuade millions of readers? That question is historical and human, and its answer — a coherent total narrative, offered at the moment the space age made visitors plausible, by an author who invited his readers to check the tablets for themselves — is given in Sections IV and XIX without condescension. Sitchin's readers were not fools, and this article does not treat them as fools. It treats them as people who were handed a set of translations and told, correctly, that the translations were the whole argument — and who were rarely shown that the translations could be looked up. // A NOTE ON SPELLINGS // Sitchin's first book was published in the United States as The 12th Planet (Stein and Day, 1976); this article uses that title for the book and "the Twelfth Planet" only in its own heading, following the hub's titling convention. Transliterations follow the dictionaries: Akkadian nēberu (also written nēbiru ), Sumerian a-nun-na , the counting unit šar (Sitchin's "shar"). Where Sitchin's own spellings differ — Nibiru, Anunnaki, Nephilim — they are kept in statements of his system, because they are part of what he taught. A word, finally, about why the system deserves a long article at all. Of all the constructions on this hub's Tier C shelf, Sitchin's is the one that engages the hub's Tier B material most directly. Churchward's Mu floats free of any checkable text; his tablets were never produced. Sitchin's Nibiru is built, brick by brick, out of texts that are produced — out of Enūma Eliš and Atrahasis, the King List and the Book of Enoch, all of which this hub treats as ancient witnesses in their own right. That makes his system the ideal test of the hub's whole discipline: the same tablet cannot be both a Tier B witness and a Tier C logbook, and the reader is entitled to see, in detail, which reading the tablet supports. The texts remain available. Any reader can check. This article is an account of what the checking finds. II. The Man — Baku, Jerusalem, New York, 1920–2010 Zecharia Sitchin was born on 11 July 1920 in Baku, in what was then the Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic, and was raised in Mandatory Palestine, where his family emigrated while he was still a child. He grew up, that is, in the landscape of the biblical texts, educated in Hebrew and in the archaeology-saturated culture of the Mandate period, and by his own account his lifelong project began there: as a schoolboy, he later said, he was troubled by the standard rendering of the Hebrew word Nephilim in Genesis 6 as "giants," when the root of the word seemed to him to speak of falling — of beings who had come down . The anecdote is his own, told in his books and interviews, and it is presented here as his own: it is the founding story he chose for himself, and like most founding stories it tidies a long, diffuse curiosity into a single scene. But the curiosity itself is not in doubt. Sitchin spent some three decades, by his account, studying the ancient Near East before he published a word of the system. His formal education was not in Assyriology. He took a degree in economics at the University of London, worked as a journalist and editor in Israel, and in 1952 emigrated to the United States, settling in New York, where he made his career as an executive in the shipping industry. The ancient languages were a private, parallel profession: he taught himself to read Sumerian cuneiform — the detail comes from his own accounts and from the profile the New York Times published of him — visited archaeological sites, and worked through the published translations and the scholarly literature as an outsider with, it should be said plainly, an outsider's real advantages as well as his real handicaps. He read widely, he read in several languages, and he was beholden to no department and no consensus. What he never held was a post in the field whose texts he re-translated, and he never published his readings in its peer-reviewed literature, where translations are checked sign by sign by other readers of the same tablets. That absence is a fact about the system's route to print , not yet a judgement on its contents; the contents are judged in Sections XII to XIV, on lexical grounds any reader can verify. // BORN // 11 July 1920, Baku Born in the Azerbaijan SSR and raised in Mandatory Palestine — the biographical frame his books and his publisher's materials consistently give. // EDUCATION // Economics, University of London A degree in economics, not in Assyriology; the ancient languages were self-taught, alongside a career first in journalism and then in shipping. // THE FIRST BOOK // The 12th Planet, 1976 Published by Stein and Day in New York — the foundation volume of the Earth Chronicles and of the whole system. // DIED // 9 October 2010, New York He died at ninety, still writing; his books by then had sold in the millions and been translated into more than twenty-five languages. Two features of the man matter for everything that follows, and both are to his credit in the plain biographical sense. The first is stamina. The Earth Chronicles ran for thirty-one years, from 1976 to 2007, through seven principal volumes and a shelf of companions, and the system they present is not a magazine speculation but a life's work, internally cross-referenced, indexed, and defended against critics in volume after volume. Whatever its standing as scholarship — and that standing is the subject of the second half of this article — it is not a casual production, and it cannot be answered casually. The second feature is his stance toward his readers. Sitchin presented himself, consistently, as a reporter rather than a prophet: not a channel, not a contactee, not the recipient of revelations, but a man reading documents and inviting the reader to read them with him. In the ecology of the ancient-astronaut literature — a shelf that includes trance readings and unproduced tablets, as this hub's Mu and Atlantis Reborn records — that stance is distinctive, and it is a large part of why his system, alone among its shelf-mates, generated a point-by-point scholarly response. He claimed the texts supported him. Texts can be checked. In the end, they were. III. The Books — The Earth Chronicles, 1976–2007 The system arrived in one book and was elaborated in a series. The 12th Planet (1976) contains the whole argument in embryo: the twelfth planet and its orbit, the Anunnaki and their arrival, the gold, the making of humanity, the collision that formed the Earth, and the seal that proved the Sumerians knew the solar system's true membership. The volumes that followed — published collectively as The Earth Chronicles — extended the same reading across the rest of the ancient world and the rest of the biblical text: The Stairway to Heaven (1980), on Egypt, Sinai, and the search for immortality; The Wars of Gods and Men (1985), on the conflicts of the Anunnaki houses and their human proxies; The Lost Realms (1990), carrying the system to the Americas; When Time Began (1993), on calendars, zodiac, and sacred time; The Cosmic Code (1998), on prophecy and the genetic themes of the first book; and The End of Days (2007), on the expected return of Nibiru and the end of the present age. Companion volumes — among them Genesis Revisited (1990), which set his readings beside the science headlines of its day, Divine Encounters (1995), and The Lost Book of Enki (2001), a continuous narrative retelling of the whole system in the voice of Enki's own memoir — filled out the shelf. The bibliography matters to this article for one reason: the system is not a rumour. It is a dated, published, page-referenced body of claims, and every claim examined below can be found in it. The books were also, by any commercial measure, a phenomenon. They sold in the millions, were translated into more than twenty-five languages, and remained in print — through a succession of paperback editions — for the rest of their author's life and beyond it. They made Sitchin, for two generations of general readers, the scholarly face of the ancient-astronaut idea: where Erich von Däniken, whose Chariots of the Gods? had appeared in 1968, offered questions and photographs, Sitchin offered translations, chronologies, and footnotes — or at least the apparatus of them, dense with cuneiform sign-names, tablet numbers, and references to the standard editions. The distinction between the two men is the subject of Section XIX. Here it is enough to register the fact that shapes the rest of this article: of all the writers in the ancient-astronaut tradition, Sitchin is the one who staked everything on the words . His system's foundation is not a photograph or a prophecy. It is a set of claimed meanings for ancient words, and meanings are the most checkable things in the world. // THE BOOKS AS PRIMARY SOURCES // In this hub's usage, Sitchin's books are Tier C primary documents: they are cited, throughout this article and in its Sources, as the record of what the system teaches — at their real dates, under their real titles — and never as authorities on the ancient world. That is the same courtesy, and the same limit, this hub extends to Churchward's Mu volumes and to the Cayce readings. A document can be a perfect source for a tradition and no source at all for the past the tradition describes; the tier system exists to keep those two uses apart. IV. The Claimed Method — Reading the Tablets Against the Translators Sitchin's claimed method deserves a section of its own, because it is the system's engine and its readers' chief reason for trusting it. The method, as he presented it across the Earth Chronicles, runs as follows. The scholars who translated the cuneiform texts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were, he argued, prisoners of an assumption: that the texts were myths — primitive religious fancies, to be rendered in the vague and elevated language of myth. Working under that assumption, they translated accordingly, softening concrete statements into metaphors and choosing, wherever a word allowed more than one sense, the sense that fit a myth. Sitchin proposed to reverse the procedure. He would go back to the words themselves — to the Sumerian and Akkadian originals, which he read, he said, directly — and translate them literally , on the working hypothesis that the texts were records: that when a tablet spoke of beings coming down from the sky, it meant that beings had come down from the sky, and that when it described a celestial battle, it was describing, in the only vocabulary its age possessed, an event in the solar system. On that hypothesis, the "myths" resolve, one after another, into history and astronomy — and the translators' vagueness resolves into the record of their refusal to see it. Stated that way, the method has a genuine rhetorical strength, and this article does not pretend otherwise. It flatters the ancient writers, whom it credits with precise knowledge faithfully recorded. It flatters the reader, who is invited to see what the professionals missed. And it contains one true premise: translation really is interpretation, and the renderings of the pioneer Assyriologists really were shaped by the categories of their age — a point Assyriology itself makes about its own history, and one reason the field perpetually re-translates its classics. Where the method fails — and the failure is total, but it is specific, and it is demonstrated word by word in Sections XII to XIV — is in the step from translate literally to translate as I do . A literal translation is not a free one. Sumerian and Akkadian words have the meanings the corpus gives them, recoverable from thousands of contexts, bilingual lists compiled by the ancient scribes themselves, and two centuries of accumulated lexicography, all of it published and all of it checkable. Sitchin's renderings repeatedly require meanings that appear in no context, no list, and no dictionary — and, crucially, he does not derive them by a stated method another reader could follow to the same result. The claim to be reading the tablets against the translations turns out, on inspection, to be a claim to be reading them against the language . Section XV follows the scholar who made that inspection his public work. // THE METHOD, AS SITCHIN PRESENTED IT // Take the ancient texts literally, as records rather than myths. Read the Sumerian and Akkadian words in their concrete senses, without the theological softening of the standard translations. Where the standard rendering yields a god, expect a person; where it yields a myth, expect an event; where it yields a marvel, expect a machine described in a pre-technical vocabulary. The system of Sections V to IX is what this method produces when it is applied, consistently, to the whole Mesopotamian and biblical corpus. The audit of Sections XII to XIV is what the corpus produces when the same words are looked up. One more element of the method must be named, because it recurs at every joint of the system: the treatment of later science as corroboration . Sitchin wrote at a moment when genetics, spaceflight, and planetary astronomy were remaking the public picture of the world, and he read the headlines as confirmations — the genetic code as the mechanism his texts had described all along, the asteroid belt as the debris his collision required, the newly discovered outer planets and their odd orbits as hints of the perturber his system predicted. Genesis Revisited (1990) is built almost entirely of such pairings. The rhetorical effect is powerful: the system seems to be perpetually catching up with the news, or rather the news with it. The logical structure, though, runs the other way. A text that is held to describe whatever science has most recently found is not being confirmed by science; it is being re-fitted to it, generation by generation — the same process this hub traced, era by era, through the modern Atlantis tradition in Mu and Atlantis Reborn . What a text actually says can only be settled in the text's own language. That settlement follows. V. The System, I — Nibiru, the Twelfth Member of the Solar System The system begins with a count. The ancient Mesopotamians, on Sitchin's reading, knew the solar system whole — not the seven visible wanderers of the standard history of astronomy, but twelve members: the Sun, the Moon, the nine planets known to modern astronomy including the then-most-distant Pluto, and one more. The twelfth member is Nibiru : a planet, in his account, larger than Earth, with a vast, elongated, tilted elliptical orbit that carries it out beyond Pluto into deep space and returns it to the inner solar system once every 3,600 years — a period he called one shar , taking the word from the Mesopotamian counting unit šar , 3,600, in which the longest reigns of the King List are expressed. Between its returns, Nibiru is lost to view in the outer dark; at each return — each "crossing," for he read the name Nibiru as the Planet of the Crossing — it passes through the planetary zone, an event the ancient world, on his reading, watched, feared, and recorded. The count of twelve is the system's foundation stone, and it is why the seal of Section X mattered so much to its author: the seal was offered as the Sumerians' own diagram of the twelve, drawn three thousand years before the telescope. Nibiru, in the system, is not a dead rock but a world in trouble, and its trouble is the plot's motor. It is the home of the Anunnaki — the great gods of the Sumerian pantheon, whom Sitchin read as a flesh-and-blood, long-lived, technologically advanced people, ruled from a royal house headed by Anu , whose sons Enlil and Enki — the two great rival brothers of the Mesopotamian texts — become, in the Earth Chronicles, the commanding officers of the Earth mission and the protagonists of its history. On Nibiru, as Sitchin reconstructed it, a thinning atmosphere was leaking the planet's heat into space, and its scientists had settled on a remedy: a shield of gold particles suspended in the upper atmosphere to hold the heat in. Gold, rare on Nibiru, had been detected on the third planet out from the Sun. The Anunnaki therefore came to Earth — not as conquerors and not, at first, as colonists, but as an expedition in search of a mineral, arriving, in the chronology Sitchin built from the Mesopotamian figures examined in Section XVI, some 450,000 years ago . Every later element of the system — the mines, the mutiny, the making of humanity, the flood, the wars of the gods — unfolds from that arrival and that need. THE COUNT OF TWELVE Sun, Moon, nine planets, and Nibiru: the solar system as Sitchin held the Sumerians knew it — and as he held seal VA 243 to depict it (§X). THE ORBIT One circuit of about 3,600 years — one shar — on a long, tilted ellipse reaching far beyond Pluto and returning through the inner system at each perihelion. THE PEOPLE The Anunnaki: in the texts a company of great gods; in the system, Nibiru's long-lived inhabitants, under the kingship of Anu and the rival commands of Enlil and Enki. THE NEED Gold — not as treasure but as technology: particles to be suspended in Nibiru's failing atmosphere as a shield against the loss of its heat. Fairness to the system requires noting how much of its appeal is architectural. Nothing in it is decorative. The orbit explains the planet's absence from modern catalogues and its periodic presence in ancient records. The gold explains the arrival, the mines explain the labour force, the labour force explains humanity, humanity explains the texts, and the texts — re-read — confirm the orbit. Each element answers the objection the previous element raises, and the whole turns, like the solar system it describes, around a single centre: the claim that the cuneiform words mean what Sitchin says they mean. That is why this article spends its second half in the dictionaries. A system this well joined cannot be loosened at its edges. It stands or falls at its keystone, and its keystone is lexical. VI. The System, II — The Arrival and the Gold The arrival, as the Earth Chronicles reconstruct it, was a colonising expedition conducted with the patience of a people whose planet returned to the inner system only once in thirty-six centuries. The first party — led, in Sitchin's narrative, by Enki — splashed down in the Persian Gulf and founded the first settlement at Eridu , the city the Sumerian King List itself names as the first seat of kingship. Seven settlements in all were established in the land that would become Sumer — Sitchin read the early city names of the lists as the stations of the mission, with a mission-control centre, a spaceport in the Sinai in his later volumes, and a command divided between Enlil, who held authority over the Earth operation, and Enki, who held the waters, the sciences, and the south. Gold was sought first where the expedition had landed: in the waters of the Gulf, from which, in Sitchin's reading of the texts' statements about Enki's domain, it was laboriously extracted. The yield was inadequate. Prospecting turned to the place the texts called the Abzu — a word the standard translations render as the subterranean freshwater deep, the domain of Enki — which Sitchin read instead as a region: south-eastern Africa, where the gold lay in the ground and could be mined. There, in his reconstruction, the deep mines were dug, and there the system's central crisis brewed. The crisis was labour. Mining, in the Earth Chronicles' first age, was done by the Anunnaki themselves — by their lower ranks, the beings the texts call the Igigi , stationed, in Sitchin's reading, in orbit and in the mines as the mission's workforce. The work went on, on his chronology, for some two hundred thousand years of Earth time — visit after visit of Nibiru, shar after shar — and at last the miners mutinied. Sitchin anchored the mutiny in a real text, and the anchor is worth pausing on, because it shows the system at its most characteristic. In the Old Babylonian epic of Atrahasis — treated in this hub as a Tier B witness in Flood Traditions — the lesser gods, the Igigi, do indeed rebel: they burn their tools, march by night on the house of Enlil, and declare that the labour imposed on them, the digging of the rivers and canals of Mesopotamia, has become unendurable. The poem's solution is the creation of humanity to bear the work instead. Sitchin took the episode over whole — the strike, the encirclement of the commander's house, the council of the great gods convened in emergency — and re-sited it: the canals became mines, the labour became the gold operation, and the poem's solution became the founding act of human history. The next section gives that act in the system's own terms. What the poem itself says, in the standard translation, is set out beside it there, because the distance between the two is the exact measure of the method of Section IV. Before the audit begins, the gold motive itself should be registered at its correct strength — which is to say, as a piece of 1970s system-building, not as a reading of any text. No cuneiform text, in any published translation, states that the gods came to Earth to mine gold, that gold was wanted for an atmosphere, or that the Abzu was a mining district in Africa; Sitchin assembled the motive from the texts' undoubted association of the gods with gold, from the Abzu's southern and watery associations in Enki's mythology, and from the requirements of his plot. That is not a criticism of the plot — as a plot it is excellent, and its excellence is a historical fact about the books' success. It is a note on the evidence: the gold, like the orbit, enters the system from the system's own needs, and is then found, on re-reading, in texts whose words are audited in Sections XII to XIV. VII. The System, III — The Making of the Lulu, the Primitive Worker The council that answered the mutiny, in Sitchin's telling, took Enki's proposal: do not import more labour, and do not concede the mines — make a worker. The raw material, he argued, was already on Earth: the ape-man, Homo erectus , evolved on the planet but lacking, in his reading, the spark that would make him trainable to the work. The Anunnaki — Enki as the mission's chief scientist and the goddess he called Ninhursag, the texts' great mother-goddess and, in the system, the mission's chief medical officer — supplied the spark by the method the twentieth century had just made thinkable: genetic intervention. They took, in his account, the genetic material of the Anunnaki themselves and combined it with the stock of Homo erectus , producing a hybrid — sterile in its first versions, on his reading of the texts' creation episodes, and at last, by a further intervention he located in the biblical Eden narrative, capable of reproducing itself. The product was the lulu — the word Sitchin took from the Sumerian lú-ùlu of the creation texts and rendered "Primitive Worker" — and its first individual was the being he identified behind the biblical Adam . The date he assigned the act, from his shar-counting chronology, was some 300,000 years ago : modern humanity, on the system, is a manufactured species, made for the mines, and every creation text in the ancient corpus is a garbled works report of its manufacture. Now the text itself, because the hub's Tier B discipline requires the two to stand side by side. In Atrahasis, as the standard translations give it — the edition of Lambert and Millard is the one this hub's Flood Traditions follows — the Igigi's revolt is answered by a creation of a quite different kind. Enki proposes that a god be slaughtered — the god Wê-ila, in the text's naming — and that the birth-goddess Nintu mix clay with the slain god's flesh and blood, so that the new creature, humanity, carries both clay and a divine element within it: a ghost, a spirit, a beating reminder of the god who died to make it. Fourteen pieces of the mixture are shaped, seven male and seven female, and the birth-goddess brings them to term. The humans take up the digging tools of the gods, and the canals get dug. The parallel Sumerian and Akkadian creation accounts — Enki and Ninmah, the creation material inside Enūma Eliš , where humanity is made from the blood of the rebel god Kingu — work with the same materials: clay, divine blood, a goddess's shaping hands, a creature made to serve. Nothing in any of them, in the standard editions, describes heredity, laboratories, or the improvement of an existing ape; the creature is made from clay , outright, as creatures are made in creation stories across the ancient world. // THE TWO CREATIONS, SIDE BY SIDE // In the texts: humanity is fashioned from clay mixed with the blood (and flesh) of a slaughtered god, shaped by a birth-goddess, to relieve the lesser gods of the labour of digging and maintaining the waterways — a theological account of what humanity is for , and of why it carries something divine in it. In the system: the same episodes are read as genetic engineering — Anunnaki genes spliced into Homo erectus by named officers of a mining mission, c. 300,000 years ago. The strike and the labour problem are genuinely in the poem. The genetics are not: they are the twentieth century's vocabulary laid over the poem's clay and blood, and no word in the poem, in the dictionaries' senses, names them. The lulu is the system's most consequential element, and its afterlife — through the ancient-astronaut media of Section XIX — has made "the Anunnaki genetically engineered humanity" the single most repeated sentence the Earth Chronicles produced. It is therefore worth stating precisely what the audit of it consists in, because it is not a quarrel about whether ancient people could imagine gods making workers: they plainly could, and did, in the plain words of the poem. The quarrel is about what the poem's words say . Sitchin's reading requires the creation vocabulary of the texts to carry technical senses — gene, hybrid, laboratory procedure — that the words bear in no attested context, while the senses they do bear, in every context, are the ones the standard translations print. A reader does not need to take Assyriology's word for that. The reader needs a dictionary, and Section XII opens one. VIII. The System, IV — Tiamat Struck: The Collision in Enūma Eliš If the lulu is the system's most repeated element, the collision is its most ambitious: nothing less than a re-reading of the Babylonian creation epic, Enūma Eliš , as an astronomical document — a record, preserved as theogony, of how the solar system actually formed. The epic, in the standard reading, tells how the young god Marduk went out to battle against Tiamat , the salt-water goddess, the mother of the first generation of gods, who had raised an army of monsters against the younger gods; how he caught her in his net, drove the winds into her, split her body, and from its two halves made heaven and earth; and how from the blood of her executed general Kingu he made humanity to serve the gods. Sitchin read every term of that combat as celestial mechanics. Tiamat, in his reading, was a planet — a watery world orbiting where the asteroid belt now runs, between Mars and Jupiter. Marduk was not, originally, a god of Babylon at all but the name the Babylonians later gave to the intruder: Nibiru itself, a planet captured into the solar system from deep space, whose arrival the epic's theogony encodes. On its first passage, one of Nibiru's moons — the texts' winds and weapons, in his reading — struck Tiamat and cracked her. The Modern Scholarly Frame — and How to Read the Chronology Now Sources I. What Tier C Means Here — A Chronology with Authors This article is classified Tier C — Modern Construction . That classification is stated here in words, as this hub requires, and it governs everything that follows. Tier C means that the subject is a documented product of the modern period, whose makers, publications, and revisions can be named and dated — not an ancient record recovered intact, and not a finding of geology or archaeology. The Theosophical chronology is, in that respect, an exemplary Tier C subject: almost everything in it can be followed, edition by edition and letter by letter, from the early 1880s to the present. The system was built principally by Helena Petrovna Blavatsky (1831–1891), co-founder of the Theosophical Society in 1875. Its first public form was given not by Blavatsky herself but by the Anglo-Indian newspaper editor A. P. Sinnett , in The Occult World (1881) and Esoteric Buddhism (1883), working from a correspondence he believed — and presented — as coming from two hidden teachers, the Mahatmas Koot Hoomi (signed “K.H.”) and Morya (signed “M.”). Its canonical form is Blavatsky’s The Secret Doctrine: The Synthesis of Science, Religion, and Philosophy , published in two volumes in London in 1888 — Volume I, Cosmogenesis , and Volume II, Anthropogenesis — presented by her as a commentary on an archaic text, the Stanzas of Dzyan . Its popular cartography was supplied by W. Scott-Elliot in The Story of Atlantis (1896) and The Lost Lemuria (1904). And its most extensive revision was supplied, a generation later, by Annie Besant and C. W. Leadbeater , whose Man: Whence, How and Whither (1913) announced itself, in its subtitle, as A Record of Clairvoyant Investigation . Every claim in this article is therefore attributed to its author. Where the text says “the Third Root Race began” without qualification, it is reporting — in compressed form — what Blavatsky, Sinnett, Scott-Elliot, or Besant and Leadbeater taught, and the surrounding paragraphs name which of them taught it. Nothing in the chronology is narrated here as established fact about the human past. Where the chronology conflicts with the geological and palaeoanthropological record — and on dates, bodies, and continents it conflicts comprehensively — that is said plainly, in §VII and elsewhere, with the evidence. Respect, in this hub, means accurate description of what a system teaches and why its makers believed it. It does not mean blurring the line between a teaching and a finding. // HOW TO USE THIS ARTICLE // Sections II–VII describe the system as Blavatsky built it, including its claimed source and its own numbers. Sections VIII–XI treat the Mahatma letters, Sinnett’s books, and the Hodgson controversy that put the letters’ authorship in dispute. Sections XII–XIV treat the systematising and clairvoyant literature that revised the chronology after Blavatsky’s death. Sections XV–XVII follow the scheme into later movements, including a brief, plain account of its misuse. Section XVIII gives the modern scholarly frame. The companion article on Lemuria tells the biography of one continent in the scheme; this article tells the biography of the scheme itself. A word on vocabulary is needed at the outset, because the system’s central term misleads modern readers. In Blavatsky’s usage, a Root Race is not a “race” in the modern biological or census sense. It is a successive, world-wide stage of humanity — a whole humanity, occupying its own continent over millions of years, with its own kind of body, its own dominant sense, and its own spiritual task — through which, in her teaching, all human souls pass in turn by reincarnation. Present humanity, of every modern people, belongs in her scheme to a single Root Race, the Fifth. That is what she taught, and it matters for §XVI. It is also true — and §XVI records it just as plainly — that her writings use the racial language and hierarchies of nineteenth-century anthropology, that some passages rank contemporary peoples as older or younger “stocks” within the scheme, and that later writers tore the vocabulary out of the system and put it to uses she did not direct. Both halves of that paragraph belong to the record, and this article keeps both. THE CLAIM, AS ITS AUTHORS MADE IT An archaic wisdom, preserved by hidden adepts (the Mahatmas), transmitted in letters and in the Stanzas of Dzyan, recording humanity’s passage through seven Root Races on a chain of seven globes, over immense cycles of time. THE DOCUMENTARY RECORD, AS SCHOLARS READ IT A synthesis constructed in 1880–1888 from the comparative religion, Orientalist scholarship, evolutionary popular science, and occult literature of Blavatsky’s own century. No independent manuscript of the Book of Dzyan has ever been produced. See §III. The table below gives the spine of the construction. Every entry is taken up in the sections that follow.
