The Claim and Its Limits This article makes one claim, and it is a claim about readers, not about poets. Between late antiquity and the end of the eighteenth century, the practitioners and theorists of alchemy developed, taught, and printed a complete way of reading Greek and Egyptian myth as a veiled account of their own art: its matter, its vessels, its fires, and the sequence of its operations. On that reading, Jason's voyage is the quest for the philosophers' stone; Medea is the art's great operator, whose cauldron performs the death and rejuvenation of the work's matter; the labours of Hercules are the operations rehearsed one by one; Atalanta, fleeing the suitor who drops golden apples in her path, is the volatile principle of the work, arrested at last by the fixed. The reading had rules, authorities, textbooks, and a dictionary. Its greatest monuments are Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1617/1618) and Dom Antoine-Joseph Pernety's Dictionnaire mytho-hermétique (1758). Its roots are older than alchemy itself: they lie in the allegorical interpretation of Homer — allegoresis — which Greek readers had practised for eight centuries before the first alchemical commentator took it up. The limits of the claim must be stated as plainly as the claim, because everything in this article depends on them. This is not an argument that Hesiod or Homer encoded alchemy. Alchemy, as a literature with a theory of transmutation, is a product of the first centuries CE; the myths it was read into are older by the better part of a millennium, and the alchemical reading of them is demonstrably, datably later than the myths themselves — Section VIII follows one such reading, the Fleece as a book of gold-making, through its attestations and shows it crystallising in the second century CE and after. Nor is this article an argument that the alchemical reading is foolish. It was practised by learned men working inside a coherent hermeneutic tradition, with stated principles and a pedagogy; it preserved, inside story-form, real knowledge of how substances behave; and it is, for the historian, a primary document of how the myths were received — which is to say, of what the myths went on doing in the world after their first audiences were gone. The archive's discipline throughout is therefore double: the alchemical reading is presented as the alchemists' reading , in their own terms and at full strength, and it is never silently promoted into the myths' original meaning. Where the tradition speaks, it is quoted or paraphrased as tradition. Where modern scholarship judges, the judgement is named as scholarship. The two voices are not mixed. WHAT THIS ARTICLE CLAIMS That a documented interpretive tradition — running from the Greek alchemical commentators through Maier to Pernety — read Greek and Egyptian myth as a veiled account of the alchemical work, and said so in print, with rules, examples, and dictionaries. The tradition is the subject; its books are the evidence. WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM That Homer, Hesiod, or Apollonius intended any such sense; that the myths were composed as alchemy; or that any alchemical decoding offered here is a key the reader should apply at the bench. Reception is not origin, and this article keeps the two apart in every section. THE TRADITION'S OWN NAME FOR ITSELF Pernety's dictionary calls its subject the mytho-hermetic : the fables of the poets explained as the metaphors and enigmas of the Hermetic philosophers. Modern scholarship, following Peter J. Forshaw and others, speaks of the mytho-hermetic tradition . This article uses both terms for the same documented practice. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published sources actually consulted in its preparation — the Suda On Line translation of the Suda's entry on the Fleece; Russell and Konstan's Heraclitus; Thomas Taylor's Porphyry; the English renderings of Maier's Arcana Arcanissima and Pernety's Dictionnaire hosted at alchemy-texts.com; Ferguson's Bibliotheca Chemica — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else is paraphrase, written as paraphrase. Why the Veil? The Tradition's Own Rationale The first thing to understand about the mytho-hermetic reading is that, inside the tradition, the veil is not an obstacle to the teaching. The veil is the teaching's form, and the tradition states its reasons openly, in its own books, in three registers that recur from the Greek commentators to Pernety. They deserve to be given exactly as the tradition gives them, because the whole method stands or falls, for its practitioners, on these reasons. Pedagogy. A story is remembered when a recipe is forgotten. The tradition held that the ancients — Egyptian priests first, Greek poets after them — possessed the art and wished to transmit it across centuries to students they would never meet; myth, memorable, pleasurable, and endlessly retold, was the durable carrier. Maier's preface to the Arcana Arcanissima (1614) states the Egyptian original of the method in terms the whole tradition repeats: the Egyptians, having obtained extraordinary things, did not want them — in the English rendering of the preface consulted for this article — “completely unknown to posterity, and yet not equally known to all”, and so devised a way of obscuring them, inventing, as Maier has it, hieroglyphics, allegories, and fables as the envelopes in which the knowledge could travel. The master teaches by veils because the veil is what survives the journey: the unprepared reader carries the story faithfully for a thousand years without knowing what he carries, and the prepared reader, arriving at last, finds the cargo intact. On this account, myth was the tradition's oral teaching vehicle before it was its written one — bench-knowledge in narrative form, passed from master to student in the telling, each retelling a lesson for whoever had ears trained to hear it. Protection of the art and of the adept. The knowledge claimed was dangerous knowledge: the making of gold touches the money supply of states, and the universal medicine touches life itself. Lawrence Principe's The Secrets of Alchemy (2013) sets out the documented pressures plainly: alchemists who announced success risked arrest and forced labour for princes; the art was illegal in many jurisdictions; and a transmuting agent in unscrupulous hands was, in the alchemists' own stated view, an economic and moral catastrophe. Pernety, introducing his dictionary, gives the adepts' own version of the argument (paraphrased from the English rendering consulted): those reputed to have known the universal medicine declared that publishing its process plainly would produce greater evils for society, through the abuses the wicked would make of it, and therefore taught it only in an enigmatic, allegorical, and metaphorical manner — intelligible, as Pernety reports their claim, only to those God wished to favour with it. Whether or not the modern reader credits the danger, the rationale is the tradition's own, stated in its own prefaces, and it explains the form of everything the tradition wrote. Protection of the unready reader. The third reason is the subtlest and, for this article's subject, the most important. A veil does not only hide; it sorts . The reader who takes the fable literally has a story, harmless and even improving. The reader who suspects an under-meaning has a puzzle, and the labour of the puzzle is itself the training: by the time he can read the Fleece as the work, he has learned the work's vocabulary, its colour-sequence, its marriage of fixed and volatile — he has become, in the tradition's terms, the kind of reader the knowledge is safe with. Pernety's dictionary preserves the Egyptian form of this sorting in its entry on the sacerdotal art of Egypt (paraphrased from the English rendering): the priestly art, it says, was taught only by hieroglyphics and mysterious terms, its true explanation given only to those who had undergone a very long trial and been judged worthy of initiation, and its secret kept — the entry reports the tradition's claim — under penalty of death. The claim is the tradition's, not this archive's; but it is the claim that made the method intelligible to itself. Deliberate obscurity, on this account, is not the enemy of teaching. It is teaching conducted at the speed of the student's fitness. // THE RULES OF THE READING // Across its two thousand years the tradition works by a stable set of rules, which later sections apply one by one. (1) The surface is a veil: the real sense is an under-meaning, Greek hyponoia . (2) Names are keys: etymology unlocks persons and places. (3) Like reads like: a story about a thing that flees, dissolves, blackens, whitens, and reddens is about whatever in the work flees, dissolves, blackens, whitens, and reddens. (4) The corpus must agree: all fables reduce to one principle — the phrase is Pernety's subtitle. (5) Obscurity is graded and intentional: failure to understand is evidence about the reader, not about the text. II. Allegoresis Before Alchemy I: Theagenes and the Defence of Homer Allegorical interpretation begins, so far as surviving evidence reaches, as an act of defence. By the late sixth century BCE the Homeric poems were already the foundation of Greek education and Greek religion — and already an embarrassment to Greek philosophy. Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570–c. 478 BCE) had attacked Homer and Hesiod in terms that survive in quotation by later authors: the poets, he charged, had attributed to the gods everything that is a reproach among men — theft, adultery, and mutual deceit (fragment 11 in the Diels–Kranz numbering, paraphrased here). If the poems were the Greeks' scripture and the poems' gods were thieves and adulterers, then either the gods or the poems had to go. Allegoresis was the third option: the poems do not mean what they say. Beneath the surface — the lexis , the wording — lies an under-meaning, a hyponoia , and in the under-meaning the gods are innocent, because they are not persons at all. They are the furniture of the physical world, wearing divine names. Theagenes of Rhegium and the Battle of the Gods The first named practitioner is Theagenes of Rhegium , a critic from the Greek city of Rhegium in southern Italy, whose floruit the ancient evidence places in the years around 529–522 BCE. His writings are lost; what we know of his method comes from a scholion — a piece of ancient commentary preserved in the margins of Homer manuscripts — on Iliad 20.67, the passage where Zeus releases the gods to fight one another over Troy: Poseidon against Apollo, Ares against Athena, Hera against Artemis, and so through the paired combatants. The scholion, which draws on Porphyry's Homeric Questions and is catalogued as testimony 8 A 2 in Diels–Kranz, reports the defence in two registers. In the physical register (paraphrased), the battle of the gods is the strife of the elements: the dry fights the wet, the hot the cold, the light the heavy; water extinguishes fire and fire dries up water, and the universe, whose parts suffer this partial destruction, remains eternal as a whole. Homer, setting out these battles, gives fire the names Apollo, Helios, and Hephaestus; water he calls Poseidon or Scamander; the moon, Artemis; the air, Hera. In the moral register, the same names are given to states of the soul: Athena is intelligence or prudence, Ares is folly, Aphrodite is desire, Hermes is speech. The scholion's verdict on the method is preserved with the method, in John A. MacPhail's translation of Porphyry's Homeric Questions (2011): the defence from the wording, holding that everything is said by way of allegory, is — as the tradition itself already knew — a very ancient one, beginning with Theagenes, the first to write about Homer. “For indeed they say that the dry fights with the wet, the hot with the cold, and the light with the heavy…” — SCHOLION ON ILIAD 20.67, PRESERVING THEAGENES' DEFENCE (DK 8 A 2), TRANS. JOHN A. MACPHAIL, PORPHYRY'S HOMERIC QUESTIONS ON THE ILIAD (2011) Two features of Theagenes' reported method matter for everything that follows in this article. First, it is systematic : it does not rescue one embarrassing verse but proposes a key — a standing table of equivalences (god = element, god = faculty) that can be applied to any passage whatever. The mytho-hermetic dictionaries of Section XIII are that table grown to six hundred pages. Second, it is defensive in form but appropriative in effect : to say that Homer's gods are really the elements is to say that Homer was, all along, a physicist — that the newest wisdom of the interpreter's own age was already present, veiled, in the oldest text. Every later allegoresis repeats that gesture with a different content. The Stoics find Stoicism in Homer; Porphyry finds Platonism; the alchemists will find the work. The gesture is Theagenes'. The Pressure Mounts: Plato's Challenge The defence was needed because the attack kept sharpening. Its most consequential form is Plato's, in Book 2 of the Republic (377e–378e, paraphrased): the tales of Ouranos and Kronos, of Hera bound by her son, of Hephaestus hurled from heaven by his father, and of the battles of the gods, are not to be admitted into the just city — and Plato adds, in the clause on which this whole article turns, whether they are composed with under-meanings or without them . The Greek word is hyponoia , the technical term of the allegorists. Plato, that is, knows the defence perfectly well and refuses it in advance: a young guardian, he argues, cannot distinguish the under-meaning from the surface, and will take the surface into his soul. The passage is the founding document of the quarrel this article traces. Allegoresis exists because Homer was indefensible read literally and indispensable read at all; and Plato's refusal — the under-meaning is no excuse — is the objection every allegorist after him, alchemical ones included, is implicitly answering. The tradition's reply, in its mature form, is the sorting argument of Section I: the veil is precisely what keeps the dangerous sense from the unready. Plato feared the surface would corrupt the young; the alchemists answered that the surface is what protects them. The Derveni Commentator and Metrodorus: The Method Widens Between Theagenes and the Stoics, two further witnesses show the method hardening into a profession. The Derveni papyrus — a carbonised book-roll recovered in 1962 from a funeral pyre at Derveni, near Thessaloniki, its copy dated to the decades around 340 BCE and its commentary older — is the earliest Greek book to survive in anything like its ancient form, and it is an allegoresis: a line-by-line commentary on an Orphic theogony, whose author insists that Orpheus spoke in riddles, deliberately and throughout, and decodes the poem into a physics of air, mind, and cosmic order (paraphrased from the papyrus's published contents). The Derveni commentator matters here for one reason: he already treats riddling obscurity as an authorial intention to be honoured, not a defect to be excused — the poet veiled his physics because the many were not to grasp it at once. That is, in embryo, the whole rationale of Section I, stated of a religious poem in the fourth century BCE. Beside him stands Metrodorus of Lampsacus (fifth century BCE), a pupil of Anaxagoras, whom the later tradition remembered for carrying the physical reading through the whole cast of the Iliad — gods and heroes alike dissolved into elements, seasons, and meteorological processes. The details of Metrodorus's table reach us in fragments and summaries and are reported here at that strength; the direction is not in doubt. By the end of the fifth century, allegoresis had a founder, a rationale, a professional literature, and a complete cast-list of equivalences. It awaited only a philosophy big enough to make it a system. The Stoics supplied it. c. 570–478 BCE XENOPHANES ATTACKS The poets attribute to the gods theft, adultery, and deceit (fr. 11 DK, paraphrased). Traditional myth, read literally, is impious: the problem to which allegoresis is the answer. fl. 529–522 BCE THEAGENES OF RHEGIUM First named allegorist. The battle of the gods at Iliad 20 is the strife of the elements; the gods' names also name faculties of the soul. Known only through the scholion drawing on Porphyry (DK 8 A 2). 5th c. BCE METRODORUS OF LAMPSACUS Extends the physical reading to gods and heroes alike, in the circle of Anaxagoras. The equivalence-table becomes a complete cast-list. Copy c. 340 BCE THE DERVENI COMMENTARY An Orphic theogony decoded line by line into physics; Orpheus held to speak in riddles on purpose, for the few. The oldest surviving Greek book is an allegoresis. c. 375 BCE PLATO REFUSES THE DEFENCE Republic 2.378d: the theomachies are excluded “whether composed with under-meanings or without” (paraphrased). The objection every later allegorist answers. III. Allegoresis Before Alchemy II: Stoics, Cornutus, and Heraclitus the Allegorist The Stoics made allegoresis a system because they needed it to be one. Stoic physics held that a single rational principle — logos , identified with Zeus — pervades the cosmos in differing degrees of tension, and that the earliest Greek speakers, naming the powers of the world, had encoded that physics in the names of the gods. Etymology, on this view, is not wordplay but archaeology: analyse a god's name, epithets, and attributes correctly, and you recover the physical insight of the first name-givers. Mikołaj Domaradzki's study of the development of Stoic allegorism states the continuity plainly: from Zeno through Cleanthes and Chrysippus to Cornutus, the Stoics assumed that the ancient mythmakers had transformed their cosmological conceptions into anthropomorphic deities, and they used etymological analysis as a research strategy — to extract, from the traditional names, the physical and moral beliefs of the ancients' world-picture. Piety, in this programme, is retrieval: philosophy recovering its own truths from under the disguise in which primitive formulation had stored them. Every element of the later alchemical method is present here except the content. Where the Stoic decodes a god into a physical principle, the alchemist will decode a hero into an operation; the conviction that the old stories are a storage technology for expert knowledge is already complete. Cornutus and the Compendium: Allegory as a Schoolbook The system's surviving textbook is the Epidrome — the Compendium of Greek Theology ( Theologiae Graecae compendium ) — transmitted under the name of Lucius Annaeus Cornutus , the Stoic philosopher of Leptis Magna who taught at Rome under Nero (his pupils included the poet Persius) and was banished by the emperor in 66 or 68 CE. The handbook, addressed to a young pupil whom it calls “my boy”, works through the pantheon from Heaven down to the Underworld, god by god, explaining each name, epithet, attribute, and myth by etymology and in terms of Stoic physics. Its opening treatment of Ouranos shows the method in miniature (paraphrased): Heaven is called ouranos , some say, because it is the “upper limit” ( ouros anō ) of all things and “marks the bounds” ( horizōn ) of nature; others derive it from “being seen above” ( horāsthai anō ); others from its looking after and guarding what it encompasses. The etymologies are, to a modern linguist, forced — and the forcing is the point to notice, because it never disappears from the tradition. An allegorical key that can be turned to any lock will open every door and certify none; Section XIV returns to that structural weakness, which the tradition's critics saw as early as its defenders did. What Cornutus establishes for this article's story is the genre : a handbook, organised as a reference work, in which the whole of myth is laid out as a table of decoded meanings for a student to learn. Pernety's dictionary is Cornutus's schoolbook rebuilt for the furnace — alphabetical where Cornutus is hierarchical, but recognisably the same instrument, seventeen centuries later. // A NOTE ON CORNUTUS'S NAME // The Epidrome comes down under Cornutus's name, and the handbooks treat it as his; a strand of modern scholarship has questioned the attribution (one study consulted for this article styles him “Pseudo-Cornutus”). This article follows the conventional attribution and flags the doubt here, once: nothing in the argument depends on which Stoic teacher held the pen. Heraclitus the Allegorist: “If He Meant Nothing Allegorically…” The defence of Homer reaches its most uncompromising ancient form in the Homeric Problems of Heraclitus the Allegorist — a grammarian and rhetorician of the late first or early second century CE, not to be confused with the Presocratic philosopher of the same name. His treatise, edited and translated by Donald A. Russell and David Konstan (Society of Biblical Literature, 2005), works through the passages of the Iliad and Odyssey that the critics had prosecuted — the battles of the gods, the adultery of Ares and Aphrodite, the laughter of Olympus — and acquits every one by allegory. The opening sentence, in Russell and Konstan's translation, states the stakes as an ultimatum: “It is a weighty and damaging charge that heaven brings against Homer for his disrespect for the divine. If he meant nothing allegorically, he was impious through and through…” — HERACLITUS, HOMERIC PROBLEMS 1, TRANS. DONALD A. RUSSELL AND DAVID KONSTAN (2005) Heraclitus's readings run in the two registers Theagenes founded, physical and ethical, and one of them points directly toward this article's subject. The song of Demodocus in Odyssey 8 — Ares and Aphrodite caught in Hephaestus's net — he reads physically, as Empedocles' cosmic powers: Aphrodite is Love ( Philotēs ) and Ares is Strife ( Neikos ), the forces that mix and separate the elements, here joined in a harmony at which the gods reasonably laugh, since the universe itself is their accord. But the same episode, as the scholarship on Heraclitus notes, he also reads as an allegory of the metalworker's art : the smith-god, the net of bonds, the union of opposed powers in a crafted thing. It is a small moment, and this article flags it as one reading among his many — but it is the moment where ancient allegoresis first touches the workshop. A myth decoded as a craft process , with a god as its operator and opposed materials as its actors, is the mytho-hermetic reading in miniature, six centuries before Zōsimos and fifteen before Pernety. The ethical register runs beside it throughout: when Athena seizes Achilles by the hair in Iliad 1 and checks his sword-hand, Heraclitus's Athena is, in paraphrase, the hero's own prudence arriving in person — the goddess as a faculty of the soul, exactly as Theagenes' table had promised. THE PHYSICAL REGISTER Gods are elements, seasons, and cosmic powers; their wars and marriages are the interactions of nature. Founded by Theagenes (fire = Apollo, water = Poseidon), systematised by the Stoics, and still the senior register in Heraclitus. THE ETHICAL REGISTER Gods are faculties and states of the soul; their interventions are psychology in person. Athena = prudence, Ares = folly, Aphrodite = desire — Theagenes' second table, and the register the Neoplatonists will raise to a metaphysics. THE INSTRUMENT: ETYMOLOGY The name is the key. Stoic etymology treats divine names as compressed physical doctrine deposited by the first speakers. Cornutus's Epidrome is its schoolbook; Pernety's dictionary, its alchemical descendant. THE FIRST WORKSHOP READING Heraclitus reads the net of Hephaestus ( Odyssey 8) not only as cosmic Love and Strife but as the metalworker's art. Myth as craft process: the mytho-hermetic reading exists here in embryo, inside respectable Homeric scholarship. IV. Porphyry's Cave of the Nymphs: The Method's Masterpiece Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–c. 305 CE), the pupil, editor, and biographer of Plotinus, wrote the most famous allegoresis of antiquity: the short treatise On the Cave of the Nymphs in the Odyssey ( De antro nympharum ), an exegesis of eleven lines of Odyssey 13 (lines 102–112) describing the cave on Ithaca where the Phaeacians set the sleeping Odysseus ashore. Homer's cave — paraphrased from the passage Porphyry expounds — is lovely and shadowy, sacred to the Naiad nymphs; it holds stone bowls and amphorae, stone looms on which the nymphs weave sea-purple cloth, ever-flowing water, bees storing honey in the stone vessels, and two doors: the northern door, by which men descend, and the southern, which is for the gods, and which men may not enter. Porphyry, following the earlier exegetes Cronius and Numenius whom he names as his authorities, begins from a difficulty that is the allegorist's charter. No such cave, he notes, is recorded by those who have described Ithaca; and it would be absurd for Homer to invent, as mere poetic licence, a cave with a door for all mankind and another for all the gods. The conclusion, in Thomas Taylor's translation of 1823 ( Select Works of Porphyry ), is that the poet — the phrase is Cronius's, as Porphyry reports him — “under the veil of allegory, conceals some mysterious signification”, and the treatise is the unveiling. The unveiling proceeds detail by detail, and its completeness is the masterpiece's claim on the reader. The cave itself is the sensible cosmos: a place beautiful but shadowed, an image of the intelligible world, into which souls descend. The Naiads, nymphs of flowing water, are souls descending into generation — for water, in the treatise's physics of symbolism, is the element of becoming and moisture, and souls on their way to birth are drawn to the moist. The bees, and the honey they store in stone vessels, are souls entering bodies, and the sweetness that binds them to incarnate life. The nymphs weaving purple cloth on looms of stone are souls weaving their flesh — the purple is blood — upon the frame of the bones: embodiment figured as a textile operation, thread by thread, on a loom of rock. And the two doors are the two solstitial gates of the soul's traffic, a doctrine Porphyry takes from Numenius: the northern gate is set under Cancer, the gate of descent , by which souls come down into generation; the southern under Capricorn, the gate of ascent , by which they return to the divine. The olive tree that stands outside the cave, at its head, belongs to Athena: wisdom stands outside the world of generation, but close beside it — and it is beneath that tree that Odysseus, the soul that has passed through the whole cycle of generation and come home, is laid down to wake. Porphyry agrees with Numenius, in paraphrase, that the Odyssey as a whole is the symbolic itinerary of a man passing successively through generation to his restoration: the wanderings are the soul's, and Ithaca is its return. “…the poet, under the veil of allegory, conceals some mysterious signification…” — PORPHYRY, ON THE CAVE OF THE NYMPHS §2, REPORTING CRONIUS, TRANS. THOMAS TAYLOR, SELECT WORKS OF PORPHYRY (1823) Three observations fix the Cave 's place in this article's argument. First, the method's unit is the detail . Porphyry does not gesture at the passage's general drift; he interrogates every noun — why stone looms, why purple, why bees, why two doors, why an olive — and treats each answer as load-bearing. The mytho-hermetic readers inherit exactly this granularity: Pernety's dictionary is the Cave 's method applied to the whole of fable, entry by entry. Second, the authorities are named and layered . Porphyry does not present the reading as his invention; he cites Cronius and Numenius, disagrees and adjudicates, and builds the treatise as a commentary on commentators. Allegoresis by his time is a tradition with a literature , and its practitioners understood themselves as links in it — as, later, the alchemical commentators would understand themselves, expounding Zōsimos as Zōsimos had expounded Democritus. Third, the decoded content is a doctrine of descent and return : something comes down into a dark enclosed place, is worked upon there, and goes up again by the other door. A reader of this hub's Zōsimos article will recognise the shape. It is the shape of the work itself — matter sealed in the vessel, spirit drawn off and returned — and it is not an accident that the generation after Porphyry produced, in the same Greek-speaking Egypt, an author who dreamed in exactly that shape and glossed his dreams as chemistry. The Neoplatonic allegorists handed the alchemical commentators a tool; they also handed them, in the Cave , a picture of what a fully decoded text looks like: a cosmos in a hollow place, with traffic passing through it by two doors. // EDITIONS OF THE CAVE // The treatise survives complete and is read in two English versions in this archive's practice: Thomas Taylor's translation (1823), quoted above, the version through which the English-speaking Hermetic tradition received Porphyry; and Robert Lamberton's modern translation, Porphyry: On the Cave of the Nymphs (Station Hill Press, 1983). Taylor's Platonist archaisms are themselves a document of reception — the Cave entered English already wearing the veil its translator thought proper to it. It remains to state the obvious, because the discipline of this article requires it. Porphyry's reading is not what Homer meant, in any sense a historian of the eighth century BCE could certify: the solstitial gates, the doctrine of the soul's descent, the Numenius behind the exegesis, are all artifacts of the Platonism of the Roman imperial age, read back into a passage whose first audiences heard a harbour, a cave, and a homecoming. Porphyry himself leaves open whether the cave ever existed — and the openness is instructive. For the allegorist, the question of the surface (was there a cave?) is strictly subordinate to the question of the sense (what does the cave mean ?), and a surface that never existed can bear a sense that is entirely real. That subordination — sense over surface, under-meaning over letter — is the charter the alchemical readers inherited, and the point at which their reading, too, must be judged: as a magnificent, systematic, and entirely retrospective act of interpretation. The next two sections watch the instrument change hands. V. The Greek Alchemical Layer: Democritus, the Aphorism, and the Commentators Alchemy enters literary history already wearing a veil, and already equipped with commentators to lift it. The earliest substantial alchemical literature in Greek is the corpus attributed to Democritus — not the atomist of Abdera (c. 460–370 BCE) but the anonymous author, or authors, of the first century CE whom modern scholarship calls pseudo-Democritus . Matteo Martelli's edition and study, The Four Books of Pseudo-Democritus (2013), dates the work to the Neronian age, the 60s CE, and reconstructs its shape: four books on dyeing — one on gold, one on silver, one on precious stones, one on purple — of which epitomised extracts survive in the treatise called Physika kai mystika , Natural and Secret Questions , and in the lists and commentaries that grew around it. The Four Books are recipe literature, but recipe literature of a peculiar kind: framed as revelation, guarded by oaths, and studded with riddling phrases that their first readers already found dark. Within a few generations the darkness had its profession. The alchemical commentators — Synesius in the fourth century, Olympiodorus in the sixth, Stephanus in the seventh — built their work exactly as the Homeric commentators had built theirs: a canonical ancient, a body of obscure utterance, and an exegesis that unfolds what the ancient meant. Synesius's dialogue commentary, addressed to the priest Dioscorus, expounds the Physika kai mystika and declares its exegetic programme openly: to disclose Democritus's thought, his processes, and his materials. The alchemists, that is, applied allegoresis to their own corpus first . Before any alchemist read the Fleece as the work, alchemists were reading Democritus as a veiled master whose sentences required a key — and the key they cut for him would fit, in time, every lock in Greek myth. The Pillar in the Temple: How the Aphorism Was Revealed The Physika kai mystika itself dramatises the veiling and unveiling of knowledge in a foundation story that Martelli's study retells and that this article gives in paraphrase, as the text's own legend. Democritus, the story runs, was initiated by the Persian magus Ostanes in Egypt; but Ostanes died before he could teach his pupils the final secret — the harmonising of natures. The pupils, gathered in the temple for a banquet, raised the master's spirit and questioned him; the spirit answered that the books were hidden in the temple. As they searched, a pillar of the sanctuary split open of itself, and inside it was the whole teaching, compressed into a single sentence. The sentence — the most quoted sentence in Greek alchemy, ascribed within the fiction to Ostanes and repeated by alchemical authors ever after — is given here in Martelli's translation: “Nature delights in nature, nature conquers nature, nature masters nature.” — PSEUDO-DEMOCRITUS, PHYSIKA KAI MYSTIKA, THE APHORISM OF OSTANES, TRANS. x: APOLLODORUS AND THE LIBRARY Athens (attributed) · the Greek world under Rome · 1st–2nd century CE // ONE HANDBOOK :: A BORROWED NAME :: THE SYSTEM BEHIND THE MYTHS // No ancient book is cited more often in this hub, and none is trusted more cautiously. The Bibliotheca — the Library — is the one comprehensive handbook of Greek myth to survive from antiquity nearly whole: three books of plain prose that run from the first gods to the death of Odysseus, arranging everything by genealogy. It is also a book whose author we cannot name, whose date we can only bracket, and whose ending we possess only in summary. This article is the source-article the rest of the hub leans on: who wrote it, when, out of what, how it reached us, and how far it can be believed. Hyginus and the Roman Side: The Fabulae XIX. Why Systematisation Matters: How a Handbook Fixes a Myth XX. Sources I. A Handbook That Swallowed a Tradition Begin with the scale of the dependence. Across this hub's Mythology Wing, the Library is cited several hundred times — for the order of Heracles' labours, for the Theban genealogies, for the passenger lists of the Argo, for who married whom and who killed whom in houses whose own poems are lost. That dependence is not a local habit. It reflects the state of the evidence itself. Greek myth was told, for a thousand years, in epic, lyric, tragedy, local history, and cult aetiology, almost all of it now fragmentary or gone. What survives entire, besides the great poems, is this one prose summary — a work with no literary pretensions at all, written in a Greek so plain that its translator J. G. Frazer could call it, in words quoted verbatim in Section XIV, generally pure, always clear, simple, and unaffected. The plainness is the point. The Library does not perform the myths. It files them. The Greek title is simply Bibliothēkē — “library”, a storehouse or book-case. Whether the title is the author's own is not known; the work is undivided in its manuscripts, and even its division into three books is an inheritance from its first printed edition (Rome, 1555, edited by Benedetto Egio, Latinised as Benedictus Aegius). Photius, the ninth-century patriarch of Constantinople, is the first writer known to mention the book, in his own Bibliotheca — a coincidence of titles that has confused cataloguers ever since — and Photius preserves an epigram that once stood at the work's head. The epigram is paraphrased here, not quoted, because this article quotes only wordings verified in the editions named in Section XX: in paraphrase, it bids the reader draw knowledge of the past from this book alone, and not trouble Homer, elegy, the tragic muse, or the Cycle, since everything the world contains is to be found in these pages. As advertising, it overshoots. As a description of what the book became — the single shelf on which the whole tradition was consulted — it is close to the truth. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — J. G. Frazer's Loeb Library (1921), for Frazer's own introductory prose, and Jacob Stern's translation of Palaephatus (1996), for one sentence in Section XVI — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient or modern author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. References to the Library follow the standard numeration: book, chapter, section (thus 2.5.1), with the Epitome cited as E. plus its own chapter and section. Three cautions govern everything that follows, the hub's standing discipline applied to its most-used source. First, the Library is a literary compilation , not a record of cult: a myth's presence in it proves a textual tradition, not a rite. Second, it is a Greek work of the Roman period , separated from most of its material by centuries; its systematising is late work on early matter. Third, where later readers — above all the alchemical tradition of Wing II — read these myths allegorically, that reading is theirs, not the compiler's: the Library explains nothing and allegorises nothing. It is a card index that outlived the library it indexed. The task of this article is to show whose handwriting is on the cards. THE WORK IN ONE VIEW Bibliotheca (“Library”), three books plus an epitome of the lost ending, in plain scholarly prose. Scope: from Uranus and Gaia to the death of Odysseus — the whole mythical history of the Greek world, ordered by descent. THE AUTHOR IN ONE VIEW Unknown. The manuscripts name “Apollodorus the Athenian, the grammarian”; scholarship since Carl Robert's dissertation of 1873 treats that identification as false and calls the writer pseudo-Apollodorus (Sections II–IV). THE DATE IN ONE VIEW After the middle of the 1st century BCE (it cites Castor of Rhodes) and, on linguistic grounds, most probably in the 1st or 2nd century CE . The range, and the arguments, are set out in Section V. THE TEXT IN ONE VIEW One principal manuscript, Parisinus Graecus 2722 (14th century), breaking off mid-Theseus; the lost ending recovered in substance from two Byzantine epitomes published in 1891 (Sections VIII–IX). II. The Author Problem: Two Men Named Apollodorus The problem can be stated in a single sentence: antiquity knew a real Apollodorus who really did write systematically about the gods and about mythical chronology, and the Library is not his work. Everything else in this section and the next two is the unpacking of that sentence — who the real man was, why the attribution was made, and why it fails. The attribution itself is old and respectable. Photius, in the ninth century, calls the author “Apollodorus the Grammarian”; the manuscripts describe him as Apollodorus the Athenian, grammarian. No ancient writer earlier than Photius is known to name the book at all — Frazer notes that the author seems to have been ignored by his contemporaries and by posterity for many generations, surfacing by name in Photius, then in the Byzantine scholars John and Isaac Tzetzes in the twelfth century, and anonymously in the scholia to Homer, Sophocles, and Euripides and in material absorbed into Zenobius' collection of proverbs. A work can be heavily used and rarely credited; the Library was excerpted the way dictionaries are excerpted, and the name that travelled with the excerpts was the famous one. That the famous name was available to be attached is itself explicable. The minor scholia on Homer — the scholia minora , schoolroom notes of uncertain date — preserve references to a comprehensive mythological work by the genuine Apollodorus of Athens, and Aubrey Diller's study of the Library 's text history (1935) traced the false ascription to a conflation arising in that scholia tradition: two repertories of myth, one by the grammarian and one anonymous, drawn together under one name. The suggestion has also been made — by Fritz Graf and others, as a possibility rather than a proof — that the compiler really was named Apollodorus: it was a common Greek name, and coincidence needs no conspiracy. This hub follows the standard convention. The author is cited as pseudo-Apollodorus , the work as the Library or Bibliotheca , and the bare name “Apollodorus” in a citation is always to be read with that silent pseudo- understood. // A NOTE ON THE NAME // Nothing in this article's use of “Apollodorus” as shorthand implies the Athenian grammarian's authorship. Where the grammarian himself is meant, he is always “Apollodorus of Athens”. Where the Library is meant, its author is pseudo-Apollodorus, whoever he was. The distinction is not pedantry: the grammarian's real works, described in the next section, took positions the Library contradicts, and arguments built on the false attribution — dating the handbook to the 2nd century BCE, or reading its silences as a Stoic's programme — collapse with it. It is worth pausing on how complete the compiler's anonymity otherwise is. His persona is almost wholly suppressed: no preface in his own voice apart from the epigram Photius transmits (itself unattributed), no dedication, no reference to a patron, a city, or an event of his own time. A handful of passages speak in the first person or pass judgement on a variant, and those few sentences are the entire surviving trace of a personality. We know his library better than we know him — Sections X–XI argue that this is the right way round: the man is recoverable, if at all, as a set of working habits visible in the text. III. The Grammarian of Athens: On the Gods and the Chronicle Apollodorus of Athens (c. 180 – after 120 BCE) was a scholar of the first rank, and the Library 's borrowed glory is his. He was a pupil of Aristarchus of Samothrace , the great Alexandrian editor of Homer, and he worked in the orbit of the Pergamene court as well as Athens; his writings, all lost except in fragments and citations, ranged across Homeric scholarship, geography, etymology, and chronology. Two of them matter here, because each is close enough to the Library 's territory to explain the confusion — and different enough from it, in method and in detail, to disprove the identity. On the Gods The Peri theōn , On the Gods , ran to twenty-four books. From its surviving fragments — collected in Müller's Fragmenta Historicorum Graecorum and now in Jacoby's Fragmente der griechischen Historiker (no. 244) — its method is plain. It was a work of interpretation : it explained the gods' natures and epithets, working freely with etymology, and it resolved the deities, in the manner Frazer summarises from the fragments, either into personified powers of nature or into deified dead men and women — the twin instruments of Hellenistic rational theology, physical allegory and euhemerism. Whatever one thinks of that method, it is a method: the grammarian had a theory of what gods are, and he argued it epithet by epithet. The Library , by contrast, contains no theory of anything. It does not explain a single epithet, resolve a single god into a power or a person, or pause over a single cult title. Frazer's contrast, paraphrased here, is exact: nothing could be further from the spirit of the mythographer — who summarises the traditional mythology without the smallest attempt to explain or criticise it — than the dissections of On the Gods . The Chronicle The Chronika , Chronicle , was a versified universal chronology in four books, composed in iambic trimeters — a metre chosen, as later readers noted, because it is easy to memorise — and dedicated to a king Attalus, generally identified as Attalus II of Pergamum. It ran from the fall of Troy (1184/3 BCE by the era it used) down to its author's own century: the original edition reached 144/3 BCE, and the work was later continued to about 119 BCE. Its importance for Greek chronology was enormous; later chronographers built on its framework for centuries. Here, if anywhere, is the seed of the false attribution: the scholia knew Apollodorus as author of a comprehensive, ordered repertory touching mythical history, and a comprehensive, ordered repertory of myth circulated under his name. But the Chronicle was a dated framework , verse, organised by years. The Library is undated prose organised by descent, and never once converts a genealogy into a year-count. The resemblance is of subject, not of book. There is a further, quieter point. Apollodorus of Athens wrote as a known scholar inside known institutions, and his fragments show a man arguing with named predecessors and correcting them. The Library 's compiler argues with nobody: where his sources disagree he notes the disagreement and moves on (Section XI). The two temperaments — the controversialist grammarian and the self-effacing filer — are not impossible in one life, but nothing requires us to unite them, and the hard evidence of the next section forbids it. IV. Why the Library Is Not His: The Case for Pseudo-Apollodorus The identification was dismantled in full by Carl Robert , De Apollodori Bibliotheca (Berlin, 1873), and Frazer's Loeb introduction accepts Robert's arguments in the main, as does the scholarship since. The case has four strands, of increasing weight. 1 · METHOD On the Gods interprets; the Library only reports. A scholar whose life-work was explaining the gods by etymology, nature-allegory, and euhemerism does not plausibly produce, in the same field, a handbook containing no explanation at all (Section III). 2 · DETAIL Robert catalogued specific discrepancies and contradictions between the grammarian's certainly attested fragments and the Library 's statements on the same points of genealogy and myth. The fragments and the handbook do not merely differ in manner; at checkable points they differ in fact. 3 · STYLE The Library 's plain, correct, slightly clogged prose — Frazer remarks on its accumulations of participles — belongs to the scholarly koine of the Roman period, with occasional late usages (Section V). It is not the instrument of Aristarchus' pupil, and its poetic tags are quotations from sources, not the versifying habit of the Chronicle 's author. 4 · THE CASTOR CITATION Decisive by itself. At 2.1.3 the Library cites the chronicler Castor of Rhodes — a contemporary of Cicero whose chronicle was brought down to 61/60 BCE , roughly a century after Apollodorus of Athens. A book cannot quote a writer not yet born. The Castor passage deserves a moment of care, because the whole dating of the work hangs from it. The citation occurs in the Argive genealogy at the opening of Book 2, where the compiler, giving the line of kings, invokes Castor's authority for the list — the passage is registered as a fragment of Castor ( FGrHist 250). Frazer's reasoning, paraphrased from his introduction, is the standard one: there is no good ground to dispute either Castor's date or the genuineness of the reference, so the middle of the 1st century BCE stands as the earliest possible date for the Library 's composition. Apollodorus of Athens, dead by about 110 BCE at the latest on any reconstruction of his life, is excluded not by taste but by arithmetic. Two escape routes from this conclusion have been tried and should be recorded, since this hub labels scholarly dispute where it exists. The first treats the Castor citation as a later interpolation. Against it: the citation sits inside a king-list of exactly the kind Castor compiled, the text shows no seam, and a theory that must delete its only fixed point to save an attribution has the burden of proof backwards. The second accepts the date and detaches the man, proposing that the compiler was a different, otherwise unknown Apollodorus. That proposal is unfalsifiable and harmless: it changes nothing about the book. What scholarship means by pseudo-Apollodorus is precisely this residue: a competent professional of the Roman-period Greek world, working from good sources, whose name, city, and circumstances are irrecoverable. V. The Date: Between Castor and the Scholia The external evidence fixes only the window's near edge. Castor gives a terminus post quem of about 60 BCE. The far edge is embarrassingly distant: the first certain evidence of the book's existence is Photius, in the 9th century CE, and the passages of the Library absorbed anonymously into scholia and into Zenobius cannot be dated closely enough to help — Zenobius worked under Hadrian, but whether the Apollodoran material entered his collection in his own time or later is not demonstrable. Frazer states the resulting position with admirable bleakness, here paraphrased: on the external evidence alone, the author might have written at any time between the middle of the 1st century BCE and the beginning of the 9th century CE. Everything narrower than that must come from the language and the contents. The linguistic argument is the one the field actually rests on. The Library 's Greek is, in the main, correct and clear scholarly prose; against that background, a small set of usages points late: the subjunctive with hina where classical usage prefers the infinitive, occasional rare words and words in unusual senses, and a few constructions paralleled in Polybius and later writers but not in classical Attic. Jean-Claude Carrière and Françoise Massonie, in the Budé edition's study of the language (1991), concluded for composition in the 2nd or even 3rd century CE . Ken Dowden, reviewing the question for the standard discussions of Greek mythography, holds that a 1st-century CE date cannot be excluded. Robert himself inclined to the earlier part of the 2nd century CE. The positions differ by a century or two; they agree in placing the book in the Roman imperial period, and the hub's working range — 1st to 2nd century CE , with the 2nd the centre of gravity — is the range the handbooks standardly print. Frazer pressed it hard: the compiler narrates Heracles driving Geryon's cattle the length of Italy, and the settlement of Greek heroes in Italy after Troy, without once naming Rome or Aeneas' landing in Latium — though he had told Aeneas' birth and escape. Frazer, paraphrased, could draw no inference but deliberate abstention, and confessed it puzzling in a subject of the Empire. The modern resolution is less dramatic: the Library is a handbook of Greek myth built from Greek sources, and its silence is its sources' and its genre's, not a political act. Roman foundation legend has its own article in this hub's plan ( Roman Founding Legends ); the date stands where the language puts it — an imperial Greek of the first two centuries CE, filing a tradition already a millennium old. VI. Structure: Three Books on a Genealogical Spine The Library opens with the words — in paraphrase — that Heaven was first ruler of the whole world, and it ends, in its complete form, with the death of Odysseus and the return of the Heraclidae. Between those points it tells, in principle, everything : every god's birth, every hero's parentage, marriage, deeds, and death, every royal house's succession. The instrument that makes “everything” organisable is genealogy . The book is not arranged by theme, by place, or by the chronology of events. It is arranged by descent : a family tree is stated, and the stories hang from its branches in the order the branches generate them. A myth enters the book when its hero is born into the narrative, and it leaves when his line is exhausted or hands over to another stem. To read the Library is to walk a vast pedigree, and most of its peculiarities — its repetitions, its doublets, its sudden compressions of famous stories into two lines while obscure marriages get a paragraph — follow from that single decision. The pedigree is the plot. The model is Hesiodic. The Theogony had already organised the divine world by generation and birth — see this hub's Theogony article — and the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women had extended the same architecture over the heroic world, arranging the heroes by the women who bore them to gods. The Library is that architecture translated into prose and completed: where the Catalogue survives in fragments, the handbook survives whole, and its skeleton is recognisably the older poem's (Section XV). Within the divine section the compiler even preserves the theogonic order — Uranus, the Titans, the Olympians, the Giants, the distribution of honours — before passing, by the bridge of Prometheus and the flood of Deucalion, into the human stems. The Stems After the gods, the heroic world grows from a small number of great stems. From Deucalion , the flood survivor, descend the Aeolian houses and so, by way of Athamas and the golden ram, the Argonauts. From Inachus of Argos descends the line of Io, Danaus, Perseus, and — by the book's longest single arc — Heracles. From Atlas descend the Pleiades' houses, including the Spartan and Trojan royal lines. The Athenian kings, the Theban houses, and the Pelopid house are worked through in Book 3. The Trojan War, when it comes in the Epitome, is not a new subject but the collision of stems already planted: Electra's descendants hold Troy, the descendants of Pelops lead the attack, and the compiler can narrate the war as a family event because he has spent three books building the family. A word on the book-divisions, since citations depend on them. The manuscripts transmit the work undivided; the division into three books is editorial, descending from Aegius' first edition of 1555, and modern scholarship has noted that it need not reflect any ancient articulation of the text — the break between Books 1 and 2, for instance, falls in the middle of the Argive material's natural run. The lost final portion, recovered through the epitomes (Section IX), is cited as the Epitome ( E. ), and a minority discussion in the scholarship treats that portion as, in effect, a fourth book's content; the hub follows the standard convention — three books, then Epitome — and so do both English translations discussed in Section XIV. Chapter and section numbers within the books are likewise editorial (Wagner's Teubner text of 1894 fixed the numeration in general use), which is why a citation such as 2.5.1 is a modern address, not an ancient one — an address, none the less, that every modern work on Greek myth shares. VII. The Books in Detail: What Stands Where The table below maps the work as it survives. It is worth reading slowly, because the hub's other articles cite the Library by these addresses constantly, and because the map itself shows the compiler's priorities: the space a subject gets is the space its genealogical fertility earns it, not the space its fame would predict. The first is the sheer weight of Book 2 . The Heracles cycle occupies a whole book — the only hero so honoured — because Heracles is the genealogical crossroads of the heroic world: Perseus' descendant, Argos' champion, the Heraclidae's ancestor, and a figure whose journeys let the compiler sweep up dozens of local traditions (monsters, kings, foundations) as episodes of one life. The Library 's ordering of the twelve labours is the ordering the tradition, and this hub, treats as canonical; the labour article examines what that means in Heracles' Labours , including the two labours — the Hydra and the Augean stables — whose counting the compiler himself reports as disputed by Eurystheus. The second feature is what is not there. There is no Roman material (Section V); almost no cult — a tomb, an altar, or a rite is mentioned when a genealogy requires it, never described for its own sake; no natural philosophy, no allegory, no etymological play of the kind the real Apollodorus practised; and remarkably little wonder as wonder — a metamorphosis is reported in the same flat sentence as a marriage. Readers who come for the myths' poetry will find the book airless. That airlessness is a scholarly virtue misread as a defect: the refusal to perform is what lets a reader see the tradition's joints, and it is why the hub cites the Library for structure and reserves its poetry for the poets. VIII. Survival I: Parisinus Graecus 2722 and the Broken Ending The Library very nearly did not survive at all. Its medieval transmission narrows, at the critical point, to a single damaged codex: Parisinus Graecus 2722 (siglum R ), a 14th-century manuscript now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris. The codex is a miscellany in disordered condition — Wagner's preface describes its Apollodoran leaves as fragments bound in confusion, some headed only “fragment of Apollodorus, as it seems” by a later hand (paraphrased here from Wagner's Latin). From this manuscript, through a copy made in the 15th century for Cardinal Bessarion, the other surviving manuscripts descend: the whole modern tradition of the text hangs from R, and where R is damaged or wrong, the text is damaged or wrong with it, unless the epitomes or a scholion can correct it. And R breaks off . Its text of the Library runs to 3.16.2 — into the Athenian section of Book 3, in the middle of the Theseus narrative, during the hero's journey from Troezen to Athens and his clearing of the road of its monsters and brigands. The sentence stops; the leaves that carried the rest are lost. Everything the complete work contained after that point — the remainder of Theseus, the whole Trojan War, the returns, the death of Odysseus, the return of the Heraclidae, which Photius' description shows to have been the work's true extent — was, in the direct tradition, simply gone. For the first three centuries of print (1555 to the 1880s), editors published a Library that ended, without explanation available to them, on the road to Athens. // WHAT “INCOMPLETE” MEANS HERE // The loss is a loss of ending , not of bulk: Books 1, 2, and most of 3 survive in the compiler's own continuous prose. But the lost portion is disproportionately load-bearing for this hub, since it contained the handbook's Troy, on which the Trojan Cycle article partly rests. Every citation of the Library for Troy is a citation of the Epitome, and should be read with the next section's cautions attached. A second caution belongs here. Several scholars have argued that even the books we possess in full may have come down in an abridged state — that the transmitted Library is itself, in part, an epitome of a fuller original. The argument rests on the work's extreme compression at points where its sources were expansive, on abrupt transitions, and on details preserved in scholia that cite the Library but are absent from our text. The position is a scholarly hypothesis, labelled as such: it is not provable from the single-manuscript tradition, and the hub does not assume it. But it should temper any argument from the Library 's silence. A silence in an epitome is not a silence in its source. IX. Survival II: The Two Epitomes and the Recovery of 1891 The ending was recovered — in summary, which is a different thing from recovered — at the end of the 19th century, from two Byzantine collections of excerpts, both published in 1891 . EPITOMA VATICANA Excerpts preserved in Vaticanus Graecus 950 (14th century), Vatican Library. Published by Richard Wagner in 1891. The collection has been ascribed — on grounds Wagner set out and later scholars have debated — to the circle, or the hand, of the 12th-century scholar John Tzetzes , who used the Library heavily in his own work. It covers the lost portion from the Theseus narrative through the end. FRAGMENTA SABBAITICA Excerpts preserved in Sabbaiticus Graecus 366 (13th century), from the monastery of Mar Saba, in the library of the Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem. Published by Athanasios Papadopoulos-Kerameus in 1891. Independent of the Vatican excerpts, drawn likewise from a complete Library , and carrying valuable scholia of its own. Wagner conflated the two collections — checking each against the other, and both against the Tzetzes scholia on Lycophron, which quote the lost portion extensively — into the composite Epitome printed in his Teubner edition, Mythographi Graeci I (Leipzig, 1894), the edition on which Frazer's Loeb rests. Frazer translated the Epitome as the work's continuation, and it is in that form — Wagner's Greek, Frazer's English — that most readers meet the Library 's Troy. The excerptors' accuracy, where it can be tested against the surviving books, has been judged good: the epitomes are faithful in substance, and their mutual agreement, from independent extraction, gives the reconstruction a double witness for much of the lost ground. But fidelity of substance is not identity of text, and the limits must be stated as plainly as the achievement. An epitome compresses: it keeps names, successions, and outcomes, and it drops connective tissue, variant-notices, and exactly the small qualifying phrases by which a reader judges a compiler's care (Section XI). The Epitome's Greek is the excerptors' Greek, at one or more removes from the compiler's. Where the two epitomes differ, the editor chooses, and the choice is a reconstruction. And the Epitome as printed is a composite : no ancient or Byzantine reader ever held precisely the text Wagner assembled. This hub's practice follows from those facts. Citations of the Epitome are cited as E. , never silently as a book number; claims resting on the Epitome alone are one grade weaker than claims resting on Books 1–3; and where the Epitome's compression flattens a variant that the prose systematizers or the scholia preserve, the variant is reported. The ending of the Library is a well-attested summary of a lost text. It is not the lost text. 9TH C. PHOTIUS First certain mention; the Library Photius knew was complete, ending with Odysseus' death and the Heraclidae's return. 12TH C. THE TZETZES CIRCLE John Tzetzes and his milieu excerpt and quote the complete work; the Vatican epitome is ascribed to this activity — the last certain handling of the full text. 14TH C. PARISINUS GRAECUS 2722 The principal manuscript copied — already, or soon to become, defective at the end; later copies descend through Bessarion's 15th-century apograph. 1555 EDITIO PRINCEPS Benedictus Aegius prints the work at Rome, divided into three books — without the ending, whose loss the edition cannot repair. 1891–94 THE EPITOMES PUBLISHED; WAGNER'S EDITION Wagner publishes the Vatican epitome, Papadopoulos-Kerameus the Sabbaitic fragments (both 1891); Wagner's Teubner text (1894) prints the conflated Epitome and fixes the modern numeration. 1921 FRAZER'S LOEB The standard English Library , with the Epitome translated as the work's completion and a commentary of parallels that made the edition a research instrument (Section XIV). X. The Compiler's Sources: A Library Behind the Library Pseudo-Apollodorus invented almost nothing, and that is his value. Behind the handbook stands a shelf of earlier Greek mythography and poetry, most of it lost, which he excerpted with a fidelity that — where checking is possible, Section XIII — proves generally high. Reconstructing that shelf is the work of two centuries of scholarship, from Robert's dissertation to R. L. Fowler's Early Greek Mythography , and its main holdings can be named with reasonable confidence. A Story Already Old When Homer Heard It Most Greek myths reach us the way a river reaches the sea: we can name the large late channels — a tragedy, an epic, a mythographer's handbook — but the headwaters are lost in a landscape of oral telling that left no texts. The Argonaut saga is unusual because its antiquity is not an inference. It is attested, inside our earliest surviving Greek poetry, as already famous. In Book 12 of the Odyssey , Circe warns Odysseus about the Wandering Rocks, the Planktai , and explains that only one seagoing ship has ever passed them: the Argo , on her way back from Aeëtes, saved because Hera loved Jason ( Odyssey 12.69–72, paraphrased). The ship is described, in the Greek, as Argo pasi melousa — the Argo “known to all”, a concern to everyone. A poet does not gloss a reference his audience will not catch. Whoever composed that passage, in the tradition that produced the Odyssey in the late eighth century BCE, expected every hearer to know who Jason was, where he had been, and why Hera protected him. The voyage was, by then, common property. The Iliad knows Jason without knowing, or without needing, the quest. It mentions Euneus, the son Jason fathered on Hypsipyle of Lemnos ( Iliad 7.467–469, 21.40–41, 23.745–747, paraphrased) — which means the Lemnos episode, a single stop on the outward voyage, was already a fixed part of the story in the epic tradition. Hesiod, around 700 BCE, knows the ending: the closing lines of the Theogony (992–1002) tell, in paraphrase, how Jason, having completed the grievous labours imposed by Pelias, carried off Aeëtes' daughter from Colchis, made her his wife, and fathered on her a son, Medeios, whom Cheiron reared in the mountains. For the Theogony itself — its poet, its date, and its place in this hub — see Theogony . Three of our oldest witnesses, then, each presuppose the saga and use a different piece of it: Homer the return past the Rocks, the Iliad the Lemnian son, Hesiod the marriage and the child. None of them tells the story whole, because none of them needed to. What follows from that distribution is the first discipline of this article. The Argonaut story is older than any surviving telling of it. There was never an original text of which Apollonius or Apollodorus is a copy. There was a saga — a Thessalian hero, a marvellous ship, a voyage to the eastern end of the sea, a golden object guarded in a king's grove, a foreign princess who betrays her father for love — circulating in song for generations before anyone whose work survives wrote a line of it. Every author in this article is therefore a version , selecting, reordering, and inventing within a tradition his audience already knew. When two versions disagree — and they disagree constantly, about who was on the ship, how Medea's brother died, and how the children at Corinth died — the disagreement is not corruption of a lost original. It is the tradition working as it always worked. Timothy Gantz's Early Greek Myth (1993), the standard guide to the literary and artistic sources, organises its Argonaut chapter on exactly this principle, source by source and century by century, and this article follows his method throughout. THE STORY AT A GLANCE Pelias, king of Iolcus in Thessaly, sends his nephew Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece from Aeëtes, king of Colchis at the eastern end of the Black Sea. Jason builds the Argo, crews her with the heroes of his generation, sails out past the Clashing Rocks, and reaches Colchis. Aeëtes sets impossible trials. His daughter Medea — in love, and in the later epic divinely made to be in love — supplies the drugs and the knowledge that carry Jason through them, drugs the guardian dragon to sleep, and flees with the Fleece, her brother, and the Argonauts. The return, the revenge on Pelias, and the catastrophe at Corinth follow. THE THREE REGISTERS OF THIS ARTICLE As throughout this hub, three kinds of claim are kept apart. (a) The myth as told: what a named text, in a named version, actually says. (b) Cult and historical footing: what inscriptions, sanctuaries, and ancient writers about ritual establish — a much thinner dossier, given at its real strength in Section XVII. (c) Later readings: the rationalisations ancient authors themselves offered for the Fleece (Section XVI) and the allegorical readings of later ages (Section XVIII). No sentence in this article claims the voyage happened. SPELLINGS USED HERE Greek names are transliterated, not Latinised: Aeëtes (not Aeetes in the article's own prose, though quotations keep their translators' spellings), Polydeuces where the Greek matters and Pollux where a Latin source is being followed, Apsyrtus (the same figure older translations call Absyrtus). Medea's name is Greek Mēdeia , traditionally connected with mēdomai , to devise or plan — the Schemer. The connection is ancient and is reported as a traditional etymology, not proved as a linguistic one. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — R. C. Seaton's Loeb Apollonius (1912), J. G. Frazer's Loeb Apollodorus (1921), David Kovacs's Loeb Euripides, H. L. Jones's Loeb Strabo, and Brookes More's Ovid (1922) — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. A word about the geography, because the myth's geography is part of its meaning. Iolcus — modern Volos, on the Pagasitic Gulf in Thessaly — was a real and ancient place, a Mycenaean centre whose palace site at Dimini and whose great tholos tombs made it, in the Bronze Age, one of the powers of the Greek mainland. Colchis was equally real: the lowland at the eastern end of the Black Sea, in modern Georgia, watered by the river Phasis (the modern Rioni), and known to the Greek world from the archaic colonising centuries onward as a source of gold, linen, timber, and slaves. Between the two lay the whole length of the Greek sea-world: the Aegean, the Hellespont, the Propontis, the Bosphorus, and the long southern shore of the Black Sea. The saga's outward route follows that real seaway station by station, which is one reason later ages kept trying to read the voyage as garbled history. Section XVII states what can and cannot be claimed on that score. The myth itself makes a simpler point with the same map: the Fleece hangs at the edge of the known world, in the keeping of a son of the Sun, and getting it is a voyage out of the human map and back. II. The Texts: Transmission and the Principal Versions Because no archaic Argonaut epic survives, the tradition reaches us through a sequence of witnesses of very different kinds, and the reader of this article is entitled to the sequence plainly laid out before the story is told from any one of them. What follows is the dossier in chronological order. Lost works are included where their existence is attested and their loss matters — which, for this saga, is often. The Archaic and Classical Witnesses Homer and Hesiod (late 8th–c. 700 BCE) give the allusions catalogued in Section I: presupposition, not narration. The lost epic Naupactia , an archaic poem named in the ancient sources and quoted by the scholia on Apollonius, treated the Argonauts at some length; only fragments and testimonia survive, but its existence shows the saga had its own epic in the archaic period. The elegist Mimnermus of Colophon (late 7th century BCE) is, on Strabo's testimony ( Geography 1.2.40), our first witness to Jason's voyage to Aia, Aeëtes' city at the edge of Ocean, in quest of the Fleece — the passage is paraphrased here from Strabo's report, the elegy itself being lost. Eumelus of Corinth , to whom the fragmentary epic Korinthiaka was attributed, gave the Corinthian version of Medea — in which she is not a refugee but a queen by inheritance — and his testimony, preserved in Pausanias and the scholia, matters greatly in Sections XV and XVII. Simonides (6th–5th century BCE) is credited in the scholia with a poem on the voyage. None of these survives whole. The archaic Argonautica is a library of titles. Pindar's Pythian Ode 4 , composed for Arcesilaus of Cyrene's chariot victory and conventionally dated to 462 BCE , is the earliest detailed account of the expedition that survives entire — and it survives entire because it is not an epic but a victory ode, into which the Argonaut story is folded for a precise local reason: Cyrene's founding line ran back through Battus to Euphemus, an Argonaut who received from the god Triton, on the Libyan leg of the return, a clod of earth that was the seed of the future colony. Pindar's telling (299 lines, the longest of his odes) is therefore radically selective. It opens with Medea herself, prophesying on Thera; it gives Jason's arrival at Iolcus and his confrontation with Pelias at length; it compresses the outward voyage almost to nothing; it expands the Colchian trials; and it closes the voyage with the dragon slain, the Fleece taken, and the Libyan episode that its Cyrene audience existed to hear. Section XI quotes its version of the trials. Pindar's Medea is already, in 462 BCE, the story's prophetic centre: the ode's first speaking voice is hers. Tragedy worked the saga's edges rather than its voyage. Euripides' Medea (431 BCE) treats only the Corinthian end, and is given its own movement in Section XV. Sophocles wrote a Colchian Women ( Kolchides ) and a Root-Cutters ( Rhizotomoi ) — the latter apparently showing Medea gathering magical herbs — both lost except for fragments and the scholia's reports; Frazer's notes to Apollodorus, consulted for this article, record both plays' bearing on the Colchian episodes. Aeschylus is credited with Argonaut titles in the ancient catalogues, likewise lost. The classical stage, in short, treated the voyage as prologue and mined the marriage for drama — a distribution of interest the whole later tradition inherited. The Hellenistic and Imperial Witnesses Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica (3rd century BCE) is the saga's one surviving epic and the backbone of Sections III–XIII: four books, some 5,835 hexameter lines, telling the voyage out, the winning of the Fleece, and the return. It is treated in full in the two sections that follow. Callimachus , Apollonius's older contemporary at Alexandria, handled Argonaut material in his Aetia in the aetiological manner — explaining rites and place-names by their Argonautic origins — and the fragments show how thoroughly the saga had become, by the third century, a quarry of local explanations. The prose mythographers of the Hellenistic age summarised the saga repeatedly; their summaries are lost, but their tradition feeds the one prose summary that survives. That summary is the Library ( Bibliotheca ) attributed to Apollodorus (1.9.16–28 for the Argonauts). The attribution is conventional and false in the simple sense: the work is not by Apollodorus of Athens, the second-century BCE scholar whose name it bears, and modern scholarship treats its author as pseudo-Apollodorus , compiling in the first or second century CE from older epic and tragic sources. What the Library gives — and why this article uses it constantly alongside Apollonius — is the saga in its handbook form: names, parentages, episodes in sequence, variants noted in a clause and passed over. Where Apollonius is a poem, with a poem's selectivity and psychology, the Library is a map of the whole tradition, including roads Apollonius did not take. Its Argonaut narrative is quoted in this article from J. G. Frazer's Loeb translation (1921) , whose dense footnotes — comparing Apollonius, the Orphic poem, Valerius Flaccus, Hyginus, Pindar, and the scholia at every episode — are themselves a conspectus of the tradition, and were read for this article alongside the text. The Roman witnesses are treated in Section XVIII: Valerius Flaccus ' unfinished Latin Argonautica (Flavian period, 1st century CE), Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 7 , which gives the fullest surviving telling of Medea's rejuvenations and the death of Pelias, and the late antique Greek Orphic Argonautica , narrated by Orpheus himself. Hyginus 's Fabulae (2nd century CE) preserve a Latin prose summary and one of the fullest crew lists. Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE, Library 4.40–56) gives a rationalising prose version, valuable precisely for its embarrassments — it is antiquity trying to make the saga respectable history, and Section XVI returns to it.
