CE or later 1,376 lines in Orpheus's own voice, dependent on Apollonius One further class of witness deserves naming before the narrative begins, because this hub's method requires it: the scholia — the marginal commentaries on Apollonius preserved in his manuscripts, compiled in late antiquity and Byzantium from Hellenistic scholarship. The scholia are where most of our knowledge of the lost versions lives: it is a scholiast who tells us what Sophocles' Colchian Women did with Apsyrtus, which return route Hecataeus proposed, and which episodes Apollonius took from which predecessor. They are cited in this article, where they are used, as scholia — ancient scholarship about the poem, not the poem — and Frazer's Apollodorus notes, which digest them at every step, are the form in which they were chiefly consulted. III. Apollonius Rhodius and Alexandria: The Scholar-Poet Apollonius was a product of the most deliberate literary institution of the ancient world. Alexandria , founded by Alexander in 331 BCE and ruled by the Ptolemies, housed the Museum — a royally salaried community of scholars — and its Library, where Greek literature was for the first time collected entire, edited, catalogued, and argued over. The poets of that world were scholars and the scholars were poets: they edited Homer in the morning and wrote learned verse, dense with Homeric allusion and recondite geography, in the afternoon. Apollonius belonged to the second generation of that world. The ancient biographical tradition — the two Lives transmitted with his poem and the Byzantine Suda entry, all of it late and all of it to be handled as tradition rather than record — makes him a native of Alexandria (some sources say Naucratis), a pupil of Callimachus , tutor to a Ptolemaic prince, and, in the best-known anecdote, a young poet whose first recitation of the Argonautica was so coldly received that he withdrew to Rhodes , revised the poem there, and won the fame that earned him the name Rhodius , “the Rhodian”. Modern scholarship repeats the outline with caution flags attached: the dates proposed for his birth run from the 290s to the 260s BCE, his floruit falls under Ptolemy II Philadelphus and Ptolemy III Euergetes (reigned 246–221 BCE), and the famous quarrel with Callimachus — the great feud of Alexandrian letters, long poem against short — is now widely doubted as biography, however real the difference of poetic programme behind it. What is not doubted is the work's character. The Argonautica is a scholar's epic: a deliberate, knowing re-composition of Homer by a man who had Homer by heart and expected his readers to have him by heart too. The poem announces that programme in its first line. In R. C. Seaton's Loeb translation (1912), the opening runs: “Beginning with thee, O Phoebus, I will recount the famous deeds of men of old, who, at the behest of King Pelias, down through the mouth of Pontus and between the Cyanean rocks, sped well-benched Argo in quest of the golden fleece.” — APOLLONIUS RHODIUS, ARGONAUTICA 1.1–4, TRANS. R. C. SEATON (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1912) Every choice in those four lines is a position taken. The invocation is to Apollo, not to the Muse of the Iliad 's opening — though the Muses are invoked a few lines later, in a doubled, self-conscious gesture, as the poet's “inspirers” or, in other renderings, his prompters and assistants: the Alexandrian poet does not pretend to be a passive mouthpiece. The heroes are “men of old”, figures of a past the poet knows he is reconstructing. And the whole quest — the mouth of Pontus, the Cyanean Rocks, the Fleece — is compressed into the proem, because the audience, like Homer's audience five centuries earlier, already knows the story and is here for the telling. Seaton's Edwardian prose, from which this article quotes Apollonius, is the Loeb version of 1912; the modern Loeb is William H. Race's edition and translation (2008) , and the most widely read modern English version is E. V. Rieu's Penguin prose translation (1959, revised by Doreen Innes, 2006). The article's narrative paraphrases are its own, checked against Seaton's text; only Seaton's wording is ever placed in quotation marks. What Apollonius did to the saga can be stated in three strokes, each of which the narrative sections below document in place. First, he made it a geography. The poem is saturated with the Hellenistic science of its city: real coastlines, real peoples, rivers whose courses are argued about, place-names explained by aitia — origin-stories — at a density no earlier epic attempts; scholars have counted some eighty aitia in the poem, many of them explaining rites and customs “still” observed in the poet's own day. The myth is pinned, deliberately, to the map of the third-century world. Second, he made Jason unheroic in a new way. Apollonius's Jason is repeatedly amēchanos — at a loss, resourceless, sunk in the helpless despondency the poem names again and again — a leader chosen by vote who leads by conciliation, diplomacy, and, at the crisis, by accepting a woman's help. Against Homer's Achilles and Odysseus the contrast is programmatic, and ancient and modern readers have argued ever since whether it is realism, irony, or decline. Third — and this is the poem's permanent achievement — he made Medea a mind. Book 3, in which Medea falls in love, argues with herself, dreams, wavers, and decides, contains the most sustained interior portrait of a woman in surviving Greek epic, and one of the earliest great studies of erotic psychology in European literature. Section XI treats it at the length it deserves. The scholar-poet of Alexandria, writing five centuries after the saga was already old, found in its foreign princess the thing archaic epic had not thought to look for: an inside. // THE RHODES STORY, FLAGGED // The tale of the failed first recitation, the withdrawal to Rhodes, and the triumphant revision comes from the ancient Lives of Apollonius, written centuries after his death. It is biography of the anecdotal kind ancient scholarship manufactured for its authors — the pattern (rejection, exile, vindication) is a stock one. This article reports it as the tradition's story about the poem's making, not as an established event. The poem's two-stage composition has been argued on internal grounds as well, and remains unproved either way. The poem's survival is itself a fact of transmission worth recording. Unlike the lost archaic Argonaut epics, the Argonautica was a school and library text: it was copied with its scholia through the Byzantine centuries, and the medieval manuscripts — the best of them the tenth- or eleventh-century Laurentian codex — preserve a text in good order. Virgil read it closely: the fourth book of the Aeneid , Dido's tragedy, is unthinkable without Apollonius's Medea, and the debt was already a commonplace of ancient criticism. When the Latin West reworked the saga in its turn (Section XVIII), it was Apollonius's version — Jason's hesitations, Medea's interior war, the long impossible return — that set the terms. IV. The Argonautica in Four Books The poem's architecture is the voyage's own shape, and Apollonius's disposition of his material across the four books is the clearest guide to where his interests lay. The outward voyage takes two books; Colchis takes one; the return — which a lesser poet would have compressed into a coda — takes the whole of the fourth, and is longer in incident than the outward journey it answers. The proportions are the argument: for Apollonius, winning the Fleece is the middle of the story, not the end of it. BOOK 1 — THE MUSTER AND THE FIRST LOSSES Proem and catalogue of the Argonauts (1–233); the farewell at Iolcus and the launching; the election of Jason as leader over Heracles' own nomination; Lemnos and Hypsipyle; Samothrace; the Doliones and the killing of Cyzicus; Mysia, the rape of Hylas, and the leaving behind of Heracles and Polyphemus. The book ends with the ship already diminished: its strongest man is gone before the Black Sea is reached. BOOK 2 — THE COAST OF PERILS Amycus and the Bebryces; Phineus and the Harpies; the passage of the Clashing Rocks; the long coasting voyage east — Mariandyni and the deaths of Idmon and Tiphys, the Amazons' shore, the island of Ares and its bronze-feathered birds, the wrecked sons of Phrixus rescued and taken aboard — and the arrival, at the book's close, in the river Phasis, under the Caucasus. BOOK 3 — MEDEA Hera and Athena enlist Aphrodite; Eros shoots Medea; the embassy to Aeëtes and the setting of the trials; Medea's night of deliberation, her meeting with Jason at Hecate's temple, the gift of the drug and the instructions; the yoking of the bulls, the sowing, the earthborn warriors. The book is the poem's centre of gravity, and Jason performs its climax entirely inside Medea's knowledge. BOOK 4 — THE FLEECE, THE FLIGHT, THE WAY BACK The dragon drugged and the Fleece taken; the pursuit; Apsyrtus lured and killed; Zeus's anger and the speaking ship's demand for purification; the impossible return up the Ister (Danube), across to the Adriatic, up the Eridanus and down the Rhodanus to Circe; the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the Phaeacians and the wedding; Libya, the carrying of the ship, Triton; Crete and Talos; Anaphe; home. Two structural features deserve emphasis because they govern how the narrative sections below cite the poem. The first is the aetiological weave. Apollonius interrupts his heroic past, constantly and on principle, to connect it with the reader's present: this altar is still sacrificed at, this rite is still performed, this people still does this because the Argonauts did that. The Doliones still mourn Cyzicus; the Mysians still call for Hylas in an annual rite the poem describes; the Apsyrtides islands still bear Apsyrtus's name. The device is Alexandrian scholarship turned into narrative form — the poem footnotes itself — and it is also, for this archive's purposes, the poem's own claim about cult: Apollonius presents these rites as real practices of his own world explained by the saga. Whether any given aition records a genuine cult fact or invents a plausible one is a question that has to be asked case by case, and Section XVII asks it. The second is the handling of the divine. Apollonius's gods are Homeric in machinery and un-Homeric in tone. Hera and Athena, Jason's patrons, conduct their campaign for him in Book 3 as a drawing-room intrigue, descending on Aphrodite and bribing the child Eros with a golden ball — a toy described in a set-piece of Alexandrian jewel-work — to shoot Medea. The scene is charming and faintly comic, and it is also the poem's theology in miniature: Medea's love, the engine of the whole quest, is at once a goddess's stratagem, a child's arrow, and — once it lands — a fully human catastrophe of loyalty divided against itself. Apollonius never lets the reader settle for one of those registers alone. Fritz Graf's essay “Medea, the Enchantress from Afar” (in Medea: Essays on Medea in Myth, Literature, Philosophy, and Art , 1997), consulted for this article, takes its start from exactly this layering: the Medea each age knows is one link in a chain of versions, and Apollonius's link is the one that forged her interior life. A note on length and scale, for proportion. At some 5,835 lines the Argonautica is a third the length of the Odyssey and little more than a third of the Iliad . In a literary culture whose most influential critic-poet, Callimachus, had made the short, dense, polished poem the mark of modern taste — and whose famous dictum held a big book to be a big evil — an epic of even this moderate size, in Homer's metre and on Homer's scale of subject, was a polemical act: a demonstration that the old form could still be written, by a scholar, out of the Library's resources. The poem's Hellenistic readers understood it so, and the scholia argue its Homeric debts line by line. V. Before the Voyage: Pelias, the One Sandal, Phrixus and the Ram Every version of the saga opens with the same two antecedent stories, and the narrative in this article follows them in the order the sources give: the crime that put the Fleece in Colchis, and the usurpation that sent Jason to fetch it. Phrixus and the Ram: How the Fleece Came to Colchis The Fleece was, first, a ram. In the account the Library gives at the head of its Argonaut narrative (1.9.1, paraphrased from Frazer's translation), Athamas, king in Boeotia, had by his first wife Nephele — Cloud — two children, Phrixus and Helle . His second wife Ino , the children's stepmother, plotted against them, and by a contrivance with the sowing of parched seed and a bribed oracle brought it about that Phrixus was to be sacrificed. At the altar, the children were rescued by a marvel: a golden-fleeced, winged ram , sent by their mother Nephele, which took them up and carried them eastward over the sea. Helle fell from its back into the strait that bears her name ever after — the Hellespont . Phrixus came safe to Colchis , where he sacrificed the ram to Zeus Phyxius, Zeus of Escape, and gave its fleece to the country's king, Aeëtes , who hung it on an oak in a grove of Ares and set a sleepless dragon to guard it. Aeëtes also gave Phrixus his daughter Chalciope in marriage — a detail the voyage will need, since Phrixus's sons are still in Colchis when the Argo arrives. The ram itself, in the catasterism attached to the story, became the constellation Aries . The fleece thus begins the saga already double: it is a rescued child's thank-offering and a king's treasure, a thing of Zeus's altar and of Ares' grove, Greek in origin and Colchian in keeping — which is to say, it is exactly the kind of object two worlds can go to war over. The tale-type deserves a sentence of its own. The wicked stepmother, the child at the altar, the animal substitute or rescuer: Greek myth tells the pattern again with Iphigenia and the deer at Aulis, and the Hebrew tradition tells it with Isaac and the ram in the thicket. The comparison is noted here as a comparison of narrative patterns, nothing more; no source known to this article derives any one of these stories from another. What the Greek version uniquely adds is the sequel: the rescued animal's skin becomes a kingdom's palladium and the goal of the next generation's quest. Pelias and the One Sandal: How Jason Was Sent Iolcus, in the saga's present, is ruled by Pelias . The Library 's genealogy (1.9.8–16, paraphrased) makes the wrong precise: Cretheus founded Iolcus; his son Aeson , Jason's father, was the line of succession; Pelias — Aeson's half-brother, a son of Poseidon — held the kingdom instead. Jason grew up in the country, in some versions under the tuition of the centaur Cheiron on Mount Pelion, the mountain that overhangs Iolcus and supplied the Argo's timbers. Pelias, consulting the oracle about his throne, was warned to beware the man with one sandal . The scene that follows is told by Pindar, Apollonius, and Apollodorus with unusual agreement. Pelias was sacrificing to Poseidon by the sea; Jason, hurrying to attend, crossed the river Anaurus and lost a sandal in the mud; he arrived with one foot bare. In Frazer's Apollodorus (1.9.16), the king, remembering the oracle, tests the young man with a question — what would he do, if an oracle had told him one of his citizens would kill him? Jason's answer, in Frazer's translation, quoted here in its short form, is the hinge of the whole saga: “I would command him,” said he, “to bring the Golden Fleece.” — PSEUDO-APOLLODORUS, LIBRARY 1.9.16, TRANS. J. G. FRAZER (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1921) Apollodorus, with a mythographer's honesty, gives two motives for the answer in a single breath: Jason spoke whether at haphazard or instigated by the angry Hera — Hera, whom Pelias had neglected to honour, arranging that Medea should one day be Pelias's curse. Pelias takes the answer as his instrument: very well, go and fetch it. The errand is a death sentence dressed as a quest, and every hearer of the saga knew it: Colchis is at the end of the world, its king is the Sun's son, and the Fleece has a dragon. Pindar's version (Pythian 4.156–168, paraphrased) dresses the same transaction in diplomacy — Jason first offers Pelias a settlement, the flocks and lands against the sceptre that was Aeson's, and Pelias, too smooth to refuse outright, produces the Fleece as the price, adding that the spirit of Phrixus himself demands its return. The two motives the tradition always keeps in play are both present from the start: the Fleece is Jason's title-deed — fetch it, and the usurper's own terms make him king — and it is his death warrant . The saga never resolves which errand he is really on. It will matter, at Corinth, that he accomplished the errand and it did not make him king. THE GENERATION BEFORE PHRIXUS AND HELLE The golden ram rescues Athamas's children; Helle falls into the Hellespont; Phrixus reaches Colchis, sacrifices the ram, and gives the Fleece to Aeëtes, who hangs it in Ares' grove under a sleepless dragon. IOLCUS PELIAS HOLDS AESON'S THRONE Pelias, warned against the one-sandalled man, receives Jason fresh from the Anaurus crossing, barefoot on one foot, and takes up Jason's own answer as the terms of his exile: fetch the Fleece. PAGASAE THE MUSTER Argus builds the Argo under Athena's direction; the heroes of the generation assemble; the ship is launched from Pagasae, Iolcus's harbour. VI. The Building of the Argo and the Speaking Timber The Argo is the saga's second protagonist, and the sources treat her building as an event of the same order as the muster of the heroes. In the Library 's account (1.9.16), quoted from Frazer's translation in the short passage that follows, Jason called in Argus, son of Phrixus — the Fleece's first owner's son, a living link between the two halves of the story — and Argus built the ship: “Argus, by Athena's advice, built a ship of fifty oars named Argo after its builder; and at the prow Athena fitted in a speaking timber from the oak of Dodona.” — PSEUDO-APOLLODORUS, LIBRARY 1.9.16, TRANS. J. G. FRAZER (LOEB, 1921) Three facts in that one sentence carry the whole weight of the ship in the saga. Fifty oars : the Argo is a penteconter , the long, narrow galley of the early Greek world, rowed by some fifty men — which is why the crew lists hover around fifty names and why “Argonaut”, Argo-sailor, names a company and not a crowd. She is, in the tradition's own estimation, a new kind of thing: the Orphic poem (Section XVIII) claims outright that she was the first ship ever built, and even the soberer sources treat her as the first long-voyage vessel, built for a journey no ship had made. Athena's advice : the goddess of craft supervises the construction, as she supervises Odysseus's raft and a hundred other makings; the ship is a work of technē , skill, and the saga insists that skill, not strength, is what the voyage runs on — a thesis the Colchian books will prove at Jason's expense. And the speaking timber : at the prow Athena set a piece of the oak of Dodona . Dodona, in Epirus in north-western Greece, was the oldest oracle of Zeus in the Greek world — older, in the Greeks' own estimation, than Delphi. Reading Aristotle Today: What the Alchemists Owed, and What They Added XVII. Sources I. The Foundation Beneath the Art: Why Aristotle Comes First This article opens a new cluster in the Alchemy wing of the Greco-Roman hub — the foundations cluster. The articles it stands beside treat the practitioners: the workshop recipes of Bolos and pseudo-Democritus in Greek Alchemy: Origins , the visions and apparatus of Zosimos of Panopolis , the professors of The Commentators . This article treats none of them. It treats the philosophy underneath all of them — the account of what bodies are, how they change into one another, and why a mixture is more than a heap — that Greek alchemy did not invent, but inherited, assumed, quoted, commented on, and eventually argued with for nearly two thousand years. That philosophy is, in its essentials, one man's: Aristotle of Stagira (384–322 BCE). The claim needs stating precisely, because it is easily overstated in both directions. Aristotle wrote no alchemical work . Nothing in his surviving corpus is a recipe, a furnace manual, or a promise to make gold. The works that travelled under his name promising exactly those things are pseudepigrapha, and Section XIV of this article flags them as such, one by one. What Aristotle wrote was a natural philosophy — a systematic account of change, matter, form, and the composition of bodies — inside which alchemy, when it emerged in Hellenistic and Roman Egypt some centuries later, found its working assumptions already built. When Zosimos speaks of bodies and spirits, when the commentators lecture on the unity of matter, when an Arabic author explains that metals grow in the earth from two opposed principles, the vocabulary, the distinctions, and often the very sentences being glossed are Aristotle's. To read the alchemists without him is to read conclusions without their premises. WHAT ARISTOTLE SUPPLIED The analysis of change into matter, form, and privation; the four elementary qualities — hot, cold, wet, dry — as powers that act and are acted on; the four simple bodies built from them; the doctrine of true mixture (mixis), in which ingredients cease to exist actually and persist potentially; the two exhalations and the underground generation of metals; and, in Meteorologica IV, the first systematic account of the homogeneous bodies and their dispositions — fusible, malleable, fissile, combustible, and the rest. WHAT HE DID NOT SUPPLY No philosopher's stone. No elixir. No sulphur–mercury theory of metals in those terms — that theory is an Arabic development whose Greek ancestry this article reconstructs carefully, and as a reconstruction, in Section XIII. No doctrine that art can perfect metals into gold stated as his own conclusion: the question of transmutation is one his framework makes discussable, not one he settles in the alchemists' favour. And no alchemical work of any kind under his own hand. A note on method, in the form this hub uses for every subject that attracts invention. Direct quotation from Aristotle in this article is verbatim only where it has been verified in a named published translation, and the translation is named at the quotation. The translations relied on are the Oxford Translation as revised in Jonathan Barnes (ed.), The Complete Works of Aristotle (Princeton, 1984) — in particular E. W. Webster's Meteorologica and H. H. Joachim's On Generation and Corruption — and H. D. P. Lee's Loeb Meteorologica (Harvard, 1952). Everything else attributed to Aristotle here is paraphrase, labelled as paraphrase , with book, chapter, and Bekker numbers given so that a reader with any standard edition — including C. D. C. Reeve's recent Hackett translations of the Physics and other works — can check the passage in minutes. Where modern scholars disagree — and on two questions in this article, the existence of prime matter and the authorship of Meteorologica IV, they disagree fundamentally — the disagreement is stated fairly, with the positions and their holders named, and no verdict is smuggled in as consensus. // THE COMPANION ARTICLES // This article is the first of a foundations cluster. Its natural companions are the hub's treatment of The Four Elements as a system in their own right, its treatment of Plato's Timaeus — the other great ancient matter theory, and Aristotle's constant interlocutor — and its treatment of the humours and Galen, where the same four qualities pass into medicine. Within the existing hub, the reader who wants to see this philosophy at work should go next to The Commentators , where Olympiodorus lectures with Aristotle open on the desk, and to Transmission , which follows the texts themselves east and west. One framing distinction governs everything that follows, and the alchemical tradition's confusion of the two is responsible for half its mythology. There is the historical Aristotle : a fourth-century BCE philosopher, Plato's pupil and critic, founder of the Lyceum, whose lecture texts survive in the corpus edited in antiquity and transmitted through Greek, Syriac, Arabic, and Latin copies. And there is “Aristotle” the authority : the name under which late-antique, Arabic, and medieval writers published works he never wrote — lapidaries, letters to Alexander, secrets of secrets — because his name had become the strongest warrant a natural-philosophical claim could carry. Both figures shaped alchemy. Only the first is the subject of Sections II–XIII. The second gets his own section (XIV), under his correct label: pseudepigraphy. II. The Corpus in Its Own Order: Physics, Generation and Corruption, Meteorologica Aristotle's natural philosophy is not a single book but an ordered course of study, and he tells the reader the order himself. The opening chapter of the Meteorologica (I.1, 338a20–339a9, in paraphrase) looks back over the works that precede it and forward to those that follow: first the Physics , on the principles of nature and change in general; then On the Heavens ( De Caelo ), on the cosmos and its fifth element; then On Generation and Corruption , on the elements, their mutual transformation, and the general processes of coming-to-be and passing-away; then the Meteorologica itself; and after it, the works on animals and plants. H. D. P. Lee's introduction to the Loeb Meteorologica sets out this sequence, and it matters for alchemy for a simple reason: the texts the alchemical tradition used most heavily are the last three members of the physical sequence — the works where general principles descend into particular kinds of body. A reader who begins, as this article does, with the Physics is following Aristotle's own syllabus. The Man, in the Minimum the Subject Requires Aristotle was born in 384 BCE at Stagira, a Greek city on the Macedonian coast; his father, Nicomachus, was physician to the Macedonian king Amyntas III. At seventeen or eighteen he came to Athens and joined Plato's Academy, where he remained for some twenty years, until Plato's death in 347 BCE. After years in Asia Minor and Lesbos — the Lesbos years, spent partly on the marine biology that fills the zoological works, are the empirical root of his natural philosophy — and a period as tutor to the young Alexander of Macedon, he returned to Athens in 335 BCE and founded his own school in the precinct of the Lyceum. He left Athens in 323, on Alexander's death, and died at Chalcis in 322 BCE. The works that survive are, on the standard scholarly account, not books he published for a general readership — those “exoteric” works, much admired in antiquity, are lost — but the treatises of the school: lecture texts, working papers, and research dossiers, edited into the corpus we have by later hands, traditionally by Andronicus of Rhodes in the first century BCE. That origin explains their manner — compressed, technical, full of cross-reference — and, in part, their textual problems, of which Meteorologica IV (Section XII) is the most consequential for this hub. Work What it establishes Why alchemy needed it Physics (Physica) Nature as an internal principle of change; the analysis of change into substratum, form, and privation (I.7–9); the four causes (II.3); potentiality and actuality; the rejection of void and of atoms as the explanation of body. The grammar of every later claim that a body becomes another: something persists, something is gained, something acts. On the Heavens (De Caelo) The fifth element (aether) of the celestial region; the four simple bodies of the sublunar region and their natural places and motions (Books III–IV). The boundary alchemy lives under: its entire theatre is the sublunar world of the four elements, beneath an unchanging heaven whose motion drives change below. On Generation and Corruption (De Generatione et Corruptione) Contact, action and passion (I.6–9); mixture, mixis (I.10); the primary tangible contrarieties and the derivation of the four simple bodies (II.1–5); elemental transformation (II.4–5). The theory of mixture — the single Aristotelian doctrine without which no theory of metallic composition, Greek, Arabic, or Latin, can be stated. Meteorologica , Books I–III Phenomena of the upper sublunar region — rain, winds, comets, earthquakes — explained through the two exhalations, vaporous and smoky (I.4; II.4); their underground effects: fossils and metals (III.6). The generation of metals inside the earth: the passage from which the whole later metallogenesis, and at several removes the sulphur–mercury theory, descends. Meteorologica , Book IV The homogeneous (homoeomerous) bodies: concoction, solidification, melting, and the catalogue of passive dispositions by which flesh, bone, wood, stone, and metal are distinguished (IV.1–12). Authorship disputed — see Section XII. Antiquity's nearest approach to a chemistry: a systematic physics of materials, read for two millennia as Aristotle's, and the direct ancestor of the commentary tradition on mixture and the minima. Metaphysics , Books VII–IX (Z, H, Θ) Substance as form, as matter, and as the compound of both; matter as potentiality, form as actuality (H.6; Θ.6–9). The metaphysical warrant behind the physical texts: why “matter” and “form” are principles of things, not ingredients in them. Two cautions belong with the table. First, the corpus order is a curricular order, not a secure chronology of composition: Aristotle revised across decades, and modern attempts to date the treatises relative to one another — the developmental readings descending from Werner Jaeger's Aristoteles (1923) — remain contested in detail. Nothing in this article depends on a developmental chronology, and none is assumed. Second, the alchemical tradition rarely read the corpus in Aristotle's order. It read it backwards, from the metals up: Meteorologica III–IV first, Generation and Corruption for the theory those books presuppose, and the Physics last, if at all. That inverted reading is itself a historical fact with consequences — it is why the Aristotle of the alchemists can look, to a reader of the whole corpus, simultaneously faithful and strangely partial. He is being read through his last chapters. III. Hylomorphism: Form, Matter, and Privation The doctrine modern scholarship calls hylomorphism — from hylē , matter, and morphē , form — is Aristotle's answer to a problem he inherited from the earliest Greek philosophy: how is change possible at all? Parmenides had argued, with a rigour Aristotle never ceased to respect, that what-is cannot come from what-is-not: being cannot arise from non-being, nor perish into it. His successors had multiplied elements, atoms, and seeds to evade the conclusion. Aristotle's solution, set out in Physics I.7–9 (in paraphrase throughout this section), is an analysis rather than a substance. Every change, he argues, involves three principles: something that underlies and persists through the change (the substratum, hypokeimenon ); a form ( eidos , morphē ) that is acquired; and a privation ( sterēsis ) — the absence of that form in the substratum — that is lost. A man becomes musical: the man persists, musicality is acquired, unmusicality is shed. Bronze becomes a statue: the bronze persists, the statue's shape is acquired, shapelessness in that respect is shed. Nothing has come from nothing. The form was not created out of void; it came to be in a matter that was already there, capable of receiving it. Matter ( hylē — the word's ordinary Greek sense is timber, wood as material) is the name for the underlying principle considered as that out of which a thing comes to be and which persists in the result. Form is the name for what the thing becomes: its structure, its defining organisation, in the limiting case its essence — what makes this bronze a statue of Hermes rather than a lump, and this organised body a human being rather than a heap of tissues. Neither principle is, in general, a separate thing. Bronze can exist without being a statue, because bronze is itself already a compound of matter and form at a lower level (Section V follows the regress down); but the form of a living thing — its soul, in Aristotle's technical use — cannot exist apart from a body it organises, and the matter of a living thing, considered precisely as its matter, is nothing but its capacity to be so organised. Matter and form are principles distinguished in analysis , correlative to one another, not two ingredients shaken together in a vessel. Every later misunderstanding of Aristotle in the alchemical tradition — and there are distinguished ones — begins by forgetting that sentence and treating his matter as a stuff among stuffs. // MATTER IS SAID IN MANY WAYS — AND THE LEVELS MATTER // “Matter” in Aristotle is relative to a level of analysis. Bronze is the matter of the statue; copper and tin, in turn, are the matter of the bronze; the homogeneous bodies are the matter of the organs; the elements are the matter of the homogeneous bodies. At each level, the matter of that level is itself a formed substance one level down. The question whether the regress terminates — whether there is a first or prime matter that is matter and nothing else — is the question of Section V, and it is a genuinely open one. What is not open is the structure: hylomorphism is a ladder, and most of Aristotle's own uses of “matter” stand on its middle rungs. The analysis distinguishes, at the same stroke, the kinds of change. In alteration , a substance persists and exchanges one quality for its contrary: the same body grows hot, then cold. In growth and diminution , it exchanges quantity; in locomotion , place. In generation and corruption — coming-to-be and passing-away without qualification — what changes is the substance itself: water becomes air, a living thing dies and its body resolves toward the elements. Here the substratum cannot be the substance that perishes, since ex hypothesi it does not persist as that substance; it is the substance's matter that underlies the exchange of substantial forms. On Generation and Corruption I.4 (319a–320a, in paraphrase) draws the line exactly there: alteration is change in the properties of a perceptible substratum that remains the same, generation is change of the whole, when nothing perceptible remains as the same substratum. The distinction is the hinge of Aristotle's chemistry, if the anachronism may be allowed once and then dropped: alteration rearranges a body's qualities, but generation replaces what the body is — and transmutation, as the alchemists would later conceive it, claims to be generation at the level of the metals. Aristotle's framework is what makes that claim formulable, and also what makes it hard: a true generation requires the old form to be genuinely lost and a new one genuinely acquired, not a surface repainted. The workshop art of colouring metals — the oldest stratum of the tradition, treated in Greek Alchemy: Origins — lives, in Aristotelian terms, on the alteration side of the line, and the whole later theoretical effort of alchemy can be read as an attempt to cross it honestly. Finally, nature itself is defined inside this analysis. A natural thing, for Aristotle ( Physics II.1, in paraphrase), is one that has within itself a principle of motion and rest — of change and of stability — whereas an artefact has its principle outside itself, in the craftsman. A bed does not beget a bed; a vine begets a vine. The definition will matter in Section XI, because Meteorologica IV's central process, concoction, is precisely the working of a thing's own internal heat upon its own matter — nature operating as an internal craftsman — and the analogy between that internal heat and the artisan's external fire becomes one of the deepest channels through which Aristotelian physics flows into laboratory practice. Art imitates nature, in this tradition, not as a slogan but as a piece of physics: the furnace is an attempt to supply, from outside, the mastery of heat over matter that a living body supplies from within. IV. The Four Causes, and Potentiality and Actuality To explain a thing, for Aristotle, is to answer the question “why?” — and “why?” has, he argues in Physics II.3 and Metaphysics V.2, four irreducibly different kinds of answer. The Greek word is aitia , conventionally translated “cause”, though “explanatory factor” is closer to its breadth. The four, stated in paraphrase, are these. The material cause : that out of which a thing comes to be and which persists in it — the bronze of the statue, the timbers of the house. The formal cause : the thing's form or essence, what it is to be that thing — the statue's shape, the house's plan, the living thing's soul. The efficient or moving cause: the primary source of the change — the sculptor, the builder, the father. And the final cause : the end, that for the sake of which — the statue as commemoration, the house as shelter, the acorn's oak. Matter and form are intrinsic to the thing explained; mover and end may stand outside it. A complete natural philosophy must be able to give all four, and Aristotle's standing complaint against his predecessors is that each school grasped one or two and mistook them for the whole. MATERIAL CAUSE That out of which. Bronze, timber, the elements, the homogeneous bodies. The alchemists' Aristotle is disproportionately the Aristotle of this cause — which is exactly what Sections IX–XIII document. FORMAL CAUSE What it is. Essence, structure, the ratio of a mixture. When a medieval author asks whether art can change a metal's species , he is asking about this cause in Aristotle's vocabulary. EFFICIENT & FINAL CAUSES That by which, and that for the sake of which. Heat is Aristotle's great efficient instrument in the sublunar world; the final cause is, by his own remark in Meteorologica IV.12, least evident precisely where matter predominates — a sentence the authenticity debate (Section XII) put to hard use. Bound to the four causes is the pair of concepts that does the deepest work in the matter theory: potentiality ( dynamis ) and actuality ( energeia , entelecheia ). Matter, Aristotle says in Metaphysics H.6 and Θ (in paraphrase), is what a thing is potentially ; form is what it is actually . The bronze is potentially a statue before the sculptor works, and the statue is that potential actualised. The concepts are not decorative. They are the machinery that will let Aristotle say, in the mixture theory of Section VIII, that the ingredients of a true mixture are present in it potentially but not actually — neither annihilated nor merely hidden — and recoverable from it because they were never actually destroyed. Nearly every sophisticated later theory of metallic composition is a variation on that one modal distinction. When the Latin tradition renders it as in potentia versus in actu , it is translating the hinge on which Aristotelian chemistry turns. It is worth pausing on what this apparatus excludes, because the exclusions are as influential as the doctrines. Aristotle rejects the void : a place with nothing in it plays no role in his physics, and his arguments against it ( Physics IV.6–9) set the terms on which atomism was refused for two millennia. He rejects atoms as the explanation of body: indivisible magnitudes cannot, he argues in On Generation and Corruption I.2 and On the Heavens III, do the work required of them — they cannot alter, cannot genuinely mix, cannot account for the continuity of growth and qualitative change. And he rejects the separate existence of Platonic Forms : form, for Aristotle, exists in the matter it informs, not in a heaven of its own. What remains, when the exclusions are made, is a continuum physics of qualities, powers, and proportions — a physics in which the smallest scale of explanation is not a particle but a ratio . The irony that later alchemy would rebuild a corpuscular theory out of Aristotelian materials — the story William R. Newman tells in Atoms and Alchemy (2006), taken up in Sections VIII and XIII — is one of the great reversals in the history of matter theory, and it begins here, in what Aristotle refused. V. Prime Matter (Prōtē Hylē): The Doctrine and the Dispute Over Whether It Exists Follow the ladder of Section III downward. Bronze is matter for the statue and form for its own ingredients; flesh is matter for the organ and a compound of elements; the elements — earth, water, air, fire — are matter for everything sublunar. But the elements themselves change into one another : water becomes air, air becomes fire, in the cycle On Generation and Corruption II.4 describes. Generation requires a substratum (Section III). What, then, underlies elemental change? When water, as a substance, perishes and air comes to be, what persists? There is no lower rung of formed body to point to. The answer given by the long tradition of Aristotle's readers — Greek, Arabic, and Latin — is prime matter : Greek prōtē hylē , “first matter”, a substratum that is the matter of the elements themselves, itself possessed of no form, no quality, no quantity, no determination of any kind — pure potentiality, never existing separately, existing only as actualised in one element or another, and persisting through their transformations as the bare capacity to be first one and then the other. On this reading, prime matter is the bottom of the ladder: matter that is not also a formed something. The key text is On Generation and Corruption II.1 (329a24–35). In paraphrase — the passage is compressed and its translation disputed at exactly the points that matter, so this article paraphrases rather than quotes it — Aristotle says that there is a matter of the perceptible bodies, out of which the so-called elements come to be, but that it has no separate existence and is always bound up with a contrariety; that the substratum, not either contrary, is the matter for both contraries; and that the principles are therefore three: the potentially perceptible body, the contrarieties, and fire, water, and the like as already-formed bodies. Metaphysics Z.3 (1029a) contributes the famous thought-experiment of stripping away: take a body and remove, in thought, its lengths, breadths, depths, and every affection, and what is left — matter, defined there by a via negativa as that which in itself is neither a particular thing nor a quantity nor any other category — cannot, Aristotle himself concludes in that chapter, be substance in the primary sense either. The traditional reading takes GC II.1's inseparable, contrariety-bound matter, informed successively by the elementary qualities, to be exactly this prime matter, and finds the doctrine already in the Physics ' analysis of change, which requires an underlying subject for every generation, elemental generation included. The Traditional Reading and Its Pedigree The traditional interpretation is not a medieval invention imposed on an innocent text. It is ancient. The Greek commentators read Aristotle this way — Simplicius, in his commentary on the Physics , treats prime matter as the substratum of elemental change — and the reading passes through the Arabic tradition into Latin scholasticism, where it becomes load-bearing: Aquinas's De Principiis Naturae (§13 in the usual citation, as the modern reference literature notes) states prime matter as pure potentiality in terms the schools would repeat for centuries. For the alchemical tradition the doctrine did specific work. If all metals share one prime matter, differentiated only by the forms and quality-ratios imposed on it, then the difference between lead and gold is, at bottom, a difference of form and proportion in a common substrate — and what differs only in form and proportion is, in principle, reformable. Prime matter is the metaphysical licence under which transmutation theory operated. It is not too much to say that medieval alchemy's theoretical respectability is the traditional reading of GC II.1, put to work. The Challenge: King, Charlton, and the Revisionists In the middle of the twentieth century the traditional reading was attacked, twice and independently, and the attack has never been fully answered or fully accepted. H. R. King, in the Journal of the History of Ideas in 1956, argued against attributing a doctrine of prime matter to Aristotle; Friedrich Solmsen replied critically in the same journal in 1958, and A. R. Lacey again in 1965. The more influential assault came from William Charlton , in the appendix on prime matter in his Clarendon edition of Physics Books I–II (1970). Charlton's case, stated here in paraphrase as his scholarly position, is that Aristotle neither needs nor holds a doctrine of a characterless substratum beneath the elements: that the analysis of change in Physics I requires a persisting subject for accidental change — a substance — and a material cause for generation, but that in substantial generation the matter that persists is always some identifiable stuff (as bronze persists through the statue's making and unmaking), and that elemental transformation can be understood without positing a further, quality-less entity beneath the elements themselves. On the revisionist alternative that King and Charlton share — the point is made explicitly in H. M. Robinson's 1974 defence, below — the elements themselves are the most fundamental kind of matter there is; the regress simply stops at them, and “the matter of the elements” in GC II.1 names not a stuff beneath them but their own material aspect, inseparable from the contrarieties that constitute them. The defence came promptly. H. M. Robinson , “Prime Matter in Aristotle”, Phronesis 19 (1974), pp. 168–188 — read in full for this article — argues, in paraphrase, that the revisionist alternative fails on the texts: that Aristotle's own principles require something to remain through a change if the change is to be a change of anything; that elemental transformation, in which no element and no perceptible body persists, therefore requires a substratum that is not itself an element; and that GC II.1, 329a24–35, read without revisionist presuppositions, posits exactly such a prime matter — a bare potentiality, existing only as actualised in a determinate element, which is what persists when one contrariety replaces another and an element's identity changes. Robinson concedes what the traditional reading always conceded: prime matter is not a body in its own right, not separable from the elements, and not a geometrical or atomistic substrate. His claim is the narrower, stronger one that the revisionists, having rejected it, have nothing coherent to put in its place as the most fundamental form of matter. Later scholarship has multiplied positions rather than converging: Mary Louise Gill's Aristotle on Substance (1989) develops a revisionist account on which the substratum of substantial change does not persist in the manner the tradition supposed; other scholars — S. Marc Cohen and Christopher Byrne among them, as the recent literature summarises — have tried to salvage a prime matter with minimal essential characteristics of its own, such as extension or corporeality; Daniel Graham has argued the notion incoherent, on the ground that what is deprived of all characteristics is simply nothing; and David Ebrey's recent work on the matter of the elements argues, in paraphrase, for a middle position: that the matter for elemental transformation is a genuine common matter, but a specific potentiality — a potentiality to become hot or cold, wet or dry — rather than a pure potentiality to become anything whatsoever. // THE POSITION OF THIS ARTICLE // The dispute is live, technical, and unresolved, and this article takes no side in it — because for the history of alchemy, the dispute has a peculiar asymmetry. Whatever Aristotle himself held, the tradition that built alchemy held the traditional reading . Simplicius, the Arabic commentators, and the Latin schools read a prime matter out of — or into — GC II.1, and it is their Aristotle, prime matter included, who stands behind Jabirian and Latin matter theory. The historian of alchemy must therefore report both facts without collapsing either: that prime matter as a characterless stuff may be a construction of Aristotle's readers rather than a doctrine of Aristotle, and that as a construction it is ancient, textually motivated, and historically enormous. Popular accounts that present “Aristotle's prime matter, the formless stuff of all things” as a settled datum of his system are repeating the tradition's Aristotle while believing they are repeating the text's. The text, at 329a, is eleven lines long and has supported two millennia of disagreement. That is the accurate sentence, and it is more interesting than the flattened one. One distinction, finally, protects the rest of this article from the dispute. Most of what alchemy took from Aristotle does not depend on prime matter at all. The quality square (Section VII), the mixture theory (Section VIII), and the exhalation theory (Sections IX–X) operate at the level of the elements and their qualities — the middle rungs of the ladder, where Aristotle's meaning is comparatively clear and the scholarly quarrels are correspondingly smaller. Prime matter is the foundation stone the tradition laid under the whole edifice. Whether Aristotle cut it himself is the question his modern readers are still, legitimately, fighting over. VI. The Elementary Qualities: Active and Passive Powers Descend now from metaphysics to physics proper. Bodies, for Aristotle, act on one another and are acted on — fire heats, water wets, a drug purges, food nourishes — and On Generation and Corruption I.6–9 lays down the conditions: action and passion require contact , and they occur between things that are alike in genus and contrary in species, which can therefore act and be acted on reciprocally until an equilibrium — a ratio — is reached. The question Book II then answers is: which contrarieties are primary for tangible body as such? Aristotle surveys the tangible differentiae — hot and cold, wet and dry, heavy and light, hard and soft, viscous and friable, rough and smooth, coarse and fine — and argues (GC II.2, 329b–330a, in paraphrase) that all the rest are reducible to four: the hot, the cold, the wet (or moist), and the dry . Heavy and light are excluded from the primary list on the principled ground that they are neither active nor passive in the relevant way — they do not, as such, act on or suffer from other bodies. The four that remain are the elementary qualities: the primary contrarieties of tangible body, from which every other tangible character derives. Within the four, Aristotle draws the distinction on which Meteorologica IV is built. The locus is Meteorologica IV.1 (378b10–13), in E. W. Webster's translation in the Oxford Translation, verified for this article: “Two of the qualities, the hot and the cold, are active; two, the dry and the moist, passive.” — Aristotle, Meteorologica IV.1, 378b, trans. E. W. Webster (Oxford Translation) The definitions behind the labels are functional, and GC II.2 (in paraphrase) supplies them. The hot is that which gathers together things of the same kind — and, by the same power, separates the unlike, which is why fire both fuses a metal and refines a mixture. The cold gathers both like and unlike indifferently: it congeals, contracts, and fixes. The moist is that which, being readily adaptable in shape, is not bounded by a boundary of its own but takes the boundary of what contains it, while yet holding together — the behaviour of fluids. The dry is the opposite: readily bounded by its own boundary, hardly adaptable — the behaviour of solids. Hot and cold are called active because they are the workers: they determine, conjoin, separate, congeal, and dissolve. Moist and dry are called passive because they are the worked-upon: the determinable material that heat and cold determine. Webster's rendering of IV.1 continues the thought in terms this article paraphrases rather than quotes: heat and cold determine, conjoin, and change things, moistening, drying, hardening, and softening them, while the dry and the moist, singly and in combination, are the subjects of that determination.
