One Leaf: What This Article Is About Every other major monument of Greek alchemy is a book, or the fragment of one: Zōsimos of Panopolis survives in memoirs, letters, and visions; pseudo-Democritus in excerpts; the commentators in lectures. The Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra — the “Gold-making of Cleopatra”, Greek Chrysopoiia Kleopatras — survives as one leaf : folio 188 verso of the Codex Marcianus graecus 299 in the Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana in Venice, the oldest surviving Greek alchemical codex, copied at the end of the tenth or the beginning of the eleventh century. The leaf contains no continuous prose at all. It contains symbols, drawings, and captions : a serpent devouring its own tail around the words ἓν τὸ πᾶν, “one is the all”; a second, concentric-ring diagram carrying the same doctrine at greater length; small star and crescent signs; and drawings of distillation apparatus — a two-armed still of the dibikos type and a device of the kērotakis type. Nothing else in the Greek corpus looks like it, and no image from the corpus has been reproduced more often. The ouroboros on this leaf is, for most modern readers, simply the ouroboros: alchemy’s universal emblem enters the visual record here. This article treats the leaf at the resolution that fame deserves and that evidence permits — which are not the same resolution, and keeping them apart is the article’s method. The leaf will be read element by element: the codex that carries it, the editions that printed it, the serpent as drawn, the three words inside it, the double ring beside it, the apparatus sketches, the star signs, and the texts — a dialogue and a teaching treatise — that travel under the same name in the same codex. Then the name itself will be examined, because “Cleopatra” is not the Ptolemaic queen and the leaf proves nothing about any queen. Then the serpent will be followed backward to its first attested appearance, on a shrine in the tomb of Tutankhamun more than a millennium and a half earlier, and forward through the Byzantine copies that degraded its inscriptions, the Renaissance engravings that multiplied it, and the modern readings that have made it mean everything from the unity of matter to the structure of the psyche. The article closes where it must: on the discipline of the single witness. Everything said here rests on one page, copied in the tenth or eleventh century from a lost original of unknown date, and the hub’s claims are sized to that fact throughout. ATTESTED IN THE RECORD The leaf exists: Marcianus graecus 299, folio 188v, in Venice. Its contents — the ouroboros enclosing ἓν τὸ πᾶν, the concentric-ring diagram with its two inscriptions and the central signs for gold, silver, and mercury, the star and crescent signs, and the apparatus drawings — are described consistently from Berthelot’s first reproduction (1885) through Sheppard’s figure-by-figure study (1962) to the present literature. The codex that carries it is dated, by handwriting, to the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century. INFERENCE, LABELLED AS SUCH The leaf’s lost original is conventionally placed in the Alexandrian milieu of the first to third centuries CE — the formative stratum of Greek alchemy, the world of Maria and the pseudo-Democritus tradition. The placement is an inference from the leaf’s company in the corpus and from the doctrine its inscriptions share with datable texts. No colophon, no dated exemplar, and no ancient citation fixes the Chrysopoeia itself to any century. INTERPRETATION, LABELLED AS SUCH What the serpent means — the unity and self-sufficiency of the matter of the work, the endless cycle of the process, the return of the many into the One — is interpretation, ancient and modern. H. J. Sheppard, in the standard study of the symbol, states the limit plainly in paraphrase: neither the early alchemists nor their later commentators gave explicit reasons for adopting the ouroboros. Section VIII keeps every reading under its own label and its own date. NOT RECOVERABLE The original leaf; its author; its date; the hand that first drew the serpent; and any biography whatsoever of the “Cleopatra” whose name the leaf bears. What survives is a Byzantine copy of a diagram, a name, and a milieu. This article claims exactly that much, and no more, for its subject. A word on the title’s key term. Chrysopoeia is Greek for gold-making: the production of gold, most commonly by the transmutation of base metals such as lead, with argyropoeia , silver-making, as its twin. It is the defining ambition-word of the art from Zōsimos to the seventeenth century, and the hub’s origins article treats chrysopoeia as a workshop practice — the yellowing of metals, step by step — in its Section X. The leaf that bears the word as its title contains no recipe for making gold. It contains the doctrine under which gold-making was thought possible, drawn as pictures, and the instruments with which the work was done, drawn beside it. Doctrine and instruments on one page: that compression is the leaf’s character, and the reason a single folio can stand, as it does in this hub, for the whole Alexandrian art in miniature. II. The Codex: Marcianus graecus 299 and the Leaf’s Place in It The leaf cannot be understood apart from its book, and its book has already been given a full treatment in this hub: the transmission article , Sections V and VI, describes the Byzantine codices and the Marcianus in detail — its dating by handwriting to the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century, its decorated opening, its table of contents listing the collection’s pieces (fifty-two entries in the count commonly reported from that table), the quires it lost and the quires its binder inverted, and the later hands that annotated it for centuries. This section does not repeat that treatment. It takes up the narrower question the leaf itself poses: where does folio 188v sit inside the codex, what surrounds it, and what does its position among working recipes tell us about what the leaf was for? The codex is an anthology, not an author’s book. Its contents span the three levels into which the scholarship divides the Greek corpus. From the oldest, pseudepigraphic stratum: works and fragments connected with pseudo-Democritus and Hermes, the lists of alchemical symbols, and the Dialogue of the Philosophers and Cleopatra . From the second level: the works of Zōsimos, dispersed through the codex in the interwoven manner the transmission article describes — the Authentic Memoirs in part, the chapters to Eusebia and to Theodorus, the Book of Sophe and Final Count materials. From the third level: the commentators, including Olympiodorus, Christianus, and the nine alchemical lectures of Stephanus of Alexandria. The Chrysopoeia leaf stands inside this company, on folio 188v, as one item among the anthology’s fifty-two — and its neighbours matter. The codex around it is, in large part, a working book: recipes for colouring metals, instructions for apparatus, procedures with charges, heats, and durations. The leaf’s mysticism, such as it is, does not float in a devotional miscellany. It sits among bench instructions, in a book compiled for readers who also needed to know how long to heat a vessel and what to seal it with. That placement is the first fact to hold against a persistent modern misreading. Because the ouroboros became famous as a free-floating symbol — detached, reproduced, tattooed, printed on book covers — the leaf is easily imagined as a piece of pure symbolism, a mandala avant la lettre. In its codex it is nothing of the kind. It is a page of apparatus and mystical designs , in H. J. Sheppard’s description of folio 188v — his words, paraphrased here from his 1962 study, call the Chrysopoeia a page of apparatus and designs of which the serpent figures form part. The drawings of the dibikos and the kērotakis-type device are not decoration added to a symbol. They are the leaf’s other half: the same page that asserts the unity of the All also shows the vessels in which the All was to be worked. Symbol and bench, on one leaf, in one hand — the conjunction is the document, and any reading that keeps only the serpent has kept only half of it. // THE LEAF’S ADDRESS // Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, Codex Marcianus graecus 299 (cited in the scholarship as M ; fuller shelfmark Marcianus graecus Z. 299), folio 188 verso. The codex reached Venice among the Greek manuscripts gathered by Cardinal Bessarion (1403–1472) and bequeathed by him to the Venetian Republic — the founding collection of the Marciana. A later copy of the Chrysopoeia material is reported at Leiden University in the modern reference literature; the Marcianus leaf remains the primary and oldest witness, and it is the witness every description in this article follows. One further codicological fact governs everything that can be said about the leaf’s drawings, and the transmission article states it for the codex’s apparatus illustrations generally: the pictures in M are Byzantine copies of late-antique exemplars, drawn by scribes who copied what they saw rather than what they used. Between the lost original of the Chrysopoeia — whenever in the first centuries CE it was composed — and the leaf in Venice stand perhaps seven centuries of copying that no surviving intermediate witness lets us inspect. The serpent’s scales, the ring inscriptions’ letter-forms, the stills’ proportions: all of it reaches us through copyists. Section III shows what happened to the leaf’s sister-images in the later codices, where the inscriptions can be watched degrading from copy to copy — Sheppard’s word for the later forms is “degenerate” — and the lesson transfers: folio 188v is the best witness to the Chrysopoeia , not a transparent window onto its original. Best is not the same as perfect, and the distinction is load-bearing for Sections V to X. Finally, the leaf’s company includes the two prose texts that share its author’s name, and a reader of the codex meets all three Cleopatras in one binding. The Dialogue of the Philosophers and Cleopatra stands in the codex’s oldest stratum; the Comarius material, in which the philosopher and high priest Comarius teaches Cleopatra the divine art and she in turn instructs the philosophers, travels with the same tradition; and a short tract On Weights and Measures is transmitted under her name in the wider corpus. Section XI treats those texts on their own terms. Here it is enough to fix the codicological point: the Byzantine compiler who gathered this anthology understood the leaf, the dialogue, and the teaching as one dossier — a name, a doctrine in pictures, and a doctrine in words. The modern habit of treating the ouroboros as a stand-alone emblem is a habit the codex itself does not share. III. How the Leaf Reached Print: Berthelot, Ruelle, and the Modern Descriptions For roughly eight centuries after its copying, the leaf’s readers were the codex’s readers: the annotating hands of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the copyists of the Paris manuscripts, and the Venetian custodians of Bessarion’s bequest. Its modern life begins, as the whole corpus’s modern life begins, with Marcellin Berthelot. In Les Origines de l’alchimie (Paris, 1885) Berthelot reproduced the leaf — Michèle Mertens’ bibliography of the codex records the reproduction precisely: “Cleopatra’s goldmaking” (M, fol. 188v), reproduced in Berthelot, Les origines de l’alchimie , plate I, and again in Mertens’ own edition of Zōsimos (plate II). Two years later Berthelot and Charles-Émile Ruelle published the Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (Paris, 1887–88), the three-volume edition — introduction, Greek text, French translation — that made the corpus a public object; the Chrysopoeia is treated there at page 128 of the first volume in the standard citation, and the leaf’s line drawing, reproduced from the Collection ’s introduction (p. 132, fig. 11 in the citation the American Research Center in Egypt gives the plate), became the form in which scholars who never saw Venice learned the page. The transmission article’s Section VIII gives the Collection its full assessment — a foundation with faults, made quickly from the principal codices — and this article simply registers the consequence for its subject: the most reproduced alchemical page in the world was, for its first modern century, known almost entirely through a nineteenth-century French line drawing of a tenth-century Byzantine copy of a lost ancient original. Three mediations deep, and famous at every depth. The modern descriptive literature on the leaf is short enough to name whole, and naming it whole is the honest way to show how thin the leaf’s scholarship is compared to its fame. F. Sherwood Taylor’s survey of Greek alchemy (1930) placed the Chrysopoeia and its author in the corpus’s formative stratum and remains a reference point for the leaf’s dating discussion. Jack Lindsay’s The Origins of Alchemy in Graeco-Roman Egypt (1970) gave the Cleopatra material its fullest narrative treatment in the older literature, including the sentence on the ouroboros quoted in Section V. The single most important study of the leaf’s imagery is H. J. Sheppard’s “The Ouroboros and the Unity of Matter in Alchemy: A Study in Origins” ( Ambix 10.2, 1962, pp. 83–96), which describes the manuscript ouroboroi figure by figure — the Marcianus serpent and ring diagram as his Figures 2 and 4, the Paris variants as Figures 3 and 5 — prints the ring inscriptions in Greek with translations, and argues the symbol’s Egyptian derivation. Sections V to VIII and XIII to XV of this article rest on Sheppard’s descriptions more than on any other single source, and cite him at each use. Lawrence Principe’s The Secrets of Alchemy (2013), the standard modern introduction, treats the leaf within its account of Graeco-Egyptian alchemy’s founding claims — the unity of matter above all — and is followed here for the framing of what the image meant to the tradition that made it. Matteo Martelli’s laboratory scholarship, cited throughout the companion Maria the Jewess article, supplies the apparatus context of Section IX. Two cautions about this literature belong in the record. The first is that the leaf has never had a modern critical edition of its own in the way Zōsimos has: there is no Mertens for Cleopatra. The Greek of its inscriptions is read from Berthelot’s printing and from the descriptions of Sheppard and his successors, not from a dedicated edition with a full apparatus of variants — one reason this article quotes the inscriptions in Sheppard’s published translations, named as his, rather than offering fresh renderings dressed as established text. The second caution is about images. The reproductions in circulation — Berthelot’s line drawing, the cleaned-up ouroboros of a thousand websites — smooth the leaf. They regularise the serpent’s scales, tidy the letter-forms, and drop the apparatus sketches and star signs that share the page, until what circulates is a logo rather than a document. A reader who wants the leaf should go to a facsimile of folio 188v itself, or to Berthelot’s plate with its mediation confessed, and should treat every simplified ouroboros — including any mental picture formed from this article’s prose — as a copy of a copy, at one more remove. // HOW TO CITE THE LEAF // Give the shelfmark and the folio, not the symbol’s fame: Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra , Codex Marcianus graecus 299, fol. 188v, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, Venice; first reproduced in Berthelot, Les Origines de l’alchimie (1885), pl. I; treated in Berthelot & Ruelle, Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs I (1887), p. 128; figures described in Sheppard, Ambix 10.2 (1962), figs. 2 and 4. A citation that names only “Cleopatra’s ouroboros” has cited the emblem and lost the document. IV. Reading the Leaf: An Inventory Before Interpretation The discipline of this article is to describe before interpreting, and this section is the description, gathered in one place so that the element-by-element reading of Sections V to X can refer back to it. The inventory follows the standard descriptions — Berthelot’s reproduction, Sheppard’s figure-by-figure account, and the summaries that descend from them — and it records only what those descriptions agree the leaf shows. Where the descriptions diverge or a detail rests on a single modern reading, the table says so. Element What the descriptions record Treated in The ouroboros A serpent devouring its own tail, drawn as a closed ring; one half of the body dark, the other light in the drawing; the scales of the body marked along its length; inside the ring, the words ἓν τὸ πᾶν. Sheppard’s Figure 2: “a simple figure of the serpent devouring its tail” (his description, paraphrased in Section V). §V, §VI The inscription inside the serpent ἓν τὸ πᾶν — hen to pan — “one is the all” in the rendering this article follows from Sheppard (“the One is the All”); also Englished “the all is one”. The Greek is the diagram’s own text and is quoted as such. §VI The double-ring diagram Three concentric circles in Sheppard’s description of the Marcianus figure (his Figure 4), which he calls a stylised representation of the ouroboros. The outer ring carries the long formula of the One and the All; the inner ring carries the sentence of the serpent and its venom; the centre encloses the symbols for gold, silver, and mercury. §VII The apparatus drawings A dibikos — a two-armed still — and an instrument similar to a kērotakis, in the wording of the standard summaries; the same device pair the transmission article records for the leaf. Drawn beside the diagrams, on the same leaf, in the same scribal campaign. §IX The star and crescent signs An eight-banded (eight-pointed) star and crescent shapes grouped on the leaf; read in one modern account as a pictorial depiction of the conversion of lead into silver — a reading, not a caption, and labelled as such in Section X. §X The title Chrysopoiia Kleopatras , “Gold-making of Cleopatra” — the attribution under which the leaf travels in the codex and in Berthelot’s edition. An attribution is a claim by the tradition, examined in Section XII; it is not a signature. §XII Three features of the inventory deserve emphasis before the reading begins, because each one disciplines a temptation. First, the leaf is mostly pictures. Its total verbal content is the title, the three words inside the serpent, the two ring inscriptions, and such captions and sign-labels as accompany the drawings — a few dozen words of Greek carrying the whole weight of the document. Every expansive account of “what Cleopatra teaches” that rests on this leaf is an expansion of those few dozen words, and Section XVI returns to the arithmetic. Second, the leaf’s elements are juxtaposed, not narrated. Nothing on the page states an order of reading, a sequence of operations, or a relation between the serpent and the stills; the relations readers find among them are supplied by readers, ancient copyists included. Third, the leaf is a copy. Every element in the table above is an element as the Marcianus scribe drew it , at the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century. The inventory describes folio 188v. What the lost original showed, no inventory can describe. ⊙ † ⊙ V. The Ouroboros: The Serpent as Drawn Begin with the animal. The serpent of folio 188v is drawn as a closed ring: the body curves full circle, the head meets the tail, and the tail is in the serpent’s mouth — the tail-devourer, which is what the Greek word means: ouroboros , from oura , tail, and -boros , eating. The drawing is, by the standards of the symbol’s later career, strikingly plain. Sheppard, describing it as his Figure 2, calls it — in the paraphrase this article uses for his description — a simple figure of the serpent devouring its tail, with the inscription in the centre. No wings, no legs, no crown, no second serpent, no dragon’s crest: the elaborations that the Paris copyists and the Renaissance engravers would add are all absent. What the Marcianus scribe drew is a snake, a circle, and three words. Two features of the drawing carry interpretive weight, and both must be stated as features of this copy before they are read as meanings. The body is two-toned. In the drawing as the descriptions record it, one half of the serpent — the upper half, including the head — is dark, and the other half is light: black and white halves meeting at the two points where the circle’s halves join. The body is scaled and dotted. The scribe marks the serpent’s scales along its length, and the standard reproductions show the small marks — dots and star-like specks — that fleck the body and its field, the kind of detail a copyist preserves because his exemplar had it, whether or not he knew what it signified. Neither feature is captioned. The leaf does not say “the dark half is night” or “the dots are stars”, and this article does not say it either, in the leaf’s voice. What can be said is what the features are, and then, separately and labelled, what readers have made of them. The making began early and has never stopped. The two-toned body has been read, in the modern literature, as a figure of duality within unity: the dark and light halves as the paired opposites — the tradition’s own vocabulary offers body and spirit, fixed and volatile, the two natures whose joining the work requires — held inside a single continuous creature that is devouring and nourishing itself at once. One widely repeated modern gloss proposes a Gnostic duality of existence for the black and white halves; the gloss is modern, its analogy to other two-toned cosmic diagrams is the glossator’s, and it is recorded here as a specimen of the reading the drawing invites, not as the drawing’s meaning. The scales and dots have attracted less commentary, and the honest treatment is the shorter one: they are the scribe’s rendering of a serpent’s body and its ornament, continuous with the way the later Paris serpents are given elaborate scale-work in red, yellow, and green (Section XV), and any finer significance — stars for a cosmic serpent, seed-dots for a scattered spirit — is speculation, labelled as such wherever this hub has met it and not adopted here. “a snake curving around with its tail in its mouth (eating itself) is an obvious emblem of unity of the cosmos, of eternity, where the beginning is the end and the end is the beginning” — JACK LINDSAY, THE ORIGINS OF ALCHEMY IN GRAECO-ROMAN EGYPT (1970), ON THE CHRYSOPOEIA OUROBOROS Lindsay’s sentence, quoted here from his published text, is the classic modern reading, and its confidence is worth examining as carefully as its content. “Obvious” is the word a symbol earns after two thousand years of readers have agreed to find it so; nothing about a snake eating itself is obvious until a tradition teaches the eye. What Lindsay’s reading gets right, and what the leaf itself supports, is the geometry : a closed curve has no beginning or end, and a creature that feeds on itself needs nothing outside itself. Those two properties — endlessness and self-sufficiency — are in the drawing, not imposed on it. Everything beyond them, including the word “cosmos”, is the reader’s contribution, Lindsay’s included. Section VIII gathers the contributions and dates them. This section’s serpent is the plainer animal: dark half and light half, scales and dots, mouth on tail, three words inside. The plainer animal is the evidence. The rest is the history of its readers. VI. ἓν τὸ πᾶν: The Three Words Inside the Serpent ἓν τὸ πᾶν hen to pan — “one is the all”; also Englished “the all is one” Inside the serpent’s ring stand three Greek words: hen , one; to , the; pan , all. The phrase is the diagram’s own text — not a caption about the serpent but words the serpent encloses and, in the drawing’s logic, protects and proclaims at once. This article quotes the Greek directly, as the brief of the leaf permits and its fame requires, and follows Sheppard’s rendering, “the One is the All”, alongside the plainer “one is the all” used in its headings; the equally common Englishing “the all is one” reverses the Greek’s order to catch its sense, and the reader will meet all three forms in the literature. The differences among them are differences of English, not of doctrine: each renders a three-word assertion that the One and the All are the same thing stated twice. The assertion was old when the leaf’s original was drawn, and its age matters to the reading, because the leaf is quoting a formula, not coining one. Sheppard’s study traces the formula’s pedigree through the Greek philosophical tradition: the doxographers attribute to Xenophanes of Colophon (sixth–fifth centuries BCE) the position that being is one and whole — Theophrastus’ summary of Xenophanes, preserved by Simplicius, is Sheppard’s exhibit — and Hippolytus preserves the compressed form of the claim, that the whole is one. A fragment Clement of Alexandria transmits as Orphic carries the same thought in verse: all things are one, and in that one all things revolve, fire and water and earth. By the second century CE the affirmation of cosmic unity was, in Sheppard’s summary, widespread: the Hermetic Poimandres has the form “all things are one”, and Gnostic works quoted by Clement carry their own variants. The leaf’s three words thus arrive with a half-millennium of philosophy behind them — Ionian monism, Eleatic argument, Stoic pantheism, Hermetic revelation — compressed into the space inside a snake. Whoever composed the Chrysopoeia did not need to explain the phrase. Its readers already carried it. Within alchemy specifically, the formula has a second, nearer pedigree, and it is the pedigree that ties the leaf to the corpus around it. A saying in the same form is attributed, in works transmitted by Zōsimos, to the early authority Chymes (also written Chemes): in the modern summary of that attribution, the all is one, and through it the all has come into being; the all is one, and if the all did not contain all, the all would not have come to be. Olympiodorus, commenting on the tradition, quotes a like saying of Chemes and connects it with Parmenides. The leaf’s ring inscription, treated in the next section, is this Chymes-form of the doctrine expanded and set in a circle: the Chrysopoeia did not invent the One-and-All formula for alchemy; it gave the formula its enduring picture. The distinction is the section’s point. ἓν τὸ πᾶν is not Cleopatra’s coinage, and the hub does not credit it to her. What the leaf contributes is the placement : the oldest surviving image in which the formula of unity is locked inside the serpent that would carry it through fifteen centuries of alchemical books. // WHY THREE WORDS CAN BE A DOCTRINE // For the working alchemist, the unity of the All was not a metaphysical ornament. It was the licence for the work itself. If all metals are modifications of one underlying matter — differing by imposed qualities, colours, and proportions — then changing one metal into another is not a violation of nature but a rearrangement within it: strip the imposed qualities back to the common matter, and impose the qualities of gold. The three words inside the serpent are that licence, stated at the length of a breath. The hub’s origins article shows the licence at work in the recipes; this leaf shows it as an emblem. A last philological note, because the leaf’s afterlife turns on it. The phrase is grammatically an equation without a verb: one — the all , the copula understood. Greek monist formulas of this shape assert identity, not resemblance: not “the one is like the all”, nor “the one rules the all”, but the one is the all. The serpent’s body performs the same assertion geometrically — one continuous creature whose end is its beginning — so that words and image say one thing in two media, each glossing the other. That mutual gloss is the leaf’s rhetorical engine, and it is why the emblem proved so portable: a reader who could not construe the Greek could still read the snake, and a reader who could construe the Greek found the snake already explained. Section XV follows the portability. Here the words stand as the scribe wrote them, inside the ring, unexplained by any caption — because in the leaf’s world, they were the explanation. VII. The Double Ring: The Fuller Formula of the One and the All Beside the serpent — in Sheppard’s ordering of the leaf’s figures, as his Figure 4 — stands the leaf’s second diagram, and it is the serpent translated into pure geometry. Sheppard describes it, in the account this section follows, as a stylised representation of the ouroboros consisting of three concentric circles. The creature has become rings; what the rings carry is text. The outer ring contains the long inscription; the inner ring contains a second, shorter inscription; and the central circle encloses the symbols for gold, silver — the silver sign, Sheppard notes in a copyist’s detail worth preserving, bearing a tail — and mercury. The diagram is a target of doctrine: two sentences in orbit around the three metals that matter most. The outer inscription, in the Greek as Sheppard prints it from the Marcianus, runs: ἓν τὸ πᾶν καὶ δι’ αὐτοῦ τὸ πᾶν καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ τὸ πᾶν, καὶ εἰ μὴ ἔχοι τὸ πᾶν, οὐδέν ἐστι τὸ πᾶν. Sheppard’s published translation, quoted here in full because it is the rendering this article has verified in his text, reads: “One is All and through it is All, and to it All, and if it has not All, All is nothing” — H. J. SHEPPARD, AMBIX 10.2 (1962), TRANSLATING THE OUTER RING INSCRIPTION OF MARCIANUS GR. 299, FOL. 188V The sentence is the three words of Section VI unfolded into a cycle. The One is the All; the All comes through it; the All returns to it; and the conditional clause closes the system with a threat: if the One has not the All — if the unity fails to contain everything — then the All is nothing. Read as process rather than as metaphysics, which is how the leaf’s bench context invites it to be read, the sentence describes a circulation with no remainder: everything in the work derives from the one matter, everything returns to it, and nothing may be lost on the way — a doctrine of the sealed vessel stated as a doctrine of the cosmos. The Chymes saying of Section VI is the same sentence in prose dress, and the resemblance is not coincidence: the ring is the tradition’s formula, versified by geometry. The renderings in circulation differ in small ways — “by it is All” for “through it”, “toward it” for “to it” — and the differences are recorded here rather than silently harmonised, because the hub’s rule is that a famous formula is quoted in a named translation or not at all. The inner ring’s inscription is stranger, and it is the leaf’s most distinctive sentence. In Sheppard’s printing of the Greek: εἷς ἐστιν ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἔχων τὸν ἰὸν μετὰ δύο συνθέματα — in his translation, quoted here: “One is the Serpent having its venom according to two compositions” — H. J. SHEPPARD, AMBIX 10.2 (1962), TRANSLATING THE INNER RING INSCRIPTION The ring diagram, that is, explains the serpent diagram. The serpent is one; its venom — ios , the word that also names the green corrosion on bronze and stands in the art’s colour vocabulary near the final purple stage, iōsis — is disposed according to two compositions, two arrangements or compounds. Sheppard’s interpretation of the sentence, given here as his interpretation and labelled as such, is that the cyclic nature of the unity is dualistic in structure: the All separates out of the One and returns into the One, and the serpent’s twofold venom figures the two phases of that cycle, the going-forth and the return — the ambivalence of a symbol that is at once the agent of dissolution and the agent of perfection. Other readers have taken the two compositions more chemically, as the two tincturing agents or the paired volatile substances of the work; the leaf does not decide between them, and this article reports Sheppard’s reading as the standard one without adopting any reading as the inscription’s settled sense. What the sentence establishes, on any reading, is that the leaf’s author thought of the serpent as one thing with a twofold action — which is also, not accidentally, a description of the art’s central reagent, the divine water of the Zōsimos tradition, one agent that both kills and revives the metals it touches. And at the centre of the rings, the point of the whole construction: the signs for gold, silver, and mercury. The placement repays a slow look. The two sentences — the All circulating through the One, the serpent’s twofold venom — do not enclose an abstraction. They enclose the work’s materials in their sign forms: the perfect metal that is the goal, the white metal that is the waystation, and the volatile spirit-metal that is the agent. Doctrine outside, materials inside; the formula as a wall around the bench. A modern reader who knows the planetary-metal correspondences of the later art will recognise the triad’s other face — sun, moon, and Mercury — and the leaf permits that recognition without requiring it: the signs are the metals’ signs, in a corpus whose symbol lists, preserved in the same codex, key those signs to the metals plai

The Commentators as Editors: How Their Choices Became the Corpus XVI. Sources I. The Phase Change: From Workshop Letter to Lecture Hall Every literature has a moment when it stops being written by its practitioners alone and starts being taught . For Greek alchemy that moment has a date-range, a city, and a cast. The date-range is the fourth to the seventh century CE. The city is Alexandria — until, at the end of the story, it is Constantinople. The cast is the generation modern scholarship calls, simply, the commentators : Synesius in the fourth century, commenting on pseudo-Democritus; Olympiodorus in the sixth, commenting on Zōsimos; the Christian philosopher known as Christianus , commenting on the whole early canon; and Stephanus of Alexandria in the seventh, lecturing on the art entire from an imperial chair. Around them stand an Anonymous Philosopher and four verse poets, and behind them all stands the figure who made their work possible and necessary at once: Zōsimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE), the last great author of the art’s first age and the first of its exegetes. The change can be stated as a change of literary form, and the form is the fact. Zōsimos wrote letters and memoirs : urgent, personal, addressed to a named patroness, Theosebeia, full of furnaces, visions, warnings against charlatans, and quotations from the ancients deployed in argument. The commentators wrote commentaries and lectures : impersonal in address, systematic in order, addressed to students, a court, or posterity, in which the ancients — Democritus, Hermes, Maria, and now Zōsimos himself — are no longer argued with but expounded from , lemma by lemma, as a school expounds Plato. Cristina Viano’s standard survey of the period, “Byzantine Alchemy, or the Era of Systematization” in the Oxford Handbook of Science and Medicine in the Classical World (2018), gives the generation its scholarly characterisation, followed throughout this article: a generation of commentators tied to the Neoplatonic milieu, whose writings were designed primarily to clarify the ideas of the previous generations — Democritus and Zōsimos above all — and which represent, in her judgement, the most advanced stage of ancient alchemical theory. Systematisation is the right word. What the workshop knew as operations, the lecture hall rebuilt as doctrine: with a history, a canon, a technical vocabulary fixed by definition, and a philosophical frame — above all the unity of matter — inside which every recipe could be discussed as an instance of a principle. This article treats the commentators as thinkers and teachers . Its companion in this hub, Transmission , treats them as carriers — the first link in the chain of codices, Syriac versions, Arabic translations, and the Latin threshold of 1144 by which the corpus survived. Both treatments are true, and they are not the same. A carrier passes a parcel; a teacher interprets it, in public, to students who will remember the interpretation as the thing itself. The commentators did not merely hand Greek alchemy to Byzantium. They decided what Greek alchemy meant — which ancients were canonical, which of their disagreements were merely verbal, which words were cover-names for which substances, and what kind of knowledge the art was: a craft, a philosophy, or, in Christianus’s daring formulation, a divine gift administered by method. Without those decisions, the codices of the transmission article would have had far less to carry, and what they carried would have meant far less to everyone who received it. The lecture hall is where the corpus acquired its table of contents in the mind before any scribe gave it one on parchment. SYNESIUS · 4TH CENTURY Dialogue commentary on pseudo-Democritus’s Physika kai mystika , addressed to Dioscorus, priest of Serapis at Alexandria. The earliest surviving work of the exegete generation; probably not Synesius of Cyrene. See Sections V–VI. OLYMPIODORUS · 6TH CENTURY On the Sacred Art : a commentary on Zōsimos’s lost On Action and on sayings of Hermes and the philosophers, containing the great doxography of the art’s founders. Identity with the Neoplatonist Olympiodorus the Younger debated. See Sections VII–IX. CHRISTIANUS · 6TH–8TH CENTURY “The Christian”: commentator on the early canon, author of the thirty chapters On Making Gold and of work on the divine water; the art reframed as a gift of God, pursued by virtue and by mathematical method. Dating unresolved. See Section X. STEPHANUS · EARLY 7TH CENTURY Nine praxeis (lectures) On the Great and Sacred Art of making gold, the last addressed to the emperor Heraclius; Alexandrian professor become, on the traditional account, ecumenical teacher at Constantinople. The Heraclius connection is questioned. See Sections XI–XII. Three disciplines govern the article, and they are stated here because this subject, more than most in the hub, punishes their neglect. First, paraphrase, honestly labelled. English translations of the commentators are scarce: Stephanus has F. Sherwood Taylor’s partial version of three lectures; Synesius is available in Matteo Martelli’s edition of the pseudo-Democritean books; Olympiodorus and Christianus are read by most scholars, as by this article, in the Greek of Berthelot and Ruelle’s Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (1887–88, cited as CAAG) and in the modern studies built on it. Accordingly, this article places no wording of Synesius, Olympiodorus, Christianus, or Stephanus in quotation marks . Their arguments are given in paraphrase, attributed to the modern scholarship that reports them. The single ancient wording quoted verbatim is the famous Ostanes aphorism on the natures, quoted from Martelli’s published translation as opened in the preparation of this article, and named as such at the point of use (Section IV). Second, identities are stated as probabilities. Three of the four principals carry an identity problem — Synesius against the bishop of Cyrene, Olympiodorus against the Neoplatonist, Stephanus against the philosopher of the same name — and each problem is handled head-on, in its own discussion, with the evidence on both sides. Third, dates are given as the scholarship gives them , with the uncertainties attached: a floruit, a range, a before 391 , a reign — never a false precision the evidence does not earn. // THIS ARTICLE AND ITS COMPANIONS // For the commentators as the first link of survival — codices, versions, translations — see Transmission , Sections II–IV. For the author they all expound, see Zōsimos of Panopolis , Section V. For the books Synesius expounds, see Greek Alchemy: Origins . For the cover-names the commentators glossed, see the hub’s Decknamen Glossary . This article cross-links to those treatments and does not duplicate them. A last framing observation belongs at the threshold, because it explains the article’s title. A lecture hall is not a neutral container. It has a curriculum, a method, an audience to be formed rather than merely informed, and an institution — a chair, a city, an emperor — that decides the teaching will continue next term. When alchemy entered that container, it gained order, method, continuity, and prestige; it also submitted to the container’s impositions: the text before the furnace, the authority before the experiment, the reconciliation of the ancients before the correction of any one of them. The four centuries of this article are the record of that bargain — on balance the making of the tradition, and, in respects Section XIV states plainly, a freezing of it. Both truths are the commentators’ legacy. II. What a Commentary Is: Lemma, Theōria, Lexis To understand what the commentators did to alchemy, the reader first needs the instrument in hand: the late-antique philosophical commentary itself, as the Alexandrian school had perfected it for Plato and Aristotle. The form was by the fourth century centuries old and highly standardised. A commentary takes a base text — the lemma text — that the school has already agreed is authoritative, and it proceeds through that text in order, in short quoted portions. Each portion, the lemma, is set down verbatim; the commentator then unfolds it. The unfolding, in the mature Alexandrian practice described in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ’s account of Olympiodorus the philosopher, was itself divided: a lecture ( praxis ) opened with the theōria , a general exposition of the passage’s meaning, scope, and place in the author’s system, and continued with the lexis , a close reading attending to wording, grammar, variants, and difficulties of detail. Before the text came the prolegomena: a standard set of introductory questions — the aim of the work, its authenticity, its order in the curriculum, its division into parts — answered for Aristotle’s treatises in a scheme the school of Ammonius had fixed. The commentary was, in short, a complete technology for keeping a dead author present as a living teacher: his words on the desk, his meaning in the professor’s voice, his system in the students’ notebooks. Three features of that technology matter for alchemy, and each will recur through this article. First, the lemma preserves by excerpting. A base text quoted inside a commentary survives in the commentator’s chosen portions, in the commentator’s order, surrounded by the commentator’s sense. Where the base text is later lost — as Zōsimos’s On Action is lost — the commentary becomes its ark and its editor at once: we have the treatise exactly as far as a sixth-century teacher needed it for his lessons, and no further. Second, commentary reconciles. The Alexandrian school held, as a working axiom, that its authorities did not fundamentally disagree: Plato and Aristotle were to be harmonised, and apparent contradictions resolved by distinguishing senses, levels, or audiences. Transferred to alchemy, the axiom became the commentators’ central labour: Democritus, Hermes, Maria, and Zōsimos name the divine water differently and describe it differently, and the commentator’s task — Christianus’s above all — is to show the one thing beneath the many names. The reconciliation is not a footnote to the doctrine. It is the doctrine, in the form the schools could teach. Third, commentary is delivered from a voice. Many Alexandrian commentaries survive as a student’s record from the voice ( apo phōnēs ) of the master: lectures heard, noted, and circulated. Stephanus’s alchemical works keep the lecture form in their very title — praxeis , lessons — and their openings and prayers keep the lecture room’s air. These are not treatises that happen to be didactic. They are courses. The Commentator’s Four Offices It helps, before meeting the men, to name the offices the form conferred on whoever held it, because the commentators exercised all four over the alchemical corpus and the corpus still bears their exercise. The commentator was an editor : he chose the base text, established its wording as he quoted it, and decided — by quotation, abbreviation, or silence — which parts of the inheritance would be read. He was a canon-maker : to comment on Democritus and Zōsimos, and not on the recipe-papyrus or the workshop notebook, was to declare where the art’s classics lay, and the declaration stuck for a millennium. He was a systematist : the prolegomena questions forced on the art the shape of a discipline — its aim, its parts, its order of study, its relation to the other sciences — whether or not the workshop had ever conceived itself in that shape. And he was a glossator of names : the lexis, the close reading of words, made him the heir and the fixer of the art’s cover-names, the Decknamen under which substances hid; his glosses, gathered, became the glossaries with which the Byzantine codices open. Section XIV takes up each office’s profit and its price. Here it is enough to see that none of the four is passive. To comment, in Alexandria, was to govern. // HOW TO READ A COMMENTATOR // Ask of any commentary three questions. What base text does it quote, and does that text survive anywhere else? What disagreements does it reconcile, and is the reconciliation the author’s or the tradition’s? And what did the commentator leave out? The answers locate the fragment in the chain: a sentence of Zōsimos may reach us only because Olympiodorus needed it for a lesson, in the form Olympiodorus’s lesson required. (The rule is this hub’s, stated in the transmission article and applied throughout this one.) One more feature of the form distinguishes the alchemical commentators from their philosophical colleagues. The philosopher commenting on Aristotle could assume his base text was trying to be clear: obscurity in Aristotle is a difficulty, not a design. The alchemist commenting on Democritus assumed the opposite. The alchemical authorities were held to have written obscurely on purpose — to hide the art from the unworthy and to exercise the minds of the worthy — and the commentators say so as a principle: Synesius attributes the training purpose to pseudo-Democritus himself, Olympiodorus and Stephanus repeat it, and the verse poets versify it (the dossier is Merianos’s, cited in Section X). A tradition whose founding axiom is that its texts mean more than they say holds a licence no Aristotelian exegete enjoyed: to find, in a recipe’s dark sentence, a philosophy its author may never have intended — and to find it honestly, by the school’s rules. Much of what is most impressive in the commentators, and much of what is most suspect, flows from that licence — including Dufault’s finding (Section VII) that the general transmutation theory is Olympiodorus’s own, projected by the form’s logic into the founders. III. The Alexandrian School: The Room the Commentators Taught In The lecture hall of this article’s title was a real place, with a succession of occupants whose names frame everything the alchemical commentators did. Alexandria in late antiquity was the Mediterranean’s school city: rhetoric, medicine, law, mathematics, and philosophy taught to an international student body, pagan and Christian together — the world Michael Griffin’s study of Ammonius and the Alexandrian school reconstructs in detail. The succession that matters here runs as follows. Hierocles of Alexandria (first half of the fifth century), a pupil of Plutarch of Athens, taught a providential, ethical Neoplatonism and commented on the Pythagorean Golden Verses — proof that commentary on a revered, riddling, verse authority was already an Alexandrian habit. Hermias , who had studied at Athens under Syrianus, held a publicly funded chair at Alexandria and commented on Plato’s Phaedrus from his master’s voice. His son Ammonius, son of Hermias (c. 435/445–517/526) inherited the chair and made the school: a pupil of Proclus, teacher of Damascius, Simplicius, Eutocius, Olympiodorus — and of the Christian John Philoponus (c. 490–570), the milieu’s emblem. Philoponus began as Ammonius’s pupil and editor, publishing his master’s lectures; he ended by turning the commentary’s own tools against Aristotle’s eternity of the world. A school in which a Christian pupil could publish a pagan master’s lectures, then refute the master’s cosmos in the master’s genre, was not a confessional enclave. It was a method with a building. That method’s religious flexibility is the milieu’s second lesson for the alchemical story. The Alexandrian school taught pagan philosophy to predominantly Christian students, for careers in the clergy and the imperial service, and it survived — as Athens’ school, closed by Justinian around 529, did not — by a practiced conciliation: the Stanford Encyclopedia ’s account of Olympiodorus stresses how his lectures accommodate his audience, rendering the gods as powers within the first cause, treating myth as language to be explained rather than doctrine to be believed, and keeping the school’s positions teachable inside an officially Christian empire. Olympiodorus the philosopher (c. 500–after 565), Ammonius’s heir and probably the last pagan to hold the Alexandrian chair without even nominal Christianity, taught students who would staff a Christian world; his own pupils — the shadowy Elias and David, and Stephanus — bore Christian names and carried the school’s pedagogy into the seventh century and to Constantinople. The alchemical commentators belong to exactly this ecology. Synesius writes to a priest of Serapis in a city whose Serapeum would fall in 391. Christianus writes as a Christian inside a corpus of pagans. Stephanus lectures with prayer, under a Christian emperor, on Hermes and Democritus. None of this is paradoxical in Alexandria. It is the school’s normal weather, and the commentators’ ease in it — their assumption that Democritus and the Gospel can be expounded by the same man, in the same week, by the same method — is Alexandrian before it is alchemical. The curriculum is the third lesson. Alexandrian study was ordered : prolegomena first, then Aristotle’s logic in its set sequence, then physics and mathematics, then Plato, toward theology as the crown; lectures were divided into praxeis , each with its theōria and lexis . Two consequences follow for alchemy. First, the commentators present the art curricularly : with prolegomena questions (its aim? its founder? its order of reading?), a canon arranged for study, and a place among the recognised disciplines — Stephanus sets it beside medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and music, the company Christianus also claims for it by method. Second, the school’s habit of writing a discipline’s history as a succession of authorities was ready-made for an art that treasured its lineage: Olympiodorus’s doxography (Section VIII) is the curriculum’s historiography applied to Hermes and Zōsimos. early 5th c. HIEROCLES AND HERMIAS Hierocles comments on the Pythagorean Golden Verses ; Hermias, Syrianus’s pupil, holds the Alexandrian chair and comments on the Phaedrus from his master’s voice. The commentary school is formed. c. 445–517/526 AMMONIUS, SON OF HERMIAS The school’s great teacher: Proclus’s pupil, fixer of the prolegomena scheme, master of Simplicius, Damascius, Olympiodorus — and of the Christian John Philoponus, who publishes his lectures and then breaks with his cosmos. c. 500–after 565 OLYMPIODORUS THE PHILOSOPHER Ammonius’s heir in the chair; commentator on Plato, Aristotle, and Paulus Alexandrinus; teacher of Elias, David, and — on the usual account — Stephanus’s generation. Whether he is also Olympiodorus the alchemist is Section IX’s question. c. 580s–640 STEPHANUS The school’s last great name teaches at Alexandria, then — on the traditional account, questioned in Section XII — at Constantinople under Heraclius (r. 610–641). The Alexandrian succession ends in the capital, with alchemy among its subjects. It remains to place the alchemical chairs — if chairs they were — inside this room honestly. No evidence shows alchemy as a funded subject of the Alexandrian school with a succession of its own; what the evidence shows is alchemical commentary written by the school’s people, in the school’s forms, for the school’s audiences : Synesius in dialogue with a temple priest, Olympiodorus (whoever exactly he was) in full prolegomena-and-doxography dress, Stephanus in titled lectures with the help of God . Viano’s formulation — a generation tied to the Neoplatonic milieu — is the correct strength, and this article keeps it. The tie is not institutional decoration. It is the explanation of the commentators’ method, their canon, their reconciliations, and their confidence that a dyeing recipe of the first century could bear, and deserved, the same exegetical reverence as the Timaeus . The workshop had produced texts. Only the school could have produced commentators . With the room furnished, the article turns to the texts on the desk — and to the first man who taught the school, by example, how to expound them. IV. Before the Commentators: Bolos, Pseudo-Democritus, and Zōsimos the First Exegete A commentary needs a classic, and alchemy’s classic was ready-made: the Four Books circulating under the name of Democritus — on the making of gold, on the making of silver, on precious stones, and on purple dyeing — gathered as the Physika kai mystika , the Natural and Secret Questions . The hub’s adjudicated position on the authorship behind that name is followed here exactly, as it is stated in full in Greek Alchemy: Origins . Bolos of Mendes , the Hellenistic compiler of the sympathy-and-antipathy tradition, flourished in the third to second century BCE and is a distinct figure from the alchemical author. The alchemical pseudo-Democritus — the anonymous writer (or writers) who composed the Four Books under Democritus’s name — is placed by Matteo Martelli’s edition ( The Four Books of Pseudo-Democritus , 2013) in the second half of the first century CE, most likely c. 54–68 CE . The older literature’s simple identification of the two — one Mendesian author, c. 200 BCE, fathering both traditions — is not followed; the dispute is stated openly wherever the hub touches it, and it is stated here: Bolos is the formative predecessor, pseudo-Democritus the Neronian-era heir who reworked the older Democritean tradition, and the commentators of this article expound the heir’s books. Nothing in their exegesis requires the two to be one man, and their own citations never settle the question modern scholarship has separated. What the Four Books bequeathed the commentators, beyond recipes, was a voice : oracular, compressed, and programmatic. Its most famous sentence is the aphorism the books ascribe to Democritus’s legendary Persian master Ostanes. This article quotes it once, verbatim, from the published translation in Martelli’s edition of the pseudo-Democritean tradition as preserved by Synesius — the one ancient wording in the article that meets its quotation rule, named here as its source: “Nature delights in nature, nature conquers nature, nature masters nature.” The sentence’s career is the commentary tradition in miniature. Zōsimos quotes it as the art’s charter. Synesius expounds it. Olympiodorus repeats Synesius’s exposition so closely — Martelli’s study of the indirect tradition shows the verbal dependence in detail, down to Olympiodorus’s apparent misreading of Synesius’s word for Democritus’s starting-points as a title of the Four Books themselves — that the chain of exegesis can be watched, link by link, in the Greek. An aphorism that no one could apply without help had created, by the sixth century, a profession of helpers. The profession’s founder, however, is not Synesius. It is Zōsimos himself . The hub’s Zōsimos article establishes the point and this section only draws its consequence: Zōsimos (fl. c. 300 CE) is the first known commentator of alchemy. His Authentic Memoirs — the corpus as Michèle Mertens delimited it in Les alchimistes grecs , Tome IV.1 (1995) — proceed by quotation and unfolding: a sentence of Democritus, an aphorism of Maria, a saying of Hermes or Agathodaimon is set down and then expounded, corrected, and applied, with rival readers refuted by appeal to the canon. Zōsimos even preserves the names of exegetes before him — a lost commentary on the Four Books by an alchemist Petasius is known because the tradition cites it — which warns the reader that “first known” means first surviving : the commentary impulse is as old as the canon it serves, and Zōsimos is its earliest extant master, not necessarily its inventor. What he invented, or at least perfected, is the posture the next four centuries inherited: the living teacher who stands between the student and the ancients, quotes them exactly, and tells the student what they meant. When Synesius, Olympiodorus, and Stephanus later perform that office for Zōsimos’s own sentences, they are paying him the precise compliment he paid Democritus. The chain has no first link we can see. It has a first link we can read, and his name is Zōsimos. BOLOS OF MENDES · FL. 3RD–2ND C. BCE The Hellenistic compiler of the Physika tradition of sympathies and antipathies. Distinct from the alchemical pseudo-Democritus on the position this hub follows; the older identification is recorded as a dispute, not adopted. See Origins , Section III. PSEUDO-DEMOCRITUS · C. 54–68 CE (MARTELLI) Anonymous author of the Four Books (gold, silver, stones, purple), transmitted in epitome in the codices and in quotation by the commentators. The commentators’ classic: the text Synesius expounds and all of them cite. ZŌSIMOS · FL. C. 300 CE Author and exegete in one: the Authentic Memoirs quote and unfold Democritus, Maria, and Hermes. The commentators’ model for the office — and, within two centuries, its principal object. THE LOST EXEGETES Petasius’s Democritean Commentaries and the other exegesis the tradition cites but does not preserve: a reminder that the surviving four commentators are the visible fraction of a larger school practice. The succession’s order is fixed by the citations, and everything later in this article hangs on it: Zōsimos does not know Synesius; Synesius is quoted, at length and sometimes verbatim, by Olympiodorus; Olympiodorus and Synesius are both quoted verbatim by Stephanus; Christianus compiles the whole early canon; and the Anonymous Philosopher, later still, lists Olympiodorus and Stephanus together as the famous ecumenical commentators (Section XIII). Democritus read by Zōsimos; Zōsimos’s method inherited by Synesius; Synesius read by Olympiodorus; both read by Stephanus; all compiled by Christianus and catalogued by the Anonymous. That is the lecture hall’s family tree — and, Section XV will argue, the corpus’s. V. Synesius to Dioscorus: Unfolding Democritus Term by Term The earliest surviving work of the exegete generation is a dialogue. Its transmitted title, in the form the editions give it, presents it as the philosopher Synesius’s notes on Democritus’s book, addressed to Dioscorus; its opening greeting, as Martelli’s work on the indirect tradition establishes, salutes Dioscorus as priest of the great Serapis in Alexandria, with God’s approval — a pagan temple’s priest, greeted in a Christianising formula, by a philosopher expounding a pagan classic. The whole Alexandrian settlement of Section III is in that one salutation. The text itself stands in Berthelot and Ruelle at CAAG II, pp. 56–69, and in Martelli’s 2011 Italian edition of the pseudo-Democritean writings with Synesius’s commentary, on which the modern study of the work rests. Its date is fixed by its addressee’s temple: the Alexandrian Serapeum was destroyed in 391 CE , and a commentary addressed to its serving priest belongs before the fall — Martelli and Viano both place the work at the beginning of the fourth century, in Zōsimos’s near aftermath, on the strength of its close affinities with his treatises as well as the dedication. The hub gives the dating in that form: fourth century, before 391, probably early in the century. A more precise year is not available and none is pretended. The dialogue’s programme is declared at its head, and Viano’s summary of the declaration is the one this article follows: Synesius states his exegetic intention openly — to disclose Democritus’s thought, the sequence of his teachings, and his processes and materials. Each element of the triad does work. Thought : the commentary’s business is not the recipes alone but the doctrine they encode. Sequence : Democritus is presented as a teacher with an ordered course, whose books unfold in a deliberate pedagogical order the commentator can recover — the curriculum idea of Section III, projected onto the founder. Processes and materials : for all its philosophy, the commentary keeps its hands on the substances; Synesius’s surviving exegesis attends chiefly, as Martelli’s study of the divine water in pseudo-Democritus shows, to the lists of solid and liquid substances the Four Books transmit, expounding their names one by one — often by a pseudo-etymological reading of the name itself, as if the word, rightly divided, would confess the thing. That is the lexis half of the Alexandrian lecture, applied to a recipe list: term by term, name by name, the master’s obscurity unfolded into a teachable inventory. Deliberate Obscurity, and the Glossary in Embryo Synesius’s most consequential doctrine is not about any substance. It is about Democritus’s style . The commentary insists — in the passages Merianos’s study collects and Martelli’s edition prints — that Democritus wrote obscurely by design : the riddling, scattered, cover-named manner of the Four Books was composed, in Synesius’s presentation of the master’s own defence, to exercise the minds and wits of its readers — to train the intelligence that could unfold it, and by the same act to exclude the intelligence that could not. The doctrine does three things at once, and the commentary tradition lived on all three for four centuries. It excuses the text: no difficulty in Democritus can count against him, since difficulty is his method. It authorises the commentator: if the meaning is deliberately folded, the unfolder is not an interloper but the text’s intended second author. And it obliges the glossary: a text that hides substances under cover-names, on purpose, permanently requires a key, and the commentator who unfolds term by term is manufacturing that key in public. Synesius is accordingly one of the chief ancient witnesses behind this hub’s Decknamen Glossary : his name-by-name exegesis of the Democritean substance lists — the divine water’s kinds distinguished, the solids and liquids identified — is among the earliest surviving strata of the cover-name tradition the glossaries of the codices would eventually freeze into lists. The glossary begins as a lecture. The dialogue form is itself a teaching decision. It lets the commentator stage the student’s difficulties as a character’s questions — Dioscorus asks, doubts, and is corrected, and every later reader is invited into Dioscorus’s chair — and it flatters the addressee into the tradition: a priest of Serapis, the great temple that was Alexandria’s pagan heart, shown learning Democritus , a generation before the temple’s destruction made the scene unrepeatable. Whether the dialogue records real conversations or invents them cannot be known; its literary fact is enough. The first alchemical commentary is a conversation between philosophy and the temple, held in the temple’s last decades, about a book already three centuries old. // SYNESIUS AS ARK // The commentator’s second service is preservation. Synesius quotes pseudo-Democritus extensively — including the substance lists and the divine-water material Martelli edits from his fragments — and preserves, in quotation, matter the codices’ epitome of the Four Books abbreviates or drops. To read pseudo-Democritus today is, in part, to read Synesius’s quotations of him: the earliest commentator is already, unavoidably, one of his author’s manuscripts. What Synesius does not do is equally diagnostic, and Dufault’s study (Section II) supplies the measure. For all his unfolding, Synesius articulates no general theory of transmutation: his Democritus gilds, colours, and doubles, and the commentary’s philosophy stays close to the names and the lists. The mystical reading of the older recipes as true transmutations — a reading the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ’s alchemy article already attributed to Synesius’s changed attitude — is, on the current scholarship, more than the text performs: the theory arrives with Olympiodorus, two centuries later, and is then read back into the whole succession. Synesius’s real historical work is quieter and more durable than a theory. He fixed the posture : Democritus as classic, obscurity as design, exegesis as the art’s second practice, the glossary as its necessary instrument. Every later commentator stands in that posture, including the ones who out-theorised him. It remains only to ask who he was — and that question, for Synesius, is a trap with a famous name in it. VI. Two Synesii: The Alchemist and the Bishop of Cyrene There are two Synesii in the late-antique record, and the tradition has spent centuries merging them. The first is the subject of Section V: an alchemical exegete of the fourth century, known only from his dialogue commentary on pseudo-Democritus. The second is one of the best-documented lives of the age: Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–c. 414), aristocrat, Neoplatonist, pupil of Hypatia at Alexandria in the 390s, ambassador to Constantinople, hymn-writer, letter-writer of genius, and from 410 the Christian bishop of Ptolemais in Libya — a man whose surviving correspondence lets us watch him think about everything from barbarian invasions to the construction of an astrolabe. The identification of the alchemist with the bishop was made early, repeated by Berthelot’s generation, and is still repeated in popular accounts and even in reference entries that should know better: the bishop’s own article in general encyclopaedias has carried the alchemical commentary among his works. It must be handled head-on, because the hub’s position — following Martelli, Viano, and Dufault — is that the alchemist is probably not the bishop , and the reasons are instructive beyond this one name. The case for the identification is not nothing, and fairness requires it first. The name matches, and it is

This glossary collects the covers — and grades, entry by entry, how well we actually know what lies underneath each one.
