What a Deckname Is — and Is Not A Deckname — German for “cover-name”, plural Decknamen — is a substitute name for a substance . Where the plain word would tell any reader exactly what to weigh out, the cover-name tells only the reader who already holds the key: a god's name for a metal, an animal product for a mineral, a colour, a place, a riddle of resemblance. The recipe that results is not nonsense and was never meant to be. It is a working instruction with the ingredient list encrypted — legible in the workshop that shared the code, opaque on the open market, and safe, or safer, in the hands of anyone who might use the knowledge badly or prosecute its owner for possessing it. The word itself is modern scholarship's, not antiquity's. It entered the literature through the German study of Arabic alchemy — Julius Ruska and Eilhard Wiedemann's “Alchemistische Decknamen” (1924) catalogued the cover-name lists preserved in Arabic manuscripts, twenty-four names apiece for iron, copper, tin, lead, mercury, and sal ammoniac, a list E. J. Holmyard showed in Nature (1926) to have a near-twin in a British Museum manuscript that adds sulphur to the set. From there the term was taken up for the whole Western tradition. Lawrence Principe's account, in The Secrets of Alchemy (2013) and in his earlier work on Boyle's secrecy, is the one this archive follows: cover-names are, in the main, practical secrecy — the secrecy of the trade secret, the dangerous process, and the initiatory community — rather than mystification for its own sake. William Newman pressed the complementary caution, in “Decknamen or Pseudochemical Language?” (1996): not every strange word is a code, and some alchemical language is genuinely descriptive, metaphorical, or confused on its own terms. Sarah Lang's recent survey of the lexicography ( Ambix , 2022) states the resulting discipline exactly: Decknamen are context-sensitive cover-words, not technical terms with one fixed meaning, and no dictionary — including this one — can abolish that sensitivity. It can only record it honestly. What a Deckname is not is equally important, and this hub draws the line in a companion article. Allegory hides a process inside a story : a king and queen marry, die, and rise; a dragon is slain; a priest is dismembered in a vessel. The narrative is the cover, and what it covers is a sequence of operations. A Deckname hides a substance inside a word : one noun stands for another noun, and what it covers is an ingredient. The two devices constantly travel together — an allegory will be stocked with cover-named substances, and a cover-name may be a miniature allegory in itself — but they fail differently and are decoded differently, and confusing them produces the worst readings in the literature. The story-side of the distinction is treated in Alchemical Allegory ; this glossary treats the word-side only. A DECKNAME One substance, deliberately renamed: “moon foam”, “the ever-fugitive”, “human excrement”. Decoded by a gloss, a lexicon, or a context tight enough to leave one possible ingredient. AN ALLEGORY One process, deliberately narrated: a marriage, a death, a resurrection in the vessel. Decoded by matching the story's sequence to an operation's sequence. See Alchemical Allegory . A PLAIN TECHNICAL TERM One substance or operation, openly named: styptēria (alum), oxos (vinegar), leukōsis (whitening). Much of the workshop vocabulary was never covered at all — the papyri prove it. A TRADE NAME A name that looks covered but is commercial: a place, a grade, a preparation — “cadmia of Thrace”, “lamellose alum”, “salt of Cappadocia”. Geography here is specification, not code. Three motives for covering a name recur in the evidence, and an entry in this glossary may owe its existence to any of them. Commerce: a process that doubles gold-coloured alloy or fixes a fast purple is worth money, and its ingredient list is the asset. Safety — the practitioner's and the public's: the covered substances of this glossary are disproportionately poisons (mercury, the arsenicals, lead compounds, corrosive vitriols), and a literature that names them in riddles restricts casual imitation, whatever else it does. Initiation: the art presented itself, from the Physika kai Mystika onward, as mystika — things disclosed to initiates — and a vocabulary that must be taught face to face is a membership test built into the text. None of the three motives requires the others, and the reader should resist the romantic inference that a covered name signals a spiritual meaning. In this corpus, a covered name usually signals a substance somebody did not want strangers to identify. That is quite interesting enough. // HAZARD NOTE — DECODED IS NOT LICENSED // Many referents in this glossary — mercury and its vapour, orpiment, realgar, cinnabar, white lead, litharge, the vitriols — are toxic, several of them cumulatively and severely. The glossary decodes historical names so that historical texts can be read. It is a reading tool, not a set of preparations, and no identification given here should be treated as an invitation to obtain or heat the substance named. II. The Evidence Base: Lexica, Commentaries, and Papyri This glossary is not a free reconstruction. The Greek alchemical corpus is unusual among ancient technical literatures in that it preserves its own dictionaries , and the entries below are drawn from those witnesses first, from workshop documents second, and from modern identification last — with the Evidence column of every entry stating which of the three is doing the work. 1. The Corpus's Own Lexica The oldest great manuscript of the corpus, the Marcianus graecus 299 (late 10th–early 11th century, Venice), opens with lists of the signs of the science — the symbols and abbreviations of the art — and contains, at folios 131r–136r, an alphabetical Lexicon on the Making of Gold ( Lexikon kata stoicheion tēs chrysopoiias ) of more than two hundred entries. Matteo Martelli's study of the alchemical lexica (2021) is the current guide: the Byzantine lexicon, as he puts it in paraphrase, condenses centuries of exegetical effort, recording identifications and equivalences that can often be traced back into the surviving treatises themselves — as when it equates kadmeia with magnēsia , or aphroselēnon (“moon foam”) with kōmaris and “light stone”. The sign-lists printed by Berthelot and Ruelle in the first volume of the Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (1887–88) belong to the same apparatus: they give the planetary names of the metals (Section III), the grades of sulphur, and glosses — krokos , for instance, as both saffron and egg yolk — on which several entries below rest. Martelli and Stefano Valente's programme for a new commented edition of a Byzantine alchemical lexicon ( Eikasmós , 2013) marks how much of this material still awaits its editor; where the lexica disagree with each other, this glossary reports the disagreement rather than electing a winner. 2. The Authors Glossing Themselves The second witness class is the tradition explaining its own words in running text. Zōsimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE) writes for his disciple Theosebeia as a commentator: he quotes the older authorities — pseudo-Democritus above all, and Maria the Jewess — and repeatedly stops to say what their covered expressions mean, because his whole project fails if she cannot follow them. Synesius , in his commentary on pseudo-Democritus addressed to Dioscorus, does the same work for the founding text: it is Synesius, as Martelli's edition shows, who preserves pseudo-Democritus's two kinds of “divine water” and who records that the water, once macerated, “is called vinegar, and Aminean wine, and the like” — an ancient author caught in the act of listing one substance's cover-names. The commentator generation as a whole is treated in The Commentators ; for this glossary their importance is simple: a gloss by Zōsimos or Synesius is evidence of a different order from a guess by us, and the Evidence column says so. 3. The Workshop Papyri: The Control Group The third witness class disciplines the other two. The Leyden Papyrus X and the Stockholm Papyrus (3rd–4th century CE, from Thebes; English translation by Earle Radcliffe Caley, 1926–27; edition by Robert Halleux, 1981) are working recipe collections that name most of their ingredients plainly — misy, alum, cadmia, cinnabar, urine, vinegar — because a bench handbook has no audience to exclude. They are therefore the control group for every claim that a word is a cover-name: if the papyri use the word openly in recipes, the word is a technical or trade term, however strange it sounds. And the papyri also preserve the single most instructive Deckname in this glossary: at the end of Stockholm recipe 51, on softening quartz, an ancient gloss explains that “human excrement” means garlic — a cover-name caught, by its own tradition, in the act of covering. Martelli notes that the gloss is probably misplaced and belonged to a recipe the collection did not include; the displacement is itself the lesson, since it shows glosses travelling separately from the texts they unlock. The papyri's full treatment is in the Egyptology division's Alchemy article; the prehistory they share with pseudo-Democritus is in this hub's origins article . // THE EVIDENCE GRADES USED IN EVERY TABLE // Ancient lexicon states it — a lexicon or sign-list of the corpus itself gives the equation. The text itself glosses it — an ancient author or papyrus note explains the name in place. Context makes it certain — no gloss survives, but the recipe's quantities, sequence, and result admit one ingredient only. Commentators' identification, probable — ancient commentators or the early scholarly tradition converge on an identification that fits, without proof. Modern conjecture, disputed — a modern proposal, contested by other specialists. UNKNOWN — no identification this glossary can verify; the entry is kept precisely so that the gap is on record. One further rule governs the Greek. Headwords are given in Greek script only where the spelling is secured by a source actually consulted for this article — the Berthelot–Ruelle sign-lists, Martelli's editions and studies, Caley's papyri, or the standard lexica. Where a name is known to this glossary only through later lists or secondary report, it is given in transliteration or in English alone, and the entry says why. A glossary of cover-names that invented its own Greek would be committing the offence it exists to document. III. The Seven Metals and Their Planetary Names The most durable cover-names in the tradition are not riddles but equivalences : each of the seven metals known to antiquity travels under the name — and the sign — of one of the seven wandering stars. In the scheme that became canonical, gold is the Sun, silver the Moon, copper Aphrodite, iron Ares, tin Zeus, lead Kronos, and mercury Hermes. A recipe could then be written in gods alone, and a sign-list could serve as its key. The equivalences are so familiar from later alchemy that their own history is usually skipped. It should not be, because the earliest surviving key does not match the canonical scheme. The history, in the brief form the evidence allows: the workshop papyri know only the first pair . In recipe 88 of the Leyden Papyrus, as Martelli notes, the signs for “sun” and “moon” are written in place of the words chrysos (gold) and argyros (silver) — the earliest witness to the planetary shorthand, and a witness to two pairings, not seven. The sign-list preserved in the Marcianus tradition and printed by Berthelot and Ruelle gives a full set of planetary names — but with two assignments the canonical scheme later reversed: there, Zeus is electrum and Hermes is tin . The list's logic is recoverable: quicksilver, a liquid metal drawn from cinnabar, had not yet taken its seat among the seven bodies , so the bright alloy electrum held Zeus's place and tin held Hermes's. The canonical scheme — Hermes for quicksilver, Zeus for tin — is the product of the later systematisation, carried by the Byzantine lexica and, in the Syriac and Arabic traditions Martelli surveys, by glossaries that list seven metallic bodies (gold, silver, iron, copper, tin, lead, mercury) alongside seven spirits . Even there the join shows: Martelli notes a standing hesitation in the sources about whether mercury belongs among the bodies or the spirits — it is listed, in different witnesses, as both. The pairings below are therefore graded individually: the Sun–gold and Moon–silver equations are as old as our earliest key; the rest are ancient, but younger, and two of them changed their metal on the way. A note on the god-names themselves: the sign-list gives each planet its Greek star-name as well — Kronos the Shining One ( Phainōn ), Zeus the Radiant ( Phaethōn ), Ares the Fiery ( Pyroeis ), Aphrodite the Light-Bringer ( Phōsphoros ), Hermes the Glittering ( Stilbōn ). These are astronomical epithets before they are alchemical ones, and their presence in the list is a reminder that the scheme is borrowed cosmology put to workshop use. The Sun's god, likewise, is Hēlios in the early lists; his equation with Apollo , and the Moon's (Selēnē's) with Artemis , belongs to the wider Greco-Roman syncretism and is the form in which the pairings are often cited. This glossary gives the names as the sign-list gives them. Cover-name (Greek, transliterated) Literal sense Referent(s) Evidence ἥλιος · Hēlios , “the Sun” The sun; the sun-god (later also cited as Apollo) Gold (χρυσός, chrysos ). The first and firmest of the planetary equivalences; the Leyden Papyrus already writes the sun-sign for gold in recipe 88. Ancient sign-list states it; papyrus use confirms it. Leyden X recipe 88 (per Martelli 2021); Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list. σελήνη · Selēnē , “the Moon” The moon; the moon-goddess (later also cited as Artemis) Silver (ἄργυρος, argyros ). Paired with the Sun–gold equation from the start; the moon-sign stands for silver in the same Leyden recipe. Ancient sign-list states it; papyrus use confirms it. Leyden X recipe 88 (per Martelli 2021); Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list. Ἀφροδίτη Φωσφόρος · Aphroditē Phōsphoros “Aphrodite the Light-Bringer” — the planet Venus as morning star Copper (χαλκός, chalkos ). The association is reinforced by geography the whole tradition knew: Cyprus, Aphrodite's island, was the Mediterranean's copper source, and “Cyprian copper” is the papyri's standard stock. Ancient sign-list states it. Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list; the pairing is stable in all later witnesses. Ἄρης Πυρόεις · Arēs Pyroeis “Ares the Fiery” — the planet Mars Iron (σίδηρος, sidēros ) — the war-god's metal: weapons, hardness, and the red of rust and blood do the mnemonic work. Ancient sign-list states it. Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list; stable thereafter. Κρόνος Φαίνων · Kronos Phainōn “Kronos the Shining One” — the planet Saturn Lead (μόλυβδος, molybdos ) — the slowest, heaviest, dullest body for the slowest planet and the aged god. Ancient sign-list states it. Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list; stable thereafter. Ζεὺς Φαέθων · Zeus Phaethōn “Zeus the Radiant” — the planet Jupiter Two referents, by period. In the Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list, Zeus is electrum — the bright natural gold–silver alloy. In the later canonical scheme, Zeus is tin (κασσίτερος, kassiteros ), the seat electrum vacated. A text's date decides which Zeus is meant; neither reading may be assumed for the other period. Ancient witnesses disagree — polysemy on record. Sign-list (electrum) against the later Byzantine, Syriac, and Arabic glossaries (tin), per Martelli 2021. Ἑρμῆς Στίλβων · Hermēs Stilbōn “Hermes the Glittering” — the planet Mercury Two referents, by period. In the Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list, Hermes is tin . In the later canonical scheme, Hermes is quicksilver (ὑδράργυρος, hydrargyros ) — the swift, elusive god for the swift, elusive liquid metal, the pairing that gives the element its modern name. See Section IV for quicksilver's own swarm of names. Ancient witnesses disagree — polysemy on record. Sign-list (tin) against the later glossaries (quicksilver), per Martelli 2021; mercury's double listing among bodies and spirits noted there. χρυσήλεκτρον / ἀσῆμον · chrysēlektron; asēmon “Gold-electrum”; asēmon : “unstamped (metal)” Electrum and its workshop heirs. Ēlektron is the natural gold–silver alloy; the sign-list's chrysēlektron is its gold-rich face. Asēmon (also written asem in Caley's translation) is the papyri's workhorse product-name: a white alloy made to stand for silver — occasionally for gold — whose recipes fill the Leyden Papyrus. The alloy that held a planet's seat in the early list ends as the imitation the whole workshop economy ran on. Ancient sign-list states the electrum terms; context makes the asem sense certain. Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list; Leyden X recipes 5–13 and passim (Caley). The lesson of the table is the glossary's lesson in miniature. Even the most “universal” code in alchemy — seven gods, seven metals — turns out to be a local, dated arrangement that shifted at exactly the point (quicksilver's promotion) where the art's theory was changing. The reader who memorises the canonical seven and applies them to the sign-list's period will misread Zeus and Hermes in every recipe. Section X returns to the rule this imposes. IV. Substances of the Work I: Mercury, Sulphur, and the Arsenicals If the metals of Section III have one cover-name each, the volatile substances have dozens. The reason is structural: the spirits — the things that rise under heat, carry colour, and flee the vessel — are the art's active agents, its most valuable and most dangerous stock, and therefore its most renamed. Mercury heads the swarm. C. A. Browne's classic survey of alchemical obscurity, summarising the Greek lexicon tradition, reports mercury described by Zōsimos as “the silvery water; the masculine-feminine; the ever-fugitive; that which hastens unto its own; and the divine water”, and lists the lexicon's further names for it — seed of the dragon, bile of the dragon, dew, milk of a black cow, sandarach, Scythian water, water of silver, water of the moon, river water, divine water, the sea and sea-water. That list is quoted here as Browne reports it, at second hand, and the entries drawn from it are graded accordingly: the swarm is real, but any single name in it carries weaker evidence than a name a papyrus glosses in place. One name in the section requires its philology up front, because it is the most famous pun in Greek alchemy. Θεῖον ( theion ) is two words wearing one spelling: theion the adjective means “divine”; theion the noun means “sulphur” (brimstone — the burning stone itself, whose fumes purified Greek sanctuaries long before they tinctured metals). The phrase θεῖον ὕδωρ ( theion hydōr ) therefore says “divine water” and “sulphur water” at once, and in the genitive — theiou hydatos — Greek grammar itself cannot tell the reader which was meant. Matteo Martelli's study of the phrase in pseudo-Democritus ( Ambix , 2009) is the definitive treatment: the alchemists, he shows, play on the polysemy deliberately, the manuscripts abbreviate the phrase with signs that deepen the ambiguity, and pseudo-Democritus in fact knows two kinds of the water, distinguished by composition — a sulphur-bearing water, and a water whose second form recalls the Leyden Papyrus's own recipe for “sulphur water” (recipe 89: lime and sulphur heated in strong vinegar or a child's urine until the liquor stands “like blood”, in Caley's translation, then decanted for use). The pun is not decoration. It is a cover-name generated by the language itself, and the tradition exploited it for a thousand years. Cover-name (Greek, transliterated) Literal sense Referent(s) Evidence θεῖον ὕδωρ · theion hydōr “Divine water” — or “sulphur water”; the Greek carries both (see introduction) A sulphur-bearing tincturing liquor , in (at least) two ancient kinds distinguished by composition: a water of sulphur, and a compounded water of the lime-and-sulphur type preserved in Leyden X recipe 89. In Zōsimos it becomes the art's central reagent — the volatile agent that draws spirits from bodies and fixes them in others. It is never, in this corpus, plain H₂O, and never one fixed recipe. Ancient authors state and distinguish it; exact composition varies by text. Pseudo-Democritus via Synesius and Moses (Martelli 2009); Leyden X recipe 89 (Caley); Zōsimos passim. ὑδράργυρος · hydrargyros “Water-silver” — liquid silver Quicksilver (metallic mercury) , extracted from cinnabar, as the sign-list itself notes. The name is descriptive, not covered — but it is the plain name underneath the whole covered swarm that follows, and the papyri use it openly (Leyden X recipes 5, 9, 13, 34). Ancient sign-list states it; context makes it certain. Berthelot–Ruelle sign-list; Leyden X (Caley). the ever-fugitive; that which hastens unto its own Epithets of flight and self-seeking (given here in translation; see Evidence) Quicksilver. The fugitive who will not stay in the fire or the hand; in the later Arabic and Latin transmission the image hardens into the runaway slave and the servant who must be caught, bound (fixed), and set to work — the whole technology of amalgamation and fixation told as a household pursuit. Covering, in this corpus, is selective, and the selection maps value and danger, not a general love of obscurity. V. Substances of the Work II: Earths, Salts, and Vitriols The second substance-family is the workshop's corrosive cupboard: alkalis, alum, and the vitriol group — the weathered copper-and-iron sulphates that antiquity mined, above all on Cyprus, and distinguished with a care modern readers must work to recover. Dioscorides and Pliny describe these minerals; Galen travelled to the Cypriot mines and collected them in layers — sōry from the lowest, chalcitis above it, misy at the top — and found his chalcitis crusted with misy twenty years later. That single observation governs the whole family's grading: these are mixtures that weather into one another , not pure compounds, and every modern chemical name offered below is a centre of gravity, not an identity. Karpenko and Norris's history of vitriol makes the complementary point: the commercial vitriol of antiquity, for all its copper associations, was in most samples iron-rich. Entries that flatten misy to one modern mineral formula are claiming more than the evidence holds; this glossary gives the formula as the leading modern candidate and grades it probable. x: DESCENTS: KATABASIS AND THE GEOGRAPHY OF THE DEAD The Edge of Ocean · Thesprotia · Cumae · And Below // GOING DOWN TO THE DEAD :: AND THE HARDER LABOUR OF COMING BACK // A handful of the living, in the Greek and Roman telling, went down into the house of Hades and returned: to ask a question, to fetch a hound, to steal a queen, to sing a wife back, to found an empire, or — once, unforgettably — to fetch a dead tragedian. This article maps the place they went to, tells each descent in full, and keeps the stories, the rites behind them, and the philosophy later built on them apart. What a Descent Taught XVII. Later Readings: The Soul’s Journey and the Alchemists XVIII. Sources I. Katabasis, Nekyia, Anabasis: The Words and the Distinctions The Greek word at the centre of this article is katabasis — from kata , “down”, and bainō , “I go” — a going-down. In its specialised modern use, which follows the ancient stories’ own shape, a katabasis is a journey by a living person down into the realm of the dead, and back. The return has its own word, anabasis , a going-up, and the pair belong together: a descent without a return is not a katabasis but a death. The Sibyl of Cumae states the asymmetry in the most quoted lines of the whole tradition, warning Aeneas before she will guide him (Virgil, Aeneid 6.126–129, trans. Robert Fagles, 2006): “The descent to the Underworld is easy. Night and day the gates of shadowy Death stand open wide, but to retrace your steps, to climb back to the upper air — there the struggle, there the labor lies.” — VIRGIL, AENEID 6.126–129, TRANS. ROBERT FAGLES (2006) Against katabasis the scholarship sets a second word, and the distinction is load-bearing for everything that follows. A nekyia (from nekys , a corpse, a dead person) is a rite for summoning and questioning the dead — an act of necromancy — in which the dead come up , or out, to the living, rather than the living going down to them. Odyssey Book 11, the oldest and most influential underworld episode in Greek literature, bears the traditional title Nekyia , and it earns it: Odysseus does not enter the house of Hades. He sails to the edge of the world, digs a pit, pours blood into it, and the dead come to him (Section VIII). Radcliffe Edmonds, in Myths of the Underworld Journey (2004), builds his analysis of the whole family of stories on the recognition that each telling is a fresh piece of work with traditional materials — his term, following Lévi-Strauss, is bricolage — and that the pattern (obstacles at the boundary, means of overcoming them, and a result that marks off one group of people from another) is constant while the meaning is remade by every teller. This article follows that discipline. Homer, Hesiod, Pindar, Aristophanes, Plato, Apollodorus, and Virgil are not chapters of one doctrine. They are successive, competing maps of the same dark country, drawn for different audiences and different purposes, and they disagree — about the rivers, about the judges, about whether anyone down there is happy — in ways this article reports rather than reconciles. Three registers must therefore be kept apart throughout, and the article’s sections are arranged to keep them so. First, the tales as told : the geography and the descents as the poems and mythographers present them (Sections II–XIII). Second, the ritual footing : the oracles of the dead, the burial customs, and the hero cults that gave the stories a footing in practice (Sections IV and XV). Third, the philosophical remaking : what Plato, and after him the whole later tradition, did with a geography they no longer simply believed (Sections XIV and XVII). A sentence drawn from one register is never allowed to do duty in another without the transfer being named. KATABASIS A living person’s descent into the realm of the dead and return: Heracles, Orpheus, Theseus (in part), Aeneas, and — in comedy — Dionysus. The return, the anabasis , is the feat; the descent itself, as the Sibyl says, is easy. NEKYIA A summoning of the dead for questioning, performed at the boundary — a pit of blood at the edge of Ocean, a tomb, a lakeside oracle. Odysseus’s rite in Odyssey 11 is the type case: the dead come to the living man, who never crosses into their country. THE TRAVELLERS Each descent in this article has a stated errand: knowledge (Odysseus), a labour imposed by a master (Heracles), theft (Theseus and Pirithous), love (Orpheus), a father and a destiny (Aeneas), a poet (Dionysus). The errand, not the scenery, is what each story is about. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — A. T. Murray’s Loeb Odyssey (1919), H. G. Evelyn-White’s Loeb Hesiod (1914), J. G. Frazer’s Loeb Apollodorus (1921), Robert Fagles’s Aeneid (2006), Benjamin Jowett’s Plato, Diane Arnson Svarlien’s Pindar (1990), and A. S. Kline’s Georgics — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author’s sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. II. Hades the God, Hades the Place Greek uses one word, Haidēs — in the older form Aïdēs , traditionally explained as “the Unseen” — for both the god who rules the dead and the realm he rules, and the ambiguity is ancient and productive. When Homer’s heroes go down “to Hades”, they go to a house and to its master at once: the Odyssey speaks throughout of “the house of Hades”, a dwelling with gates, a threshold, and a household, ruled by the god and his queen. Keeping the two senses apart is the first act of map-making, because the god has a biography and the place has a geography, and they are not the same story. The God Hades the god is a son of Kronos and Rhea, brother of Zeus and Poseidon, and in the division of the cosmos that the Iliad puts into Poseidon’s mouth (15.187–193, paraphrased) the three brothers cast lots for their domains: Zeus drew the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the murky darkness below — the dead and the underworld — while earth and Olympus remained common to all. He is, in the Theogony ’s family tree treated in this hub’s Theogony , “strong Hades, pitiless in heart, who dwells under the earth” (Hesiod, Theogony 455, Evelyn-White’s rendering, paraphrased in context here). His epithets mark his double nature. As receiver of the dead he is polydegmōn and polyxenos , “host of many” — the one host no guest refuses. As keeper of the earth’s buried wealth he is Ploutōn , Pluto, “the Wealthy One”, the name under which Rome received him as Dis; the euphemism is transparent and was already felt as one in antiquity — wealth is the polite name for the power nobody wishes to name plainly. His queen is Persephone, daughter of Demeter, whose abduction and divided year are the charter myth of Eleusis told in this hub’s Mysteries ; in the underworld she is no victim but a sovereign, dread Persephone, whose permission every traveller in this article must in the end obtain. Two features of the god matter for the descents. First, he is not a devil. Greek tradition gives Hades no programme of tormenting the dead for its own sake, no rebellion against Zeus, and almost no myths of his own initiative at all beyond the abduction of Persephone: he is a gaoler-king administering an allotment, bound by the same order of things as his brothers, and — crucially — capable of being petitioned, bargained with, and on one famous occasion moved by a song (Section XI). The punishments of Tartarus (Section VI) fall on those who offended gods , not on ordinary human sinners. Second, he is nearly invisible in cult. Where Zeus and Poseidon had temples in every city, Hades had almost none — the famous exception, the sanctuary at Elis where a temple of Hades was opened once a year and entered only by its priest, is reported by Pausanias (6.25, paraphrased) precisely as a curiosity. Greeks sacrificed to him, when they did, with averted faces and offerings struck into the ground. The god of the dead was honoured by being left alone, and his realm was imagined in the same spirit: not worshipped, not explored, and — except by the travellers of this article — not visited. The Place Hades the place, in the earliest texts, is less a country than a condition. Homer’s dead are psychai , breath-souls, strengthless heads (the Odyssey ’s recurring phrase, in Murray’s translation) who flit like shadows or dreams, witless until they drink blood, and housed in a murk — Erebos is Homer’s word for the darkness in and under which they gather — that has a gate, a meadow, and almost no interior architecture. Its location is correspondingly vague, and the vagueness is geographical in two directions at once. It is below : heroes go down to it, it lies under the earth at a depth Hesiod will presently measure (Section VI). And it is beyond : Odysseus reaches its threshold by sailing across Ocean to the land of the Cimmerians, where the sun never shines (Section VIII), so that the realm of the dead sits at the edge of the world’s map as well as under its floor. Later tradition multiplied entrances and stitched the two directions together — caves and lakes in the known world, at Tainaron, at Heraclea, at Avernus, where the upper world was held to open downward (Section XV) — but the Homeric picture never lost its authority: a house at the world’s edge and under its foundations, whose inhabitants are what is left of people when strength, memory, and voice have gone out of them. // NOT HELL // The single most important correction a modern reader needs is negative. Homeric Hades is not a place of moral judgement for ordinary people: there is no heaven for the good and no hell for the bad in Odyssey 11, only the same grey twilight for kings and hirelings, which is why Achilles’ verdict on it (Section VIII) is so bleak. Judgement, reward, and punishment enter the map slowly — Sections V–VII and XIV trace the entry — and are never, in the pagan tradition, universalised into the two-destination scheme later ages take for granted. The population of the place, as the tradition assembles it, divides into kinds, and the descents meet them in a fairly stable order that Virgil will eventually codify (Section XII): the unburied, who cannot properly enter; the untimely dead — infants, the unmarried, those cut off early; the great company of ordinary shades in the meadow; the heroes, who keep something of their earthly pursuits and grievances; the exceptional sufferers, punished for offences against gods; and, at the brightening margin, the exceptional blessed. The staff of the place is equally stable: Charon at the crossing (Section IV), Cerberus at the gate (Sections IV and IX), the judges in their court (Section V), Hermes in his one underworld office — psychopompos , conductor of souls, who in Odyssey 24 (paraphrased) leads the suitors’ ghosts down with his golden wand, squeaking like bats — and Hecate at the crossroads and thresholds, honoured already in Hesiod above all the Titan-born (see Theogony , Section VII). What the tradition never supplies is a survey. Every traveller sees a part, from a path, in the dark, and the maps disagree because the journeys did. III. The Rivers of the Dead An underworld with a geography needs water, and the tradition supplied it river by river, over centuries. The finished system — five named rivers, each with a character and an office — is so familiar from later literature that it is easy to mistake it for a Homeric given. It is not. The rivers enter the texts one or two at a time, and the full fivefold scheme is a late systematisation, completed by Plato and canonised by Virgil. Tracing the entries in order is the cleanest demonstration in this article of how the geography of the dead was built . Styx: The First River, and an Oath Before It Is a Crossing The oldest underworld river is the Styx , and in Hesiod — its fullest early treatment, Theogony 775–806, paraphrased from Evelyn-White’s translation — it is not yet primarily a river of the dead at all. Styx is a goddess, eldest daughter of Ocean, who lives apart from the gods in a glorious house vaulted with great rocks and propped to heaven with silver pillars, far under the earth, where a branch of Ocean flows through the dark night: a tenth part of Ocean’s water is allotted to her. Her office is the gods’ oath. When strife arises on Olympus, Zeus sends Iris with a golden jug to fetch the famous cold water of Styx, and a god who pours a libation of it and swears falsely lies breathless for a full year, cut off from nectar and ambrosia, and exiled from the gods’ councils for nine more. The river of the dead begins, in other words, as the cosmos’s instrument of truth — the water by which even gods are bound — and its dreadfulness is juridical before it is topographical. Homer knows Styx in the same register: gods swear by “the down-flowing water of Styx”, and the Iliad (8.369, paraphrased) can use “the gates of Hades and dread Persephone” and Styx together as the limit of Heracles’ labours. Only later does Styx settle into the role the handbooks give it, as the river Charon ferries — and even then the texts disagree about which river the ferry crosses (Section IV). Acheron and Cocytus: The Homeric Pair Homer’s own underworld rivers, named where Circe gives Odysseus his sailing directions ( Odyssey 10.513–515, paraphrased from Murray’s translation), are Acheron , the river of woe, and its two tributaries: Pyriphlegethon , the river blazing with fire, and Cocytus , the river of wailing, which Circe calls a branch of the water of Styx; all three flow together into Acheron at a rock where the traveller is to dig his pit. That is the whole Homeric river-system: a confluence at the edge of Ocean, described in four lines, as a landmark for a rite. Acheron had a double life the other rivers never quite matched, because there was a real Acheron — a river of Thesprotia in north-western Greece, flowing through a gloomy gorge into an Acherusian lake near the coast — and the real river anchored the mythic one to a visitable place, with an oracle of the dead on its banks (Section XV). Cocytus, “Wailing”, stays mostly a name and a sound: the river whose name is what the dead do beside it. Pyriphlegethon and Lethe: Fire and Forgetting Pyriphlegethon — Phlegethon in its shortened Latin form — is Homer’s fire-river, and Plato will give it the fullest ancient description: a stream that issues into a vast region of fire, forms a boiling lake of water and mud larger than the sea, coils many times around the earth, and plunges at last into Tartarus, throwing up jets of fire — the lava streams of the upper world are its offshoots — wherever it nears the surface ( Phaedo 113a–b, paraphrased; Section XIV). Lethe , Forgetfulness, is the latest arrival and the most consequential. As a personified power she is old — Hesiod makes Lethe a daughter of Strife ( Theogony 227, paraphrased) — but as an underworld river or plain whose water the dead drink and forget, she belongs to the developed eschatologies: to the gold tablets’ geography, where the forbidden spring is hers by implication and the chosen water is Memory’s (the tablets’ own treatment is in The Mysteries , Section IX, and is not duplicated here); to Plato’s Myth of Er, where the souls cross the plain of Lethe and drink from the river of Unmindfulness before rebirth (Section XIV); and to Virgil, whose Anchises points out the souls at Lethe’s stream who must forget everything before they can return to bodies (Section XII). A river that erases the traveller is the tradition’s most elegant invention: the underworld’s final defence is not a wall but a drink. River Name means Earliest full treatment Office in the developed map Styx “Hateful, shuddering” Hesiod, Theogony 775–806: a goddess under the earth, the gods’ oath-water The boundary river; the oath; in many later accounts, the ferry crossing Acheron “River of woe” Odyssey 10.513: the river into which Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus flow The crossing Charon makes in Virgil and most later tradition; also a real river in Thesprotia with an oracle of the dead Cocytus “Wailing” Odyssey 10.514: a branch of Styx flowing into Acheron The river of lamentation; in Plato, a route by which the curably wicked are carried back from Tartarus Pyriphlegethon “Blazing with fire” Odyssey 10.513; fully described in Plato, Phaedo 113a–b The fire-river coiling round the earth and into Tartarus; source of volcanic fire Lethe “Forgetfulness” Personified in Hesiod, Theogony 227; as underworld water, the gold tablets, Plato’s Republic 10, and Virgil The water of forgetting, drunk before rebirth; the counter-image of the tablets’ Pool of Memory The systematisation, when it comes, is Plato’s. In the Phaedo ’s closing myth (111c–114c, paraphrased throughout; Section XIV) the four great rivers — Ocean, Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, and Cocytus, the last there called the Stygian river, whose lake is Styx — are set into a single hydraulic machine: all flow into and out of Tartarus, which pierces the whole earth, on a great oscillation, like breathing, and each takes the character of the soil it passes through. Virgil inherits the Platonic completeness and gives it a traveller’s itinerary: Acheron’s flood, the Stygian marsh, Cocytus winding round the grove before the descent, Lethe in Elysium. The reader should hold the chronology firmly. Homer gives a confluence of three streams at the world’s edge; Hesiod gives an oath-river in a silver-pillared house; Plato gives a system; Virgil gives a route. The five-river underworld of the handbooks is the sediment of eight centuries, and this article cites each river, wherever it can, from the stratum in which it actually appears. IV. The Crossing: Charon, the Obol, and Cerberus Between the living and the dead the tradition sets water, and on the water a boatman. Charon — his name has no agreed etymology, and the flashing-eyed Charon of Etruscan demonology, Charun, is a cousin whose exact relation to the Greek ferryman is debated — is absent from Homer and Hesiod altogether. He enters the record in the archaic epic tradition and in art: the lost epic Minyas knew him, the great fifth-century painting of the underworld by Polygnotus in the Lesche of the Cnidians at Delphi — described in detail by Pausanias (10.28, paraphrased) — showed him poling his boat on Acheron with the dead aboard, and Attic white-ground lekythoi of the fifth century BCE, the oil-flasks placed in graves, show him again and again: an old, rough, unshaven working man in a short tunic and cap, standing in his skiff with the pole in his hands, receiving a shade at the reed-fringed shore, sometimes from Hermes’ hand. The iconography is the theology. Charon is not a judge and not a tormentor; he is a ferryman doing a job, and his one condition is the condition of his trade: the fare. The Obol: A Literary Fare with an Archaeological Footing The fare was an obol — a small coin, a sixth of a drachma — and the custom of placing it with the dead is the point at which this article’s geography touches the ground most firmly. Greek and Latin literary sources name the coin, call it Charon’s naulon , his boat-fare, and specify its placement in or on the mouth of the corpse; Aristophanes makes the fare a joke his whole audience is expected to get (Section XIII), and later writers from Virgil’s commentators to Lucian treat it as common knowledge. Archaeology confirms that the custom behind the joke was real, and also corrects its tidy form. Coins are found in burials across the Greek and Roman world from the fifth century BCE onward — in the mouth, yes, but also on the eyes, in the hand, and beside the head; of various denominations, not always the single obol of the texts; sometimes several, sometimes purpose-made thin gold pieces, the danakai , that were never currency at all; and in only a minority of burials, never universally. The honest summary, which this article adopts, is the one the brief for it prescribes: the obol is a practice with archaeological footing, stated as such — a real and widespread funerary custom that the literature simplified into a single coin in the mouth for a single ferryman. The simplification itself is evidence: a culture does not joke about a fare, or mint imitation coins for the dead, unless the crossing and its cost are part of its furniture of thought. What the archaeology will not support is the reverse inference, that every coin in a grave is a ferry fare and every Greek expected to pay one; grave coins did other work too, as offerings and as wealth, and the specialists who study them (the modern literature runs from Kurtz and Boardman’s Greek Burial Customs through the studies gathered under the heading of “Charon’s obol” as an archaeological term of art) warn against letting the ferryman claim them all. // THE UNBURIED: THE FARE’S OTHER SIDE // The crossing had a second condition, stricter than the coin: burial. In Virgil’s systematisation (Section XII) the unburied crowd the near bank and may not cross for a hundred years, and the rule is already the emotional engine of Odyssey 11, where the first shade Odysseus meets is Elpenor — unburied on Circe’s roof, begging for his mound and his oar (Section VIII). The dead who had received their rites belonged below; the unburied belonged nowhere. Greek horror at the unburied corpse — the premise of Sophocles’ Antigone — is the same belief in its civic form: burial is the passport, and the obol is small change beside it. Cerberus at the Gate Past the crossing stands the gate, and at the gate the dog. Cerberus — Greek Kerberos ; Hesiod ( Theogony 310–312, paraphrased) makes him a child of Typhaon and Echidna, brother to the Hydra and the Nemean lion — is in Hesiod “the brazen-voiced hound of Hades, shameless, fifty-headed, eater of raw flesh”. Homer knows him without the name, as simply “the hound” whom Heracles was sent to fetch ( Iliad 8.368; Odyssey 11.623, paraphrased). Later tradition regularised the heads to three — Apollodorus (2.5.12, paraphrased) gives him three dogs’ heads, a dragon’s tail, and serpents’ heads along his back — and gave him his famous double office, which the Latin tradition states as a maxim and the Greek stories everywhere imply: he fawns on those who enter and devours those who try to leave. Cerberus is the anabasis problem with teeth. The descent is easy; the gate-dog faces the other way. How the travellers get past him is therefore a diagnostic of each story: Heracles wrestles him, bare-handed, by his master’s permission (Section IX); Orpheus sings him to sleep in the later tellings; the Sibyl throws him a honey-cake drugged with soporific herbs, and Virgil’s three throats gape, take it, and sink (Aeneid 6.417–425, paraphrased); and Aristophanes, characteristically, leaves him offstage and gives the door to a doorman with a grudge (Section XIII). c. 700 BCE HESIOD’S STAFFING Styx in her silver-pillared house as the gods’ oath; Cerberus, fifty-headed and brazen-voiced, named among Echidna’s brood. No Charon yet, no judges, no fare. 5th c. BCE CHARON IN ART AND ON STAGE Polygnotus paints the ferryman on Acheron at Delphi; white-ground lekythoi show him receiving shades; coins begin to appear in burials in numbers the archaeology can count. In 405 BCE Aristophanes puts him on stage to collect a fare and make his passenger row. 4th c. BCE PLATO SYSTEMATISES The Phaedo sets the rivers into one machine and posts judges at the parting of the roads; the Republic ’s Myth of Er adds the spindle, the lots, and Lethe. The geography becomes an eschatology. 29–19 BCE VIRGIL CODIFIES THE ROUTE Aeneid VI walks the whole map in order — entrance, rivers, Charon, the unburied, Cerberus, the regions of the dead, Tartarus, Elysium, Lethe — and every later Western underworld, Dante’s included, is built on Virgil’s itinerary. V. Judges, Meadows, and the Ordinary Dead: The Asphodel Meadow Most of the dead, in the early tradition, go nowhere in particular, and the name of nowhere is the asphodel meadow . Asphodel — a grey-white lily of poor Greek soils, food of the poor in life — carpets the Homeric underworld: Achilles strides away over it rejoicing at his son’s fame ( Odyssey 11.538–539, in Murray’s translation), Orion drives the wild beasts he slew across it (11.572–575), and in Odyssey 24 (paraphrased) the suitors’ ghosts are led down past Ocean, the White Rock, the gates of the Sun, and the land of dreams to the meadow where the spirits dwell. It is not a punishment and it is not a reward. It is a pasture for shades: flat, dim, and endless, the visual form of a belief that death levels everyone into the same thin continuation. The meadow’s population keeps its earthly shape and, in the heroes’ case, its earthly preoccupations — Orion hunts, Minos judges, Heracles’ phantom carries its bow — but without body, strength, or, until blood is drunk, full wits. That is the baseline of Greek eschatology, and every brighter or darker region in this article is an exception carved out of it. The Judges Judgement enters the meadow early but narrowly. In Odyssey 11 (567–571) Odysseus sees Minos , the glorious son of Zeus, golden sceptre in hand, seated and giving judgement to the dead, who sit and stand about him through the wide-gated house and ask for his decisions — in Murray’s translation, paraphrased here only in arrangement. The scene is a king holding court, not a tribunal of souls: Minos settles the dead’s disputes as he settled the living’s in Crete, and Homer gives no hint that he assigns anyone’s eternal lot. The developed bench of three — Minos , Rhadamanthys , and Aeacus — is a later construction, assembled from figures each of whom begins elsewhere. Rhadamanthys, Minos’s brother, is in Homer already exceptionally placed: the Odyssey (4.563–565, paraphrased) sets him in Elysium, and Pindar will make him the assessor of the judge of the dead and counsellor in the Isles of the Blest (Section VII). Aeacus, grandfather of Achilles, famed in life for justice and for praying Athens out of a drought, becomes in the developed tradition the underworld’s doorkeeper and judge of Europeans — Aristophanes demotes him, unforgettably, to Pluto’s porter with a score to settle (Section XIII). Plato completes the bench and gives it jurisdiction: in the Gorgias myth (523a–524a, paraphrased) Zeus appoints his three sons — Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Aeacus — as judges of the dead at the parting of the roads, because judgements in the old days, delivered on clothed and living defendants, were corrupted by fine appearances; henceforth the dead are judged naked, soul by soul, by dead judges, and sent right to the Isles or left to Tartarus. The Phaedo (113d, paraphrased) has the dead conducted to a place of judgement and sorted — the middling to Acheron and the lake, the incurable to Tartarus, the curably wicked to Tartarus for a year and out again by the rivers, the exceptionally holy to the upper earth. Between Homer’s court scene and Plato’s tribunal lies the whole moralisation of the Greek afterlife, and it happens, characteristically, not in cult but in philosophy (Section XIV). MINOS Cretan king and lawgiver, son of Zeus. In Homer he holds court among the dead with a golden sceptre; in the developed tradition he presides over the bench of three, and Virgil gives him a court of the falsely condemned, shaking the urn and summoning the silent council (Section XII). RHADAMANTHYS Minos’s brother, the just man of Crete. Placed by Homer in Elysium; by Pindar at Kronos’s right hand in the Isles of the Blest; by Plato on the bench, judging the dead of Asia. Virgil sets him in Tartarus itself, hearing and punishing confessed frauds (Section XII). AEACUS King of Aegina, grandfather of Achilles and Ajax, proverbial for justice. Keeper of the keys and judge in the developed scheme; in Aristophanes’ Frogs , Pluto’s doorman, still furious at Heracles for stealing the dog. THE ORDINARY DEAD No verdict at all, in the early map: the asphodel meadow, strengthless and dim, for farmer and king alike. The ordinariness is the point — and the pressure that slowly produced every exception in Sections VI, VII, and XIV. One further class of the dead stands between the meadow’s anonymity and the exceptions, and the descents keep meeting them: the untimely and the unquiet — the aōroi who died before their season (infants, the unmarried, the slain), the ataphoi who died unburied, and the biaiothanatoi who died by violence. Greek belief, documented across the necromancy evidence assembled by Daniel Ogden in Greek and Roman Necromancy (2001), held such dead to be restless, near the surface, and available: they are the ghosts necromancers could most readily raise, the shades who crowd Odysseus’s pit and Charon’s bank, and the population Virgil will presently arrange in its own border regions (Section XII). The geography of the dead, in short, has a sociology, and it is the sociology of the living: those whom life left unfinished are imagined as unfinished in death, lingering at the boundary where the travellers pass. VI. Tartarus Below Hades Below the house of Hades lies somewhere worse, and the tradition is precise about the depth. Tartarus — in Hesiod’s Theogony one of the first things to come into being (116–120), a pit in the depth of the wide-pathed earth — receives its measure at the close of the Titanomachy, when the defeated Titans are hurled down and bound there (720–726). In Evelyn-White’s Loeb translation (1914): “For a brazen anvil falling down from heaven nine nights and days would reach the earth upon the tenth: and again, a brazen anvil falling from earth nine nights and days would reach Tartarus upon the tenth.” — HESIOD, THEOGONY 722–725, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) The image is a surveyor’s: the cosmos is symmetrical, heaven-to-earth as earth-to-Tartarus, nine days’ fall each way, and Tartarus is as far below the underworld as the underworld is below the sky. Around it, Hesiod continues (726–735, paraphrased), runs a fence of bronze, and night spreads in a triple line about it like a neck-circlet; above it grow the roots of the earth and the unfruitful sea; Poseidon fixed gates of bronze upon it, and the Hundred-Handers — Gyes, Cottus, and great-souled Obriareus — live there as trusty warders of Zeus. A little further on (736–745, paraphrased) the sources and ends of earth, Tartarus, sea, and heaven stand all in order in a dank gulf which even the gods abhor, with gates of marble and a threshold of bronze that no one who enters crosses again within the year. Tartarus in Hesiod is a prison , built for defeated gods, and its inmates are the Titans: beings who cannot die, held in the only custody that can hold them. That origin governs its whole later history. Tartarus is never, in the early tradition, where bad people go. It is where dangerous powers are kept. The human inmates arrive by a specific door: offences against gods in person. The three sufferers Odysseus glimpses in Odyssey 11 (576–600, Murray’s translation, paraphrased here) are the type cases, and each is a cosmic, not a moral, offender. Tityos , the giant son of Earth, lies stretched over nine roods while two vultures tear his liver, because he laid violent hands on Leto, Zeus’s wife, as she passed through Panopeus toward Delphi. Tantalus stands in a pool that shrinks from his chin whenever he stoops to drink, under fruit trees whose branches the wind tosses to the clouds whenever he reaches — Homer, notably, does not say what his crime was; the later tradition supplies the banquet of his son Pelops and the theft of the gods’ nectar and ambrosia. Sisyphus strains to thrust his monstrous stone to the crest of the hill, and as often as he is about to heave it over, the weight turns it back and the ruthless stone rolls down to the plain, and he braces and thrusts again, sweat streaming, dust rising from his head — Homer again gives no charge sheet; the trickster who chained Death and talked his way back from the dead belongs to the later accretions. The pattern is exact: these are not sinners in a general hell but particular, named transgressors against the divine order, punished in person, forever, in a place Odysseus can see but — significantly — does not enter and is not said to be beneath: in the Odyssey the sufferers are simply there , in the same visual field as the meadow, and the hard stratification of Hades above and Tartarus below is Hesiod’s and Plato’s work, not Homer’s. // IXION, AND THE WHEEL THAT IS NOT IN HOMER // Later lists of the great sufferers add Ixion, bound to his fiery wheel for attempting Hera, and the Danaids with their leaking jars. Neither is in Odyssey 11: Ixion’s wheel is Pindaric ( Pythian 2, paraphrased) and the Danaids’ water-carrying belongs to the developed tradition Plato already plays with in the Gorgias . The catalogue of the damned, like the river-system, grew by accretion — a standing warning against citing “the Greek Tartarus” as if it were a single text. Plato takes Tartarus over and rebuilds it as the engine of his eschatology: the chasm that pierces the whole earth, into which all rivers flow and out of which they surge ( Phaedo 112a–c, paraphrased), the pit into which the incurable are cast by their fitting destiny and never emerge, while the curably wicked are carried out again after a year on the currents of Cocytus and Pyriphlegethon to beg their victims’ forgiveness at the Acherusian lake (113e–114c, paraphrased; Section XIV). Virgil takes it over in turn as the fortress-prison on the left-hand road, with its triple wall, its river of fire, its gate of adamant, and Tisiphone on watch night and day — and, notably, has the Sibyl describe it from outside: Aeneas, a living man on a sanctioned errand, does not go in (Section XII). The descent tradition’s deepest place is thus the one place its heroes are shown but never taken. Even katabasis has a floor it does not cross, and the floor is Tartarus. VII.
