Sources I. The Problem: A Famous Text with No Ancient Manuscript Begin with the embarrassment, because the embarrassment is the subject. The Emerald Tablet — in Latin the Tabula Smaragdina , the Smaragdine Table — is the most quoted document in the whole history of Western alchemy. Medieval commentators treated it as the art’s foundational charter; Renaissance printers set it at the head of collections; Isaac Newton translated it with his own hand and commented on it. It speaks in the voice of Hermes Trismegistus , and it was read for centuries as a survival from the deepest antiquity of Egypt — a text older than Plato, older than Moses on some reckonings, cut into green stone by the thrice-greatest sage himself. And yet: no ancient Greek manuscript of the Tablet exists, and no ancient Latin one either. No Greek author of antiquity quotes it. No papyrus carries it. The philosophical Hermetica gathered in the Corpus Hermeticum — the subject of this hub’s Hermetica article — do not contain it, and Brian Copenhaver’s standard modern edition of those treatises does not print it, because it does not belong to that Greek family at all. The Tablet’s trail, followed honestly backward, does not end in a temple library in pharaonic or even Roman Egypt. It ends in an Arabic book. The book is the Kitāb sirr al-khalīqa wa-ṣanʿat al-ṭabīʿa — the Book of the Secret of Creation and the Craft of Nature , known also as the Kitāb al-ʿilal , the Book of Causes — an encyclopaedic Arabic treatise on natural philosophy, compiled in the late eighth or early ninth century CE , which presents itself as the work of Balīnūs , or Balīnās: the Arabic form of the name of Apollonius of Tyana , the first-century Greek sage and wonder-worker. At the end of that book, after its formal close, stands the Tablet: a short sequence of aphoristic sentences in the voice of Hermes, prefaced by a narrative of how Balinas found them — in a subterranean vault, beneath a statue of Hermes, on a tablet of emerald held by an old man seated on a golden throne. That narrative, that book, and that Arabic text are the earliest witnesses the Tablet has. Everything else — the Jabirian quotation, the Secret of Secrets recension, the twelfth-century Latin translations, the vulgate text that conquered Europe, Newton’s English — is downstream of the Arabic centuries this article covers. This is not a marginal scholarly opinion. It is the settled result of the twentieth-century rediscovery of the Arabic sources, begun by E. J. Holmyard in 1923 and established by Julius Ruska ’s Tabula Smaragdina (Heidelberg, 1926), the foundational modern study, which demonstrated that the Arabic versions precede the Latin by some three centuries and that the Latin wording cannot be projected backward onto an imagined Greek original. Ursula Weisser ’s critical edition of the Sirr al-khalīqa (Aleppo, 1979) and her monograph on the pseudo-Apollonian book (Berlin, 1980) gave the earliest witness its standard text. Paul Kraus , in his great study of the Jabir corpus (Cairo, 1942–43), fixed the book’s place in the intellectual world of early Abbasid science. Modern syntheses — Lawrence Principe’s The Secrets of Alchemy (2013) among them — present the Arabic provenance as the starting point of any responsible account. This article follows that scholarship, and states its limits where the scholarship states them. WHAT SURVIVES Four Arabic recensions of the Tablet, preserved in treatises of the 8th–10th centuries — chiefly the Sirr al-khalīqa and the pseudo-Aristotelian Sirr al-asrār ( Secret of Secrets ) — and Latin translations from the 12th century onward. WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE Any Greek or Latin manuscript of the Tablet from antiquity; any quotation of it by an ancient author; and the emerald object itself, which no writer outside the frame story has ever claimed to have seen. THE EARLIEST WITNESS The Tablet as an appendix to the Kitāb sirr al-khalīqa of pseudo-Apollonius (Balinas), compiled in Arabic in the late 8th or early 9th century and certainly complete by the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn (813–833). THE COUNT The Tablet’s text runs to thirteen sentences in the usual segmentation — fourteen in editions that divide the closing sentences . That is the archive’s agreed formulation, stated here and kept throughout; see the Egyptology division’s Alchemy . Three disciplines govern what follows, and they are the same disciplines this hub’s Transmission article applies to the Greek corpus. First, witnesses before stories. Where a claim rests on a text, the text is named with its recension and its editor. Second, the frame is labelled as frame. The vault narrative is the Sirr al-khalīqa ’s own account of where its Tablet came from; Section III tells it as the text tells it, and neither endorses it as an excavation report nor apologises for its literary power. Third, quotation is rationed and sourced. The Tablet is quoted in this article only from published translations of the Arabic that are named at the point of quotation — Holmyard’s 1923 rendering of the Jabirian version and Joseph Azize’s translation of Ruska’s Arabic text — and everything else is labelled paraphrase. The famous Latin wording, the Verum sine mendacio and its descendants, belongs to the post-1144 story; it appears here only as a contrast, never as the Arabic original’s voice. // WHERE THIS ARTICLE SITS // This hub’s Transmission article follows the Greek alchemical corpus east through Syriac and Arabic and west through the Latin door of 1144. This article is its companion piece for a single text: the Tablet’s Arabic centuries, from the vault of the frame story to the threshold of Hugo of Santalla’s Latin. The Egyptology division treats the same Arabic centuries from the Egyptian side in its Islamic Egyptology — including its adjudicated account of the Hermetic migration ( §VIII ) and of Ḥarrān and its Hermes ( §XIV ) — and its Alchemy article states the Tablet’s sentence count in the form this article keeps. The full Latin and Renaissance career of the Tablet, Newton’s translation included, belongs to the archive’s later wings; for Newton’s own handling of the text see the Egyptology division’s Newton article. This article’s scope stops at the Latin threshold. II. Balinas: Apollonius of Tyana in His Arabic Afterlife The name on the Tablet’s first book is a borrowed one, and the borrowing is the first fact to get straight. Apollonius of Tyana (c. 15 – c. 100 CE) was a historical figure: a Greek Neopythagorean sage from Tyana in Cappadocia, remembered as a travelling teacher, ascetic, and worker of wonders, whose life the sophist Philostratus wrote up in the early third century at imperial commission. In the Greek and Roman world his reputation was contested — philosopher to his admirers, charlatan and magus to his detractors — but it was as a master of hidden powers that he passed into the literatures of the Near East. In Syriac and then in Arabic he became Balīnūs or Balīnās , and the Arabic Balinas is a larger figure than the Greek Apollonius ever was: in the formulation of Mohammad Karimi Zanjani Asl’s study of the Sirr al-khalīqa ’s influence (2016), Apollonius was known in the Islamic period both as “Lord of the Talismans” ( ṣāḥib al-ṭilasmāt ) and as a Neo-Pythagorean-Hermetic philosopher. Arabic tradition credited him with founding talismanic images that protected cities, with books on the talismanic art, and with a body of wisdom reaching back behind Islam to the sages of the ancient world. A name like that is an author-function: to sign a book “Balinas” was to claim for it the authority of the ancient talisman-master himself. The author of the Sirr al-khalīqa was not Apollonius. The book is an Arabic composition of the late eighth or early ninth century — some seven centuries after its supposed author’s death — and modern scholarship accordingly calls its writer pseudo-Apollonius : Weisser’s 1980 monograph is titled, precisely, Das “Buch über das Geheimnis der Schöpfung” von Pseudo-Apollonios von Tyana , “The ‘Book of the Secret of Creation’ of Pseudo-Apollonius of Tyana”. The pseudepigraphy is not a fraud in the modern sense so much as a convention of the literature: the Arabic Hermetic and occult-scientific corpus is thick with works signed by Hermes, by Aristotle, by Plato, by Apollonius, in which the ancient name certifies the teaching’s pedigree. But the convention has a consequence the reader must hold firmly. When the Sirr al-khalīqa says “Balinas found” or “Balinas said”, the speaker is an anonymous Arabic author of the early Abbasid centuries writing in character — and the character he is writing is himself presented, inside the book, as a finder and transmitter rather than an inventor. The Tablet thus arrives doubly framed: a text by Hermes, found by Balinas, written down by an author who is neither. Section III unpacks that frame; this hub’s article on the legendary lives of the sages treats the Balinas persona and its congeners at length — see Legendary Lives . One more strand of the Arabic Apollonius matters for the Tablet’s story, because it explains why this sage, of all the ancients, is the one made to find Hermes’ book. In the Arabic tradition Balinas is not merely a sage who might plausibly enter a vault; he is the sage of talismans — of made objects in which celestial powers are lodged — and the Tablet, in its Arabic form, calls the One Thing it describes the father of the talismans ( abū al-ṭilasmāt ). The discoverer and the discovery match. The book that bears Balinas’s name is a cosmology of how powers descend into things and are bound there; the short text at its end names the principle of that binding. Whoever assembled the Sirr al-khalīqa — whether he composed the Tablet, inherited it, or received it from the Greek or Syriac materials the book elsewhere draws on — set it in the keeping of the one ancient name under which such a text most naturally travelled in Arabic. The attribution is literary. It is also, as construction, exact. // NAMES, KEPT STRAIGHT // Apollonius of Tyana : the historical 1st-century Greek sage. Balīnūs / Balīnās (Balinas) : his Arabic name and persona, Lord of the Talismans. Pseudo-Apollonius : the modern scholarly label for the unknown Arabic author who wrote under that name. Hermes Trismegistus : the voice of the Tablet itself, and — inside the frame story — the enthroned old man who holds it. Four figures, three of them textual functions; the article keeps them distinct throughout. The Arabic Balinas had a readership, and it was not a fringe one. Asl’s 2016 survey traces citations of Apollonius across Islamic sources in field after field, notes that Jābir ibn Ḥayyān himself refers in the Kitāb al-Aḥjār to “the Muslim advocates of Balinas” ( aṣḥāb Balīnās al-islāmīyūn ) — evidence, Asl argues, that the Sirr al-khalīqa was already famous in the Arabic-speaking world very early — and follows the book’s reception into the Ismāʿīlī tradition and into a fourth/tenth-century Arabic commentary by ʿAwn b. al-Mundhir , preserved in a unique manuscript and in a Persian translation that preserves parts of the commentary the Arabic excerpt has lost (Section XI). A pseudepigraph that attracts commentators within two centuries is not a curiosity. It is a classic in the process of becoming one, and the Tablet rode inside it. III. The Frame in Full: The Vault Beneath the Statue of Hermes The Sirr al-khalīqa does not simply contain the Tablet. It stages its discovery, and the staging deserves to be told in full — as the text’s own frame story, labelled as such — because for a thousand years the staging was the Tablet’s provenance: this is the account every later reader, Arabic, Latin, and Renaissance, received along with the text, and the account that fixed the Tablet’s imagined object-form (a slab of emerald, in a tomb, in dead hands) in the tradition’s imagination. The book’s introduction presents the account as transmitted teaching. What the priest Sājiyūs of Nablus set down — the frame is his dictation, treated in Section IV — concerns the entrance of Balinas into a hidden chamber. In the narrative as the Arabic text tells it, Balinas enters a vault or crypt situated beneath a statue of Hermes — in the recensions’ geography, at Tyana, the sage’s own city. The chamber is a place where a talisman has been set up: Balinas has come, in the logic of the story, to the guarded heart of an ancient installation of power. Passing into the darkness, he comes upon an old man seated on a throne of gold . The seated figure is Hermes himself, long dead and enthroned in his vault. In his hands the old man holds a tablet of emerald — a slab of green stone, the lawḥ from which the text’s later Latin name, Tabula , descends — and before him rests a book . Balinas takes up what he has found: the tablet, and with it the book. The wisdom passes, in the story’s terms, from the keeping of the dead sage into the hands of the living one. The introduction, as Kraus read it and as Asl’s translation of Weisser’s edition (p. 7) presents it, ties the two found objects to the two halves of the book’s own full title — a detail of construction too neat to be accidental. On the emerald tablet, in the frame’s account, stand the words “this is the art of nature”; on the book found with it, “this is the secret of creation and the science of the causes of things”. The Sirr al-khalīqa wa-ṣanʿat al-ṭabīʿa — the Secret of Creation and the Craft of Nature — thus presents itself as the book from the vault, and the Tablet as its companion piece: the book expounds the causes of things openly, at encyclopaedic length, while the tablet compresses the art of nature into a page of aphorisms. Kraus’s celebrated reading builds on exactly this division of labour, and states it as his interpretation, not the text’s: the Tablet, he argued, says in veiled terms what the book never spells out — the making of the elixir — and its few lines are, in his phrase, the key to the book of Balinas (Kraus 1942, pp. 302–303; Asl 2016, pp. 443–444). Whether or not the elixir reading is accepted, the structural point stands on the text itself: the Tablet stands after the formal close of the Sirr al-khalīqa (Kraus 1942, p. 302), as an appendix — the vault’s second object, appended to the first. An old man on a golden throne, a tablet of emerald in his hands, and a book before him: the frame gives the Tablet a finder, a place, and a material — everything, that is, except a date. — the frame story of the Sirr al-khalīqa, in paraphrase Two features of the frame repay attention before its literary character is assessed. The first is the language claim . In the recension Ruska printed, the words on the tablet are introduced as written in Syriac, in the first — the primordial — language : Azize’s translation of Ruska’s Arabic gives the preamble’s sense as a tablet of emerald “written in Syriac, in the first language”, in the keeping of the enthroned shaykh . The claim does double work inside the fiction — it makes the text older than Arabic, older than Greek, coeval with the first speech of mankind — and it has done double work in the scholarship ever since, since a Syriac intermediary behind the Arabic is one of the live hypotheses about the book’s sources (Section VI). But a claim inside a frame story is evidence of what the framer wanted believed, not of what happened; this article reports it as the text’s claim, at exactly that strength. The second feature is the throne . The old man is not lying in a sarcophagus; he is seated , enthroned, holding the tablet as a king or a god holds an emblem of office. The iconography is that of the sage as ruler of hidden things — the same enthroned Hermes who presides, in the parallel Arabic discovery narratives of Section XI, over the Book of Crates ’ temple vision. The frame is composed, in other words, out of the tradition’s own furniture. And that is the assessment. The vault narrative is a discovery narrative — a recognised literary device of Hermetic and alchemical writing, in which a new or newly presented text is authorised by being found : hidden by an ancient sage against a corrupt age, preserved in a tomb, a vault, a pyramid, a statue’s hollow, and recovered by a worthy finder. The device is older than Islam — late-antique Hermetica already deposit their teachings in temples and stelae — and the Arabic literature of the ninth and tenth centuries is full of it. To call the frame a device is not to call it a lie in any interesting sense; it is to locate it in its genre. What the frame establishes historically is not that Balinas entered a vault — the historical Apollonius had been dead seven centuries when the book was compiled — but that the book’s compiler understood the Tablet as a thing received : older than its finder, hidden rather than composed, and written in a language older than the one in which he presented it. Every element of that self-understanding is a claim, and Section XIV weighs the claims one by one. The narrative itself, told as the text tells it, is this section’s whole duty. // NO EMERALD HAS EVER BEEN PRODUCED // No emerald slab answering to the frame’s description survives in any museum, treasury, or inventory; no fragment, rubbing, or independent eyewitness account exists. “Emerald” itself, in ancient and medieval usage, named a family of green stones — true emerald, green jasper, even green granite among them — but the point is prior to mineralogy: the object belongs to the frame story. The historical Emerald Tablet is a text , and its earliest witnesses are Arabic manuscripts, two of which the scholarship cites by shelfmark: the Leipzig manuscript Vollers 832 , carrying the oldest recension (A) of the Sirr al-khalīqa , and Paris, Arabe 2300 , carrying the younger recension (B). IV. Sājiyūs of Nablus: The Priest Who Transmits the Account Between Balinas and the reader stands a third figure, easy to overlook and structurally indispensable: the transmitter. The Sirr al-khalīqa presents itself not as Balinas’s autograph but as an account dictated and explained by a priest of Nablus — the ancient Shechem, in Palestine — who comments on the words and the discovery of Balinas. The frame’s chain of custody is therefore three links long before the text even begins: Hermes writes; Balinas finds; the priest of Nablus transmits and expounds. It is the Arabic book-culture’s instinct for the isnād , the chain of transmission, applied to a Hermetic discovery: a teaching is worth what its chain is worth, and so the book supplies one. The priest’s name is itself a small lesson in the state of the evidence. The manuscripts do not give it cleanly. Kraus read it, with a question mark, as Sājiyūs (Sagijus in the older Latinising literature), and also considered a reading as [He]sychius ; older scholars took the figure for a Sergius (Kraus 1942, p. 272 n. and pp. 273, 280; Asl 2016, p. 442). The older secondary literature — the summaries that descend from Ruska through Holmyard’s generation — accordingly speaks of a recension “dictated by Sergius of Nablus”, and that form of the name still circulates; this article uses Sājiyūs, following Kraus and Asl, and records the alternatives because the instability is the fact. Martin Plessner and Julius Ruska took the priest for an invention of the author — one more layer of the frame. Kraus, by contrast, found the detail plausible enough to look for the book’s roots in the Hellenising circles of Syria: a Christian priest of a Palestinian town, expounding a pagan sage’s book, in a milieu where Greek learning survived in Syriac dress. Both judgements are inferences from the same damaged name. Neither upgrades the frame into a report. The Christian colouring of the transmitted account is, however, a datum of the text and not only of its modern readers. Azize, translating Ruska’s Arabic preamble in full, notes that the relevant passage opens with a Trinitarian invocation — in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God — which authenticates, in literary terms, the transmitter’s priesthood, and that the tablet’s claimed Syriac wording places the whole narrative within a Christian frame of reference: Syriac was, by the eighth and ninth centuries, the prestige language of the Christians of the Islamic world. His inference — offered as inference — is that the account as we have it passed through Christian hands, whatever the religion of the Tablet’s first composer. The observation aligns with what the Sirr al-khalīqa ’s modern editor concluded from a different direction: Weisser, following Fuat Sezgin’s judgement, held that the Arabic book rests on a translation made by this same Nablus priest from a Greek original — a position Section VI states with its rivals. For the present section the point is narrower. The book’s own presentation makes its transmitter a Syriac-reading Christian priest of Palestine. In a transmission history, that is the receiving culture signing its work. // THE CHAIN, AS THE BOOK GIVES IT // Hermes , enthroned in the vault, holds the tablet and the book. Balinas enters, finds, and takes them up. Sājiyūs of Nablus dictates and comments. The anonymous compiler of the Sirr al-khalīqa sets the account at the head of his cosmology and the Tablet at its end. Four stations, of which only the last is historical without qualification — and the book is honest, in its way, about the arrangement: it never claims Balinas wrote the Tablet. It claims he found it. Finding is the frame’s whole thesis. V. The Sirr al-khalīqa: A Cosmology of Causes What kind of book carries the Tablet at its end? The Sirr al-khalīqa is an encyclopaedic treatise on natural philosophy cast as a cosmogony : an account of how the world is made, ordered, and caused, from its first principle down through the heavens to the sublunary world of minerals, plants, animals, and man. Its alternative title, Kitāb al-ʿilal — the Book of Causes — is the accurate one. After a prologue on the unity of God and on creation, the book lays out a cosmology that descends the ladder of being: the heavenly spheres and their motions; the elements and the four natures — hot, cold, moist, and dry — of which all lower things are mixtures; the generation of minerals in the earth, of plants, of animals; and finally the human being, in whom the whole system is recapitulated. Every phenomenon, in the book’s method, is traced to its material cause: a fitting mixture of the natures, in due proportion, under the influences of the world above. The relations of sympathy and antipathy between beings — why this substance acts on that one, why this talisman binds that power — are explained by the same mixtures: things agree or quarrel because their natures do (Kraus 1942, pp. 272, 282 n., 303; Asl 2016, pp. 442–443). The architecture matters for the Tablet’s reading. A short text that says the upper is from the lower and the lower from the upper, that all things come from one thing by one ordering, and that a single power ascends from earth to heaven and descends again, is — inside this book — not a riddle pasted onto an unrelated cosmology. It is the cosmology’s own grammar, compressed to aphorism. The spheres act on the mixtures below; the mixtures, rightly prepared, receive and return the action; the whole is one ordered system of causes, and the book’s six treatises (the maqālāt into which Weisser’s edition divides the work) unfold at length what the Tablet’s sentences state in shorthand. This is why the question that has exercised the scholarship — whether the Tablet is an extraneous appendix to the Sirr al-khalīqa or an integral part of it, cosmogonic in sense or alchemical from the outset — is a real question with evidence on both sides. The Tablet stands after the book’s formal close, which suggests attachment; its matter is the book’s matter, which suggests belonging. Kraus’s key-to-the-book reading (Section III) is the strongest form of the belonging case. The prudent statement, and this article’s, is that the Tablet’s earliest surviving context is this cosmology, that it reads coherently as the cosmology’s epitome, and that its later career as a free-standing alchemical charter began when readers detached it from the book that framed it — a detachment the Jabirian quotation (Section X) already performs. THE PROLOGUE The unity of God and the act of creation: the book opens as theology before it proceeds as physics, in the manner of the early Abbasid cosmological treatise. THE SPHERES The heavenly order and its influences — the “above” whose powers descend into every mixture below, and the frame within which talismans, the book’s patron art, are intelligible. THE NATURES Hot, cold, moist, and dry — the book calls the elemental qualities “natures” — whose mixtures and proportions cause the properties of minerals, plants, animals, and men. THE APPENDIX After the formal close: the Tablet, presented as the vault’s second object — the art of nature in aphorisms, where the book has given the secret of creation in treatises. The book’s sources are as layered as its frame. Weisser’s edition — established from four principal manuscripts out of sixteen she appraised — prints, among its supplements, extracts from the Greek bishop Nemesius of Emesa ’s work on the nature of man (c. 400 CE), and the scholarship has long noted the Sirr al-khalīqa ’s kinship with Syriac cosmological writing of the ninth century, the Book of Treasures of Job of Edessa among the comparanda named in the older literature. A cosmology compiled in Arabic around 800 that digests a fourth-century Greek bishop, breathes the air of Syriac school culture, and signs itself with a first-century pagan sage’s Arabic name is not an anomaly of the Abbasid translation age. It is a typical product of it — and it is precisely the kind of product in which a short Hermetic text of uncertain, probably late-antique, ancestry would come to rest. The book is the Tablet’s earliest home. It is also the best evidence for the milieu that made the Tablet, as we have it, possible. VI. Dating the Book: Ruska, Kraus, Weisser — and an Early Doubter The Sirr al-khalīqa is conventionally placed in the eighth to ninth centuries CE , in the Arabic world of the early Abbasid caliphate. Behind that bland range stand three landmark datings, and the differences among them are instructive, because each scholar was dating a slightly different thing. Ruska (1926), who first established the book as the Tablet’s earliest witness, allowed that its underlying material might reach back to the sixth–eighth centuries — a judgement about the sources the compilation digests, Greek and Syriac materials of late antiquity. Kraus (1942–43) placed the compilation itself under the caliph al-Maʾmūn (reigned 813–833). Weisser (1980), in the standard critical study, settled on a compilation around 750–800 . The formulation the evidence supports, and the one this article uses throughout, is the composite one: compiled in Arabic in the late eighth or early ninth century, and certainly complete by the end of al-Maʾmūn’s caliphate in 833 . The archive’s Egyptology division dates it the same way — “before 833” — in its Alchemy article. Was the book composed in Arabic, or translated into it? Here the scholarship divides, and the division must be reported rather than resolved. Weisser, agreeing with Sezgin’s judgement in the Geschichte des arabischen Schrifttums , held that the Arabic text is a translation — made by the Nablus priest of Section IV — of a Greek original of the sixth century , now lost; on her dating, the Arabic version belongs around 815–816, in al-Maʾmūn’s reign. Reviewers of her edition already registered the alternative: that the book was composed in Arabic from older materials , its Greek and Syriac ingredients worked into an Arabic original — a position argued on grounds of style, and placed by one early reviewer as late as the middle of the ninth century. The current reference position keeps both doors open: the Secret of Creation , the Tablet’s earliest source and its likely original context, was either wholly or at least partly compiled from earlier Greek or Syriac materials . What no party to the debate claims is a surviving Greek or Syriac manuscript of the book — still less of the Tablet. The lost original, if it existed, is an inference from the Arabic text’s character, and Section XIV keeps it at that strength. c. 15 – c. 100 CE APOLLONIUS OF TYANA The historical Greek sage whose Arabic afterlife, as Balinas, Lord of the Talismans, will lend the book its name — seven centuries before the book exists. c. 400 CE NEMESIUS OF EMESA The Greek bishop whose work on the nature of man is among the identifiable late-antique ingredients digested in the Sirr al-khalīqa — evidence of the Greek materials behind the Arabic compilation. c. 750–833 THE SIRR AL-KHALĪQA COMPILED Weisser: c. 750–800. Kraus: under al-Maʾmūn, 813–833. Either way: an Arabic book of the early Abbasid centuries, complete by 833, with the Tablet at its end — the text’s entry into documented history. 9th–10th c. THE JABIR CORPUS QUOTES IT The Second Book of the Element of the Foundation , in the corpus dated c. 850–950, carries a shortened Tablet and ascribes its knowledge of it to Balinas’s book (Section X). 10th c. THE SIRR AL-ASRĀR RECENSION The pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets takes the Tablet over, probably from the Sirr al-khalīqa , into the most widely read Arabic book of counsel of the Middle Ages (Section XI). c. 1145–1151 HUGO OF SANTALLA The Sirr al-khalīqa is translated into Latin at Tarazona as the Liber de secretis naturae — the Tablet’s first Latin home (Section XIII). The most striking witness to the dating debate is also the oldest — older than Ruska by a thousand years. The Ismāʿīlī writer Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī (d. 933/934) records that his contemporary and opponent, the philosopher-physician Abū Bakr al-Rāzī — Rhazes, the greatest clinician of the Arabic Middle Ages — told him the book was a recent work , by an author who lived under al-Maʾmūn (813–833) and merely took the name of Balinas . The report survives at second hand, in an adversary’s record of a debate, and this article gives it at that strength. But its existence matters beyond its precision: by the early tenth century, a leading Arabic man of science was already making, in public controversy, exactly the judgement modern scholarship makes — that the attribution to Apollonius is a literary device and the book a product of al-Maʾmūn’s age. The pseudepigraphy fooled the tradition’s devotees for a millennium. It did not fool its first critical readers, because it was never really designed to: it was designed to place the book, and placing is a claim a contemporary could check against the book-trade of his own Baghdad. The modern dating debate — 750–800 against 813–833 — is, in the end, an argument over a single generation, conducted within the frame Abū Bakr al-Rāzī already drew. // HOW TO DATE A PSEUDEPIGRAPH // Date the compilation , not the name on it, and not the oldest ingredient in it. The Sirr al-khalīqa contains material with late-antique roots (Ruska’s sixth–eighth centuries), was compiled as the book we have in the late eighth or early ninth (Weisser; Kraus), and is quoted by the Jabir corpus of c. 850–950 — three different dates for three different objects, all of them true, none of them interchangeable. Most popular datings of the Tablet go wrong by silently substituting one for another. VII. The Book’s Teaching: Natures, Mixtures, and the First Sulphur–Mercury The Sirr al-khalīqa ’s cosmology is a physics of mixture . All things below the moon are composed of the four elemental principles — in the book’s own idiom, the four natures : heat, cold, moisture, and dryness — combined in differing proportions, and their combinations account for the properties of things and for the relations of sympathy and antipathy between them. A substance is what its mixture is; an operation is an adjustment of a mixture; a talisman is a mixture prepared, under the right celestial configuration, to receive and hold a power from above. Creation itself, in the book’s cosmogony, is the first and greatest act of ordering: the one God disposes the natures into the spheres, the elements, and the generated world, so that the whole of nature is a single system of balances — proportions held, disturbed, and restored. Later Arabic science would give that intuition a technical name and an arithmetic, the mīzān , the Balance, of the Jabir corpus (Section X). In the Sirr al-khalīqa it is still cosmology rather than calculus — but the direction is set: the world is intelligible because it is proportioned , and it is workable because its proportions can be known. Within that physics sits the book’s most consequential single doctrine. Its mineralogy holds — in Kraus’s identification (1942, p. 1 n. 1 and p. 283) — the oldest known statement of the theory that the metals are formed in the earth from sulphur and mercury mixed in due proportion: the two principles whose varying purity and balance make lead lead and gold gold. The Jabirian corpus took the theory over from the Balinas book, built its metallurgy on it, and through Arabic sources it passed into the alchemy of the Latin Middle Ages, where it stands at the foundation of the Summa ascribed to Geber. Why Testing Exists: Value You Cannot See This article belongs to the Foundations cluster of the Alchemy wing, alongside the hub's treatments of Aristotle and matter theory and the four elements . Those articles treat what Greek thinkers believed metals are . This one treats the prior, more urgent question that every buyer, banker, temple treasurer, and king had to answer before theory mattered at all: is this piece of metal what it claims to be? A gold stater, a silver tetradrachm, a votive crown, and an ingot fresh from the smelter are all, in the end, promises. The metal's value lies inside it, where no eye can reach. Testing — dokimasia in Greek, the word that also names the scrutiny of a magistrate before he takes office — is the set of procedures by which the ancient world forced the inside of a piece of metal to give evidence about itself. The pressure that built the procedures was fraud, and fraud was not an aberration in the system. It was a standing condition of it. Gold and silver are valuable precisely because they are scarce, soft, fusible, and — the decisive property — mixable . Gold accepts silver and copper into itself in any proportion and stays handsome. Silver accepts copper and lead and stays bright. A plated core wears a skin of the real thing and passes every test of the eye. From the moment Lydia struck the first coins in the seventh century BCE, every handler of precious metal worked in an environment where some fraction of what passed through his hands was lying to him, and where the profit on a successful lie was the difference between the face value of the piece and the value of the cheap metal inside it. The tests in this article are the counter-technology, developed over roughly a thousand years, and they are best read as an arms race: each procedure answers a fraud, and each fraud that survives is a map of the procedure's blind spot. The Greek language preserves the whole story in one word. Basanos (βάσανος) is, first, the touchstone itself: the dark stone on which gold is rubbed so that its streak can be judged. From the stone the word spreads outward — to a test or trial of genuineness in general, to an examination under torture (the stone's interrogation of the metal transferred to the interrogation of a witness), and in poetry to any ordeal that reveals what a person is made of. Bacchylides, writing in the fifth century BCE, already uses the figure in paraphrase: as the Lydian stone tries gold, so truth tries the excellent man. Plato, in the Gorgias (486d, in paraphrase), has Callicles wish for just such a stone for souls: if his soul were gold, he says, he would be delighted to find one of the stones with which gold is tested, and to have it confirm that his soul had been well tended. The metaphor only works because the procedure was familiar, quick, and trusted. Nobody builds a moral philosophy on an instrument his audience has never seen used. DOKIMAZEIN — TO TEST, TO APPROVE The verb dokimazein means to put to the proof and, on proof passed, to approve. Athens used the same word-family for the scrutiny of incoming officials ( dokimasia ), for the vetting of new citizens, and for the assaying of coin. The dokimastēs of Section IX is literally “the Approver”: a man whose verdict turned a lump of stamped silver into money that had to be accepted. KIBDĒLOS — THE COUNTERFEIT The standing Greek word for debased or forged coin, and by extension for anything spurious or untrustworthy in a person. The coinage law of 375/4 BCE (Section IX) uses it as a legal category: a coin that is kibdēlon is cut in half on the spot and forfeited to a goddess. Fraud was common enough to need a noun, a law, and a salaried official. A note on method, because this article makes a promise its subject would approve of: it tests its own claims. No direct quotation appears unless it was verified in the named translation cited at the quotation, and quotations are kept short; everything else is labelled paraphrase. The anchor translation for Theophrastus is D. E. Caley and John F. C. Richards, Theophrastus: On Stones (Ohio State University Press, 1956), checked against the full text, and the quotation is credited to them. Pliny is quoted from H. Rackham's Loeb translation of the Natural History (vol. IX, Books 33–35, 1952). Vitruvius is given in Morris Hicky Morgan's translation of the Ten Books on Architecture (Harvard University Press, 1914). Caley's translations of the Leyden and Stockholm papyri. // A WORD THIS ARTICLE WILL KEEP USING HONESTLY // Reconstruction. Ancient texts rarely give a complete bench procedure; they were written for men who already knew the work. Where this article assembles a full sequence of operations from an ancient hint plus the later assay literature and modern replication, the assembled steps are labelled reconstruction in the text. What an ancient author states, what archaeology shows, and what a modern assayer supplies are three different kinds of evidence, and they are not interchangeable. The article keeps them apart — which is, in the end, what an assay is. The article's route is the route of a piece of suspect metal through a well-run ancient city. First the quick, non-destructive screen: the touchstone (Sections II–III). Then the quick destructive-adjacent screens: fire, breath, and the hot shovel (Section IV). Then the heavy procedures of the refinery, which consume a sample in order to tell the truth about the whole: cupellation (Section V) and parting (Sections VI–VII). Then the one famous test that is not a workshop procedure at all but a piece of natural philosophy — Archimedes and the crown — examined as rigorously as the workshops examined metal (Section VIII). Then the state steps in: Athens institutionalises testing in law, with a public tester, set hours, set penalties, and a chisel (Sections IX–X). And finally the loop closes where this hub began, in the workshops of Roman Egypt, whose recipe books — the Leyden and Stockholm papyri — write the whole tradition down as bench instructions, tests included (Section XI). The reader who wants the workshop world in its own right should read this article beside The Workshop Root: Bolos of Mendes and the Physika kai Mystika , where the recipe tradition that the papyri inherit is treated in full. II. The Anchor Text: Theophrastus, On Stones §§4, 45–47 The earliest surviving technical account of precious-metal testing in Greek is three short sections of a lecture treatise: Theophrastus of Eresus (c. 371–c. 287 BCE), Aristotle's successor as head of the Lyceum, in his On Stones ( Peri lithōn , De lapidibus ), written toward the end of the fourth century BCE. The treatise — in form closer to lecture notes than to a finished book, as both of its modern editions note — is the earliest scientific work on minerals to survive, and its testing passages (§§45–47 in the standard numbering, prepared for by §4) are the anchor text for everything in Sections III and IV of this article. They repay slow reading, because Theophrastus is not merely reporting a trick. He is doing something recognisably philosophical with it: asking how the stone knows. §4 — The Stone Enters the Classification Theophrastus classifies stones first by their ordinary differences — colour, hardness, smoothness, density — and then by their powers ( dynameis ): what a stone can do to other things, or suffer from them. In Caley and Richards's translation, the powers include stones that colour water, stones that petrify what is placed in them, stones with the power of attraction, and — in the sentence this article exists to unpack — stones that, as he puts it, “can test gold and silver, such as the stone called the Heraclean and the one called the Lydian”. Two cautions belong to that sentence. First, the pairing is slightly loose: the Heraclean stone is elsewhere in the treatise the lodestone, the magnetic stone whose power is attraction, and the commentators — Eichholz's commentary discusses the passage at length — have long noted that Theophrastus here runs the attracting stones and the testing stone together in one breath. The testing stone proper is the Lydian stone. Second, the classification itself is the point: for Theophrastus, testing gold is a natural power of a kind of stone, on the same list as magnetism. Assaying begins, in the surviving literature, as natural history. §45 — Two Ways of Knowing: Fire and Friction Section 45 opens the dedicated discussion, and it opens with a puzzle Theophrastus immediately dissolves. The stone that tests gold seems, he says in paraphrase, to have the same power as fire, since fire tests gold too — and some people are puzzled that two such different things should do the same work. They should not be, he answers, because the two do not do the same work in the same way. In Caley and Richards's wording: “Fire works by changing and altering the colors, and the stone works by friction” — and the stone, he goes on in paraphrase, seems to have the power of picking out, of discriminating, the essential nature of each metal rubbed on it. The distinction is exact, and this article is organised around it. Fire-testing (Section IV) is a reaction test: heat the metal and read what the heat does to its surface. Stone-testing (Section III) is a sampling test: abrade a trace of the metal onto a standard surface and read the trace. Theophrastus, in three sentences, has already separated the two great families of quick assay that the next two thousand years would elaborate. §46 — The Improved Stone and the Ladder of Small Weights Section 46 is the most technically dense passage on testing to survive from the classical Greek world, and it deserves to be followed clause by clause, in paraphrase. A much better stone, Theophrastus reports, has now been found than the one used before. The improvement is specified in three stages: STAGE ONE — PURIFIED GOLD The older stone, in paraphrase of §46, detected purified gold: it could tell refined gold from what was not gold. A yes-or-no instrument. STAGE TWO — TERNARY ALLOYS The new stone also detects gold and silver alloyed with copper: it works on the three-metal mixtures of real commerce, not only on the refiner's pure product. STAGE THREE — QUANTITY PER COIN It shows, in Theophrastus's phrase as usually rendered, how much is mixed in each stater. The verdict is no longer genuine or false but a proportion, read off against a ladder of very small weights. The ladder is the passage's famous crux, and it must be handled carefully. In paraphrase: indications are obtained from the smallest possible weight; the smallest unit is the krithē (a barleycorn, as a weight), then the kollybos (a tiny coin and weight), then the quarter-obol, then the half-obol — and from these the precise proportion is determined. On the Attic standard an obol weighed about 0.72 grams, so the ladder's upper rungs are roughly a third and a sixth of a gram, and its lowest rungs are fractions of those. What the ladder is , physically, Theophrastus does not say: he does not describe a set of comparison needles, and any account that pictures him handling a modern assayer's needle-case is importing later equipment into his text. What the passage establishes — and it is enough — is that by his lifetime the streak test was being read quantitatively , against graded standards fine enough to argue about fractions of an obol in a stater. Eichholz's commentary treats the passage as evidence for comparison against standard alloys; Caley, himself a chemist, discusses in his commentary how the later, fully documented needle method (Section III) achieves exactly the discrimination Theophrastus claims, and where its real limits lie. The honest summary is: the text proves graded comparison existed; the surviving text does not describe the grading hardware. // THE CLAIM AND ITS LIMITS // Theophrastus's §46 claims a great deal for the improved stone — discrimination down to the smallest weights in the ladder. Pliny, three and a half centuries later, repeats the tradition in superlatives (Section III). Modern assayers who have worked the touchstone method under controlled conditions find it genuinely discriminating in trained hands — the later literature commonly credits it with about a carat (one twenty-fourth part) on gold under good conditions — but not infallible, and not independent of the operator. Read the ancient claims as the testimony of men impressed by a real skill, stated without error bars. The skill was real. The error bars are this article's addition, and they are labelled as such wherever they appear. §47 — Where the Stones Come From, and Why One Face Is Better Section 47 grounds the instrument in a place and a material, in paraphrase. All such stones are found in the river Tmolos — the mountain stream of Lydia, in the Sardis region, the same Tmolus whose slopes fed the gold-bearing Pactolus (Section VI). They are smooth by nature, like pebbles, but flat rather than round, and in size about twice the largest pebble. Then comes the detail that proves Theophrastus is reporting workshop practice and not book-learning: the upper surface of the pebble, the face that has lain toward the sun, tests better than the lower face. His explanation, in paraphrase, is physical and testable: the upper surface is drier, and moisture prevents the stone from picking out the metal; in hot weather, too, the stone tests worse, because it gives out moisture and the metal slips. An instrument whose performance varies with which face is up, with damp, and with the weather is not a philosopher's invention. It is a bench tool, described by someone who had watched it misbehave. Section III builds the full procedure on this foundation — and keeps Theophrastus's failure modes in it, where they belong. One last framing point. Theophrastus wrote around 315–300 BCE. Bacchylides had used the Lydian stone as a poetic commonplace a century and a half earlier; the Sardis refinery (Section VI) had been rubbing gold on touchstones two and a half centuries before that. Theophrastus is therefore not an inventor reporting a novelty. He is a systematiser reporting a mature craft — mature enough to have already produced an improved instrument, a quantitative reading, and a literature of complaints about damp stones. The Greek world's testing tradition is older than its earliest surviving description of it, and every date in this article should be read with that lag in mind. III. The Touchstone at Work: Drawing and Reading the Streak The touchstone test is the most durable assay ever devised. It is attested in Lydia by the sixth century BCE, described by Theophrastus in the fourth, repeated by Pliny in the first century CE, presupposed by the recipe papyri in the fourth century CE (Section XI), and still sold today, in essentially its ancient form, as a jeweller's kit: a black stone, a set of graded needles, and a trained eye. This section gives the procedure in full — first what the stone is, then the operation step by step, then who used it and where, then how it fails. Steps that the ancient sources state are marked as stated; the connective bench detail that the ancient sources omit and the later assay literature supplies is marked reconstruction , per the rule set out in Section I. The Stone Itself The ideal touchstone, as the tradition from Theophrastus to the modern manuals describes it, must satisfy four requirements at once, and the geology follows from them. It must be hard — harder than gold and silver, so that the metal, not the stone, is what wears away in the rubbing. It must be fine-grained and very slightly abrasive , with a matte, even texture that takes a clean streak the way fine sandpaper takes a mark, without gouging or polishing. It must be black, or nearly so , because the evidence is a film of metal a few thousandths of a millimetre thick, and gold, silver, and copper can only be told apart by colour if the background swallows all reflected light. And it must be chemically inert , indifferent to the metal, to handling, and to heat. The rocks that meet the specification are dense, black, siliceous stones: the material the mineralogical tradition calls basanite or Lydian stone — a velvety-black, flinty jasper-like rock, in modern terms a fine chert or lydite — with dense basalt and black slate as serviceable seconds. Pliny, in Rackham's translation of Natural History 33.126, gives the stone's dossier in paraphrase: the touchstone (Latin coticula ) was formerly, on Theophrastus's authority, found only in the river Tmolus, but in Pliny's day was found in many places; some call it the Heraclian stone, others the Lydian; the pieces are of moderate size, not exceeding about four inches long by two broad; and the face that has lain toward the sun is better than the face that lay on the ground — Theophrastus §47, faithfully transmitted. The name Lydian is itself the provenance record: the stone is named for the kingdom that invented coinage, as if the map remembered what the texts forget to say — that the test and the coin were born in the same place, of the same need. The Procedure, Step by Step Step 1 — Prepare the stone (partly reconstruction). The working face must be clean, dry, and free of old streaks. Theophrastus §47 states the governing facts: use the drier, sun-facing surface; expect worse performance from a damp stone and in damp, hot weather, when the stone sweats and the metal slips instead of biting. The later bench practice (reconstruction) adds the maintenance the texts assume: old streaks are scoured off — pumice and water in the later manuals — the face is wiped dry, and the stone is kept out of the tester's sweating hand as much as the work allows. A greasy or wet stone gives a pale, broken streak, and a pale streak reads as poor metal: the commonest false fail in the method is a dirty instrument, not a bad coin. Step 2 — Draw the streak (stated in substance). Take the piece to be tested — coin, ingot, ornament, or a droplet of metal melted down for the purpose, as at Sardis (Section VI) — and rub a corner or edge of it firmly across the stone in one steady stroke, with even pressure, so as to lay down a continuous band of metal. Pliny's image, in Rackham's translation, is that the experts use the stone “like a file”, taking a scraping from the piece with it. The later manuals (reconstruction) standardise the mark — a streak on the order of a centimetre or two long and a few millimetres wide is the working size in the modern literature — and insist on what any practitioner learns in a day: pressure and speed must match between the unknown streak and the comparison streaks, because a hard rub lays down more metal and a richer colour than a light one, and the reading is a comparison, not a measurement of the streak alone. Only a few milligrams of metal are transferred. The piece is, for practical purposes, undamaged — which is why this test, alone among the accurate ones, could be applied to a finished coin or a temple crown without destroying the thing tested. That single property explains its thousand-year career. Step 3 — Draw the comparison streaks (the principle stated by Theophrastus §46; the hardware reconstruction). Beside the unknown streak, rub streaks from standards of known composition — in the fully documented later practice, the touch-needles : slim rods or star-mounted points, each tipped with an alloy of certified fineness. A working needle set is a ladder. For gold, the later sets run in carats (twenty-fourths): needles alloyed with silver, needles alloyed with copper, and needles alloyed with both, because a gold–silver alloy and a gold–copper alloy of the same fineness lay down different colours — silver pales the streak toward a greenish white, copper warms it toward red — so a one-dimensional ladder cannot identify a three-metal mixture. The tester picks the needle whose fresh streak looks nearest the unknown, lays it down alongside, and then brackets: a finer needle, a poorer needle, until the unknown is pinned between two standards or matched outright. Theophrastus §46 proves that graded comparison against very small weight-steps was the ancient aim; the Sardis evidence (Section VI) shows a gold needle of known purity in actual refinery use; the organised needle-case itself, with its carat numbering, is documented only in the later assay literature, and this article does not antedate it. Step 4 — Read the streaks (stated). The reading is colour, judged side by side on the same stone, in the same light, at the same moment. Pure gold lays a deep, rich yellow. Silver in the alloy bleaches it, step by step, through pale yellow toward the greenish-white of electrum and the white of silver itself. Copper reddens it. A streak that matches a standard in hue and in the way it catches the light is read as that standard's fineness; a streak between two standards is read as between them. Pliny, in Rackham's translation (NH 33.126), states the experts' claim without flinching: “When experts using this touchstone, like a file, have taken with it a scraping from an ore, they can say at once how much gold it contains and how much silver or copper, to a difference of a scruple” — a scruple being the Roman scrupulum , a twenty-fourth of an ounce, about 1.1 grams. Read soberly, the claim is that a master could call a ternary alloy's recipe to within a small weight-step, on sight. The modern verdict (Section II's caution) is that the method in practised hands is good to roughly a carat on gold — remarkable for a test that takes ten seconds and consumes nothing — and that Pliny's “never mistaken” is the voice of the tradition admiring its masters, not a laboratory error estimate. // WHAT THE ANCIENT TEST DID NOT HAVE: THE ACID DROP // Every modern touchstone kit includes acid — a drop of nitric acid (or, for higher carats, an aqua regia mixture) laid across the streaks, which eats the poorer streak faster and turns a colour judgement into a survival race. That step is not ancient. The Greek and Roman world had no mineral acids to drop (Section VII): nitric acid is a medieval preparation, unambiguous only in the Latin pseudo-Geber writings of the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. The ancient reading was colour alone, unaided — which is precisely why it demanded a master, why Theophrastus marvels at it, and why its verdicts were argued about. Any picture of a Greek assayer with an acid bottle is an anachronism of about fifteen hundred years. Who Used It, and Where The touchstone's users can be placed, from the evidence, at every level of the metal economy. At the top, the refinery : at Sardis, after cementation, the parted gold was assayed on the stone against a needle of known purity before it was collected and sent into the city (Section VI) — the test as quality control on a state-grade product. In the middle, the mint and the banker's table : the Athenian public tester sat among the bankers' tables in the Agora (Section IX), and while the law that placed him there specifies his cut, not his stone, the streak is the only rapid, non-destructive screen a man examining coin after coin all day could have used to decide which pieces deserved the chisel; that sentence is an inference from the workflow, and is labelled as one. At the bench level, the goldsmith : the recipe papyri presuppose the stone throughout — most nakedly in a recipe (Leyden X, No. 38, Section XI) for a gilding that, in Caley's translation, neither touch nor rubbing on the touchstone will detect, a fraud specified precisely by the test it is engineered to beat. And in the culture at large, the poet and the philosopher : Bacchylides and Plato (Section I) reach for the stone when they need an image of a verdict that cannot be flattered, bribed, or argued with — only read. An instrument does not acquire that metaphorical career by being rare. How the Touchstone Fails The failure modes define the rest of this article, because every later procedure exists to cover one of them. FAILURE ONE — IT READS ONLY THE SKIN A streak is a sample of the surface, a few milligrams deep at most. A plated coin, a gilded copper ring, a surface-enriched alloy (Section VI) all present honest metal to the stone and base metal to the world. The stone cannot see a core. Only the cut can (Section X). FAILURE TWO — IT CANNOT COUNT THREE METALS AT ONCE Colour is one channel of information; a gold–silver–copper mixture has two independent variables. Different recipes can lay down near-identical streaks. The needle ladder narrows the possibilities; it does not close them. Pliny's scruple is a master's boast, not a method's guarantee. FAILURE THREE — THE INSTRUMENT DRIFTS Moisture (Theophrastus §47), grease, worn or clogged stone, mismatched rubbing pressure, poor light: each shifts the reading. The test's accuracy lives in the operator's discipline, and dies with it. FAILURE FOUR — IT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT WEIGHT A clipped, sweated, or underweight coin of honest metal passes the stone perfectly. Fineness and weight are separate promises, kept by separate instruments: the stone for the first, the balance for the second. The dokimasia needed both (Section IX). Hold those four failures in mind. Cupellation answers the second (it counts, by weighing what survives). Parting answers it completely (it separates the metals so each can be weighed alone). The cut answers the first. The balance answers the fourth. The Greek testing system is not a collection of tricks; it is a set of instruments whose blind spots interlock — and the men who ran it knew the interlocking, because the frauds that beat one test and died on another are recorded in their own books. IV. Fire as the Second Witness: Colour, Breath, and the Hot Shovel Theophrastus §45 set the terms: fire tests by changing and altering the colours . Fire-testing is the touchstone's elder sibling — cruder, partly destructive, and available to anyone with a charcoal fire and an eye. Its principle is differential behaviour under heat. Pure gold is, among common metals, uniquely indifferent to fire: it melts (at 1,064 °C, in modern measurement) without oxidising, without tarnishing, and comes out of the fire the colour it went in. Its usual companions are not indifferent. Silver stays bright at a red heat but its copper content oxidises and darkens; copper reddens and then blackens with scale; lead oxidises, softens, and slumps far below the others' melting points; tin sweats out early. Heat a suspect piece strongly and watch it, and the alloy confesses in colour and in texture what the cold eye could not see. Pliny gives the doctrine its Roman form in Natural History 33.59–60, in paraphrase of Rackham's translation: gold is the one substance that loses nothing by fire, even in conflagrations and on funeral pyres; indeed it improves the more often it is fired, and fire serves as a test of its goodness, the gold taking on a red hue like fire itself — and this process, Pliny says, is called assaying. He adds the refiner's detail that gold, for purification, is roasted with lead — a sentence that points straight at cupellation (Section V). The Procedure, as the Recipe Papyri Write It Down The fullest surviving bench statement of the fire test is not in a philosopher or an encyclopaedist but in the workshop book this article ends with: Leyden Papyrus X, Nos. 43 and 44, in Caley's translation, here paraphrased closely because the recipes are short and their logic is the whole content. To test gold (No. 43): remelt the metal and heat it strongly. If it is pure, it keeps its colour after heating and stays bright like a coin. If it turns white , it contains silver. If it becomes rougher and harder , it contains copper or tin. If it blackens and softens , it contains lead. To test silver (No. 44): heat or melt it as with gold. If it stays white and brilliant, it is pure. If it turns black , it contains lead. If it turns hard and yellow , it contains copper. That is the complete procedure: one furnace, one heating, four or three colour-and-texture verdicts. Note what it is and is not. It is a screen for gross adulteration — Caley's assessment, carried in the Egyptology division's treatment, is that such recipes detect gross adulteration only — and it is qualitative : it names the adulterant but cannot weigh it. Note also its cost: the piece must be remelted. The fire test in this form can be applied to bullion, to scrap, to a sample — never to a finished coin whose stamp is its value. The touchstone screens the coin; the fire judges the melt. The division of labour between Sections III and IV is a division between objects, not just between techniques. Pliny's Silver Tests: The Shovel and the Breath For silver, Pliny (NH 33.127, in paraphrase of Rackham) preserves two further tests, and — characteristically — the fraud that defeats one of them. The shovel test : lay a shaving of the silver on a white-hot iron shovel. A shaving that stays perfectly white is passed as good silver; if it turns red, it is of the next quality down; if black, it is worthless. The chemistry, in modern terms, is the oxidation behaviour of the alloy's copper on the hot iron: the whiter the residue, the less oxidisable metal was in the shaving. Then Pliny's warning, in paraphrase: fraud has found its way even into this test — if the shovels are kept in urine, the shaving is stained during the burning and a base shaving counterfeits whiteness. The detail is precious evidence, worth more than the test itself: by the first century CE the testing of silver was an adversarial practice with a literature of counter-measures, in which even the instrument could be prepared in advance by the cheat. The breath test follows in the same section, in paraphrase: breathe on polished silver; genuine silver at once films with moisture and then dissipates the vapour. It is a test of surface and polish more than of composition — the weakest instrument in this article, recorded here because Pliny records it, and because its presence in his list shows the truth about the whole family: ancient testing was a bundle of screens of very unequal power, and the skill lay in knowing which screen a given suspicion required. // THE SAME LOGIC, APPLIED TO A PIGMENT // Pliny's fire logic was general-purpose. In NH 33.121 (in paraphrase of Rackham) he reports that cinnabar from the Sisapo mines is assayed by means of gold made red-hot: adulterated cinnabar blackens against the hot gold, genuine cinnabar keeps its colour — and, if no gold is available, a sheet of red-hot iron serves the same turn, detecting lime adulteration. A standard hot surface, a suspect sample, a colour verdict: the shovel test with the roles reversed. The Greek world's testing habit was not confined to coin metal; it was how a material culture without chemistry interrogated any substance whose value hid inside it. Fire's verdicts, then, are fast, legible, and shallow. They sort the grossly false from the plausible in minutes, at the price of the sample's form. To go further — to turn this metal contains copper into this metal contains eleven parts of copper in the hundred — the assayer must stop watching surfaces and start destroying samples methodically, weighing what the destruction leaves behind. That is fire assay proper, and its engine is the subject of the next section: a bath of molten lead, a porous cup of bone ash, and a bead that brightens at the end like a signal lamp. V. Cupellation: The Lead That Carries Everything Away Cupellation is the quantitative heart of ancient assaying, and the oldest of its heavy procedures: archaeology carries it back to the third millennium BCE in Asia Minor, where it was invented to win silver from lead ores, and it remained, with remarkably little change, the standard fire assay for gold and silver into the modern laboratory. Its principle is a piece of chemical luck so convenient that it looks designed. Melt lead in a stream of air at a bright red heat and it oxidises, steadily and completely, into molten lead oxide — litharge (PbO). Melt gold or silver in the same air at the same heat and they do not oxidise at all. And molten litharge is a solvent and a vehicle: as it forms, it dissolves the oxides of the base metals present — copper, tin, iron, antimony, bismuth — and carries them away with itself. So: alloy the precious metal with a generous excess of lead, hold the melt hot in moving air, and the lead becomes a river that flows out of the vessel taking every base metal with it, until nothing is left in the vessel but the precious metal, alone, in a bead that can be weighed. What the bead weighs, against what the sample weighed, is the fineness. The touchstone estimates; cupellation counts .
