A System, Not a List: What the Tetrad Is This article opens a new cluster in the Alchemy wing of the Greco-Roman hub: the Foundations . The wing's other articles begin where the texts begin — with a workshop, a recipe collection, a named practitioner at a bench. This cluster begins one level down, with the matter-theory those practitioners took for granted. An Alexandrian worker who heated a body to drive off its moisture, who sealed a vessel so that what rose would condense and fall back, who spoke of a metal's body and the spirit that could be drawn out of it and fixed in it again, was not inventing a physics on the spot. He was using one — the oldest continuously used physics in the Western record, the doctrine that the perceptible world is compounded of four elements : fire, air, water, and earth . The first thing to understand about the tetrad is that it is a system , not a list. A list of four stuffs would be a curiosity. What Empedocles proposed in the fifth century BCE, what Plato mathematised in the fourth, and what Aristotle rebuilt into the most durable natural philosophy of antiquity is a machine for explaining change: a small stock of permanent constituents, a rule for how they combine, a pair of motive powers or an equivalent mechanism to do the combining, and — in the Aristotelian form that antiquity, medicine, and alchemy actually inherited — a derivation of the four stuffs themselves from two pairs of contrary qualities , the hot and the cold, the wet and the dry. Once the qualities are in place, the elements stop being four brute facts and become the four possible answers to a two-question test. That derivation, drawn as a square, is the single most consequential diagram in this article, and Section X gives it in full. Stated in advance, exactly as this hub states it everywhere: Fire is hot and dry; Air is hot and wet; Water is cold and wet; Earth is cold and dry. THE FOUR, AS STUFFS Empedocles' four “roots” (rhizōmata): fire, air (aithēr, the bright upper air), water, and earth — eternal, ungenerated, imperishable, and never transformed into one another. Everything else is their mixture and separation. See Sections IV–V. THE FOUR, AS QUALITY-COMPOUNDS Aristotle's four “simple bodies”: each is prime matter qualified by one term from each contrary pair — hot or cold, wet or dry. So defined, the elements can transform into one another, by the exchange of a quality. See Sections IX–X. The difference between those two cards is the plot of this article. For Empedocles, the roots are primitive and changeless, and the world's variety is arrangement. For Aristotle, the qualities are primitive, the elements are compounds of them, and the world's variety includes genuine transformation of element into element — the very thing Empedocles' scheme forbade and the very thing an art of transmutation would later need its physics to allow. Plato stands between them, giving the tetrad a mathematics — proportion first, then geometry — and a craftsman to impose it. The Stoics and Galen then carry the scheme into the two domains where it would live longest, cosmology and medicine; and the alchemists of Roman Egypt receive it, at the end of that long transmission, not as a theory to be debated but as the grammar in which operations are described. Section XIV, the article's closing substantive section, follows the tetrad into their hands. A note on method, in the form this hub uses wherever the sources invite invention. No direct quotation is given in this article unless it is explicitly attributed to a named published translation that was consulted for it. In practice the article paraphrases throughout, and paraphrases of ancient texts are labelled as paraphrase in the text. The handful of short verbatim quotations — from Empedocles fragment 6 in the translation printed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 's Empedocles entry, from Plato's Timaeus in Benjamin Jowett's translation, and from Aristotle's On Generation and Corruption in H. H. Joachim's translation — are each flagged at the point of use, with the translator named. Fragment numbers for the Presocratics follow the standard Diels–Kranz numbering (DK 31 for Empedocles), cited through the standard modern translations and discussions listed in the Sources. Where scholars dispute a point — and on Empedocles they dispute nearly every point — the dispute is stated as a dispute, with the main positions named, rather than silently settled. // WORDS FOR “ELEMENT” // Empedocles did not call his four “elements”. His word is rhizōmata , “roots”. The Greek word later standard for element, stoicheion (plural stoicheia ), originally means a letter of the alphabet — one item in an ordered row — and its application to the physical constituents is first securely attested in Plato's circle and after. Aristotle, looking back, credits Empedocles with being the first to distinguish the four clearly ( Metaphysics A 4, 985a31–3, in paraphrase), while using the later vocabulary to do it. This article follows the same convention: “roots” for Empedocles' own conception, “elements” for the doctrine in general, and “simple bodies” where Aristotle's technical usage is in view. One framing caution, because popular accounts blur it. The four elements of this article are not the elements of modern chemistry, and the resemblance of the word conceals an opposite conception. A modern element is defined by atomic structure and is, in ordinary chemical process, exactly what does not change into another element. The ancient tetrad, in its Aristotelian form, is defined by sensible qualities and is exactly what does change: water heated and rarefied becomes air-like, air condensed becomes water-like, and the theory's whole point is to make such changes intelligible rather than miraculous. Nor are the ancient “elements” simply the stuffs of everyday experience under their everyday names. Aristotle is explicit, in paraphrase of On Generation and Corruption II.3, that the simple body corresponding to fire is “such-as-fire”, not the flame on the hearth — ordinary fire is an excess, a kind of boiling of the hot and dry, as ice is an excess, a freezing of the cold and wet. The tetrad names four poles of a qualitative space, approximated by familiar stuffs, not four samples in jars. Keep that in view and most of the scheme's apparent naivety dissolves; what remains is a serious, wrong, and extraordinarily productive theory of matter. II. Before Four: The Single-Stuff Theories and the Problem of Change The tetrad was an answer, and it cannot be understood without the question. Greek natural philosophy before Empedocles had spent a century asking what the world is fundamentally made of, and its first answers were singular. The tradition Aristotle reports, and modern scholarship reconstructs with due caution from his reports and the surviving fragments, runs as follows — each item here is a paraphrase of the standard account in Kirk, Raven and Schofield's The Presocratic Philosophers (2nd ed., 1983), the reference this article follows for the early material. THALES OF MILETUS (fl. c. 585 BCE) Water as the originating stuff (archē): the earth floats on water; moisture nourishes all things; the seeds of things are moist. Known almost entirely through Aristotle's retrospective report, and to be handled as such. ANAXIMANDER (c. 610–c. 546 BCE) Not a familiar stuff but the “indefinite” (to apeiron): an unbounded, ageless source from which the opposites — hot and cold, wet and dry among them — are separated out, and to which they return. The opposites, note, are already doing cosmological work a century before the tetrad. ANAXIMENES (fl. c. 545 BCE) Air (aēr) as the basic stuff, other stuffs arising from it by rarefaction and condensation: rarefied, air becomes fire; condensed, it becomes wind, cloud, water, earth, and finally stone. One stuff, one mechanism, a graded series — the direct ancestor of every later density-based account. HERACLITUS OF EPHESUS (fl. c. 500 BCE) Fire as the emblem and measure of a world that is process before it is stuff: all things exchange for fire and fire for all things, as goods for gold and gold for goods (DK 22 B 90, in paraphrase). Whether Heraclitus held a material monism at all, or a doctrine of ordered change in which fire is first among equals, is disputed; the tetrad's authors read him, in any case, as fire's partisan. Each single-stuff theory faces the same embarrassment, and Aristotle states it against all of them in On Generation and Corruption II: if everything is really one stuff, then the manifest differences among things — hot against cold, dry against wet, heavy against light — must be explained as modifications of that stuff, and the modifications quietly become the real theory. Anaximenes' mechanism is the honest version of the problem: rarefaction and condensation are already two opposed processes doing the work that opposed qualities would later do openly. Pluralism — the move Empedocles makes — simply promotes the modifications to constituents: instead of one stuff in many states, several stuffs in many mixtures. Parmenides: The Challenge That Set the Terms The pluralists were not only answering the Milesians. They were answering Parmenides of Elea (born c. 515 BCE), whose poem mounted the most consequential argument of the century: in paraphrase of fragment DK 28 B 8, what-is cannot have come from what-is-not, for what-is-not cannot be thought or said; what-is therefore neither comes to be nor perishes, is one, continuous, ungenerated and imperishable, and the world of birth, death, motion, and variety that the senses report is, strictly, unintelligible. The argument is a trap with three exits, and the next generation of Greek physics can be read as a choice among them. Accept the logic and multiply the unchangeable: posit not one Parmenidean being but several, each satisfying Parmenides' conditions — ungenerated, imperishable, unalterable in itself — and let apparent change be their rearrangement. That is Empedocles' exit, and the atomists' after him. Or accept the logic and rebuild change itself on a new analysis, distinguishing the senses in which a thing can come to be. That, two generations later, is Aristotle's exit. Plato, characteristically, takes both roads in different works. The tetrad is born, in other words, as a Parmenidean pluralism : four little beings, each eternal, doing together what the one Being could not do alone — underwrite a changing world without anything ever, at bottom, being born or dying. Empedocles states the inheritance himself, in paraphrase of fragments DK 31 B 8 and B 12: there is no birth of any mortal thing, nor any end in destructive death, but only mixture and the separation of what has been mixed; and nothing can come to be from what in no way is, nor can what-is be destroyed, for wherever it is, there it will always be. “Birth” and “death” are names men give to the mixtures and separations. The sentence could be Parmenides' in its logic; its physics is the tetrad's charter. What the roots and their powers are, the next three sections set out. // WHY THIS PREHISTORY MATTERS TO THE WING // Two habits of thought that alchemy never loses are already visible here. First, the explanation of manifest difference by a small set of opposed powers — hot/cold, wet/dry, rarefying/condensing — rather than by an open-ended list of substances. Second, the conservation instinct: nothing in the work is created or annihilated; it is separated, recombined, purified, and fixed. When a late-antique recipe speaks of a body “dying” and being “revived”, it is speaking Empedocles' licensed fiction — the names men give to mixture and separation — with full theoretical backing. See Section XIV. III. Empedocles of Acragas: The Poet, the Poems, and the Evidence Empedocles was a citizen of Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily, born in the early fifth century BCE — conventionally c. 495–c. 435 BCE, the dates used in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 's entry, which this article follows — into an aristocratic family: his grandfather, of the same name, is remembered as an Olympic victor in the horse races. The biographical tradition, preserved chiefly in Diogenes Laertius' Lives (Book VIII), written some seven centuries later, makes him a democratic champion who broke an oligarchic council of the Thousand and refused a kingship, a physician and founder of the Sicilian medical tradition, a rhetorician credited by Aristotle with the invention of rhetoric, and a wonder-worker who presented himself, in his own verse, as a god gone among mortals. The same tradition kills him picturesquely — leaping into the crater of Etna, which obligingly returned one of his bronze sandals — and modern scholarship is unanimous that the leap is legend, manufactured out of the poems' own imagery. The safe biographical sentence is short: a wealthy Acragantine of the democratic side, active in the decades after the fall of the Sicilian tyrannies, who wrote didactic hexameter poetry of extraordinary force on nature and on purification, and whose physics — unusually for a Presocratic — was still being argued with, line by line, by Plato and Aristotle a century later. That last fact is why his evidence base is comparatively good. Empedocles wrote, according to the ancient tradition, two poems: On Nature ( Peri physeōs ), addressed to his disciple Pausanias, setting out the roots, the powers, the cosmic cycle, and a biology; and the Purifications ( Katharmoi ), addressed to his fellow citizens, setting out a doctrine of the fallen divine being (daimōn), its exile and transmigrations, and the pure life that shortens the road back. Neither poem survives whole. What survives is some 450 lines, preserved as quotations in later authors — Aristotle and his commentators above all, but also Plutarch, Sextus Empiricus, Clement of Alexandria, and the doxographical tradition descending from Theophrastus — plus one physical windfall: the Strasbourg Papyrus , fragments of a papyrus roll of the poem, identified in the Strasbourg University Library and published by Alain Martin and Oliver Primavesi in 1999, which recovered lines of On Nature previously unknown and confirmed the ordering of others. // ONE POEM OR TWO? A LIVE DISPUTE, STATED FAIRLY // Whether On Nature and the Purifications are two poems or one project in two registers has been contested since Catherine Osborne's 1987 challenge to the two-poem orthodoxy, with Brad Inwood, Simon Trépanier, and others developing single-work or closely-unified readings. The Strasbourg Papyrus materially strengthened the unity side: it contains lines traditionally assigned to the Purifications in physical continuity with the physical poem, showing that if there are two works they are far more closely related than the older picture — physics here, religion there — allowed. The two-poem division remains the conventional filing system, and this article uses the traditional titles for convenience, as the reference literature does. But the reader should register what the dispute means for the tetrad: the roots and the powers are not, for Empedocles, a secular mechanism onto which a religion was later pasted. Love and Strife are cosmic powers and moral facts in a single vision, and the same poem that proportions bone out of earth, water, and fire also legislates against bloodshed. The alchemical tradition, which would later refuse exactly this separation, was in that respect a faithful heir. The fragments are cited, by universal modern convention, from Hermann Diels and Walther Kranz, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (6th ed., 1951–52), where Empedocles is chapter 31: A-texts are ancient testimony about him, B-texts are the fragments themselves, numbered B 1 to B 154 in the usual count. Every DK number in this article was checked against the discussions in Kirk–Raven–Schofield and the Stanford Encyclopedia entry listed in the Sources. Two warnings travel with the numbering. A fragment is a quotation torn from a poem: its context is lost, its placing in the poem is reconstruction, and in a handful of famous cases the reconstruction is contested. And the translations differ — sometimes, on contested lines, materially. This article therefore paraphrases Empedocles as a rule, and quotes verbatim only the one passage flagged in Section I. c. 495 BCE BIRTH AT ACRAGAS Empedocles born into a wealthy family of Acragas in Sicily, a generation after Parmenides, in the Greek West that produced both the Eleatic argument and its pluralist answers. c. 450 BCE THE POEMS On Nature and the Purifications composed in hexameters. The four roots and the two powers enter the record — the tetrad's birthday, so far as surviving evidence allows one to be assigned. c. 435 BCE DEATH Aristotle reports that he died at sixty. Place and manner are unknown; the Etna leap is an ancient legend, not a report. 4th c. BCE PLATO AND ARISTOTLE ARGUE WITH HIM The tetrad's two great systematists take Empedocles as their point of departure — Plato by adopting and geometrising the four, Aristotle by adopting and rebuilding them (Sections VII–XI). 1999 THE STRASBOURG PAPYRUS Martin and Primavesi publish the papyrus fragments: new lines of the physical poem, and the strongest physical evidence yet for the closeness of the physical and purificatory material. IV. The Four Roots: Rhizōmata The doctrine, in its author's own opening move, is a list with divine names. The one verbatim quotation this article permits itself from Empedocles is the list itself, fragment DK 31 B 6, given here in the translation printed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 's Empedocles entry: “Hear first of all the four roots of all things: Zeus the gleaming, Hera who gives life, Aidoneus, and Nêstis, who moistens with her tears the mortal fountain.” EMPEDOCLES, DK 31 B 6, AS TRANSLATED IN THE STANFORD ENCYCLOPEDIA OF PHILOSOPHY The names are a riddle the tradition began solving immediately and has never quite finished. That Nestis — a Sicilian water goddess — is water is secured by her tears and her fountain. The other three assignments have been disputed since antiquity: the doxographer Aëtius identifies Hera with air and Aidoneus with earth, while other ancient reports distribute the names differently, and modern editors still flag the passage as contested. The majority modern reading, reflected in Kirk–Raven–Schofield and the reference literature, takes gleaming Zeus as fire (or as the bright aithēr in its fiery aspect), life-bearing Hera as air in Aëtius' scheme or earth in a rival one, and Aidoneus — Hades under a euphemistic name — as the remaining term. What is not disputed is the referent set: the four roots are fire, air, water, and earth , confirmed by fragments (B 17, B 21, B 109 among them) that name the stuffs plainly. The divine names do interpretive work beyond camouflage. Each root, bearing a god's name, is presented as in some sense alive and active — a point recent scholarship (Catherine Rowett's work is the reference usually cited) has pressed against the older picture of the roots as inert matter awaiting external forces. The roots are not billiard balls. They are powers in their own right, which is one reason the boundary between “stuff” and “force” in Empedocles has always been hard to police. What a Root Is: The Parmenidean Specification Each root satisfies, individually, the conditions Parmenides laid down for what-is. In paraphrase of B 17 and its companion fragments: the roots are equal to one another and the same in age ; each presides over its own province and has its own character; nothing is added to them and nothing is taken away; they do not come to be and they do not perish; running through one another they become now this and now that, while remaining, in themselves, continually the same. Three consequences define the system. 1. NO TRANSMUTATION A root never becomes another root. Fire does not turn into water, in Empedocles, ever. All change is mixture and separation of changeless constituents — the exact point on which Aristotle will break with him (Section IX). 2. NO VOID Nothing is empty of the roots; the whole is full. Motion is therefore not motion into emptiness but interchange of place — the roots “incessantly exchange their places”, in the B 17 paraphrase — a plenum physics, against which atomism's void is the rival solution to the same Parmenidean problem. 3. PROPORTION IS IDENTITY What a compound is is fixed by the ratio of roots in it. Bone, blood, flesh, and the rest differ not in kind of stuff but in recipe — see the ratios in Section V. The painter's palette, not the sculptor's block, is the system's governing image. A word on “air”. Empedocles' word for the second root is aithēr , the bright upper air, the shining medium of the heavens — not aēr , the murky lower atmosphere of mist and cloud. The distinction is old in Greek (Homer's gods dwell in aithēr above the aēr) and it matters twice over in this article. It matters for Empedocles, whose air-root is a celestial, luminous stuff, nearer to fire in character than the damp exhalations of the lowlands. And it matters for Aristotle, who will take the word aithēr over for something else entirely — the fifth body of the heavens (Section XI) — while demoting his air-element to the aēr register. Readers who meet “aether” in later alchemical and occult literature are meeting a word with at least three ancient jobs, and the jobs must not be conflated: Empedoclean bright air, one root among four; Aristotelian celestial body, expressly not one of the four; and the Stoic and later usages, which differ again (Section XII). Finally, the roots are perceptible in kind . Fragment B 109, in paraphrase, states the system's epistemology in one line: by earth we perceive earth, by water water, by air bright air, by fire destroying fire, by Love Love, and by Strife baneful Strife. Like is known by like, because the perceiver is himself a mixture of the very constituents he perceives, and perception works — as the fragments on effluences and pores (B 84, B 89 in the standard discussions) elaborate — by the fitting of emanations from objects into the pores of the sense organs, where the mixture answers to the mixture. The doctrine is worth pausing on because of its long echo: a cosmos in which like acts on like, knows like, and is drawn to like is a cosmos already organised by sympathy , and sympathy — systematised by the Stoics, catalogued by Bolos of Mendes — is the workshop physics of the earliest alchemy. The line from B 109 to the Physika tradition is drawn in Section XIV. V. Love and Strife: The Motive Powers Roots alone would be a warehouse. Empedocles' second posit makes them a world: two powers, as eternal and as unoriginated as the roots themselves, that move them. Love (Philia, Philotēs; also named Aphrodite and Kypris in the fragments) unites: it brings the unlike roots together into mixtures, blends them, and at the limit gathers all things into one. Strife (Neikos) separates: it drives the roots apart, sorts like to like, and at the limit holds each root in its own unmixed mass. Fragment B 17 — the longest continuous passage of the physical poem to survive, and the text every account of Empedocles is built on — states the alternation, in paraphrase: a twofold tale; at one time all things grow together to be one alone out of many, at another they grow apart to be many out of one; double is the birth of mortal things and double their destruction, the one born and destroyed by the coming together of all things, the other nourished and scattered by their separation; and these things never cease from their continual exchange, now through Love all coming together into one, now each borne apart by the hatred of Strife. The Cosmic Cycle and the Sphere Extended over cosmic time, the alternation becomes a cycle with two poles. At one pole, Love is wholly dominant: the roots are completely intermingled, their differences dissolved in a uniform, motionless, divine whole that Empedocles calls the Sphere (Sphairos) — in paraphrase of the fragments that describe it (B 27–B 29), a rounded whole rejoicing in its circular solitude, without limbs, branches, or strife, equal to itself on every side. At the other pole, Strife is wholly dominant: the roots stand completely separated, each in its own region, a world unmade into four pure masses. Between the poles the powers wax and wane against each other under what B 17 calls, in paraphrase, a broad oath and a fixed alternation of time — and in the intermediate conditions, where mixture is partial and unstable, ordered worlds like ours arise, with heavens, earth, sea, plants, animals, and men. Our world, on the traditional reading, is one such intermediate: a cosmos in which Strife is increasing, or Love is, depending on which half of the cycle we inhabit. // ONE COSMOGONY OR TWO? THE CYCLE DISPUTED // The symmetrical reading just given — a two-part cycle with a cosmogony and a zoogony in each half, once under waxing Strife and once under waxing Love — is the traditional interpretation, associated above all with Denis O'Brien's Empedocles' Cosmic Cycle (1969) and M. R. Wright's edition (1981). It has been challenged by interpreters who find in the fragments evidence for only one cosmogony and one zoogony per cycle, and the Strasbourg Papyrus has been enlisted by both sides. The dispute is technical, turns on the placing and reading of a small number of lines, and remains open. What no party disputes is the machinery: two powers, opposed in effect, alternating in dominance, with complete mixture and complete separation as the cycle's poles and the ordered world as an intermediate state. This article presents the traditional symmetrical cycle as the standard account and flags it, here, as an interpretation — the same discipline it applies to the one-poem question in Section III. How the Powers Work: Mixture in Proportion Love's work is specified by the system's most famous analogy, fragment B 23, in paraphrase: as painters, trained in their craft, take pigments of many colours in their hands and mix them in harmony, more of some and less of others, and from them produce forms resembling all things — trees, men and women, beasts and birds and water-nurtured fish, and long-lived gods — so let not your mind be deceived that there is any other source for the countless mortal things that are seen; know this clearly. A handful of pigments, unlimited pictures: the analogy is the pluralist programme in a single image, and it fixes the role of proportion at the centre of the physics. The fragments give recipes. Bone (B 96, preserved by the commentator Simplicius and reported in the standard discussions) is compounded, in paraphrase, of two parts earth, two parts water, and four parts fire, compacted by the gluing power of Harmony — Love under her joiner's name. Blood and flesh (B 98) are mixtures of the four roots in approximately equal parts. Thought itself is located in the blood around the heart, where the mixture is most nearly equal and therefore most receptive to all its constituents alike. A thing's nature is its ratio; change the ratio and you change the thing, without any root having been created, destroyed, or transmuted. It is difficult to overstate how much of the later tradition — medical mixture theory, alchemical proportioning, the whole language of the “right mixture” — is already present in this move. Two further pieces of the physics deserve record, because both show Empedocles arguing from apparatus and observation, not only from Parmenidean logic. The first is the clepsydra (fragment B 100): a girl playing with a bronze water-lifter, closing its neck with her hand and plunging it into water — the water does not enter, because the air inside, pressing on the perforated base, holds it back; release the hand, the air escapes, and the water rushes in to take its place. In paraphrase of the fragment's point: air is a body. It occupies space, resists, and can be displaced only as another body takes its room — a demonstration, in a child's toy, of the plenum doctrine of Section IV, and one of the earliest surviving pieces of experimental argument in Greek science. The second is the doctrine of effluences and pores : all things give off streams of fine particles, and perception, magnetism, respiration, and the action of one body on another at a distance are explained by whether those streams fit the pores of the receiving body. The mechanism is crude and the reach is enormous: here, in embryo, is a general theory of selective interaction — why this acts on that and not on the third thing — which the later language of sympathy, antipathy, and specific affinity will inherit. // ARE LOVE AND STRIFE FORCES, GODS, OR STUFFS? // Aristotle already complains, in paraphrase of his criticisms in the Metaphysics and On Generation and Corruption , that Empedocles uses Love inconsistently — as a cause of good and of unity, yet also as a separator of like from unlike when it gathers the Sphere — and that he gives no account of what moves the powers themselves. Modern readers divide over whether Love and Strife are material constituents alongside the roots (they are sometimes spoken of in spatial terms, Love “equal in length and breadth” amid the roots in B 17), incorporeal forces, or divine agents of a kind the stuff/force distinction does not fit. The honest statement is that Empedocles' ontology is sixfold — four roots, two powers — and that the powers are sui generis in his poem: eternal, spatially extended, morally valenced, and mechanically effective at once. Later systems will tidy this away: Plato replaces the pair with a craftsman and mathematical structure, Aristotle with form, privation, and an unmoved mover, the Stoics with a single active principle. The untidiness is the price of the invention, and the invention — separate the constituents from the causes of their combination — is permanent. What Empedocles does not give the tetrad is as important as what he gives it. He gives it no fixed assignment of the contrary qualities — hot, cold, wet, dry — as the roots' defining properties. The roots have characters, and fragments associate them with qualities in passing (the sun bright and hot, earth heavy and hard, in the paraphrase of B 21's survey of the roots' appearances), but there is no scheme in the surviving fragments that defines each root by a quality-pair, and none should be retrojected into them. The quality-pair derivation is Aristotle's construction, built two generations later for his own purposes (Section IX), and the medical writers of the intervening period supply its other parent. To that parallel tradition — without which the square of Section X cannot be understood — the article now turns. VI. The Medical Parallel: Opposites, Powers, and the Hippocratic Body The tetrad has two birthplaces. One is the Eleatic argument of Section II. The other is the sickroom. Greek medicine of the fifth century BCE was independently converging on the same explanatory shape — a small set of opposed powers whose balance is health and whose imbalance is disease — and the mature element-theory of the fourth century, the one Galen and the alchemists inherit, is a fusion of the philosophical and medical lines. The fusion is so complete in later sources that separating the parents takes deliberate effort; this section makes the effort, because one of the most common errors in popular accounts is to read the finished fusion back into the fifth century. Alcmaeon of Croton (early fifth century BCE) is the tradition's starting point: in paraphrase of the testimony (DK 24 B 4), health is the isonomia — the equal rule, the political equality — of the powers in the body: wet and dry, cold and hot, bitter and sweet, and the rest; disease is the monarchia , the sole rule, of any one of them. The list is open-ended and the powers are qualities, not stuffs; but the grammar is complete already. The body is a polity of opposites; therapy is constitutional reform. Empedocles, working in the same Greek West and himself remembered as a physician, gives the Sicilian medical tradition its cosmology; the Hippocratic writers give the cosmology a clinic. On the Nature of Man and the Four Humours The Hippocratic Corpus — some sixty treatises, by many hands, of the late fifth and fourth centuries BCE — is not a system, and its authors disagree with each other vigorously. One treatise in it, however, became canonical for the whole later tradition: On the Nature of Man , attributed by Aristotle's school to Polybus, Hippocrates' son-in-law. In paraphrase of its central doctrine: the human body contains blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile ; these are its constitution, and through them it suffers pain and enjoys health; health is when these constituents are duly proportioned to one another in strength and bulk and well mixed; pain is when one of them is in defect or excess, or is separated in the body and not mixed with the others. The treatise goes on to correlate the four humours with the seasons — phlegm, cold and wet in character, increasing in winter; blood in spring; yellow bile in summer; black bile in autumn — and with the ages of life. It also argues, against monist physicians, that the body cannot be one stuff, for one stuff could not feel pain or generate opposites. // WHAT THE HIPPOCRATIC TEXT DOES — AND DOES NOT — SAY // Two precisions, both load-bearing. Assessment: What This Stratum Is and Is Not XXI. Sources I. A Workshop, Not a System: What This Stratum Is Greek alchemy does not begin with a theory of the universe. It begins with a set of workshop procedures for making inexpensive materials look, weigh, ring, and wear like expensive ones: copper alloys coloured yellow until they pass for gold, white alloys that pass for silver, clear quartz coloured green until it passes for emerald, and wool coloured with cheap dyestuffs until it passes for Tyrian purple. The oldest stratum of the Greek alchemical tradition — the material gathered under the names of Bolos of Mendes and of the pseudo-Democritus , the anonymous author (or authors) who wrote as Democritus of Abdera — is a craft literature. Its founding text, the Physika kai Mystika , is lost as a complete work and survives only in fragments, epitomes, and quotations. What those fragments contain, overwhelmingly, is recipes. That plain statement needs defending, because later centuries loaded this material with meanings it did not originally carry. There is, in this stratum, no philosopher's stone . There is no elixir of life , no universal medicine, no programme for the perfection of the soul through the perfection of metals. Those ideas belong to later developments — to the generation of Zosimos of Panopolis around 300 CE, who quotes pseudo-Democritus constantly and builds something larger on him, and to the Arabic and Latin traditions after that. What the Bolos / pseudo-Democritus stratum does have is three things that proved durable: a fourfold organisation of the art (gold, silver, stones, purple); a physical framework — sympathy and antipathy between “natures” — that purported to explain why the recipes work; and an initiatory frame story , in which the recipes are temple secrets revealed by a Persian master. Craft, physics, and legend arrive together, in the same short texts. Keeping them distinct, while showing how they interlock, is the work of this article. A note on method, because this archive's standing rule for repeatable processes applies here with full force: the recipes are presented below as workshop texts , step by step, in the sequence the sources give, with quantities where the sources give quantities. Where a modern chemical explanation helps the reader see what a procedure actually does to the metal or the stone, that explanation is offered — and is flagged, every time, as a modern explanation . The practitioners did not think in terms of oxidation, selective dissolution, or copper salts, and this article does not dress modern chemistry in their clothes. Conversely, where the ancient text explains itself — in terms of natures delighting in, conquering, and mastering one another — that explanation is given in its own terms, in Section XVII. The fullest surviving parallels to this recipe tradition, the third- to fourth-century CE workshop papyri from Thebes, receive their complete treatment in the Egyptology division — in the Zosimos article (§§IX–X) and in the Alchemy article (§XXIV) — and are used here to illuminate the earlier material, not duplicated. ATTESTED A recipe tradition organised in four books — on gold, on silver, on precious stones, on purple — ascribed to Democritus, quoted extensively by Zosimos, Synesius, and the later Greek commentators; substantial recipe overlap with the Leyden Papyrus X and the Stockholm Papyrus. DEBATED AMONG SPECIALISTS The date of Bolos (3rd or 2nd century BCE, conventionally c. 200 BCE); whether Bolos himself wrote any of the alchemical recipes; and the date of the alchemical pseudo-Democritus, whom Matteo Martelli's edition places in the second half of the 1st century CE, most likely c. 54–68 CE. LEGEND, LABELLED AS SUCH The initiation of Democritus by the Persian mage Ostanes in the temple at Memphis; the dead master's books discovered inside a temple column; the evocation of Ostanes from Hades. These are the texts' own frame stories, reported in Section VII as the tradition's self-presentation, not as biography. NOT PRESENT IN THIS STRATUM No philosopher's stone; no elixir; no transmutation doctrine in the later sense of a universal agent perfecting all metals; no apparatus literature of the kind Maria the Jewess and Zosimos introduce. The art here makes surfaces, alloys, and imitations — and says so. II. Mendes and the Delta: The World Behind the Recipes Mendes — Egyptian Djedet, Greek Mendēs — was a substantial city of the north-eastern Nile Delta, capital of the sixteenth Lower Egyptian nome, sacred to the ram god Banebdjedet. By the Hellenistic period it sat inside the most technically accomplished craft economy of the Mediterranean world. Egypt's temple and palace workshops had been working gold, silver, electrum, bronze, faience, glass, and coloured stones for three thousand years before Bolos; its dyers handled linen and wool with mordants and vat dyes of great sophistication; and its Delta ports traded with Phoenicia — the source of the murex purple that gave the fourth book of the pseudo-Democritean corpus its subject — and with the Aegean, Cyprus, and the Levant. The recipes in this tradition presuppose that economy at every line: Cyprian copper, Chian earth, Cappadocian salt, Italian antimony, misy and sory from the mines, Cadmean earth from Cyprus, saffron from Cilicia and Cnidus. The ingredient lists are trade maps. Over that Egyptian craft base lay a Greek intellectual superstructure. After Alexander's conquest (332 BCE) and the founding of Alexandria, Greek natural philosophy — above all the atomism of Democritus , the physics of the Stoics with its cosmic sympathy , and the pharmacology descending from Theophrastus and Dioscorides — met Egyptian workshop practice in the same cities and, this article will argue following Jack Lindsay's The Origins of Alchemy in Graeco-Roman Egypt (1970), in the same texts. The characteristic product of that meeting is a recipe that comes with a reason: not merely “do this,” but “do this, because this nature delights in that one.” F. Sherwood Taylor, in his histories of Greek alchemy, made the same point from the other side: the earliest alchemical writings are continuous with the technical papyri and the dyers' and goldsmiths' handbooks, and only gradually acquire the mystical vocabulary of the later corpus. // WHY EGYPT, WHY THEN // The conjunction that produced this literature — hereditary temple crafts, a monetised market hungry for precious materials, Greek philosophical vocabularies available for hire, and a book trade that rewarded famous ancient names — existed in Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt and nowhere else in quite that form. The recipes' geography is not an accident of survival; it is the tradition's birthplace showing through. One more feature of the setting matters for everything that follows: precious materials were expensive, tested, and policed . Gold and silver coinage and plate were assayed — the Leyden Papyrus includes recipes for testing the purity of gold, silver, and tin, and for detecting adulteration — and the same handbook that teaches a workman how to double his asem teaches him how the fraud can be found out. The line between the legitimate jeweller stretching a costly material, the dyer imitating a costly colour openly for a cheaper market, and the counterfeiter was drawn differently in antiquity than a modern reader expects; the papyri themselves frequently acknowledge that their products are imitations. Section XX returns to the question of fraud. For now it is enough to hold the economic fact: a technology that could make eight drachmas of silver-white alloy do the work of sixteen was worth money, worth writing down, and worth keeping secret — which is precisely the social setting the word mystika describes. III. Bolos of Mendes: The Man and the Dating Problem Almost everything known about Bolos comes at second or third hand, and the honest way to present him is to present the dossier and its cracks together. The Byzantine encyclopedia known as the Suda (10th century CE) contains two entries under the name Bolos: one for a Pythagorean philosopher of Mendes who wrote on marvels, potent remedies, and astronomical phenomena, and one for a Bolos of the school of Democritus, author of an Inquiry and a Medical Art containing material on natural sympathies. The Roman agricultural writer Columella (1st century CE), who cites a Bolos of Mendes on farming matters, supplies the passage from which scholars have generally concluded that the two Suda entries concern one man : a Mendesian writer of the Democritean persuasion, with Pythagorean colouring, who compiled works on natural properties, medicine, and agriculture. The standard modern reference summary — the Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry on Bolos of Mendes, consulted for this article — concludes the same, and adds the judgement that in antiquity Bolos was “widely read,” his reputation as an authority in natural history at times rivalling Aristotle's. The date is genuinely debated, and this article gives it as a range. Bolos is conventionally placed around c. 200 BCE — floruit in the 3rd or 2nd century BCE. The fixed points are these: he appears to have known Theophrastus' Historia Plantarum (Theophrastus died c. 287 BCE), which puts him after the early 3rd century; and he was already an authority for writers of the later Hellenistic and early Roman periods. Beyond that, precision dissolves. Matteo Martelli, in The Four Books of Pseudo-Democritus (2013) — the standard modern edition of the alchemical material — reviews the proposals for Bolos' date at pages 37–41 and treats the conventional placement as exactly that: conventional. Some discussions of the Democritean material have argued for later dates for parts of the corpus circulating under his name. The reader should therefore hold two dates separately, because the tradition itself separates them: Figure Conventional date Basis Status Democritus of Abdera c. 460–370 BCE The historical atomist; wrote no alchemy Secure as a person; irrelevant as an author here except as a borrowed name Bolos of Mendes fl. 3rd–2nd c. BCE (often given c. 200 BCE) Knowledge of Theophrastus; Suda entries; Columella's citation Debated within roughly a century either way The alchemical pseudo-Democritus Second half of 1st c. CE, most likely c. 54–68 CE (Martelli) Martelli 2013, pp. 29–31, on the language, sources, and transmission of the Four Books Modern scholarly dating; older literature often simply equated him with Bolos Zosimos of Panopolis fl. c. 300 CE His own corpus; the first alchemical author whose works survive substantially in his own name Broadly secure; see the hub's Zosimos article The distinction in the last three rows is the single most important piece of housekeeping in this article. An older generation of scholarship — Max Wellmann's 1928 study of the Physika of “Bolos Demokritos,” followed by E. J. Holmyard, Robert Multhauf, and Jack Lindsay — identified the alchemical pseudo-Democritus with Bolos: one Mendesian author, c. 200 BCE, standing at the head of both the sympathy literature and the recipe literature. That identification was criticised already by Wilhelm Kroll in 1934, and by P. M. Fraser, Jackson Hershbell, and Jean Letrouit after him; Martelli's edition treats the alchemical author as an anonymous writer of the Neronian period who inherited and reworked an older Democritean tradition to which Bolos had contributed. This article follows the current position: Bolos is the tradition's Hellenistic fountainhead; the surviving alchemical text is a Roman-period product of that tradition . Where the older literature is quoted below, the equation it assumes is flagged. IV. The Works Under Bolos' Name: Sympathies, Things Made by Hand, Farming None of Bolos' works survives complete. What survives is a wake: citations, excerpts, and attributions in Pliny the Elder, Aelian, Columella, the Hermetic compilations, and the Byzantine agricultural collection known as the Geoponica . From that wake, four bodies of material can be reconstructed with reasonable confidence. 1. On Sympathies and Antipathies — the Physika Bolos' best-known and most influential work circulated under titles rendered as Natural Properties ( Physika ) and as On Sympathies and Antipathies . Its project, as the Dictionary of Scientific Biography summary puts it, was to catalogue observed biological and ecological relationships — which creatures, plants, and stones help, harm, attract, or repel one another — and to explain them through supposed affinities and aversions between the entities concerned, figured almost as conscious “loves and hates.” The remora that stops the ship, the elephant's fear, the herb that counteracts the venom: the Physika gathered hundreds of such pairings, largely marvellous in content, and organised them by a single explanatory principle. Section XVII examines that principle as the physics of the later recipe books; here the point is bibliographical. The sympathy framework is Bolos' signature contribution to the tradition, and it is older than any surviving alchemical recipe ascribed to the Democritean school. 2. Cheirokmēta — Things Made by Hand The Cheirokmēta — the title means, roughly, “things made or effected by hand,” artificial or hand-worked products — was usually cited under Democritus' name rather than Bolos' own. It dealt, on the surviving evidence, with medical and magical herbs and with agricultural practices: the manipulation of natural materials by art to produce effects nature alone does not supply. The word matters for the history of alchemy beyond this article: cheirokmēta is also the title Zosimos gives to parts of his own encyclopedic corpus, a deliberate act of affiliation with the Democritean workshop tradition, treated in the Egyptology division's Zosimos article (§V). Already in the title, hand-work — cheir , the hand — is the point: these are things made, not things found. 3. On Farming — the Georgika and the Geoponica Debt Bolos wrote on agriculture — a work cited by Columella as On Farming ( Peri geōrgias ) — and the Democritean agricultural material descending from him was excerpted for a millennium. Wellmann's 1921 edition assembled eighty-two surviving fragments of the Democritean Georgika . The tenth-century Byzantine Geoponica , the great surviving Greek farming compilation, drew heavily and repeatedly on the Democritus/Bolos tradition: its precepts on grafting, pest control, weather signs, and sympathetic plant lore carry the Mendesian compiler's fingerprints throughout, transmitted through intermediaries such as Vindonius Anatolius and Cassianus Bassus. H. J. Rose's 1933 study of the folklore of the Geoponica states the attribution plainly, in the form this article adopts: the supposed extracts from Democritus treating of magic, sympathy, and antipathy have been referred — plausibly, in Rose's word — to Bolos of Mendes, an author of the Alexandrian period. The agricultural afterlife matters here because it shows the scale of the pseudepigraphic machine: by the time the Geoponica was compiled, “Democritus” on farming meant Bolos' tradition, and nobody involved found that remarkable. 4. On Stones, and the Rest of the Dossier A On Stones ( Peri lithōn ) is also ascribed to Bolos: a catalogue of precious and semiprecious stones and their powers, in the manner that foreshadows the later lapidary tradition — the direct ancestor, in spirit, of the stones book of the Four Books , where the interest shifts from the stone's occult virtues to the workshop problem of counterfeiting its colour (Section XIV). Separate writings on medicine, on the history of the Jews, and on other subjects were credited to him in antiquity as well; of most of them, few identifiable fragments remain. The dossier as a whole describes not a specialist but a compiler-encyclopedist of the hidden properties of things — exactly the profile that could plausibly stand behind a recipe collection organised by sympathy, and exactly the profile that made his adopted name worth borrowing. V. Why Democritus? The Pseudo-Democritus Problem Democritus of Abdera (c. 460–370 BCE) was the co-founder, with Leucippus, of atomism: the doctrine that reality consists of indivisible atoms moving in void, and that the sensible qualities of things — colour, taste, heat — are arrangements, not essences. He wrote nothing about making gold. Yet by the Hellenistic period his name had become a magnet for precisely the literature he never wrote: works on sympathies, on agriculture, on stones, on the making of precious materials. Modern scholarship files all of it under pseudo-Democritus , and the question is why this name, of all names, attracted the workshop corpus. Three reasons, mutually reinforcing, are visible in the evidence. First, suitability of doctrine. Atomism makes material transformation thinkable in a way few other Greek systems do: if the difference between copper and gold is a difference of arrangement and admixture, then an art that rearranges and admixes is, in principle, imitating nature's own method. Later alchemists who presented their theories as interpretations of Democritus were exploiting a real affinity between the borrowed name and the borrowed doctrine. Second, the traveller legend. From the first century BCE onward, Greek and Roman authors increasingly credited early philosophers with formative journeys to Egypt, Persia, and Babylon. Democritus was swept into that pattern early and thoroughly: he was said to have learned from the Chaldaeans, from the Magi who accompanied Xerxes, and above all from Ostanes , the legendary Persian mage. A philosopher who had been initiated in Egypt and Persia could plausibly possess Egyptian temple recipes; the legend manufactured the credentials the recipes required. Third, the economics of authority. In a manuscript culture, an anonymous recipe is a claim; a recipe by Democritus is an inheritance. The name sold, protected, and authorised the text — and, once attached, was defended by every copyist and commentator whose own work leaned on it. // PSEUDEPIGRAPHY IS NOT A SCANDAL HERE // Ancient readers did not experience attribution the way modern scholarship does. A work “of Democritus” could mean: from his school, from his tradition, in his manner, or simply — shelved under his name. The fraud question is real for individual recipes sold as gold-making (Section XX), but the borrowed name itself was a normal literary institution of the Hellenistic book world, applied to Pythagoras, Hermes, Zoroaster, and Moses with the same freedom. The consequence for the reader of this archive is a discipline of naming. In what follows, “Democritus” inside a summary of an ancient claim means the figure the ancient text presents; pseudo-Democritus means the anonymous historical author(s) of the alchemical Four Books as modern scholarship reconstructs them; and Bolos means the Mendesian compiler of the 3rd–2nd century BCE, whose relation to the alchemical text is that of fountainhead to a later redaction — close, formative, and not identity. Martelli's edition is the authority followed for that three-way distinction throughout this article. VI. The Physika kai Mystika: A Lost Book and Its Fragments The founding text of Greek alchemy does not exist. That sentence is not a flourish; it is the bibliographical situation, and this article states it as plainly as the task of the archive requires: the Physika kai Mystika is a lost work . No manuscript of the complete Four Books survives. What survives, on Martelli's reconstruction, is a set of epitomised extracts preserved in two extant treatises — the Physika kai Mystika itself, in the abridged form transmitted by the Byzantine alchemical corpus, and a separate treatise On the Making of Silver ( Peri asēmou poiēseōs ) — together with a collection of substance lists, the Katalogoi , and a sediment of quotations, summaries, and paraphrases in Zosimos, Synesius, pseudo-Olympiodorus, Stephanus, Christianus, and the anonymous commentators. The oldest great manuscript of the corpus, the Marcianus graecus 299 (10th–11th century, Venice), already contains the work in epitome: even our earliest witness is a digest of a digest, a thousand years downstream of its author. The Title, Translated Carefully Physika kai Mystika (Φυσικὰ καὶ μυστικά) is conventionally Englished in several ways, and the differences are not cosmetic. Lawrence Principe, in The Secrets of Alchemy (2013), discusses the title directly: it is often translated “Physical and Mystical Things,” but that rendering misleads, because Greek mystika in this period did not mean “mystical” in the modern sense of inward spiritual experience; it meant things to be kept secret — the adjective of the mysteries, of what is disclosed only to initiates. Principe's preferred rendering is “Natural and Secret Things” : physika , matters of nature, and mystika , the secret parts of the craft — secret, on his reading, in the practical sense that lucrative artisanal processes are trade secrets. Other translators, keeping the initiatory colouring of mystika in view, render the title “Natural and Initiatory Matters.” This article uses Physika kai Mystika untranslated after this section, and asks the reader to hold both halves of the word's range at once: these are nature-recipes that present themselves as initiates' knowledge. The frame story of Section VII shows the text insisting on the second half; the recipes of Sections X–XV show the first half doing the work. Berthelot and Ruelle: How the Fragments Reached Us in Print The modern study of the text begins with Marcellin Berthelot and Charles-Émile Ruelle's Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (Paris, 1887–88) — the edition, French translation, and vast introductory study that first made the Greek alchemical corpus, pseudo-Democritus included, available as a whole. Berthelot's accompanying Les origines de l'alchimie (1885) argued the thesis that still structures the field: that alchemical doctrine grew out of the documented practices of Egyptian goldsmiths, dyers, and glassworkers — out of imitation and falsification techniques preserved in the Leyden papyrus — rather than descending from pure speculation. The English renderings of the Physika kai Mystika quoted and paraphrased in this article follow the Berthelot–Ruelle text as transmitted in that edition (the Marcianus manuscript being their principal witness); Martelli's 2013 edition, with its own text and translation of the Physika kai Mystika , the On the Making of Silver , the Katalogoi , and Synesius' commentary, is the current scholarly standard and the authority for the datings and attributions used here. // READING A FRAGMENTARY TEXT HONESTLY // Because the work survives in epitome, arguments from its silence are worthless: that the surviving extracts say little about (for example) stones compared with gold reflects, as Martelli notes, the interests of the later excerptors, who privileged gold- and silver-making — not necessarily the proportions of the lost original. Every claim in Sections VIII–XV is therefore framed as a claim about the transmitted tradition, whose centre of gravity we can see, rather than about a book we cannot open. VII. The Frame Story: Ostanes, Memphis, and the Column in the Temple What follows in this section is the text's own frame story — the legend the tradition tells about itself. It is labelled legend throughout, because that is what it is: a charter myth for a recipe book, composed to explain where secret knowledge comes from and why the reader may trust it. The summary given by Synesius (c. 373–414 CE) in his commentary-letter on Democritus' book — preserved and edited by Martelli — runs, in paraphrase, as follows. Democritus came from Abdera in Thrace, a natural philosopher who investigated all natural questions; but he became truly wise when he went to Egypt and was initiated in the temple of Memphis, together with the Egyptian priests, by the great Ostanes , the Persian mage. From Ostanes he took his first principles, and he composed four books on dyeing: on gold, on silver, on stones, and on purple. The initiation claim does double duty in the legend: it gives the Greek philosopher Egyptian temple credentials — Memphis being among the most venerable cult centres of Egypt, seat of Ptah, patron of craftsmen — and Persian magical credentials in a single scene, welding the two prestige traditions of secret knowledge into one pedigree. The Physika kai Mystika 's own opening narrative, as transmitted in the Berthelot–Ruelle text, is stranger and more specific, and is paraphrased here closely because its details became canonical for the whole later tradition. The author and his fellow pupils had gathered their master's teaching on the diversity of matter and were labouring to make the natures agree when the master died before they were initiated — before, that is, he had imparted the final secret. They attempted to evoke him from Hades . The shade, constrained, could say almost nothing: in the Berthelot–Ruelle rendering, its whole utterance is the sentence, “The books are in the Temple.” Returning to the temple and finding nothing by inquiry, the pupils were later feasting together in the sanctuary when a column suddenly opened — and inside it, where no one had told them anything was hidden, they found the master's books, and in them the whole of his writing gathered into a single short formula: the aphorism of the natures, treated in Section XVIII. The narrative then pivots, without transition, into recipes — as if to say: the formula is the theory, and the rest of the book is what it looks like at the bench. // WHAT A FRAME STORY IS FOR // Read functionally, the legend solves three practical problems for a trade-secret text. It explains why the knowledge is written at all (the master died; the books are his testament). It explains why it is incomplete (the initiation never happened; the reader, like the pupils, must work out the compositions for himself). And it sets the price of entry: the recipes that follow are temple property, to be handled as initiates handle sacred things. Every later alchemical preface that complains of a dead master, a hidden book, or an oath of secrecy is spending currency minted here. Ostanes himself belongs to the legend's furniture. A figure of that name — a Persian magus attached, in various accounts, to the courts of Xerxes or of Alexander — recurs across Hellenistic magic, astrology, and pharmacology as the fountainhead of Persian secret wisdom for Greek readers. Martelli's discussion (pp. 69–73) treats the Ostanes of the Four Books as a literary authority-figure of that tradition, not as a recoverable historical teacher. The archive's rule applies: the initiation at Memphis is evidence — excellent evidence — for how the Roman-period craft imagined its own origins. It is not evidence for an event in the life of a fifth-century atomist who, on the chronology alone, had been dead for some four centuries when the scene is set. VIII. The Four Books: Gold, Silver, Stones, Purple Synesius' summary, Zosimos' citations, and the surviving epitomes agree on the architecture of the lost work. The Four Books were four books on dyeing : BOOK I — ON GOLD Chrysopoeia , gold-making: how to give base metals a yellow tinge — to dye them gold — and how to augment and double gold itself. The longest shadow in the tradition; the surviving Physika kai Mystika epitome is dominated by it. BOOK II — ON SILVER Argyropoeia , silver-making: whitening copper, iron, tin, and lead into silver-like bodies, and the manufacture of asem , the white alloy that stood in for silver. A separate epitome, On the Making of Silver , preserves this book's line of transmission. BOOK III — ON STONES The dyeing of stones: colouring rock crystal and other cheap transparent minerals to pass as emerald, ruby, beryl, amethyst, and the rest; improving and imitating pearls. Preserved most fully not in the epitomes but in the Stockholm Papyrus (Section XIV). BOOK IV — ON PURPLE The dyeing of wool purple: genuine murex dyeing and, at greater length, its imitation with lichens, madder, alkanet, and other cheaper dyestuffs fixed with mordants. The Physika kai Mystika as transmitted opens with purple recipes (Section XV). Two features of that table deserve emphasis. First, the unity of the four subjects. To a modern reader, metallurgy, gemmology, and textile dyeing are three trades. To this tradition they are one art, because they are one operation — the fixing of a precious colour in a receptive body — performed on four kinds of matter. The same vocabulary ( baphē , dyeing; katabaphē , immersion-dyeing) runs through all four books; the same mordant-like auxiliaries (alum, urine, vinegar, brine) recur in the metal recipes and the wool recipes alike; and the same explanatory refrain follows the recipes in every book. Section IX takes up that unity as the tradition's central idea. Second, the centre of gravity is imitation. Each book is organised around a precious material and the problem of producing its appearance — and, so far as the workshop could manage it, its working properties — from cheaper stock. The art begins, and in this stratum remains, the production and imitation of precious materials. Later alchemy's claim to transmute in earnest is a reinterpretation of this workshop inheritance, not its original content. The preserved extracts, as Martelli notes, skew heavily toward Books I and II: the later Greek alchemists who excerpted and commented on pseudo-Democritus cared about gold and silver above all, and the stones and purple books survive disproportionately through the parallel papyrus tradition rather than through the commentary tradition. That skew is itself a historical datum — it is the moment the fourfold workshop art begins to narrow into the gold-obsessed art of the later corpus — and it is why this article leans on the Leyden and Stockholm papyri for Sections XIV and XV: they preserve, in working form, the half of the Four Books that the commentators let slip. IX. The Language of the Art: Baphē — Everything Is a Dyeing The technical vocabulary of the Four Books is the vocabulary of the dye-house, and learning to hear it is the fastest way into the practitioners' own understanding of what they were doing. The master-word is baphē (βαφή): a dipping, a dyeing, the colour taken up by a body immersed in a prepared liquor. A metal treated with a yellowing preparation is not, in the text's own terms, transmuted; it is dyed . The recipes speak accordingly of dyeing silver yellow to make it gold, of dye liquors ( bammata ) compounded to a wax-like consistency and smeared on leaf, of immersion times counted in days, of colours that must “penetrate to the centre” of the leaf, and of results judged by whether the colour pleases and whether it resists fire. The wool-dyer's criteria — fastness, depth, evenness — are the gold-maker's criteria, unchanged. Around that master-word cluster the operation-words of the bench. Projection ( epibolē in the later vocabulary; the epitome speaks of throwing or projecting a preparation onto a molten or heated body) is the moment a prepared powder or paste meets the metal. Fixing is the rendering of a volatile ingredient — above all mercury — non-volatile by combination, so that it stays in the work instead of flying off in the fire. Whitening and yellowing name the two great colour-operations on metals, exactly parallel to bleaching and dyeing in the cloth trade. And presiding over the whole vocabulary stands the word physis , “nature”: every ingredient and every metal is a nature, with its own affinities, and a recipe is a choreography of natures. When the epitome pauses after a recipe to remark that salt cleans copper inside and out, that mercury whitens a body within and on its surface, that a drop of oil can destroy a quantity of purple and a little sulphur burn many bodies — it is thinking, in its own idiom, about penetration, dosage, and disproportionate effect. The idiom is not ours. It is not empty, either.
