A Timing Science: What This Article Covers This article belongs to the Foundations cluster of the Alchemy wing — the small group of articles that sets out the intellectual machinery the Alexandrian art presupposed — and its subject is the machine the whole ancient world used to answer one question: when? When will this life turn? When will this sickness break? When should this voyage, this marriage, this building, this operation begin? Greek astrology, in the form this article treats it, is best understood not as a fortune-telling sideline of ancient religion but as the Hellenistic world's timing science : a complete, teachable, internally consistent system for correlating the configurations of the heavens at a chosen instant with the character and course of whatever began at that instant — a child, an illness, a city, a question, a work. The system's working life runs, roughly, from the second century BCE , when its characteristic synthesis first becomes visible in Ptolemaic Egypt, to the sixth or seventh century CE , when its last Greek practitioners were still writing in a world already transformed. Between those bounds it was practised from Spain to Mesopotamia, in Greek and Latin and Demotic, by court astrologers and by street-corner consultants, and it generated one of the largest technical literatures of antiquity. Three of its books anchor this article, because between them they show the system from three sides: the didactic poem of Dorotheus of Sidon (first century CE), the electional authority; the nine-book Anthology of Vettius Valens (second century CE), the working practitioner's handbook; and the Tetrabiblos of Claudius Ptolemy (second century CE), the attempt to give the whole art a foundation in natural philosophy. Around those three stand the modern accounts on which this article chiefly rests: Tamsyn Barton's Ancient Astrology (1994) and Roger Beck's A Brief History of Ancient Astrology (2007). A note on method, because this subject, like the Hermetica treated elsewhere in this wing, attracts invention. No quotation appears in this article unless it was verified in the named translation and is attributed to that translation at the point of quotation. In practice there are only two verbatim quotations, both short, both from F. E. Robbins's Loeb translation of the Tetrabiblos , read in full for this article. Everything else — the contents of Dorotheus's poem, of Valens's handbook, of Ptolemy's first book — is given as labelled paraphrase , following the translations and modern accounts named in Section XV. Where the evidence is disputed — and on Dorotheus's date, on his text's road through Persian into Arabic, and on the standing of Ptolemy's defence, it genuinely is — the dispute is stated as a dispute, in Sections IX and XII, rather than settled by editorial sleight of hand. GENETHLIALOGY The science of births (Greek geneseis ): casting and interpreting the configuration of the heavens at a person's birth — or, more rarely, conception — to read character, fortunes, and the timed course of a life. The dominant form of Greek astrology, and the trunk from which the other branches grow. KATARCHAI — BEGINNINGS From katarchē , a beginning: the astrology of inceptions. Read a beginning that has happened, to judge how the thing begun will fare; or, in the properly electional use, search forward for the beginning whose heavens promise the outcome wanted, and start then. Dorotheus is its founding authority (Section IX). GENERAL ASTROLOGY Genethlialogy's methods applied to collectives — peoples, cities, kingdoms — and to weather and crops: the direct heir of the Babylonian omen tradition, and the branch Ptolemy treats in his Book II before turning to individuals. INTERROGATIONS Questions put to the astrologer and answered from the heavens at the moment of asking — the ancestor of later horary astrology. In the earliest surviving treatment, Dorotheus's fifth book, interrogations and elections are not yet cleanly separated, and the blur is itself evidence (Section IX). One framing distinction governs everything that follows, and Beck's account states it with useful bluntness. Ancient astrologers did not, in the main, observe the sky at the moment of a birth. They calculated it — from tables, often years after the event, reconstructing where the Sun, Moon, and five visible planets had stood in relation to each other, to the zodiac, and to the local horizon and meridian of the birthplace at the birth hour. Astrology therefore presupposed astronomy: the better the tables, the more exact the chart, and the system's two greatest surviving authors stand on opposite sides of that dependence — Ptolemy, who wrote the ancient world's standard astronomical tables in the Almagest and then the Tetrabiblos to interpret what they computed, and Valens, who consumed such tables the way a physician consumes a pharmacopoeia. The modern habit of filing astronomy as the science and astrology as its embarrassing parent is, as Beck argues, a poor guide to the ancient material, in which the two formed a single predictive enterprise of greater and lesser certitude. This article follows the ancient filing. // WORDS: ASTROLOGY AND ASTRONOMY // Greek astrologia and astronomia were used with little of the modern distinction for much of antiquity; the same author could write both, and Ptolemy calls the predictive art simply the second of the two “means of prediction through astronomy”. “Horoscope” likewise needs its ancient sense recovered: Greek hōroskopos is the hour-marker — the degree, and then the sign, rising at the birth hour — before it is the whole chart, and only later the newspaper paragraph. This article uses “horoscope” for the chart and “Ascendant” or “Hour-Marker” for the rising point itself. The article's route is the system's own logic. Section II gives the Babylonian upstream in the brevity the hub's division of labour requires. Section III describes the Egyptian synthesis. Section IV presents the Thema Mundi , the mythical horoscope of the world's birth in which the system encoded its own rationale. Sections V–VII set out the working apparatus — signs and planets, places and aspects, lots, decans, and terms, and the time-lord techniques that turned a static chart into a dated life. Section VIII asks what a consultation actually delivered. Sections IX–XI take the three anchor authors in turn. Section XII states the standing dispute over Ptolemy's defence. Section XIII follows astrology into medicine. And Section XIV closes the loop this cluster exists to close: astrology as the timing science of the alchemical art itself — the elections by which a work was begun, and the planetary days and hours by which the workshop kept celestial time. II. The Babylonian Upstream, Kept Brief This section is deliberately brief. Mesopotamia is another hub's ground: the Before Kemet hub's Mesopotamia wing treats Babylonian celestial divination in the fullness it deserves, and the reader who wants the upstream in depth should begin with that hub's Babylonian Sky Science and its companion Omens and Medicine . What a reader of the Greek system needs in hand is only the shape of the inheritance — three gifts, and one decisive absence. The first gift is the omen tradition itself. For well over a millennium, Mesopotamian scribes recorded celestial phenomena — eclipses, halos, planetary appearances and disappearances, unusual colours and conjunctions — and read them as signs addressed, in the first instance, to the king and the land: war, harvest, flood, plague, the fate of armies. The great omen series Enūma Anu Enlil , running to some seventy tablets in its standard form, organised thousands of such protases and apodoses — if the Moon does this, then that will befall — and the scholarly apparatus of the Assyrian and Babylonian courts existed to match the night's sky against the series and warn the king in time. Two features of that world passed intact into the Greek system: the conviction that the heavens are legible , a text written in moving lights; and the professional figure of the scholar who reads them for a client whose fate is at stake. What changed, in transmission, was the client. The second gift is mathematical: the zodiac of twelve equal signs . Across the fifth century BCE, Babylonian astronomers regularised the constellations along the ecliptic into twelve signs of thirty degrees each — a coordinate grid, independent of the uneven star-pictures, against which any planet's position could be stated exactly and computed in advance. With the zodiac came the sexagesimal arithmetic, the period relations, and eventually the ephemerides that made the Greek astrologer's retrospective calculation possible. Almost everything in Sections V–VII that involves a number — degrees, terms, rising times, planetary periods — is Babylonian in its ancestry, however Greek its dress. The third gift is the proof of concept: the Babylonian horoscopes . From the late fifth century BCE, Babylonian scribes began applying the sky to individuals, recording the positions of the Moon and planets at a child's birth. The earliest known example is dated to 410 BCE ; a small corpus — some thirty tablets, chiefly from Babylon and Uruk, running into the first century BCE — survives. These texts are terse: a birth date, planetary positions in the zodiac, sometimes brief prognostic notes. But the conceptual move is complete in them. The heavens at this person's first moment are worth writing down, because they bear on this person's life. Genethlialogy exists, in embryo, on clay. // THE DECISIVE ABSENCE // What the Babylonian horoscopes do not have is the apparatus that makes a chart a chart in the Greek sense: no Ascendant as the pivot of interpretation, no twelve places counted from the rising sign, no developed doctrine of aspects between signs, no lots, no time-lords. The Babylonian gift was the legible sky, the zodiac, and the idea of the birth moment. The interpretive machine built on those gifts is the Hellenistic invention — and the invention, on the evidence, happened in Egypt. How the transmission ran — through the Persian period, through Babylonian scholars working in a Greek-speaking world, through figures such as Berossus, the Babylonian priest who wrote in Greek and was said to have taught on Cos — is a genuinely murky historical problem, on which Barton is properly cautious: flashes of evidence amid will-o'-the-wisps, in the phrase of her reviewer Alexander Jones, summarising her brief and honest chapter. This article does not pretend to clear the murk. It notes only that by the time Greek astrology becomes fully visible, in the second half of the first century BCE, it already has the shape it will keep for the rest of antiquity — and that its own foundation stories point, unanimously, not to Babylon but to Egypt. III. The Hellenistic Synthesis in Egypt The Greek system was made in Egypt — in the temples, cities, and bilingual scholarly culture of the Ptolemaic kingdom and its Roman successor — out of three strands that had never before been one thing. Babylon supplied the zodiac, the planetary periods, and the omen habit of mind. Greece supplied the geometry — the circle divided, the aspects as angular relations, the spherical cosmos of concentric spheres — and, in time, the philosophy: Stoic fate and cosmic sympathy, Platonic cosmology, Aristotelian physics of qualities. Egypt supplied the third strand, and the one modern accounts most easily underrate: the decans , the thirty-six star-groups whose successive risings had marked the hours of the Egyptian night since the early second millennium BCE, together with the temple setting, the priestly scholars, and the immense prestige of Egyptian antiquity in Greek eyes. The decans return, as working apparatus, in Section VI; their role here is as evidence of where the synthesis happened. When the decans were folded into the zodiac — three to a sign, one for each ten degrees — two civilisations' timekeeping became a single instrument. The system's own memory of its founding is preserved by the fourth-century astrologer Firmicus Maternus, and it is Egyptian to the core. In paraphrase of Firmicus's account: the art descended from Hermes — Mercury, in his Latin — through Asclepius, and was set out in books by Nechepso , a pharaoh, and Petosiris , his priest. Modern scholarship treats Nechepso and Petosiris as the pseudepigraphal authors — real books circulated under those august names — of a foundational astrological literature composed in Greek in, most probably, the second century BCE . Fragments and citations of the Nechepso–Petosiris material survive throughout the later tradition, and its eclipse lore in particular can be set beside its Mesopotamian prototypes. The attribution pattern matters beyond the two names. Like the Hermetica of the companion article, early Greek astrology authorised itself by antiquity and by Egypt: Hermes as inventor, a pharaoh and a priest of Thoth as first expositors. Whether a historical Petosiris — a high priest of Thoth of that name is known around 300 BCE — stands anywhere behind the books cannot be recovered, and this article does not pretend otherwise. What is recoverable is the claim, and the claim is a map of the synthesis: Greek technique, wearing Egyptian authority, built on Babylonian data. // DENDERA, IN PASSING // The famous sculpted zodiac from the temple of Hathor at Dendera (c. 50 BCE) — the twelve signs set among Egyptian decans and constellations — is the synthesis carved in stone, and it is the Egyptology division's object, not this article's. It is named here only to fix the point in the reader's eye: by the mid-first century BCE, an Egyptian temple ceiling could display the Babylonian zodiac naturalised among Egypt's own stars. Egyptology owns the monument; this article owns what practitioners did with the system it pictures. Alexandria is the conventional name for the synthesis's home, and the convention is reasonable — the city was Ptolemaic Egypt's intellectual capital, the natural meeting point of Greek, Egyptian, Babylonian, and Jewish learning — subject to the same warning the Hermetica article issues for its own texts: the surviving astrological papyri come from temple libraries and town rubbish heaps up and down the Nile, and “Alexandria” names a culture more securely than a street address. What can be said without qualification is the chronology. Astrological literature in Greek is being cited, excerpted, and argued with from the first century BCE onward; Greek horoscopes on papyrus survive from the first century CE; and by the second century CE the system exists in the great handbooks — Dorotheus behind them, Valens and Ptolemy at their head — in essentially the form Sections V–VII now set out. c. 1600 BCE and after THE OMEN SERIES The celestial omens gathered in Enūma Anu Enlil: the sky read for king and land. CE EASTWARD: PAHLAVI AND ARABIC Dorotheus and Valens are translated into Middle Persian, and from Persian (and Greek) into Arabic — the road by which the Greek system reached Baghdad, and eventually returned west in Latin dress. The hub's transmission history follows that road elsewhere; Section IX states what it did to Dorotheus's text. IV. The Thema Mundi: The System's Charter Horoscope Every mature system carries a picture of itself at its most intelligible, and Greek astrology's picture is a horoscope: the Thema Mundi , the “theme” — the chart — “of the world”. It purports to be the configuration of the heavens at the birth of the cosmos itself, and it is transmitted in late-antique sources, above all Firmicus Maternus ( Mathesis III.1) and Macrobius's Commentary on the Dream of Scipio (I.21). It was used in teaching, and its function in the tradition is exactly the function of a charter: from its placements, the system's otherwise arbitrary-looking rules can be read off , as if deduced. Whether it was truly the system's generative starting point — a construction from which the rules were derived — or a later rationalisation built to display rules already in use, is a live question in the modern literature, and this article states it as open. What is not in question is the chart itself, which is perfectly definite. Point Placement What the placement encodes Ascendant 15° Cancer The world rises in the Moon's sign, at the solstitial sign of high summer — generation and embodiment stand at the chart's pivot. Moon Cancer, its domicile The nearer luminary in the sign it rules, on the Ascendant: the Moon as lady of the body and of fortune. Sun Leo, its domicile The farther luminary in the sign it rules, in the sign following the Ascendant — the two brightest signs of the northern year given to the two lights. Mercury Virgo First of the five planets in zodiacal order from the luminaries, in one of its two domiciles — and, instructively, impossibly far from the Sun (see below). Venus Libra In domicile; sextile to the Moon's sign — the geometry that will mark Venus's configurations as harmonious. Mars Scorpio In domicile; square to the Sun's sign — the geometry that will mark Mars's configurations as harsh. Jupiter Sagittarius In domicile; trine to the Sun's sign — the geometry of beneficence at its most harmonious. Saturn Capricorn In domicile; opposed, across the wheel, to the Ascendant sign itself — the geometry of the great malefic's hostility to life and light. Read as a teaching diagram, the chart does three pieces of work at once. First, it grounds the domiciles : the assignments of signs to planetary rulers — the Moon to Cancer, the Sun to Leo, and the five planets each to two signs disposed symmetrically outward from the luminaries, Mercury to Virgo and Gemini, Venus to Libra and Taurus, Mars to Scorpio and Aries, Jupiter to Sagittarius and Pisces, Saturn to Capricorn and Aquarius — are simply the Thema Mundi's placements, generalised. Second, it grounds the aspects : standing in the world's first chart, Jupiter's sign beholds the Sun's by trine and Venus's beholds the Moon's by sextile, while Mars's beholds the Sun's by square and Saturn's opposes the Moon's — and the tradition's valuation of the aspects, harmonious trine and sextile against harsh square and opposition, together with the benefic and malefic natures that go with them, can be exhibited as geometry visible in the charter. Third, it fixes the chart's orientation : the world is a night chart, the Sun below the horizon in the second sign from the Ascendant, with the Moon on the Ascendant — a disposition the tradition read as fitting for a cosmos whose sublunar life is generated, embodied, and fortune-governed before it is illuminated. Later summaries add the planetary joys and further schemes to the diagram's yield; the three yields above are the load-bearing ones, and they are enough to show the kind of object the Thema Mundi is. // AN IMPOSSIBLE CHART, AND WHY THAT IS THE POINT // The Thema Mundi never happened, and cannot have. Mercury is never more than about twenty-eight degrees from the Sun; the charter puts Mercury a full sign — thirty degrees — away, and at the canonical fifteen degrees of Virgo against the Sun's fifteen of Leo the separation is exactly that impossible thirty. Venus's elongation is likewise strained past its limit in strict degree versions. The ancients who taught from the chart were astronomers enough to know this. The Thema Mundi is not a failed observation but a diagram — a mythical charter in the precise sense that its truth is structural, not historical. It tells the student not what the sky once did, but why the rules are shaped as they are. Treating it as a datable event, as some late-antique and many modern popular accounts do, mistakes the genre — the same mistake, in miniature, as treating the Hermetica 's Hermes as a datable author. One further resonance deserves a sentence, because it ties the charter to the synthesis of Section III. The Ascendant at fifteen degrees of Cancer has repeatedly been connected, in modern discussion, with Sothis — Sirius, whose heliacal rising in the Egyptian summer marked the New Year and the coming inundation, and whose sign in the seasonal calendar is Cancer's season. The connection is suggestive and unprovable: the heliacal rising is not a fixed tropical degree across latitudes and centuries, and no surviving ancient text states the link outright. This article records it as what it is — a modern hypothesis that would, if true, set Egypt's oldest time-signal at the very pivot of the Greek world's first chart — and builds nothing on it. V. The Working Apparatus I: Signs, Planets, Sect, and Dignity A Hellenistic chart is a configuration of seven planets — Sun, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, in the descending “Chaldean” order of their spheres — disposed in twelve signs , in twelve places , in aspect to one another, and graded by a battery of conditions. This section takes the first layer: the signs and the planets themselves. Section VI takes the places, aspects, and calculated points. The vocabulary is dense, and it is given here in full because the anchor authors of Sections IX–XI are unintelligible without it — Valens's first book is, in large part, simply this vocabulary written out at handbook length. The Twelve Signs The signs are thirty-degree divisions of the ecliptic, named for the constellations they once roughly matched, and read in the Greek system as bundles of contrary qualities. They are masculine or feminine in alternation from Aries; they are tropical (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn — the signs of the equinoxes and solstices, where the Sun “turns”), solid (Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius), or bicorporeal / double-bodied (Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces); they group by triplicity into the four elemental families — fiery (Aries, Leo, Sagittarius), earthy (Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn), airy (Gemini, Libra, Aquarius), watery (Cancer, Scorpio, Pisces) — and each carries a freight of further predicates in the handbooks: human or bestial, vocal or mute, fruitful or barren, straight-rising or crooked-rising, and the regions of the world and parts of the body assigned to it. Valens's sign chapters (Anthology I.2, in Riley's translation, in paraphrase) show the genre at full stretch: Aries is Mars's house, masculine, tropical, fiery, governing — and also, by its degrees, stormy in its first portion, mild in its middle, plague-bearing in its last, with the lands from Babylon to Egypt parcelled out among its parts. The modern reader should take the density itself as the datum: a sign, for a Hellenistic practitioner, was not a symbol but a dossier. The Seven Planets: Natures and Sects The planets likewise are dossiers, but dossiers with an internal order. Each planet has a nature — a characteristic mode of action, which Ptolemy will ground in the physical qualities (Section XI) and Valens simply catalogues: what the planet signifies in a nativity, from persons and professions to materials, colours, tastes, and the parts of the body it rules. In Riley's translation of Valens I.1, in paraphrase: the Sun indicates kingship, intellect, the father, public reputation, and rules the head, the right eye, and the heart, and among materials gold; the Moon indicates the body, the mother, fortune, voyages, and rules the left eye, the stomach, and the breasts, and among materials silver and glass; Saturn makes its natives, in Valens's unsparing catalogue, care-worn, solitary, downcast, and brings humblings, obstacles, imprisonment, and grief — and also, well placed, great ranks and the management of others' property. The catalogue style is the point: a planet's meaning is a field , and interpretation is the art of narrowing the field by condition and context — the superabundance problem of Section VIII already visible in the raw material. BENEFICS Jupiter and Venus — the greater and lesser benefic — with the Moon generally counted kindly: planets whose tempered, fertile natures (in Ptolemy's physics, their share of the hot and the moist) incline their significations toward increase, union, and preservation. MALEFICS Saturn and Mars — the greater and lesser malefic: planets of excess, Saturn of cold and Mars of dry heat in Ptolemy's grounding, whose significations incline toward separation, damage, and loss. Both handbooks insist the labels are defaults, not destinies: a malefic in good condition, in its own sect, can bestow the greatest positions, and a benefic ill placed reverses — Valens says so in as many words (Anthology I.1, in paraphrase). SECT — HAIRĒSIS, THE PARTY OF THE CHART Every chart is a day chart (Sun above the horizon) or a night chart (Sun below it), and the planets are partisans: Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn belong to the day party; Moon, Venus, and Mars to the night party; Mercury is a turncoat, diurnal when it rises before the Sun, nocturnal when after. A planet in sect — of the chart's ruling party — is a citizen in its own city; a planet out of sect is an exile, and its significations, benefic or malefic, are graded accordingly. Sect is the single most consequential grading in the system, and the first thing a Hellenistic reading establishes. THE COMMON PLANET Mercury stands outside the benefic–malefic and, by its turncoat rule, half outside the sect division: common, convertible, taking the character of its company and condition. Its Valens dossier is correspondingly the longest and most various — letters, accounts, markets, theft, interpretation, and every systematic craft from medicine to divination. Dignity: A Planet at Home, Honoured, or Abroad A planet's power to deliver its significations is graded, above all, by its relation to the sign it stands in — its dignities , a layered system in which the Thema Mundi (Section IV) is the deep charter. By domicile , the planet rules the sign: the Moon in Cancer, Mars in Scorpio, a planet in its own house, disposing of its own resources. By exaltation , the planet is honoured in a particular sign and degree — the Sun in Aries (exalted at 19°), the Moon in Taurus (3°), Jupiter in Cancer (15°), Saturn in Libra (21°), and their opposites as falls — a guest of honour in another's house. By triplicity , the planet shares rule of an elemental family, with day and night rulers distinguished — a grading that carries unusual weight in Dorotheus, where the triplicity lords of the luminary in a nativity are read in sequence for the thirds of a life. And beneath these, two finer gratings — the decans and the terms — divide every sign internally; they are treated with the places and lots in Section VI, where they belong as apparatus. The contrary conditions complete the scheme: a planet in the sign opposite its domicile is in detriment (exile), opposite its exaltation in fall (humiliation) — the vocabulary of honour and disgrace is the tradition's own, and it is social through and through. A Hellenistic chart is a court: seven great persons, each at home, honoured, visiting, or exiled, in party or out of it, beholding or blind to one another. The metaphor is not decoration. It is how the handbooks teach the eye to read. VI. The Working Apparatus II: Places, Aspects, Lots, Decans, and Terms The Twelve Places (Topoi) The places — later tradition's “houses” — are the twelve-fold division of the chart counted from the Ascendant, and in the Hellenistic mainstream they are whole-sign : the entire sign containing the Ascendant degree is the first place, the next sign the second, and so on, with the degree of the Ascendant and the degree of the Midheaven (which may fall in the ninth, tenth, or eleventh sign) retained as sensitive points inside the scheme. Degree-based quadrant divisions of the kind later astrology favours exist at the tradition's margins, but the whole-sign frame is the one Dorotheus, Valens, and the papyrus horoscopes presuppose. Each place is a topic of life, and the set, in Beck's summary table and the handbooks' standard list, runs as follows. Place Later name Topic, in the handbooks' standard sense I — The native: body, life, character, the helm of the chart II Gate of Hades Livelihood, possessions, resources III Goddess Siblings, kin, short journeys, the Moon's joy IV Subterranean Parents, home, property, endings, Saturn's region below V Good Fortune Children, pleasures, Venus's joy VI Bad Fortune Illness, injury, labour, Mars's joy VII Setting Spouse, partners, opponents — the other party VIII Idle Place Death, inheritances, others' goods IX God Travel, divination, religion, the Sun's joy X Midheaven Action, profession, rank — what the native does XI Good Spirit Friends, hopes, patrons, Jupiter's joy XII Bad Spirit Enemies, suffering, confinement, Saturn's joy Two structural rules give the table its dynamics. The four angles or centres — the places anchored to Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and subterranean point (I, X, VII, IV in sign terms, with the pivots falling where they fall) — are the chart's strong places, where planets act with full force; the places cadent from the angles (III, VI, IX, XII) are weak, their planets fallen away from power; and the succedent places (II, V, VIII, XI) stand between. And the places are further graded by their aspect to the Ascendant (below): the places that behold the first — III, IV, V, VII, IX, X, XI by the whole-sign aspects — are operative, while II, VI, VIII, and XII, which stand in aversion to it, are the chart's dark rooms, their topics harder for the native to command. The reader will note that the tradition's bleakest topics — illness, death's place, enemies — cluster precisely in the averted places. The geometry is the doctrine. Aspects: Beholding and Aversion Planets and signs relate by aspect — literally, by seeing . The recognised configurations, reckoned by sign and refined by degree, are: conjunction (same sign, bodily presence); sextile (two signs apart, 60°); square (three apart, 90°); trine (four apart, 120°); and opposition (six apart, 180°, diameter). Signs one or five apart — 30° and 150° — stand in aversion : they do not behold each other, and planets so placed are, in the vivid technical vocabulary, blind to one another, unable to witness, assist, or restrain. Around this simple scheme the handbooks build a refined optics: planets apply and separate, cast rays, stand in superior or inferior aspect (the planet earlier in zodiacal order “overcomes” the later), are contained, besieged, or attended — Valens's term is doryphory , spear-bearing, for the planets that attend a luminary as a king's guard attends the king. The valuation of the aspects themselves — trine and sextile harmonious, square and opposition harsh — is, as Section IV showed, read off the Thema Mundi; and their elemental logic reinforces it, trines joining signs of one triplicity, squares and oppositions joining signs at cross-purposes of quality. Ptolemy, characteristically, keeps the geometry and discards much of the optics (Section XI). The Lots (Klēroi) The lots are calculated points — not bodies, not stars, but places on the zodiac derived by formula from the chart's own factors, each assigned a topic. The scheme's charter idea is projection: take the arc between two factors, and lay it off from a third. The two great lots govern the system's division of a human being. The Lot of Fortune (Greek Tychē ) — by day, the arc from Sun to Moon laid off from the Ascendant; by night, the reverse arc — belongs to the Moon, the body, and everything that befalls a person: health, material circumstance, the given. The Lot of Spirit (Greek Daimōn ) — the complementary arc, by day from Moon to Sun — belongs to the Sun, the mind, and everything a person does : intention, action, career. Around these the tradition multiplies lots for the topics of a life — of Eros and of Necessity, of the father, the mother, siblings, marriage, children, debt, accusation, and dozens more; the standard early scheme counts seven lots, Fortune's the most important, as Beck notes in his appendix on the subject, worked from a real papyrus

Later Readings, and a Note on the Alchemical One XXV. Sources I. A Cycle That Had to Be Made Every schoolchild can be taught to recite them, and that is precisely the fact that needs explaining. The twelve labours of Heracles — Greek Hēraklēs , Roman Hercules — present themselves to a modern reader as a single, ancient, self-evident list: lion, hydra, hind, boar, stables, birds, bull, mares, girdle, cattle, apples, Cerberus. The list feels as if it must always have existed, in that order, since the Bronze Age. It did not. The labours began as separate local stories , attached to separate places — a lion troubling Nemea, a water-serpent in the marsh at Lerna a few miles away, a boar on an Arcadian mountain, a cattle-king in Elis — each story intelligible on its own, each claiming Heracles for a landscape that wanted a Heracles story of its own. Heracles was the most portable of Greek heroes: because he had wandered everywhere in the course of his service, any community could plausibly locate an episode in its own territory, and a great many did. The cycle is what happened when that scattered, competitive, ever-growing material was at last gathered, counted, and closed. The Greek word matters. A labour is an athlos (plural athloi ): not work in the sense of employment, but a contest — an ordeal undertaken for a prize, the word from which athlete descends and which belongs to the vocabulary of the games. Emma Stafford, in the study of Heracles on which this article draws throughout, makes the point that the term underlines Heracles' character as the athlete par excellence : his service is imagined not as drudgery but as a series of prize-contests, each with its own rules, its own conditions of victory, and — crucially, as Sections VIII and XI show — its own possibility of being disallowed , like a result struck from the record by a judge. The collective name for the twelve, dōdekathlos (“the twelve-contest”), is itself a later convenience: Stafford notes that the word was not used in antiquity for the set, however ancient the set became. Even the cycle's title is an editorial act. Three layers must be kept apart throughout this article, and the hub's method requires them to be named whenever they threaten to blur. First, the myth as told : the stories themselves, in the versions given by named ancient authors — Homer and Hesiod mentioning individual feats in passing, Euripides listing a divergent set in a choral ode, Diodorus Siculus narrating a full career in the first century BCE, and the mythographer conventionally called Apollodorus giving, in the first or second century CE, the ordered prose account that has become the standard. Second, the cultic and historical footing : what can be said from sanctuaries, sculpture, inscriptions, and historians about Heracles as an object of worship — the metopes at Olympia, the dual cult Herodotus describes at Thasos, the festivals and gymnasia of Section XXIII. A story about Heracles is not evidence for his cult, and his cult is not evidence for any story. Third, the later allegorical reading : the interpretations imposed on the finished cycle by moralists, Stoics, Neoplatonists, and eventually alchemists, who read the twelve as a map of the soul's or the Work's progress. That third layer is real history — the history of reception — but it is not what the stories originally meant, and this article confines it to Section XXIV and to the companion treatment in Alchemical Allegory , keeping the labours themselves in their own terms. THE CYCLE AT A GLANCE Twelve athloi performed in the service of Eurystheus, king of Tiryns and Mycenae. In Apollodorus' account ten were commanded; two of the ten were disallowed; two more were imposed; twelve were performed. The first six belong to the Peloponnese; the last six carry Heracles to Crete, Thrace, the Black Sea, the far west, and finally under the earth. THE ORDER USED HERE This article follows Apollodorus, Library 2.5 , in J. G. Frazer's Loeb translation — the order modern retellings standardly use. Where Diodorus, Euripides, Hyginus, or the Olympia metopes order or select differently, the difference is stated in place, not silently harmonised. THE EARLIEST COMPLETE SET Not a poem but a building: the twelve metopes of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, c. 470–457 BCE, six over each porch. Section III examines what that fixes — the number, and a membership — and what it does not: a narrative order, and any text. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted: Frazer's Apollodorus, C. H. Oldfather's Diodorus, the Pausanias text as given in the Perseus Digital Library, and A. D. Godley's Herodotus. Everything else rendering an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. A word on the hero himself, since the cycle cannot be understood without the oddity of its performer. Heracles is the son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene (Greek Alkmēnē ), wife of Amphitryon, and a descendant through both parents of Perseus. His name is usually analysed as “glory of Hera” ( Hēra + kleos ) — an irony the tradition exploits relentlessly, since Hera is his persecutor from before his birth to the pyre, and since one strand of the tradition, preserved in Diodorus (4.10.1, paraphrased in Section IV), explains the name by the glory he won precisely through the serpents Hera sent to kill him. He was born, in the name he first bore, Alcides ( Alkeidēs ), after his grandfather Alcaeus; Apollodorus (2.4.12) reports that the Pythian priestess at Delphi first called him Heracles at the moment she assigned him his service. For the wider institutions within which he sits — hero cult at the tomb, epic fame in song, and the unique doubleness of a hero worshipped also as a god — see this hub's Heroes and Epic , whose Sections IV–V treat Heracles in brief; the present article is the full treatment of the labours themselves, and the two are written to be read together without duplication of their central arguments. II. The Sources and Their Orders No single ancient author is the source for the twelve labours. What survives is a shelf of partial witnesses, spread over a thousand years, which agree on a core and disagree — instructively — on order, membership, and framing. An honest account of the cycle is therefore an account of its witnesses first. The Early Witnesses: Episodes Without a List The Iliad knows Heracles as a figure of the generation before the Trojan War, already dead, already the type of the suffering hero: it knows his servitude to Eurystheus, imposed through Hera's trickery over his birth (19.95–133), it knows Eurystheus sending him to fetch the hound of Hades (8.362–369), and it knows that even Heracles, dearest of men to Zeus, could not escape death (18.117–119). It lists nothing. Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) knows more episodes, but knows them as genealogy : the labours enter the poem where their victims belong in the family tree of monsters. So the cattle of Geryon appear at lines 287–293, in the line of Phorcys and Ceto; Cerberus at 310–312, the Hydra of Lerna — reared by Hera in her anger and killed by Heracles with the help of Iolaus — at 313–318; and the Nemean lion, offspring of Echidna, reared by Hera and settled in the hills of Nemea as a plague to men, at 327–332, all paraphrased from the Evelyn-White translation used in this hub's Theogony article. The pseudo-Hesiodic Shield of Heracles and the fragmentary Catalogue of Women add further episodes. The pattern is constant: in the earliest surviving literature the labours exist, severally and vividly, and the cycle does not. Lyric and drama filled individual episodes out into whole works. Stesichorus of Himera (early sixth century BCE) composed a Geryoneis — a substantial lyric poem on the Geryon labour alone, fragments of which survive on papyrus and show the monster given a voice, a mother, and a pathos no summary preserves. Pindar and Bacchylides touch labours in passing, as exempla. A fragment of Pindar has even been thought to preserve part of the word (dōd)ekatos , “twelfth”, in a Heracles context — Stafford reports the suggestion and its fragility together: only part of the word survives, and a possible reference is not a canon. Antiquity itself credited the gathering of the labours into one poem to the lost epic Heraclea of Peisander of Rhodes , dated variously to the seventh or sixth century BCE. That Peisander wrote a Heraclea in at least two books, that later writers treated him as the poet who fixed Heracles' familiar equipment of club and lionskin, and that a tradition made him the first to number the labours at twelve, are all attested claims about a lost poem. The poem is gone; its contents cannot be checked; and this archive records the attribution as an ancient attribution, not as a fact about what Peisander's text contained. Euripides' Chorus: A List That Is Not the List The most instructive divergent witness is also one of the most beautiful. In Euripides' Heracles (c. 416 BCE), while the hero is believed lost in Hades, the chorus of old Thebans sings his deeds as a kind of funeral eulogy in advance (lines 359–424 in the usual numeration; the ode is also cited as 348–441). Read in the translation hosted by the Center for Hellenic Studies and in the excerpts collected in Timothy Gantz's Early Greek Myth source-chapters, the ode runs, in paraphrase: first, the lion, whose skin he wears; then — where Apollodorus will put the Hydra — the Centaurs , shot down with his bow; then the golden-horned hind ; then the mares of Diomedes ; then Cycnus , the guest-murdering son of Ares, killed by the river Anaurus; then the Hesperides , the slain dragon, the calming of the sea, and the bearing of the heavens for Atlas , treated as a sequence of its own; then the expedition against the Amazons for the queen's girdle; then, only now, the Hydra , burned and its venom taken for his arrows, coupled with Geryon ; and last, as the play's own action requires, the descent for Cerberus , from which the chorus fears he will not return. Of the canonical twelve, the boar, the stables, the birds, and the Cretan bull are absent altogether; three parerga — the Centaurs, Cycnus, and the sea-calming — stand in their place; and the Hesperides labour is split in two around them. A modern scholarly summary of the ode counts twelve deeds , of which eight are canonical labours. Euripides, writing two generations after the Olympia metopes had carved a twelve, still felt free to compose a different twelve for the stage — because his list is not a catalogue but a song, shaped to a dramatic moment, and because the canon, even then, bound sculptors more tightly than it bound poets. Diodorus: The Full Career, Rationalised The first surviving continuous prose account of the whole career is Diodorus Siculus, Library of History Book 4 (first century BCE), read for this article in C. H. Oldfather's Loeb translation. Diodorus opens with a remarkable methodological apology (4.8, paraphrased): myth should not be scrutinised with the same sharp eye as contemporary events; audiences applaud Centaurs and three-bodied Geryon in the theatre though persuaded no such beings existed; and Heracles, who “brought under cultivation the inhabited world” by his labours, deserves to have his benefactions remembered rather than picked apart. The apology announces the treatment. Diodorus' Heracles is a civilising benefactor on a world tour: his labours are interleaved with the founding of cities, the draining of marshes, the clearing of beasts from Crete and Libya, the making of roads over the Alps, and the punishment of lawless rulers — a euhemerising, almost historical progress, in which the cattle-raid on Geryon becomes a full military expedition with an army, a fleet, and campaigns in Iberia, Celtica, and Italy on the way home (4.17–24, paraphrased). Diodorus' order differs from Apollodorus' at three paired points, and the differences are most clearly shown in the table in this section. His third labour is the boar and his fourth the hind , where Apollodorus has hind third and boar fourth. His fifth is the birds and his sixth the stables , where Apollodorus has stables fifth and birds sixth. And at the end the swap is structural: Diodorus makes Cerberus the eleventh labour (4.25–26) and the apples of the Hesperides the twelfth and last (4.26–27), where Apollodorus ends with Cerberus. Diodorus also differs in substance at points the table cannot show. His Heracles undertakes the service under a bargain struck before his birth (Section IV); his madness comes after Zeus has already ordered the service and Heracles has refused the first summons (4.10.6–4.11.1, paraphrased); he does not operate Apollodorus' disqualification arithmetic — the Hydra and the stables are not struck from his count, and the twelve are twelve from the outset, not ten-plus-two; his Augeas labour is commanded to be done without the help of any other man and carries no wage bargain (4.13.3); his Diomedes is fed to his own mares by Heracles directly (4.15.3–4); and his Hippolyta labour ends not with a queen killed through Hera's rumour but with a full Amazon battle, a list of named Amazon champions, and Melanippe ransoming herself with the girdle (4.16, paraphrased). Neither account is a corruption of the other. They are two late, learned reconciliations of a tradition that had never been single. Apollodorus: The Standard Order and Its Status The account modern retellings follow is the Library ( Bibliothēkē ) attributed to Apollodorus — in current scholarly usage, Pseudo-Apollodorus, since the work, a systematic prose handbook of Greek myth in three books and an epitome, is now generally dated to the first or second century CE and cannot be by Apollodorus of Athens, the second-century BCE scholar whose name it carries. Its Heracles narrative runs from 2.4.8 to 2.7.8, and the labours occupy 2.5.1–2.5.12 : one numbered section per labour, in the order this article follows. Apollodorus' virtues are compression and completeness: he gives variants where he knows them (“Acusilaus says… but some say…”), names the authorities embedded in his narrative, and preserves, inside the story, the disqualification mechanism that explains the number twelve (Section VI). His order became the standard not because it is the oldest — it is among the latest of our witnesses — but because his handbook survived entire and was mined by everyone after him. Hyginus, in the Latin Fabulae 30 (attributed to a writer of the Roman imperial period), gives a bare list of the same twelve with the boar and hind, and birds and stables, swapped in the manner the table shows — a reminder that even list-makers working from the finished canon did not agree on its internal sequence. # Apollodorus, Library 2.5 Diodorus, Library of History 4.11–27 Hyginus, Fabulae 30 (summary list) 1 Nemean lion Nemean lion Nemean lion 2 Lernaean Hydra Lernaean Hydra Lernaean Hydra 3 Ceryneian hind Erymanthian boar Erymanthian boar 4 Erymanthian boar Ceryneian hind Ceryneian hind 5 Augean stables Stymphalian birds Stymphalian birds 6 Stymphalian birds Augean stables Augean stables 7 Cretan bull Cretan bull Cretan bull 8 Mares of Diomedes Mares of Diomedes Mares of Diomedes 9 Girdle of Hippolyta Girdle of Hippolyta Girdle of Hippolyta 10 Cattle of Geryon Cattle of Geryon Cattle of Geryon 11 Apples of the Hesperides Cerberus Apples of the Hesperides 12 Cerberus Apples of the Hesperides Cerberus The table is the argument of this section in miniature. Membership is stable across the prose witnesses — the same twelve feats, a canon already centuries old when they wrote. Sequence is not stable: three independent swaps separate Diodorus from Apollodorus, and Hyginus agrees with Diodorus on the first two swaps and with Apollodorus on the last. Any retelling that presents the order of the labours without naming its source is therefore presenting one ancient editor's decision as if it were the myth itself. This article names its source — Apollodorus — and flags the variants where they matter. III. Olympia: All Twelve in Stone, c. 460 BCE The earliest surviving complete set of twelve is not a text at all. The Temple of Zeus at Olympia — the great Doric temple of the Panhellenic sanctuary in Elis, built c. 470–457 BCE in the decades after the Persian Wars — carried, above the porches at either end of its inner building, twelve carved metopes , the square relief panels of the Doric frieze: six over the east porch, six over the west, one labour to a panel. Heracles was the inevitable subject. Olympia was his sanctuary in a special sense: tradition made him the founder of the Olympic Games (Diodorus 4.14 gives him the founding as an interlude in the labours themselves, after the Cretan bull), the labours were athloi — contests — in the home of contests, and the temple of his father Zeus was the natural frame for the son's ordeals. The metopes survive, fragmentary but substantially recoverable, divided between the Archaeological Museum at Olympia and the Louvre; their subjects are identified by the surviving sculpture itself and by the description of the traveller Pausanias, who saw them in place in the second century CE. “Most of the labours of Heracles are represented at Olympia. Above the doors of the temple is carved the hunting of the Arcadian boar, his exploit against Diomedes the Thracian, and that against Geryones at Erytheia; he is also about to receive the burden of Atlas, and he cleanses the land from dung for the Eleans. Above the doors of the rear chamber he is taking the girdle from the Amazon; and there are the affairs of the deer, of the bull at Cnossus, of the Stymphalian birds, of the hydra, and of the Argive lion.” — PAUSANIAS, DESCRIPTION OF GREECE 5.10.9, AS GIVEN IN THE PERSEUS TEXT Pausanias' sentence is the key document, and it repays the close reading the Perseus Digital Library's entry on the Olympia metopes gives it. He names eleven labours. Cerberus — which the findspots and the surviving fragments show did occupy a panel — is missing from his list, an inadvertent omission in an otherwise careful inventory. He lists the porches in the order he viewed them, not in narrative order. Reconstructing a reading order for the twelve is therefore a scholarly construction, and it has been constructed in more than one way. Read as a visitor approaching and entering would encounter them — west porch first, each porch left to right — the sequence runs: Nemean lion, Hydra, Stymphalian birds, Cretan bull, Ceryneian hind, Amazon's girdle; Erymanthian boar, mares of Diomedes, Geryon, Hesperides (Atlas with the apples), Cerberus, Augean stables . That reconstruction, associated with Martin Robertson's argument from the findspots, gives a satisfying frame — lion first, as everywhere; the local Elean labour, the stables, last, as a capstone in the sanctuary's own territory — and the Oxford Handbook of Heracles' survey of the lists reports the suggestion, credited to Boardman and Gantz, that the stables' anomalous last place reflects exactly that local pride: Elis honouring its own labour at the climax. But the same survey lists the metopes' order with the stables twelfth precisely as a deviation from every literary list, and other arrangements of the panels have been defended, including a rearrangement after earthquake damage. The honest summary is: the membership is certain, the count is certain, the original reading order is argued . What, then, do the metopes fix? They fix the number. By about 460 BCE, at the most Panhellenic address in Greece, the labours were publicly and monumentally twelve — not ten, not an open series. They fix a membership : the twelve panels are the twelve of the later canon, the same feats Apollodorus and Diodorus and Hyginus list, with no Centaurs, no Cycnus, no Antaeus among them — the side-feats are already, in stone, side -feats. They fix an iconography : Athena appears as Heracles' divine helper in several panels — with the birds, with the stables, at the Hesperides — a visual theology of assisted labour that the texts distribute more sparingly; and the Heracles of the metopes is notably weary in places, a labouring, burdened figure — seated, resting, receiving the apples from Atlas with Athena's support — rather than a triumphant strongman, an interpretation in marble of what an athlos costs. And they fix a terminus : whatever Peisander may or may not have done two centuries earlier, the canon demonstrably exists, complete, by the middle of the fifth century BCE. What they do not fix is equally important. They do not fix a narrative: a metope shows a moment, not a story, and several panels — the hind, the bull — are unintelligible as narrative without a text or a guide, as Pausanias' own glosses show he understood. They do not fix the order in which the labours were performed , since their arrangement answers to architecture and to a visitor's path, not to chronology — the stables last at Olympia are first-six in every text. They do not fix the frame: nothing at Olympia tells a viewer why Heracles labours, whether for purification, by Zeus's bargain, or in Euripides' bleaker sequence. And they do not prove that the canon was created by the temple. Stafford's formulation, reported in Heroes and Epic and followed here, is that the Olympia metopes are the first clear instance of the collection of twelve, and that it has been suggested the number was in part dictated by the twelve spaces the architecture offered — six and six. That suggestion cuts both ways, and should be allowed to: a temple needing twelve panels would canonise a twelve; a tradition already counting twelve would give a temple its programme. The evidence shows the two in place together around 460 BCE and cannot, by itself, say which summoned the other. // THE HEPAISTEION COMPARISON // A generation later, the Temple of Hephaestus at Athens (c. 450 BCE) carved Heracles again — but only nine labours, in its own order (lion, Hydra, hind, boar, mares, Cerberus, Amazons, Geryon across two panels, Hesperides), as the Oxford Handbook's list-survey records. Even after Olympia, a major temple could select rather than recite. The canon was available; it was not yet a straitjacket. One further witness belongs in this section because it is stone's contemporary and shows the canon still molten. Sophocles' Trachiniae ( Women of Trachis , date debated within the fifth century) has Heracles, in agony, address his own arms and recall what they subdued (1089–1100, paraphrased from the excerpts in Gantz): the Nemean lion, the Lernaean Hydra, the army of Centaurs, the Erymanthian beast, the three-headed hound of Hades underground, and the dragon that guarded the golden fruit at the ends of the earth. Five labours and a parergon , chosen for a dying man's retrospect, in no canonical order. Tragedy, lyric, and prose each kept their own Heracles long after the sculptors of Olympia had agreed on twelve panels. The canon was a fact about the tradition; it was never a law over it. IV. The Frame: Hera, the Delayed Birth, and Eurystheus First The labours have a master, and the master has a grievance written into the order of births. The frame story, in its fullest form at Apollodorus 2.4.8–2.4.12 and Diodorus 4.9, is this. Zeus lay with Alcmene in the likeness of her absent husband Amphitryon — Diodorus (4.9.2–3, paraphrased) adds that Zeus prolonged the night to three times its length, and insists, in his rationalising manner, that the union was for the sake of begetting a benefactor, not from desire. Alcmene bore twins of different fathers: Iphicles , Amphitryon's son, and Heracles , Zeus's. But before the birth Zeus had announced among the gods — in the Iliad 's telling (19.95–133), in answer to Hera's prompting of a boast he could not retract — that the descendant of Perseus born that day would rule over his neighbours. Hera, who hated the child of her husband's infidelity before he existed, hastened to Argos, delayed Alcmene's labour by binding the birth-goddesses, the Eileithyiae, and brought Eurystheus , son of Sthenelus and grandson of Perseus, into the world first — a seven-month child, Apollodorus says (2.4.5, paraphrased). Zeus's word stood. The weaker cousin was king of Tiryns and Mycenae by divine pronouncement; the stronger was, by the same pronouncement, born to be ruled by him. The whole servitude is contained in that delivery room: the labours are what happens when cosmic precedence is settled by a trick of timing. Diodorus gives the frame a contractual form that Apollodorus does not (4.9.5, paraphrased): Zeus, outmanoeuvred but unwilling either to break his word or to abandon Heracles, persuaded Hera to agree that Eurystheus should indeed be king, but that Heracles, after serving him and performing twelve labours of Eurystheus' prescribing, should receive the gift of immortality. In Diodorus, therefore, the number is twelve from before the hero's birth, the service is a bargain between gods, and immortality is its stated prize from the start. In Apollodorus, by contrast, the oracle will speak of ten labours and twelve years (2.4.12), and the twelve of the finished cycle will be produced by Eurystheus' disqualifications, inside history, by a king's spite. The two frames cannot both be the tradition's single original; they are two different explanations of the same finished fact — that there were twelve, and that they ended in godhead — one theological and prospective, the other legalistic and retrospective. This article reports both, in their places, and builds its narrative on Apollodorus' frame while flagging Diodorus' at every point where they diverge. The infant's first ordeal came at eight months, or in some tellings sooner. Hera sent two serpents into the twins' cradle; Iphicles screamed, and Heracles — so Apollodorus 2.4.8 and Diodorus 4.10.1, paraphrased — seized a serpent in each hand and strangled them, and was found in the morning holding the dead snakes. The scene is among the most painted in all Greek art, and its function in the frame is precise: the persecution that will drive the man begins with the child, and the child's answer to it — bare hands, no weapon, a grip that does not relax — is the template of the first labour and the last. Diodorus (4.10.1) adds his etymology: the Argives, learning what had happened, named the boy Heracles because he had gained kleos , glory, through Hera — the persecutor unwillingly supplying both the trials and the name they glorified. Other traditions make the naming Delphic (Apollodorus 2.4.12) or an attempted propitiation of Hera. The sources disagree about the name as they disagree about so much else; they agree that the name and the hatred belong together. Grown, Heracles was educated — Apollodorus (2.4.9, paraphrased) lists his teachers and the gifts of the gods, a sword from Hermes, bow and arrows from Apollo, a golden breastplate from Hephaestus, a robe from Athena, and the club he cut for himself — and he first made his name in war, not in service. The Minyans of Orchomenus exacted a yearly tribute of a hundred cattle from Thebes for the killing of their king Clymenus; Heracles mutilated the tribute-collectors when they came, defeated the Minyan army, killed their king Erginus, and imposed a double tribute in reverse (Apollodorus 2.4.11; Diodorus 4.10.3–5, paraphrased). Creon, king of Thebes, gave him his eldest daughter Megara in marriage as a prize of valour. Heracles had a wife, three sons by her — Therimachus, Creontiades, and Deicoon in Apollodorus' naming — a city grateful to him, and a reputation without equal in Greece. It is at exactly this point, with everything to lose, that the frame closes on him. How it closes is the subject of the next section, and it is the point on which the tradition most consequentially disagrees with itself. BEFORE THE BIRTH ZEUS'S PRONOUNCEMENT The Perseid born that day shall rule. Hera hears it, and acts on it ( Iliad 19.95–133; Apollodorus 2.4.8; Diodorus 4.9.4). THE BIRTH EURYSTHEUS FIRST Alcmene's labour delayed; Eurystheus, a seven-month child, born first and king by the word of Zeus. Twins born to Alcmene: Iphicles and Heracles. INFANCY THE SERPENTS Hera's two snakes strangled in the cradle, one in each hand — the hero's method, announced before he could speak. YOUNG MANHOOD THE MINYAN WAR AND MEGARA Thebes freed from the Minyan tribute; Erginus killed; marriage to Megara, Creon's daughter; three sons. The life the madness will destroy is complete. V. The Madness and the Chronology Problem In the standard account — the account this hub's Heroes and Epic summarises, and the one Apollodorus and Diodorus both, in their different ways, presuppose — the sequence is: madness first, labours after, as expiation. Hera sent a madness ( lyssa ) upon Heracles. In Apollodorus (2.4.12, paraphrased) he flung his own children by Megara, and two children of Iphicles, into the fire; Megara herself survives in this version, to be given in marriage to Iolaus after the labours (2.6.1). In Diodorus (4.11.1–2, paraphrased) he tried first to kill Iolaus, who escaped, and shot his children with his bow, believing them enemies; on recovering, he recognised “the mistake he had made through a misapprehension” — the historian's careful phrasing is reported here as paraphrase of Oldfather's rendering — grieved, shunned company, and at last resolved to undergo the dangers. Condemning himself to exile, the Apollodoran Heracles was purified by Thespius and went to Delphi to ask where he should dwell. The labours, on this construction, are a sentence and a purification: the service is what a polluted man owes, and its completion is what makes him clean — and, the oracle adds, immortal. Euripides reverses it. In the Heracles (c. 416 BCE) the labours are already complete when the play begins. Heracles has been absent on the last of them, the descent for Cerberus; in his absence the usurper Lycus has seized Thebes, killed Creon, and marked Megara, the children, and old Amphitryon for death. Heracles returns — with Cerberus still in tow, a stage property of appalling casualness — rescues his family, and kills Lycus. Then , at the summit of the completed career, Hera acts: Iris and Lyssa, Madness personified, appear above the house, and Lyssa — in one of the most extraordinary scenes in Greek tragedy — protests : she recites Heracles' services to gods and men, the monsters cleared from land and sea, and declares she does not wish to drive this man mad. Iris, speaking for Hera, overrules her. Lyssa obeys against her will, and Heracles, in the madness, believing he is assaulting the house of Eurystheus, kills Megara and all three children . He wakes bound to a pillar, amid the bodies, to Amphitryon's telling. What follows — his resolve to live rather than die, Theseus' arrival and offer of purification and a home in Athens, the famous exchange in which Heracles rejects the poets' tales of gods' adulteries and chains as unworthy of belief even as he submits to necessity — is tragedy's deepest exploration of the hero. But for the historian of the cycle, the play's first fact is its chronology: the crime the labours were supposed to expiate has not yet happened when the labours end . The service, in Euripides, cannot be a penance. It is undertaken, the play's background suggests, under a prior obligation to Eurystheus unconnected with blood-guilt — and the madness is not its cause but its ghastly sequel, Hera's answer to a completed success. // THE CHRONOLOGY PROBLEM, STATED HONESTLY // The two sequences are irreconcilable, and no ancient source reconciles them. Apollodorus and Diodorus: madness → purification → Delphi → service as expiation. Euripides: service → return in triumph → madness → a second, unexpiated catastrophe answered not by further labours but by Theseus' friendship and the decision to endure. Which is older cannot be demonstrated from surviving evidence: Euripides is by centuries the earlier surviving author, but he was famous in antiquity for innovating against received myth, and a tragedian's reversal is exactly the kind of stroke his audience was trained to notice. The scholia and later critics already debated such Euripidean innovations. This article follows the Apollodoran sequence for its narrative, because the article's subject is the cycle as a cycle — and flags, here and in Section XXII, that the Euripidean sequence exists, is earlier in survival, and makes a different and arguably darker sense: that the labours purchase nothing, and Hera's hatred is not a debt to be discharged but a condition of the hero's existence. Euripides returned to the family in the Heracleidae ( Children of Heracles , usually dated c. 430 BCE, though dates into the 420s have been argued). There Heracles is already dead, and the persecution has descended a generation: Eurystheus, through his herald Copreus — the same herald who conveys the labours' commands in Apollodorus — demands that Athens surrender the hero's children, who have fled from city to city with Iolaus, now an old man, and with Alcmene.
