Two Families Under One Name: Philosophical and Technical Hermetica This article belongs to the Alchemy wing of the Greco-Roman hub, but it is not, strictly speaking, an article about alchemy. It is the wing's philosophical sibling. The alchemical texts treated elsewhere in this hub — above all in the article on Zosimos of Panopolis — were written in the same cities, in the same centuries, and under the same presiding name as the texts treated here: Hermes Trismegistus , Hermes the Thrice-Greatest. To understand why a furnace manual and a dialogue about the divine Mind could both be ascribed to Hermes, the reader first needs the distinction on which all modern scholarship of the subject rests. Writings ascribed to Hermes fall, in the conventional scholarly division, into two families. The philosophical Hermetica are religious and philosophical treatises — dialogues, discourses, hymns, and prayers — concerned with God, the making of the cosmos, the nature and fate of the human soul, and the knowledge ( gnōsis ) by which the soul finds its way back to its source. The technical Hermetica are practical works: astrological treatises and catalogues, alchemical recipes and allegories, magical procedures, and writings on the hidden properties of plants, stones, and animals. The Cyranides , the astrological works that circulated under Hermes' name from the Hellenistic period onward, and a large body of alchemical pseudepigrapha all belong to the second family. The division is a modern filing system, not an ancient wall. Garth Fowden, in The Egyptian Hermes (1986), argued persuasively that both families are best understood as responses to a single milieu — the complex Greco-Egyptian culture of Ptolemaic, Roman, and early Christian Egypt — and later scholarship has repeatedly noted that the two kinds of text shared readers, copyists, and assumptions. A reader who copied a philosophical dialogue about rebirth might also copy an astrological catalogue; the alchemist Zosimos, writing around 300 CE, appears to quote or echo the philosophical treatises even as he writes about apparatus and operations. The families are distinguished here because their histories differ — the philosophical treatises have a datable Greek manuscript tradition, a famous Renaissance translation, and a famous scholarly redating, and that history is this article's subject — not because ancient readers kept them in separate rooms. THE PHILOSOPHICAL HERMETICA The Corpus Hermeticum; the Latin Asclepius; the Hermetic excerpts preserved by Stobaeus, including the Kore Kosmou; the Vienna fragments; the Armenian Definitions; and the three Coptic Hermetica of Nag Hammadi Codex VI. Theology, cosmology, anthropology, and the way of knowledge and rebirth. THE TECHNICAL HERMETICA Astrological, alchemical, magical, and medical writings under Hermes' name, some of them older than the philosophical treatises — astrological Hermetica may reach back to the second or third century BCE. Practical in aim: elections, remedies, operations, and the sympathies of things. The technical family has its own article in this hub: The Technical Hermetica treats the Kyranides , Hermetic astrology and iatromathematics, and the alchemical writings under Hermes' name. This article keeps the philosophical family. A note on method, because this subject attracts invention as few others do. No direct quotation from a Hermetic treatise is given in this article unless it is explicitly attributed. In practice, the article paraphrases throughout, and every paraphrase of a treatise's contents is labelled as paraphrase in the text or follows the standard modern account in Brian P. Copenhaver's Hermetica (Cambridge, 1992) — the Greek Corpus Hermeticum and the Latin Asclepius in a new English translation, with notes and introduction — which is the backbone translation and scholarly introduction for everything that follows. Where a famous phrase is discussed, it is discussed as a phrase, not smuggled in as a quotation. Readers who want the treatises' own words should go to Copenhaver; this article's job is the texts' identity, date, and afterlife. // THE EGYPTIAN SIDE, ELSEWHERE // The Egyptology division of this archive treats the same literature from the Egyptian end: see its Corpus Hermeticum article for the treatises read inside an Egyptian frame, and its Hermeticism article for the wider tradition. This article complements rather than repeats them: its centre of gravity is the Greek textual tradition, the dating question, and the European reception. One further framing point. The Hermetica are routinely described, in popular writing, as “ancient Egyptian wisdom”. That description is itself a historical artefact — it is what late-antique, medieval, and Renaissance readers believed, and the belief had enormous consequences — but it is not what the evidence supports about the texts' composition. The treatises were composed in Greek , in Roman Egypt , in the second and third centuries CE . Holding both facts at once — what the texts are, and what they were taken to be — is the whole discipline of this article, and Sections V, XII, and XIII return to the tension between them from three directions. II. What the Corpus Hermeticum Is The Corpus Hermeticum (conventionally abbreviated CH) is a collection of seventeen short Greek treatises ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus. The name is slightly misleading, and Copenhaver's introduction is among the many scholarly accounts that say so: corpus normally suggests the whole body of an author's surviving work, whereas this collection is a small selection from a much larger Hermetic literature, most of it lost. The individual treatises were quoted by authors from the second and third centuries onward; the collection as a collection is first attested much later, in the writings of the Byzantine philosopher Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), and it was Byzantine editors who gathered the treatises into the form in which the Renaissance would receive them. The Numbering, Stated Accurately Modern editions number the treatises I–XVIII , but there are seventeen of them, because number XV is vacant . The gap is an artefact of early-modern editing, not a lost or suppressed book: an early printed edition placed extraneous material — excerpts drawn from Stobaeus and other sources — at that point in the sequence, and later editors removed it while leaving the surrounding numbers undisturbed. The collection therefore runs I–XIV and then XVI–XVIII. Any account that treats “the missing Book XV” as a mystery to be explained by concealment has mistaken a printer's and editor's accident for a fact about antiquity. The treatises are not chapters of one book. They differ in length, form, speaker, and — as Section VII sets out — in doctrine. Most are dialogues or discourses in which Hermes instructs a disciple: his “son” Tat (whose name derives, by a Greek route, from Thoth himself), Asclepius (the Greek name under which the deified Egyptian sage Imhotep was known), or King Ammon (the god Amun in human, royal form). One treatise is spoken by Mind ( Nous ) to Hermes; one is a letter; one, the last, is a panegyric of kings in which Hermes does not appear at all. The standard critical Greek text is the Budé edition prepared by A. D. Nock and A.-J. Festugière (four volumes, 1945–1954), on which Copenhaver's English translation rests. No. Usual short title or description Form and speakers I Poimandrēs Visionary revelation: Poimandrēs, the divine Mind, instructs the narrator II To Asclepius Discourse on motion, place, and God; Hermes and Asclepius III The Sacred Discourse Brief creation account in Hermes' voice IV The Mixing Bowl (Krater), or the Monad Hermes to Tat: the bowl of Mind sent down for human immersion V That God Is Invisible and Entirely Visible Hermes to Tat VI That the Good Is in God Alone Addressed to Asclepius VII That Ignorance of God Is the Greatest Evil Short sermon-like exhortation VIII That Nothing That Is Is Destroyed Hermes to Tat, on change and so-called destruction IX On Understanding and Sensation Hermes to Asclepius X The Key Hermes to Tat: a compact overview of the teaching XI Mind to Hermes Nous itself instructs Hermes XII On the Mind Shared in Common Hermes to Tat XIII On Rebirth (Palingenesia) Secret dialogue on a mountain: Hermes leads Tat through rebirth XIV To Asclepius: Health of Mind A letter from Hermes to Asclepius XV — vacant — No treatise: an early-modern editorial insertion, later removed XVI Definitions of Asclepius to King Ammon Asclepius instructs King Ammon; also preserved in an Armenian version XVII Fragmentary dialogue Tat addresses a king (speaker attributions vary by edition) XVIII On the Soul Hindered by the Body A praise of kings; no Hermetic dialogue frame Two consequences of that table deserve emphasis. First, the Corpus is an anthology assembled over time , not a work composed at a sitting: its treatises were probably written by different hands, and their gathering into one collection was the work of later editors. Second, the Renaissance division of labour follows directly from the numbering: Marsilio Ficino translated treatises I–XIV ; the remaining three, XVI–XVIII , were translated later by Lodovico Lazzarelli (1447–1500). When a Renaissance or early-modern source speaks of Ficino's Pimander , it means the fourteen treatises of his 1463 translation — not the whole modern Corpus (Section X). III. Beyond the Corpus: Asclepius, Stobaeus, Vienna, and Nag Hammadi The Corpus Hermeticum is the most famous part of the philosophical Hermetica, but it is not the whole of it. Four further bodies of material complete the picture, and each matters to a different part of this article's story: the Asclepius is the text the Latin Middle Ages actually knew; the Stobaeus excerpts preserve Hermetica that would otherwise be lost; the Vienna fragments show the literature still being copied on papyrus in Roman Egypt itself; and the Nag Hammadi texts, recovered only in 1945, changed modern scholars' sense of who read Hermes and where. The Latin Asclepius The Asclepius is a long Hermetic dialogue that survives complete only in Latin . It is a translation of a lost Greek original known as the Perfect Discourse (Greek: Logos teleios ), and it was transmitted in the Middle Ages among the works of Apuleius of Madaura, to whom it is not now attributed. In paraphrase: Hermes instructs Asclepius on God, the cosmos, and the human being — presented, in a celebrated passage, as a great wonder, a being who joins the mortal and the divine — and the dialogue contains two passages that dominate its later history. The first describes the Egyptian art of making gods: drawing powers into statues so that the images become, in the text's terms, animated bodies inhabited by invited spirits. The second is a prophecy, cast as a lament, that Egypt will one day be abandoned by its gods and its temples left desolate. Augustine quoted both at length (Section VIII); the first made the Asclepius the most theologically dangerous Hermetic text in the Latin tradition, and the second let Christian readers hear, in a pagan voice, a foretelling of paganism's end. The Stobaeus Fragments and the Kore Kosmou In the fifth century CE, the anthologist John of Stobi — Stobaeus — compiled a vast anthology of extracts from Greek authors for the education of his son. Among its contents are dozens of Hermetic excerpts, conventionally cited as the Stobaean Hermetica (SH). Some duplicate material known from elsewhere; many preserve Hermetic writing found nowhere else. The most substantial is the Kore Kosmou — the title means, roughly, the Virgin (or Pupil, or Maiden) of the World — preserved as Stobaean excerpts XXIII–XXIV in the usual numbering. In paraphrase: the goddess Isis instructs her son Horus in how souls were created and embodied — made to assist in the ordering of living things, grown proud and transgressive, and in consequence bound into bodies, with a promised return for those who live worthily of their origin. The Kore Kosmou is the most overtly mythological of the surviving philosophical Hermetica, and its Isis–Horus frame is a standing reminder that the literature's Egyptian dramatis personae are not confined to Hermes himself. The Vienna Fragments The Vienna Hermetica are four short Greek fragments on papyrus — papyri now in Vienna, dating to the late second or third century — preserving parts of what was once a collection of Hermetic discourses of Hermes to Tat, one of them conventionally titled On Energies . Their importance is out of proportion to their size. They are physical witnesses from Roman Egypt itself, close in date to the treatises' composition, and they show the dialogues circulating as a collection of discourses — not only as isolated tracts — already in antiquity. Related witnesses include the Definitions of Hermes Trismegistus to Asclepius , preserved in an Armenian translation, which some scholars regard as among the earliest Hermetic philosophical material, possibly reaching back toward the first century CE. The Nag Hammadi Hermetica In 1945, near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt, a buried jar yielded thirteen codices of mostly Gnostic and Christian-related writings in Coptic. Codex VI contains three Hermetic texts, all translated from Greek originals: NH VI,6 — THE DISCOURSE ON THE EIGHTH AND NINTH A previously unknown initiatory dialogue: a teacher leads a disciple, through prayer and sung vowel sequences, toward a vision of the eighth and ninth spheres above the seven planetary zones. The most explicitly initiatory Hermetic text to survive whole. NH VI,7 — THE PRAYER OF THANKSGIVING A Hermetic prayer of gratitude for saving knowledge, also known independently in Greek (in the Greek Magical Papyri) and in Latin (at the close of the Asclepius). A scribal note records that those who prayed then embraced and shared a meal. NH VI,8 — ASCLEPIUS 21–29 A Coptic version of a central portion of the Asclepius (the Perfect Discourse), covering — among other material — the prophecy of Egypt's desolation. A control on the Latin text, and proof the dialogue circulated in Egypt in Coptic dress. The find mattered for two reasons. It proved, in physical form, that Hermetic writings were copied and read in fourth-century Egypt alongside Gnostic and Christian texts — the readers were neighbours, and in some cases evidently the same people. And the Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth , with its guided ascent, its hymnody, and its instruction that the teaching be written up and deposited in a temple, gave scholars their strongest single exhibit for the argument — associated above all with Jean-Pierre Mahé's work on the Hermetica of Upper Egypt and developed by Fowden and others — that the philosophical Hermetica reflect a lived devotional practice, not merely a literary game played with Egyptian scenery. How far that argument extends to the Corpus treatises themselves remains debated (Section V); that the debate exists at all is a post-1945 fact. IV. Hermes-Thoth in Brief This section is deliberately brief. The figure behind the treatises — how the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth became one thrice-greatest sage — is treated at length, from the Egyptian side, in the Egyptology division's Hermeticism article, and the treatises' Egyptian frame is the subject of its Corpus Hermeticum article. What follows is only what a reader of the Greek tradition needs in hand. When Greeks settled in Egypt after Alexander's conquests, they practised what modern scholarship calls interpretatio graeca : reading foreign gods through Greek equivalents. The Egyptian Thoth (Egyptian Ḏḥwty ) — ibis-headed god of writing, reckoning, and sacred knowledge, scribe of the gods, who in Egyptian myth records, mediates, and heals — was identified with Hermes , the Greek messenger, herald, and patron of speech and interpretation. Thoth's chief cult city, Khmunu, became in Greek Hermopolis , the City of Hermes. The compound figure, Hermes Trismegistus — Hermes the Thrice-Greatest, the epithet generally explained as rendering the repeated Egyptian superlatives (“great, great”) applied to Thoth — emerges in the Hellenistic and Roman periods as author, revealer, and patron of all sacred learning. The identification carried a curriculum with it. Around 200 CE the Christian writer Clement of Alexandria described, in paraphrase, a procession of Egyptian priests carrying forty-two books of Hermes held to be indispensable to the cult — books on hymns, ritual, astronomy and astrology, geography, medicine, and the training of priests. Clement's list is a Christian author's report, not a temple catalogue, but it shows the shape of the reputation the Hermetica inherited: Hermes was not the author of a book but of a library , and a library administered by priests. That reputation is the seed of everything later — of the technical Hermetica as much as the philosophical, since astrology, medicine, and ritual all stood on Clement's shelves — and it is why new writings on any sacred subject could plausibly appear under Hermes' name for centuries. Authorship, in this tradition, is authorisation. // ONE FIGURE, THREE REGISTERS // God: Thoth-Hermes, worshipped at Hermopolis and across Roman Egypt. Sage: the legendary priest-king and lawgiver whom Cicero's catalogue of five Hermeses already sends fleeing to Egypt with letters and laws. Author-function: the name on the title of any text claiming revealed, Egyptian, and therefore ancient authority. The treatises move among all three registers without marking the transitions, which is one reason their later readers could find in them a prophet, a philosopher, or a magus, as the reader required. V. Dating and Milieu: Greek Texts from Roman Egypt The scholarly consensus that Copenhaver's Hermetica represents — and that the standard reference literature shares — dates the philosophical Hermetica to the first three centuries CE, chiefly the second and third , composed in Greek in Roman Egypt . No philosophical Hermetic treatise is generally accepted as earlier than the turn of the era, and the Definitions (Section III), sometimes placed toward the first century CE, mark the early edge of the range rather than an exception to it. The technical Hermetica are a different chronological story — some astrological Hermetica may go back to the second or third century BCE — and conflating the two families' dates is the single most common error in popular accounts of “Hermes”. The evidence for the dating is cumulative, and Section XII shows it being assembled, in essence, as early as 1614. The treatises' Greek is the Greek of the Roman imperial period, with the vocabulary of later Greek philosophy. Their intellectual furniture — the divine Mind, the mediating Word, the craftsman, fate working through the planetary spheres, the soul's kinship with God — is the furniture of the period's popular Platonism. No author before the Christian era quotes or mentions them. Their earliest certain readers are the writers of the second and third centuries and the copyists of the Vienna papyri (Section III). And their world — temples still standing, statues still animated in cult, a priestly culture writing in Greek under Roman rule — is the world of Roman, not pharaonic, Egypt. The Ingredients MIDDLE PLATONISM The dominant ingredient: a supreme God beyond easy predication; Mind (Nous) as first principle and revealer; a craftsman figure ordering the cosmos; the soul's descent into body and its possible return. The Hermetica are unintelligible except as popular, devotional Platonism of the imperial period. STOICISM A living cosmos pervaded by divine reason and breath; fate (heimarmenē) as the connected order of causes; sympathy among the parts of the whole. Stoic physics supplies much of the treatises' cosmology even where their soteriology is Platonic. JEWISH AND BIBLICAL ECHOES The Poimandrēs creation account (Section VI) works with material closely parallel to the Greek Genesis — light separated from darkness, a creative Word, the command to increase and multiply. Scholarship generally explains this through the shared Alexandrian world of the Septuagint and of Philo, not through direct dependence in either direction between the treatises and the New Testament. EGYPTIAN RELIGION The dramatis personae, the temple settings, the statue animation of the Asclepius, the Isis of the Kore Kosmou. How deep this ingredient goes — living priestly tradition or literary colouring — is the field's central live debate, summarised below. How Egyptian? The Fowden Question A.-J. Festugière, whose edition still underlies the modern text, read the Hermetica as essentially Greek philosophy in Egyptian dress: the Egyptian names and settings, on his account, lend sanctity to doctrines drawn from the Greek schools. Fowden's The Egyptian Hermes (1986) mounted the counter-case that has structured discussion since: that the Hermetica, philosophical and technical together, arise from a genuinely Egyptian, if thoroughly Hellenised, milieu — the world of the Egyptian temples and their priestly intellectuals under Roman rule, for whom Greek was a working language and Greek philosophy a usable idiom, but whose institutions, practices, and gods were their own. The Nag Hammadi evidence (Section III), the Demotic and temple parallels assembled by Mahé and others, and more recent work — notably Christian Bull's The Tradition of Hermes Trismegistus (2018), which presses the Egyptian priestly continuity further still — have moved the centre of gravity toward Fowden, without dissolving the question. The position this article adopts, because it is the position the evidence currently supports, is the double one stated in Section I: Greek in language and philosophical idiom, Roman in date, Egyptian in milieu and in more than decoration. Casaubon (Section XII) was right about the date. He was not required to be right about everything else. // ALEXANDRIA, WITH A WARNING // Alexandria is the conventional shorthand for the Hermetica's world, and this article's title keeps it — the city was Roman Egypt's intellectual capital and the natural home of its Greek-Egyptian-Jewish exchanges. But the treatises name no city, and the Nag Hammadi and Panopolis evidence points up the Nile as well as to the Delta. “Alexandria” in Hermetic contexts should be read as the name of a culture, not as a proven street address. A last point of milieu, easily missed because the texts are so bookish: the dialogues presuppose circles . A teacher, a small company of disciples — Tat, Asclepius, Ammon — secrecy enjoined, hymns sung in common, a meal after prayer in the Nag Hammadi note. Fowden called the pattern, in paraphrase, a way of Hermes: a graded spiritual path pursued in small Hermetic communities. Whether those communities were formal lodges, temple circles, or reading groups gathered around a charismatic teacher cannot be recovered, and this article does not pretend otherwise. But the social form inscribed in the texts — master, initiates, silence, hymn — is itself evidence, and it is the form the later Hermetic tradition, from the Renaissance academies onward, instinctively reproduced. VI. Poimandrēs (CH I): The Vision, the Making, and the Way Back The first treatise is the Corpus's most famous, and the one from which the whole collection took its Renaissance name: Ficino titled his translation the Pimander after it. Its Greek title names its revealer: Poimandrēs , the being who appears to the narrator. The name's own etymology is disputed — a Greek reading takes it as “shepherd of men”; a widely discussed modern proposal derives it from an Egyptian phrase for the knowledge of Re — and the dispute is a miniature of the whole Hermetic question (Section V). What follows is a paraphrase of the treatise's thirty-two short sections, following the account in Copenhaver's translation and the standard scholarly summaries. It is not a quotation, and no sentence in it should be cited as the treatise's wording. The Vision (§§1–3, in paraphrase) The narrator relates that once, when his thought was turned toward the things that are, his understanding rose to a great height while his bodily senses were held back, as in the heaviness of sleep after food or labour. A being of boundless size appeared, called him by name, and asked what he wished to hear and see. Asked who he was, the being named himself Poimandrēs, the Mind (Nous) of the sovereign power, and offered to teach what the narrator desired. The narrator asked to learn the things that are, to understand their nature, and to know God. The revelation that follows is the answer. The Making of the Cosmos (§§4–11, in paraphrase) The narrator saw an unbounded light — serene and joyful — and then, in counterpoint, a darkness coiling downward that became a moist, troubled nature, smoking and giving out an inarticulate sound. From the light a holy Word (Logos) came upon the moist nature; pure fire leapt up from it, light and eager; air followed; earth and water remained mingled below. Poimandrēs explained, in paraphrase: the light is Mind, the narrator's god, older than the moist nature that emerged from darkness; the Word that comes from Mind is the son of God; and the two are not separate from the life they give. Then Mind — described as male-and-female, being life and light — brought forth by a word a second Mind, a craftsman (demiurge), who formed seven governors (administrators) enclosing the sensible world in circles; their government is what is called fate. The Word rose to join the craftsman Mind, its kin; the heavy elements left below produced living creatures without reason; and the ordered cosmos stood complete: elements below, governors above, and all of it held within Mind. The Human (§§12–19, in paraphrase) Mind, the father of all, then brought forth a Human (Anthrōpos) in his own image, beautiful and bearing the father's likeness, and loved him as his own child, granting him authority over the craftsman's works. The Human, entering the craftsman's sphere, received from each of the seven governors a share of its nature, and then broke through the vault of the spheres and leaned down through the cosmic framework to show the form of God to downward-tending nature. Nature saw the reflection of that form in her own element and smiled with love; the Human, seeing in nature a form like his own, reflected in her waters, loved it and willed to dwell in it — and act and will coincided: he took up residence in the form without reason. Nature embraced her lover, and they were mingled. Hence the treatise's anthropology, in paraphrase: the human being alone among living creatures is double — mortal through the body, immortal through the essential Human; subject to fate, yet carrying within an authority above the framework of the spheres. In time, the first androgynous generation was divided into male and female, with the divine command to increase and multiply; and the treatise draws its ethical line at once: whoever has recognised himself knows where he comes from and returns to life and light, while whoever has loved the body that came from the error of desire wanders in darkness. The Way Back (§§20–32, in paraphrase) The return reverses the descent. At death, in paraphrase, the body is surrendered to alteration, the senses return to their sources, and the soul rises through the framework of the spheres, giving back at each of the seven zones what it had received: at the first, the energy of growth and decline; then, in succession, the scheming of evil, the deceit of desire, the arrogance of rule, unholy daring, the evil impulses of wealth, and the falsehood that lies in wait. Stripped of all the governors' workings, the soul enters the eighth region — the ogdoadic nature — where it joins the powers in hymning the Father, and those who have ascended are made powers themselves and come to be in God. That, the treatise says in paraphrase, is the good end for those who have knowledge: to be made god. The vision closes in mission and worship: Poimandrēs mingles with the powers; the narrator, empowered, goes out to preach to those sunk in drunkenness, sleep, and ignorance of God, calling them to sobriety and to a share in immortality; some mock and depart, others are taught; and the treatise ends with the narrator's hymn and prayer — thanksgiving for knowledge received, and a plea not to fall away from it and to bring light to those of his kind still in ignorance. // TWO READING WARNINGS // First: “fall” is the interpreter's word, not the treatise's. The Human of §§12–15 is not expelled and does not rebel; he leans down in love, and the text's tone toward the descent is wonder as much as lament. Second: the seven zones of the ascent are not named as planets in the text; calling them the planetary spheres rests on their identification with the seven governors of §9 — a standard and reasonable identification, but an identification all the same. Both warnings are the kind of distinction Copenhaver's notes exist to preserve, and both are routinely lost in popular retellings. Why this treatise, of the seventeen, carries the tradition: it contains the whole Hermetic plot in miniature — revelation by Mind, a cosmos made through Word and craftsman, a humanity double in nature, salvation as self-knowledge, and an ascent that undoes the descent zone by zone. Every later Hermetic text, and most later Hermetic readers , are footnotes to one or another of its movements. VII. A Constellation, Not a System: The Other Treatises Read straight through, the Corpus Hermeticum does not agree with itself, and honest accounts — Copenhaver's introduction among them — say so plainly. Some treatises speak warmly of the cosmos as a beautiful, living, divine order, a “second god” through whom the first God can be contemplated; others speak of the body and the material world as a burden and a prison from which the soul must escape. Scholarship has long described these as an optimistic and a pessimistic strand within the literature — world-affirming and world-fleeing Hermetism — with the pessimistic strand standing nearest to Gnosticism. The inconsistency is not a defect to be explained away. It is the expected product of an anthology of different authors writing devotional philosophy for different circles across two centuries, and Fowden's suggestion (Section V) — that some apparent contradictions mark stages of a graded path rather than rival doctrines — can be held alongside it. What the Corpus offers is a constellation of related treatises, not a system; the system was supplied later, by its readers. Three treatises beyond the first repay naming here, because later sections and the companion articles lean on them. CH IV, the Mixing Bowl (in paraphrase): God sent down a great bowl — a krater, the mixing vessel of a Greek symposium — filled with Mind, and a herald invited all who could to immerse themselves; those who did gained knowledge and became complete in mind, while those who refused the message remained at the level of reason alone. CH X, the Key , offers the Corpus's most compact overview of its own teaching, a summary dialogue that ancient and modern readers alike have used as a map of the whole. CH XIII, On Rebirth — a secret dialogue on a mountain — is the Corpus's initiatory centrepiece (in paraphrase): Hermes leads Tat through a rebirth ( palingenesia ) accomplished in silence and contemplation, in which twelve tormentors that bind the soul to matter — ignorance, grief, lust, injustice, greed, deceit, envy, anger among them — are driven out and ten divine powers enter in their place, and the reborn Tat answers with a hymn. Together with the Nag Hammadi Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth (Section III), CH XIII is the chief evidence that Hermetic knowledge was imagined not as information but as transformation. 2nd–3rd c. BCE EARLIEST TECHNICAL HERMETICA Astrological writings under Hermes' name begin to circulate in Hellenistic Egypt — the technical family's early edge, centuries before the philosophical treatises. c. 200 CE CLEMENT'S FORTY-TWO BOOKS Clement of Alexandria describes the forty-two indispensable books of Hermes carried in Egyptian priestly procession — the reputation the literature inherited, in a Christian report. 2nd–3rd c. CE THE PHILOSOPHICAL TREATISES COMPOSED The Corpus treatises, the Perfect Discourse behind the Asclepius, and their companions are written in Greek in Roman Egypt; the Vienna papyri copy Hermetic discourses in the same centuries. c. 300 CE ZOSIMOS READS HERMES The alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis writes in Upper Egypt, echoing the philosophical Hermetica inside alchemical teaching — the two families in one reader. See Zosimos of Panopolis . 4th–5th c. CE LATIN ASCLEPIUS; STOBAEUS; NAG HAMMADI COPIES The Perfect Discourse circulates in its Latin dress as the Asclepius; Coptic Hermetica are copied into what becomes Nag Hammadi Codex VI; Stobaeus anthologises Greek Hermetic excerpts, including the Kore Kosmou. 11th c. THE COLLECTION ATTESTED Michael Psellos knows the Corpus as a collection in Byzantium — the first attestation of the anthology as such. 1463 / 1471 FICINO TRANSLATES; TREVISO PRINTS Ficino completes his Latin Pimander (CH I–XIV) in April 1463; the editio princeps is printed at Treviso in 1471. See Section X. 1614 CASAUBON REDATES Isaac Casaubon's Exercitationes against Baronius argues the treatises into the Christian era on philological grounds. A hero in Greek epic was something else: a name carried by song into every city in the Greek world. This article keeps those two institutions apart, because the Greeks lived with both at once, and because confusing them is where most popular accounts of Heracles, Theseus, and Jason go wrong. Two Institutions, One Word: Hero Cult and Epic English uses one word, hero , for two Greek things that a Greek of the Classical period would have experienced as quite different arrangements. The first is hero cult : a set of rituals performed at a fixed place, usually a tomb, for a dead figure believed to retain power after death and to exercise it, for good or ill, over the community that lived around that place. The second is epic : song — later, text — that carried the deeds of figures such as Achilles, Heracles, and Jason across the whole Greek-speaking world, detaching them from any single tomb or town and making them the common property of Greeks everywhere. The same name could live in both arrangements at once. Heracles had tombs and shrines where he received the offerings due to the dead, and he also strode through poems sung from Ionia to Sicily. Those are not two aspects of one thing. They are two institutions, with different geographies, different economics, and different kinds of authority, and this article treats them separately throughout. The distinction was given its sharpest modern form by Gregory Nagy in The Best of the Achaeans (1979; second edition 1999). In the account that follows from Nagy's analysis — paraphrased here, not quoted — hero cult is local : it belongs to a particular polis or locality, it is anchored to a physical tomb, and the honour it confers (Greek timē ) is delivered by the worshipping community in ritual, again and again, for as long as the cult is maintained. Epic, by contrast, is Panhellenic : it circulates beyond any one city, sheds local peculiarities as it travels, and confers a different kind of honour — kleos , the glory of being heard of, which the song itself creates and renews at every performance. A hero could be enormous in cult and minor in epic, or the reverse. Most heroes, in fact, were purely local: the Greek landscape was dense with named and unnamed heroes — founders, ancestors, athletes, war dead, figures known only as “the hero” of a particular shrine — who never appear in any surviving poem at all. Epic's cast list is the small, famous tip of a very large cultic iceberg. Walter Burkert's Greek Religion (German original 1977; English translation by John Raffan, 1985) remains the standard synthesis of the cultic side, and its chapter on the heroes sets out the framework this article uses: the hero is a dead human being — unlike a god, a hero has a biography that ends in a death, often a violent or uncanny one — whose power operates from the grave, within a limited territory, and who must be kept well-disposed by offerings. Heroes could help: they healed, they protected cities, they appeared in battle. They could also harm, and a neglected or angered hero was a danger precisely because he was near. The gods of Olympus, treated in this hub's Olympians article, were by contrast deathless, mobile, and worshipped everywhere under shared names. The hero's defining features are therefore the opposite of the Olympian's: mortality, locality, and a grave. HERO CULT Local and place-bound. Centred on a tomb or heroon . Maintained by a specific community. Confers timē through repeated ritual. The hero is dead, near, and capable of helping or harming his own people in particular. PANHELLENIC EPIC Mobile and supra-local. Carried by singers, then by texts. Maintained by performance traditions that cross city boundaries. Confers kleos — fame in song — which survives as long as the song is sung, anywhere. WHERE THEY MEET A Panhellenic figure could acquire local cults (Heracles everywhere; Achilles at specific tombs and islands), and a local cult figure could be absorbed into epic's cast. The traffic ran both ways, but the institutions never merged. WHERE THEY DO NOT MEET Most cult heroes have no epic. Most epic narrative — the journeys, combats, and speeches — was never ritual. A story about a hero is not evidence for his cult, and a cult is not evidence for the truth of any story told about him. One further distinction governs everything below. The gods had a genealogy and a theogony : Hesiod's poem explained where they came from and how their order was established, once, in the deep past. Heroes had no theogony. They were generated continuously by Greek communities — by a remarkable death, a remarkable tomb, an oracle's instruction, a city's political need — throughout the Archaic and Classical periods and beyond. Hero cult is therefore not a fossil survival from a single primitive age. It is a living institution that kept producing new heroes, including, as Section VII shows, in the full daylight of the fifth century BCE, for reasons an Athenian politician could have explained to you. II. The Anatomy of Hero Cult: Tomb, Heroon, and Offering A hero's cult place is called a heroon (Greek hērōion ). In form it could be many things: an actual tomb, Bronze Age or recent; a mound; a small walled precinct ( temenos ) with an altar; a chapel-like building housing a tomb or a cenotaph; or, in later periods, a substantial shrine with dining rooms, because hero festivals, like festivals of the gods, commonly involved a shared meal. What identifies a heroon archaeologically is not its architecture but its deposits: votive offerings — pottery, figurines, miniature weapons, inscribed dedications naming the honorand — accumulated at a spot treated as the hero's point of contact with the living. The earliest cult place whose honorands are named by objects found on the site is the shrine on the ridge at Therapne above Sparta, conventionally called the Menelaion, where dedications to Menelaus and Helen begin around c. 700 BCE . That date matters: it puts named, epic-connected hero cult at the same horizon as the fixation of the Homeric poems themselves (Section XIII), and the question of which came first — epic fame or tomb cult — is one of the genuinely open questions in the study of early Greek religion. Offerings Poured Down: The Textbook Model Older handbooks, following a real strand of ancient evidence, drew a sharp ritual contrast. To the Olympian gods one performed thysia : sacrifice on a raised altar ( bōmos ), the victim's head drawn up toward the sky, the god receiving the smoke of the burning thigh-bones and fat, and the worshippers feasting on the meat. To heroes and the powers below the earth one performed enagizein (the noun is enagisma ): offerings directed downward , into a low hearth ( eschara ) or a pit ( bothros ) dug into the ground, the victim's head pressed down, blood and libations — wine, oil, honey, water, collectively choai — poured into the earth for the dead power to receive, and in the extreme form the victim burned entire ( holocaust ), with nothing eaten. The hero, on this model, is a chthonic power — of the earth, chthōn — and is fed the way the dead are fed: downward. // WORDS FOR THE DEAD // Chthonic (from chthōn , earth) marks powers addressed as belonging to the ground and what is under it. Enagizein is the verb ancient authors use for making offerings to the dead and to heroes as dead; thyein is the ordinary verb of sacrifice to gods. Herodotus uses exactly this pair of verbs for the two cults of Heracles (Section V) — the vocabulary itself encodes the distinction. The Revision: What Hero Shrines Actually Did The textbook model is an ancient idea , attested in ancient texts, and it describes some real rituals. As a description of what most hero sanctuaries actually did, it has been substantially revised. Gunnel Ekroth's study of the sacrificial rituals of Greek hero cults (2002, from her Stockholm dissertation) examined the epigraphic and archaeological record sanctuary by sanctuary and concluded — in the finding for which her work is now standardly cited — that the main ritual at hero cults of the Archaic to early Hellenistic periods was in fact thysia , ordinary sacrifice followed by communal dining, with the meat eaten by the worshippers; that low hearths, pits, holocausts, and the vocabulary of enagizein are documented only rarely in hero contexts before the Roman period; and that the neat Olympian/chthonic opposition owes as much to later lexicographers and scholiasts, systematising a distinction, as to Archaic practice. This article therefore states both layers honestly: the downward offering is how Greek writers themselves conceptualised feeding a hero, and Herodotus' contrast in Section V proves the concept was alive in the fifth century; but the excavated and inscribed record shows hero cults feasting like everyone else. An honest archive reports the idea and the practice, and does not let either erase the other. Tombs of Strangers: The Eighth-Century Evidence Hero cult in the broad sense emerges in the archaeological record in the eighth century BCE , the same century in which the Homeric poems were taking shape. Across Greece, offerings begin to appear at tombs of the Bronze Age — Mycenaean chamber tombs and tholoi a half-millennium old by then — whose occupants the offerers cannot have known by any continuous tradition. Scholars distinguish, following J. N. Coldstream and Anthony Snodgrass, between tomb cult (veneration directed at an ancient grave as such) and hero cult proper (veneration of a named hero at his recognised shrine), and Carla Antonaccio's work on the archaeology of ancestors argued that much eighth-century tomb cult was about claiming land and ancestry in a period of community formation, not about Homer. Whether the spread of epic caused the turn to ancient tombs — communities identifying their local graves with epic heroes they had heard sung — or whether both are parallel products of the eighth century's social transformations, remains debated. What is not debated is the synchronism, and the most spectacular single piece of evidence for the world that produced it predates the eighth century altogether. It is the subject of the next section. III. Lefkandi: The Toumba Building and the Debate Over It Lefkandi, on the west coast of Euboea between Chalkis and Eretria, was one of the most prosperous communities of the Greek Early Iron Age — the period older scholarship called the Dark Age. On the hill called Toumba (“the mound”), excavations by the British School at Athens and the Greek Archaeological Service, reported in a preliminary account by Mervyn Popham, Evi Touloupa, and Hugh Sackett in 1982 and fully in the Lefkandi publication series, uncovered something without parallel for its date: a very large apsidal building, roughly 47 metres long and 10 metres wide in the excavators' reconstruction, oriented east–west, with a porch at the east end, a great central room, smaller rooms toward the apsidal west end, mudbrick walls on a stone socle, a thatched roof, and — in the original reconstruction — a surrounding veranda of wooden posts that has often been noted as a distant anticipation of the peristyle of the later Greek temple. The building is dated to the mid-tenth century BCE, c. 1000–950 BCE , and it stood only briefly. Beneath the floor of the central room lay two deep shafts. One held the skeletons of four horses , apparently sacrificed and thrown or driven in headfirst, two of them still wearing iron bits. The other, larger shaft held a double burial. A man, cremated, his ashes wrapped in a fringed linen cloth — itself an extraordinary survival — and placed in a bronze amphora imported from Cyprus that was already an antique, perhaps a century old, when it was buried; beside the urn, an iron sword, a spearhead, and a whetstone. Next to it, inhumed in a wooden coffin or on a bier, a woman, wearing gold: earrings, hair spirals, a necklace with faience and rock-crystal beads, and an antique gold pendant of Near Eastern manufacture far older than the burial itself; an iron knife with an ivory handle lay near her head. The excavators and most subsequent readers have taken the knife, the simultaneity of the burials, and the woman's inhumation beside a cremated man to raise the possibility — it is no more than that — that she was killed to accompany him. East of the shafts, a rock surface scorched by fierce fire with a circle of postholes has been interpreted as the site of the cremation pyre. After the burial, the building was demolished and the whole structure was covered by a great mound of earth — the Toumba itself. Around and against that mound, in the decades that followed (broadly c. 950–825 BCE ), the community buried its dead in a rich cemetery, the Toumba cemetery, as if the mound had become a focus of prestige and memory. It is this sequence — monumental building, princely burial, deliberate mounding, subsequent burials clustering at the spot — that led the excavators to call the structure a heroon : a building erected over a hero's grave, and the burials beneath it the earliest candidate in Greek archaeology for the burial of a man his community then treated as a hero. // THE INTERPRETATION DEBATE, STATED PLAINLY // The heroon reading is influential but not uncontested, and this archive does not present it as settled. Alexander Mazarakis Ainian argued, in a line of interpretation developed across his work on early Greek rulers' dwellings, that the Toumba building is better read as the house of a living ruler — a chieftain's hall — in which the burials were subsequently made, rather than a shrine built for the dead: on this reading the building's life came first and the heroisation, if any, attached to a former residence. Others have questioned details of the reconstruction, including the height of the building and whether the outer posts formed a veranda or a fence. What no interpretation disputes is the sequence of building, rich burial with horse sacrifice, demolition, and mound, or its date. The debate is about what the building was for — and it is a useful first lesson in how much of hero cult's early history rests on readings of mute earth and postholes. Why Lefkandi anchors this article is its date and its shape. Around 950 BCE — two centuries before the Menelaion dedications, in a Greece without temples in the later sense, without writing in general use, and without the Homeric poems in any fixed form we can point to — a community staged a funeral of Homeric splendour: cremation, an antique bronze vessel for the ashes, sacrificed horses, gold, and a mound. Readers of the Iliad will recognise the grammar: it is the funeral of Patroclus, with its pyre, its sacrificed horses, and its mound, enacted in the real world at roughly the era when the epic tradition was forming. Whether Lefkandi shows epic reflecting life, life imitating a sung tradition already in circulation, or both drawing on a shared heroic funeral custom, cannot be decided from one site — and scholars have argued all three. The safe statement is the strongest one the evidence allows: the institution that hero cult would become — a powerful dead man, a marked place, a community organising its memory around both — is materially present at Lefkandi by the middle of the tenth century BCE, before any text in this article was written down. Heracles: The Labours Before There Were Twelve Heracles (Greek Hēraklēs , Roman Hercules) is the limiting case of every generalisation in this article, because he overflows both institutions. His name is usually analysed as “glory of Hera” — an irony the tradition itself exploits, since Hera, his divine stepmother, is his persecutor throughout: it is Hera who delays his birth so that his cousin Eurystheus is born first and rules (the story the Iliad itself tells, at 19.95–133), Hera who sends the snakes into his cradle, and Hera who drives him mad to kill his own wife and children, the crime for which, in the standard later account, the labours are imposed as purification and service. His mortal mother is Alcmene; his father, in the tradition, is Zeus. He is therefore exactly the hero of Section I at maximum scale: a mortal man with a death — a terrible one, by poison and fire (Section V) — who nonetheless ends among the gods. Every Greek city could claim some episode of his wanderings, which is one reason he, and not a more local figure, became the Panhellenic hero par excellence : his myth had to be portable, because he had been everywhere. A Series in Search of a Number The labours — Greek athloi , contests or ordeals — are tasks imposed by Eurystheus, king of Tiryns and Mycenae, on a Heracles bound to serve him. The crucial historical fact about them is that the set was fluid for centuries . The Iliad knows the servitude to Eurystheus and names individual tasks, including the descent for Cerberus, the hound of Hades (8.362–369), and presents Heracles' whole career as the type of the hero who suffered and died despite being dearest to Zeus (18.117–119); it nowhere lists twelve. Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) knows several labours as separate episodes woven into its monster genealogies — the cattle of Geryon (287–293), the Hydra of Lerna, reared by Hera and killed by Heracles with Iolaus' help (313–318), Cerberus (310–312), the Nemean lion (327–332) — again with no numbered cycle. Individual labours circulated as individual stories: Stesichorus' lyric Geryoneis (early sixth century BCE) made a whole poem out of the Geryon episode alone. Antiquity itself credited a lost epic, the Heraclea of Peisander of Rhodes (dated variously to the seventh or sixth century BCE), with first gathering the labours into a single poem; the poem is lost, and what it contained cannot be checked, so the credit is recorded here as ancient attribution, not as fact. The earliest complete set of twelve that survives is not a text at all. It is sculpture: the twelve metopes of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, built c. 470–457 BCE , whose carved panels — six over the east porch, six over the west — displayed twelve labours, one to a panel, in the temple of the sanctuary where Heracles was honoured as the legendary founder of the Olympic Games. Emma Stafford's study of Heracles, on which this paragraph draws, makes the point precisely: the canonical twelve do not seem to be established before the Classical period, and the Olympia metopes are the first clear instance of the collection — it has even been suggested that the number was in part dictated by the twelve spaces the architecture offered. A cycle that modern readers meet as timeless was, on the evidence, fixed late, in stone, at a Panhellenic sanctuary: epic's fluid tradition crystallised by a temple's decoration. Cerberus Hades Added with the apples; the hound is taken without weapons and returned Ten, Then Twelve: The Mythographer's Arithmetic The fullest surviving prose account is the Library (2.4.8–2.5.12) of the author conventionally called Apollodorus — the work is now generally dated to the first or second century CE and attributed to an unknown mythographer, “Pseudo-Apollodorus”; it is cited here in J. G. Frazer's Loeb translation. The Library itself — its author problem, its survival, and how far it can be trusted — is the subject of Apollodorus and the Library . In Apollodorus' telling, the oracle at Delphi directs Heracles to serve Eurystheus and perform the labours imposed, and the arithmetic of the cycle is explained inside the story: Eurystheus refused to count two of the completed ten. The Hydra was disqualified — in Frazer's translation of Apollodorus 2.5.2, Eurystheus said the labour “should not be reckoned among the ten because he had not got the better of the hydra by himself, but with the help of Iolaus” — and the cleansing of the Augean stables was disqualified because Heracles had bargained for a wage. Two further tasks were therefore imposed, the apples of the Hesperides and the capture of Cerberus, bringing the performed total to twelve (Apollodorus 2.5.11). The episode is worth dwelling on because it shows what kind of object the “twelve labours” are: not a datum of the myth but a negotiated count , rationalised after the fact by a mythographer reconciling a ten-task servitude with a twelve-item canon that his culture had already fixed. Other sources vary the order, substitute episodes, and preserve labours the canon excludes; Heracles also performed a penumbra of further deeds — the parerga , “side-works” — on the way to and from the labours proper. The canon is real, but it is a late editorial fact about the tradition, and this archive dates it as such: fluid in Homer and Hesiod, gathered by degrees in Archaic poetry and art, complete in stone at Olympia around 460 BCE, and canonised in prose by Apollodorus half a millennium later still. V. Heracles Between Hero and God: Thasos and the Apotheosis Heracles died — in the tradition, horribly. Deianeira, his wife, fearing to lose him to a captive girl, sent him a tunic smeared with what she believed was a love-charm: the blood of the centaur Nessus, whom Heracles had shot with an arrow dipped in the Hydra's venom. The tunic burned into his flesh. Carried to Mount Oeta, he built his own pyre and had it lit; the tradition then divides his end: the mortal part burned away, and Heracles himself was taken up to Olympus, reconciled with Hera, and married to her daughter Hebe, Youth. Hesiod's Theogony already ends his story that way (950–955), and the Odyssey 's underworld scene contains the same doubleness — Odysseus meets Heracles' eidōlon , his phantom, in Hades, while “he himself” feasts among the immortal gods (11.601–604; the lines were already suspected by some ancient scholars, and their status is still discussed). The myth, in other words, could not decide whether Heracles was dead or divine, because Greek religion had decided, in practice, that he was both — and it maintained two cults to prove it. The proof-text is Herodotus. In Histories 2.44, investigating whether the Greek Heracles was a man or an ancient god, Herodotus reports travelling to Tyre in Phoenicia, where he found a great temple of Heracles — the Phoenician Melqart — whose priests dated it to the city's foundation, 2,300 years before his visit; and to the island of Thasos in the northern Aegean, where he found a temple of Heracles founded by Phoenicians who had settled the island while searching for Europa, five generations, he calculates, before the birth of the Greek Heracles son of Amphitryon. His conclusion, in A. D. Godley's Loeb translation, is quoted here verbatim because it is the single most important sentence in the ancient evidence for this article's whole subject: “Therefore, what I have discovered by inquiry plainly shows that Heracles is an ancient god. And furthermore, those Greeks, I think, are most in the right, who have established and practise two worships of Heracles, sacrificing to one Heracles as to an immortal, and calling him the Olympian, but to the other bringing offerings as to a dead hero.” — Herodotus, Histories 2.44.5, trans. A. D. Godley (Loeb Classical Library) Every element of Section II is present in that sentence. The two worships are distinguished by verb and by attitude: sacrifice ( thyein ) to Heracles the immortal, the Olympian; offerings as to the dead ( enagizein ) to Heracles the hero. Herodotus is not confused by the doubleness; he approves of it, as the correct ritual response to a genuinely double being. The Thasos evidence adds the historical layer: the island's Heracles cult was, on Herodotus' own report, Phoenician in foundation and older than the Greek hero — the Greek Heracles had absorbed, by the process scholars call interpretatio graeca , the cult of the Tyrian god Melqart, whose worship the Phoenicians carried across the Mediterranean. Heracles the hero-god is thus not only a mythological paradox but a documented case of cults merging across cultures, with the seams still visible to a travelling historian in the fifth century BCE. The pattern generalises. Heracles received cult as a god, as a hero, and in some places in both capacities at neighbouring altars; he was worshipped as a healer, as a protector of gymnasia and of travellers, as Alexikakos, Averter of Evil. Asclepius shows the same trajectory — a hero of epic, killed by Zeus's thunderbolt in the early tradition, who by the Classical period received cult of fully divine scale at Epidaurus and across the Greek world, the world of the healing sanctuaries and dream incubation treated in this hub's Mysteries and Healing Cults article. The boundary between hero and god, which the textbook model draws as a line, was in practice a slope, and the greatest heroes slid up it. What never changed was the grammar underneath: even the deified Heracles kept his tomb-traditions and his hero-offerings somewhere, because his story — unlike a god's — contained a death. Apotheosis did not erase the hero. It added a second register on top of the first, and Greek cult, characteristically, kept paying both. VI. Theseus: Athens Builds Its Hero If Heracles shows a hero outgrowing every local boundary, Theseus shows the opposite process, and shows it with unusual clarity because it happened late, fast, and in a city that kept records: Theseus is, in large part, an Athenian construction . That statement needs care. Theseus is not an invention from nothing — he appears, briefly and marginally, in early epic: the Iliad names him once, in a catalogue of great fighters of a former generation (1.265), and the Odyssey knows his Cretan adventure with Ariadne (11.321–325) and his descent to the underworld with his friend Peirithous (11.631). But in Homer he is a minor figure, a name in other heroes' stories. The Theseus who dominates Athenian art, festival, and self-understanding — the unifier of Attica, the slayer of the Minotaur, the founder of Athenian institutions, the democratic king who (in Euripides' Suppliants ) lectures a Theban herald on the virtues of democracy — is the product of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, built up by Athens as the city's own answer to Heracles. The Growth of a Cycle The material record dates the growth. The Metropolitan Museum's survey of Theseus in Athenian art, a standard summary of the iconographic evidence, traces the pattern: the earliest surviving representation of Theseus in art, on the François Vase of c. 570 BCE , already shows the Cretan episode, but depictions remain few before c. 540 BCE; between c. 540 and 525 they multiply, centred on the Minotaur; after c. 525 the repertoire diversifies into a full cycle of deeds — above all the journey from Troezen to Athens along the Saronic Gulf, on which the young Theseus clears the road of a series of murderous brigands: Periphetes the Club-bearer, Sinis the Pine-bender, the Crommyonian sow, Sciron, Cercyon the wrestler, Procrustes of the bed. The structural point is unmistakable, and Plutarch's Life of Theseus states the motive inside the story itself: the young hero, fired by the fame of his cousin Heracles, deliberately chooses the dangerous land route to earn a fame like his, and kills each brigand by the method the brigand had used on travellers. The road cycle is a set of labours, composed on the Heraclean model, for a hero who needed labours. Athens was equipping its founder with the standard heroic curriculum — a generation or two after the democracy's foundation, at exactly the moment when a young, ambitious, newly self-conscious city most needed a founder who could stand beside the Panhellenic Heracles whom Dorian Sparta and other rivals claimed as their own ancestor. // THE SYNOIKISMOS // Theseus' greatest political deed, in Athenian tradition, was the synoikismos : the unification of the many settlements of Attica into a single political community centred on Athens, with one council-house and one magistracy. Thucydides (2.15) reports the tradition and treats it as the origin of Athens' unified structure. Whether any historical unification happened under a king named Theseus is unverifiable; what the attribution does is give the unified state a founder, a date in the heroic age, and a charter older than any rival's. The literary record matches the vases. Bacchylides, writing for Athenian performance in the early fifth century BCE, devoted two dithyrambs (Odes 17 and 18) to Theseus: Ode 17, the Youths or Theseus , dramatises the voyage to Crete and Theseus' dive to the sea floor to prove his descent from Poseidon — a scene vase-painters took up in the same decades — and Ode 18 stages Aegeus in dialogue with a chorus of Athenians as news of the unknown young hero's road-deeds reaches the city. Tragedy then made Theseus the voice of Athens itself: in Euripides' Suppliants (c. 423 BCE) he embodies Athenian democracy, asylum, and the burial of the dead as civic doctrine, and in Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus (produced posthumously, 401 BCE) he is the just king who receives the polluted outcast and guarantees his grave. None of this is Bronze Age survival. It is a Classical city writing its values backwards into a heroic founder, in full view of the documentary record — which is precisely what makes Theseus the best case study in this archive for how heroic tradition is made . Two cautions complete the picture. First, “constructed” does not mean “fake” in the sense of a fraud perpetrated on a gullible public: myth-making of this kind was the normal technology by which Greek cities thought about themselves, and the Athenians who promoted Theseus also genuinely worshipped him, as the next section shows. Second, Theseus never displaced Heracles in cult the way he did in Athenian civic imagery; Heracles kept his Attic shrines, and Theseus himself, in the myth, was said to have rededicated most of his own precincts to Heracles on his return from the underworld, keeping only four (Plutarch, Theseus 35.2, citing Philochorus). The rivalry was real but it was a rivalry of emphasis and patronage, conducted by festivals, buildings, and bones. VII. Cimon, Skyros, and the Bones of Theseus The promotion of Theseus reached its most concrete act in 476/5 BCE . After the Persian Wars, Athens — now head of the Delian League — consulted Delphi, and the Pythia instructed the Athenians to bring home the bones of Theseus from the island of Skyros, where the hero, exiled from Athens in the myth, had been killed by King Lycomedes, and to bury and guard them honourably in Athens. The general Cimon , son of Miltiades, conquered Skyros from its Dolopian inhabitants in the League's early campaigns (Thucydides 1.98 records the conquest and enslavement) and, in the story told by Plutarch in both the Life of Theseus (36) and the Life of Cimon (8), set himself to find the grave. The account that follows is Plutarch's, in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb translation, and it is quoted, not paraphrased, so that the reader can see exactly what kind of evidence a hero's relic was. “Cimon took the island… and being ambitious to discover the grave of Theseus, saw an eagle in a place where there was the semblance of a mound, pecking, as he says, and tearing up the ground with his talons. By some divine ordering he comprehended the meaning of this and dug there, and there was found a coffin of a man of extraordinary size, a bronze spear lying by its side, and a sword.” — Plutarch, Life of Theseus 36.1–2, trans. Bernadotte Perrin (Loeb Classical Library) Plutarch continues (36.2, in Perrin's translation, paraphrased only in the connective tissue here): the relics were carried to Athens on Cimon's trireme and received “with splendid processions and sacrifices, as though Theseus himself were returning to his city”, and the hero was laid to rest “in the heart of the city, near the present gymnasium”, where his tomb became “a sanctuary and place of refuge for runaway slaves and all men of low estate who are afraid of men in power, since Theseus was a champion and helper of such during his life”. The chief festival, the Theseia , was celebrated on the eighth day of the month Pyanepsion, the anniversary in the myth of Theseus' return from Crete, and Theseus received honours on the eighth day of every month.
