Two Poems, Three Kinds of Object Every other article in this hub treats a poem as a window: through the Theogony we look at the gods' generations, through the epics we look at heroes, their cults, and their cities. This article turns the glass around and looks at the window itself. Its subjects are two poems — the Iliad , 15,693 lines in twenty-four books, and the Odyssey , 12,110 lines in twenty-four books, both in dactylic hexameter, both attributed by antiquity to a singer named Homer — considered not as stories but as texts : physical and institutional objects with a manufacture, a transmission, and an editorial history longer than that of any other works in European literature. The tales themselves are told elsewhere in this hub — the war and its aftermath in The Trojan Cycle , the homecoming hero in Odysseus — and the Homeric Question is sketched, from the heroes' side, in Heroes and Epic , Sections XI–XIII, to which this article is the full companion. What follows is the textual treatment that sketch promised. The organising distinction of the article should be stated at once, because every confusion in the two-hundred-year argument about Homer comes from collapsing it. A Homeric poem is three different kinds of object, and a fact true of one is not automatically true of the others. 1 · THE POEM AS EVENT A performance: a singer, an audience, an occasion — a feast, a festival, a competition. In this mode the poem has no fixed wording. It exists the way a jazz standard exists, as a story and a technique, realised afresh each time. Most of the poems' prehistory, and the whole of their formulaic technique (Sections IV–VI), belongs to this mode. 2 · THE POEM AS TEXT A written object: letters on papyrus, then parchment, then paper, then print. In this mode the poem has a wording that can be copied, miscopied, compared, edited, and argued about line by line. The fixation of the poems in writing, the Alexandrian editions, and the medieval manuscripts (Sections X–XIII) belong to this mode. 3 · THE POEM AS INSTITUTION A social fact: the schoolbook of the Greek world, the syllabus of rhetoric, the quarry of moral examples, the text that had to be explained — by allegory when its gods embarrassed its readers. Canonisation, schooling, and the Roman answer to Homer (Sections XIV–XV) belong to this mode. WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS “Who wrote the Iliad ?” has three different answers depending on the mode: a tradition of singers (event), an unknown chain of scribes and editors (text), and the Greek educational system that decided this poem, above all others, would be preserved (institution). Scholarship goes wrong when it demands one answer do the work of all three. A note on dates, since this article will give many. The dating debate is a debate , and it is reported as one throughout. The conventional position places the monumental crystallisation of the two poems in the later eighth century BCE — the Iliad first, commonly somewhere in the range c. 750–700 BCE , the Odyssey somewhat later, with responsible estimates for its final shaping running into the early seventh century. The margins matter: linguistic arguments have placed the Iliad as early as the mid-eighth century and its fixation as late as the sixth; M. L. West argued for a single Iliad -poet working around the middle of the seventh century (Section IX). What is being dated, in any of these proposals, is a crystallisation — the moment when a fluid tradition hardened into something like our poems — not the tradition's materials, which are demonstrably older, in places centuries older, than any date proposed for the poems themselves. Herodotus, our earliest external witness, placed Homer and Hesiod “not more than four hundred years” before his own time — around 850 BCE by his arithmetic — which tells us that by the fifth century the poets were already figures of a founding past whose date had to be guessed. We are still guessing, with better instruments and the same absence of documents. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — A. T. Murray's Loeb translations of the Iliad (1924) and Odyssey (1919), and Benjamin Jowett's translation of Plato's Republic — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient or modern author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. Line references are to the standard numeration of the Greek text. One more preliminary. The two poems were not, in antiquity, the whole of “Homer.” The name attracted attributions the way a magnet attracts filings: the poems of the Epic Cycle, the Homeric Hymns , the comic Margites , the mock-epic Battle of Frogs and Mice all travelled under it at one time or another, and ancient scholars already disputed the attributions. The Iliad and Odyssey are the two poems whose Homeric authorship no ancient critic seriously withdrew — though a small Hellenistic school, the chorizontes , the “separators”, argued they were by different poets, a position whose ghost still walks in Section IX. When this article says “the Homeric epics”, it means these two, and the question of what their shared name is worth is part of its subject. II. The Iliad as Architecture: A Few Weeks Around a Wrath The Iliad is not the story of the Trojan War. It is the story of a few weeks in the war's tenth year, cut out of the whole with a precision that is itself the poem's first lesson in what kind of object it is. The war's beginning — the judgement of Paris, the abduction of Helen, the gathering at Aulis — is never narrated; it is presupposed, recalled in speeches, present as the audience's prior knowledge. The war's end — the wooden horse, the sack of Troy, the deaths of Achilles and Paris — is never narrated either; it is foreshadowed, prophesied inside the poem by dying men and knowing gods, and left to other poems of the Cycle to tell. What the Iliad narrates is an episode, and it announces the episode, not the war, as its subject in its first word: mēnin , wrath. “The wrath sing, goddess, of Peleus' son, Achilles, that destructive wrath which brought countless woes upon the Achaeans, and sent forth to Hades many valiant souls of heroes, and made them themselves spoil for dogs and every bird; thus the plan of Zeus came to fulfillment, from the time when first they parted in strife Atreus' son, king of men, and brilliant Achilles.” — HOMER, ILIAD 1.1–7, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1924) The proem is a table of contents compressed into seven lines. The poem's subject is a single emotion and its consequences: Achilles, dishonoured by Agamemnon's seizure of his prize Briseis, withdraws from the fighting and asks his mother Thetis to persuade Zeus to let the Trojans win until the Achaeans learn his worth. The “plan of Zeus” that the proem names is that arrangement, and the poem is the working-out of its cost. The narrated time is short — some fifty days by the usual reckoning of the poem's internal chronology, with the great mass of the action, the battles in which the Achaeans are driven back to their ships, Patroclus enters the fight and is killed, and Achilles returns in fury to kill Hector, concentrated into a handful of days in the middle. Around that narrow spine the poem builds the widest possible frame: because the fighting pauses, advances, and wheels across the whole plain, and because gods, councils, catalogues, embassies, games, and funerals fill the intervals, the episode comes to contain a whole world — a society at war, viewed entire, inside a story about one man's anger. The Shape in Books The twenty-four books (on the division itself, an editorial artefact, see Section XII) fall into movements a reader can hold in the mind. Books 1–9 : the quarrel and the withdrawal; the great Catalogue of Ships in Book 2, which musters the whole Achaean host and the Trojan allies as if the war were beginning, though it is ending; the duel of Paris and Menelaus and the meeting of Hector and Andromache (Books 3 and 6), which show what the war is about and what it costs at home; the long first day of battle; and in Book 9 the embassy to Achilles — Odysseus, Phoenix, and Ajax pleading with him to accept Agamemnon's gifts and return — which he refuses, in the poem's most famous speech, on grounds that go beyond the quarrel: no wealth, he says, is worth his life. Books 11–17 : the second great battle, in which the Achaean champions fall wounded one by one, the wall is breached, the ships themselves are fired, and Patroclus — Achilles' companion, wearing Achilles' armour — turns the battle, kills Sarpedon, and is killed by Hector with Apollo's help. Books 18–22 : Achilles, grief displacing wrath at the Achaeans with wrath at Hector, receives new armour from Hephaestus — its shield, described at length in Book 18, carries an image of the whole world of peace and war — is reconciled with Agamemnon, and drives the Trojans to their walls, where Hector, alone outside them, faces him and dies. Books 23–24 : the funeral games for Patroclus, in which the Achaean host reassembles as a society of contests and prizes; and Book 24, in which Priam, guided by Hermes, crosses the battlefield by night to ransom his son's body, and the two enemies — the killer and the father — weep together in Achilles' tent. The poem ends not with a death but with a funeral: Hector's burial, and a truce. THE WRATH, IN FOUR PHASES Wrath at Agamemnon (Books 1–9) · wrath displaced and refused , while the cost mounts (9–16) · wrath at Hector , grief turned outward (18–22) · wrath spent , in the ransom scene where Achilles recognises his own father in Priam (24). The emotion announced in line 1 is the plot's engine and its subject of study. RING COMPOSITION, AT THE LARGEST SCALE Book 1 opens with a father, Chryses, coming to ransom his child and being refused; Book 24 closes with a father, Priam, coming to ransom his child and being received. The frame is exact, and it is the Unitarians' oldest exhibit (Section VIII): whoever or whatever made this poem, its first and last movements were designed against each other. WHAT THE POEM EXCLUDES No judgement of Paris, no horse, no sack, no death of Achilles — the war's famous furniture is present only as memory and prophecy. The exclusions are the design: the poem takes the war's whole meaning and declines to narrate the war. THE CATALOGUE OF SHIPS (2.484–877) A muster-list of contingents, commanders, and ship-counts for both armies — the poem's most overtly traditional, least narrative block, and for the Analysts a prime candidate for an originally independent piece. Its geography has been argued over for a century as evidence for the tradition's Bronze Age memories; its presence, whatever its origin, shows the monumental poem absorbing a list the way a cathedral absorbs a Roman wall. The architecture matters for the textual question because it is the strongest evidence on one side of it. A poem of 15,693 lines whose first and last books mirror each other, whose central refusal (Book 9) is prepared in Book 1 and answered in Book 19, whose hero's death is everywhere prophesied and nowhere shown, does not look like an accidental accumulation. How that design is compatible with the poem's equally demonstrable making out of inherited, formulaic materials is the problem Sections V–IX work through. III. The Odyssey as Architecture: A Return Organised Around Recognition The Odyssey is built on the opposite plan. Where the Iliad narrows ten years of war into weeks around one emotion, the Odyssey takes a ten-year homecoming — the nostos of Odysseus from Troy to Ithaca — and narrates only its final phase directly, some forty days of story-time, folding the ten years of wandering into a tale the hero tells about himself, in the middle of the poem, to hosts who have asked who he is. And where the Iliad 's first word names its subject, the Odyssey 's first word names its man — and then withholds his name for a hundred and fifty lines more of story, as if the poem were already practising its governing device: this is a poem about identity, and identity in it is something disclosed, tested, and recognised, never simply stated. “Tell me, O Muse, of the man of many devices, who wandered full many ways after he had sacked the sacred citadel of Troy. Many were the men whose cities he saw and whose mind he learned, aye, and many the woes he suffered in his heart upon the sea, seeking to win his own life and the return of his comrades. Yet even so he saved not his comrades, though he desired it sore, for through their own blind folly they perished — fools, who devoured the kine of Helios Hyperion; but he took from them the day of their returning. Of these things, goddess, daughter of Zeus, beginning where thou wilt, tell thou even unto us.” — HOMER, ODYSSEY 1.1–10, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1919) The epithet Murray renders “of many devices” is polytropos — of many turns, many ways, many selves — and modern translators' divergent renderings of that one word (Lattimore's “man of many ways”, Fagles's “man of twists and turns”, Emily Wilson's “complicated man”, in their well-known versions) are a first, miniature lesson in this article's closing theme: even the most stable text in the world arrives in a modern language only through an editor's and a translator's judgement. The proem, like the Iliad 's, is a programme. The hero is defined by two activities — seeing cities and learning minds, suffering and seeking to save — and by one failure, the loss of every companion, which the poem assigns at once to the companions' own folly. The whole poem is the expansion of those ten lines. The Shape in Books The Odyssey runs two plots in parallel and joins them late. Books 1–4, the Telemachy : Ithaca without its king — Penelope besieged by suitors who feast in the hall and court her on the assumption that Odysseus is dead; Telemachus, the son who was an infant when his father sailed, sent by Athena on a journey to Pylos and Sparta to seek news, a journey that is also his education into his father's world; the suitors plot to ambush him on his return. Odysseus does not appear. Books 5–8 : the hero at last, released from Calypso's island by divine order, shipwrecked by Poseidon, washed ashore among the Phaeacians, where — still unnamed — he hears a singer sing of Troy, and weeps, and is asked who he is. Books 9–12, the Apologoi : Odysseus answers with the wanderings told in the first person — the Lotus-Eaters, the Cyclops, Circe, the descent to the dead, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the cattle of the Sun — the poem's most famous episodes, all of them a tale within the tale, whose teller is the tradition's most accomplished liar, a fact the poem itself underlines. Books 13–24 : Ithaca, in disguise. Athena lands him home; the second half of the poem is a long, tightening sequence of recognitions , each one earned and each one different: by the swineherd Eumaeus he is not recognised but sheltered; by Telemachus he reveals himself, by design; by his old dog Argus he is recognised instantly, and the dog dies; by the nurse Eurycleia he is recognised by the scar on his thigh, and silenced; by Penelope he is tested — the trial of the bow, the slaughter of the suitors, and then her own counter-test, the secret of the immovable bed built around a living olive tree, by which she makes him prove that he is himself. The poem ends with the recognition by his father Laertes and Athena's imposition of peace on the suitors' kin. BOOKS 1–4 THE TELEMACHY Ithaca in the king's absence; the suitors in the hall; Telemachus' journey to Pylos and Sparta. The hero is present only as a question: is he alive, and what would his return mean? BOOKS 5–8 THE PHAEACIAN BOOKS Calypso releases Odysseus; the raft, the storm, Scheria. An unnamed guest hears his own deeds sung by Demodocus and weeps — the poem's portrait of what epic does to the man it is about. BOOKS 9–12 THE APOLOGOI The wanderings in the hero's own voice: Cyclops, Circe, the dead, the Sirens, the cattle of the Sun. Ten years folded into four books of first-person tale — told, the poem reminds us, by a man famed for tales that are not true. BOOKS 13–24 ITHACA: THE RECOGNITIONS Disguise, testing, and disclosure, person by person: Telemachus, Argus, Eurycleia, the bow contest, the suitors' slaughter, Penelope's test of the bed, Laertes. The poem's second half answers its first word: the man of many turns is known, at last, by the one turn that cannot be counterfeited. Set the two architectures side by side and the pairing that antiquity already felt becomes visible. The Iliad is centripetal: everything is drawn into the gravity of one emotion in one place. The Odyssey is centrifugal and then homebound: its hero is scattered across the whole sea of the world and gathered back, person by person, token by token. One poem is organised around a wrath; the other around a recognition — around the question of how you know that the stranger at the door is who he claims to be. That second question, the reader will notice, is also the question this article asks about the poems themselves. The Odyssey is, among other things, a poem about identifying a much-travelled, much-retold, disguised original. Its scholars have been doing to it, for two thousand years, exactly what Penelope does to Odysseus. IV. The Language No One Spoke: The Epic Kunstsprache Open either poem at any line and you are reading a language that was never anyone's mother tongue. Homeric Greek — the epic dialect — is an artificial poetic language, a Kunstsprache (the German term, “art-language”, is standard in the scholarship), whose base is the Ionic Greek of the eastern Aegean, but which preserves, layered into it, forms from Aeolic Greek, archaisms older than either dialect, and occasional traces reaching back toward the Greek of the Bronze Age. No city spoke it. No audience, even in the eighth century BCE, used it to buy bread. It existed for one purpose: to sing hexameters in. Deborah Steiner's Cambridge introduction to the Odyssey , consulted for this article, puts the point in the form this archive adopts: no Greek ever spoke the language that Homer and his characters use; the poet composed in an artificial idiom, an amalgam reflecting the successive stages through which the oral tradition had passed, from the late Bronze Age down to about 700 BCE. The amalgam was not a defect or an accident. It did three kinds of work at once, and Steiner's summary, paraphrased here, names all three. First, metrical utility : a singer composing in the strict dactylic hexameter needs, for many ideas, more than one word-shape — a long form and a short form, a form beginning with a vowel and one beginning with a consonant — and the mixed dialect supplied doubles and triples for the same notion, each fitting a different slot in the line. Where the spoken language had levelled two forms into one, the epic language kept both, because the metre needed both. Second, Panhellenic portability : a language belonging to no one city could be sung in every city without sounding foreign or parochial; the Kunstsprache is the linguistic form of the Panhellenism described in Heroes and Epic — epic shedding local peculiarity as it travels. Third, elevation : the very artificiality and archaic colouring of the diction set the heroic world at a distance from the audience's everyday speech, the way a liturgical language sets worship at a distance from conversation. The heroes sound older than the listeners because, linguistically, they are. The Ghost Letter: Digamma The single most telling fossil in the language is a letter that is not there. Early Greek possessed a consonant, the w -sound written with the letter digamma (ϝ), which Ionic Greek lost early and which the transmitted text of Homer nowhere writes. Yet in a great many lines the metre behaves as if the sound were still present: a vowel that should shorten before a following vowel does not shorten, a syllable that should be light scans heavy, precisely where a word — wanax , “lord”; woinos , “wine”; wergon , “work” — once began with the lost consonant. The eighteenth-century scholar Richard Bentley first argued systematically that the missing letter explained the anomalies, and the argument has held: the tradition preserved, in the rhythm of its phrases, the ghost of a sound its singers' own dialect had ceased to pronounce. A written composition by a single eighth-century author, inventing freely, would have no reason to respect a consonant nobody could hear. A tradition of phrases handed down, fitted to the metre, and conserved because they worked, has every reason. The digamma is the Kunstsprache's certificate of age: proof, inside the language itself, that parts of the poems' verbal fabric are older — much older — than the poems. Layer in the language What it is Why it is there Ionic base The dialect of the eastern Aegean islands and coast, the tradition's last home before fixation The poems crystallised in an Ionic-speaking milieu; the base layer is the youngest Aeolic forms Words and endings from the neighbouring Aeolic dialect, kept beside their Ionic equivalents Either an earlier Aeolic phase of the tradition or long contact between the two dialect areas — the question is debated; the forms themselves are metrical alternatives the singer needs Archaisms Old endings, uncontracted vowels, obsolete words (the epic glossai that already needed glossaries in antiquity) Fossilised inside formulae whose metrical shape protected them from modernisation The digamma's ghost Metrical effects of a lost w -sound, unwritten in the text Phrases coined while the sound was alive, transmitted by ear long after Ionic speakers dropped it Attic overlay A thin later colouring in the transmitted forms The text's centuries in Athens and in Attic-writing scriptoria (Sections X and XIII) — the youngest layer of all, and a textual, not a compositional, fact This is why the language is evidence and not merely colour. A literary dialect that no one spoke, stocked with doublets no single speaker would maintain, haunted by a letter no copyist wrote, is not the sort of thing an author invents at a desk. It is the sort of thing a profession accumulates over centuries — a singers' technology, refined generation by generation for a single task. The next section takes that technology apart at the level of the individual line. V. Formula and Type-Scene: How the Line Is Built “Oral-formulaic” is the most used and least pictured term in Homeric studies. This section pictures it. It names the two mechanisms — the formula at the scale of the phrase, and the type-scene (Lord's theme ) at the scale of the episode — and shows each at work in passages any reader can check. The Formula, and the Epithet System Milman Parry's definition of the formula, as standardly cited from his published work and repeated in every account since, is: a group of words which is regularly employed under the same metrical conditions to express a given essential idea . The clearest instance is the noun-epithet combination. Achilles is “swift-footed” even when he is sitting in his tent refusing to move — which, for nine books, he is. Odysseus is “much-enduring” and “of many devices”; Dawn is “rosy-fingered” at every arrival; the sea is “wine-dark”; Hera is “white-armed” and “ox-eyed” in different metrical positions. A reader meeting these phrases for the first time in a modern novel would call them repetitive. Parry's demonstration — the argument of his Paris theses of 1928 — was that they form a system , and that the system has two properties no individual stylist's habits explain. The first property is economy , or thrift. For a given character, in a given grammatical case, in a given metrical slot in the line, the tradition normally keeps exactly one formula. If a singer needs Achilles as the subject of a sentence in the last part of the hexameter, one phrase is ready; if he needs him in another case or another slot, a different single phrase is ready for that. The stock is a fitted toolkit: near-complete coverage of the common needs, with almost no duplication. No poet composing in writing rations himself this way — a writer can pause, revise, and vary. A tradition of singers composing at performance speed must ration itself this way, because a choice between two equivalent phrases is a hesitation the metre does not forgive. The second property is extension : the system is too large, too consistent, and too interlocking to be one man's stock. It covers gods, heroes, ships, sea, earth, speaking, dying, arming, feasting — the whole furniture of the heroic world — in thousands of phrases, many of them demonstrably old (the digamma's ghost haunts the formulae above all). Parry's conclusion, in its careful form, was not that Homer was unoriginal. It was that the medium is traditional: Homer composes the way a jazz musician improvises — in a language of ready phrases whose readiness is the precondition of the performance's speed, and whose traditional character says nothing, by itself, about the quality of what a master does with it. Figure Characteristic formulae (Murray's renderings) What the system shows Achilles “swift-footed Achilles”; “brilliant Achilles”; “Peleus' son Achilles” Different formulae for different cases and slots; the running epithet is used while he sits out the war — the phrase belongs to the name, not to the moment Odysseus “much-enduring brilliant Odysseus”; “of many devices”; “sacker of cities” A hero defined by endurance and versatility gets a whole family of formulae, distributed by metre Hera “white-armed Hera”; “ox-eyed queen Hera” Two formulae, one goddess: the famous apparent exception, resolved by position — each occupies a different metrical slot, so the economy holds Dawn “rosy-fingered Dawn”; the full line “when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared” A whole-line formula: the singer's standard way to start a new day, used scores of times across both poems Speech introductions “Then answered him…”; “and to him spoke…”, completed by the addressee's name-formula Half-line frames with interchangeable name-blocks: the clearest view of the system's joinery — frame plus fitted piece, assembled at speed The Type-Scene: Arming, Feasting, Sacrifice What the formula is to the phrase, the type-scene is to the episode: a recurrent action with a fixed sequence of elements, which the singer expands or contracts to fit the occasion. Walter Arend's 1933 study of the “typical scenes” in Homer catalogued them — arrivals, departures, sacrifices, feasts, dreams, assemblies, armings — and Lord, developing the same observation from the South Slavic material, called the unit a theme . The textbook case is the arming scene . Four times in the Iliad a hero arms in full, and the sequence does not vary: greaves first, then the corselet, then sword, shield, helmet, and last the spear — Paris in Book 3 (3.328–338), Agamemnon in Book 11 (11.15–55), Patroclus in Book 16 (16.130–154), Achilles in Book 19 (19.364–424). What varies is the weight the scene is given, and the variation is the meaning. Paris arms briefly, in the basic sequence — he is dressing for a duel he will not finish. Agamemnon's arming swells to three times the length, each piece described, because the king is arming for his day of glory. Patroclus arms in Achilles' armour through the standard sequence — and then reaches the spear, the Pelian ash spear that only Achilles can wield, and leaves it behind: the one deviation from the pattern, placed exactly where a practised audience would feel it, tells them the impersonation will fail before a blow is struck. Achilles' own arming, finally, is interrupted and expanded by the description of the new shield itself, the poem's largest single object. The type-scene is thus not a shortcut that flattens the poetry. It is an instrument of emphasis: the pattern creates the expectation, and the singer plays meaning off the pattern — exactly as a congregation hears the one changed word in a familiar liturgy. The feast works the same way at smaller scale. Again and again the poems mark a meal with the same sequence — the animal slaughtered and butchered, the thigh-pieces wrapped in fat and burned for the gods with wine poured over them, the rest roasted on spits, the company eating “until desire for food and drink is satisfied”, in the recurring formula — and the sequence does social work each time: a feast is how this world ratifies an arrival, seals a truce, honours a guest, buries a dead man. When the suitors feast in Odysseus' hall, the same elements recur in a house where every obligation of the feast — the host's right, the guest's duty — is inverted, and the audience that knows the pattern knows the verdict before the bow is strung. A lay reader who has grasped these two mechanisms — the formula filling the line, the type-scene filling the episode, both inherited, both variable under a master's hand — has grasped what “oral-formulaic” means concretely. The next question is how anyone knows that living singers actually work this way. That knowledge has a date, a place, and a recording machine. VI. Parry and Lord: The Singers of Tales The argument so far rests on inference from the texts. Milman Parry (1902–1935) refused to leave it there. Having demonstrated, in his 1928 Paris theses on the traditional epithet and in the papers that followed, that Homeric diction is a formulaic system of a scale and thrift implying generations of traditional singers, he set out to test the implication against a living tradition: if the theory was right, somewhere in the modern world singers should still be composing long heroic songs in performance, by formula and theme, without writing — and their practice should illuminate Homer's at every point where the texts are ambiguous. The place he chose, following the earlier work of the Slovene scholar Matija Murko, was the mountain country of Yugoslavia — Bosnia, Herzegovina, Montenegro, and the Sanjak — where Muslim and Christian singers called guslari , accompanying themselves on the one-stringed gusle , still sang heroic songs of the frontier wars in coffee houses and at weddings and Ramadan evenings. In the field seasons of 1933–1935 , Parry, with his assistant Albert B. Lord (1912–1991) and the local singer and fixer Nikola Vujnović, recorded hundreds of songs on aluminium discs with a specially built recording machine, and took down many more by dictation — building the collection now held at Harvard as the Milman Parry Collection of Oral Literature. The fieldwork was designed as an experiment with controls. The same singer was recorded singing the same song on different occasions, and the versions compared. Singers were asked whether they repeated a song “word for word, without changing anything” — the claim oral singers characteristically make — and the recordings showed what that claim means in practice: the story is held constant with great fidelity, the themes recur in their order, the formulae recur by the thousand, and the wording, the length, and the degree of ornament vary with the audience, the occasion, and the singer's form on the day. A song sung in fifteen minutes for a restless coffee house could be sung in an hour for a patient patron. The song is the same song. It is never the same text. That distinction — identity at the level of story and technique, multiformity at the level of wording — is the fieldwork's central finding, and everything in the modern Homeric settlement is built on it. // AVDO MEĐEDOVIĆ // The tradition's master, a farmer and butcher from Bijelo Polje in Montenegro, was recorded and dictated to in 1935. His Wedding of Smailagić Meho runs to over 12,000 lines — Odyssey length — and his dictated songs are longer and more ornate than his sung ones, because dictation gave him time. Lord treated Avdo as the fieldwork's “Homer”: proof that a single non-literate singer, working in a mature tradition, can sustain monumental scale. Parry died in December 1935, in a hotel accident in Los Angeles, at thirty-three, with the great comparative book unwritten. Lord returned to Yugoslavia in 1935 and again in the 1950s, re-recording singers Parry had recorded — some of them singing the same songs twenty years on, to the same claim of word-for-word fidelity and the same measurable variation — and in 1960 published The Singer of Tales , the book that set out the theory whole: how a singer learns (first listening and absorbing, then applying the technique to songs of his own, then singing before a critical audience); what the formula and the theme are and how they interlock; how composition-in-performance actually proceeds, neither memorisation nor free improvisation but fluency in a specialised grammar of song; and what follows for Homer. x: THE HOMERIC HYMNS Delos · Delphi · Eleusis · Olympus · c. 700–400 BCE and after // THIRTY-THREE HYMNS :: ONE NAME :: NO AUTHOR // Thirty-three poems in epic hexameters, addressed to the gods, transmitted under the name of Homer and written by nobody we can name. Between the great epics and the lyric age they stand as the Greek world's other archaic scripture: the place where a god, rather than a hero, gets a birth, a character, and a life-story. This article treats the corpus as a corpus — its making, its narrow escape from loss, its four great narrative hymns and its twenty-nine shorter ones, and the editions in which a modern reader can hold it. The Corpus: Thirty-Three Hymns Under One Name The Homeric Hymns are a collection of thirty-three poems in dactylic hexameter, each addressed to a god or goddess, preserved together in the medieval manuscripts under the title Homērou hymnoi — “Homer's hymns.” They range in length from three lines to five hundred and eighty. Four of them — to Demeter, to Apollo, to Hermes, to Aphrodite — are substantial narrative poems, among the most important mythological texts in Greek. One, to Dionysos, survives only as the tail of a poem whose body is lost. The remaining twenty-eight are short pieces, most of them under sixty lines, several under ten: invocations, portraits, miniature myths, festival pieces. Taken together the thirty-three run to some 2,345 lines in the standard numeration — roughly a fifth of the Odyssey — and they were composed, on the arguments set out in Section X, across several centuries, by many hands, in many places. The corpus is an anthology, not a work. The first discipline this article observes is the one its title already enforces. “Homeric” is an ancient classification, not an authorship claim. The hymns are Homeric in the sense A. W. Verrall put in 1894, in the remark Nicholas Richardson's standard commentary still quotes: the collection is Homeric in the only useful sense the word can bear — it has come down labelled “Homer” from the earliest times of Greek book-literature. The poems share with the Iliad and Odyssey their metre, their artificial epic dialect, and much of their formulaic stock; on that kinship see The Homeric Epics , Sections IV–V. Antiquity, which attributed to Homer everything written in that manner — the Epic Cycle, the comic Margites , the mock-heroic Battle of Frogs and Mice — attributed the hymns to him too, and the earliest surviving reference to any of them, Thucydides in the fifth century BCE, quotes one as Homer's without a flicker of doubt (Section II). No modern scholar defends the attribution. The hymns are anonymous, and their anonymity is not a gap in our knowledge to be apologised for: it is the normal condition of archaic Greek song, in which the tradition, not the individual, was the author of record. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations consulted for this article — H. G. Evelyn-White's Loeb translation of the hymns (1914) and Benjamin Jowett's translation of Thucydides — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. Line references are to the standard numeration of the Greek text as printed in the editions discussed in Section XI. What kind of thing is a “hymn” here? The Greek word hymnos in its archaic use means a song of praise addressed to a god — as distinct from the epic narrative whose subject is heroes, and from the later literary hymns of Callimachus, which are book-poems written for readers. The Homeric hymns stand at the head of the Greek hymn tradition and are built, in their developed form, on a three-part frame that the handbooks standardly describe. First an invocation : the singer calls on the Muse or names the god, often with the god's epithets, birthplace, and parentage — the god's identifying dossier, compressed into the opening lines. Then a central section of praise , which in the long hymns expands into full narrative: the god's birth, deeds, acquisitions, and the winning of his or her province and honours. Then a close : a farewell to the god — chaire , “hail, rejoice” — a prayer for favour or victory in the contest, and, characteristically, a promise to pass on to another song. That closing promise is the corpus's signature, and Section II takes it up: it is the fossil of the hymns' original function. THE LONG HYMNS Four narrative poems: to Hermes (580 lines), Apollo (546), Demeter (495), and Aphrodite (293) — preceded in the collection by the fragment of a fifth, to Dionysos, which must once have been of comparable scale. These are treated one by one in Sections IV–VII. THE SHORT HYMNS Twenty-eight pieces from 3 to 59 lines: second and third hymns to gods already honoured at length (Dionysos three times in all, Aphrodite three times, Hermes, Artemis, Athena, Hestia, the Dioscuri twice each), and single short hymns to gods the long poems pass by — Ares, Pan, Helios, Selene, Earth. Surveyed, with the full table of the thirty-three, in Section VIII. WHAT THE CORPUS IS NOT Not a liturgy. The hymns were not, so far as the evidence shows, the service-book of any cult: they are festival and contest pieces, sung by professional singers, and their relation to actual worship is the indirect one examined in Section IX. Literary myth and cult practice are kept distinct throughout this article, as throughout this hub. THE THIRTY-FOURTH PIECE The manuscripts append to the hymns a short piece To Hosts ( Eis xenous ), four lines reminding the hearer that hospitality is a sacred duty watched by Zeus. It is not a hymn and is not counted among the thirty-three; editors print it as an epigram of the collection. Its presence is itself evidence — a professional singer's pointed parting word to the household that was about to feed him. The corpus's position in this hub should be stated plainly. Elsewhere the hymns appear as witnesses raided for a story: the Mysteries article draws on the Hymn to Demeter for the charter myth of Eleusis, the Olympians article on several hymns for the gods' portraits, and Descents on the Demeter hymn's geography of the underworld. This article is the corpus's own home: the hymns treated, as the epics are treated in their article, as texts — objects with a manufacture, a transmission that nearly failed, and an editorial history. Where a hymn's cult meaning is the point, the article says so and sends the reader to the article that treats it; the textual treatment stays here. II. Prooimia: Preludes Sung Before Epic The single most important ancient statement about the hymns is also the earliest reference to any of them. In the winter of 426/5 BCE the Athenians purified Delos and refounded its festival, and Thucydides, describing the old Ionian gathering on the island, proves its antiquity from Homer ( History 3.104). He quotes two passages of what we call the Hymn to Apollo — the Ionians in their long robes assembling for boxing, dance, and song (Hymn 3.146–150), and the praise of the Delian maidens' choir ending in the singer's self-portrait as the blind man of Chios (3.165–172) — and he introduces the first quotation with a generic label: the verses, he says, are “from the prooimion to Apollo” ( ek prooimiou Apollōnos ). Prooimion means a prelude: an opening piece sung before the main performance. Thucydides, our first witness, thus tells us three things at once — that the hymn circulated under Homer's name, that it was already old and authoritative in the fifth century, and that its kind was understood to be the prelude kind. “The blind old man of Chios' rocky isle.” — THE SINGER'S SELF-PORTRAIT, HYMN TO APOLLO 172, AS QUOTED BY THUCYDIDES 3.104, TRANS. BENJAMIN JOWETT The prelude function explains the corpus's most distinctive formal feature. Hymn after hymn ends with the same gesture: the singer bids the god farewell, asks for favour, and announces the transition — in paraphrase, “and I will remember you, and another song too.” The closing line of the Hymn to Demeter (495), of the Hymn to Apollo (546), and of the Hymn to Hermes (580) is that formula, and the Hymn to Aphrodite closes more explicitly still: having begun from the goddess, the singer will pass on to another song. Read as literature these endings are abrupt. Read as the working parts of a performance they are exact: the hymn was the singer's opening number, sung to the god of the festival or of the singer's choosing, after which the rhapsode passed to the main business of the day — the recitation of epic, his own or the tradition's, the Iliad and Odyssey and the other poems treated in The Homeric Epics . The god is honoured first, the audience warmed, the singer's voice and credentials displayed — the blind man of Chios passage is precisely a credential, a request to be remembered — and then the epic begins. Two cautions belong here, and the scholarship insists on both. First, the prelude theory fits the short hymns best: a five-line invocation to Athena is a plausible curtain-raiser, while a 580-line comic epic about Hermes is a strange warm-up for anything. The long hymns are better understood as festival and contest pieces in their own right — the main event of a rhapsode's appearance at a god's festival, competing for a prize — which grew out of the prelude form and kept its frame. Some scholars have accordingly proposed that parts of the short-hymn stock are excerpts: the invocation and close of longer hymns, cut down to prelude length by singers who needed the frame without the narrative. That is a hypothesis, labelled as such; it cannot be proved for any individual piece, but it explains the corpus's odd shape — many frames, few full bodies — better than any alternative. Second, the word prooimion in Thucydides is applied to one hymn; extending it to the whole collection, as Martin West does in the introduction to his Loeb edition — “the so-called Homeric Hymns are a collection of thirty-three such prooimia ”, in paraphrase of his formulation — is an inference from the closing formulae and the genre's shape, not a quotation of ancient testimony. The inference is strong and standardly made; it remains an inference. Rhapsodes and the Homeridae The singers who performed such pieces were rhapsodes : professionals who recited epic verse at festivals and contests, staff in hand, in competition for prizes — the class of performer described, from the texts' side, in The Homeric Epics , Section X. Around the name of Homer there had formed, by the sixth century BCE, a guild or clan of such performers, the Homeridae of Chios, who claimed descent from the poet and custody of his works. The guild matters to this corpus because one hymn, the Hymn to Apollo, is attached by an ancient source to a named member of it — Cynaethus of Chios — and because the hymn's own blind singer of Chios was read by antiquity as Homer himself, performing inside the Homeridae's home tradition. Section V takes up that tangle. Here it is enough to register the institutional fact: the hymns survive because a profession sang them, and the profession had a corporate interest in the name under which they travelled. Hesiod supplies the complementary picture from the singer's side. The proem of the Theogony — treated as a text in Theogony and the Succession Myth — is itself a hymn, to the Muses, over a hundred lines long, standing before a didactic epic exactly as a prooimion stands before a recitation; and the Works and Days opens with a shorter hymn to Zeus. The boundary between “hymn” and “epic” in archaic practice was thus a seam inside a performance, not a wall between kinds. The Homeric Hymns are what that seam looks like when the preludes are gathered up, written down, and preserved as a book. III. Transmission: A Narrow Survival The Iliad survives in hundreds of manuscripts and a blizzard of papyri; it was the schoolbook of the Greek world, and its transmission, traced in The Homeric Epics , Sections XI–XIII, is correspondingly broad and deep. The hymns had no such luck. They were nobody's schoolbook. They travelled as an appendix to Homer — copied in the company of the epics, the Battle of Frogs and Mice , the epigrams, and the fragments of Hesiod — and their whole medieval tradition hangs on a thread that this section follows from the archetype to the printed page. The account here follows the stemma as set out in the introduction to M. L. West's Loeb edition (2003), checked against the Allen–Halliday–Sikes commentary tradition. The Archetype and Its Two Branches All surviving manuscripts of the hymns are fifteenth-century copies, and all descend from a lost archetype whose text already bore the collection in its present order — an order that is itself a fact of the transmission, not of the poems' composition: somebody, at some date we cannot fix, gathered these thirty-three pieces into this sequence, and every copy we have inherits that act of gathering. From the archetype the tradition divides. On one side stands a lost hyparchetype, conventionally sigled Ψ (psi), probably of the twelfth or thirteenth century, from which twenty-eight manuscripts descend in three families. On the other side stands a single manuscript, sigled M , copied in the fifteenth century by the scholar-scribe Ioannes Eugenikos, probably in Constantinople sometime after 1439. Every other manuscript begins the collection at Hymn 3, to Apollo. M alone begins at Hymn 1. // THE 1777 DISCOVERY // M's modern history is the most famous accident in the hymns' survival. The codex reached Moscow — how, is not securely documented — and there, in 1777 , the German philologist Christian Friedrich Matthaei found it in the imperial archive; a later anecdote, repeated in the scholarship with varying confidence, places it in a barn among farm animals, and the anecdote is given here as anecdote, not as record. Matthaei's transcription reached David Ruhnken, whose editions of the Hymn to Demeter appeared in 1780 and, in the form that held, 1782. The codex itself later came to Leiden, where it now rests as Universiteitsbibliotheek BPG 33 H — the Codex Leidensis that was the Codex Mosquensis . The two names in the literature denote one book. What M uniquely preserves is the head of the collection. Its first hymn, to Dionysos, it preserves only in ruins: a gathering — a quinion, in West's account — had fallen out of the codex before it was copied or found, carrying away the body of the Dionysos hymn, so that only its last twenty-one lines stand on the page where the second hymn begins. And the second hymn is the Hymn to Demeter: 495 lines of major archaic poetry that survive in exactly one manuscript , unknown to the entire tradition — to antiquity after a point, to Byzantium, to the Renaissance, to the first printers — until 1777. The editio princeps of Homer, printed at Florence in 1488 by Demetrios Chalkokondyles, included the hymns as the Ψ tradition had them: beginning at Apollo. For nearly three centuries of print, the corpus that scholarship studied lacked its first two members. The Demeter hymn's arrival in 1782 was an event in European letters — it fed the Romantic rediscovery of Greek religion — and it rests, textually, on one fifteenth-century book and the care of its one modern finder. Damage Inside the Survivor Even M is not intact. One of its leaves — folio 35, in the modern study of the codex by Oliver Thomas ( Mnemosyne 68, 2015) — was already damaged in antiquity's aftermath: part of the leaf was lost, taking with it stretches of the Demeter hymn around lines 387–404, 437, and 462–479, and a later reader pasted in a repair sheet and inked in replacement text, partly over the original scribe's letters. Editors distinguish that repairing hand (siglum m ) from Eugenikos' own, and treat its supplements as what they are — an early reader's conjectures, some formulaic and plausible, none authoritative. The consequence deserves emphasis, because it is the kind of fact this hub exists to keep visible: at several points in one of the most-read religious poems of archaic Greece, the text in every modern edition is a repair, and the apparatus, not the page, is where the poem's true state can be seen. Lines are also missing or corrupt elsewhere in the hymn; Richardson's commentary (Section XI) marks the lacunae, and honest translations mark them too. The rest of the transmission is quieter. The Ψ families transmit Hymns 3–33 with the ordinary quota of scribal error and a thin scholia tradition — nothing like the Alexandrian commentary mass that attended the epics, for the hymns were never edited by Aristarchus' school with the same intensity, and no ancient commentary on them survives whole. What antiquity quoted, it quoted piecemeal: Thucydides' two passages of the Apollo hymn (Section II) are the prize exhibit, valuable precisely because they let editors check the medieval text of those lines against a fifth-century BCE witness — and the check shows small divergences, the ordinary drift of a text copied for a thousand years. The hymns' survival, in sum, is the opposite of the epics': narrow where theirs is broad, late where theirs is anciently attested, and at its head dependent on a single book found once, in one archive, in 1777. 5TH C. BCE THUCYDIDES QUOTES THE APOLLO HYMN The earliest surviving reference to any hymn: two passages of Hymn 3 quoted as Homer's prooimion to Apollo (Section II). 12TH–13TH C. THE Ψ HYPARCHETYPE The lost ancestor, on West's stemma, of the twenty-eight manuscripts that transmit Hymns 3–33 — the collection already lacking its head. AFTER 1439 M IS COPIED Ioannes Eugenikos writes the codex now Leiden BPG 33 H, the sole witness to Hymns 1 and 2; a gathering is already lost from its Dionysos hymn. 1488 THE FLORENCE PRINCEPS Demetrios Chalkokondyles prints Homer at Florence, hymns included — from Hymn 3 onward. The Demeter hymn remains unknown to print for almost three more centuries. 1777 · 1782 MATTHAEI FINDS M; RUHNKEN PRINTS DEMETER The Moscow discovery, and Ruhnken's edition of the Hymn to Demeter (1782, superseding his 1780 issue): the corpus recovers its head. 1936 · 2003 THE MODERN TEXTS Allen, Halliday & Sikes' Oxford edition and commentary (2nd ed. 1936); West's Loeb text and translation (2003). Section XI. IV. The Hymn to Demeter as Text The Hymn to Demeter ( Hymn 2, 495 lines ) is the collection's second poem and its most consequential survival. This hub's Mysteries article treats what the poem founded — its standing as the charter myth of Eleusis, the kykeon, Iambe's jests, the closing blessing on the initiated — and that cult reading is expressly left there. This section treats the poem as a made object: its date as argued, its architecture as built, and the underworld geography it assumes, with the narrative given in the summary the textual argument needs and no more. The Date, as Argued The hymn is conventionally dated to the late seventh or the sixth century BCE . The arguments, stated as arguments: its language and formulaic stock are of the same stratum as the epics' later layers and Hesiod's, which sets a broad archaic frame; it knows Eleusis as a place of local princes rather than as an Athenian state sanctuary, which most scholars take to precede, or to ignore, Athens' absorption of the cult — an argument from silence, and labelled as such whenever it is used; and it shows no trace of the Orphic and later theological developments that a Hellenistic pastiche would be expected to betray. N. J. Richardson's commentary (Oxford, 1974), the standard modern treatment, places the poem in that late-seventh-to-sixth-century window, and Richard Janko's statistical study of epic diction ( Homer, Hesiod and the Hymns , 1982) put the Demeter hymn earliest among the four long hymns on his linguistic measures. The window is a consensus range, not a date; Section X returns to the method and its limits. The Architecture: Four Movements The poem is built in four movements, and its architecture is the tightest of any long hymn — a story of a loss that empties heaven and earth, resolved only when the cosmos renegotiates the terms. It opens in mid-catastrophe: the proem names Demeter and her daughter in a single sentence that already contains the crime. “I begin to sing of rich-haired Demeter, awful goddess — of her and her trim-ankled daughter whom Aidoneus rapt away, given to him by all-seeing Zeus the loud-thunderer.” — HOMERIC HYMN TO DEMETER 1–3, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) First movement: the rape and the search (roughly lines 1–87). Persephone, gathering flowers with the daughters of Ocean — the narcissus, grown by Earth as a snare at Zeus's will, is the trap's centrepiece — is seized by Hades in his chariot as the earth splits open. Her cry reaches her mother. Demeter tears her headdress, casts off her dark veil, and searches land and sea for nine days, torches in her hands, tasting neither ambrosia nor nectar, never washing. Hecate, who heard the cry but saw nothing, meets her at dawn of the tenth day; together they go to Helios, who sees all things, and Helios tells the truth whole: Zeus gave the girl to his brother. The movement's engine is knowledge withheld and then granted — the poem's gods know, and the mother must find out. Second movement: Eleusis (roughly lines 87–302). Demeter, in anger at Zeus, withdraws from Olympus and wanders in disguise — an old woman past childbearing — to Eleusis, where she is taken into the house of Celeus as nurse to the infant Demophon. The episode's centre is the failed immortalising: anointed with ambrosia by day, hidden in the fire by night, the child is being burned free of mortality when his mother Metaneira spies and cries out, and the working breaks. The goddess stands revealed in radiance, rebukes the household's folly, and commands a temple and altar below the citadel, promising to teach her rites. As narrative this is the poem's human panel — grief, service, a mother's error answering a mother's loss — and as foundation it is the charter the Mysteries article expounds; here it is enough to mark its structural place: the goddess, robbed of her daughter, nearly makes a mortal child a god, and the failure turns her grief outward into institution. Third movement: the famine and the embassy (roughly lines 302–404). Seated in her new temple, Demeter makes a year “most terrible”: the earth will not sprout, the plough is dragged in vain, and mankind starves — which threatens the gods themselves, whose honours are fed by mortal sacrifice. The leverage is the poem's theology in one mechanism: the grain-goddess's grief is a strike that empties heaven's altars. Zeus sends Iris; Demeter refuses. He sends the whole company of the gods with gifts; she refuses them all, vowing never to let fruit rise until she sees her daughter. Zeus yields the only way left: Hermes goes down to Hades to bring Persephone up. Hades consents — and, smiling, gives his queen a pomegranate seed to eat, so that she cannot stay above forever. The underworld of this movement is the traditional house of Hades below the earth, reached by the messenger god and left by chariot; for the geography of Greek descents as a system, see Descents , where this hymn's version takes its place among the katabasis texts. Fourth movement: the settlement and the foundation (roughly lines 404–495). Mother and daughter meet in a recognition scene the poem plays at full emotional stretch — Persephone springs from the chariot, Demeter runs to her “like a maenad down the mountain,” in paraphrase of the simile — and then, in the embrace, asks the question on which the world turns: did you eat anything below? The pomegranate confessed, Zeus's settlement arrives by Rhea, the grandmothers' envoy: for a third part of the year Persephone will go down to darkness, for two parts she will stay above with her mother and the gods. Demeter restores the fruit to the Rhaian plain, teaches her mysteries to the Eleusinian princes — Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, Celeus are named — and returns to Olympus. The closing lines bless the mortal who has seen the rites and darken the lot of the uninitiated after death, and the singer signs off with the corpus's formula: he will remember the goddess, and another song too. A HYMN TO TWO GODDESSES West's introduction makes the point editors now standardly repeat: the poem is in substance a hymn to Demeter and Persephone, the presiding pair of Eleusis, and its narrative is the foundation myth of their Mysteries. The daughter is not a subplot; the poem's subject is the bond the rape broke and the settlement re-made on new terms. THE POMEGRANATE AS MECHANISM The seed is the plot's legal instrument: food eaten in the house of the dead binds the eater to the house. The poem states the rule through its working, not as doctrine — Persephone herself reports that Hades “secretly put in my mouth pomegranate-food, honey-sweet, and compelled me against my will,” in paraphrase — and the settlement's thirds of the year are its consequence. WHAT THE POEM DOES NOT SAY It never describes the rites it founds. The Mysteries' content was secret, and the hymn — a public, festival poem — keeps the secret perfectly: it gives the myth, the temple, the teachers, and the blessing, and of the drōmena themselves, nothing. The distinction between the charter myth, which is literature, and the cult practice, which is not recoverable from it, is the Mysteries article's standing caution, repeated here because this poem is where readers most often blur it. A TEXT WITH HOLES The poem we read is M's poem, repaired: the damaged folio (Section III) cuts into the reunion movement itself, and the supplements of the repairing hand stand in the text of lines around 387–404, 437, and 462–479. Where a translation prints those lines smooth, an editor has chosen the repair; the Greek page, honestly read, has gaps. V. The Hymn to Apollo: Two Hymns Joined at a Seam The Hymn to Apollo ( Hymn 3, 546 lines ) is the longest of the hymns after Hermes, the earliest attested (Section II), and the only one whose composite nature is visible to the naked eye. It falls into two halves that differ in subject, in geography, in the god they celebrate, and in the audience they address — and between them, at line 179, there is a join that scholarship since Ruhnken has treated as the seam where two hymns were stitched into one. The Allen–Sikes commentary's judgement, paraphrased, states the consensus the subsequent literature has refined but not overturned: the hymn in its present form reads as continuous, but the continuity lies only on the surface, and the abrupt transition at verse 179 cannot be missed. The Delian Half (Lines 1–178) The first half celebrates Apollo of Delos : the god of the island festival, of the bow, of music and the assembled Ionians. It opens with a theophany in the house of Zeus — Apollo enters Olympus with his bow, and the gods tremble and rise from their seats until Leto unstrings the weapon and seats her son — then turns to the birth. Leto, pregnant by Zeus and hounded by Hera's jealousy, wanders the Aegean seeking a land that will receive her son; the lands refuse, fearing the proud god who will scorn them. Little Delos, poor and rocky, accepts — after bargaining, in one of the hymn's most human passages, for a temple and honours, and exacting from Leto a great oath that Apollo will honour her above all islands. The birth follows: Hera detains Eileithyia, the birth-goddess, until Iris fetches her with promise of a golden necklace; the god is born, the goddesses wash and swaddle him, and — in the detail every account keeps — he takes not the breast but nectar and ambrosia from Themis, bursts his swaddling bands, and speaks at once, claiming the lyre, the bow, and the declaring of Zeus's will to men. The half closes with the Delian festival itself — the Ionians assembled, the maidens' choir that can mimic every voice — and the singer's farewell and self-portrait, the blind man of rocky Chios, quoted by Thucydides and quoted in Section II above. Then, at line 178, the singer takes leave. The poem has ended. The Pythian Half (Lines 179–546) Except that it begins again. Line 179 opens a second invocation — “How shall I hymn you who are so well hymned?” in paraphrase — and a second subject: Apollo of Delphi , the oracular god, and the founding of his shrine. The god strides from Olympus seeking a site for his oracle, passing the cities and springs of Boeotia; at Telphusa's spring he chooses his place and lays foundations, but the nymph, jealous for her own honours, deceives him into moving on to a wilder site below Parnassus. There he kills the monstrous she-dragon that ravaged the district — the serpent later tradition names Python, whose rotting ( pythesthai ) in the sun gives Pytho its name in the hymn's own etymology — and returns to punish Telphusa, stopping her spring with rocks. Then, lacking priests, he provides them by piracy of a benevolent kind: taking the shape of a dolphin — the delphis from which the hymn derives Delphinios and Delphi — he leaps aboard a Cretan merchant ship, terrifies the crew by his transformations and the ship's miraculous sailing, and brings them round to Crisa, Delphi's port, where he reveals himself and appoints them his ministers: they are to guard his temple, speak righteousness, and live, as he dryly promises, on the sacrifices of others. The hymn ends with his charge to them and the closing formula. Birth and choir have given way to foundation, dragon-slaying, and the institution of a priesthood: a different poem, for a different sanctuary, with a different Apollo. TWO GODS, ONE NAME The Delian Apollo is the Ionian festival god, archer and musician, born on an island sanctuary shared by a sea-going confederacy. The Pythian Apollo is the mainland oracular god, dragon-slayer and founder, whose priests are landsmen imported by sea. The hymn that joins them is a theological act: one Apollo, both shrines, each half validating the other. THE SEAM AT 179 The Delian half ends with a complete close — farewell to the god, the singer's sphragis, a prayer — and the Pythian half begins with a fresh invocation and a new question. Two closes and two openings in one poem are the formal signature of the join. Editors since Ruhnken print the division; the manuscripts know nothing of it. WHO JOINED THEM, AND WHEN Thucydides already knew the Delian passages as part of a hymn to Apollo in the fifth century BCE, and the Pythian half is certainly much older than Thucydides; the Allen–Sikes argument, paraphrased here, infers that the unity of the document extends back at least to the end of the fifth century. The join is therefore archaic or early classical, not a Byzantine editor's work. THE BLIND MAN OF CHIOS The sphragis at lines 165–172 — the singer asking the Delian maidens to remember him and to answer any future stranger that the sweetest singer is the blind man of Chios — was read by antiquity as Homer's self-portrait, and it is one of the root-texts of the blind-Homer tradition. Modern scholarship treats it as a rhapsode's signature within the Homeridae's tradition (below), not as biography of the epics' author. Cynaethus of Chios One ancient source names an author. A scholion on Pindar's second Nemean ode reports that the school of Cynaethus of Chios was prominent among the Homeridae and put out many compositions under Homer's name, and that Cynaethus himself composed the hymn to Apollo; the same notice dates his first recitation of the Homeric poems at Syracuse to the sixty-ninth Olympiad, 504–501 BCE. The notice is late, scholiastic, and uncorroborated, and this article reports it as such — a tradition, not a document. But it has proved unusually productive. Walter Burkert's well-known argument (in Arktouros , 1979) proposed that the combined hymn was made for a datable occasion: the double festival of Apollo held by Polycrates of Samos in 522 BCE , honouring Delian and Pythian Apollo together — precisely the two Apollos of the hymn's two halves — and that a Chian Homerid, Cynaethus, was the combining hand, joining a Delian hymn to a Pythian one for the festival that needed both. The proposal elegantly explains the join, the date fits the scholion's floruit within a generation, and M. L. West has argued in support of Cynaethus' authorship of the combined hymn. It remains a proposal: other scholars date the Delian half a century or more earlier and treat the join as anonymous and gradual. What is not in dispute is the shape of the evidence — two hymns, one seam, an archaic joiner, and a Chian guild in whose keeping the Homer-name travelled. VI. The Hymn to Hermes: The Divine Comedy The Hymn to Hermes ( Hymn 4, 580 lines ) is the longest of the hymns and the funniest poem in archaic Greek. Its subject is the youngest Olympian's first day of life, and its tone — reverent toward no one, delighted with its hero's criminal brilliance — makes it the corpus's standing proof that a hymn need not be solemn to be a hymn. Hermes is born at dawn in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, to Zeus and the nymph Maia, a shy goddess living apart from the gods' company. By evening of the same day he has invented the lyre, stolen his brother Apollo's cattle, invented fire-making, sacrificed, lied to Apollo, been hauled before Zeus, and settled the affair in an exchange of gifts that fixes both brothers' provinces forever. The hymn is a biography as negotiation: a god with no honours acquires them, by theft, music, and charm, in twenty-four hours. The Tortoise and the Lyre The newborn god's first act is an invention. Stepping over the threshold of the cave — he does not stay in his cradle past the poem's first movement — Hermes finds a tortoise, and greets it, in paraphrase, with the poem's first joke: alive, it is a charm against witchcraft; dead, it will sing beautifully. He cuts off its limbs, scoops the shell, stretches ox-hide over it, fits horns and a crossbar, and strings it with seven sheep-gut strings — the first lyre, made between morning and noon by a god a few hours old.
