Closing the Loop: The Shared Physics of Medicine and Alchemy XVI. Sources I. A Physics Shared by Body and World: What This Article Is This article belongs to the Foundations cluster of the Alchemy wing, and it is — like its companion on the Hermetica — not, strictly speaking, an article about alchemy. It is an article about the physics alchemy inherited. Before a Greek, Arabic, or Latin alchemist could say what a furnace does to a metal, he needed a language for what a body is : what it is mixed from, why one mixture is healthy and another diseased, why one substance heats and another cools, and by how much. That language was built by physicians. Its elements are four qualities — the hot, the cold, the wet, and the dry — its bodily bearers are the four humours , and its grammar is mixture : Greek krasis , the word that gives us, through Latin temperamentum , the temperament of a patient, of a drug, and eventually of a metal. The story has two great stations, six centuries apart. At the first, an anonymous treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, On the Nature of Man (late fifth or early fourth century BCE), states the four humours — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — as the constituents of the human body, bound to the four qualities and to the turning seasons. At the second, Galen of Pergamum (129–c. 216 CE), physician to gladiators and to emperors, takes that treatise as canonical, comments on it line by line, and builds around it the most durable medical system of the pre-modern world: a classification of temperaments, a theory of disease as imbalance, and — the part this hub most needs — a pharmacology in which every simple drug and food is graded, in degrees from the first to the fourth, by its power to heat, cool, dry, or moisten . When the Arabic and Latin alchemists later speak of correcting a metal's temperament, of a substance too hot in the third degree or a body suffering a cold and wet dyskrasia, they are speaking Galen's quantified language, whether they know it or not. THE QUALITY SQUARE The frame everything in this article hangs on. Fire is hot and dry; Air is hot and wet; Water is cold and wet; Earth is cold and dry. Two pairs of opposites — hot/cold, wet/dry — generate exactly four combinations, and the four elements, the four humours, the four seasons, and the four temperaments are all read off the same square. See The Four Elements . THE CANONICAL MAPPING Blood answers to Air: hot and wet. Yellow bile answers to Fire: hot and dry. Black bile answers to Earth: cold and dry. Phlegm answers to Water: cold and wet. This mapping — completed by Galen and the tradition after him, as Sections VI–VII and X explain in detail — is used consistently throughout this hub, and throughout this article. A note on method, because this subject, like the Hermetica, attracts confident invention. No direct quotation appears in this article unless it is verbatim in a named translation, and the translation is named at the quotation. The Hippocratic quotations are from W. H. S. Jones's Loeb translation of On the Nature of Man ( Hippocrates , vol. IV, Loeb Classical Library, 1931), checked against the Greek text's standard chapter divisions. Everything else — Galen's arguments, the Hippocratic treatises' contents, scholars' positions — is paraphrase, and is labelled as paraphrase or attributed by name where a position is one scholar's rather than the field's. The scholarly frame follows Vivian Nutton's Ancient Medicine (2nd ed., 2013); the Galen scholarship follows R. J. Hankinson (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Galen (2008), and P. N. Singer's translations in Galen: Selected Works (Oxford World's Classics, 1997) and, with Philip van der Eijk, Galen: Works on Human Nature , vol. I: Mixtures (Cambridge, 2018). // WHERE THIS ARTICLE SITS // The Foundations cluster supplies the theory the workshop texts assume: Aristotle on matter and the qualities for the physics, The Four Elements for the square itself, this article for the body's mixtures and the degrees of drugs, and the Technical Hermetica for the Hermetic medicine — iatromathematics, sympathies, and the healing art under Hermes' name — that grew on the same soil. One warning before the detail. The four-humour system is usually met today as a diagram — four coloured boxes, four personality types, a curiosity. The diagram is the end of the story, not its beginning, and it flattens two things this article works to keep separate. First, the treatise that states the humours does not itself contain the whole diagram: On the Nature of Man gives the humours, their qualities, and their seasons, but the explicit binding of each humour to an element, and the full scheme of the ages of life, are completions due to Galen and the tradition after him (Sections VII and X state exactly which parts are whose). Second, the system's real historical power was never the diagram. It was the degrees : the claim that qualitative action could be measured on a scale, matched against a measured imbalance, and corrected by contraries of equal strength. That claim — medicine as applied, quantified mixture-theory — is what alchemy took over whole. Section XII is therefore the centre of this article, and it is written to be used, not merely read. II. Before the Humours: Alcmaeon and the Equality of Powers The humours were not the beginning. Behind On the Nature of Man stands a century of Greek thinking in which health had already been defined — not as the presence of a healthy substance, nor as the absence of a disease-thing, but as a relation among powers . The earliest surviving statement of that definition is also the most beautiful, and it comes from the Greek west, from Croton in southern Italy, a city famous for its physicians and its Pythagorean associations. Alcmaeon of Croton (fl. c. 500 BCE) Alcmaeon, son of Peirithous , wrote — probably in the first half of the fifth century BCE, possibly earlier — a book of which only fragments and reports survive. He is credited in the ancient testimony with identifying the brain, not the heart, as the seat of understanding, and with tracing channels ( poroi ) from the sense-organs to it. But the fragment that matters here is his definition of health, preserved by the doxographer Aëtius and conventionally numbered DK 24 B4. In the standard modern rendering (as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's Alcmaeon article): the equality — isonomia , the term for equal political rights in a well-ordered city — of the opposing powers that make up the body, “the wet, the dry, the hot, the cold, the sweet, the bitter etc.”, preserves health, whereas the monarchy of any one of them produces disease. Three features of that sentence deserve to be dwelt on, because all three run through everything that follows. First, the powers are plural and open-ended : Alcmaeon's list ends with an “etc.” — hot and cold, wet and dry, but also bitter and sweet and, by implication, whatever other opposed powers the body contains. Nothing in the fragment fixes their number at four, and the later fourfold schemes are a narrowing of Alcmaeon's open field, not a quotation of it. Second, health is a constitution , described in the political vocabulary of the Greek city: equality of powers against the tyranny of one. Disease is not an invader but a coup — one power ruling alone. Third, and most consequentially, the account is dynamic : the body is a standing balance of opposed tendencies, continually re-struck, and the physician's art is the art of restoring a balance that nature is always in the process of losing. Every later definition in this article — the Hippocratic “duly proportioned”, Galen's eukrasia — is Alcmaeon's political metaphor with the politics worn smooth. // WHAT ALCMAEON DOES NOT YET HAVE // No humours: his powers are qualities and flavours, not fluids. No fixed tetrad: the list of opposites is illustrative, not closed. No elements: nothing is said about fire, air, water, and earth. What he contributes is the form of the theory — health as proportioned equality among opposed powers, disease as one power's excess — into which the humours, the elements, and the degrees will later be poured. Alcmaeon also stands at the head of a second line that matters to this hub: the line of medical philosophy written as natural philosophy . His book addressed physiology, psychology, embryology, sleep, and death inside a single account of nature, and Aristotle thought him worth a treatise of refutation. The Hippocratic writers inherit that ambition — a medicine that is also a physics — and Galen completes it. When the alchemists, centuries later, write treatises in which the furnace and the body obey one set of principles, they are working in a genre Alcmaeon's generation invented. III. Empedocles and the Four Roots If Alcmaeon supplied the form, Empedocles of Acragas (c. 494– c. 434 BCE) supplied the number. His poem On Nature — fragments of which survive, quoted by Aristotle, Plutarch, and the later commentators — taught that all things are mixtures of four “roots” ( rhizōmata ): fire, air, water, and earth , eternal and unchanging in themselves, combined and separated in endless proportions by two cosmic powers, Love, which unites, and Strife, which divides. The full treatment of the four elements — their history before and after Empedocles, their Aristotelian transformation, and their alchemical career — belongs to the companion article, The Four Elements , and is not repeated here. What this article needs is only the medical consequence, and it is large. Empedocles was remembered in antiquity as a physician as well as a philosopher and wonder-worker, and his Sicilian milieu produced a medical tradition of its own: Philistion of Locri , a generation or two later, is reported to have built the human body explicitly from the four elements and to have explained health as their proportion and disease as the excess of one — Alcmaeon's isonomia, now with Empedocles' four roots as the powers whose equality is at stake. Plato, who knew Philistion's Sicilian medicine, took a version of the scheme into the Timaeus , where the body is compounded of the four elements and its diseases are traced to their excess, deficiency, and displacement. The channel matters more than the detail: by the time the Hippocratic writers were at work, a fourfold physics of the body was already in circulation, with a Sicilian and a Platonic branch, and any new medical system had to position itself against it. That positioning is exactly what On the Nature of Man does, and it does it by refusal as much as by adoption — a point the secondary literature, following Jacques Jouanna's study of the treatise, is emphatic about, and which Section VI states in full. The treatise's author will not say that man is fire, air, water, or earth. His constituents are not the cosmic roots but the body's own fluids. The fourfold pattern is retained; the Empedoclean content is declined. The binding of humour to element, one-to-one, which the later diagram treats as the system's foundation, is therefore a later synthesis — Galen's and his successors' — of two originally distinct fourfolds: Empedocles' roots of all things, and the Hippocratic humours of the body. The synthesis was so successful that its seams vanished. This article keeps them visible, because the hub's alchemical texts live precisely on the seam: it is only once humour and element are identified that a medicine of the body and a physics of metals become one science. // A SECOND ROOT: BREATH AND BLOOD // Empedocles also gave the tradition two durable images: respiration through the pores of the skin as well as the lungs, demonstrated by his famous clepsydra analogy, and blood — especially the blood around the heart — as the seat of thought. Neither survives into the Galenic system in its Empedoclean form, but both show how early the questions were set that the humoral theory would answer in its own terms: how the inside of the body trades with the outside, and where in the mixture the person resides. IV. The Quality Physics Beneath: Aristotle's Four Qualities Between Empedocles and Galen stands the thinker who turned the four roots into a physics of qualities , and without whom the degrees of Section XII are unintelligible: Aristotle (384–322 BCE). The full account — prime matter, form, the four causes, and the sublunary theory of mixture — is the subject of the companion article, Aristotle on Matter, Form, and the Qualities . Here, only the load-bearing pieces. In On Generation and Corruption Aristotle argues, in paraphrase, that the tangible qualities reduce to two pairs of opposites: hot and cold , which he treats as active powers — they act on other things, combining and separating — and wet and dry , which he treats as passive — they are acted on, the wet being readily shaped and the dry retaining its shape. The four simple bodies are then defined by one quality from each pair: fire is hot and dry, air hot and wet, water cold and wet, earth cold and dry — the quality square of Section I, now with a physical rationale. Because each element shares a quality with its neighbours (fire and air share heat; air and water share wetness), the elements can transform into one another by the replacement of a single quality, and because qualities admit of more and less , mixtures are not all-or-nothing: a body is hotter or colder, wetter or drier, by degree . Every later use of the word “degree” in medicine and alchemy lives in that Aristotelian space — qualities as intensities on a continuum, not as labels pasted on things. ACTIVE: HOT AND COLD The pair that does things. Heat concocts, ripens, thins, and separates the unlike; cold condenses, thickens, and fixes. In the body, innate heat is the engine of digestion — food is literally “cooked” (Greek pepsis , concoction) into blood. In the furnace, the same pair does the same work on metals and minerals. PASSIVE: WET AND DRY The pair that is worked on . The wet yields, flows, and takes form; the dry resists, holds form, and crumbles rather than flows. A body's wet–dry balance is its texture: the softness of phlegm, the friability of black bile's earthy dregs, the fusibility of a metal, the dryness of a calcined powder. Aristotle also supplies the second indispensable notion: mixture proper ( mixis ) , as distinct from mere juxtaposition. In a true mixture, on his account, the ingredients do not survive intact side by side, nor is one simply destroyed: they blend into a single homogeneous body whose qualities are a new, intermediate disposition of theirs, recoverable in principle because the ingredients persist potentially . Galen's whole doctrine of krasis — and the alchemists' conviction that a mixture's qualities can be adjusted rather than merely averaged — presupposes this analysis. A temperament, for the tradition that follows, is not a recipe of parts but a state of a blended whole, and it can therefore be shifted, by regimen, by drugs, or by fire, along the continua of the qualities. Hold that sentence; Sections VIII, XII, and XV are its unfolding. V. The Hippocratic Corpus: A Library, Not a Man Everything in Sections VI–VIII is drawn from writings that travel under one man's name, and the first duty of an honest account is to say what that name does and does not mean. Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460–c. 370 BCE) was a real physician, famous in his lifetime — Plato names him, with respect, as a byword for the medical art, and Aristotle mentions him as an example of a man great not in stature but in his science. Of writings securely by his own hand, we possess none that can be proved . What we possess is the Hippocratic Corpus : some sixty treatises in the Ionic dialect of Greek — textbooks, lectures, case-books, surgical manuals, polemics, speeches, aphorism collections — composed by many authors, in many places, over more than a century, and gathered under Hippocrates' name in the Hellenistic age, most plausibly in connection with the great library at Alexandria in the third century BCE. Vivian Nutton's Ancient Medicine , the frame this article follows, treats the Corpus throughout as what it demonstrably is: not a book but a library , and a quarrelsome one. The treatises disagree with each other, openly and on fundamentals. On Ancient Medicine attacks the importation of philosophical postulates — the hot, the cold, the wet, the dry, wielded as explanations — into medicine. On Regimen builds health on two constituents, fire and water. On the Sacred Disease argues that epilepsy is no more divine than any other disease and traces it to phlegm obstructing the vessels of the brain. The Epidemics record case after case with a clinician's reticence about theory altogether; the surgical treatises are content with hands and instruments; Airs, Waters, Places founds an environmental medicine on winds, waters, and the seasons of a city. The number of humours, where humours are counted at all, is not everywhere four. Any sentence that begins “Hippocrates believed…” and ends with a doctrine should therefore be read as shorthand — for “a Hippocratic author believed”, or, very often, for “Galen needed Hippocrates to have believed” (Section IX). The shorthand is unavoidable; this article uses it only where the text flags it. The one volume the reader of this article needs is the fourth: Jones's 1931 volume, which prints On the Nature of Man first, with the short Regimen in Health that antiquity already attached to it, and the Aphorisms — the Corpus's most quoted product — a few signatures later. It is a fitting arrangement. The treatise, the regimen, and the aphorisms are the three forms in which Hippocratic medicine conquered the world: a theory, a way of life, and a pocketful of sentences. // THE “HIPPOCRATIC QUESTION”, STATED PLAINLY // Scholars have argued since antiquity over which, if any, Corpus treatises are by Hippocrates himself; Galen already had his canon of the genuine, the interpolated, and the spurious, and modern scholarship has not converged on a list. The position taken here, following Nutton and the standard reference literature, is the minimal one the evidence compels: the Corpus is multi-author; no treatise in it is proved to be Hippocrates' own; and the one treatise whose authorship antiquity lets us discuss with a name attached is the subject of the next section — where the name attached is not Hippocrates'. VI. On the Nature of Man: The Four Humours Stated On the Nature of Man (Greek: Peri physios anthrōpou ) is a short treatise — fifteen chapters in the usual division, with the appended Regimen in Health sometimes counted as its continuation — and it carries more subsequent history per page than any other medical text of antiquity. It is here, and, in this explicit form, only here in the Corpus, that the four humours are stated as a complete system. Jacques Jouanna, the treatise's modern editor, calls it in his study of the four-humour theory's legacy the only treatise of the Corpus to which an author's name can be attached — and the name is Polybus . The Authorship Dispute The attribution rests on Aristotle. In the History of Animals (III.3), discussing the description of the blood-vessels, Aristotle cites an account he ascribes to Polybus — and the account he describes corresponds to the vessel-description embedded in On the Nature of Man . Later biographical tradition made Polybus Hippocrates' pupil and son-in-law, and on that basis the treatise entered the Corpus as the work of the master's own household: close enough to Hippocrates to carry his authority, distinct enough to explain why the master himself never quite says this elsewhere. Galen, for his part, held the treatise's core to be genuinely Hippocrates' own, and his commentary on it is one of the foundation documents of the whole later system (Section X). Modern scholarship has been less comfortable at every joint of the story. The treatise as transmitted is probably composite — the anatomical chapters sit awkwardly with the humoral ones, and Jones, in his Loeb introduction, already treated its parts as of different dates, placing the opening section somewhere between about 440 and 400 BCE. The Polybus attribution itself is widely accepted — it is the best ancient testimony we have — while the son-in-law relationship has recently been challenged as a Hellenistic biographical invention, of the kind ancient lives of famous men manufacture to reconcile competing attributions: on that challenge, Polybus the author is real, but his marriage into the house of Hippocrates, and with it any “Coan school” succession built on the marriage, is not evidence but embroidery. This article's usage follows the evidence as it stands: the treatise is attributed to Polybus on Aristotle's testimony ; it is a Hippocratic treatise by collection, not a proved work of Hippocrates; and Galen's contrary conviction is reported as Galen's. The Argument of the Treatise (chs. 1–6, in paraphrase) The treatise opens as a polemic, and its first target is monism — the doctrine that man is one thing. Its author declines, in paraphrase, to discuss the nature of man beyond its bearing on medicine: those who say man is air, or fire, or water, or earth — some one element and nothing else — share, he argues, a single idea under different names, and their disagreement about the name betrays the idea. Physicians who say man is blood only, or bile only, or phlegm only, commit the same error in medical dress. Against both he sets a simple, devastating test: if man were a unity, he could never feel pain, for there would be nothing in him for the one thing to suffer from ; and the cures for his diseases would be one, whereas in fact they are many. Plurality is therefore not a theory but a clinical observation. The body contains many constituents, which heat, cool, dry, and wet one another beyond nature and so engender diseases — many constituents, many forms of disease, many healings. Chapter 4 then names the constituents, in the sentence on which two millennia of medicine are a commentary. Jones's Loeb translation, verbatim: “The body of man has in itself blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile; these make up the nature of his body, and through these he feels pain or enjoys health.” — ON THE NATURE OF MAN, CH. 4, TRANS. W. H. S. JONES (LOEB, 1931) The chapter continues, in paraphrase: he enjoys the most perfect health when these constituents are duly proportioned to one another in compounding, in power, and in bulk, and are perfectly mingled; pain is felt when one of them is in defect or in excess, or is isolated in the body and not compounded with the others — for the place it has left is diseased by the emptying, and the place where it floods is diseased by the excess. Alcmaeon's isonomia (Section II) has acquired fluids, proportions, and a pathology of separation : disease is not only too much or too little, but a humour standing apart , unmixed — a formulation Galen will never improve on, only annotate. Chapter 5 adds the empirical proofs, in paraphrase: the four are visibly distinct in colour and to the touch — not equally warm, cold, dry, or moist — and each can be drawn off separately, by a drug that purges phlegm, by a drug that purges bile, by the black bile a purge brings away, and by the blood that flows from a wound, on any day of the year. The humours are not postulates. They are what comes out of the patient. // WHAT CHAPTER 4 DOES NOT SAY // It does not name the elements. Fire, air, water, and earth are the treatise's opponents' candidates in chapter 1, not its own constituents in chapter 4; the humours are bound, in the treatise itself, to the qualities and the seasons , not one-to-one to the cosmic roots. Jouanna's study is the standard modern statement of this point, and Galen's commentary is where the element-binding is made explicit (Section X). The canonical mapping of Section I is therefore historically layered, and this article dates each layer rather than projecting the finished diagram back into 400 BCE. VII. Seasons, Ages, and the Turning Year Chapter 7 of On the Nature of Man is the treatise's most original movement, and the one that turns a list of fluids into a medicine. Its claim, in paraphrase: the four constituents are always all present in the body, but each waxes and wanes with the year, increasing in the season akin to its own nature and decreasing in the season opposed to it — as the year itself participates in all the qualities, hot, cold, dry, and moist, none of which could persist for a moment without the others. The body is a small year. Its weather changes on schedule, and the physician who knows the schedule can see a disease coming with the season that feeds its humour. The Seasons in the Treatise (ch. 7, in paraphrase) Phlegm increases in winter , the author argues, because phlegm is the coldest constituent of the body — you may test it by touch against bile and blood — and winter is its kin: in winter men's sputum and nasal discharge are fullest of phlegm, swellings turn white, and diseases run phlegmatic. In spring, blood increases : the cold relaxes, the rains come, and the season is moist and warm, most akin to blood's nature — spring and summer bring dysenteries and nosebleeds, and men are then hottest and red. In summer, bile rises and holds its strength into autumn: men vomit bile spontaneously, purges bring away the most bilious matter, and fevers and complexions declare it, while phlegm, opposed by the dry warmth, is at its weakest. In autumn, black bile is greatest and strongest , and blood is at its least, autumn being dry and already chilling, contrary to blood's nature; then, as winter returns, the chilled bile shrinks and phlegm grows again with the rains and the long nights. The proof offered is a purge experiment, in paraphrase: give the same man the same drug four times in the year, and he will vomit the most phlegmatic matter in winter, the moistest in spring, the most bilious in summer, and the blackest in autumn. The qualities assigned are the canonical ones, and they are the treatise's own: blood hot and wet, yellow bile hot and dry, black bile cold and dry, phlegm cold and wet. The humours, qualities, and seasons columns are On the Nature of Man itself, chapters 4 and 7. The element column (*) is the Galenic completion: asserted in Galen's commentary and in his treatise On the Elements According to Hippocrates , and universal thereafter. The ages column (†) is likewise a completion: the Hippocratic treatise ties predominance to age only in passing — remarking, of the quartan fever it ascribes to black bile, that the humour predominates in those between about twenty-five and forty-two — and it is Galen, in the commentary and in On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato , who extends that single remark into the full fourfold scheme: the child hot and wet and abounding in blood, the youth hot and dry, maturity cold and dry under black bile, old age cold and wet and phlegmatic, life itself a slow cooling and — in the old — a final drowning of the innate heat. The temperament column (‡) is the latest layer of all, and Section X returns to it: the four character-names are the medieval and early-modern crystallisation of hints in Galen, not a table Galen himself ever drew in this form. What the treatise itself builds on the seasons is practical, and it is the germ of all later regimen literature. If each humour waxes in its season, then diet and way of life must be counter-seasonal : the regimen must be adjusted through the year so as to oppose the rising humour before it rules — the doctrine the appended Regimen in Health works out as a seasonal calendar of foods, exercise, baths, and evacuations. The physician of this tradition does not wait for the coup Alcmaeon feared. He governs against it, quarterly, in advance. In that preventive, calendar-bound, quality-counting practice — medicine as the management of a mixture through time — both Galenic dietetics and, at one remove, the alchemist's timed regimen of the furnace (gentle heat in its spring, fierce heat in its summer) have their common ancestor. VIII. Krasis: Mixture as the Body's Individual Nature The Hippocratic treatise speaks of the constituents being “duly proportioned” and “perfectly mingled”. The word the tradition will use for that state — and for the individual constitution that results — is krasis : literally a mixing, as of wine with water in the mixing-bowl ( kratēr ) from which the word derives. Latin renders it complexio and temperamentum — a due tempering — and the double translation survives in our own double vocabulary: a person's complexion was originally their mixture, not their skin, and their temperament was the mixture itself, not the moods it was later blamed for. Krasis is the hinge concept of this article, because it operates at every scale the system touches: a humour has a krasis of qualities, a body has a krasis of humours, an organ has its own krasis within the body's, a drug has a krasis that will act on all of them — and, in the alchemical transfer of Section XV, so does a metal. EUKRASIA — THE GOOD MIXTURE Health as a state, not a substance: the constituents proportioned in power and bulk and perfectly mingled ( On the Nature of Man , ch. 4). Crucially, eukrasia is individual : each body has its own due proportion, set by its nature, age, sex, place, and season — which is why Galen can speak of a latitude of health rather than a single point (Section XI). DYSKRASIA — THE BAD MIXTURE Disease as disproportion: a constituent in defect or excess, or separated and unmixed. Dyskrasia names both the humoral imbalance and — in Galen's wider usage — any departure of a part's quality-mixture from its due state, even where no humour is at fault: a part can simply be too hot, too cold, too wet, or too dry. That wider usage is what makes the degree pharmacology of Section XII a complete therapeutics. Two Hippocratic consequences follow immediately, and both are stated in the treatise's ninth chapter, the locus of the whole tradition of cure by contraries. In paraphrase of its argument: diseases arising from repletion are cured by evacuation, and those from evacuation by repletion; diseases from exercise by rest, and from idleness by exercise; and the physician must set himself against the established character of the disease, the constitution, the season, and the age — relaxing what is tense and tensing what is relaxed — for in this way the diseased part will best come to rest, “and this, in my opinion, constitutes treatment”. The Jones translation's shortest sentence in the chapter is the one the next two thousand years quoted: diseases due to repletion, it says verbatim, “are cured by evacuation” — and its pair, by repletion. Contraria contrariis — opposites are cured by opposites — is the Latin tag the Middle Ages put on this chapter, and it is a fair tag. But note what the chapter adds that the tag drops: the contrary must be chosen against four variables at once — disease, constitution, season, age. Cure is contrariety calibrated to a mixture . The entire Galenic development of this insight consists in giving that calibration a scale. Regimen — diaita , a word covering food, drink, exercise, bathing, sleep, and the whole ordered conduct of life — is the calibration applied daily, and in the Hippocratic world it is the senior partner of drug therapy, not its handmaid. The reasoning is internal to the theory: food is the body's daily intake of qualities, concocted into blood and so into the humours themselves; a food's krasis therefore feeds the mixture continuously and gently, where a drug strikes it occasionally and hard. Galen will formalise exactly this relation — foods alter the body little and gradually, drugs alter it much and at once, and the same substance can cross the line by dose and preparation — in On the Properties of Foodstuffs and the opening books of the Simples (Section XII). Introduction — Scope of This Hub This hub covers the Greek and Roman world as a single, long civilisation with two languages, many cities, and one continuous argument with itself about the gods, about nature, and about what human beings can make and remake. It begins in the Bronze Age background — Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece, the palace worlds whose languages, gods and crafts stand behind everything later Greeks told about their own past — and it ends at a threshold in 1144 CE , when an Arabic alchemical book was put into Latin and the art that Alexandria had founded entered the Latin West. Between those points lie the archaic and classical city-states, the Hellenistic kingdoms, the Roman absorption of the Greek world, and the long late-antique centuries in which Greek learning was copied, commented on, and carried into new hands. The hub has a defined place in this archive, and it is worth stating plainly. It follows the Egyptology division — the reader who arrives from Egyptology will find the story picked up where the pharaonic and Ptolemaic material leaves it — and it follows the Before Kemet hub, which treats everything before dynastic Egypt and tiers its evidence as attested, ancient-traditional, and modern-constructed. This hub needs no tier system of that kind, because its whole period is documented: there are texts, inscriptions, buildings and workshop remains throughout. What it needs instead — and what its method section sets out — is discipline of a different kind: the discipline of distinguishing a poem from a cult, a Greek original from a Roman reception, and a verified quotation from a paraphrase. One debt of continuity deserves emphasis. The Egyptology division already treats Egyptian alchemy, the Hermetica, and Zōsimos of Panopolis from the Egyptian side: see its Alchemy article for the sacred art of Kemet, its temple crafts and its recipe papyri. The alchemy wing of this hub carries that same history forward — from the point where Greek-speaking practitioners in Roman Egypt turned Egyptian craft knowledge, Greek natural philosophy and a new apparatus tradition into the discipline the later world would call alchemy, and onward through its Byzantine, Syriac, Arabic and Latin transmission. The two treatments are companions, not duplicates: Egyptology asks what the art was in Egypt; this hub asks what the Greek and Roman world made of it, and where it went next. The mythology wing now carries the great story-cycles in full — the Argonauts, the labours of Heracles, Theseus, Perseus, the wanderings of Odysseus, the Trojan and Theban cycles, the descents to the dead, the makers and fire-stealers, Cupid and Psyche, and the legendary lives of the sages. There is a reason beyond completeness. In the alchemical tradition these stories were not decoration: they were a teaching vehicle , passed from master to student — much of the transmission oral — with their lessons deliberately obscured by allegory , so that the tale could be heard by anyone and understood only by those prepared for it. That is the tradition's own account of why it veiled its teaching in story, and this hub documents it as such: Wing I tells the myths whole, as texts with their transmission and their cult footing stated honestly, and Wing II's Alchemical Allegory sets out how the alchemists themselves read them — a documented interpretive tradition with its own rules, presented as the alchemists' reading, never as the myths' original meaning. The wing has since grown the two shelves it was missing. Rome now has its own mythology here — the founding legends, the Aeneid read whole rather than in its sixth book alone, and the mysteries of Mithras — and the sources themselves have been put on the shelf as subjects: Apollodorus's Library , the prose systematizers Herodotus, Pausanias and Plutarch, Ovid's Metamorphoses , tragedy, the Works and Days , the Homeric Hymns, the Bronze Age tablets behind the Olympians, and the Baal Cycle of Ugarit, the Levantine corpus that stands behind the succession myth. A reader can now judge every source Wing I leans on from an article in this hub. // THE HUB IN ONE LINE // Mythology is read here as literature and as lived religion; alchemy is read here as philosophy and as bench work. Neither wing is allowed to swallow the other, and neither is reduced to the other. A note on names and spelling. Greek words are transliterated consistently throughout the hub, with macrons marking long vowels where the standard scholarly spelling carries them: Zōsimos , kērotakis , tribikos , chēmeia . Personal names follow the familiar Latinised forms (Hesiod, Plutarch, Ptolemy) except where the Greek form is itself the subject. Dates are BCE and CE throughout; a date preceded by c. is approximate, and a date given as a range is a floruit or a construction period, not a pair of anniversaries. Where scholars disagree about a date that matters — the dating of the alchemical pseudo-Democritus is the standing example — the timeline says so in the entry itself rather than silently choosing a side. Finally, a note on what this hub is not. It is not a retelling of the myths for their own sake, though the myths are told here carefully and in full. It is not a celebration of alchemy as lost super-science, nor a dismissal of it as fraud: the recipe literature is explicit that many of its products were imitations, and the hub reports that plainly, because a tradition honest about its own imitations deserves to be read honestly. And it is not a general history of Greece and Rome — politics and war appear on the timeline where they change the conditions of cult, of learning, or of the art, and not otherwise. // A DELIBERATE EXCLUSION // Anatolia — the Hittite and Hurrian world — appears in this hub comparatively, where its succession myth illuminates Hesiod's (see the Theogony article), and not as a subject in its own right. That is a decision, not an oversight: Anatolia feeds no alchemical line this archive follows, and a comparative section is its proportionate home here. II. The Two Wings The hub is organised in two wings . The division is not decorative: the two wings use different primary evidence, ask different questions, and are held to the same standard by different means. Wing I works from poems, hymns, inscriptions, sanctuaries and ritual calendars. Wing II works from treatises, recipe collections, apparatus descriptions and manuscripts. Every article in the index belongs to one wing, and the timeline is written so that a reader can follow either wing down its length — or watch the two converge, as they do in Alexandria, where the god Hermes of Wing I becomes Hermes Trismegistus, the named author of Wing II's philosophy. WING I MYTHOLOGY — gods, heroes and epics as texts and as cult. The succession myth and the Olympian order; the heroes and the epics that carry them; and the mystery cults — Eleusinian, Orphic, Dionysian, Samothracian — where myth stopped being only a story and became something a person underwent. A myth is treated first as a text : who composed it, in what genre, surviving in what edition. It is treated second as cult : who sacrificed, processed, swore, initiated, and where. The wing's standing warning is that the two do not map onto each other neatly, and any sentence that confuses a poet's invention with a city's practice is rewritten until it no longer does. WING II ALCHEMY — the Alexandrian art and its transmission. The art that Greek-speaking Egypt built out of older Egyptian and Near Eastern craft: pseudo-Democritus and the Physika kai Mystika , Maria the Jewess and the apparatus tradition, Zōsimos and the vision literature, the Hermetica, and the commentators who carried the corpus through Byzantium into Syriac and Arabic and finally through the Latin door of 1144. Workshop procedure stands at the centre of this wing: furnaces, stills, the kērotakis , quantities, sequences, tests. A claim about what alchemists believed is only admitted here alongside the evidence of what they actually did at the bench. WING I — ITS KEY DISTINCTION Literary myth is not cult practice. Homer and Hesiod are evidence for what archaic audiences heard; calendars, decrees and sanctuary remains are evidence for what cities did. Burkert's Greek Religion is the wing's model for holding the two together without merging them. WING II — ITS KEY DISTINCTION Recipe is not theory, and theory is not recipe. The Leyden and Stockholm papyri describe making and testing saleable imitations; Zōsimos describes vessels, vapours and visions in one breath. The wing keeps both registers visible and names which one a given text is speaking in. The wings meet at three points, and the hub marks each meeting rather than blurring it. They meet in Hermes : Olympian messenger in Wing I, thrice-greatest sage and supposed author in Wing II. They meet in the mysteries , where Wing I's cult history borders the initiatory language Wing II later borrowed. And they meet in Alexandria itself — a Greek city on Egyptian soil, ruled from a Macedonian court, taxed by Rome — the one place where a single practitioner could plausibly read Hesiod in the morning and tend a kērotakis in the afternoon. Plato's Atlantis, treated in the Before Kemet hub at Plato's Atlantis , is the archive's standing example of a Wing I text that later ages misread as a Wing II-style technical record; it is cross-referenced there and not duplicated here. III. Method — The Rules of This Hub Every archive in this project keeps its rules on its hub page, where a reader can hold the articles to them. These are the rules of the Greco-Roman hub. They are stricter than they look, and they bind the timeline below as much as the articles it indexes. // THE HUB'S RULE // No invented quotations anywhere in this archive. A sentence inside quotation marks is a verified quotation from a named published translation, or it does not appear. Everything else is labelled paraphrase — including this hub's own summaries of the arguments it admires most. Texts are named in named editions and translations. Hesiod is cited from M. L. West's editions of the Theogony and the Works and Days ; the Greek alchemists from Berthelot and Ruelle's Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs and from Michèle Mertens's Les alchimistes grecs ; the Corpus Hermeticum from Brian Copenhaver's Hermetica . Where an article relies on a different edition, that edition is named on the article. A claim that cannot be traced to a named text is not made. Literary myth is distinguished from cult practice. That a god does something in a poem establishes that the poem says it. It does not establish that any Greek sacrificed, processed or prayed on that basis. Cult claims in this hub rest on cult evidence: inscriptions, calendars, votives, sanctuary archaeology, and ancient authors writing about ritual as ritual — Pausanias describing a sanctuary, a decree regulating a festival, Plutarch writing as a priest of Delphi. Greek and Roman reception are distinguished. Rome did not simply inherit Greece; it translated, renamed, re-founded and sometimes invented Greek material for Roman purposes. Zeus and Jupiter, Heracles and Hercules, the Greek chēmeia and the Latin alchimia that reached the West through Arabic — in each pair the second term is a reception, with its own date and its own agenda, and this hub dates receptions separately from their sources wherever the difference matters. The Atlantis of Plato and the Atlantis of later centuries are, by this rule, two different subjects. Quotations are only from verified published translations, and are named as such. No wording is reconstructed from memory, none is silently modernised, and none is manufactured to give an argument a classical accent it has not earned. Where a famous saying turns out to be a later paraphrase — a common fate of alchemical maxims in particular — the hub says so and prints the paraphrase labelled as paraphrase, with its actual, later source where that source is known. Speculation is labelled as speculation. The date of Homer, the identity of Bolos of Mendes, the historicity of Maria the Jewess, the authorship of works ascribed to Stephanus of Alexandria: on each of these the scholarship is divided or the evidence thin, and this hub presents them as open questions with the main positions named, not as settled facts with the disagreement footnoted away. A reader should be able to tell, from any sentence in this hub, whether they are standing on a document, on a scholarly consensus, or on an argument. // A NOTE ON THE ALCHEMICAL SOURCES // Pseudepigraphy is the normal condition of Wing II's library, not an embarrassment to be explained away. Works travel under the names of Democritus, Hermes, Moses, Cleopatra and Aristotle that their named authors did not write. This hub cites such works as pseudo- Democritus, the Hermetica ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, and so on — the attribution is part of the historical evidence, and silently treating it as authorship would falsify the record the hub exists to keep. IV. The Greco-Roman Timeline Fifty-three entries, from the palace of Knossos to the great Byzantine codex that preserved the Greek alchemists. Read it as two interleaved histories: the Wing I history of gods, poems and cults, and the Wing II history that begins, quietly, in Hellenistic Egypt and ends by walking out of the Greek world altogether — into Syriac, into Arabic, and at the threshold, into Latin. Every date was checked for this hub against the standard references named in the Sources section; approximate dates are marked as approximate. c. 2000–1450 BCE Minoan Crete — the first Aegean palace civilisation. On Crete, a non-Greek-speaking people — Minoan is a modern name, taken from the legendary King Minos — built unfortified palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, administered in the undeciphered Linear A script. Their art, their sea trade and their religious imagery — bulls, double axes, goddess figures — formed the deep background that later Greek myth remembered, transformed, as the age of Minos, the labyrinth and the Minotaur. c. 1600–1100 BCE Mycenaean Greece — Greek-speaking palace kingdoms. On the mainland, fortified palace centres at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes and Athens ruled through a redistributive bureaucracy whose accounts survive in Linear B — deciphered in 1952 as an early form of Greek. The tablets already name gods the classical world would worship, among them Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysos. Around 1450 BCE the Mycenaeans took over Knossos, and Minoan and Mycenaean culture fused in the late palaces. c. 1350–1190 BCE Ugarit and the Baal Cycle. At Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast, a cosmopolitan port between Egypt, Hatti and Cyprus, scribes copy the great mythic tablets in a thirty-sign alphabetic cuneiform: Baal's combat with Sea, his palace, his death at the hands of Mot and his return. The cycle is the fullest surviving Levantine mythology, and its succession and sea-combat patterns stand behind the Greek succession myth this hub traces in Hesiod. The city falls with the collapse that follows. c. 1200–1100 BCE The Bronze Age collapse. Within a few generations the palace system failed across the eastern Mediterranean: Mycenaean centres were destroyed or abandoned, the Hittite Empire fell, and trade networks contracted sharply. In Greece, Linear B writing was lost entirely, and the centuries that followed — poorer, smaller in scale, and without writing — are conventionally called the Greek Dark Age. The causes of the collapse remain debated; its reality, in the ground, is not. c. 800 BCE The Greek alphabet adapted from Phoenician script. Greek communities adapted the Phoenician consonantal script and, decisively, repurposed some of its signs as vowels — producing the first fully alphabetic writing system. Within a generation or two, writing in Greek was being used not only for accounts and ownership marks but for verse: some of the earliest surviving Greek inscriptions are poetic. The recovery of writing is the precondition for everything Wing I studies. c. 750–700 BCE Homer and Hesiod — the foundational poems take shape. The Iliad and Odyssey , composed in an oral-formulaic tradition and conventionally attached to the name Homer, reached something close to their surviving form in the later 8th century BCE; their exact dating remains debated. Hesiod of Ascra, a near-contemporary, composed the Theogony — the first systematic Greek account of the gods' generations — and the Works and Days . Between them, these poets gave the Greek world its shared divine genealogy and its heroic past. 776 BCE Traditional date of the first Olympic Games. Later Greek chronographers fixed the first Olympiad, and with it the starting point of Greek historical dating, to 776 BCE, when the victor list for the games at Olympia begins with Koroibos of Elis, winner of the stadion foot-race. The sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia was older than the games' traditional start, and the date is best understood as the beginning of a reliable victor record rather than the invention of the festival itself. 734–733 BCE Greek colonisation reaches Sicily — Naxos and Syracuse founded. In the great archaic movement of settlement around the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts, Chalcidians founded Naxos in Sicily in 734 BCE and Corinthians founded Syracuse the following year, by the traditional chronology Thucydides reports. The colonies carried Greek cults, calendars and myths into new landscapes — and brought Greek speakers into permanent contact with the peoples, crafts and materials of Italy, North Africa and the Near East. 594/593 BCE Solon, archon of Athens. Chosen as archon and mediator in a crisis of debt and faction, Solon cancelled debts, abolished debt-bondage for Athenians, reordered political rights by wealth classes, and — unusually — set his reforms down in verse, from which later authors quote him. His settlement did not create democracy, and tyranny followed within a generation; but it established the principle, foundational for classical Athens, that law is a public, written thing standing above faction. 508/507 BCE Cleisthenes' reforms — Athenian democracy founded. After the fall of the Peisistratid tyranny, Cleisthenes reorganised the Athenian citizen body into ten new tribes drawn across the old regional divisions, with a Council of Five Hundred preparing business for the assembly of citizens. The reforms are conventionally taken as the founding act of Athenian dēmokratia — a citizen body, excluding women, slaves and resident aliens, governing itself through assembly, council and courts. 490 BCE Marathon — the first Persian invasion repelled. A Persian expeditionary force sent by Darius I landed at Marathon to punish Athens and Eretria for aiding the Ionian Revolt. On the plain of Marathon, Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated it decisively; Herodotus gives the Athenian dead as 192, a figure the burial mound on the field still commemorates. Marathon became, in Athenian memory, the founding victory of the democracy's self-image — the generation of the Marathonomachai, the Marathon-fighters. 480 BCE Thermopylae and Salamis — Xerxes' invasion turns. Xerxes' far larger invasion crossed into Greece in 480 BCE. A Greek rearguard under the Spartan king Leonidas was destroyed holding the pass of Thermopylae; Athens was evacuated and its Acropolis burned. Weeks later, in the straits of Salamis, the allied Greek fleet — its largest contingent Athenian, its strategy Themistocles' — destroyed the Persian fleet in confined water where numbers told against the invader. The invasion was not over, but its momentum was broken. 479 BCE Plataea and Mycale — the Persian Wars end in Greece. In 479 BCE a pan-Hellenic army under the Spartan Pausanias defeated the Persian land force left in Greece at Plataea in Boeotia, and Greek forces destroyed the Persian fleet beached at Mycale across the Aegean on, by tradition, the same day. Mainland Greece was free of Persian occupation. The wars' memory — a small world of free cities defeating an empire — shaped Greek, and then European, political imagination out of all proportion to the forces engaged. 478 BCE The Delian League founded. Athens and its Aegean allies formed a league, its treasury on Delos and its purpose the continuation of war against Persia, with members contributing ships or money. Within a generation the league had become, in substance, an Athenian empire: the treasury moved to Athens in 454 BCE, allied contributions became tribute, and the league's funds underwrote the building programme that remade the Acropolis — a fact Athens' critics, ancient and modern, have not let it forget. c. 450 BCE Empedocles of Acragas — the four roots. A Sicilian philosopher-poet, writing in verse a generation before Socrates, set all nature on four eternal “roots” — fire, air, water and earth — mixed and parted by two powers, Love and Strife. Plato and Aristotle will each rebuild the scheme rather than replace it, and the tetrad Empedocles fixed underwrites, in the end, the physics of the alchemists. 447–432 BCE The Parthenon built on the Athenian Acropolis. Under Pericles' leadership Athens rebuilt the sanctuary the Persians had burned, raising the Parthenon — temple of Athena Parthenos, designed by Iktinos and Kallikrates, its sculpture overseen by Pheidias — between 447 and 432 BCE. It housed Pheidias' colossal gold-and-ivory Athena and functioned in part as the treasury of the Athenian state. As cult building, war memorial and imperial statement at once, it is Wing I's central case of a temple that is also an argument. c. 460–370 BCE Hippocrates and the Hippocratic corpus. Under the name of the Coan physician, some sixty treatises by many hands bind the body's four humours — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile — to the same qualities that order the elements: hot, cold, wet and dry. Temperament, the body's individual mixture of those qualities, becomes the shared physics of Greek medicine and, centuries later, one of alchemy's parent languages. 431–404 BCE The Peloponnesian War. Athens and Sparta, at the head of their respective alliances, fought a generation-long war recorded by Thucydides and, after his history breaks off, by Xenophon. Plague devastated Athens from 430 BCE; the Athenian expedition to Sicily ended in catastrophe in 413 BCE; and in 404 BCE, starved by blockade after its fleet was destroyed at Aigospotami, Athens surrendered. The war ended Athenian empire and began a century in which no Greek state could hold the hegemony all of them sought. 399 BCE The trial and death of Socrates. An Athenian jury convicted Socrates, aged about seventy, on charges of not recognising the gods of the city, introducing new divinities, and corrupting the young; he was executed by drinking hemlock. Socrates wrote nothing. His pupil Plato made the trial and death — in the Apology , Crito and Phaedo — the founding scene of Western philosophy: a city that could kill its questioner, and a questioner who would not stop questioning to save his life. 387/386 BCE Plato founds the Academy at Athens. On returning to Athens, Plato established his school in the grove of the hero Akademos outside the city walls — the institution whose name every later academy borrows. There Aristotle studied for twenty years before founding his own Lyceum in 335 BCE. The Academy endured, through many changes of doctrine, for over nine centuries: its closure in 529 CE is one of this timeline's closing entries, and the span between the two dates is a fair measure of Greek philosophy's institutional life. 384–322 BCE Aristotle — matter, mixture, and the subterranean fire. Plato's pupil of twenty years founds his own school, the Lyceum, in 335 BCE, and gives the world below the moon its lasting physics: form realised in matter, mixture as a true union of qualities, and — in the Meteorologica — metals generated within the earth from a moist exhalation, the Greek root from which the sulphur–mercury theory will grow. 338 BCE Chaeronea — Macedon masters Greece. At Chaeronea in Boeotia, Philip II of Macedon defeated the combined forces of Athens, Thebes and their allies; the Theban Sacred Band was annihilated where it stood. In 337 BCE Philip organised most Greek states into the League of Corinth under Macedonian leadership, formally to make war on Persia. The independent foreign policy of the classical polis — the world that had produced Marathon, the Parthenon and Socrates' jury — was effectively over. 336–323 BCE Alexander the Great — reign and conquests. Succeeding his assassinated father at twenty, Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and in eleven years destroyed the Achaemenid Persian Empire — Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela — took Egypt without a battle, and campaigned as far as the Indus before his army refused to go further. He died at Babylon in 323 BCE, leaving no adult heir. His conquests carried Greek language, cities and cults across the Near East and created the Hellenistic world in which Wing II begins. 331 BCE Alexandria founded in Egypt. On the western edge of the Nile Delta, Alexander founded the city that bears his name — laid out, by tradition, with his own hand marking its streets. Under the Ptolemaic dynasty it became the largest Greek city in the world and its greatest centre of learning, governing Egypt through a Greek-speaking court while ruling an Egyptian countryside of temples and villages. No single place matters more to this hub: Alexandria is where Wing I's gods were re-imagined and Wing II's art was invented. early 3rd century BCE The Museum and Library of Alexandria founded. Under Ptolemy I Soter and Ptolemy II Philadelphus — the project is associated with Demetrius of Phalerum, an exiled Athenian statesman formed in Aristotle's school — Alexandria acquired the Mouseion, a royally salaried research community, and its famous Library. Scholars there edited Homer and the tragedians into the texts we still read, and Callimachus catalogued the collection in his Pinakes . Royal patronage of learning on this scale was itself a Hellenistic invention. c. 300 BCE Euclid's Elements — Alexandrian science at full stretch. Working in Alexandria around 300 BCE, Euclid organised geometry into the axiomatic Elements , the most durable textbook in the history of science. He stands here for a constellation: Eratosthenes, librarian at Alexandria, who measured the Earth's circumference from shadow lengths; Aristarchus, who proposed a heliocentric system; Herophilus and Erasistratus, who founded systematic anatomy. Hellenistic Alexandria did not only preserve Greek learning — it extended it further, faster, than the classical world ever had. c. 250 BCE Apollonius Rhodius composes the Argonautica . In Ptolemaic Alexandria, a scholar-poet of the Library retold the oldest of Greek voyage-tales — Jason, Medea and the Golden Fleece — as a learned epic in four books. The saga was already archaic when the Odyssey mentioned the Argo as "known to all"; Apollonius's poem is the fullest surviving telling, and the form in which the story reached every later reader, the alchemical readers included. c. 200 BCE Bolos of Mendes — the name behind pseudo-Democritus. Bolos, a Hellenised Egyptian writer from Mendes in the Delta, flourished around 200 BCE — the floruit is also given as the 3rd century BCE — writing on sympathies and antipathies in nature under the authority of the philosopher Democritus. Later scholarship has attached his name to the alchemical Physika kai Mystika . The connection is genuinely disputed: the surviving alchemical text, in the form we have it, is now generally placed much later, in the 1st century CE. This hub therefore treats Bolos and the alchemical pseudo-Democritus as related but distinguishable problems — see the timeline entry for the 1st century CE below, and the Wing II article on the origins of the art. 146 BCE Corinth destroyed — Rome absorbs mainland Greece. After defeating the Achaean League, the Roman general Mummius sacked Corinth — among the richest and oldest Greek cities — and its territory was annexed; Macedonia had already become a Roman province. Greece kept its language, its schools and its prestige, and Roman aristocrats would soon be sending their sons to Athens to be educated. But political sovereignty had passed, permanently, to Rome: the Greek world would be governed from outside itself for two thousand years. 31 BCE Actium — Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra. Off the western coast of Greece, the fleet of Octavian — the future Augustus — defeated the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII of Egypt. The battle decided the Roman civil wars and, with them, the fate of the last great Hellenistic kingdom. Antony and Cleopatra fled to Alexandria and held it for one more year; the Hellenistic age, conventionally dated from Alexander's death in 323 BCE, ends with theirs. 30 BCE Alexandria falls — Egypt becomes a Roman province. Octavian entered Alexandria in 30 BCE; Antony and Cleopatra died by their own hands, and Egypt was annexed not as an ordinary province but as the emperor's personal possession, governed by an equestrian prefect and closed to senators. Alexandria remained a Greek metropolis — restless, brilliant, and now the intellectual capital of a Roman world. It is under Roman rule, in this Greek city on Egyptian soil, that alchemy as a written discipline appears. 19 BCE Virgil's Aeneid published after his death. Virgil (70–19 BCE) left the Aeneid unfinished, and Augustus had it published as it stood. Its sixth book — Aeneas's descent to the dead, guided by the Cumaean Sibyl — is the most complete underworld the ancient world produced: the geography of Hades, its judges, punishments and Elysian rewards systematised into a single journey, and the katabasis tradition's Roman summa. c. 8 CE Ovid's Metamorphoses — the myths become a handbook. Ovid (43 BCE–17/18 CE) completes his fifteen-book chain of some 250 tales of transformation, from Chaos to the apotheosis of Caesar, shortly before Augustus exiles him to Tomis. The poem's versions — many of them Ovid's own inventions — displace their rivals, and the Metamorphoses becomes the form in which the Latin West, and after it Europe, actually reads Greek myth. 1st century CE The Physika kai Mystika in its surviving form — the Roman-era workshop. The oldest substantial alchemical treatise we possess, the Physika kai Mystika ( Natural and Secret Questions ) ascribed to Democritus, survives as epitomised extracts of a work in four books on dyeing — metals gold and silver, stones, and wool purple. Recent scholarship places its anonymous alchemical author in the second half of the 1st century CE, often c. 54–68 CE, centuries after both Democritus and Bolos. Its subject throughout is the workshop operation the Greeks called baphē , dyeing or tinting: giving a base material the colour, and so the appearance and standing, of a precious one. Theory and recipe are already inseparable in it. 1st–3rd century CE Maria the Jewess and the apparatus tradition. Known only through quotation and report — above all by Zōsimos, who treats her as an ancient authority — Maria is placed by the tradition that cites her somewhere in the first three centuries CE, in Alexandria. To her are credited the descriptions or inventions that define early alchemical equipment: the tribikos , a three-armed still; the kērotakis , a sealed reflux vessel in which metal leaf was exposed to vapours; and the gentle water bath that still bears her name in the French bain-marie . Whether one historical woman stands behind the attributions cannot be proved; that the attributions shaped fifteen centuries of laboratory practice is not in doubt. late 1st–4th century CE Mithraism — the Roman mystery cult. Along the frontiers, in the ports and in Rome itself, initiates meet in cave-shaped temples before the image of Mithras slaying the bull, ascending through seven grades under a Pater. The cult leaves hundreds of mithraea, inscriptions and monuments — and no scripture, liturgy or insider account at all, so that everything known of it is read off stone, image and the reports of outsiders. Suppressed with the other pagan cults at the fourth century's end, it remains the Roman world's most widespread mystery — and its most silent. c. 46 – after 119 CE Plutarch of Chaeronea — priest, biographer, Platonist. Plutarch, who served for many years as a priest of Apollo at Delphi, wrote the Parallel Lives — paired biographies of Greek and Roman statesmen that became Europe's schoolbook of antiquity — and the wide-ranging essays of the Moralia , including major works on Isis and Osiris and on the Delphic oracles. He is this hub's model Roman-era Greek witness: a man of the classical tradition writing, observantly and from inside, about cults far older than it. 2nd century CE Ptolemy of Alexandria — the ancient cosmos systematised. Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria — his dated astronomical observations run from 127 to 141 CE — composed the Almagest , the mathematical astronomy that governed the science until Copernicus, together with the Geography , the Tetrabiblos on astrology, and works on optics and harmonics. His synthesis drew on Babylonian records and Greek geometry alike. Through Arabic and then Latin translation, Ptolemy — not any classical Athenian — was the Greek scientist the medieval world actually read. 1st–2nd century CE The Library of pseudo-Apollodorus — myth becomes a system. An unknown compiler — not Apollodorus of Athens, the grammarian whose name the work carries — orders the whole Greek mythic tradition into three books on a genealogical spine, from the first gods to the returns from Troy. The handbook becomes the tradition's reference form: the source through which the cycles reach most later readers, and the single work this hub cites most. 129–c. 216 CE Galen of Pergamum — temperament systematised. Physician to Marcus Aurelius and the most prolific medical author of antiquity, Galen canonises the four humours and grades every simple drug by degrees
