What Legend Is Evidence For: The Genre’s Lesson for This Archive XIX. Sources I. Legend Is Not Myth: The Genre and Its Three Layers The other articles of this hub’s first wing deal in myth : stories of gods and heroes, set in what Latin scholarship calls in illo tempore — “in that time”, the undatable time before history, when Ouranos ruled and Kronos swallowed his children. No one asks when, in what year, the castration of Ouranos happened, because the story does not claim a year. Its persons are not the kind of beings who have biographies. The Theogony article of this hub treats Hesiod’s poem accordingly: as a text with a date, carrying a story without one. This article deals in legend , and legend is a different genre with a different contract. A legend attaches wonders to a named person in datable time : a man who was born on Samos, taught at Croton, and died — somehow — in the Greek West around 490 BCE; a philosopher from Acragas in Sicily who flourished in the 440s BCE; a wandering sage from Tyana in Cappadocia who stood, or is said to have stood, before the emperor Domitian; a king who really did conquer the Persian Empire and really did die at Babylon in June 323 BCE; a slave on Samos whose killing the people of Delphi really did, on our earliest evidence, have to pay for. The wonders are not the difference. Gods work wonders in myth, and these men work wonders in legend. The difference is the frame : legend insists that its wonder-worker had a birthplace, a floruit, contemporaries who could have contradicted the story, and a grave — or, in the most telling cases, a conspicuously missing one. That frame is what makes legend, paradoxically, the more historical of the two genres — not because its wonders are true, but because its growth is datable. A myth arrives whole, from a past that cannot be stratified. A legend arrives in layers, and the layers have authors and dates. We possess, for Pythagoras, a mocking couplet by a contemporary, a paragraph of sober report from Aristotle’s lost work on the Pythagoreans, a reincarnation memoir retailed by a pupil of Plato, and three full Lives written seven to eight centuries after the man died — and the wonders grow, measurably, at every step. The accretion is itself a document. Read in sequence, the sources for a legendary life are a core sample through the religious imagination of eight hundred years, and each stratum can be dated by the hand that laid it down. LAYER (a): THE RECOVERABLE PERSON What the earliest and least interested evidence supports: a birthplace, a school, a public career, a death in roughly datable circumstances. This layer is always thinner than readers want it to be, and this article reports it at its real evidential strength — including, where the strength is low, saying so. LAYER (b): THE LEGEND’S GROWTH The wonders, in the order the sources add them, each with its author and its date. A golden thigh in a fragment of Aristotle is a different kind of fact from a golden thigh in a Life written in 300 CE, and the article never lets the second borrow the authority of the first. LAYER (c): WHAT THE LEGEND WAS FOR Legends are made by communities that need them: a school proving its founder was more than human, a city claiming a sage, a court commissioning a pagan holy man, a conquered people making the conqueror their own king’s son. The function is not a debunking afterthought. It is, most of the time, the explanation of why the story exists at all. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — R. D. Hicks’s Loeb Diogenes Laertius (1925), A. D. Godley’s Loeb Herodotus, F. C. Conybeare’s Loeb Philostratus (1912), and M. R. Wright’s Empedocles fragments (1981) — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author’s sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. The five lives chosen here were not chosen at random, and their order is an argument. Pythagoras is the type case: a founder about whom almost nothing contemporary survives, whose legend can be stratified with unusual precision thanks to Walter Burkert’s Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (German 1962; English 1972), the study on which all modern work on the question rests. Empedocles is the harder case: a philosopher whose own surviving verses present him as a fallen god, so that the legend is not simply added to the man — the man supplied its script, and his biographers quarrelled over his death already in antiquity. Apollonius of Tyana is the commissioned case: his legend survives essentially in one magnificent, problematic book, written to order for an empress more than a century after his death. Alexander is the maximal case: the best documented life of the ancient world, and also the most thoroughly fictionalised, in a Romance that out-circulated every sober history ever written about him. Aesop is the limiting case: a person whose recoverable core shrinks to four or five facts, and whose legend is therefore almost pure — the storyteller absorbed into his own genre. The Egyptology division of this archive holds the great Egyptian parallel, a historical official of the Third Dynasty whom later ages made a god: Imhotep . The discipline is the same on both sides of the archive, and it is stated once here so that it does not have to be re-argued in every section: a legend is evidence — not for the wonders it reports, but for what its tellers needed the sage to be. // A WORD ON “LEGEND” // The word is used in this article in its scholarly sense, from Latin legenda , “things to be read” — a narrative tradition attached to a person, neither certified history nor free invention. It carries no verdict on any single episode. Some legendary episodes preserve real events in costume; most do not; the genre analysis does not depend on deciding each one, and this article decides only where the evidence actually decides. One more preliminary, because the five lives share it. In every case the legend grows in the same direction: outward in space and upward in rank . The sage travels further than any contemporary could check — to Egypt, to Babylon, to India, to Ethiopia, to the Ocean and the ends of the earth — and he rises in ontological rank as he goes, from gifted teacher to prophet, from prophet to theios anēr , a divine man, from divine man to a being of a third order between gods and men, and finally, in the boldest tellings, to a god who has condescended to walk about in a body. The pattern is so regular that its exceptions are informative: where a source refuses the promotion — a historian who insists the sage died obscurely in exile, a biographer who hedges a resurrection with “apparently dead” — the refusal is datable too, and it is usually the sound of a rival community talking. Legend is a competitive genre. Schools, cities, and eventually religions bid against one another for the sage, and the bids are the evidence. II. How a Legend Grows: Strata, Dates, and the Discipline of This Article Before the lives, the method — because in this subject the method is most of the content. A legendary life is never one text. It is a tradition : a sequence of tellings, each retelling the last with additions, and the additions are rarely innocent. The working tool of this article is therefore stratigraphy, borrowed from the archaeologists: lay the sources out in chronological order, identify what each layer adds, and refuse to read a late layer’s material back into an early one. Applied consistently, stratigraphy dissolves most of the famous “mysteries” of these lives into ordinary literary history. Pythagoras did not become more mysterious as the evidence improved; the evidence got later, and later evidence is wonderfuller. The mystery is an artefact of reading the strata in the wrong order — beginning, as the late Lives invite us to begin, at the top of the pile. The Five Strata, as They Recur in Life After Life First stratum: contemporaries and near-contemporaries. Brief, oblique, often hostile or amused. Xenophanes mocks Pythagoras for recognising a friend’s soul in a beaten puppy; Heraclitus sneers at his learning as a patchwork; Herodotus mentions Aesop once, in passing, to date somebody else. This stratum is gold precisely because it is not trying to build a legend: a joke only works if the audience already knows the reputation it plays on, so a contemporary joke is evidence for the reputation, dated to the joker’s lifetime. Second stratum: the fourth century BCE. The generation of Plato and Aristotle collects, systematises, and — crucially — already marvels. Aristotle’s lost treatise On the Pythagoreans , known from fragments, reported the golden thigh and the bilocation without endorsing them, in the tone of a man cataloguing what the school believed. His pupils and Plato’s — Aristoxenus, Dicaearchus, Heraclides Ponticus — wrote the first connected accounts, and each had a programme: Aristoxenus, himself from Pythagorean Tarentum, rationalised; Heraclides, a Platonist with a taste for the marvellous, embroidered. Almost everything in the later Lives that is not pure late-antique invention can be traced to this stratum’s workshop. Third stratum: Hellenistic biography and the novel. Between roughly 300 BCE and 100 CE the lives become literature: Hermippus, Satyrus, Neanthes, and their kind supply teachers, travels, trials, last words, and deaths shaped to fit the subject’s philosophy — the phenomenon Ava Chitwood’s Death by Philosophy (2004) documents for the early philosophers, in which a thinker’s doctrines are mined to manufacture his biography, above all his death. The Life of Aesop and the Alexander materials assembled in this stratum belong as much to the history of the ancient novel as to biography. Fourth stratum: the imperial Lives. In the second and third centuries CE the legendary life becomes a major literary form with religious stakes: Diogenes Laertius compiles his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (early third century CE, dates debated); Philostratus writes Apollonius for the Severan court; Porphyry and Iamblichus write Pythagoras for a paganism that now has a rival. These texts are routinely mined as if they were archives. They are better read as arguments — each with a named author, a known milieu, and a discernible opponent. Fifth stratum: translation and world conquest. Some lives escape the Greek world entirely. The Alexander Romance passes into Latin, Syriac, Armenian, Arabic, Persian, Ethiopic, Hebrew, and every European vernacular. Apollonius passes into Arabic as Balīnās, master of talismans, and into Byzantine civic folklore as the wards on Constantinople’s gates. Aesop passes into everything, everywhere, and is still passing. At this stratum the legend no longer needs the person at all; it has become a free-floating author-function, a name under which new wonders can be filed indefinitely. c. 570–490 BCE THE PERSONS OF THE EARLIEST STRATUM Pythagoras active at Croton (from c. 530 BCE); Aesop’s floruit falls in the reign of Amasis of Egypt (570–526 BCE) on Herodotus’s evidence. Their contemporaries Xenophanes and Heraclitus already treat Pythagoras as a figure of fun and fame — the legend’s first datable layer is a joke. c. 494–c. 434 BCE EMPEDOCLES OF ACRAGAS The one figure in this article who authors his own legend in advance: the Purifications present their speaker as a fallen daimōn now restored to godhood among men. Every later account of his death is a commentary on those verses. 356–323 BCE ALEXANDER OF MACEDON The historical conqueror. His court historian Callisthenes dies in disgrace in 327 BCE; the fictionalising of the campaigns begins within the conqueror’s own generation, in writers who had marched with him. 1st century CE APOLLONIUS OF TYANA A Neopythagorean teacher of the Roman imperial age. Philostratus’s chronology puts his birth a few years before the common era and his death in the reign of Nerva (96–98 CE); modern handbooks often give c. 15–c. 100 CE. The discrepancy is the evidence’s, not this article’s, and is reported as such in Section XI. c. 200–330 CE THE GREAT COMPILATIONS Within little more than a century: Diogenes Laertius compiles the philosophers’ lives; Philostratus completes the Life of Apollonius after Julia Domna’s death in 217; Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305) and Iamblichus (c. 245–c. 325) write their Pythagorean Lives; the Greek Alexander Romance reaches the form in which a Latin translation could be made of it (Julius Valerius, c. 320 CE). The legendary life becomes, in these decades, a dominant genre of Greek prose. 303 CE and after THE LEGEND AS WEAPON Sossianus Hierocles, an official of the Diocletianic persecution, sets Apollonius against Christ; Eusebius of Caesarea writes the rebuttal. From here the legendary lives are ammunition in a religious war, and their preservation — and much of their subsequent fame — follows from that use. // THE STANDING CAUTION OF THIS ARTICLE // A late source is not a lying source, and an early source is not an honest one; both are sources for their own moment . When Diogenes Laertius, writing around seven centuries after Pythagoras, reports a wonder and names a fourth-century authority for it, the report is good evidence that the fourth century told that wonder — which is a real and interesting fact. It is not evidence that the wonder occurred in the sixth century BCE. Every section below therefore cites wonders in the form “X reports, in [date], that…” wherever the distinction matters, and the reader should treat any sentence in any other book of the form “Pythagoras did…” followed by a marvel as a stratigraphic error until proven otherwise. III. Pythagoras I: The Recoverable Man — Samos, Croton, and the School Layer (a), the person. Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, was a Samian who emigrated to Croton in southern Italy at about the age of forty, around 530 BCE , and there founded the community that made him famous. His conventional dates, c. 570–c. 490 BCE, are modern scholarly estimates, not records — the heading of Diogenes Laertius’s Life in Hicks’s Loeb edition gives “c. 582–500 B.C.”, a reminder that even the frame dates have moved by a decade within modern scholarship. He wrote nothing that survives, and on the dominant modern view, following Burkert, he wrote nothing at all: the verses and treatises circulating under his name are the school’s later products, fathered on the founder by the normal pseudepigraphy of the tradition. What the earliest evidence — Plato, Aristotle, and the fourth-century writers who had access to the school’s own memory — supports is a founder of a way of life : Plato’s single mention of him, in the Republic (600a–b, paraphrased), says exactly that and nothing more marvellous: Pythagoras was loved for a manner of life that his followers, called Pythagoreans still in Plato’s day, continued to live by, distinguished from other men. It is the most valuable sentence about Pythagoras written in antiquity, because it is the least interested in him. The way of life had a politics. At Croton, Pythagoras and his associates — Diogenes Laertius (8.3), in Hicks’s translation, gives the figure of nearly three hundred — were “held in great estimation” and governed so effectively, the same passage says, that the constitution was in effect an aristocracy, a government of the best. The Pythagorean societies of the Greek cities of Italy were political clubs as well as religious communities, and they ended as political clubs end: in violence. The tradition preserves two waves of anti-Pythagorean rising, one in Pythagoras’s own last years at Croton and a worse one around the middle of the fifth century BCE, when Pythagorean meeting-houses across southern Italy were burned and their members killed or scattered. The school’s dispersion is, ironically, part of why we know anything about it: Philolaus of Croton (c. 470–c. 385 BCE), a refugee generation’s heir, was the first Pythagorean to publish the doctrines in a book — the book Plato is said to have bought at a famous price — and it is Philolaus, not the founder, to whom the earliest attributable Pythagorean philosophy belongs. What the founder himself taught, at the strength the evidence will bear, is this. He taught the immortality and transmigration of the soul : that the soul survives death and is reborn, in human and in animal bodies, and that conduct in this life answers for the next. He taught a discipline of ritual purity and dietary restriction , of which abstention from animal flesh — grounded in the kinship of all ensouled life — is the best attested and was already, in the fifth century, the school’s public trademark, mocked on the comic stage. He taught by authority rather than argument : the school’s later formula, autos epha — “he himself said it” — preserves the memory of a master whose pronouncements closed questions. And he founded a community bound by friendship, common property, and graded secrecy , in which candidates underwent a long probation — the tradition says five years of silence, listening without seeing the master — before full admission. Burkert’s stratigraphic verdict, which this article follows, is that this religious founder is the historical Pythagoras, and that the mathematician-philosopher of the handbooks — the theorem, the musical ratios as a system, “all things are number” — is a construction of the following centuries: Aristotle, our earliest systematic witness, attributes the number-doctrine not to Pythagoras but to “the so-called Pythagoreans”, and the doctrines he describes match the generation of Philolaus. The distinction is Burkert’s central one, between the lore — the acusmata, the ritual rules, the master’s charisma — and the science , which the school developed after him and the legend then donated to him. BCE); Aristotle’s reports Strong — mocked by contemporaries, which requires the doctrine to be his public trademark Dietary and ritual rules; the bean prohibition Aristotle’s On the Pythagoreans , fragments on the acusmata; comedy Strong for the school; the founder’s own observance is the tradition’s claim Political influence at Croton; violent reaction Fourth-century historians via the later Lives; the mid-5th-century burnings are independently remembered Moderate — outline secure, episodes embroidered The theorem; “all is number”; the harmony of the spheres as his system Attributed to “the Pythagoreans” by Aristotle; to Pythagoras personally only in late sources Weak for the man; strong for the school’s later generations (Philolaus onward) Any writing by Pythagoras Diogenes Laertius (8.6) already reports the denial and the counter-claim side by side Not established; the surviving “works” are pseudepigrapha Even his death comes in the two registers at once. Diogenes Laertius (8.39–40, paraphrased from Hicks’s translation) gives first the dramatic version: fleeing the burning of Milo’s house at Croton, Pythagoras reached a field of beans and stopped, saying he would be captured rather than cross it — the bean prohibition of Section VI made fatal — and his pursuers cut his throat. He then gives Dicaearchus’s version, in the next breath: Pythagoras died a refugee in the temple of the Muses at Metapontum, after forty days’ fasting. A death by his own doctrine, or a death in sanctuary exile: the tradition could not decide, because both deaths meant something, and meaning, in this genre, outbids fact. The Metapontine ending has the better early authority — Dicaearchus was Aristotle’s pupil — and the bean-field ending has the better story. The legend kept both, as it usually does. IV. Pythagoras II: Already a Wonder-Worker — The Reports of Aristotle’s Generation Layer (b) begins early — startlingly early. The standard picture of legend as a slow fungus on a sober original fails for Pythagoras in an instructive way: the wonders are not late. They are present, fully formed, in the fourth century BCE , within a long lifetime of the man’s death, in the reports of Aristotle himself. Aristotle wrote a treatise On the Pythagoreans , now lost; a famous fragment of it (fr. 191 Rose), preserved through later quotation — in Aelian, in Apollonius’s Mirabilia , and in Iamblichus’s Life — catalogues the school’s presentation of its founder, and the catalogue is worth giving in full, in paraphrase, because every later Life is an expansion of this single paragraph. Aristotle reported that the Pythagoreans divided rational beings into three kinds — gods, men, and beings like Pythagoras; that Pythagoras had a golden thigh , which he displayed; that he was seen on the same day and at the same hour at both Metapontum and Croton ; that when a deadly snake bit him, he bit it back and killed it; that as he crossed a river — the Nessus in Diogenes’s version, the Casas in others — the river addressed him aloud , greeting him by name; and that the people of Croton identified him as the Hyperborean Apollo , Apollo come from the fabulous far north. Diogenes Laertius, compiling seven centuries later, retails the core of the same catalogue in his own voice, and his wording — Hicks’s Loeb translation (1925) — may stand here for the tradition’s settled form: “Indeed, his bearing is said to have been most dignified, and his disciples held the opinion about him that he was Apollo come down from the far north. There is a story that once, when he was disrobed, his thigh was seen to be of gold; and when he crossed the river Nessus, quite a number of people said they heard it welcome him.” — DIOGENES LAERTIUS, LIVES 8.11, TRANS. R. D. HICKS (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1925) Three observations keep this stratum honest. First, Aristotle reports; he does not endorse. The fragment’s frame is ethnographic — this is what the Pythagoreans say and teach about their master — and Aristotle elsewhere treats the school’s doctrines with cool philosophical distance. But reportage is not nothing: a sober catalogue of c. 330 BCE proves the wonders were the school’s public doctrine about its founder within two generations of his death, taught while men whose grandfathers had known him were still alive. The legend of Pythagoras is not a medieval or even a late-antique growth. It is, in its essentials, a product of the school itself, and nearly contemporary with the school’s founding generation. Second, the wonders are specific in kind . A golden thigh is not a generic marvel; in Greek terms it is a mark of the more-than-human, the body of a being whose substance is not ordinary flesh — the same logic by which heroes in epic have ichor, not blood, in their veins. Bilocation — Metapontum and Croton are some sixty kilometres apart — asserts freedom from the body’s ordinary limits. The speaking river asserts that nature itself recognises him. Together they do not say “this man was clever”; they say “this man was misclassified as human”, which is precisely what the three-kinds doctrine — gods, men, and such as Pythagoras — states in propositional form. Third, the Hyperborean Apollo identification ties the founder to Apollo’s cult geography: the Hyperboreans, the blessed people beyond the north wind, were Apollo’s own, and Abaris, their priest, was said to have flown to Greece on Apollo’s arrow. The later Lives make Abaris visit Pythagoras and hand him the arrow in recognition. The school’s founder is being slotted into an existing sacred map, not invented from nothing. The contemporary stratum beneath Aristotle is thinner and ruder, and it corroborates the reputation from the other side. Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570–c. 475 BCE), an older contemporary, wrote the puppy verses Diogenes preserves (8.36, in Hicks’s verse rendering): Pythagoras, passing a man beating a puppy, cries out — “Stay, smite not! ’Tis a friend, a human soul; I knew him straight whenas I heard him yelp!” The joke is datable evidence of the first class: by Xenophanes’ lifetime, Pythagoras’s transmigration doctrine was famous enough to be a punchline, and the punchline already casts him as the man who recognises souls across bodies — the seed from which Heraclides’ reincarnation memoir (Section V) will grow. Heraclitus of Ephesus (fl. c. 500 BCE), quoted by Diogenes at 8.6, attacks from another flank: Pythagoras practised inquiry beyond all other men, Heraclitus concedes in Hicks’s rendering, but made of his selections “a wisdom of his own, showing much learning but poor workmanship” — polymathy without understanding, the charge of a rival sage who plainly regards Pythagoras as the competition. And Empedocles , a generation later, praises in verse a man of surpassing knowledge whose mind reached across ten and twenty lifetimes of men — unnamed in the fragment (DK 31 B129), but identified by the ancient tradition, plausibly, as Pythagoras: the reincarnation doctrine reflected back as a compliment between wonder-workers. Hostile, amused, and admiring witnesses agree on the one thing that matters for layer (a): the reputation — soul-expert, master of a devoted school, claimant to knowledge beyond the human filing system — is contemporary. The golden thigh is the reputation, mineralised. // WHY A THIGH? // The golden thigh puzzled ancient rationalisers too, and the later tradition supplied occasions for its display: shown to Abaris as a credential, shown at the Olympic Games, bared by accident when Pythagoras was disrobed, as Diogenes has it. Burkert’s discussion treats the motif within the shamanic and Apolline complex of the early legend — the marked body of the man who travels between worlds. What can be said without theory is the stratigraphic fact: the thigh is in Aristotle’s fragment, and nothing in the tradition is older than the stratum that contains it except the jokes. Layer (c), what this stratum was for, is already visible. A school that taught by autos epha — the master said it — needed a master whose saying settled things, and a master of the third kind, neither god nor man, settles things better than a clever Samian emigrant could. The wonders are the school’s constitution in narrative form. They also armed it against a specific vulnerability: Pythagoras left no writings, so his authority could not be checked against a text; it could only be embodied in a person, and the person had therefore to be extraordinary. Every founder-legend in this article solves an institutional problem of exactly this shape, and Pythagoras’s solves it first and most influentially. V. Pythagoras III: Memory Across Lives — Heraclides Ponticus and the Reincarnation Chain The single most influential addition to the legend was made by Heraclides Ponticus (c. 390–c. 310 BCE), a pupil of Plato and one of the most inventive writers of the fourth century — astronomer, literary critic, and retailer of marvellous narratives that antiquity itself already read with raised eyebrows. Diogenes Laertius (8.4–5) introduces the story with an attribution that deserves to be quoted in its grammar even in paraphrase: this is what Heraclides of Pontus tells us Pythagoras used to say about himself. A first-person memoir of previous lives, at two removes: Heraclides reports what Pythagoras claimed to remember. The chain, as Diogenes retails it in Hicks’s translation (paraphrased here, with the structure kept exact), runs as follows. Pythagoras had first been Aethalides , a son of Hermes, and Hermes had offered him any gift except immortality; Aethalides chose memory — to retain, through life and through death, the recollection of everything he experienced. So the soul passed, with its memory intact, into Euphorbus , the Trojan hero whom Menelaus killed in the Iliad — and Euphorbus could still recount the soul’s earlier wanderings, its lives in plants and animals, and what it had seen in Hades. When Euphorbus died, the soul entered Hermotimus of Clazomenae, who proved the story empirically: travelling to the temple of Apollo at Branchidae, he identified the shield Menelaus had dedicated there on his voyage home from Troy, by then rotted away to its ivory facing alone. Hermotimus died and became Pyrrhus , a fisherman of Delos, who still remembered the whole sequence. Pyrrhus died, and the soul became Pythagoras — who remembered everything. 1. AETHALIDES THE GIFT OF MEMORY Son of Hermes. Offered any gift but immortality, he chooses unbroken memory across death — the device that makes the whole chain, and the doctrine behind it, narratable in the first person. 2. EUPHORBUS THE TROJAN HERO The soul in heroic time, killed by Menelaus ( Iliad 17). The chain annexes the epic past: Pythagoras’s previous life is checkable, in principle, against Homer — and against a physical object, the dedicated shield. 3. HERMOTIMUS THE PROOF AT BRANCHIDAE Hermotimus identifies Menelaus’s shield, rotted to its ivory facing. The legend here invents its own verification scene — memory tested against an artefact in a temple, the ancient world’s nearest approach to a museum label. 4. PYRRHUS THE FISHERMAN OF DELOS A nobody between the hero and the sage. The humble incarnation matters: the chain does not only collect famous lives; it demonstrates the doctrine’s democracy of souls, high and low in alternation. 5. PYTHAGORAS THE REMEMBERER The present life, in which the chain becomes known — because this incarnation, uniquely, can tell it. The doctrine of transmigration acquires an eyewitness. As narrative engineering, this is superb, and its functions (layer c) are legible. Transmigration is an unfalsifiable doctrine until someone remembers; Heraclides’ Pythagoras remembers, and the story supplies the memory with a mechanism (Hermes’ gift), a proof (the shield), and a pedigree that runs through Homer himself. The chain also quietly promotes its hero: his soul is not merely old, it is documented , with a heroic incarnation and a divine father in its past. And it converts the school’s central doctrine into the founder’s autobiography — the strongest form of authority a doctrine can have in a culture that trusts witnesses over arguments. The stratigraphic discipline applies with full force. Heraclides wrote a full century and a half after Pythagoras died; he is also the source, in the Empedocles tradition (Section X), for a vanishing-and-apotheosis death, and ancient critics already classed him among the paradoxographers, the retailers of wonders. None of that makes the chain worthless as evidence. It makes it evidence of a precise thing: that by the later fourth century BCE, within Plato’s own circle’s penumbra, the Pythagoras tradition was producing first-person reincarnation narrative of a sophistication the founder’s contemporaries never record. Xenophanes’ puppy shows the doctrine was his; the chain shows what the doctrine became in the hands of a literary man. Between those two data points lies the whole growth of the legend’s second stratum — and the distance between them is exactly what this article means by a layer. // HOW TO READ A CHAIN LIKE THIS // Ask three questions of any such set-piece. Who first tells it, and how long after the events? (Heraclides; about 150 years.) What work does its machinery do? (It makes an uncheckable doctrine checkable-looking, by attaching it to a temple object and a Homeric name.) What did the teller’s other work look like? (Heraclides specialised in marvellous narratives of souls, heavens, and resurrections.) None of the answers refutes the story. Together they file it — correctly — as fourth-century school literature, not sixth-century memoir. VI. Pythagoras IV: The Akousmata — A School Held Together by Riddles Between the person and the wonders stands the stratum that Burkert taught scholarship to take most seriously, because it is the hardest to invent retrospectively: the akousmata , also called symbola — the short, strange oral precepts that initiates memorised and lived by. Diogenes Laertius (8.17) lists them in Hicks’s translation, and the list’s flavour is its own evidence: do not stir the fire with a knife; do not step over the beam of a balance; do not sit down on your bushel; do not eat your heart; do not help a man off with a load, but help him on; do not leave the pan’s imprint on the ashes — the list runs on: no swallows under the roof, no birds with hooked claws, do not turn back at the frontier when you go abroad. (Paraphrased from the list at 8.17–18; the individual precepts quoted are Hicks’s renderings.) Diogenes then immediately supplies allegorical explanations

A Cluster of Makers: Why These Stories Are Told Together Greek myth has no department of technology. There is no single poem of the forge, no epic of the workshop, no hymn in which the arts are handed over in one ceremony and the account closed. What there is, instead, is a cluster — a knot of stories, told by different poets across eight centuries, in which fire changes hands, things are made, and the making always costs somebody something. At the centre of the cluster stands Prometheus , the Titan who divided an ox so that men would eat meat and gods would receive smoke, who stole the fire Zeus had hidden and carried it down to earth smouldering in a hollow stalk, and who was chained to a rock at the edge of the world while an eagle ate his liver out of him, day after day, for longer than any human punishment could last. Beside him stands Hephaestus , the only Olympian who works: a god with a forge, bellows, an anvil, and a limp, who made the armour of heroes, the sceptre of Zeus, a net fine as spiderweb to catch adulterers, golden handmaidens who could speak, and — on Zeus's orders — the first woman herself. And beside both of them, at the human end of the scale, stands Daedalus , a mortal with no fire to steal and no forge in heaven, only his hands: the Athenian craftsman who built a wooden cow for a queen's unnatural desire, a labyrinth to hide the monster that desire produced, and finally a pair of wings, feather by feather, to escape the king who had imprisoned him in his own design. Between the Titan and the smith-god, the cluster has a hinge, and her name is Pandora . She is not a maker but a made thing — earth and water kneaded by Hephaestus at Zeus's command, dressed by Athena, graced by Aphrodite, given speech and a lying nature by Hermes, and sent down to Prometheus's brother as the gods' answer to the theft of fire. Hesiod calls her, without softening it, the price of fire: men got the flame, and in exchange they got her, and with her the jar whose opening let toil, disease, and sorrow loose in the world, leaving only Hope shut under the rim. Any honest account of this cluster has to keep her in it, because the poets keep her in it. In Hesiod the stories of Prometheus, of fire, and of the first woman are not three stories. They are one transaction, told twice, and the transaction is the founding charter of the human condition as the archaic Greeks understood it: men eat cooked meat, work for their bread, marry, sicken, and die, and the gods receive the smoke of bones — and all of it was settled in a single exchange of tricks between Zeus and the one Titan clever enough to deal with him. The cluster matters to this archive for a further reason, and the reason should be stated at the outset rather than smuggled in at the end. These are the myths that every later fire-working tradition — bronze-founders and goldsmiths in antiquity, and in due course the alchemists, whose art is fire applied to matter under a philosophy — has reached for when it wanted ancestors. A stolen fire that makes all arts possible; a god whose lameness is the mark of the smith in every early society; a craftsman whose name became the name of an artistic period; a woman fashioned out of earth by a divine artisan: the materials are almost suspiciously well suited to a metalworker's mythology, and later ages noticed. This article will make that claim visible — it is a real fact about the myths' afterlife, and Section XXIII closes with it — without endorsing it as the myths' meaning. The myths came first. Hesiod was not encoding a metallurgy, and the Prometheus Bound is not a guild charter. What the texts say, in their own order and their own voices, is the subject of everything that follows; what later fire-workers made of them is one section at the end, clearly fenced. PROMETHEUS Titan, son of Iapetus. The trickster of Mecone, the thief of fire, the chained sufferer of the Caucasus — and, in the tragedy that bears his name, the inventor of number, writing, ships, medicine, and metallurgy itself. Sections III–XII. PANDORA The first woman, fashioned from earth and water by Hephaestus and gifted by all the gods, sent to Epimetheus as the price of fire. Her jar — not her box — is the cluster's darkest object. Sections XIII–XIV. HEPHAESTUS The lame smith of Olympus, thrown from heaven twice in two different tellings, whose forge produced the shield of Achilles, the self-moving tripods, and the golden handmaids. Patron of smiths at Athens and Lemnos. Sections XV–XIX. DAEDALUS The mortal maker: Athenian exile, builder of the Labyrinth, inventor of the wings that killed his son, and in the end a name so identified with early art that art history still calls a whole style “Daedalic”. Sections XX–XXII. One thread runs through all four figures, and it is worth naming before the details begin, because the texts themselves keep returning to it. In this cluster, making is never innocent and never free . Prometheus's every gift to men is answered by a counter-stroke from Zeus. Hephaestus's masterworks are made on commission, under obligation — a debt of gratitude to Thetis, an order from Zeus, a husband's revenge. Daedalus's three great works are a cow that enables a monstrous birth, a prison that consumes Athenian children, and wings that save the maker and kill his son. Even Pandora, the made thing, is a weapon. The Greek imagination, at its most archaic, did not separate the wonder of craft from its price; the same word, technē , covers the art that builds a ship and the art that builds a snare, and Hesiod uses the vocabulary of cunning — mētis , dolos , the wile and the trap — for Prometheus, for Hephaestus, and for the fashioned woman alike. That is the cluster's real unity, and it is a sterner and more interesting unity than any later guild-mythology made of it. II. Texts, Translations, and the Three Registers of This Article Following the rule of this hub, the article distinguishes three registers throughout, and the reader is entitled to know at any point which one a sentence is standing in. (a) Myth as told : what a named ancient text says, cited to that text, in a named translation where it is quoted. (b) Cult footing : what Greeks actually did — altars, festivals, temples, torch races — resting on cult evidence: inscriptions, calendars, sanctuary remains, and authors such as Pausanias writing about ritual as ritual. (c) Later readings : what subsequent ages made of the stories — the tragedian who turned Hesiod's trickster into a culture-bringer, the philosopher who turned him into an allegory of human nakedness, the Romantics who turned him into a rebel saint, and the alchemical tradition that read the whole cluster as veiled instruction. The three registers constantly touch; the article's business is to keep them from being confused. The primary texts, in the order the article uses them, are these. Hesiod , Theogony and Works and Days (c. 700 BCE), in H. G. Evelyn-White's Loeb translation of 1914 — the hub's standard Hesiod, quoted throughout; the Prometheus episode of the Theogony (lines 507–616) is treated briefly in this hub's Theogony article, Section IX, and at full length here. Homer , Iliad and Odyssey , in A. T. Murray's Loeb translation: the Iliad for Hephaestus's two falls and the shield of Achilles, the Odyssey for the net that caught Ares and Aphrodite (the Odyssey 8 song read in Ian Johnston's translation, and paraphrased from it). Prometheus Bound , transmitted under the name of Aeschylus, in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb translation of 1926 — with the play's authorship treated as the open question it is (Section X). Plato , Protagoras , in Benjamin Jowett's translation. Apollodorus , Library and Epitome (first or second century CE), in J. G. Frazer's Loeb translation of 1921 — the great prose handbook that preserves the cluster's fullest continuous narratives, above all for Daedalus. Ovid , Metamorphoses Book 8 (c. 8 CE), in Brookes More's translation of 1922, for the wings of Daedalus in their most influential telling. And Pausanias , Description of Greece (second century CE), in W. H. S. Jones's Loeb translation, for the cult evidence and for Daedalus's works as a traveller could still see them. Scholarship is cited where it is used: Jean-Pierre Vernant's reading of Mecone above all, and Mark Griffith's authorship study; Timothy Gantz's Early Greek Myth (1993) stands as the standard handbook of the variant tradition, against whose frame the variants used here were checked in the primary texts themselves. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from the named published translations listed above and in the Sources, each identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. Greek names are transliterated, not Latinised (Hephaestus, not Vulcan; Heracles, not Hercules), except inside quotations, where the translator's spelling stands — Frazer, for example, writes “Hercules”, and quotations from him keep it. c. 700 BCE HESIOD The Theogony and Works and Days : Mecone, the theft of fire, the fashioned woman, the jar, the eagle and the liver. The cluster's foundation text, and the only one in which all its elements appear as a single transaction. 8TH CENTURY BCE HOMER The Iliad and Odyssey in their surviving form: Hephaestus's falls, his forge and masterworks, the shield of Achilles, the net — and, in a single simile, Daedalus's dancing-floor for Ariadne, his first appearance in Greek literature. 5TH CENTURY BCE PROMETHEUS BOUND · PLATO The tragedy transmitted as Aeschylus's turns the trickster into the inventor of all the arts (its date and authorship are disputed; Sections IX–X). Plato's Protagoras retells the theft as an allegory of man's unprovided nature. c. 8 CE OVID Metamorphoses Book 8: Daedalus and Icarus in the telling that fixed the story for the Latin West and for European art — feathers graded small to large, thread at the midrib, wax at the base, and the warning to fly the middle course. 1ST–2ND CENTURY CE APOLLODORUS · PAUSANIAS The Library and Epitome give the cluster its fullest prose narratives; Pausanias, travelling Greece five centuries after Plato, records the altars, the torch race, and the wooden images still ascribed to Daedalus's own hand. III. Prometheus Before the Theft: A Titan of the Second Generation Prometheus is a Titan by birth and an anomaly by conduct. Hesiod introduces him in the catalogue of the children of Iapetus , the Titan who married the Oceanid Clymene ( Theogony 507–511): their sons are Atlas, who holds up the heaven at the borders of the earth; Menoetius, whom Zeus blasted with the thunderbolt for his presumption and sent down to Erebus; Prometheus , “clever, full of various wiles” in Evelyn-White's rendering; and Epimetheus , the scatter-brained brother, “who from the first was a mischief to men who eat bread”, because it was he who first took from Zeus the woman the god had formed. The family's character is set in four lines: strength punished (Atlas), pride punished (Menoetius), cleverness punished (Prometheus), and folly rewarded with a wife (Epimetheus). Apollodorus's Titan list gives the brothers a different mother, Asia ( Library 1.2.3) — a variant worth registering, because it is typical of the tradition: the framework is stable, the details migrate. The tragedy Prometheus Bound makes a bolder change, giving Prometheus a mother who is Themis , identified with Earth herself, from whom he has inherited his foreknowledge — a parentage that serves the play's purposes, since its Prometheus must be able to know the future he refuses to sell to Zeus. The names themselves are a matched pair, and the Greeks heard them as such. Promētheus is the Forethinker — the one who sees beforehand, from pro- , before, and the root of mētis , counsel or cunning intelligence. Epimētheus is the Afterthinker — the one who understands afterwards, when the evil thing is already his, as Hesiod says of the moment he accepted Pandora. Whether the names generated the characters or the characters the names is a question the evidence cannot answer, and this article does not pretend otherwise; what is certain is that by Hesiod's time the pair functioned as a diagram of two kinds of mind, and that every later telling, Plato's included, works the diagram. Prometheus's own defining quality, in Hesiod, is mētis itself: the supple, devious, trap-setting intelligence that Greek thought opposed to brute force ( biē ) — and the drama of his story is that he meets, in Zeus, the one mind in the cosmos more encompassing than his own. Hesiod's episode ends on exactly that moral, stated flatly: it is not possible to deceive or to go beyond the will of Zeus ( Theogony 613, paraphrased). The tragedian will take the same figure and invert the moral's sympathy entirely. Both Prometheuses are in this article, in their places. One further element belongs to the dossier before the narrative begins, because later tradition made so much of it: Prometheus as maker of mankind itself . Hesiod never says it. In Hesiod, men already exist when Prometheus divides the ox at Mecone; the Titan is their advocate and trickster-patron, not their creator. The fashioning of men from earth and water enters the tradition later — it is the opening of Apollodorus's account ( Library 1.7.1), it stands behind Ovid's creation scene ( Metamorphoses 1.82ff.), and Pausanias records the local claim at Panopeus in Phocis, where two stones of clay-coloured earth were shown as the remnant of the clay from which Prometheus moulded the whole race, and were said to smell like human flesh ( Description of Greece 10.4.4, paraphrased). Frazer's note to Apollodorus collects the parallels. The creator-Prometheus is thus a genuine ancient development, not a modern embroidery — but it is a development, and the distinction matters for Section XXIII: the alchemical tradition's Prometheus, fashioner of man from earth, is Apollodorus's and Ovid's figure, not Hesiod's. “Prometheus moulded men out of water and earth and gave them also fire, which, unknown to Zeus, he had hidden in a stalk of fennel.” — APOLLODORUS, LIBRARY 1.7.1, TRANS. J. G. FRAZER (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1921) Frazer's single sentence, written down some eight centuries after Hesiod, contains the whole later dossier in miniature: the making, the gift, the stalk, the punishment that follows in the next breath. Hesiod's own telling is slower, stranger, and begins not with a making but with a meal. IV. Mecone: The Divided Ox The Theogony tells the Prometheus story backwards, and the structure is worth noticing. Hesiod first gives the punishment — the binding, the eagle, the release by Heracles (lines 521–534) — and only then explains what it was for, beginning with the scene at Mecone (lines 535–560). Mecone itself is otherwise almost unknown: later tradition identified it with Sicyon, on the Corinthian gulf, and a scholiast on Pindar preserves the equation. What happens there, Hesiod says, is a settlement : “when the gods and mortal men had a dispute at Mecone” (Evelyn-White) — in the poem's chronology, this is the moment when the relations between the newly enthroned Olympians and mankind were being fixed, and the fixing takes the form of a division of meat. Prometheus comes forward, cuts up a great ox, and sets out two portions, “trying to deceive the mind of Zeus”. The division is the heart of the story, and Hesiod describes it with a butcher's precision. For men: the flesh and the rich inner parts, laid on the hide and covered over with the ox's paunch — the best of the animal, hidden inside its least appetising wrapping, a stomach. For Zeus: the white bones, dressed up with cunning art and covered with shining fat — nothing edible at all, arranged to look like the richer portion. Each heap is a lie about its contents, in opposite directions. Zeus speaks first, and his speech is the crux on which two millennia of interpretation have turned. In Evelyn-White's translation: “Son of Iapetus, most glorious of all lords, good sir, how unfairly you have divided the portions!” — HESIOD, THEOGONY 543–544, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB, 1914) Prometheus, smiling softly and not forgetting his cunning trick, invites him to take whichever portion his heart bids. And then Hesiod does something remarkable: he insists, in so many words, that Zeus was not deceived . Zeus, “whose wisdom is everlasting, saw and failed not to perceive the trick”, and already in his heart was planning mischief against mortal men. With both hands he took up the white fat; and when he saw the white bones craftily tricked out beneath it, wrath came to his spirit (lines 545–558, paraphrased from Evelyn-White). The poem then draws the aetiology in one sentence, and it is the sentence for which the whole episode exists: because of this , the tribes of men on earth burn white bones to the deathless gods on fragrant altars. That is Greek sacrifice as every classical Greek knew it in practice. At a thysia , the animal's thigh-bones, wrapped in fat, were burned on the altar for the god, who received the smoke and savour; the meat was roasted and eaten by the worshippers. Hesiod's story is the charter myth of that practice — the explanation, in narrative form, of why the gods get the inedible part. This hub's Theogony article (Section IX) gives the episode in its place within the succession narrative; the treatment here is the full one. // WAS ZEUS FOOLED? // The text says he was not — twice. Yet the story's machinery requires a grievance, and some modern editors, M. L. West among them, have held that Hesiod has reworked an older version in which Zeus was genuinely deceived, and has left the seams showing: a god who knowingly chooses bones and then rages at the sight of them is a figure under strain. Vernant's reading (Section V) accepts the text as it stands and makes the knowing choice the whole point. The article reports both; the poem, as transmitted, says Zeus perceived the trick. Three features of the episode deserve emphasis before the interpretation begins. First, the setting is a meal shared, or about to cease to be shared. Gods and men are together at Mecone, settling their relations — the last scene, in Hesiod's implied chronology, of the age when the two kinds ate at one table. The division of the ox is simultaneously the end of that commensality: from now on gods and men will eat apart, differently, the one kind receiving smoke, the other meat, and sacrifice will be the regulated channel between them. Second, the trick is a division, not a theft. Prometheus does not steal the meat; he apportions it, and invites Zeus to ratify the apportionment by choosing. What is founded at Mecone is a distribution — a permanent allocation of shares between kinds — and Greek sacrifice will re-enact that allocation at every altar. Third, the portion men receive is the perishable one. Meat rots; it must be eaten at once; it nourishes a body that itself perishes. The gods' portion — bone, fat, smoke — is precisely what does not nourish, because the gods do not need nourishing: they are deathless, and their share is the incorruptible residue. Hesiod does not spell out this symbolism. Vernant did, and Section V follows him. V. Reading Mecone: Vernant and the Founding of the Human Condition The most influential modern reading of the Mecone episode is that of Jean-Pierre Vernant , set out in his essay on the myth of Prometheus in Hesiod (collected in Myth and Society in Ancient Greece ) and developed across the collaborative volume The Cuisine of Sacrifice Among the Greeks (edited by Marcel Detienne and Vernant). Vernant's reading is structural: he treats the episode not as a folktale about a clever Titan and a touchy god, but as a coded account of what a human being is , in the Greek system of categories — and his first move is to take Hesiod's insistence seriously. Zeus is not fooled. Zeus sees the trick, and chooses the bones anyway, because the bones are the portion appropriate to gods . On this reading the division is not a swindle that happens to have permanent consequences; it is the founding act itself, performed jointly by the trickster who proposes it and the king who ratifies it, and what it founds is the distance between gods and men. Prometheus, intending to cheat heaven on mankind's behalf, in fact fixes mankind's place in the order of things — below the gods, above the beasts, and defined by the gap on both sides. The story's conclusion in the Theogony — it is impossible to go beyond the will of Zeus — is on Vernant's reading not a pious tag but the episode's thesis. The details lock together, in Vernant's hands, into a single system. The portions: men receive meat, the food of mortals, which feeds a body subject to hunger and death; the gods receive bones wrapped in fat, burned into smoke — the part of the animal that does not decay, for beings who do not die. To eat meat is to declare oneself mortal; every sacrifice thereafter repeats the declaration. The fire: because men eat meat, and eat it cooked, they need fire — which is why the withholding and theft of fire follow the division as its direct consequence, and why sacrifice, cooking, and the hearth form one complex. The woman: because men are mortal, they cannot continue themselves except through women and birth; Pandora is therefore not an arbitrary extra punishment but the third term of the same system — sacrifice, agriculture (men must now work the earth for grain, the bios Zeus hid), and marriage are the three institutions of the mortal condition, and Hesiod's two poems distribute them between the same small group of stories. Vernant notes, too, the system's sly internal rhyme: Prometheus hides the good meat inside a stomach — and woman, in Hesiod's sour presentation, is herself figured as a belly, an appetite lodged in the household, consuming what the man's labour wins from the earth. The trick at Mecone and the counter-gift of Pandora are made of the same material. // HOW THIS ARCHIVE USES VERNANT // Vernant's reading is presented here as what it is: the most powerful modern interpretation of the episode, argued from the text's own structure, and widely (not universally) accepted. It is scholarship, register (c) — a later reading — not a recovery of what Hesiod's first audience consciously thought. Where this article's own exposition leans on the structural pattern (sacrifice, fire, marriage as one system), the leaning is Vernant's, and it is attributed. The counter-position — that Hesiod has imperfectly reworked a simpler tale in which Zeus really was deceived — is stated in Section IV and remains a live alternative in the editions. One consequence of Vernant's reading matters for everything that follows in this article. If Mecone founds the human condition, then the theft of fire is not a second, separable adventure but the completion of the first: the division gave men meat, and meat without fire is carrion. Prometheus's theft is, structurally, the trickster finishing his own job — and Zeus's counter-stroke, the fashioned woman, is likewise the completion of the settlement, the term that makes the mortal package whole. That is why Hesiod's two poems can split the story between them and why neither telling feels incomplete on its own terms: each is working the same system from a different side. It is also why the cluster gathered in this article coheres. Fire, in the Greek telling, is never just a substance. It is the middle term between gods who need nothing and beasts who cook nothing — the technology that makes men men, delivered by theft, and paid for in full. VI. Fire Withheld and Fire Stolen: The Fennel Stalk Zeus's answer to Mecone is not thunder but withholding . In the Theogony (lines 561–564, paraphrased), angry in spirit, he refuses to give the power of unwearying fire to the ash-tree race of mortal men who live on the earth. The Works and Days tells the same stroke from the economic side (lines 42–50): the gods have hidden the bios , the means of life, from men — otherwise a man could work one day and live a year — and Zeus, angered because Prometheus deceived him, hid fire itself. The two withholdings belong together: livelihood and fire are both things men once, in the poem's fiction, might have had without labour, and now must win by labour or by theft. Prometheus chooses theft. In both poems the instrument is identical and is named with care: he steals the fire back in a hollow fennel stalk — Greek narthēx — “so that Zeus who delights in thunder did not see it” (Evelyn-White, Works and Days 50–52). The detail is not decoration. The giant fennel ( Ferula communis ) grows a tall, thick stalk whose dry white pith, once kindled, smoulders slowly for hours without flame — a natural, portable slow-match, used around the Mediterranean in historical times precisely for carrying live fire from place to place. Frazer's note on Apollodorus 1.7.1 describes the stalk — some five feet high, the pith catching and holding fire like a wick — and the identification has never been seriously doubted. The myth's central prop is a piece of real fire-technology: the theft was imagined by people who knew exactly how you would carry a coal across a landscape without letting it die. Zeus's speech on discovering the theft, in the Works and Days , is the hinge on which the whole cluster turns, because it announces Pandora in the same breath as the fire: “Son of Iapetus, surpassing all in cunning, you are glad that you have outwitted me and stolen fire — a great plague to you yourself and to men that shall be. But I will give men as the price for fire an evil thing in which they may all be glad of heart while they embrace their own destruction.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 54–59, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB, 1914) “So said the father of men and gods, and laughed aloud” — and the laugh is the most frightening sound in Hesiod. The exchange is now explicit, and Hesiod's own word for it is a commercial one: anti pyros , in return for fire , the price of fire. Fire for woman, gift for counter-gift, in an economy of revenge in which every benefit is invoiced. Prometheus's own share of the plague — “a great plague to you yourself” — is the subject of the next section. But one observation belongs here, because it disciplines the romantic reading in advance: in Hesiod, the theft of fire is not celebrated. It is not said to be just, or noble, or even, on balance, good for men, who receive with it the necessity of labour, the company of Pandora, and the contents of her jar. Hesiod's Prometheus is a benefactor whose benefactions are indistinguishable from disasters, and Hesiod's Zeus is a king whose punishments are the constitution of the world. The defiant, admirable Prometheus — the one the nineteenth century would worship — had to wait for the tragedian of Section IX, and even he is more complicated than his admirers. // THE STALK IN THE TRAGEDY // The fennel stalk survives into Prometheus Bound , where the Titan, alone on his rock, names it as the instrument of the theft: he stole the “secret fount of fire” hidden in a fennel stalk — in Smyth's translation, the fire that proved to mortals “a great instructor in arts and a means of much progress” ( Prometheus Bound 107–111, paraphrased in wording, the stalk and its role exact). By the fifth century the prop needed no explanation. It had become the theft's signature. VII. The Punishment: Chains, Eagle, and Liver Hesiod gives the punishment before its cause, in the catalogue of Iapetus's sons, and his account ( Theogony 521–525) is the tradition's bedrock. In Evelyn-White's translation: “And ready-witted Prometheus he bound with inextricable bonds, cruel chains, and drove a shaft through his middle, and set on him a long-winged eagle, which used to eat his immortal liver; but by night the liver grew as much again everyway as the long-winged bird devoured in the whole day.” — HESIOD, THEOGONY 521–525, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB, 1914) Every element of the sentence is doing work. The bonds are inextricable — the punishment is engineered, not merely imposed. The shaft through his middle fixes him to the rock as a stake fixes a victim: he is not chained to a mountain he might move around, but pinned, displayed. The eagle is long-winged , a creature of the far sky for a punishment at the far edge of the world. And the liver is immortal — the organ regrows by night exactly as much as the bird devours by day, so that the punishment is calibrated to be literally endless: not a long torment but a perpetual one, a machine for suffering with no terminal state. Hesiod does not name the place. The location the tradition settled on is the Caucasus — Apollodorus states it flatly: Zeus ordered Hephaestus to nail Prometheus's body to Mount Caucasus, “which is a Scythian mountain”, and there he remained bound for many years while the eagle devoured the lobes of his liver ( Library 1.7.1, paraphrased). The tragedy's opening scene is set in a Scythian wilderness of crags, at the earth's limit, which later readers identified with the Caucasus; the name then attached itself to the whole story. The geography is the meaning: the punishment happens where the ordered world runs out. Two features of the developed tradition deserve separate notice. The smith is the gaoler. In Apollodorus, it is Hephaestus who does the nailing, on Zeus's orders; in Prometheus Bound , the play opens with Hephaestus on stage, hammer in hand, compelled by Power and Force — Kratos and Bia, Zeus's enforcers — to rivet his own kinsman to the rock, protesting as he works. The maker of Pandora is made to be the maker of the fire-thief's chains: the cluster's figures keep being set to work against one another, and Section IX returns to the scene. The eagle has a pedigree. Apollodorus, in the Heracles narrative, identifies the bird as the offspring of Echidna and Typhon ( Library 2.5.11) — the monster-parents of Cerberus, the Hydra, and the Chimaera. The punishment is thus staffed from the same brood as the labours of Heracles, which is fitting, since it is Heracles who ends it. A word, finally, on the liver itself. Greek thought located the passions and the life in the liver — it is the organ of Prometheus's cousin Tityos's identical punishment in the underworld, where two vultures eat the liver of the giant who assaulted Leto ( Odyssey 11.576–581). The parallel is ancient and was already available to Hesiod's audience: a liver that regrows for a bird that returns is the underworld's own machinery, installed above ground, at the world's edge, for a god who could not be killed and so had to be kept . VIII. The Release: Heracles on the Caucasus The punishment ends, as Hesiod tells it, by the will of the god who imposed it. Heracles, the valiant son of Alcmene, on his journey to the apples of the Hesperides, shot the eagle and delivered the son of Iapetus from his cruel plague — “not without the will of Olympian Zeus” , Hesiod is careful to say ( Theogony 526–534, paraphrased from Evelyn-White). Zeus, though he had been angry, ceased from his wrath, and the poem gives his reason without embarrassment: so that the glory of Heracles, his son, might be yet greater over the earth. The release of Prometheus is, in Hesiod's economy, an episode in Heracles's career and an act of Zeus's policy. There is no rebellion in heaven, no storming of the Caucasus against the king's will. The king relents, on schedule, for dynastic reasons — and Prometheus's centuries of torment turn out to have been, among other things, a glory-reserve held against his deliverer's arrival. It is a colder ending than the tragedy's, and a more Hesiodic one. Apollodorus's prose account ( Library 2.5.11) adds the machinery by which the release was squared with heaven's bookkeeping, and the addition is characteristic of the handbook tradition's tidiness. Heracles, crossing to the mainland on his way to Atlas, shot on the Caucasus the eagle, offspring of Echidna and Typhon, that was devouring the liver of Prometheus, and released him — after Prometheus had chosen for himself the bond of olive , a token bond, a wreath or ring of olive-wood worn as the sign that the sentence was commuted rather than annulled; and to Zeus Heracles presented Chiron , the immortal centaur, who had been incurably wounded by one of Heracles's own arrows and longed to die but could not, being deathless. Chiron, though immortal, consented to die in Prometheus's stead (the exchange is told at 2.5.4 as well, with the parties reversed in the telling: there Prometheus offers himself to Zeus to become immortal in Chiron's place, and so Chiron died). An immortality, in the handbook's arithmetic, cannot simply be cancelled; it must be transferred. The freed Titan then paid his rescuer in the currency he was richest in — information: it was Prometheus who advised Heracles not to fetch the apples
