A Figure Who Survives Only in Quotation Maria the Jewess is the earliest named woman in the history of chemical technology, and she is known to us in the most precarious way a historical figure can be known: entirely at second hand. No work of hers survives. No treatise, no letter, no recipe collection travels under her name in any manuscript that a modern editor can print as hers. What survives is a body of quotation, paraphrase, and attribution inside the works of later writers — pre-eminently Zosimos of Panopolis , the earliest alchemical author whose own writings survive in bulk, who flourished around 300 CE and who cites her, repeatedly and with reverence, as an authority of the past. Everything else — the Arabic and Latin dialogues that speak in her voice, the sayings that gather under her name, the portrait engravings of the Renaissance — is later tradition building on that quoted core. This article is written to that evidentiary shape, and it asks the reader to hold the shape in mind throughout. When it says “Maria describes” or “Maria specifies”, it means: a text transmitted by Zosimos, or by a later compiler drawing on the same tradition, presents this description or specification as Maria's . That is not a pedantic hedge. It is the difference between the two things this archive exists to keep apart: what the record attests, and what later ages made of it. Maria is an unusually pure case of the distinction, because in her case the record is so thin and the later making so rich. A woman who may have lived in Alexandria in the first, second, or third century CE became, across seventeen centuries, a prophetess, a sister of Moses, a daughter of Plato, the inventor of the still, and the eponym of the double boiler. The quoted authority underneath all of that is real, and she is remarkable enough without the embroidery: the tradition's chief named source for the design of chemical apparatus, quoted by the first surviving alchemical author as one of the sages of the art. The companion treatment in this archive should be named at the outset, because the two articles divide the labour deliberately. The Egyptology division's profile of Zosimos of Panopolis treats the apparatus from inside Zosimos' corpus: the kērotakis step by step in its §XI, the tribikos, dibikos, and ambix in its §XII, and Maria and the bain-marie attribution in its §XIII. The present article is the companion piece from the other side: Maria herself as a figure and an authority, the apparatus tradition that bears her name considered as her tradition and traced through its transmission, and the modern scholarship — from Berthelot's edition to Taylor's reconstructions to the most recent work of Raggetti and Martelli — that has tried to recover her from the quotations. Where the two articles overlap, this one does not repeat the other's wording; it cross-refers, and it adds what belongs to Maria's own dossier: her names, her contested dates, her later identifications, her attributed doctrine and dicta, and the long afterlife of her bath. ATTESTED IN THE RECORD Zosimos, writing around 300 CE, quotes and cites a Maria — “the divine Maria”, in the tradition's rendering of his epithet — as a past authority among the sages, and credits her specifically with descriptions of apparatus: the kērotakis, the tribikos, and the heated bath that later bears her name. Later Greek authors, including the commentator Christianos and the Olympiodorus tradition, cite her in the same capacity. INFERENCE, LABELLED AS SUCH Her dates (conventionally the 1st–3rd centuries CE), her Alexandrian setting, and her priority over the authorities Zosimos pairs her with. None of these is stated by any surviving source as a fact about her life; all are reconstructed from the way Zosimos speaks of her as belonging to the past. See Section III. LATER TRADITION, LABELLED AS SUCH Her identification with Miriam, sister of Moses; the title Prophetissa in its full prophetic sense; the Arabic and Latin dialogues in which she teaches a prince named Aros; the Axiom of Maria in its familiar numbered form; and the claim that she discovered hydrochloric acid, which historians of chemistry do not accept. Each is treated in its own section below, under its own label. NOT RECOVERABLE Any sentence she certainly wrote, in her own wording, in Greek. The fragments reach us through excerptors, translators, and copyists across more than a millennium, and this article quotes nothing as her ipsissima verba. Where a saying is given in a named published translation, the translator is named; everything else is labelled paraphrase. II. The Names: Hebraea, Prophetissa, the Copt She travels under a cluster of names, and the cluster itself is evidence — of the different cultures that claimed her. In Greek she is Maria . In Latin she is Maria Hebraea , “Maria the Hebrew woman” — the Jewess of the English title — and Maria Prophetissa (also spelled Prophetissima), “Maria the Prophetess”. In the Arabic tradition she appears as Māriyya al-Qibṭiyya , “Maria the Copt”, and in one Arabic title as a daughter of the Queen of Sheba — an ancestry no Greek source gives her. The early medieval Latin dialogue tradition calls her, in its full style, Maria Prophetissa, sister of Moses . Each name does different work, and keeping them apart is the first discipline of her dossier. Hebraea is the earliest and the most nearly descriptive of the names. It marks her, in the Greek and Latin sources that use it, as a Jewish woman — a member of the large, learned Jewish community of Roman Alexandria, in the city where Greek philosophy, Egyptian craft practice, and Jewish scriptural learning had been in conversation for centuries. Zosimos' own framing of the art's pedigree, as the scholarship summarises it, distinguishes two wisdoms, that of the Egyptians and that of the Hebrews; Maria stands at the head of the Hebrew line as Hermes and the Egyptian authorities stand at the head of the other. Whether the historical woman behind the quotations was in fact Jewish is a question Section VI takes up through Raphael Patai's thesis and the caution it has attracted; what can be said without controversy is narrower: the tradition consistently names her so , from Zosimos onward, and no ancient source names her anything else. Prophetissa is a title of honour that grew. In the alchemical usage of the word, a prophet is not primarily one who foretells; it is one who reveals — who discloses the hidden working of nature and the art, as the prophets of scripture were held to disclose hidden things of God. The title fits the function Maria performs in the texts that cite her: she does not merely report procedures, she pronounces on the art's inner logic, in short authoritative utterances that later writers treat the way theologians treat proof-texts. But the title also invited the identification that Section V examines: a prophetess named Maria, sister — in the Latin dialogue's style — of Moses, slides very easily into being Miriam. The slide is the tradition's, not the record's, and it tells us more about the medieval appetite for biblical pedigrees than about the Alexandrine authority Zosimos quoted. The Copt belongs to her Arabic afterlife. In the Arabic transmission she is naturalised as an Egyptian — a Copt — and supplied with dialogues, letters, and a royal interlocutor that the Greek fragments do not contain. Lucia Raggetti's study of Maria in the Arabo-Islamic tradition (2022) and Matteo Martelli's study of her Practica in early modern alchemy (2022), both in the Brill volume Gendered Touch , are the current scholarly guides to this stratum: the Arabic Maria is not a translation of the Greek Maria but a re-creation of her, in which the quoted authority of Zosimos' pages becomes a speaking teacher in her own right. The historian's rule for all three names is the same: a name is evidence for the community that used it, at the date it used it — Hebraea for the Greek-Latin tradition's memory of her origin, Prophetissa for the medieval tradition's estimate of her authority, the Copt for the Arabic tradition's adoption of her as one of its own. // A NOTE ON SPELLING // This article writes Maria (the Greek and Latin form) rather than the English Mary , and transliterates her apparatus consistently: kērotakis for the reflux chamber, tribikos for the three-armed still, ambix for the still-head, balneum Mariae for the bath. The variants a reader will meet elsewhere — kerotakis, tribicos, bain-marie — are the same words at different points in their transmission, not different devices. One further name belongs in this section because it is so often mistaken for hers. The Arabs knew her, the tradition reports, as the “Daughter of Plato” — an honorific that in Western alchemical texts was also used for white sulphur, so that a reader of the later literature must sometimes decide, from context, whether “the Daughter of Plato” in a given sentence is the woman or the substance. The confusion is itself a small parable of her transmission: in a literature of cover-names, even an authority's honorific could be reabsorbed into the code. What never gets reabsorbed is the plain ethnic — Hebraea, the Jewess — which follows her from Zosimos to the title of this article without interruption. III. Dates and Place: Inference, Not Record Maria has no dates. No source gives her birth, her death, her floruit, her city council, her patron, or a single datable event of her life. The dates assigned to her in modern reference works — the first to third centuries CE — are an inference, and this section states the inference plainly so that the reader can see exactly how much, and how little, it rests on. The inference has three legs. First, she is past for Zosimos. Zosimos, flourishing around 300 CE, speaks of her consistently as an authority of an earlier generation — one of the sages whose writings he expounds, in the same posture in which he expounds the Democritus tradition. She must therefore predate about 300 CE, and the tone of the citations — classic, not contemporary — suggests she predates him by a margin, though the texts nowhere say by how much. Second, she belongs to the formative stratum of the art. The authorities among whom Zosimos and the later tradition place her — the pseudo-Democritus tradition descending from Bolos of Mendes, Agathodaimon, Hermes — belong, in their historical kernels, to the first centuries BCE and CE; the apparatus she is credited with describing belongs to the same early stratum of the Greek alchemical corpus. Third, the Alexandrian setting is inferred from the milieu: Alexandria in Roman Egypt is where the Greek alchemical tradition, on all the evidence assembled in this hub's origins article , took shape, and it is the city the tradition associates with her. No surviving sentence of Zosimos says “Maria of Alexandria” in so many words. Within the inferred range, scholars have placed her differently, and the differences should be reported rather than averaged away. F. Sherwood Taylor, in his survey of Greek alchemy (1930) and his later writings, treated her as one of the first alchemical writers and placed her work no later than the first century CE ; Edmund Oscar von Lippmann, the great German historian of alchemy, is cited for the same early placement, and Marilyn French followed it in her history of women. Other scholars, more cautious about how much pastness Zosimos' tone can bear, leave the whole span open — first to third centuries — which is the formulation the current reference literature, and this article, adopt. The honest summary is a bracket with a direction: before Zosimos, probably well before him, in the first centuries of the Roman Empire, in Egypt — most plausibly Alexandria . Anything more precise is a scholar's estimate wearing the clothes of a fact. 1st–3rd c. CE THE INFERRED FLOURISH The conventional bracket for Maria's activity, inferred from Zosimos' treatment of her as a past authority. Taylor and Lippmann argued for the early end of the range; the bracket as a whole remains the cautious consensus. c. 300 CE ZOSIMOS QUOTES HER Zosimos of Panopolis, the earliest alchemical author whose works survive in bulk, cites Maria among the sages and draws on her for the apparatus descriptions in the treatises transmitted as On Apparatus and Furnaces . This is the fixed point from which all dating of Maria is reckoned backward. 8th c. CE SYNCELLUS' CHRONOLOGY The Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus presents Maria as a teacher of Democritus whom she met in Memphis in the time of Pericles — a placement in the fifth century BCE that no modern scholar accepts, and an early specimen of the tradition's habit of pushing her ever further into a prestigious past. 10th c. CE THE FIHRIST LISTS HER Ibn al-Nadīm's Kitāb al-Fihrist , the great Baghdad index of books, counts Maria among the most famous alchemists and credits her with preparing caput mortuum , a purple pigment — evidence that her name carried authority in the Arabic tradition independently of the Greek manuscripts. 13th–14th c. THE NAME ENTERS LATIN The Latin balneum Mariae , “Maria's bath”, is attested in the Latin alchemical literature — Arnold of Villanova is the name the tradition attaches to its early use — and becomes the standard term from which the French bain-marie descends. 1617 MAIER'S PORTRAIT Michael Maier's Symbola aureae mensae duodecim nationum includes Maria Hebraea among its twelve sages of alchemy, with the engraved portrait by which she is still most often pictured — an image made some fourteen centuries after her inferred lifetime, and evidence only for her Renaissance standing. The Syncellus entry in that timeline deserves a sentence of its own, because it shows the failure mode this article is written against. A chronicler who makes Maria the teacher of Democritus in the age of Pericles has not made a dating error of the ordinary kind; he has done what the tradition always does with its founders, which is to convert authority into antiquity . The same conversion, in reverse, is what the modern bracket refuses: Maria's authority in Zosimos is a fact; her antiquity beyond the bracket is not. A reader who meets a precise date for Maria anywhere — a birth year, a reign, a synchronism — is meeting the tradition, not the record. IV. Maria in Zosimos: Among the Sages The whole Maria dossier rests on one relationship: Zosimos read her, revered her, and said so. This section sets out what that relationship looks like from inside his corpus — briefly, because the full in-corpus treatment is the Egyptology article's §§XI–XIII, to which the reader is referred for the apparatus in Zosimos' own arrangement ( Zosimos of Panopolis, §§XI–XIII ). What belongs here is the character of the citation: how a commentator uses an authority, and what that use certifies. Zosimos places Maria in the company he reserves for the founders: with Hermes, with the Democritus tradition, with Agathodaimon. The tradition renders his epithet for her as “the divine Maria” , and the reference literature summarises his posture as counting her among the sages . Both phrases are reported here as the tradition's renderings of his Greek, not as quotations verified in a critical edition for this article; the posture itself, however, is not in doubt, because it is structural. Zosimos is a commentator — the first known commentator of alchemy — and a commentator's authorities are his credentials. When he expounds an apparatus construction, the name he reaches for is Maria's. In the formulation the scholarship repeats from his text, in paraphrase: many constructions of apparatus were written by Maria . She is his authority specifically on apparatus , as Democritus is his authority on the art's theory and antiquity. That division of labour in his citations is the single most important fact about her: in the earliest surviving alchemical literature, the hardware has a named mistress, and the name is hers. The citations have a texture that distinguishes them from honorific name-dropping, and the texture is worth dwelling on because it is the strongest internal evidence that a real, technically specific body of writing stands behind them. Zosimos does not quote Maria for sentiments alone; he quotes her for specifications — the thickness of a still tube measured against a frying pan, the paste that seals a joint, the behaviour of a vapour in a closed chamber. Taylor, in his 1937 study of the origins of Greek alchemy in Ambix , made the point in the form in which it has been repeated ever since, here paraphrased: the most extensive passage Zosimos quotes from her shows a practical worker, and confirms that the name Maria is not a mere ascription but that of a real woman who knew the inside of a workshop. Taylor's inference — from the concreteness of the quoted matter to the reality of its author — is an inference, and Section VI records the caution that attaches to building biography on it. But as a reading of the citations' character it has carried the field: nobody invents a patron saint and then equips her with tolerances. Zosimos also quotes her on the art's central reagent. The divine water — theion hydōr , the phrase that puns in Greek on “divine” and “sulphur” — runs through his treatises as the volatile, sulphur-bearing agent that draws spirits out of bodies and fixes them into others, and the tradition associates Maria's teaching with its preparation and use, including a silver-sulphide colouring process of the kind the workshop papyri also preserve. Section VII takes up the doctrine in her name; here it is enough to note the shape of the debt. Zosimos' Maria is quoted on the two things his own work is about: the vessels in which spirits are handled, and the water that carries them. Apparatus and reagent, hardware and agent — the whole practical system of the Authentic Memoirs is expounded under her authority, and his visions and doctrines are, as the Egyptology article shows, meditations on the processes her apparatus performs. // HOW TO READ A ZOSIMOS CITATION OF MARIA // Three questions sort the material. Is Zosimos quoting, paraphrasing, or merely invoking her name for authority? The specifications — tube thicknesses, lutes, charges — behave like quotation or close paraphrase of a technical source; the doctrinal utterances behave like a tradition already proverbial. Is the passage in the securest stratum of his corpus — the Authentic Memoirs as delimited by Michèle Mertens' 1995 edition — or in a later excerpt travelling under his name? And does any independent witness (the Syriac tradition, the Arabic tradition, a later Greek commentator) carry the same attribution? Where all three answers are favourable, the Maria dossier is as firm as ancient technical history gets. Where they are not, this article says so at the point of use. V. Miriam the Prophetess: The Later Identification At some point in the tradition's long life, Maria the Alexandrine authority became Miriam the biblical prophetess — the sister of Moses and Aaron who sings at the Red Sea. The identification is everywhere in the later literature: the Latin dialogue styles her soror Moysi , sister of Moses, in its very title; Renaissance and early modern writers repeat the kinship as fact; popular accounts repeat it still. This section states the identification, dates it as well as the evidence allows, and gives the reasons no historian of alchemy accepts it as biography. The mechanism of the identification is transparent, and it is the standard mechanism by which the alchemical tradition manufactured antiquity for its authorities. The art's founders were routinely supplied with biblical or heroic pedigrees: Hermes was fused with Thoth and pushed toward the Flood; Moses himself was enrolled as an alchemist on the strength of the golden calf he ground to powder; Democritus was given a Persian master and an Egyptian initiation. A revered woman authority named Maria — Miriam in Hebrew — who bore the title Prophetissa was an irresistible candidate for the same treatment, because scripture already contained a prophetess of exactly that name, attached to exactly the nation the epithet Hebraea assigned her to. The identification costs the tradition nothing and buys it everything: an authority older than Greek philosophy, sanctified by scripture, and female in a canon short of women. Syncellus' fifth-century-BCE Maria, teaching Democritus at Memphis (Section III), is the same purchase made by a different route. Against the identification, the record is silent in the decisive way. Zosimos, who had every motive to glorify his authority and who retails origin-myths freely elsewhere, does not identify his Maria with Moses' sister. The kinship appears in the later strata — the Arabic and Latin dialogue tradition and the writers who draw on it — centuries after the quotations that constitute her dossier. The chronology the identification requires is also the chronology the whole tradition requires its readers not to examine: a woman of the Exodus era, conventionally placed in the second millennium BCE, cannot be the quoted source of a Greek-writing commentator's apparatus specifications, and no scholar defends the literal claim. What the identification does establish is real, and worth keeping: by the early medieval period, Maria's authority in the tradition was so great that the tradition reached for the highest pedigree it knew. The sister-of-Moses title is a measurement of her standing, taken by the Middle Ages. It is not a fact about her family. A companion inflation should be recorded beside it, because the two travel together in popular writing: the claim that Maria discovered hydrochloric acid . It circulates widely; it is not accepted by historians of chemistry, and no text in her dossier supports it. The mineral acids belong, on the evidence, to a much later stratum of the art — the Latin and Arabic traditions of the central Middle Ages — and attributing one to Maria is the Syncellus move again: authority converted into priority. This archive does not repeat the claim as fact, and flags it here so that a reader who meets it elsewhere knows its standing. VI. Patai's Maria: The Thesis, and the Caution Around It The fullest modern brief for a historical Maria — a real Jewish woman alchemist of Roman Egypt, author of real treatises, standing at the head of a Jewish participation in alchemy that runs from antiquity to the nineteenth century — is Raphael Patai's The Jewish Alchemists: A History and Source Book (Princeton University Press, 1994). Patai (1910–1996), a Hungarian-born ethnographer and historian of wide linguistic range, devoted two consecutive chapters to her: chapter 5, “Maria the Jewess” (pp. 60–80), assembling everything the traditions say of her, and chapter 6, “Zosimus on Maria the Jewess” (pp. 81–91), working through the quotations themselves. His opening verdict on her stratum of the tradition is the book's most quoted sentence about her, paraphrased here: she stands among the first non-fictitious alchemists of the West. Patai's Maria is not a cover-name or a goddess in disguise; she is a working author whose lost treatise On Furnaces and Apparatuses — the title the tradition associates with her material, and the title Zosimos' own apparatus memoirs also bear — was excerpted by Zosimos and echoed for a millennium and a half afterward. Patai's case deserves to be stated at its strongest, because it is built from the dossier itself rather than from enthusiasm. The quotations in Zosimos are technically concrete in a way that honorific invention rarely is (Section IV). The ethnic is consistent across independent traditions — Greek, Arabic, Latin — that had no shared motive for inventing a Jewish foundress. Alexandria's Jewish community was large, Hellenised, and intellectually productive in exactly the inferred centuries, so the figure the quotations imply is a figure her setting could readily have produced; and women practitioners are independently attested in the early alchemical milieu — Cleopatra the Alchemist, Theosebeia, Paphnutia — so a woman authority is not an anomaly requiring special explanation. On Patai's reading, the burden of proof lies on the sceptic: a tradition this consistent about a person this specific is more economically explained by a person than by a personification. The scholarly caution around the book is equally a matter of record, and fairness requires it in the same detail. The review of Patai in the Bulletin for the History of Chemistry (vol. 26, 2001), while acknowledging the range of sources he commands, makes the structural observation that has followed the book since: what the reader can follow through its forty chapters is not a continuous Jewish tradition but a discontinuous line of individual authors and masters who were — in the reviewer's careful phrasing — perhaps or surely Jewish, identified through fragmented sources that relate to Jews, in the review's words, possibly but not always with certainty. Applied to Maria, the caution bites at exactly one joint: the step from the tradition consistently calls her a Jewess and quotes her as an authority to a specific historical Jewish woman wrote these treatises is a step the surviving evidence invites but does not compel, because every link in it passes through excerptors with their own uses for her. Later readers have pressed the same point from the other side, noting places where Patai holds an attribution more confidently than his own quoted authorities — Gershom Scholem's expressed doubts about one later manuscript in the book are the famous instance — would warrant. This article's position is the one the evidence supports when both statements are kept whole. Patai's collection of the Maria dossier remains indispensable — no other single work assembles the Greek, Arabic, and Latin witnesses to her as completely — and his central intuition, that the quotations preserve a real practitioner's writing, is shared in substance by Taylor before him and by the current scholarship's working practice. His biographical confidence exceeds what the dossier can certify. Maria as a historical Jewish woman alchemist of Alexandria is the best explanation of the evidence, held by this archive as a well-grounded probability; Maria with a biography — dates, a school, a life — is Patai's construction, and it is labelled as his wherever this article draws on it. The distinction is not a courtesy. It is the same distinction Sections III and V enforce against Syncellus and the sister-of-Moses tradition, applied even-handedly to a scholar the archive respects. // TWO QUESTIONS, NOT ONE // “Was there a Maria?” and “Was Maria Jewish?” are separate questions with separate evidence. The first is answered by the quotations' technical character and consistency. The second rests on the ethnic the tradition never varies — strong as tradition, unverifiable as record, since no independent document of her life exists against which to check it. Patai answers both with one confidence; the archive answers them separately. VII. The Doctrine Attributed to Her: Bodies, Spirits, and the Divine Water Maria is quoted for hardware, but the tradition also credits her circle with the vocabulary in which the hardware's work was understood — and the vocabulary matters here because the apparatus sections that follow are unintelligible without it. The analysis of substances into bodies and spirits , with soul standing between them in the idiom her tradition bequeathed, is summarised in the reference literature as her characteristic teaching, transmitted through Zosimos: metals are spoken of in lifelike terms, as having bodies that can be killed and spirits that can be drawn out of them, carried elsewhere, and fixed again. A spirit, in this idiom, is a volatile agent — the vapour of sulphur, of mercury, of an arsenic compound — that bears a quality with it: a colour above all. To tincture a metal is to draw a spirit out of one body and fix it into another so that the receiving body wears the spirit's colour permanently, as wool wears a dye. The full doctrinal exposition, in Zosimos' proportions, is given in the Egyptology article's §XV; what follows here is only what a reader of Maria's apparatus needs in hand. Three consequences of the doctrine shape everything attributed to her bench. First, the work is vapour-work. If the active agents are spirits — things that rise under heat and flee if not confined — then the central engineering problem of the art is containment: vessels that keep the fume in, return it to the work, and expose the body to it for as long as the tincture takes. The kērotakis (Section X) is that problem solved in one direction, the still (Sections XII–XIII) in another. Second, the work is read by colour. A fixed spirit announces itself as a changed surface: blackening, whitening, yellowing, purpling — the sequence the theory names melanōsis , leukōsis , xanthōsis , iōsis — and the operator judges the process by watching the metal's colour the way a dyer judges a vat. Third, the work is gentle where it can be. Spirits that flee violence must be coaxed: slow heats, capped heats, heats held for hours and days. The water bath (Section VIII) is that temperament built into a vessel. The doctrine's other famous element — the union of opposites, metals spoken of as male and female whose joining produces a new entity — is attributed to Maria in the later tradition and is treated, with its textual standing, in Section XV among her dicta. Here it is enough to mark its function in her system as transmitted: it is the theoretical counterpart of the bench practice. Two fumes, two gums, two natures are brought together in a sealed vessel under a governed fire, and what comes out is neither of them. A reader who keeps that shape in mind — two bodies, one vessel, a governed heat, a new colour — has the whole of Maria's attributed doctrine in the form in which her apparatus embodies it. // HAZARD NOTE — THE SPIRITS ARE POISONS // The volatile agents of Maria's tradition — mercury vapour, sulphur fumes, arsenic compounds — are cumulative poisons, and the apparatus described in Sections X and XII was designed to concentrate them in sealed, heated vessels. The procedural accounts in this article are historical documentation of what the texts describe, written so that the tradition can be understood. They are not buildable instruction sets, and nothing in them should be attempted. The water bath of Section VIII is the one device in the article whose modern descendants are in ordinary safe use, in laboratories and kitchens that owe the form — and the name — to her tradition. VIII. The Balneum Mariae: The Water Bath, Step by Step The balneum Mariae — Latin for “Maria's bath”, French bain-marie — is the gentlest device in this article and, by any measure of continuous use, the most successful piece of chemical technology to come out of antiquity. Its principle can be stated in one sentence: the vessel holding the material is heated not by the fire but by a surrounding bath of water, and water at ordinary pressure cannot exceed its boiling point, so the inner vessel's temperature is capped, even, and self-governing for as long as the bath is kept topped up. Everything in this section is an unfolding of that sentence — how the bath is built, how it is run, why the physics protects the work, and what the alchemical laboratory used it for. The attribution itself is stated with the archive's usual care at the end of the section: the bath is Maria's in the tradition's naming and in its alchemical laboratory form; water-bath heating as such is older than Maria, and no careful scholar claims she invented hot water. THE BALNEUM MARIAE — CONSTRUCTION AND OPERATION, AS TRANSMITTED 1 · The outer vessel. A broad, open vessel — copper, bronze, or earthenware in the ancient descriptions; the form is indifferent to material so long as it holds water over a fire — forms the bath proper. It is sized to the work: large enough to receive the inner vessel with water standing around it on every side, deep enough that the water can cover the inner vessel to the level of its contents. 2 · The water. The outer vessel is filled with water — in the laboratory tradition, plain water for the standard bath. The water is the device's governor: it is not a container detail but the working part, the medium that will absorb the fire's violence and deliver only its gentleness. 3 · The inner vessel. The vessel holding the material to be heated — a flask, a cucurbit, a small still-pot, a dish of matter to be digested or slowly evaporated — is set down into the water, resting on the bath's floor or on a ring or grid that holds it steady and, in the developed forms, keeps its base off the hottest metal. Its charge sits below the waterline outside, so that the whole working part of the vessel is jacketed. 4 · The fire. A furnace or brazier under the outer vessel is lit and brought up slowly. The fire heats the bath, not the charge. The operator's skill is exercised on the bath alone: a steady, moderate heat, maintained for the length of the operation — hours for a digestion, the better part of a day for a slow coction — with the draught governed so the water simmers rather than rages. 5 · The cap. x: MITHRAISM: THE ROMAN MYSTERIES OF MITHRAS Rome · Ostia · The Rhine and Danube Frontiers · c. 90–400 CE // A CULT WITHOUT A SCRIPTURE :: ROOMS — IMAGES — OUTSIDERS // Mithraism was the most widely distributed mystery cult of the Roman world, and it left no book. No scripture, no liturgy, no myth told by an initiate, and no explanation of its central image survives from inside the cult — only hundreds of cave-shaped rooms, a strikingly uniform picture of a god killing a bull, some thousands of short dedications, and the remarks of outsiders, most of them hostile. This article is therefore built the way the evidence is built: rooms first, image second, outsiders third, and every interpretation labelled with the name of whoever made it. What Cannot Be Known XV. Sources I. The Evidence Problem, Stated First Every other article in this hub's Mysteries sequence rests, at some point, on a text written by someone who stood inside the tradition it describes. Eleusis has the Homeric Hymn to Demeter ; the Orphic current has the Derveni commentary and the gold tablets; the Isis cult has Apuleius, an initiate writing a novel about initiation. Those articles are gathered in The Mysteries , and the reader who comes to Mithras from them should be warned at the threshold: for Mithraism there is no equivalent text. Not a damaged one, not a fragmentary one — none. The cult flourished for roughly three centuries, in hundreds of communities, across an empire that produced paper the way it produced pottery, and it has not left one sentence of its own theology. What survives falls into four classes, and the whole discipline of the subject consists in not confusing them. 1 · BUILDINGS The mithraea themselves: small, cave-shaped, bench-lined halls, identified in the hundreds across the empire. They tell us where the cult met, how many could meet at once, and how the room was arranged. They say nothing, directly, about what the men in the room believed. 2 · IMAGES Above all the tauroctony, the bull-slaying relief or painting that stood at the end of every mithraeum, in some seven hundred surviving examples of remarkable consistency. An image is evidence of what a cult showed its initiates. It is not a caption, and this cult left no caption. 3 · INSCRIPTIONS Roughly a thousand short texts: dedications of altars, reliefs, and buildings, usually giving a man's name, his grade, his unit or profession, and the god's titles — Deo Soli Invicto Mithrae , “to the Unconquered Sun-God Mithras”, is the standard formula. They are prosopography, not doctrine: they tell us who, where, and when, almost never what was taught. 4 · OUTSIDERS A handful of passages in authors who were not initiates: a Neoplatonist philosopher allegorising a cave, three Christian writers attacking a rival, a biographer repeating a story about pirates. Each has an agenda, each is treated in Section X under his own name, and none may be read as a report from inside. The standard corpus makes the imbalance concrete. Maarten Vermaseren's Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae (1956–1960) — the CIMRM, still the reference collection, cited by number throughout the scholarship — runs to some 2,400 entries of monuments and inscriptions, and the decades since have added substantially to it. Manfred Clauss's survey of the material counts, in round numbers, about a thousand inscriptions and seven hundred examples of the bull-slaying scene from some 420 find-spots. Against that mass of stone and paint, the insider literature of Mithraism is zero pages long. Two lost works are known by title and a few paraphrased lines — histories of the mysteries by authors named Euboulus and Pallas, cited by Porphyry — and even they were, so far as the citations show, accounts about the cult rather than scriptures of it. The gap is not an accident of survival alone. A cult that met in rooms built for a few dozen men, admitted by graded initiation, and guarded its rites as mysteries appears simply never to have circulated a written theology for a copyist to preserve. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Because the subject invites invented scripture, this article quotes almost nothing. The one extended quotation is the list of grade-names in Jerome's letter, given in Section VIII from the standard text of the letter. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense — Porphyry, Plutarch, Justin, Tertullian, Firmicus, the Avestan hymn — is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase, with the author and work named at the point of use. Modern scholars' positions are likewise paraphrased and named, never ventriloquised. The consequence should be carried through every section that follows. When a handbook states flatly what Mithraists “believed” — that the bull-slaying released life into the world, that the soul climbed seven planetary spheres, that the initiate was promised resurrection — the reader is entitled to ask which of the four classes of evidence the statement rests on, and the honest answer is almost always the same: on an inference, drawn by a named modern scholar, from images and rooms, sometimes assisted by an outsider with an agenda of his own. Inference is not worthless; some of it is very strong. But in this subject the distance between the stone and the sentence built on it is the whole story, and this article keeps that distance visible. It is the same discipline this hub applies at Eleusis, where the secret was also kept — with the difference that at Eleusis we at least possess the myth the initiates heard. For Mithras we possess the furniture. II. The Phenomenon: A Cult of the Roman World Strip the interpretation away and the phenomenon itself is solid, datable, and mappable. A mystery cult — initiatory, oath-bound, meeting in dedicated rooms under a hierarchy of grades — centred on a god named Mithras , appears in the Roman world in the late first century CE , spreads with remarkable speed along the empire's military and commercial arteries, flourishes through the second and third centuries, and is extinguished in the course of the fourth. Its remains run from Hadrian's Wall to the Euphrates, and from the Danube to North Africa. It was, by distribution, the most successful of the Roman mysteries — the one a traveller in 250 CE was most likely to find, in some small vaulted room behind a barracks or a warehouse, in almost any garrison town or port of the Latin West. The Chronology, at Its Real Strength The earliest literary notice is a line of Statius, in the first book of the Thebaid (c. 80s–90 CE), which speaks — in paraphrase — of Mithras twisting the horns of an unruly bull beneath the rocks of a Persian cave: the god, the bull, and the cave are already together, in a Roman poem, by about 90 CE. The earliest datable monuments belong to the same generation: dedications and mithraea of the Flavian and Trajanic periods, clustering — and this matters for Section XI — in Rome and its port Ostia and on the Rhine and Danube frontiers, not in the Greek East. Through the second century the evidence thickens everywhere in the West; the mithraeum at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates, founded by Palmyrene archers in Roman service, carries dated dedications of 168 and 171 CE and shows the cult fully formed at the empire's eastern edge within a lifetime of its first certain appearance in Italy. The third century is the peak by every count — of new mithraea, of dedications, of named initiates. The fourth century is contraction, then suppression, treated in Section XIII. Two earlier notices are often promoted into evidence for a first-century-BCE cult, and both must be kept at their real weight. Plutarch, writing about 100 CE, says in his Life of Pompey (24) that the Cilician pirates suppressed by Pompey in 67 BCE performed secret rites, among them rites of Mithras, which — he adds — continued to his own day. That is a claim made a century and a half after the event, by a writer with a taste for eastern colour, and no first-century-BCE mithraeum, relief, or inscription has ever been found to support it. It may preserve a genuine memory of Mithras-worship in Cilicia; it cannot document the Roman mystery cult, whose archaeology begins, abruptly and fully formed, some 150 years later. Similarly, Dio Cassius's story of the Armenian king Tiridates at Nero's court in 66 CE, addressing the emperor as one who had come to worship him “as Mithras”, attests the god's name and its Iranian royal associations in the East. It attests nothing about mysteries in Rome. The distinction between the name Mithras circulating in the eastern Mediterranean and the Roman mystery cult of Mithras is the single most important chronological distinction in the subject, and Section XI returns to it. c. 90 CE STATIUS; THE FIRST MONUMENTS Statius's Thebaid names Mithras, the bull, and the cave. The earliest datable dedications and mithraea belong to the Flavian–Trajanic generation, in Rome, Ostia, and the frontier provinces. 168–171 CE DURA-EUROPOS Dated dedications in the mithraeum of the Palmyrene archers on the Euphrates: the cult, complete with grades and tauroctony, at the empire's eastern frontier. 3RD CENTURY THE PEAK The great majority of mithraea are built, adapted, or redecorated; the epigraphic record of named initiates is densest; Ostia accumulates its exceptional cluster of sanctuaries (Section V). 4TH CENTURY CONTRACTION AND SUPPRESSION Fewer foundations, some violent destructions, some careful burials of cult images; imperial law turns against sacrifice in 391–392; the last mithraea close, are wrecked, or are built over (Section XIII). The Map, and What It Argues The distribution is not even, and its unevenness is itself evidence. The densest provinces are the military zones of the Rhine and upper Danube — Germania Superior, Raetia, Noricum, the Pannonias — together with Italy , Britain along the northern frontier, Dacia , and the port cities of the West. The Greek East, by contrast, is strikingly thin: a scatter of monuments in Asia Minor, very little in Greece itself, a modest presence in Syria largely explained by Roman garrisons like Dura. A cult diffusing westward out of Persia through Anatolia over centuries should be thickest where it started. The Mithraic map is thickest where the Roman army and the Roman customs service were thickest, and its earliest datable cluster sits in the capital's own port. Whatever Mithraism was, its vehicle was Roman: the legion on transfer, the customs official on posting, the merchant and the imperial slave moving along the empire's internal routes. The cult's own sociology (Section III) is written in its map. One more feature deserves emphasis: the cult's uniformity . A mithraeum in Britain and one in Syria are recognisably the same institution — same plan, same image, same grades in the same order — though there was no Mithraic church, no central authority, and no scripture to enforce the pattern. How a textless cult standardised itself so tightly is a genuine puzzle. The most economical answer the evidence allows is that the pattern travelled with the men: soldiers and officials initiated in one post founded or reshaped the community at the next. That is an inference, and it is labelled as one; the uniformity it explains is a fact of the archaeology. III. Who the Initiates Were — and the Question of Women The inscriptions, thin as they are on doctrine, are rich in names, and Manfred Clauss's prosopography, Cultores Mithrae (1992), assembled them into the cult's social portrait: in round terms, a thousand or more named adherents whose status or profession can be read from the stones. The portrait is consistent from province to province. SOLDIERS AND VETERANS The largest single bloc: legionaries, auxiliaries, officers up to a middling rank, and veterans settled near their old stations. The frontier density of the mithraea (Section II) is this bloc made architectural. The older picture of Mithraism as the soldiers' religion nonetheless overstates it: soldiers are a plurality of the named adherents, not the whole, and in a civilian port like Ostia they are scarcely present at all. THE IMPERIAL SERVICE Imperial slaves and freedmen of the emperor's household administration, and — conspicuously in the Danube provinces — the staff of the customs service, the portorium : clerks, station-managers, and their slaves, whose postings moved them along the same routes the cult travelled. Mithraism maps onto the empire's junior bureaucracy as faithfully as onto its army. MERCHANTS, SLAVES, FREEDMEN Traders in the ports; privately owned slaves, who appear as dedicators in their own right and sometimes in the grades; freedmen in numbers. A slave and a freeborn officer could stand in the same grade hierarchy, ranked by initiation rather than by birth — one of the cult's real attractions, and one of the few social facts about it that the stones state plainly. WHO IS MISSING The high aristocracy is almost entirely absent for the cult's first two and a half centuries. A small group of senatorial adherents appears only in the later fourth century at Rome, in the milieu of the last pagan revival — the exception that marks how thoroughly Mithraism had been a cult of the empire's middle and lower ranks. The communities were correspondingly small. A mithraeum's benches (Section IV) seat a few dozen reclining diners at most, and the membership lists that survive fit that scale: the bronze membership tablet from Virunum in Noricum, dated to 184 CE and recording names added year by year, lists a community numbered in the dozens, not the hundreds. Mithraism was not a mass movement with local branches; it was a network of small, intense, face-to-face cells, each gathered around its Pater , its Father — the senior grade who presided over a community (Section VIII) — and bound to the next cell by the mobility of its members and the uniformity of its forms, not by any organisation above the cell. There is no evidence for Mithraic provinces, synods, or any authority beyond the individual Pater. The Question of Women, at Its Real Strength The standard statement — Mithraism was an all-male cult — is one of the best-supported negative claims in the study of ancient religion, and it should still be stated precisely, because its support is of a particular kind. It rests on total epigraphic silence across a large corpus : among the thousand-plus named adherents, dedicators, and grade-holders in the inscriptions, and in the membership lists such as Virunum's, every name is male. Not nearly every name — every name. Cumont drew the conclusion in 1899 from the corpus he had just assembled, and a further century of finds has not produced a female initiate's dedication to set against it. For Ostia specifically, where the record is densest, the modern study of the cult there reports no evidence of even marginal female participation. Against that silence stand exactly the kinds of scraps that keep a question technically open. A passage of Porphyry ( On Abstinence 4.16), describing the animal names of the grades, has been read as assigning women a corresponding animal designation — the passage is compressed, its text and reference disputed, and it may concern the symbolism of the grades rather than the admission of women. A funerary inscription from North Africa appears to style a woman with a feminine form of the Lion grade, lea , “lioness”; its context is ambiguous and it may not be Mithraic at all. The scholar David Jonathan argued in 2000 that women were involved with Mithraic groups in at least some places; Aleš Chalupa's review of the whole dossier concludes that the traditional position still stands. The archive's verdict follows the evidence's weight: the cult of the mithraea was, so far as a large and consistent record can show, a cult of men ; the two or three ambiguous scraps are recorded here because the discipline of this hub is to show the counter-evidence, not because they balance the corpus. What women in an initiate's household knew, believed, or practised at home is beyond the evidence entirely, and this article does not speculate on it. IV. The Mithraeum: A Cave Built Indoors The primary record of Mithraism is a room. The initiates called it, among other names, a spelaeum — a cave — and the word is the plan: a mithraeum is a cave manufactured indoors, in whatever material a town offered, inside buildings that from the street looked like nothing at all. Mithraea are found inserted into warehouses, baths, houses, barracks, and the basements of later churches; purpose-built examples are usually half-buried. Almost none presents a temple front to the street. The cult that left no book also built no skyline: its architecture is interior, windowless, and turned inward, and that is the first thing its remains say about it. The Standard Plan With local variation, the plan repeats from Britain to Syria. A rectangular hall, commonly in the range of ten to twenty metres long. Down each long side runs a continuous masonry bench or podium, raised, sloping slightly, on which the initiates reclined for the communal meal, facing inward across a central aisle . At the far end, in an apse or niche — often framed as a cave-mouth, sometimes roughened with pumice or tufa to imitate rock — stood the cult image : the tauroctony, as relief, painting, or free-standing group (Sections VI–VII). Before it, one or more small altars . The vault, where it survives or can be reconstructed, was in some cases painted with stars; the room was lit by lamps and by whatever light the doorway admitted, and in some mithraea by small openings contrived to throw a shaft of light toward the image — the specific claims made for particular light-effects at particular sites are modern reconstructions and are labelled as such in the site reports. Many mithraea add an ante-room for preparation and storage; some have a well or water basin, consistent with the water-miracle scene in the god's image-cycle (Section VII) and with ritual washing, though the use made of the water is nowhere described. Element What the archaeology shows What it does not show The benches Reclining places for a communal meal, sized for a few dozen men at most; animal bones, pottery, and drinking vessels in the debris of many mithraea confirm regular eating and drinking in the room The menu's ritual meaning, the words spoken, or whether the meal re-enacted the banquet of Mithras and Sol shown in the images — all inference The cave form Windowless or near-windowless halls, vaulted, often sunken; the cult image set in a rock-like niche; the room called a cave in the sources Why a cave. Porphyry's cosmic explanation (Section X) is a philosopher's interpretation, offered two centuries into the cult's life The cult niche The tauroctony at the room's focus, flanked in many examples by the torchbearers as statues in their own niches What was said or done before the image at any particular rite Capacity Communities of a few dozen; the room enforces the small, graded, face-to-face character of the cult (Section III) Whether smallness was doctrine, economics, or both — the stones do not distinguish Feasting remains At a few sites, notably the mithraeum at Tienen in Belgium, large deposits of animal bone and broken pottery indicate communal feasts on a considerable scale at festivals The calendar of those festivals, which is unrecorded for the cult as a whole Two consequences follow from the plan, and both are firmer than most of what is said about Mithraic belief. First, the cult's centre of gravity was a meal eaten together in a ranked room : whatever else initiation conferred, it issued in a seat on a bench, in grade order, before the image. The Christian witnesses (Section X) who fixate on the Mithraic meal — bread, a cup, words spoken over them — were reacting to something architecturally real. Second, the room was a total environment : a man reclining in it saw the bull-slaying before him, the torchbearers beside it, stars (where painted) above him, and his graded fellows around him, and nothing of the ordinary street-world at all. Modern readings of the mithraeum as a model of the cosmos (Sections X and XII) begin from this real enclosure; how far the initiates themselves theorised it is the part that cannot be recovered. Contrast the public temple of this hub's Roman Religion article: civic cult was conducted outdoors, before a crowd, at an altar in front of a god's house. The mithraeum inverts every term — indoors, hidden, initiates only, its image lit artificially in a built cave. That inversion is the mystery-form itself, shared with the cults of The Mysteries ; Mithraism gave the form its most standardised architecture. V. Ostia: The Urban Case If the frontier mithraeum shows the cult in its military setting, Ostia — Rome's port, excavated as few Roman towns have been — shows it in the city, and Ostia is where the numbers become startling. Giovanni Becatti's catalogue of the Ostian mithraea, published in 1954 in the official excavation series, already listed fifteen; subsequent work has raised the count, and totals of seventeen or eighteen identified mithraea now circulate in the literature, the variation depending on how doubtful cases are counted. Either figure makes the point: in a town of perhaps fifty or sixty thousand people, archaeologists can walk the streets and point to a mithraeum every few blocks. No other town preserves anything like the density, because no other town of the cult's heartland survives as completely — Rome itself certainly held more mithraea, but Rome is buried under Rome. The Ostian examples display the cult's whole urban repertoire. They are tucked into the ground floors of apartment blocks, into warehouses near the Tiber wharves, into the substructures of baths, into a converted house; one was installed in the premises of a guild, the rope-makers, under a patron named Fructosus. They are, with few exceptions, adaptations , not new buildings: a long room, a pair of benches, a niche, an altar — the kit of parts of Section IV, fitted into whatever shell the town provided. The dedicators are the port's working population: merchants, warehouse staff, slaves and freedmen, the occasional official. The army, dominant on the frontiers, is marginal here, because Ostia was not a garrison town. Ostia is therefore the standing correction to the “soldiers' religion” slogan: in the cult's most thickly documented community, Mithraism appears as a religion of the commercial and servile city. THE MITHRAEUM OF FELICISSIMUS A modest adapted room of the later third century, famous for one object: the black-and-white mosaic laid down its central aisle in seven panels of symbols, panel by panel the fullest material statement of the seven grades (Section VIII). The dedicatory panel names Felicissimus, the man who paid for the pavement. THE MITHRAEUM OF THE SEVEN SPHERES Named for its mosaic of the planetary spheres; its benches carry mosaics of the zodiac signs. It is among the most explicitly cosmic interiors the cult has left, and it is cited — with due caution — in every discussion of the astral readings (Section XII). THE MITHRAEUM OF THE SEVEN GATES Named for a mosaic showing seven gates. The name has inevitably been connected with the seven-gated ladder that the pagan critic Celsus, quoted by Origen, ascribed to the mysteries (Section VIII); the connection is a modern association, attractive and unprovable, and is labelled as such in the literature. THE PAINTED MITHRAEA The Mithraeum of the Painted Walls ( Pareti Dipinte ) and others preserve wall-painting where most sites preserve only masonry — processions and cult scenes comparable to the richer cycle at Santa Prisca in Rome (Section VIII). What Ostia proves, beyond density, is plurality without unity . Fifteen or more mithraea in one town cannot have been one congregation meeting in fifteen places; they were fifteen communities, founded at different dates by different patrons, presumably recruiting from different streets, workplaces, and households, with no Ostian Mithraic authority above their several Fathers visible in any record. The cult reproduced by fission and fresh foundation, not by organisation. And yet a man initiated in one Ostian mithraeum would have found the room, the image, the grades, and the meal of any other immediately familiar. Holding those two facts together — cellular independence, formal uniformity — is the sociological form of the problem stated in Section II, and no surviving evidence resolves it further. A last Ostian caution: the town's mithraea are mostly of the third century , the earliest belonging to the Antonine age, a generation after the cult's first appearance at Rome. Ostia shows the cult in maturity, at its densest — not at its origin. VI. The Tauroctony I: The Central Group and the Animals At the end of every mithraeum stood the same picture. Its modern name, tauroctony — Greek for “bull-slaying” — is a scholars' coinage; no ancient Mithraic term for the image survives, which is fitting, since no ancient explanation of it survives either. Some seven hundred examples are known, in marble relief, local stone, stucco, and paint, from the great carved altarpieces of the Rhine to small plaques in Dacia; and their agreement is the most extraordinary fact in Mithraic studies. Across three centuries and an empire, workshops that cannot have been in contact reproduce one composition, figure for figure, with the fidelity of a coin type. This section and the next read the image element by element, under a strict rule, stated once and kept throughout: first what the image shows, then — separately, and under a scholar's name — what has been inferred from it. The Central Group: What Is Shown A young man kneels on the back of a bull that has been forced to the ground. His left knee presses into the bull's spine; his right leg extends back to pin the bull's hind leg. His left hand grips the bull's muzzle or horns and hauls its head up and back; his right hand drives a short sword or dagger into the bull's neck, at the shoulder. His head is turned away from the killing — characteristically, he looks back over his shoulder, toward the figure of Sol in the corner of the scene. He wears the costume the Roman world read as Persian: a soft pointed cap (the “Phrygian” cap), a long-sleeved tunic, trousers, and a cloak that billows behind him, in finer examples studded with stars or lined with the signs of the zodiac. The setting is a cave, shown as a rocky arch over the group. This is Mithras, and the composition — the kneeling killer astride a bull, the averted face — is not an Iranian invention: art historians have long noted its descent from a classical Greek type, the bull-slaying Victory (Nike) known from Hellenistic sculpture, adapted and re-cast. The cult's central image, in its very anatomy, is a Greco-Roman artwork. The Animals: What Is Shown Element What the image shows Status of the usual interpretation The dog A dog leaps up at the wound in the bull's neck, toward the flowing blood Constellation Canis (Major or Minor) in the astral readings (Section XII); “companion of the god” in narrative readings. Both are inferences; the image gives the dog no label The snake A snake moves toward the wound alongside the dog, in many examples rising from a crack in the ground Read as the constellation Hydra by the astral school; as an earth-creature receiving the blood by others. Inference in both cases The scorpion A scorpion fastens on the bull's genitals Scorpius in the astral readings; a strike at the bull's generative power in fertility readings. The placement is a fact; both meanings are inferred The raven A bird, usually identified as a raven, perched on the rock or the god's cloak, or flying in; sometimes shown near Sol, as if carrying a message between Sol and Mithras Corvus in the astral readings; Sol's messenger in narrative readings reconstructed from the side panels. The messenger role is plausible and unproven The wheat Ears of wheat sprout from the tip of the bull's tail, in some examples from the wound itself The image's clearest statement that life of some kind comes out of the killing — and the limit of its clarity. Grain, not a doctrine, is what is shown; the star Spica in the astral readings The cup and the lion A cup or crater and a lion appear in a minority of reliefs, notably from the Rhine and Danube provinces, set below or beside the central group Crater and Leo in the astral readings; the lion also matches the Leo grade (Section VIII). Their regional distribution is a fact; their meaning is inferred Three disciplines follow from the table. First: no ancient text explains any of these figures ; every identification — dog as constellation, snake as earth, scorpion as autumn — is a modern proposal, and the proposals disagree. Second: the one thing the image itself insists on is a paradox, a killing from which grain grows. Fertility-from-death is shown ; every fuller statement of it is a reconstruction, Cumont's in the first instance (Section XI). Third: there is no evidence that any bull was ever killed in a mithraeum. The rooms are far too small, their debris is feasting debris — chicken and other small-animal bone predominates where faunal remains have been analysed — and the tauroctony is a picture, not the record of a rite. // THE AVERTED FACE // Mithras's turned head has generated a literature of its own: reluctance, obedience to Sol's command, refusal to watch a necessary act. The image shows the turn; it also shows, in many examples, a ray or a direct line of sight linking Sol to Mithras, which makes “looking toward Sol” the minimal description. Everything beyond the minimal description — the god's emotions, his orders, his reluctance — is supplied by the interpreter. This article supplies none of it. VII. The Tauroctony II: Torchbearers, Sol and Luna, the Ring of Signs The central group does not stand alone. It is framed by a fixed company of witnesses and, in the grander reliefs, by the machinery of the sky itself. These framing elements are, if anything, more consistent than the animals, and they are the elements on which the cosmic readings of the image (Section XII) principally rest. Cautes and Cautopates Flanking the group stand two small figures dressed as Mithras himself — same cap, tunic, and trousers — each holding a torch. Cautes , conventionally on the viewer's right of the scene, holds his torch pointing up . Cautopates , on the left, holds his pointing down . Both commonly stand with legs crossed, in a posture as fixed as the torches. Their names are genuinely ancient — they appear in dedications — and they are the tauroctony's only named supporting figures. In a number of examples, about fifty catalogued cases, their positions are reversed, Cautopates taking the right and Cautes the left; the reversal is a fact of the corpus whose significance, if any, is unknown. In the mithraeum itself the pair often stood as statues in niches flanking the cult image, so that the initiate dining in the room sat, in effect, inside the picture. What they mean is inference, and the inferences should be kept in their lanes. Raised and lowered torch most plainly suggest sunrise and sunset, dawn and dusk, rising and setting light; from there interpreters have gone on to spring and autumn, birth and death, life and the underworld, the two equinoxes. All of these are readings of a visual antithesis that the image certainly intends — the pair is too deliberate to be decoration — and none of them is confirmed by any Mithraic word. Where later writers, ancient and modern, have allegorised the torchbearers, this archive reports the allegory as theirs. The image gives two torches, one up, one down, and two names. It gives no more. Sol, Luna, and the Zodiac Ring In the upper corners of the relief — Sol on the viewer's left, Luna on the right — the busts of the Sun and Moon look on. In elaborate examples Sol appears in his four-horse chariot mounting upward, Luna in her two-horse chariot descending, each preceded by a torch-bearing youth, Phosphorus with torch raised before the Sun, Hesperus with torch lowered before the Moon: the Cautes-and-Cautopates antithesis written across the sky. Around the whole scene, in many reliefs, runs an arch or ring bearing the twelve signs of the zodiac , sometimes with the signs carved in full, sometimes abbreviated; stars stud the god's cloak and the cave's vault. The god's own titles, in the dedications, bind him to the sun: Sol Invictus Mithras , the Unconquered Sun Mithras, and Mithras and Sol appear together throughout the side scenes as allies who meet, clasp hands, and dine. Here the line between showing and inferring can be drawn with unusual precision, and this article draws it. Shown: the scene is set under the sun and moon, inside the zodiac, among stars; its god is named with the sun's title; its room was a cave that a philosopher contemporary with the cult could describe as an image of the cosmos (Section X). The tauroctony is, demonstrably, a cosmic image — that much is in the carving, not in the interpreter. Not shown: any specific astronomical doctrine — which stars, which event, which teaching about the soul's road through the spheres. Those specifics are the work of the modern astral school (Section XII), and they stand or fall as modern arguments. The distinction matters because the cult's imagery is often raided, in both directions, by readers who want the zodiac ring to prove a whole astronomy, or who want to dismiss the astronomy because the whole cannot be proved. The ring proves a frame. The frame is real. What was taught inside it is gone. The Side Scenes: A Myth in Pictures On the grander reliefs the tauroctony is surrounded by small panels, read in sequence, which give the god something no text gives him: a story. They kept the secret. This article is about the shape of what they kept — and about the honesty required when the centre of the evidence is, by design, missing.
