Sources I. The Secrecy Problem: What Can and Cannot Be Known Every other article in this archive begins from something that survives: a building, a text, a dated inscription. This one begins from an absence, and the absence is not an accident of preservation. It is the subject. The Greek mysteries — mysteria , from a root connected with closing the eyes or the lips — were rites whose central content was aporrheton : forbidden to be spoken. Initiates were bound not to reveal what took place, Athenian law backed the prohibition with the death penalty for profanation, and the remarkable fact, on which Walter Burkert’s Ancient Mystery Cults (1987) still rests its opening chapters, is that the prohibition worked. Across many centuries and tens of thousands of initiates — farmers, slaves, emperors, children — no initiate published an account of the central rites of Eleusis. The secret outlived the cult. When the sanctuaries were closed in the 390s CE, the knowledge simply stopped being transmitted, and what had been seen in the Telesterion at night was seen no more. This has a consequence that any honest treatment must state before it states anything else: the content of the mysteries is not recoverable, and no modern book — including this article — can tell the reader what initiation “really was” from the inside. Anyone who claims otherwise is selling something. What scholarship can recover, and recover well, is everything around the secret: the myths that framed it, the calendar that scheduled it, the buildings that housed it, the officials who ran it, the crowds who underwent it, the fees they paid, the road they walked, and the effects they reported afterwards in the general terms the rules allowed — that they feared death less, that they counted themselves blessed, that something had been seen which changed the terms of a life. The shape of the rite is documented. Its centre is not. The Three Categories — and Why They Are Only Categories Ancient writers who discuss mystery ritual in general terms divide it into three components, conventionally given in Greek: dromena , things done or enacted; deiknymena , things shown; and legomena , things said. The triad is genuinely ancient and genuinely useful — it tells us that initiation was not a lecture and not a creed. Something was performed, something was displayed, something was spoken, and the initiate’s part was to undergo the whole: the standard modern summary, following Aristotle’s reported remark that initiates were expected not to learn something ( mathein ) but to experience something ( pathein ), rests on a fragment preserved by the late writer Synesius, and it is labelled as such here. But the triad must not be mistaken for a description. It is a table of contents for a book that was never written. We know the headings under which the secret was filed. We do not know what stood under them. ATTESTED: THE SHAPE OF THE RITES Festival calendars, processions, sacrifices, purifications, fasting, the ritual drink, the buildings and their capacities, the priestly families and their offices, eligibility rules, fees, and the existence of graded initiation — all documented in inscriptions, archaeology, and uncontroversial literary references. REPORTED, WITH WARNINGS: HOSTILE AND LATE WITNESSES Specific claims about the secret content come overwhelmingly from Christian polemicists of the 2nd–3rd centuries CE — Clement of Alexandria and Hippolytus of Rome above all — who were not initiates, wrote to discredit the rites, and reported at second or third hand. Their testimony is used in this article only with the warning attached, every time. ATTESTED AS OBJECTS, DEBATED AS MEANINGS The Orphic gold tablets, the Derveni papyrus, the Villa of the Mysteries paintings, and the Samothracian buildings are physical survivals. What they meant — which cult they belonged to, what ceremony they served — is argued about by the specialists cited, and the arguments are reported here as arguments. NOT KNOWN, AND NOT RECOVERABLE What was shown in the Telesterion at the climax; what was said there; what the sacred objects ( hiera ) in their chest actually were; the names of the Samothracian gods as initiates learned them; and the inner experience of any single initiate at Eleusis or Samothrace. No source that was inside and bound by the rule describes any of it. A note on method, because this archive’s readers are entitled to it. Three kinds of evidence are kept apart throughout what follows. First , the public and archaeological record: inscriptions, excavated buildings, official calendars, court speeches, and historians writing about public events. Second , the charter myths and literary works — the Homeric Hymn to Demeter , Euripides’ Bacchae , Apuleius’ novel — which are real texts that can be read, but which are poems, plays, and fiction, not ritual manuals; each is treated as what it is. Third , the hostile witnesses: when Clement or Hippolytus is the source for a claim, the sentence says so, in so many words, before the claim is given. The reader should apply the same test to every other account of the mysteries they ever meet. Ask of any vivid detail: who reports this, when, and were they in the room? For the centre of the mysteries, the answer is always no. // THE WORDS // An initiate of the first grade was a mystes (plural mystai ) — traditionally connected with closing the eyes. The guide who sponsored and instructed a candidate was the mystagogos . Initiation itself was a telete ; the higher Eleusinian grade, open only in a later year, was the epopteia , “the viewing”, and those who had attained it were epoptai , “those who have seen”. The vocabulary itself encodes the secret: the highest knowledge the cult offered was something seen, not something stated. One more preliminary. The mysteries treated here were not a single religion, and “the mystery cults” is a modern umbrella, useful and dangerous in equal measure. Eleusis was a state cult of Athens, run by hereditary priestly houses under civic oversight, as public in its administration as it was secret in its centre. The Dionysian initiations were largely private and portable, spread by associations and by travelling initiators. The rites attached to Orpheus’s name were carried by texts and by freelance ritual experts. Samothrace was an island sanctuary of gods whose very names were withheld. What unites them is a form — voluntary initiation, graded and secret, promising the initiate a changed relation to death or danger — not a doctrine. Burkert’s definition, in paraphrase, remains the working one for this article: mysteries are initiation ceremonies in which admission is personal and voluntary, the rite is secret, and the initiate expects benefits that public cult does not confer on the uninitiated. Where a section’s subject strains that definition, the strain is noted rather than smoothed over. II. Eleusis: The Charter Myth — The Homeric Hymn to Demeter Eleusis lies some twenty kilometres north-west of Athens, on the coast road toward Megara, and its sanctuary of Demeter and her daughter was already old when Athens became a great city. The myth that the initiates themselves treated as the foundation story — the cult’s charter — survives in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter , a poem of 495 lines in the epic dialect, conventionally dated to the late seventh or sixth century BCE. It is called Homeric because it is written in Homer’s metre and manner, not because Homer wrote it; its author is anonymous. The standard English version used in this article is H. G. Evelyn-White’s Loeb translation of 1914, and the summary below is a summary: the poem is paraphrased, not ventriloquised, and the one passage quoted is quoted from that named translation. The poem opens with the abduction. Persephone — the Daughter, Kore , “the Maiden” — is gathering flowers with the daughters of Ocean when the earth opens and Hades, lord of the dead, carries her off in his chariot, with Zeus’s prior consent, which Zeus does not advertise. In Evelyn-White’s translation (1914), the first lines run: “I begin to sing of rich-haired Demeter, awful goddess — of her and her trim-ankled daughter whom Aidoneus rapt away, given to him by all-seeing Zeus the loud-thunderer.” — Homeric Hymn to Demeter , lines 1–3, trans. H. G. Evelyn-White (Loeb Classical Library, 1914) Demeter hears her daughter’s cry, tears her headdress, and searches the earth for nine days with torches in her hands, neither eating nor washing. Hecate, who heard but did not see, joins her; Helios, who sees everything, finally tells her the truth. Demeter withdraws from Olympus in anger and comes, disguised as an old woman, to Eleusis, where she sits by the Maiden Well and is taken into the house of King Celeus as nurse to his infant son Demophon. There the poem gives the cult two of its most durable ritual echoes — offered here as the correspondences scholars standardly draw, not as proof of what any rite contained. Offered red wine in the house, the goddess refuses it as unlawful for her in her grief and asks instead for a drink of barley meal and water mixed with pennyroyal: the kykeon , the very drink the initiates would later take to break their fast (lines 207–211). And the servant Iambe, with jests, makes the grieving goddess smile and laugh — the mythic counterpart, in the usual reading, of the ritual mockery exchanged on the procession road (Section III). The nursing goes wrong, as divine nursing in Greek myth tends to. Demeter, loving the child, anoints him with ambrosia and hides him in the fire at night to burn away his mortality; his mother Metaneira spies, cries out, and breaks the working. The goddess reveals herself in terrifying radiance, rebukes the household, and commands that a great temple and altar be built for her below the citadel of Eleusis — and that the people be taught her rites, which she herself will show them. Then she withdraws to her new temple and makes a year of famine: no seed sprouts, the plough is dragged in vain, and because mortals are dying, the gods themselves face the loss of sacrifice and honour. Zeus sends Iris, then the whole company of gods with gifts; Demeter refuses them all. Only when Hermes is sent down to Hades and Persephone is brought up — having eaten, in Hades’ house, a pomegranate seed, which binds her to return — does the story resolve. The settlement, brokered by Rhea, divides the year: a portion below with her husband, the greater part above with her mother. Demeter restores the grain, teaches the princes of Eleusis — Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, and Celeus are named — her mysteries, and the poem ends by pronouncing blessed the mortal who has seen them, and wretched the uninitiated, who has no share in such things after death. That closing blessing, in paraphrase, is the hymn’s own statement of what initiation was for; the poem does not say what the rites were, and its silence on the point is itself part of the evidence for Section I. // HOW TO READ A CHARTER MYTH // The Hymn explains why the cult exists, where it sits, which families serve it, and what mood it enacts — grief, search, fasting, laughter, restoration. It does not describe the initiation, because its audience included the uninitiated and its author kept the rule. Correspondences between poem and festival (the kykeon, the jesting, the torches, the search) show that rite and story were woven together; they do not license the reverse inference, common in popular writing, that the initiates “acted out the myth” scene by scene in the Telesterion. No ancient source says they did. Two cautions about the Hymn’s date and authority belong in the record. First, the poem in its surviving form knows nothing of Iacchos, the processional god so prominent in the later festival, and its Eleusinian princes do not map neatly onto the historical priestly houses — signs, in Kevin Clinton’s and others’ readings, of a poem composed for the sanctuary at a particular stage of its development and later treated as timeless. Second, the Hymn survived antiquity by a thread: it is preserved in a single fifteenth-century manuscript, discovered in Moscow in 1777, with a gap in the text where leaves were lost. The charter myth of the best-attended mysteries of the ancient world reached us in one copy. The archive notes the fact because it is the secrecy problem’s literary twin: even the public frame of the cult very nearly vanished. III. Eleusis: The Festival — Lesser Mysteries, the Sacred Way, the Nine Days Eleusinian initiation was not an event but a curriculum, spread over at least two seasons and, for the highest grade, two years. Its public timetable is among the best-documented festival programmes in Greek religion, reconstructed from inscriptions, calendars, and literary references assembled in the standard modern studies — George Mylonas’s excavation history, Kevin Clinton’s work on the sanctuary and its officials, and Burkert’s synthesis. The day-by-day scheme below follows that reconstruction; where a detail rests on a single late source, the text says so. The Lesser Mysteries at Agrai The preliminary initiation — the myesis in its first stage — belonged to the Lesser Mysteries, held in the Athenian month Anthesterion (roughly February–March) at Agrai, a suburb of Athens on the banks of the Ilissos. Tradition explained their existence with a story: they were instituted, it was said, so that Heracles, polluted by bloodshed and foreign besides, could be purified and made eligible for the greater rites. The story is an aetiology, not a record, but the rite’s function is clear enough from its place in the sequence: purification and preliminary instruction, including, on the usual reconstruction, the sacrifice of a piglet by each candidate and washing in the river. Only those who had passed through the Lesser Mysteries could proceed to the Greater; the minimum interval was a matter of months, and Clinton’s study of the stages argues that preliminary initiation could also be performed at other times and places, including the City Eleusinion in Athens — a reminder that even the “fixed” curriculum had working flexibility. The Greater Mysteries in Boedromion The Greater Mysteries fell in Boedromion (roughly September), over some nine days, and were administered as a state festival: the archon basileus, Athens’s king-archon for sacred affairs, held overall responsibility, assisted by overseers ( epimeletai ), some elected and some drawn from the priestly houses. The festival’s skeleton, in the standard reconstruction, is this. On 14 Boedromion the sacred objects — the hiera , carried in their covered containers by the sanctuary’s personnel — were escorted from Eleusis to the Eleusinion at the foot of the Athenian Acropolis. On the 15th came the prorrhesis , the formal proclamation by the hierophant and the torch-bearer from the Painted Stoa, which opened the festival and pronounced its exclusions (Section V), and the gathering ( agyrmos ) of the candidates. A day of purification followed, famous for its summons — paraphrased here as “to the sea, initiates” — when the mystai went down to the sea at Phaleron, each washing in the salt water and washing the piglet each had brought for sacrifice. Days of sacrifice and rest in Athens intervened. Then, on the 19th, came the procession itself. Stage When and where What is attested Lesser Mysteries (preliminary myesis) Anthesterion (c. Sept.), Athens The hierophant’s prorrhesis pronounces the exclusions; candidates assemble under their sponsors ( mystagogoi ) Sea purification 16 Boedromion, Phaleron Initiates bathe in the sea; each sacrifices a piglet The procession 19 Boedromion, Athens to Eleusis by the Sacred Way, c. 20 km The hiera carried back to Eleusis; the crowd escorting Iacchos; ritual jesting ( gephyrismoi ) at the bridge over the Cephissus The night of the telete Night of 20–21 Boedromion, the Telesterion, Eleusis Fasting broken with the kykeon; the initiates enter the hall at night. What followed inside is the secret: see Sections I and V Closing rites 22–23 Boedromion, Eleusis and Athens Libations for the dead with the twin vessels called plemochoai ; the festival disperses Epopteia (second grade) A subsequent year’s Greater Mysteries, Eleusis Returning mystai admitted as epoptai , “those who have seen”; its content beyond the first grade is not described by any permitted source The procession deserves its own paragraph, because it was the festival’s public face and the part of the mysteries that all Athens — initiate or not — could watch. The crowd walked the Sacred Way westward out of the city, escorting the hiera home and carrying the image and the name of Iacchos, the youthful processional god whose cry the marchers took up; Aristophanes’ Frogs (produced 405 BCE) stages a chorus of blessed initiates singing to Iacchos in the underworld, which tells us how the procession sounded in the Athenian imagination, though a comedy is evidence for atmosphere, not for liturgy. At the bridge over the Cephissus, bystanders — or, in some accounts, appointed jesters — shouted ritual abuse at the passing notables, the gephyrismoi or “bridge jests”, an apotropaic mockery the tradition itself connected with Iambe’s jesting in the Hymn. The procession reached Eleusis toward evening, by torchlight, and the night that followed — dancing and an all-night vigil ( pannychis ) in the sanctuary’s outer court, on the usual reconstruction — belonged still to the public and semi-public festival. The fast was broken with the kykeon. Then the doors of the Telesterion closed on the initiates, and the documentation, by design, stops. // THE KYKEON, WITHOUT THE LEGEND // The kykeon’s recipe is one of the few ritual details the Hymn itself supplies: barley meal and water, mixed with pennyroyal (lines 207–211, paraphrased here from Evelyn-White’s translation). It was an ordinary Greek drink — Homer’s heroes drink versions of it — and the Hymn gives it no added ingredient. The famous modern proposal that the Eleusinian kykeon was dosed with ergot, the fungus of infected grain, comes from R. Gordon Wasson, Albert Hofmann, and Carl Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978). It is an ingenious hypothesis about an unrecorded ingredient; no ancient source mentions it, no residue analysis has established it, and Burkert and the mainstream of scholarship treat the experience of the mysteries as explicable by the rite itself — fasting, night, crowd, expectation, darkness, and light — without pharmacology. This article records the hypothesis as a modern proposal, not as a finding. IV. Eleusis: The Telesterion and Its Priests The building at the cult’s centre is as unusual as the rite it housed. A Greek temple is a god’s house, built to be looked at from outside; the Telesterion was a hall built to contain a crowd in the dark. In its final form — the product of repeated rebuilding from the archaic period through the fourth century BCE — it was a roughly square roofed hall of some fifty metres to a side, its roof carried on a forest of internal columns arranged in rows, with tiers of steps running around all four interior walls on which the initiates stood or sat, facing inward. Estimates of capacity run into the thousands. Near its centre stood a small, separate structure, the anaktoron , which the excavators identified as the holy of holies from which the hierophant emerged at the climax and in which the hiera were kept; the identification is the excavators’, descending from the early Greek excavation of the site, and the building’s phases are debated in detail, but the broad picture — a stepped auditorium around a small central chamber, rebuilt on the same footprint for centuries — is the archaeology’s settled core. The building’s history carries one of the site’s live scholarly arguments, and it is reported here as Clinton and his critics have framed it. Mylonas, the sanctuary’s great twentieth-century excavator, traced the Telesterion’s line back to a Mycenaean megaron on the site and read the cult as continuous from the Bronze Age. Clinton’s re-examination questioned both the megaron’s identification as a cult building and the inference of unbroken continuity; the earliest certainly cultic phases are archaic. The difference matters beyond Eleusis: a Bronze Age pedigree makes the mysteries a survival, an archaic monumentalisation makes them a creation of the same centuries that produced the Hymn. This article follows the cautious position: occupation on the site is old, monumental cult building is archaic and later, and continuity of worship across the gap is asserted by tradition rather than demonstrated by stratigraphy. The Two Houses The rite was served by two hereditary Athenian houses, and their division of labour is epigraphically and literarily secure. The Eumolpidai , who traced their line to Eumolpus — the Hymn’s Eleusinian prince, eu-molpos, “the fair singer” — supplied the hierophant , “the one who shows the sacred things”, the chief officiant of the mysteries, who alone, in the standard accounts, entered the anaktoron and brought forth the hiera , and whose voice proclaimed the sacred formulas. The Kerykes , the “Heralds”, supplied the second and third great officers: the dadouchos , the torch-bearer, second in rank, whose torches lit the night procession and the search that recalled Demeter’s; and the hierokeryx , the sacred herald, who pronounced the proclamation and the ritual silences. Priestesses of Demeter and Kore held office alongside them, and the whole establishment ran under civic law: officials accounted to Athens, the festival’s finances were administered and audited, and decrees about the mysteries were passed by the Assembly like decrees about harbours or grain. Burkert’s point deserves repeating here, because it corrects the romantic picture: the most secret rite in Greece was also a budgeted, staffed, and inspected department of a democracy. Its neighbours in this hub’s story — the public face of the Olympians and the succession myth of the Theogony — were the religion everyone could see; Eleusis was what the same civilisation kept behind a door. c. 7th–6th c. BCE THE HYMN AND THE ARCHAIC SANCTUARY The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is composed; the sanctuary at Eleusis is monumentalised in stone in the archaic period, in the orbit of an Athens absorbing Eleusis into its territory. 480 BCE PERSIAN DESTRUCTION The sanctuary is burned in the Persian invasion; rebuilding follows, in phases associated with Kimon and then with Pericles’ architects, producing the great classical Telesterion. 415 BCE THE PROFANATION SCANDAL The mutilation of the Herms and the alleged mock celebrations of the mysteries in private houses convulse Athens on the eve of the Sicilian expedition. See Section VI. 4th c. BCE THE FINAL TELESTERION The porch of Philon and the last great building phase give the hall its final form; the festival is pan-Hellenic in reach and administered under detailed sacred law. Roman period EMPERORS AS INITIATES Augustus, Hadrian, and Marcus Aurelius are among the Roman initiates the sources name; the sanctuary is embellished with the Greater and Lesser Propylaia. Initiation remains, in form, the Athenian rite. 391–396 CE CLOSURE AND DESTRUCTION The Theodosian decrees close the pagan sanctuaries; Eunapius, a pagan writer hostile to the Christian empire, records a last hierophant’s prophecy of ruin, and Alaric’s Goths sack Eleusis in 396. The chain of transmission ends. V. Eleusis: Who Could Be Initiated — and the Night Itself Against every modern instinct about ancient exclusiveness, Eleusis was open. The proclamation that opened the festival excluded, in the standard formulation preserved by the later sources, two classes only: those who could not understand Greek — the bar was linguistic, a matter of being able to undergo a rite conducted in Greek — and those with blood on their hands, the ritually polluted, above all unexpiated murderers. Everyone else could be initiated: Athenians and foreigners, men and women, the free and the enslaved. Slaves were initiated at Eleusis alongside their masters, a fact documented in the scholarship on slave participation in Athenian religion and remarkable enough in a slave society to be worth stating plainly: the mysteries did not merely tolerate the unfree, they admitted them to the same night, the same hall, and the same hope as the citizen who owned them. Women were initiated in large numbers and in their own right — the Hymn’s goddesses had a cult whose initiates were never a male preserve — and children were occasionally initiated, sometimes, in the city’s practice, a single child “from the hearth” on the community’s behalf. Initiation was not free: fees, the piglet, travel, and days away from work were real costs, and cost, not status, was the practical filter. But the formal position stands, and antiquity noticed it: the one Athenian institution that promised a better lot after death made the promise without asking who your father was. What the initiates hoped for is stated, in permitted general terms, by a chain of respectable witnesses who were themselves initiates and kept the rule while praising the rite. Pindar, in a fragment (fr. 137) paraphrased here, calls blessed the man who has seen these things before going beneath the earth, for he knows the end of life and its god-given beginning. Sophocles, in a fragment (fr. 837) likewise paraphrased, calls thrice-blessed those mortals who have seen the rites and then go to Hades, for to them alone is there life there; to the others, every evil. Cicero, an initiate, wrote in the Laws (2.14.36, paraphrased) that Athens had given humanity nothing better than the mysteries, by which men were civilised and learned not only to live joyfully but to die with a better hope. These are evaluations, not descriptions — praise in the superlative, content withheld — and they are exactly what the secrecy rule predicts initiates would produce. Plutarch, in a fragment of his work On the Soul (fr. 178, paraphrased), comes closest to phenomenology while still keeping the rule: he compares the soul’s experience at death to initiation — wandering, exhaustion, fear, then light, meadows, voices, dancing, and sacred sights — an analogy, offered by an initiate-philosopher as analogy, which later writers have too often quoted as if it were a leaked transcript. It is not one. The Night: The Two Hostile Leaks Everything specific that is “known” about the climax inside the Telesterion derives, in the end, from two Christian writers of the decades around 200 CE, both hostile, neither an initiate. They are given here with their warnings attached, because they will be met everywhere else without them. Clement of Alexandria , in his Protrepticus or Exhortation to the Greeks (2.21.2), a work whose purpose is to turn Greeks away from their cults by exposing them, preserves what he presents as the Eleusinian synthema — the formula or password by which initiates recognised one another. In G. W. Butterworth’s Loeb translation (1919), as Clement reports it, the formula runs: “I fasted; I drank the kykeon; I took from the kiste; having done my task, I placed in the basket, and from the basket into the kiste.” Three warnings are mandatory. Clement is a hostile witness writing polemic, some six centuries after the classical festival’s floruit. The kiste (a lidded chest) and the kalathos (the “basket” of the translation) were containers whose contents no permitted source ever names, so the formula, even if genuine, certifies that initiates handled sacred objects — it does not say what the objects were. And scholars have questioned whether Clement’s formula belongs to Eleusis proper or to a related Demeter rite he has conflated with it. The formula is quoted in this article only as Clement’s report, for what it is: the shape of a password, preserved by an enemy. Hippolytus of Rome , in his Refutation of All Heresies (5.8.39–40), writing a generation after Clement and likewise to discredit, reports — inside an exposition of the Naassene Gnostic sect, whose doctrines he is refuting, not in a description of Eleusis for its own sake — that the Athenians, initiating at Eleusis, display to those admitted to the highest grade “an ear of grain in silence reaped”. The phrase is famous, and its fame has outrun its credentials. Hippolytus was not in the room; his information serves a Gnostic allegory he is attacking; and a climax that turns out to be a single ear of wheat serves a polemicist’s argument — that the pagans’ great secret was a trifle — suspiciously well. None of that makes the report false: grain is Demeter’s gift, and a silent showing is precisely the kind of non-verbal climax the vocabulary of epopteia , “the viewing”, predicts. Burkert treats the report with corresponding care — possible, unprovable, and unusable as a foundation. This article does the same. The ear of grain is Hippolytus’s claim, flagged as a hostile, second-hand claim, and nothing in what follows is built on it. // WHAT CANNOT BE RECOVERED // It follows that the most-repeated “facts” about the Eleusinian climax — the ear of grain, a staged re-enactment of the rape and return of Persephone, a sacred marriage, a psychedelic sacrament — are, respectively, a hostile report, a modern inference, a conjecture without an ancient source, and a modern hypothesis. The ancient evidence establishes that thousands of people, over more than a millennium, underwent something at night in that hall which they valued above almost everything and would not describe on pain of death. The historian’s task is to hold both halves of that sentence at once. Dropping the second half produces credulity; dropping the first produces the pretence that there was nothing to keep secret. VI. 415 BCE: The Herms, the Profanation, and the Price of the Secret The secrecy’s social weight is best measured by what happened when Athens thought it had been broken. In the spring of 415 BCE the city was launching the Sicilian expedition, the great armada against Syracuse that would end, two years later, in the destruction of Athenian power. On a single night, shortly before the fleet sailed, most of the herms of Athens — the square stone pillars topped with the head of Hermes that stood at doorways and street corners all over the city — were mutilated, their faces smashed. Thucydides, our contemporary source ( History 6.27–28, paraphrased throughout this section), reports that the act was read as an omen for the expedition and as evidence of a conspiracy to overthrow the democracy; large rewards were offered, and immunity was promised to any informer, citizen, resident alien, or slave. The informers, when they came, spoke less about the herms than about something else: private performances, in houses, of mock celebrations of the Eleusinian mysteries — drinking parties at which, it was alleged, men had acted out the rites, with one of them playing the hierophant and showing the sacred things to the uninitiated. The name at the centre of the allegations was Alcibiades, the expedition’s most brilliant and most distrusted commander. Thucydides (6.28) is careful in a way his summarists often are not: he reports the charges, notes that Alcibiades’ enemies magnified them for political ends, and records that Alcibiades demanded immediate trial and was refused — his enemies preferring to let him sail and recall him when his army’s protection was gone. The state ship Salaminia was duly sent to Sicily to fetch him; Alcibiades escaped at Thurii in Italy, defected to Sparta, and was condemned to death in his absence, his property confiscated and sold — the inscribed accounts of the sales survive in part — and a curse pronounced against him by the priests and priestesses of Eleusis, a curse the tradition says one priestess, Theano, refused to utter, on the ground that she was appointed to bless, not to curse (the detail is Plutarch’s, Alcibiades 22, written five centuries later, and is flagged as such). Andocides’ speech On the Mysteries , delivered in 400 or 399 BCE in his own defence on a related charge, remains our fullest courtroom window onto the affair: denunciations, imprisonments, men executed or exiled, and a city that had, for a season, treated a ritual offence as treason’s twin. Three lessons are drawn in the scholarship and are drawn here. First, the charges were believable to contemporaries precisely because everyone knew there was a secret to profane: parody requires an original, and the panic of 415 is independent evidence for the rite’s reality and its hold on the city. Second, profanation was prosecuted as a capital crime against the community, not as a private impiety — the mysteries were the city’s own, and their violation on the eve of a national expedition was read as an attack on the expedition and the constitution alike. Foundations: The Air Alchemy Breathed This article belongs to the Foundations cluster of the Alchemy wing, and like its sibling on the Hermetica it is not, strictly speaking, an article about alchemy. No furnace is lit in it, no apparatus is drawn, no metal changes colour. Its subject is prior to all of that: the philosophy inside which Alexandrian alchemy became thinkable as a sacred science rather than a workshop trick. When Zosimos of Panopolis , writing around 300 CE, dreams of altars that are also men, of metals that suffer, die, and rise, and of a cosmos in which every material thing is bound to every other by hidden kinship, he is not inventing a private mythology. He is drawing, often without citation, on the common intellectual stock of his century — and the largest single deposit in that stock is the philosophy modern scholarship calls Neoplatonism . The word itself is modern. No ancient philosopher called himself a Neoplatonist; Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus all understood themselves simply as Platonists — interpreters of Plato, recovering what Plato had meant. The modern label marks a real difference of temper and system all the same. Between roughly 250 and 530 CE the Platonic tradition produced something Plato himself had not: a complete, hierarchical metaphysics in which all reality proceeds from a single, utterly simple first principle — the One — through the divine Intellect and Soul , down to the last dregs of matter, and in which the human soul’s whole task is the journey back. That metaphysics is the first half of this article’s subject. The second half is what happened to it when one of its greatest systematicians concluded that the journey back could not be made by thought alone, and that the gods themselves had provided the missing vehicle: theurgy ( theourgia ), literally “god-work” — rite understood not as human bargaining with the divine but as divine action performed through human hands, materials, and names. NEOPLATONISM The systematic Platonism of Plotinus (204/5–270) and his successors: reality as an ordered procession from the One through Intellect and Soul to matter; salvation as the soul’s contemplative return ( epistrophē ) to its source. The metaphysical frame of nearly all late-antique learned religion, pagan and — by adoption and argument — much Christian and later Islamic and Jewish thought besides. THEURGY The ritual system defended above all by Iamblichus (c. 245–c. 325) in the De Mysteriis : divinely instituted rites — sacrifice, invocation, divination, the consecration of statues — held to purify and elevate the embodied soul by the gods’ own power working through material tokens ( symbola , synthēmata ) sown through the cosmos. Not, in its own account, coercion of the gods: receptivity prepared, divinity received. Why an alchemy hub needs this article can be put in one sentence each for its two halves. From Neoplatonism, alchemy inherited its cosmos : a living, hierarchically ordered whole in which the lowest things genuinely participate in the highest, so that work done on matter could be, in principle, work done on reality itself and not mere tinkering with appearances. From theurgy, it inherited its method’s dignity : the conviction that material operations — the right substance, prepared the right way, at the right time, under the right name — are not a descent from philosophy into superstition but one of the places philosophy happens. The alchemist who seals a vessel, times an operation by the heavens, and addresses the work in prayer is not a philosopher who has lapsed. In the world this article describes, he is applying the metaphysics. // THE EGYPTIAN TREATMENT, ELSEWHERE // The Egyptology division of this archive treats Neoplatonism in its own right, from the Egyptian end: see its Neoplatonism article for the philosophy read inside an Egyptian frame — Plotinus’s own Egyptian birth, the Alexandrian setting, and the tradition’s long entanglement with the temples and wisdom of Kemet. This article complements rather than repeats it: its centre of gravity is the Greco-Roman philosophical treatment — the texts, the arguments, and the quarrel over theurgy — and it deliberately leaves the Egyptian-side material to the division that owns it. A note on method, because this subject, like the Hermetica, attracts invention. No direct quotation from Plotinus, Iamblichus, or any other ancient author is given in this article unless it is explicitly attributed to a named modern translation. In practice the article paraphrases throughout, and every paraphrase is labelled as paraphrase in the text or follows the standard modern accounts named in the Sources: for Plotinus, the Enneads in A. H. Armstrong’s Loeb translation (seven volumes, 1966–1988) and in the Cambridge edition edited by Lloyd P. Gerson (2018); for Iamblichus, the De Mysteriis in the translation of Emma C. Clarke, John M. Dillon, and Jackson P. Hershbell (2003). Where scholars disagree — and on the central questions of this article they disagree sharply — the disagreement is stated as disagreement, with the parties named. Readers who want the philosophers’ own words should go to Armstrong, Gerson, and Clarke–Dillon–Hershbell; this article’s job is the system, the quarrel, and the consequences. One framing caution before the system itself. It is tempting to tell this story as a decline: pure philosophy first, ritual superstition after — the so-called “irrational turn” of late antiquity. That telling has a distinguished pedigree, and Section XV gives it its due. But it is a verdict , not a fact, and the revisionist scholarship of the last half-century — John Dillon’s work on Iamblichus, Gregory Shaw’s Theurgy and the Soul , Ilinca Tanaseanu-Döbler’s Theurgy in Late Antiquity — has made the opposite case with the texts open on the desk: that Iamblichus’s turn to rite follows from premises Plotinus himself supplied, argued with philosophical rigour, and that the difference between the two men is a disagreement inside Platonism about one precise question — how far the soul falls when it enters a body. This article states both readings and adjudicates where the evidence allows. It does not smuggle either verdict into its descriptions. II. Plotinus and Porphyry: The Life, the School, the Book Plotinus (204/5–270 CE) was born in Roman Egypt — the tradition gives Lycopolis, in the Delta, though he himself refused to speak of his birthplace, his parents, or his birthday, and the refusal is part of the evidence. Nearly everything known of his life comes from one source: the Life of Plotinus written by his pupil Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305) as the preface to Porphyry’s edition of the master’s writings. The Life is a devoted pupil’s work, not a neutral record, and this article treats its anecdotes as Porphyry’s testimony rather than as court evidence. But it is testimony of the first order, from a man who lived in the circle for some six years, and its main lines have never been seriously displaced. In paraphrase of Porphyry’s account: Plotinus came to philosophy at twenty-eight, in Alexandria, working through the city’s famous teachers in disappointment until he was brought to Ammonius Saccas , the Platonist who taught without writing — and recognised his teacher at once, remaining with Ammonius for eleven years. At thirty-nine he joined the emperor Gordian III’s Persian expedition in the hope of reaching the philosophers of Persia and India; the expedition collapsed with Gordian’s murder, and Plotinus escaped to Antioch and then to Rome , where from about 244 he taught for the rest of his life. He began to write only at about fifty. Porphyry’s famous opening judgement — in paraphrase, that Plotinus seemed ashamed of being in the body, and would not sit for a portrait, since a portrait would be an image of an image — is the biographical seed of the whole philosophy that follows: a man for whom embodiment was the problem to which thought was the answer. The school in Rome was a circle more than an institution: lectures built around the reading of Plato and Aristotle and their commentators, open discussion in which, Porphyry says, the master welcomed interruption and objection, and a household that took in orphans and administered their property with an exactness Porphyry praises — the otherworldly teacher as meticulous trustee. Plotinus wrote in Greek, badly spelled and worse punctuated by his own cheerful admission, in treatises that read as the school’s internal arguments set down: objections raised and answered, positions tried, abandoned, resumed. He died in 270, in Campania, having withdrawn as illness — probably a form of leprosy, on the usual modern reading of Porphyry’s symptoms — made company difficult. Porphyry records his last words, addressed to his physician Eustochius; the Greek permits two construals, and translations divide between a confession (“I am striving to give back the divine in myself to the divine in the All”) and an exhortation (“Strive to bring back the god in you to the divine in the universe”). The ambiguity is preserved here deliberately: it is a small, exact emblem of how much of Plotinus reaches us already interpreted. Porphyry the Editor: How the Enneads Were Made Plotinus left no book. He left fifty-four treatises , written across the last seventeen years of his life, in no published order. The book the world reads — the Enneads — is Porphyry’s construction, made some thirty years after the master’s death, around 301 CE. Porphyry tells us in the Life (chapters 24–26) exactly what he did, and the candour is the point: he edited, titled, divided, and arranged. To reach the number fifty-four he split some long works into several treatises and joined others; he then grouped the fifty-four into six sets of nine — six enneads , from the Greek ennea , nine — and disposed the whole in three volumes . The arrangement is not chronological. It is a curriculum: an ascent for the reader, deliberately modelled on the ascent the philosophy describes. Ennead Porphyry’s province for it What the reader climbs through I Ethics — the human being Happiness, virtue, beauty, the good and primary evil, suicide, dialectic: the treatises of conduct and first orientation II Physics — the cosmos The heaven, the stars’ agency, matter, potency and act, providence begun: the sensible world as Soul’s product III Physics continued — the cosmos in detail Fate, providence completed, the guardian spirit, love, nature’s contemplation, eternity and time IV Soul The soul’s essence, its descent and undescended part, sensation, memory, the soul’s impassibility V Intellect The three primary hypostases, the knowing hypostases, the intelligibles not outside Intellect, intelligible beauty VI Being — and what is beyond it The kinds of being, number, free will, the Good or the One: the summit treatises, closing with VI.9, on the Good Two features of the edition matter for everything after. First, Porphyry also preserved, in the Life , the chronological order in which the treatises were actually written — twenty-one before his own arrival in Rome, twenty-four during his years in the circle, nine after his departure for Sicily — so modern scholarship can read Plotinus twice over: in the master’s developing order, or in the pupil’s pedagogical one. Citations in this article follow the universal convention: Ennead, treatise, chapter — thus V.1 is the first treatise of the Fifth Ennead, “On the Three Primary Hypostases”, the tenth treatise in chronological order and the system’s own best summary. Second, the Life itself became the tradition’s front door. Every later Platonist, and every modern reader since, has met Plotinus through Porphyry’s framing: the ashamed-of-the-body sage, the four ecstasies (Porphyry reports that in their six years together Plotinus attained union with the One four times, Porphyry himself once) — a biography that is already an interpretation, and one its subject, who would not even sit for a portrait, might have declined to authorise. The editor is the first commentator. Remember that when Section VII reaches the pupil’s second career: as the questioner whose doubts provoked the theurgic turn. // READING PLOTINUS NOW // The Greek text rests on the Henry–Schwyzer critical editions. In English, the two scholarly standards are Armstrong’s Loeb (Greek facing English, seven volumes) and the Gerson-edited Cambridge Enneads of 2018 — the first complete new English translation in over seventy-five years, made by a team (Boys-Stones, Dillon, Gerson, King, Smith, Wilberding) for terminological consistency. Stephen MacKenna’s older version (1917–1930) remains the most beautiful and the least literal. This article’s paraphrases follow Armstrong and Gerson; no sentence of Plotinus is quoted here in any translator’s words without the translator being named. III. The Three Hypostases: One, Intellect, Soul The system can be stated in a single paragraph, and Plotinus states it himself, in paraphrase, at the opening of V.1: there are three primary realities — hypostases , the word means something like “that which stands under”, a real, subsistent level of being — and everything else is their product, image, or failure. At the summit, the One ( to Hen ), also called the Good. Below it, Intellect ( Nous ), the realm of true being and of Plato’s Forms. Below Intellect, Soul ( Psychē ) — first the World Soul that animates the cosmos, then, as its powers and offspring, the souls of stars, of daimones, of human beings, of animals and plants. Below Soul, the sensible world of bodies; and at the very floor, matter , of which Section V treats. The hierarchy is not a ladder built once and left standing. It is a continuous, eternal dependence: each level exists, at every moment, by looking toward the level above it. The One: Beyond Being, Beyond Predication The One is not a being. That is the first and hardest sentence of the system, and Plotinus means it strictly: being involves form, form involves determination, determination involves duality — a thing and its form, a thinker and a thought — and the first principle can contain no duality at all, or it would not be first. The One is therefore beyond being ( epekeina tēs ousias — Plato’s own phrase for the Good in the Republic , which Plotinus takes as his charter), beyond intellect, beyond self-knowledge: it does not think, because thinking divides; it does not will in our sense, because willing implies a lack or an object. Every name for it — One, Good, First, Cause, Father — is, in Armstrong’s and Gerson’s shared rendering of Plotinus’s repeated warning, a pointer and not a description: we say what it is not, and the negations are truer than the affirmations. And yet it is, in the treatise’s famous phrase as both translations render the sense, the productive power of all things ( dynamis pantōn ): not one item in the inventory of reality but the reason there is an inventory. The paradox is deliberate and structural. A first principle that could be described would be one more thing among things; the One explains everything precisely by being nothing in particular. Intellect: Being Thinking Itself From the One — Section IV examines the “from” — comes Intellect , the second hypostasis, and with Intellect, being itself begins. Intellect is Plato’s realm of Forms gathered into a single living mind: it does not have thoughts about the Forms from outside, as a scholar consults a catalogue; it is the Forms, thinking itself, each Form transparent to all the others, thinker and thought one act. Plotinus’s V.5 insists, against any picture of the intelligibles as external standards, that the intelligibles are not outside Intellect : truth is not correspondence to something elsewhere but the identity of mind and being. Intellect is eternal, not in the sense of lasting a very long time but of standing outside time altogether — all its life at once, nothing awaited, nothing lost. It is also the first multiplicity: perfectly unified, but a unity that contains the articulated whole of what can be — being, sameness and difference, rest and motion, the great kinds of Plato’s Sophist — and so it stands one step, and exactly one step, below the absolute simplicity of the One. Soul: The Amphibious Hypostasis From Intellect comes Soul , the third hypostasis, and the system’s great mediator. Soul faces both ways. Turned upward, it contemplates Intellect and receives the Forms as rational principles ( logoi ) — the same contents Intellect holds timelessly, unfolded by Soul into sequence, discourse, and life. Turned downward, it gives those principles body: the World Soul pours them into the cosmos as nature, growth, sensation, and motion, and individual souls administer individual living things. Soul is the origin of time : in the celebrated account of III.7, in paraphrase, time is the life of Soul in movement — Soul, unable to hold Intellect’s all-at-once, spreading it out into before and after, and the sensible cosmos is that spreading made visible. Hence the description of soul that the whole later tradition, Iamblichus included, inherits: amphibious . The human soul lives in two worlds at once, intelligible and sensible, and its misery and its dignity are the same fact — it can forget which world is home. Everything in Sections VI–X of this article is a dispute about exactly how amphibious, and how forgetful, the soul can be. THE ONE Beyond being and thought; absolutely simple; the Good; productive power of all things. Known, if at all, by negation and by union — not by description. Enneads V.1, V.4, VI.9 are its charter treatises. INTELLECT (NOUS) Being itself as self-thinking mind; the Forms internal to it; eternal, all-at-once, the first multiplicity-in-unity. The soul’s true home and the object of its contemplation. Ennead V throughout. SOUL (PSYCHĒ) Image of Intellect; source of time, life, and the sensible cosmos; amphibious between the intelligible and the bodily. World Soul above, individual souls below — distinct, yet not severed. Ennead IV throughout. A scholarly caution, owed to John Dillon’s The Middle Platonists (1977; revised 1996) above all: none of this was invented from nothing in 250 CE. The raw materials — a supreme principle beyond the demiurge, a mediating world-soul, the Forms as God’s thoughts, the language of procession and return — were assembled across the four centuries of Middle Platonism that Dillon’s book maps: Plutarch of Chaeronea, Alcinous, Numenius of Apamea (whose triad of gods stands nearest to Plotinus’s scheme), the Neopythagoreans, and behind them the Alexandrian Judaism of Philo. Plotinus’s originality is not the parts but the engineering: the strict derivation of each level from the contemplation of the one above, the location of the Forms inside Intellect, and the uncompromising simplicity of the One. “Neoplatonism” names the moment a tradition’s materials became a system — which is why the tradition’s later members, quarrelling over the system, could all plausibly claim to be restoring Plato. IV. Emanation and Return: Procession, Contemplation, Ascent How does anything come from the One? Plotinus’s answer, developed across V.4, V.1, and III.8 and paraphrased here, refuses the two obvious models. Not making : the One does not deliberate, choose, or act in time, and a first principle that decided to create would already be two things — a decider and a decision. Not diminution : the One is not divided among its products like a loaf among guests, and it loses nothing by their existence. The model Plotinus reaches for, in image after image, is overflow from perfection : as the sun gives light without being spent, as a spring flows without deciding to, as heat radiates from fire — what is perfect produces, necessarily and eternally, an external activity that is its image, while its internal activity remains itself, undiminished. Modern scholarship calls the doctrine emanation ; Plotinus’s own preferred vocabulary is procession ( proodos ) and the double activity — each reality has an activity that constitutes it and an activity that flows from it, and the second is the next level of the world. The mechanism, stated as precisely as paraphrase allows, is contemplation ( theōria ). What flows from the One is at first indefinite — a kind of unformed seeing, an intelligible matter — and it becomes Intellect by turning back toward the One and contemplating it; the turning (the return, epistrophē ) is what gives it form, limit, and being. The pattern then repeats at every level: Intellect, contemplating the One, produces Soul as its external activity; Soul, contemplating Intellect, produces the ordered cosmos; and in the audacious generalisation of III.8, everything produces by contemplating — even nature, even plants, even the earth itself, in a quiet, dreamlike contemplation that issues in form. Production and return are not two events but one structure seen from two ends: the world is the hypostases’ contemplation, externalised; salvation is the same contemplation, recovered by the one part of the world that can recover it deliberately — the human soul. The Return: Philosophy as the Way Back For Plotinus the soul’s return is an inward journey with a strict itinerary, and its vehicle is philosophy practised as a way of life. In paraphrase of I.6 (On Beauty) and VI.9 (On the Good, or the One), the ascent runs: from beautiful bodies, which are form shining in matter, to the beauty of souls and practices; from there to Intellect, beauty itself, where the soul discovers that what it loved in fragments it is , in its own highest part; and beyond Intellect — beyond even the duality of thinker and thought — to the One, in a union ( henōsis ) that Plotinus describes, in the treatises’ most famous movement, as no longer seeing but being one with the seen, the centre coinciding with the centre. The treatise I.2 adds the ethical engine: the virtues purify, civic virtues first, then the higher, purificatory virtues that make the soul like god — Plato’s Theaetetus programme of homoiōsis theōi , assimilation to god, given a metaphysical staircase to climb. Dialectic (I.3) is the discipline that steadies the climb. Nothing in the itinerary requires a temple, a priest, an offering, or a name of power. It requires attention. Hold that fact: it is the exact point at which Iamblichus will dissent — not from the itinerary’s destination, but from its sufficiency for passengers as embodied as we are. c. 170–180 CE THE CHALDAEAN ORACLES COMPOSED A Greek hexameter revelation, ascribed to Julian the Chaldaean and his son Julian the Theurgist, in the reign of Marcus Aurelius — the text that will become the theurgic tradition’s scripture (Section XIII). 204/5 CE PLOTINUS BORN IN EGYPT Traditionally at Lycopolis; the philosopher himself, per Porphyry, declined to commemorate the fact. For the Egyptian frame, see the Egyptology division’s Neoplatonism . 232–243 WITH AMMONIUS AT ALEXANDRIA Eleven years under Ammonius Saccas, the unwriting teacher; then the Persian expedition with Gordian III, its collapse, and the move to Rome. 244–270 THE ROMAN SCHOOL; THE TREATISES Teaching at Rome; writing begins c. 253. Porphyry joins the circle in 263, leaves for Sicily in 268; Plotinus dies in Campania in 270. c. 301 PORPHYRY PUBLISHES THE ENNEADS Fifty-four treatises edited, titled, and arranged in six enneads, prefaced by the Life — the form in which Plotinus reaches all posterity. c. 280–305 LETTER TO ANEBO; DE MYSTERIIS Porphyry’s questions to the Egyptian priest Anebo; Iamblichus’s reply under the name Abamon — the charter of theurgy (Sections VII–VIII). Dating within these decades is debated. 412–485 PROCLUS Head of the Athenian school from c. 437; the great systematiser of the theurgic Platonism Iamblichus founded (Section XIV). 529 CE THE ATHENIAN SCHOOL ENDS Justinian’s measures against pagan teaching; Damascius and six colleagues depart for Persia. The hub timeline’s closing entry for the ancient schools — and, as Section XIV notes, a more complicated event than the date suggests. V. Matter as Privation — and the Honest Tension Every system has a floor, and Plotinus’s is the strangest item in his philosophy. Matter ( hylē ) is what Soul’s productive activity finally reaches and cannot inform completely: pure receptivity without any form of its own, no quality, no quantity, no shape — in the analysis of II.4 (On Matter), a kind of non-being that is nevertheless not nothing, since bodies are manifestly of something. Plotinus’s language for it is relentlessly privative: matter is indefiniteness, unmeasuredness, the absence of limit and form; it is known, in a notorious phrase of the tradition’s paraphrase, only by a kind of bastard reasoning that thinks it by thinking everything else away. And in I.8 (On What Are and Whence Come Evils) Plotinus draws the conclusion his premises force: if the Good is the measure of all value, then matter, as the utter privation of form and measure, is evil itself — not a substance that does evil, not a rival god (Plotinus is no dualist; there is no evil principle enthroned beside the One), but evil as darkness is the absence of light: primary evil, with the soul’s vices as secondary evils, the infections a soul contracts by attending to the formless. The doctrine is rigorous, and it is also — stated now as plainly as this article can state it — a standing problem for any philosophy of material transformation , and therefore for alchemy itself. Three tensions deserve honest statement rather than apologetic softening. The Three Tensions First, the tension of value. If matter is privation and primary evil, then matter is not, in itself, perfectible: there is nothing in it to perfect. Form comes to it wholly from above, as light falls on a mirror that contributes only the reflecting. An alchemy that claims to ennoble matter — to ripen lead toward gold as toward a nature matter itself is striving for — is speaking a language Plotinus’s floor does not obviously license. What the system licenses is imposition : form mastering a recalcitrant substrate, never the substrate’s own fulfilment. Second, the tension of practice. Plotinus’s own ethics points away from the workshop. The philosopher’s task is purification — loosening the soul’s attention from the bodily — and the sensible world, however beautifully ordered as Soul’s image, is the place one learns to stop mistaking for home. A lifetime spent perfecting furnaces is, on a strict Plotinian accounting, a lifetime spent polishing the mirror. The historical alchemists knew the counter-texts inside the system — nature’s own contemplative production in III.8, the World Soul’s ungrudging government of the cosmos, the doctrine that the sage does not flee the world but ceases to be ruled by it — and they built on those. But they built against the grain of I.8, and intellectual honesty requires saying so. Third, the tension inside Plotinus himself. The same philosopher who calls matter primary evil also insists, against the Gnostics in II.9, that the cosmos is beautiful, divine, and the best possible image of the intelligible; that the stars are gods; that to despise this world is to misunderstand its maker, who is Soul, who is good. Matter as substrate of the cosmic body is not the same topic as matter as bare privation, and Plotinus holds both analyses at once — the cosmos as splendid, its ultimate substrate as a kind of nothing that anchors evil. Later Platonists felt the strain. It is one of the pressures that pushed Iamblichus and Proclus toward a more positive account of the material vehicle: if the gods themselves sow tokens of their presence into stones and plants (Section XI), then matter, however lowly, is not mere privation — it is a receptacle prepared by divinity for divinity . Theurgy, among its other work, is Neoplatonism repairing its own floor. // WHAT THIS ARTICLE DOES NOT CLAIM // It does not claim that Plotinus was an alchemist, that the Enneads teach transmutation, or that alchemy “is” applied Neoplatonism. The Alexandrian art is older than Plotinus — its roots are the subject of the hub’s Greek Alchemy: Origins article — and its practitioners drew on Stoic, Hermetic, Egyptian, and craft traditions as well as Platonic ones. The claim is the narrower, documented one: that from the third century onward the art was practised and defended inside a Neoplatonic cosmos, by men who increasingly spoke its language, and that the fit was never perfect. The seam shows, and this section has shown it on purpose. VI. The Undescended Soul: Plotinus’s Wager Buried in the technical treatises of Ennead IV is the single doctrine on which the whole theurgic controversy turns. In IV.8 (On the Descent of the Soul into Bodies) Plotinus confronts the obvious objection to his own system: if the soul has descended into body, fallen among sensations, passions, and forgetting, how can philosophy — the soul’s own act of thinking — possibly lift it out? His answer, in paraphrase, is the wager of his entire soteriology: the soul has not descended entirely . Something of it — its highest part, the soul insofar as it is turned toward Intellect — remains always in the intelligible world, contemplating, unfallen. We are not aware of it because awareness is monopolised by the descended part’s traffic with the body, as a man in a noisy room does not hear the music that never stopped. But the link was never cut. Ascent, therefore, is not travel to a foreign country; it is attention redirected — waking, as the tradition’s paraphrase has it, to what we already are. Contemplation suffices because the contemplator’s summit never left the place contemplation seeks. The doctrine does enormous work. It explains how a fallen soul can know the intelligible at all (its summit is there); how virtue is possible without grace (the ladder’s top rung is already in our hands); why Plotinus can treat ritual as, at best, an irrelevance and, at worst — his reported refusal of a temple invitation, in Porphyry’s telling, on the ground that the gods ought to come to him, not he to them — a category error about where divinity is found. It also carries a cost that his successors itemised: it makes embodiment curiously unreal. If the true soul never descends, then the person who suffers, errs, and dies is a kind of shadow-administration, and the drama of salvation becomes a drama of noticing. Porphyry, who loved the doctrine, spent a career negotiating its pastoral difficulties. Iamblichus, who had been Porphyry’s own pupil, rejected it outright — and the rejection, not any love of ritual for its own sake, is the engine of the De Mysteriis . Sections VII to X follow the argument in its own order: the question, the text, the counter-doctrine, and the rite that the counter-doctrine requires. // A DOCTRINE WITH A LONG AFTERLIFE // The undescended soul did not die with its critics. It recurs wherever Platonism needs an unfallen point of contact between the human and the divine — in the Christian doctrine of the soul’s highest part in some medieval readers of Augustine and Dionysius, in Renaissance Platonism, and in modern depth psychology’s borrowings from Plotinus. Its rival, the fully descended soul, has an equally long posterity: every tradition that insists salvation must arrive from outside the soul’s own resources, because the soul’s resources are exactly what is damaged, is arguing Iamblichus’s side of this quarrel whether it knows his name or not. VII. Porphyry Between Two Worlds: The Letter to Anebo Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–c. 305) is the hinge figure of this whole history, and the hinge creaks. Editor of Plotinus, author of the Isagoge that would introduce Aristotle’s logic to a millennium of students in Greek, Syriac, Arabic, and Latin, biographer of Pythagoras, vegetarian controversialist, and the most formidable pagan critic Christianity faced in the third century — he was also, by his own honest record, a man divided about ritual . In the Philosophy from Oracles he collected divine utterances as authorities; in On Abstinence he restricted blood sacrifice and assigned the higher gods a worship of pure intellect; in the treatise On the Return of the Soul , known through Augustine’s extensive reports, he is found — in Augustine’s paraphrase — conceding that theurgy might purify the soul’s lower, pneumatic part for a return to the aetherial regions, while denying that any rite could purify the intellectual soul or bring it to the Father; and complaining that a universal way of salvation had not been found. The concessions and the denials are both his. Later tradition, which likes its debaters consistent, has repeatedly ironed him flat; the texts will not allow it. The document that matters here is a letter . At some point late in his career — proposals range across roughly 280–305, and the dating remains genuinely unsettled — Porphyry addressed a set of questions to an Egyptian priest named Anebo , otherwise unknown to history. The letter survives only in the use made of it by its answerer, quoted and paraphrased point by point, so that its contents are known the way a demolished building is known from the surveyor’s report on its demolition. The questions, as they can be reconstructed, are not hostile; they are worse than hostile, they are perplexed , and they come from inside the tradition. x: THE WANDERINGS OF ODYSSEUS Scheria · The Court of Alcinous · Odyssey Books 9–12 // THE APOLOGOI :: THE SEA-TALE STRATUM OF THE ODYSSEY :: A TALE WITHIN THE TALE // For four books the Odyssey stops and listens. A shipwrecked guest at a foreign king's table tells how he lost everything — twelve ships, every companion, ten years — in a world of lotus, giants, witches, sirens, and the cattle of the Sun. The teller is Odysseus, the poem's most accomplished liar. The poem knows it, his hosts half-know it, and the tale works anyway. This article reads the wanderings as what they are in the poem: a first-person performance, built out of far older sea-tales and folktales, whose truth the Odyssey itself invites its audience to question.
