Sources I. A Tale Within the Tale: The Apologoi and Their Frame Books 9–12 of the Odyssey have a collective name, and the name itself is a warning about how to read them. They are called the Apologoi (singular Apologos ; Greek apologoi , from apologeomai , to speak in one's own defence, to give an account of oneself): the tales Odysseus tells, in the first person, to King Alcinous and the Phaeacian court on the island of Scheria. Everything else in the Odyssey is told by the poem's primary narrator, the voice that invokes the Muse in Book 1 and that the audience is trained to trust. The wanderings are not. They reach the audience at one remove, filtered through a character inside the poem — and not just any character, but the character the poem has already established, repeatedly and with evident delight, as a master of plausible falsehood. That single formal fact organises this whole article. The episodes are told here in full, in the poem's order, with their line references; but they are told throughout as Odysseus's account of his wanderings, which is the only form in which the poem ever gives them. The frame matters, and the poem builds it carefully. Odysseus has been washed ashore on Scheria, naked and salt-caked, after Poseidon's storm wrecked his raft from Calypso's island (Book 5) and the princess Nausicaa found him on the beach (Book 6). He has been received as a suppliant by Queen Arete and King Alcinous (Book 7), feasted, and entertained at the games and at the songs of the blind singer Demodocus (Book 8) — where, twice, songs about Troy make the unknown guest weep, and Alcinous, watching, finally asks the question the whole first movement of the poem has been delaying: who are you, and what have you suffered? Odysseus answers at the end of Book 8 and the opening of Book 9 by naming himself — Odysseus, son of Laertes, known among men for all manner of wiles, in A. T. Murray's Loeb translation of the self-introduction (9.19–20, paraphrased in the connective summary here) — and then, at Alcinous's request for his woes, he begins: first the raid on the Cicones, then everything that followed, in a single sustained performance that fills the night. The performance is interrupted once, in the middle of Book 11, when Odysseus pauses, the spellbound court responds, and Alcinous begs him to continue until dawn (11.330–384; Section II). It ends at the close of Book 12, where Odysseus refuses to retell the Calypso story on the ground that he told it the night before and that it is, in Murray's rendering of 12.450–453, an irksome thing to tell again a plain-told tale (paraphrased; the passage is discussed in Section XIII). The Phaeacians then do exactly what the tale was, in part, designed to make them do: they load him with gifts beyond anything Troy would have given him and carry him, sleeping, home to Ithaca in one of their marvellous ships (Book 13). Three scopes must be stated at the outset, because this hub divides its Homeric material deliberately. First , this article covers only the wanderings: the Apologoi of Books 9–12, with the Scheria frame that holds them and the Calypso episode that closes them. The Odyssey as a whole text — its composition, its place in the epic tradition, its canonisation — belongs to this hub's Homeric Epics article, and is cross-linked there rather than duplicated here; the hero and epic background is at Heroes and Epic . Second , Book 11, the nekyia — Odysseus's consultation of the dead at the edge of Ocean — is treated here only as the wanderings' structural pivot (Section IX). The underworld itself, its geography, its dead, and the wider Greek tradition of descents to Hades belong to this hub's Descents to the Underworld article, and the reader who wants the nekyia in full should go there. Third , three different objects are kept apart throughout, and the article's argument depends on keeping them apart: (a) the poem's tale — what Odysseus says happened, in the order he says it; (b) the folktale and sea-tale stratum behind it — the older, travelling stories of blinded ogres, forbidden bags, and man-eating harbours out of which the poem's episodes were built (Sections V and XV); and (c) the later history — the attempts, ancient and modern, to pin the voyage to a real map (Section XIV), and the allegorical readings that turned Circe and the Sirens into dangers of the soul (Section XVI). A sentence that confuses (a) with (b), or (b) with (c), misdescribes all three. THE APOLOGOI AT A GLANCE Odyssey 9–12. Speaker: Odysseus, in the first person. Audience inside the poem: Alcinous, Arete, and the Phaeacian court at Scheria. Occasion: a feast, at night, in return for hospitality and in hope of conveyance home. Extent: the three years of wandering between Troy and Calypso's island — the other seven years of the ten-year return are spent, almost motionless, on Ogygia. THE ITINERARY, IN THE POEM'S ORDER Ismarus (Cicones) · the Lotus-Eaters · the Cyclopes and Polyphemus · Aeolia and the bag of winds · Telepylus (Laestrygonians) · Aeaea and Circe · the house of Hades at Ocean's edge · Aeaea again · the Sirens · Scylla and Charybdis · Thrinacia and the cattle of the Sun · Charybdis again · Ogygia and Calypso. Sections III–XIII follow this order exactly. SPELLINGS AND NAMES USED HERE Transliteration follows the hub's practice, with macrons where standard: mētis (cunning intelligence), nostos (homecoming), xenia (guest-friendship), kleos (glory in song). The false name is Outis — Murray's Loeb translation renders it “Noman”; most modern translations (Lattimore, Fagles, Wilson) render it “Nobody”. Quotations keep Murray's spelling; the article's own text uses Outis / Nobody and notes the difference where it matters. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — A. T. Murray's Loeb translation of the Odyssey (1919) for Homer, and H. L. Jones's Loeb translation of Strabo for the Eratosthenes saying — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. Line numbers follow the standard numeration of the Greek text, preserved in all modern editions and translations. A word on chronology inside the tale, because retellings routinely flatten it. The wanderings proper — from the sack of Ismarus to the wreck on Thrinacia — occupy, on the poem's own showing, roughly three years : a year of it is spent at Circe's table alone (10.467–475; Section VIII), and the rest is sailing, storm, and disaster in quick, brutal succession. The remaining seven years are the stillness of Ogygia (Section XIII). Odysseus's ten-year return is therefore not ten years of adventure. It is three years of catastrophe followed by seven years of enforced rest — a shape the poem underlines by making the catastrophe the part Odysseus narrates himself, at length and in detail, and the rest the part he refuses to narrate twice. II. The Narrator Who Lies for a Living: Truth-Status at Scheria The Odyssey does not hide what kind of narrator it has given its central tale. Odysseus is introduced by the poem's own narrator as a man of many turns ( polytropos , 1.1) and of many wiles; Athena, his patron goddess and the poem's other great intelligence, greets him on Ithaca with open admiration for his deceitfulness, in a scene (Book 13) where god and hero recognise each other as fellow practitioners. More to the point, the poem's second half is a gallery of Odysseus's fictions: the so-called Cretan tales , the elaborate false autobiographies he delivers, in disguise, to the swineherd Eumaeus (Book 14), to Penelope herself (Book 19), and to others — tales that mix real places, real names, and real episodes of his own past with invented voyages, invented shipwrecks, and an invented self, and that the poem's narrator explicitly marks as lies made to resemble truth. A listener who has read the whole poem therefore knows, before judging the Apologoi , two things at once: that Odysseus can invent a sea-voyage indistinguishable in texture from a true one, because the poem shows him doing it repeatedly; and that the wanderings tale, unlike the Cretan tales, is never marked false by the primary narrator. The poem leaves the question open on purpose. This section sets out the evidence on both sides, because the hub's rule — stated on its index page — is that a reader should be able to tell, from any sentence, whether they are standing on a document, on a scholarly consensus, or on an argument. Here the document itself is double. The Audience Within the Poem The Phaeacians are not neutral hearers, and the poem does not treat them as such. Scheria is itself a threshold place: a people, in their own account, who live far apart in the wash of the waves, the farthermost of men, visited by no other mortals (the description Strabo later seized on, Geography 1.2.18, when arguing about where Homer meant the wanderings to lie; Section XIV) — a fairy-tale court of magical ships, perpetual feasting, and gardens where fruit never fails, suspended between the wonder-world of the wanderings and the real, dangerous Ithaca of the poem's second half. Odysseus's tale is told there , to them , and it has work to do there. He is a suppliant and a guest. He needs gifts, and above all he needs a ship and an escort home — the one service the Phaeacians, ferrymen of men, are uniquely able to give. The tale is his credential and his payment in one: it establishes who he is (the sacker of Troy, whose kleos has reached heaven), it explains why a great man has arrived with nothing, and it entertains the court through the night in the manner the court most values. None of this makes the tale false. All of it makes the tale interested — told by a man with everything to gain from telling it well — and a careful reader, ancient or modern, is entitled to notice. The poem stages its own verdict on the performance, and stages it in the most ambiguous place possible: the interruption in Book 11 (11.330–384). Odysseus breaks off after the catalogue of heroines, pleading the lateness of the hour. Dead silence falls on the hall; the court sits spellbound. Arete speaks first, praising the guest and urging generosity. Then Alcinous gives the judgement on which so much modern discussion turns. In paraphrase of Murray's translation (11.363–368): looking at Odysseus, the king says, the Phaeacians do not take him for a knave or a cheat of the kind the dark earth breeds in plenty — men who fashion lies out of things no one can test; on the contrary, there is a shapeliness on his words and a noble mind within them, and he has told his tale knowingly, like a singer — the sorrows of all the Argives, and his own. Alcinous then asks for more, and Odysseus, flattered and encouraged, resumes. Every element of the compliment cuts two ways, and scholars have said so for generations. To acquit a man of being a fabricator of untestable lies, in those terms, is to name exactly the suspicion the tale invites — the wanderings are, by construction, untestable: every witness except the teller is dead. To praise a prose performance as being like a singer's is to class it with song — with Demodocus's performances earlier that day, which the poem treats as inspired entertainment, not as deposition. The poem's audience-within-the-poem believes him, or performs belief, and rewards him. The poem's audience outside the poem is left to decide whether Alcinous is a good judge. It is worth adding that Alcinous has already shown himself a fallible reader of his guest: in Book 8 he watched Odysseus weep at Demodocus's songs and said nothing in public until the evening. The court that certifies the tale is a court the poem has taught us to watch as carefully as the tale itself. // LIES LIKE TRUTH, TWICE OVER // Hesiod's Muses boast that they know how to speak many false things as though they were true, and how to utter true things when they will ( Theogony 26–28; see this hub's Theogony article). The Odyssey gives the same double competence to a mortal. The parallel is not accidental colour: in both poems the audience is warned, at the threshold of a great traditional tale, that verisimilitude is a skill, not a guarantee. What Corroboration the Poem Does — and Does Not — Supply Against pure scepticism, the poem supplies a frame of corroboration, and it is fair to set it out. The primary narrator, who never lies to the audience, confirms the tale's endpoints and several of its fixed points independently of Odysseus's telling. Book 1's council of the gods presupposes the Calypso detention and the anger of Poseidon; Book 5 narrates the Ogygia departure, the raft, and the storm in the narrator's own voice, matching the outline Odysseus later gives; the prophet Theoclymenus and the shade of Teiresias, within the tale itself, make predictions the outer poem proceeds to fulfil — above all the warning about Thrinacia, whose fulfilment Odysseus narrates and whose consequences (the loss of the last ship and crew, the late and solitary return in another's ship, the woes in the house) are the poem's own plot. The curse of Polyphemus (Section V) is, in effect, the wanderings' table of contents, and the outer poem honours it item by item. A reading that treats the Apologoi as wholesale invention must explain why the poem bothers to underwrite them so carefully. For scepticism, the poem supplies the teller. The Cretan tales prove capability; the Scheria occasion proves motive; and the tale's texture — its folktale anatomy, set out in Section XV — proves that its materials are the common stock of travelling sailors' and storytellers' tales, not a logbook. Modern scholarship has occupied every position between the poles. W. B. Stanford, in his mid-twentieth-century edition and commentary on the Odyssey , treated the wanderings' geography with famous reserve — on 9.80–81, where Odysseus is swept past Cape Malea and Cythera, Stanford commented, in the words standardly quoted from his edition, that these are the last clearly identifiable places in Odysseus's wanderings, after which he leaves the sphere of geography and enters wonderland (paraphrased here as to its bearing; the sentence is quoted in the geographical literature and discussed in Section XIV). The Oxford commentary tradition — A. Heubeck's commentary on Books 9–12 in A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey , vol. II (Heubeck, Hoekstra, and others; Oxford, 1989), the English version of the Fondazione Lorenzo Valla commentary — reads the Apologoi episode by episode with constant attention to their traditional and folktale elements, without requiring a verdict on the narrator's veracity: the commentary's question is how the tales are made, not whether their teller is lying. The narratological literature, and studies of truth and lying tales in the poem (the discussion in Greece & Rome on true and lying tales is representative), converge on the position this article adopts: the poem deliberately sustains both readings. Odysseus's wanderings are presented as true within the fiction — the gods act on them, prophecies turn on them, the plot is built from them — and simultaneously presented as the kind of story this particular man, on this particular night, for these particular stakes, would be uniquely able to invent. The invitation to ask is part of the text. An honest archive reports the invitation rather than accepting or declining it on the reader's behalf. // HOW THIS ARTICLE CITES THE WANDERINGS // Throughout Sections III–XIII, narrative statements are the poem's tale (stratum (a)): “Odysseus tells”, “in his account”, “the poem has him say”. Where a claim belongs to the folktale stratum (b) or to later localisation and allegory (c), the text says so and names the source. No episode is presented as history. No episode is dismissed as “mere” invention either: a folktale stratum is evidence — for the storytelling world that made the poem — of exactly the kind this hub exists to record. III. Ismarus and the Cicones: The Last Raid of the War The wanderings begin, pointedly, in the world the audience already knows: not wonderland, but war (9.39–61). From Troy the wind carries Odysseus's twelve ships to Ismarus , a city of the Cicones in Thrace — a real people in a real place, Trojan allies in the Iliad 's catalogue. What Odysseus does there, in his own telling, is simply what an Achaean commander did at Troy for ten years: he sacks the city, kills the men, and divides the women and treasure equally among his crews, taking care, he says, that no man go defrauded of his share. Then the tale's first lesson is administered. Odysseus orders an immediate departure. His men refuse — in his phrase, in Murray's rendering, the others in their great folly did not hearken (paraphrase of 9.43–44) — and settle to drink wine and slaughter sheep and cattle on the beach. The Cicones meanwhile summon their inland neighbours, more numerous and better fighters, skilled from chariots and on foot. Battle is joined at the ships at dawn. The Achaeans hold through the morning; when the sun turns toward the unyoking of oxen, the Cicones prevail. Six men from every ship — seventy-two men in all, on the poem's arithmetic — are killed. The rest escape to the ships, and Odysseus will not sail until each of the dead has been called on three times, the ritual cry over comrades whose bodies cannot be recovered. The episode is the wanderings in miniature, and it is placed first for a reason. Every later disaster repeats its structure with the volume turned up: a landing that begins in success or safety; a failure of discipline or judgement — sometimes the men's, sometimes, as with the Cyclops, unmistakably Odysseus's own; a price paid in lives; a narrower escape. The Cicones episode also establishes the tale's moral accounting. Odysseus narrates his own generalship favourably — his order was right, his division was fair, his piety to the dead was exact — and blames the loss on his men's folly. A listener alert to Section II's problem will notice the pattern early, because it recurs: in Odysseus's telling, disaster is very often the crew's disobedience and escape is very often his foresight. Sometimes the poem's own detail supports him. Sometimes, as at Thrinacia (Section XII), it supports him only partly. The Cicones give the audience a baseline: this is still the heroic world, where the enemy are men, the weapons are spears, and the dead can be counted. A storm off Malea (9.67–81) — two nights and two days driven before the North Wind, sails torn to shreds, then a fair start spoiled at the cape where the current and wind beat him back past Cythera — carries the fleet out of that world. Nine days of direful winds follow. On the tenth day they make landfall somewhere no map in the poem will ever name again. Stanford's wonderland begins here. EPISODE LEDGER — THE CICONES Text: Odyssey 9.39–61. Ships: 12. Lost: 6 men per ship (72 in all). Cause, in the teller's account: the crews' refusal to re-embark after the sack. Folktale anatomy: none — this is heroic warfare, continuous with the Iliad . Its function is contrast: the last episode in which the dangers are human, countable, and governed by the customs of war. MARON'S WINE: THE DETAIL THAT TRAVELS At Ismarus Odysseus spares Maron, priest of Apollo, with his wife and child, and receives in return gold, a silver mixing-bowl, and twelve jars of sweet, unmixed wine of extraordinary strength — a cup diluted in twenty measures of water (9.196–211, paraphrased). The wine is not local colour. It is the weapon that will blind the Cyclops, carried out of the war-world into the wonder-world in a goatskin. The tale plants its instruments early. IV. The Lotus-Eaters: Forgetting the Way Home The first wonder is the gentlest, and in some ways the most frightening (9.82–104). The fleet reaches the land of the Lotus-Eaters ( Lōtophagoi ), who eat a flowery food. Odysseus sends two men and a herald inland to learn who the inhabitants are. The Lotus-Eaters do them no violence at all. They simply give them lotus to taste — and the lotus abolishes the mission, the fleet, and Ithaca in a single act of eating. In Murray's translation (9.94–97), the passage quoted here is the episode's whole mechanism: “And whosoever of them ate of the honey-sweet fruit of the lotus, had no longer any wish to bring back word or to return, but there they were fain to abide among the Lotus-eaters, feeding on the lotus, and forgetful of their homeward way.” — HOMER, ODYSSEY 9.94–97, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1919) Odysseus's response is force. He drags the three men back to the ships weeping, ties them beneath the rowing benches, and orders the rest aboard at speed, lest anyone else eat and forget. Then they row away. The episode takes twenty-three lines. No one dies. Nothing is fought. And yet the tale has stated, in its purest form, the danger against which the entire Odyssey is organised: not death but forgetting — the loss of nostos , the homeward way, as a desire. Every subsequent episode is a variation. Circe's drugs make men forget their native land (10.236, in the potion's stated effect). Calypso offers a life so complete that home becomes unnecessary. The Sirens offer a knowledge that makes sailing on pointless. Even the dead, in Book 11, are defined by having forgotten almost everything except grief. The lotus is the theme with the machinery stripped away: a food that deletes purpose. Later tradition could not leave so blank a wonder alone. Herodotus (4.177) already places Lotus-Eaters on the Libyan coast as a real people, and Polybius, as Strabo reports him ( Geography 1.2.17), identified their land with the island of Meninx off North Africa — the first moves in the long localisation game examined in Section XIV. Botanical candidates for the lotus — jujube, date-palm products, and others — have been proposed ever since. The poem itself identifies nothing and needs nothing: its lotus is defined purely by its effect, which is why the episode survives every attempt to identify the plant. // HOW TO READ A TWENTY-THREE-LINE EPISODE // Brevity in the Apologoi is not unimportance. The poem spends over four hundred lines on the Cyclops and twenty-three on the lotus because the Cyclops is a story and the lotus is a principle. Where Odysseus lingers, he is performing; where he is terse, he is often stating the terms on which everything else will be judged. The Lotus-Eaters, Aeolus's refusal, and the Laestrygonian catastrophe are all told short, and all three are load-bearing. V. The Cyclops Polyphemus: Outis, the Stake, and Poseidon's Curse The Cyclops episode (9.105–566) is the longest, most famous, and most consequential of the wanderings — the one episode whose consequences drive the rest of the poem — and it is also the episode where the folktale stratum lies closest to the surface (Section XV). Odysseus tells it in full scenic detail: the land of the Cyclopes, the offshore Goat Island, the cave, the wine, the stake, the sheep, the naming, the curse. This section follows his telling closely, because the detail is where the poem's art and the tale-type's bones show through together. A People Without Xenia The Cyclopes are introduced as an anti-society (9.105–115, paraphrased from Murray). They are an overweening and lawless folk. They neither plant nor plough; the earth bears for them unsown — wheat, barley, and vines — and Zeus's rain increases it. They have no assemblies for counsel and no appointed laws; each lives in a hollow cave on the mountain peaks and is lawgiver to his own wives and children, and they reck nothing one of another. Every term is a negation of the Greek city: no agriculture, no assembly, no law, no neighbourliness — and, as the offshore island passage adds (9.116–141), no ships and no shipwrights, though the island across the water lies fertile and unused, a colonist's prospectus read aloud over an empty landscape. The ethnography is a thought-experiment: what men would be without the institutions that make men. The answer walks in at evening. Polyphemus (Greek Poluphēmos ) is a monstrous man, like a wooded peak of the mountains standing alone; he pastures his flocks apart, mingles with no one, and has his heart set on lawlessness. Odysseus, against his companions' urging to steal cheese and lambs and go, waits in the cave to see the man and to test whether he will give the gifts of hospitality — a decision the teller himself concedes, in a rare admission, was wrong: verily it would have been better far to have listened (paraphrase of 9.228–230). The giant returns, drives in his milking flocks, and closes the cave with a door-stone so vast that twenty-two four-wheeled wagons could not shift it. The trap is architectural. Whatever happens now happens inside. The interview that follows is the poem's set-piece on xenia , guest-friendship, the sacred law of Zeus the strangers' god (9.250–278, paraphrased). Odysseus pleads as a suppliant: we are Achaeans from Troy, driven off course; reverence the gods; Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and strangers. Polyphemus answers with the anti-creed: the Cyclopes reck not of Zeus who bears the aegis, nor of the blessed gods, since they are better far than they; he would spare neither Odysseus nor his men to shun Zeus's wrath, unless his own heart bid him. He then asks, cunningly, where the ship is moored — and Odysseus, cunning answering cunning, lies: Poseidon wrecked it on the rocks; these men alone escaped. The lie saves the ship and the men outside. Then the giant seizes two of the company, dashes them to the ground like puppies, cuts them limb from limb, and eats them — entrails, flesh, and marrowy bones, leaving nothing, as a mountain lion eats. In the morning he eats two more, drives out his flocks, and replaces the stone. Odysseus considers killing him in his sleep and rejects the plan for the tale's most practical reason: no hands but the giant's can move the door-stone. A dead Polyphemus is a sealed tomb. The hero must not kill the monster; he must make the monster open the door. Everything that follows — the wine, the name, the blinding, the sheep — is engineering in service of that single constraint. The Wine, the Name, and the Stake On the second evening the giant eats two more men — six are now dead — and Odysseus offers him Maron's wine, undiluted, in an ivy bowl (9.345–362, paraphrased). The Cyclops drains it, asks for more, drains it again, and a third time — thrice he drained it in his folly — and, pleased, promises his guest a stranger's gift and asks his name. The answer is the most celebrated sentence in the wanderings. In Murray's translation (9.366–367): “Noman is my name, Noman do they call me — my mother and my father, and all my comrades as well.” — HOMER, ODYSSEY 9.366–367, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB, 1919) The Greek is Outis — ou tis , “not anyone”, welded into a proper name and declined like one. Murray's “Noman” and the modern “Nobody” both carry the first joke. The second joke is untranslatable, and commentators from the ancient scholia onward have marked it: when the blinded giant's neighbours later ask whether mē tis — “no one”, in the other Greek negative — is doing him violence (9.410), the words mē tis sound as mētis , cunning intelligence itself, the quality that is Odysseus's essence and standing epithet ( polymētis , Odysseus of many counsels). The man who has named himself No One is, at that instant, most completely mētis — and the poem lets the pun stand in the Greek for those who can hear it, as the Heubeck commentary on Book 9 and the Stanford commentary tradition both note in their discussions of the passage (reported here as commentary, not quoted). The giant, delighted, delivers his guest-gift: Noman he will eat last, and the others before him; this shall be thy gift (9.369–370, paraphrased). Then the wine takes him. He reels backward, vomits wine and pieces of human flesh, and sleeps. The blinding (9.371–394) is told with a craftsman's relish, and its two similes are workshop similes. The stake is a length cut from the Cyclops's own olive-wood club — a staff as great, the men thought, as the mast of a black twenty-oared merchantman — smoothed, sharpened by Odysseus, and hardened in the fire; the four men chosen by lot, with Odysseus as fifth, drive the glowing point into the single eye and lean on it and whirl it, as a man bores a ship's timber with a drill kept spinning by a thong. The eyeball hisses round the stake as a great axe or adze hisses when a smith plunges it in cold water to temper it — for therefrom comes the strength of iron (9.391–394, paraphrased from Murray). The giant wrenches out the bloody stake and bellows; the neighbouring Cyclopes gather outside in the dark and call in: what ails him, is someone driving off his flocks, is someone slaying him by guile or by force? From inside, Polyphemus gives the only answer his information allows him. In Murray's translation (9.408): “My friends, it is Noman that is slaying me by guile and not by force.” — HOMER, ODYSSEY 9.408, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB, 1919) The neighbours reason correctly from what they hear: if no man is doing him violence, alone as he is, then the affliction is sickness sent by great Zeus, which cannot be escaped; let him pray to his father Poseidon (9.410–412, paraphrased). And they go home. Odysseus's heart, he says, laughed within him that his name and his blameless mētis had so beguiled. The escape at dawn completes the design: rams bound in threes with withes, a man slung beneath the middle ram of each trio, and Odysseus himself clinging by his hands beneath the belly of the greatest ram, the flock's leader. The blind giant sits in the doorway and feels along the backs of every animal as it passes — and speaks, in the episode's most quietly devastating passage, to the ram that goes last, burdened with its fleece and with the narrator himself, wondering why it lags, and whether it grieves for its master's eye (9.447–460, paraphrased). The poem gives the monster tenderness at the exact moment of his defeat, and gives it to a sheep. It is one of the places where the Apologoi exceed any folktale source that can be reconstructed for them. The Boast and the Curse: The Wanderings' Engine What happens next is the hinge on which the whole poem turns, and the teller does not acquit himself. Safe aboard, at the distance a man's shout carries, Odysseus taunts the blinded giant with mocking words. The Cyclops tears off a mountain peak and hurls it; the splash drives the ship back almost to shore; the men pole off and row. At twice the distance Odysseus calls out again — and this time his comrades beg him, one after another, not to provoke the savage man (9.494–499, paraphrased). He answers, he says, with angry heart, and gives the curse the one thing it needs: a name, a father's name, and an address. In Murray's translation (9.502–505): “Cyclops, if any one of mortal men shall ask thee about the shameful blinding of thine eye, say that Odysseus, the sacker of cities, blinded it, even the son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca.” — HOMER, ODYSSEY 9.502–505, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB, 1919) The giant groans — an old prophecy, he says, is come upon him: the seer Telemus foretold he would lose his sight at Odysseus's hands, and he had always looked for some tall and comely man, not this puny weakling who blinded him with wine (9.506–521, paraphrased). Then he prays, stretching both hands to the starry heaven, to Poseidon his father — and the prayer (9.528–535) is the wanderings' engine, quoted here in Murray's translation in its operative part: “Grant that Odysseus, the sacker of cities, may never reach his home, even the son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca; but if it is his fate to see his friends and to reach his well-built house and his native land, late may he come and in evil case, after losing all his comrades, in a ship that is another's; and may he find woes in his house.” — HOMER, ODYSSEY 9.528–535, TRANS. A. T. MURRAY (LOEB, 1919) The dark-haired god, the poem says in the teller's own words, heard him (9.536). Every clause is then cashed out by the poem: late — ten years; in evil case — naked, alone, asleep in a foreign ship; after losing all his comrades — Thrinacia and the storm (Section XII); in a ship that is another's — the Phaeacian ferry; and woes in his house — the suitors. The blinding did not doom the voyage; ogres in folktales are blinded every day, and no god avenges them. The boast doomed it, because it converted an anonymous trick into a named injury to a named god's son, and a curse, in this poem's theology, requires a target. Odysseus's need for kleos — for the deed to be attached to his name, sung with his name in it — is the same need that made him tell the whole tale at Scheria, and the poem lets the audience feel both costs at once. How to Read This Article: Myth Is Not Cult This article makes one distinction on every page, and the reader who holds onto it will not be misled by the rest: myth is what was told about the gods; cult is what was done for them. The two overlap, influence each other constantly, and are not the same thing. A story in Homer about Zeus quarrelling with Hera is literature, composed for performance across the whole Greek-speaking world. A sacrifice to Zeus Xenios — Zeus as protector of guests — at a particular altar, on a particular day, by a particular community, is cult. The first travels. The second stays home. Walter Burkert, whose Greek Religion (German original 1977; English translation by John Raffan, 1985) is the backbone of this article, built his account on exactly that priority: ritual practice, sanctuaries, festivals, and inscriptions first, with the poems read as one kind of evidence among others — brilliant, early, and Panhellenic, but not a service book. Jon D. Mikalson's Athenian Popular Religion (1983) does the same work for one city, reconstructing what ordinary Athenians actually did from calendars, decrees, and dedications rather than from tragedy. François de Polignac's Cults, Territory, and the Origins of the Greek City-State (French original 1984; English translation 1995) adds the political dimension: a city's sanctuaries, especially the ones placed out in its territory, were part of how the city defined and held itself together. Three working rules follow, and this article states them once, here, rather than repeating a warning in every paragraph. First, when a practice is attested only in a late author, or only in authors hostile to it, the article says so in place — the traditions about Zeus Lykaios in Section IV are the standing example. Second, no speech is put in a god's or a poet's mouth that cannot be checked: direct quotations below are short, named, and drawn from published translations identified in the Sources; everything else is paraphrase and is written as paraphrase. Third, dates that carry an argument are checked dates — above all the date of the Altar of the Twelve Gods at Athens in Section II. PANHELLENIC Shared across the Greek world: the Homeric and Hesiodic poems, the great sanctuaries at Olympia and Delphi, the idea of the Twelve. Panhellenic does not mean uniform — it means portable, recognisable everywhere. LOCAL Belonging to one city, deme, or sanctuary: a specific epithet, a specific festival date, a specific image. Most lived religion was local. A worshipper did not sacrifice to “Apollo” in the abstract but to Apollo Pythios, Delios, or Didymeus, in that place. LITERARY Shaped by a poem, play, or philosophical dialogue for its own purposes. Plato's two Aphrodites in Section VII are a philosophical construction built on real cult titles — real as evidence for Plato, not automatically as evidence for cult. LATE OR HOSTILE ATTESTATION Some famous “facts” about Greek cult rest on a single late writer, a Christian polemicist, or a traveller reporting what he was told and pointedly refusing to confirm it. The label is kept attached wherever it applies. The archive treats the Egyptian pantheon the same way — as a working system of local forms under shared names rather than a fixed cast list — in its Egyptian pantheon article, and the comparison is instructive in both directions. Egypt's gods were gathered into families and enneads by theologians; Greece's were gathered into a family of twelve by poets, cities, and, eventually, one altar in the Athenian Agora. How that gathering happened is the first real subject of this article. II. The Twelve as a System: How the Dodekatheon Formed The Greek word is dodekatheon (δωδεκάθεον): dodeka , twelve, plus theoi , gods. It names a grouping, not a creed. No Greek council ever voted a canonical list into existence, no text was closed, and no priesthood policed the membership. The Twelve formed the way most Greek institutions formed: a number hardened into convention while the names inside it stayed negotiable. The Altar in the Agora, 522/1 BCE The earliest firm anchor for the cult of the Twelve as a group is a building. In the north-western part of the Athenian Agora stood the Altar of the Twelve Gods , a walled, open-air altar enclosure on the Panathenaic Way. Thucydides (6.54.6–7) records, in the course of his digression on the tyrannicides, that it was dedicated by Peisistratos the Younger — son of Hippias, grandson of the tyrant Peisistratos — during his year as eponymous archon. That archonship is conventionally dated to 522/1 BCE , and the date is the one used throughout this hub. Thucydides pairs it with a second dedication by the same man, an altar in the precinct of Apollo Pythios, whose dedicatory inscription he says could still be read in his own day, though the letters were fading. In Richard Crawley's translation the inscription runs, in part: “Pisistratus the son of Hippias dedicated this memorial of his archonship in the sacred precinct of the Pythian Apollo.” The Agora altar's own inscription, Thucydides notes, had by then been obscured when the Athenians enlarged one side of the altar. Two details about that altar matter more than its masonry. It became the central milestone of Athens : distances from the city were measured from it, which placed the Twelve, quite literally, at the point from which Athenian space was reckoned. And it functioned as a place of supplication and refuge — a suppliant seated at the Altar of the Twelve Gods was under the collective protection of the group. The Twelve, that is, appear in the record first not as a portrait gallery but as a civic institution: a single address at which the city's gods could be approached together. Athens was not alone, and 522/1 BCE was not necessarily first — it is simply the earliest securely dated attestation. Around the same generation, the Homeric Hymn to Hermes has the newborn Hermes divide a sacrifice of two stolen cattle into twelve portions beside the river Alpheios, the river of Olympia — a passage regularly read as reflecting a twelve-god grouping at Olympia itself (the hymn is paraphrased here, not quoted). At Olympia the grouping took a distinctively local architectural form: six twin altars , for six pairs of gods, described by Pausanias (5.14.4–8). Pindar, in the fifth century, likewise knows a cult of the Twelve at Olympia. By the Classical period the idea of twelve gods honoured together is established across the Greek world — at Delos, Chalcedon, Magnesia on the Maeander, Leontinoi in Sicily, and elsewhere — while the membership of the twelve continues to vary from place to place. // WHY TWELVE? // No ancient source explains the number, and modern explanations — twelve months, a complete and surveyable company, Near Eastern precedent for groups of twelve gods in Asia Minor, which Burkert notes — remain explanations offered by scholars, not testimony. What is attested is the pattern itself: the number is fixed; some names vary. Burkert's summary, in paraphrase: the Greeks assembled their most important gods in a society of twelve, and within that fixed number Hestia and Dionysos in particular change places. The List, and Its One Famous Vacancy The list most often given — the list carved, in effect, on the east frieze of the Parthenon, where twelve seated gods watch the Panathenaic procession — runs: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Apollo, Artemis, Hephaistos, Athena, Ares, Aphrodite, Hermes , and a twelfth seat contested between Dionysos and Hestia . Burkert's own presentation of the Twelve in Greek Religion includes Dionysos and notes Hestia as the frequent substitute; other lists, and other cities, reverse the choice. The fluidity is structural, not accidental. Hestia is the hearth — present in every house and every prytaneion, honoured first and last in sacrifice by custom, but almost without mythology, temples of her own, or a dramatic personality for epic to work with. Dionysos is her opposite: late-arriving in the epic picture, overwhelming in cult, theatre, and private devotion. A list shaped by epic tends to keep Hestia; a list shaped by lived Classical religion tends to make room for Dionysos. Neither list is wrong. They are answers to different questions. Local variation went further than that one swap. At Olympia the twelve included the river-god Alpheios, paired with Artemis, and Kronos and Rhea, the older generation, paired together — members no Athenian list would have produced. At Kos, Herakles and Dionysos appear among the twelve while Ares and Hephaistos drop out. Hades is the systematic exclusion : brother of Zeus and Poseidon, one of the three gods among whom the cosmos itself was divided, yet not an Olympian, because his realm and residence are under the earth and he does not come up to Olympus. Plato, characteristically, plays with the boundary — in the Laws he associates the twelve with the twelve months and assigns the last month to Pluto — but that is Plato legislating for an ideal city, and it is reported here as such, not as Greek practice. Three things, on the evidence. It gave the bewildering plurality of Greek cult a surveyable shape — a company a city could honour at one altar and an artist could seat on one frieze. It expressed a genealogy : the Twelve are a family, two generations of them, the children of Kronos and Rhea and the children of Zeus, whose internal order mirrors the succession myth told in full in this hub's Theogony article. And it left the edges open, so that a city could adjust the company to its own gods without breaking the form. A pantheon with a negotiable twelfth seat is not a failed system. It is a federal one. III. What “Olympian” Meant: Olympus in Homer and Hesiod Olympian is, in the first instance, an address. Mount Olympus — the real, massive mountain on the border of Thessaly and Macedonia, its summit habitually hidden in cloud — gave the gods their collective surname: the Olympioi , those of Olympus. But already in the earliest poems the address will not sit still, and the instability is worth describing precisely, because later tradition flattened it into a simple picture of gods in a palace on a peak. In Homer , Olympus oscillates. At moments it is plainly the mountain: gods travel to and from it, Zeus sits on its highest peak, and its weather is the mountain's weather raised to perfection — in a famous passage of the Odyssey (Book 6), paraphrased here rather than quoted, Olympus is described as a place never shaken by wind, wet by rain, or touched by snow, spread instead with cloudless brightness. At other moments Olympus functions simply as heaven , the sky itself, interchangeable with ouranos . The Homeric gods eat, drink, sleep, quarrel, hold assemblies, and watch the war at Troy as spectators at games; their society is a great household and court projected upward, and Zeus presides over it less as an omnipotent monarch than as the strongest member of a fractious family whose other members he must threaten, deceive, and conciliate by turns. That portrait — anthropomorphic, political, often comic — is the one epic fixed for the whole tradition, and Section IV onward repeatedly sets it against what cult was doing in the same centuries. In Hesiod , Olympus is above all the prize and seat of a succession . The Theogony tells how the Olympians, under Zeus, defeated the Titans and confined them below the earth, after which Zeus distributed honours among the gods — the poem's word is timai , portions of honour and function, and that distribution, more than any palace description, is Hesiod's picture of the Olympian order: a cosmos parcelled out among recognised powers, each with its province. The full account, with the Titanomachy and the Prometheus episode that Section X takes up, is given in the hub's Theogony: The Birth of the Gods and the Order of the World article and is not repeated here. // OLYMPIAN VS CHTHONIAN // Greek itself marks a second axis beside the Olympian one: chthonios , “of the earth” ( chthon ). Chthonian powers — Hades, Persephone, Demeter in some aspects, the dead, the Erinyes — received different ritual handling from Olympians: offerings poured down or burned whole rather than shared as a meal, darker victims, evening rather than morning rites, in the conventional scholarly summary. The contrast is real but was never a tidy dualism; individual cults mix the modes, and Burkert and later scholars warn against turning it into a system tidier than the evidence. It is used in this article as a tendency, not a law. One more qualification completes the picture. “Olympian” was never a closed caste. Gods not among the Twelve — the Muses, the Graces, Hebe, Eileithyia, Iris — are also said in poetry to live on Olympus, and Herakles, a mortal hero, ends there by apotheosis, a story the hub's Heroes and Epic article follows. Residence, membership of the Twelve, and importance in cult are three different things that the single word “Olympian” lazily merges. Keeping them apart is most of what it means to read Greek religion accurately. IV. Zeus: One God, Many Altars — Olympia, Dodona, Lykaios Zeus is the test case for this article's whole method, because no god shows a wider gap between the epic portrait and the cult map. In Homer he is the cloud-gatherer, father of gods and men, holder of the scales and the thunderbolt, whose nod shakes Olympus. In cult he is all of that and, simultaneously, a crowd of more specific figures, each reached under a title: Zeus Xenios , guardian of the guest; Zeus Horkios , of oaths; Zeus Ktesios , of the household's stores; Zeus Meilichios , the “gentle” Zeus of expiation, pictured at Athens as a great bearded snake; Zeus Soter , the Saviour, to whom the third and final libation of a drinking party was poured. A Greek did not experience these as different gods, nor quite as one god with hobbies. The name held them together; the epithet told you which Zeus you were dealing with, and what he could be asked to do. Section IX formalises the point. Olympia: Zeus of the Games Zeus's greatest Panhellenic sanctuary was not on Mount Olympus at all. It was Olympia in Elis, in the north-western Peloponnese — a sanctuary (the Altis) rather than a city, where the Olympic Games were held in his honour every four years. Its cult centre was not originally a temple but the great ash altar of Zeus : a mound built up, Pausanias reports, from the ashes of the thighbones burned there, generation upon generation — sacrifice accumulated into architecture. The Classical temple (completed 456 BCE) housed Pheidias's colossal gold-and-ivory statue of the seated Zeus, counted among the Seven Wonders; but the ash altar remained the ritual heart, and the sequence is the lesson. At Olympia the Olympian god par excellence was worshipped at a heap of the remains of his own sacrifices. Dodona: Zeus of the Oak At Dodona in Epirus, in the north-west of Greece, Zeus spoke differently: through the rustling of a sacred oak , through doves, and through his priestesses and priests, in what Greeks themselves regarded as their oldest oracle. Homer already knows it — Achilles prays in the Iliad to Zeus of Dodona and mentions his interpreters, the Selloi, who sleep on the ground and do not wash their feet (paraphrased). The excavated lead tablets from Dodona show what an oracle was actually for in ordinary life: not prophecies of empires but small, anxious questions, scratched on lead and folded — whether a journey is safe, whether a marriage will prosper, whether the questioner's illness comes from a god, to which god one should sacrifice to do well. Dodona's Zeus, in other words, was consulted as a practical adviser by private people, a role the epic portrait never shows him filling. Lykaios: The Dark Traditions, Stated Carefully On Mount Lykaion in Arcadia stood another ash altar of Zeus — Zeus Lykaios — with a temenos Pausanias says it was forbidden to enter, athletic games (the Lykaia), and a rain rite in drought, in which the priest stirred the spring Hagno with an oak branch. Excavation of the altar has confirmed burnt animal bone, overwhelmingly sheep and goat, accumulating from as early as the Mycenaean period into Hellenistic times. So far, attested. Around this cult, however, gathered the most sinister traditions attached to any Olympian sanctuary, and this article states them with their credentials attached. The founding myth told of King Lykaon, who served human flesh to Zeus at a banquet and was turned into a wolf — an aition , a story explaining a name and a rite, told in several inconsistent versions. Plato , in the Republic (565d–e), refers to a tale — he calls it a mythos — that at the Lykaia human entrails were mixed with the sacrificial meat and that whoever tasted them became a wolf. Pausanias (8.2; 8.38), writing in the second century CE, reports the wolf-transformation story of the boxer Damarchos, says of the sacrifice on the altar that he has his suspicions but will not pry — his stance, in paraphrase, is to let the rite be as it has been from the beginning — and retails the Lykaon myth while remarking that, unlike the men of Lykaon's age, he himself finds parts of it hard to credit. The fullest lurid version comes latest of all, in Porphyry (third century CE), citing Theophrastus, in a philosophical work arguing against animal sacrifice. A human skeleton of about the eleventh century BCE was reported in 2016 from within the altar's ash; the excavators presented the find cautiously, and specialists have been explicit that a burial in an ash altar does not by itself prove sacrifice. // WHAT CAN AND CANNOT BE SAID ABOUT LYKAION // Attested: an ancient ash altar, centuries of animal sacrifice, games, a forbidden precinct, and a cluster of wolf and human-flesh stories reaching back at least to Plato. Not attested: that human sacrifice was a regular, historical practice of the Classical cult. The stories may preserve a memory of an initiation rite of Arcadian youths (Burkert's influential reading connects the wolf tales with a rite of passage of epheboi ), a ritual tasting under taboo, or simply the reputation a remote mountain cult acquires among lowlanders. The honest sentence is the uncomfortable one: the Greeks themselves told these stories about Lykaion, at increasing length as the sources get later, and no source lets us watch the rite. V. Apollo: Delphi, Delos, and Didyma Apollo is the most Greek of the gods in Burkert's famous judgement — and the one whose epic portrait comes closest to his cult reality, because both centre on the same things: prophecy, music, archery and plague held in one hand, purification, and the founding of cities. Even so, “Apollo” in practice meant three great oracular and festival centres, each with its own title, personnel, and clientele, and a scatter of local Apollos besides — Apollo Lykeios , Smintheus (“of the mice”, already in the Iliad 's first scene), Alexikakos (Averter of Evil), the Apollo of the Athenian Pyanepsia with its bean-stew and hung branches. Delphi: Apollo Pythios At Delphi , on the slopes of Parnassos, Apollo Pythios — the title from Pytho, the place's older name, and from the Python, the serpent of the foundation myth — spoke through the Pythia , a local woman who delivered the god's responses from the inner chamber of his temple. Delphi's real historical function was as the Greek world's clearing-house of authoritative advice: colonies were founded on its word, laws and cults were sanctioned by it, wars and constitutions were referred to it. The responses preserved in literary sources range from the genuinely oracular-ambiguous to the plainly manufactured after the event, and the modern scholarly consensus — associated above all with Joseph Fontenrose's critical catalogue — is that the famous verse riddles belong largely to legend, while the historical Pythia mostly answered the question put to her, often in a form closer to a sanctioned yes or no. Delphi also staged the other side of Apollo: purification. The murderer, the polluted city, the plague-stricken community came to the god who both sent plague and cleansed it. Delos: Apollo Delios Delos , the small Cycladic island where myth placed Apollo's birth (with his sister Artemis, from Leto), was his festival home: Apollo Delios , the Delia, and, in the fifth century, the Delian League's treasury and the Athenian purification of the island — graves removed, births and deaths banned on it — that turned piety into imperial theatre, as Thucydides reports. Delos shows the Panhellenic festival Apollo: choruses sent by cities, a gathering of Ionians, the god as the patron of a whole maritime league of worshippers rather than of any one city's territory. Didyma: Apollo of the Branchidai Didyma , south of Miletos in Asia Minor, housed Apollo Didymeus in one of the largest temples ever attempted in the Greek world — an oracle administered in its early centuries by the Branchidai , a priestly clan claiming descent from Branchos, the god's beloved. Destroyed in the Persian sack of Miletos (494 BCE) and revived after Alexander, Didyma reminds the reader that Apollo's oracular network was plural and competitive: Delphi's primacy was a primacy among rivals, not a monopoly. A city or a king chose his oracle, and the choice itself was politics. // THE GOD WHO DID NOT LIE, AND DID NOT HELP PLAINLY // Apollo's oracular title Loxias — the Oblique, the Slanting One — is the cult's own admission of how his answers worked. Croesus of Lydia, in Herodotus's famous account (paraphrased), tested the oracles, asked the best of them whether to attack Persia, was told he would destroy a great empire, attacked, and destroyed his own. Herodotus has the god defend the answer as correct. Whatever the story's history, its theology is exact: the risk in an oracle lay in the interpretation, and the god's honour was preserved by transferring the error to the hearer. VI. Athena, Hera, and Poseidon: Gods of Particular Cities Athena Polias and the Counsellor of Epic In epic, Athena is Zeus's favourite child and the gods' strategist: she walks beside Odysseus and Diomedes, engineers victories, and embodies metis — cunning intelligence — as a divine personality. In Athens she was something both narrower and more concrete: Athena Polias , “Athena of the City”, whose ancient olive-wood image ( xoanon ) in the Erechtheion was the city's true palladium, dressed, bathed, and carried in procession at the Plynteria and Kallynteria, and presented each year at the Great Panathenaia with a newly woven robe, the peplos , on which Athenian women and girls had worked the Gigantomachy. The Parthenon's Athena — the gold-and-ivory Parthenos — was the famous statue; the Polias was the sacred one. Athens also knew her as Athena Promachos (“who fights in front”, the colossal bronze whose spear-tip sailors could see from Sounion, Pausanias says), Athena Nike on her bastion by the Propylaia, Athena Ergane of the craftspeople, and Athena Hygieia of health. De Polignac's reading of the Acropolis and its outlying sanctuaries remains the standard frame: the goddess's city temple and her territorial shrines together mapped what Athens was. The epic counsellor and the Polias are recognisably one goddess — intelligence, craft, the defended city — but a worshipper met the second, not the first, and met her on the Acropolis, not on Olympus. Hera of Argos and Samos Epic's Hera is too often reduced to the jealous wife of the comedy of Olympus. Her cult geography tells a grander story. Her oldest and greatest mainland sanctuary was the Heraion of Argos , set in the Argive plain between Argos and Mycenae, where she was the Argives' sovereign goddess — Hera Argeia — served, in the historical period, by a priestess whose years of office were used as a dating system by historians (Thucydides dates an event by the priestess Chrysis's tenure). Herodotus preserves the Argive tale of the priestess Cydippe's sons, Kleobis and Biton, who pulled their mother's cart to the Heraion themselves and died in the temple after her prayer — told by Solon, in Herodotus, as the second-happiest of human lives (paraphrased). On Samos , her island birthplace by local claim, the Heraion was one of the largest temples in the Greek world, its cult image bound up with the local lygos (chaste-tree) and an annual festival in which the image was carried to the shore, hidden, and sought again. Hera's provinces in cult — marriage, the female life-cycle, the sovereignty of particular cities — are continuous with epic but weighted entirely differently: the shrew of the poems was, at Argos and Samos, a queen in her own right, older in her sanctuaries than the literary marriage that subordinated her. Poseidon: Earth-Shaker, Horse-Tamer, Loser of Athens Poseidon's epic titles — Earth-Shaker ( Ennosigaios ), Dark-Haired, lord of the sea who received his province by lot with his brothers — map directly onto cult: earthquakes in a seismic land were his doing, and he was worshipped at Helike in Achaea until the city was destroyed by earthquake and wave in 373 BCE, an event Greeks read as his anger at a violated sanctuary. As Poseidon Hippios he was god of horses and of the horse-racing aristocracies of Thessaly and Boeotia; at the Isthmus of Corinth the Isthmian Games were his. Athens preserved, in the contest myth carved on the Parthenon's west pediment, the memory of his defeat: Poseidon struck the Acropolis rock with his trident (the mark was shown in the Erechtheion, beside a salt well) and offered the horse, or the salt spring; Athena offered the olive, and the city chose the olive. The loser was not expelled — he was housed, honoured, and given his marks to show in the winner's own temple. Greek polytheism settled its contests the way its cities settled theirs: the defeated god kept a seat. VII. Artemis, Aphrodite, and Demeter: Local Forms, Panhellenic Names Artemis of Brauron and Artemis of Ephesos No contrast in this article is sharper than Artemis's two faces. At Brauron on Attica's east coast, Artemis Brauronia received the service of little Athenian girls, the arktoi (“bears”), who spent a period at her sanctuary before puberty, in a rite the sources connect with a bear killed for the goddess and with the taming of the wildness of girlhood; the sanctuary's inventories of dedicated garments — real clothing, catalogued on stone, much of it from women in the dangers of childbirth — are among the most human documents of Greek religion. This Artemis is the huntress of the wild margins and the guardian of transitions: birth, puberty, the passage from girl to woman. At Ephesos in Asia Minor, the same name covered a goddess Greek visitors themselves found foreign. Her temple, the Artemision, was counted among the Seven Wonders; her cult image, known from Roman-period copies, is a frontal, columnar figure in a stiff, panelled garment hung with animals and signs, wearing a high mural crown — and across her chest, rows of rounded, pendant forms. Those forms are traditionally called her many breasts (Latin scholarship named her multimammia ), and the description “many-breasted” is so embedded in the literature that this article must both use and correct it. The objects have no nipples ; modern scholarship has proposed, in turn, that they represent breasts, eggs, dates or other fruits, gourd-shaped amber pendants actually excavated at the site, or the scrota of sacrificed bulls hung on the image as fertility offerings — the bull interpretation was taken up by Burkert among others, and disputed by Robert Fleischer, the image's chief modern student. The accurate statement is that the Ephesian image wears rows of breast- like pendants whose intended referent is unresolved, on a figure whose ancestry is Anatolian as much as Greek: a great mother and city-goddess of Asia, wearing a Greek name. To call her simply the epic huntress grown fertile is to miss what Ephesos itself knew — that its Artemis was its own. Aphrodite: Paphos, Ourania, Pandemos Aphrodite's cult came into Greece from the east, and the Greeks knew it. Herodotus (1.105) traces her oldest sanctuary to Ascalon and its transmission through Cyprus and Kythera; Pausanias repeats a version of the same itinerary. Her great Cypriot home was Paphos , where she was worshipped not in a human-shaped statue but, Tacitus reports, as a conical stone — an aniconic image of a kind older than Greek figural art — and where her title was simply the Paphian . Her names Kypris and Kythereia are her addresses worn as epithets. The distinction the tradition made famous is between Aphrodite Ourania , “the Heavenly”, and Aphrodite Pandemos , “of All the People”. It must be handled in two layers. In cult , Pandemos at Athens was a civic title: the goddess of the whole demos united, worshipped with Peitho (Persuasion), her foundation ascribed to Theseus's unification of Attica — a political Aphrodite, patroness of the community's cohesion, honoured with full civic respectability. In philosophy , the titles were rebuilt into a doctrine: in Plato's Symposium (180c–185c), the speaker Pausanias — a character in the dialogue, not the travel writer — argues that there are two Aphrodites and two Loves: the elder, motherless Ourania, daughter of Ouranos, inspiring love directed to the soul; and the younger Pandemos, daughter of Zeus and Dione, inspiring common, bodily love (paraphrased). Xenophon's Symposium plays with the same pair while doubting whether they are two goddesses or two titles of one. The philosophical contrast — heavenly versus vulgar love — became enormously influential in later thought, and it is routinely read back into cult, where it does not belong in that form: the Athenians who sacrificed to Aphrodite Pandemos were honouring the unity of their people, not patronising prostitution, whatever later moralists made of the name. Demeter: The Grain and the Grief Demeter is the least Olympian in manner of the Twelve: her mythology is a single great story — the rape of her daughter Persephone, her search, her famine, and the compromise of the seasons, told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter — and her cult is that story institutionalised. As Demeter Thesmophoros , “Lawgiver”, she was honoured at the Thesmophoria , the widely celebrated autumn festival of married women, from which men were excluded, involving fasting, obscene jesting, and the retrieval of rotted offerings from underground chambers — the details reported by later scholiasts and to be handled with the usual caution for secret rites described by outsiders. Her other great institution, the Mysteries of Eleusis, where Demeter's grief became a promise held out to initiates about their own death, belongs to this hub's Mysteries article and is treated there in full. What belongs here is the structural point: Demeter's power in cult rests on the two things her myth joins — the grain that feeds the city and the daughter who returns from the dead — and no other Olympian binds agriculture and eschatology together in a single figure. VIII. Hephaistos, Hermes, Ares, Dionysos, and Hestia Hephaistos: The Smith at Home in Athens and Lemnos Epic's Hephaistos is the lame craftsman of Olympus, maker of Achilles' shield and of the gods' houses, a figure of pathos and comedy — thrown from Olympus, caught in his own net with Ares and Aphrodite for the gods' laughter. Cult gave him a dignity the comedy conceals. In Athens he shared the Hephaisteion, the best-preserved temple in Greece, above the Agora's metalworking quarter, with Athena Ergane: the two patrons of craft, honoured together at the Chalkeia, the smiths' festival, by the artisans who were their real congregation. His other home was volcanic Lemnos , where myth dropped him when he fell from heaven and where his sons or priests, the Kabeiroi, presided over mysteries of their own. Hephaistos is the clearest case of a god whose cult constituency was occupational: you met him at the forge. Hermes: Herms, Roads, and Thresholds Hermes's commonest cult object was not a temple statue but the herm : a squared stone pillar with the god's head and an erect phallus, set at doorways, crossroads, gymnasia, and boundaries throughout the Greek world — apotropaic, lucky, and so much a part of Athens's fabric that the mutilation of the Herms in 415 BCE, on the eve of the Sicilian expedition, was treated as an attack on the city itself and investigated as a conspiracy (Thucydides 6.27–29). The god of the herm is the god of passages: roads and travellers, heralds and merchants, thieves and luck, the gymnasium's young men, and — as Psychopompos , Guide of Souls — the road down to the dead. Epic's charming trickster-herald and cult's stone guardian of every threshold are the same function seen from two sides: Hermes is whoever and whatever gets you across. x: OVID AND THE METAMORPHOSES Sulmo · Rome · Tomis · 43 BCE – 17/18 CE // ONE POEM :: FIFTEEN BOOKS :: SOME 250 TRANSFORMATIONS // The Metamorphoses is the poem this hub cites more than any other single work — and, until now, the poem it had never stopped to introduce. Fifteen books, some two hundred and fifty myths, one unbroken song from Chaos to the deification of Julius Caesar: this article treats the poem itself — its maker, its making, its sources, its inventions, and the long afterlife in which a Roman poet's chain of transformations became the Latin West's handbook of myth.
