Editions and Translations: What the Modern Reader Holds XIV. Sources I. The Handbook That Was Used Everywhere and Introduced Nowhere Count the citations and a pattern emerges. Across the fifteen Wing I articles of this hub — the Olympians, the heroes, the cycles of Thebes and Troy, the descents, the makers and fire-bearers — one Latin poem is reached for again and again as the working source: the Metamorphoses of Publius Ovidius Naso , known to every later age simply as Ovid . The register of this hub counts some sixty-eight mentions of the poem. It supplies the fullest surviving telling of tale after tale treated elsewhere in these pages. And yet, until this article, it had no page of its own. It was used everywhere and introduced nowhere. That imbalance is not an accident of this archive. It reproduces, in miniature, the poem's whole historical position. For well over a thousand years the Metamorphoses was the place where the Latin West got its Greek myths — the handbook on the school desk, the quarry of poets, painters, and moralists — and a handbook is precisely the kind of book that gets used rather than examined. Readers mined it for stories and passed over the questions this article asks: who made it, out of what, by what technique, with what inventions of his own, and by what strange route a poem about pagan transformation survived, and was even cherished, inside a Christian culture that had every institutional reason to suppress it. The poem's bare dimensions should be fixed first, because everything else in this article hangs on them. The Metamorphoses is a Latin narrative poem in fifteen books and 11,995 lines of dactylic hexameter — the metre of Homer and of Virgil — comprising some 250 myths , the count varying a little with how a counter divides nested tales. It was essentially complete by 8 CE , the year of its author's ruin. Its announced span is the whole of time: from the first origin of the world to the poet's own days. Its announced subject is stated in its first line: bodies changed into new forms. “Of bodies changed to other forms I tell; / You Gods, who have yourselves wrought every change, / Inspire my enterprise and lead my lay / In one continuous song from nature's first / Remote beginnings to our modern times.” — OVID, METAMORPHOSES 1.1–4, TRANS. A. D. MELVILLE (OXFORD WORLD'S CLASSICS, 1986) Four Latin lines do all of that work, and Section IV will take them apart word by word. Here it is enough to register what the proem promises and what it withholds. It promises continuity — one song, unbroken — and totality: nothing from Chaos to Caesar is outside the brief. It withholds a hero. Homer's proems name a wrath and a man; Virgil's names arms and a man. Ovid's names a process. The protagonist of the Metamorphoses is metamorphosis itself, and every character in the poem, god or mortal, is temporary — a form the song passes through on its way to the next form. That single decision, announced in four lines, is what makes the poem unlike any epic before it and what made it, afterwards, so uniquely usable as a handbook: a poem organised by a process rather than a person can absorb any story that exhibits the process, and can be raided for any story without breaking. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations consulted for this article — principally A. D. Melville's Oxford World's Classics translation (1986) — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders Ovid's or another author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. Line references are to the standard numeration of the Latin text as printed in Tarrant's Oxford Classical Text (2004). Where this article reports a scholarly dispute, it names the positions rather than silently adopting one. A word, too, about the title. Ovid himself, in the poems he later wrote from exile, refers to the work by its subject — the changed forms, mutatae formae . The Greek title by which the whole world now knows it, Metamorphoses , is not attested in Ovid's own usage; it appears in Latin authors of the following generations, Seneca and Quintilian among them, and then hardens into the book's name. The point is small and worth making in an archive that cares about the difference between a work and its reception: even the title on the spine is part of the afterlife, not of the poem as its author left it. The plan of the article follows the hub's standing method. The life comes first, told with a constant distinction between what is independently known and what Ovid himself claims — a distinction that matters more for this poet than for almost any other, because our fullest source for Ovid's life is Ovid, writing verse, in exile, with a case to plead. Then the poem: its architecture, its map, its linking technique, its sources, and — the section on which the hub's other articles silently depend — the versions that are Ovid's own inventions and that displaced every rival. Then the tone, and the sharpest statement this hub can give of its founding distinction between literary myth and cult practice. Then the afterlife, medieval and Renaissance, presented strictly as reception. And finally the editions and translations by which a modern reader actually holds the poem. II. A Life in Outline: Sulmo, Rome, and the Elegiac Career Publius Ovidius Naso was born on 20 March 43 BCE at Sulmo — modern Sulmona — a town in the Apennine country east of Rome, in the year after the assassination of Julius Caesar and on the eve of the triumviral wars that ended the Republic. The date deserves a moment's attention. Ovid was born into the wreckage of one Rome and grew up entirely inside another: he never knew the Republic as a working system, and he was a small child when Octavian, the future Augustus, became sole master of the Roman world after Actium in 31 BCE. Virgil and Horace, the great poets of the preceding generation, had lived through the civil wars as adults and carried the scars in their work. Ovid did not. He is the first great Roman poet for whom the Augustan settlement was not a deliverance but simply the weather. His family was equestrian — the second rank of the Roman propertied order, below the senatorial — and prosperous. He tells us, in the verse autobiography he wrote in exile ( Tristia 4.10, the single most important source for his life, and a poem, with all the cautions that implies), that he and his elder brother were educated at Rome for public careers, and sent to Athens and to travel in Asia Minor and Sicily as finishing. The brother, who had the family's hopes riding on him, died at twenty. Ovid was steered toward the law courts and held minor public posts. He also tells us — and here the archive's caution applies in full, because the story is suspiciously perfect — that verse would not leave him alone: whatever he tried to write came out in metre. “My father often said, 'Why try a useless / Vocation? Even Homer left no wealth'. / So I obeyed, all Helicon abandoned, / And tried to write in prose that did not scan. / But poetry in metre came unbidden, / And what I tried to write in verses ran.” — OVID, TRISTIA 4.10.21–26, TRANS. A. D. MELVILLE Read that as what it is: not a transcript but a self-portrait, composed half a century later by a ruined man explaining to posterity how he became a poet. The outline is credible — equestrian son, rhetorical education, a start in public life, a turn to poetry — and parts of it are corroborated by the shape of the career that followed and by contemporary references. The polish is Ovid's. This article will keep returning to that formula, because it is the honest one for almost everything in this section: the outline is credible; the polish is Ovid's . The Elegiac Career What Ovid made his name with was not epic but love elegy — the short, witty, erotically frank poetry in the elegiac couplet, the metre of a long hexameter line answered by a shorter pentameter, that he would handle with a technical ease no Latin poet matched. The Amores , poems to a mistress he calls Corinna, appeared first in five books and were then revised down to the three books that survive. The Heroides gave voice, in verse letters, to the abandoned heroines of myth — Penelope to Ulysses, Dido to Aeneas, Ariadne to Theseus, Medea to Jason — a work this hub's Psyche and descent articles draw on for the heroines' side of stories the epics tell from the men's. A short poem on women's cosmetics, the Medicamina Faciei Femineae , survives in part. A tragedy, Medea , was famous in antiquity and is lost entire — the archive's standing reminder that survival is an accident, not a judgement. Then came the works that made him, by his forties, the most famous living poet in Rome — and one of them made his ruin. The Ars Amatoria , the Art of Love , is a mock-didactic poem in three books teaching, with a straight face and perfect technique, how to find, win, and keep a lover in Augustan Rome. Its sequel, the Remedia Amoris , taught the cure. These poems were written into the teeth of the emperor's public programme: Augustus had legislated, from 18 BCE onward, to promote marriage and to criminalise adultery, presenting moral restoration as a pillar of his regime. Ovid's defence, later, was that his verses addressed themselves to courtesans and excluded respectable married women by explicit disclaimer. Whether that disclaimer was ever more than a fig-leaf is a question Section III takes up. What is not in doubt is the fame: by the first years of the first century CE, Ovid stood with the dead Virgil and Horace as one of the three canonical poets of the Augustan age — the only one of the three who had never had to earn the regime's favour, and the only one who would be destroyed by the regime's displeasure. Two great hexameter projects occupied his maturity, and they were conceived as a pair. The Fasti took the Roman calendar, month by month, and filled its festivals with their aetiological myths and rites — the closest thing in his work to an engagement with actual Roman cult practice, and treated in this hub's Roman Religion . The Metamorphoses took the whole mythical past. Six books of the Fasti survive, covering January to June; the poem was left unfinished, or its second half lost. The Metamorphoses was complete — though, on its author's later testimony, not finally revised — when, in 8 CE , the blow fell. Ovid was fifty years old. He would never see Rome again. WHAT IS INDEPENDENTLY KNOWN The dates and the frame: born 43 BCE at Sulmo to an equestrian family; a career in love elegy that made him Rome's most famous living poet; two hexameter projects, the Fasti and the Metamorphoses, in hand by the first decade CE; relegation by Augustus in 8 CE to Tomis on the Black Sea; death there in 17 or 18 CE without recall, under Augustus or under Tiberius. The bare events are corroborated by later Roman references, Pliny the Elder and Statius among them. WHAT OVID HIMSELF CLAIMS Nearly everything with colour in it: the father who called poetry a useless vocation, the prose that scanned against his will, the perfection of his own education, the innocence of his error, the savagery of Tomis and the barbarism of its people, and the burning of the Metamorphoses at his departure. Each claim comes from the exile poetry, written to plead a case. Each may be true. None can be taken as a neutral record. THE THREE MARRIAGES Ovid mentions three marriages, the first two brief and unsuccessful, the third — to a woman with connections to the powerful Fabii — lasting. The detail comes from Tristia 4.10 and is generally accepted, since it serves no obvious pleading purpose. His wife remained in Rome during the exile and worked, through those connections, for his recall. The exile poems' addresses to her are among their most affecting, and most rhetorical, pieces. THE NAME Publius Ovidius Naso: Naso means 'nose', and Ovid plays on it. The modern habit of calling him simply 'Ovid' follows English usage; French says Ovide, Italian Ovidio. Nothing in the life turns on the name — except that the exile poems sign it, again and again, as if repetition could keep the man attached to the city that had expelled him. III. The Exile to Tomis: Carmen et Error In 8 CE , by the personal decision of the emperor Augustus, without trial before the Senate or any court that Ovid names, the most famous poet in Rome was ordered out of the city and relegated to Tomis — modern Constanța, on the Romanian coast of the Black Sea. The legal form matters. This was relegatio , not the harsher exilium : Ovid kept his Roman citizenship and his property, which is itself evidence — the penalty of a man being removed, not destroyed. But the destination was the edge of the world as a Roman of his class felt it: a Greek-founded port town in Moesia, exposed to Getic and Sarmatian raiding, with winters Ovid describes — rhetorically, but not, it seems, wholly fancifully — as freezing the sea and the wine alike. The cause, in Ovid's own famous compression, was twofold: carmen et error — a poem and a mistake ( Tristia 2.207). The whole of Tristia 2, a single long verse letter addressed to Augustus himself, is Ovid's defence, and it is from that defence, and from scattered lines across the nine books of exile poetry that followed — the five books of Tristia and the four of Epistulae ex Ponto — that everything claimed about the cause must be quarried. There is no surviving official record. There is no prosecution speech. There is only the defendant's plea, written in verse, by the most accomplished rhetorician among Latin poets. The archive's discipline therefore applies at full strength: what follows separates, at each step, the attested from the pleaded from the guessed. The Carmen The poem is identified, by Ovid's own defence, as the Ars Amatoria . In Tristia 2 he answers, at length, the charge he reports against himself — paraphrased here, not quoted: that he had made himself a teacher of obscene adultery. His answer runs on several rails at once. The Ars , he says, explicitly excluded married women and addressed the class of women with whom affairs were not adultery under the law. Poetry is not conduct: no reader, he argues, was ever corrupted by a book who was not corruptible already, and he marshals the whole of Greek and Latin literature, from Homer onward, as precedents for erotic verse that no regime had punished. And the poem was old: the Ars had been published around the turn of the era, some seven to ten years before the blow fell. That last point is the one modern scholarship leans on hardest. A poem cannot plausibly be the whole cause of a punishment inflicted a decade after its publication, in a city where it had circulated freely the whole time. The carmen , on the standard modern reading, was the charge that could be named — the standing offence, available whenever the regime wanted it. Something else supplied the occasion. The Error The something else is the error , and about the error Ovid says, deliberately and repeatedly, almost nothing. The sum of what he lets fall, assembled from the exile poems and stated here as the paraphrase it is: it was not a crime but a blunder; it was done without premeditation; it involved having seen something he should not have seen; it was worse, in its consequences to him, than the poem; and he must be silent about it, because to reopen it would reopen the emperor's wound. Each of those details is a pleading detail, shaped by a man who needed Augustus to believe two incompatible things at once — that the offence was trivial, and that it was too dangerous to describe. The second claim, if true, explains the first's vagueness. It also makes the whole account unverifiable, which a sceptical reader is entitled to note may have been convenient. Modern theories have filled the silence with the politics of the imperial house, and they should be labelled as what they are: speculation, named as such . The year 8 CE was also the year of the disgrace of Augustus's granddaughter, Julia the Younger , exiled for adultery as her mother Julia the Elder had been a decade before; a long scholarly tradition has therefore guessed that Ovid's error was some entanglement in, or knowledge of, the younger Julia's circle or her fall. Other reconstructions have proposed an offence at court, a religious indiscretion, or knowledge of a conspiracy. None of these is supported by any ancient testimony beyond Ovid's own hints, and the hints were written to be suggestive rather than informative. A minority position, held by some twentieth-century scholars and now generally set aside, questioned whether the exile happened at all and read the Tomis poems as a literary fiction; the consensus of current scholarship treats the exile as historical — the references in Pliny and Statius, and the sheer cost of the fiction to a real career, weigh against the hypothesis — while treating nearly every detail Ovid gives about it as advocacy. This article follows that consensus and labels it as one. // THE EVIDENCE, PLAINLY // Known: the relegation, its date (8 CE), its place (Tomis), its legal form, and its permanence — Augustus died in 14 CE unrelenting, and Tiberius did not recall the poet, who died at Tomis in 17 or 18 CE. Claimed by Ovid: the two causes, carmen et error, and every particular of both. Guessed by moderns: everything about the error's content. Any account of Ovid's fall that presents a specific content for the error — a scandal witnessed, a plot uncovered, a princess compromised — as fact has exceeded the evidence, and the reader should treat it accordingly. One exile claim concerns this article directly, and it is the most literary of all. Ovid says that in his despair at the sentence he burned his own copy of the Metamorphoses — and that the poem survived because other copies were already in circulation among his friends ( Tristia 1.7). He adds that the work therefore went out into the world without its author's final revision, and asks the reader's indulgence for its faults on that ground. The story may be true. It is also, as scholars have long noticed, a perfect Ovidian gesture: Virgil, on the famous ancient account, had ordered the unfinished Aeneid burned on his deathbed, and the order was countermanded. Ovid's burned-and-saved poem claims the same pathos for a book its author was still alive to disown. What is certain is only the textual consequence he alleges, and which the manuscript tradition, with its doublets and uneven passages, does something to support: the Metamorphoses we have may lack the last pass of its author's hand. Section XIII returns to what that means for editors. IV. The Architecture: A Carmen Perpetuum from Chaos to Caesar Return to the four lines of the proem, in Melville's translation as quoted in Section I, and read them as a contract. Of bodies changed to other forms I tell : the subject is not a hero, a war, or a city, but a class of events — transformations — and the poem will be exactly as unified, and exactly as loose, as that subject makes it. You Gods, who have yourselves wrought every change : the gods are invoked not as a Muse, in the epic manner, but as fellow-practitioners — they are inside the subject, its chief agents and some of its victims, not above it. In one continuous song : the Latin is carmen perpetuum , a continuous, unbroken poem — and the phrase is a polemical one, aimed at the Callimachean aesthetics of the short, polished, discontinuous piece, which Ovid's generation had inherited as orthodoxy. From nature's first remote beginnings to our modern times : the span is universal history, prima ab origine mundi ad mea tempora — from the world's first origin to my times. The poem ends, that is, within a year of its author's birth, with the deification of Julius Caesar, and gestures beyond him to Augustus and to Ovid himself, whose closing lines claim a transformation of his own. The Latin repays one more look, because its most discussed word is a weaving term. The verb in the proem's last line, deducite — 'lead down, draw out' — is the verb for drawing out a thread in spinning, and Callimachus had used its Greek equivalent for the finely-spun, slender poem. Ovid asks the gods to draw his song out fine and continuous at once : a carmen perpetuum that is also a carmen deductum . The apparent contradiction is the poem's programme in miniature. It will have epic's scale and elegy's finish, the whole of mythical time and the polish of the miniature, fifteen books and not a line in them that feels like bulk. Scholars who call the poem an anti-epic, a mock-epic, a collective poem of epyllia, or simply unclassifiable — all of these labels are current, and the disagreement is genuine — are each fastening on one side of that founding double claim. The Frame: Chronology as Scaffolding What holds 250 myths in one song? Not plot: no character survives more than a book or two, and most survive a few hundred lines. The poem's spine is chronology — or rather, the appearance of chronology, deployed with great freedom. The song begins before time, with Chaos, and moves steadily forward: creation, the ages of mankind, the flood and the repopulation of the earth; then the generations of the gods' loves and the founding houses of Greek myth; then the great heroic complexes — Thebes, Perseus, the Argonauts, Heracles, Theseus; then Troy, and after Troy the wanderings and the Italian sequel that Roman myth required; then early Rome, Numa and the kings giving way to history's edge; and at the end the one transformation Ovid's first readers had themselves lived within memory of — a murdered Roman statesman becoming a god, Julius Caesar's soul carried to the stars. The frame lets the poem claim the dignity of universal history, a genre much in fashion in the first century BCE, while the matter inside the frame remains defiantly unhistorical: a chain of marvels wearing chronology as a travelling cloak. Brooks Otis, in Ovid as an Epic Poet (1966), gave the standard four-part analysis of the whole, and it remains the map most accounts start from — stated here as one scholar's structure, widely used and sometimes contested: Books I–II , the 'Divine Comedy', creation and the early dealings of gods with the new world; Books III to VI.400 , 'The Avenging Gods', the great cycles of divine punishment, Thebes foremost; Books VI.401–XI , 'The Pathos of Love', the long central stretch in which human passion, not divine wrath, drives the transformations; and Books XII–XV , 'Rome and the Deified Ruler', Troy to Caesar. The value of Otis's divisions is not that Ovid announced them — he did not — but that they register a real drift any full reading feels: the poem's centre of gravity moves, book by book, from gods to humans to Rome, and its transformations move with it, from cosmic acts to punishments to the strange mercy and cruelty of desire, until at the end a political apotheosis is told in exactly the grammar evolved for Daphne's laurel and Narcissus's flower. Within that drift sits the poem's most self-conscious set piece, and its only extended philosophy: the speech of Pythagoras in Book XV, in which the Samian sage — presented, note, as a character inside a Roman poem, instructing King Numa — expounds a doctrine of universal flux. All things change; nothing perishes; the soul migrates; empires rise and fall like seasons. Scholars dispute, and have disputed for a century, how straight the speech is meant to be taken: whether it is the poem's philosophical key, placed near the end to gloss everything before it, or one more virtuoso performance, a borrowed voice sustained for hundreds of lines past any doctrinal need. The dispute is flagged here because the hub's method requires it, and because later readers — including, in their own way, the alchemical readers of Section XI — repeatedly took Pythagoras's speech as the poem's thesis. Ovid gives no ruling. He gives the speech, at enormous length, to a character, inside a tale, near the end of a poem about change — and moves on to Caesar. // HOW TO READ THE POEM'S UNITY // New readers often ask whether the Metamorphoses is 'really' one poem or an anthology in disguise. The archive's practical answer: it is a chain, and it should be read as a chain. The links are the meaning as much as the links' contents — Ovid's transitions, echoes, and pairings argue, tale by tale, that no story in the collection is only itself. But the chain can be entered anywhere, which is exactly how fifteen centuries of handbook-users entered it. Both readings are native to the work. V. The Map of the Fifteen Books What follows is the poem book by book — not a retelling, which the hub's tale-articles already supply, but a map: what each book contains, where its weight falls, and which of this hub's pages a given stretch of Ovid feeds. The line counts are those of the standard text. Stories habitually overrun book boundaries — Phaethon begins in Book I and crashes in Book II, Perseus begins in Book IV and fights on into Book V — and the overruns are part of the design: the books are scroll-units, not episodes, and Ovid makes the seams show on purpose. Roman Religion; Aeneid (companion) XV (879 lines) Numa and Pythagoras; Pythagoras's speech on universal change; Hippolytus; Cipus; Aesculapius comes to Rome; the deification of Julius Caesar; the poet's epilogue. Roman Religion; Legendary Lives Three features of the map deserve emphasis. First, the Trojan War , the gravitational centre of all earlier epic, is astonishingly compressed: Ovid reaches Troy only in Book XII, gives the war a handful of episodes, and hurries past the Iliad 's whole matter in a fraction of a book. The slight is deliberate and it is a manifesto — the old epic's centre will not be this epic's centre. Second, the Aeneas material of Books XIII–XIV retells Virgil's Aeneid at speed and at an angle, compressing six Virgilian books of wanderings into a rapid itinerary and lavishing its space instead on the erotic and metamorphic byways — Circe, Scylla, Pomona — that Virgil's poem had sailed past. Scholars call this stretch the 'little Aeneid', and argue, still, over whether its tone is homage, rivalry, or parody; the prudent verdict is that in Ovid those three are rarely separable. This hub's companion article, The Aeneid , treats the Virgilian original as a text in its own right. Third, the map shows the poem's geography of sympathy . The early books belong to gods and their victims; the middle books — the longest imaginative stretch — belong overwhelmingly to women, lovers, artists, and the otherwise powerless, whose transformations are the poem's emotional core; and only at the end does the song arrive at the men of Roman public history, who are handled, by comparison, briefly and coolly, until Caesar's star. A reader who wants to know what the Metamorphoses is about , beneath its announced subject, could do worse than follow that distribution of attention. It is also the distribution that determined the poem's afterlife: what the Middle Ages and the Renaissance took from Ovid, overwhelmingly, was the middle — the loves, the losses, and the changes of shape by which passion becomes landscape. VI. Chain-Linking: Frames, Narrators, and Tales Within Tales A chain of 250 stories needs links, and Ovid's links are the most studied joinery in Latin literature. The technical problem is real. A carmen perpetuum must never be felt to stop and restart; yet every tale in it is, by nature, a separate piece with its own beginning and end. Ovid's solutions form a repertoire, and learning to see them is learning to read the poem as he built it rather than as the handbook tradition dismembered it. The Repertoire of Links CHRONOLOGY AND KINSHIP The plainest link is the frame itself: the next tale is the next generation, the next reign, the next stage of the journey. Cadmus founds Thebes, and Theban tales follow because Thebes now exists to have them. Aeneas sails, and each landfall licenses the local tale. The link claims only sequence — but sequence, sustained for fifteen books, feels like history. THE SHARED WORD OR IMAGE A transformation ends in a tree, and the next tale begins under trees; a tale closes on a name, and the next opens by explaining the name. Ovid delights in links that are frankly verbal — a pun, an echo, a repeated epithet — as if to confess that the chain's unity is a poet's artefact, not the world's. The confession is part of the pleasure he offers: the reader is invited to admire the join. CAUSE, CONSEQUENCE, AND CONTRAST One tale's ending is the next tale's premise: a punishment creates the monster the next hero meets; a death plants the flower the next lover wears. Or the link is antithesis — a tale of lust punished followed by a tale of lust rewarded, a pious pair saved set against an impious house destroyed — and the juxtaposition does the arguing that a narrator's moral would only flatten. THE TALE WITHIN THE TALE The strongest link of all is to hand the narration over. A character inside the poem tells the next stories, and the frame — who is telling, to whom, and why — becomes a story in itself, with its own desires and its own unreliability. The rest of this section is given to the great instances, because they are where Ovid's technique and his themes fuse completely. The Daughters of Minyas (Book IV) Book IV opens inside a frame that comments on the whole enterprise. The daughters of Minyas refuse to join the festival of Bacchus; they stay at their looms, working on a holy day, and pass the time — as the poem's own readers do — by telling each other tales of transformation. One sister proposes, considers, and rejects several stories in a breath, in a miniature parody of a poet choosing his matter, before settling on Pyramus and Thisbe . Her sisters follow with the loves of the Sun, and Salmacis and Hermaphroditus. The frame is pointed at every level. These are women narrating, in defiance of a god, while practising the textile art that Arachne's tale (Book VI) will make the poem's emblem of narrative itself — for weaving, texere , is Latin's standing metaphor for composing a text. And their reward, when Bacchus's vines invade the loom and the sisters are turned to bats, is the poem's wryest judgement on its own activity: storytelling will not save the storyteller. The tales remain; the tellers squeak in the rafters. Orpheus the Narrator (Books X–XI) The poem's largest internal performance is given to Orpheus . Having lost Eurydice a second time — the descent itself is treated in this hub's Descents — the singer withdraws to a Thracian hillside, and the trees gather to hear him: the catalogue of the audience is a grove of former persons, each tree a transformation already told or yet to come. Orpheus announces a programme — songs of boys loved by gods, and of girls punished for forbidden desire — and delivers, across the rest of Book X, the poem's most famous sequence: Ganymede, Hyacinthus, Pygmalion, Myrrha, Venus and Adonis, Atalanta. The Oldest Monster-Slaying Cycle Perseus is the hero of what is, on the surviving evidence, the oldest fully formed monster-slaying cycle in Greek myth. Heracles, treated in this hub’s Heroes and Epic article, would eventually outgrow him in fame and in the sheer number of his deeds; Theseus would be built up, late and deliberately, as Athens’s answer to both. But the Perseus story was already old, complete, and Panhellenic when our earliest texts were composed. Hesiod’s Theogony (c. 700 BCE) presupposes the whole beheading in a handful of genealogical lines — the Gorgons’ parentage, Medusa’s mortality, her union with Poseidon, and the two beings who spring from her severed neck — without bothering to narrate it, because no listener needed it narrated. The pseudo-Hesiodic Shield of Heracles (early sixth century BCE) can use Perseus in mid-flight, head in bag, Gorgons in pursuit, as a piece of decoration on another hero’s shield: an image inside an image, chosen because every viewer would know it at a glance. A story does not get used as wallpaper until it has been famous for a long time. The cycle’s shape is worth stating before its parts, because the parts were assembled over centuries and do not all come from the same stratum. A king of Argos, warned that his daughter’s son will kill him, locks the daughter away; a god reaches her anyway, as a shower of gold; mother and infant are cast into the sea in a chest and wash ashore on an island, where a fisherman raises the boy. Grown, the boy is trapped by the island’s king — who wants the mother — into promising an impossible gift: the head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose face turns onlookers to stone. Aided by Hermes and Athena, the hero extorts directions from three ancient sisters who share a single eye and a single tooth, collects a kit of magical equipment from nymphs, flies to the edge of the world, and beheads the one mortal Gorgon while looking only at her reflection. From the wound spring a winged horse and a golden-sworded giant. On the way home the hero petrifies a Titan, rescues a princess chained to a rock for a sea-monster, fights off her former betrothed, returns to petrify the king who sent him, and finally — seeking his grandfather in friendship — kills him by accident with a discus, fulfilling the oracle he never tried to fulfil. He then exchanges kingdoms rather than inherit a throne stained by kin-killing, founds or fortifies Mycenae, and becomes the ancestor of the Perseid dynasty, of the kings of Persia in one Greek telling, and, through his great-grandson’s line, of Heracles himself. Three features distinguish this cycle from the other great heroic careers, and this article returns to each. First, it is a story about equipment. Perseus performs almost no feat by unaided strength. He wins by information (extorted from the Graeae), by borrowed tools (sandals, wallet, cap, sickle, shield), and by a technique — indirect vision — that is itself a kind of tool. The tale is, in a sense the Greeks themselves seem to have felt, a story about how a mortal handles powers too dangerous to meet directly. Second, its central object outlives its killing. Medusa’s head does not stop working when Medusa dies. It petrifies Atlas, Phineus, Polydectes, and a hall full of men; it ends its career fixed at the centre of Athena’s aegis; and its face, the gorgoneion , becomes the most widely reproduced protective image in Greek art — the monster’s face as a device for warding off monsters. Third, the cycle is a charter. Perseus is Argos’s hero and Mycenae’s founder; his descendants rule the Argolid in the mythic king-lists; Herodotus reports his temple and his two-cubit sandal in Egypt and retails the claim that the Persians take their very name from his son. The story explains who rules, where cities came from, and how Greeks, Egyptians, and Persians are related — which is to say, it does the political and genealogical work that Greek myth existed, in large part, to do. THE HERO AT A GLANCE Perseus, son of Zeus and Danaë, daughter of Acrisius, king of Argos. Raised on Seriphos by the fisherman Dictys. Slayer of Medusa; rescuer and husband of Andromeda; founder, in the tradition, of Mycenae; ancestor of the Perseids and, in the line of his son Alcaeus, great-grandfather of Heracles. THE CYCLE AT A GLANCE Oracle and bronze chamber · the shower of gold · the chest at sea · Seriphos · Polydectes’s trap · the Graeae · the nymphs’ gifts · the beheading by reflection · Pegasus and Chrysaor · Atlas · Andromeda and the sea-monster · the wedding fight · Polydectes petrified · the discus at Larissa · Mycenae founded · the Perseid dynasty. SPELLINGS USED HERE Familiar forms are used in the text (Perseus, Medusa, Pegasus), with the Greek given at first mention where it matters: Danaë, the Graiai (Graeae), kibisis (the wallet), harpē (the sickle-sword), gorgoneion (the Gorgon-face as image), kētos (the sea-monster, Latin Cetus). Long vowels are marked with macrons where the standard scholarly spelling carries them. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — Frazer’s Apollodorus, Evelyn-White’s Hesiod, Murray’s Iliad , Godley’s and Macaulay’s Herodotus, Svarlien’s and Sandys’s Pindar, and Jones’s Pausanias — and are identified at the point of quotation. Ovid, for whom this article paraphrases throughout, is never quoted. Everything else that renders an ancient author’s sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. A note on method, because this hero needs it more than most. The Perseus story survives in no single ancient telling that is both early and complete. The fullest continuous account, Apollodorus’s Library 2.4.1–5, is a prose handbook of the first or second century CE — some eight centuries after Hesiod — which itself draws heavily on the fifth-century BCE mythographer Pherecydes of Athens, whose account survives only in fragments and in the scholia that preserve it. Between those poles stand lyric allusions (Pindar, Simonides, Bacchylides), a lost tragedy (Aeschylus’s Phorcides ), a Roman epic retelling that rearranges and embroiders freely (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4–5), historians with their own agendas (Herodotus), a periegete cataloguing cult places (Pausanias), and an enormous body of images — vases, pediments, coins, shield devices — that sometimes preserve episodes the texts have lost and sometimes contradict the texts we have. This article therefore keeps three layers visibly apart throughout, as this hub’s method requires: (a) the myth as told, source by source, with the telling dated; (b) the cultic and historical footing — what was actually worshipped, built, or claimed, and on what evidence; and (c) the later readings, ancient and modern, that have been laid over the tale. Where a famous detail belongs to a late layer — Medusa’s rape and transformation in Ovid, Bellerophon’s fall from Pegasus in Euripides — the article says so at the point where the detail appears, not in a footnote afterwards. II. The Sources and Their Layers: How the Tale Survives The epic stratum (c. 700–550 BCE). Homer barely touches Perseus, and the near-silence is itself evidence: the Iliad knows the Gorgon as a terror fixed on Athena’s aegis and on Agamemnon’s shield, and knows Perseus himself only as an ancestor in genealogies, while the Odyssey fears the Gorgon’s head in the underworld without naming Medusa at all. Homer’s one full heroic inset of this cycle’s world is not Perseus but Bellerophon, told by Glaucus in Iliad 6 — and treated in Section XI of this article, because the tradition itself attached Bellerophon’s career to Perseus’s as its sequel. Hesiod’s Theogony (c. 700 BCE) gives the Gorgons their genealogy and Medusa her death in eleven lines (270–294, treated in Sections VIII and X). The pseudo-Hesiodic Shield of Heracles , a poem of the Hesiodic tradition now dated to the first half of the sixth century BCE — it is not by Hesiod, and was already suspected in antiquity — gives the earliest extended picture of the hero, in its description of the shield Heracles carries into battle (lines 216–237, quoted in Section VII). The lost Hesiodic Astronomy ( Astronomia ), a star-poem attributed to Hesiod in antiquity and surviving only in fragments and citations — among them citations preserved in the Catasterismi tradition discussed in Section XVII — belongs to the same Hesiodic penumbra: it matters to this article not for any Perseus narrative, of which no fragment survives, but as the earliest named Greek attempt to organise the sky the Perseus family would later fill, and as a warning about how much of the Hesiodic corpus is a name attached to scraps. The lyric and tragic stratum (sixth–fifth centuries BCE). The lyric poets use Perseus the way lyric uses myth: as a paradigm, compressed to the episode the occasion needs. Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BCE) composed a lyric treatment of Danaë in the chest at sea — the fragment, preserved by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in which Danaë laments over the sleeping infant, is among the most famous scraps of Greek lyric; it is paraphrased, not quoted, in Section IV, since this article did not consult a complete published translation of it. Pindar gives the cycle two of its sharpest early attestations. In Pythian 10 (498 BCE, for Hippocleas of Thessaly) Perseus feasts among the Hyperboreans, the blessed people beyond the north wind, in a passage quoted in Section II’s table below and discussed in Section VI. In Pythian 12 (490 BCE, for Midas of Acragas, victor in the flute contest) Pindar tells how Athena invented the flute’s “many-headed tune” by imitating the Gorgons’ lament over their beheaded sister — the aetiology that ties Medusa’s death to a living Greek musical practice (Section VIII). Aeschylus staged the Graeae episode in his lost Phorcides — the title is the other name of the Graeae, the Phorcides, daughters of Phorcys — of which only fragments and testimonia survive; what can responsibly be said about it is said in Section VI, and it is handled there strictly as fragments, not as a play we can summarise. Aeschylus’s surviving Prometheus Bound (authorship and date both debated in modern scholarship) gives, in Io’s itinerary, a set-piece description of the Graeae and Gorgons in the far east — three swan-shaped ancient maids with one eye and one tooth between them, and near them their winged, snake-haired sisters, whom no mortal may look on and live (paraphrased from Prometheus Bound 791–800). Sophocles and Euripides both wrote plays on the Andromeda episode — Euripides’ Andromeda (412 BCE) was famous enough for Aristophanes to parody it the next year — and both plays are lost except for fragments. The mythographic stratum. The fifth-century BCE logographer Pherecydes of Athens gave the Perseus story its first surviving systematic prose form (fragments 10–12, preserved chiefly in the scholia to Apollonius Rhodius), and modern scholarship — the case is set out in Ulrike Kenens’s study of the mythographical tradition from Pherecydes to Tzetzes — treats Apollodorus’s account as a skilled adaptation of Pherecydes, modernised, abridged, and contaminated with other sources. That lineage matters: the connected narrative modern readers meet in handbooks is not a late invention but a classical prose telling, twice epitomised. Apollodorus — properly Pseudo-Apollodorus, since the Library is not by the Athenian scholar of that name — wrote in the first or second century CE; his Library 2.4.1–5, read for this article in J. G. Frazer’s Loeb translation (1921), is the backbone of Sections III–XV, and is cited as Apollodorus throughout, with the dating caveat stated here once and holding everywhere. The Roman stratum. Ovid’s Metamorphoses (c. 8 CE) retells Perseus across the end of Book 4 and the opening of Book 5 — out of chronological order, beginning with Atlas and Andromeda and giving the Medusa expedition as a flashback told by Perseus himself at his own wedding feast. Ovid’s version is the source, direct or indirect, of most of what the later world “knows” about Perseus: the Atlas metamorphosis as a set piece, the coral aetiology, the Libyan snakes born from dripping blood, the wedding battle expanded into a small epic of slaughter, and above all the story of Medusa herself as a beautiful maiden raped by Neptune in Minerva’s temple and punished by the goddess with serpent hair. None of that last story is in Hesiod, Pindar, Pherecydes, or Apollodorus. This article follows Ovid closely where he is the source and flags him every time; Sections XII and XVIII keep his layer distinct. Hyginus’s Latin handbooks ( Fabulae and De astronomia , second century CE) preserve further variants and the fullest surviving star-lore (Section XVII). The modern scholarship. Two works organise the modern study of this cycle, and this article leans on both, as the brief for it required. Timothy Gantz, Early Greek Myth: A Guide to Literary and Artistic Sources (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993) , chapter 10, “Perseus and Bellerophontes”, assembles every literary and artistic attestation in chronological order; the source-pages for that chapter, maintained in the University of Georgia’s Gantz Myth Sources project, were read for this article and supply several of its fragment references, including the Aeschylus Phorcides testimony. Daniel Ogden, Perseus (Routledge, 2008) , in the Gods and Heroes of the Ancient World series, is the first scholarly monograph in English devoted to the whole Perseus myth in over a century; its publisher’s description and the published review literature were consulted for this article, and its organisation of the material — family saga, Medusa and the Gorgons, Andromeda, reception — stands behind the present article’s own. Ogden’s two 2013 volumes on dragons, Drakōn and the sourcebook Dragons, Serpents, and Slayers , treat Medusa and the Ethiopian sea-serpent as dragon-slayings, a framing discussed in Section XVIII. Where this article reports a scholarly position, it names its holder; where the sources disagree, it says so. CE Mycenae’s foundation stories; the Perseus shrine on the Argos road; Argive cult traces III. Acrisius, the Oracle, and Danaë in the Bronze Chamber The story begins, as so many Greek heroic stories begin, with an oracle a king tries to evade. Acrisius , king of Argos, son of Abas and descendant — through Lynceus and Danaus — of Io’s line, had a daughter, Danaë , and no sons. Apollodorus opens the account (2.4.1, in Frazer’s translation) with the consultation itself: Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he should get male children, and, in Frazer’s wording, the god answered that “his daughter would give birth to a son who would kill him”. The answer converts a dynastic disappointment into a death sentence: the grandson he might have welcomed as an heir is announced, before conception, as his killer. Acrisius’s response is architectural. Still in Frazer’s account, paraphrased here except where quoted: he built a brazen chamber beneath the ground and there guarded Danaë — a prison of bronze, underground, designed to make the prophecy physically impossible by making access to the girl impossible. The tradition preserves two accounts of how the chamber was breached, and Apollodorus, characteristically, reports both and lets them stand. In the first, Danaë was seduced by Proetus , Acrisius’s own twin brother — whence, Apollodorus notes, arose the brothers’ famous quarrel, the feud that split the Argolid between Argos and Tiryns and that frames the whole Argive heroic age (Bellerophon, too, will be exiled from Proetus’s court; see Section XI). In the second account, the one that conquered the world’s imagination, Zeus came to Danaë in the form of a stream of gold poured through the roof into her lap. Frazer’s Apollodorus gives it in one clause — Zeus “had intercourse with her in the shape of a stream of gold which poured through the roof into Danae’s lap” — and the economy is the point: bronze walls and an underground room are a defence against men, and the story is precisely about the futility of defending against a god. Pindar already knows the golden conception as a byword: in Pythian 12 he calls Perseus, in Diane Arnson Svarlien’s translation, the son of Danaë “who they say was conceived in a spontaneous shower of gold”. The image — wealth, divinity, and irresistible penetration in a single emblem — became one of the most painted scenes in Western art, a later life noted in Section XVIII; in the Greek sources it is stated plainly and passed over quickly, one marvel among many. // THE BROTHERS’ FEUD // Acrisius and Proetus quarrelled, in one strand of the tradition, from the womb, and their feud divided the Argolid: Acrisius held Argos, Proetus took Tiryns, Midea, and the coast. The Perseus cycle is unintelligible without that division — it explains Proetus’s alternative paternity for Perseus, Bellerophon’s exile, and the exchange of kingdoms with which Perseus’s own story ends (Sections XI and XIV). What Acrisius does next defines him. Learning that Danaë has borne a child, Perseus , he refuses to believe Zeus is the father — Apollodorus is explicit that the refusal, not the birth, drives the act — and, unwilling or unable to kill daughter and grandson outright under his own roof, he puts them in a wooden chest ( larnax ) and casts it into the sea. The distinction matters to the story’s moral machinery. Exposure — abandoning the unwanted to the elements, the sea, the mountainside — is the standard Greek mythic device by which a killer delegates the killing to fortune and keeps his own hands formally clean; Oedipus on Cithaeron and Paris on Ida are the famous parallels. The sea, in these stories, regularly refuses the commission. The chest becomes a cradle, the intended drowning a voyage, and the oracle’s machinery — which no precaution has ever yet slowed — moves mother and child out of Argos altogether, to the small island where the next act of the king’s avoidance will be played out by other hands. Danaë’s own voice in the chest survives, in Simonides’ fragment, as the tradition’s emotional centre for this episode; it is treated with the voyage itself in the next section. // TWO PATERNITIES, KEPT APART // Apollodorus reports the Proetus seduction and the shower of gold as alternatives (“as some say” / “but some say”), and this article keeps them so. The divine paternity is the version the rest of the cycle assumes — Perseus acts throughout as Zeus’s son, and Herodotus 6.53 notes that the Greek king-lists run back to Perseus precisely because no mortal father is named for him, as Amphitryon is named for Heracles — but the Proetus version is old, consequential for the Argive feud, and not a late rationalisation to be tidied away. IV. The Chest, the Sea, Seriphos, and Dictys The chest was washed ashore, Apollodorus says, on Seriphos — a small, rocky Cycladic island, proverbially poor, whose inhabitants later Greek comedy treated as a byword for insignificance; the choice of landfall is part of the story’s design, since the hero of Argos must grow up where no one knows his name. There Dictys — his name is the Greek word for a net, and Apollodorus presents him at his work — took up the boy and reared him. Dictys is a fisherman, and in most tellings the chest comes up in his nets: the sea that was meant to kill the child delivers him instead to the humblest possible protector, a working man whose only resources are kindness and obscurity. The pattern is the exposure-story’s standard reversal, but the Seriphos setting gives it a particular edge. Perseus grows up not merely hidden but provincial — an Argive prince and a god’s son raised as a fisherman’s fosterling on an island the great world ignored — and everything that follows, Polydectes’s contempt, the boast at the feast, the impossible gift demanded of a young man with nothing, depends on that social fact. The emotional register of the voyage is supplied by Simonides . His Danaë fragment (fragment 543 in Page’s Poetae Melici Graeci ), preserved because Dionysius of Halicarnassus quoted it as a model of pathetic composition, gives Danaë a lament over the sleeping child in the dark, pitching chest: she speaks to the infant who sleeps through the wind and the bronze-nailed box, contrasting his untroubled rest with her own waking terror, in lines that ancient critics already treated as the supreme example of a mother’s voice in lyric. This article paraphrases the fragment rather than quoting it — no complete published translation of it was opened in the research for this article, and the hub’s rule is that quotation marks are earned, not approximated — but its existence and its fame belong in the record: by the early fifth century BCE, the chest episode was already being treated not as adventure but as pathos, and the cycle’s centre of feeling was the mother, not the hero. Gantz’s source-collection (chapter 10) places the fragment at the head of the Danaë testimonia, and Ogden’s monograph likewise gives the Simonides passage its weight as the earliest surviving interior telling of any part of the Perseus story. Dictys had a brother: Polydectes , king of Seriphos. The two brothers are the island’s whole moral geography — the fisherman who takes in, and the king who takes. Apollodorus’s arrangement is spare: Dictys rears Perseus; Polydectes rules; Danaë lives, in effect, under her rescuer’s protection in her rescuer’s brother’s kingdom. For as long as Perseus is a child, the arrangement holds. The story’s second act begins at the moment it cannot hold any longer — when the fosterling is grown, and stands between the king and the king’s desire. Before turning to that act, the geography deserves one note, because later sections depend on it. Seriphos is real, small, and near; the Gorgons’ country, to which Perseus will be sent, is at the edge of the world, beyond Ocean, in the neighbourhood of Night. The quest’s geography is a geography of increasing remoteness — island, then the Graeae in the twilight, then the nymphs, then Ocean’s shore — and the hero’s equipment (Section VII) is precisely the kit required to traverse that gradient and come back. ARGOS THE ORACLE AND THE CHAMBER Acrisius, told his daughter’s son will kill him, immures Danaë in an underground bronze chamber. Zeus reaches her as a stream of gold; in the alternative version, Proetus seduces her. Perseus is born. THE SEA THE CHEST Acrisius, refusing to believe the divine paternity, casts Danaë and the infant Perseus into the sea in a wooden chest — exposure in place of direct kin-killing. SERIPHOS DICTYS The chest washes ashore on Seriphos. The fisherman Dictys takes up the boy and rears him. His brother Polydectes is king of the island. MANHOOD THE OBSTACLE Perseus grown to man’s estate stands between Polydectes and Danaë. The king devises the trap of the wedding contributions (Section V). V. Polydectes’s Trap and the Impossible Task Apollodorus tells the trap’s mechanism with a mythographer’s economy (2.4.2, paraphrased from Frazer’s translation). Polydectes fell in love with Danaë but could not get access to her, because Perseus was grown to man’s estate. The son is the obstacle; the king’s problem is therefore not how to woo but how to remove — honourably, publicly, and at no risk to himself. His device is a feast with a fiction attached. He called together his friends, Perseus among them, under the pretext of collecting contributions toward a wedding gift for Hippodamia, daughter of Oenomaus — the princess of Pisa whose suitors raced her father for her hand and died for losing; the pretext is pointed, since a gift-collection for that wedding is a demand no guest can refuse without shame, and the company will be expected to contribute horses, the standard prestige-gift of heroic society. Perseus, who has no horses and no wealth — the fisherman’s fosterling at the king’s table — covers his poverty with the one currency he has, a boast: he declared, in Frazer’s rendering, that he would not stick even at the Gorgon’s head. It is the rash promise of a young man cornered in public, and Polydectes had designed the corner. The king required the others to furnish horses; from Perseus, who had offered more, he required exactly what had been offered. Bring the Gorgon’s head. The task’s impossibility deserves to be stated flatly, because the cycle’s later wonders can make it sound merely difficult. The Gorgons live beyond Ocean at the world’s edge; their whereabouts are unknown to mortals; they can fly; and their faces turn anyone who looks at them to stone — which is to say, the ordinary heroic method, walk up and fight, is suicide by definition, and even finding them requires information no human source possesses. Polydectes is not sending Perseus on a hard errand. He is sending him to a death that will look like the consequence of his own boast, leaving Danaë unprotected and the king blameless. Pindar, in Pythian 12, compresses the whole Seriphos situation into the deliverance it produced: Perseus, in Svarlien’s translation, repaid Polydectes with a deadly wedding-gift “for the long slavery of his mother and her forced bridal bed” — a phrase that confirms, from the early fifth century BCE, both the marriage-pressure on Danaë and the story’s own sense of the head as a gift answering a gift. The eranos, the contribution-feast, is answered by an anti-eranos: the one contribution that destroys the collector. // THE BOAST AS BOND // Greek heroic narrative treats a public boast as a binding act: what a man says he will do, at a feast, before witnesses, he must do or be shamed past recovery. Polydectes’s trap works because the obligation is real. Perseus cannot withdraw the offer without ceasing to be the person the story needs him to be — and the king, who understands the code perfectly, simply holds him to his word. What saves the enterprise is that Perseus is not, in fact, without resources: he is Zeus’s son, and the Olympian order has its own interest in the Gorgon. Apollodorus states the guidance in a clause — under the guidance of Hermes and Athena he made his way to the daughters of Phorcys — and the pairing is exact. Hermes is the god of roads, thresholds, theft, and clever acquisition, the divine escort who knows the way to places mortals cannot find; Athena is the goddess of craft, technique, and the disciplined use of tools, whose own emblem the Gorgon’s head will become. Between them they embody the quest’s whole method: find out, equip, indirection . Neither god fights Medusa for him. What they provide is a route and, at the kill itself, a guided hand (Section IX). The hero’s part is to execute — and, first, to interrogate the only beings who know the way onward: the Gorgons’ own sisters, the ancient ones of the twilight, the Graeae. VI. The Graeae: One Eye, One Tooth The Graeae — Greek Graiai , the Grey Ones, also called the Phorcides — are, in Hesiod’s genealogy ( Theogony 270–273), daughters of the sea-god Phorcys and Ceto , grey from birth: Pemphredo and Enyo are the two Hesiod names, and a third, Dino, joins them in Apollodorus and later sources. They are the Gorgons’ sisters and, in the tradition Aeschylus staged, their appointed lookouts — the outer defence of the Gorgon country, posted where the twilight begins. Their defining feature is the one every retelling keeps: the three sisters possess between them one eye and one tooth , which they pass from hand to hand in turn. Apollodorus, in Frazer’s translation, states it without ornament: the three “had but one eye and one tooth, and these they passed to each other in turn”. Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound gives the same economy a geography — the ancient maids dwell where neither sun nor moon ever looks on them (paraphrased) — and the detail is more than grotesque decoration. Beings who share a single organ of sight are beings whose perception itself has a gap in it: a moment, at every handover, when the eye is in transit and no one is seeing. Perseus’s first exploit is to find that gap and put his hand in it. Apollodorus’s account of the exploit (2.4.2) is the canonical one, and this article follows it in paraphrase with its key terms quoted from Frazer. Perseus got possession of the eye and the tooth — seized them, the fuller tradition in Pherecydes and the scholia makes clear, in the instant of passing — and when the sisters demanded them back, he named his price: he would return them if they would show him the way to the nymphs who held the quest’s equipment. The extortion is worth pausing on, because it sets the cycle’s ethical tone and Ogden’s monograph remarks on the pattern: Perseus’s characteristic act is not the frontal blow but the seizure of leverage. He takes hostage the two things his victims cannot live without — their sight and their eating — and trades them for information. The Graeae comply; he returns eye and tooth, as agreed; and the bargain, faithfully kept on both sides, moves him one station further out: from the sisters who know the way, to the nymphs who hold the tools. The tale’s logic is a chain of custodians, each guarding the next link, and the hero’s skill is the skill of working the chain. Aeschylus’s Phorcides: Handling a Lost Play Aeschylus made a tragedy of this episode — the Phorcides — and the play is lost. What survives is testimony: fragments and reports preserved by later authors, collected as fragment 262 in Stefan Radt’s edition of the tragic fragments ( Tragicorum Graecorum Fragmenta , vol. 3) and assembled in Gantz’s source-pages for the Perseus chapter, which were read for this article. The fullest testimony comes through Eratosthenes’ star-lore (the Catasterismi tradition, Section XVII), and in the translation given in Gantz’s sources it reports, in substance, this: that Perseus took the curved blade of adamant from Hephaestus; that, as Aeschylus says in the Phorcides , the Gorgons had the Graeae as their lookouts, who had one eye between them and handed it round as each went on guard; that Perseus, watching carefully, stole the eye as it was handed over and threw it into the Tritonian lake; and that, coming upon the Gorgons asleep, he took Medusa’s head. Two differences from Apollodorus stand out and are recorded here as differences, not harmonised: in the Aeschylean version as reported, Perseus does not bargain — he destroys the eye, throwing it into Lake Tritonis (in Libya, in the far west), blinding the lookouts permanently; and the adamantine blade comes from Hephaestus , not Hermes. The vase-painting record studied by J. H. Oakley in his 1988 article “Perseus, the Graiai and Aeschylus’ Phorkides ” ( American Journal of Archaeology 92.3) — an Attic red-figure pyxis lid in Athens (National Museum 1291) and related images of Perseus with the Graeae — has been connected with the play’s staging and influence. Beyond this, honesty requires the archive’s standard formula: the play’s plot, structure, and treatment are not recoverable , and any account that summarises the Phorcides as if it could be read is inventing. What the fragments establish is narrower and still valuable: that by the mid-fifth century BCE the Graeae episode was important enough to carry a tragedy, and that its tragic form was harsher than the mythographic one — theft and blinding, not a bargain kept. Pindar’s Pythian 10 adds one further station that the prose accounts omit, and its omission from Apollodorus should be noted rather than explained away. In the ode for Hippocleas (498 BCE), Perseus, guided — the poem stresses Athena’s favour — journeys to the Hyperboreans , the people beyond Boreas, the north wind, who live in feasting and freedom from disease and old age. x: THE PROSE SYSTEMATIZERS: HERODOTUS, PAUSANIAS, PLUTARCH Halicarnassus · Lydia · Chaeronea · c. 440 BCE – c. 180 CE // INQUIRY :: PERIEGESIS :: BIOGRAPHY // Almost every cult fact in this hub — every rite described, every image identified, every local legend attached to a place — reaches us through prose, and most of it through three prose writers: Herodotus, who asked where the gods came from; Pausanias, who walked Greece and wrote down what stood there and what was said about it; and Plutarch, who tried to make the myths philosophically respectable. This article is their source-critical home: what each man was doing, how each man's evidence works, and why the hub trusts each of them for different things.
