What “Systematizer” Means Here The poets came first, and this hub has treated them as texts in their own right: Homer in The Homeric Epics , Hesiod in Theogony and the Succession Myth . But a poem is not the only machine antiquity built for organising myth. From the fifth century BCE onward, prose took up the same material and did different work with it. Prose could ask questions a hexameter could not: Who told you this? Did you see it yourself? What stands on the spot now? What does the story mean? The three writers of this article are the three great prose answers to those questions, and “systematizer” is this hub's word for what they share: each of them took the inherited mass of Greek myth — local, contradictory, unowned — and forced it into a system , an ordered whole with a principle of arrangement that a reader can inspect. The systems differ, and the difference is the article's subject. Herodotus organised myth by inquiry ( historiē ): he travelled, asked, compared peoples, and reported what was said, arranging the gods themselves into a history of transmission — who had them first, who borrowed them, who named them. Pausanias organised myth by place ( periēgēsis , a “leading around”): he walked mainland Greece sanctuary by sanctuary and city by city, and pinned each story to the altar, image, tomb, or spring where it was told. Plutarch organised myth by person and meaning : in the Lives he fitted the legendary founders into biography beside documented statesmen, and in the essays he asked what the stories signify — the question that makes him the ancestor of every allegorist this hub treats in Wing II. HERODOTUS · INQUIRY The organising question is whence? Myth becomes evidence in an investigation: reports are collected, compared, and sometimes judged. The system is a history of peoples and their customs, in which the gods have a transmission history like a trade good. PAUSANIAS · PERIEGESIS The organising question is where, and what is there? Myth becomes topography: every story is anchored to a visible object or a performed rite at a named place. The system is a map of Greece made of sanctuaries. PLUTARCH · BIOGRAPHY AND PHILOSOPHY The organising questions are what was he like? and what does it mean? Myth becomes character in the Lives and doctrine in the essays. The system is a moral and metaphysical order, into which the old stories must be made to fit — or be explained until they do. WHY THE HUB NEEDS ALL THREE Between them the three cover the whole life of a Greek cult fact: its earliest surviving report (often Herodotus), its state on the ground in the high Roman period (Pausanias), and its philosophical afterlife (Plutarch). No one of them can substitute for the others, and Section XVI states the hub's rules for keeping their evidence apart. A fourth prose systematizer stands behind all three in this hub's architecture and has an article of his own in this same phase of building: Apollodorus , whose Library organised myth by genealogy into the handbook every later writer plundered — see Apollodorus and the Library . The difference is instructive. Apollodorus systematised the stories ; Herodotus, Pausanias, and Plutarch systematised the evidence — testimony, place, and interpretation. That is why they, and not the handbook tradition, carry the weight of this hub's cult claims, and why they get the source-critical treatment here. A name-mention count across the hub's files makes the dependence plain: Pausanias is named some 135 times, Herodotus some 130, and Plutarch structures the whole of Theseus . An archive that leans that hard on three witnesses owes its readers an account of the witnesses. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — A. D. Godley's Loeb Herodotus, George Rawlinson's Herodotus, and Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb Plutarch — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. References of the form “2.53” are to book and chapter of the Histories ; Pausanias is cited by book, chapter, and section; Plutarch's essays by their Latin titles and, for On Isis and Osiris , by the standard Moralia pagination (351C–384C). One caution governs everything that follows, and it is the hub's standing discipline applied to its own favourite sources. None of the three is a neutral recording instrument. Herodotus has a thesis about Egypt. Pausanias has a canon of what counts as worth recording, and it excludes most of the living Roman present. Plutarch has a philosophy, and he bends stories toward it openly. To use them well is not to strip those agendas away — they cannot be stripped — but to know, for each claim, which agenda produced it and what the claim is therefore evidence of . A Herodotean sentence is excellent evidence for what a fifth-century inquirer could be told. A Pausanian sentence is excellent evidence for what stood at a place in the second century CE and what its custodians said. A Plutarchan sentence is excellent evidence for what an educated Platonist priest could make of a myth around 100 CE. Confusing those three evidentiary values is the single commonest error in popular writing on Greek religion, and this article exists to make it harder to commit here. II. Three Writers, Three Centuries, Three Projects The three were not contemporaries, collaborators, or even readers of one another in any simple line. Six centuries separate the first from the last, and the Greek world each wrote in was a different world. c. 484 – c. 425 BCE HERODOTUS OF HALICARNASSUS A Greek of a mixed Greek-Carian city on the Anatolian coast, writing in the generation after the Persian Wars, in a world of independent city-states. His Histories — the inquiry into the wars between Greeks and barbarians — ranges over the whole known world and treats Egypt, Babylon, Scythia, and Libya as fully as Greece. He is the earliest of the three by half a millennium, and for many cults his is the earliest prose testimony that survives at all. fl. c. 150 – 180 CE PAUSANIAS OF LYDIA A Greek of Roman Asia Minor — probably from the region of Magnesia under Sipylus, an inference from his intimate knowledge of Lydia rather than a stated fact — writing under the Antonine emperors, when Greece was a museum- province of the Roman Empire. His Periegesis ( Description of Greece ) in ten books walks the mainland in the age of Hadrian's and Herodes Atticus' building programmes, and systematically prefers the old Greece to the new. c. 46 – after 119 CE PLUTARCH OF CHAERONEA A Greek of a small Boeotian town, educated at Athens, widely travelled, a priest of Apollo at Delphi, writing under Trajan and Hadrian — a generation or two before Pausanias, whom he does not appear to have known. His Parallel Lives pair Greek with Roman statesmen from Theseus to the early Empire; his essays (the Moralia ) range over philosophy, religion, and antiquarian lore. He is the only one of the three who is himself a cult official, and it shows. The order of this article is chronological, but the order of dependence in the hub runs the other way. When a cult is described in this archive — the rites at Eleusis in The Mysteries , the images of the Olympians , the hero-shrines of Theseus — the description on the ground is usually Pausanias'; the earliest check on it is Herodotus'; and the interpretation layered over it in later antiquity is usually Plutarch's. Reading the three in chronological order, as this article does, is reading the evidence in the order it was produced; using them in the hub means running the film backward, from the latest fullest description to the earliest testimony, and noticing what each stage added. Each of the next three parts of the article takes one writer in three movements: the man and the shape of his book; his method, stated in his own practice; and the characteristic failure mode a reader must discount. The comparison, the hub's rules of use, and the editions follow. III. Herodotus: The Inquirer and His Book Herodotus opens his work by naming himself, his city, and his purpose: the book is a historiēs apodexis , a “display of inquiry”, meant — in paraphrase of his famous first sentence — to keep human deeds from being erased by time and to explain the cause of the war between Greeks and barbarians. The word historiē is the programme. It does not yet mean “history” in the modern disciplinary sense; it means asking and finding out , and the inquirer ( histōr ) was originally a man who knows because he has asked and seen. Everything in the nine books — the division into nine, named for the Muses, is later editorial work, not his — is the record of an inquiry: wars, yes, but also rivers, customs, animal lore, king-lists, temple inventories, and the origins of the gods. The structure matters for the myth-reader. The Histories is built of logoi — accounts, each attached to a people or a place: the Lydian logos, the Persian logos, and, longest and most consequential for this hub, the Egyptian logos of Book 2, a self-contained treatise on Egypt's land, customs, kings, and religion that runs to nearly a fifth of the whole work. Myth enters Herodotus not as narrative ornament but as data inside logoi : when he reports what the Egyptians say about Heracles, or what the priestesses of Dodona say about the doves, he is filing testimony. His myth-material is therefore always attributed — someone, somewhere, says this — and the attribution is part of the evidence. This is a different thing from Hesiod's inspired catalogue or Homer's Muse-given song, and it is the birth of the source-critical habit this hub tries to practise. His travels were real and wide — Egypt up the Nile to Elephantine by his own account (2.29), Babylon, the Black Sea coast, Tyre, Cyrene — though the modern debate about how much he saw, and how much he took from books and talk, is genuine and is flagged in Section V. His informants were typically the people a Greek traveller could actually reach: priests through interpreters, temple staff, local notables, other travellers. He names classes of sources more often than individuals: “the priests of Hephaestus at Memphis”, “the priestesses at Dodona”, “the Egyptians say”. A reader who keeps asking who could have told him this, and what did they want him to believe? is reading Herodotus the way Herodotus asks to be read — because he asks exactly that question about his own informants, repeatedly, in the text. THE SHAPE OF THE HISTORIES Book 1: Lydia, Persia's rise, Croesus. Book 2: Egypt. Book 3: Persia and the conquest of Egypt. Book 4: Scythia and Libya. Book 5–6: the Ionian revolt and Marathon. Books 7–9: Xerxes' invasion, Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea. The war narrative is the spine; the ethnographic logoi are the ribs, and the ribs carry most of the myth. THE MAN Born at Halicarnassus in Caria, a Dorian Greek city under Persian rule; exiled in the city's politics; travelled the eastern Mediterranean; associated in later life with the Athenian colony of Thurii in Italy, where he probably died. The biographical tradition about him is late and unreliable in detail; the book is the man we have. THE REPUTATION Cicero called him the father of history — and in the same breath noted the fables. Later antiquity split: admirers of his inquiry against critics, Plutarch among them, who wrote a whole essay On the Malice of Herodotus accusing him of bias. Both verdicts are in the record from early on; the modern scholarly verdict (Section V) is a argued middle: a genuine inquirer working with the informants and the critical tools his century had. IV. Book 2: The Egyptian Logos and the Gods from Egypt Book 2 is the reason Herodotus is a founding source for this hub, and its central claim is the boldest in all Greek prose about religion. Having described Egypt's land and customs, Herodotus turns to its gods and states, as the conclusion of his inquiries, that the names of nearly all the Greek gods came to Greece from Egypt (2.50). In paraphrase of Godley's Loeb rendering: he holds it proven that the names came from the barbarians, and from Egypt above all; the Egyptians, he says, were the first of mankind to use divine names, to build altars, images, and temples, and to carve figures in stone (2.4, 2.50). Greek religion, on this account, is a reception — an imported system, naturalised so long ago that the Greeks had forgotten the import. It is the first surviving statement of the diffusionist thesis about Greek myth, and every later version of that thesis — including the Egyptology hub's careful, evidence- tiered version of it — is written in its shadow. The claim is built up in stages through the book, and the stages are worth separating, because they do not all stand at the same strength. The Stages of the Argument The nameless gods of the Pelasgians (2.52). Before the names came, Herodotus says, the Pelasgians — his name for the pre-Greek or earliest Greek population — sacrificed to gods they called simply theoi , “gods”, without surnames or personal names, because they had not yet heard any. The word itself he derives, in a characteristic folk etymology, from the gods having “set all things in order”. The named, personalised Olympian system is thus, for Herodotus, a second stage in Greek religion — and the names that define it are the import. Heracles, the test case (2.43–44). Herodotus argues at length that the Greek hero Heracles, son of Amphitryon, must be distinguished from an ancient god Heracles whom the Egyptians reckoned among their twelve gods — and that the Greeks took the name from Egypt and applied it to the hero. He clinches the argument, in his own presentation, by travel: he went to Tyre in Phoenicia, where there is a famous temple of Heracles, and was told the temple was founded when Tyre was, some 2,300 years before his visit; and he saw a second Tyrian temple of “Thasian Heracles”, and went to Thasos too, where the Phoenicians had founded a Heracles cult five generations before the Greek hero's birth. Whether or not the argument persuades a modern reader — the Egyptian god behind it is presumably Khonsu or Shu, identified with Heracles by interpretatio graeca — its form is remarkable: a theological claim tested by autopsy at three sites. This is inquiry doing the work that myth used to do. Dionysus and the rites (2.49). The worship of Dionysus, Herodotus says, came to Greece later than the other gods' names, introduced — as he reconstructs it — by Melampus, who learned the rites from Cadmus of Tyre and the Phoenicians, who had themselves received them from Egypt; the phallic processions of Dionysus are his exhibit. And at 2.51 the ithyphallic images of Hermes are traced not to Egypt but to the Pelasgians, with the explanation lodged in the mysteries of Samothrace — a reminder that Herodotus' diffusionism is not a single-source dogma: different elements have different routes, and he tracks them separately. The mysteries and the silences (2.171). Book 2 also gives this hub one of its most-quoted Herodotean habits: the reverent refusal. Describing the rites at Saïs for the god he will not name in that connection — Osiris — Herodotus says, in paraphrase, that although he knows the details he will keep a pious silence about them; and on the rites the Greeks call Thesmophoria he will say only that they were brought from Egypt by the daughters of Danaus, and no more. The silence is itself evidence of two things: that mystery cult imposed real reticence even on a foreign inquirer, and that Herodotus observed it — a datum the Mysteries article leans on when it weighs what can and cannot be known about Eleusis. // READING THE EGYPTIAN CLAIM TODAY // Herodotus' thesis that Greece's gods came from Egypt is presented in this hub as Herodotus' thesis — a fifth-century Greek construction built from priestly informants, interpretatio (the Greek habit of matching foreign gods to Greek names), and genuine observation of Egypt's vastly older temple culture. Modern scholarship accepts real Egyptian and Near Eastern influence on Greek religion in specific, demonstrable channels, and rejects the wholesale derivation of the Olympian names. The Egyptology hub's treatment of the same encounter — including its adjudication of the Osiris material in Osiris , Section XIX — is written from the Egyptian evidence outward, and the two hubs' accounts should be read as complements, not duplicates: Herodotus tells us what a Greek could conclude; the Egyptian record tells us what was there. One more feature of Book 2 deserves emphasis, because it is the seed of this whole article. At 2.3 Herodotus remarks — again in paraphrase — that all men know equally about the gods: which is to say, nobody's theology is knowledge. The Egyptian priests have older records, longer king-lists (2.142 counts 341 generations of kings and priests, more than eleven thousand years), and older temples; but on the nature of the gods themselves, Egyptian and Greek stand in the same ignorance, and what each people has is what is said . That levelling remark is the philosophical ground of the discipline examined next. V. “I Report What Is Said”: Herodotus' Discipline and Its Limits Herodotus states his rule of evidence twice in programmatic places, and the two statements are not identical — the gap between them is where his method lives. At 2.123, closing an Egyptian account of the soul's transmigration, he remarks, in paraphrase of the standard renderings, that whoever finds such stories credible may believe them; for his own part, throughout the whole work, he keeps to the rule of recording what is said by each party. At 7.152, in the middle of the war narrative, he states the rule at full strength, and this article quotes it in Rawlinson's translation: “For myself, my duty is to report all that is said; but I am not obliged to believe it all alike — a remark which may be understood to apply to my whole History.” — HERODOTUS, HISTORIES 7.152, TRANS. GEORGE RAWLINSON (1862) The rule sounds like abdication — report everything, judge nothing — but Herodotus' practice is better than his formula. In the text he judges constantly: he marks stories he disbelieves (“the Greeks tell many things without due investigation, among them this silly tale”, of Heracles in Egypt, 2.45 — paraphrase); he gives rival versions side by side and sometimes declares for one; he tests claims against geography, chronology, and probability, most famously doubting the Phoenician circumnavigation of Africa on every point except the one detail — the sun on their right hand — that a modern reader recognises as the strongest proof they really did it (4.42). The discipline is therefore better described as a two-tier system : the record is comprehensive and attributed; the judgement is intermittent, personal, and flagged when it occurs. For a myth-source this is nearly ideal. The hub can take the report as testimony — this was said, by these people, at this date — without inheriting the inquirer's verdicts, and can take his verdicts as a fifth-century critical intelligence at work, without mistaking them for facts. The Limits The limits are equally definite, and the article names them so that the hub's citations can be discounted correctly. Informants. Herodotus worked through interpreters and through the class of Egyptians who talked to Greeks. His Egyptian priests were real, but they were also performing Egypt for a Greek audience — a performance with its own antiquarian pride and its own inventions, as the Egyptology hub's source criticism shows in detail. When Herodotus reports that the Egyptians told him a thing, the claim that survives scrutiny is the telling . Interpretatio. His comparative method requires foreign gods to wear Greek names — the Egyptian god at Sais is “Athena”, the Theban god is “Zeus” — and the equations are his or his informants' Greek grid laid over foreign material. The grid is evidence for Greek religious thought; it is weak evidence for the foreign cult underneath it, which is why this hub cross-checks every Herodotean Egyptian claim against the Egyptian record before using it. Chronology. Herodotus believes in deep Egyptian time and reports its figures faithfully — and the figures are priestly constructions, not records. His Greek chronology, built from genealogies counted at three generations to the century, is a rational instrument applied to legendary material: it produces dates that look like history for persons who belong to myth. The hub therefore never cites a Herodotean date for a mythic event as a date; it cites it as Herodotus' computation. The source-citation debate. Modern scholarship has fought over how far the citations themselves can be trusted. Detlev Fehling's Herodotus and His ‘Sources’ (German 1971; English 1989) argued that the source attributions follow literary patterns so regular that they should be read as a fiction of the genre rather than as records of real inquiries. W. Kendrick Pritchett's The Liar School of Herodotos (1993) answered with a point-by-point defence, marshalling the archaeological and epigraphic confirmations of Herodotean reports. The dispute is not settled , and this hub's position is the working middle the evidence supports: Herodotus travelled and inquired genuinely, and also shaped, compressed, and on occasion ventriloquised his authorities, as every ancient historian did. Citations in this archive therefore read “Herodotus reports that the Egyptians say”, never simply “the Egyptians held”. VI. Histories 2.53: Canon-Formation in One Sentence The most consequential single sentence Herodotus wrote about religion stands at 2.53, at the end of the Egyptian argument. The Greeks, he has been saying, learned the gods' names from Egypt only recently, as human affairs go — and then he says who it was that turned the imported names into the Greek pantheon the world knows. This article quotes the sentence in A. D. Godley's Loeb translation: “For Hesiod and Homer I suppose were four hundred years before my time and not more, and these are they who made a theogony for the Hellenes and gave the titles to the gods and distributed to them honours and arts, and set forth their forms.” — HERODOTUS, HISTORIES 2.53, TRANS. A. D. GODLEY (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1920) Read it slowly. Herodotus does not say that Homer and Hesiod recorded the theogony, or received it. He says they made it — poiēsantes theogoniēn , the verb of the poiētēs , the poet as maker. In his account, the Greek divine order — who the gods are, what they are called, which honours and crafts belong to each, what they look like — is a literary artefact , assembled by two poets at a datable moment, four hundred years and not more before his own time. The gods are older than the poems; Herodotus has spent Book 2 arguing their names are Egyptian and immemorial. But the system — the pantheon as a cast of named, titled, specialised, visualised persons — is the poets' work. This is, so far as surviving texts go, the first statement in European literature that a religion's canonical form was authored . Herodotus immediately draws the corollary, and it is as sharp as the claim. The poets said to be earlier than Homer and Hesiod — Orpheus and Musaeus and their kind — were, in his opinion, actually later (2.53.3). Antiquity of attribution is not antiquity of fact; a poem travelling under an immemorial name may be a recent composition wearing it. The sentence at 2.53 thus does two pieces of canon-critical work at once: it dates the canonisation (the two poets, four centuries back), and it supplies the test by which pretenders to greater antiquity are detected and redated. This hub's own treatment of the Orphic material, and of the Homeric Hymns ' travelling attribution, runs on exactly this Herodotean track. For the hub's method, 2.53 is the charter text, and it cuts in two directions. In one direction it licenses the archive's whole procedure: if the pantheon's canonical form is a made thing with makers and a date, then it can be studied as a made thing — its seams found, its sources traced, its local variants distinguished from the Panhellenic overlay the poets spread over them, as the Olympians article does throughout. In the other direction it warns : what Homer and Hesiod made was a theogony for the Hellenes — a Panhellenic literary system — and cult on the ground, in the sanctuaries Pausanias walked, was always older, stranger, and more local than the system. The gap between the poets' pantheon and the practised religion is precisely the gap this hub exists to map, and Herodotus, in one sentence, is the first writer to mark both its sides. // HOW THE HUB CITES HERODOTUS // Herodotus is cited for early testimony and reception : what was being said about a god or rite by the fifth century BCE, and what a critical Greek intelligence of that century made of it. He is not cited as an authority on Egyptian religion in himself — for that, the Egyptology hub's record governs — nor for the state of any Greek cult in periods after his own. A Herodotean myth-report is evidence with a date, a place, and an informant-class attached; the hub keeps all three attached. VII. Pausanias: The Periegete and His Ten Books Pausanias wrote one work, and it is unlike anything else that survives from antiquity. The Periegesis Hellados — Description of Greece , or more exactly a “leading-around of Greece” — is a ten-book account of mainland Greece organised as a journey: it begins at Cape Sunium, comes up to Athens, and proceeds region by region through the Peloponnese and central Greece, ending at Delphi. At every stop it does the same three things: it describes what stands there (temples, images, altars, tombs, paintings, inscriptions); it tells what is said there (the local myths, hero-legends, and historical memories attached to the objects); and it records what is done there (the rites, festivals, and customs still performed). No other ancient text attempts the whole of a country's sacred topography in this way, and none of the partial parallels survives. Pausanias is, quite literally, irreplaceable: for hundreds of cults, images, and local myths he is the only witness there will ever be. Book Region What it carries for this hub 1 Attica Athens and Eleusis: the Acropolis images, the Agora, the Eleusinian sanctuary and its rites as far as a non-initiate account may go 2 Corinthia and the Argolid Corinth, Mycenae (Section X), Argos and the Heraion, Epidaurus and the Asclepius cult, Troezen — the Theseus country 3 Laconia Sparta, the throne of Apollo at Amyclae, the Hyacinthia, the cults of Helen and the Dioscuri 4 Messenia The Messenian national history and the mysteries of Andania — the longest historical excursus in the work 5–6 Elis and Olympia The fullest ancient description of a single sanctuary: the Altis, the temple of Zeus, the victor statues, the Olympic cult machinery 7 Achaia The Achaean cities, the oracle of Heracles at Bura, the Trophonius-adjacent lore of the coast 8 Arcadia The hub's richest single book for primitive cult: Demeter at Phigalia, Despoina at Lycosura, the Lykaia, aniconic and animal-formed images 9 Boeotia Thebes and the Theban sanctuaries, the oracle of Trophonius at Lebadea, the Muses of Helicon 10 Phocis and Delphi Delphi entire: the Sacred Way monument by monument, Polygnotus' paintings of the underworld in the Lesche of the Cnidians, the Pythian cult The scope is as deliberate as the method. Pausanias covers the mainland — the Greece of the classical city-states — and not the islands, not Crete, not the Greek cities of Asia Minor from which he himself came. The omission is not an accident of survival; the work as transmitted is complete in its design, and the design is a statement: the Greece that matters is the old Greece, the landscape in which the myths happened. Within that scope he is guided by a selection principle he states in his own way throughout — he records, as he repeatedly puts it in paraphrase, the things most worth telling ( logou axia ), and passes over the rest without apology. What counts as worth telling is the subject of Section IX; the method by which the telling was produced is the subject of the next section. Of the man himself almost nothing is known outside the book — no ancient biography, no portrait, no certain date. The work's internal references place its composition across roughly the middle decades of the second century CE, with material gathered over years of travel; he mentions seeing places far beyond Greece — Babylon's ruins, Jerusalem, Rome, Egypt — in passing, always in service of a comparison. The anonymity is fitting. Pausanias effaces himself more completely than almost any ancient author: no proem survives in which he states his programme at length, no first-person manifesto like Herodotus' opening or Plutarch's proems. The system must be inferred from the practice, and the practice is consistent enough — across ten books and some thousands of entries — to infer it with confidence. VIII. Pausanias' Method: Autopsy, Guides, and the Exegesis of Images Pausanias' method has three working parts, and this hub's confidence in him rests on all three being visible in the text, operating entry by entry. 1 · Autopsy: He Went and Looked The first-person verbs of seeing run through the work like a watermark: I saw , it still stands , in my time . Pausanias measures with his eyes — he gives the relative sizes of images, the materials, the state of preservation, the order of monuments along a road — and he corrects predecessors against the ground. Where a thing he expected is absent, ruined, or different, he says so. This is the quality that made the nineteenth-century excavators treat him as a colleague (Section X): his descriptions are checkable , and they were checked, and the checking is the foundation of his modern reputation. The hub's rule follows from it: a Pausanian description of an object's existence, material, and location is the strongest class of literary evidence this archive handles. 2 · Local Informants: Guides, Priests, Exegetes What Pausanias could not see, he asked about on the spot. His named classes of informant are the local ones: the exegetai — the official or semi-official explainers attached to sanctuaries, whose job was precisely to expound the images and rites to visitors — priests and temple staff, guides, and “the people of the place” whose account he introduces with formulas like “the Corinthians say”. The localness is the value. A story Pausanias files from Lycosura is the story Lycosura told about itself in the second century CE, attached to the image Lycosura showed; it is not a Panhellenic handbook's smoothing. This hub's articles repeatedly prefer Pausanias' local version to Apollodorus' systematised one for exactly this reason (see Apollodorus and the Library on the contrast), and repeatedly note where the local version contradicts the literary canon — the contradiction is the signature of genuine local tradition. He is not a passive recorder of his informants. He reports rival local accounts side by side; he occasionally marks a story as one he does not believe, or as one he accepts only because of its antiquity; and on the most sensitive material — the content of mystery rites — he maintains the same reverent silence as Herodotus, most famously at Eleusis, where he relates, in paraphrase, that a dream forbade him to describe what lies within the sanctuary wall, and that the uninitiated are in any case barred from learning what they are barred from seeing (1.38.7). The silence is methodological gold: it shows a witness who knows the difference between what he may report and what he may not, which is the precondition of trusting what he does report. 3 · Exegesis: The Object Expounded The distinctively Pausanian act is the exegesis of the object : he stands before an image, a relief, a painting, and expounds it figure by figure, identifying each personage and telling the myth that explains the grouping. The great set-pieces are famous: the Chest of Cypselus at Olympia (5.17–19), a cedar chest covered in carved and inlaid mythological scenes, which he describes band by band; the throne of Apollo at Amyclae (3.18–19), a sculptural programme wrapped around an archaic cult image; and above all the paintings of Polygnotus in the Lesche of the Cnidians at Delphi (10.25–31) — the sack of Troy and the underworld, expounded figure by figure for chapters, our fullest surviving encounter with classical painting. In these passages Pausanias is doing what the sanctuary exegetes did, at literary length and with a scholar's cross-references: reading images as texts. For a hub whose subject is the meeting of myth and cult object, this is the single most useful ancient skill, and Pausanias is its only surviving master-practitioner. // WHY THE HUB NAMES HIM THE MODEL CULT WITNESS // The hub's standard for a cult claim is: a named place, a visible object or performed rite, a local account attached to it, and a witness who distinguishes what he saw from what he was told. A Tale at the Centre of a Novel The story modern readers call Cupid and Psyche is not a free-standing myth, a hymn, or a fragment of epic. It is an inset tale — a story inside a story — occupying Books 4.28 to 6.24 of the Metamorphoses of Apuleius , the Latin novel also known, from Augustine onward, as The Golden Ass . It sits at the novel's midpoint and takes up roughly a fifth of its whole length: some sixty chapters in which the main narrative — a young man named Lucius, turned into an ass by bungled magic and passed from master to master — stops altogether, and an unnamed old woman in a bandits' cave tells a kidnapped girl a fairy tale. That the most philosophically suggestive love story to survive from classical antiquity arrives in this packaging is not an accident to be apologised for. It is, as Sections V and XVI argue, part of what the tale means and part of why scholars still argue about it. Three different objects must be kept distinct throughout this article, because the secondary literature constantly runs them together. First, (a) the tale as Apuleius tells it : a continuous narrative, in his own exuberant Latin, whose plot Sections VI–XIV retell in full and in order. Second, (b) its frame and function inside the novel : who tells it, to whom, in what circumstances, and how its pattern of curiosity, punishment, wandering, and rescue mirrors — and in places pointedly fails to mirror — the story of Lucius that surrounds it (Sections V, XV, and XVI). Third, (c) its allegorical afterlife : the seventeen centuries in which readers from Fulgentius to Raphael's patrons to the alchemical interpreters of myth treated Psyche, whose name is simply the Greek word psychē , “soul”, as the soul personified, and her trials as the soul's own itinerary (Sections XVIII–XIX). Apuleius is responsible for the first. He is partly responsible for the second. The third is the work of his readers, and this article attributes it to them, not to him. A note on names and spellings. The heroine's Greek name is Psychē (Ψυχή); her husband is, in Apuleius's Latin, Cupīdō — Cupid — also called Amor , “Love”; his Greek counterpart is Erōs. His mother is Venus, Greek Aphrodite. This hub's convention of preferring Greek forms is set aside in this article wherever Apuleius's own Latin is the subject, because the tale is a Latin literary artefact, not a Greek myth that happens to be written down in Rome: Venus, Cupid, Jupiter, Juno, Ceres, and Proserpina are the names the text itself uses, and they are the names used here, with Greek equivalents given where the argument needs them. Transliterated Greek carries macrons where the standard form requires them ( psychē , erōs in its long vowel, hēdonē ). THE TALE AT A GLANCE Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4.28–6.24. Told by an unnamed old woman to the kidnapped Charite in the bandits' cave, overheard by Lucius in ass's form. The longest inset tale in the novel, at its structural centre. THE STORY AT A GLANCE Psyche, a mortal whose beauty empties Venus's temples, is exposed on a crag to a prophesied monster, carried by Zephyr to a palace, and married to an unseen husband. Persuaded by her sisters to look at him by lamplight, she finds Cupid — and loses him. Wandering, she submits to Venus and performs four tasks, the last a descent to Proserpina. Restored by Cupid, she is made immortal, married on Olympus, and bears a daughter, Voluptas — Pleasure. THE AUTHOR AT A GLANCE Apuleius (c. 124 – c. 170 CE), of Madauros in Numidia: rhetorician, travelling lecturer, and self-described Platonist philosopher, tried for magic at Sabratha and acquitted or at least uncondemned, author of the Apologia , the Florida , philosophical works on Plato and on the god of Socrates — and of the Metamorphoses . See Section II, and this hub's Legendary Lives , where his biography is treated among the wonder-working sages of antiquity. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Direct quotation is kept to a minimum and is always named in place. Short phrases are quoted from P. G. Walsh's translation, The Golden Ass (Oxford World's Classics), as identified at the point of quotation. One passage of Book 11 is quoted from William Adlington's translation of 1566, the first English Golden Ass , likewise named in place. Everything else that renders Apuleius's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. No quotation in this article is invented, reconstructed, or silently modernised. II. Apuleius of Madaura: The Life That Survives Almost everything known about Apuleius's life comes from Apuleius — principally from the speech he published in his own defence, the Apologia , and from the Florida , a collection of excerpts from his public lectures. That has two consequences a reader should hold from the start. The outline is unusually vivid for a second-century author, because its source is a brilliant self-presenter speaking for effect. And it is unusually unverifiable, because for most of it there is no second witness. Later tradition even borrowed his Christian name from his fiction: no ancient source gives him the praenomen Lucius ; medieval manuscripts began calling him Lucius after Lucius, the hero of his novel, and the habit stuck. He is Apuleius of Madauros — Apuleius Madaurensis — and that is how the ancient evidence knows him. He was born about c. 124 CE at Madauros (also spelled Madaura; modern M'Daourouch, in Algeria), a Roman colonia in Numidia, inland from the North African coast — the same town where Augustine of Hippo would receive part of his early education two and a half centuries later. Apuleius describes himself, in a famous phrase of the Apologia (paraphrased here), as half Numidian and half Gaetulian, born on the border between the settled province and the peoples beyond it, and he is plainly proud rather than apologetic about the mixed origin. His father had been a duumvir , one of the colony's two chief magistrates, and left his two sons an inheritance of nearly two million sesterces — a substantial provincial fortune. The son spent much of his share, by his own cheerful admission, on the two things that made him: travel and study. The education was the best the Roman world offered, and it was bilingual. After schooling at Carthage , the great city of Roman Africa, he went to Athens , where he studied Platonist philosophy among much else, and then to Rome , for Latin rhetoric and, most likely, a period of practice in the courts. He travelled widely in Asia Minor and Egypt, pursuing philosophy and religion — and, what matters for his novel, pursuing initiation. He presents himself, in the Apologia and elsewhere, as an initiate of several Greco-Roman mysteries, the Dionysian among them; he held a priesthood of Asclepius at Carthage, and Augustine reports that he served as sacerdos provinciae , priest of the province of Africa. The man who would write the ancient world's most famous fictional initiation, in Book 11 of the Metamorphoses , was by his own account a serial initiate in real life. How much weight that autobiographical fact can bear is one of the questions of Section XVI. His fame in his lifetime rested not on the novel — which may be late work, and whose ancient readership is hard to measure — but on oratory. Apuleius was a star of the movement modern scholarship calls the Second Sophistic : the revival of virtuoso Greek (and, in his case, Latin) display rhetoric that filled theatres across the empire, in which a travelling sophist lectured on philosophy, literature, natural curiosities, and anything else a crowd would pay to hear treated brilliantly. The Florida preserves the flavour: openings of lectures on subjects from the parrot to the death of Socrates, each a small performance of learning worn lightly. Statues were voted to him at Carthage and elsewhere. S. J. Harrison's standard modern study is titled, exactly, Apuleius: A Latin Sophist (2000), and the title is the biography in three words: a Greek-educated intellectual performing, in Latin, in the provinces, for an empire-wide culture of display. // PLATONICUS // Later antiquity also knew him as Apuleius Platonicus — Apuleius the Platonist. The label is earned by the philosophical works transmitted under his name: De Platone et eius dogmate (“On Plato and His Teaching”), a handbook of Platonic doctrine; De deo Socratis (“On the God of Socrates”), on the daimones , the intermediary spirits between gods and men — a category to which, in Plato's Symposium , Love himself belongs; and a Latin version of the pseudo-Aristotelian De mundo , whose attribution to Apuleius is debated. The Platonism is not a veneer on the novelist. It is the other half of one career. The date of his death is not recorded. The conventional dates c. 124 – c. 170 CE , used in this article and across the reference literature, mark a birth that can be triangulated from his career and a death that cannot: he was certainly alive and active after his trial in the late 150s, and some evidence has been taken to show him still writing in the 170s or even the 180s. “c. 170” is a scholarly convenience, not a datum, and it is flagged as such here because the dating of the Metamorphoses itself (Section IV) partly depends on it. III. The Apologia: A Platonist on Trial for Magic The most famous incident of Apuleius's life is the one that connects him, in his own person, to the world of his novel: he was tried for practising magic. The episode is worth setting out in some detail, both because it is exceptionally well documented — his defence speech survives entire — and because this hub returns to it in Legendary Lives , where the trial is read alongside the other ancient proceedings against wonder-workers and philosophers. On his way toward Alexandria, Apuleius fell ill at Oea (modern Tripoli) and was taken into the house of Sicinius Pontianus , a friend from his Athens student days. Pontianus's mother, Aemilia Pudentilla , was a wealthy widow. With Pontianus's consent — indeed, on the account Apuleius gives, at his encouragement — Apuleius married her. Pontianus then died, and Pudentilla's relatives, who stood to lose control of her fortune, turned against the marriage. The charge they constructed, brought formally in the name of her younger son Pudens, a boy, and driven by her brother-in-law Sicinius Aemilianus, was that Apuleius had won Pudentilla by magic : love-charms, spells, and sinister nocturnal rites. A subsidiary charge of responsibility for Pontianus's death was aired and quickly dropped. The case was heard at Sabratha , in 158 or 159 CE , before the proconsul of Africa, Claudius Maximus. The Apologia — its full title is Pro se de magia , “In His Own Defence, Concerning Magic” — is the speech Apuleius delivered, afterwards published in the expanded form in which it survives. It is a performance of the Second Sophistic turned to forensic ends, and its strategy is the one that matters for this article. Apuleius does not deny being interested in the things his accusers call magic. He re-describes them. The fish he bought and dissected were for natural philosophy, in the line of Aristotle and Theophrastus. The mysterious object kept wrapped in a cloth in his host's household shrine was an emblem of his initiations, which a pious man does not exhibit to the profane. His verses on a tooth-powder, his mirror, his poverty, his good looks, his eloquence itself — each item of the prosecution's picturesque case is taken up, mocked, and refiled under philosophy, medicine, or religion. And at the centre of the speech stands Plato: Apuleius presents himself to Claudius Maximus, a judge he flatters as a philosopher, as a fellow-Platonist whose pursuits are being traduced by rustics who cannot tell a philosopher from a sorcerer — magus in the Persian sense, he notes, is the name of a priestly caste and a student of divine things, and only in the vulgar sense a criminal enchanter. // WHAT THE VERDICT WAS, WE DO NOT KNOW // No record of Claudius Maximus's judgement survives. That Apuleius resumed a public career at Carthage, was honoured with statues, and published the speech as a trophy is strong circumstantial evidence of acquittal, and acquittal is the usual scholarly inference. It remains an inference. The Apologia as we have it is also a literary revision of whatever was said in court, at a length no court sat through; it is evidence for the trial and, at least as much, for the self Apuleius wished to project after it. Two consequences of the trial run through the rest of this article. The first is chronological: the Apologia never mentions the Metamorphoses , and its accusers — who ransacked their man's life for anything disreputable — make no use of a novel full of witches, transformations, and a heroine who opens a forbidden box in the underworld. Harrison and others have argued from that silence that the novel is later work, the product of the years after 159; the argument is suggestive, not conclusive, but it is one reason the novel is generally placed late in Apuleius's career, in the 160s or after (Section IV). The second consequence is thematic, and it is the reason the trial belongs in an article about Cupid and Psyche at all. The author of the tale had stood in a real court and argued, in public, that the line between philosophy, religion, and magic is a line drawn by interpretation — that the same acts are piety or sorcery according to the story told about them. His novel, which tells the same pattern of curiosity, suffering, and rescue first as a robbers' fairy tale and then as an Isiac conversion, is that argument turned into fiction. Section XVI takes up the point. IV. The Metamorphoses: Lucius, the Ass, and the Greek Original The Metamorphoses is a novel in eleven books , narrated in the first person by Lucius , a well-born, well-educated young Greek travelling in Thessaly — the part of Greece proverbial for witchcraft — out of an appetite the novel names in its first pages and never lets him forget: curiositas , curiosity, the desire to see and to practise magic. At Hypata he attaches himself to Photis, a slave-girl in the household of the witch Pamphile; watches Pamphile anoint herself and turn into an owl; persuades Photis to steal the ointment; and is given, by her mistake in the dark cupboard, the wrong pot. He becomes not a bird but an ass — retaining, in the novel's central device, a human mind, human memory, and human shame inside an animal that cannot speak. The antidote is simple: eat roses. The rest of Books 3–10 is the story of how hard roses are to reach when you are other people's property: stolen by bandits, sold to priests of the Syrian Goddess, to a miller, a cook, a gardener, and others, Lucius is beaten, starved, threatened with gelding and with worse, and hears — an ass's long ears are the novel's great listening device — the inset tales, confessions, and scandals that fill the book, of which Cupid and Psyche is the longest and the first. In Book 11, at Cenchreae, the port of Corinth, he prays to the moon, and Isis answers (Section XV). The work's own title is Metamorphoses — transformations. The familiar alternative, The Golden Ass (Latin Asinus aureus ), is Augustine's name for it, four centuries on, and “golden” most likely commends the book — a splendid, precious ass-story — rather than describing the animal. It is the only Latin novel to survive complete from antiquity : Petronius's Satyrica survives in substantial fragments, Apuleius entire. Its language is itself an exhibit — an exuberant, archaicising, neologising Latin, dense with diminutives, alliteration, and rhythmic prose, which E. J. Kenney's commentary on Cupid and Psyche (Section XX) elucidates passage by passage and which no translation reproduces. Readers of Walsh's fluent English should know they are reading a domesticated Apuleius; the original is stranger, funnier, and more difficult. The Greek Original of the Ass-Story Apuleius did not invent the ass-story. Behind the Metamorphoses stands a lost Greek work, the Metamorphoseis attributed to an otherwise unknown Lucius of Patrae , known to us from a summary by the ninth-century Byzantine scholar Photius ( Bibliotheca , cod. 129). A shorter Greek version survives entire: Lucius, or the Ass (the Onos ), transmitted among the works of Lucian and generally treated as an epitome — an abridgement — of Lucius of Patrae's text. The relationship among the three is the settled framework of modern scholarship, established in its essentials by Ben Edwin Perry's Princeton dissertation of 1920: the lost Greek Metamorphoseis is the common source; the Onos abbreviates it; Apuleius expands it, freely and massively, into eleven books. What is Apuleian in the expansion can be identified by comparison where the Onos runs parallel — and the comparison is decisive for this article's subject at two points. The Onos contains no Cupid and Psyche, and no Isis book. Its Lucius regains human form by roses obtained without any goddess's epiphany, and the story ends in the bedroom, not the temple. The tale at the centre and the conversion at the end — the two features of the Latin novel on which its whole later reputation rests — are, on the comparative evidence, Apuleius's own contributions: either his inventions, or material he imported from elsewhere into a frame that lacked them. Section XVII asks what “elsewhere” might have been for the tale. Date. When in his career Apuleius composed the novel is not known, and this article reports the range rather than a year. Proposals run from a youthful work before the trial of 158–159 to a climax of his maturity in the 170s or even the 180s; Harrison has argued that Book 11 parodies, among other targets, the Sacred Tales of Aelius Aristides, published between 171 and 176, which if accepted would put the novel's completion after the mid-170s (Section XVI). The conventional shorthand “late second century CE”, and the dating of the tale to about the 160s–170s in most modern editions, should be read with those margins. What is not in doubt is the text's survival route: the novel was edited in late antiquity (a subscription records editorial work at Rome and Constantinople at the end of the fourth century), was known to Augustine, Macrobius, and Fulgentius, then narrowed to what appears to have been a single line of descent — some forty surviving manuscripts, all or nearly all descending from the eleventh-century Monte Cassino codex Laurentianus 68.2, the editor's “F”. Boccaccio knew the Cupid and Psyche story by about 1370; the Metamorphoses was printed in 1469. The tale's modern life begins there (Section XIX). The Frame: An Old Woman, a Kidnapped Bride, and an Ass Listening Before the tale can be retold, its telling must be described, because Apuleius has built the telling into the tale's meaning. The narrative levels are three deep. Apuleius writes a novel narrated by Lucius. Lucius, in ass's form in the bandits' cave, overhears an old woman. The old woman tells Charite a story about Psyche. The most elevated material in the book reaches the reader through the book's most compromised channels, and every level of the frame comments on the one inside it. The circumstances are these (Book 4). The bandits who stole Lucius from Hypata have raided a wedding and carried off Charite , a rich young bride, snatched on her wedding day for ransom and penned in their cave alongside the ass. Charite weeps without stopping. The bandits' old woman — their cook and housekeeper, an anus , in the Latin a stock figure of the garrulous, wine-loving old nurse — sets herself to comfort the girl, and offers her, in the narrator's presentation, a pretty tale, an old wives' story: fabula . Lucius stands by with his ears up. When the tale ends, sixty chapters later, he gives the reader his review, in paraphrase: he was sorry, by Hercules, that he had no tablets and stylus to take down tam bellam fabellam — so charming a little story ( Metamorphoses 6.25). The ass is the tale's first literary critic, and his verdict is aesthetic, not doctrinal: bella fabella , a beautiful little tale. What the framing licenses, first, is genre . An old woman's tale to a frightened girl may be a fairy tale — may have a king and queen with three daughters, a speaking tower, a helpful ant, a wedding among the gods — without the novel's world having to vouch for any of it. Apuleius, the most self-conscious of Latin stylists, gets the resources of Märchen , the folk tale — its impossible tasks, its animal helpers, its repetitions in threes — at one remove, attributed to a narrator whose authority is precisely nil. Modern folklore scholarship (Section XVII) has taken the hint embedded in the frame and treated the tale as the literary refashioning of a folk tale: P. G. Walsh's influential formulation describes Apuleius transforming a Märchen into a Kunstmärchen , an art-tale, and E. J. Kenney's commentary traces, passage by passage, the poetic, philosophical, and iconographic materials worked into the folk-tale armature. What the framing licenses, second, is irony — and the irony cuts against the comfort the tale is told to give. The old woman's story is meant to assuage Charite: its heroine is exposed to a monster, lives with an unseen husband, suffers, and is at last married in heaven and made immortal. Charite's own story, resumed the moment the tale ends, grants her a rescue by her husband Tlepolemus — and then, in Books 7–8, brings both of them to squalid, violent deaths, Tlepolemus murdered by the rival Thrasyllus and Charite dying by her own hand after blinding him. The fairy tale's happy ending is told to the one character in the novel whose marriage will end worst. Scholars from John J. Winkler onward have made this counterpoint central: the tale is a mise en abyme , a miniature mirror of the whole novel — curiosity punished, wandering, divine rescue, deification — held up inside a narrative that refuses, at Charite's level, to let the pattern come true. Whether the mirror consoles, deceives, or instructs is left, characteristically, to the reader; and the old woman herself, after the captives' failed escape attempt — in which she recaptures the fleeing ass and is dragged and beaten for her pains — hangs herself from a tree rather than face the bandits' vengeance (6.30–31). The teller does not long survive her tale either. // HOW TO READ THE RETELLING THAT FOLLOWS // Sections VI–XIV retell the tale as Apuleius tells it, in his order, at his length, keeping his proportions — including the long palace sequence and the full detail of the fourth task, which most summaries compress. Chapter references (4.28, 5.22, 6.20, and so on) are to the Metamorphoses . Where Apuleius's text is ambiguous or where translations differ materially — the naming of Venus's handmaids is the standing example — the difference is flagged rather than silently resolved. Allegorical interpretation is excluded from the retelling by design and confined to Sections XVIII–XIX, where it belongs: it is the tale's afterlife, not its plot. VI. Beauty and Venus's Anger: The Tale Opens The tale opens as fairy tales open (4.28). In a certain city there lived a king and a queen — Apuleius names neither the city nor the royal pair, and never will — who had three daughters of conspicuous beauty. The two elder were lovely enough to be praised in human terms. The youngest, Psyche , was beautiful beyond what the poverty of human speech could praise, and the tale's first movement is not about her at all but about what her beauty did to the cult of a goddess. Crowds travelled from neighbouring cities and from across the sea to gaze at her. The temples of Venus were deserted; her shrines went without garlands; the honours owed to the goddess were transferred, entire, to a mortal girl, who was worshipped as Venus herself present on earth — some said a new Venus, some said the goddess's own daughter by an unseemly union. Psyche did nothing to procure any of this. That is the tale's first moral datum, and its allegorical readers have always had to reckon with it: the catastrophe begins not in anything the soul does but in what is done to it, and with it. Venus's response (4.30–31) is staged as an offended deity's soliloquy, in which the goddess recites her own antiquity — she is the primal parent of nature, older than the order that now slighted her — and her humiliation at being supplanted by a mortal namesake. She summons her son: Cupid , the winged boy-god, armed with torch and arrows, whose character the novel has already fixed at 4.30 as a delinquent — a corrupter of marriages, a public nuisance whom his mother herself describes as needing discipline. The commission she gives him is quoted here in Walsh's translation, as reproduced in the study literature: Venus orders him to “punish harshly this girl's arrogant beauty” (Walsh, The Golden Ass , Oxford World's Classics, p. 76) — by making Psyche burn with love for the lowest and most wretched man alive, a man so ruined in fortune, standing, and body that no creature on earth is his equal in misery. The punishment is precisely fitted to the offence: the girl worshipped as the goddess of love is to be destroyed by love, at its most degrading. Cupid goes — and Cupid fails, or refuses, or is himself the first casualty; Apuleius leaves the mechanism famously light. In the tale's telling, the god sent to wound Psyche is wounded by his own weapon: he scratches himself on his own dart, whose property is to make the wounded fall in love with the first thing seen, and what he sees is Psyche. He falls deeply in love with her and disobeys his mother's order outright. Nothing further is said at this point; the god withdraws, and the story returns to the girl, who is discovering that to be worshipped as a goddess is a sentence of solitude. Suitors came to look, and went away to marry other women. Her sisters, the merely beautiful, married kings. Psyche, the divine, sat at home a virgin widow of a marriage no one dared attempt, sick at heart, hating in herself the beauty that everyone else adored — the first of the tale's several inversions, in which every gift arrives as its opposite. // THE TWO VENUSES // Apuleius the Platonist had a doctrine ready for this doubling, and he states it in the Apologia itself: Venus is twofold — a heavenly Venus who presides over chaste, philosophical love, and a common Venus who presides over bodily desire, each producing her own kind of lover. The tale does not announce the doctrine, and this article does not impose it on the plot. But the doubling of Venus in Psyche — a mortal girl carrying the goddess's name and honours while the goddess rages — is exactly the kind of figure a Platonist reader of Apuleius's formation would have seen double. See Section XVIII. The king, suspecting divine anger, does what kings in tales do: he consults an oracle, the Milesian oracle of Apollo. The answer he receives is the engine of the whole plot, and it is deliberately double-edged — a genuine prophecy, fulfilled to the letter by the story that follows, and at every point susceptible of the disastrous misreading that Psyche's sisters will later press on her. She is not to be married to a mortal at all. VII. The Oracle and the Mountaintop Bridegroom The oracle's response (4.32–33) directs the king to dress his daughter in funeral bridal attire, expose her on a high rocky crag, and expect as a son-in-law no human being but a fierce, barbaric, snake-like monster — in Walsh's rendering, quoted in the study literature, a “fierce, barbaric, snake-like monster” (Walsh, p. 78) — who flies with wings, harasses the whole world with fire and iron, makes Jupiter himself tremble, and is feared by the gods above and the powers of Styx below. Every clause is true of Cupid, read correctly: winged, armed, a tyrant even over gods, the one power to whom Jupiter will in the end have to negotiate. Every clause is also, read with the eyes of fear, a description of a dragon. The tale will turn, at its crisis, on which reading Psyche believes. What follows (4.34–35) is told as a funeral that is also a wedding, and Apuleius lingers on the merging of the two rites: the procession through the city with torches lowered and wedding hymns turned to dirges, the parents conducting their daughter to the crag as to a tomb, the whole people in mourning. Psyche's own speech to her parents, as the Walsh-based summaries report it, already understands her case better than they do: they should have wept for her earlier, she tells them — my one undoing has been the title of Venus bestowed on me (paraphrase of 4.34, following Walsh, p. 79). She is left alone on the peak, trembling and weeping, at the exact point where the tale's machinery changes key. The expected monster does not come. What comes is a wind. 4.28–31 BEAUTY AND VENGEANCE Psyche is worshipped as a new Venus; the goddess's temples empty. Venus commissions Cupid to make her love the most wretched of men. Cupid, wounded by his own dart, falls in love with her himself and disobeys. 4.32–35 THE ORACLE AND THE CRAG Apollo's oracle promises a winged, serpent-like bridegroom feared by gods and Styx. Psyche is processed in funeral bridal dress to a rocky peak and exposed. 5.1–4 ZEPHYR AND THE PALACE Zephyr carries her to a meadow and a palace of invisible servants. An unseen bridegroom comes to her by night and forbids her to seek to see him. 5.5–24 THE SISTERS; THE LAMP Two visits inflame the sisters' envy; at the third persuasion Psyche takes lamp and knife to the bed, sees Cupid, spills the oil, and loses him. 5.25–6.8 WANDERINGS Psyche finds Pan, engineers her sisters' deaths, is refused by Ceres and Juno, and surrenders herself to Venus's service. 6.10–21 THE FOUR TASKS The grains (the ants); the golden wool (the reed); the Styx water (the eagle); the box of Proserpina's beauty (the tower's instructions) — opened, and the Stygian sleep. 6.22–24 OLYMPUS Cupid pleads before Jupiter; Psyche receives ambrosia and immortality; the wedding banquet is held; a daughter is born, Voluptas. VIII. Zephyr and the Invisible Palace Zephyrus , the West Wind — Zephyr — lifts Psyche gently from the crag, in a descent described as a caress rather than a fall, and lays her in a flowering meadow, where she sleeps (4.35–5.1). She wakes at the edge of a grove and finds, in the tale's most sustained piece of description, a palace that is plainly not of human building: golden columns, a carved ceiling of citrus wood and ivory, silver walls embossed with animals wild and tame, jewelled mosaic floors, and no one in it at all. A disembodied voice — the palace itself, or its staff, speaking — tells her that all of it is hers: in Walsh's rendering, “Lady, all these things are yours” (Walsh, p. 81). She bathes; a table serves itself; invisible musicians sing and play; she is, as Apuleius puts it in paraphrase, attended by a household of voices. Kenney's commentary notes how deliberately the description straddles the mortal and divine: the house reads like an imperial palace and like a god's dwelling built for converse with human beings at once. It is the first of the tale's several places that are also states — a paradise whose single rule is that its giver must not be seen. That night, in darkness, her unknown bridegroom comes to her — the Walsh-based summaries keep Apuleius's phrase, her unknown bridegroom — makes her his wife, and leaves before dawn (5.2). The pattern settles: days of solitary luxury, nights of a presence she may hear and touch but never see. He is gentle; he is also absolute on the single point. She must not seek to know what he looks like; she must not even ask. The prohibition is the palace's counterpart to the oracle: the same unknown, stated as a command instead of a prophecy. For a while — Apuleius is vague about duration, as fairy tales are — Psyche accepts the terms, and even comes to love the darkness that at first frightened her. What breaks the settlement is not doubt. Rome is the city that told its myths about itself — in prose, on the record, with dates attached — and then built an empire on the telling. This article treats those charter legends as what they are: legends, with a textual history that can be traced stratum by stratum, from a closing passage of Hesiod to the antiquarian arithmetic that fixed a birthday for a city. Legend is not failed history. Read properly, it is evidence of the first order — for the people who needed it. GRECO-ROMAN HOME > THE FOUNDING LEGENDS OF ROME // ARCHIVE CONTENTS // I.
