Sources I. A City That Wrote Its Own Beginning Rome is unusual among the cities of this hub, and the unusualness is the subject. The myths of Thebes, of Argos, of Troy itself, come down to us chiefly in poems — in epic, tragedy, and lyric, where a story's business is to be sung, not to be believed on oath. Rome's founding stories come down chiefly in prose histories : in Livy's first book, in the Roman Antiquities of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in Plutarch's paired Lives of Romulus and Numa. These are works that present themselves as records. They give regnal years. They synchronise the fall of Troy with Olympiads. They argue, in the open, about which of two rival dates for the city's birthday is correct. The Roman foundation legend is therefore not best approached as a tale that happens to have been written down. It is a constructed civic past : assembled by named writers, at datable moments, out of Greek myth, local cult, family pride, and chronological arithmetic, and revised whenever the city's needs changed. This article follows the construction, stratum by stratum, and keeps the scaffolding visible throughout. That discipline requires three distinctions to be held at every step, and the reader should hold the article to them. First, legend is distinguished from cult practice : that Romans sacrificed to the Penates at Lavinium is a fact of religion, attested and datable; that Aeneas carried those Penates out of burning Troy is the legend the cult carried, and belongs to a different order of claim. Second, the Greek original is distinguished from the Roman reception : the earliest surviving notice connecting Italy with the heroic age is Greek, is about Odysseus rather than Aeneas, and knows nothing of Rome by name; the Aeneas-centred, Rome-centred version is a later synthesis, and the seams show. Third, speculation and scholarly dispute are labelled as such, with positions named : where modern scholarship divides — over the Capitoline Wolf's date, over Andrea Carandini's Palatine wall, over how much of the king list can be salvaged — this article gives the division, not a verdict dressed as consensus. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — H. G. Evelyn-White's Loeb translation of Hesiod's Theogony (1914) and the Perseus text of Livy Book 40 — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. The stories of Livy Book 1, Dionysius, and Plutarch are retold, never dressed in invented quotation marks. The shape of the whole, before the detail. A Trojan refugee, Aeneas , escapes the sack of Troy and comes by sea to Italy, where he founds Lavinium and leaves his household gods, the Penates, in its keeping. His son founds Alba Longa , whose line of kings — the Silvii — reigns, the tradition says, for some four centuries, bridging the gap between Troy's fall and the eighth century. From that line, through a dispossessed king, a violated Vestal, and a she-wolf, come the twins Romulus and Remus ; Romulus survives the augury contest and the killing of his brother, and founds Rome on the Palatine on 21 April of a year the scholars would eventually fix as 753 BCE. Seven kings follow in sequence — Romulus, Numa, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius, Tarquinius Superbus — until the last is expelled in 509 BCE and the Republic begins. Every element of that paragraph is load-bearing in Roman identity, and almost every element can be shown to be a join: two originally separate legends (a Trojan Aeneas in Latium; a local founder Romulus) riveted together by the Alban king list, which exists, as Section V argues, largely in order to be the rivet. The poem that fused the whole into Rome's permanent self-image, Virgil's Aeneid , has its own article in this hub — The Aeneid — and this article's last narrative duty, in Section XIV, is to hand the story over to it. THE THREE PRINCIPAL WITNESSES Livy , Ab Urbe Condita Book 1 (late first century BCE): the canonical Roman telling, brisk, sceptical at the edges, apologetic where the story shames Rome. Dionysius of Halicarnassus , Roman Antiquities Books 1–4 (published from 7 BCE): a Greek writing Rome's past for Greeks, fuller, more antiquarian, and our best preserver of the lost early historians. Plutarch , Lives of Romulus and Numa (c. 100 CE): biography, not history, and invaluable precisely because he reports variants his sources disagreed on. II. The Greek Stratum: Odysseus' Sons, Stesichorus, Hellanicus The Aeneas legend did not begin as Rome's. It began as a Greek habit of mind: the habit of mapping the peoples of the western Mediterranean onto the genealogies of heroic myth, so that a foreign nation became legible as somebody's descendants. Greeks had been planting colonies in Italy and Sicily since the eighth century BCE; the mythic map was drawn over the colonial one, and Italy filled up with the offspring and the landfalls of Homeric heroes. The earliest surviving text in the whole dossier belongs to this Greek stratum, and its hero is not Aeneas. It is Odysseus. Hesiod's Closing Lines: Latinus, Son of Odysseus The Theogony ends — in lines 1011–1016, whose place in the poem is discussed below — with the children Circe bore to Odysseus. In Evelyn-White's Loeb translation (1914), consulted for this article, Circe “loved steadfast Odysseus and bare Agrius and Latinus who was faultless and strong”, and the sons, the passage concludes, ruled over the famous Tyrrhenians, far off in a recess of the holy islands. Three facts in those lines carry the whole Greek stratum. Latinus is the eponym of the Latins — the people of Latium, Rome's own people — here given a Greek father and a divine mother. The Tyrrhenians are the Etruscans, the Latins' powerful northern neighbours, folded into the same genealogy. And the father is Odysseus : in the earliest surviving version, Italy's peoples descend not from Troy's survivor but from Troy's destroyer — from the Greek hero whose wanderings the Odyssey had already scattered across the western sea. Rome is not named. Aeneas is not mentioned. The connection between Latium and the heroic age is older than the connection between Latium and Aeneas, and it runs through the other side of the Trojan War — a point worth holding, because the finished Roman legend, in which Rome is Trojan to the core, can make its Greek and Odyssean beginnings invisible. // THE STATE OF THE HESIODIC TEXT // The closing lines of the Theogony are not beyond dispute. The line naming a third son, Telegonus , is bracketed by editors as a probable interpolation, and the whole Circe passage has been regarded by some scholars as an addition rather than Hesiod's own — the genealogical catalogue at the poem's end shades into the separate Catalogue of Women , and its seams were visible in antiquity. The passage is reported here as the tradition transmits it, attributed to Hesiod, with the caveat stated: what is certain is that the lines are early — archaic Greek, not Roman-era fabrication — and that they attest a Greek, pre-Roman linking of Latium to the Odyssean world. The Odyssean line did not die when the Aeneas line rose. Dionysius ( Roman Antiquities 1.72), cataloguing the rival accounts with an antiquarian's patience, reports the historian Xenagoras for a version in which Odysseus and Circe have three sons — Romos, Antias, and Ardeas — who found three cities and give them their names: Rome itself, in this telling, is an Odyssean foundation, named for a son of Circe. The detail is precious precisely because it lost. It shows the foundation of Rome still unsettled property in the Greek imagination, available to be assigned to whichever hero a given author's scheme required, centuries before the Roman state fixed its own version and exported it back to the Greek world as fact. Stesichorus: Aeneas Sails West Aeneas enters the western story, so far as surviving evidence goes, with the lyric poet Stesichorus of Himera in Sicily (c. 630–555 BCE), whose Sack of Troy treated the city's fall at a scale the epic Cycle's version — told in this hub's Trojan Cycle — did not exhaust. The poem is lost, but a marble relief of the early Empire, the Tabula Iliaca Capitolina , illustrates the sack “according to Stesichorus”, as its inscription says, and shows Aeneas at the ships, embarking with Anchises, his son, and the household gods, bound — the scene's standard interpretation — for Hesperia , Italy. The attribution rests on that inscription and the relief's iconography, and is reported at that strength. But the geography is eloquent: a Sicilian Greek poet is the first witness we can name who sends Troy's refugee toward Italy. The Etruscans took the story up early — Aeneas carrying Anchises appears on vases from southern Etruria from the late sixth century BCE — material evidence that it circulated in Italy, in non-Roman hands, generations before any Roman wrote it down. Hellanicus: Aeneas Founds Rome The decisive Greek step — Aeneas not merely reaching Italy but founding Rome — is credited by Dionysius (1.72) to Hellanicus of Lesbos , the great mythographer of the later fifth century BCE. In the account Dionysius attributes to him, Aeneas came to Italy in company with Odysseus — the two wanderers of the two strata travelling together, in a synthesis that already betrays a systematiser at work — and founded the city, naming it after Romē , one of the Trojan women who had sailed with him: Romē, weary of wandering, persuaded the other women to burn the ships, stranding the expedition in Italy for good. Dionysius attributes a similar account to Damastes of Sigeum , Hellanicus' contemporary. Two features deserve emphasis. First, in Hellanicus there is no chronological gap : Aeneas founds Rome himself, within a generation of Troy's fall — the four-century problem the Alban king list would later be built to solve (Section V) does not yet exist, because no one has yet fixed Troy's fall and Rome's founding far enough apart to create it. Second, the founder's city is named for a woman, and a ship-burner at that: the eponymous Romē is one of several rival eponyms the Greek tradition generated — Romos the son of Odysseus, Romus a son of Aeneas in other accounts — of which the Roman tradition's own candidate, Romulus, is only the one that won. The name of Rome was as contested in antiquity as its date would be. What the Greek stratum bequeathed to Rome was not a story but a field of stories , from which Roman writers would select, suppress, and systematise — the subject of the next section. III. The Roman Stratum: Naevius, Ennius, Fabius Pictor, Cato Rome began writing its own past in the third century BCE, in the generation of the Punic Wars — the moment when the city, suddenly a Mediterranean power, needed a past commensurate with its present and legible to the Greek world it was defeating and joining. The Roman stratum of the foundation legend is the work of four writers across roughly a century. All four are lost except in fragments and citations. All four can be placed, and their contributions distinguished, with reasonable confidence — and the distinctions matter, because they show the legend still molten, its central genealogies not yet fixed, well into the second century BCE. c. 235 BCE NAEVIUS, BELLUM PUNICUM Gnaeus Naevius' epic on the First Punic War — the war his own generation fought — reached back, in a long retrospective movement, to the fall of Troy and Aeneas' flight to Italy: the storm at sea, Venus pleading her son's cause before Jupiter, the sojourn at Carthage that later tradition would make the tragedy of Dido. The poem's surviving fragments establish the architecture Virgil would inherit two centuries later: a Roman war explained by a Trojan origin, the present rooted in the mythic past. In Naevius' genealogy, as the fragments and later testimony are usually read, Romulus stood close to Aeneas — his grandson, in the version most often reconstructed — with no Alban centuries between them. The gap had still not been opened. c. 180–170 BCE ENNIUS, ANNALES , BOOK 1 Quintus Ennius' eighteen-book epic of Roman history opened with the fall of Troy and devoted its first book to Aeneas, to his daughter Ilia — mother of the twins by Mars, in Ennius' telling, and herself Aeneas' daughter, which makes Romulus Aeneas' grandson by the direct line — to Ilia's famous dream, reported to her sister in a passage later critics quoted with admiration, and to the twins, the augury, and Romulus' eventual taking-up into heaven. Ennius gave Rome its first great poetic past, and his chronology was generous to the point of vagueness: later readers computed from his verses a founding centuries earlier than any annalist would allow. What Ennius fixed was not dates but descent : the founder of Rome was of Aeneas' blood, immediately. c. 216–200 BCE FABIUS PICTOR, HISTORY OF ROME (IN GREEK) Quintus Fabius Pictor, a Roman senator who had fought in the Hannibalic War and been sent on an embassy to Delphi, wrote the first prose history of Rome — in Greek, for a Greek-reading world that needed Rome explained. His history ran from Aeneas to his own day, and the foundation narrative in the form the later tradition inherits — Aeneas in Latium, Lavinium, Alba, the Alban kings, the twins, the founding — is substantially his construction, or his systematisation of materials older than himself. For the twins' story Plutarch names his Greek source: Diocles of Peparethus , whose account, Plutarch says, Fabius followed in most respects — a reminder that even Rome's first historian was working from Greek mythography. Fabius dated the founding to the first year of the eighth Olympiad, 748/7 BCE (Section VIII): the first Roman date, and already a computation, not a memory. c. 168–149 BCE CATO, ORIGINES , BOOK 1 Marcus Porcius Cato — the Censor — wrote the first history of Rome in Latin, and its first book treated the foundations of Rome and of the Italian peoples city by city: Aeneas' landing, the Aborigines who already held Latium, King Latinus, the marriage alliance, Lavinium, Alba. Cato's handling, so far as the fragments let us judge, was already rationalising at the edges — peoples and places explained by migration and merger rather than by miracle — and his chronology became the tradition's anchor: Rome founded 432 years after the fall of Troy , which Dionysius, comparing Eratosthenes' date for Troy (1184/3 BCE), converts to the first year of the seventh Olympiad, 752/1 BCE. With Cato, the two ends of the story — Troy and Rome — are both dated, and the distance between them is a stated number. The Alban king list exists to fill exactly that number of years. Stand back from the four and the pattern is clear. The poets came first , and for the poets the descent from Aeneas was direct and the centuries did not matter. The historians followed , and for the historians centuries were the whole problem, because Greek chronography — the discipline Eratosthenes had just founded — supplied a date for Troy's fall (1184/3 BCE) that no genealogical compression could reconcile with an eighth-century Rome. Between Naevius' grandson-Romulus and Livy's fifteen Alban kings lies the entire labour of the Roman stratum: the invention, or elaboration, of a middle. Two cautions belong here. “Invention” need not mean cynical fabrication: king lists, genealogies, and synchronisms were the ordinary instruments by which the ancient world organised a past it possessed as stories, and Fabius and Cato used them in good faith on materials they believed. And the strata did not stop moving with Cato: the later annalists — Calpurnius Piso, Valerius Antias, Licinius Macer — kept adjusting numbers, names, and motives, and Dionysius and Plutarch preserve their variants. The systematisation this hub's Prose Systematizers article traces in Apollodorus and his kind was, in Rome, a centuries-long civic project, and its product — the smooth narrative of Sections IV–XII below — should be read with the joins kept in view. IV. Lavinium and the Penates: Aeneas on the Ground If the Aeneas legend has a home address, it is not Rome. It is Lavinium , on the coast of Latium some thirty kilometres south of the city, at modern Pratica di Mare — and the priority is itself a piece of evidence. A legend invented at Rome, for Rome, would have brought Aeneas straight to the Palatine. Instead the tradition lands him down the coast, marries him to a local king's daughter, seats his gods in a Latin town that is not Rome, and makes Rome a granddaughter-city, founded two removes later. Traditions that preserve inconvenient geography are usually older than the interests they inconvenience: the Lavinium stage of the story looks like a genuinely Latin, pre-Roman or not-only-Roman possession, which Rome adopted — and then, characteristically, put under state supervision. The story as Livy (1.1–2) and Dionysius (1.55–65) tell it, in paraphrase. Aeneas, escaping Troy with his father, his son Ascanius, and the gods of his house, wanders the Mediterranean and comes at last to the Laurentine shore of Latium. The land is held by Latinus , king of the Aborigines, the people already there. War threatens, then does not: Latinus, warned by an oracle that his daughter Lavinia is destined for a foreign bridegroom, makes alliance and marriage instead — though Lavinia had been promised to Turnus , king of the neighbouring Rutuli, and the war comes anyway, through Turnus' resentment and, in the fuller tellings, the meddling of Juno and the Fury Allecto: that war, its duels, and Turnus' death at Aeneas' hands are the matter of the Aeneid 's second half, and are told in this hub's Aeneid article. Aeneas founds a city and names it Lavinium for his wife. He reigns briefly — three years in Livy's reckoning — and dies, killed in battle against the Rutuli and their Etruscan allies at the river Numicus, or simply vanishing there; the tradition promoted him, in death, to a god of the place, Aeneas Indiges , the native-born god, with a hero-shrine on the Numicus' bank. THE PENATES The Penates were the gods of the store-cupboard and the household's continuity — in the legend, the gods Aeneas rescued from Troy and carried to their destined home. Their Roman cult was seated at Lavinium: Dionysius (1.67–68) describes the sanctuary and its sacred objects, Trojan in origin as the Lavinates maintained, and records the practice that tied Rome to the place permanently — Roman magistrates, on taking office, travelled to Lavinium to sacrifice to the Penates and to Vesta. The legend is legend; the sacrifice was real, annual, and official. On the Penates' place in lived Roman religion, see Roman Religion . THE THIRTEEN ALTARS Excavation at Pratica di Mare uncovered a sanctuary of thirteen altars in a row, built and rebuilt between the sixth and second centuries BCE — a federal cult place of the Latin peoples — and, nearby, a monumentalised tomb of the fourth century BCE which its excavators identified with the heroon , the hero-shrine, of Aeneas that Dionysius describes. The identification is an interpretation, and is reported as one; what is not interpretation is that Lavinium was a major Latin sanctuary, of archaic date, organised around cults the literary tradition connects with Aeneas and the Penates. Here, unusually, legend and spade point at the same town. WHY LAVINIUM MATTERS TO THE METHOD Lavinium is the strongest case in this article for the middle position of Section XV. The cult is archaic and real; the federal altars are archaic and real; the magistrates' pilgrimage is historically attested. None of it makes a Trojan refugee of the twelfth century BCE historical. What it makes historical is a Latin community of the archaic period that already understood its origins through a figure the Greek world called Aeneas — the legend at work, early, in cult, before any Roman historian touched it. Ascanius — called also Iulus , the name from which the Julian family would derive itself (Section XIV) — succeeded, and in the tradition's spacing founded Alba Longa a generation after Lavinium, leaving Lavinium itself to his stepmother Lavinia and her unborn son. With that move the story leaves the coast for the Alban hills, and leaves narrative for something stranger: a list. V. Alba Longa: The King List as a Bridge State the problem plainly, because the tradition states it plainly once its own dates are set side by side. Troy fell, on Eratosthenes' accepted computation, in 1184/3 BCE . Rome was founded, on the date that became canonical, in 753 BCE . Between Aeneas, who must reach Italy within years of Troy's fall, and Romulus yawns an interval of 431 years — some fourteen generations — for which the heroic story supplied nothing. Romulus had to be of Aeneas' blood, and the blood had to be carried, reign by reign, across the gap. Alba Longa , the “long white city” under the Alban Mount, is the bridge built to carry it, and its king list is the bridge's roadway. This article states the construction as construction, following the broad consensus of modern scholarship: whatever Alba was in archaic Latium — and the Alban hills held an important settlement zone, with cemeteries to prove it — the list of its kings, in the form Livy and Dionysius transmit, is a literary-chronographical artefact, assembled to fill a measured interval. King (Livy 1.3) The name's tell Function in the list Ascanius / Iulus Aeneas' son; “Iulus” anchors the Julian claim Founds Alba a generation after Lavinium Silvius Latin silva , “wood”: born in the woods, where Lavinia fled a jealous Ascanius Gives every later king the surname Silvius Aeneas Silvius The founder's name, recycled Fills a generation Latinus Silvius The bride's father's name, recycled Credited with founding Latin colonies Alba Silvius The city's own name, enthroned Fills a generation Atys / Capetus Livy's Atys is Dionysius' Capetus — the lists already disagree Fills a generation Capys Silvius A Trojan name (the Capys of the Iliad ) Fills a generation Capetus Silvius A near-duplicate of Capys — padding visible in the join Fills a generation Tiberinus Silvius Drowned in the river Albula, which takes his name: the Tiber Explains a river's name; fills a generation Agrippa Silvius A Roman name of later fame, retrojected Fills a generation Romulus Silvius The founder's name, pre-echoed; struck by lightning in Dionysius Fills a generation Aventinus Silvius Buried on the hill that takes his name: the Aventine Explains a hill's name; fills a generation Proca — Father of the last two: Numitor and Amulius Numitor (and Amulius ) The rightful king and the usurping brother Sets up the twins' birth (Section VI) Read the table as a chronographer, not as a chronicler, and its workmanship declares itself. The names are eponyms and recyclings : the city (Alba), the river (Tiberinus), the hill (Aventinus), the wood (Silvius), the two great names of the generation before (Aeneas, Latinus) used again, a Trojan name for colour (Capys), and a doublet (Capys, Capetus) where the padding had to thicken. Dionysius' list (1.71) is longer than Livy's and differently stocked — he counts the Alban dynasty at some fifteen kings across 432 years, reigns averaging close to the chronographer's conventional generation-length — and the disagreement between the two lists is itself the evidence: a transmitted record does not wobble like this; a constructed bridge, rebuilt by each engineer to his own span, does. Nor is the device a Roman eccentricity. King lists that stretch a line of rulers across an otherwise empty interval are among the oldest instruments of ancient chronography — the reader of this hub's Antiquity division will know the type from the Antediluvian King Lists of Mesopotamia, where the spans are filled with reigns of fabulous length rather than with extra kings. Rome's list is the same instrument in a sober, republican dress: no king reigns an impossible number of years; there are simply enough kings. // WHAT THE BRIDGE CARRIES // Once the list is seen as a bridge, several famous features of the tradition rearrange themselves as its cables. Romulus must descend from Aeneas through Alba — hence his mother is an Alban princess, not a Roman one. Rome must be Alba's daughter — hence the twins are exposed, recognised, and first employed on Alban business, and hence Rome will later destroy Alba utterly and absorb its people and noble families (Section XI): the daughter-city devouring the mother is the bridge being dismantled behind the crossing. And the Julian family, claiming descent from Iulus, stands at the bridge's far end with its pedigree running the whole length of the roadway (Section XIV). None of this makes Alba Longa nothing. The Alban hills held one of archaic Latium's richest settlement zones; the Latin peoples held their common festival, the Feriae Latinae , on the Alban Mount under Jupiter Latiaris into the Empire; and Rome's claim to head the Latin League was argued, in diplomacy and in war, through its Alban descent. A constructed list can be laid over a real landscape, and usually is: construction works best with genuine materials. What the construction cannot do is testify. The Silvii, as individuals, are the least historical persons in this article — and the tradition, to its credit, barely pretends otherwise: it gives most of them no deeds at all, only names and years, the exact silhouette of a bridge. VI. Romulus and Remus: The Twins, the Wolf, the Foster-Parents At the bridge's end the list stops and the story — the most famous foundation tale in the western world — begins. It is told here as Livy (1.3–5), Dionysius (1.76–84), and Plutarch ( Romulus 3–8) tell it, in paraphrase, with the variants kept where the sources keep them: in the open. Proca , king of Alba, left two sons. Numitor , the elder, inherited the throne; Amulius , the younger, seized it — drove his brother out, killed his brother's son, and neutralised his brother's daughter Rhea Silvia (the tradition also calls her Ilia ) by making her a Vestal Virgin, sworn to a chastity whose breach was death: a dynastic problem solved by a religious office. The solution failed. Rhea Silvia became pregnant, and declared — Livy (1.4) reports her claim and immediately brackets it, remarking in paraphrase that she named Mars as the father perhaps because she believed it, perhaps because a god made a nobler author of the fault — by Mars . Amulius imprisoned her and ordered the twin boys she bore to be thrown into the Tiber. The river was in flood; the servants, unwilling or unable to reach the deep water, left the basket at the flood's edge below the Palatine, by the wild fig tree called the Ficus Ruminalis . The waters fell, the basket grounded, and a she-wolf , coming down from the hills to drink, heard the crying, suckled the twins, and licked them clean — until Faustulus , the king's herdsman, found the scene, took the boys home, and gave them to his wife Acca Larentia to raise among the shepherds of the Palatine. LUPA : THE WORDPLAY THE SOURCES THEMSELVES SUPPLY Latin lupa means a she-wolf. It also means, in the slang of the street, a prostitute — the word survives in lupanar , a brothel. Livy, in the very chapter that tells the wolf story (1.4), records the rationalising alternative without blinking: some, he says in paraphrase, hold that Larentia was called lupa among the shepherds because she made her body common, and that this is the origin of the marvellous tale. The pun is not a modern scholar's debunking. It is in the canonical text, in the first century BCE — evidence that the tradition carried its own demystification alongside its miracle from the moment we can read it whole. Plutarch ( Romulus 4) reports the same doubleness. ACCA LARENTIA, TWICE OVER The foster-mother's name belongs also to a figure of Roman cult: an Acca Larentia honoured at the Larentalia festival in December, with a tomb in the Velabrum where the state made offerings to the dead. Antiquarians already debated whether the heroine of the cult and Faustulus' wife were one person, two, or a name that had migrated between a cult and a story. The debate is reported here unresolved, as the sources leave it: a tidy specimen of legend and cult practice (distinguished, per Section I, as method) growing through one another until the roots cannot be separated. THE RECOGNITION Grown, the twins lived as shepherds and hunters, feuding with the herdsmen of the deposed Numitor. In a clash at the Lupercalia, or in an ambush over cattle in the variant tellings, Remus was captured and hauled before Numitor; the old king, questioning a young man whose bearing did not match his station, heard the story of the basket and the wolf, and Faustulus, arriving with the basket itself, confirmed it. Romulus marched on Alba, Remus rose inside it, Amulius was killed, and Numitor restored. The recognition scene is the hinge of the whole legend — the point where the Alban story and the Roman story are bolted together in narrative, as the king list bolts them in chronology. Grandfather restored, the twins declined to live at Alba as subjects, and resolved to found a city of their own on the hills where they had been exposed and raised — the Palatine country, already filling, in the tradition's telling, with the shepherds, outlaws, and runaways who followed them. But a city can have only one founder and one name, and the twins were equal in birth, in age, and in following. The tradition is unanimous on how they agreed to settle it, and unanimous on nothing else: they would take the auspices , and the gods would choose between them by birds. What the birds decided, and what it cost, is the next section — the darkest in the legend, and the one where the sources' disagreements are most instructive. VII. The Augury Contest and the Fratricide Augury — the reading of the gods' will in the flight of birds — was no decorative detail in Roman life; it was constitutional machinery, and remained so into the late Republic (see Roman Religion ). The legend accordingly settles its succession crisis by the state's own instrument. The twins took their stations: Remus on the Aventine — or, in a variant, at a place called Remoria — and Romulus on the Palatine. The agreed sign was vultures. To Remus, first, came six . To Romulus, after, came twelve . And there the sources' agreement ends, because the result was double: Remus had priority , Romulus number . Each party proclaimed its own man, Livy (1.6–7) says in paraphrase, the one side claiming by time, the other by the count of birds; argument became quarrel, quarrel a fight. Rome's first constitutional crisis was an ambiguity in its own sacred law, and it was resolved, as the legend insists on remembering, by blood. Who Killed Remus? The Variants, Kept Visible On the manner of Remus' death the tradition does not speak with one voice, and this article follows the hub's discipline of keeping the variants in the open rather than silently electing one. VARIANT A · THE WALL (LIVY'S “MORE COMMON” ACCOUNT) The founding proceeded: Romulus ploughed the sacred furrow, the pomerium , round the Palatine — the plough lifted and carried where gates were to be, in Plutarch's detailed account ( Romulus 11) — and the first walls rose. Remus, in mockery of the work, leapt over the half-built wall. Romulus killed him on the spot, with the words Livy reports in paraphrase as the tradition's grim charter: so perish everyone who shall hereafter leap over my walls. In this variant the fratricide is an act of foundation law: the wall is sacred from its first course, and its sanctity is consecrated by the founder's own brother's blood. VARIANT B · THE MELEE (LIVY'S OTHER ACCOUNT; DIONYSIUS) Livy himself gives, first and more briefly, the version in which the killing belongs to the augury quarrel itself: words came to blows between the two followings, and Remus fell in the fighting — killed by no named hand, a casualty of the disputed omen. Dionysius (1.87) tells a version of this type at length, with the battle between the twins' parties fought out and Faustulus himself among the dead. Here the fratricide is not an execution but a civil brawl — less theatrical, and in its way darker: the city begins not with a sentence pronounced but with a riot over a religious technicality. VARIANT C · CELER'S SPADE (PLUTARCH; OVID) Plutarch ( Romulus 10) reports, among the accounts he canvasses, the version in which the killer was not Romulus at all but Celer , the overseer of the wall-work, who struck Remus with his spade or mattock for the mocking leap — and Romulus, in this telling, buried his brother with public grief, on the Remoria, and concealed his anger at Celer. Ovid's Fasti (Book 4) tells the Celer version and follows it with Remus' ghost, appearing to the aged Faustulus and Acca Larentia to ask for a festival of the dead: the origin, in Ovid's aetiology, of the Lemuria. In this variant Rome is founded not by a fratricide's hand but by a fratricide it must mourn — and the founder's guilt is displaced, conveniently, onto a subordinate. Not Greek Myth in Latin Dress: Religion as Doing Begin with the sentence this hub requires every reader of Roman religion to hold onto, because almost every popular account violates it: Roman religion is not Greek mythology retold in Latin. The companion article on the Olympians shows what Rome did with the Greek gods — it matched them, name by name, to its own older Italic and Etruscan powers, in the process modern scholarship calls interpretatio romana , and then let Greek stories flow into the Roman names. That matching is real, and Sections XII–XIII of this article return to it. But the matching happened inside a religious system that was already Roman in its structure, its personnel, and its purposes before the Greek myths arrived in bulk — and that system, not the stories, is the subject here. A reader who knows the Aeneid and the Metamorphoses knows what educated Romans read. This article is about what Romans did : who sacrificed, on which days, in which words, under whose authority, with what consequence if a word was missed. The modern account on which this article principally rests — Mary Beard, John North, and Simon Price, Religions of Rome (Cambridge, 1998), in two volumes, a history and a sourcebook of documents in translation — opens with a deliberate provocation of exactly this kind. Its history runs for more than a thousand years, from the eighth-century BCE hamlet on the Tiber to the Christian capital of the fourth and fifth centuries CE, and it insists throughout that the story is one of change : new gods admitted, old rites revived or reinvented, priesthoods opened, closed, and politicised. John Scheid’s An Introduction to Roman Religion (French original 1998; English translation by Janet Lloyd, 2003), the second backbone of this article, makes the complementary point from the ritual side: Roman religion is best approached through its acts — sacrifices, vows, auspices, processions — and through the documents those acts generated, rather than through any supposed Roman creed, because there was no creed to reconstruct. Neither work treats “Roman religion” as a set of beliefs Romans held in their heads. Both treat it as something Romans performed , in public and at home, correctly or incorrectly, with the correctness open to inspection. That is the sense of the word orthopraxic , which this article uses in its precise, limited meaning. Greek cult, as the Olympians article shows, was already various — city by city, altar by altar, epithet by epithet, with no central authority to standardise it. Roman public cult, by contrast, developed a single civic centre, a small number of priestly colleges charged with advising the Senate, an inscribed calendar that told the whole community which days allowed which business, and a body of sacred law ( ius divinum ) administered like other law. To call Roman religion orthopraxic is not to say Romans felt nothing, believed nothing, or cared only for form — Section III takes up that caricature directly. It is to say that the system’s test of a religious act was whether it had been done rightly : the right person, the right victim, the right words, the right day, the right place. Belief was not examined. The performance was. THE GREEK STORY-WORLD Poets — Homer, Hesiod, the tragedians — carry the theology. Gods have biographies, quarrels, loves, and childhoods. Cult is local and plural, and no single city’s practice binds another’s. See the hub’s Theogony and Olympians articles. THE ROMAN RITUAL SYSTEM Priestly colleges, magistrates, and the Senate carry the practice. Gods have functions, temples, festival dates, and priesthoods. Public cult is civic and documented, and a flawed performance is a defective act to be repeated, not a private failure of faith. INTERPRETATIO ROMANA The naming of a foreign god by a Roman name — Jupiter for Zeus, Mars for Ares, Isis kept as Isis — is treated in this hub as a Roman administrative-religious act: an identification made by priests, generals, and the Senate, with legal and cultic consequences, not as the translation of a myth from one language to another. WHERE THE EVIDENCE LIVES Less in narrative poetry than in calendars on stone and plaster, priestly records, senatorial decrees preserved on bronze, dedications, and antiquarian writers — Varro, Livy, Ovid’s Fasti , Plutarch’s Roman Questions — who describe rites as rites. Section XVI lists what was actually used. A last framing fact, because it explains the article’s shape. Rome had no word that maps cleanly onto the modern English word “religion.” The Latin religio named, in its core uses, scrupulous obligation — the care owed to the gods, the binding force of an oath or a rite, sometimes the anxiety that a duty had been neglected. Superstitio , by contrast, named excess: religion done too much, too fearfully, or by the wrong people in the wrong way — a social judgement as much as a theological one, and one Romans applied freely to foreign cults and to their neighbours. Pietas named dutifulness toward gods, parents, and fatherland in a single breath, which is why Virgil’s hero is pius Aeneas in all three relations at once. A vocabulary in which duty to the gods and duty to the family and the state share one word is not a vocabulary that separates “religion” from the rest of life. Roman religion had no outside. That is precisely why its priests were senators, its calendar was the civic calendar, and its most characteristic documents are legal ones. II. Numen, Function, and the Gods Without Stories A Roman god, in the oldest stratum of the system, is a numen : a divine power, a capacity to act, attached to a function, a place, or a moment — and very often to nothing else. The word matters. Numen (from nuere , to nod) is in origin the nod itself, the sign of assent and power, before it is a person. Greek gods, even in cult, keep the gravitational pull of their epic biographies: Zeus who sacrificed at Olympia is still the Zeus who quarrelled on Olympus. A large class of Roman divine powers never acquired a biography at all, and the absence is not a gap in the record. It is the point of this section, and in a sense of the whole article: a Roman power could be fully real in cult — with a temple, a festival, a priest, and a date — and have no myth whatsoever. Janus: The God of the Door Has No Greek Double Janus (Iānus) is the standing example. God of beginnings, doorways, passages, and the hinge-moment between states, he is depicted with two faces looking opposite ways — the image is a function drawn, not an episode from a life. He has no Greek equivalent: the interpretatio, which found a Roman partner for nearly every Olympian, found none for Janus, and he remained himself. His month, Iānuārius, opens the year; his shrine in the Forum, the Janus Geminus, stood with its doors open in wartime and closed in peace — a condition so rare that its occurrences were remembered as events, under Numa by tradition, in 235 BCE, and three times under Augustus, who advertises the closures in his own account of his reign (paraphrased). Invocations of the gods in formal prayer regularly began with Janus, as Ovid’s Fasti Book 1 stages at length, because beginnings belonged to him by office. Of a childhood, a marriage, a quarrel, a journey — the normal furniture of a Greek god — Janus has effectively none. He is a door that is also a god, and Rome found nothing missing in that. Terminus, Fides, and the Powers of Single Acts Terminus is a boundary stone that is a god. His festival, the Terminalia (23 February), was kept by neighbouring landholders at the boundary itself, with offerings at the stone; the Capitoline temple’s foundation legend, told by Livy and others (paraphrased), made the point into theology: when the site was cleared and the older shrines were formally deconsecrated, Terminus alone — in some versions with Juventas, Youth — refused to move, and his shrine was therefore built into Jupiter’s temple, under an opening in the roof, because Terminus would not be housed under cover. Rome’s boundaries, the story says in ritual form, do not yield — not even to Jupiter. Around Janus and Terminus stands a whole population of such powers: Fides , Good Faith, with a temple on the Capitol; Concordia , Concord, whose temple in the Forum was rebuilt at successive political crises as an argument in stone; Spes , Hope; Salus , Safety; Virtus and Honos , Valour and Honour, worshipped in paired temples so that the worshipper passed through Honour to reach Valour — the architecture itself preaching. The priestly lists known as the indigitamenta carried the principle to its limit: minute powers for the stages of a child’s life, a crop’s growth, a door’s parts — hinge, panel, and threshold each with its own name. Augustine, who preserves much of this material from Varro in order to mock it in the City of God , is thus, unwillingly, one of its chief witnesses; the mockery is Christian polemic, the lists are Roman priestly practice as Varro recorded it, and Section XVI keeps the two apart. The systematiser who lets us see this world whole is also its great loss. Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), the most learned Roman of his age, devoted the sixteen books on divine affairs of his Antiquitates rerum humanarum et divinarum — Antiquities of Human and Divine Things — to the Roman system as a system: who performs the rites, where, when, what is performed, and finally to which gods — the order Augustine reports in City of God Book 6, in the course of refuting it. The work is lost. It survives in fragments and, above all, inside Augustine’s hostile summary, which preserves Varro’s famous threefold division of theology ( theologia tripertita ): the mythical theology of the poets, the natural theology of the philosophers, and the civil theology of the cities — what the people, and above all the priests, must know and perform. Varro’s own allegiance, on Augustine’s evidence (paraphrased), was plain: the civil theology is the one a citizen lives under, and Varro wrote, in effect, its handbook. Every modern account in Section XVI works in Varro’s shadow and through his loss: Rome produced exactly one great systematiser of its own religion, and his book reached us dismembered inside the work of the man who set out to destroy its world. The archive notes the pattern because it recurs — the Arval records of Section IV and the calendar inscriptions of Section VIII are the compensating evidence, documents the system made about itself, in stone, without an author to lose. III. Pax Deorum, Pietas, and Exact Performance The condition Roman public religion existed to maintain had a name: pāx deōrum , the peace of the gods — the state of right relations between the Roman community and its divine powers, in which the gods were neither angered nor neglected and the community could expect their favour, or at minimum their neutrality. Its breach had names too: ira deum , the anger of the gods, inferred after the fact from defeat, plague, famine, or prodigy; and the work of restoring the peace — expiation ( piaculum ), vows, games, processions, new temples, imported gods — fills the annalistic record that Livy preserves. The logic is sometimes described as a contract, and the description is fair if its limits are kept. The pax was not negotiated once; it was a standing condition, maintained by a calendar of owed performances, monitored by signs, and repaired, when it broke, by further performances whose adequacy the event itself would judge. Rome’s empire, in the Romans’ own explanation, was the longest-running evidence that the maintenance worked. Instauratio: When a Rite Fails, Begin Again Exactness had a technical consequence that displays the system better than any definition. If a public rite was flawed — a word misspoken, a victim that bolted or struggled, an ill-omened sound interrupting the prayer, a magistrate who stumbled in the formula — the act was not a prayer that had failed to persuade. It was a defective performance , a vitium , and the remedy was instauratio : the rite, festival, or games were performed again, entire, from the beginning. Livy’s history is studded with instaurations of the great games for faults no modern reader would notice — a dancer who stopped, a chariot driver who lost a rein, a rope that broke — each recorded because each cost the state a full repetition at public expense (paraphrased throughout). The presiding magistrate sacrificed with covered head ( capite velato ), a flute-player played continuously to drown out ill-omened sounds, and an attendant prompted the formula word by word from a written text so that nothing depended on memory: Plutarch, in the Roman Questions (Question 10, in Frank Cole Babbitt’s Loeb translation, paraphrased here), explains the covered head in part as a precaution lest any ill-omened sound reach the worshipper’s ears while praying — the anxiety is procedural before it is anything else. A religion that stations a man with a book beside its chief officiant, to catch a mispronunciation, has told you where it locates the sacred: in the performance, done rightly. Pietas is the virtue that operated the system, and its range is the system’s range: dutifulness to the gods, to parents and ancestors, and to the fatherland, felt as a single obligation with three objects. Its opposite was not unbelief — Rome had no instrument for detecting unbelief and no procedure that required it — but neglegentia , neglect: the festival not kept, the vow not paid, the auspices not taken, the ancestral rite allowed to lapse. Scheid’s introduction is particularly good on this point (paraphrased): impiety at Rome, in the cases that produced action, is almost always a failure of performance or a violation of sacred property and persons — theft from a temple, injury to a priest or a Vestal, a rite performed by someone not entitled — not a wrong opinion about the gods’ nature. Philosophers could argue that the gods did not exist, or did not care, in books that other senators read; what no one could do with impunity was stop the city’s rites or botch them in office. The boundary is worth stating exactly, because Section XIII’s suppressions and Section XV’s bans both turn on it: Rome policed acts. Sacrifice stood at the centre of the acts, and its Roman form should be pictured concretely. The public victim — ox, sheep, or pig, according to the god and the occasion, unblemished and garlanded — was led in procession to an outdoor altar before the temple (the temple itself was the god’s house and the treasury of the cult, not a congregational hall; the rite happened outside it), sprinkled with salted meal ( mola salsa , prepared under the Vestals’ charge) and wine, and stunned and slaughtered by attendants while the officiant, head covered, pronounced the prayer naming the god and the purpose. The entrails ( exta ) were inspected — a failed inspection, like a flawed formula, voided the act and required repetition — then cooked and offered; the meat was eaten by the participants or distributed, so that a great public sacrifice was also a distribution of meat through the city. Scheid’s account of public sacrifice, and the Arval protocols of Section IV which record sacrifices victim by victim and god by god, agree on the essential impression: this was skilled, staffed, expensive public work, closer in its organisation to a civic ceremony than to a congregational service, and it was done, on the great days, by the same men who governed. IV. The Priesthoods as Civic Offices: Pontifices and the Pontifex Maximus Rome’s public priests were not a clergy in the later sense: no separate caste, no pastoral charge, no doctrine to teach, no congregation to lead in weekly worship. They were civic office-holders — overwhelmingly senators, holding priesthood alongside consulships, commands, and governorships, often several priesthoods across a career — whose religious function was expertise: to know the sacred law, to advise the Senate and magistrates on it, to keep the calendar and the records, and to perform or supervise the rites assigned to their college. The arrangement is unintelligible if priesthood is imagined as a vocation set apart from politics. At Rome it was one of the forms politics took. Julius Caesar’s election as pontifex maximus in 63 BCE was a major political contest, fought with heavy bribery on all sides, because the office was worth a career; Augustus, who waited politely for the incumbent to die rather than depose him, made the chief priesthood thereafter a permanent attribute of the emperor. The gods’ business and the state’s business had the same personnel because, in the Roman arrangement, they were the same business conducted in two registers. The College of Pontifices The pontifices formed the senior college. Under their head, the pontifex maximus , they held a general superintendence of sacred law: the calendar and its intercalations, the formulae of vows, dedications, and devotions, adoptions and wills insofar as they touched ancestral rites, the discipline of the Vestals and the appointment of the flamines, and the keeping of records — the chief pontiff’s annual notice-board of events, the annales maximi , stands behind Rome’s earliest historical writing. Formally attached to the college’s world were the rex sacrorum , the “king of the sacred rites” who inherited the deposed kings’ ritual duties and ranked first in ceremonial precedence while holding almost no power; the fifteen flamines (Section VI); and the Vestal Virgins (Section VI). The college’s membership tells the political story in miniature: originally patrician, it was opened to plebeians by the lex Ogulnia of 300 BCE — one of the landmark concessions of the Conflict of the Orders — enlarged by Sulla, and refilled by Caesar and the emperors. A priesthood that a rising order fights for two centuries to enter is not a retreat from public life. It is one of public life’s prizes, and the fight over it is evidence for how much the expertise was worth. The Fratres Arvales , the Arval Brothers — twelve priests of senatorial rank, serving for life, whose grove and temple of the goddess Dea Dia lay on the Via Campana outside the city — inscribed their Acta , their protocols, on tablets fixed to the temple walls. The surviving records, recovered in bulk in the nineteenth century, span in their datable entries from 21 BCE to 304 CE and document, in formulaic detail, what a Roman priesthood actually did across three centuries: the election of officers, vows undertaken and discharged for the emperor’s safety, sacrifices specified by date, place, god, and victim, expiations for such incidents as a tree struck by lightning in the grove or iron brought into it against the rule — the expiation itself requiring named substitute victims and the removal of the offending iron — and, in the record for 218 CE, the text of the Carmen Arvale , the Brothers’ archaic hymn to the Lares and Mars, already so old that its Latin was barely intelligible to the men who sang it, preserved because the protocol of that year happened to write it down. V. Signs and Permission: Augures, Auspicia, Haruspices, and Prodigies No Roman public act of consequence was supposed to begin until the gods had been asked — not what would happen, but whether they assented to the act proposed, on that day, by that magistrate. The asking was the auspicia , the auspices; the discipline that governed it was the augural law; and its experts were the augures . The distinction between the magistrate and the augur is the institution in miniature. The auspices belonged to the magistrate by virtue of his office — a consul, praetor, or general held the auspicia as he held command ( imperium ), and took them himself, at dawn, in a ritually delimited space ( templum in its original sense: a zone marked out in the sky and on the ground for observation). The augur was the consultant beside him: keeper of the discipline’s precedents, entitled to declare a flaw ( vitium ) in the proceedings, and possessed of the formidable right of obnuntiatio — announcing unfavourable signs and thereby halting a public assembly. Elections, legislation, the departure of an army, the founding of a colony, the dedication of a temple: all ran under auspices, and an act done against them, or after a declared flaw, was religiously void in a way that Roman politics repeatedly exploited and Roman courts repeatedly had to judge. Impetrative and Oblative: Signs Asked For and Signs Sent Roman theory, as Scheid sets it out (paraphrased), divided signs into two kinds. Auspicia impetrativa were sought : the magistrate defined the question and the field of observation and watched for the specified birds — their species, number, direction, flight, and cries — or, in the army’s practical shorthand, fed the sacred chickens ( pulli ) and read their appetite. The answer was narrow by design: assent or refusal, for that act, that day; the auspices expired at nightfall, at the crossing of a boundary, at any flaw in the taking. Auspicia oblativa were unsought : signs that presented themselves — lightning, an eclipse, a stumble, a sneeze, a chance word — which the magistrate could accept as significant or formally decline to notice, a discretion without which government would have seized up daily. The system was thus neither a fortune-telling machine nor a fraud, in its own terms: it was a procedure for obtaining divine permission, with rules for what counted, who could ask, and how long the answer lasted — permission, notably, not prediction. What the gods thought of the outcome was a question the auspices did not put. The Etruscan Discipline: Haruspices, Livers, and Lightning Beside the Roman auspices stood a second, foreign science that Rome adopted without ever quite naturalising: the disciplina Etrusca , the Etruscan discipline, practised by haruspices . Its three fields were the inspection of victims’ entrails, above all the liver, whose lobes and markings were read against a model of the divided sky; the interpretation of lightning, classified by quarter, colour, and consequence in a doctrine of great elaboration; and the expiation of prodigies. The discipline’s prestige was proverbial — Rome’s first kings are Etruscan in the tradition, and the city’s early sacred architecture and regalia carry Etruscan workmanship — and its practitioners were summoned from Etruria by the Senate well into the Republic. Yet the haruspices long remained consultants without a college : the Senate took their responses ( responsa ) and ordered the expiations they prescribed, but the experts themselves stood outside the collegiate priesthoods, organised as an ordo of sixty only under the Empire — Claudius, Tacitus reports (paraphrased), proposed formal state support for the college of haruspices lest the ancient Italian discipline decay through neglect. The pattern recurs in Section XIII: Rome uses a foreign religious expertise, honours it, pays for it — and keeps the authority to decide in Roman hands. Prodigies: The Senate as Clearing-House of the Uncanny A prodigy ( prodigium ) was an event out of nature’s order reported to the Senate as a sign that the pax deorum was broken: rains of stones or blood, speaking oxen, statues sweating, two-headed calves, lightning striking a temple, a wolf in the Forum. The procedure that followed is the Roman system at its most characteristic, and Livy’s annalistic lists — year after year of prodigies and their expiations — are its archive. The Senate decided which reports to accept as public prodigies (private wonders were the owner’s problem); it referred the accepted ones to the appropriate experts — pontifices, haruspices, or the keepers of the Sibylline Books (Section VII); it decreed the prescribed remedy — a procession, a hymn sung by twenty-seven virgins through the city, nine days of rites ( novemdiale sacrum ), games, a temple vowed, a foreign god fetched; and it had the remedy performed at public expense and entered in the record. Modern readers meet these lists as curiosities. In their own setting they are a government’s incident log: the uncanny, routed through committee, answered with budgeted ritual, and filed. Beard, North, and Price’s treatment stresses what the lists also show — that the system contracted in the late Republic, as prodigy-reporting from an Italy-wide network thinned and elite writers grew ironic about the machinery their grandfathers had operated in earnest. The machinery’s decline is part of its history, and Section XV returns to it. VI. Bound by Taboo: Flamines, the Flamen Dialis, and the Vestal Virgins If the colleges show Roman priesthood as civic expertise, the flamines show its other pole: priesthood as bondage to a single god and a single ritual programme. A flamen was the priest of one deity — the word is traditionally connected with kindling the sacrificial flame — and the fifteen flamines, three major and twelve minor, served Jupiter, Mars, and Quirinus at the head of a list that reaches down to gods like Pomona of the orchards and Volturnus of the river, several of whom had little cult beyond their flamen’s rites. The three major flamines belonged to the archaic stratum of the system — Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus is the old triad that precedes the Capitoline arrangement of Section XII — and they were required to be patricians married by the archaic rite of confarreatio , because the office was held, in a real sense, by the couple: the flamen’s wife, the flaminica , had her own ritual duties, her own dress, and her own taboos, and for the greatest of them her death ended his tenure. The Flamen Dialis: Rigour Made Visible The flamen Dialis , priest of Jupiter (Diespiter — hence Dialis ), lived under the most famous set of taboos in Roman religion, preserved in Aulus Gellius’s Attic Nights (10.15), drawing on earlier antiquarian and juristic authorities — the list is paraphrased here from the tradition Gellius reports. He might not ride a horse, nor look upon an army drawn up, nor swear an oath, nor wear a ring except one broken in form, nor have a knot anywhere on his person, nor touch or name a goat, raw meat, ivy, or beans; his hair might be cut only by a free man and with a bronze blade; the clippings of his hair and nails were buried beneath a fruitful tree; he might not sleep away from his own bed for more than a fixed span of nights; his bed’s legs were smeared with clay and no one else might sleep in it; he wore his pointed cap ( apex ) and his festival dress — a heavy woollen cloak of prescribed manufacture, woven by his wife — not on feast days only but as his constant public condition, a man permanently dressed for a rite. He was married by confarreatio, could not divorce, and if his wife died he resigned: the priesthood was a marriage’s office. Modern accounts sometimes present the taboos as picturesque survivals. In the system’s own terms they are better read as the flamen’s job description written on his body: Jupiter’s priest was kept, by rule, in a state of continuous ritual readiness and continuous separation from the contaminations of war, death, and the ordinary — the system’s rigour, made visible in one encumbered senator. The rigour had a price the record does not hide. The office stood vacant from 87 BCE to 11 BCE — seventy-five years in which no flamen Dialis served — because, after the suicide of the incumbent Cornelius Merula in the Marian troubles, no eligible patrician could be found, or would accept, a life so constrained and a career so limited: the flamen was barred by his taboos from much of the military and provincial service on which senatorial careers were built. Augustus, in his general restoration of the priesthoods, refilled the office in 11 BCE and adjusted its conditions by decree — the antiquarian tradition behind Gellius’s list itself reflects, as Scheid notes, a dossier assembled from specific rulings rather than a single priestly rule-book. The vacancy is the honest counterweight to any romance about Roman piety: the most sacred priesthood in Rome was, for three generations, a post the aristocracy declined to take, and the system ran on without it. What revived it was not a surge of devotion but an emperor’s programme of restoration — religion, again, administered. The Vestal Virgins: The Hearth of the State The Vestal Virgins ( virgines Vestales ) were six in number, chosen as girls between six and ten years old from families free of defect and with both parents living, taken — the ritual word is captio , a “taking” — by the pontifex maximus, and bound to thirty years of service: ten learning, ten performing, ten teaching, by the conventional scheme the sources report. Their charge was the cult of Vesta , the hearth: the undying fire in her round temple in the Forum, which might never go out — if it did, the Vestal responsible was scourged by the chief pontiff and the fire rekindled by friction from wood, as a new fire — the sacred storehouse ( penus Vestae ) whose contents no outsider might see, the preparation of the salted meal for public sacrifice, and the keeping of objects on which the state’s safety was believed to ride, among them, by tradition, the Palladium, the ancient image said to have come from Troy. The Vestals’ legal position was unique in Rome: removed from their father’s power without entering a husband’s, they could own property, make wills, and give evidence, were preceded by a lictor, and carried a sanctity that made injury to their persons a capital sacrilege and an accidental meeting with them, on the road, a reprieve for a condemned man being led to execution. The other face of that sanctity was its penalty. A Vestal who broke her vow of chastity committed incestum — a pollution of the state’s hearth, treated as a prodigy in a person — and was buried alive in an underground chamber near the Colline Gate with a lamp and small provisions, a rite carefully framed so that the city did not, in form, kill her; her lover was beaten to death in the Forum. The recorded cases are few across a thousand years and cluster at moments of public crisis — after the disaster at Cannae in 216 BCE two Vestals were condemned, in a season that also saw expiations of a far darker kind recorded by Livy with visible discomfort — and modern historians read the prosecutions as the system’s pressure-valve: when the pax deorum was felt to be broken beyond ordinary repair, suspicion fell on the guardians of the fire. The Vestals embody, in one institution, the household and the state fused: Vesta’s fire is the city’s hearth, as the fire of Section X is the family’s, and its keepers are daughters of no household because they are daughters of the city’s. Their end dates the old system’s end as precisely as any event can: the fire was extinguished and the order dissolved under Theodosius I in 394 CE, in the legislation treated in Section XV. VII. War Made Lawful: Fetiales, Vows, and the Sibylline Books Rome’s most distinctive theological claim was that its wars were just — not merely successful, but iusta , lawful in the sight of gods and men — and it maintained a priesthood whose whole charge was to make that claim procedurally true. The fetiales were twenty priests, keepers of the ius fetiale , the sacred law between peoples: they advised on treaties and their violation, demanded restitution for injuries, and performed the rites by which war was declared and peace sworn. Their procedures, which Livy sets out in Book 1 as archaic inheritances from the kings, are the clearest surviving specimen of Roman religion as law: a sequence of prescribed speeches, at prescribed stations, before prescribed witnesses, after
