Why Wing II Needs a Physics: The Operating Vocabulary This article belongs to the Foundations cluster of the Alchemy wing — Wing II — of the Greco-Roman hub. It is not an article about an alchemist, an apparatus, or a recipe. It is an article about the physics that the wing’s other articles keep presupposing, usually in a single unexplained word. When the article on Greek alchemy’s origins says that Bolos of Mendes catalogued the sympathies and antipathies of things, when the article on Zosimos of Panopolis says that a sublimed vapour is a pneuma and that a tincture is that spirit fixed in a body, and when the article on alchemical allegory says that the Stoics first taught Greek readers to decode a god into a physical principle, all three are spending a currency they did not mint. The mint was the Stoa. The claim of this article is a limited and a checkable one. Between roughly 300 and 200 BCE, in Athens, three successive heads of one philosophical school — Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BCE), Cleanthes of Assos (c. 331–232 BCE), and Chrysippus of Soli (c. 279–206 BCE) — built, and their successors maintained and argued over, a complete physics of a continuous, living, rational cosmos. In that physics a single material breath, the pneuma , pervades all matter; its tension, tonos , is what makes a stone one stone, a plant alive, an animal ensouled, and a human being rational; bodies can blend wholly through one another without either ceasing to be itself; and because the whole is one animal held together by one breath, what happens in one part can genuinely affect a distant part — the doctrine the Greeks called sympatheia , sympathy, literally a suffering-with or feeling-with. That is the doctrine, and the vocabulary, that the Hellenistic workshop inherited. The inheritance matters because sympathy, in the alchemical texts, is not a decorative metaphor. In Bolos it is offered as the reason a recipe works. In Zosimos the rising vapour is not like a spirit; in his Greek register it is a pneuma , a body fine enough to leave a body and to carry a quality into another body and fix it there. A reader who meets those claims without the Stoic physics behind them will read them as poetry, or as magic in the loose modern sense of the word. A reader who has the physics can see what their authors saw: a workshop application of the most systematic natural philosophy of the Hellenistic age. Recovering that difference — between a metaphor and a mechanism, as its users understood mechanism — is this article’s whole job. WHAT THIS ARTICLE IS The physics beneath Wing II’s operating vocabulary: the two principles, the designing fire, pneuma and tension, total mixture, cosmic sympathy, the conflagration and recurrence, and fate and providence in the brief form the physics requires — followed by the handover of that vocabulary to Bolos, to Zosimos, and to the allegorists. WHAT THIS ARTICLE IS NOT Not a life of Zeno, Cleanthes, or Chrysippus; not an account of Stoic logic or of Stoic ethics, except where the physics touches them; and not a claim that every alchemist was a Stoic. The alchemists were borrowers and adapters, and Section XV keeps the borrowing and the adapting distinct. A note on method, placed here because this subject, like the Hermetica treated in the companion article on the Hermetica , attracts confident quotation of texts that do not survive. No complete work of Zeno, Cleanthes, or Chrysippus on physics survives. Chrysippus alone was credited in antiquity with hundreds of books; not one of them comes down to us whole. What survives is testimony: summaries, paraphrases, and short quotations preserved inside the books of later writers — doxographers, commentators, physicians, church fathers, and, very often, the Stoics’ philosophical opponents. The backbone modern collection of that testimony, in new English translations with commentary, is A. A. Long and D. N. Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers (Cambridge, 1987), cited throughout this article as Long & Sedley , or by their section numbers (44 for the principles, 46 for God, fire, and the cosmic cycle, 47 for elements, breath, tenor, and tension, 48 for mixture, 52 for everlasting recurrence, 55 for causation and fate). Accordingly: verbatim quotation in this article is confined to passages whose wording is verified in a named translation, and the translation is named at the quotation. Everything else that reports a Stoic doctrine is paraphrase, and is presented as paraphrase. Where the ancient testimony disagrees with itself — and it does, on points this article is required to cover — the disagreement is stated, not smoothed over (Section XIV). // THE FOUNDATIONS CLUSTER // This article assumes, and repeatedly points to, its cluster companions: Aristotle on matter and mixture , for the Peripatetic physics the Stoics were answering; atomism , for the Democritean and Epicurean physics of particles and void that is Stoic continuism’s great rival; and Greek astrology , for the astral art that Stoic sympathy was used to underwrite. Read together, the four give Wing II its floor: what matter was, what the rival accounts of it were, and what followed from choosing this one. One further framing point, and it governs every section that follows. Stoic physics is not a detachable “science” module inside an otherwise ethical philosophy. The Stoics themselves divided philosophy into logic, physics, and ethics and then insisted, in the comparisons Diogenes Laertius preserves, that the parts are not separate: philosophy is compared, in paraphrase of Diogenes Laertius 7.39–40, to a living animal — logic the bones and sinews, ethics the flesh, physics the soul — and to an egg, and to a fertile field whose wall is logic, whose fruit is ethics, and whose soil and trees are physics. The comparisons are not ornaments. A school that held the cosmos to be one animal held its own philosophy to be one animal too, and it placed physics where the soul goes: innermost, animating, and impossible to remove without killing the whole. The modern popular Stoicism of handbooks and maxims, which keeps the ethics and discards the physics, would have struck the early Stoa as a dissection, not an abridgement. This article restores the discarded part — not because the ethics needs rescuing, but because the alchemists did not discard it. They took the physics, and left the maxims. II. The Evidence: A System Rebuilt from Other People’s Books Every statement in Sections III–XIII rests on evidence of a peculiar kind, and the reader is entitled to know its shape before being asked to trust any of it. The shape is this. Of the early Stoa’s own writings, what survives whole can be listed quickly: Cleanthes’ short Hymn to Zeus , preserved inside an anthology, is the famous exception that proves the rule. For the rest — for Zeno’s On Substance and On the Universe , for Cleanthes’ physical writings, for the enormous Chrysippean corpus on which the system chiefly rests — we have titles, summaries, and fragments: passages quoted, paraphrased, mocked, or refuted by later authors who had the books in front of them and had their own reasons for opening them. The Witnesses, in Rough Order of Usefulness The single most serviceable witness is Diogenes Laertius , whose Lives of Eminent Philosophers , written in the third century CE, devotes its seventh book to the Stoics. At 7.132–160 Diogenes gives a continuous, school-manual summary of Stoic physics: the division of the subject, the two principles, the elements, the cosmos and its ruling part, fate, divination, primary matter, mixture, the soul and its parts. The summary is compressed, occasionally garbled in transmission, and five centuries younger than Zeno — and it is still, by a wide margin, the closest thing to a Stoic physics textbook that antiquity left us. This article cites it constantly, by book and section, and quotes it, where it quotes it at all, in the Loeb translation of R. D. Hicks (1925), named at the quotation. A second English version, the older translation of C. D. Yonge (1853, reissued 1895), was also read in full for the physics sections in preparing this article, and is useful precisely because its divergences from Hicks mark the places where the Greek is hard. One such place matters and is flagged where it occurs: at 7.134 the tradition is unanimous that both principles are bodies, and renderings that make the principles incorporeal should be treated as a translator’s or copyist’s slip against the whole drift of the system (Sections III and XIV). Around Diogenes stands a crowd of witnesses, each with an angle. The doxographer conventionally called Aetius preserves placita — school positions in a line or two — including the celebrated definition of the Stoic god as designing fire and breath that Section V quotes from Long & Sedley’s translation. Stobaeus , anthologising in the fifth century CE, preserves long extracts from the Stoic Arius Didymus and others, including the two-kinds-of-fire testimony of Section V. Cicero , in On the Nature of the Gods , On Fate , and On Divination , gives Latin, first-century-BCE expositions and critiques of Stoic theology, providence, and divination that are among our fullest sources for Sections X–XIII — written by a sceptical Academic who understood the system he was attacking. Plutarch , in On Stoic Self-Contradictions and On Common Conceptions Against the Stoics , quotes Chrysippus extensively in order to convict him of inconsistency, and thereby preserves him. Alexander of Aphrodisias , the great Aristotelian commentator of the late second and early third centuries CE, wrote a whole treatise, On Mixture ( De mixtione ), against the Stoic theory of total blending, and a treatise On Fate against Stoic determinism; hostile, exact, and indispensable, he is the chief source for Section IX. Galen , the physician, preserves Stoic doctrine on breath, soul, and mixture inside medical polemic. Sextus Empiricus , Philo of Alexandria , Nemesius , Origen , Eusebius quoting the otherwise lost Aristocles, Aulus Gellius , Hippolytus — the list in Long & Sedley’s index of sources runs to dozens of names, and Sections III–XIII draw on the testimony under the names given there. // READING HOSTILE TESTIMONY // A doctrine reported by its refuter is evidence twice handled. Alexander wants blending to be absurd; Plutarch wants Chrysippus to contradict himself; the church fathers want the conflagration to be a pagan error awaiting correction. The modern method — Long & Sedley’s, and this article’s — is not to discard such witnesses, which would discard most of the evidence, but to read them against one another: where a hostile summary, a neutral doxography, and a sympathetic exposition converge on the same doctrine, the doctrine is as secure as anything in Hellenistic philosophy can be. Where they diverge, this article says so. The two principles, pneuma and tension, total blending, sympathy, and the conflagration all pass the convergence test. Several details inside them do not, and Section XIV collects the failures honestly. The Modern Reconstruction The testimony was first collected entire by Hans von Arnim in Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta (1903–1905), conventionally cited as SVF — the great Greek and Latin quarry from which all later work builds. Long & Sedley (1987) re-selected, re-translated, and commented the principal sources thematically, and their Stoic physics sections — 43, the scope of physics; 44, principles; 45, body; 46, God, fire, and the cosmic cycle; 47, elements, breath, tenor, and tension; 48, mixture; 49, place and void; 50, continuum; 51, time; 52, everlasting recurrence; 53, soul; 54, theology; 55, causation and fate — are the map this article follows. Two further modern works are used where they are apt, and their angles are different enough to be worth naming at the outset. S. Sambursky, The Physics of the Stoics (first published 1959) reads Stoic physics with a physicist’s eye, and is responsible, more than any other modern book, for the influential picture of pneuma as a continuum or field-like medium whose tension is a physical state of the body it informs — a picture Section XIV both uses and warns against taking for an ancient self-description. David E. Hahm, The Origins of Stoic Cosmology (1977) works in the opposite direction: not what Stoic physics resembles in modern science, but where it came from — arguing, in summary, that the Stoics built their cosmology by combining materials drawn from Plato’s Timaeus and receptacle and world-soul doctrines and from Aristotle’s accounts of generation, causation, and the divine, together with Presocratic elemental models, into a system neither predecessor would have owned. Where this article makes a claim about origins, it is Hahm’s kind of claim; where it makes a claim about structure, it is more often Sambursky’s or Long & Sedley’s. The three do not always agree, and the article does not pretend they do. Finally, a caution about the word “system” itself. Zeno founded, Cleanthes developed, Chrysippus — in the ancient tag, without whom there would have been no Stoa — systematised. But the school then lived for five more centuries, and later Stoics changed their minds in public: about the seat of the cosmos’s ruling part, about whether souls survive and for how long, about divination, and, most consequentially for this article, about whether the cosmos burns at all (Sections XII and XIV). “The Stoics hold” in what follows therefore means, unless a name is given, “the early Stoa as the testimony reconstructs it, with Chrysippus as its weightiest voice”. Where a doctrine belongs to one man against another, the men are named. That discipline — names, not just schools — is the difference between a reconstruction and a legend, and this article observes it throughout. III. Only Bodies Act: Corporealism and the Two Principles Stoic physics begins with a criterion of reality, taken over from a famous passage of Plato’s Sophist (247d–e) and then hardened. In paraphrase of the Stoic position as Long & Sedley present it (sections 27 and 45): to be, in the full sense, is to be able to act or to be acted upon; and only a body — a three-dimensional solid with resistance — can act or be acted upon. The conclusion is uncompromising. Only bodies exist. God is a body. The soul is a body. Qualities, virtues, breath, fire — if they do anything, they are bodies. A small class of incorporeals — place, void, time, and lekta , the sayables or meanings of speech — are allowed a lesser status, subsistence rather than existence, precisely because they neither act nor suffer action. Everything that does work in the world is solid, extended, and resistant. This corporealism is the load-bearing wall of the whole physics: remove it, and pneuma becomes a metaphor; keep it, and pneuma must be a stuff. Within the world of bodies, explanation bottoms out at two principles ( archai ). Diogenes Laertius states them at 7.134, in the passage on which this whole section rests. In the Loeb translation of R. D. Hicks (1925), quoted verbatim: They hold that there are two principles in the universe, the active principle and the passive. The passive principle, then, is a substance without quality, i.e. matter, whereas the active is the reason inherent in this substance, that is God. For he is everlasting and is the artificer of each several thing throughout the whole extent of matter. — DIOGENES LAERTIUS 7.134, TRANS. R. D. HICKS (LOEB, 1925) = LONG & SEDLEY 44B Unpack the sentence, term by term, because everything else in this article is commentary on it. The passive principle ( to paschon ) is unqualified substance ( apoios ousia ), matter: that which underlies everything, has of itself no quality, no form, no motion, and no resistance to being shaped, and can neither come to be nor perish. The active principle ( to poioun ) is the logos — reason — inherent in matter, and it is identified, without embarrassment and without remainder, with God . God, on this account, is not a craftsman standing outside his material, as the demiurge of Plato’s Timaeus is pictured standing outside his. The Stoic God is in the matter, everlasting as it is, and crafts each thing, in Diogenes’ phrase, throughout the whole of it. Diogenes immediately adds the pedigree: the doctrine is laid down, he says in paraphrase, by Zeno in On Substance , by Cleanthes, by Chrysippus towards the end of the first book of his Physics , by Archedemus, and by Posidonius. This is not one man’s speculation. It is the school’s foundation deed, signed by five names across two centuries. THE PASSIVE PRINCIPLE — TO PASCHON Unqualified substance; matter (hulē). No quality, form, or motion of its own. Ungenerated and indestructible. That which is acted upon, shaped, divided, and qualified — never, in the actual world, found alone and bare. THE ACTIVE PRINCIPLE — TO POIOUN Logos, reason inherent in matter; God; Zeus; designing fire; pneuma. Everlasting as matter is. That which acts: crafts, qualifies, coheres, moves, and orders each thing throughout the whole extent of matter. Three consequences follow at once, and the article will keep returning to all three. First, both principles are bodies. That is the point on which the testimony, read whole, is firm — Long & Sedley’s section 44 is built on it — and it is what makes the Stoic God a physical doctrine rather than a theology pasted onto a physics. A bodily God can be mixed with bodily matter, can be present in different degrees and tensions in different places, and can literally be the breath in an animal’s chest and the coherence in a stone. An incorporeal God could do none of those things except by metaphor, and the Stoics, who allowed incorporeals to subsist but never to act, had closed the metaphorical door on purpose. Second, the principles are inseparable. They are distinguished in thought; they are never found apart in fact. There is no moment, not even at the conflagration of Section XII, at which bare matter sits waiting to be informed, and no place at which the active principle floats free of a material vehicle. The pair is an analysis of the one world, not an inventory of two worlds. Third, the principles are everlasting, and the elements are not. Diogenes draws exactly this contrast at 7.134, in paraphrase: principles and elements differ, in that the principles are ungenerated and indestructible, whereas the elements are destroyed at the conflagration; and the principles are unformed, whereas the elements have taken form. Keep the contrast in hand. It is what allows the cosmos to be, at once, eternal in its constituents and periodic in its arrangements — the hinge on which Section XII turns. It is worth pausing on how strange the passive principle is, since later alchemy inherits a cousin of it. Unqualified substance is not any kind of stuff. It is not wet, dry, hot, cold, bright, dark, heavy, or light; each of those is a qualification the active principle has imposed. Nor is it a heap of particles: Stoic matter is continuous, infinitely divisible without ever reaching an indivisible minimum — the doctrine of the continuum in Long & Sedley’s section 50 — and the school’s rejection of atoms is not an oversight but a theorem (Section IX). Diogenes returns to primary matter at 7.150, in paraphrase of the Yonge and Hicks renderings alike: the substance of all things is primary matter; matter as a whole neither increases nor decreases, though the matter of particular things does both; and body is finite, changeable, and divisible without end. A substrate that never appears unqualified, is never exhausted, and has no smallest part: the Stoics were aware that such a thing is known by reason rather than displayed to sense, and they accepted the consequence. What sense displays is always the blend — the peculiarly qualified individual, this stone, this plant, this person — in which the two principles are already, and inseparably, at work. // NOT PLATO’S CRAFTSMAN, NOT ARISTOTLE’S FORM // The Stoic pair is easiest to misread as a re-labelling of an older pair: Plato’s demiurge and receptacle, or Aristotle’s form and matter. Hahm’s Origins shows how much material the Stoics genuinely took from both — and the differences are the doctrine. Aristotle’s form is not a body and does not travel through its matter; Plato’s craftsman works from outside, on a model he did not make. The Stoic active principle is a body, is inside, and is its own model: the seminal principles of Section V are not Forms in a separate heaven but reasons carried in the fire itself. See the cluster companion, Aristotle on matter and mixture , for the position being answered. A last distinction, without which the next two sections blur. Principles explain; elements compose. The two principles are the world analysed into agent and patient. The four elements — fire, air, water, earth — are the first formed bodies into which, and out of which, the world’s furniture is actually made and unmade. Confusing the two levels is the commonest beginner’s error in reading Stoic physics, and the school’s own summary in Diogenes is careful about it in a way popular accounts rarely are. God is not a fifth element, and matter is not a zeroth one. They are what elements, and everything made from elements, are made of — the active breath and the passive body it breathes through, all the way down. IV. The Four Elements in Stoic Dress The Stoics kept the canonical four elements of Greek physics — fire, air, water, earth — and redressed every one of them. The redressing, not the list, is the doctrine. Three changes matter: the elements are qualified from the start; they are divided into active and passive pairs; and fire is promoted from first among equals to the element from which the others derive and into which they resolve. Diogenes states the qualifications at 7.137. In paraphrase, following both the Hicks and the Yonge renderings: the four elements together are unqualified substance — matter — but taken singly, fire is the hot, water the moist (or wet), air the cold, and earth the dry. The sentence has troubled editors — the companion discussion in modern scholarship of how elements can be both matter and qualified is genuine, and is noted in Section XIV — but its physical intent is plain enough. An element, for the Stoics, is not a neutral building block awaiting a quality. It is a primary quality carried by a body: heat, cold, wetness, dryness in their purest available forms. That is why elemental change, for the Stoics, is real transformation rather than rearrangement. When air condenses to water, nothing has been shuffled; a body has changed its tension and its quality, through and through — a claim that only makes sense inside the mixture theory of Section IX, and that the atomist alternative, treated in the atomism article , exists precisely to deny. Element Primary quality (DL 7.137, paraphrase) Role Fire The hot Active. Pre-eminent: the element from which the others are generated and into which the cosmos resolves at the conflagration. In its designing form, the vehicle of the active principle itself. Air The cold Active. With fire, constitutes pneuma. Its contractive, condensing work supplies unity and resistance; the medium of sound, of vision’s tensed cone, and of the soul’s messengers. Water The moist / wet Passive. With earth, the sustained and shaped pair: the material the active elements hold together, nourish, and qualify. Earth The dry Passive. The densest element, settled at the centre of the spherical cosmos; the sediment, in Diogenes’ image at 7.137, of the rest. The active–passive division of the elements is the two principles reappearing at the elemental level. The testimony is explicit: a passage of Nemesius, cited in the modern collections and discussed in Long & Sedley’s section 47, reports in paraphrase that the Stoics held some elements to be active and others passive — fire and air active, earth and water passive — the upper, rarer pair doing the sustaining and the lower, denser pair being sustained. The architecture is fractal, and deliberately so: agent and patient at the level of principles; active and passive at the level of elements; and, in Section VIII, tenor, nature, and soul as grades of the same agency at the level of things. A Stoic explanation is recognisable across the centuries by exactly this signature — the same two-handed pattern, applied at every scale, with nothing left over that acts from outside the pattern. Fire’s promotion needs its own paragraph, because Wing II lives downstream of it. In the cosmogony Diogenes summarises at 7.135–136 and 7.142 — paraphrased in Section V — the world is not assembled from four co-eternal elements. Substance turns, at the beginning of a cosmic cycle, from fire through air into moisture; the thick part of the moisture settles as earth, the thin part is rarefied as air and, rarefied further, kindles again as fire; and from the mixture of the elements so produced come plants, animals, and the rest. Fire is therefore both the first state of the whole and the last: at the conflagration everything resolves into it, and out of it the ordered world condenses again. Diogenes’ arrangement at 7.137, in paraphrase, gives the settled cosmos its onion of spheres: highest, the fire called aether, in which the sphere of the fixed stars is generated, then the planetary sphere, then air, then water, and earth, like a sediment, at the centre of all. Note what this is not. It is not the Aristotelian cosmos of a fifth, celestial element moving naturally in circles above a corruptible sublunary world. The Stoic heaven is fire — the same element that burns in a hearth, in its purest and most designing state — and the stars, in testimony Diogenes and Stobaeus preserve, are intelligent, fiery, and nourished by exhalations from sea and earth. One physics, from the fixed stars to the sediment: that monism, as much as any single doctrine, is what the alchemists bought when they bought the Stoa. // WHY THE WORKSHOP CARED ABOUT ELEMENTS // A recipe tradition that heats, condenses, sublimes, and dissolves is, whether it says so or not, a technology of elemental change. Stoic elemental theory told the Hellenistic workshop three usable things: that change of quality is real and total, not a rearrangement of changeless grains; that the active agents in any operation are the hot and the cold, fire and air, working on the wet and the dry; and that the rarest, most fiery fraction of a body is also its most powerful. The dyeing, gilding, and purple recipes of the Physika kai Mystika tradition are not Stoic treatises — but their operations are exactly the operations this physics describes best. V. The Designing Fire and the Seminal Principles The active principle has a biography inside the school, and the biography explains the vocabulary Wing II inherited. Zeno’s characteristic name for the active principle, on the testimony, was fire — not the destructive fire of the hearth but a creative, craftsmanlike fire. Cleanthes developed the fiery theology, located the cosmos’s ruling part in the sun, and gave the school its one surviving complete poem, the Hymn to Zeus , in which the universal logos steers all things. Chrysippus then refined fire into the subtler and more versatile instrument the mature system runs on: pneuma , breath, fire blended with air. Section VI takes up the refinement. This section keeps the fire, because two of the system’s central notions — the designing fire and the seminal principles — are stated in its language and never quite lose its accent. The definition is Aetius’, and it is the second of this article’s two verbatim quotations. In Long & Sedley’s translation ( The Hellenistic Philosophers , 1987, section 46A), quoted verbatim: The Stoics made god out to be intelligent, a designing fire which methodically proceeds towards creation of the world, and encompasses all the seminal principles according to which everything comes about according to fate, and a breath pervading the whole world, which takes on different names owing to the alterations of the matter through which it passes. — AETIUS 1.7.33, TRANS. LONG & SEDLEY (1987) 46A “Designing fire” renders pyr technikon : fire that works technikōs , with art, as a craftsman works — methodically, the translation says, proceeding by a road towards the production of a world. Diogenes gives the same phrase in his own summary at 7.156, in paraphrase: nature is a designing fire, proceeding methodically to creation, a fiery breath proceeding according to art. The contrast class is stated in a testimony of Zeno preserved by Stobaeus (1.213, in Long & Sedley’s section 46), here in paraphrase: there are two kinds of fire — the undesigning kind, which converts its fuel into itself, and the designing kind, which causes growth and preservation, as in plants, where it is their nature, and in animals, where it is their soul; and such, Zeno is reported as saying, is the fire that constitutes the substance of the stars. Hold the contrast firmly. Stoic fire is not combustion with a compliment attached. It is a defined technical term: the hot, active body in its ordering, preserving, life-giving employment, as distinct from the same element in its consuming employment. When later alchemical writing distinguishes a fire that cooks from a fire that destroys — a distinction the workshop literature makes constantly — it is spending this Stoic coin, whether or not the writer could have named the mint. The Seminal Principles (Spermatikoi Logoi) A designing fire that merely heated would explain a warm world, not an ordered one. The ordering is done by the seminal principles — spermatikoi logoi , seminal reasons — which the Aetius definition says the fire encompasses, and according to which everything comes about. The governing image is biological, and Hahm’s Origins is the modern account that takes the biology most seriously: as a seed contains, in miniature and in programme, the whole future organism and the timetable of its unfolding, so the primordial fire contains the logoi of all things — the rational formulae, carried materially in the fire itself, from which each kind of thing, and in the Chrysippean strong version each individual thing and event, develops in its appointed sequence. Diogenes states the cosmogonic form of the image at 7.135–136, in paraphrase: God, being alone at the beginning, turns the whole of substance through air into water; and as the seed is enveloped in the seminal fluid, so God, the seminal principle of the world, remains in the moisture, making matter serviceable to himself for the successive stages of creation, and then creates first the four elements. Eusebius, quoting Aristocles, preserves the conflagration-side statement (Long & Sedley 46G), likewise in paraphrase: at fated times the whole world is conflagrated and reconstituted, and the primary fire is as it were a seed, possessing the principles of all things and the causes of past, present, and future events, whose nexus and succession is fate. Two warnings about the seminal principles, both necessary. First, they are not Platonic Forms . A Form, in the Platonic scheme the Stoics knew and rejected, is incorporeal, separate, and contemplated by a craftsman who copies it into matter from outside. A spermatikos logos is corporeal, inseparable, and inside: a portion of the designing fire’s own rational structure, differentiated by the matter it is developing. Proclus, in antiquity, already tried the equation of seminal principles with Forms, and modern scholarship — the point is standard in the commentary tradition Long & Sedley represent — rejects it. Second, the principles are not a blueprint consulted once . Because the fire that carries them never leaves the world it made, the logoi remain at work as the world’s continuing natures: the seminal principle of an oak is not exhausted in the acorn, and the seminal principle of the cosmos is not exhausted in the cosmogony. Development, growth, generation, decay — the whole traffic of nature — is the seminal principles still proceeding methodically. That is why one Greek word, physis , can mean both the nature of a single plant and Nature as the governing whole, and why Section VIII’s ladder can place the plant’s physis and the sage’s reason on a single scale of one breath’s tension. PYR TECHNIKON — DESIGNING FIRE The active principle under its elemental description: intelligent, methodical, productive. Contrasted with undesigning fire, which only consumes its fuel. The substance of the stars; in plants, their nature; in animals, their soul (Zeno, in Stobaeus, paraphrased above). SPERMATIKOI LOGOI — SEMINAL PRINCIPLES The rational programmes carried in the designing fire, according to which each thing develops in sequence. Corporeal and immanent, not separate Forms. At the conflagration, the primary fire as seed holds the principles of all things, past, present, and future. Diogenes gathers the identifications into a single sentence at 7.135, in paraphrase: God and mind and fate and Zeus are one thing, called by many names. The sentence is the school’s theology in miniature, and Section XIII will need it: the many names are not many gods, and not mere aliases either, but the one active principle named from its several employments — as reason, as craftsman, as the chain of causes, as the ruler of the whole. The Other Half of the Promise This article exists because another article in this hub made a promise and then, quite properly, kept only half of it. The hub’s Hermetica article opens — in its Section I, “Two Families Under One Name” — by dividing everything written under the name of Hermes Trismegistus into two families. The philosophical Hermetica are dialogues, discourses, hymns, and prayers about God, the cosmos, and the soul’s way back to its source. The technical Hermetica are practical works: astrological treatises and catalogues, alchemical recipes and allegories, magical procedures, and writings on the hidden properties of plants, stones, and animals. The Hermetica article then follows the first family — the Corpus Hermeticum , the Asclepius , Ficino, Casaubon — because that family has the datable manuscripts, the famous translation, and the famous redating. The second family was named, carded, and left at the door. This article is the second family’s article. It picks up exactly that promise, and the Hermetica article remains what it was designed to be: the owner of the Corpus in this hub, to which the reader should go for the seventeen treatises, the Poimandrēs , and the Renaissance. Nothing in what follows retells that story. What follows instead is the bench-level literature of the same world. Where the philosophical treatises ask what the soul is and where it is going, the technical writings ask narrower and more urgent questions. Under which decan was this child born, and which part of his body will suffer for it? On which day will this fever turn? Which plant, gathered under which star, answers to this pain? What image, cut into which stone and set above which herb, will hold the illness off? Which hour is fit to begin the work in the furnace, and which is not? The answers were issued under the same name as the dialogues — Hermes, the thrice-greatest — and they were issued earlier. Some of the astrological Hermetica may reach back to the second or third century BCE , centuries before the earliest philosophical treatise that scholarship will accept. The technical family is not the philosophical family’s degeneration, still less its appendix. On the chronology the evidence supports, it is closer to being its elder sibling: the dialogues about escaping fate were written into a world that already possessed, under Hermes’ name, a large literature for calculating fate in detail. THE PHILOSOPHICAL FAMILY — ELSEWHERE The Corpus Hermeticum, the Latin Asclepius, the Stobaean excerpts, the Vienna fragments, and the Nag Hammadi Hermetica: theology, cosmology, and rebirth through knowledge. Owned, in this hub, by the Hermetica article, whose Section I states the two-families division this article completes. THE TECHNICAL FAMILY — HERE Astrological, medical, magical, and alchemical writings under Hermes’ name: the Nechepso–Petosiris tradition, the Liber Hermetis, the decan books, the iatromathematical fragments, the Kyranides, and Hermes as the alchemists cited him. Practical in aim: elections, remedies, operations, and the sympathies of things. A note on method, in the same terms the sibling article set for itself. No direct quotation from a technical Hermetic text is given in this article unless it is explicitly attributed to a named translation. The technical corpus survives largely in fragments, excerpts, and layered compilations, often in Latin or Arabic dress over lost Greek, and its wording is correspondingly easy to fake and hard to check. The article therefore paraphrases throughout, and says so where it paraphrases. The one extended exception is the prologue of the Kyranides in its seventeenth-century English dress (Section IX), quoted briefly, verbatim, and under its translator’s title, because that wording can be verified against the printed book. Everything else is labelled paraphrase or follows a named modern account — Fowden, Festugière, and the specialist literature listed in Section XVI. And the standing warning of this hub applies here with double force, because the technical literature invites it: these are pseudepigrapha . No text treated in this article was written by a historical Hermes Trismegistus, for there was no such historical person: there was a god — Thoth in Greek dress — a legendary sage built upon the god, and an authorising name under which priests, astrologers, physicians, and compilers published their work for the better part of a thousand years. “Hermes says” in a technical text means what “Hermes says” means in a philosophical one: a writer, whose name we almost never know, claimed the oldest authority his culture afforded. The hub says this plainly everywhere, and this article says it first rather than last, because the technical texts wear their attributions more variously than the dialogues do — a king of Egypt, a Persian king, an Alexandrian rhetor writing to his daughter, a physician taught face to face by a god — and each costume is part of the evidence, not a distraction from it. // WHERE THIS ARTICLE SITS // This is a Wing II foundations article. It stands behind the hub’s named practitioners — behind Zosimos of Panopolis and the other alchemists — as the literature of the world they worked in, and beside two companion foundations: the hub’s account of Greek astrology , which owns the technical astronomy and the horoscope’s machinery, and its account of the humours and Galen , which owns the medical theory against which Hermetic medicine defined itself. Pointers to both recur below, and mark the seams rather than filling them twice. The plan of the article follows the family’s own centre of gravity. Sections II–III define the category and inventory the corpus. Sections IV–VI take the astrological Hermetica, the family’s oldest and largest branch, from its fountainhead tradition through the Liber Hermetis to the decans in which its Egyptian inheritance is most visible. Sections VII–VIII take the medical branch — iatromathematics, the medicine of the stars — in theory and in its surviving Hermetic texts. Sections IX–XI give the Kyranides , the family’s best-surviving single book, the three sections its scale earns: its structure, its layered composition, and its actual use. Sections XII–XIII take the alchemical Hermetica and the magical borderland briefly — briefly, because this hub treats alchemy in its own articles and the Egyptology division treats the magical papyri in theirs. What “Technical” Means: Sympathy, Election, and the Working Text “Technical” is a scholar’s word, and it should be unpacked before it hardens. It does not mean mechanical, and it does not mean modern. It renders the sense of the Greek technē — an art, a craft, a body of procedures that can be taught, looked up, and applied — and it marks the difference of use between the two Hermetic families. A philosophical treatise is read, meditated, and argued with; a technical treatise is consulted . It is built for the moment of need: the consultation, the sickbed, the workshop, the engraving bench. Its characteristic forms follow from that use — the catalogue, the table, the alphabetised entry, the aphorism, the recipe, the list of correspondences — and its characteristic question is never “what is true?” in the abstract but “what answers to what, and what do I do now?” Festugière’s Occult Sciences The modern study of the family begins, as so much Hermetic study does, with A.-J. Festugière . The first volume of his La révélation d’Hermès Trismégiste (1944) — L’astrologie et les sciences occultes , “Astrology and the Occult Sciences” — remains the founding survey of the technical corpora, and its taxonomy is still the one the reference literature repeats. Among the works of the occult sciences, Festugière distinguished three great kinds, with three different early edges: astrology , beginning in the third or second century BCE; alchemy , beginning in the second or first century BCE; and magic , recorded in papyri of the fourth to seventh centuries CE that reproduce sources obviously much more ancient. Medicine, in the form of astrological medicine, runs through all three rather than standing as a fourth kind: the decan that governs a body part also governs its diseases, its plants, and the stones cut for its cure. Festugière’s judgement on the two families’ relation was severe, and it is part of the record. He held, in paraphrase of his position, that the philosophical Hermetica had only slight connections with the technical: the occult texts he was ready to credit to the Egyptian priesthood, while the philosophical treatises he read as the work of Greek writers of modest culture dressing Greek doctrine in Egyptian costume. On that reading the families share a name and little else — two literatures, two milieux, one borrowed brand. The severity matters because the correction of it is the second founding moment of the field, and because something of Festugière’s instinct survives in every library catalogue that shelves the Corpus Hermeticum under philosophy and the Kyranides under folklore. Fowden’s Single Milieu Garth Fowden , in The Egyptian Hermes (1986), argued the counter-case that has structured discussion since — the same argument the sibling article adopts for the philosophical family, stated there and applied here to both. The two families, on Fowden’s account, are distinct but interdependent : products of a single, complex Greco-Egyptian milieu — the world of Ptolemaic, Roman, and early Christian Egypt, and above all of its temples and their priestly intellectuals, for whom Greek was a working language and Greek learning a usable idiom, but whose institutions, gods, and practices were their own. The families shared readers, copyists, and assumptions; a man might copy a dialogue on rebirth and a catalogue of decans in the same season, and the alchemist Zosimos, around 300 CE, quotes Hermes in both registers without marking any border (Section XII). More recent work has tightened the connection further still: Christian Bull’s study of the Physica of Hermes (2018) argues, in paraphrase, that a technical treatise known to Zosimos likely stands behind passages of the philosophical Perfect Discourse and the Kore Kosmou — that the traffic between the families ran at the level of composition, not merely of readership. The position this article adopts is Fowden’s, for the reason the sibling article gave: it is the position the evidence currently supports. The division is real as a division of kinds of text and histories of transmission . It is not a wall, and antiquity did not observe it. SYMPATHY AND ANTIPATHY The family’s physics in two words. Things that share a star, a decan, a letter, or a nature attract, reinforce, and cure one another; things opposed repel and harm. The Kyranides’ own full title, in paraphrase, announces a book of physical virtues, sympathies, and antipathies — the doctrine is on the title page. ELECTION — KATARCHĒ The family’s practical core. Every undertaking has a moment at which it must begin if it is to prosper: the hour to gather the herb, cut the stone, begin the treatment, start the work. Technical astrology is, in large part, the art of finding that moment — and Hermetic astrology is its oldest Greek literature. CORRESPONDENCE LISTS The family’s characteristic page. Star to plant, decan to stone, sign to limb, letter to bird, fish, herb, and gem: knowledge stored as alignment, so that the practitioner who knows the row knows the remedy. The list is not a primitive table of contents. It is the theory, in storage form. THE AUTHORISING NAME The family’s title page. Hermes, a pharaoh, a priest, a Persian king: attribution as authorisation. A technical claim — this stone cures, this hour avails — needed an authority older than argument, and Egypt, in Greek eyes, was where such authority lived. One more definition, because the family’s modern reputation suffers from its absence. To call these texts “occult” — Festugière’s word, and the tradition’s — is to say that they traffic in hidden properties : virtues in stones, plants, and animals that no inspection of their manifest qualities reveals, and that operate by sympathy rather than by contact mechanics. It is not to say that their users experienced them as a separate, shadowy domain set against ordinary knowledge. For the physician who consulted a decan table, the astrologer who elected an hour, and the compiler who alphabetised the virtues of birds, this was ordinary knowledge — the working natural philosophy of the world Wing II’s practitioners inhabited. The hub’s foundations cluster exists to make that world legible: the Greek astrology article supplies its sky, the humours and Galen article its learned medicine, and this article its Hermetic working library. // A DATING WARNING, BEFORE THE INVENTORY // The technical family has no Casaubon moment and no single corpus to date, and its dates must be handled text by text. Three different things are routinely confused: the date a tradition claims (a pharaoh of the seventh century BCE), the date its material may reach back to (in places, the second or third century BCE), and the date of the compilation or manuscript that actually survives (often Byzantine, sometimes a millennium later). This article keeps the three apart wherever it gives a date, and gives ranges where the scholarship gives ranges. Fowden’s own caution stands at the head of the subject: our earliest firm testimonies to Hermetic astrology belong to the first century BCE, however much older the material they testify to may be. III. A Working Library, Not a Book: The Shape of the Corpus The philosophical Hermetica can be tabled in a page: seventeen treatises, a Latin dialogue, a set of excerpts. The technical Hermetica cannot, and the reason is itself informative. There was never a technical corpus in the Byzantine editors’ sense — no Psellos gathered the decan books between two covers. What survives is a working library : hundreds of treatises, excerpts, catalogues, and fragments, in Greek, Latin, Arabic, and the languages beyond them, scattered through astrological miscellanies, medical handbooks, alchemical codices, and magical papyri, much of it anonymous or pseudonymous, much of it still unedited in the manuscripts where the great cataloguing projects of a century ago recorded it. Modern scholarship is candid that the technical Hermetica — Greek, Arabic, and Latin together — remain largely unexplored beside the philosophical treatises. Section XIV. Three features of that inventory deserve emphasis before the detail begins. First, its chronological sprawl : the family’s composition runs from the Hellenistic centuries to the high Middle Ages without a break — Hermetic technical writing was still being produced, translated, and expanded in the twelfth century, long after the philosophical treatises had settled into their Byzantine corpus. Second, its linguistic sprawl : Greek is the family’s first language, but Latin and Arabic are not mere afterlives — the Liber Hermetis survives only in Latin, the Kyranides was reworked in both, and a large Arabic Hermetic literature, some of it translated from Greek or through Persian and Syriac intermediaries, some of it composed in Arabic under the name, awaits the study the Greek material has had. Third, its anonymity in practice : for every text that trumpets Hermes on its title, the astrological codices carry a dozen excerpts headed simply “from Hermes”, “the Egyptian says”, or nothing at all, whose Hermetic paternity is a cataloguer’s inference. The family is best imagined not as a shelf of books but as a sediment — layers of attributed, excerpted, and reattributed working material, in which the name Hermes functions less like an author’s signature than like a stratum marker: this layer claims Egypt, antiquity, and revelation. // HOW TO READ THE SECTIONS THAT FOLLOW // Each branch is treated in the same order: the claim the texts make about themselves, the state in which they actually survive, the machinery they teach, and the use to which a working reader put them. Where the hub has a fuller treatment — Greek astrology’s machinery, Galenic medicine’s theory, the Emerald Tablet’s Arabic home, the alchemists’ own articles — the section says so and stops at the seam. The seams are the hub’s map, not its gaps. IV. Nechepso and Petosiris: The Fountainhead Tradition Greek astrology, when it tells its own origin story, does not begin with Hermes alone. It begins with a king and a priest . The king is Nechepso — the name under which the historical pharaoh Necho II (reigned 610–595 BCE), of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, entered the astrological tradition. The priest is Petosiris — “gift of Osiris” — a name borne by a famous high priest of Thoth of about 300 BCE, though whether the astrological author was meant to be that man, or another of the name, cannot be known. Under these two names there circulated, from the second century BCE , a body of astrological writing that later antiquity treated as the fountainhead of the art: the oldest, most authoritative, and most oracular stratum of Greek astrology, from which the named astrologers of the Roman centuries — Dorotheus, Valens, Hephaistio, and their fellows — drew and against which they measured themselves. The attribution needs its plain statement, in the hub’s manner: the Nechepso–Petosiris texts are pseudepigrapha . Anonymous works of the Hellenistic centuries were fathered on a pharaoh five hundred years dead and on his legendary priest, and the fathering was the point. But the tradition is Hermetic at its root, and says so in its own genealogy. The Latin astrologer Firmicus Maternus , in the fourth century CE, gives the chain of transmission in paraphrase: the material originates with the legendary sage Mercury — Hermes — passes to Asclepius, and is then elaborated by the Egyptian pharaoh Nechepso and the high priest Petosiris. The fragments themselves ascribe the knowledge they convey to the authority of Hermes: Petosiris, in the tradition’s frame, took his revelation from Hermes, and the king was guided by the priest into a vision that granted him horoscopic truth. Hermes stands behind the king and the priest as Thoth stands behind Egyptian writing itself — not the working author of the handbook, but the god of the archive from which the handbook was supposedly copied. Every later Hermetic astrological text lives somewhere downstream of that arrangement. What Survives, and in Whom Of the fountainhead itself, nothing survives whole. What survives is a debris of fragments and testimonies — quotations, paraphrases, and respectful citations embedded in the astrologers who used the work — collected by Ernst Riess in 1892–1893 and brought up to date by Stephan Heilen in the present century; a complete modern edition of the fragments is still lacking. The chief quarries are the Anthology of Vettius Valens (second century CE), who cites the king and Petosiris by name at the foundations of his system — the Lot of Fortune’s calculation, in Valens’s account, stands at the opening of the king’s thirteenth book, expounded, as Valens complains in paraphrase, in an enigmatic fashion that later writers have never stopped reinterpreting — and the Apotelesmatika of Hephaistio of Thebes (about 415 CE), whose first book closes with a long excerpt on eclipse delineation that shows the fountainhead’s oldest layer at work. Proclus and John Lydus preserve further fragments in late antiquity. The modern reference classification groups the fragments under four heads, and the grouping is a fair map of the early art’s whole range: ASTRAL OMENS General indications from eclipses, comets, halos, winds, and the heliacal rising of Sirius, developed in Ptolemaic Egypt from Mesopotamian prototypes — the Babylonian inheritance in Egyptian dress, and the stratum by which scholars dated the whole to the second century BCE. THE REVELATION AND THE HOROSCOPE The vision-text in which the king, guided by Petosiris, receives horoscopic truth, and the doctrines that flow from it — lots, places, and the reading of a nativity. The fountainhead of horoscopic astrology proper, whose machinery the hub’s Greek astrology article owns. ASTROLOGICAL BOTANY AND DECANIC MEDICINE A treatise on astrological botany for medical purposes, and another on decanic medicine — the fountainhead already flows into the sickroom. The medical branch of the family (Sections VII–VIII) begins here, in the second century BCE, inside the astrological corpus itself. NUMEROLOGY AND THE LOTS Treatises on significant numbers and on the calculated places — the Lots — by which a chart’s abstract geometry was turned into judgements about fortune, spirit, and the times of a life. Two scholarly cautions belong with the fountainhead, and this article records both rather than smoothing them. The first is the older scholarship’s temptation, now resisted: to assign every anonymous early fragment — every “the ancients say”, every “the Egyptians hold” — to Nechepso and Petosiris, making one lost handbook explain all of early astrology. Joachim Friedrich Quack’s work on the Demotic evidence has shown, in paraphrase of his argument, that a rich Egyptian astrological tradition existed beyond the two names, and that the works attributed to them were not necessarily one and the same book. The fountainhead is a tradition, not a codex. The second caution runs the other way: fragmentary survival is not insignificance. When Valens, the most practical astrologer of antiquity whose work survives whole, builds his Lots on the king’s thirteenth book and argues with Petosiris’s Definitions across six centuries of supposed distance, the deference is itself the datum. The Nechepso–Petosiris texts were to Greek astrology what Hermes was to the whole Hermetic library: the authority that did not need to be read entire to be obeyed — which is fortunate, since they could not be. // THE EGYPTIAN SIDE OF THE FOUNTAINHEAD // The names were not Greek inventions pasted onto Egypt from outside. Necho II was a real Saite pharaoh; Petosiris was a real priestly name, borne by the high priest of Thoth whose tomb at Tuna el-Gebel is among the famous monuments of the early Ptolemaic age; and Demotic astrological material under Nechepso’s name has been identified in Egyptian sources. The pseudepigraphy worked because it was plausible: Egypt had priest-astrologers, temple archives, and a star science older than Greece’s, and the Greek handbook claimed, in Greek, to be their translation. The fountainhead tradition also fixes the family’s geography and social setting at its source. This is the astrology of Ptolemaic Egypt : Babylonian omen lore and mathematical schemes, Egyptian calendar and decan lore, and Greek geometrical and philosophical habits of system, meeting in the temples and the Alexandrian libraries of a kingdom where all three were in daily contact. The Salmeschoiniaka — the “Wandering of the Influences”, perhaps Alexandrian, perhaps of the same second or third century BCE — belongs to the same moment: configurations of stars read as powers moving through the zodiac. The Art of Eudoxus , preserved on a papyrus of the second century BCE and already citing Hermes as an authority, shows the arrangement in physical form within a generation or two of the fountainhead’s composition. When the philosophical Hermetica were written, four centuries later, Hermes the astrologer was already ancient. Hermes the theologian was the newcomer. V. Hermetic Astrology Proper: The Liber Hermetis and the Catalogue Tradition Beside the fountainhead tradition — Hermetic by genealogy, royal and priestly by attribution — there stands a second astrological stratum that bears Hermes’ name on its own title: the astrological Hermetica proper. Its principal survivor is the Liber Hermetis , the “Book of Hermes”, and its survival states the family’s condition in one line: the book exists only in Latin , in an early translation conventionally dated to the fourth or fifth century CE, of a Greek compilation whose elements may be traced to the second or third century BCE. The Greek is lost. What the Latin preserves is not a treatise but a compilation of compilations — a gathering of short, freestanding chapters on the working topics of the art, of the kind a practitioner’s handbook accumulates: the thirty-six decans of the twelve signs with their forms; the bright stars and their natures; the lots; the twelve places; the climacteric years, those dangerous years of a life at which the astrologer was expected to look twice; and the consideration of the figure of a nativity as a whole. The standard edition is Wilhelm Gundel ’s of 1936 — Neue astrologische Texte des Hermes Trismegistos , “New Astrological Texts of Hermes Trismegistus” — and the book is read today in the Latin Gundel printed, in the English translation Robert Zoller made from it for the Project Hindsight recovery of Hellenistic astrology. Its first chapter, on the decans, is the bridge to Section VI, and the oldest stratum of decan lore in the family’s Greek line. Around the Liber the catalogue tradition spreads in every direction, and its scale is the point. The great modern map of it is the Catalogus Codicum Astrologorum Graecorum — the CCAG — the twelve-volume catalogue and edition of the Greek astrological manuscripts undertaken under Franz Cumont’s leadership and published at Brussels between 1898 and 1953. The CCAG’s editors scoured the libraries of Europe for astrological codices and printed, volume by volume, the excerpts those codices contained; and through its pages the Hermetic stratum runs like a seam: chapters headed with Hermes’ name on the decans, on the fixed stars, on inceptional astrology — the katarchai , the elections of Section II — on the prognosis of the sick, on thunder and earthquakes, excerpted, re-excerpted, and bound among the works of Valens, Hephaistio, Rhetorius, and the Byzantine compilers. Much of this material has never been translated, and some of it has never been edited since the CCAG printed it. To speak of “Hermetic astrology” as a book is therefore a convenience. It was a stratum of the astrological manuscript tradition , continuously mined by the tradition’s working astrologers, who treated “Hermes” the way their successors treated a standard authority: as the name you cite when the doctrine is older than your other sources. The Weather Shelf and the Omen Books The stratum’s humblest members repay a paragraph, because they show the family’s range at its widest. The Brontologion — the thunder book — sets out, in paraphrase of its scheme, what thunder portends in each month of the year: a calendar of the sky’s noises, descended from the Babylonian omen series through the same Egyptian mediation as the fountainhead’s astral omens. The Peri seismōn , “On Earthquakes”, relates earthquakes to the astrological signs under which they occur. Neither text pretends to philosophy; both pretend to Hermes, or travel in his company; and both were copied for centuries because the need they answer — a public event, a frightened city, a ruler who must be told what the sign means — never went away. The technical Hermetica include the literature of the consultation as well as of the study, and the omen books are where the family touches the oldest divinatory practice of the ancient Near East most directly. What Hermetic Astrology Is Not A boundary should be drawn here, because the name invites confusion. Not every Greek astrological text is Hermetic, and the hub does not claim them. Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos , Valens’s Anthology , Dorotheus’s poem, and Firmicus’s Mathesis are the art’s great systematic books, written under their authors’ own names, and they belong to the hub’s Greek astrology article, which owns the horoscope’s machinery — the places, the aspects, the lots, the time-lords — in full. The Hermetic astrology of this article is the attributed stratum those authors themselves cite as older than themselves: the fountainhead behind Valens, the decan books behind the medical writers, the catalogues behind the compilers. The relation is the one Section IV established. The systematists are the family’s readers and witnesses, and it is largely in their pages that the family survives. 3rd–2nd c. BCE THE FOUNTAINHEAD AND ITS COMPANY The Nechepso–Petosiris texts are composed in Ptolemaic Egypt; the Salmeschoiniaka perhaps at Alexandria; the Art of Eudoxus papyrus already cites Hermes as a technical authority. 1st c. The Footing: Bronze Age Thebes and the Kadmeia XX. Sources I. The Other Great Cycle: Thebes Against Troy Greek epic had two great theatres, and the Greeks themselves paired them. When Hesiod, in the Works and Days , came to the fourth of his five races of mankind — the race of heroes, the demigods — he named exactly two wars as the events that destroyed them: some, he says, fell at seven-gated Thebes , fighting for the flocks of Oedipus, and others at Troy , for rich-haired Helen's sake ( Works and Days 161–165, paraphrased; the passage is treated in this hub's Theogony article). The pairing stuck. Thebes and Troy are the twin poles of the heroic age: the two cities whose falls closed it, sung in two families of epic poems, and remembered ever after as the measure of what the age of heroes had been. But the two cycles are opposite in shape, and the opposition is the subject of this article. The Trojan cycle is centrifugal : a coalition gathers from all over Greece, sails outward to a foreign shore, and fights an external enemy for ten years. Its violence, however terrible, is directed at strangers, and its survivors scatter homeward across the whole Greek world. The Theban cycle is centripetal . Almost nothing in it travels. A Phoenician prince arrives from outside and founds a city; after that founding act, the story never really leaves Thebes again — it only descends, from generation to generation of one royal house, each generation's disaster prepared by the one before. The enemy is never finally foreign. The dragon Cadmus kills is the city's own tutelary monster, sacred to Ares. The men who spring from its teeth kill each other before they can kill anyone else. The god who tears the royal house apart in the second generation is the house's own grandson, born in its own palace. The king who saves the city from the Sphinx destroys it by the saving, because the throne and the marriage bed he wins are his father's and his mother's. And the cycle's two wars — the Seven and the Epigoni — are both, at bottom, a quarrel between two brothers over one inheritance, fought the second time by the sons of the first war's dead. Troy is a family destroyed by a war. Thebes is a war generated, twice over, by a family. The house has a genealogy, and the cycle is unintelligible without it. In outline — the narrative sections below fill in every link — it runs as follows. Cadmus , son of the Phoenician king Agenor, founds Thebes and marries Harmonia , daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. Their children are a son, Polydorus , and four daughters — Autonoe, Ino, Semele, and Agave — every one of whose stories ends in a child destroyed. Polydorus's line continues through Labdacus to Laius , and from Laius to Oedipus . Oedipus's children by Jocasta — Eteocles, Polynices, Antigone, and Ismene — are the cycle's last full generation: the brothers kill each other, Antigone dies for burying one of them, and the kingship passes to the collateral lines, to Creon and to Eteocles' son Laodamas, until Polynices' son Thersander is restored by the Epigoni's victory — a restoration that lasts only until Thersander himself is killed on the road to Troy, handing the Theban story over, at its very end, to the Trojan one. Four generations from Cadmus to Oedipus; a fifth to the Epigoni. The article follows them in order. GENERATION I — THE FOUNDERS Cadmus of Tyre and Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. The founding acts: the cow followed, the dragon killed, the teeth sown, the Kadmeia built, the alphabet — in Herodotus's account — brought with the Phoenicians who came with Cadmus (Sections III–VI). GENERATION II — THE DAUGHTERS Semele blasted by Zeus's lightning; Ino mad, her son dead in the sea; Autonoe's son Actaeon torn apart by his own hounds; Agave's son Pentheus torn apart by his own mother. The house's second act is a catalogue of children destroyed (Sections VII–VIII). GENERATION III–IV — THE LABDACIDS Labdacus, Laius, Oedipus: the oracle defied, the child exposed, the father killed at the crossroads, the mother married, the truth recognised. Then Oedipus's sons, the curse, and the two wars (Sections IX–XVII). THE FOUR LAYERS OF THIS ARTICLE Throughout, four things are kept distinct: (a) the myth as told; (b) the lost epic tradition behind the telling; (c) the cult and archaeological footing at real Thebes; and (d) tragedy's remaking of all three in fifth-century Athens. A sentence that confuses the layers is, by this hub's rule, a sentence rewritten. One more framing point, because it governs the tone of everything below. The Theban cycle is the darker of the two great cycles not because its body count is higher — Troy's is higher — but because its horrors are domestic and hereditary . Its characteristic act is not the duel but the recognition: the moment a character learns what relation they actually stand in to the person they have killed, married, eaten, or torn apart. Its characteristic instrument is not the spear but the inherited object — a necklace, a robe, a silver table, a golden cup — passed down the generations and ruining each new owner in turn. And its characteristic theology is the oracle fulfilled by the very steps taken to escape it. A reader who keeps those three signatures in mind — recognition, inheritance, and the self-fulfilling oracle — holds the key to the whole cycle, from the dragon's teeth to the fall of the city. II. How the Cycle Reaches Us: Epics, Tragedies, and a Handbook No Theban epic survives. That single fact shapes everything a modern reader can know about this cycle, and it must be stated before any of the story is told. The Trojan cycle lost most of its poems too, but it kept the Iliad and the Odyssey — two enormous, complete archaic epics around which everything else can be arranged. The Theban cycle kept nothing whole. Its poems — the Oedipodea , the Thebaid , the Epigoni , and the Alcmaeonis — survive as a handful of quoted lines, a few ancient testimonies about their length and authorship, and the use later writers made of them (Section XVIII gives the full inventory). What we possess instead is the cycle at second and third hand, in three great bodies of material, each with its own date and its own agenda. First Body: The Early Notices — Homer and Hesiod The earliest surviving Greek literature already treats the Theban stories as old, famous, and available for allusion rather than narration. Homer never tells a Theban story whole, but the poems are salted with references that assume an audience who knows them: the Iliad 's Catalogue of Ships lists not Thebes itself but Hypothebai , “Lower Thebes” ( Iliad 2.505) — as if, already in the epic present, the great city of the cycle stood diminished beside its own lower town, a detail ancient and modern readers alike have connected with the Epigoni's sack. The Iliad knows Tydeus's embassy to Thebes and his ambush on the way home (4.376–398), Zeus's love for Semele (14.323–324), and funeral games held at Thebes for the dead Oedipus (23.679–680). The Odyssey 's catalogue of heroines in the underworld gives the oldest surviving connected account of Oedipus's marriage: Odysseus sees Epicaste — the name the later tradition standardises as Jocasta — who in ignorance married her own son, and hanged herself when the gods made the truth known, leaving Oedipus to rule the Cadmeans in sorrow under his mother's Furies ( Odyssey 11.271–280, paraphrased). Note what Homer does not have: no blinding, no exile, no Sphinx, no plague. The archaic Oedipus of the Odyssey remains king after the revelation. Much of what a modern reader thinks of as “the myth of Oedipus” is later than Homer, and this article flags the joins where they matter. Hesiod, for his part, supplies the Sphinx's parentage — she belongs to the monster-brood of Echidna, a bane to the Cadmeans, in the Theogony 's catalogue (326–332; see this hub's Theogony article) — and the heroes-at-Thebes passage of the Works and Days quoted in Section I. Second Body: Tragedy — The Fifth-Century Remaking The cycle's second life, and the one that fixed its modern shape, is Athenian tragedy. All three great tragedians worked the Theban material repeatedly, and seven Theban plays survive entire — more than for any other cycle. Aeschylus produced a connected Theban trilogy in 467 BCE — Laius , Oedipus , and Seven Against Thebes , with the satyr play Sphinx — of which only the Seven survives. Sophocles returned to the house three times across forty years, in three unconnected productions: Antigone (c. 442/441 BCE), Oedipus the King (conventionally c. 429 BCE; the date is an estimate, not a record), and Oedipus at Colonus (written near his death in 406 BCE and produced posthumously in 401 BCE). Euripides treated the material in the Phoenician Women (c. 411–409 BCE), the most densely populated retelling of the whole saga that survives from antiquity; in the Suppliants (c. 423 BCE), on the recovery of the Argive dead; in the Bacchae (produced posthumously, c. 405 BCE), on Pentheus; and in lost plays including a Chrysippus and an Antigone whose ending differed from Sophocles'. Tragedy is not a transparent window on the epic cycle. Each tragedian selects, compresses, invents, and — above all — re-motivates : motives that epic left to curse and oracle are re-examined as character, law, and civic argument. Where this article follows a tragedian's version against the handbook tradition, it says so. Third Body: The Handbook — Apollodorus, and the Traveller Pausanias The fullest continuous prose account of the cycle is the Library ( Bibliothēkē ) attributed to Apollodorus — in modern usage Pseudo-Apollodorus , since the work, dated to the first or second century CE, cannot be by the second-century BCE Athenian scholar of that name. Book 3, chapters 4–7, tells the Theban story from Cadmus to Alcmaeon in a single unbroken genealogical narrative, drawing on the lost epics, on early prose mythographers such as Pherecydes (whom it names where he differs), and on tragedy, and noting variant traditions as it goes. This article takes Apollodorus, in J. G. Frazer's Loeb translation, as its narrative spine — not because the Library is the oldest source (it is among the latest) but because it is the only source that tells the whole story in order, and because its habit of flagging variants (“some say”) lets a careful reader see the tradition's seams. Alongside it stands Pausanias , the second-century CE traveller whose Description of Greece devotes the first half of Book 9 to Thebes: its mythical history, its seven gates, its springs, tombs, and sanctuaries, described as things a visitor could still be shown. Pausanias is this article's chief witness for layer (c) — what the stories looked like when they had hardened into a landscape — and, in his argument at 9.5.10–11 about Oedipus's children, a rare ancient voice doing source-criticism on the cycle itself. // THE PROCLUS GAP, STATED PLAINLY // Readers of the Trojan cycle rely on the prose summaries of the Epic Cycle written by Proclus and preserved, through Photius, for the Trojan poems. No such summary survives for the Theban poems. Proclus's Chrestomathy evidently covered them — his summary of the Cypria begins by succeeding the Epigoni , the last Theban poem — but Photius, excerpting Proclus in the ninth century, dropped the Theban summaries, and they are lost. For the Theban epics we have fragments and testimonies only. Any account that purports to give the contents of the Oedipodea or the Epigoni in detail is reconstructing them from Apollodorus, tragedy, and scholia, and should be read as reconstruction. This article marks that boundary wherever it is crossed.
