Cadmus: The Search for Europa and the Oracle's Cow The cycle begins, uniquely among Greek foundation stories, with a failure. Cadmus does not set out to found a city. He sets out to find his sister. The story, as Apollodorus tells it ( Library 3.1.1–2 and 3.4.1, in Frazer's translation, paraphrased here except where quotation is marked), begins in Phoenicia. Agenor , king in Phoenicia, has by Telephassa a daughter, Europa , and three sons — Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix. Zeus, desiring Europa, takes the shape of a tame bull, breathes saffron from his mouth (the detail is Apollodorus's), tempts her onto his back, and carries her across the sea to Crete, where she bears Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys — the Cretan royal house, and with it the whole Cretan cycle treated in this hub's Heroes and Epic article's background, is the Theban cycle's first offshoot. Agenor sends his sons to search for their sister, with orders not to return without her. The search disperses the family across the map, and the dispersals are eponyms: Phoenix gives his name to Phoenicia, Cilix to Cilicia, Thasus — a companion or kinsman in the party — to the island of Thasos. Cadmus and his mother Telephassa settle for a time in Thrace. Europa is never found. She was never findable: a god had taken her, and the search was, from the first, a sentence of permanent exile disguised as an errand. Telephassa dies in Thrace. Cadmus buries her, is hospitably received by the Thracians, and goes to Delphi to ask the god about Europa. The answer he receives is the cycle's first oracle, and it establishes the pattern every later oracle in the saga will follow: it refuses the question asked and substitutes the answer that matters. In Frazer's translation of Apollodorus 3.4.1, the god told Cadmus not to trouble about Europa, but to be guided by a cow, and to found a city wherever she should fall down for weariness. Cadmus journeys through Phocis, falls in with a cow among the herds of Pelagon, and follows behind her across Boeotia until, at the place where Thebes now is, the cow sinks down. The founder does not choose the site; he is led to it, on foot, behind an animal, at walking pace, by an oracle that has first cancelled his life's errand. Greek foundation stories are full of such guidances — a crow, a goat, a fish — but the Theban version has a characteristic bleakness: the city begins at the exact point where the search for the lost sister is abandoned, and the founder's obedience consists in stopping. // THE COW AND THE NAME // Ancient writers themselves connected the cow with the country's name: Boeotia was popularly derived from bous , an ox or cow. The derivation is a folk etymology, not a linguistic fact, and this article reports it as the ancients' own wordplay — the kind of pun by which Greek tradition habitually welded a story to a landscape. Pausanias (9.12.1) adds that the cow Cadmus followed bore on each flank a white mark like the full moon: the guide was signed, for those who needed a sign. Cadmus's first act on the site is a sacrifice: he wishes to offer the cow to Athena. Sacrifice requires water. He sends companions to draw it from a nearby spring — the spring of Ares — and the companions do not come back. With that errand, told in a sentence by Apollodorus, the founding turns violent, and the cycle's true subject announces itself: at Thebes, even water is guarded, and everything the house takes from the land must be paid for in kind. The next section takes up the spring, the dragon, and the most consequential sowing in Greek myth. IV. The Dragon of Ares, the Sown Men, and the Founding of the Kadmeia The spring — later Theban topography knew it as the spring of Ares, and Pausanias's Thebes still pointed out its waters — was guarded by a dragon : a great serpent, which some said was the offspring of Ares (Apollodorus 3.4.1). It killed most of the companions Cadmus had sent for water. Cadmus, in indignation, killed the dragon in his turn. Euripides' Phoenician Women (638–675, paraphrased), in the long ode in which the chorus recalls the founding, gives the killing a single vivid means: Cadmus destroyed the serpent with a stone, showering blows on its head — the founder fights not with a hero's sword but with the weapon of a man caught unprepared at a spring. The killing is the founding act, and it is also the founding debt. The dragon was Ares' creature, in some tellings Ares' child; its death is a homicide within the divine household into which Cadmus is about to marry, and it will be expiated, pursued, and finally — in the founder's own serpent metamorphosis — literally embodied, across the rest of his story (Section VI). Then comes the sowing. By Athena's advice, Cadmus sowed the dragon's teeth in the earth. From the ground rose armed men — Spartoi , the Sown Men, from speirein , to sow. What the earth of Thebes produces, when seeded with the teeth of its own guardian serpent, is soldiers; and the soldiers' first act is to kill one another. Apollodorus reports two versions of how the slaughter began, and keeps both: in one, the Spartoi fell to fighting of themselves, some in a chance brawl and some in ignorance; in the other, which he attributes to Pherecydes, Cadmus, seeing armed men growing from the ground, flung stones among them, and each, supposing himself pelted by the man beside him, came to blows with his neighbour. Five survived: Echion, Udaeus, Chthonius, Hyperenor, and Pelorus — names that are themselves a programme: Echion is “snake-man”, Chthonius and Udaeus are “earth-men”, Pelorus is “monstrous”. From these five, the tradition held, descended the noble houses of Thebes: the Spartoi are the city's aristocracy, autochthonous in the most literal sense Greek myth affords — not merely born in the land, but grown from it, out of a dragon's jaw. The Theban aristocrat's pedigree, as the myth frames it, runs: earth, dragon, tooth, soldier. The city's first crop is a battle in which the crop destroys itself; five men are the harvest. Every later Theban war — brothers, Seven, Epigoni — is already present in miniature in the founding furrow: Thebans killing Thebans, on Theban soil, at the moment of the city's birth. The debt to Ares was paid in service. Apollodorus (3.4.2) says Cadmus atoned for the slaughter by serving Ares for an “eternal year” — and adds the gloss, in Frazer's rendering, that the year was then equivalent to eight years of our reckoning. Only after the servitude does the founding complete itself: Athena procures Cadmus the kingship, and Zeus gives him a wife. The city he builds on the hill above the spring takes his name: the Kadmeia (Cadmea), the citadel of Thebes — a name the real citadel of the real city kept into the historical period and beyond, so that Xenophon, describing the Spartan seizure of the Theban acropolis in 382 BCE, calls it simply the Cadmea ( Hellenica 5.2, paraphrased). The walls of the wider city belong, in the tradition, to a later generation — to Amphion's lyre (Section IX) — and the distinction is worth keeping: Cadmus founds the citadel and the royal house; the seven-gated circuit that defines the cycle's geography is a second foundation laid over his. THE FIVE SURVIVORS Echion · Udaeus · Chthonius · Hyperenor · Pelorus. Ancestors, in the tradition, of Thebes's Spartoi families. Echion marries into the royal house itself — his wife is Cadmus's daughter Agave, and their son is Pentheus (Section VIII). THE OTHER SOWING The dragon's teeth were not all sown at Thebes. In the Argonautic tradition, Athena gave half the teeth to Aeëtes of Colchis, and Jason, at the far end of the world, sows the other half and faces the same crop of armed earthborn men — the Theban founding replayed as a hero's task. See Heroes and Epic , Section VIII. THE SPRING The spring of Ares, where the dragon kept guard, remained a named place in the storied topography Pausanias walked (Book 9). Thebes's myths are unusually well-anchored in named waters: Dirce, Ismenus, and the spring of Ares all carry episodes of the cycle. THE DEBT STRUCTURE Founding at Thebes is never free. The cow is sacrificed; the companions are killed; the dragon's death is expiated by eight years' servitude; the sown men mostly die. The cycle's accounting begins here: every acquisition in this saga is entered twice, once as gain and once as debt. V. The Alphabet: Herodotus and the Cadmean Letters Cadmus brought Thebes one more thing besides a citadel, and it is the only gift in the cycle that is an unmixed good — though the claim for it must be stated with exact care. The claim is Herodotus's . In Histories 5.57–58, tracing the Athenian clan of the Gephyraeans back to Phoenician settlers who, by his enquiry, had come with Cadmus to the land now called Boeotia, Herodotus writes, in A. D. Godley's Loeb translation: “These Phoenicians who came with Cadmus and of whom the Gephyraeans were a part brought with them to Hellas, among many other kinds of learning, the alphabet, which had been unknown before this, I think, to the Greeks. As time went on the sound and the form of the letters were changed.” — HERODOTUS, HISTORIES 5.58.1, TRANS. A. D. GODLEY (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY) Herodotus continues (5.58.2, paraphrased) that the Greeks who then lived around the Phoenicians — for the most part Ionians — learned the letters from them, altered a few of their forms, and called the characters Phoenician , “as was quite fair”, in Godley's rendering, seeing that the Phoenicians had brought them into Greece. And he offers evidence of the kind he trusts: autopsy. In 5.59 he reports that he has himself seen Cadmean letters ( Kadmēia grammata ) in the temple of Ismenian Apollo at Thebes in Boeotia, engraved on certain tripods and for the most part resembling Ionian letters; and he transcribes the tripods' dedications, the last of them ascribed to Laodamas, son of Eteocles — that is, to a king of the cycle's own fifth generation (5.59–61, paraphrased). The historian who is so often accused of credulity is here doing something precise: attributing a technology to a carrier, naming the mechanism of its adaptation, and citing inscribed objects he claims to have inspected, in the very city the myth says the carrier founded. Now the frame must be set beside the claim, and this hub's own timeline supplies it: the Greek alphabet was adapted from the Phoenician script around c. 800 BCE (see the hub index timeline ), when Greek communities took over the Phoenician consonantal signs and, decisively, repurposed some of them as vowels. That is the archaeological and epigraphic record: no Cadmus stands in it, and no single act of importation can be dated or placed. The myth, by contrast, gives the alphabet a Phoenician prince, a name, a route, and a city. The two accounts should be stated together, in exactly these terms and no further: the myth gives the alphabet a Phoenician prince, the record gives it to Phoenician trade, and the two are not as far apart as usual. A technology that the record attributes to sustained contact between Greek speakers and Phoenician carriers is attributed by the tradition to a Phoenician who came and stayed. Herodotus, standing between the two, reports the tradition as tradition — “as I think” is his own hedge, in Godley's translation — and anchors it to letters he says he saw cut in bronze at Thebes. This article leaves the matter exactly there. // CADMUS OF TYRE // Herodotus knows Cadmus as a Tyrian: at 2.49 he writes of “Cadmus of Tyre and those who came with him from Phoenicia to the land now called Boeotia” (Godley's translation, paraphrased in the connective wording here) as the channel through which Melampus learned the worship of Dionysus. The alphabet passage is not an isolated fancy; it belongs to Herodotus's settled view that Cadmus's Phoenicians were a real vector of eastern learning into Greece — letters and a god among the cargo. There is a fittingness the tradition itself surely felt. The cycle that would become the most written of Greek sagas — the saga of the lost epics, of the shield inscriptions Eteocles reads aloud, of the letters on Polynices' shield in Aeschylus, of an oracle culture that ran on inscribed tripods — traces its city's founding to the man Greek tradition credited with bringing writing itself. Whether or not any historical kernel stands behind the attribution, the shape of the claim is the shape of the cycle: at Thebes, everything, even the alphabet, arrives as an import that takes root and turns native. The Levantine world those Phoenicians came from — its cities, its scribal schools, and its own great mythic corpus, the Baal Cycle of Ugarit — is treated in Ugarit and the Baal Cycle , this hub's account of the tradition on the alphabet's home shore. VI. Cadmus and Harmonia: The Wedding, the Necklace, and the Serpent End After the servitude to Ares, the founding is crowned with a marriage that no other Greek hero is granted. Zeus gives Cadmus to wife Harmonia , daughter of Aphrodite and Ares — Hesiod's Theogony (933–937) already lists Harmonia among the children Ares and Aphrodite had together — and Apollodorus (3.4.2) describes the wedding in terms that make it the cycle's one moment of unshadowed splendour, in paraphrase: all the gods quitted the sky, and, feasting in the Kadmeia, celebrated the marriage with hymns. Later tradition amplified the scene into the first wedding on earth attended by the Olympians in person, with the Muses singing the epithalamium and the gods bringing gifts; Diodorus Siculus (4.2 and 5.49, paraphrased) preserves versions of that amplification. The bride was, note, the daughter of the two divinities the founding had most engaged: Ares, whose dragon Cadmus killed and whom Cadmus then served, and Aphrodite, whose line the marriage joins. Harmonia's very name — Fitting-Together, Concord — proclaims what the union was meant to be: the Phoenician stranger fitted into the Greek land, war and love reconciled, the debt to Ares discharged in kinship. The cycle will spend four generations demonstrating what that name was worth. The Necklace Among the wedding gifts was the object that outlasts every person in this article. Apollodorus (3.4.2, paraphrased, with the variants he himself records): Cadmus gave Harmonia a robe and the necklace wrought by Hephaestus — which some say was given to Cadmus by Hephaestus, but Pherecydes says was given by Europa, who had received it from Zeus. The Library does not call the necklace cursed; it simply follows it, and the following is the curse. The necklace descends with the royal house. Generations later it is in the treasury of Thebes, and Polynices, exiled, takes it with him — with the robe — as his portable wealth (Apollodorus 3.6.1). At Argos he uses it to bribe Eriphyle, and the bribe sends her husband Amphiaraus to his death and, in the next generation, sends her sons to war and Eriphyle herself to death at her son's hand (Sections XIV and XVII). Alcmaeon gives necklace and robe to his first wife; his second wife demands them; the lie he tells to recover them gets him murdered; his young sons avenge him, and the necklace's last recorded act in the tradition is its dedication — Pausanias (8.24 and 9.31, paraphrased) knew of the necklace of Harmonia shown among the dedications at Delphi, the poisoned gift finally taken out of circulation by being given to a god. Later writers, scholiasts especially, supplied the necklace with an explicit malice — Hephaestus, in those accounts, made it in bitterness at Aphrodite's adultery with Ares, so that her daughter's line would never prosper — but that explanation is a later rationalisation of a pattern the older sources simply display: at Thebes, the wedding gift and the ruin are the same object, and no one who owns it keeps it safely. The Children, and the End in Illyria To Cadmus and Harmonia were born, in Apollodorus's list (3.4.2), daughters Autonoe, Ino, Semele, and Agave , and a son, Polydorus . The marriages are a map of the house's alliances: Ino to Athamas, king of Boeotian Orchomenus; Autonoe to Aristaeus, the culture-hero of herding and bees; Agave to Echion, one of the five Spartoi — the founder's daughter wedded to the earthborn, the two foundings of Thebes joined in one bed. Their stories are the next two sections. Of Cadmus and Harmonia themselves, the end is strange and, in its way, gentle. In old age the couple leave Thebes — the throne passes down the line toward Polydorus's descendants and, in the immediate term, to Agave's son Pentheus — and go out to the Encheleans in Illyria, who make Cadmus their king after an oracle promises them victory under his leadership (Apollodorus 3.5.4, paraphrased). There a son, Illyrius, is born to them, eponym of the Illyrians. And there, at the last, the debt of the spring is called in, in the mildest possible form: Cadmus and Harmonia are turned into serpents , and Zeus sends them to the Elysian fields. The founder becomes the animal he killed. Ovid's telling ( Metamorphoses 4.563–603, paraphrased) makes the metamorphosis Cadmus's own weary inference — if a serpent's life is so precious to the gods, he muses, let him stretch out into a serpent's length — and gives Harmonia the choice to join him in the shape rather than be left human without him. Euripides, in the Bacchae 's closing prophecy (1330–1339, paraphrased), has Dionysus foretell the same end with a harder edge: Cadmus, become a serpent, with Harmonia a serpent beside him, will lead a barbarian host against Greece and sack many cities, until at last he is brought to the land of the blessed. Even the founder's apotheosis is double: a serpent's exile, then blessedness; a barbarian invasion, then rest. The cycle permits no one an unmixed ending — but it permits its founders, alone among its kings, an ending that is not a catastrophe. ACT I THE FOUNDING Europa lost; the cow followed; the dragon killed; the teeth sown; eight years' service to Ares; the Kadmeia founded; the wedding of Cadmus and Harmonia, with the necklace among the gifts. ACT II THE DAUGHTERS AND PENTHEUS Semele, Ino, Autonoe, and Agave each lose a child or a mind to a god; Dionysus, the house's own grandson, returns unrecognised and destroys Pentheus, the house's king. ACT III OEDIPUS Laius defies the oracle; Oedipus is exposed, saved, and returns to kill his father, answer the Sphinx, and marry his mother; the truth is recognised; the blind exile dies a holy death at Colonus. ACT IV THE TWO WARS Oedipus's curse divides his sons; the Seven fail before the seven gates; Antigone dies for a burial; ten years on, the Epigoni — the After-born — succeed, and Thebes falls. VII. The Daughters' Generation: Semele, Actaeon, Ino, and Agave The house of Cadmus has no ordinary second generation. Polydorus's line — the male line that will produce Laius and Oedipus — runs on quietly in the background of the sources, while the foreground belongs to the four daughters and to what the gods did to each of them. Apollodorus tells their stories consecutively (3.4.3–3.5.2), and told consecutively they form a single pattern with four variations: in each, a god enters the house from outside the ordinary rules — as lover, as offended majesty, as madness, as the family's own unrecognised child — and in each, the price is paid by a child. Semele and the Thigh of Zeus Zeus loved Semele and lay with her unknown to Hera, having promised — the fatal formula — to do for her whatever she asked. Hera, deceiving her, persuaded her to ask that Zeus come to her as he came when he was wooing Hera herself: in his full state, with his lightnings. Bound by his promise, Zeus came to her chamber in a chariot with thunder and lightning and launched a thunderbolt; Semele died of fright; and Zeus snatched the six-month child from the fire and sewed it into his own thigh, from which, at term, Dionysus was born a second time (Apollodorus 3.4.3, paraphrased). The sisters of Semele then spread the report that she had lain with a mortal man and lied about Zeus, and that the thunderbolt was her punishment — a piece of family slander that the tradition never forgets, because Dionysus's whole Theban career (Section VIII) is its refutation. Reception: Herodotus and the Greeks' Own Systematisation XVII. Sources I. A Poem That Organised a Pantheon The Theogony — Greek Theogonia , “the birth (or begetting) of the gods” — is a poem of 1,022 lines of dactylic hexameter, attributed to the Boeotian poet Hesiod and conventionally dated to about c. 700 BCE . It is, with the Iliad and Odyssey attributed to Homer and Hesiod's own Works and Days , among the earliest Greek literature to survive entire. Its subject is nothing less than everything: how the world began, where the gods came from, why Zeus rules them, and how the present order of heaven and earth was won. Where Homer's epics assume a settled Olympian family and get on with the story of heroes, the Theogony explains how that family came to exist — and it explains it as a story of violent succession, in which the kingship of heaven passes from Ouranos (Sky) to Kronos to Zeus, each ruler overthrown or threatened by his own children, until Zeus finds the means to make his rule permanent. The poem's method is genealogy. Hesiod organises the teeming, contradictory mass of local Greek myth — every town and island had its own gods, heroes, and stories, and they did not agree with one another — into a single family tree, in which every god has parents, siblings, and a place. Rivers and winds, Sleep and Death, Victory and Strife, monsters and abstractions all receive a parentage and therefore a position in one cosmos. That systematising achievement is the poem's historical importance, and an ancient reader already saw it clearly: Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BCE, credited Homer and Hesiod jointly with giving the Greeks their theogony (Section XVI). The family tree was never a creed — no priesthood enforced it, and local variants cheerfully persisted alongside it — but it became the shared map on which Greek myth was drawn ever after. Two cautions belong at the front, because this article returns to both. First, the poem is a text with a history: it was composed in an oral-traditional medium, written down at some point we cannot date exactly, and transmitted through papyri and medieval manuscripts whose disagreements modern editors must judge (Sections III–IV). The 1,022-line poem a reader buys today is a scholarly reconstruction, very close to what ancient readers had, but not a stenogram of a performance around 700 BCE. Second, its central story is not a Greek invention ex nihilo. The succession myth — a sky-god deposed, a castration, a swallowed stone, a storm-god who finally rules — has close and detailed relatives in the Hurrian-Hittite Kumarbi cycle, copied in cuneiform centuries before Hesiod. Sections XIII–XIV set out those parallels in full, and also set out, fairly, what they do and do not prove. The wider habit of telling the deep past as a sequence of divine reigns is older than Greece altogether: the reader of this archive has already met it in the Egyptian and Mesopotamian materials gathered at Divine Dynasties and the Antediluvian King Lists , where gods and impossibly long-lived kings rule before ordinary history begins. Hesiod's poem is the Greek entry in that ancient genre — and, characteristically, it is the entry that ends the sequence for good, in a kingship that will never be succeeded. THE POEM AT A GLANCE 1,022 hexameter lines in the artificial epic dialect. Structure: proem to the Muses (lines 1–115); first things and first generations (116–452); the succession narrative, from the castration of Ouranos to the enthronement of Zeus (154–885, interleaved with catalogues); the marriages of Zeus and the closing catalogue of goddesses and mortals (886–1022). THE STORY AT A GLANCE Chaos, Gaia, Tartaros, and Eros come first. Gaia bears Ouranos, who hides his children inside her; her youngest son Kronos castrates him and rules in his place, swallowing his own children to keep the throne; the youngest of them, Zeus, is hidden on Crete, forces Kronos to disgorge the rest, defeats the Titans in a ten-year war, survives the monster Typhoeus, and secures his rule by swallowing Metis (Counsel) herself. SPELLINGS USED HERE Greek names are transliterated, not Latinised, throughout this hub: Ouranos (not Uranus), Kronos (not Cronus), Titanomachy. The Evelyn-White translation quoted in this article spells the name “Cronos”; quotations keep their translator's spelling, and the difference is noted where a quotation is given. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — H. G. Evelyn-White's Loeb translation of Hesiod (1914) and A. D. Godley's Loeb translation of Herodotus — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. II. Hesiod and Ascra: The Poet in His Own Poems Almost everything said about Hesiod's life comes from Hesiod. No contemporary record of him exists; the later ancient biographies — the Lives transmitted under the names of Proclus (fifth century CE) and Tzetzes (twelfth century CE), and the entertaining fiction of the Contest of Homer and Hesiod — add little that can be checked and much that plainly cannot. What the poems themselves tell us, in the first person, is this. Hesiod's father was a seafaring trader from Cyme in Aeolis , on the coast of Asia Minor, who gave up the sea, crossed to mainland Greece to escape poverty, and settled at Ascra in Boeotia , a village near Thespiae under Mount Helicon, which the poet himself describes in the Works and Days in famously unflattering terms — a wretched place, bad in winter, harsh in summer (paraphrase of Works and Days 633–640). Hesiod and his brother Perses inherited the farm, quarrelled over the division, and fell out; the Works and Days is addressed to Perses in the aftermath of that quarrel, though the Theogony itself never mentions it. Of the poet's own formation the Theogony gives one scene, and it is the scene with which the poem opens (Section V): while Hesiod was shepherding his lambs under holy Helicon, the Muses of Olympus met him, addressed him with startling rudeness, gave him a staff of laurel, and breathed a divine voice into him, commanding him to sing of the gods. Whether the encounter is vision, convention, or a poet's way of claiming authority for traditional material, it is the earliest surviving first-person account in Greek literature of a poet receiving his art — and it locates that art precisely, on the slopes of Helicon above Ascra. The Works and Days adds one more autobiographical datum: Hesiod crossed the sea exactly once, the short hop from Aulis to Chalcis in Euboea, where he competed at the funeral games of Amphidamas and won a tripod, which he dedicated to the Heliconian Muses ( Works and Days 646–662, paraphrased). The games have sometimes been used to date him — Amphidamas was connected in tradition with the shadowy Lelantine War — but the connection is too uncertain to bear much weight, and modern dating rests on other grounds (Section III). // A POET, NOT A PRIEST // Hesiod presents himself as a working farmer and occasional competitor in song, not as a priest, prophet, or temple official. Greek religion had no scripture and no clergy charged with doctrine. The Theogony 's authority was the authority of a much-sung, much-copied poem — which proved, in the event, to be authority enough. Two works are securely his in the judgement of modern scholarship: the Theogony and the Works and Days . Antiquity attached more to his name — the Catalogue of Women , a vast genealogical poem bridging gods and heroes, and the Shield of Heracles among them — and modern editors print those as pseudo-Hesiodic: products of the same Boeotian, genealogical tradition, composed in his manner and under his authority, mostly in the sixth century BCE. The distinction matters for this article at exactly one point: the Theogony 's final two lines hand the song over to the subject-matter of the Catalogue (Section XII), so the two poems were already being read as a continuous Hesiodic corpus in antiquity, whoever wrote the continuation. III. Date, Dialect, and Oral-Traditional Making Date. The conventional date of about c. 700 BCE is a scholarly estimate, not a record, and honest accounts give its margins. Hesiod must come after the formation of the Homeric epics' tradition and before the mid-sixth century, when his poems are being quoted and imitated. Within that span, specialists have argued for placements across the late eighth and early seventh centuries: Richard Janko's statistical study of epic diction argued for roughly 700–665 BCE; M. L. West, in later work, argued for roughly 680–660 BCE; the reference literature commonly settles on “c. 730–700” or simply “c. 700”. This article uses c. 700 BCE as the conventional midpoint and flags it as conventional. Herodotus, our earliest external witness, placed Hesiod and Homer together “not more than four hundred years” before his own time (Section XVI) — which, counted from the mid-fifth century, would put them around 850 BCE, earlier than any modern estimate. The discrepancy is itself instructive: Herodotus was guessing from tradition, as we guess from language and archaeology, and his guess shows how quickly the poets had become figures of a remote, founding past. Dialect and metre. The poem is composed in dactylic hexameters — the metre of Homer — and in the same artificial epic language: a literary dialect based on Ionic Greek, enriched with Aeolic and archaic forms, that no one ever spoke in the street. It was the shared professional medium of Greek epic singers, and Hesiod, an Aeolic-speaking Boeotian by upbringing, commands it completely. Formulaic phrasing — the fixed epithets and ready-made line-parts (“wise Zeus”, “Earth the loud-crashing Earth-Shaker” and the like, in Evelyn-White's renderings) — runs through the poem exactly as it runs through Homer. That formulaic texture is the fingerprint of an oral tradition : generations of singers composing in performance with a inherited stock of phrases fitted to the metre. Oral or written? How a poem of this texture became the fixed text we have is debated, and the debate should be reported rather than settled. One influential position, associated with Gregory Nagy, treats Hesiodic poetry as oral composition that crystallised only gradually, through repeated performance and eventual transcription. Another, associated with M. L. West and Glenn Most, holds that Hesiod himself was aware of the newly available technology of alphabetic writing — Greece had adopted and adapted the Phoenician alphabet in the eighth century — and used it in composing poems of a length and intricacy that suggest deliberate, revisable construction; the recent Cambridge commentary by Jenny Strauss Clay and Athanassios Vergados (2025) argues the written-composition case from word- and sound-play sustained across long stretches of text. The positions are not as far apart as their labels suggest: an oral-traditional technique , learned by ear, is fully compatible with a literate poet writing a poem down. What is certain is the milieu — the decades around 700 BCE when Greek epic, newly writable, was being fixed in the forms in which it would be transmitted for the next two and a half millennia. The Surviving Text: Transmission and Editions No autograph, and nothing like one, survives. The Theogony reached the modern world by the usual precarious route of Greek literature: performance and copying in antiquity, quotation and commentary by Hellenistic scholars at Alexandria and elsewhere, papyrus copies in Roman Egypt — fragments of Hesiod on papyrus, several from Oxyrhynchus, attest the poems' circulation in the ancient world and occasionally preserve readings older than the medieval tradition — then medieval manuscripts, copied in the Byzantine world, from which all modern editions descend. The medieval tradition is comparatively rich but not perfectly uniform: manuscripts differ in wording at many points, a handful of lines are suspected by editors as interpolations, and at one famous place — the birth of Hephaestus, lines 929a–t in modern numeration — the tradition preserves what looks like a second, alternative version of a passage already given a few lines earlier, a doublet that Evelyn-White prints in brackets and most editors treat as evidence of the text's fluid early life. None of this threatens the poem's overall shape: the 1,022-line Theogony of modern editions is, in substance, the poem ancient readers knew. It does mean that every modern Theogony is an editor's judgement, line by line, among attested variants. The edition that set the modern standard is M. L. West's Hesiod: Theogony , edited with prolegomena and commentary (Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1966) — a Greek text based on a fresh survey of the whole manuscript tradition, with a critical apparatus, and prolegomena that discuss the nature of theogonic literature across cultures, the poem's Near Eastern relationships, its genealogical principles, its date, its transmission, and its language and metre. West's conviction, stated already in that 1966 volume and developed for the rest of his career, that early Greek literature must be read as part of an eastern Mediterranean world, frames Sections XIII–XIV of this article. For readers of English, the standard translations include H. G. Evelyn-White's Loeb Classical Library version (1914) , from which this article's quotations are taken; Richmond Lattimore's translation (University of Michigan Press, 1959) ; and West's own translation in the Oxford World's Classics Hesiod: Theogony and Works and Days . Line numbers in this article follow the standard numeration used by all of these editions. // READING THE LINE NUMBERS // Citations in the form “lines 453–506” refer to the Greek text's standard line numeration, which every modern edition and translation preserves. Evelyn-White's prose translation prints the line ranges at the head of each paragraph, which makes his version the most convenient one for following the references in this article. A last point of method. Because the poem is a genealogy, it is not a continuous story: narrative episodes — the castration, the swallowing, the war — are separated by long catalogues of births, and the same figure may be introduced twice, in two different family lines, with two different parentages. The most famous case is the Moirai, the Fates, who are born once from Night (lines 211–225) and again from Zeus and Themis (lines 901–906). Editors do not “fix” such doublets, and readers should not be troubled by them: Hesiod is weaving inherited lists together, and the seams are part of the evidence for how the poem was made. V. The Proem: Helicon, the Muses, and “Lies Like Truth” The poem opens not with the cosmos but with its own credentials. The first 115 lines — the proem , or hymn to the Muses — fall into three movements. First (lines 1–21), the Heliconian Muses themselves: they hold the great and holy mountain, dance on soft feet around a deep-blue spring and the altar of Zeus, wash in the streams of Permessus, the Horse's Spring (Hippocrene), and Olmeius, and go veiled in mist by night through the world, singing. Their song, as Hesiod summarises it, is already the whole poem in miniature: Zeus and Hera, Athena and Apollo, Artemis and Poseidon, Themis, Aphrodite, Hebe, Dione, Leto, Iapetus and Kronos, Dawn and Sun and Moon, Earth and Ocean and black Night — the cast of the theogony, named before it is explained. Second (lines 22–35) comes the encounter on the mountain, treated below. Third (lines 36–115) the Muses are hymned at length in their Olympian home: their birth from Zeus and Mnemosyne (Memory) — nine nights, nine daughters — their names (Clio, Euterpe, Thaleia, Melpomene, Terpsichore, Erato, Polymnia, Urania, and Calliope, “the chiefest of them all”, in Evelyn-White's rendering), their power to gladden Zeus and to make a grieving man forget his sorrows when a singer chants the deeds of old, and finally Hesiod's commissioning prayer: tell me these things from the beginning, Muses, and tell me which of them first came to be . The poem's whole programme is in that question. The proem is not decoration; it is the poet asking, on the record, for a cosmogony. The Encounter, and the Famous Passage The encounter scene (lines 22–34) is told with deliberate plainness. The Muses, Hesiod says, once taught him glorious song while he was shepherding his lambs under holy Helicon — and their first words to him were an insult. In Evelyn-White's Loeb translation (1914), the passage runs: “Shepherds of the wilderness, wretched things of shame, mere bellies, we know how to speak many false things as though they were true; but we know, when we will, to utter true things.” — HESIOD, THEOGONY 26–28, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) The Muses then plucked and gave him a staff — a shoot of sturdy laurel, in Evelyn-White's rendering — breathed into him a divine voice to celebrate what shall be and what was aforetime, and commanded him to sing of the race of the blessed gods, but always of the Muses themselves first and last (lines 29–34, paraphrased). The insult and the boast together have been discussed ever since. “Mere bellies” reduces the shepherd-poet to an appetite: a creature who sings, as shepherds were proverbially thought to do, for his supper. The boast is more unsettling. The goddesses who are the poem's source announce that lying convincingly is among their competences, and that truth is something they utter when they will . Hesiod does not resolve the problem he has raised. He simply begins — leaving every later reader, from Plato onward, to decide which parts of what follows are the truth and which are the lies like truth. It is an extraordinarily self-aware opening for an “archaic” poem, and this archive takes it as the poem's own instruction for how to read it: a traditional account, claiming divine warrant, that warns its audience in its first breath not to confuse the warrant with a guarantee. // A NOTE ON THE GREEK // The key word of the passage, etymoisin (in pseudea polla legein etymoisin homoia ), means “like true (or real) things”. Translators render the line variously — “many false things as though they were true” (Evelyn-White), “many lies that pass for truth”, “many fictions like to truths” — but the sense is stable across renderings: fictions indistinguishable from fact, produced on purpose, by experts. Only Evelyn-White's wording is quoted in this article; the variants are given here, unquoted, to show the range. VI. The Beginning: Chaos, Gaia, Tartaros, Eros Asked which came first, the Muses answer with four names (lines 116–122). In Evelyn-White's translation: “Verily at the first Chaos came to be, but next wide-bosomed Earth, the ever-sure foundations of all the deathless ones who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus, and dim Tartarus in the depth of the wide-pathed Earth, and Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods…” — HESIOD, THEOGONY 116–120, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB, 1914) Each of the four needs a word. Chaos is not “disorder” in the modern sense. The Greek word is connected with gaping and yawning: Chaos is a gap , an open chasm or empty interval, the space in which things can subsequently be. The poem never says Chaos was made, or by whom; it simply “came to be” first. Gaia , Earth, wide-bosomed, is the solid ground of everything and the poem's most consequential character: mother of gods, plotter of revolutions, and the one figure who advises every successful challenger. Tartaros is the pit beneath the earth, named already here, at the beginning, because the poem will need it at the end — as the prison of the defeated. And Eros , Love or Desire, “who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men” (Evelyn-White), is not yet the winged boy of later art but a cosmic force: the principle of union and generation, without which a genealogy cannot start. A theogony — a poem made of begettings — puts Desire among its first principles as a matter of mechanics. Generation then proceeds by two methods, both of which the poem keeps distinct. Parthenogenesis : Gaia, alone and “without sweet union of love”, bears starry Ouranos (Heaven), equal to herself, to cover her on every side; the long Hills; and Pontus, the barren Sea (lines 126–132, paraphrased). From Chaos come Erebus (Darkness) and black Night; Night, united with Erebus, bears Aether (bright upper air) and Day (lines 123–125). Union : Gaia then lies with the Ouranos she has made, and bears the first great divine family — deep-swirling Oceanus; Coeus and Crius; Hyperion and Iapetus; Theia and Rhea; Themis and Mnemosyne; gold-crowned Phoebe and lovely Tethys; and last, youngest and most terrible, Kronos the wily , who hated his father from the first (lines 133–138). After the twelve Titans come two further, stranger broods of Earth and Heaven: the one-eyed Cyclopes — Brontes (Thunder), Steropes (Lightning), and Arges (the Bright One) — smiths who in due course will give Zeus his thunderbolt; and the Hundred-Handers , Cottus, Briareos, and Gyes, each with a hundred arms springing from his shoulders and fifty heads (lines 139–153). The poem has now assembled, before any conflict begins, both the ruling family and the two sets of imprisoned giants whose release will decide its war. FIRST: THE FOUR BEGINNINGS Chaos (the gap) · Gaia (Earth) · Tartaros (the pit below) · Eros (Desire, the force of union). None is created by another; the poem begins with them, not before them. GAIA ALONE Ouranos (Heaven) · the Hills · Pontus (Sea) — borne without union, so that Earth has a cover, a landscape, and a surrounding deep. GAIA AND OURANOS: THE TWELVE TITANS Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rhea, Themis, Mnemosyne, Phoebe, Tethys — and Kronos, the youngest. Then the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers. CHAOS AND NIGHT From Chaos: Erebus and Night. From Night, alone or with Erebus: Aether and Day — and, in the poem's darkest catalogue, Doom, Death, Sleep, the Fates, Nemesis, and Strife with all her children (Section VII). VII. Ouranos and Kronos: Concealment, the Sickle, and the Castration The succession begins with an act of suppression. Ouranos, the poem says, hated his children from the first — the Hundred-Handers above all — and as each was born he hid it away in a secret place of Gaia and would not let it come up into the light; and Ouranos rejoiced in his evil doing (lines 154–158, paraphrased). Gaia, straitened and groaning within, becomes the first revolutionary. She fashions the element of grey flint into a great jagged sickle, lays her plan before her sons, and asks which of them will punish their father's outrage. Fear seizes them all, and none speaks — except the youngest. Kronos the wily takes courage and answers that he will undertake the deed, since he does not reverence a father of evil name who first thought of doing shameful things (lines 159–172, paraphrased). Gaia hides him in ambush, puts the sickle in his hands, and tells him the whole plot. What follows (lines 176–206) is the poem's most famous act of violence, and its most consequential piece of cosmology. Ouranos comes at night, longing for love, and spreads himself full upon Gaia — Heaven covering Earth as he does each night. From his ambush Kronos stretches out his left hand, seizes his father with it, and with the great long sickle in his right hand swiftly lops off his father's genitals and casts them away behind him. The separation is the point: Heaven is cut away from Earth and stays away, and the world acquires the open space between ground and sky in which everything else will happen. But in Hesiod nothing generative is wasted. The bloody drops that fall to Earth are received by Gaia, and in due season she bears from them the strong Erinyes (the Furies, avengers of kindred blood), the great Giants in gleaming armour, and the Meliae , the ash-tree nymphs. The severed flesh itself, cast into the sea, drifts long on the surge; white foam gathers around it, and in the foam a maiden grows — Aphrodite , who comes first to Cythera and then to Cyprus, and whose names the poem explains one by one: Aphrodite, the foam-born; Cytherea, because she reached Cythera; Cyprogenes, because she was born in billowy Cyprus; and Philommedes, because she sprang from the genitals. Eros and Himeros (Desire) attend her from her birth, and her allotted portion among gods and men — the whisperings of maidens, smiles and deceits, sweet delight and love — is fixed in the same breath (paraphrased from lines 188–206). The goddess of love is thus, in Hesiod's scheme, older than Zeus and older than the Olympian order altogether: a daughter of the first revolution. One more detail of the episode carries forward. Ouranos, the poem says, gave his sons the name Titans in reproach — connecting the name, by the poem's own folk etymology, with straining and presumptuous overreaching — and declared that vengeance for their deed would come afterwards (lines 207–210, paraphrased). The prophecy is structural. Every ruler in this poem is warned, and the warning is always accurate; the only question the poem asks is whether the third ruler can break the pattern. The Generations Between: Night, Sea, and the Titan Houses (Lines 211–452) Between the castration and the next act of the succession, Hesiod suspends the narrative for some two hundred lines of catalogue — the filling-out of the cosmos, family by family. Night , lying with none, bears the dark powers: hateful Doom and black Fate and Death; Sleep and the tribe of Dreams; Blame and painful Woe; the Hesperides who guard the golden apples beyond Ocean; the Destinies and ruthless Fates, Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos; Nemesis (Indignation); and after her Deceit and Friendship and hateful Age and hard-hearted Strife (Eris) — who in turn bears painful Toil and Forgetfulness and Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words, Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin, and Oath, who most troubles men when anyone wilfully swears a false oath (lines 211–232, paraphrased). It is a moralised cosmos: the miseries of human life are given birthdays and addresses alongside the gods. Pontus , the Sea, fathers Nereus the truthful Old Man of the Sea, and, with Gaia, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto, and Eurybia. From Nereus and Doris come the fifty Nereids ; from Thaumas and Electra, Iris the rainbow-messenger and the Harpies; from Phorcys and Ceto, the grey-born Graiae, the Gorgons — from whose severed neck, when Perseus beheads Medusa, spring Chrysaor and the winged horse Pegasus — and the monstrous Echidna , half nymph and half snake, whose brood by Typhaon fills the monster-catalogue of Greek myth: Orthus the hound of Geryon, fifty-headed Cerberus the hound of Hades, the Hydra of Lerna, the fire-breathing Chimaera, the Sphinx, and the Nemean lion (lines 233–332, paraphrased). From Oceanus and Tethys flow the rivers of the world and three thousand Oceanid daughters, chief among them Styx , whose oath will bind the gods themselves (lines 333–370). The Titan houses intermarry and fill the sky: Hyperion and Theia bear Helios (Sun), Selene (Moon), and Eos (Dawn); Eos bears the winds Zephyrus, Boreas, and Notus, and the morning star; Crius and Eurybia bear Astraeus, Pallas, and Perses; Styx, joined to Pallas, bears Zelus (Emulation), Nike (Victory), Kratos (Strength), and Bia (Force) — the four who will have no house apart from Zeus, because Styx was the first to come to Olympus when Zeus summoned allies against the Titans, and was rewarded beyond all (lines 371–403). Coeus and Phoebe bear Leto and Asteria; Asteria bears Hecate , to whom Hesiod devotes the poem's longest single hymn of praise (lines 411–452): Zeus, the poem insists, did Hecate no wrong and took nothing away of all that was her portion among the former Titan gods, but confirmed her shares in earth, heaven, and sea — an older goddess carried intact into the new order, honoured, as the passage repeats, above all. The catalogue has done its work: when the war comes, the reader already knows every house, every allegiance, and every prize. VIII. Kronos in Power: The Swallowing, the Stone, and Zeus Hidden on Crete Kronos rules, and repeats his father's crime in a new form. He has learned from Gaia and starry Ouranos that he is destined to be overcome by his own son, strong though he is; so, married to his sister Rhea , he swallows each of their children as it comes forth to its mother's knees — Hestia, Demeter, gold-shod Hera, strong Hades, the loud-crashing Earth-Shaker Poseidon, and, as the sixth pregnancy approaches, Zeus himself is intended (lines 453–467, paraphrased). Where Ouranos hid his children in Earth, Kronos hides his in himself: concealment has moved inward, and the devouring father becomes the poem's emblem of a kingship that maintains itself by consuming its future. Unceasing grief seizes Rhea — and Rhea, like Gaia before her, goes to the older generation for help. She beseeches her own parents, Gaia and Ouranos, to devise a plan that the birth of her child may be concealed and retribution overtake Kronos both for his father and for the swallowed children. They hear her, tell her all that is destined, and send her to Lyctus, in the rich land of Crete (lines 468–478, paraphrased). The Cretan episode (lines 479–491) is told in a few lines and echoed for millennia. Gaia herself receives the newborn Zeus from Rhea in wide Crete, carries him by night to Lyctus, and hides him in a remote cave beneath the secret places of the holy earth on thick-wooded Mount Aegeum — so Hesiod names the place; later Greek tradition attached Zeus's infancy to other Cretan mountains, Dicte and Ida, and surrounded it with the armed Curetes who clashed their spears to drown the crying, none of which is in Hesiod. To Kronos, Rhea gives instead a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes . He takes it in his hands and thrusts it down into his belly — and does not know, the poem says with relish, that in place of the stone his son is left behind, unconquered and untroubled, soon to overcome him by force and drive him from his honours (paraphrased from lines 485–491). The reversal, when it comes (lines 492–506), is managed by the same counsellor. As Zeus grows to full strength, Kronos the wily is beguiled by the deep suggestions of Gaia and brings up again his offspring, vanquished by the arts and might of his own son — vomiting up first the stone he had swallowed last. Zeus sets the stone fast in the wide-pathed earth at goodly Pytho, beneath the glens of Parnassus, to be a sign thenceforth and a marvel to mortal men: the poem's own aetiology for a sacred stone displayed at Delphi, later tradition's omphalos, the navel of the world. And Zeus frees from their deadly bonds the brothers of his father — the Cyclopes, sons of Ouranos, whom Ouranos in his foolishness had bound — who in gratitude give him thunder, the glowing thunderbolt, and lightning, which great Gaia had hidden before. In them, the poem says, he trusts, and rules over mortals and immortals (paraphrased from lines 492–506). The instruments of rule are, characteristically, a gift from the generation his grandfather oppressed and his father left bound. Zeus's first political act is a liberation; his second, in the next movement of the poem, will be a war. LINES 154–210 OURANOS DEPOSED Kronos, hidden in ambush by Gaia, castrates Ouranos with the flint sickle. From the blood: Erinyes, Giants, Meliae. From the foam: Aphrodite. Ouranos names his sons Titans and foretells vengeance. LINES 453–478 KRONOS SWALLOWS HIS CHILDREN Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon are swallowed at birth. Rhea appeals to Gaia and Ouranos, who send her to Lyctus in Crete. LINES 479–491 THE STONE FOR THE CHILD Zeus is hidden in a cave on Mount Aegeum. Kronos swallows a swaddled stone in his place. LINES 492–506 THE DISGORGING Beguiled by Gaia's counsels, Kronos vomits up the stone first, then the children. Zeus sets the stone at Pytho (Delphi) and frees the Cyclopes, who give him the thunderbolt. IX. Prometheus, the Sacrifice at Mecone, and the First Woman Before the war, Hesiod pauses on the other Titan house whose story defines the human condition: the sons of Iapetus (lines 507–616). Atlas, who through hard constraint upholds the wide heaven with unwearying head and arms at the borders of the earth; Menoetius, blasted by Zeus's thunderbolt down to Erebus for his presumption; scatter-brained Epimetheus, who first took from Zeus the fashioned woman; and clever Prometheus , full of various wiles.
