A Hero Made to Order: Theseus and Athens Every Greek city had heroes, but Athens, in the course of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, did something more systematic with hers than most: it built one. Theseus — son of Aegeus, king of Athens, or of the god Poseidon, depending on which parentage a given passage needs — is, in the form in which the tradition hands him down, a comparatively late and deliberately political hero. Heracles, the hero against whom Theseus is constantly and explicitly measured in the sources themselves, is Panhellenic and archaic: he belongs to Argos and Thebes and Tiryns, he is already fully formed in Homer and Hesiod, and no single city owns him. Theseus, by contrast, barely appears in Homer at all — a handful of lines, one of them suspected already in antiquity of having been inserted to please Athens (Section II) — and then, from about 570 BCE onward, his deeds multiply in Athenian vase-painting with a speed and in a pattern that scholars have long read as promotion rather than survival. First the Cretan adventure, then, around 520 BCE, a whole new cycle of “Attic deeds” along the road from Troezen, laid out as a deliberate counterpart to the labours of Heracles. In the fifth century the tragedians take him up as Athens' spokesman — the king who argues for democracy in Euripides' Suppliants and buries other men's dead at the cost of a war. In 476/5 BCE the Athenian general Cimon conquers an island, finds an outsized coffin, and brings home what the city receives, with processions and sacrifices, as the hero's bones. A sanctuary is built for them in the heart of Athens. A great festival, the Theseia, is attached to his name. The sequence is not a legend slowly accreting. It is, at several identifiable points, hero-making as statecraft — and the remarkable thing is that the ancient sources, read carefully, let us watch it happen. This article therefore keeps three things apart on every page, and asks the reader to keep them apart too. (a) The myth as told : the connected story of the tokens, the road, the Labyrinth, the black sail, the unification of Attica, the Amazons, Phaedra, the descent, and the death on Scyros, as Plutarch, Apollodorus, and the poets give it. (b) The cultic, civic, and historical footing : what can be dated and placed — vase-painting from c. 570 BCE, the festival calendar, the recovery of the bones in 476/5 BCE, the Theseion, the paintings Pausanias saw, the synoecism as a claim made by Thucydides and the Atthidographers. (c) The later readings : what subsequent ages made of the material — the philosophers' argument over Theseus's ship, the Amazonomachy read as an allegory of the Persian Wars, Sir Arthur Evans reading the palace at Knossos as the Labyrinth, and the modern scholarly argument, associated above all with H. J. Walker's Theseus and Athens (1995), about when and why Athens promoted its hero. Confusing these three layers is the one error that makes Theseus unintelligible. Keeping them apart makes him one of the most instructive figures in Greek myth, because in his case the machinery that usually hides behind a hero is unusually visible. A word on the hero's character as the tradition itself presents it, because the civic portrait is only half of him. The Theseus of the full story is brave, public-spirited, and repeatedly careless or worse with the people closest to him: he abandons Ariadne, whose help saved his life, on Naxos — or loses her, or is forced to leave her; the sources cannot agree, and Section IX gives the disagreement in full. His forgetfulness kills his father. His credulity, armed with a curse borrowed from Poseidon, kills his son. His last great enterprise, undertaken at fifty, is the abduction of a child, Helen, and an attempt to abduct a goddess, Persephone, which ends with him stuck fast in the underworld while Athens is invaded and his throne is taken. Athens knew all of this — its own tragedians staged the worst of it — and promoted him anyway. That too is part of what this article is about: a city's hero did not have to be blameless. He had to be theirs , and he had to have founded the things they valued. Theseus unified Attica, humbled Crete, repelled the Amazons, sheltered suppliants, and — in the telling Athens settled on — handed power to the people. The rest could be carried. THE HERO AT A GLANCE Son of Aegeus (or Poseidon) and Aethra of Troezen. Raised at Troezen; proves himself by lifting the rock and taking his father's sword and sandals; clears the Isthmus road of six killers; sails to Crete as one of the tribute youths — or as a volunteer — kills the Minotaur, and escapes by Ariadne's thread; becomes king, unifies Attica, fights the Amazons, loses his son Hippolytus through Phaedra's accusation and his own curse; descends with Pirithous to seize Persephone and is rescued by Heracles; is driven from Athens and killed on Scyros. THE CIVIC HERO AT A GLANCE Founder, in Athenian telling, of the unified Attic state (the synoecism), of the Panathenaea in its enlarged form, of the Oschophoria, the Pyanepsia, and the Synoikia festival; patron of suppliants, slaves, and the poor; apparition at Marathon in 490 BCE; bones recovered by Cimon in 476/5 BCE and enshrined in the Theseion; chief festival, the Theseia, on 8 Pyanepsion. SPELLINGS USED HERE Greek names are transliterated, not Latinised, throughout this hub: Pirithous (not Peirithous, except inside quotations, where the translator's spelling is kept), Scyros, Crommyon. The Minotaur's name is Greek Minōtauros , “the bull of Minos”. Ariadne's thread is called a clew in this article, for reasons Section VIII explains. QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE Passages in quotation marks are given only from named published translations actually consulted for this article — Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb Plutarch, J. G. Frazer's Loeb Apollodorus, R. C. Jebb's Bacchylides, and E. P. Coleridge's Euripides — and are identified at the point of quotation. Everything else that renders an ancient author's sense is paraphrase, and is written as paraphrase. II. The Sources, and Why They Disagree No single ancient author tells the whole Theseus story, and the authors who tell parts of it disagree with one another constantly — about whether the tribute went to Crete every year or every nine years, about whether Theseus was chosen by lot or volunteered or was picked out by Minos in person, about what happened to Ariadne, about whether the Labyrinth held a monster at all. This is not a defect in the evidence to be apologised for. It is the evidence. Theseus was a living civic tradition for a thousand years, retold by epic poets, lyric poets, tragedians, local historians of Attica (the Atthidographers), vase-painters, and eventually biographers, and every retelling served the teller's city, genre, and moment. The honest method — the one this hub uses throughout — is to name the source at the claim and let the disagreements stand visible, rather than to blend the versions into a smooth composite that no ancient reader ever possessed. The Early Traces: Homer, Hesiod, and a Suspect Line Theseus is a shadow in the earliest poetry. The Iliad mentions him once in passing, in a list of heroes of a former generation whom Nestor had known ( Iliad 1.265, paraphrased). The Odyssey names him twice: Ariadne, Odysseus says in the underworld, was carried from Crete toward Athens by Theseus but slain by Artemis on Dia before he had joy of her ( Odyssey 11.321–325, paraphrased) — the oldest surviving sentence about the Cretan adventure, and already a version in which Ariadne simply dies. The second Odyssey passage, the line “Theseus, Peirithous, illustrious children of Heaven”, seen among the heroes in Hades ( Odyssey 11.631, in the wording Plutarch quotes), was already suspected in antiquity: Plutarch reports the claim of Hereas of Megara that Peisistratus inserted that line into Homer, and removed from Hesiod a line about Theseus's passion for Aegle, in each case to gratify the Athenians ( Theseus 20.2, paraphrased). The report is itself a piece of Megarian polemic against Athens and cannot be verified; but its existence shows that by the Hellenistic period, scholars understood perfectly well that Theseus's presence in the old poems might be an Athenian editorial product. An epic Theseid also existed — Plutarch dismisses one episode from it, the Amazons' counter-attack at Theseus's wedding to Phaedra, as having “every appearance of fable and invention” ( Theseus 28.1, paraphrased) — and a fragmentary epic on the descent of Pirithous, ascribed to Hesiod and known to Pausanias, told the underworld adventure (Section XV). Of the early Theseus poetry, what survives entire is not epic but lyric: Bacchylides' two dithyrambs (Section VII). The Classical Witnesses: Bacchylides, Tragedy, Thucydides Bacchylides of Ceos (born c. 510 BCE) wrote at least two dithyrambs on Theseus for Athenian performance. Ode 17 puts him on the ship to Crete, defying Minos and diving for the ring that proves his divine birth (Section VII). Ode 18 is a small drama in itself: a dialogue between Aegeus and a chorus of Athenians, as news arrives, deed by deed, of the unknown young man clearing the road from Troezen — Theseus approaching his own city as a rumour before he arrives as a person. The two poems, recovered from an Egyptian papyrus published in 1897, are the earliest substantial Theseus texts we have, and they are already Athenian civic pieces, written for the festivals of the city whose hero they celebrate. Tragedy made Theseus Athens' moral spokesman. In Euripides' Suppliants (c. 423 BCE) he debates a Theban herald on democracy versus tyranny and goes to war to recover the unburied Argive dead (Sections XII and XVII). In the same poet's Hippolytus (428 BCE, first prize) he is the tragedy's instrument of destruction, cursing his innocent son on a dead woman's written word (Section XIV). Aeschylus, in his lost Eleusinians , had Theseus recover the Argive dead by persuasion rather than battle — Plutarch prefers that version and says so ( Theseus 29.4–5, paraphrased). Sophocles gives the aged, exiled Theseus a last gracious appearance in the Oedipus at Colonus , sheltering the blind Oedipus on Attic soil. The tragedians' Theseus is not consistent — Euripides' two plays alone give a democrat-philosopher and a catastrophic father — because each play needs a different Athens, and Theseus is the shape Athens takes on stage. Thucydides , the historian, gives the synoecism its first explicit surviving statement (2.15, paraphrased): before Theseus, Attica was a scatter of independent townships with their own magistrates and council-chambers; Theseus abolished the local governments, established one council-chamber and prytaneum in Athens, and instituted the Synoikia festival in commemoration — though the inhabitants, Thucydides adds drily, went on living on their own land as before. It matters that the first explicit account of Theseus's greatest political deed appears not in poetry or art but in a work of critical history of the late fifth century BCE; modern scholarship (Section XII) has drawn the obvious inference about when the synoecism story itself took shape. The Systematisers: Apollodorus, Plutarch, Pausanias The connected narrative this article follows comes chiefly from two late, learned compilations. The Library (Greek Bibliotheca ) transmitted under the name of Apollodorus — a mythographic handbook of the first or second century CE, not by the second-century BCE scholar whose name it bears — tells the Theseus story in Library 3.15–16 and in the Epitome (1.1–24), the surviving summary of its lost final book. Apollodorus is terse, sequential, and invaluable: where Plutarch debates his sources, Apollodorus simply gives the story, occasionally noting a variant (“or, as some affirm, he offered himself voluntarily”). His Frazer translation (Loeb, 1921) is the version quoted here. Plutarch (c. 46–after 119 CE) made Theseus the subject of the first of his Parallel Lives , paired with Romulus — founder of Athens against founder of Rome. His opening is the most honest statement of method any ancient biographer of a hero ever wrote: having reached periods where, in his image, geographers write “what lies beyond is full of marvels and unreality, a land of poets and fabulists”, he asks his readers' indulgence where fable obstinately refuses to submit to reason (paraphrased from Theseus 1). The Life that follows is a critical anthology as much as a narrative: Plutarch names his authorities — Hellanicus, Philochorus, Pherecydes, Cleidemus, Demon, Ion of Chios, Aristotle — reports their disagreements, occasionally rationalises (the Minotaur becomes, in Philochorus's Cretan version, a general named Taurus; the underworld becomes a Molossian king named Aidoneus with a wife called Phersephone and a dog called Cerberus), and flags invention where he smells it. His Life of Cimon gives the recovery of the bones a second telling. Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb translation (1914) is the version quoted here, and this article follows Plutarch's chapter numbers throughout. Pausanias , the second-century CE traveller, supplies the cultic and monumental record: the Theseion and its paintings (1.17.2–3), the Amazonomachy and the Marathon painting in the Stoa Poikile, where Theseus rises from the underworld among the fighters (1.15.3), Ariadne asleep in a painting on the Acropolis as Theseus sails away and Dionysus arrives (1.20.3), and, far away at Delphi, Polygnotus's great underworld painting, in which Theseus and Pirithous sit in their chairs, Theseus holding both swords while Pirithous gazes at the now useless blades (10.29.9) — all paraphrased here from Pausanias's Description of Greece . Pausanias is this article's standing reminder that Theseus was not only read. He was looked at, walked past, sacrificed to, and taken refuge with, in specific buildings on specific streets. // ON THE MODERN SCHOLARSHIP CITED // Three modern works frame this article's second and third layers. Timothy Gantz, Early Greek Myth (1993), is the standard source-by-source survey, and its ninth chapter assembles the Theseus testimonia in chronological order — the basis for the claim, made repeatedly below, that a given episode is early, late, or Athenian. H. J. Walker, Theseus and Athens (Oxford University Press, 1995), argues the promotion thesis in its fullest form: that the Theseus cycle was substantially built up in the sixth century, in the Athens of the Peisistratids and then of the young democracy, as a civic counterweight to Heracles. Walter Burkert, Greek Religion (English translation 1985), supplies the framework for hero-cult used in Section XVII: the hero as a dead man of power, worshipped at a tomb, in a city that has reasons of its own for keeping him. Where these scholars disagree with each other — and on Theseus they do — the text says so rather than silently choosing. III. Birth at Troezen: Two Fathers and the Tokens Under the Rock The story begins, as Athenian stories about legitimacy tend to, with a childless king and an ambiguous oracle. Aegeus , king of Athens, had no children. Consulting Delphi, he received the celebrated riddling response — in Perrin's translation of Plutarch, the verse runs: “Loose not the wine-skin's jutting neck, great chief of the people, / Until thou shalt have come once more to the city of Athens” ( Theseus 3.3). Not understanding it, Aegeus stopped at Troezen , on the Saronic coast of the Argolid, and repeated it to his host Pittheus , son of Pelops, a man reputed the wisest of his time. Pittheus understood — the oracle forbade Aegeus to lie with a woman before reaching Athens — and, by persuasion or guile (Plutarch's alternatives, Theseus 3.4, paraphrased), brought it about that Aegeus lay instead with Pittheus's own daughter, Aethra . Apollodorus is blunter: Pittheus, understanding the oracle, made Aegeus drunk and caused him to lie with Aethra ( Library 3.15.6, paraphrased). The dynastic point is plain in both versions. Pittheus, by one night's hospitality, attached the childless Athenian royal house to his own; and the child, if child there was, would be at once Aegeus's heir and Pelops's great-grandson. Before leaving, Aegeus hid a sword and a pair of sandals under a great rock that had a hollow just large enough to receive them, and told Aethra alone the secret: if she bore a son, and the son, grown to manhood, could lift the rock and take out what lay beneath, she was to send him to Athens with the tokens, in secrecy — for Aegeus feared the fifty sons of Pallas , his nephews, who plotted against the childless king and despised him (Plutarch, Theseus 3.5, paraphrased). The tokens — Greek gnōrismata , “recognition-things” — are the story's founding device, and they are worth pausing on. Greek myth is full of exposed infants recognised by trinkets; Theseus's tokens are the adult, civic version of the same machinery. The sword and sandals do not merely identify a lost child. They are a test (the rock must be lifted), a credential (they must be produced in Athens), and a claim (they assert, against fifty rival nephews, that this stranger is the king's son). When the recognition finally happens, in Section V, it happens by the sword alone, at a banquet, at the last possible moment — the story spends its founding device with a dramatist's economy. The Second Father Aethra bore a son. But whose? The tradition, characteristically, refuses to choose, and the refusal is functional. Plutarch reports that Aethra kept the truth concealed and that Pittheus spread the report that the boy was begotten by Poseidon — a claim Troezen had every reason to welcome, since Poseidon was the city's patron, honoured with first-fruits and stamped, as a trident, on its coinage ( Theseus 6.1, paraphrased). Apollodorus preserves the mechanism in its most startling form: on the same night that Aegeus lay with Aethra, Poseidon also lay with her ( Library 3.15.7, paraphrased). The double paternity is a known Greek pattern — Heracles is son of Zeus and of Amphitryon in the same way — but in Theseus's case it does specific work for the rest of the story. The mortal father gives him the Athenian throne and the plot. The divine father gives him his sea-affinity (the dive in Bacchylides, Section VII), his standing with Poseidon — who grants him, in the tradition Euripides uses, three curses, one of which he will spend on his own son (Section XIV) — and his calendar: Athens honoured Theseus on the eighth day of the month, Poseidon's day (Section XVII). Even the boy's upbringing is doubled. He is reared at Troezen by Pittheus, with a tutor, Connidas, to whom the Athenians still sacrificed a ram on the day before the Theseia in Plutarch's own time ( Theseus 4.1, paraphrased) — a minor cult detail that shows how completely the hero's biography had been furnished with commemorations, down to his schoolmaster. The name itself attracted ancient etymology: Plutarch reports that the boy was called Theseus either because the tokens had been “placed” ( tithēmi , to place) in hiding for him, or because Aegeus “acknowledged” him at Athens — two derivations offered side by side, neither endorsed ( Theseus 4.1, paraphrased). Modern philology treats the name as pre-Greek, like so much else in the story — the hero, his city, and his monster all carry names older than the Greek language that tells of them. What is certain is the sequence the story now sets running. The boy grows up at Troezen displaying, with his strength, “a firm spirit united with intelligence and sagacity” (Perrin's wording, Theseus 6.2, paraphrased in the surrounding text). Aethra brings him to the rock, tells him the truth, and bids him take the tokens and go — by sea, the safe way, as both she and Pittheus beg him to do. He lifts the rock easily. And he refuses the sea. // THE HAIRCUT OF A HERO // Plutarch pauses, before the journey, on a tonsure. It was the custom, he says, for youths coming of age to go to Delphi and offer their hair to the god; Theseus went, and sheared only the front of his head, as Homer says the Abantes did, so that enemies could not seize him by it in close fighting — and this cut was called the Theseis after him ( Theseus 5, paraphrased). A place at Delphi was still called the Theseia from his visit. The detail is small and characteristic: even the hero's haircut had become an Athenian institution with a name. IV. The Road to Athens: The Six Labours of the Isthmus The land road from Troezen to Athens — across the Isthmus of Corinth and through the Megarid — was, in the story's geography, infested. Plutarch frames the age itself as the problem: it produced men of extraordinary strength and endurance who used their powers for nothing fitting, exulting in cruelty and holding reverence and justice to be the virtues of cowards ( Theseus 6.4, paraphrased). Some of these Heracles had destroyed on his travels; others had crouched out of his sight, and when Heracles fell into misfortune and servitude to Omphale in Lydia, the old villainies burst out again in Greece, there being none to restrain them ( Theseus 6.5, paraphrased). Pittheus, describing each miscreant in detail, tried to persuade his grandson to sail. The persuasion failed for the reason the whole cycle exists: Theseus had long been secretly fired by the glory of Heracles . He listened most eagerly to those who had seen the hero; he dreamed of his achievements by night; and he judged it dreadful that his famous cousin — the two were kin, Aethra and Alcmene being first cousins through Pelops's children — should purge land and sea while he himself arrived at Athens by the safe route carrying, as proofs of his birth, “only sandals and a sword unstained with blood” (Perrin's wording, Theseus 7.1, closely paraphrased). He set out by land, determined, Plutarch says, to do no man any wrong, but to punish those who offered him violence. The six encounters that follow are the labours of the road , and their pattern is exact. In almost every case Theseus kills the killer by his own method : the clubber is clubbed, the pine-bender is torn apart by bent pines, the foot-washer is kicked into the sea, the bed-stretcher is fitted to his own bed. Plutarch states the principle openly and attributes it to the model: Theseus did this in imitation of Heracles, who punished those who offered him violence in the manner in which they had plotted to serve him ( Theseus 11.1, paraphrased). The justice of the road is talionic — measure for measure — and it is also, read civically, a programme: the future founder of the unified state begins by making its one land approach safe for travellers. The road from the Peloponnese to Athens runs through the story in the order the encounters are given below: Epidaurus, the Isthmus, Crommyon, the Megarian cliffs, Eleusis, Erineus. 1. PERIPHETES, THE CLUB-BEARER — EPIDAURUS First, in Epidaurian territory, Periphetes, who fought with an iron-bound club and was called the Club-bearer (Korynetēs), laid hold of Theseus and tried to stop his progress; Theseus grappled with him and slew him (Plutarch, Theseus 8.1; Apollodorus, Library 3.16.1, paraphrased). Pleased with the club, Theseus took it and carried it ever after — as Heracles carried the lion's skin: the weapon of the vanquished, in the victor's hands, made invincible. Apollodorus adds that Periphetes was a son of Hephaestus, lame like his father. 2. SINIS, THE PINE-BENDER — THE ISTHMUS On the Isthmus, Sinis bent pine trees down, fastened his victims to them, and let the trees tear them apart. Theseus slew him in the very manner in which he had destroyed many men — without practice or acquaintance with the device, showing, Plutarch says, that valour is superior to all device and practice ( Theseus 8.2; Apollodorus, Library 3.16.2, paraphrased). The sequel is darker than the labour: Sinis's daughter Perigune fled and hid among rushes and wild asparagus, vowing never to trample them if they saved her; Theseus pledged her safety, and she bore him a son, Melanippus ( Theseus 8.2–3, paraphrased). The road-clearer's first conquest is also the story's first of many women taken along the way. 3. THE CROMMYONIAN SOW — CROMMYON The sow of Crommyon, called Phaea — whether after the old woman who reared it, as Apollodorus has it, the creature was no insignificant beast but fierce and hard to master. Theseus went out of his way to encounter and slay it, Plutarch says, so that he might not seem to perform all his exploits under compulsion, and because the brave man ought to attack villainous men in self-defence but seek occasion against the nobler beasts ( Theseus 9.1; Apollodorus, Library 3.16.2, paraphrased). Some rationalisers, Plutarch notes, made Phaea a female robber nicknamed Sow for her life and manners. In Apollodorus the sow is a child of Echidna and Typhon — of the monster-brood catalogued in this hub's Theogony article. 4. SCIRON — THE MEGARIAN CLIFFS On the borders of Megara, Sciron robbed passers-by from the cliffs that bear his name; in the prevalent tradition he insolently thrust out his feet and bade strangers wash them, then kicked them, mid-washing, into the sea below, where a great turtle waited in some tellings. Theseus hurled him down the cliffs himself (Plutarch, Theseus 10.1; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.2, paraphrased). Plutarch immediately reports the counter-tradition: Megarian writers, “waging war with antiquity”, insisted Sciron was no robber but a chastiser of robbers, respectably married into the families of Aeacus and Cychreus, and that Theseus killed him later, in war, not on this journey ( Theseus 10.2–3, paraphrased). The labour, that is, was already contested local history in antiquity: what Athens remembered as road-clearing, Megara remembered as murder. 5. CERCYON — ELEUSIS At Eleusis, Cercyon the Arcadian challenged passers-by to wrestle and killed them in the bout. Theseus out-wrestled him and killed him (Plutarch, Theseus 11.1; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.3, paraphrased — in Frazer's wording, he lifted him up on high and dashed him to the ground, the wrestler's throw that later tradition made the invention of scientific wrestling itself). The place matters: Eleusis, later home of the Mysteries treated in this hub's Mysteries article, enters the Theseus story first as a strong man's killing-ground on the Athens road. 6. PROCRUSTES — ERINEUS Last, at Erineus, Damastes, surnamed Procrustes — “the Stretcher” — who kept a bed (two beds, in Apollodorus: a short one and a long one) and fitted his guests to it, stretching the short and lopping the tall. Theseus killed him by compelling him to make his own body fit his bed, as he had been wont to do with strangers (Plutarch, Theseus 11.1; Apollodorus, Epitome 1.4, paraphrased). The name outlived the story: a “Procrustean bed” is still English for a standard imposed by violence on things that do not fit it — the one labour of the six whose villain, not whose hero, the language kept. A Cycle Built Backwards Now the second layer, because with the road labours it is unusually well documented. In Athenian vase-painting, the Cretan adventure — Theseus and the Minotaur — appears from about c. 570 BCE ; the road labours as a cycle , the so-called Attic deeds, appear from about c. 520 BCE , suddenly and as a set. The dating is the art historians' (the sequence is conveniently summarised in the scholarship cited in Section XVIII: Minotaur and Centaur fights from c. 570, the Attic deeds from c. 520, monumental public compositions from c. 480–420). The implication drawn by Walker and others is that the cycle was assembled at that moment — older, separate strong-man tales of the Isthmus and the Megarid gathered, ordered along a road, and issued as a set, precisely so that Athens' hero should have what Heracles had: a canonical series of labours, performed in his own territory, on his way to his own city. The sculptural programmes then canonised the pairing: on the Athenian Treasury at Delphi (c. 490 BCE) and on the Hephaisteion above the Athenian Agora, the deeds of Theseus are carved in direct counterpart to the labours of Heracles, metope answering metope. None of this makes the individual tales new — Sciron, Sinis, and Procrustes may each be old local figures, and Megara's protest (above) proves the Sciron story was old enough to fight over. What the late sixth century added was the frame : one hero, one road, six labours, one destination. The frame is the politics. The journey ends in a rite, not a fight. At the river Cephisus, men of the Phytalidae met the bloodstained traveller, purified him from bloodshed at his request with the customary rites, made propitiatory sacrifices, and feasted him in their house — the first kindness, Plutarch says, that he met with on his journey ( Theseus 12.1, paraphrased). Theseus remembered it: the Phytalidae were later given charge of his own sacrifices at Athens (Section X). And so, purified, on the eighth day of the month then called Cronius and later Hecatombaeon, he entered Athens — a city, Plutarch says, full of confusion and dissension, and a royal household in a distressing condition. V. Arrival: Medea's Cup, the Recognition, and the Marathonian Bull The household's distress had a name. Medea , fled from Corinth, was living with Aegeus, having promised by her sorceries to cure his childlessness. She learned who the arriving stranger was before Aegeus did; and Aegeus, old, ignorant of his son, and afraid of everything because of the faction in the city, was persuaded by her to entertain Theseus as a guest and take him off by poison (Plutarch, Theseus 12.2, paraphrased). Apollodorus adds the errand that precedes the banquet: Medea persuaded Aegeus to beware of the stranger as a traitor, and Aegeus, not knowing his own son, sent him first against the Marathonian bull — the bull that was ravaging the Marathonian Tetrapolis, in some accounts the very bull of Crete, Heracles' seventh labour, released and wandered north (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.5, paraphrased; Plutarch places the bull after the recognition, at Theseus 14 — the sources differ on the order, and the difference is noted here rather than harmonised). Theseus killed the bull. Then came the banquet, and the poison, which Aegeus had received that same day from Medea. The recognition is the story's most perfectly constructed scene, and both systematisers tell it the same way. Theseus, at the table, chose not to announce himself, but to give his father the means of discovery: when the meats were served, he drew his sword — the sword from under the rock — as if to carve with it, and brought it to his father's notice. Aegeus perceived it, dashed down the proffered cup of poison, questioned his son, embraced him, and formally recognised him before an assembly of the citizens, who received him gladly for his valour (Plutarch, Theseus 12.2–3, paraphrased; in Apollodorus, Epitome 1.6, Frazer's wording has Aegeus dash the cup from his hands on recognising the sword). Plutarch adds the aetiological garnish his readers expected: the spilled poison, they said, marked the spot where the enclosure in the Delphinium later stood, by Aegeus's house. Medea, her plot exposed, was expelled — in Apollodorus's word — and vanishes from the Athenian story as suddenly as she entered it. Recognition made Theseus heir, and heirship made him a target. The sons of Pallas , who had expected the kingdom on Aegeus's childless death, went to war: exasperated, Plutarch says, that Aegeus should be king at all, as an adopted son of Pandion unrelated to the house of Erechtheus, and that an immigrant stranger should now succeed him ( Theseus 13.1, paraphrased). They divided into two bands — one marching openly from Sphettus, one in ambush at Gargettus — but their herald, Leos of Agnus, betrayed the plan; Theseus fell on the ambush and slew them all, and the other band dispersed. Plutarch preserves the feud's fossil in local custom: the township of Pallene, he says, still would not intermarry with Agnus, nor allow heralds to cry their customary “Hear, ye people!” ( Akouete leō ) there, for hatred of the word that sounds like the traitor's name ( Theseus 13.3, paraphrased). The episode is worth its space because it states the charge against Theseus that the rest of his career must answer, in Athens' own telling: he was a foreigner . The hero of Athens was born at Troezen, of a Troezenian mother, and arrived as an immigrant with a sword. The civic myth does not hide this. It builds on it — the outsider who becomes the founder is a stronger claim than a founder who was never anything else — and Section XVI shows the charge returning, fatally, at the end. The Marathonian bull, in Plutarch's ordering, belongs here: Theseus, desiring to be at work and to court the people's favour, went out against the bull that was doing no small mischief to the Tetrapolis, mastered it, drove it alive through the city in display, and sacrificed it to Delphinian Apollo ( Theseus 14.1, paraphrased). The Second Foundation: A Dialogue That Became a World This article belongs to the Foundations cluster of the Alchemy wing, and it treats the wing's second foundation. The first is the four-element scheme itself — fire, air, water, and earth as the roots of all bodies — which the hub treats in its own article on the four elements . That scheme is older than Plato: it is Empedocles' inheritance. What Plato's Timaeus did, around 360 BCE, was to give the four roots a physics — to say what an element is, why there are exactly four of them, how they pass into one another, and what kind of cosmos they compose when a rational maker orders them toward the good. Nearly everything the later tradition meant by “element theory” — in Greek alchemy, in Arabic natural philosophy, in Latin scholasticism, and in the Hermetic literature this wing exists to document — descends from that act of foundation, whether its heirs were developing Plato's construction or, as Aristotle did, rebuilding the house while keeping its address. The companion article on Aristotle's matter theory treats the rebuilding; this article treats the original building. The Timaeus is also, by a wide margin, the most continuously read work of Greek philosophy in the pre-modern world. Other Platonic dialogues vanished from the Latin West for a thousand years; Aristotle's treatises travelled by Syriac and Arabic roads and arrived in Latin Europe late and in pieces. The Timaeus never went away. It was commented on in Plato's own school, quarrelled over by his immediate successors, translated in part by Cicero, translated again — with a vast commentary — by Calcidius, epitomised by Galen and carried in that form into Arabic, expounded at enormous length by Proclus, glossed by the masters of Chartres, and read by every educated European who read any Plato at all until Ficino's complete Plato of 1484 finally gave the West its other dialogues back. For most of its history, “Plato” effectively meant this one dialogue, and “Plato's cosmology” meant the cosmos it describes: a living, ensouled, spherical world, made by a good craftsman in the likeness of an eternal model, out of elements that are geometrical solids at bottom. A note on method, in the form this hub's readers will recognise from the wing's other articles. Direct quotation from the Timaeus is given only where it has been verified in a named modern translation, and the translation is named at the quotation. The two translations relied on throughout are F. M. Cornford's, published with his commentary as Plato's Cosmology (1937), and Donald J. Zeyl's (Hackett, 2000). Everything else that reports the dialogue's contents is paraphrase , labelled as such where the wording matters, and keyed to the dialogue's Stephanus pagination — the page-and-letter references (29d, 53c, and so on) by which every edition of Plato has been cited since the sixteenth century. The Timaeus attracts confident misquotation more than almost any ancient text, because so many later systems have wanted its authority for doctrines it does not quite contain. This article's discipline is the opposite one: where the dialogue is strange, disputed, or silent, the article says so, and the disputes are stated as disputes. THE DIALOGUE Written c. 360 BCE, among Plato's late works. Dramatically a sequel to a conversation resembling the Republic's, and the first panel of an unfinished trilogy: Timaeus on the cosmos and human nature, Critias on ancient Athens and Atlantis, and a Hermocrates that was never written. Almost the whole of it is one speech by Timaeus of Locri. THE SPEECH'S THREE MOVEMENTS Modern editions divide Timaeus' discourse (27d–92c) into three parts: the works of Intellect (29d–47e); the works of Necessity (47e–69a), prefaced by the “second beginning” that introduces the receptacle; and the two causes cooperating in the making of the human being (69a–92c). This article follows that division. One framing point before the frame itself. The Timaeus is routinely described in popular writing as Plato's “creation myth”, and the description is not wrong, but it conceals the dialogue's double nature. It is at once a story — a god makes the world, in an order, for reasons — and a piece of technical natural philosophy, containing the most detailed physical theory any Greek author produced before Aristotle: a geometry of matter, a mathematical harmonics of soul, a physiology, a pathology, and a theory of sensation. Its author knew the two registers were in tension, and he built the tension into the text: the speaker announces in advance that his account can only be a likely story (Section IV). Holding both facts at once — that this is a myth that knows it is one, and that it is also the ancient world's most serious cosmology — is the whole discipline of reading it, and Sections IV and V return to the tension from the two directions of the oldest scholarly quarrel it provoked. // WHY THIS ARTICLE SITS IN THE ALCHEMY WING // The alchemists treated elsewhere in this hub did not inherit their elements from Empedocles directly. They inherited them as Plato had rebuilt them — corpuscular, geometrical, transformable by rule — and as Aristotle, Galen, and the Arabic tradition then reworked the Platonic scheme. A reader who wants to know why Alexandrian alchemy speaks of bodies dissolving, recombining, and ripening toward perfection needs the dialogue in which transformation first became arithmetic. That dialogue is this one. II. The Frame: One Absent, a Festival, and a City Set in Motion The dialogue opens with an absence. Socrates counts his companions — one, two, three — and asks, in paraphrase, where the fourth is: a member of yesterday's company is missing, kept away by indisposition (17a). The three present are Timaeus , Critias , and Hermocrates , and the conversation they are about to have is explicitly a repayment. Yesterday, in a discussion the dialogue summarises at 17c–19b — a city ordered much as the Republic 's ideal city is ordered, with its classes, its common arrangements, and its guardians — Socrates played host and speaker. Today the guests are to entertain him in return, and Socrates states what he wants from the entertainment: not another portrait of the ideal city at rest, but the city in motion — set down in the world, at war, negotiating, fighting, behaving as the living thing his static description could not show (19b–c, in paraphrase). The programme the three guests agree on divides the labour in the order of being itself. Timaeus will speak first, beginning with the origin of the cosmos and ending with the nature of human beings; Critias will then take those human beings, set them in the Athens of nine thousand years ago, and show the ideal city in action against Atlantis; Hermocrates was to speak third (27a–b, in paraphrase). Of the three panels, the first exists — it is this dialogue — the second exists unfinished as the Critias , and the third was never written. The setting, on the usual reading of the dramatic clues, is Athens during the Panathenaea, the great festival of Athena — a fitting stage for a story in which Athens herself will be the heroine. The Speakers TIMAEUS OF LOCRI Presented (20a, in paraphrase) as a visitor from Locri in southern Italy, a man of wealth and standing who has held his city's highest offices and reached, in Socrates' introduction, the summit of philosophy — above all of astronomy and the study of the nature of the universe. Whether a historical Timaeus of Locri wrote anything is doubtful; a treatise On the Soul of the World later circulated under his name, but it is a much later summary of this dialogue, not its source. Plato's Timaeus is best read as a constructed authority: the Pythagoreanising astronomer-philosopher the speech requires. CRITIAS AND HERMOCRATES Critias — the dialogue leaves it genuinely uncertain whether the notorious Critias of the Thirty Tyrants or his grandfather is meant, and scholarship has argued both — is the keeper of the Atlantis story, which he claims descends from Solon. Hermocrates, the Syracusan general who had defeated Athens in Sicily, is present chiefly as the promised third speaker: a standing reminder that the trilogy's last panel, which might have judged the other two, is missing. The frame matters to everything that follows, for two reasons. The first is literary: nearly all of what the world knows as “Plato's cosmology” is placed in the mouth of a guest, in a speech Socrates commissions and then does not interrupt. The Timaeus is a monologue wearing a dialogue's frame, and its pronouncements arrive with an authority no Socratic cross-examination is allowed to test. Ancient and modern readers alike have disagreed about how far Plato stands behind his speaker — the question runs underneath the dispute of Section IV — but the form itself is a fact: this is doctrine delivered, not doctrine debated. The second reason is structural. The promised sequence — cosmos first, then the city in history — makes cosmology the foundation of politics in the trilogy's design: you cannot show the good city in motion until you know what kind of world it moves in, and what kind of animal the human being is who moves it. Timaeus' speech honours the commission exactly. It ends, as Section XII shows, with the human body and soul — the point at which Critias was to take over. // HOW TO READ THE REFERENCES // References in the form 29d or 53c–55c are to the Stephanus pagination: the page numbers of Henri Estienne's 1578 Geneva edition of Plato, subdivided by the letters a–e, which all modern editions print in their margins. They are the coordinates of Plato scholarship. A reader with any translation — Cornford, Zeyl, or another — can find every passage this article discusses by those numbers alone, whatever the page of the translation itself. III. Atlantis, in One Section This article gives Atlantis exactly one section, deliberately. The full treatment — the story's sources, its geography, and its enormous modern afterlife as a supposed lost continent — belongs to the Antiquity division's article on Plato's Atlantis , and the reader who wants Atlantis should go there. What a reader of the Timaeus needs is only the story's function inside this dialogue, which is smaller, stranger, and more interesting than the legend built on it. Within the frame, the Atlantis story is Critias' contribution, and in the Timaeus he only summarises it (20d–25d); the full telling was reserved for the Critias . In paraphrase of the summary: Critias recounts a tale he heard from his grandfather, who had it from Solon, who had it from Egyptian priests at Saïs. The priests told Solon that the Greeks are children in memory, that cataclysms periodically destroy civilisations and their records, and that nine thousand years before Solon's time there existed an Athens of the very constitution Socrates described yesterday — and an island power, Atlantis, larger (in the text's phrase) than Libya and Asia together, situated beyond the Pillars of Heracles. Atlantis made war on the peoples within the straits; primeval Athens, alone and abandoned by her allies, defeated the invasion and liberated the Mediterranean world; and afterwards, in a single day and night of catastrophe, earthquakes and floods swallowed the Athenian army and sank Atlantis beneath the sea, leaving the Atlantic unnavigable for its mud. Critias insists, repeatedly and in terms, that the story is not a fiction but true (20d, 26e, in paraphrase) — an insistence modern readers have taken both as Plato's wink and as his earnest, and which the Antiquity division's treatment examines at length. Inside the trilogy's design, the story's job is plain: it is the city in motion Socrates asked for. The ideal constitution, which the Republic could only describe at rest and which critics could dismiss as a pattern laid up in heaven, is here given a past: it once existed, it fought, and it won. Atlantis is its necessary opposite — wealth, sea-power, and imperial appetite grown past measure — and the war between them is the frame's whole point, the exhibit the cosmology is commissioned to support. Timaeus' speech, which follows immediately, is therefore not an interruption of the Atlantis story. It is its foundation: first the world and the human animal must be made, before the city made of those animals can be shown in action. Readers who come to the Timaeus for Atlantis alone invert the dialogue's own priorities; the dialogue spends five Stephanus pages on Atlantis and sixty-five on the cosmos. This article follows the dialogue. IV. A “Likely Story”: The Status of the Account and the Oldest Dispute in Platonism Before Timaeus says anything about the world, he says something about his own speech, and the whole later history of the dialogue is contained in the warning. The discourse opens (27d–28a) with a distinction that governs everything: between what always is and never becomes , grasped by understanding with a reasoned account, and what becomes and never fully is , grasped by opinion with unreasoning sense-perception. The cosmos belongs to the second class: it is visible, tangible, bodily, and therefore a thing that has become (28b–c). And from the classification Timaeus draws the methodological consequence (29b–d, in paraphrase): accounts are akin to the things they set forth. An account of what is eternal and unchanging can itself be stable and irrefutable; an account of a likeness — and the cosmos is a likeness, an eikōn , of an eternal model — can only be a likely account, an eikōs logos or eikōs mythos : in the phrase every translation must wrestle with, a “likely story” . The wordplay is untranslatable and deliberate: eikōs , likely, is the adjective of eikōn , image. A discourse about an image can be no more exact than its subject permits. The warning is not a shrug, and Section IV's first duty is to state its force accurately, because two opposite misreadings of it are endemic. On one side, “likely story” is quoted as if Plato were confessing that the cosmology is mere poetry, to be enjoyed and not believed. The text does not support the shrug: Timaeus undertakes to give an account “no less likely than anyone else's” (29c, in paraphrase), the account is to merit belief ( pistis , 29c) even though it cannot command the certainty reserved for knowledge of eternal things, and the speaker repeatedly marks the points at which he is exceeding what human beings can settle (for instance at 53d, where a definitive account of the elementary triangles is reserved to a god and to the man dear to a god). On the other side, the warning is ignored altogether, and the speech is mined as flat doctrine. That reading is equally unsupported: the dialogue itself grades its own epistemic status, and any honest account of its teaching must carry the grade with the teaching. The modern scholarly consensus, represented by the Stanford Encyclopedia's treatment of the dialogue, reads the contrast as one between apodeictic certainty about intelligible matters and warranted plausibility about empirical ones — not as a licence to treat the cosmology as either scripture or decoration. The Dispute: Did the World Begin? The second and deeper dispute concerns not the account's certainty but its tense . Timaeus speaks throughout of the cosmos as something that came to be : the craftsman took over a pre-existing disorder and ordered it (30a); time itself came into being together with the heavens (38b); the world soul was compounded, divided, and joined to the body in a narrated sequence of operations. Taken at face value, the dialogue teaches a temporal creation — a before, an act, and an after. But Plato's own school split on the question immediately, and the split is the oldest documented quarrel in Platonism. THE METAPHORICAL READING: THE OLD ACADEMY Speusippus, Plato's nephew and successor, and Xenocrates, the Academy's third head — with Crantor, the dialogue's first commentator, often named beside them in the ancient reports — held that the generation of the cosmos is narrated “for the sake of instruction”: as a geometer draws a figure in stages to make its structure intelligible, so the dialogue assembles in time what in reality exists eternally and all at once. On this reading there was no first moment and no pre-cosmic chaos; the “before” of the story is an analytical device, showing what the world would be without the ordering presence of intellect. The reading became the prevailing view among later Platonists, Plotinus and Proclus included. THE LITERAL READING: ARISTOTLE Aristotle, who studied in the Academy for twenty years, read the dialogue literally — and attacked it on that reading. In On the Heavens (I.10, 279b–280a) and Physics VIII he argues against a cosmos that began but will never end, and against a beginning of time itself (Physics 251b), treating Plato as the one thinker who made the world generated yet indestructible. Aristotle knew the metaphorical defence and names it — only to reject it: the geometrical analogy, he argues, fails, because a diagram's stages coexist in the finished figure, whereas a generated cosmos's beginning is a real event. Plutarch and Atticus later defended the literal reading within Platonism itself. Modern scholarship has inherited the quarrel entire, and this article states its modern form rather than pretending it closed. A. E. Taylor's commentary (1928) and, most influentially, Cornford's Plato's Cosmology (1937) defended the metaphorical reading: Cornford held that the creation narrative is a myth in form, that time cannot have begun since “before time” is incoherent, and that the pre-cosmic disorder represents, in story-form, the element of necessity in a world that has always depended on a reason it did not choose. Harold Cherniss pressed the Academy's testimony to the same side. Against them, Gregory Vlastos's defence of the literal reading (from 1939 onward) reopened the case: Vlastos argued that the text's temporal language is too sustained and too specific to be waved away, and that Plato — unlike his successors — was willing to hold that the cosmos genuinely began, its order imposed on a motion that genuinely preceded it. The contemporary literature remains divided along recognisably the same lines: David Sedley's Creationism and Its Critics in Antiquity (2007) defends a robustly literal, creationist Plato, and Sarah Broadie's Nature and Divinity in Plato's Timaeus (2012) likewise takes the craftsman's agency with full seriousness, while other recent interpreters seek positions between the poles — a real dependence of order on intellect, without a datable first morning. The position of this article is the one the evidence supports: the dispute is genuine, it is twenty-four centuries old, it was already a dispute among men who had heard Plato lecture, and no summary that settles it in a sentence can be trusted. What can be said without controversy is what the dispute is about : whether the world's dependence on reason is a fact of its history or a fact of its structure. Both parties agree on the dependence. They disagree about the tense. // A SECOND DISPUTE HIDING INSIDE THE FIRST // Entangled with the question of generation is the question of the craftsman himself. Is the demiurge a distinct divine agent, literally deliberating and building? A personification of the world soul's rationality? A figure for the intelligible model's own causal presence in the world? The dialogue never says, and the options map only loosely onto the literal–metaphorical divide: one can hold a literal creation by a figurative craftsman, or an eternal cosmos ordered by a real god. The Stanford Encyclopedia's survey concludes that the craftsman's intellect cannot simply be identified with the world soul (which is itself his product) or with a form (forms are objects of thought, not thinkers), and leaves him, in its phrase, sui generis. Readers should know that the most famous person in the dialogue is also its least identified. V. The Demiurge and the Model The argument that produces the craftsman is short and is given at 28a–29b (in paraphrase throughout this section). Everything that becomes, becomes by some cause. The cosmos is visible, tangible, and bodily; therefore it is perceptible; therefore it belongs to the class of things that become; therefore it has a cause — a maker. A maker works by looking to a model. If the model he looks to is eternal and unchanging, his work will be beautiful; if to something generated, it will not. The cosmos is the most beautiful of generated things; therefore its maker looked to the eternal. The maker receives his enduring name at 28a: the demiurge ( dēmiourgos ) — in ordinary Greek, a craftsman, a skilled public worker, the word for a potter or a smith raised to cosmic scale. Cornford and Zeyl both render him “the craftsman”; older translations' “Demiurge” has become his proper name in the literature, and this article uses both. His motive is stated at 29e–30a, in the dialogue's most consequential piece of theology (in paraphrase): he was good, and in the good no envy or grudging ever arises; being free of envy, he wanted everything to become as like himself as possible. He found the visible world not at rest but moving in a discordant and disorderly fashion, and he brought it from disorder into order, judging order to be in every way better. Two features of this famous passage deserve emphasis, because later ages repeatedly flattened them. First, the craftsman does not create from nothing. He takes over what is already there — the verb matters — and his work is ordering, not summoning into existence. Whatever the Timaeus teaches, it is not creatio ex nihilo , and the medieval readers who found Genesis in it (Section XIII) were reading with an effort the text itself does not make. Second, his goodness is defined negatively and precisely: it is the absence of phthonos , grudging. The Platonic god is not a jealous god. In a religious landscape full of divine envy, the sentence is a manifesto, and the Hermetic and Neoplatonic traditions both built on it. The Model: The Living Thing The model to which the craftsman looks is named at 30c–31b (in paraphrase): the Living Thing ( zōon ) — the intelligible original that contains within itself all intelligible living things, as the cosmos contains all visible ones. The argument for the cosmos's unity runs off the model's: as the model is one and complete, embracing every kind of living being in the intelligible order, so its image must be one and complete, embracing every kind in the visible order. There cannot be two cosmoses, because there is no second model for a second cosmos to copy, and a cosmos that left some kind of creature outside itself would be, to that extent, an image of something less than the whole. Whether the Living Thing is a single form or an ordered constellation of forms — the form of Animal somehow containing the forms of all species — is a question the dialogue raises by its phrasing and does not resolve, and the scholarly literature (the Stanford Encyclopedia's survey states both options) leaves it open. What is not open is the structural role: the model is the standard by which every subsequent detail of the construction is justified. The cosmos has the features it has because the best possible image of that original, in this medium, must have them. The medium imposes its first requirement at once (31b–32c, in paraphrase). The image must be bodily: therefore visible and tangible; therefore it must contain fire , by which things are seen, and earth , by which they are solid to the touch. But two extremes cannot be joined without a mean, and because the cosmos is a solid, not a plane, it requires two means — air and water — set in continuous proportion: as fire is to air, so air is to water, and as air is to water, so water is to earth. The four elements enter the dialogue, on its first presentation of them, not as a chemist's list but as a proportion — a bond ( desmos ) of mathematical friendship holding the world's body together. The point is foundational for this hub's subject, and it is worth pausing on: in the Timaeus , the fourfold scheme of the elements is justified geometrically before it is described physically. The elements of Section X, built from triangles, are the same doctrine at a deeper level — body resolved into number all the way down. What Intellect makes, it makes as a mathematician makes; the works of Necessity, when they come, will be what resists the proof. // THE CRAFTSMAN'S LIMITS // The demiurge of the Timaeus is not omnipotent, and the dialogue is careful about it. He works in a medium he did not make, with materials whose properties he does not choose, toward a perfection the medium only partly permits. The results are therefore always of the form: the best possible under the conditions . Later Platonism, embarrassed by a limited god, progressively allegorised the limitation away; later theology, reading the dialogue through Genesis, denied it outright. The text's own position is the craftsmanlike one, and it is the source of the dialogue's characteristic explanatory pattern — purpose achieved through constraint, intellect “persuading” necessity (48a) rather than abolishing it. VI. The World Soul and Its Harmonic Ratios A cosmos that is an image of a Living Thing must itself be alive, and a living thing that is to be intelligent must have a soul; intellect, Timaeus argues, cannot be present in anything apart from soul (30b, in paraphrase). The craftsman therefore compounds a world soul before he finishes the world's body, and places it at the centre, stretched throughout the whole and enveloping it from outside (34b, 36e, in paraphrase) — older than the body it animates, and its mistress, though the narrative, for instruction's sake, described the body first. The compounding of the soul (35a–b) is the dialogue's most metaphysically dense passage. In Zeyl's translation — the one verbatim quotation this article permits itself at length, verified in his 2000 edition's text as widely reprinted — the craftsman mixes, for each of the soul's three ingredients, an intermediate between the indivisible and the divisible: “In between the Being that is indivisible and always changeless, and the one that is divisible and comes to be in the corporeal realm, he mixed a third, intermediate form of being, derived from the other two. Similarly, he made a mixture of the Same, and then one of the Different, in between their indivisible and their corporeal, divisible counterparts. And he took the three mixtures and mixed them together to make a uniform mixture, forcing the Different, which was hard to mix, into conformity with the Same.” — Timaeus 35a–b, translation Donald J. Zeyl (2000). The mixture is thus made of Being , Same , and Different , each blended across the divide between the intelligible and the bodily — which is precisely what a soul must be, if it is to know both orders: akin to the indivisible in its grasp of what is eternal, akin to the divisible in its commerce with what becomes. The cognition of the world soul is then explained mechanically, and beautifully, by its geometry. The craftsman splits the blended strip lengthwise into two, crosses them like the letter X, and bends each into a circle: the circle of the Same , revolving uniformly in its own plane, and the circle of the Different , set at an angle and divided into seven unequal circles — the orbits of the moon, the sun, and the five planets known to Greek astronomy (36b–d, in paraphrase). When the soul's circles, in their revolutions, make contact with anything of the order of Being, judgements of sameness and difference run through the whole soul and constitute its knowledge; contact with the divisible order yields true opinion (37a–c, in paraphrase). Cosmology and epistemology are one mechanism: the heavens are the world soul thinking, made visible. The Division: Soul as a Scale Between the compounding and the bending comes the passage for which the dialogue was studied as a musical text for two thousand years: the harmonic division of the soul-stuff (35b–36b). In paraphrase of its procedure: the craftsman first cuts from the mixture a series of portions in two interleaved progressions — the doubles, 1, 2, 4, 8, and the triples, 1, 3, 9, 27 — the seven numbers the text gives in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27. (Ancient commentators, Crantor among them as Plutarch reports, arranged the series in the shape of the letter lambda, Λ , the doubles down one leg and the triples down the other, with 1 at the apex; the arrangement is a commentator's diagram, not Plato's drawing, and it is labelled as such here.) He then fills the intervals: into each double and triple interval he inserts the two means, harmonic and arithmetic, which generate the ratios of the fifth (3:2) , the fourth (4:3) , and the tone (9:8) ; and he fills each fourth with tones, leaving in each a residual interval, the leimma — the “leftover” — whose ratio is 256:243 , the Pythagorean semitone. The result is a continuous scale spanning four octaves and a major sixth, built into the substance of the soul itself. Interval Ratio Where it arises Octave 2:1 The double progression: 1–2, 2–4, 4–8 Fifth 3:2 The arithmetic mean within the octave (and the triple step 2–3) Fourth 4:3 The harmonic mean within the octave Tone 9:8 The difference of fifth and fourth; the unit that fills each fourth Leimma 256:243 The residue left in each fourth after two tones are inserted Double octave and beyond 4:1; the series to 27 The triple progression 1–3–9–27 extends the scale's compass Why build a soul out of a scale? The dialogue's answer is its deepest piece of psychology. The soul knows by recognition of ratio : its revolutions are attuned to the ratios that structure the intelligible world, and the visible heavens — whose periods are those same ratios embodied in motion — are given to embodied souls as the instrument by which their own disordered revolutions may be re-attuned (47a–e, 90c–d, in paraphrase; Section XII returns to the therapy). The world soul is therefore not a metaphor laid over the astronomy. It is the claim that one and the same mathematical order runs in the heavens, in the knowing soul, and in the music that moves between them — the claim from which the whole later doctrine of the harmony of the spheres descends, and the reason the Timaeus was read for centuries as the charter text of mathematical harmonics, from the Pythagoreanising commentators through Boethius to Kepler, who took the dialogue's solids and its ratios together as the programme of his Harmonices Mundi (1619). // A WARNING ABOUT THE NUMBERS // The seven numbers and the ratios named above are the dialogue's own, and they are not in dispute. Almost everything beyond them is: the exact reconstruction of the scale (which octave species Plato intended, and in which direction it ran), the total number of terms in the fully filled series, and the question whether the division describes a musical scale at all or a more general mathematics of proportion have been argued from Crantor to the present commentary literature — Proclus's discussion of 35b–36b alone fills a volume of his commentary. This article gives the construction the text states, and declines, as the text's best modern translators do, to pretend the reconstruction is settled. VII. Time, the Heavenly Gods, and the First Human Souls The first movement of the discourse closes with the furnishing of the cosmos: time, the heavenly gods, and the mortal kinds. Each is treated here briefly, because each matters to the foundations this article documents, and none is its centre. Time, the Moving Image The model is eternal, and eternity — abiding in unity — cannot be given whole to a generated thing. So the craftsman makes, in the dialogue's most famous single figure (37d, in paraphrase), a moving image of eternity : time, proceeding according to number, of which days and nights, months and years are the parts, and for whose measurement and guardianship the heavenly bodies are made as instruments (38c, in paraphrase). The fixed stars are divine and eternal living beings, each a sphere of fire turning in place (40a–b); the planets — named in the dialogue's order as the moon, the sun, Venus and Mercury in the sun's train, and the three outer wanderers whose names the text leaves to those who know them (38c–d) — run their courses in the circle of the Different, at speeds and inclinations fitted to their ratios. Time, on this account, is not a container the cosmos sits in. It is a feature the cosmos has, generated with it — which is exactly why the question of Section IV, whether anything can be “before” the cosmos, is so much harder than it looks. The Younger Gods and the Delegation The heavenly bodies are gods — the dialogue calls them so without embarrassment (38e, 40d) — and to them the craftsman delegates the making of mortal creatures, in an address reported at 41a–d (in paraphrase): gods of gods, his works, of whom he is maker and father; what he has bound cannot be unbound except by his will, and his will is a greater bond than their composition. He compounds the immortal part of the mortal creatures himself — individual souls, mixed in the same bowl as the world soul but from the remnants of its mixture, second and third in purity (41d) — assigns each soul to a star, teaches them the laws of destiny, and leaves the weaving of mortal bodies around them to the younger gods.
