The Genre That Carried the Myths Ask where a fifth-century Athenian actually encountered the stories this hub retells — Oedipus and his house, in The Theban Cycle ; the sack of Troy and its long aftermath, in The Trojan Cycle ; Medea at Corinth, in The Argonauts — and the honest answer is not “in Homer.” Epic was recited, certainly, and Homer stood at the centre of schooling. But the living, current, argumentative form in which myth was remade year by year, before the largest audience any Greek literary genre ever commanded, was tragedy : the competitive drama staged at Athens' festivals of Dionysos. For roughly a century and a half, from the late sixth century BCE to the end of the fifth, Athenian poets produced new tragedies by the hundred, almost all of them built from the inherited mythic stock, and almost all of them lost. What the city watched, argued about, quoted in its lawcourts and assemblies, and carried in its memory was this genre. When a later Greek — or a Roman, or a modern reader — speaks of what “the myth says” about Medea or Helen or Oedipus, the version being cited is, far more often than is realised, the version a tragedian fixed on the Athenian stage. That claim has three parts, which the sections keep distinct. First, tragedy was an institution before it was a literature: a state-run religious festival, financed by a tax on the rich, judged by lot-drawn citizens, attended as an act of citizenship (Sections II–IV). Second, it was a craft with a documented technical history — one actor, then two, then three; the chorus's share shrinking; scene-painting — known chiefly from one fourth-century witness, Aristotle, whose testimony must be weighed as retrospection, not as a contemporary record (Sections V–VI). Third, it was the ancient world's most powerful engine of mythic revision : a machine that took variant-rich stories, forced each poet to embody one version before the whole city, and thereby canonised some versions and buried others — including, in the hardest case examined here, a Medea that may be one poet's invention and is now simply “the myth” (Sections VII–XI). The plays' survival, by school-selection and manuscript accident, closes the article (XIII–XIV). // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // This article quotes no ancient text verbatim. Tragedy is a genre whose famous lines circulate in dozens of competing translations, and the hub's rule — quotation only from a verified published translation, named in place — is met here by the stricter course: every rendering of an ancient author's sense is written as paraphrase and labelled as paraphrase at the point of use. The editions from which the paraphrases are made are named in Section XIV and in the Sources. A word on what tragedy was not. It was not, in the first instance, cult . The plays were performed in a sanctuary, in the god's presence — his image was carried into the theatre, his priest sat in the front row — and that frame matters (Section II). But a tragedy is a literary artefact, composed by a named poet for a prize, and its gods are characters in an argument, not objects of worship. The hub's distinction holds throughout: sacrifice, procession, and dithyramb are cult practice; the tetralogy beside them is literature, and the two must not be collapsed into a claim that tragedy “was ritual.” Equally, a tragedy is not a transcript of what Athenians believed. It is what three competing poets could make their fellow citizens sit through, weep at, and vote for — and the difference between belief and prize-winning representation is precisely the space in which tragedy did its work on myth. THE SCALE OF THE LOSS The three tragedians whose work survives complete — Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides — wrote, on the ancient catalogues' figures, some three hundred plays between them, and they were three among dozens of competing poets. Thirty-two tragedies survive whole. Section XIII accounts for the arithmetic and for the selection that produced it. THE STAKES FOR THIS HUB Where Wing I retells a myth, the version retold is usually a tragedian's. The Prometheus Bound discussed in Makers and Fire , the descents catalogued in Descents , the house of Atreus, the house of Laius — all passed through this genre's hands, and bear its fingerprints. One more preliminary, of method. The evidence is uneven: magnificent for the plays themselves, inscriptional for the festival (victor-lists, the production records called didascaliae , choregic monuments), and thin for the early history, where we depend on one fourth-century theorist and late biographical traditions of mixed reliability. Where a cherished fact rests on a single late witness, the article says so at the point of use. II. The City Dionysia: A Festival Before It Was a Theatre The City Dionysia — the Great Dionysia, held in the month Elaphebolion , roughly March into April — was Athens' grandest festival of Dionysos, and the home of tragic competition. Its timing was itself a civic statement. By Elaphebolion the winter seas had reopened; the city was full of foreign envoys, allied delegations, traders, and visitors, and Athens staged the festival, in part, before that international audience. The god honoured was Dionysos Eleuthereus , named for Eleutherae, the border town from which his cult image was said to have come to Athens; his sanctuary lay on the south slope of the Acropolis, and the theatre grew up inside it. The god of the festival — his myths, his ecstasies, and his initiatory cults — is treated in this hub in The Mysteries ; what belongs here is the festival as the city ran it. The festival ran for several days, and its exact day-by-day order is reconstructed — the word should be noted — from inscriptions, orators, and scholia that do not always agree; the sequence given here is the standard modern reconstruction, stated at that strength. It opened with the pompē , the great procession: the god's image, escorted out of the city and brought back by torchlight in a re-enactment of his first arrival, was carried through streets lined with offerings to his sanctuary, and bulls were led to sacrifice and a public feast. Citizens marched in their orders; resident foreigners marched too, in distinguishing dress; colonies and allies sent offerings. The procession was the festival's cultic heart, and it preceded the plays: whatever tragedy later became, it grew up inside a rite in which the city first presented itself, ranked and ordered, to its god. The Civic Ceremonies Around the performances the city wrapped ceremonies that had nothing to do with drama and everything to do with the occasion. In the theatre, before the assembled allies, the year's tribute from the subject-allies of Athens' empire was displayed, talent by talent — a deliberate exhibition of power. Generals poured libations; public honours were proclaimed. And the war orphans — sons of citizens killed in the city's service, reared at public expense — were paraded in full armour provided by the state and given seats of honour: the democracy exhibiting its side of a bargain, that the city raises the sons of those who die for it. That this ceremony shared a programme with Persians and Antigone is the frame that tells us what a tragedy was: not entertainment after the serious business, but one instrument among several by which the assembled city defined and argued about itself. The Dithyramb Before the dramas came the dithyramb , the choral hymn to Dionysos, organised by the ten tribes of the citizen body. Each tribe fielded two choruses — one of men, one of boys — fifty voices each: a thousand citizen performers in all, in tribal competition. The dithyramb matters here for two reasons. It is the likeliest matrix from which tragedy grew, on Aristotle's account (Section VI); and it shows the festival's deep grammar: competition was not an ornament on worship but the form worship and citizenship jointly took — tribe against tribe, poet against poet, choregos against choregos, in the god's honour, before the whole city. The dithyrambic prize was a bronze tripod, set on monuments along the Street of the Tripods east of the theatre; one still stands in Athens, that of the choregos Lysicrates , dated 335/4 BCE — a fourth-century stone witness to a competition structure already two centuries old. THE ARCHON'S CHOICE The festival was administered by the archon eponymous , Athens' chief civil magistrate. Months ahead, he selected the competing poets — in the tragic contest, three — and assigned each a choregos. A poet refused a chorus was, for that year, silenced: the archon's grant was the gate through which every tragedy had to pass, and ancient tradition preserves the refusals and favouritisms as political acts, which they were. THE JUDGES Prizes were awarded by judges drawn by lot from lists submitted by the tribes, sworn, and sequestered against bribery and pressure — and even so, the count was hedged: on the standard account of the procedure, only a portion of the judges' ballots, drawn by lot from those cast, determined the result. The detail matters for Section X: a poet's recorded placing — first, second, third — is the output of a partly randomised procedure, not a clean plebiscite of the audience. THE AUDIENCE, AT HONEST STRENGTH That the audience was overwhelmingly citizen, male, and seated by tribe is secure. Whether women attended is a genuine scholarly dispute: no surviving source states the matter plainly either way, arguments from silence point in both directions, and responsible accounts now state the question as open. This article states it as open. Comedy belonged to the festival too — five comic poets in competition, admitted to the City Dionysia in 486 BCE by the standard dating; its evidence for tragedy is so valuable that it gets its own section below (Section XII). Tragic and comic contests were parts of one programme, before one audience, under one god. Tragedy was not a shelf in a library. It was three days in a crowded sanctuary, between a procession and a drinking-party, in a city talking to itself. III. The Tetralogy, the Choregia, and the Theatre of Dionysos The unit of tragic competition was not the play but the tetralogy . Each of the three selected poets presented, on his day, three tragedies followed by a satyr play — four plays in sequence, from morning into the afternoon, in daylight, in the open air. The three tragedies were often, especially in the earlier fifth century, connected: a trilogy on one mythic sequence, as the Oresteia is (Section VII). But connection was a choice, not a rule — Sophocles, the ancient tradition reports, abandoned the writing of connected trilogies, and Euripides' tetralogies were normally four treatments of unrelated stories. The satyr play that closed the set was a different register entirely: a burlesque on a mythic theme, performed by a chorus of satyrs — the half-animal companions of Dionysos — with the myth's heroes travestied in their company. It returned the audience, after three plays of suffering, to the god of the festival in his earthiest form, and it reminded them whose occasion this was. Of the hundreds of satyr plays produced, exactly one survives complete: Euripides' Cyclops , a drunken travesty of Odysseus' encounter with Polyphemus — its survival, and what it does and does not let us generalise from, is taken up in Section XIII. The Choregia: Paying for the Chorus A tetralogy was expensive, and the city did not pay for it directly. It taxed it. Under the liturgy system — the mechanism by which Athens funded public services from private wealth — the archon appointed a wealthy citizen as chorēgos , sponsor, for each poet. The choregos recruited the chorus and paid for its training, costumes and masks, the piper, and the rehearsal space, across months of preparation; the state supplied the theatre and, by arrangements that shifted over the period, the principal actors. The poet himself directed: he composed the music, choreographed the dances, trained the chorus, and in the early period acted in his own plays. Choregia was a burden — a major production could cost in the range of a trireme's fitting-out, the other great liturgy — and simultaneously one of the chief honours a rich Athenian could win, because the prize was shared: victor-lists name poet and choregos together, and choregic monuments are the sponsor's self-advertisement in stone. The splendour of the chorus that embodied Theban elders before the city was thus a rich man's competitive display — a fact about tragedy's material basis that its texts, read in silence, conceal. Element Form Note The tetralogy Three tragedies + one satyr play, one poet, one day Trilogies connected in theme early; unconnected sets normal later. Judged as a set: the prize went to the poet, not to a single play. The actors At most three speaking actors, all male, masked; multiple roles by doubling One actor in the earliest form; two from Aeschylus, three from Sophocles, on Aristotle's testimony (Section VI). An actors' prize was added at the City Dionysia in the mid-fifth century. The chorus Twelve, later fifteen, citizen performers; song and dance to the aulos (double pipe) The chorus sings the odes between episodes and remains present throughout — the community inside the play, commenting, fearing, misjudging. The poet Composer, director, choreographer; early on, also actor The Greek word is didaskalos , “teacher”: a production is a didaskalia , a “teaching” of the chorus. The records kept under that name are our production archive. The Theatre The Theatre of Dionysos stood — and its remains stand — on the south slope of the Acropolis, within the god's sanctuary, beside his temple. Its elements are the elements of every Greek theatre: the theatron , the “seeing-place”, a great semicircular bowl of seating rising up the slope; the orchestra , the circular dancing-floor at its foot, where the chorus performed; and the skēnē , the stage building behind the orchestra, whose front served as the plays' backdrop — a palace door, a temple, a tent — and whose roof and doorways the action used. Two cautions govern everything said about this building. First, the theatre a visitor sees today is largely the stone rebuilding associated with the statesman Lycurgus, around 330 BCE, with later Roman alterations: the fifth-century theatre of Aeschylus and Sophocles was a more provisional structure of wooden seating on the same slope, and its capacity — estimates for the stone theatre run into the range of fourteen to seventeen thousand — should not be projected back onto the wooden original, which held, on most reckonings, several thousand fewer. Second, the stagecraft the texts imply was achieved with simple means: a wheeled platform, the ekkyklēma , rolled out to display interior scenes — characteristically, corpses; and a crane, the mēchanē , that swung a god or a flying hero over the stage building. The second of those machines gives this article one of its key terms in Section IX. Neither machine is described by any fifth-century source; both are inferred from the plays and mocked, helpfully, by comedy. The inference is standard, and is stated here as inference. Performance conditions followed from the architecture. Plays were given once, in daylight, without intervals, the chorus's odes marking the joints of the action. Masks covered the whole head; costume distinguished king from messenger, Greek from foreigner, god from mortal, at distances where facial expression was useless anyway. Three actors, by rapid changes of mask and dress, populated plays with a dozen speaking parts — which is why tragic scenes are overwhelmingly confrontations of two, the third actor's entrances husbanded for maximum pressure. The form's famous economy is the direct imprint, on the texts we still read, of a hillside, a daylight sky, three masked men, and fifteen dancing citizens. IV. The Lesser Dionysia: Lenaia and the Rural Festivals The City Dionysia was the summit, but it was not the whole mountain. Athens and Attica kept a calendar of Dionysiac festivals, and two of them carried dramatic competitions of their own. They matter to the record because some canonical facts about tragedy — including the first performance of the comedy that judges tragedy in Section XII — belong to them, and because they show the genre operating at other scales: mid-winter, inward-looking, and local. The Lenaia The Lenaia fell in Gamelion , roughly January — mid-winter, when the seas were closed and the audience was Athens talking to itself, without the allied delegations and foreign visitors of the spring festival. Its sanctuary, the Lenaion, lay somewhere in the city — its exact site is disputed and unknown — and its competitions were administered by the archon basileus , the “king archon”, rather than the eponymous archon. Comedy was the Lenaia's senior genre: comic competition there is older than the tragic contest, which was added around the 430s BCE on the usual dating. Tragedy at the Lenaia was a smaller affair — two poets, on the standard reconstruction, with two tragedies each and no satyr plays. Yet the festival's inwardness gave it a distinctive evidentiary value. Aristophanes' Frogs , the richest ancient document on tragedy's standing in its own city, was produced at the Lenaia of 405 BCE (Section XII) — a play about the tragic stage, performed in winter, to the home crowd, weeks after the deaths of both Euripides and Sophocles had emptied that stage. Aristophanes jokes, in a parabasis paraphrased here, that at this festival there are no tribute-bearing allies to flatter: the Lenaia was where Athens spoke most freely, because nobody else was listening. The Rural Dionysia The Rural Dionysia belonged not to the city but to the demes — the villages and townships of Attica — and fell in Poseideon , roughly December. Each deme kept its own festival and procession, and the larger demes maintained theatres and staged plays: Piraeus had a notable theatre and festival; Eleusis, Ikarion, Thorikos and others are attested with performances of varying ambition. Ikarion carries a particular charge, as the named home deme of Thespis (Section V). The rural programmes mixed new work with revivals and formed the base of a pyramid whose apex was the City Dionysia; the deme theatres — Thorikos preserves one of Attica's earliest stone theatres — are the archaeology of the genre's diffusion. From 386 BCE a decree added revivals of old tragedies to the City Dionysia's programme: the first formal admission that the genre now had classics (Section XIII). // HOW TO HOLD THE CALENDAR // Poseideon (c. December): Rural Dionysia in the demes. Gamelion (c. January): Lenaia — comedy first, tragedy added later, home audience. Elaphebolion (c. March–April): City Dionysia — three tragic poets, three tetralogies. The plays this hub cites by year — Persians 472, Oresteia 458, Medea 431 — are City Dionysia dates unless otherwise stated. V. Origins: Thespis and the Limits of the Record Every account of tragedy's origin must begin by confessing the shape of its evidence. The genre emerges, fully competitive and state-run, in records of the late sixth century BCE; the process by which it emerged occupies the preceding decades, for which we have no contemporary documents at all. What we have is a tradition — assembled by later Greeks from records, memories, and inference — and one great theorist, Aristotle, writing in the fourth century with access to production records now lost. The tradition's central figure is Thespis , and the honest treatment of Thespis is this article's test case for handling the whole origin question: he must be presented at exactly the strength of his attestation — no stronger, and no weaker. The attestation, in summary, is this. The Parian Marble , a chronological inscription carved on Paros in the third century BCE, records — in the entry conventionally dated to the years around 534 BCE — that Thespis was the first to produce a tragedy at Athens and to win the prize, in the tradition's phrasing a goat. Aristotle's Poetics , earlier and weightier, describes the mechanism of the beginning without naming Thespis at all: tragedy arose, he says, from the leaders of the dithyramb — the solo voice that led off the choral hymn stepping out, answering the chorus, and becoming, in that exchange, the first actor (Section VI). Later sources fill in the man: Thespis of Ikarion , the Attic deme with its own Dionysiac traditions (Section IV); Thespis as the inventor of the acted prologue and speech, in Themistius' much later summary of the Aristotelian tradition; Thespis in Horace's Art of Poetry , a Roman poet's version, touring the villages with a wagon, his players' faces smeared with wine-lees. A list of his play-titles survives in the Byzantine Suda . And the word for actor in Greek, hypokritēs — literally “answerer” — fits Aristotle's mechanism exactly: the one who answers the chorus. // THE THESPIS TRADITION, AT HONEST STRENGTH // What is solid: by the later sixth century BCE, tragic competition existed at the City Dionysia, and Greek tradition from the third century BCE onward attached its invention to a named man, Thespis, at a date around 534 BCE. What is not solid: every biographical particular. The wagon, the wine-lees, the village tours are late literary colouring; the surviving play-titles and the four lines quoted under Thespis' name were already suspected in antiquity — a tradition reported by Diogenes Laertius holds that the Thespian corpus was forged by Heraclides Ponticus in the fourth century BCE. Modern scholarship divides between treating Thespis as a historical innovator whose achievement the tradition simplified, and treating him as the kind of culture-hero figure to whom Greek tradition habitually assigned inventions. This article presents him as the tradition's named founder, at that strength, and builds nothing further on the details. The deeper question — what tragedy grew from — has attracted answers of very different evidential kinds, and they should be sorted, not blended. Aristotle's account is formal: tragedy developed from the dithyramb's improvisations, passing through a phase he calls satyric — close to the satyr play in metre and dance — before acquiring, late, its dignity and its iambic metre. Whatever its gaps, this is a fourth-century scholar's reconstruction from records, and it is the account with the best claim on our assent. The etymology of tragōidia , “goat-song”, is a fact of language in search of a referent: the goat may be the prize (as the Parian Marble's tradition suggests), the sacrifice at which the song was sung, or an animal whose guise the singers wore — all three explanations are ancient or modern guesses, and none is provable. The ritual-origin theories of the early twentieth century — the Cambridge ritualists' derivation of tragedy from a ritual of the dying and reviving year-spirit — are presented in modern handbooks as speculation that outran its evidence, and this article does not build on them; the hero-cult hypothesis (tragedy from lament at heroes' tombs) rests on the true observation that the plots are overwhelmingly hero-myths, but plots are not origins. What can be said without speculation is narrower and sufficient: tragedy appears in the record as a choral performance for Dionysos that acquired, at a date tradition fixes around 534 BCE, an actor who spoke against the chorus — and that single acquisition, dialogue, is the seed of everything in this article. Between Thespis and Aeschylus the record offers names almost without texts: Choerilus , competing by the 520s; Pratinas of Phlius, credited with shaping the satyr play as a separate form; and Phrynichus , the first tragedian of whom real historical notices survive. His Capture of Miletus , staged within a year or two of Miletus' fall to Persia in 494 BCE, dramatised a catastrophe so raw that — Herodotus reports, in paraphrase — the theatre burst into tears, the city fined the poet a thousand drachmas for reminding it of its own sorrows, and the play was banned. The story is the earliest evidence that tragedy could treat near-contemporary history — the precedent for Persians (Section VII) — and that the city policed the stage's emotional power when it turned on the audience itself. Phrynichus' Phoenician Women treated the Persian defeat from the enemy court's side, and Aeschylus, who is said to have acknowledged the debt, took its opening as his own Persian play's model. VI. Aristotle's Poetics: The Earliest Theory, Read as Retrospection Our earliest theory of tragedy is also our earliest history of it, and it is the same book: Aristotle's Poetics , composed in the fourth century BCE — most plausibly in the 330s–320s, when its author was teaching in Athens — roughly two centuries after Thespis and a full lifetime after the deaths of Sophocles and Euripides. The Poetics survives incomplete: the treatise on tragedy is substantially whole; the companion treatment of comedy is lost. What it says about tragedy's development, in its fourth chapter, is the foundation on which every modern account is built, and it must be read with its date held firmly in mind. Aristotle is not a witness. He is a researcher — the first, and for this subject the only one whose work survives — reconstructing a two-hundred-year process from production records, from the plays, and from a philosophical commitment to seeing arts as organisms that grow toward their natural form. His history is therefore evidence of two things at once: of what the records available in the fourth century showed, and of what a fourth-century teleologist made of them. The sections below use him constantly and trust him accordingly: completely on the technical sequence, cautiously on the motives, and not at all where his theory needs a fact the record cannot have given him. The Technical Sequence Aristotle's developmental claims, paraphrased from Poetics chapter 4, are these. Tragedy began in improvisation, from the leaders of the dithyramb; in its early phase it was satyric in character, with short plots and a dancing metre, and it acquired seriousness late, exchanging that metre for the iambic — the metre, Aristotle notes, closest to speech. Aeschylus raised the number of actors from one to two, reduced the chorus's part, and made dialogue take the leading role. Sophocles added the third actor and scene-painting. Thereafter tragedy stopped developing, in Aristotle's phrase, when it had attained its natural form. The sequence is corroborated in its broad effect by the plays themselves: the earliest extant Aeschylus is markedly more choral than the latest Euripides, and no surviving scene requires a fourth speaking voice. But the neatness should provoke caution. Attributing each step to a single named innovator is the pattern Greek tradition imposed on every art's history — compare Thespis in Section V — and scene-painting is credited elsewhere, in the tradition preserved by Vitruvius, to the painter Agatharchus working for Aeschylus , a generation before Aristotle's Sophoclean date. The conflict is recorded here, unresolved: Aristotle is the earlier and better source, and the article builds on the sequence, not on the attributions. THE RANKING OF THE PARTS Plot ( mythos ) first, character second, then thought, diction, song, and spectacle last — Aristotle's hierarchy, paraphrased from Poetics chapter 6. Its consequence for this hub is direct: for Aristotle, the story-structure is the tragedy, and the inherited myth is raw material for plot-making. The poet, he says in chapter 9, should be a maker of plots rather than of verses — and is not bound to the received stories, though the famous names anchor belief. THE CRITICAL INSTRUMENTS Reversal ( peripeteia ), recognition ( anagnōrisis ), and suffering are Aristotle's names for plot's moving parts, and his exhibit for their perfect conjunction is Sophocles' Oedipus the King , which the Poetics treats throughout as the genre's paradigm. That a single play should stand as the model of the form — for a theorist writing a century later — is itself a canonising act, and Section XIII shows the school tradition completing it. Aristotle's famous definition — tragedy as the imitation of a serious, complete action, effecting through pity and fear the katharsis of such emotions — is paraphrased here, not quoted, and every term in it, katharsis above all, has been disputed for centuries. Note also what the Poetics omits: the festival entire. His tragedy floats free of the Dionysia — no choregia, no judges, no procession — and that silence is the standing warning against reading the genre through theory alone. Two of Aristotle's judgements deserve separate statement, because later sections lean on them. In chapter 13, paraphrased, he names the finest tragic figure: a man neither wholly good nor bad, brought down not by vice but by some hamartia — a word whose rendering, as “error” rather than moral “flaw”, is one of the field's consequential translation disputes, flagged here rather than settled. And in chapter 15, paraphrased, he lays down that a plot's resolution should arise from the plot itself and not from a machine — naming Euripides' Medea as the offending exhibit, since Medea's escape is effected by the Sun's chariot rather than by anything the action has prepared. That sentence is the birthplace of deus ex machina as a critical reproach; Section IX returns to it. Aristotle's Euripides is in any case a study in a divided mind: the most criticised of the three in the Poetics , and yet named there — paraphrased here — the most tragic of the poets, because his plays end in the misery the genre exists to show. VII. Aeschylus: History on Stage and the One Surviving Trilogy Aeschylus (c. 525/4–456/5 BCE), of Eleusis, is the first tragedian whose work survives. The ancient catalogues credit him with some seventy to ninety plays; his first production came around 499 BCE and his first victory in 484; he fought at Marathon — his epitaph, in the tradition the biographies preserve, commemorated the battle and not the poetry — and he died at Gela in Sicily, having produced plays for the Sicilian tyrant Hieron as well as for Athens. Seven plays survive under his name. One of the seven, the Prometheus Bound , is now widely held not to be his: the case — metrical, lexical, dramaturgical — is set out in this hub's Makers and Fire , Sections IX–X, whose labelling this article adopts: transmitted under Aeschylus' name, authorship disputed, with a substantial modern case for a later production, possibly by his son Euphorion, staged under the father's name. The reader should carry that label through every generalisation about “Aeschylus” in what follows. Persians: The Enemy's Court, Eight Years After The Persians of 472 BCE — choregos, the young Pericles, on the production record — is the only surviving tragedy on a historical subject, and it is very near-contemporary history: Salamis was fought in 480, eight years before, and men who had rowed in it sat in the audience. The play is set at the Persian court at Susa, among the defeated: Queen Atossa, the chorus of elders, the ghost of Darius raised to judge his son's folly, Xerxes returning in rags. The messenger speech narrates Salamis entirely from the losing side, so the audience heard its own victory as the enemy's catastrophe, in the enemy's mouth. Two disciplines govern the reading. First, Phrynichus' precedent (Section V) shows the mode was dangerous: history on stage could be fined when it hurt wrong. Aeschylus' solution — the victory framed as the gods' punishment of royal overreach — let the city celebrate itself at one remove, through pity. Second, the play is not documentary: its Persia is a Greek construction, its Darius a mouthpiece for Greek political wisdom. Persians is evidence for how Athens wished to remember Salamis in 472 — a different, and in some ways richer, thing than evidence for Salamis. The Oresteia: The One Surviving Trilogy In 458 BCE Aeschylus presented the Oresteia — Agamemnon , Libation Bearers , Eumenides , with the satyr play Proteus , now lost — and won first prize. It is the only complete trilogy to survive from the entire genre, and its survival lets us see, once, what the connected form could do at full stretch. The story is the house of Atreus, whose full cycle is told in this hub in The Trojan Cycle : Agamemnon, home from Troy, murdered by Clytemnestra; Orestes, commanded by Apollo, returning to kill his mother; the Furies — the Erinyes, ancient powers of blood-vengeance — pursuing the matricide to Athens, where the third play moves the action out of myth's Argos into the audience's own city and founds, on stage, a court. The trilogy's architecture is its argument: an inherited curse working itself out through three generations of reciprocal killing is not answered by a fourth killing but by an institution — a homicide court, a jury of citizens, a tied vote, and the persuasion of the Furies themselves, who are not destroyed but housed, given a shrine in Athens and a new name, Eumenides , the Kindly Ones. Three Languages, One Art: What Transmission Changed XIX. Sources I. Transmission Is the Story: What a Text Has to Survive Every other article in this wing of the archive is about something somebody wrote, made, or believed. This one is about the narrower and stranger question of how any of it is still here to be read. Greek alchemy was composed, in the main, between the first and the seventh centuries CE, in a Greek-speaking Egypt that then passed under Byzantine, Persian, and Arab rule in quick succession. No autograph survives. No papyrus codex of Zosimos of Panopolis survives. What survives is a chain: late-antique teachers who turned workshop writings into commented school texts; Byzantine compilers who gathered those texts into codices, the oldest of which was copied some seven centuries after Zosimos wrote; Syriac translators who carried a selection of the corpus into the Christian East; Arabic translators and authors in Baghdad who received it, rebuilt it, and made it the foundation of a new literature; and, at the end of the chain, a single dated Latin translation — 11 February 1144 — through which the art entered a Latin West that, by its translator’s own account, did not yet know what alchemy was. Transmission, in this article, is therefore not a synonym for copying. Each link in the chain did something to what it passed on. The commentators systematised: they decided which ancients agreed with which, and taught the art as a doctrine with a history. The compilers selected: a codex is an argument about what belongs together, and the Greek corpus as we have it is a Byzantine editorial product, not a Roman one. The translators re-founded: the Arabic tradition did not merely keep Greek alchemy alive, it rebuilt the art’s theory, its classification of substances, and its literary forms, so that what Latin Europe received in the twelfth century was Greek alchemy as Arabic scholarship had preserved, corrected, and extended it — the formulation Lawrence Principe’s The Secrets of Alchemy (2013) argues across its transmission chapters, and the one this article follows. Preservation was never passive. It was a series of interventions, each of which can be studied, and some of which can be dated. Three disciplines of evidence govern what follows, and they are worth stating at the front because the subject invites romance. First, shelfmarks before stories. Where a claim rests on a manuscript, the manuscript is named — Marcianus graecus 299, Parisinus graecus 2325, Parisinus graecus 2327, Cambridge Mm. 6.29 — and dated as the catalogues date it, as a range where the dating is palaeographical. Second, catalogues say only what catalogues say. Where the evidence for a transmission is a catalogue entry — William Wright’s Cambridge catalogue for the Syriac Zosimos, Ibn al-Nadim’s Fihrist for the Arabic — the article reports the entry and does not build a narrative on top of it. Third, the tradition’s own account of its transmission is labelled as tradition. The story that a Byzantine monk taught an Umayyad prince, who thereby founded Arabic alchemy, is the alchemical tradition’s account of itself. It is historically precious and historically unverified, and Section XIV treats it at exactly that strength. THE GREEK LINK Commentators of the 4th–7th centuries — Synesius, Olympiodorus, Christianus, Stephanus — turn the early treatises into a commented, teachable corpus; Byzantine compilers gather that corpus into codices, of which the Marcianus graecus 299 (late 10th–early 11th c.) is the oldest survivor. THE SYRIAC LINK A documented but narrow bridge: twelve treatises attributed to Zosimos survive in Syriac in a 15th-century Cambridge codex, alongside Democritean and workshop material of the same Greek kind as the Leyden and Stockholm papyri. The wider Greek-to-Syriac translation culture, exemplified by Sergius of Reshaina, is the context — not, on present evidence, an alchemical channel in itself. THE ARABIC LINK Baghdad’s translation movement (8th–9th c.) carries Greek alchemy into Arabic, substantially through Syriac. Zosimos survives in Arabic in works with no complete Greek counterpart; the Jabir corpus (c. 850–950) systematises the inheritance into an Arabic creation that is not a translation of anything. THE LATIN LINK Before 1144, essentially no Latin alchemical literature exists. On 11 February 1144 Robert of Chester completes the Liber de compositione alchemiae , the Morienus dialogue, from Arabic — the first dated Latin alchemical translation. Gerard of Cremona and Toledo follow within a generation. The hub’s companion articles carry the persons; this article carries the road between them. For Zosimos himself, see Zosimos of Panopolis in this hub and the Egyptology division’s fuller Zosimos , whose Sections VII and VIII treat the Syriac and Arabic transmissions in detail; for the apparatus whose drawings anchor the codex tradition, see Maria the Jewess ; for the name under which the whole art travelled, see Hermetica ; and for the Arabic centuries treated from the Egyptian side, the Egyptology division’s Islamic Egyptology , whose Sections VII–VIII state the archive’s adjudicated position on the Syriac evidence and the Jabir corpus — a position this article follows and does not outrun. II. The Commentators: The Art Becomes a School Text The first transmission of Greek alchemy happened inside Greek. Between the age of the early treatises — the works circulating under the names of pseudo-Democritus, Hermes, Agathodaimon, Isis, Cleopatra, Maria, and Ostanes, composed roughly between the first and third centuries — and the age of the codices stands a generation of writers whose work was not to invent but to explain : the commentators. Scholarship on the Byzantine period of the art, notably Cristina Viano’s survey of Greco-Egyptian alchemy and the work gathered under the heading of the era of systematisation, treats this generation as the moment alchemy acquired a doctrine: a set of agreed questions, a canon of ancients whose apparent disagreements had to be reconciled, and a philosophical frame — above all the unity of matter — within which workshop operations could be discussed as theory. The sequence, as Michèle Mertens sets it out in her study of Graeco-Egyptian alchemy in Byzantium, has three levels. The oldest level is the pseudepigraphic stratum itself: the prestigious names of the first to third centuries. The second level is Zosimos of Panopolis (active around 300 CE), in whom technical preoccupation and religious reflection are already fully mixed, and who himself cites, quotes, and argues with the first level — a transmitter inside the tradition before he is an authority of it. The third level is the exegetes: Synesius in the fourth century, commenting on pseudo-Democritus; Olympiodorus in the sixth; Stephanus of Alexandria in the seventh; a commentator known simply as the Christian (Christianus, the Christian Philosopher) in the seventh or eighth; and an Anonymous Philosopher somewhat later. Close to Stephanus stand four alchemical poems in verse, ascribed to Heliodorus, Theophrastus, Hierotheus, and Archelaus and dated to the seventh or eighth centuries — the art, by then, had a literature in every register the schools used: treatise, commentary, lecture, and poem. What commentary does to a technical literature deserves a paragraph of its own, because everything later in this article is a variation on it. A commentator selects a base text and declares it authoritative. He breaks it into lemmata — short quoted passages — and surrounds each with explanation, which means the base text now survives inside another man’s book, in the order and the excerpts the commentator chose. He reconciles: where Democritus and Zosimos appear to disagree about the divine water, the commentator’s task is to show the fundamental accord beneath the different names, and the reconciliation becomes doctrine in its own right. And he teaches: the commentary is a school form, addressed to students, delivered as lectures, and copied as a course. An art that exists as commentary is an art that has become scholastic — portable between cities, teachable to strangers, and dependent for its survival on institutions that copy books. That dependence is the precondition of everything in Sections V to IX. // WHO WERE THEY? // The identification of the alchemical Olympiodorus and Stephanus with their namesakes, the Neoplatonic commentators on Plato and Aristotle, was long doubted on the ground that serious philosophers would not write on gold-making. The identification is now commonly accepted in the scholarship this article follows (Viano; Mertens). Its consequence matters: alchemy in late antiquity was not a marginal craft literature but part of the philosophical school curriculum of Alexandria. The geography moved as the commentary tradition matured. Synesius and Olympiodorus belong to Alexandria, still the Mediterranean’s great school city, where the Neoplatonic commentators taught Aristotle and Plato in a curriculum alchemy now sat beside. Stephanus, as Section IV details, carried the Alexandrian school to Constantinople under Heraclius: the last great Alexandrian teacher became an imperial professor in the capital. After him, the tradition’s Greek life is Byzantine and bookish — Michael Psellos in the eleventh century, the monk Kosmas, Nikephoros Blemmydes in the thirteenth — a sequence of readers, excerptors, and compilers rather than of new system-builders. The art’s creative Greek centuries were the commentators’ centuries. Its Byzantine centuries were the copyists’, and it is to the copyists’ books that we now turn — after two sections on the commentators themselves, because the codices cannot be understood without knowing whose lectures they contain. III. Olympiodorus and Christianus: Commentary as Method Olympiodorus (sixth century) wrote the commentary that best shows the method at work. Its base text was a lost treatise of Zosimos, the Kat’ energeian — On Action — together with sentences drawn from other ancient alchemists. Around that base Olympiodorus built something Zosimos had not attempted: a doxography , a structured survey of opinions, in which the doctrines of nine monist Presocratic philosophers — the early Greek thinkers who had each proposed a single principle of all things — are set beside the alchemical doctrine of the unity of matter. The comparison is the argument. If Thales’ water, Anaximander’s boundless, and the rest can be read as early statements of the one underlying matter, then alchemy’s founding claim — that metals differ by imposed qualities on a common substrate, and can therefore be changed — is not a workshop superstition but the laboratory form of the oldest Greek philosophy. Viano’s study of the passage (on De arte sacra , §§18–27) shows the doxography following the standard pattern of Neoplatonic surveys of opinion: Olympiodorus is doing to Zosimos exactly what his school did to Aristotle, and with the same purpose — to exhibit a tradition as a single, developing, self-consistent teaching. The practical consequence for transmission is easily missed. Because Olympiodorus quotes his base text in lemmata, fragments of Zosimos’ lost Kat’ energeian survive inside the commentary that the treatise itself does not. The commentator is thus an involuntary archivist: later copyists who transmitted Olympiodorus transmitted pieces of Zosimos with him, selected by a sixth-century teacher’s syllabus. When modern editors reconstruct Zosimos, they work substantially from such embedded quotation — from the Authentic Memoirs in the codices, from Olympiodorus’ lemmata, and from the Syriac and Arabic witnesses of Sections X and XII. The corpus is a mosaic of other people’s quotations to a degree classical literature rarely matches, and Mertens’ warning stands over the whole field: in the alchemical manuscripts the works of each author are interwoven with one another, copied one after another without gaps, their titles and subheadings not always distinguished, so that even locating where one work ends and another begins is editorial work, not reading. Christianus and the Divine Water The commentator known as Christianus — the Christian Philosopher — is the generation’s most shadowy figure and, for the historian of transmission, one of its most instructive. His surviving work, preserved in the Greek corpus and printed in Berthelot and Ruelle’s Collection (CAAG II, pp. 395–421 in the standard citation), is a compilation in thirty chapters On the Divine Water , dedicated to a Sergius — identified in the reference literature as probably Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople under Heraclius — and organised as commentary, chapter by chapter, on precise themes and questions in the early authors: pseudo-Hermes, Zosimos, pseudo-Democritus. His dating is debated: the reference tradition places him broadly between 500 and 800; Mertens puts the Christian in the seventh or eighth century; recent work on his text’s strikingly early description of Indian lac — the resin whose dye and shellac manufacture his procedures describe — has argued for the early seventh century, in Heraclius’ reign. This article gives the range and flags the debate rather than choosing a decade the evidence does not settle. Christianus’ theme is the commentators’ theme in its purest form: the divine water , the active, dissolving agent of transformation, and the scandal that the ancients name it in many ways while meaning, he argues, one thing. Where pseudo-Democritus speaks in general of a unique kind and Zosimos of multiple material kinds, Christianus undertakes to show that all multiplicity leads back to the one unity — the same reconciliation Olympiodorus performed with Presocratics, performed here within the alchemical canon itself. Berthelot, editing the text, noted the method with a historian’s ambivalence: the compilation follows the general Byzantine system of drawing extracts and summaries from early authors — the method of Photius and of Constantine VII’s excerpting projects — which conserves fragments and dismembers texts in a single operation. That sentence could stand as the epigraph of this whole article. Byzantine transmission saved Greek alchemy by taking it apart. // HOW TO READ A COMMENTATOR // Ask of any commentary three questions. What base text does it quote, and does that text survive anywhere else? What disagreements does it reconcile, and is the reconciliation the author’s or the tradition’s? And what did the commentator leave out? The answers locate the fragment in the chain: a sentence of Zosimos may reach us only because Olympiodorus needed it for a lesson, in the form Olympiodorus’ lesson required. IV. Stephanus of Alexandria at the Court of Heraclius Stephanus of Alexandria (fl. c. 580 – c. 640) is the last of the great commentators and the hinge between the Alexandrian school and the Byzantine world. He studied at Alexandria, probably under Elias, in the circle of Christian successors to Olympiodorus the philosopher; he was teaching and writing commentaries there in the 580s. Shortly after the accession of the emperor Heraclius in 610 he moved to Constantinople — whether by imperial invitation is not known — and took up a chair as oikoumenikos didaskalos , ecumenical professor, at the Imperial Academy, teaching Plato, Aristotle, the quadrivium, astrology , and alchemy. Among his students was Tychicus of Trebizond, himself the teacher of the Armenian polymath Anania Shirakatsi: the Alexandrian curriculum, alchemy included, now radiated from the capital of the empire. Stephanus died sometime before Heraclius’ own death in 641. His alchemical work survives as nine Lectures ( Praxeis ) On the Great and Sacred Art of Making Gold, associated with Heraclius’ court and commonly described as dedicated to the emperor. The lectures comment on the ancient alchemists in a highly rhetorical style — Viano’s characterisation — and they do something none of the earlier commentators had done so fully: they set alchemy explicitly among the other mathematical and natural disciplines, linking it with medicine, astrology, mathematics, and music. The art is presented not as a craft secret but as one member of a system of knowledge, expounded from a professor’s chair, in a capital, under an emperor’s name. Whatever the workshop reality behind the rhetoric, the institutional fact is the transmission fact: by the early seventh century alchemy had a place in the highest teaching establishment of the Greek world. A discipline with a chair gets copied. A discipline without one gets lost. Two cautions belong to Stephanus, and this article keeps both. The first is authorship. The identification of the alchemical Stephanus with the Alexandrian professor of philosophy is, in Mertens’ formulation, not absolutely certain but quite probable; the alchemical lectures’ style has led some scholars to hesitate, and F. Sherwood Taylor, who translated the first three lectures against the Marcianus, accepted the identification. The second caution is editorial. Stephanus was not printed in Berthelot and Ruelle’s Collection (see Section VIII): his lectures were edited separately, by Julius Ludwig Ideler in the Physici et medici graeci minores (Berlin, 1841–42) from a faulty copy of the Marcianus, and Taylor’s partial re-edition of 1937–38, collating Ideler against the Marcianus itself, covers only the first three of the nine lectures. The most famous Greek alchemical author of the seventh century is still read, in large part, through a nineteenth-century edition its own editor’s materials compromised — a standing reminder that “the Greek corpus” names a set of manuscripts and a history of editions, not a stable book. 4th c. SYNESIUS Commentary on pseudo-Democritus addressed to Dioscorus: the earliest surviving work of the exegete generation, presenting later theory as interpretation of the Four Books . 6th c. OLYMPIODORUS Commentary on Zosimos’ lost Kat’ energeian , with the Presocratic doxography aligning alchemical unity of matter with the oldest Greek philosophy. 7th c. STEPHANUS AT CONSTANTINOPLE After 610 Stephanus teaches at the Imperial Academy under Heraclius; the nine alchemical Lectures belong to this court setting. The alchemical poems ascribed to Heliodorus, Theophrastus, Hierotheus, and Archelaus cluster in the same seventh-to-eighth-century milieu. 7th–8th c. CHRISTIANUS AND THE ANONYMOUS The Christian Philosopher’s thirty chapters On the Divine Water and the Anonymous Philosopher’s work continue the exegete line; compilation by excerpt becomes the tradition’s normal mode. 7th–8th c. THE CORPUS IS GATHERED The compendium of alchemical writings from which the surviving Greek codices descend is commonly placed in Constantinople in the seventh or eighth century: ancients, Zosimos, commentators, poems, and apparatus material bound into one editorial whole. That last entry is the bridge to the codices. The Greek alchemical corpus — some forty authors in the usual count, spanning a millennium of composition — is not a library that survived; it is an anthology that was made , most plausibly in Constantinople in the seventh or eighth century, in the world the commentators had created. The makers chose the order, the attributions, and the inclusions. Everything the Byzantine, Syriac, Arabic, and eventually Latin traditions knew of Greek alchemy, they knew through that anthology and its descendants — or, in the Arabic case (Section XII), through Greek exemplars older than the anthology’s surviving copies, which is a different and luckier story. V. The Byzantine Codices: How a Corpus Becomes a Book A corpus becomes a book at the moment someone pays for parchment, rules the pages, and decides what goes in. For Greek alchemy that moment came repeatedly — the tradition knows a large number of medieval manuscripts — but the whole surviving tradition hangs on three principal witnesses, or four: Mertens’ formulation, which this article follows, distinguishes the Marcianus graecus 299, the Parisinus graecus 2325, and the Parisinus graecus 2327, with the Laurentianus graecus 86.16 as a possible fourth whose exact relation to the Parisinus 2327 remains unresolved. All other known Greek alchemical manuscripts appear to derive from these. The contents of the corpus range, in Mertens’ summary, from the beginning of our era to the fifteenth century: the codices are not snapshots of a moment but sedimented libraries, in which a first-century pseudepigraph, a third-century memoir, a seventh-century lecture, and a fifteenth-century addition can stand quire to quire. The three principal witnesses differ from one another in ways that are themselves evidence, and Mertens’ comparison is worth following closely because it shows three different ideas of what the corpus was for. The Marcianus is the most beautiful of the alchemical manuscripts: a prestige object, its first title inscribed in a pyle — a magnificently decorated frame painted in four colours — and its pages carrying the lavish illustrations, above all the apparatus drawings and the Chrysopoeia leaf, for which the tradition is famous. The Parisinus 2325, by contrast, presents important omissions: its copyist, Mertens judges, was more interested in the technical content than in the philosophical and doctrinal texts, and organised the material as a workshop handbook. The Parisinus 2327 encloses a larger collection than either, including a number of texts peculiar to itself whose origin is unknown. A courtly showpiece, a practitioner’s handbook, an expanded anthology: the same corpus, three reading publics. Transmission history is, in part, the history of who a book was copied for . The stemmatic caution in that table is not pedantry. Mertens records that the relations between the three principal manuscripts have not been conclusively clarified despite wide discussion: whether B and A derive from M, whether M and A are independent of one another (Viano’s judgement: very probably independent), whether L copies A or shares its exemplar — these questions decide, for any given passage, which reading is evidence and which is a copyist’s accident. An editor of Zosimos works the way a restorer works: with the witnesses side by side, and with the Syriac and Arabic versions as further witnesses to Greek exemplars now lost. The seven-century gap Mertens names — Zosimos active about 300, the oldest manuscript about 1000 — is filled with exactly this kind of subterranean copying, during which, as she puts it, it is difficult to know what was happening. The codices are the gap’s far shore. VI. Marcianus graecus 299: The Oldest Surviving Greek Alchemical Codex The Marcianus graecus 299 — cited in full as Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, graecus 299 (Collocazione 584), and in the scholarship simply as M — is the oldest surviving Greek alchemical codex and the single most important witness to the corpus. Its dating is palaeographical: according to its handwriting, Mertens concludes, it probably dates from the end of the tenth or the beginning of the eleventh century. This article gives the range in that form wherever the codex is dated, because the range is what the evidence supports: no colophon survives to fix a year, and the familiar shorthand “tenth-century” in popular accounts rounds one end of a two-generation window. The codex is a large book — roughly three hundred folios in the usual descriptions — and it opens as a planned edition: a table of contents stands at its head, listing the collection’s pieces (fifty-two entries in the count commonly reported from that table), most of them devoted to what the Byzantine tradition called the Sacred Art. The table is also the codex’s wound made legible. It corresponds only partially to the manuscript’s present contents, because the book was, in Mertens’ phrase, the victim of several accidents: it lost several quires, and some of those that remain were inverted by the binder. H. D. Saffrey’s demonstration, which Mertens endorses, is that the table of contents is in fact that of the manuscript before its various misfortunes — a catalogue of a fuller book than the one on the shelf. The Marcianus thus documents its own losses. We know, in part, what Greek alchemy we no longer have, because its oldest codex lists it. What Is Inside The contents span the corpus’s three levels. From the oldest stratum: works of and fragments connected with pseudo-Democritus and Hermes, the lists of alchemical symbols, and the Dialogue of the Philosophers and Cleopatra . From the second level: the works of Zosimos, dispersed through the codex in the interwoven manner described in Section III — the Authentic Memoirs in part (the Marcianus preserves, for example, the first lesson of the Visions where the Parisinus 2327 preserves all three), the chapters to Eusebia and to Theodorus, the Book of Sophe and Final Count materials — the four groups Mertens distinguishes across the witnesses, no one of which any single codex contains entire. From the third level: the commentators, including the nine alchemical lectures of Stephanus of Alexandria and the work of Olympiodorus and Christianus. And on folio 188v, the most reproduced single page in the history of alchemy: the Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra , the one-leaf diagram of concentric circles, the ouroboros enclosing the motto hen to pan — the One, the All — with the symbols of gold, silver, and mercury, and drawings of the dibikos and of a kerotakis-type apparatus. Those apparatus drawings are the codex’s second great gift, and the one this hub’s Maria the Jewess article depends on. The Greek texts describe the kerotakis — the sealed reflux apparatus in which metals were bathed in vapours — and the tribikos , the three-armed still attributed to Maria, in words; the Marcianus tradition draws them. The drawings in M and its descendants are the source from which every modern reconstruction of the kerotakis and tribikos begins: the Egyptology division’s Zosimos treats the apparatus step by step in its Sections XI–XII, and its Section XIV states the necessary limit — the drawings are Byzantine copies of late-antique exemplars, made by scribes who drew what they saw rather than what they used, and their evidence is real but mediated. A drawing copied for seven centuries is a rumour with a pedigree. Section IX takes up what that pedigree does to technical information. // READING THE MARCIANUS // The standard modern description is Otto Lagercrantz’s, in the second volume of the Catalogue des manuscrits alchimiques grecs (Brussels, 1924–32), with an edition of the table of contents; Saffrey’s study of the codex’s history and structure is the key modern analysis. The most recent full catalogue entry is E. Mioni’s, in the Marciana’s catalogue of its Greek manuscripts (Rome, 1981). Taylor’s collation of Stephanus against M showed how much an edition can gain — and how much it can lose — from a single witness. One more fact about M belongs in a transmission article, because it governs the codex’s modern fate. A number of later hands, most dated to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, annotated the manuscript throughout: headings, captions, and notes in semi-uncial scripts supplement the main text. The Marcianus was not a sealed relic. It was a working book for at least four centuries after its copying — read, glossed, and handled in the same centuries in which B, A, and L were copied from the tradition it heads. The corpus’s Byzantine life did not end when its oldest codex was made. It continued in the margins. VII. Paris and Florence: Parisinus graecus 2325, Parisinus graecus 2327, and the Laurentianus The Parisinus graecus 2325 (B), of the thirteenth century, is the tradition’s practitioner. Where M is a monument, B is a tool: its copyist’s omissions fall, as Section V noted, on the philosophical and doctrinal texts, and its organisation serves the workshop. The point for transmission history is that selection is interpretation. A thirteenth-century reader who wanted the corpus’s recipes without its metaphysics could have them, because a thirteenth-century copyist had already decided the metaphysics was ballast. Every later reader of B inherited that decision invisibly. When modern scholars complain that the Greek tradition transmits Zosimos in abbreviation, B is one of the mechanisms: abbreviation was a service copyists performed for readers, and its cost was borne by posterity. The Parisinus graecus 2327 (A) is the tradition’s expansion. A colophon fixes what palaeography cannot for M: the codex was copied in June 1478 at Candia (Khandak) in Crete by Theodoros Pelecanos of Corfu, passed through the hands of the Corcyrean collector Antonius Eparchus, and was acquired soon after by the royal library at Fontainebleau — the ancestor of its present home in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. A is the largest of the witnesses: it contains the complete Visions of Zosimos (lessons 1–3, ff. 84v–88v) where M holds only the first lesson, and it preserves a number of texts found in no other manuscript, whose origin Mertens records as unknown. Its construction is composite: the first half is reported as a copy of B, the second half drawn from another, not yet located source. And it carries the tradition’s most famous single image after the Chrysopoeia: Pelecanos’ own drawing of the ouroboros, dated by the codex to 1478 — a fifteenth-century scribe’s rendering of a symbol his exemplars had carried for a thousand years, and a perfect emblem of the codex tradition itself: faithful in outline, contemporary in hand. The Laurentianus graecus 86.16 (L), in Florence’s Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, was completed in December 1492 by the scribe Antonius Dranganas. It too preserves the Visions entire (ff. 90v–95v). Its scholarly interest is its unresolved position: Mertens’ introduction to her Zosimos edition leaves open whether L is a copy of A or whether the two are gemelli — twins, copied independently from a shared exemplar. The difference decides L’s evidentiary value. If L copies A, its agreements with A prove nothing; if the two are twins, their agreements witness their lost common source, and their disagreements locate errors in one line or the other. That the question remains open, for the corpus’s fourth witness, in the standard edition, is the honest state of the field — and a useful inoculation against any account of the Greek tradition that speaks of “the text” as if it were one thing. WHAT B TEACHES Selection is loss with a rationale. The 13th-century handbook’s omissions show a living readership sorting the corpus by use — and show modern readers that an abbreviated witness may abbreviate its exemplar, not the author. WHAT A TEACHES Lateness is not worthlessness. The 1478 codex preserves whole texts its 10th-century senior lacks. In a tradition this thin, the youngest principal witness can be, for a given work, the only complete one. WHAT L TEACHES Uncertainty is data. An unresolved stemma is not a failure of scholarship but its accurate report: the tradition’s branching is partly unrecoverable, and editions that hide that fact overstate what anyone knows. WHAT ALL FOUR TEACH Survival was narrow. Four codices, copied across five centuries in Constantinople’s orbit, Crete, and Florence, carry a literature composed across a millennium. The margin between the Greek alchemy we have and none at all is four books wide. VIII. Berthelot and Ruelle: The Corpus Enters Modern Scholarship For five centuries the corpus lived the life described above: copied, excerpted, annotated, and read by a narrowing circle. Its entry into modern scholarship has a date and two names. In 1887–88 the chemist Marcellin Berthelot and the Hellenist Charles-Émile Ruelle published in Paris the Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs — the Collection of the Ancient Greek Alchemists, cited ever since as CAAG — in three volumes: an introduction, the Greek text, and a French translation. The edition rested principally on the great codices, the Marcianus and the Paris manuscripts, and it made the corpus, for the first time, a public object: any scholar in any library could now read Olympi

They remembered it as a circle: a ring of epics running from the wedding at which Strife threw her apple to the death of Odysseus at the hands of his own son. Two of the ring's poems survive. The rest are known from summaries, fragments, and the plays and pictures that fed on them — and at the ring's centre stands a real mound in north-west Anatolia that has been dug, argued over, and misread for a hundred and fifty years. This article keeps the tradition, the texts, and the ruin in three separate registers, and says at every point which register it is speaking in. A War Too Big for Two Poems Ask a modern reader what the Iliad is about and the answer comes back as the Trojan War. The poem itself refuses the compliment. It covers a few weeks of the war's tenth year — a quarrel in the Greek camp, a withdrawal, a death, a revenge, a funeral — and it ends not with Troy taken but with Troy's greatest defender buried, the city still standing, its fall still in the future and known to every listener in advance. The Odyssey likewise covers the war only in retrospect: songs sung at feasts, veterans' reminiscences, a wooden horse recalled in a Spartan hall and in the underworld. Between them, the two surviving epics narrate perhaps a tenth of the story the Greeks told about Troy. The rest — why the war began, how the fleet was gathered, what it cost to launch it, how Achilles died, how the city actually fell, what happened to the victors on the way home, and how the last of the heroes died — was carried by six further epics, composed in the same dactylic hexameter and the same artificial epic dialect, which together with the Iliad and Odyssey formed the Trojan section of what antiquity called the Epic Cycle (Greek Epikos Kyklos , “the epic circle”). Those six poems are lost. The Cypria told everything before the Iliad : the divine decision to have a war, the Judgement of Paris, the flight of Helen, the mustering at Aulis, the sacrifice of Iphigenia, and nine years of raiding. The Aethiopis continued from Hector's funeral through the coming of the Amazons and of Memnon to the death of Achilles. The Little Iliad carried the story from the contest for Achilles' arms to the building of the Wooden Horse and the firing of the Greek camp. The Iliou Persis — the Sack of Ilium — told the night itself: the Horse opened, the altars violated, the city burned. The Nostoi , the Returns , followed the victors home into storm, shipwreck, and, in Agamemnon's case, a bath and a murderer. And the Telegony closed the ring after the Odyssey , with Odysseus's further voyages and his death, unknowing, at the hand of the son Circe had borne him. Read in sequence, the eight poems gave a Greek listener the whole war, from a quarrel among goddesses at a wedding to the extinction of the heroic generation. The Iliad and Odyssey were later lifted out of that ring — canonised, commented on, made the centre of Greek education — and the ring itself was allowed to perish. Sections II–III set out what exactly survives of it, and by what fragile route. This article therefore works in three registers, and it marks them as it goes, because nearly every confusion in the vast popular literature on Troy comes from sliding between them. First, the tradition as told: the story the Greeks themselves organised and retold for a thousand years, in epic, tragedy, painting, and cult. Told whole, in cycle order, it occupies Sections IV–XII. Second, the texts: the lost poems as historical objects — who was said to have composed them, when, how they were summarised and excerpted, and how much of them a modern reader can actually recover. That is the business of Sections II–III and of the poem-by-poem sections that follow, and it is a much thinner record than the story's fame suggests. Third, the archaeology: the mound of Hisarlik in the Troad, its nine superimposed settlements, and the Hittite documents that name a kingdom in the right place at the right time. That record, treated in Sections XVI–XVIII at its real strength — neither inflated into proof of the poems nor dismissed because it cannot prove them — supports a Bronze Age citadel, repeatedly destroyed, one of whose destructions is compatible with a war around the date Greek tradition assigned. It does not support, and no honest reading of it has ever supported, the war as told: ten years, a thousand ships, and named heroes are literature, built — this is the part the spade does warrant — on a real place. The verdict section (XIX) holds those two statements apart, because the distance between them is precisely the subject. THE RING AT A GLANCE Eight poems in story order: Cypria (11 books) · Iliad (24) · Aethiopis (5) · Little Iliad (4) · Iliou Persis (2) · Nostoi (5) · Odyssey (24) · Telegony (2). Seventy-seven books of hexameter. Two poems survive entire; six survive as prose summaries, fragments, and echoes. WHAT “LOST” MEANS HERE No complete cyclic poem has existed for well over a millennium. What we have is: the prose summaries of Proclus (Section II); a few hundred quoted lines and half-lines preserved by later authors; the parallel prose narrative of Apollodorus's Library and Epitome ; and the Cycle's vast reflex in archaic and classical art and tragedy. Reconstruction is possible; recovery is not. SPELLINGS USED HERE Greek names are transliterated, not Latinised, as throughout this hub: Ilios (not Ilium, except in the poem-title Iliou Persis as conventionally printed), Aias (not Ajax, except where a quoted translation or an established English title requires it), Alexandros for Paris's second name. Quotations keep their translators' spellings, including Evelyn-White's “Ilium” and “Ajax”.
