One boundary should be drawn before proceeding. The Iliad and Odyssey as texts — their composition, their oral-formulaic making, their fixation and canonisation — are the subject of this hub's companion article, The Homeric Epics , and of the Homeric sections of Heroes and Epic . Here the two poems appear in their other capacity: as members of the ring, two segments of a longer story that the tradition told whole. Where this article touches them, it is to mark where they sit in the sequence and what they presuppose — the Iliad opens in the tenth year because the Cypria had already told the first nine — not to re-argue their making. II. How We Know the Lost Poems: Proclus, Photius, and the Fragments Everything in Sections IV–XI rests on a chain of transmission that is short enough to state in full, and every reader of the Trojan Cycle should know its links and its weak points. The cyclic poems themselves circulated in antiquity as texts: they were read, quoted, mined by tragedians, illustrated by painters, and eventually excerpted into handbooks. By late antiquity they were already rare, and at some point in the Byzantine centuries the last complete copies perished. What survived the poems is a set of prose summaries of their contents, attributed to a certain Proclus and drawn from his Chrestomathy — a “useful reading” handbook of literary history in four books. Who this Proclus was is genuinely uncertain: candidates canvassed in the scholarship include a grammarian of the second century CE and the Neoplatonist philosopher Proclus (c. 412–485 CE), and the question is not settled. The summaries' value does not depend on settling it. They are businesslike plot abstracts, poem by poem and book-count by book-count, and wherever they can be checked against surviving fragments and against the poems' reflexes in art and tragedy, they check out as faithful — compressed, colourless, but faithful. The summaries themselves reach us by two narrow channels. The summary of the Cypria is preserved in a number of Iliad manuscripts. The summaries of the remaining five Trojan poems survive essentially in one: the tenth-century Venetus A manuscript of the Iliad , where they were copied into the scholarly apparatus as a guide to the whole saga surrounding the poem. A third witness stands behind both: the ninth-century patriarch and scholar Photius , whose Bibliotheca (codex 239) epitomises Proclus's Chrestomathy and confirms its contents — and also tells us that Proclus's Cycle was larger than the Trojan ring. In Photius's account the Epic Cycle ran from the union of Heaven and Earth, through the Titanomachy and the Theban poems (the Oedipodea , Thebaid , Epigoni , and Alcmaeonis ), and only then to Troy: a complete epic history of the mythical world, of which the Trojan War was the final, climactic chapter. This article treats the Trojan section, as the hub's brief requires, but the reader should register the frame: for the tradition that assembled the Cycle, the war at Troy was not the beginning of anything. It was the end of the heroic age — the event after which, as the Cypria 's own opening fragment puts it, the earth was emptied of the heroes. The Fragments, and Apollodorus Beside Proclus Around the summaries cluster the fragments : lines and passages of the actual poems quoted by later authors — scholiasts explaining Homer, Athenaeus at his dinner-table of learning, Pausanias describing paintings, Plato, Herodotus, the lexicographers. They amount, for all six poems together, to a few hundred lines at most, and they are not a random sample: later authors quoted what served their own purposes, so the fragments skew toward the quotable, the curious, and the disputed. Modern editions — those of Bernabé, Davies, and West are the standard three — gather fragments and testimonia poem by poem, and M. L. West's The Epic Cycle: A Commentary on the Lost Troy Epics (2013) is the first comprehensive commentary: it works through every fragment and testimonium and attempts, poem by poem, to reconstruct each lost epic's plan and course from the summaries, the fragments, and the evidence of early art and literature combined. West's further suggestion, reported here as his, is that both Proclus and Apollodorus ultimately derive their accounts from digests of the cyclic epics made in the Hellenistic period — which, if right, means our two prose witnesses are cousins, not independent checks on each other. Apollodorus is the second witness, and the fuller storyteller. The Library ( Bibliotheca ) attributed to Apollodorus — a mythographic handbook of the first or second century CE, by an author modern scholarship calls Pseudo-Apollodorus — retells Greek myth in continuous prose from the beginnings to the end of the heroic age, and its surviving continuation, the Epitome , covers the Trojan War in detail (Epitome 3–7): the Judgement, the oath of Helen's suitors, the muster, Aulis, the war's course, the Horse, the sack, the returns, Agamemnon's murder, and Odysseus's death. The Epitome agrees with Proclus's summaries in sequence and in most particulars, and diverges in some — it names killers where Proclus is silent, and preserves conditions and episodes (the theft of the Palladium as a stated condition of the city's fall, Nauplius's false beacons) that the summaries compress away. Where Proclus and Apollodorus agree, the cyclic poem almost certainly stood behind both. Where they disagree, or where a tragedian disagrees with both, this article says so: the tradition was never a single fixed text, and its variants are evidence, not embarrassment. The sack of Troy offers the sharpest cases (Section IX). // THE EVIDENCE LADDER, STATED ONCE // For any given episode of the lost poems, the evidence ranks as follows. Highest: a surviving fragment of the poem itself, quoted by a named ancient author. Next: Proclus's summary, checked against Apollodorus. Next: Apollodorus alone, or a tragedian's or painter's version, which may reflect the cyclic poem or may innovate freely. Lowest: late mythographers and Roman poets — Hyginus, Dictys, Dares, Virgil — whose versions are evidence for the tradition's afterlife, not for the cyclic poems. The famous details that fail this ladder are flagged where they occur: the apple inscribed “for the fairest”, Achilles' vulnerable heel, and Laocoön crushed with both his sons are all later than the Cycle, and none of them is used in this article as cyclic evidence. Were the Cyclic Poems Made to Fill Homer's Gaps? Antiquity's own verdict on the cyclic poems was condescending, and it has stuck. Aristotle, in the Poetics (1459a–b, paraphrased), praises Homer for taking not the whole war but one unified part of it, and faults the Cypria and Little Iliad by contrast: they are episodic, strung around a person and a period rather than a single action, so that — his famous count — only one tragedy, or two at most, can be made from the Iliad or the Odyssey , while many have been made from the Cypria and more than eight from the Little Iliad , whose episodes he lists: the Award of the Arms, Philoctetes, Neoptolemus, Eurypylus, the Begging, the Laconian Women, the Sack, the Sailing of the Fleet, Sinon, the Trojan Women. Callimachus, in a much-quoted epigram (fr. 465 Pfeiffer, paraphrased), declares his hatred of the cyclic poem and of everything common and much-travelled. From these judgements grew the modern assumption, dominant into the twentieth century, that the cyclic epics were late, derivative patchwork — composed after Homer, by lesser poets, precisely to fill the gaps before, between, and after the two masterpieces. Jonathan Burgess's The Tradition of the Trojan War in Homer and the Epic Cycle (2001) is the systematic challenge to that assumption, and its argument is reported here as the current revaluation's core. Burgess's evidence is chiefly the archaic visual record: surveying Trojan War scenes in early Greek art, he shows that episodes from outside the Iliad and Odyssey — the Judgement, the death of Achilles, the sack, the escapes and returns — predominate in archaic representation, while scenes securely tied to the Homeric poems specifically emerge surprisingly late. His conclusion, in the image his reviewers quote: if the tradition of the Trojan War were a tree, the Iliad and Odyssey would initially have been a couple of branches, and the Cycle's material the trunk. On this view the cyclic poems are not Homeric spin-offs but free-standing compositions drawing on a broad, stable, extra-Homeric tradition — “pre-Homeric” in the sense that their material took shape before Homer became the tradition's centre, whatever the dates of the particular texts that were eventually written down and summarised by Proclus. West, for his part, dates the six Trojan cyclic poems as texts to roughly 630–560 BCE — after the Homeric poems' formation, but squarely in the archaic world that also produced the earliest Trojan art. The two positions are compatible where it matters for this article: the story the Cycle tells is older than its surviving arrangement, the poems were independent works and not appendices, and their loss is a loss of archaic literature, not of footnotes to Homer. III. The Ring on the Shelf: The Cycle Poem by Poem The table below is the article's map. Attributions are the ancient ones, transmitted with the summaries and the fragments; they are attributions, not title-pages, and several were disputed already in antiquity — the Cypria was ascribed variously to Stasinus of Cyprus, to Hegesias (or Hegesinus) of Salamis, and to Cyprias of Halicarnassus, and one persistent ancient story made it Homer's own work, given to Stasinus as a dowry with his daughter. The floruits antiquity assigned (Arctinus placed at the 27th Olympiad, 776 BCE, in the Eusebian tradition) sit uneasily beside the later dates modern linguistic and historical arguments favour; West's c. 630–560 BCE for the poems as composed texts is given in the final column as the modern working estimate. What is not in dispute is the sequence: Proclus's summaries dovetail — each poem's summary ends where the next begins — and that dovetailing, whether it reflects the poems' original design or a later editor's arrangement of them into a cycle, is what makes the ring a ring. The first is its completeness as design . The seams are deliberate: the Cypria ends with the distribution of the two captive women, Chryseis and Briseis, whose seizure and return drive the Iliad 's plot, and with Zeus's plan to relieve the Trojans by detaching Achilles — the very mechanism of the Iliad 's opening. The Aethiopis begins, on Proclus's showing, exactly at the Iliad 's last line's aftermath: Hector buried, the Amazon arriving. The Telegony begins with the burial of the suitors, the business the Odyssey 's final book leaves unfinished. Whoever stitched the ring — the poets themselves accommodating famous neighbours, or Hellenistic editors regularising a corpus — stitched it tightly. The second feature is its asymmetry of survival . The two poems that survived are the two that antiquity's schools adopted; the six that perished include the war's beginning, its end, and its entire moral reckoning in the returns. A reader who knows only Homer knows the wrath and the wanderings. The Cycle's reader knew the consequences — and it is the consequences, as Sections XIII–XIV will show, that classical Greece could not stop staging and ritualising. BEFORE THE RING: THE WIDER CYCLE Photius's Proclus began with the Titanomachy and the Theban poems. The Trojan ring is the larger Cycle's final movement — the gods' wars and Thebes' destruction precede it, so that Troy's fall closes the age of heroes altogether. For the divine succession that opens the sequence, see this hub's Theogony . THE POEMS' OWN DATES Ancient floruits (Arctinus at 776 BCE) are traditional, not documentary. West's working dates for the six Trojan poems as texts, c. 630–560 BCE, rest on language, on their relations to the Homeric poems, and on their reflexes in datable art. Burgess's argument concerns the tradition's age, which is a different and older quantity. IV. Cypria I: The Plan of Zeus, Eris, and the Judgement of Paris The Cypria — eleven books, the longest of the lost poems — does not begin with Helen or Paris. It begins with a decision in heaven, and the poem's surviving first fragment states it with a bleakness that frames the entire Cycle. The fragment is preserved by a scholiast on Iliad 1.5, commenting on Homer's phrase “the plan of Zeus was fulfilled”, and is quoted here in Evelyn-White's translation (1914): “There was a time when the countless tribes of men, though wide-dispersed, oppressed the surface of the deep-bosomed earth, and Zeus saw it and had pity and in his wise heart resolved to relieve the all-nurturing earth of men by causing the great struggle of the Ilian war, that the load of death might empty the world. And so the heroes were slain in Troy, and the plan of Zeus came to pass.” — CYPRIA FR. 1, PRESERVED BY THE SCHOLIAST ON ILIAD 1.5, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB, 1914) In Proclus's summary, Zeus plans the war in council with Themis . The instrument is a wedding. Peleus, a mortal, is to marry the sea-goddess Thetis — herself, in another Cypria fragment, a bride assigned to a mortal because she had refused Zeus and Zeus had sworn it in anger — and the gods feast at the marriage on Mount Pelion. Strife (Eris) arrives at the feast and starts a dispute among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite as to which of them is fairest. Proclus says no more than that: no apple is mentioned in the summary, and the golden apple inscribed “for the fairest” — the detail every modern retelling leads with — belongs to later versions of the story (it is in Hyginus and in Lucian, not in Proclus, and the inscription is later still). The archive records the apple as the tradition's most successful later addition, and the summary's plainer quarrel as the cyclic evidence. Zeus will not judge his wife, his daughter, and Aphrodite himself. At his command Hermes leads the three to Alexandros — Paris — a king's son herding on Mount Ida above Troy, and Alexandros, in Proclus's blunt phrase, “lured by his promised marriage with Helen, decides in favour of Aphrodite”. Apollodorus (Epitome 3.2, paraphrased) spells out the three offers as the tradition standardised them: Hera offered rule over all men (in some tellings, kingship of Europe and Asia), Athena victory in war, Aphrodite the marriage with Helen, the most beautiful woman alive. Paris chose the woman. The bribes are the point: the Judgement is not a beauty contest misjudged but a choice among three lives — empire, glory, desire — and the herdsman chose desire, and the world paid. Helen, and How She Came to Be Helen The Cypria also carried Helen's own strange origin, in a fragment preserved by Athenaeus (viii. 334 B, in Evelyn-White's translation, paraphrased here except for the sense): Helen was the child of Zeus and Nemesis — Retribution herself — who fled the god across land and sea, changing shape from fish to beast to beast, until Zeus caught her; the egg that resulted passed, in the fuller tradition, to Leda of Sparta, and Helen hatched from it, “a marvel to men”. Other accounts made Helen simply Leda's daughter by Zeus in swan form; the Cypria 's version, with Nemesis as mother, is the darker and arguably the more programmatic one: the woman over whom Europe and Asia would fight was Retribution's child. Grown, Helen was already a prize contested by heroes before Paris: Theseus had carried her off as a girl, in the cyclic tradition the scholia preserve, and her brothers Castor and Polydeuces (the Dioscuri) had rescued her, sacking Aphidna and Athens in the process. She was then married to Menelaus of Sparta — chosen from a crowd of suitors under the oath that Section V describes — and it was as Menelaus's wife, queen in his palace, and mother of his daughter Hermione, that Paris found her. The Flight Proclus's summary of the abduction is a masterpiece of compression, and this article follows it step by step (paraphrased from Evelyn-White's rendering). Aphrodite, her promise to redeem, directs Alexandros to build ships. His brother Helenus , who has the gift of prophecy, foretells what will come of the voyage; his sister Cassandra prophesies likewise, and is — here as always in her story — not believed. Aeneas sails with him at Aphrodite's order. Alexandros lands in Lacedaemon, is entertained first by the sons of Tyndareus and then by Menelaus in Sparta, and at a feast gives gifts to Helen. Menelaus then sails for Crete, leaving Helen — the detail is Proclus's own, and it is devastating in its domesticity — with instructions to furnish the guests with all they require until they depart. Aphrodite brings Helen and Alexandros together; after their union they load very great treasures aboard and sail by night. Hera raises a storm; they are driven to Sidon, which Alexandros sacks; from Sidon he sails to Troy and celebrates his marriage with Helen. (Herodotus, at 2.117, cites the Cypria itself against the storm voyage: in the poem as he read it, Alexandrus reached Ilium from Sparta in three days with a fair wind — a reminder that even the cyclic text had variants, and that Herodotus used the poem as a documentary source for the story's geography.) Meanwhile, in a parallel strand the poem wove in, Castor and Polydeuces are caught stealing the cattle of Idas and Lynceus; Castor is killed, the killers are killed, and Zeus grants the brothers their strange shared immortality, each alive on alternate days — Helen's brothers thus removed from the war their sister is about to cause, and translated out of the mortal story at the moment it begins. Iris brings the news to Menelaus. The wronged husband comes home to an empty palace, stolen treasure, and a guest-friendship violated in his own hall. The war now needs only its machinery. // GUEST-FRIENDSHIP: THE CRIME INSIDE THE CRIME // Paris was Menelaus's xenos — his guest, bound by the sacred reciprocity Zeus himself protected as Zeus Xenios. The abduction was therefore not only adultery and theft but sacrilege against the institution that made travel, diplomacy, and civilisation possible. Greek tellings never let the point drop: it is why the war is, in the tradition's own terms, just — and why its conduct, Section IX, is so damning when the avengers commit sacrileges of their own. V. Cypria II: The Oath, Aulis and Iphigenia, and the Road to Troy The Oath of Tyndareus Why did all Greece sail? The tradition's answer is a contract. When Helen came of age, her suitors — in Apollodorus's catalogue (Library 3.10, paraphrased), a roll of the heroic age's kings and champions — competed for her at Sparta, and her father Tyndareus, fearing that the losers would make war on the winner, bound them all by oath, on the advice (in Apollodorus's telling) of Odysseus, who extracted Penelope's hand as his fee for the idea. The suitors swore, standing on the cut pieces of a sacrificed horse, that they would defend the chosen husband against any who wronged him in respect of the marriage, and would join in exacting redress. Menelaus was chosen. Years later, when Paris carried Helen off, the oath fell due — and the Cypria 's muster is the oath being collected. The mechanism matters to the tradition's moral architecture: the expedition is not a riot of volunteers but a coalition bound by a sworn instrument, led by Menelaus's elder brother Agamemnon , king of Mycenae, as commander-in-chief. It also explains the coalition's reluctant members — above all Odysseus, who had devised the oath and now feigned madness to escape it, yoking mismatched animals and sowing salt (the fuller tradition, in Apollodorus and Hyginus), until Palamedes exposed him by laying the infant Telemachus in the plough's path. Proclus's summary records the exposure laconically: the leaders, gathering the host, detect Odysseus “when he pretends to be mad, not wishing to join the expedition, by seizing his son Telemachus for punishment at the suggestion of Palamedes” (Evelyn-White's rendering, paraphrased in compression). Odysseus never forgave Palamedes; the Cypria itself contained Palamedes' death — drowned, Pausanias reports from his reading of the poem (10.31.2, paraphrased), by Odysseus and Diomedes while he was out fishing. The coalition's cleverest man murdered its most inconvenient witness before the war had properly begun, and the cyclic poem said so. Aulis: The Omen, the False Start, and the Stag The host gathered at Aulis , the Boeotian harbour opposite Euboea, and there the tradition sets its first great omen. As the army sacrificed, a serpent darted from the altar, climbed a plane tree, and devoured a sparrow and her eight nestlings in the nest — nine birds — before Zeus turned it to stone where it clung. Calchas, the expedition's seer, read the sign: nine years of war, and Troy taken in the tenth. The Iliad itself preserves the omen, in Odysseus's retelling (2.308–330), which is one of the clearest places where the surviving poem leans on the cyclic story it presupposes. The fleet sailed — and landed in the wrong country. In Mysia , far south of the Troad, the Greeks stormed Teuthrania taking it for Troy, and were met by Telephus , the local king, a son of Heracles, who killed Thersander and was himself wounded in the thigh by Achilles before Dionysus tripped him with a vine. A storm scattered the fleet on its withdrawal, and the expedition dissolved homeward — Achilles to Scyros, where he married Deidameia, daughter of Lycomedes, a marriage whose son, Neoptolemus, will end the war his father could not. Eight years passed, in the tradition's arithmetic. Telephus's wound would not heal; an oracle told him that his wounder would heal him, and he came to Argos, where Achilles scraped rust from the very spear that had wounded him into the wound, and Telephus in return guided the fleet to Troy. The episode — the wounder as healer — became one of the tradition's most durable images, and Telephus's son Eurypylus will repay the debt in blood in Section VIII. Iphigenia at Aulis The fleet mustered a second time at Aulis, and now the story produces the episode by which the whole war's cost is first measured. Agamemnon, hunting, shot a stag and boasted that he surpassed even Artemis . The goddess, in anger, sent storms that pinned the fleet in harbour. Calchas declared her anger and its price: the army could not sail until Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to Artemis. The girl was fetched from Mycenae on a lie — she was told she was being brought to marry Achilles. And then, in Proclus's summary of the Cypria , the poem performs the first of the tradition's great rescues: at the altar, Artemis snatched Iphigenia away, transported her to the land of the Taurians on the Black Sea, and made her immortal, setting a stag on the altar in her place. The army saw a deer die and sailed. // TWO IPHIGENIAS, AND THE ARCHIVE KEEPS BOTH // The substitution is the Cypria 's version, and it is not the only one the Greeks told. Aeschylus's Agamemnon (458 BCE) remembers Iphigenia as really killed — gagged, lifted over the altar “like a goat”, her saffron robe slipping, her eyes pleading (paraphrased) — and makes the killing the moral engine of the whole Oresteia : it is why Clytemnestra waits ten years with an axe. Euripides staged both versions in two plays: in Iphigenia among the Taurians the rescued girl is found alive, a priestess compelled to sacrifice strangers; in Iphigenia at Aulis she goes willingly to a death the transmitted ending then undoes with a reported substitution — an ending scholars have long suspected of being a later addition to Euripides' text. The cyclic poem, the tragedians, and the mythographers do not agree, and no ancient authority reconciled them. Section XIII returns to what tragedy did with the disagreement. Tenedos, Lemnos, and the First Man Ashore Released, the fleet sailed to Tenedos , the island off the Troad, and there the expedition shed another indispensable man. At a feast, Philoctetes — the archer who held the bow and arrows of Heracles, without which, though the Greeks did not yet know it, Troy could not fall — was bitten by a snake. The wound festered and stank until the army could not bear it, and Philoctetes was put ashore on Lemnos and left there, alone with his bow, for ten years. Proclus records the abandonment in one clause; Sophocles built one of his greatest plays out of the moral filth of it (Section XIII). At the same feast, Achilles quarrelled with Agamemnon over a late invitation — the Cypria 's small rehearsal for the great quarrel of the Iliad . Then the fleet crossed to the Troad. The Trojans contested the landing; Protesilaus , first of the Greeks to leap ashore, was killed by Hector — the first Greek death of the war, fulfilling the oracle that the first to land would be the first to die. Achilles killed Cycnus, a son of Poseidon invulnerable to iron, and drove the Trojans from the beach. The Greeks sent Menelaus and Odysseus as envoys into Troy to demand Helen and the treasure back — the tradition's formal last chance of peace, preserved also in the Iliad 's recollections — and the Trojans refused. The army assaulted the walls, failed, and settled into the war the Cypria spends its remaining books narrating: nine years of raiding the Troad and its allied cities, Lyrnessus and Pedasus and the cities of Aeneas's country among them, Achilles killing Troilus, a son of Priam, in Apollo's sanctuary (a killing the archaic painters loved and the tradition counted among the war's darkening acts), Patroclus selling Priam's son Lycaon in

x: UGARIT AND THE BAAL CYCLE Ras Shamra, Syrian Coast · Flourished c. 1450–1190 BCE · Recovered 1928–29 // THE MISSING MIDDLE TERM :: SEA — PALACE — DEATH :: EVERY PARALLEL GRADED // Between Egypt and Greece there stands a city that neither hub of this archive can do without and neither, until now, has treated on its own ground. Ugarit — a Bronze Age port on the Syrian coast, destroyed around 1190 BCE and dug out of its mound in 1929 — left behind the only substantial mythology the Levant ever wrote about itself: the Baal Cycle, six broken tablets in an alphabet of thirty wedge-signs, in which a storm god fights the Sea for a kingship he never quite secures, builds a palace, dies, and returns. This article tells that story, introduces the city and the script that preserved it, and then does the harder thing: it weighs, one by one and at their real strength, the famous parallels — Hesiod's succession myth, Leviathan, Psalm 29, Zeus of Mount Kasios — and grades each as transmission, inheritance, or resemblance. After Ugarit: The Phoenician Continuation and Sanchuniathon XVII. Sources I. The Missing Middle Term This archive has twice needed Ugarit already, and twice borrowed it in passing. The Theogony article, explaining where Hesiod's succession of sky-gods — Ouranos deposed by Kronos, Kronos deposed by Zeus — could have come from, reached east to the Hurrian Kumarbi cycle and to the storm-god mythology of the Levantine coast. The Theban Cycle article opened its gates to Cadmus, the Phoenician prince who carries the alphabet into Greece. Both doors open onto the same corridor, and at the corridor's centre stands a city this article exists to describe. Ugarit is the missing middle term of the eastern Mediterranean: the place where the mythic materials that later surface in Hesiod, in the Hebrew Bible, and in Phoenician tradition can be read, for once, in a local hand, in a local language, on tablets fired in the city's own destruction. The claim needs its limits stated at once, because this article's whole discipline (Sections XIII–XV) is the grading of such claims. Ugarit is not the source of Greek myth, and the Baal Cycle is not a draft of the Theogony . What Ugarit gives us is something rarer and more useful than a source: a dated, localised, fully documented instance of the mythological world the whole region shared — a control sample. Before 1929, the religion of Bronze Age Canaan was known almost entirely through its enemies: the Hebrew Bible's polemics against Baal, and late Greek and Roman reports of Phoenician custom filtered through centuries of retelling. After 1929, scholars held the thing itself — myths, epics, rituals, god-lists, and offering calendars written by the worshippers, in their own script, in the decades before the city fell. Every comparison made in this hub between Greek, Hebrew, and Egyptian material runs differently once that control sample exists. That is Ugarit's importance, and it does not need inflating. WHAT UGARIT IS A Late Bronze Age port-kingdom at Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast, north of modern Latakia; harbour at Minet el-Beida; destroyed c. 1190 BCE in the upheavals of the Bronze Age collapse and never reoccupied on the old scale — which is precisely why its archives survived in place. WHAT IT LEFT Thousands of clay tablets: royal correspondence, treaties, law, trade records, school exercises, and a literary corpus — myths, epics, hymns, rituals — in an alphabetic cuneiform of some thirty signs, deciphered within two years of the first finds. WHAT THE BAAL CYCLE IS The longest and fullest of the Ugaritic poems: six tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6 in the standard edition) telling how Baal, the storm god, defeats Yam the Sea, wins a palace on Mount Saphon, is swallowed by Mot, Death, and returns. Told in full in Sections VII–IX. HOW THIS ARTICLE PROCEEDS City first, then script, then text, then story, then pantheon, then the other epics — and only then the parallels, each graded: demonstrable transmission , shared inheritance , motif resemblance , or unproven . The grading scheme is set out in Section XV and applied in XIII–XIV. A word on names and spellings. The language of the tablets is called Ugaritic , a Northwest Semitic language closely related to the Canaanite dialects from which Hebrew and Phoenician descend. Its consonantal script leaves most vowels unwritten, so the vocalisation of names is partly reconstructed: the storm god's name, written bʿl , is read Baʿlu , conventionally Baal — a word that is also a title, “lord, master”, a fact that matters whenever the Hebrew Bible uses it. The sea is Yam (also “Prince Yam, Judge River”); death is Mot ; the craftsman god is Kothar-wa-Khasis , “Skilful-and-Wise”; Baal's mountain is Saphon (Ugaritic Ṣapānu ), the peak north of the city that Greeks would later call Mount Kasios. Where this article renders lines of the poems in English, it paraphrases the standard published translations named in Section XVII and says so; the discipline is the hub's usual one, and the tablet texts are too broken, and their renderings too contested, for quotation to be offered lightly. // QUOTATIONS IN THIS ARTICLE // Passages in quotation marks are limited to wordings this article can stand behind: Samuel Sandmel's published definition of “parallelomania” (1962), quoted in Section XV, and the King James rendering of Isaiah 27:1, quoted in Section XIII. Everything from the Ugaritic tablets themselves is given as close paraphrase of the translations of Coogan & Smith, Wyatt, and Pardee named in Section XVII, and is written as paraphrase. Divine epithets in quotation marks — “Rider on the Clouds”, “Bull El” — are the conventional renderings of fixed Ugaritic formulas as printed in those translations. II. The City: A Plough, a Tomb, and Claude Schaeffer Ugarit was not lost the way Troy was lost, under legend; it was lost the way a working port is lost, by abandonment, and it was found by accident. In the spring of 1928 , a Syrian farmer ploughing near the bay of Minet el-Beida , on the coast north of Latakia, struck a stone slab with his ploughshare. Beneath it lay a vaulted tomb with rich goods. The find was reported to the antiquities authorities of the French Mandate, which then administered Syria, and in 1929 a French expedition under Claude F. A. Schaeffer arrived to investigate. Schaeffer began at the harbour necropolis, and then did the thing that made his reputation: he looked inland, less than a kilometre away, at the large artificial mound the locals called Ras Shamra — “Fennel Headland” — and moved the excavation there. The mound vindicated him within days. Inscribed clay tablets began coming up in the first season: some in the familiar Akkadian cuneiform, the diplomatic script of the age, and some in a script no one had ever seen — wedge-shaped signs like Mesopotamian cuneiform, but far too few of them, only about thirty, to be a syllabary. The tablets also named the place. Ras Shamra was Ugarit , a kingdom previously known only from other people's archives — from the Amarna letters of fourteenth-century Egypt, from Hittite treaties, from Egyptian lists — a name without a city. Schaeffer directed the excavations for some four decades, and French and later joint French-Syrian missions have worked the site, with interruptions for war, ever since. What they uncovered was a full Late Bronze Age capital: a royal palace of some ninety rooms with its own archives, private houses of merchants and officials with theirs, and on the acropolis two great temples, of Baal and of Dagan , with the house of the high priest — and its library — between them. The timing of the discovery deserves emphasis, because it explains the find's outsized effect. The tablets appeared at the moment when biblical scholarship, Assyriology, and classics were all short of exactly the same thing: a primary source for the Levant between Egypt and Mesopotamia. The script was deciphered with a speed that still looks miraculous — independently, in 1930 , by Hans Bauer , Édouard Dhorme , and the excavations' own epigrapher Charles Virolleaud , working from the reasonable guess that a thirty-sign system must be an alphabet and that the language behind it was Semitic. Within a few years the mythological tablets were being published and translated, and the scholarly map of the ancient Levant had been redrawn. It is not an exaggeration — this article will make the grading argument carefully in Section XV, but the point here is a consensus of the field — to call the Ras Shamra archives the most consequential single find for the study of Levantine religion in the twentieth century. c. 1450–1200 BCE THE CITY'S GREAT AGE Ugarit flourishes as a trading port under, successively, Egyptian and then Hittite overlordship; the palace, temples, and archives accumulate. The literary tablets belong to its last century and a half. c. 1190 BCE DESTRUCTION The city is burned and abandoned in the Bronze Age collapse — the era of the Sea Peoples' movements. Letters from the last king's reign speak of enemy ships and burning towns. Ugarit is never rebuilt as a city. 1928 THE PLOUGH A farmer breaks into a tomb at Minet el-Beida. The find is reported to the French Mandate authorities. 1929 SCHAEFFER AT RAS SHAMRA The French expedition moves from the harbour to the tell; tablets in Akkadian and in an unknown alphabetic cuneiform appear in the first season. 1930 DECIPHERMENT Bauer, Dhorme, and Virolleaud independently crack the alphabet; the language proves to be a previously unknown Northwest Semitic tongue, promptly named Ugaritic. One more fact about the discovery belongs here, because the whole article depends on it. Ugarit's tablets survived because the city burned. Unbaked and lightly baked clay is perishable; a library caught in a conflagration is fired hard, like pottery, and the destruction that ended Ugarit in about 1190 BCE kiln-fired its archives in place. The texts a modern reader holds were, many of them, still in the rooms where scribes had shelved them — in the palace, in the high priest's house by the temples, in the villa of the official Rapanu, whose private archive of diplomatic correspondence is famous in its own right. Later seasons added more: a substantial archive found in rescue excavations in 1973, and over three hundred further tablets in a single building in 1994. The corpus is still growing, and its editions are still being revised; Section VI takes up what that means for the Baal Cycle itself. III. A Port Between Four Worlds To understand why this city's myths matter beyond its walls, begin with its geography. Ugarit stood about a kilometre from the sea on a fertile coastal plain, backed by wooded hills that supplied the cedar and resin the ancient world prized, and faced, across a short crossing, by the island of Cyprus — the copper island, Alashiya of the letters. Its harbour at Minet el-Beida served ships running every route the Late Bronze Age knew: south to Egypt , east up the Euphrates corridor to Mesopotamia , north into the orbit of Hatti , the Hittite empire in Anatolia, and west to Cyprus, the Aegean, and beyond. The kingdom it ruled was modest — a coastal strip and its hinterland — but the port was a hinge, and hinges get traffic from every door they join. Politically, Ugarit lived its great age as a gifted vassal. In the Amarna age its kings corresponded with pharaohs; around 1350 BCE Niqmaddu II accepted Hittite overlordship, sealing a treaty with the great king Suppiluliuma I that fixed an annual tribute in gold, silver, and fine garments — and, in the crisis that followed, Hittite arms saved Ugarit from a coalition of its neighbours, and Hittite favour enlarged its territory. Vassalage, for Ugarit, was a business model: the tribute bought protection, the protection kept the harbour open, and the harbour's customs made the tribute cheap at the price. The palace archives preserve the arrangement from the inside — treaties, royal letters, legal decisions, tax and trade records — and they show a kingdom negotiating, in writing, with every power in its world. EGYPT, TO THE SOUTH The old imperial presence: diplomatic correspondence in the Amarna age, Egyptian goods and Egyptianising art in the city, and a long Egyptian familiarity with the Levantine storm god — the same Baal whom Egypt had already identified with its own Seth, as the Egyptology hub's article on Set sets out. The identification is older than Ugarit's fall and outlasts it. HATTI, TO THE NORTH The overlord of Ugarit's last century and a half: treaty partner, court of appeal, and the conduit through which Hurrian myth — the Kumarbi material of Section XIII — circulated in the same scribal world Ugarit belonged to. CYPRUS AND THE AEGEAN, TO THE WEST Copper from Alashiya, Mycenaean pottery in Ugarit's houses, merchants from across the sea resident in the port. The craftsman god of the Baal Cycle, Kothar-wa-Khasis, keeps his workshops at Kaphtor — Crete — and at Memphis in Egypt: the poem's own geography is the port's trade map, divinised. MESOPOTAMIA, TO THE EAST The scribal mother-culture: cuneiform itself, the Akkadian language of diplomacy, Sumerian as the classical language of the schoolroom, and a stock of mythic and scholarly material that Ugarit's scribes copied, translated, and shelved beside their own. The end came fast, and the tablets catch its edge. In the decades around 1200 BCE the whole eastern Mediterranean system convulsed — the Bronze Age collapse: palaces burned from Greece to Anatolia, trade routes failed, and peoples on the move by sea, the Sea Peoples of the Egyptian records, raided down the Levantine coast. Letters from Ugarit's last king, Ammurapi , and correspondence with the king of Alashiya speak of enemy ships, of towns burned, of Ugarit's own troops and fleet absent in Hittite service when they were needed at home. Sometime around 1190 BCE the city was destroyed and abandoned. Unlike Tyre and Sidon to the south — whose survival is the subject of Section XVI — Ugarit was never refounded. Its mound slept under farmland for three thousand years, which is why a farmer's plough, and not a successor city's foundations, was what found it. // ON THE DESTRUCTION DATE // The date of Ugarit's fall is conventionally given as c. 1190 or c. 1185 BCE; the precision is archaeological, not documentary — no tablet says “in this year the city fell”, and the last letters are undated appeals in a crisis whose year we infer from the wider chronology of the collapse. This article writes “c. 1190 BCE” and means the margin honestly: within a decade or so, in the generation around 1200 BCE. IV. The Writing: An Alphabet in Wedges The second marvel of Ras Shamra, after the archives themselves, is the script they are written in. Mesopotamian cuneiform — the wedge-impressed writing of Sumer and Akkad — is a magnificent and laborious system: hundreds of signs, each standing for a syllable or a whole word, the life's study of a professional scribal class. The scribes of Ugarit took the technique — a reed stylus pressed into wet clay — and discarded the system. In its place they built an alphabet : a small set of signs, each standing for a single consonantal sound, with which anything in their language could be written. The standard count is thirty signs : twenty-seven consonants, and three forms of the first letter, aleph , differentiated by the vowel that follows it — a small, telling breach of pure consonantal writing, and the only vowels the script bothers to mark. The invention has to be placed carefully. Ugarit's scribes did not invent the alphabet from nothing: alphabetic writing on the consonantal principle had existed in the Levant, in rough experimental forms scratched on stone and pottery, for centuries before them — the inscriptions from Sinai and Canaan that Egyptologists and Semitists group as Proto-Canaanite. What Ugarit did was to systematise it: to give the alphabet a fixed signary, a fixed order, a scribal school to teach it, and a literature to write in it. We know the order was fixed because the school tablets preserve it: abecedaries from Ugarit list the letters in a sequence recognisably ancestral to the order still used by the Phoenician, Hebrew, and — through them — Greek and Latin alphabets. A second abecedary from the city preserves a different order, the one later standard in South Arabia; Ugarit's schoolroom, characteristically, knew both. When a modern reader recites A-B-C, the sequence descends, through Phoenician and Greek hands, from the tradition these tablets document. Feature Mesopotamian cuneiform Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform Sign inventory Hundreds of signs in active use Thirty signs What a sign stands for A syllable, or a whole word (logogram) A single consonant; three alephs also mark a following vowel Direction Left to right Left to right Medium Clay, stone, metal Clay, almost exclusively Who could learn it A professional class, after years of schooling Still a professional class at Ugarit — but the system itself can be learned in days, and that portability is its historical destiny (Section XVI) Two cautions belong with the celebration. First, the alphabet at Ugarit remained a scribal instrument: there is no evidence of a generally literate population, and the clay medium tied it to the palace and the school. The alphabet's democratising career belongs to its later life on papyrus, ink, and stone in the Phoenician cities. Second, the Ugaritic signary itself died with the city. No later script descends from its wedge shapes — the shapes were an artefact of clay. What travelled west was the principle and the order , carried in the linear letter-forms of the Phoenicians, whose twenty-two-sign alphabet is a cousin, not a child, of Ugarit's thirty. Keeping those two cautions in view is the difference between the alphabet's real history — remarkable enough — and the inflated version in which Ugarit single-handedly teaches the world to write. V. The Archives and the School of Four Languages The tablets were not found in one library but in a scatter of archives across the city, and the scatter is itself information: writing at Ugarit was not a temple monopoly or a palace secret but the operating system of a trading kingdom. The royal palace held the state's papers — treaties, the king's correspondence with great kings and with his own officials, legal rulings, lists of taxes, rations, and personnel. The house of the high priest , on the acropolis between the temples of Baal and Dagan, held the scholarly and religious library: the mythological and epic tablets, rituals, god-lists, omen and scholarly texts, and school exercises. Private houses held the rest: the archive of Rapanu, a high official whose correspondence reached across the known world; merchants' letters and accounts; the papers of men whose business required records in several languages at once. The languages are the point. Ugarit's archives are written in at least seven or eight tongues — Ugaritic, Akkadian, Sumerian, Hurrian, Hittite, Egyptian, and texts in the still-undeciphered Cypro-Minoan script among them — and in several scripts. But the school , the institution that trained the men who wrote all this, worked principally in four languages , and its exercises survive to prove it: lexical lists aligning Sumerian words with their Akkadian and Hurrian and Ugaritic equivalents, column by column, the Bronze Age equivalent of a four-language dictionary drilled into apprentices; syllabaries; copies of Mesopotamian classics; practice alphabets. A graduate of that school could draft a treaty in Akkadian for the Hittite court, a letter in Ugaritic for a local merchant, and a ritual list for the temple — and could shelve, in the high priest's library, a copy of the Baal Cycle made by a master of the same craft. THE PALACE ARCHIVES The state in writing: international correspondence, vassal treaties, royal edicts, court cases, administrative lists. Mostly Akkadian, the diplomatic lingua franca — Ugarit's outward face. THE HIGH PRIEST'S LIBRARY The city's memory of itself: the mythological poems including the Baal Cycle, the epics of Kirta and Aqhat, rituals, sacrifices lists, god-lists, and the school texts. Mostly Ugaritic, in the alphabetic script — the inward face. THE PRIVATE ARCHIVES Rapanu's diplomatic files; merchants' houses with letters, contracts, and accounts in multiple languages. Proof that the scribal system served commerce as well as crown and cult. WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE MYTHS The Baal Cycle was not folk-tale taken down by an antiquarian. It was a library text , copied in a school tradition, shelved with the rituals of the cult that worshipped the same gods — literature and liturgy in one room. Section VI follows from this. That last point deserves a paragraph of its own, because it governs how the poems should be read. Alongside the myths, the high priest's library held the working documents of the cult: lists of sacrifices naming the same gods in the same families, ritual calendars, a famous list of the gods of Ugarit in fixed order — the pantheon's official table of precedence, so to speak — and texts for the rites of the royal ancestors. Myth and cult at Ugarit are therefore not two separate subjects that a modern writer may choose between; they are two shelves of one library. But they are still different shelves , and the hub's standing discipline applies with full force here: the Baal Cycle is a literary text — a poem, with a poem's licences — and it is not a transcript of any rite, nor a creed, nor a report of what a worshipper at the Baal temple was required to believe. What the cult documents can do is corroborate the pantheon: the gods of the poems are the gods of the offering lists, under the same names and epithets. What they cannot do is turn the poem into liturgy. Section XI will use them in the first way and refuse the second. VI. The Baal Cycle as a Text: Six Tablets, One Scribe, Many Gaps The Baal Cycle survives on six clay tablets , cited in the standard edition — Die keilalphabetischen Texte aus Ugarit , whence the abbreviation KTU — as KTU 1.1 through 1.6 . Each tablet is written in columns on both faces, in a fine, dense alphabetic cuneiform, and the poem they carry is long: in modern translation the cycle runs to some fifty pages of verse. The division of the story across the tablets is clean at the level of the three great movements: tablets 1–2 carry the conflict with Yam; tablets 3–4 the building of the palace; tablets 5–6 the conflict with Mot. Within that frame, the sequence of episodes — and in places the sequence of the tablets' own fragments — is a reconstruction, and this section's business is to state plainly what that means. The cycle is unusual among ancient poems in carrying its copyist's name. A colophon — the scribal signature set at the end of the work, preserved on the sixth tablet — names the scribe Ilimilku of Shubbani, describes him as the pupil of Attanu-puruleni , chief of priests and chief of herdsmen, and places his work under a King Niqmaddu of Ugarit. Ilimilku's name stands in the colophons of the Kirta and Aqhat poems as well: the great literary tablets of Ugarit come, so far as their signatures tell us, from one master's hand, in one priestly school, in one reign. He is a copyist and editor, not claimed by the colophon as the poems' inventor — the compositions are anonymous and, in their materials, certainly older than their tablets, though by how much is unprovable. Ugarit gives us, almost uniquely for its world, a myth with a dateable manuscript ; it does not give us an author. // WHICH NIQMADDU? THE DATING ARGUMENT, STATED HONESTLY // The colophon's king is named only “Niqmaddu”. Ugarit had several kings of the name. The traditional identification is with Niqmaddu II , the treaty partner of Suppiluliuma I — which would put Ilimilku's copies in the fourteenth century BCE . Other scholars, arguing from the archaeology of the find-spots and from the tablets' associations, have placed Ilimilku later, in the thirteenth century BCE , under a subsequent Niqmaddu. The disagreement is live and unresolved; textbooks divide. What is not in dispute is the bracket: the tablets are Late Bronze Age, copied in the city's last century and a half, and fired in its destruction around 1190 BCE. This article dates the copies to “the reign of a King Niqmaddu, fourteenth to thirteenth century BCE”, and treats any more precise date offered elsewhere with the suspicion it has earned. The state of the text is the third fact, and the one readers of smooth modern translations most need to hear. The six tablets are broken : corners lost, surfaces abraded, whole columns missing, and one tablet of the six surviving only in fragments whose placement is argued from the story's logic. A responsible edition prints the text the way an archaeologist draws a pot — solid line where the shard exists, dotted line where the profile is restored — and the standard translations mark, or ought to mark, the gaps: passages where a column's sense can be guessed from context, passages where parallel passages elsewhere in the poem (Ugaritic verse is built of repeated formulas, and a messenger scene lost on one tablet often survives word for word on another) let an editor restore a line with fair confidence, and passages that are simply gone. Key moments fall in the damage. The opening of the cycle is fragmentary; the manner of Baal's return from death is nowhere narrated in surviving text (Section IX); the poem's end, if the sixth tablet is its end, is a hymn to the sun goddess rather than a resolution. None of this makes the cycle unreadable — its three movements are clear, its great scenes intact — but every retelling, this one included, is a retelling of a reconstruction , and the seams should show. The honest order of operations is the one this article follows: first the story as the tablets, gaps marked, actually tell it; then, separately and labelled, the readings scholars have built on it. VII. The Cycle Told I: Baal Against Yam, the Sea The poem opens in a contest for kingship. The gods assemble at the mountain of El , the aged father of the pantheon, at the source of the rivers, and into that assembly come the messengers of Yam — Sea, also named Prince Yam and Judge River — with a demand framed as a claim of right: that the assembly hand over Baal , the storm god, son of Dagan, whom Yam calls his slave and his captive. El, astonishingly, concedes. In the surviving lines the old god answers, in the translations' close paraphrase, that Baal is indeed Yam's slave, that he shall bring tribute like the other gods and the sons of Athirat. The concession defines the poem's political problem at a stroke: El holds the seniority, but not the will; the kingship of the gods is vacant in everything but title, and Yam — the sea, the flood, chaos with a throne-claim — has moved to take it by procedure before Baal takes it by force. Baal's answer is violence, and the poem's first great scene is the forging of its instruments. The craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis , “Skilful-and-Wise”, whose workshops lie at Kaphtor (Crete) and at Memphis in Egypt, is summoned, and under Baal's hands he fashions two clubs — and names them, as a smith in this world names a weapon the way a king names a son. The first is Yagrush , “Driver”: it is to leap from Baal's hand like an eagle, Kothar instructs, and strike Prince Yam between the shoulders. It does, and Yam does not fall — he reels, his joints tremble, but he stands. Kothar fashions the second, Ayyamur , “Chaser”, with the instruction that it strike Judge River between the eyes. It does, and Yam collapses to the ground. Baal moves to finish him; it is Anat and Athtart , the goddesses, who in the text restrain the kill and proclaim the kingship: Baal is king, in the formula the translations render as a cry that his kingship is for ever. (The club-names and the two-blow structure are among the cycle's best-preserved passages; the paraphrase above follows Coogan & Smith and Wyatt closely.) Baal's fixed epithets are the poem's thesis in miniature: he is “the Mightiest Baal” — Aliyn Baal , Baal the Triumphant — and “Rider on the Clouds” , the storm god whose chariot is the weather itself. Both formulas matter beyond Ugarit: the second is applied, in the Hebrew Bible, to Israel's god — Psalm 68 bids praise to the one who rides upon the clouds — a verbal inheritance examined at its proper grade in Section XIV. Note what the victory does not do. Yam is defeated, dragged out, and (on the most common reading of a damaged passage) finished off by Anat's hand or scattered — but Baal's kingship, though proclaimed, is not yet housed, recognised, or safe. El has not been deposed; he has merely been shown up. The assembly has not ratified anything. And Baal himself names the deficiency in the poem's second movement, in the complaint that drives it: the other gods have houses, courts, palaces — Baal has no house like the gods, no court like the sons of Athirat . In the world of this poem, kingship is not real until it is architecture. A god without a palace is a claimant camping on his mountain. The whole middle of the cycle is the story of getting the building permit for heaven — and the permit office is El's. VIII. The Cycle Told II: A Palace, and the Quarrel of the Window The palace campaign is fought with diplomacy, not clubs, and its general is a goddess. Baal sends to Athirat — Asherah of the Hebrew texts, El's consort and the mother of the gods — the gifts and the flattery the occasion requires, and Athirat, pleased and (the poem is candid) calculating the advantages, undertakes the embassy to El. She rides to the source of the rivers on her ass, with her servant Qadesh-wa-Amrur leading, and El, seeing her come, receives her with the poem's characteristic blend of ceremony and appetite. Her petition is granted: El authorises a house for Baal. The building is Kothar-wa-Khasis's work, and the poem dwells on its materials with a merchant city's love of inventory — cedar from Lebanon and Sirion, the finest timber of the coast, and bricks that are not clay: the house is built, in the poem's splendid hyperbole, of silver and gold, its structure fired in a furnace of precious metal for six days until on the seventh the work stands complete. Baal rejoices, and slaughters oxen and sheep for the feast of dedication. The Window Into this triumph the poem inserts its strangest quarrel. Kothar proposes to set a window — an opening, a lattice — in the palace, and Baal refuses, twice, with a vehemence the text does not fully explain. The refusal is one of the cycle's famous cruces, and the explanations on offer should be labelled as explanations, not readings: that Baal fears Yam's or Mot's entry through the opening (the poem elsewhere shows Mot threatening to come to the palace); that he fears for his daughters, the rain-maidens Pidray and Tallay, whom an enemy might spy or seize through it; that the window is the storm god's proper vent — the aperture through which rain and thunder issue — and Baal's resistance is a piece of divine psychology the poem leaves deliberately dark. What the text does say is the outcome: Kothar predicts Baal will reconsider, Baal does reconsider, and the window is installed — whereupon Baal opens it and, in the poem's phrase as the translations render it, lets his voice go forth in the clouds: thunder, rolling over the mountains, the earth shaking, his enemies fleeing to the woods and the high places. The storm god's palace is complete when it can sound. Whatever the quarrel meant to its first hearers, its narrative function is exact: the last fitting of the house is the weapon of its owner. The feast follows — the gods summoned to Saphon, seventy of them, the sons of Athirat, fed on oxen and rams and wine in quantities the poem counts with pleasure — and then the poem turns, deliberately, to the unfinished business. Baal tours his cities, taking them town by town in a catalogue of dominion, and comes back to the one power his kingship has not faced. Yam was chaos by water; there remains chaos by privation. Baal sends his messengers, Gapn and Ugar — “Vine” and “Field”, the storm god's twin heralds — down to the throne of Mot , Death, in his city in the underworld, with an invitation that is also a claim of rank: Mot is to come up, acknowledge Baal's kingship, and feast. The messengers are instructed, in a passage every translation remarks, not to approach too near: lest Mot take them as a morsel, lest he swallow them as a lamb is swallowed. It is the poem's way of telling us that the invitation was never going to be accepted — and that Baal knows it. IX. x: HESIOD'S WORKS AND DAYS Ascra · Boeotia · c. 700 BCE // WORKS :: DAYS :: JUSTICE — WORK — THE YEAR // The Works and Days is the other half of Hesiod: 828 lines of hexameter addressed to a brother who cheated him, in a village the poet himself calls good at no season. Out of that quarrel it builds the Greek world's first surviving didactic poem — a myth of why men must labour, a doctrine of justice enforced by Zeus, a working farmer's calendar keyed to the stars, and a catalogue of lucky and unlucky days. The Theogony tells how the world was ordered; this poem tells what it costs to live inside the order, in the iron age, on a small farm.
