The Poem and Its Occasion: A Quarrel at Ascra The Works and Days ( Erga kai Hēmerai ) is a poem of 828 lines in dactylic hexameter, attributed to Hesiod and conventionally dated to around 700 BCE — the same broad horizon as the Theogony , with the relative order of the two poems debated and no external document to settle it. It is not a narrative. Nothing in it happens in sequence the way things happen in the Iliad ; its unity is the unity of an address. One man is speaking, throughout, to another man, and everything in the poem — myth, fable, calendar, proverb, curse — is something the speaker is saying to him , for a reason the poem states in its first forty lines and never lets the reader forget. The addressee is Perses , the poet's brother. The occasion, as the poem itself gives it (lines 27–41, paraphrased here), is a lawsuit that is already over. The two brothers had divided their inheritance — the farm their father left at Ascra — but Perses, Hesiod says, seized the greater share and carried it off, “greatly swelling the glory” of the local lords who judged the case, the “bribe-swallowing” or “gift-devouring” kings ( dōrophagoi basileis ) who loved to judge such a cause. Perses then squandered what he had taken — the poem's portrait of him is of a man who hangs about the courthouse and the marketplace, living on litigation and on other men's goods, and who has now come back, in want, to the brother he wronged. Hesiod's answer is the poem: no more handouts, no second bite at the estate, but instruction instead — “let us settle our dispute here with true judgement”, and let the settlement be a year's food honestly earned. // HOW MUCH OF THIS IS BIOGRAPHY? // The quarrel is known only from the poem, and scholars are divided over its status. One line of reading takes it at face value: the allusiveness of the references — the dispute is mentioned obliquely, never narrated in full — is what a real grievance, known to its first audience, would look like. A second line, associated in modern scholarship with Gregory Nagy's account of Hesiod as a traditional poetic persona, treats “Hesiod” and “Perses” as roles the tradition speaks through, and the quarrel as the poem's enabling fiction rather than a court record. This article reports the quarrel as the poem presents it, and flags the dispute where it matters: nothing in the poem's teaching depends on whether a historical Perses lost a historical lawsuit. The place matters as much as the persons. Ascra was a village in Boeotia , in the valley below Mount Helicon — the mountain where, in the Theogony 's proem, the Muses met the shepherd Hesiod and gave him his song. The Works and Days supplies the family's route there (lines 633–640, paraphrased): the poet's father had been a seafaring trader from Cyme in Aeolis , on the coast of Asia Minor, who fled not riches but “wretched poverty, which Zeus lays upon men”, crossed the sea, and settled near Helicon in Ascra — a place the poem characterises, in its most quoted piece of local colour, as bad in winter, sultry in summer, and good at no time. The family is thus immigrant stock, one generation removed from the sea, farming marginal land under a mountain. The poem's economics are the economics of that holding: a small farm, worked by its owner with a slave or two and a yoke of oxen, one bad season away from begging at neighbours' doors — which is exactly the fate the poem predicts for Perses and labours to prevent for itself. The third party to the address is the kings themselves. The poem speaks to Perses, but it is built to be overheard: the fable of Section V is told explicitly “for princes who themselves understand”, and the justice teaching of Section VI turns and addresses the gift-devouring judges directly, by name and by crime. The basileis of the poem are not Homer's warrior-kings; they are the local aristocracy of an early Greek village, the men who sit in judgement in the agora and whose verdicts, in a world without written law codes or professional courts, are the law for a smallholder. Hesiod's charge against them is precise: they take gifts — bribes — and give crooked judgements. His counter-weapon is the poem's central doctrine, that judgement is watched: Zeus sees, Justice reports, and a city that harbours crooked verdicts starves for them (Section VI). The Works and Days is therefore a double address from its first lines — a brother warned to work, and a bench warned to judge straight — and its famous mixture of farming instruction and moral thunder is not a mixture at all. Both halves answer the same occasion. Perses must stop living by litigation because litigation, in Ascra, is corrupt; and the kings must stop corrupting it because the poem's god keeps accounts. THE POEM IN NUMBERS 828 lines of dactylic hexameter in the standard modern text (M. L. West's edition; some older editions count 832, the difference lying in lines judged spurious or transposed). Proem: lines 1–10. The two Strifes: 11–26. Prometheus and Pandora: 42–105. The Five Ages: 109–201. The hawk and the nightingale: 202–212. The justice teaching: 213–285. Proverbs and precepts: 286–382. The farming calendar: 383–617. Sailing: 618–694. Social and ritual precepts: 695–764. The Days: 765–828. A POEM WITHOUT A NARRATOR'S DISTANCE Where the Homeric narrator effaces himself behind the Muse, the Works and Days is saturated with its speaker: his farm, his father, his lawsuit, his one sea crossing, his prize tripod. Whether that “I” is autobiography or persona (see the note in this section), it is the earliest sustained first-person voice in Greek literature, and the didactic tradition it founds (Section X) inherits the posture: the teacher who has done the work he prescribes. THE TITLE Erga kai Hēmerai — “Works and Days” — names the poem's two great practical masses: the works , the tasks of the farming year in their seasons (Section VII), and the days , the lucky and unlucky dates of the month (Section IX). The title is ancient and apt, but a reader who stops at it will miss the poem's first three hundred lines, in which neither works nor days appear: the title describes the manual, not the sermon that authorises it. A note on quotations, in line with this hub's standing method. Passages in quotation marks in this article are given from H. G. Evelyn-White's Loeb translation of the Works and Days (1914), consulted in full for this article, and are identified at the point of quotation. All other renderings of the poem's sense are paraphrase, written as paraphrase. Line numbers follow the standard numeration of the Greek text as printed by West. II. The Proem and the Two Strifes: Hesiod Correcting Hesiod The proem is ten lines long — against the Theogony 's hundred and fifteen — and it does different work. The Theogony opens on Helicon, with the Muses' gift and the poet's commissioning. The Works and Days opens in Pieria, the Muses' older northern home, and what it asks them to sing is not the poet but their father: Zeus, and Zeus specifically as the power that levels. Through him, the proem says, men are famed or unfamed, spoken of or unspoken of, as Zeus wills; he makes the strong man low and raises the obscure, straightens the crooked and blasts the proud. Then, in a single pivot, the hymn becomes a prayer with an address and a petition: Zeus is asked to hear, to see, and to make judgements straight with righteousness — and the poet turns to his brother: “And I, Perses, would tell of true things.” “Muses of Pieria who give glory through song, come hither, tell of Zeus your father and chant his praise. Through him mortal men are famed or un-famed, sung or unsung alike, as great Zeus wills. For easily he makes strong, and easily he brings the strong man low; easily he humbles the proud and raises the obscure, and easily he straightens the crooked and blasts the proud — Zeus who thunders aloft and has his dwelling most high. Attend thou with eye and ear, and make judgements straight with righteousness. And I, Perses, would tell of true things.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 1–10, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) Every element of the poem is already in those ten lines. Zeus the leveller is the god of the justice teaching: the power that raises the obscure is the power a defrauded smallholder invokes against gift-fed judges. The petition for straight judgements names the lawsuit without narrating it. And the closing promise — true things , told to Perses — sets the poem's register: this is not the Muses' ambiguous gift of the Theogony , where the goddesses boast that they can speak lies like the truth as readily as truth itself. The Works and Days claims, for its instruction, plain veracity — the claim every didactic poem after it will repeat, and the reason the proem's Zeus is a god of this world, of verdicts and harvests, rather than of cosmic genealogy. The Revision: One Eris Becomes Two What follows is the most remarkable act of self-correction in early Greek poetry. The Theogony knows one Eris — Strife — a daughter of Night, mother of Toil and Famine and Sorrows, of Battles and Murders and Quarrels and Lies, a wholly malign power in the genealogy of the world's evils. The Works and Days opens its argument by taking that back. “So, after all, there was not one kind of Strife alone, but all over the earth there are two” (lines 11–12, Evelyn-White). The correction is performed in the open, in the poem's first movement, by the same poetic voice that had sung the single Eris — whether the two poems are by one historical man revising himself, or by a tradition revising its own inheritance, the text presents the doubling of Eris as a discovery announced to the audience: after all , we were wrong; there are two. “So, after all, there was not one kind of Strife alone, but all over the earth there are two. As for the one, a man would praise her when he came to understand her; but the other is blameworthy: and they are wholly different in nature. For one fosters evil war and battle, being cruel: her no man loves; but perforce, through the will of the deathless gods, men pay harsh Strife her honour due. But the other is the elder daughter of dark Night, and the son of Cronos who sits above and dwells in the aether, set her in the roots of the earth: and she is far kinder to men. She stirs up even the shiftless to toil; for a man grows eager to work when he considers his neighbour, a rich man who hastens to plough and plant and put his house in good order; and neighbour vies with his neighbour as he hurries after wealth. This Strife is wholesome for men. And potter is angry with potter, and craftsman with craftsman, and beggar is jealous of beggar, and minstrel of minstrel.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 11–26, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) The doctrine is the poem's engine, and it should be read exactly. The bad Eris is the Strife of the Theogony : war, battle, and — the poem will make the application explicit — the strife of the courthouse, contention over other men's goods. The good Eris is her elder sister, set by Zeus himself in the roots of the earth, and her province is emulation: she works not by hatred but by comparison. A man idles until he sees his neighbour's field ploughed, his neighbour's barn filling; then envy — the poem does not flinch from the word's family — becomes industry. Potter against potter, craftsman against craftsman, beggar against beggar, singer against singer: the same rivalry that, aimed at a lawsuit, ruins a household, aimed at a furrow, feeds it. The two Strifes are the poem's moral physics in miniature. There is one human energy, competition, and it has exactly two lawful and unlawful objects: your neighbour's work , which you may strive to match, and your neighbour's goods , which you may not strive to take. Perses' whole error, and the kings' whole crime, is the confusion of the two. // A GENEALOGICAL PUZZLE, FLAGGED // The good Eris is here called “the elder daughter of dark Night” — Night is Eris's mother in the Theogony too. But in the Theogony Night's brood is unrelievedly dark, and no second, beneficent Eris appears. Readers should not harmonise the two poems into a single system the texts themselves do not offer: the Works and Days passage reads, and has been read since antiquity, as a revision of the earlier scheme, not a supplement to it. The hub's Theogony article treats the single Eris in her genealogical place; this article treats the pair. The contradiction is Hesiod's own, and it is evidence — of a poet, or a tradition, willing to correct its theology when the theology failed to describe the moral world. The application to Perses follows at once (lines 27–41, paraphrased). Let the mischief-loving Strife not hold your heart back from work while you peer and listen at the courthouse. A man who has a year's food stored has little concern with quarrels and courts; a man who has not, has nothing else. Perses has had his verdict and spent it; there will be no second chance to deal so again. What remains is the good Strife's road: store the year's grain first, and then, if he must contend, let him contend with his neighbour's harvest and not with his brother's title deeds. The famous aside that closes the passage — that the gift-swallowing lords do not know “how much more the half is than the whole”, nor the good there is in mallow and asphodel, the poor man's wild greens — compresses the whole ethic into a proverb: half a farm worked is worth more than a whole farm stolen and squandered, and a dinner of foraged greens eaten in independence outranks a fortune held by fraud. The poem then asks the question its myths exist to answer: if work is the human lot and emulation its spur, why is life like this? Why is the means of life hidden, why must bread be sweated for at all? The answer is a story about fire. III. Prometheus and Pandora: Fire, the Jar, and Hope The poem's first myth (lines 42–105) is an aetiology — an account of origins that explains a present condition. The condition is stated first, before the story: “the gods keep hidden from men the means of life” (line 42, Evelyn-White's rendering). But for that hiding, a man could work one day and live a year on it, hang up his rudder over the smoke, and let the fields rest. Life is not like that, and the poem says why. Zeus hid the means of life in anger, because Prometheus deceived him — the deception, told in full in the Theogony , is the division of the sacrifice at Mecone, where Prometheus portioned an ox so that men kept the meat and the gods received the bones wrapped in fat. Zeus, undeceived in the long run and furious in the short, hid fire . Prometheus stole it back — in the Works and Days ' version, as in the Theogony 's, carried down to men hidden in a hollow fennel-stalk, the slow-smouldering pith of the giant fennel that Mediterranean peoples used as a portable ember — and Zeus, seeing the theft, pronounced the price. The full treatment of Prometheus, the sacrifice, and the fire-theft across both poems is in this hub's Makers and Fire article; what belongs here is the form the story takes when its purpose is not cosmic order but the explanation of toil. “Son of Iapetus, surpassing all in cunning, you are glad that you have outwitted me and stolen fire — a great plague to you yourself and to men that shall be. But I will give men as the price for fire an evil thing in which they may all be glad of heart while they embrace their own destruction.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 54–59 (ZEUS TO PROMETHEUS), TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) The “evil thing” given “as the price for fire” is the first woman. In the Theogony she is never named; the Works and Days names her, and the naming is the poem's addition to the myth. Zeus orders the manufacture as a piece of divine craftsmanship, itemised god by god (lines 60–82, paraphrased from Evelyn-White's text): Hephaestus is to mix earth with water and fashion a maiden's shape, lovely as the goddesses; Athena is to teach her needlework and the weaving of the varied web, and to clothe her; Aphrodite is to shed grace on her head, and with it “cruel longing and cares that weary the limbs”; Hermes is to put in her a shameless mind and a deceitful nature, and to give her speech. The Graces and Persuasion hang gold necklaces on her; the Hours crown her with spring flowers. And Hermes names her: Pandora — “because all they who dwelt on Olympus gave each a gift, a plague to men who eat bread”. The name is a Greek compound, pan + dōron , “all-gifted” — the woman endowed by all the gods — though the poem's gloss already bends it toward the darker sense: the gift that is a plague. // THE POEM'S SEXISM, STATED PLAINLY // The Pandora of the Works and Days is presented by the poem itself as a “beautiful evil” — the phrase is the Theogony 's ( kalon kakon , Theogony 585) for the same figure — a snare manufactured to punish men, endowed by her makers with deceit as a design specification. The misogyny is not an imposition of modern readers; it is the text's own framing, and it runs through the poem's later precepts on wives and women (Section IX). This archive reports it as what it is — the sexual politics of an archaic Greek farming poem, in which woman enters the world as a divinely engineered cost, set against the man's labour as its counterpart — and distinguishes that literary and theological construction from any evidence about real women's lives or cult roles in archaic Boeotia, on which the poem is not a witness but an interested party. Hermes delivers the finished gift to Epimetheus , Prometheus' brother — Afterthought, as his name says, to his brother's Forethought. Prometheus had warned him never to accept a gift from Olympian Zeus, but to send it back, for fear it might prove harmful to men. Epimetheus took the gift, and afterwards, when the evil thing was already his, he understood. Then comes the act on which the whole aetiology turns (lines 90–105). Before it, the tribes of men lived on earth free from ills, from hard toil, and from the heavy sicknesses that bring men to their deaths. But the woman took the great lid off the jar with her hands, and scattered what was inside: sorrows and mischief for men. The diseases now wander the earth silently, by day and by night, of themselves — Zeus took away their voices, so they give no warning. “So is there no way to escape the will of Zeus.” The Jar: Pithos, Not Box The vessel is a pithos : a large clay storage jar, of the kind Greek households used — often sunk into the floor of a storeroom — for grain, oil, and wine, and which could stand as tall as a person. It is not a box, a casket, or a chest, and nothing in Hesiod's Greek suggests one. The universal modern phrase “Pandora's box” is a Renaissance artefact, and its origin can be named with unusual precision. Erasmus of Rotterdam , retelling the story in Latin in his Adagia (1508), in illustration of the proverb Malo accepto stultus sapit — “from experiencing trouble a fool is made wise” — rendered the Greek pithos as pyxis , a small box or casket. The attribution of the mistranslation to Erasmus's 1508 retelling is the standard scholarly account, repeated in the reference literature (the Oxford University Press's own discussion of the myth states it in those terms); a minority tradition has also named the Italian humanist Giglio Gregorio Giraldi (Lilius Giraldus) as a source of the box, and the honest summary is that the pyxis enters the story in sixteenth-century Latin retelling, with Erasmus as its best-documented and most influential carrier. The consequences were not trivial. A jar is a household fixture, too big to carry, part of the furniture of the storeroom — the evils were, so to speak, already in the house. A box is a portable, lockable, openable object, a thing of curiosity; the Renaissance image of Pandora with her casket rewrote the myth's mechanics, shifting its centre toward the woman's curiosity — a motive Hesiod never states. Hesiod does not say why Pandora lifted the lid. He does not say she was curious, or that she had been forbidden to open it. The jar is simply there, in Epimetheus' house, and she opens it. Later tradition supplied the prohibition and the curiosity; the poem supplies neither, and the difference is a standing lesson in this archive's discipline: the famous version of a myth is usually a sediment of retellings, and the earliest text is stranger and barer than all of them. Elpis Under the Rim: The Poem's Open Question “Only Hope remained there in an unbreakable home within under the rim of the great jar, and did not fly out at the door; for ere that, the lid of the jar stopped her, by the will of Aegis-holding Zeus who gathers the clouds. But the rest, countless plagues, wander amongst men; for earth is full of evils and the sea is full.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 96–101, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) One thing did not escape. Elpis — Hope, or Expectation; the Greek word covers both the cheerful and the neutral sense, anticipation of what is coming, good or bad — remained under the rim of the jar, stopped by the lid, “by the will of Zeus”. Hesiod does not explain the detail, and it has been argued over ever since, because the poem's whole theodicy pivots on how it is read. The positions, stated as the scholarship standardly states them, are these. On the consoling reading , hope is preserved for mankind: the evils escaped into the world, but hope stayed in the house, within human reach — the one good thing men keep at home while the plagues wander abroad. On the pessimistic reading , hope is withheld from mankind: it alone of the jar's contents did not get out, shut in by Zeus's express will, so that men suffer their evils without even the mitigation of expectation — or, in a darker variant of the same reading, elpis was itself one of the jar's ambiguous contents, and its retention is a further cruelty, since hope in Hesiod's world is not reliably a blessing: the idle man of line 498 (in Evelyn-White's rendering) “waits on empty hope”, and the poem repeatedly treats hope as the pauper's snare, the substitute for stored grain. A third line of scholarship notes that elpis in early Greek is as often foreboding as comfort, and declines to decide the passage's valence at all. This article flags the question as genuinely open: the text gives the fact — elpis stayed, by Zeus's will — and no interpretation, and any retelling that presents the staying of hope as straightforwardly good news has added something Hesiod withheld. What the myth explains, taken whole, is the poem's premise. The means of life are hidden; fire was bought at the price of a beautiful evil; diseases walk silently; there is no way to escape the will of Zeus. Therefore — the poem's logic is relentless — a man works, or he starves, and the only choice the world offers is between the good Strife's labour and the bad Strife's litigation. The next myth widens the frame from the household to the whole of human history: if this is the iron present, what were the past ages, and how did the world get from there to here? IV. The Five Ages: Metal, Heroes, and Iron The second myth (lines 109–201) is introduced as “another tale”, to be laid up in Perses' heart: how gods and mortal men sprang from one source. It is the famous account of the Five Ages — five successive races of men, each made by the gods, each living its character, each covered by the earth before the next. Four of the races are named for metals, in descending order of worth: gold , silver , bronze , iron . The fifth name on the list is not a metal at all, and its presence is the scheme's most discussed feature. The races are not, strictly, ages in the text — Hesiod's word is genos , a race or generation, each separately created, not one humanity declining through time — though “the Five Ages” is the conventional English title and is used here with that caution attached. Race Lines Character End and afterlife Gold 109–126 Made by the Olympians in the reign of Cronos. They lived like gods, without sorrow, toil, or grief; old age did not come on them; the earth bore fruit unforced, in abundance. They died as if overcome by sleep. They became daimones — pure spirits on the earth, guardians of mortal men, watchers of judgements and cruel deeds, givers of wealth. Silver 127–142 “Less noble by far”, unlike gold in body and spirit. A child stayed a hundred years at his mother's side, a simpleton; grown, men lived briefly and in sorrow, for they could not keep from wronging one another, and would not serve the gods or sacrifice. Zeus, angry at the withheld honour, hid them away. They are the blessed spirits of the underworld, of second order, but honoured still. Bronze 143–155 Sprung from ash trees; terrible and strong; devoted to the works of Ares and to violence; they ate no bread. Their armour, houses, and tools were bronze; there was no black iron. They destroyed themselves by their own hands, and went nameless to the dank house of Hades, leaving no name behind them. The Heroes 156–173 “Nobler and more righteous” than bronze: a god-like race of hero-men, called demigods, the race before our own. War destroyed them — at seven-gated Thebes, for the flocks of Oedipus, and at Troy, for Helen's sake. The survivors dwell apart, in the Isles of the Blessed by deep Ocean, where the earth bears fruit three times a year, and Cronos rules over them. Iron 174–201 The poet's own race. Men never rest from labour and sorrow by day, nor from perishing by night; yet even these have some good mingled with their evils. Not ended yet — but Zeus will destroy this race too, in the days when the poem's closing signs come to pass (see the text below). The Heroic Anomaly The scheme's logic is metallic decline: each race worse than the last, gold to silver to bronze to iron, value falling as the metal cheapens. The heroic race breaks the series twice over . It is not a metal, and it is not worse than what precedes it — it is expressly “nobler and more righteous” than the bronze race before it, an improvement inserted into a decline. The explanation is not far to seek, and scholarship states it plainly: the heroes could not be omitted, because Greek tradition — the whole epic inheritance, the wars at Thebes and Troy that the Theban and Trojan cycles sing — placed a race of demigods immediately before the present age of ordinary men, and Hesiod's audience knew their names. A purely metallic scheme would have had to erase them; the poem instead interrupts its own pattern to accommodate them, and the interruption is the most valuable thing in the myth for a historian of tradition. It shows the scheme being fitted to inherited material that resists it — Hesiod, or the tradition behind him, bending a tidy four-metal decline around the untidy fact of the heroes. The hub's Heroes and Epic article treats the heroic race from the heroes' side; here the point is structural: the anomaly is not a flaw in the poem but a fossil of its making, the seam where an abstract scheme and a concrete tradition were stitched together. Note, too, what the heroic race's wars are. Thebes and Troy: the two great subjects of the epic cycles, the wars for the flocks of Oedipus and for Helen. The Works and Days , the poem of the small farm and the lawsuit, contains in its second myth a compressed table of contents of heroic epic — and places it one generation back, in a better world, now closed. The heroes are gone to the Isles of the Blessed, at the ends of the earth, where Cronos — the deposed king of the golden race's heaven — rules over them, released from his bonds. The present is defined by their absence. “Thereafter, would that I were not among the men of the fifth generation, but either had died before or been born afterwards. For now truly is a race of iron, and men never rest from labour and sorrow by day, and from perishing by night; and the gods shall lay sore trouble upon them. But, notwithstanding, even these shall have some good mingled with their evils.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 174–179, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) The iron race is described twice: first in its present condition — ceaseless labour, sorrow by day, perishing by night, some good mingled with the evils — and then, in the poem's most prophetic passage (lines 180–201, paraphrased), in its future degeneration, the signs by which its end will be known. Zeus will destroy this race also, when children are born already grey at the temples. Father will not agree with children, nor guest with host, nor brother with brother — the poem's audience cannot have missed that the first symptom of the world's end is the poem's own occasion, the broken bond between brothers. Men will dishonour their ageing parents and chide them with bitter words, not knowing the fear of the gods; they will not repay the cost of their nurture. Might will be right; the oath-keeper, the just, and the good will win no favour, while the evil-doer and the violent man are praised. Envy, foul-mouthed and scowling, will walk with all wretched men. And then the end: “And then Aidos and Nemesis, with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods: and bitter sorrows will be left for mortal men, and there will be no help against evil.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 200–201, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) Aidos — Shame, Reverence, the inward check that makes a man regard another's rights — and Nemesis — Indignation, the outward check, the community's anger at wrong — are the last two moral powers left on earth in the iron age, and the poem ends its myth of history with their departure. The personifications belong to the world of the Olympians article in this hub, where the lesser powers around Zeus's throne are set out; here their function is diagnostic. As long as Aidos and Nemesis remain, the iron age, for all its labour and fraud, is still a moral world: men can still be ashamed, and wrong can still provoke. Their leaving is the true end of the race — not a catastrophe of nature but the extinction of the two feelings on which the poem's entire teaching depends. The Works and Days is addressed, from beginning to end, to men presumed still capable of both. The myth's function in the address is now complete. Pandora explained why the individual man must work; the Five Ages explain where his working life sits in the history of the world — in the last and worst of the races, but not yet at its end, with good still mingled in the evil and Aidos still on earth. What remains is to convert the diagnosis into conduct. The poem does it in two strokes: first a fable, addressed over Perses' head to the kings; then the doctrine of justice, addressed to everyone. V. The Hawk and the Nightingale: Greek Literature's First Fable At line 202 the poem changes instrument. “And now I will tell a fable for princes who themselves understand” — the word is ainos , a tale with a point, a story that means something other than what it says and trusts its hearer to draw the meaning. What follows (lines 203–212) is eleven lines long, and it is the earliest animal fable to survive in Greek literature: the ancestor, in the form we have it, of the whole Aesopic tradition that would later attach itself to the name of Aesop. A hawk, carrying a nightingale high up among the clouds, gripped in his talons — the nightingale, the songbird, pierced by the crooked talons, crying pitifully — addresses her, and the speech is the whole fable. There is no narrative beyond the grip and the speech; there is no moral appended. The hawk speaks, and the poem moves on. “Thus said the hawk to the nightingale with speckled neck, while he carried her high up among the clouds, gripped fast in his talons, and she, pierced by his crooked talons, cried pitifully. To her he spoke disdainfully: 'Miserable thing, why do you cry out? One far stronger than you now holds you fast, and you must go wherever I take you, songstress as you are. And if I please I will make my meal of you, or let you go. He is a fool who tries to withstand the stronger, for he does not get the mastery and suffers pain besides his shame.' So said the swiftly flying hawk, the long-winged bird.” — HESIOD, WORKS AND DAYS 203–212, TRANS. H. G. EVELYN-WHITE (LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY, 1914) The fable's difficulty is its point, and it has troubled readers since antiquity: whose voice is the hawk's, and what is Perses — or the princes — supposed to learn? The hawk's doctrine is naked: the stronger holds, the weaker goes where he is taken, resistance adds shame to pain. Read as the poet's own advice, the fable would counsel submission to power — and would flatly contradict the justice teaching that follows immediately, in which violence is ruin and Justice beats Outrage in the end. The standard scholarly resolutions, stated as positions, are these. On the ventriloquism reading , the hawk speaks the kings' own doctrine back to them: this is what your crooked judgements sound like from underneath, in the talons; the fable is addressed to princes “who themselves understand” precisely so that they will recognise their own voice in the predator's mouth, and recoil. On the warning reading , the fable is for Perses: this is the world as the strong describe it, and the brother who relies on courts and litigation is the nightingale — a singer, like the poet himself, whose art is no defence against t

Two Articles, One Alchemist: The Division of This Archive This archive treats Zōsimos of Panopolis twice, deliberately, and the reader is owed a plain statement of the division before anything else. The companion article, in the Egyptology division — Zosimos of Panopolis — is the biographical and practical profile. It covers his name and his city, his life and his addressee Theosebeia, the survey of the Cheirokmēta corpus, the Syriac and Arabic transmissions, the workshop world of the Leyden and Stockholm papyri, the recipes and what happens when they are repeated, the kerotakis and the tribikos step by step, the attribution of that apparatus to Maria, and the manuscript drawings. None of that ground is re-covered here. A reader who wants the man, the city, or the still should go there first, and this article will send them back at every point where the two subjects touch. This article's ground is narrower and, in its own way, stranger. It treats Zōsimos as a Greek author : a writer of Greek prose, working in the Greek genre of the commentary, preserved in Greek codices, and read for a thousand years by Greek readers who cited him the way philosophers cite Plato. Its subjects are the Greek manuscript tradition and the modern editions built on it; the place Zōsimos holds in the commentary tradition that runs through Synesius, Olympiodorus, and Stephanus of Alexandria; the dream treatises known as the Visions , read closely as Greek allegorical text; his doctrine stated in its own Greek philosophical vocabulary — sōma and pneuma , the divine water, the tincture; and the religious landscape of his century, in which a workshop art and a philosophy of salvation occupied the same page. Where the companion article asks what Zōsimos did , this one asks what he wrote , and what his writing did to the readers who inherited it. One convention governs the whole article and should be stated at the threshold. No wording from the Visions is placed in quotation marks in this article. The dream treatises are narrated throughout in labelled paraphrase, following the standard scholarly accounts — above all Howard M. Jackson's edition and translation of the Omega tractate and his work on the other treatises, Michèle Mertens' critical edition of the Authentic Memoirs , and the recent Oxford text, translation, and commentary on the Visions . The reason is the archive's standing rule: an ancient text is quoted only from a named published translation verified in the preparation of the article, and the Visions ' English transmission — scattered across Berthelot and Ruelle's French, F. Sherwood Taylor's pioneering study, and the translation embedded in Jung's essay — does not offer a single rendering that this article can responsibly present as the text. Paraphrase, honestly labelled, loses the music and keeps the facts. The Sources section (XVI) names every rendering a reader may consult to recover the music for themselves. THE COMPANION ARTICLE COVERS The name and the city; the life and Theosebeia; the corpus survey; the Syriac and Arabic transmissions; the Leyden and Stockholm workshop world; the recipes repeated; the kerotakis and tribikos step by step; Maria's attribution; the drawings; a first doctrine survey. See Zosimos of Panopolis in the Egyptology division. THIS ARTICLE COVERS Zōsimos in the Greek commentary tradition; the Greek codices, above all Marcianus graecus 299; Berthelot and Ruelle and Mertens as the modern textual basis; the Visions read closely as Greek allegory; sōma , pneuma , the divine water, and baphē in their Greek register; the canon of authorities; the Omega tractate and the Final Account as eschatological framing; workshop and theurgy. A note on names and spelling, since this article's subject is a text and its words matter. The author is Zōsimos throughout, with the long vowel marked, following the transliteration practice of the scholarship this article rests on. Greek technical terms are transliterated consistently and glossed at first use: sōma (σῶμα), body; pneuma (πνεῦμα), spirit or breath; baphē (βαφή), a dyeing, hence a tincture; theion hydōr (θεῖον ὕδωρ), the divine — and sulphurous — water of Section XI. His floruit is given as c. 300 CE , the consensus bracket established by Mertens and refined by Jackson: he must postdate the authorities of the third century whom he cites, and he must predate the destruction of the Alexandrian Serapeum in 391 CE, which the Omega tractate mentions in terms that imply it still stood. Nothing in this article requires a more precise date, and none is pretended. II. A Greek Author: Zōsimos the Commentator To call Zōsimos a Greek author is not a remark about his passport. Panopolis was an Egyptian city, and the companion article treats its Egyptian depth in full. It is a remark about his genre . Zōsimos writes in the forms that Greek intellectual life had perfected over six centuries: the letter that is really a treatise, the memoir that is really a commentary, and above all the exegesis — the patient unfolding of what an ancient authority meant by words that have gone dark. His predecessors in the art, so far as they survive, wrote recipes framed as revelations. Zōsimos writes about those recipes: he quotes Democritus and glosses him, cites Maria and explains her, weighs Hermes against Agathodaimon, and corrects the readings of his contemporaries by appeal to the canon. The scholarship's sharpest formulation of the point — that Zōsimos is the first known commentator of alchemy — is also the key to his Greekness. Commentary is the characteristic literary act of the later Greek world, the form in which Alexandrian scholarship preserved Homer, in which the Neoplatonists preserved Plato and Aristotle, and in which, from Zōsimos onward, the alchemists preserved one another. That placement has a consequence readers of the companion article should carry into this one. When later Greek writers cite Zōsimos, they do not cite him as a recipe-book. They cite him as an authority to be interpreted — which is to say, they treat him exactly as he treated Democritus. The commentary tradition is a chain of such treatments, and Section V follows Zōsimos's own link in it link by link. But the chain begins with his self-fashioning. A writer who presents his work as exegesis of the ancients is claiming two things at once: that the ancients are canonical, and that he is their authorised reader. Both claims were accepted. Within two centuries the exegetes were expounding Zōsimos's sentences with the same reverent ingenuity he had spent on the sentences of the Democritean books, and the Byzantine compilers who assembled the alchemical corpus placed his memoirs near its head — the position of a classic. // COMMENTARY AS A GENRE // A Greek commentary ( hypomnēma ) does not summarise its author; it proceeds lemma by lemma, quoting a phrase and then unfolding it — philologically, philosophically, and, in the alchemical case, operationally. Zōsimos's memoirs keep that shape even when their subject is a furnace: a sentence of Maria or Democritus is set down, and the memoir is the unfolding. His successors return the compliment in kind. His Greek is the learned Greek of late-antique Egypt — the koinē of the schools, dense with the technical vocabulary of the workshops and increasingly coloured by the religious vocabularies of his milieu: Hermetic, Gnostic, and biblical turns of phrase all surface in his prose without any one of them owning it. That mixture is itself a datum of the textual tradition. Byzantine copyists, excerptors, and commentators were not neutral conduits for such a text: they abbreviated what bored them, expanded what puzzled them, and occasionally Christianised what scandalised them, and the modern editor's first task — Mertens' task, in the edition Section IV describes — is to distinguish the Panopolitan's voice from the chorus of his transmitters. The Zōsimos of this article is therefore, of necessity, the Zōsimos of the critical editions: a fourth-century author reconstructed from tenth- to fifteenth-century books by twentieth-century philology. The reconstruction is good. But the article never lets the reader forget that it is a reconstruction, because the distance between the dreamer of c. 300 and the codices of c. 1000 is precisely this article's subject. One further Greek frame deserves naming here, because Sections X to XII depend on it. Zōsimos writes as a philosopher , and says so in the tradition's own terms: the practitioners of the art call themselves philosophers, and the art itself is styled the divine and sacred art. His matter-theory is not a workshop pidgin but a provincial dialect of the common philosophical language of his age — the language of body and spirit, of natures that act and are acted upon, of a substrate that receives form — which Plato's Timaeus , Aristotle's Meteorologica , and the Stoic physics of pneuma had made available to any educated Greek writer. When Olympiodorus, two centuries later, sets Zōsimos's authorities in a doxographical table beside Thales, Heraclitus, and the other early physicists (Section V), he is not flattering the alchemists. He is filing them where, by their own vocabulary, they had asked to be filed: among the investigators of nature, whose first principles were the business of philosophy. III. The Greek Manuscripts: Marcianus Graecus 299 and the Codex Tradition Every word of Zōsimos read in this article descends through a small family of Byzantine codices, and the family has a head. Marcianus graecus 299 — shelfmark M in the editions — is a parchment codex of the late tenth or early eleventh century, now in the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice, and by common consent the oldest and most important surviving manuscript of Greek alchemy. Mertens' study of the Byzantine reception of the art begins from it for a reason: M is not merely the earliest witness to the corpus, it is the most beautiful — its opening title set in a pylē , a magnificently decorated frame painted in four colours, its pages carrying the lavish illustrations for which the codex is famous. It is also a damaged book. It lost several quires in its long life, and some of the quires that remain were bound in the wrong order by a binder who did not know what he was handling. The oldest Zōsimos we possess is thus a splendid, mutilated, misbound Constantinopolitan anthology, copied some seven centuries after its author's death — a fact that should temper every sentence ever written about what Zōsimos “said”, including the sentences of this article. The corpus M transmits was not Zōsimos's creation. The Greek alchemical corpus — some forty authors, from the pseudo-Democritean books of the first century to the Byzantine systematists of the seventh — was probably first assembled at Constantinople in the seventh or eighth century , when an unknown compiler (or a succession of them) gathered the art's classics into a single library between covers. Zōsimos stands near the centre of that library, and the Visions have a precise address within it: the dream treatises survive in more than forty manuscripts in total, but M preserves only the first of the three lessons, and the first complete copy of the Visions is the latest of the great witnesses — a point to which the textual history of Section VI returns. The hub's transmission article treats the codex tradition of the hub's texts as a whole; this section confines itself to what the Zōsimos reader needs in hand. Siglum Manuscript Date Note for the Zōsimos reader M Marcianus graecus 299, Biblioteca Marciana, Venice Late 10th–early 11th c. The oldest and most important alchemical codex; lavishly decorated; quires lost and some inverted by the binder; preserves the Omega tractate's second recension and the first Visions lesson only. B Parisinus graecus 2325, Bibliothèque nationale, Paris 13th c. The second great witness; differs from M in contents, arrangement, and state of preservation. A Parisinus graecus 2327, Bibliothèque nationale, Paris Copied 1478 The first complete copy of the Visions ; its apparatus drawings are the most reproduced in the literature. L Laurentianus graecus 86.16, Florence 15th c. Completes the usual set of principal witnesses cited by the editions. Three features of this tradition shape everything downstream, and each will matter when the Visions are read in Sections VII and VIII. First, excerpting : the Byzantine transmitters did not only copy Zōsimos, they abridged him, and Mertens' introduction is blunt that parts of the corpus under his name are more or less summarised extracts owed to Byzantine compilers — the author's connected argument replaced by a digest of its striking sentences. Second, dislocation : in the Authentic Memoirs as transmitted, the three sections of the work known as On Excellence — the Visions — are interrupted by shorter chapters on chemical procedures that are clearly not part of it, so that the dream treatise reaches us already dismembered by its own manuscript tradition, a circumstance Section VI takes up. Third, illustration : the codices carry the apparatus diagrams and the famous single leaf of Cleopatra's Chrysopoeia (Marcianus graecus 299, folio 188v), so that the Greek tradition transmits Zōsimos's world in pictures as well as words — the companion article treats the drawings and their limits, and this article simply notes that the pictures, like the words, are Byzantine copies of lost originals, not photographs of the fourth century. How did such a book survive at all? The Marcianus reached Venice among the Greek manuscripts gathered by Cardinal Bessarion (1403–1472), the Byzantine scholar-cardinal who spent his last decades rescuing Greek books in the shadow of Constantinople's fall in 1453 and bequeathed his library to the Venetian Republic — the founding collection of the Marciana. The alchemical codex was part of that rescue. There is a fittingness the archive notes without labouring: a corpus assembled in Constantinople, copied in Constantinople, and carried west by a Constantinopolitan exile is the material form of the Greek tradition itself — continuous, endangered, and dependent at every stage on individual readers who thought the old art worth the parchment. The transmission article follows that thread through the hub's other texts; for Zōsimos, the thread runs M, B, A, and L, and then — in 1887 — into print. IV. The Modern Text: From Berthelot and Ruelle to Mertens The modern Zōsimos begins with a chemist. Marcellin Berthelot, the great French thermochemist, turned in the 1880s to the Greek manuscripts in Paris and Venice with a historian's question — what did the ancients actually know about matter? — and, with the philologist Charles-Émile Ruelle, produced the Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (Paris, 1887–88): three volumes of Greek text with French translation that made the corpus generally readable for the first time. The Collection remains, more than a century on, the only edition of most of the corpus's treatises, and every later worker — Taylor, Jung, Jackson, Mertens — stands on it. It is also, by the standards Mertens would later set, an inclusive edition: Berthelot and Ruelle printed under Zōsimos's name much that travelled under it in the manuscripts, without the sustained attempt to separate the Panopolitan's authentic work from the extracts, summaries, and false attributions that a millennium of copying had attached to it. The reader of the Collection meets a Zōsimos larger, looser, and in places later than the historical author. That is not a reproach; it is the normal first state of a recovered literature, and the century of scholarship since has been the slow correction of it. The correction, for Zōsimos, is Michèle Mertens' Les alchimistes grecs , Tome IV.1: Zosime de Panopolis: Mémoires authentiques (Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1995) — Greek text, French translation, and an introduction of over a hundred pages that remains the foundation of all modern work on the author. Mertens sorted the manuscript jumble into four groups of works attributable to Zōsimos with certainty : the Authentic Memoirs ; the Chapters to Eusebia ; the Chapters to Theodorus ; and the group formed by the Book of Sophe and the Final Account . The companion article sets out the four groups and their contents in full; for this article's purposes the load-bearing group is the first. The Authentic Memoirs — thirteen short treatises, also transmitted under the title On Apparatus and Furnaces — open with the programmatic On the Letter Omega and contain, as their tenth to twelfth memoirs, the three dream treatises known as the Visions . That single paragraph of orientation is all the corpus survey this article permits itself; the detail lives in the companion article , and the cross-link, not repetition, is the archive's method. Alongside Mertens stands the one full English monograph-edition devoted to a single Zōsimos tractate: Howard M. Jackson, Zosimos of Panopolis on the Virgin: Zosimus' Tractate “On the Letter Omega” (Missoula: Scholars Press, 1978; Texts and Translations 14, Graeco-Roman Religion 5) — Greek text, English translation, and commentary on the tractate that stands at the head of the Authentic Memoirs , together with Jackson's studies of the author's other treatises. Jackson's dating argument (pp. 4–5 of that edition) is the one this article's header follows: the tractate's mention of Julius Africanus, who died in 240, and its reference to the Serapeum of Alexandria, destroyed in 391, set the outer limits within which Mertens' floruit of about 300 CE sits. Jackson also bequeathed the field a caution that Section XIV will use: his reading of the Omega tractate's “propitious tinctures” as a doctrine of astrologically favourable times was challenged by Daniel Stolzenberg, who argued that Zōsimos's point runs the other way — the genuine tinctures are precisely those not dependent on times, demons, or fate. The disagreement is recorded here at the point where the edition is introduced, because it is the model of how this article handles its sources: the modern authorities are named, their readings are attributed to them, and where they disagree, the disagreement — not a silent choice between them — is what the reader is given. // HOW TO CITE ZŌSIMOS // Modern scholarship cites the Authentic Memoirs by Mertens' memoir numbers (the Visions are Memoirs X–XII) and the older literature by the volume and page of Berthelot and Ruelle's Collection (the Visions stand in its third volume). Jung's essay cites the Berthelot text throughout. A reference that gives neither edition is, in this field, a reference that cannot be checked — the archive treats such references, wherever it meets them, as paraphrase at best. The newest layer of the textual basis deserves its sentence. The Visions received a full modern text, translation, and commentary in Joshua Werrett's Oxford doctoral thesis of 2024, The Visions of Zosimos of Panopolis , which reads the three dreams in their scientific, religious, and literary contexts together and argues — against both the purely psychological and the purely technical readings — for a real dream worked up with a poet's freedom. This article follows the Oxford commentary's narrative of the visions in Sections VII and VIII, in paraphrase, alongside Mertens and Jackson. The textual tradition of Zōsimos is thus still an open workshop: a corpus assembled in the eighth century, copied in the eleventh, printed in the nineteenth, delimited in the twentieth, and re-edited in the twenty-first. The Greek tradition did not end at Constantinople. It changed its address. V. The Commentators Read Zōsimos: Synesius, Olympiodorus, Stephanus Greek alchemy's third age — after the founders of the first centuries and the systematiser of c. 300 — is the age of the commentators, and its shape is the strongest evidence for the claim of Section II: that Zōsimos had become a classic. Cristina Viano's standard periodisation, followed in the handbooks, names the succession plainly. The commentators are a generation tied to the Neoplatonic schools, whose writings were designed primarily to clarify the ideas of the previous generations — Democritus and Zōsimos above all — and whose work represents, in Viano's judgment, the most advanced stage of ancient alchemical theory. They do not bring new recipes. They bring exegesis : the conviction that the old texts contain a coherent philosophy of nature, and that the commentator's task is to draw it out. Zōsimos is both their model for that conviction — he had practised it on Democritus — and its principal object. Synesius: The Dialogue with Dioscorus The succession opens in the fourth century with the commentary transmitted under the name Synesius : a dialogue addressed to Dioscorus, a priest of Serapis at Alexandria, expounding the Physika kai mystika of pseudo-Democritus. Two cautions attach to the name, and the scholarship states both. The alchemical Synesius is probably not Synesius of Cyrene, the Neoplatonist bishop of Ptolemais, though the attribution may have been intended to borrow his lustre; and the dialogue's value for this article lies less in its authorship than in its posture. Its author declares his exegetic intention openly — to disclose Democritus's thought, the sequence of his teachings, and his processes and materials — and in doing so he works downstream of Zōsimos in two senses: chronologically, since the relative chronology established by the citations puts Zōsimos first, Synesius after him, and Olympiodorus after both; and methodologically, since the commentary he writes is the genre Zōsimos founded for the art. He also preserves, in quotation, fragments of the older literature — pseudo-Democritus among them — that would otherwise be lost, which is the commentator's second service to the tradition: he is an ark as well as an interpreter. The hub's Greek alchemy origins article treats the Democritean books themselves; here the point is the relay — Democritus read by Zōsimos, Zōsimos's method inherited by Synesius, Synesius read verbatim by Olympiodorus, and all three read by Stephanus. Olympiodorus: Commentary as Doxography In the sixth century, Olympiodorus produced the tradition's most ambitious surviving commentary: an exegesis of a lost treatise of Zōsimos, the Kat' energeian — On Action , or According to Action — together with sayings of Hermes and the other philosophers, transmitted under the title On the Sacred Art . Whether the alchemical Olympiodorus is identical with Olympiodorus the Younger, the Alexandrian Neoplatonist who commented on Plato and Aristotle, is a genuinely open question — Cristina Viano's study of his Aristotle commentary sets out the case for identity, and the handbooks record it as possible rather than proven — but the commentary's character is not in doubt. Its centrepiece is a doxography : a systematic comparison in which the first principles ( archai ) of nine early Greek physicists — Thales' water, Heraclitus' fire, the air of Diogenes of Apollonia, and their fellows — are set beside the principles of the alchemical art, and Hermes, Chymes, Agathodaimon, and Zōsimos himself are enrolled among the art's founding physicists. The gesture deserves a moment's attention. A doxography is how Greek philosophy wrote its own history: to give a school a doxography was to declare it a philosophy with a past. Olympiodorus, commenting on Zōsimos, writes alchemy into the succession of Greek natural philosophy at exactly the point where the Neoplatonic schools were writing that succession for themselves. Olivier Dufault's study of transmutation theory in the corpus adds the necessary cold water: of the three authors he examines — Zōsimos, Synesius, Olympiodorus — only Olympiodorus's commentary articulates something approaching a general theory of transmutation, and the tidy “theory of the art” that later centuries attributed to the Greek alchemists wholesale is largely the commentators' construction, projected backward onto founders who worked, as Zōsimos did, by analogy, aphorism, and dream. The construction is not a fraud. It is what commentary is — and Zōsimos, who had done the same service for Democritus, could hardly have complained at receiving it. Stephanus of Alexandria: The Nine Lectures The chain reaches its Byzantine culmination in Stephanus of Alexandria , the universal philosopher and public professor who lectured at Constantinople under the emperor Heraclius (r. 610–641) on Plato, Aristotle, geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, and music — and on alchemy. His alchemical work consists of nine Praxeis , lectures on the making of gold, together with a letter to Theodore interpolated among them; F. Sherwood Taylor's translation and commentary (published in Ambix in the 1930s) remains the standard English point of entry, and Taylor's introduction records both the attribution debate — some scholars held the alchemical lectures pseudepigraphal, or as late as the ninth century — and the evidence that settles the lectures' place in the chain: Stephanus quotes Olympiodorus and Synesius verbatim and comments on pseudo-Democritus, so that the whole succession stands inside his text in order. In Stephanus the commentary tradition becomes a curriculum. The lectures are addressed, ultimately, to an emperor; they open with prayer; they move through the authorities in sequence; and they treat the art's theory as a branch of the same philosophy the professor taught in the morning on Aristotle. Zōsimos's memoirs, written three centuries earlier as letters to a patroness in Upper Egypt, have become — by the ordinary Greek machinery of citation, commentary, and lecture — a set text of the imperial capital. That transformation, and not any single doctrine, is the Greek tradition's deepest fact about him. SYNESIUS · 4TH CENTURY Dialogue commentary to Dioscorus on pseudo-Democritus's Physika kai mystika ; declares his exegetic programme openly; probably not Synesius of Cyrene. Cites the tradition Zōsimos founded, and is himself quoted verbatim by Olympiodorus. OLYMPIODORUS · 6TH CENTURY Commentary On the Sacred Art on Zōsimos's lost On Action and the sayings of Hermes and the philosophers; builds the great doxography aligning nine Presocratic archai with the art's principles; possibly identical with the Alexandrian Neoplatonist commentator. STEPHANUS · EARLY 7TH CENTURY Nine Praxeis (lectures) on gold-making and a letter to Theodore, under Heraclius; quotes Synesius and Olympiodorus verbatim; the commentary tradition become an imperial curriculum. Taylor's Ambix translation is the standard English entry. THE ANONYMOUS SUCCESSORS After Stephanus the chain continues anonymously — the Christian philosopher, the Anonymous Philosopher, and the Byzantine excerptors who cite Stephanus as already ancient — until the compilers fold the whole succession into the corpus the Marcianus preserves. Citation has become custody. A last observation closes the section, because it disciplines the ones that follow. The commentators cite Zōsimos constantly and quote him selectively: what they needed from him was authority for doctrine — for the unity of matter, for the reading of Democritus, for the dignity of the art — and not the dream treatises, which they largely leave alone. The Visions survived not because the commentary tradition cherished them but because the corpus compilers copied whole books rather than excerpts alone. Their modern fame is therefore doubly accidental: preserved by the anthologists of the eighth century, completed only in the codex of 1478, printed by Berthelot, and made famous in 1937 by a psychologist. The next four sections read them as what they are in the Greek text — the visionary core of the Authentic Memoirs — and keep their strange afterlife, Jung included, in its labelled place. VI. The Visions as Greek Text: On Virtue and the Dream Treatises The Visions are three short dream narratives transmitted as Memoirs X, XI, and XII of the Authentic Memoirs in Mertens' numbering, under the title Peri aretēs — On Excellence , or On Virtue — and known in the older literature also as On the Composition of the Waters , from the technical discourse that frames them. Their position in the memoir sequence is itself an editorial fact worth pausing on: as the text reaches us, the three sections of On Excellence are interrupted by shorter chapters on chemical procedures that are clearly not part of the work, so that the Byzantine transmission delivers the dream treatise in pieces, separated by recipes. Whether that dislocation happened in the corpus's assembly or in later copying, its effect on readers has been real: for most of their history the Visions were encountered as fragments embedded in a technical anthology, and the modern editions earn their keep partly by reassembling them into the single, carefully structured work — discourse, dream, waking interpretation, dream again — that their internal cross-references show them to be. Their textual condition is the second fact. The Visions survive in more than forty manuscripts — a wide tradition by the standards of Greek technical literature — but the tradition is lopsided: the oldest witness, Marcianus graecus 299, preserves only the first lesson, and the first complete copy is Parisinus graecus 2327, copied in Crete in 1478. The text of the second and third dreams therefore rests on witnesses a full millennium younger than their author, and every narrative detail in Sections VII and VIII is given as the standard accounts — Mertens, Jackson's studies, the Oxford commentary, and the translation tradition behind Jung's essay — agree in reporting it. Where the accounts diverge in detail, this article follows the majority report and says nothing it cannot ground. That is the philological price of reading these texts at all, and it is cheaper than the alternative, which is not reading them. // DREAM OR LITERATURE? // Whether Zōsimos actually dreamed the Visions has been debated since Taylor noted their strongly oneiric character in 1937. Jung held that the vision might well have been an actual happening. The Oxford commentary's position — a real dream, worked up with a poet's freedom — is the current scholarly resting point. The question matters for biography; for the reading of the text, what matters is that Zōsimos presents the dreams as dreams, interprets them inside the narrative, and builds doctrine on the interpretation. The frame matters as much as the dreams. On Excellence does not begin with the altar. It begins with a discourse — the most quoted sentences Zōsimos ever wrote, given here in paraphrase — on the composition of the waters: the movement and growth of things, their embodying and disembodying, the drawing of spirit out of body and the bonding of spirit within body, all of it expressly said to proceed not from foreign natures imported from outside, but from a single nature acting upon itself, one kind containing both the hard shells of minerals and the moist pulp of plants. Only then, in the treatise's famous transition — in paraphrase: as I was saying these things, I fell asleep — does the dream begin. The structure is the doctrine. The discourse states the theory of pneuma in the abstract; the dream then shows it, in persons; and the dreamer's own waking gloss, which closes the first lesson, identifies the vision with the discourse — he asks himself, in paraphrase, whether what he has seen is not precisely the composition of the waters, and concludes that he has understood rightly. Greek allegory rarely announces its own key so openly. Zōsimos hands the reader the key, turns it himself, and then dreams again — as if to say that the understanding, once won, must be tested against further visions. Sections VII and VIII follow that sequence exactly. A word on the title's key term before the narrative begins. Aretē — excellence, virtue — is in this text a technical as well as a moral word: it names the perfected state toward which both the metal and the dreamer are travelling, the condition of a thing that has become fully what its nature fits it to be. The men in the visions are repeatedly described, in paraphrase, as seeking to attain excellence and becoming spirits in the attempt. Keeping the double sense in view — the excellence of a tincture that has taken perfectly, and the excellence of a soul that has been perfected — is the whole art of reading these three short texts, and the sections that follow will not separate the senses, because Zōsimos does not.
