The Philosopher Who Wrote a Perfume Book: The Paradox Stated This article belongs to Wing II of the Arabic hub — the wing of the Art itself, of workshops, operations, and recipes — and it begins with a man who is usually filed in Wing I's world, among the translators and transmitters. Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī (c. 801–873) is remembered, correctly, as the first great philosopher to write in Arabic: the court thinker who set himself to show that the Greek sciences — metaphysics, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, logic — could be thought and said in the language of Baghdad. The medieval bio-bibliographers called him faylasūf al-ʿarab , “the philosopher of the Arabs”, and the title has stuck for eleven centuries. What the title conceals, and what this article exists to recover, is that the same man also wrote the earliest surviving Arabic book devoted wholly to a chemical craft: the Kitāb Kīmiyāʾ al-ʿIṭr wa-l-Taṣʿīdāt , the Book of the Chemistry of Perfume and Distillations , a workshop manual of one hundred and seven recipes for scented waters, perfumed oils, compounded court perfumes, incense pastilles, cosmetics — and, most remarkably, for convincing imitations of the costliest aromatics on earth. The paradox is not that a philosopher wrote recipes. In the ninth-century Abbasid world, the distance between the philosopher's study and the perfumer's bench was shorter than a modern reader expects, and Section II will show al-Kindī moving across the whole range of the sciences as a matter of course. The paradox is sharper than that, and it is the frame of everything that follows. Al-Kindī also wrote — the attribution is standard in the medieval lists of his works and is accepted in the modern literature — a treatise against alchemy : a short work warning its reader against the deceptions of the alchemists, arguing that the transmutation they promised, the making of gold and silver out of baser stuffs by art, was not a difficult art but an impossible claim, and that those who sold it were, in effect, frauds. One author; two chemical books; opposite verdicts. The perfume book practises chemistry on nearly every page — weighing, grinding, macerating, distilling, subliming, compounding — while the refutation denies the period's most famous chemical promise. Any account of early Arabic chemistry that quotes only one of the two books has misrepresented its author. Held together, the two books draw a line, and the line is al-Kindī's own. On one side of it stands chrysopoeia — gold-making, the claim to change the species of a metal, to make a substance be what by nature it is not. That claim al-Kindī rejects, on grounds Section III sets out: human art, in his philosophy, works on what nature supplies; it does not confer new substantial natures. On the other side of the line stands everything art legitimately can do with substances: separate them, purify them, dissolve and recombine them, extract their virtues into water and oil, imitate a costly product's sensible qualities out of cheaper materials. That work al-Kindī not only permits but documents, at a level of procedural detail no earlier Arabic text matches. The perfume book is what chemistry looks like when a rigorous philosopher decides where its honest boundary runs — and then writes down, recipe by recipe, everything on the honest side of the boundary. This hub files the book, accordingly, neither as alchemy manqué nor as a curiosity at philosophy's margin, but as what it declares itself to be in its title: a kīmiyāʾ , a chemistry — of perfume. THE REFUTATION A short treatise against the alchemists' transmutation claims, listed among al-Kindī's works by the medieval bio-bibliographers: gold-making by art is impossible, and its sellers deceive. See Section III. Paraphrased throughout in this article; no wording is quoted. THE PERFUME BOOK Kitāb Kīmiyāʾ al-ʿIṭr wa-l-Taṣʿīdāt : 107 recipes for distilled waters, perfumed oils, compounded perfumes, incense, cosmetics, and imitations of musk and ambergris. The period's great practical book of chemical craft. See Sections IV–XI. THE LINE BETWEEN THEM Art may separate, purify, extract, and compound; it may imitate a product's sensible qualities. Art may not change a substance's species. The distinction is al-Kindī's own, and it is this article's frame. THE ACCESS Karl Garbers's edition and German translation of 1948 ( Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes ) is the standard scholarly access to the Arabic text, and the edition this article follows. See Section IV. A note on method, in the form this archive uses wherever the sources invite invention. No direct quotation is given in this article from al-Kindī's Arabic, and no recipe wording is reproduced or reconstructed. The procedures of Sections V–XI are paraphrases , drawn from Garbers's edition and from the descriptions of the book in the secondary literature listed in the Sources, and they are labelled as paraphrase and summary where they appear. Ingredients, sequences, apparatus, and endpoints are given at the fullest detail the secondary literature supports; weighed proportions are described as the book's practice — the recipes do specify quantities, in the weight-units of the period — without this article inventing figures Garbers's text was not re-collated to verify line by line. Where the popular literature credits this book, or its century, with achievements the text does not contain — above all, the distillation of alcohol — the article says so at full length and at the claim's real evidentiary strength (Section XII). Contested claims are stated as contested; the text's actual contents are stated precisely. That discipline is not a hedge laid over the article. It is, the reader will find, al-Kindī's own. // NAMES AND TRANSLITERATION // Arabic words are given in scholarly transliteration with diacritics throughout: al-Kindī, kīmiyāʾ , ʿiṭr (perfume), taṣʿīd (distillation/sublimation — see Section V on the word's range), ghāliya , ʿūd (agarwood), kuḥl . The article sign (al-) is not capitalised mid-name. Dates are CE. Where a product name's identification is uncertain, the uncertainty is stated rather than a confident gloss supplied. II. Al-Kindī: Life, Court, and Corpus The biographical record for al-Kindī is respectable by ninth-century standards and thin by modern ones: no contemporary life survives, and the outline below follows the medieval bio-bibliographical tradition — Ibn al-Nadīm's Fihrist (compiled 987) above all, with the later biographers behind it — as sifted in the modern reference literature. Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī was born about 801 , probably at Kufa in Iraq, into the Arab tribe of Kinda — a lineage of old South Arabian royal ancestry of which he was plainly proud, and which mattered in a court culture where the great translation enterprise was staffed largely by Syriac Christians, Persians, and Sabians: al-Kindī was, conspicuously, an Arab Muslim at the centre of a multi-confessional republic of letters. His father had been governor of Kufa under the early Abbasids. The son was educated at Basra and then at Baghdad, the new Abbasid capital, and it was at Baghdad that his career was made. His patrons were caliphs. Under al-Maʾmūn (r. 813–833) — the caliph whose court gave the translation movement its most famous institutional form, treated in this hub's companion article on the Baghdad translation movement — al-Kindī rose into the circle of court scholars, and under al-Maʾmūn's successor al-Muʿtaṣim (r. 833–842) he stood high enough to be appointed tutor to the caliph's son Aḥmad, to whom several of his works are dedicated. The position was real and it was precarious, as court positions were. Under al-Mutawakkil (r. 847–861), whose reign turned against the rationalist theology al-Kindī's philosophy had served, he fell from favour; the biographical tradition preserves the famous, perhaps embroidered, episode of his library being confiscated — and, through the intercession of rivals-turned-intercessors, restored. He died at Baghdad about 873 , in his early seventies, having outlived the great age of his own influence. The anecdotes are flagged here as the tradition gives them; the secure skeleton is birth, tribe, two caliphal patrons, a tutorship, a fall, and a death date, and this article builds on nothing more. The Corpus: An Encyclopedist of Greek Science in Arabic What al-Kindī wrote is, in range, the translation movement become a single mind. The Fihrist 's list of his works runs to some two hundred and sixty titles — the count varies slightly by how composite items are divided — of which a substantial minority survives. The list is itself a map of the Greek scientific inheritance as Baghdad received it, reworked now as original Arabic composition: works on metaphysics (including the famous On First Philosophy , addressed to al-Muʿtaṣim), on the soul and the intellect, on logic and the classification of the sciences; on arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and the astrolabe; on music theory, where his treatises apply Greek harmonic science to the ʿūd; on medicine and pharmacology, including the formulary known as the Aqrabādhīn , which Martin Levey translated (see Sources); on optics, meteorology, tides, and the fabrication of swords; on theology, composed in defence of the rationalist doctrines his caliphal patrons favoured. He commissioned and supervised translations as well as writing — the Arabic version of Plotinus that circulated as the Theology of Aristotle emerged from his circle — and he revised the work of the translators around him with a philosopher's impatience for terminological sloppiness. The Arabic scientific lexicon whose forging the translation-movement article describes was, in part, forged on his desk. Two features of that corpus matter for the perfume book's place in it. The first is that al-Kindī's interest in the productive arts was systematic, not incidental. A philosopher who wrote on sword steels, on glass, on the preparation of drugs, and on the classification of the sciences — in which the practical arts have their assigned places — did not stoop when he wrote on perfume; he filed a craft where his system said crafts belong, among the arts that work on nature's materials by knowledge of their properties. The second is that his pharmacological writing gives the perfume book a sibling. The Aqrabādhīn — a formulary of compound medicines, organised by preparation and ailment — and the Chemistry of Perfume share a literary skeleton: terse, imperative, quantitative recipes, ingredient by ingredient, operation by operation, with the preparer's judgement invoked exactly where a quantity cannot be fixed in advance. Levey, who worked on both texts, treated them together as the twin witnesses to al-Kindī's practical chemistry, and this article follows him: the perfume book is the formulary's secular twin, the same hand writing for the dressing table and the incense burner what the Aqrabādhīn writes for the sickroom. c. 801 BIRTH Born probably at Kufa, of the tribe of Kinda; his father a governor of Kufa under the early Abbasids. Educated at Basra and Baghdad. 813–833 UNDER AL-MAʾMŪN Rises at the court of al-Maʾmūn, in the decades of the translation movement's greatest caliphal patronage. 833–842 UNDER AL-MUʿTAṢIM Tutor to the caliph's son Aḥmad; On First Philosophy dedicated to al-Muʿtaṣim. The height of his court standing. after 847 THE FALL Out of favour under al-Mutawakkil; the tradition's episode of the confiscated and restored library belongs to these years and is reported here as tradition, not as verified fact. c. 873 DEATH AT BAGHDAD Dies at Baghdad, leaving a corpus of some two hundred and sixty listed works — among them a refutation of the alchemists and the Chemistry of Perfume . III. The Refutation: What Al-Kindī Said Against the Alchemists The medieval lists of al-Kindī's works include, among the physical and philosophical treatises, a short work directed against the alchemists: a warning against their deceptions, and an argument that the thing they claimed to do could not be done. The treatise is known to modern scholarship through the bio-bibliographical record and the discussions of it in the standard histories of Arabic alchemy (Ullmann's survey, listed in the Sources, gives the dossier its canonical form); it does not survive as a widely read text in the way the perfume book does, and this section therefore reports its position — which the record states consistently — in paraphrase, without quotation and without reconstructing its wording. The position, stated at the strength the record supports, is this. The alchemists claim to produce gold and silver from substances that are not gold and silver. That production, if it were real, would be the changing of one natural species into another by human art. But art does not work that way: the artisan disposes, combines, separates, and adorns materials whose natures nature has already fixed; he does not confer natures. What the alchemists actually deliver, when their products are examined, is resemblance — alloys, surface treatments, and admixtures that present the colour, weight, or ring of the noble metals without being them — and the sale of resemblance as identity is deception, whether or not the seller believes his own pitch. The treatise's burden, on the standard account, is thus double: a physical impossibility claim and an ethical one, and the two are connected. The claim is impossible; therefore the trade in it is fraud. The philosophical root of the impossibility claim is worth drawing out, because it explains — what otherwise looks like mere inconsistency — how the refutation and the perfume book come from one mind. In the metaphysics al-Kindī built out of his Greek materials, natural substances have their forms and properties from nature's own ordering, ultimately from God; human making operates downstream of that ordering, on mixtures and accidents. An art can change what a body looks, smells, and feels like — its colour, odour, texture, consistency — because those are qualities that mixture governs. An art cannot change what a body is in species, because species is not a mixture-effect. Gold is not lead plus the right colour; it is a distinct nature, and no arrangement of lead's accidents sums to it. This is, the reader should note, very nearly the Aristotelian quality-physics of the Greco-Roman hub's foundation articles turned against chrysopoeia: if the elements and their qualities are the alphabet, then compounding spells new mixtures , not new letters — and gold, in al-Kindī's handling, is a letter, not a word. Later Arabic critics of alchemy — Ibn Sīnā's famous denial that the alchemists can produce true species, a century and a half on — argue in this same Kindian register, and the perfume book's author stands at the head of that sceptical line as surely as the Jābirian corpus stands at the head of the affirmative one. This hub's article on al-Rāzī follows the argument's next great round, in which a practising chemist of genius answers the philosophers from the bench. // THE REFUTATION, STATED AT ITS REAL STRENGTH // Three precisions govern everything said about this treatise in this article. First, its target is transmutation — the production of the noble metals — not chemical practice as such; nothing in the record suggests al-Kindī condemned the distillation, compounding, and imitation his own perfume book teaches, and the perfume book itself is the proof he did not. Second, the treatise's argument is reported here in paraphrase from the secondary literature's consistent account of it; its wording is not quoted, because this article quotes no text it has not verified in a named edition. Third, the modern reader should resist filing the refutation as “science against superstition” in modern dress. Al-Kindī's objection is metaphysical before it is empirical: species cannot be made because of what species are , in a philosophy he held for reasons that have nothing to do with laboratory failure. The bench evidence — that alchemical gold failed the touchstone and the assay — supports the argument in his presentation, but the argument does not rest on the bench alone. Now turn the refutation over, and its reverse side is a licence. If art's legitimate field is exactly the field of mixture and sensible quality — colour, odour, texture, consistency — then the arts that work that field most skilfully are not alchemy's poor relations. They are the model of what human making, honestly understood, is. Perfumery is that field's purest case. A perfume is nothing but managed sensible qualities: an odour, compounded of odours; a texture, compounded of oils and waxes and ground aromatics; an effect on the wearer and the room that exists entirely at the level where art is sovereign. And imitation — the manufacture, from cheap materials, of a product whose sensible qualities convincingly match a costly original — is, within this philosophy, not a guilty secret but the field's characteristic triumph: resemblance sold as resemblance, to a buyer who knows musk is dear and wants its effect at a price he can pay, deceives no one. The line between the refutation and the recipes is thus not a wall between two interests. It is a single principle seen from two sides: pass off an imitation as the species itself, and you are the fraud of the refutation; compound an imitation openly, as a perfume, and you are the craftsman of the Kīmiyāʾ al-ʿIṭr . Section IX, on the imitation recipes, returns to this point with the products in hand. IV. The Book: Survival, Edition, and Genre The Kitāb Kīmiyāʾ al-ʿIṭr wa-l-Taṣʿīdāt — the title is also transmitted with the second element in the fuller form wa-l-taṣʿīdāt , “and the distillations / sublimations”, on which see Section V — survives, on the standard account, in a very small manuscript tradition: Garbers edited the text from a single Istanbul manuscript copy, and the book's modern life descends from that narrow thread. The circumstance is worth pausing on, because it is typical of the practical literature this wing studies and atypical of the philosophical literature of Wing I. Al-Kindī's metaphysics was copied because schools taught it; his perfume book was copied, when it was copied, because workshops and courts used it, and used books wear out, are discarded when their recipes are absorbed into later compilations, and survive by accident. That this one survived at all — complete enough to edit, with its recipe sequence and its quantities intact — is the accident on which the present article, and every modern account of Abbasid perfumery, depends. The standard access is Karl Garbers's edition of 1948 : Kitāb Kīmiyāʾ al-ʿIṭr wat-Taṣʿīdāt: Buch über die Chemie des Parfüms und die Destillationen von Yaʿqūb b. Isḥāq al-Kindī , published in the Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes (vol. XXX, no. 2, Leipzig: Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft / Brockhaus), giving the Arabic text with a German translation and commentary. Garbers's count of the contents — one hundred and seven recipes — is the figure this article's subtitle carries and the literature repeats. Martin Levey's studies of early Muslim chemistry, and his translation of al-Kindī's medical formulary (the Aqrabādhīn , University of Wisconsin Press, 1966), brought the perfume book into the Anglophone history of chemistry, where it has since stood as the type specimen of ninth-century Arabic practical chemistry: cited by Ullmann in his survey of the natural and secret sciences in Islam (1972), and by every subsequent history of distillation and of perfume that works from the texts rather than from legend. Readers who want the recipes themselves go to Garbers; this article, which paraphrases and summarises throughout, is a map to his edition, not a substitute for it. Genre: A Workshop Manual What kind of book is it? Not a treatise. The Chemistry of Perfume has no preface of theory, no classification of odours, no natural philosophy of smell — nothing, in short, of the apparatus a modern reader expects the philosopher of the Arabs to supply, and its absence is the point. The book is a workshop manual : a sequence of recipes in the imperative mood, each opening on its product — a water, an oil, a compound, an incense — and proceeding through materials, quantities, preparation, operation, and endpoint in the fewest words the operation allows. Its closest relatives are not al-Kindī's own philosophical works but the recipe literature of late antiquity: the workshop papyri of Roman Egypt (the Leyden and Stockholm papyri, treated in the Egyptology division), whose dyers' and metalworkers' recipes share the same grammar of weighed ingredients and unadorned imperatives, and the formulary tradition of Greek and Syriac medicine, in which al-Kindī's own Aqrabādhīn also stands. The perfume book is what that ancient genre looks like transplanted to a ninth-century Abbasid court city, stocked with the aromatics of an Indian Ocean trade, and written up by a man who weighed his words as carefully as his musk. TERSE Recipes are compressed to the operations themselves. Explanation, where it occurs, is functional: what to do when a product falls short, how to judge an endpoint, how to correct a batch — the tacit knowledge of a bench, written down only where writing can carry it. IMPERATIVE The grammatical mood is the command: take, grind, steep, distil, knead, set aside. The implied reader is a practitioner — a court perfumer, a pharmacist, a skilled servant of a great household — not a student of theory. QUANTITATIVE Ingredients are weighed, in the period's units (the mithqāl and the dirham and their fractions), and sequences are timed and repeated by count — so many steepings, so many distillations. The book's chemistry is a chemistry of measure, continuous with its author's mathematics. PRODUCT-ORGANISED The sequence runs by product class — waters, oils, compounds, incenses, then the cosmetic margins — not by raw material or by theory. Sections VI–X of this article follow the book's own organisation for that reason. V. The Workshop in Words: Apparatus, Heating, and the Vocabulary of Taṣʿīd The book's title carries its technical programme in its second noun. Taṣʿīd (plural taṣʿīdāt ) is the verbal noun of a verb meaning, at root, “to cause to ascend” — and in the chemical vocabulary of the period it covers, without distinguishing them as sharply as modern usage does, the two great operations in which a substance is made to rise as vapour and be recovered in a purer or more potent form: distillation , in which a liquid is vaporised and its vapour condensed and collected as liquid, and sublimation , in which a solid is vaporised and its vapour deposited again as solid on a cooler surface above. Garbers's German renders the title's word with Destillationen , and English accounts follow him with “distillations”; both renderings are correct for most of the book's contents and slightly narrow for all of them, since the recipes' ascending operations include the purification and concentration of solids by rising vapour as well as the drawing off of waters and oils. This article keeps the Arabic word in view wherever the distinction matters, and states, for each operation described, whether what rises is a liquid's vapour or a solid's — the text's own practice, which distinguishes by product and apparatus what its title gathers under one word. The Still and Its Parts The apparatus of the ascending operations is the alembic — Arabic al-anbīq , a loanword whose Greek ancestor, ambix , names the cup-shaped head of the stills of Roman Egypt. The instrument al-Kindī's recipes presuppose is the direct descendant of the apparatus the Greco-Roman hub's article on Maria the Jewess reconstructs for the first centuries CE, and the continuity is material, not metaphorical: a lower vessel or cucurbit (Arabic qarʿa , the “gourd”) holding the charge; a head set over it, in which the vapour gathers; a delivery path — in the developed form, a descending tube — along which the vapour passes and cools; and a receiver ( qābila ) in which the distillate collects. The joints are luted — sealed with clay or a prepared lute — so that the vapour's only road out is the road to the receiver; a charge whose vapour escapes at the joints is a charge wasted, and the recipe literature's attention to sealing, here as in Alexandria, is the attention of men paying for their aromatics by the mithqāl. Materials are the period's usual ones: glass for receivers and for charges that must be watched, glazed earthenware and metal for the bodies of stills that stand in direct fire. The perfume book names parts and presupposes the rest; the reconstruction above follows the standard accounts of the early Arabic still in Forbes's history of distillation, corrected and supplemented by Levey and Ullmann (see Sources, and Section XII on where Forbes's larger claims outrun his evidence). // TAṢʿĪD: ONE WORD, TWO OPERATIONS // Modern chemistry separates distillation (liquid → vapour → liquid) from sublimation (solid → vapour → solid) without remainder. Ninth-century Arabic did not, because the bench did not: the same still, the same fire, and the same verb serve both, and the operator distinguishes them by what he charged and what he collects. When this article says a recipe “distils”, a liquid was charged; when it says a recipe “sublimes” or “raises”, a solid was. The title's taṣʿīdāt covers both, and any translation that silently narrows it to one has already begun to misdescribe the book. Heating Regimes: Water Bath and Direct Fire Fire management is the stillman's whole art, and the recipes distinguish, as the whole pre-modern distillation literature distinguishes, two working regimes. The first is direct fire : the cucurbit stands in or over the flame, the charge heats fast and hard, and the operator's skill is the skill of restraint — too fierce a fire scorches an aromatic charge, drives the vapour over faster than the head can cool it, and carries the still's contents, in the worst case, out of the receiver and into the room. Direct fire suits robust charges and bulk work: waters drawn from petals and water in quantity, where the charge is mostly water already and scorching is guarded against by the charge itself. The second regime is the water bath : the vessel holding the charge stands in a larger vessel of heated water, so that the charge can never exceed the bath's gentle ceiling, and delicate aromatics — oils, fine waters, anything whose virtue is a volatile fragrance that fierce heat destroys — are worked slowly and safely. The water bath descends, through the same Alexandrian line as the still itself, from the apparatus tradition attached to Maria's name (the bain-marie of the later European kitchen and laboratory is her name worn smooth by a millennium of use), and its presence in the perfume workshop is the apparatus ancestry of Section XIV in miniature: Baghdad's perfumer heats his oils as Alexandria taught the world to heat them. Between the two regimes the recipes also know the gentler heat-sources of the pre-modern bench — warm ash, sand, and the sun itself, the last of them a working instrument in a climate like Baghdad's, where a sealed vessel of oil and aromatics set in the sun is a slow maceration apparatus that costs no fuel at all (Section VII). // READING THE RECIPES THAT FOLLOW // Sections VI–X present the book's procedures class by class, in paraphrase. Three conventions hold throughout. Quantities are described as the book's practice (weighed, in mithqāls and dirhams) without invented figures. Endpoints are given as the literature reports them — a distillate that runs clear and fragrant, an oil that has taken the scent, a paste of the right consistency — since endpoints, not timings, are how a pre-thermometer bench knows it is done. And every procedure is labelled, in the text or in Section XI's table, as a summary of Garbers's edition and the secondary literature — never as the book's own wording, which this article nowhere reproduces. VI. Distilled Waters: Rose Water and the Aromatic Waters The book's ascending operations begin, as Abbasid perfumery itself began each season, with the flowers. The distilled aromatic waters — rose water at their head — are the perfume workshop's bulk products and its foundation stocks: waters that carry a flower's fragrance in a form that keeps, travels, and can be used as it stands (for the skin, for the hands after eating, for flavouring and for medicine) or worked further, as the solvent and vehicle of compounded preparations. The procedures below are paraphrases and summaries of the recipes as Garbers's edition and the secondary literature describe them; the sequence, the apparatus, and the endpoints are the book's, the wording is this article's. Rose Water: The Type Procedure Take fresh rose petals — the recipes presume the fragrant damask-type roses of the period, gathered with their scent at its height, and the literature is unanimous that stale or wilted petals make a water not worth the fuel. Charge the cucurbit with the petals and with water, the petals covered and the vessel filled well short of the head, so that boiling cannot throw the charge into the vapour path. Set the head, lute the joints, and bring the still to a gentle, steady heat: the water vaporises, the vapour carries the petals' volatile fragrance with it — the phenomenon a modern chemist calls steam distillation, in which the aromatic principles, though barely soluble and higher-boiling than water, ride over with the steam — the vapour condenses in the head and delivery tube, and the distillate runs into the receiver as a clear, intensely fragrant water. The endpoint is judged by the product, not the clock: the run is collected while it comes over fragrant and is stopped, or the receiver changed, when the fragrance thins — the later, weaker runnings are kept apart, for lesser uses or for reworking, and are not allowed to dilute the first quality. The finished water is stored stoppered, in glass, away from heat and light. Two refinements, both characteristic of the book's bench intelligence, recur in the accounts of these recipes. The first is repeated distillation — cohobation , in the later literature's term: a water judged too weak is returned to the still, alone or over a fresh charge of petals, and distilled again, each pass concentrating the fragrance the charge can be made to yield. The second is the grading of the product by its runnings, just described: the still does not produce “rose water” in the abstract but a sequence of fractions of declining strength, and the perfumer's art is in part the art of the cut — of knowing which receiver holds the perfume and which holds the wash. Both refinements matter beyond perfumery. Fractionation by successive cuts and concentration by redistillation are, in embryo, the two techniques on which the whole later history of distillation turns — including, centuries later and in other hands, the distillation of wine, whose absence from this book Section XII examines in full. The Other Waters, and What Distillation Is For Rose is the type, not the whole class. The book's distilled waters extend across the aromatic materia of the Abbasid market — waters drawn from other fragrant flowers and from aromatic woods, leaves, and spices, by the same charge-heat- condense-collect sequence, adjusted for the material: delicate flowers worked gently and quickly, denser materials given longer and hotter runs, some materials steeped in the water before the fire is lit so that the charge goes onto the heat already yielding its virtue. The class as a whole teaches the operation's purpose in this book, and the purpose should be stated plainly, because Section XII depends on it. Distillation here is an extraction and preservation technology. It moves a fragrance out of a perishable material — a petal that will rot in days — into a stable, portable, saleable medium, and it concentrates the fragrance in the moving. What it is never asked to do, in any recipe of this book, is to isolate a single chemical substance for its own sake, still less to produce an intoxicating spirit. The waters are products, not reagents; the still is a perfumer's tool, not yet — in this text, in this century — the alchemist's engine of separation that it would later become. That restraint is not a failure of imagination. It is the exact boundary al-Kindī's philosophy draws (Section III), observed at the bench: art extracting and compounding nature's qualities, and claiming nothing more. // THE GEOGRAPHY IN A BOTTLE // Rose water was already, in al-Kindī's century, an article of long-distance trade as well as of local manufacture: the rose water of Jūr in Fars (Persia) was famous across the caliphate and exported as far as the trade routes ran, and the roses of Ṭāʾif in the Hijaz supplied Arabia's own market. A Baghdad recipe for rose water thus sits inside an economy — local distillation competing with celebrated imports — of exactly the kind Section XIII reconstructs for the costlier aromatics. VII. A Physician at the Bench: Why al-Rāzī Reads Differently Open the Kitāb Sirr al-asrār — the Book of the Secret of Secrets — beside any text of the Jābir corpus, and the difference is felt before it can be argued. The Jābirian books, treated in this division in The Jābir Corpus , speak in the voice of a master veiling doctrine for initiates: the science of the Balance weighs letters as well as substances, authorities are layered on authorities, and the imam stands behind the teaching as its guarantor. Al-Rāzī's book speaks in a different voice entirely. It begins by sorting the materials of the workshop into classes. It goes on to describe the furnaces, vessels, and hand tools the work requires. Only then does it give procedures, in numbered succession, with the order of operations stated and the signs of success and failure noted. There is no science of letters here. There is no imam. There is a list, a bench, and a sequence — and the list comes first. That order is the article's subject. Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakarīyāʾ al-Rāzī (865–925) — Rhazes, Rasis, and Albubator in the Latin spellings — was by profession a physician, and by the testimony of the Arabic biographical tradition one of the most successful of his age: director of the hospital of his native Rayy, then of a hospital in Baghdad, author of the vast medical notebook-encyclopedia that Latin Europe would read as the Continens . His alchemy carries the habits of that profession into the workshop. A physician of the Galenic school lived by classification: diseases sorted by kind, drugs sorted by power and degree, cases recorded whether the outcome flattered the doctor or not. Al-Rāzī's Secret of Secrets does to the mineral workshop what his medicine did to the clinic. Substances are sorted by what they observably do under treatment. Instruments are inventoried before they are used. Procedures are written so that another worker can repeat them — and can tell, when the result fails, at which step it failed. THE JĀBIRIAN MANNER Doctrine dispersed and veiled by design; the Balance of letters; esoteric exegesis; authority descending from the imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq. Knowledge is guarded, and the guarding is part of the teaching. See The Jābir Corpus . THE RĀZIAN MANNER Doctrine inventoried and ordered for use; classification by behaviour in fire; apparatus described before procedures; failure assigned to method. Knowledge is arranged, and the arrangement is the teaching. The present article. None of this makes al-Rāzī a modern chemist before his time, and this article will not call him one. He believed in the elixir. He believed base metals could be transmuted into silver and gold, he organised his book around that belief, and the third part of the Secret of Secrets is a repertoire of elixir procedures. The modernity that older popular writing claimed for him — the laboratory rationalist who had quietly stopped believing what his contemporaries believed — is a mirage, and Section XVII returns to it. What distinguishes al-Rāzī is not disbelief. It is discipline about belief : transmutation, for him, is not a wonder to be credited on a master's word but a result to be produced by a stated method, from classified materials, in described apparatus — and if the result does not come, his own preface argues, in paraphrase, that the fault lies in the worker's procedure and not in the Art's principle. That sentence, paraphrased again at its proper place in Section XIV, is the most consequential sentence in Arabic alchemy. It converts failure from a refutation into a diagnosis. A note on method, in the form this archive uses wherever a text invites invention. No direct quotation from al-Rāzī is given in this article. Everything the Secret of Secrets says is given in paraphrase, labelled as paraphrase, and the paraphrases follow the standard modern access to the work: Julius Ruska's edition and German translation, Al-Rāzī's Buch Geheimnis der Geheimnisse (Berlin, 1937), cited throughout simply as Ruska's edition. Where a famous saying circulates in popular writing under al-Rāzī's name and cannot be verified in the edited text or in a named scholarly translation, it is not printed here — not even to be refuted at length. The discipline is the same one the Greco-Roman division applies in Fire and Assay : what a text states, what a later tradition reports, and what a modern writer wishes it had stated are three different kinds of evidence, and they are not interchangeable. // NAMES AND TRANSLITERATION // Arabic terms are given in scholarly transliteration with diacritics throughout: al-Rāzī, Sirr al-asrār , arwāḥ (spirits), ajsād (bodies), aḥjār (stones), zājāt (vitriols), bawāriq (boraces), amlāḥ (salts), khārṣīnī (the zinc body). Latin name-forms — Rhazes, Rasis — are used only where the Latin reception is itself the subject (Section XVI). Dates are CE. The article's route follows the book's own order, because the order is the argument: the man and his independence (Sections II–III), the book as a document and its three-part structure (Sections IV–V), the classification in full (Sections VI–IX), the inventory and operations (Sections X–XI), three worked procedures in labelled paraphrase (Sections XII–XIII), and doctrine, critics, afterlife, and assessment (Sections XIV–XVII). For the theory al-Rāzī inherited, read beside this article The Sulphur–Mercury Theory ; for the mineral-acid question, which this article touches only to police its boundary, Mineral Acids and Practice — where the canonical position stands in full: the mineral acids belong to the Latin pseudo-Geber, not to al-Rāzī and not to Jābir. II. The Man and the Record: Rayy, Baghdad, and the Hospitals Al-Rāzī was born in Rayy — ancient Rhages, on the southern edge of the Elburz foothills, near modern Tehran — in 865 by the dating this archive follows, and he died there in 925. The biographical tradition, preserved in Ibn al-Nadīm's Fihrist , in al-Bīrūnī's bibliography of his works, and in the later medical biographers, gives a life in two careers. The young al-Rāzī, on the tradition's telling, worked first in his father's world of exchange — he is remembered as having been a money-changer — and came to medicine and philosophy as an adult, studying at Rayy and then in Baghdad. The anecdotal colour of the early life (the lute-playing youth, the turn to study) belongs to the biographers' stock of conversion stories and is filed here as anecdote. What is firm is the second career's outline, because it is corroborated by the works themselves and by the institutions they name. He directed the hospital of Rayy, and then a hospital in Baghdad — the biographical sources associate the Baghdad post with the great hospital foundation of the caliph al-Muʿtaḍid's era — and he wrote medicine on a scale that still staggers. The Kitāb al-Ḥāwī , the Comprehensive Book on medicine, is less a composed treatise than a lifetime's clinical notebook, assembled after his death from his papers: case upon case, excerpt upon excerpt from Greek, Syriac, Persian, and Indian authorities, each tagged with its source and often with al-Rāzī's own dissent recorded beside it. Latin Europe, which received it in the thirteenth century as the Liber Continens , treated it as an authority of the first rank for three hundred years. The Kitāb al-Manṣūrī , dedicated to the same Samanid governor of Rayy who received the Secret of Secrets (Section IV), is the opposite kind of book: a compact, ordered handbook of medicine in ten treatises, whose Latin form, the Liber ad Almansorem , became a European textbook. And the treatise on smallpox and measles — the first clinical differentiation of the two diseases to survive — shows the same mind at the bedside that the Secret of Secrets shows at the bench: observe the distinguishing signs, record them in order, let the classification do the work. PHYSICIAN FIRST Hospital director at Rayy and at Baghdad; the al-Ḥāwī (Latin Continens ) as a career's clinical archive; the al-Manṣūrī as its ordered handbook. The alchemy was written by a man whose day work was diagnosis, regimen, and the hospital ward. THE CASE-HISTORY HABIT Al-Rāzī's medical writing is famous for its case records — presentations, treatments, outcomes, including outcomes that failed. The Secret of Secrets ' habit of noting the signs by which a procedure's success or failure is known is the same habit, moved from ward to workshop. THE DISSENTING READER His Doubts About Galen ( al-Shukūk ʿalā Jālīnūs ) argues, respectfully and in detail, that the greatest medical authority of antiquity was wrong on stated points — on evidence al-Rāzī says he observed himself. Deference to authority was not in his method, in any field. THE RECORD'S KEEPERS What is known of the life rests chiefly on Ibn al-Nadīm's Fihrist (tenth century), on al-Bīrūnī's catalogue of al-Rāzī's writings (Section XV), and on the medical biographers. The catalogue counts well over a hundred works across medicine, philosophy, and the sciences — most now lost, the alchemical books among the survivors. Two cautions govern the biography. Chronologically, al-Rāzī (865–925) stands a generation after the translation movement's great age and roughly contemporary with the Jābir corpus's later strata: he is not Jābir's pupil, in any sense the evidence supports, but a reader of the Jābirian books who chose to write otherwise. And the tradition's report of his sight failing late in life — cataract is the usual account — is widely attested as fact, while the speeches attached to it vary by source and are literature, not record. 865 BORN AT RAYY Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakarīyāʾ al-Rāzī born at Rayy. The early money-changing career and the adult turn to medicine belong to the biographical tradition and are reported here at that strength. LATE 9TH C. HOSPITALS AT RAYY AND BAGHDAD Directs the hospital of Rayy, then a hospital at Baghdad. The clinical career that produced the al-Ḥāwī notebooks and the smallpox-and-measles treatise. c. 900–915 THE SAMANID DEDICATIONS The Kitāb al-Manṣūrī in medicine and the Kitāb Sirr al-asrār in alchemy are dedicated to Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Manṣūr ibn Isḥāq, Samanid governor of Rayy (Section IV). 925 DEATH AT RAYY Dies at Rayy, his sight failed, leaving the al-Ḥāwī papers to be assembled by others. The Latin afterlife of the medicine — and, separately, of the alchemy — begins two centuries later (Section XVI). Why does the biography matter to a bench manual? Because the Secret of Secrets is unintelligible as a courtly or initiatory text and fully intelligible as a professional one. Its author earned his living by a learned art practised in institutions with stores, instruments, assistants, and records, and the book's opening moves — inventory the materials, describe the instruments, then and only then prescribe — are those of a man who had run a dispensary. Section III takes up the other half of his independence, the philosophical half: al-Rāzī held, on stated grounds, that no inherited authority was entitled to his assent without examination. The workshop book and the heretical metaphysics are one mind at two benches. III. The Five Eternals: Philosophical Independence and Its Price Al-Rāzī's philosophy survives mostly in the reports of men who opposed it — a fact that must be stated before any of it is summarised, because it sets the evidence's strength. His own philosophical books are largely lost. What remains is the doxographical record: summaries, refutations, and debate-reports by Ismaili, Muʿtazilite, and later writers, from which modern scholarship — Shlomo Pines's studies and Lenn E. Goodman's work are the standard modern accesses named in the Sources — has reconstructed a system startling in its independence. At its centre stands the doctrine by which al-Rāzī is still known to historians of philosophy: the five eternals . In paraphrase of the doctrine as the reports agree in giving it: there are five eternal, uncreated principles — God, the Soul, Matter, Time, and Place . God did not create the world from nothing at a moment of His choosing. The Soul, eternal but unwise, desired embodiment and entangled itself in eternal Matter; God, in wisdom and mercy, fashioned the ordered world from that pre-existent matter as the theatre in which souls could learn, suffer, and finally be released from embodiment altogether. Every term of that paraphrase was a provocation. An eternal Matter beside an eternal God limits creation in a way no orthodox theology, Muslim, Christian, or Jewish, could accept. An absolute Time and an absolute Place — durations and extensions that exist whether or not any world fills them — cut against the Aristotelian physics the Baghdad schools were then absorbing, in which time is the measure of motion and place the boundary of a containing body. And the Soul's fall through desire, with release through knowledge, owes more to the Platonist and gnostic currents of late antiquity than to the Qurʾān. Al-Rāzī held these positions, on the reports, knowingly and in public disputation. The Ismaili missionary Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī — a namesake, not a relative — debated him at Rayy, on the reports preserved in Abū Ḥātim's own Aʿlām al-nubuwwa , over prophecy itself: al-Rāzī is there made to argue, in paraphrase, that reason is given to all men equally and that a God who singled out prophets would set men at each other's throats — an argument whose exact wording is Abū Ḥātim's report of an opponent he aimed to refute, and which this article therefore gives only as a reported position, not as a quotation and not as a transcript. // HOSTILE WITNESSES: HOW THE PHILOSOPHY SURVIVES // The five eternals are known chiefly through opponents — Abū Ḥātim's debate-report, the refutations of later theologians, and doxographical summaries such as those Pines and Goodman analyse. Hostile transmission cuts both ways, and the article states both. It can distort: a refuter sharpens the position he refutes. But it also corroborates the doctrine's outline, because writers who agree on nothing else agree that al-Rāzī taught five eternals and denied creation from nothing. The outline is firm; the fine wording is lost with the books. Later charges that al-Rāzī denied prophecy outright, or mocked revelation, belong to the polemical layer and are flagged again in Section XV: they tell the historian what his enemies needed him to have said, which is evidence about them as much as about him. What has this to do with alchemy? Three things. First, matter is eternal and therefore lawful : in a world fashioned from pre-existent matter, the Art's transformations are rearrangements of what eternally is — the conservation instinct the Greco-Roman division traces from Empedocles onward, here held as metaphysics. Second, no authority closes a question : the man who wrote Doubts About Galen was not going to accept an elixir procedure because Jābir's name stood over it. The Secret of Secrets ' silence about the Jābirian veiling — no Balance of letters, no imam, no dispersed doctrine — is a philosophical position enacted as an editorial one. Third, knowledge releases : in the five-eternals myth, in paraphrase, souls are freed by learning what they are and what matter is. His alchemy is humbler — it promises gold, not salvation — but it shares the premise that liberation, of a metal or of a soul, comes by knowledge of natures, methodically acquired. Atomism, Briefly and Carefully The reports also credit al-Rāzī with a form of atomism: matter, in paraphrase of the doxography, composed of indivisible particles with void between them, defended against Aristotelian continuum physics and opposed after him by al-Bīrūnī and Ibn Sīnā (Section XV). The doctrine reaches us entirely through critics' summaries, its details vary between reports, and Pines's reconstructions differ on its originality and centrality. It is stated here at report strength only. Nothing in the Secret of Secrets ' procedures requires it, and the procedures are not argued from it in the text: the metaphysics explains the man's independence, not the recipes. IV. The Book and Its Patron: Sirr al-asrār and Kitāb al-Asrār The Kitāb Sirr al-asrār , the Book of the Secret of Secrets , was written for a patron, and the patron matters because he fixes the book's kind. The dedication, as Ruska's edition gives it, is to Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Manṣūr ibn Isḥāq , the Samanid governor of Rayy — the same al-Manṣūr who received the medical Kitāb al-Manṣūrī . Al-Manṣūr was no initiate of an alchemical circle. He was a provincial governor of the Samanid amirate, a man of the court world, who wanted — on the preface's own presentation, in paraphrase — the Art set down for him completely and intelligibly: its materials, its instruments, and its procedures, without the deliberate obscurity in which, the preface complains, earlier writers had wrapped it. A book commissioned by a governor from his physician is a commission for usable knowledge. The Secret of Secrets ' famous clarity is not an accident of temperament alone. It is what the patron paid for. That preface argument deserves its own statement, because Section XIV builds on it. In paraphrase of Ruska's text: earlier masters spoke of the Art in riddles and dispersed fragments, so that a reader could spend a life assembling what any one of them knew; he will instead set down the whole in order — substances, apparatus, procedures — and he defends the Art against its despisers on a single ground: that men who failed at it failed in the doing, through ignorance of the materials, the measures, or the order of operations, and that a failure of procedure is not a disproof of principle. The argument's shape — completeness promised, obscurity blamed, failure reassigned to method — is not in dispute among the book's modern readers (Section XVII). Two Books, Not One: al-Asrār and Sirr al-asrār The bibliography must now be untangled, because al-Rāzī wrote two closely related alchemical books and the tradition — Arabic, Latin, and modern — has repeatedly tangled them. The Kitāb al-Asrār , the Book of Secrets , is the shorter and, on the usual scholarly account, the earlier of the two: a compact presentation of the same classification, apparatus, and procedure material. The Kitāb Sirr al-asrār , the Book of the Secret of Secrets , is the fuller work: it carries the dedication to al-Manṣūr, expands the apparatus and procedure sections, and presents itself as the complete statement. The two overlap extensively — whole stretches of substance-description and procedure run parallel — and manuscripts and catalogues have not always kept their titles apart, a confusion Ullmann's catalogue of the Arabic scientific literature (1972) does much to sort. The distinction this article observes is therefore stated plainly: where the fuller, dedicated text is meant, Sirr al-asrār is meant, and Ruska's edition is the access; where the shorter companion is meant, it is named Kitāb al-Asrār in so many words. Stapleton and Husain's pioneering English study of 1927 worked principally from the Asrār material, which is one reason the shorter book is disproportionately familiar to English readers. KITĀB AL-ASRĀR — BOOK OF SECRETS The shorter companion work. Same sixfold classification, same bench orientation, more briefly stated. The principal basis of Stapleton and Husain's 1927 English presentation of al-Rāzī's chemistry. KITĀB SIRR AL-ASRĀR — SECRET OF SECRETS The fuller, dedicated work: preface to al-Manṣūr ibn Isḥāq, expanded apparatus list, expanded procedures. The subject of this article, in Ruska's 1937 edition. NOT THIS BOOK: THE PSEUDO-ARISTOTELIAN SECRET The famous Latin Secretum secretorum — the pseudo-Aristotelian mirror for princes, letters to Alexander on kingship, physiognomy, and regimen — is a different work that shares half a title. It is not al-Rāzī's book, contains no laboratory, and must never be cited as if it did. The confusion is old, common, and refused throughout this archive (see Section XVI). RUSKA 1937: THE STANDARD ACCESS Julius Ruska, Al-Rāzī's Buch Geheimnis der Geheimnisse (Berlin, 1937): Arabic text edited from the manuscript tradition with German translation and commentary. Every paraphrase of the Sirr al-asrār in this article follows Ruska's edition, and is labelled paraphrase accordingly. A word on the title itself. Sirr al-asrār , "the secret of secrets", sounds like the deepest veiling of all — and the book then proceeds, with almost comic directness, to inventory the workshop. Al-Rāzī keeps the genre's title and declines the genre's method: the secret, his preface argues in paraphrase, was never a riddle. It was a procedure nobody had yet written down in order. V. Three Parts: Substances, Apparatus, Procedures The Secret of Secrets , in Ruska's edition, is built in three parts, and the build is the most quoted fact about it — rightly, because no earlier surviving Arabic alchemical book is built so. Part One treats the substances : the complete materia of the Art, classified and described kind by kind — the six mineral classes of Sections VII–VIII, then the vegetable and animal substances of Section IX — with the marks by which each kind is known, chosen, and tested. Part Two treats the apparatus : the furnaces, vessels, and tools of Section X, described as instruments with specifications, before any procedure is allowed to presuppose them. Part Three treats the procedures : the operations of Section XI applied, in the worked sequences of Sections XII–XIII, to the preparation of spirits and bodies and finally to the composition of elixirs. Substances, apparatus, procedures: the order of a pharmacopoeia, of a surgical manual, of a hospital formulary — of every genre, that is, in which al-Rāzī's medical profession had already learned to write — applied for the first time, at this completeness, to the alchemical workshop. Part Contents What the part does I. Substances The six mineral classes — spirits, bodies, stones, vitriols, boraces, salts — then vegetable and animal substances, each kind described with its identifying marks and its behaviour under treatment Fixes the vocabulary of the whole book: a procedure in Part Three can name a substance and be understood, because Part One has already said what the name covers and how the stuff behaves in fire II. Apparatus Furnaces (athanor, blast furnace, self-feeding furnace), crucibles, alembics and cucurbits, the descensory, the blind alembic and aludel, baths, bellows, and the hand tools Fixes the instrumentarium: nothing in Part Three is done in a vessel Part Two has not described — the manual's equivalent of a surgical text describing its instruments before its operations III. Procedures The operations — calcination, sublimation, distillation, solution, coagulation, fixation, ceration, and their companions — applied to spirits, bodies, and compound preparations, rising to the elixir procedures Fixes the method: sequences in stated order, with the signs of completion and the remedies for failure, so that a second worker can repeat the work and locate his own errors Why does the structure make this the most laboratory-facing Arabic alchemical text that survives ? The claim needs its qualifiers. It is about surviving texts: earlier Arabic alchemy survives in fragments too broken to compare as books. It is about structure , not truth: a book can be perfectly laboratory-facing and its elixir procedures still unworkable, as Section XVII weighs. And it is comparative within the Arabic tradition: the Jābir corpus contains vastly more procedure, but dispersed and veiled by design across hundreds of treatises, where al-Rāzī concentrates his whole art between two covers in bench order. With those qualifiers, the claim stands on the structure alone: no other surviving Arabic alchemical book lets a reader answer, from the book itself, what a laboratory asks every morning — what have we got, what do we work with, and what do we do, in what order? // HOW TO READ THE SECTIONS THAT FOLLOW // Sections VI–IX give Part One, Sections X–XI give Part Two and the operations of Part Three, and Sections XII–XIII give Part Three's procedures as worked examples. The division mirrors the book's own, deliberately: a reader who works through the article in order has handled the substances before meeting the furnaces, and the furnaces before the procedures — which is how al-Rāzī insists the Art itself be learned. Cross-references to the Greco-Roman division's Fire and Assay article mark where the Arabic laboratory inherits Greek testing discipline; references to Maria the Jewess mark where its apparatus descends, through Alexandria, from the oldest named workshop in the tradition. VI. Classification by Bench Behaviour: The Analytical Point Part One of the Secret of Secrets divides the mineral substances of the Art into six classes . The division is usually quoted as a list — spirits, bodies, stones, vitriols, boraces, salts — and left there, as if it were a piece of medieval tidiness. It is considerably more than that, and this section states the article's analytical point before the classes themselves are given, so that the detail of Sections VII–VIII can be read as evidence for it. Al-Rāzī's classes are defined by bench behaviour: by what the substances do when the workshop treats them. A spirit is not a substance with a volatile essence contemplated in the abstract. It is a substance that rises — that sublimes or evaporates under fire and can be caught above. A body is a substance that stands — that endures the furnace, melts without fleeing, and can be cast, hammered, and weighed after firing as it was before. A stone is a mineral that does neither: it neither flees nor properly melts, and the Art must break, calcine, or dissolve it by indirection. The salts dissolve in water; the boraces melt and make other things melt with them; the vitriols bite, colour, and yield sharp waters on distillation. Each class is a prediction: treat a member so, and it will answer so . Classification, in this book, is compressed procedure. The contrast that proves the point is with the classifications al-Rāzī did not use. He did not classify by the four elements or the four qualities, though that scheme was available to him from the whole Greek tradition this archive's Greco-Roman division describes — a scheme that sorts by essence, by a body's supposed inner constitution of hot, cold, wet, and dry. He did not classify by the Jābirian Balance, by letters and their numerical weights. He classified the way his own medicine classified drugs in the Galenic manner: by powers known through effects, graded by observation. A Galenic simple is hot in the second degree because of what it observably does to a body. A Rāzian substance is a spirit because of what it observably does in a furnace. The epistemology is one and the same, and it is why Stapleton, himself a chemist, could recognise so many of al-Rāzī's substances from their described behaviours in 1927: behaviour-descriptions survive translation in a way that essence-descriptions do not. A text that says a substance is phlegmatic tells a modern reader nothing testable. A text that says it rises in the aludel, melts in the crucible, or dissolves in water and recrystallises on evaporation has told him where to look. // A CLASS IS A PROMISE ABOUT FIRE // Read the six classes as six fire-verdicts. Spirits flee the fire upward. Bodies endure it and melt in place. Stones resist it and must be broken down. Vitriols decompose in it, colouring and corroding. Boraces flow in it and carry other things into flow. Salts mostly fear water more than fire: they dissolve, and can be recovered by drying. The scheme is not modern chemistry — sulphur and mercury share a class with sal ammoniac, which no modern table would allow — but it is a workshop truth: those four really are the things in the store-room that will leave by the chimney if the vessel is not sealed. Two limits must be entered in fairness. The classes are not perfectly behavioural: the bodies are the seven metals of the ancient canonical list, a traditional roster, and the spirits carry theoretical freight from the sulphur–mercury doctrine (Section XIV), mercury and sulphur being the Art's principles as well as two volatile store-room substances. The classification is behaviour organising tradition, not replacing it; and within the classes the descriptions mix bench marks with lore, as every pre-modern materia medica does. The analytical point survives both limits: the sorting principle is operational — volatility, fusibility, solubility, behaviour in fire. Sections VII–VIII now give the classes in his order. VII. The Six Mineral Classes I: Spirits and Bodies The Spirits (arwāḥ): The Volatile Four The spirits , arwāḥ (singular rūḥ ), are four in number, and the fourfold list is one of the most stable in the whole book: mercury, sulphur, the arsenic sulphides, and sal ammoniac . In paraphrase of Ruska's text, what unifies them is stated operationally: they are the substances that cannot be held in open fire — they rise, evaporate, or sublime away, and the whole technology of sealed vessels, alembics, and aludels (Section X) exists in large part to catch them. Mercury ( zaybaq ) flees as vapour and amalgamates the bodies it touches. Sulphur ( kibrīt ) burns and rises, and carries the Art's colouring and hardening powers. The arsenics ( zarnīkh ) — the yellow sulphide, orpiment, and the red sulphide, realgar, counted as kinds of one spirit — sublime to a deadly, whitening vapour: the workshop's great whitening agent and its great poison, in one. Sal ammoniac ( nūshādir ) sublimes clean, without residue when pure, and serves the Art as a volatile salt that can carry other substances up with it and bite into metals' surfaces. Four substances, one behaviour, and — not coincidentally — the four most dangerous things in the store-room. The class is a safety warning as well as a taxonomy. Class Members (principal) Unifying bench behaviour Spirits — arwāḥ Mercury; sulphur; arsenic sulphides (orpiment, yellow; realgar, red); sal ammoniac Volatility: rise, evaporate, or sublime under fire; must be worked in closed or luted vessels and caught above; act on bodies by vapour and amalgam Bodies — ajsād Gold; silver; copper; iron; lead; tin; khārṣīnī (zinc) Fixity with fusibility: endure fire, melt without fleeing, solidify again unchanged in kind; can be cast, filed, hammered, calcined, and revived Stones — aḥjār Marcasite; magnesia; malachite; tutty; talc; haematite; lapis lazuli; gypsum; glass; and their companions (Section VIII) Resistance: neither flee nor truly melt; must be calcined, ground, dissolved, or fluxed before the Art can use what is in them Vitriols — zājāt The vitriols by colour: green, white, yellow, red, and black kinds (names vary; Section VIII) Astringent, colouring, corrosive earths: dissolve in water, decompose in fire, and yield sharp distilled waters; the dyer's and ink-maker's minerals as much as the alchemist's Boraces — bawāriq Natron; tinkār (borax); and the borax kinds, incl. Armenian borax and the borax called of bread Fluxing: melt readily and make the substances mixed with them melt and join; the solderer's and refiner's helpers; clean metals' surfaces in the melt Salts — amlāḥ Common salt; sal alkali (qilī); salt of lime; salt of ashes; bitter salt; salt of urine; and their companions (Section VIII) Solubility: dissolve in water, recrystallise on evaporation or coagulation; bite, preserve, and — in calcination mixtures — help break bodies down The Bodies (ajsād): The Seven Metals The bodies , ajsād (singular jasad ), are the seven metals of the ancient canon, in the order the text's descriptions presuppose: gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, tin — and the seventh, khārṣīnī , the metal the Arabic tradition associated with China ( Ṣīn ), identified in the modern literature, following Stapleton and Ruska, with zinc or a zinc-rich alloy. The identification deserves its caution stated: metallic zinc was not isolated as a European laboratory product until the early modern period, but zinc-rich metals and zinc ores were traded from the East far earlier, and al-Rāzī's descriptions of khārṣīnī — in paraphrase, a body resembling tin in some marks and iron in others, brittle where tin is soft — fit a zinc-bearing metal better than any other candidate the commentators have offered. This article gives the identification as the standard one, flagged as an identification, not as a certainty the text itself states. What unifies the bodies, in paraphrase of the class's treatment, is fixity with fusibility : a body can be melted in the crucible, cast into a mould, and taken out the same metal it went in — which no spirit survives and no stone achieves. Each body is described by its bench marks: colour, weight in the hand, ring and hardness, behaviour at file and hammer, its melting heat relative to its companions, and the company it keeps — which spirits attack it, which salts calcine it, which fluxes clean it. How This Bibliography Is Organised This page is a hub utility page, and it carries no wing badge of its own : it spans both of the hub's wings at once — Wing I, Transmission , and Wing II, The Art — and a single badge would mislabel half of what it lists. Instead, the wing discipline is applied at the level of the sections. The Antiquity division's bibliography sorts its sources by its three evidence tiers; this hub has no tiers, and its natural sort is different. It sorts by wing and by kind : first the primary texts themselves, in the editions and translations the hub reads them in (§II), and then the modern scholarship, divided between the wing whose questions it answers (§III for Transmission, §IV for The Art). A work that serves both wings — Manfred Ullmann's handbook is the standing example — is entered where its weight in this hub chiefly falls and cross-noted in its grounds line, not duplicated. Primary texts come first for a reason that is specific to this field, and the reader should understand it before using the list. Arabic alchemy is read, even by specialists, through a narrow gate. Of the Jābirian corpus — some two hundred surviving treatises — only a small fraction exists in a modern critical edition, and a smaller fraction still in any European-language translation. Al-Rāzī's great alchemical summa is accessible in a German rendering of 1937 and in piecemeal English studies, not in a complete modern English edition. Ibn Umayl's major work waited until the twenty-first century for its full critical presentation. A bibliography of this hub that listed “Jābir, works” or “al-Rāzī, Secret of Secrets ” without naming which edition, whose translation, and how much of the text that edition actually covers would be concealing the single most important fact about the evidence: its partiality. Section II therefore names editions and translations as precisely as the articles use them, and its grounds lines say, entry by entry, what remains unedited and untranslated. Where the hub says a work “remains untranslated”, that is a statement about the whole work; excerpts, extracts, and paraphrases in the secondary literature do not contradict it, and the entries distinguish them. The governing rule of the page is the archive's honesty rule, stated on the hub index and applied here without exception: an entry appears only if the hub's articles actually rest on it. Nothing is listed for decoration, for completeness of the field, or because a bibliography of Arabic alchemy is “supposed” to contain it. Every entry below is harvested from an article's Sources section or from the hub index's own method and sources discussion, and every entry carries a tag line naming the article or articles it grounds. Where several articles rest on the same work — Paul Kraus's Jābir ibn Ḥayyān stands behind the Jābir article, the sulphur–mercury article, and the hub's dating practice throughout — the work is consolidated into a single entry in its home section and every article that uses it is tagged. Within each section the entries run in a deliberate order: §II follows the hub's own reading order, from the catalogue tools through the great corpora to the reference works; §§III–IV run alphabetically by author, as a working shelf should. // CONSULTED, READ, RESTED ON // Three verbs do different work in this hub, and the bibliography keeps them apart. A work is rested on when an article's claim would fall without it: it is tagged to that article. A work is read when it was worked through in full for an article, whether or not a single claim finally cites it. A work is consulted when it was opened for a check — a date, a catalogue number, a manuscript shelfmark — and used at exactly that strength. Where an article's Sources section records the weaker relation (“as cited in”, “via the discussions in”, “consulted for the catalogue numbers”), the entry below preserves the limitation rather than upgrading it. A citation here is a measurement, not a compliment. Each entry gives the citation as the scholarship standardly gives it — author, title, year, and journal or publisher where those are certain — followed by one grounds line on what the work grounds in this hub: the text it makes readable, the claim it carries, the dating it fixes, or the account for which it is the cited authority. The grounds lines are written to be checked. A reader who wants to test any claim in this hub should be able to walk from the claim, to the article's Sources section, to this page, and out to the work itself without a gap — and, just as important, should be able to see at each step how much of the work the hub is standing on: the whole monograph, one chapter, a catalogue entry, a translated excerpt. In a field where a famous name can conceal a three-page excerpt, that visibility is the bibliography's main service. §II — THE TEXTS THEMSELVES Editions, translations, and the catalogue tools that stand in for editions where none exist. This section is deliberately short and deliberately precise: it is the whole of the hub's direct access to its primary literature, and its grounds lines mark, without softening, how partial that access is. §§III–IV — THE MODERN FIELD The scholarship the articles argue with and build on, sorted by wing. Wing I's shelf is a history-of-transmission shelf — translation movements, bridge cities, the Latin door. Wing II's shelf is a history-of-the-art shelf — the corpus studies, the laboratory histories, the editions' companions. Several names stand on both shelves; each is entered once. How a reader uses the page follows from how it is built. Start from the claim, not from the shelf: find the article, read its Sources section for the strength at which each work is cited there, and then find the work here for its full citation and its grounds. A reader who starts from the shelf instead — who wants to know, before reading an article, what kind of evidence it stands on — can read the tag lines in reverse: collect every entry tagged to an article and the article's evidentiary skeleton is on the table, editions first and interpretations after, each at its named strength. Both directions are deliberate. A bibliography that only supports the first is a footnote apparatus; one that only supports the second is a reading list. This page is built to be the first, and to be usable, with its limits visible, as the second. A last word on transliteration, because a bibliography is where inconsistent spelling does its quiet damage. Arabic names and titles are given throughout in the hub's scholarly transliteration, with macrons and diacritics retained: Jābir ibn Ḥayyān , al-Rāzī , Ibn Umayl , Kitāb sirr al-asrār , Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ . Where a cited work's own title page uses an older or simpler spelling — Holmyard's “Geber”, the Memoirs ' “Muhammad ibn Umail” — the entry gives the work's title as published and the hub's transliteration in the grounds line, so that a catalogue search under either form will find the book. Latinised names (Geber, Rhazes, Senior Zadith) are treated as what they are: separate publication identities, cross-referenced, never silently merged with the Arabic names they descend from. The fullest statement of why that separation matters is §V's standing-corrections note; the bibliography enforces it entry by entry. II. Primary Texts — Editions and Translations The entries in this section are not “the primary sources” in the abstract. They are the material forms in which the primary sources reach this hub: a catalogue raisonné that functions as an edition-tool for a corpus no complete edition exists for; a 1928 Paris edition that is still the printed Arabic text of the Jābirian treatises it covers; a 1937 German rendering that remains the fullest modern access to al-Rāzī's summa; a 1933 journal memoir that gave the scholarly world its first substantial Ibn Umayl in English; a twenty-first-century edition series that has finally superseded it. Read the dates as part of the evidence. Much of this hub's primary shelf was built between 1928 and 1948, by a small generation of scholar-editors — Holmyard, Ruska, Stapleton, Garbers, Kraus — whose work has been extended but, in several cases, never replaced. The hub says so where it is so, because a claim resting on a 1933 excerpt is a different kind of claim from one resting on a 2009 critical edition, and the reader is entitled to know which kind they are holding. Two conventions govern the section. First, coverage is stated, not implied : where an edition covers part of a work, the entry names the part; where a translation is of excerpts, the entry says excerpts. Second, the Latin witnesses are filed here, with the Arabic ones, when the hub reads them as primary evidence — the Turba Philosophorum in Ruska's edition, Morienus in Stavenhagen's translation, and pseudo-Geber's Summa in Newman's — because the hub's threshold articles treat the Latin texts as primary documents of the transmission, not as secondary literature about it. They are labelled Latin at every mention. Nothing in this section is a modern paraphrase dressed as a text: where the hub's knowledge of a work comes through a modern study rather than an edition, the study is the entry, in §§III–IV, and the grounds line there says so. Kraus, Paul. The catalogue raisonné of the Jābirian corpus, in Jābir ibn Ḥayyān: Contribution à l'histoire des idées scientifiques dans l'Islam , vol. I: Le corpus des écrits jābiriens (Cairo: Institut français d'archéologie orientale, 1943) — the numbered inventory of the treatises ascribed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, with manuscript witnesses, incipits, and cross-references, used in this hub as an edition-tool: the means by which a treatise is identified, counted, and located where no modern edition of it exists. The companion monograph is entered as scholarship in §IV. Grounds the corpus's count, its collection structure, and every treatise identification in the Jābir article. Wing I — Transmission: Modern Scholarship Wing I asks how the art travelled : by what roads, in whose hands, under whose patronage, and at what cost in vocabulary and meaning. Its scholarship is therefore a shelf of histories — of a translation movement, of two bridge cities, of a Hermetic tradition's Arabic career, of a second translation movement, three centuries later, that carried the rebuilt art into Latin. The shelf's centre of gravity is Baghdad. Dimitri Gutas's account of the Graeco-Arabic translation movement as a social phenomenon — funded, staffed, and argued over, not a caliph's whim — is the wing's model and its most-tagged entry; George Saliba's revision of the same movement's origins and afterlife is its standing interlocutor; and Franz Rosenthal's older survey remains the shelf's orientation volume, the form in which two generations of readers first met the classical heritage in Islam. Around that centre stand the city studies (Tamara Green on Harran), the prophet-of-science study (Kevin van Bladel on the Arabic Hermes), the handbook that covers both wings (Ullmann), the Latin-door studies (Charles Burnett), and the medical-institution literature (Michael Dols, Vivian Nutton) on which the hub's Gundeshapur account is held at its real evidentiary strength. A discipline note, because Wing I's questions invite a characteristic error. Transmission history is written from survivals: translators' prefaces, catalogues like the Fihrist (§II), colophons, and the manuscripts that happen to remain. Every work below is cited in this hub for what its evidence can carry, and the hub's own rule — stated on the index and repeated in the Gundeshapur article — is that a late source's institutional splendour is reported as that source's claim, not as the institution's history. Where the scholarship itself divides — on the scale of the Bayt al-Ḥikma, on the depth of Gundeshapur's academy, on how much of Harran's Hermetica is Harranian — the articles state the division with the positions named, and this bibliography tags the works on each side.
