Wing II — The Art: Modern Scholarship Wing II asks what the Arabic world made of the art it received: the Jābirian system of the balance, the sulphur–mercury theory, al-Rāzī's laboratory order, al-Kindī's perfumery, the Brethren's filing of the art inside a complete philosophy, Ibn Umayl's allegorical commentary. Its scholarship is accordingly a shelf of corpus studies, laboratory histories, and field surveys, and it has a clear patriarch. Paul Kraus's two volumes of 1942–43 — the catalogue entered as a tool in §II, the monograph entered here — redated the Jābirian corpus, reconstructed its system, and set the questions the field still argues: the shelf's other Jābir entries (Sezgin's counter-dating, Haq's systematic exposition, Lory's studies) are all, in one way or another, answers to Kraus. Around the corpus studies stand the bench histories — Stapleton's papers, Levey's pharmacological and perfumery work, Multhauf's and Forbes's histories of chemistry and distillation — and the two modern syntheses, Newman's and Principe's, in which the Arabic art takes its argued place in the longer history of chymistry. Holmyard's Alchemy of 1957 stands on the shelf as what it is: the field's classic English survey, by the editor of §II's 1928 texts, read in this hub as a document of the scholarship's own history as much as an authority for its claims. The wing's discipline is the index's workshop rule, and it shapes what these entries are cited for . A claim about doctrine is admitted in Wing II alongside the evidence of practice; the scholarship below is therefore tagged not only to the articles it informs but, in its grounds lines, to the kind of evidence it supplies — system, bench, or both. The Brethren of Purity were transmitters too — their encyclopedia is one of the great relay stations of Greek science into Arabic high culture — but this hub rests on them for what they filed : the place their system assigns to minerals, metals, and the art itself. That is a Wing II question, asked of a Wing II kind of evidence, and the scholarship that answers it is shelved here, beside the Oxford editions (§II) through which the hub reads the epistles themselves. Two Cities, One Bridge: Why Ḥarrān and Gundeshapur Belong Together The Greek art did not travel from Alexandria to Baghdad in a straight line, and it did not travel by itself. Between the last Alexandrian commentators and the first Arabic systematisers stands a corridor of cities, schools, and bilingual households in which Greek learning was kept in working order for three centuries by people who were, for the most part, neither Greek nor Muslim: the Syriac-speaking Christians of Mesopotamia and Persia, and — the corridor’s strangest and most instructive survival — the pagan community of Ḥarrān. This article treats the corridor’s two great nodes together, and the pairing is deliberate. Ḥarrān (the Roman Carrhae, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, near the Syrian border) is the bridge’s northern, Hermetic pier. Gundeshapur (Jundaysābūr, Syriac Beth Lapat, in Khuzistan in south-western Iran) is its southern, medical pier. Different religions, different empires, different languages of daily life — but the same structural job. Each city held a body of Greek knowledge inside a non-Greek civilisation, in a form that civilisation could use, until Baghdad was ready to ask for it. The pairing also disciplines the evidence, because the two cities fail in opposite directions in the popular literature. Ḥarrān attracts romance: a moon-god temple standing into the Islamic centuries, pagan philosophers in Arabic dress, Hermes worshipped under the caliphs. The romance has a real core — the Ḥarrānians were pagans, they did honour Hermes, and they did produce one of the translation movement’s greatest scholars — but the core is wrapped in medieval self-presentation and modern over-reading, and Sections IV to VI of this article separate the layers as carefully as the sources allow. Gundeshapur attracts inflation of the opposite kind: not romance but institutional fantasy, a fully organised “university” with faculties and an observatory, projected back into Sasanian Persia on the strength of sources written centuries later. Its real core — a hospital, a medical tradition, a dynasty of physicians the caliphs summoned by name — is impressive enough without the fantasy, and Section XIII states plainly what is solid and what is not. ḤARRĀN — THE NORTHERN PIER An ancient cult city of the moon god Sîn whose pagan community survived the Christianisation of the Roman East and the Islamic conquest, adopted the Qurʾānic name “Sabian” in the ninth century, and sent Baghdad its mathematicians, astrologers, and translators — Thābit ibn Qurra above all. See Sections II–IX. GUNDESHAPUR — THE SOUTHERN PIER A Sasanian royal city in Khuzistan, refounded with Roman prisoners, seat of Church of the East synods and of a Syriac medical tradition patronised by Khosrow I; home of the Bukhtīshūʿ family, whose summons to Baghdad in the eighth century physically carried the Galenic inheritance into the caliphal capital. See Sections X–XIII. THE SYRIAC SYSTEM — THE ROAD ITSELF Edessa, Nisibis, Reshaina, and the monasteries and schools between them: the institutional network that made Greek-to-Syriac translation a profession three centuries before Greek-to-Arabic translation existed, and through which the two-step transmission — Greek into Syriac, Syriac into Arabic — ran. See Sections XIV–XV. BAGHDAD — THE FAR BANK The Abbasid capital, where the corridor delivered its cargo to the translation movement : Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq’s circle, the Banū Mūsā’s patronage, and the caliphal hospitals. What Baghdad made of the cargo is the subject of this hub’s Jabir corpus article; this article ends at the delivery. A note on method, in the form this archive uses wherever the sources invite invention. No direct quotation is given in this article. Ancient and medieval texts are paraphrased throughout, and paraphrases are labelled as paraphrase where the wording matters. Where a claim rests on a single medieval reporter — and in Ḥarrān’s case many of the most vivid claims rest on exactly one — the reporter is named in the text, so the reader can weigh the claim at its true strength. Where modern scholars disagree, the disagreement is stated as a disagreement, with positions attached to names: Tardieu, Green, and van Bladel on Ḥarrān; Dols and Nutton on Gundeshapur. The Greco-Roman hub’s Transmission article treats the Syriac and Arabic reception from the Greek corpus’s side, in its Sections X and XI; this article consolidates and deepens that treatment from the bridge cities’ side, and follows its adjudications — above all, that Sergius of Reshaina is the context of the Syriac alchemical manuscripts, not, on surviving evidence, their translator. // NAMES AND SPELLINGS // Ḥarrān is the Arabic form of a name the city carried for millennia (Akkadian Ḫarrānu, “road, caravan route”; Greek Karrhai, Latin Carrhae). Gundeshapur is the Arabic Jundaysābūr, from Middle Persian Gundēšābuhr; its Syriac ecclesiastical name is Beth Lapat. Transliteration in this article follows the archive’s Arabic-hub convention, with ḥ, ṣ, ṭ, ʿ, and ʾ marked and long vowels macroned: Ṣābiʾa, Thābit ibn Qurra, Bukhtīshūʿ, Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq. Dates are CE throughout, with c. where approximate. The article’s shape follows the road. Sections II to IX walk Ḥarrān from its Bronze Age moon cult to its Baghdad diaspora. Sections X to XIII walk Gundeshapur from Shāpūr’s prisoner-city to the Bukhtīshūʿ summons. Sections XIV and XV step back to the Syriac system that connected both cities to each other and to Baghdad. Section XVI inventories the cargo — medicine, philosophy, astronomy and astrology, and the alchemical corpus — and asks what the crossing filtered out and what it transformed. Section XVII closes with the honest gaps: the things about these two cities that cannot now be known, stated as plainly as the things that can. II. Ḥarrān: The City of the Moon God Ḥarrān stands on the plain of the Balikh river, a tributary of the Euphrates, at the meeting of roads: north to Edessa (modern Şanlıurfa) and the Anatolian passes, west to the Euphrates crossings and Syria, east along the Khabur to upper Mesopotamia, south down the Balikh to Raqqa and the desert road to Iraq. The Akkadian name itself — Ḫarrānu, a road or caravan journey — advertises the function. A city at a crossroads in northern Mesopotamia is never only a city; it is a customs post, a garrison, a market, and a sanctuary for the travellers of four directions, and Ḥarrān was all four for an extraordinarily long time. It appears in the Hebrew Bible as the city where Abraham’s father Terah settled and died on the migration from Ur; in Assyrian records as a royal city and provincial capital; and in the second millennium BCE already as a cult centre of the moon god. The moon god is the city’s constant. Sîn , the great moon god of Mesopotamia whose other seat was Ur in the south, was worshipped at Ḥarrān in the temple called Eḫulḫul — Sumerian É-ḫúl-ḫúl, conventionally rendered “House of Joys” or “House of Rejoicing”. The temple’s antiquity is documented in royal inscriptions across two millennia: Assyrian kings of the early first millennium BCE record its restoration, and its most famous rebuilding belongs to the last king of Babylon, Nabonidus (r. 556–539 BCE), whose devotion to Sîn of Ḥarrān was a matter of family piety — his mother, Adad-guppi, was a lifelong devotee of the Ḥarrān moon god, and her autobiographical inscription, one of the most personal documents to survive from the ancient Near East, records her prayers at Ḥarrān and her son’s restoration of Eḫulḫul after its destruction in the wars of the seventh century BCE. When Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE, Ḥarrān’s cult was already ancient beyond the memory of any living tradition in the city. It would outlast, in recognisable continuity of place and priesthood, the Persian, Macedonian, and Parthian empires. Carrhae: The Roman Catastrophe The classical world knew the city as Carrhae , and knew it for a disaster. In 53 BCE the Roman triumvir Marcus Licinius Crassus, invading Parthia in search of a conquest to match his colleagues’, was drawn onto the open plain near Carrhae and destroyed there by the Parthian general Surena: the Roman heavy infantry, unable to close with horse-archers who retired as they shot and were resupplied with arrows by camel train, were shot to pieces over two days; Crassus was killed in a parley turned violent, his son Publius died with his Gallic cavalry, and some twenty thousand Romans were killed and ten thousand captured, with the legionary eagles lost — a humiliation Rome remembered for centuries and avenged, in her own accounting, only when the standards were recovered by diplomacy under Augustus. Plutarch’s Life of Crassus is the fullest ancient narrative. For this article the battle matters for two reasons. It fixed Ḥarrān in the classical imagination as a place at the edge of the Roman world, in the contested marches between Rome and Persia — which is what, strategically, it remained for seven hundred years. And it illustrates the city’s permanent condition: empires fought over Ḥarrān because of where it stood, and the city’s own institutions — temple, priesthood, market — survived each change of garrison. The moon god’s city outlasted its conquerors as a matter of routine. 2nd mill. BCE THE MOON CULT ESTABLISHED Ḥarrān is a cult centre of Sîn and a station on the upper Mesopotamian road network; the Eḫulḫul temple stands at the city’s heart. r. 556–539 BCE NABONIDUS RESTORES EḪULḪUL The last Babylonian king rebuilds the moon temple, fulfilling, in his inscriptions’ telling, the vow of his mother Adad-guppi, the god’s devotee. 53 BCE CARRHAE Crassus’ invasion of Parthia is annihilated on the plain by Carrhae; the lost eagles become a byword for Roman disaster in the East. 363 CE JULIAN AT ḤARRĀN The emperor Julian, marching to his Persian war, sacrifices at Ḥarrān — a pagan emperor honouring a still-pagan city on the eve of the Christian empire’s consolidation. c. 639–640 CE THE ISLAMIC CONQUEST Ḥarrān surrenders to the Arab armies during the conquest of the Jazīra. The city passes under Muslim rule with its pagan community intact — the precondition of everything in Sections IV–IX. One geographical fact deserves emphasis before the narrative moves on, because it explains Ḥarrān’s later intellectual character. The city stood in the Syriac-speaking world. Its countryside, its Christian neighbours, and much of its own population spoke Syriac; its learned pagan families were, by the early Islamic centuries, trilingual in the pattern the bridge required — Syriac at home and in the street, Greek in the inherited books, Arabic increasingly in administration and ambition. A Ḥarrānian scholar of the ninth century did not need to learn the bridge’s languages as foreign tongues. He had been raised standing on the bridge. III. Carrhae to the Caliphate: A Pagan City Inside Successive Empires The Christianisation of the Roman Empire transformed Ḥarrān’s neighbours and largely passed Ḥarrān by. Edessa, a day’s journey north, became one of the great Christian cities of the East, its schools and martyria famous across the Syriac world. Ḥarrān, by contrast, is reported again and again in late-antique sources as a stronghold of the old religion: the emperor Julian’s visit in 363 CE, when he sacrificed in the city on his march to Persia, was a pagan emperor’s deliberate courtesy to a pagan population; Procopius, writing in the sixth century, still treats the Ḥarrānians as pagans in a Christian empire; Syriac Christian writers of the fifth and sixth centuries complain of Ḥarrān’s idolatry in the tone men use for a neighbour’s incorrigible habit, not a dying one. The city had Christian inhabitants and, in time, bishops; it was never a pagan enclave in the sense of a place without Christians. But its civic identity — temple, priesthood, festival calendar, the great temple of Sîn on its mound — remained pagan long after paganism had ceased to be a public option almost everywhere else in the Roman East. Why Ḥarrān held out is a question the sources answer only obliquely, and this article assembles the oblique answers and labels the assembly as interpretation. The city’s frontier position mattered: it lay in the war zone between Rome and Persia, changed hands, and was repeatedly more valuable to its rulers as a loyal garrison and market than as a mission field. The moon cult’s antiquity and civic centrality mattered: to suppress Eḫulḫul was to suppress the city’s reason for existing, and no emperor needed that fight. And Ḥarrān’s paganism was, by late antiquity, an educated paganism: the city’s leading families cultivated Greek philosophy alongside the old cult, in the pattern of the late-antique pagan intelligentsia from Athens to Alexandria, which gave the community intellectual defences — a theology, a cosmology, an account of its own rites as philosophy enacted — that mere custom would not have supplied. How much of that philosophical colouring was old and how much was a late-antique renovation is one of the disputes Section VI takes up. That the colouring existed, by the Islamic period, is not disputed. Under Islam: The Protected Anomaly Ḥarrān surrendered to the Arab conquerors of the Jazīra around 639–640 CE, on terms of the kind the conquest generation standardly granted: the population kept its property and its worship on payment of tribute. For Jews and Christians the arrangement had a clear Qurʾānic and legal frame — they were ahl al-kitāb , People of the Book, entitled to the protected ( dhimmī ) status. For pagans it had, in principle, no frame at all: the early Islamic legal tradition was divided on whether non-scriptural communities could hold protected status, and the Ḥarrānians’ astral cult — temples, images, planetary worship — was precisely the shirk , the association of partners with God, that the Qurʾān condemns most severely. Yet the Ḥarrānians were not, in the event, converted by force or expelled. They persisted as a recognisable pagan community under Muslim rule for centuries — taxed, occasionally harassed, periodically required to explain themselves, and repeatedly able to do so. The explanation they eventually gave, and the name they gave it under, is the subject of the next three sections, and it is the single most consequential act of self-definition in this archive’s transmission history: the moment a community talked its way, with a borrowed name and a borrowed prophet, into legal existence. // WHAT “SURVIVAL” MEANS HERE // Survival does not mean unchanged. The Ḥarrān of the ninth century was not the Ḥarrān of Nabonidus: its temple cult had absorbed Hellenistic astrology, Greek philosophy, and Hermetic literature; its language was Syriac and Arabic, not Akkadian; its god was addressed in philosophical as well as cultic terms. What survived was continuity of community, cult-place, and self-ascription — a pagan population that still knew itself to be the moon god’s city — across fourteen centuries of other people’s empires. Continuity of that kind is rare enough in the record to need no exaggeration. The community’s later fate can be stated briefly here, to keep the article’s main narrative in the bridge centuries. Ḥarrānian pagans are still visible in the sources of the tenth and eleventh centuries; the city’s great temple survived, in some form, into the Islamic period — medieval travellers describe its remains, and the site of the Great Mosque of Ḥarrān, built under the Umayyads and enlarged under the Abbasids, is traditionally identified with the temple precinct, a succession of sanctuary by sanctuary that the archaeology of the mound has not been able either to confirm in detail or to dismiss. Mongol destruction in the thirteenth century ended the city’s long urban life; the modern village of Harran, with its famous beehive houses, sits beside the ancient mound. The bridge, by then, had long since delivered its traffic: Ḥarrān’s scholars were in Baghdad, and Ḥarrān’s name was in the catalogues. IV. The Sabian Question: A Name in the Qurʾān Three times, the Qurʾān names a community called al-Ṣābiʾa — the Sabians. The verses (Q 2:62; Q 5:69; Q 22:17, in paraphrase) place them in distinguished company: those who believe, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians — whoever of them believes in God and the Last Day and does right has his reward with his Lord, and no fear shall be upon them. In Q 22:17 the Sabians appear again in the list of communities God will judge between on the Day of Resurrection, this time alongside the Magians (Zoroastrians) and the polytheists. The verses establish that the Sabians exist, that they are a recognised religious community of the Qurʾān’s world, and that they stand, somehow, on the scriptural side of the line that separates the saved from the idolaters. The verses do not say who the Sabians are. Everything else — two centuries of early Islamic exegesis, a monumental nineteenth-century monograph, and one of the neatest problems in the religious history of the Near East — follows from that silence. The early Muslim commentators themselves disagreed. In the exegesis collected by al-Ṭabarī and his successors, the Sabians of the Qurʾān are variously identified, in paraphrase of the reports he transmits: as a community between Judaism and Christianity; as worshippers of angels; as a group that prayed toward a qibla not Jerusalem’s; as the followers of a prophet of their own; or as the baptising sects of the southern Iraqi marshes — the communities among whom the Mandaeans , the gnostic baptists of the Shatt al-Arab region whose religion survives to this day, are the strongest modern candidates. The Mandaean identification rests on real correspondences: the Mandaeans’ self-designation in Arabic sources is indeed Ṣābiʾa , their religion is centred on repeated baptism (the root ṣ-b-ʾ in Aramaic carries the sense of immersing or baptising), and their home is the Iraq of the Qurʾān’s first audience. A related candidacy attaches the name to the Elchasaites, the Jewish-Christian baptist movement of the same Mesopotamian world. Modern scholarship on the Qurʾānic Sabians — the survey in Section VI gives the positions — broadly agrees that the Qurʾān’s Sabians were a baptist community or communities of Iraq, most plausibly connected with the Mandaean-Elchasaite milieu, and broadly agrees on the negative point that matters most for this article: whatever the Qurʾānic Sabians were, they were not, in the first instance, the pagans of Ḥarrān. Ḥarrān is in upper Mesopotamia, hundreds of miles from the marshes; its cult was astral and temple-based, not baptist; and no source before the ninth century calls its people Sabians. The name arrived in Ḥarrān late, and it arrived, on the tradition’s own telling, as a solution to a problem. // TWO SABIAN POPULATIONS, ONE NAME — THE ARCHIVE’S RULE // Nineteenth-century scholarship, above all Daniel Chwolsohn’s Die Ssabier und der Ssabismus (1856), established the distinction this archive observes throughout: the Qurʾānic Sabians — a baptist community of southern Iraq, plausibly Mandaean or Elchasaite — and the Ḥarrānian “Sabians” — the pagan community of Ḥarrān, which bore the name from the ninth century as a matter of legal self-designation. Where this hub writes “Sabian” of Ḥarrān, it means the Ḥarrānian community under its adopted name, and says so. Where it means the Qurʾān’s community, it says Qurʾānic Sabians. Conflating the two is the founding error of the older literature, and a surprising amount of modern popular writing still commits it. The legal stakes of the name explain why it was worth adopting. Protected status under Islamic law turned on scriptural standing: a community with a prophet and a revealed book could be tolerated as dhimmī ; a community of naked idolaters could not, on the stricter readings. A pagan community that could present itself as the Qurʾān’s own Sabians — named in the Book, promised reward in the Book — acquired, at a stroke, a Qurʾānic charter for its existence. It would still need a prophet and a book to complete the presentation. Ḥarrān, as the next section’s story shows, found both: the prophet was Hermes, whom Islamic tradition already identified with the Qurʾānic prophet Idrīs and, behind him, with the biblical Enoch; the book was the Hermetic corpus itself, the writings of Hermes, which a pagan philosophical community could present — not wholly cynically, since it genuinely revered them — as its scripture. Whether the transaction happened in a single dramatic interview in 830 CE, as the famous anecdote tells it, or accreted across a generation of negotiation, is the question Section V examines. That some such transaction happened — that the name is adopted, not inherited — is the consensus position of the modern scholarship this article follows, and it is stated here without hedging: the identification of the Ḥarrānians with the Qurʾānic Sabians is a legal-political act of self-designation, not a simple continuity. What remains genuinely disputed is how much stood behind the presentation — how much real Hermetic paganism the name covered. That dispute is Section VI. V. 830: Al-Maʾmūn Passes Through Ḥarrān The story, as the tradition tells it, has the completeness of a parable, and this article tells it first exactly at that strength — as the tradition reports it — before examining its credentials. The source is the Baghdad bookseller and bibliographer Ibn al-Nadīm , whose Fihrist (completed 987 CE) contains, in its account of the Sabians, the narrative paraphrased here from Bayard Dodge’s English translation ( The Fihrist of al-Nadīm , 1970). In or about the year 830 CE, the caliph al-Maʾmūn (r. 813–833), travelling through Ḥarrān on his way to campaign against the Byzantines, was struck by the appearance of the city’s pagan notables — their dress and their long hair, in the account’s telling, unlike anything Muslim, Christian, or Jewish — and demanded to know what religion they were. They answered that they were Ḥarrānians. The caliph pressed through the recognised categories: Are you Jews? Christians? Magians? Have you a book, a prophet? To each, in effect, no. His verdict, in paraphrase of the Fihrist ’s report, was an ultimatum: you are unbelievers and idolaters, whose blood it is lawful to shed; choose one of the recognised religions before I return from this campaign, or be put to the sword. The caliph marched on. The Ḥarrānians, in terror, scattered to consult — some converted to Islam or Christianity outright — and the remnant took counsel with a Ḥanafī jurist of the city, a shaykh learned in the law, who gave them the advice on which their survival turned, in paraphrase: when the caliph returns, say to him, We are the Sabians — for that is a name God has mentioned in the Qurʾān; profess it, and you will be safe. They did. And, the account continues, they completed the presentation the jurist’s advice implied: they took Hermes as their prophet and the writings of Hermes as their book. Al-Maʾmūn died in 833, before any return visit could test the claim; the name held; and the Ḥarrānians entered Islamic law and literature as the Sabians. It is a superb story. It is also, in the form we have it, a story told a century and a half after the event by a Baghdad bibliographer whose business was books, not archives, and transmitted in a chapter whose other contents — lists of Sabian writings, Hermes titles, doctrines — show Ibn al-Nadīm working from the Ḥarrānian community’s own later self-presentation. The modern discussion of its historicity divides, and the positions should be named. The maximal reading accepts the anecdote’s core: a real confrontation under al-Maʾmūn, a real ultimatum, a real juridical improvisation, with the dialogue’s polish conceded to the telling. Its defenders note that the story is circumstantially plausible — al-Maʾmūn did campaign through the Jazīra toward Byzantium in these years; his court was simultaneously the great patron of Greek translation, which made Ḥarrān’s Greek-holding pagans both suspect and valuable; and a community’s legal re-badging under pressure is a documented pattern of the period, not a novelist’s invention. The minimal reading treats the interview as an etiological story — a community’s foundation charter for a name it had in fact adopted gradually, dramatised into a single scene with a caliph, a deadline, and a clever jurist, the three furniture-pieces of Near Eastern legal folklore. Its defenders note the story’s folktale symmetry, the absence of any contemporary corroboration, and the convenience of the ending: the caliph conveniently dies before the claim is examined. The middle position , where much current scholarship in practice stands, holds that the anecdote preserves the memory of a real ninth-century process — the Ḥarrānians’ adoption of the Sabian name under legal pressure, very plausibly in al-Maʾmūn’s reign and plausibly sharpened by a real royal progress through the city — in a literary form that cannot be pressed for its details. This article adopts the middle position and writes accordingly: the 830 scene is cited as the tradition’s account, reported by Ibn al-Nadīm , and the adoption of the name is cited as the fact the account exists to explain. // THE OTHER WITNESSES // Ibn al-Nadīm is the fullest source for the 830 story, but the Ḥarrānian Sabians are described independently by a shelf of medieval authors: al-Bīrūnī in The Chronology of Ancient Nations (c. 1000 CE), who distinguishes the Ḥarrānian Sabians from what he calls the true Sabians of the south; al-Masʿūdī in The Meadows of Gold ; al-Shahrastānī in the Book of Religions and Sects (12th c.), the fullest heresiographical account; and the geographer-historian al-Dimashqī (14th c.). Their agreements establish the community’s existence and self-presentation; their disagreements — on doctrine, temples, and the name’s history — are the raw material of Section VI. One consequence of the adoption deserves its own paragraph, because it structures everything the medieval sources say afterwards. Once the Ḥarrānians were “Sabians”, they had to be able to perform Sabianism in the recognised scriptural shape: a prophet, a book, a doctrine of God that Muslim interlocutors could file. The community’s spokesmen — and it produced formidable spokesmen, Thābit ibn Qurra first among them — accordingly presented their religion in a form modern scholars call its philosophical register: one supreme God, remote and unknowable; beneath him the celestial intelligences and the planetary governors, honoured not as gods but as mediators and cosmic administrators; Hermes the prophet-philosopher, thrice great in the tradition’s genealogy; the stars’ cult as the visible liturgy of an invisible monotheism. How far that register describes what Ḥarrānian families actually did at the temple — and how far it is a translation, made under interrogation, of an older astral polytheism into the only theological language their rulers would accept — is not a question the sources let us answer cleanly. It is, in modern dress, the whole Sabian question, and it is to the modern argument that the article now turns. VI. Sabians, Ḥarrānians, Platonists: The Modern Debate Modern study of the Ḥarrānian Sabians begins with Chwolsohn’s Die Ssabier und der Ssabismus (1856), two volumes that collected the Arabic sources wholesale and drew the distinction Section IV adopted: the Qurʾānic Sabians and the Ḥarrānian name-bearers are different populations, and the Ḥarrānians’ claim to the name is a medieval transaction. Chwolsohn’s collection remained the field’s quarry for a century. The modern debate proper opens in 1986, with Michel Tardieu’s article on the Qurʾānic Sabians and the “Sabians” of Ḥarrān, and it is Tardieu’s thesis — brilliant, specific, and contested — that still organises the argument. The thesis, stated fairly, has three parts. First, the Qurʾānic Sabians are to be identified with the baptist milieu of southern Iraq — on Tardieu’s reading, the Elchasaites in particular. Second, the Ḥarrānians who took the name were not generic pagans but the heirs of Greek Neoplatonism : a community of pagan philosophers, in continuity — Tardieu argued — with the Athenian Academy’s diaspora after 529, whose religion was a philosophical paganism centred on Hermes and the Platonic theology, and whose “Sabianism” was that philosophy’s Arabic public dress. Third, and most consequentially for the history of philosophy, Tardieu proposed Ḥarrān as the missing link between the late-antique Greek schools and the Arabic philosophical tradition: the channel through which Athenian Neoplatonism reached Baghdad. He connected the proposal to the philosopher Simplicius, one of the 529 refugees of Section XI, suggesting Ḥarrān as the refugees’ eventual place of settlement and teaching. The thesis was received as Tardieu’s work usually is: with admiration for its learning and resistance to its construction. The critics’ objections, assembled across the following decades, are of three kinds. Evidential: no source places Simplicius or any Athenian refugee teaching at Ḥarrān; the link is an inference from Ḥarrān’s later philosophical colouring, and the colouring has nearer sources — Alexandria’s curriculum reached upper Mesopotamia through the Syriac schools for centuries without needing an Athenian transplant. Historical: Ḥarrān’s paganism has a documented local root — the Sîn cult, the astral religion of Mesopotamia — far older than any Academy, and the burden of proof lies on deriving the community from Athens rather than from its own temple. Methodological: Tardieu’s reading takes the Ḥarrānians’ philosophical self-presentation — the register Section V described, produced under legal interrogation — at face value as a description of the community’s religion, where the sources warrant treating it as, at least in part, a presentation. The thesis in its strong form — Ḥarrān as the Academy in exile — has not carried the field. Its weaker legacy is permanent: no one now writes about Ḥarrān without reckoning with the Greek philosophical stratum in its religion, and the 529 refugees’ story (Section XI) is no longer told without a footnote asking where, exactly, Simplicius went home to. TARDIEU (1986): THE PLATONIST ḤARRĀN The Ḥarrānian “Sabians” are pagan Neoplatonists, heirs of the Athenian school tradition; the Qurʾānic Sabians are Iraqi baptists; the name-transfer joins two unrelated groups, and Ḥarrān is Platonism’s bridge to Baghdad. Strong form not sustained; the philosophical stratum it identified is undisputed. GREEN (1992): THE MOON GOD’S CITY Tamara Green’s The City of the Moon God (1992) restores the local root: Ḥarrān’s religion as the long survival of Mesopotamian astral cult — Sîn, the planets, the temple — successively redressed in Hellenistic, philosophical, and finally Islamic-era language. Continuity of cult first; philosophy as its late-antique idiom, not its origin. VAN BLADEL (2009): THE ARABIC HERMES Kevin van Bladel’s The Arabic Hermes (2009) studies the Hermes tradition’s passage from Greek through Syriac into Arabic and places Ḥarrān inside that Syriac-Mesopotamian world: the community’s Hermeticism is real but is the local, Syriac-mediated Hermeticism of upper Mesopotamia, not an Athenian import; its learned men are products of the Syriac school culture as much as of any Greek survival. THE CONSENSUS FLOOR Agreed across positions: the Sabian name is adopted, not inherited; the community was genuinely pagan and genuinely learned; Hermes stood at its centre; its scholars really did carry Greek learning to Baghdad. Disputed: the proportions — how much cult, how much philosophy, how much presentation — in the compound. This article’s adjudication, following the three positions above and stating it as the archive’s, is as follows. On the name: settled. The Ḥarrānians are not the Qurʾānic Sabians; the identification is a ninth-century legal-political act of self-designation, whether or not the 830 scene happened as Ibn al-Nadīm tells it. On continuity: Green’s local root is the sound base — a Mesopotamian astral cult with unbroken civic continuity at Ḥarrān is documented from Nabonidus to the Islamic sources in a way no Athenian transplant is. On the Hermetic and philosophical stratum: real, but routed as van Bladel routes it — through the Syriac world Ḥarrān actually lived in, enriched by the same Greek school culture that reached Edessa and Nisibis, rather than through a single dramatic transplant from Athens. On survival’s extent: honestly disputed, and stated here as disputed — the medieval descriptions attest a living cult with temples, festivals, and sacrifices into the tenth century and beyond, while how much of the philosophical Hermeticism was practised religion and how much was the learned self-image of a scholarly caste within the community cannot be recovered from sources written, almost all of them, by outsiders or by the caste itself. Section VII now describes that Hermeticism at the strength the sources support: medieval descriptions, named as such. VII. Ḥarrān’s Hermeticism: Temples, Planets, and Hermes–Idrīs At the centre of Ḥarrānian religion, as the medieval sources describe it, stands Hermes . The identification that made him available to a community living under Islam was already old and already triple: the Greek Herme

A Man Known Only by His Books: The Thinness of the Record Begin with what is not known, because with Ibn Umayl the not-known is most of the biography. Muḥammad ibn Umayl al-Tamīmī was an Egyptian alchemist who flourished in the tenth century CE — the floruit this article uses, c. 900–960 , is the conventional scholarly placement, inferred from the authorities he quotes, from the authorities who quote him, and from the internal evidence of his works, not from a dated document of his life. No contemporary biography of him survives. The Arabic biographical literature that preserves lives, teachers, journeys, and death dates for physicians, philosophers, and transmitters in abundance preserves, for Ibn Umayl, essentially the name, the tribal nisba al-Tamīmī, the Egyptian setting, and the books. He has no anecdotes. He has no recorded master whose biography can be used to date him, no recorded pupil whose career carries his teaching forward under his name, no court, no patron, no city quarter, no tomb. The thinness of the record must be stated plainly, in the form this archive uses wherever the sources invite invention: almost nothing is documented about Ibn Umayl’s life, and this article invents none of it. What survives is a body of writing — substantial, systematic, and unlike anything else in the Arabic alchemical corpus in its concentration on a single procedure: commentary. Where the Jābir corpus builds a system, where al-Rāzī builds a workshop classification, Ibn Umayl builds readings. His characteristic act is to take a text or an image that he presents as inherited — a poem, a pictured tablet, a saying ascribed to Hermes or Democritus or Maria — and to unfold it, term by term, into the doctrine and practice of the art as he understands it. The man disappears behind the method so completely that the method has to serve as the biography: a reader trained in the Greek sources, writing in Egypt in the first half of the tenth century, in Arabic, for readers he expects to need the ancients explained — and explained at a length that suggests the explanation, not the poem, is the real book. WHAT THE RECORD GIVES The name Muḥammad ibn Umayl al-Tamīmī; an Egyptian milieu; a tenth-century floruit (c. 900–960 in this article’s convention); a small shelf of Arabic works, one of them very large; a Latin afterlife under the name Senior Zadith. WHAT THE RECORD DOES NOT GIVE Birth and death dates; teachers and pupils by secure attestation; travels, patrons, offices, or incidents. Every fuller life of Ibn Umayl in popular literature is a construction from the works, and should be read as one. THE LATIN NAME In Latin he is Senior Zadith — Senior, the Elder, rendering an Arabic honorific of seniority, with Zadith a Latinised deformation whose exact Arabic substrate is itself a small philological problem. The Latin name is a reception fact, not a second identity: see Section XIV. THE EGYPTIAN SETTING Egypt is not decoration in his works. The temple vision of Section III is set in an Egyptian temple landscape, and his pictured tablet belongs to the same Egyptian furniture of vaults, statues, and pictured writing that the Greco-Roman hub’s Emerald Tablet article traces through the Arabic discovery narratives. A note on method, in the form this hub uses wherever a tradition speaks in quotations. No invented quotation is given in this article. Ibn Umayl’s Arabic is paraphrased throughout, and paraphrases are labelled as paraphrase in the text. Where a published translation exists and is named — above all the extracts translated by H. E. Stapleton and his collaborators in 1933, and the modern Corpus Alchemicum Arabicum editions discussed in the Sources — the article names that access as the reader’s route to the wording, rather than dressing a paraphrase in quotation marks. The discipline matters doubly here, because Ibn Umayl’s own books are built out of quotations of earlier authorities, many of them otherwise lost: a modern article that invented his wording would be falsifying the very evidence — his value as a quoting witness — that makes him important. // HOW TO DATE A MAN WITHOUT A LIFE // The floruit c. 900–960 rests on termini, stated here so the reader can weigh them. He quotes authorities of the ninth century and the compilation known as the Turba (Sections IX–XI); he is himself quoted and used by later Arabic authors; and the Latin translations of the twelfth century and after presuppose an Arabic author already canonical. Termini give a window, not a birthday, and this article keeps the window labelled as one. One further caution belongs at the front, because it governs the article’s centre. Ibn Umayl is the Arabic continuation of a subject the Greco-Roman hub has already treated from the Greek and Latin side: the alchemical reading of inherited images. That hub’s article, Alchemical Allegory , documents how readers trained in the art read Greek myth as a veiled account of the work, and it states its discipline in terms this article adopts without alteration: the alchemical reading is presented as the alchemists’ reading , a documented interpretive tradition, and it is never silently promoted into the inherited images’ original meaning. Ibn Umayl stands inside that discipline perfectly — indeed, he is one of its earliest systematic practitioners in any language — because his subject is not, in the first instance, myth at all. His subject is alchemical texts and alchemical images themselves, which he holds to have been composed in symbols deliberately, by ancients who meant the symbols to be decoded. Whether the ancients meant any such thing is a separate question, and Sections VI and XVI keep it separate. What is not in question is that Ibn Umayl believed it, built a method on it, and left in his books the fullest surviving demonstration of the method at work. II. The Works: A Shelf in Three Titles Three works carry Ibn Umayl’s name in the tradition, and a fourth element — the sheer mass of quotation inside the first of them — is in practice a fourth work in its own right. This section files the shelf. The detailed treatment of each title occupies the sections named in the cards; the point here is the shape of the whole: a commentary, a key to images, and an epistle — three forms, one procedure. 1. AL-MĀʾ AL-WARAQĪ WA-L-ARḌ AL-NAJMIYYA The Silvery Water and the Starry Earth — his major work: a commentary ( sharḥ ) on an alchemical poem, unfolding its images into doctrine, and quoting the earlier authorities at a scale that makes the book a library of lost Greek alchemy in Arabic dress. Sections III–VIII. 2. KITĀB AL-MIFTĀḤ FĪ AL-ṢUWAR The Book of the Key to the Images — a shorter work whose title states the programme exactly: the pictured figures of the art, the ṣuwar , require a key, and the book supplies one. Section XII. 3. RISĀLA AL-SHAMS ILĀ AL-HILĀL The Epistle of the Sun to the Crescent Moon — a short allegorical epistle in which the two luminaries, the art’s standing pair, speak the doctrine in person. Known above all through its Latin life. Section XIII. THE FOURTH PRESENCE: THE QUOTATIONS Inside the Māʾ al-waraqī stands a second, shadow corpus: extended quotations of Hermes, Democritus, Zosimos, Maria, and the Turba, many preserved nowhere else in this form. Modern scholarship mines Ibn Umayl as a witness to Greek alchemy precisely because of this stratum. Section VII. Transmission of the Shelf The works survive in Arabic manuscripts, in the partial modern editions and translations listed in the Sources, and — for the Māʾ al-waraqī and the Risāla — in Latin versions that gave their author a second, European career as Senior Zadith (Section XIV). The transmission is uneven in a way the reader should register. The Latin West received Ibn Umayl early and read him hard; the modern Arabic editions arrived late, and the full critical presentation of the Māʾ al-waraqī is a twenty-first-century achievement of the Corpus Alchemicum Arabicum project (CALA), whose editions of Ibn Umayl — issued under the title The Book of the Explanation of the Symbols for the work known as al-Māʾ al-waraqī wa-l-arḍ al-najmiyya , 2003–2009 — are the current scholarly access named in this article’s Sources. Between Stapleton’s 1933 extracts and the CALA volumes, most readers who cited Ibn Umayl cited him at second hand, through the Latin Senior or through Ullmann’s catalogue. The article’s claims are held at the strength that layered transmission supports, and the layers are named wherever a claim depends on one of them. III. The Temple Vision: Statues, a Tablet, and an Egyptian Ekphrasis The Māʾ al-waraqī opens its authority-claim not with an argument but with a scene, and the scene must be told as what it is: Ibn Umayl’s own report , presented in his book as the account of how the pictured wisdom at the centre of his commentary came to be seen. This section expounds the vision narrative as he reports it, labelled as his report throughout. It is not presented as an excavation, a travel record, or a verifiable event, and nothing in this article builds a historical claim on its having happened. What it establishes — and this is considerable — is how a tenth-century Egyptian alchemist framed the origin of the images he spent a book decoding. In paraphrase of Ibn Umayl’s report, then: he recounts entering an Egyptian temple — in some accounts of the narrative the place is specified as the temple (in other tellings, the pyramid) at Būsīr — and finding, in its inner chamber, statues: ancient figures in stone, among them a sage figure holding, or presenting, a tablet . The tablet is the vision’s centre. It is covered not with a running text but with figures — pictured forms, in the report’s terms the pictured, hieroglyphic writing of the ancients: human and symbolic figures arranged as a pictured doctrine. The Greco-Roman hub’s Emerald Tablet article, treating the same passage from the Tablet’s side, states the point in the form this article keeps: in Ibn Umayl’s discovery story a stone table rests on the knees of Hermes in the secret chamber of a pyramid, and the table in the picture is inscribed with pictured writing rather than with the Emerald Tablet’s text, which the treatise quotes separately. Figure and text are two different objects in the vision, and the distinction governs everything Ibn Umayl does with them. The figures on the tablet, as his ekphrasis — his formal verbal description of a pictured work — unfolds them, form a small company of the art’s standing persons and things: an old man, the sage; younger figures; birds; the sun and the moon; a tree; the apparatus and postures of the work rendered as a pictured scene. The exact inventory varies in emphasis between the report’s parts and its later Latin retellings, and this article does not force a single canonical list where the tradition itself is fluid. What matters for the method is the form of the whole: a scene , with actors in relation — above and below, old and young, flying and fixed, male and female, sun and moon — whose relations, not merely whose identities, are the doctrine. A list of symbols can be glossed word by word. A scene must be read , and reading a scene, posture by posture and relation by relation, is exactly the labour the commentary then performs on the poem (Section V) and the Book of the Key performs on the images directly (Section XII). // THE VISION, FILED AT ITS REAL STRENGTH // The temple vision is a discovery narrative , of the same literary family as the vault beneath the statue of Hermes in the Sirr al-khalīqa and the temple vision of the Book of Crates , both treated in the Greco-Roman hub’s Emerald Tablet article: an ancient wisdom is found, hidden in a sacred Egyptian place, in the keeping of a sage figure, in pictured or aphoristic form. To file the vision in that family is not to call Ibn Umayl a liar. It is to locate his report in its genre — the genre in which, in his world, a book of the ancients announced where it came from. The historical content of the report is the framing , and the framing is genuine evidence: for what a tenth-century Egyptian alchemist thought the art’s pictured sources looked like, where he thought they were kept, and why they needed a commentator. Two features of the ekphrasis repay attention before the article follows the commentary proper. The first is its Egyptian specificity . The vision is not set in a generic ancient ruin. Its temple, its statues, its pictured writing, and — in the Būsīr specification — its named Egyptian locality place the pictured doctrine in the monumental landscape Ibn Umayl’s readers could still see standing around them. Egypt, for this author, is not the art’s remote mythical homeland. It is the building he reports walking into. The Egyptology division’s treatment of Zosimos of Panopolis — the Greek alchemist of Roman Egypt whose visions Ibn Umayl quotes (Section VII) — is the archive’s dossier for the older, Greek-language form of the same Egyptian alchemical world, and the continuity of place between Zosimos’ Panopolis and Ibn Umayl’s temple is a continuity the tradition itself insisted on. IV. The Poem He Comments: Sharḥ as Form The Māʾ al-waraqī wa-l-arḍ al-najmiyya is, in form, a sharḥ — a commentary — and the form is the first thing to understand about it, because Arabic literary culture gave the commentary a dignity and a set of conventions that a modern reader, accustomed to treat commentary as a secondary genre, will otherwise miss. A sharḥ takes a base text — a matn — whose authority is presupposed, quotes it piece by piece, and unfolds each piece: glossing its words, supplying its ellipses, resolving its ambiguities, and marshalling the earlier authorities who bear on its sense. Qur’ānic exegesis, legal commentary, grammatical commentary, and philosophical commentary all work in this form. Ibn Umayl’s originality is to apply the full apparatus of the sharḥ — lemma by lemma, authority by authority — to an alchemical poem, and thereby to claim for the art the same textual seriousness the form confers everywhere else it is used. The base text, stated at exactly the strength the scholarship supports: the Māʾ al-waraqī comments an alchemical qaṣīda , a formal ode in monorhyme, which the work presents as the composition of the author’s master — his teacher figure, the sage under whose authority the poem, and through it the commentary, stands. The ascription is part of the work’s own presentation, and this article reports it at that strength: the poem is ascribed, within the tradition Ibn Umayl transmits, to his master ; the master’s secure historical identification is not established by the surviving evidence, and the article does not supply one. That restraint is not pedantry. A commentary tradition habitually attaches its base text to an authoritative name, and the name’s function — to certify the poem as received doctrine rather than the commentator’s invention — is performed whether or not the attribution can be independently verified. What can be verified is the poem’s role: it is the skeleton on which the whole large book is hung, verse by verse. THE MATN The base poem: an alchemical qaṣīda whose verses, quoted as lemmata through the commentary, carry the doctrine in the covered register — tree, birds, sun and moon, the old man, the waters and earths of the art’s standing imagery. THE SHARḤ The commentary: Ibn Umayl’s prose unfolding of each lemma — gloss, paraphrase, decoding into operations and substances, and a marshalling of earlier authorities in support. The commentary outweighs the poem by an order of magnitude; the poem is the occasion, the sharḥ is the book. THE AUTHORITIES Quoted, not merely named: Hermes, Democritus, Zosimos, Maria, the sages of the Turba, and others, produced as witnesses that the decoding of each image is the ancients’ own sense and not the commentator’s fancy. Section VII. THE CLAIM OF THE FORM By casting the art as matn and sharḥ, Ibn Umayl claims for alchemy a canon, a tradition, and a school discipline: there is a text, the text is difficult, the difficulty is intended, and the intended sense is recoverable by method. The relation between poem and commentary is the reverse of the modern reader’s expectation, and Ibn Umayl’s book is unintelligible until the reversal is grasped. The poem does not need the commentary because the poem is badly written. On Ibn Umayl’s stated theory (Section VI), the poem is written exactly as the ancients wrote everything that mattered: in symbols, rumūz , deliberately — plain enough to be carried faithfully by any copyist, dark enough to be useless to any reader who lacks the key. The commentary is the key, delivered in the only form a key to a whole poem can take: the poem again, slowly, with every lock shown open. Nor is the commentary a mere glossary. A glossary would equate each image with a substance and stop. Ibn Umayl’s sharḥ does that, and then keeps going — into the sequence of operations the images encode in their order, into the proportions and regimens the authorities attach to them, and into extended doctrinal digressions in which the poem disappears from view for pages at a time under the weight of the tradition the commentator is determined to deposit alongside it. The book is a commentary the way a cathedral is a chapel: the form is real, and it has been built out, deliberately, into a summa. It follows that the commentary cannot be sampled fairly by its lemmata. Read for the poem alone, the Māʾ al-waraqī looks repetitive: image, gloss, image, gloss. Read as its author built it — as a systematic decoding in which each gloss is checked against the authorities and against every other gloss — it is the most complete surviving statement of how the Arabic art understood its own symbolic language at the moment that language was at its richest. The next section follows the decoding at work, image by image, at the level of the standing examples the brief of the book itself puts in the foreground: the tree, the birds, the sun and the moon, and the old man. V. Allegory as Method I: Every Image Decoded The centre of this article is a procedure, and it is time to watch it run. Ibn Umayl’s commentary takes each image of the commented poem — and, behind the poem, each figure of the temple tablet — and decodes it into the art’s operations and substances. The decoding is systematic in a precise sense: the same image, recurring, receives the same decoding; the decodings are required to cohere with one another across the whole poem; and each decoding is supported, where the commentator can support it, by a quoted authority who used the image in the same sense. What follows is the procedure’s grammar, given through its standing examples. The individual equations are reported as Ibn Umayl’s decodings — the tradition’s readings, in the discipline of Section I — in paraphrase, without invented quotation. The Tree A tree, in the poem’s imagery, is a growing thing with roots below and branches above, drawing what is beneath into what is displayed. In Ibn Umayl’s decoding, in paraphrase, the tree figures the work’s matter in its growth: a single stock from which the operations branch, rooted in the body from which the work begins and bearing, in its branches and fruit, the multiplied forms the one matter puts on through the regimen. The decoding is behavioural before it is verbal: a tree is the right picture for the matter because the matter, in the vessel, behaves as a tree behaves — it is fed from below, it differentiates upward, it is pruned and grafted by the operator’s hand, and its fruit is not the stock it grew from. The commentator’s task, as he performs it, is to walk the image’s parts — root, trunk, branch, leaf, fruit — and assign each its operational sense, so that a verse about a tree becomes, under the gloss, a paragraph of bench instruction. Whether the poem’s author planted the instruction there is Section XVI’s question. That Ibn Umayl extracts it, consistently, is the text’s fact. The Birds Birds fly, and in the art’s behavioural vocabulary flight is the signature of the volatile: what rises from the body under heat, what leaves the vessel’s floor for its dome, what must be caught, condensed, and returned if the work is not to lose its spirit to the air. Ibn Umayl’s decoding of the poem’s birds, in paraphrase, works this register in full: birds that rise and birds that fall, birds that fight and birds that are caught, figure the volatile principle in its states — escaping, circulating, fixed at last. The image is one of the oldest in the art’s covered language, and the commentator’s authorities run with it: the volatile as bird is already at home in the Greek corpus he quotes. The decoding’s discipline is visible in its constraints. A bird that flies cannot, in Ibn Umayl’s reading, figure the fixed body; a bird brought down cannot figure a spirit still escaping. Behaviour keys the equation, and the equation, once keyed, is held steady across the poem. The Sun and the Moon The paired luminaries are the art’s most durable couple, and Ibn Umayl decodes them as the work’s two great principles in their celestial dress: the sun for the hot, dry, active, gold-bearing principle the Arabic tradition theorises in its sulphur doctrine, the moon for the cold, moist, receptive, silver-bearing principle of its mercury doctrine — the pair whose theory this hub treats in its own right in Sulphur–Mercury Theory . In the commentary, in paraphrase, their risings, settings, eclipses, and conjunctions in the poem figure the operations in which the two principles meet: the conjunction of sun and moon is the art’s marriage, the union of the active and the receptive from which the work’s offspring — the stone, the elixir, in the tradition’s several vocabularies — is born. The Risāla al-shams ilā al-hilāl (Section XIII) is this decoding promoted to a whole work: the sun writes to the crescent moon, and the letter is the doctrine of their union. The Old Man The old man is the tablet’s and the poem’s presiding figure, and Ibn Umayl’s decoding of him is the method’s most characteristic move, because the figure operates on two levels at once and the commentator keeps both. As a person of the scene, the old man is the sage — Hermes, in the tablet’s identification as the Emerald Tablet article records it; the ancient master, in the poem’s — the authority from whom the pictured doctrine descends. As a term of the decoding, in paraphrase, his age, his posture, and his attributes are themselves glossed into the work’s matter and regimen: age figures what is ancient, fixed, and enduring in the work; the seated stillness of the statue figures fixation; what he holds figures what the doctrine delivers. The double operation — the old man as the teaching’s source and as one of its terms — is not a confusion in Ibn Umayl. It is the method’s signature: in a fully symbolic text, even the author-figure inside the picture is part of the picture, and is read. Allegory as Method II: Rumūz — Why the Ancients Hid the Art A method this elaborate needs a theory, and Ibn Umayl supplies one — the tradition’s own theory of obscurity, stated in his books with a completeness that makes him its most useful witness. In paraphrase of his stated position, held consistently across the commentary: the ancients — Hermes and the sages who followed him — possessed the art entire, and they wrote it down in symbols , rumūz (singular ramz ): a ramz is a sign, a hint, an allusive token, a word or image that points at its sense without stating it. They did so deliberately , and for two reasons that Ibn Umayl’s tradition always gives together. The symbols hide the art from the unworthy — from readers who would misuse the knowledge, cheapen it, or come to harm by it — and they teach the worthy, who recognise in the symbol a sense they are prepared, by study and by the bench, to receive. Obscurity, on this theory, is not the ancients’ failure to communicate. It is their chosen instrument of communication, calibrated to sort their readers. The continuity with the Greco-Roman hub’s allegory article is exact, and it is worth drawing in the open. That article’s first section sets out the rationale the mytho-hermetic tradition gives for the veil, in three registers: pedagogy — a story is remembered when a recipe is forgotten; protection of the art and of the adept — the knowledge was valuable, dangerous, and in many places illegal; and protection of the unready reader — the veil sorts, and the labour of lifting it is itself the training. Ibn Umayl’s theory of the rumūz is the same rationale, stated five to seven centuries earlier, from inside the Arabic art, about the art’s own texts rather than about Greek myth. The sorting argument is his argument. The pedagogy of the puzzle is his pedagogy. Where the later European tradition would claim that the Egyptian priests devised hieroglyphics, allegories, and fables as envelopes for a knowledge they wished neither wholly hidden nor equally known to all, Ibn Umayl — an Egyptian, commenting a poem by the pictured tablet of an Egyptian temple — states the doctrine of his own tradition in his own terms, without needing the fables of Greece to carry it. The Arabic hub’s allegory article and the Greco-Roman hub’s are therefore not two articles about two resemblances. They are two chapters of one documented history: the history of an interpretive conviction — that the ancients spoke in symbols on purpose — which the Greek commentators applied to Democritus, Ibn Umayl applied to the whole inherited corpus, and Maier and Pernety applied, after him, to the whole of myth. RAMZ (PL. RUMŪZ) A symbol, hint, or allusive sign. The term is the theory’s technical word: the ancients’ utterances are rumūz, and the commentator’s art is their unfolding. Ibn Umayl’s CALA title — The Book of the Explanation of the Symbols — is this word, translated. THE HIDING From the unworthy: the covetous, the careless, the merely curious, and the dangerous. The symbol is a lock whose key is fitness — study, discipline, and the master’s or the commentary’s guidance. THE TEACHING To the worthy: the symbol instructs by requiring labour. A sense the reader has decoded is a sense the reader owns; the rumūz are a curriculum disguised as a wall. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR READING If the ancients spoke in rumūz deliberately, then a plain reading of an ancient alchemical text is, by definition, a misreading — and disagreement among decoders is a problem of keys, not of the texts’ good faith. Section XVI weighs what that consequence costs. One refinement of the theory is Ibn Umayl’s in emphasis, and it distinguishes his commentary from a mere codebook. The symbols, on his showing, are not arbitrary. A ramz is not a random word assigned to a substance by convention, as a password is assigned; it is drawn from the covered thing’s behaviour and appearance — the bird for the volatile because the volatile flies, the tree for the growing matter because the matter grows, the sun and moon for the two principles because the principles act as the luminaries act, in conjunction and in phases. This is the behavioural keying that the Greco-Roman allegory article identifies, in the Greek corpus, with the aphorism ascribed to Ostanes — nature delights in nature, nature conquers nature, nature masters nature, in Matteo Martelli’s translation — transferred to reading: a decoding is right when the story’s agents behave as their decoded natures behave. Ibn Umayl’s rumūz stand under the same rule. It is the rule that gives his commentary whatever discipline it has, and the rule whose limits — resemblance is cheap, and a determined decoder is rarely refused — Section XVI must weigh on the other side. VII. A Library in One Author: The Quotation of the Ancients If Ibn Umayl had decoded his poem in his own voice alone, he would be a curiosity of method. He is instead a major source for the history of alchemy, because the commentary is built as an anthology : at every lemma, the decoding is supported by extended quotation of the earlier authorities, quoted at a length and with a fidelity of attribution that turn the Māʾ al-waraqī into a library of Greek alchemy in Arabic dress. Passages of authors whose Greek is lost, fragmentary, or preserved only in epitome survive in Ibn Umayl’s Arabic in fuller form than anywhere else, and modern editors of the Greek corpus read him, in consequence, as a witness — a tenth-century Arabic manuscript tradition testifying to Greek texts of the first centuries CE. This section files the library’s main shelves and states, shelf by shelf, the strength at which a quoting witness can be used. Authority quoted Who stands behind the name What Ibn Umayl’s quotation preserves Hermes Hermes Trismegistus, the art’s founding sage in its own presentation Sayings and the Emerald Tablet material (Section VIII); the presiding authority of the temple tablet, whose pictured figures the commentary reads. Democritus The pseudo-Democritean corpus — the Physika kai mystika tradition of the 1st century CE, not the atomist of Abdera in person Recipe-doctrine and riddling utterance in Arabic transmission, of the corpus the Greek commentators had already treated as a veiled canon. Zosimos Zosimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE), the first alchemical author whose works survive in bulk in Greek Material cognate with the Greek Zosimos, including visionary and doctrinal matter, in Arabic dress — a control on the Greek tradition and a supplement to it. See the Egyptology division’s Zosimos . Maria Maria the Jewess, the art’s legendary apparatus-maker, known in Greek through quotation in Zosimos and the commentators Sayings ascribed to Maria in the Arabic line — part of the small dossier by which her doctrine, as distinct from her apparatus, can be traced at all. The Turba The assembled sages of the Turba Philosophorum , speaking in dialogue Quotations that are among the earliest dated evidence for a Turba-like Arabic text — the terminus evidence of Sections IX–XI, and the single most consequential shelf in the library. The use of a quoting witness requires a discipline, and the discipline should be stated as plainly for Ibn Umayl as this archive states it for any anthologist. A quotation in a commentary is evidence, in the first instance, for what the commentator had in front of him — for the form in which a text circulated in tenth-century Egypt, in Arabic, in the manuscripts available to one reader. It is evidence, at one remove and with the translation’s losses priced in, for the earlier text itself. And it is not transparent evidence: a commentator quotes what his lemma needs, trims what it does not, and — the sharpest hazard — may quote in the wording his own decoding requires, since the authorities are produced to support the gloss. None of this is an accusation against Ibn Umayl in particular; it is the standing condition of anthological evidence, and the modern scholarship that mines him — Stapleton’s generation first, the CALA editors in our own — works with the condition priced in, checking his quotations against the surviving Greek wherever Greek survives to check them against. Where the check can be run, his value rises: the Arabic Zosimos material, set beside the Greek, shows a witness transmitting a real tradition, not inventing one. Where the check cannot be run — where Ibn Umayl is the only witness — his quotations are used at the strength of a single, interested, tenth-century testimony, and this article so uses them. The library’s existence also corrects a lazy picture of the Arabic art as a fresh start. Ibn Umayl’s commentary presupposes, on every page, an Arabic-reading audience for whom Hermes, Democritus, Zosimos, and Maria are already authorities whose sayings settle arguments — an audience, that is, standing at the end of the translation movement this hub’s Wing I describes, in a culture where the Greek corpus had been naturalised in Arabic deeply enough to be commented like a canon. The Jābir corpus had built its system partly out of the same inheritance; Ibn Umayl’s distinct contribution is to make the inheritance itself the subject — to write the book in which the tradition explains, authority by authority, what it thinks its founders meant. A tradition that produces its own commentator has reached a particular stage of self-consciousness. Ibn Umayl is Arabic alchemy becoming conscious of its library. VIII. An Encyclopedia Written by a Brotherhood The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ — the Brethren of Purity, in full the Brethren of Purity and the Friends of Fidelity ( Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ wa-Khullān al-Wafāʾ ) — are the anonymous authors of the most ambitious encyclopedia produced in the medieval Islamic world: the Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ , the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity . The work comprises, in the form in which the manuscript tradition overwhelmingly transmits it, fifty-two epistles arranged in four divisions, together with a summary compendium, the Risālat al-Jāmiʿa (the Comprehensive Epistle), which presents itself as the key that gathers the whole. Taken together, the epistles attempt nothing less than a complete curriculum of the knowledge available to a tenth-century Iraqi intellectual: arithmetic and geometry, astronomy and music, logic, natural philosophy in all its branches, psychology, metaphysics, and finally theology, law, and the doctrine of the soul's return. No comparable single work of the period attempts the same total coverage inside a single, deliberately ordered design. The design is the point, and it is what separates the Rasāʾil from a mere miscellany. The Brethren do not collect knowledge the way a bookseller collects stock. They order it, as a path. The reader begins with number — the most abstract, most certain, and, in their Pythagorean conviction, most purifying of the sciences — and ascends through the study of nature and of the soul to the study of the divine law and the fate of the soul after death. Knowledge, in their presentation, is not an end in itself. It is a discipline of purification ( ṣafāʾ , the purity of their own name, is the programme as much as the title): the soul, sunk in the body and in ignorance, is cleansed by learning the true structure of the world it inhabits, until it can recognise that structure as the image of its own, and ascend. The encyclopedia is therefore simultaneously a work of science, a work of philosophy, and a work of spiritual direction — and any account that reduces it to only one of those three has already misdescribed it. For this hub — Wing II, The Art — the Brethren matter for a specific and documentable reason. Their encyclopedia is one of the earliest surviving Arabic works to give the practical arts, the crafts, and among them the arts that handle matter — metallurgy, the lore of minerals, and alchemy itself — a formal, argued place inside a complete philosophy of knowledge. They do not write alchemical recipe books. They do something, for the historian of the art, almost as valuable: they tell us where a learned Iraqi brotherhood of the tenth century filed alchemy — among which sciences, under which cosmology, subject to which ends, and with what degree of honour. Section XII, this article's centre, sets out that filing in full, with the cautions its evidence requires. The sections before it build the cabinet the filing sits in: the work's structure (Section II), its disputed authorship and date (Sections III–IV), its contested religious identity (Section V), its cosmology (Sections VI–IX), and its classifications of knowledge and of labour (Sections X–XI). THE WORK The Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ : fifty-two epistles in four divisions — mathematical (14), natural (17), psychological and rational (10), theological and nomological (11) — plus the summary Risālat al-Jāmiʿa . See Section II for the full table. THE AUTHORS Anonymous by design. A Basra-centred circle of the tenth century, on the mainstream dating; the names tradition attaches to it are preserved by Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī and are stated, as tradition, in Section III. THE SYSTEM Neoplatonic emanation — God, Intellect ( ʿaql ), Soul ( nafs ), matter, world — framed by Pythagorean number doctrine and organised throughout by the correspondence of macrocosm and microcosm. Sections VI–IX. THE ART'S PLACE Minerals and metals are treated inside natural philosophy, on an Aristotelian frame; alchemy is treated with respect among the crafts and sciences, and expressly subordinated to the purification of the soul. Section XII. A note on method, in the form this archive uses wherever the sources invite invention. No direct quotation is given in this article. The Rasāʾil are paraphrased throughout, and paraphrases are labelled as paraphrase in the text; where a doctrine is summarised, the summary is the modern scholarship's, cited in the Sources, and not a rendering of an Arabic sentence presented as if it were one. The reason is practical as well as principled: the epistles' Arabic is ornate, rhymed in places, and dense with technical vocabulary whose translation is itself a scholarly act — the ongoing Oxford edition discussed in Section XV exists precisely because no adequate complete English translation previously did. An archive that invented smooth English sentences and put them in the Brethren's mouths would be falsifying its evidence. What can be stated exactly — the work's structure, its classifications, the positions of the modern scholars who dispute its authorship, date, and allegiance — is stated exactly, and the disputes are stated as disputes, with the positions named, rather than silently settled. That discipline governs Sections III–V in particular, and the reader should hold the article to it. // NAMES AND TRANSLITERATION // Transliteration follows the scholarly system used across this division, with diacritics throughout: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Rasāʾil, ʿaql (Intellect), nafs (Soul), ṣūra (form), mādda (matter). The article element (al-) is not capitalised mid-name. Personal names given in full at first mention — Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī, Abū Sulaymān al-Bustī al-Maqdisī — are shortened thereafter only where the reference remains unambiguous. Dates are CE. One framing caution, because popular accounts blur it in both directions. The Brethren are sometimes presented as a secret society of occultists, custodians of a hidden alchemical doctrine, and sometimes, at the opposite pole, as harmless popularisers who merely repackaged Greek science for a general reader. The surviving text supports neither caricature. The Rasāʾil are learned, technically demanding, and philosophically serious; they are also deliberately written to be intelligible beyond a narrow circle of specialists, in a clear expository Arabic, with examples drawn from the market, the workshop, and the animal world. Their secrecy — and there is secrecy: the authors withhold their names and repeatedly enjoin the reader, in paraphrase, not to cast the work before those unprepared for it — is the secrecy of a brotherhood with a teaching mission and a prudential sense of its own heterodoxy, not the secrecy of a laboratory notebook. What they hid was who they were. What they taught, they taught in the open architecture of an encyclopedia. II. The Rasāʾil: Fifty-Two Epistles in Four Divisions The fourfold structure is stated by the work itself, in its opening epistles and its internal tables of contents, and it is stable across the manuscript tradition: the variations among manuscripts concern the ordering and subdivision of individual epistles, not the four divisions or the total of fifty-two. The divisions ascend. The first treats the mathematical sciences ( al-ʿulūm al-riyāḍiyya ) — the propaedeutic disciplines, in the Greek quadrivium's lineage, by which the soul is first trained and purified. The second treats the natural sciences ( al-ʿulūm al-ṭabīʿiyya ) — the physical world, from the heavens to minerals, plants, animals, and the human body. The third treats the psychological and rational sciences ( al-ʿulūm al-nafsāniyya al-ʿaqliyya ) — the soul, the intellect, and the intelligible world. The fourth treats the theological and nomological sciences ( al-ʿulūm al-ilāhiyya al-nāmūsiyya ) — divine law, prophecy, politics, death, and resurrection. The ascent is pedagogical, psychological, and soteriological at once: each division presupposes the one before it, and the whole is traversed, in the Brethren's repeated image, as a ladder.
