Three features of the table deserve emphasis, because each corrects a common misreading. First, the epistles named above are representative, not exhaustive: individual manuscripts and modern editions differ slightly in the titles they give particular epistles, and the numbering used here is the standard numbering of the modern editions and of the Oxford series discussed in Section XV. Second, logic stands inside the mathematical division , as its closing sequence: for the Brethren, as for the late-antique Greek curriculum they inherit, logic is not a separate philosophy but the instrument that completes the propaedeutic training. Third — and this is the table's most consequential entry for the present hub — the epistle on the crafts stands inside the mathematical division too , as Epistle 8, among the propaedeutics. The practical arts are not an appendix to the Brethren's system. They are part of its foundation course. Section XI gives that placement its full weight. The Jāmiʿa and the Question of a Fifty-Third Text Alongside the fifty-two stands the Risālat al-Jāmiʿa , the Comprehensive Epistle, which summarises the whole work's doctrine in condensed form and presents itself, in paraphrase, as the fruit of the fifty-two and the key to their inner sense; a still more condensed Jāmiʿat al-Jāmiʿa also circulates in the tradition. The Jāmiʿa 's relation to the main corpus — whether it is the Brethren's own summary, a near-contemporary epitome by their circle, or a later distillation that the tradition attached to the corpus — has been debated, and the debate is noted here rather than settled: the mainstream of modern scholarship treats the Jāmiʿa as belonging to the Brethren's own milieu and as an authentic guide to how the corpus understood itself, while allowing that its textual history is not identical to that of the fifty-two. For the purposes of this article the point is structural: the tradition itself felt the need of a map to the encyclopedia, and supplied one from inside the encyclopedia's own world-view. The Jāmiʿa is that map, and its strongly esoteric, cyclical, and prophetological emphases are among the exhibits in the Ismāʿīlī debate of Section V. A CURRICULUM, NOT AN ANTHOLOGY The epistles cross-refer constantly, in paraphrase: what was established in the epistle on arithmetic will be assumed in the epistle on music; the doctrine of matter and form (Ep. 15) governs the epistles on minerals, plants, and animals that follow it. The work is written to be read in order, as a course. GREEK SCIENCE, REFRACTED The content is, in large part, the Greek scientific inheritance in Arabic dress — Euclid and Ptolemy, Aristotle and Galen, Nicomachus and the Neoplatonists, received through the translation movement treated in this division's Baghdad Translation Movement article — but refracted through a religious brotherhood's programme: selected, ordered, and moralised for the soul's ascent. The refraction metaphor is exact, and worth keeping. A refracted beam is the same light, bent. The Brethren's astronomy is Ptolemaic astronomy; their logic is the Aristotelian Organon in its late-antique school order; their arithmetic is Nicomachean; their emanation scheme is the Neoplatonism of the Arabic Plotinus and Proclus materials. What the brotherhood adds is the bending medium: a doctrine of the soul's fall and return, a cyclical view of sacred history, a brotherhood ethic, and a conviction that number is the signature of the world's maker. Greek science enters the Rasāʾil as knowledge and leaves it as a path of salvation. That transformation — not any single doctrine — is the Brethren's originality, and it is why a hub devoted to the transmission of the art cannot pass them by: for two centuries and more, east and west, the Rasāʾil were one of the principal vehicles by which the Greek inheritance actually circulated, in a form ordinary learned readers could and did read whole. III. Who Wrote Them? The Names al-Tawḥīdī Preserved The Rasāʾil name no author. That anonymity is deliberate, maintained across fifty-two epistles by writers perfectly capable of naming themselves had they wished to, and it has made the question of authorship a permanent scholarly problem rather than a soluble one. Everything the tradition knows — or thinks it knows — about the authors' identities comes from outside the work, chiefly from one precious external witness: Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī (died after 1023), the great prose stylist and court intellectual of Baghdad, who in his Kitāb al-Imtāʿ wa-l-Muʾānasa (the Book of Enjoyment and Conviviality) reports, in the account modern scholarship relies on and paraphrases here, that the epistles were composed by a group of scholars associated with Basra , and gives their names. Name, as Preserved by al-Tawḥīdī What the Tradition Adds Abū Sulaymān Muḥammad ibn Maʿshar al-Bustī al-Maqdisī Presented in the reports as a leading figure of the circle — often taken, in the later tradition, as the group's senior or spokesman. The nisbas point to Bust and to Jerusalem (al-Maqdisī, “the Jerusalemite”). Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Hārūn al-Zanjānī Named by al-Tawḥīdī among the composers; the nisba points to Zanjan in north-western Iran. Independently little documented, like most of the group. Abū Aḥmad al-Mihrajānī Named by al-Tawḥīdī; the name is also read al-Nahrajūrī in some reports and editions — a textual instability in the external tradition itself, noted here because it measures how thin the biographical evidence is. Al-ʿAwfī Named by al-Tawḥīdī by nisba alone. No secure independent biography survives. Zayd ibn Rifāʿa The best documented of the five: a scholar and secretary in Baghdad, personally known to al-Tawḥīdī, who reports conversations with him. His presence anchors the circle's floruit in the later tenth century — see Section IV. The table must be read at its real evidentiary strength, which this section now states plainly. Al-Tawḥīdī is a near-contemporary witness of the first rank — he moved in the same Baghdad intellectual world, knew Zayd ibn Rifāʿa, and had no obvious motive to invent a Basra circle out of nothing. His testimony is the reason the mainstream of modern scholarship speaks, as this article does, of a Basra-centred group of the tenth century. But his report is still a report: it is one man's account, given in a work of literary conversation, of a group that had chosen anonymity; the names cannot be checked against authorial statements in the Rasāʾil themselves, because there are none; and the biographies of four of the five men are, beyond al-Tawḥīdī and the later bio-bibliographical tradition that largely repeats him, effectively blank. The honest statement is the one the scholarship, at its most careful, makes: the ascription to a Basra circle including these men is the traditional ascription, preserved by al-Tawḥīdī, widely accepted as substantially credible, and not independently verifiable in detail. Later sources add further names and associations — the tradition also connects the epistles' circulation with Baghdad figures and, in the west, with the circle of al-Majrīṭī (Section XV) — but additions of that kind extend the work's reception history, not its authorship. // ANONYMITY AS EVIDENCE // The Brethren's anonymity is itself a datum, and scholars have read it in opposite directions — which is why this article reports the readings rather than choosing between them. On one reading, anonymity is prudence: a group whose doctrines sat uneasily with the orthodoxies around it — Muʿtazilite, Ashʿarite, Imami, and Ismāʿīlī claims all had enforcers in tenth-century Iraq — protected its members by publishing as a brotherhood. On another reading, anonymity is doctrine: the work presents itself, in paraphrase, as the teaching of a purified collectivity rather than of any individual master, and the effacement of the authors enacts the effacement of the self the teaching recommends. The two readings are not exclusive, and the text gives material to both. What neither licenses is the romantic inference, common in popular accounts, from anonymity to a vast secret organisation: the external evidence supports a circle of scholars, not an order with chapters, and this archive files the Brethren accordingly. Basra, in any case, is the right kind of place for such a circle, and the geography deserves a sentence of its own. Tenth-century Basra was a great port and a greater crossroads of doctrine: the birthplace of Muʿtazilite theology, a centre of Arabic grammar and philology, a meeting point of Persian, Arab, and Indian Ocean worlds, and — with Baghdad a few days north — plugged directly into the Abbasid capital's patronage and book trade. A group of philosophically inclined scholars, in correspondence and conversation with Baghdad (Zayd ibn Rifāʿa's career is exactly that pattern), composing an encyclopedia that fuses Greek science with a universalist religious programme, is entirely at home in that city. The Rasāʾil 's own internal geography — the work addresses a dispersed brotherhood of readers, “wherever they may be” in the paraphrase of its recurring address — suggests the circle understood itself as the centre of a network rather than as a local school. Authorship, on the evidence, is best pictured as a small group writing collectively over a period of years, revising one another, and issuing the result under a collective name. Which is, after all, what the title page — had the work had one — would have said. IV. When? Dating the Epistles, Stated as a Debate No question about the Brethren has consumed more scholarly ink, relative to the evidence available, than the date of the Rasāʾil — and the reason is structural. The work names no author and dates no event unambiguously; its contents can be paralleled in authors of several centuries; and its doctrines, if they could be dated, would date movements — above all Ismāʿīlism (Section V) — whose own chronologies are partly built on it. The debate therefore has to be stated as a debate, with its proposals ranged and its mainstream identified, and that is what this section does. Proposals in the literature have ranged across more than a century. 9th c. THE EARLIEST PROPOSALS Some earlier scholarship, reasoning from the epistles' apparently primitive state of certain doctrines and from parallels with ninth-century authors, placed composition in the ninth century, in whole or in an early stratum. Such datings now command little support as accounts of the corpus as transmitted, though the possibility that the circle reworked older materials is not excluded by any party. early–mid 10th c. FORMATION OF THE CIRCLE The period in which, on the mainstream view, the Basra circle formed and the bulk of the epistles were composed. Internal references and the state of the astronomy and philosophy the work presupposes sit comfortably here; nothing in the corpus requires a date after the 970s. c. 960s–980s COMPLETION, ON THE MAINSTREAM PLACEMENT The placement this article adopts as the mainstream: the epistles were completed by about the 960s to 980s. The anchor is external: al-Tawḥīdī's testimony (Section III) places the composers, and Zayd ibn Rifāʿa in particular, in the later tenth century, and the work must precede its documented diffusion around and after the year 1000. late 10th c. THE LATEST PROPOSALS Datings toward the very end of the tenth century have been argued from the work's relations to contemporary Ismāʿīlī and court circles. They remain minority positions for the corpus as a whole, but they mark the debate's outer bound: no serious proposal places the Rasāʾil as transmitted in the eleventh century. The mainstream placement — composition in the middle decades of the tenth century, the corpus complete by roughly the 960s–980s — rests on the convergence of three independent considerations, and it is worth setting them out because convergence, not any single proof, is what the date actually rests on. First, the external testimony: al-Tawḥīdī (died after 1023) treats the epistles and their composers as matters of his own lifetime's recent past, and the men he names belong to the later tenth century. Second, the internal state of the sciences: the astronomy, medicine, and philosophy the epistles presuppose are those of the post-translation-movement world — the world after Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq (died 873) and his circle, treated in this division's Baghdad Translation Movement article — with no clear dependence on the eleventh century's authors. Third, the reception: by the early eleventh century the epistles are being quoted, attacked, and carried west (Section XV), which requires the corpus to have existed, complete enough to travel, by about the year 1000. A date much earlier than c. 900 strains the first consideration; a date much later than c. 980 strains the third. The middle is where the evidence leaves room, and the scholarship — de Callataÿ's and Netton's surveys, cited in the Sources, give the debate's current state — has settled there, without the settlement amounting to proof. // WHY THE DATE MATTERS BEYOND ITSELF // Two neighbouring chronologies hang on this one. The Jābirian alchemical corpus is dated by this hub, as a canonical position, to c. 850–950, itself a debated range (Section XIV): on the mainstream datings of both corpora, the Jābirian writings and the Rasāʾil are near-contemporaries in the same Iraqi world, and the question of influence between them is a real question precisely because neither can be shown to be simply prior. And the Ismāʿīlī daʿwa 's intellectual history is partly reconstructed from the epistles: date them early and they become a source of Ismāʿīlī doctrine; date them late and they become its echo. Section V states that entanglement without pretending to cut it. A last precision. To date “the Rasāʾil ” is to date a corpus that may not have been composed at a sitting. A collective work of fifty-two epistles, produced by a circle over years, can contain strata: epistles drafted earlier and revised, materials taken up from the circle's reading, a summary (the Jāmiʿa ) added when the whole was already substantially complete. Scholars who have argued for composite composition are not thereby arguing against the mainstream placement of the finished corpus; they are describing how a work of this kind normally comes to be. This article's usage follows the scholarship's: the date given is the date of the corpus as transmitted, and claims about individual epistles' dates are made, where they are made at all, epistle by epistle and with their evidence attached. V. The Ismāʿīlī Question Are the Brethren of Purity Ismāʿīlīs? The question has been asked since the medieval period — medieval opponents already filed the Rasāʾil among the literature of the daʿwa , the Ismāʿīlī mission — and it remains the single most contested question in the scholarship. It is contested because the evidence genuinely points in two directions, and this section's obligation is to exhibit both directions at full strength, name the scholars who hold the main positions, and take no side silently. The archive's practice, here as in the Greco-Roman hub's disputed datings, is to state the dispute as the finding. The Case for an Ismāʿīlī Connection The affinities are real, numerous, and structural — not a matter of a stray phrase. In paraphrase of the doctrines as the modern literature (Netton; de Callataÿ; El-Bizri's volume, all in the Sources) catalogues them: the Rasāʾil teach a cyclical prophetology — sacred history unfolds in cycles ( adwār ), each inaugurated by a prophet-legislator (a nāṭiq , “speaker”) and interpreted by his legatee and the imams who follow, in a heptadic pattern of sevens that is characteristic of early Ismāʿīlī thought. They practise a systematic esoteric interpretation ( taʾwīl ) of scripture and law, distinguishing the exoteric ( ẓāhir ) from the esoteric ( bāṭin ) sense in the manner of the daʿwa . Their cosmology (Section VI) is the Neoplatonic emanation scheme that contemporary Ismāʿīlī thinkers — al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī, al-Sijistānī — were simultaneously elaborating in recognisably kindred forms. Their organisation — a graded brotherhood, enjoined to discretion, devoted to a teaching mission ( daʿwa is the ordinary Arabic word for such a call, and the epistles use the vocabulary of calling and summons freely) — resembles the mission's structure. And their later reception is heavily Ismāʿīlī: the epistles were preserved, copied, and revered in Ismāʿīlī communities, above all in Yemen and India, to a degree no other medieval readership matches (Section XV). A case built on that catalogue is not a weak case. The Case for an Ecumenical Self-Presentation Against it stands the work's own self-presentation, which is — also structurally, also pervasively — ecumenical . The Brethren declare, in paraphrase of their programmatic passages (Epistle 44 is the locus usually cited, on the Brethren's own doctrine), that they do not oppose any science, shun any book, or cling fanatically to any single school: their fellowship presents itself as open to the truths of all religions and all philosophies, gathering what is sound in each. The Rasāʾil cite and use Muʿtazilite, Sufi, Christian, Jewish, Persian, and Indian materials alongside the Qurʾan and the Greek corpus, with a catholicity that sits awkwardly with a confessional mission's discipline. Distinctively Ismāʿīlī doctrines in their hard form — the named imamology of the Fatimid daʿwa , allegiance to a living imam of the line — are, on the reading of the scholars who stress this side, absent or held at a level of generality compatible with several Shiʿi and even non-Shiʿi positions. And the circle's Basra milieu was one in which Muʿtazilite theology and a broad philosophical culture supplied an alternative home for exactly such a programme. On this side of the argument, the affinities of the first case are explained as shared milieu : emanationism, cycles, and esotericism were in the tenth-century Iraqi air, breathed by Ismāʿīlīs and non-Ismāʿīlīs alike, and resemblance is not membership. S. M. STERN Samuel Miklos Stern, in studies of the 1960s (notably on the authorship question and the epistles' relations to the Ismāʿīlī movement), argued the connection with the early Ismāʿīlī daʿwa in a strong form, treating the Rasāʾil as a document of the movement's intellectual world and a key to its early doctrine. His work set the terms in which the modern debate is still conducted. YVES MARQUET Yves Marquet, across a series of studies of the epistles' philosophy and their Shiʿi character, likewise stressed the Ismāʿīlī — in his analysis, specifically early, pre-Fatimid or Qarmaṭian-adjacent — colouring of the work's prophetology and esotericism, while attending closely to its philosophical sources. IAN RICHARD NETTON Netton's Muslim Neoplatonists (1979; 2nd ed. 1991) — the standard English monograph on the Rasāʾil 's thought — reads the Brethren as Neoplatonists whose system incorporates Ismāʿīlī- resonant elements without being reducible to a party document; his analyses of their emanationism and their eclectic method underwrite Sections VI–VIII of the present article. GHOLAM REZA DE CALLATAŸ De Callataÿ's Ikhwan al-Safa': A Brotherhood of Idealists on the Fringe of Orthodox Islam (2005) gives the position its most quoted modern formulation: the Brethren stand, in his reading, on the fringe — idealists with deep Ismāʿīlī affinities and an ecumenical programme that no confessional label fits without remainder. His edition and translation work on individual epistles anchors the current scholarship. The positions, ranged, are these. A strong-Ismāʿīlī reading (Stern; Marquet, in their different keys) makes the epistles a product of the daʿwa 's world and an instrument of its teaching. A fringe or affinities reading (de Callataÿ's formulation is the most influential) grants the affinities in full and denies that they amount to membership or commission: a brotherhood of idealists, formed in a milieu saturated with Ismāʿīlī ideas, pursuing a universalist programme of its own. A milieu reading, present across the literature and given systematic form in Nader El-Bizri's edited volume The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ and their Rasāʾil (2008), relocates the question: the epistles are a document of tenth-century Iraqi intellectual culture as a whole, in which Ismāʿīlī, Muʿtazilite, Sufi, and philosophical currents interpenetrated, and the demand for a single confessional label is the anachronism. This article adopts no one of these as its own. It reports — because the fact is itself historically important — that the Rasāʾil 's reception was decisively shaped by Ismāʿīlī communities who preserved and canonised them, whatever the authors' own allegiance was; that the text's self-presentation is ecumenical in terms no reading may silently discard; and that the scholarly question remains, in the current literature, open. Readers who need the debate's full dossier will find it in the Sources. // NO SIDE SILENTLY TAKEN // Accordingly, this article's usage is fixed and the reader may check it against every page: the Brethren are described as a Basra-centred brotherhood with strong Ismāʿīlī affinities and an ecumenical self-presentation. They are not described, anywhere in this hub, simply as “the Ismāʿīlī encyclopedists”, and their doctrines are not cited, anywhere in this hub, as official Ismāʿīlī doctrine. Where a doctrine of theirs parallels a doctrine of the contemporary daʿwa , the parallel is stated as a parallel. The discipline costs a few easy sentences. It buys the only thing this archive sells: statements the evidence will carry. VI. Emanation: God, Intellect, Soul, and the World The Rasāʾil 's cosmology is, in its skeleton, the Neoplatonic emanation scheme that Arabic philosophy received from the Greek tradition — the scheme whose Greek ancestry this archive treats in the Greco-Roman hub's Neoplatonism and Theurgy article, to which the present section is the Arabic sequel. The Brethren take the scheme over through its Arabic mediations — the paraphrase-tradition of Plotinus (the so-called Theology of Aristotle ) and of Proclus (the Book of the Pure Good , known in Latin as the Liber de causis ) — and restate it, in paraphrase of their recurrent expositions, as follows. God — the Creator, the One — is utterly transcendent, beyond the attributes language can predicate, the source from which all being flows without diminution of the source. From God proceeds, as the first originated being, the Universal Intellect ( al-ʿaql al-kullī ): perfect, actual, the locus of the forms of all things. From the Intellect proceeds the Universal Soul ( al-nafs al-kulliyya ): the living principle that moves the heavens and animates the world, desiring and striving toward the Intellect from which it came. From the Soul proceeds prime matter ( al-mādda al-ūlā ), and thereafter second matter, the absolute body, the spheres, the elements, and the whole sublunary order of generation and corruption. Being descends by degrees; and the soul of man, a fragment or efflux of the Universal Soul sunk in a body, ascends by the reverse road — which is the road the encyclopedia itself paves. x: Arabic Transmission · The Art · The Latin Threshold // FROM HARRAN AND BAGHDAD TO TOLEDO :: 7TH–14TH CENTURY // The Greek art's second life in Arabic: how alchemy was carried across languages and empires, translated, criticised and rebuilt into a systematic discipline — with its own theory of the balance, its own laboratory order, and its own literature — and how, at the far end of that long labour, it was handed on to Latin Europe. WING I — TRANSMISSION WING II — THE ART ARABIC HOME // ARCHIVE CONTENTS // I. Introduction — Scope of This Hub II. The Two Wings III. Method — The Rules of This Hub IV. The Arabic Timeline V. Article Index — Wing I — Transmission — Wing II — The Art VI. Sources and Further Reading I. Introduction — Scope of This Hub This hub covers the Arabic-language career of alchemy from the seventh century to the fourteenth — roughly, from the Arab conquests that brought Egypt, Syria and Iraq under new rulers to the moment when the art the Arabic world had rebuilt passed, in Latin dress, into the hands of European readers who would remake it again. Its subject is a transformation, not a relay race. The Greek alchemy of Alexandria — pseudo-Democritus, Maria the Jewess, Zōsimos, the commentators — did not simply survive in Arabic translation. It was rebuilt : given a new technical vocabulary ( kīmiyāʾ for the art, iksīr for the agent that perfects metals), a new master theory in the doctrine of the balance ( mīzān ), a new classification of substances and apparatus, and a literature many times larger than the Greek corpus it inherited. What Latin Europe received in the twelfth century was not Alexandria's art preserved in ice. It was Baghdad's, Basra's and Cairo's art, alive and argued over. The hub has a defined place in this archive, and it is worth stating plainly. It follows the Egyptology division, which treats the Egyptian crafts and the earliest alchemy from the Egyptian side, and it follows the Greco-Roman hub, whose Wing II carries the Alexandrian art from its Greek beginnings to a closing threshold: 1144 CE , the year of the first dated Latin alchemical translation. This hub's relation to that threshold is deliberately different. It begins before it — with the conquests of the seventh century and with the Syriac bridge that had been carrying Greek learning eastward for two hundred years before Islam — and it runs past it , following the Arabic tradition through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and out through the Latin translations it fed, to the threshold of the Latin art itself around 1300. Where the Greco-Roman hub ends at the Latin door, this hub walks through it — once, briefly, and only to show what was carried across. The Egyptology division's own later-period treatment, its Islamic Egyptology article, is the companion piece from the Egyptian side. Two standing cautions govern everything in this hub, and they are stated here, up front, rather than buried in the method section. The first concerns the hub's name. This is an Arabic-language hub, not an ethnic one. Arabic was the learned language of a civilisation far wider than Arabia, and many of this hub's central authors were not Arabs: al-Rāzī and al-Bīrūnī were Persians; Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq was a Nestorian Christian from al-Ḥīra whose first scholarly language was Syriac; Thābit ibn Qurra was a Sabian of Harran; the translators of Cordoba included Jews working between Arabic, Hebrew and Romance. Others were Syriac Christians, Sabians, Jews and converts of every background, writing in the one language that reached from Cordoba to Nishapur. Throughout this hub, "Arabic" names the language of the texts — nothing more, and nothing less. The second caution concerns a name. The Arabic corpus ascribed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān and the Latin works ascribed to Geber are different bodies of work , written in different languages, in different centuries, with different doctrines — most sharply on the mineral acids, which belong to the Latin side of the divide. The Latin Summa perfectionis of pseudo-Geber, composed around 1300, is one of the most accomplished alchemical treatises ever written; it is not a translation of Jābir, and its author — a Latin writer working, on William Newman's showing, in a Franciscan milieu — borrowed the great name precisely because it carried authority. This hub never confuses the two : "Jābir" in these pages means the Arabic corpus and its school; "pseudo-Geber" means the Latin author. Where older popular writing merges them into a single legendary figure, the hub says so and separates them again. // THE HUB IN ONE LINE // Wing I asks how the art travelled — who translated it, where, and under whose patronage. Wing II asks what the Arabic world made of it — at the bench, in theory, and on the page. Neither wing is a footnote to the other. A note on names and spelling. Arabic words and names are transliterated consistently throughout the hub, with macrons marking long vowels and the standard diacritics retained: Jābir ibn Ḥayyān , al-Rāzī , Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq , Thābit ibn Qurra , mīzān (the balance), iksīr (the elixir), kīmiyāʾ (alchemy). The letters ʿ and ʾ mark the consonants ʿayn and hamza and are part of the spelling, not decoration. Book titles are given in transliteration with an English rendering at first use — Kitāb sirr al-asrār , the Book of the Secret of Secrets — and thereafter by whichever form the scholarship standardly uses. Dates are CE throughout this hub; a date preceded by c. is approximate, a date given as a range is a lifespan or a floruit, and where scholars disagree about a date that matters — the dating of the Jābirian corpus is the standing example — the timeline says so in the entry itself rather than silently choosing a side. Finally, a note on what this hub is not. It is not a chapter in a story about Europe: the Arabic tradition is treated here as an end in itself, judged by its own texts and its own questions, and the Latin translations appear because the Arabic authors' afterlife is part of their history — not because translation into Latin is what made them matter. It is not a celebration of a "golden age" in the decorative sense: the period this hub covers contains credulity, forgery, court flattery and failed transmutations alongside its genuine achievements in distillation, classification and laboratory discipline, and the hub reports both registers. And it is not a general history of the medieval Islamic world — caliphs, conquests and dynasties appear on the timeline where they change the conditions of learning, of patronage, or of the art, and not otherwise. // SCOPE NOTE — DELIBERATE EXCLUSIONS // The Latin West after the translations — the post-1144 Latin art, from the translators' immediate readers to pseudo-Geber and beyond — is reserved for a future Latin hub, and appears here only at the threshold where the Arabic tradition hands its books across. India and China, whose alchemical traditions are older than, parallel to, and largely independent of the one told here, will have their own hubs later in the archive's sequence; they are not treated as annexes of this one. This hub treats the Arabic-language world only — but it treats all of it, from Harran to Cordoba. II. The Two Wings The hub is organised in two wings . The division is not decorative: the two wings use different primary evidence, ask different questions, and are held to the same standard by different means. Wing I works from translators' prefaces, bio-bibliographical catalogues, court and library records, and the manuscripts that survive at the ends of long journeys. Wing II works from treatises, recipe collections, classifications of substances and apparatus, and the commentaries in which the tradition argued with itself. Every article in the index belongs to one wing, and the timeline is written so that a reader can follow either wing down its length — or watch the two converge, as they do in ninth-century Baghdad, where the translators' city becomes, within a generation, the city of the Jābirian school. WING I TRANSMISSION — how the Greek art reached the Arabic world. Before there could be an Arabic alchemy there had to be a road: the Syriac schools of Edessa and Nisibis, where Greek medicine and philosophy had been taught in Syriac since the fifth century; the pagan star-city of Harran and the medical academy of Gundeshapur, the two bridge cities where Greek, Syriac, Persian and Arabic learning met; and then Baghdad, where the early ʿAbbāsid caliphs funded the largest organised translation enterprise of the pre-modern world. At the far end of the wing stands the Latin door itself — Toledo, Sicily, and the translators of the twelfth century — treated here from the Arabic side: as the moment the Arabic tradition's own books began a second transmission, into a second new language. WING II THE ART — the Arabic golden age itself. The Jābirian corpus and its science of the balance; the sulphur–mercury theory that gave the art its lasting account of what metals are; al-Rāzī's laboratory discipline — his classification of substances, his ordered apparatus, his procedures written to be repeated; al-Kindī's chemistry of perfume, where distillation becomes an industry of scent; the encyclopedia of the Brethren of Purity, in which the art takes its place in a complete map of knowledge; the allegorical commentators, above all Ibn Umayl, who read the ancients' images as the work's own portrait; and the workshop record itself — the furnaces, stills, salts and corrosive waters of the bench. Workshop procedure stands at the centre of this wing: a claim about what the Arabic alchemists believed is only admitted here alongside the evidence of what they actually did. WING I — ITS KEY DISTINCTION Translation is not transmission. A text rendered into Arabic is not yet a tradition rebuilt: transmission happened when translators coined a technical vocabulary, when patrons paid for the same work twice to get it right, when readers commented, abridged and argued — when the translated art acquired Arabic masters of its own. Gutas's Greek Thought, Arabic Culture is the wing's model for that distinction. WING II — ITS KEY DISTINCTION System is not credulity. The Jābirian balance is a rigorous, quantified theory — and it stands in the same corpus, sometimes on the same page, as bench procedures for sublimation, calcination and solution that any modern chemist can follow. The wing reports both registers at full strength and refuses to explain either one away by means of the other. The wings meet at three points, and the hub marks each meeting rather than blurring it. They meet in Baghdad , where Wing I's translation movement created the readership — and the library — that Wing II's Jābirian school presupposes on every page. They meet in the figure of Jābir himself, or rather in the corpus that bears his name: a Wing II achievement whose own account of itself reaches back through Wing I's territory, claiming a master, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, who died before the translation movement began — a claim the hub reports as the corpus's own account, and dates by the scholarship, not by the claim. And they meet at Toledo , where Wing I's road ends and Wing II's books begin their Latin life: the Liber de septuaginta that Gerard of Cremona translated is Jābir's Book of Seventy , and a reader who wants to know what crossed the threshold in 1144 and after must hold both wings open at once. The Greco-Roman hub's Transmission article tells the same crossings from the Greek side; the two accounts are companions, not duplicates. III. Method — The Rules of This Hub Every archive in this project keeps its rules on its hub page, where a reader can hold the articles to them. These are the rules of the Arabic hub. They are the Greco-Roman hub's rules, carried into a tradition whose sources raise the same problems in sharper forms — a larger pseudepigraphic literature, a longer chain of translation, and a modern popular literature considerably less careful than either. // THE HUB'S RULE // No invented quotations anywhere in this archive. A sentence inside quotation marks is a verified quotation from a named published translation, or it does not appear. Everything else is labelled paraphrase — including this hub's own summaries of the arguments it admires most. Texts are named in named editions and translations. The Jābirian corpus is cited from Paul Kraus's Jābir ibn Ḥayyān and from the editions and studies that build on it; al-Rāzī's Secret of Secrets from the scholarship on the Kitāb sirr al-asrār — the early English renderings of Stapleton and his collaborators, and Syed Nomanul Haq's Names, Natures and Things ; the translation movement from Dimitri Gutas's Greek Thought, Arabic Culture . Where an article relies on a different edition, that edition is named on the article. A claim that cannot be traced to a named text is not made. Quotations are only from verified published translations, and are named as such. Arabic alchemical prose reaches most readers through two or three layers of translation, and each layer is a place where wording can be silently improved. No wording in this hub is reconstructed from memory, none is silently modernised, and none is manufactured to give an argument an antique accent it has not earned. Where a famous saying turns out to be a later paraphrase — a common fate of sayings attached to Jābir in particular — the hub says so and prints the paraphrase labelled as paraphrase, with its actual, later source where that source is known. The Arabic tradition is judged by its own texts, not by what Latin Europe made of them. Latin reception is evidence for Latin history. That pseudo-Geber's Summa systematised the sulphur–mercury theory more cleanly than any Arabic text does not make the Arabic texts failed drafts of the Summa ; that the Latin West read al-Rāzī chiefly as "Rhazes" the physician does not shrink the Arabic al-Rāzī to a physician. Each tradition is first described in its own terms, in its own order, by its own standards of success — and only then compared. Speculation is labelled as speculation. The dating of the Jābirian corpus, the existence of a historical Jābir behind it, the authorship of the Ghāyat al-ḥakīm , the nature of Baghdad's Bayt al-Ḥikma: on each of these the scholarship is divided or the evidence thin, and this hub presents them as open questions with the main positions named — Kraus's dating of the corpus to c. 850–950 is stated as Kraus's dating, and the older picture of a single eighth-century author is stated as the corpus's own account of itself, not as the hub's. A reader should be able to tell, from any sentence in this hub, whether they are standing on a document, on a scholarly consensus, or on an argument. Workshop procedure stands at the centre for Wing II. The Arabic corpus is unusually rich in bench evidence: al-Rāzī lists his substances by class and his apparatus by function; the Jābirian books describe sublimation, calcination, solution and coagulation as ordered operations; al-Kindī's perfume book is a formulary meant to be worked from. Claims about doctrine in this wing are therefore always checked against the operations the same texts prescribe. Where a theory and a procedure conflict, the hub reports the conflict rather than harmonising it — the conflict is itself evidence about how the tradition actually worked. // A NOTE ON THE ALCHEMICAL SOURCES // Pseudepigraphy is the normal condition of Wing II's library, not an embarrassment to be explained away. Works travel under the names of Jābir, Hermes, Aristotle and Apollonius — Balīnās, in his Arabic afterlife — that their named authors did not write; the Secret of Creation is Apollonius's only by ascription, and the books of Jābir are a school's corpus gathered under a master's name. This hub cites such works as the Jābirian corpus, the Hermetica ascribed to Hermes, the Ghāya ascribed to al-Majrīṭī, and so on — the attribution is part of the historical evidence, and silently treating it as authorship would falsify the record the hub exists to keep. IV. The Arabic Timeline Forty entries, from the closing of the school of Edessa to the Latin pseudo-Geber's Summa perfectionis . Read it as two interleaved histories: the Wing I history of roads, cities and translators, which runs ahead of the art it carries; and the Wing II history that begins, in earnest, in ninth-century Iraq and ends by walking out of the Arabic world altogether — into Latin, at Toledo and Palermo. Every date was checked for this hub against the standard references named in the Sources section; approximate dates are marked as approximate, and disputed dates carry their disputes inside the entry. 489 CE The school of Edessa closed — the Syriac road opens. The emperor Zeno closed the Christian school of Edessa in Mesopotamia, whose teachers had been rendering Greek theology, logic and medicine into Syriac for generations. Its scholars moved east, beyond the Byzantine frontier, to Nisibis in Persian territory, and refounded their school there. The move set the pattern for three centuries: Greek learning travelling east in Syriac dress, preserved by the Church of the East, and waiting — though no one yet knew it — for Arabic readers. d. 536 CE Sergius of Reshaina — the first great Syriac translator. Sergius (d. 536), a physician-priest of Reshaina trained at Alexandria, translated Galen, Aristotle's logic, and the works of pseudo-Dionysius into Syriac, and wrote commentaries of his own. His versions — and the curriculum they served, in which Aristotle's Categories opened the road to medicine and philosophy — fixed the shape of the Syriac bridge: Greek science ordered for teaching, in a Semitic language, east of the empire that had produced it. c. 550s CE Gundeshapur under Khusraw I — the Persian refuge. In Khuzistan, the Sasanian royal city of Gundeshapur (Jundaysābūr) became, under Khusraw I Anūshirvān (r. 531–579), a meeting place of Greek, Syriac and Persian learning: Nestorian Christian physicians taught and practised there, and the philosophers who left Athens after Justinian closed its school in 529 were received at the Persian court. The academy's scale in later Arabic retelling is probably embellished; its medical school and its Syriac-speaking physicians are not. Wing I's article on the bridge cities weighs both. 641 CE The Arab conquest of Egypt completed. Arab armies under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ took Egypt from the Byzantine Empire between 639 and 642; Alexandria capitulated by treaty, and the conquest is conventionally dated to 641 CE. Syria, Iraq and Persia had already fallen or were falling. The conquerors ruled, at first, through the existing Greek, Syriac and Coptic administrations — and inherited, intact, the cities, libraries and craft traditions in which the Greek art had been born. For this hub the conquest is not an ending but a change of custody. c. 683 CE Masarjawayh translates Aaron of Alexandria — Arabic medicine begins. Masarjawayh, a Jewish physician of Basra, is credited in the Arabic bio-bibliographical tradition with translating the medical Pandects of Aaron of Alexandria — a seventh-century Alexandrian priest-physician — from Syriac into Arabic, conventionally dated to about 683, in the reign of the Umayyad caliph Marwān I. It is the first medical translation into Arabic the tradition records: a Greek work, by a Syriac road, into the new language of learning. The pattern of the next two centuries is already complete in it. d. 704 CE Khālid ibn Yazīd — the prince of the legend. Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya (d. 704), an Umayyad prince passed over for the caliphate, is remembered by the Arabic tradition as the first patron of translation from Greek and Coptic, and as a student of alchemy under the monk Morienus — Marianos, in the legend's Greek form. The Morienus story, in which the art passes from Stephanus of Alexandria through Morienus to Khālid, is legend , as the Greco-Roman hub also flags it: built on real names, unsupported by contemporary evidence. What is documented is the tradition's need for a founding prince — and the Latin career the legend later had, when the dialogue of Morienus and Khālid became, in 1144, the first alchemical book of the Latin West. 762 CE Baghdad founded. The ʿAbbāsid caliph al-Manṣūr founded Baghdad on the Tigris in 762 as his dynasty's new capital — a round city of palaces, markets and, very soon, translators. Built at the meeting of the Syriac-speaking east and the Persian administrative tradition, staffed by secretaries and physicians drawn from both, Baghdad became within two generations the largest city in the world and the capital of its learning. Every Wing II achievement in this hub happens in Baghdad's orbit, or in argument with it. d. 765 CE Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq — the corpus's claimed master. Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad al-Ṣādiq (d. 765), sixth imam of the Shīʿa, is named by the Jābirian corpus as Jābir's master and the source of its teaching. That is the corpus's own account of itself , and this hub reports it as such: Jaʿfar was a real and revered teacher in Medina, and later tradition credits him with learning of many kinds, but no contemporary evidence connects him to an alchemical school, and the corpus that claims his authority was composed, on the dating the scholarship standardly uses, a century and more after his death. The claim matters — it is the corpus's charter — and it is a claim, not a document. 765 – c. 825 CE The Bukhtīshūʿ physicians summoned from Gundeshapur. In 765 al-Manṣūr, ill and dissatisfied with his physicians, summoned Jurjis ibn Bukhtīshūʿ, head of the medical school at Gundeshapur, to Baghdad. Jurjis came, was cured of any wish to leave by the caliph's favour, and founded a dynasty: for six generations the Bukhtīshūʿ family — Nestorian Christians, Syriac-speaking, Galen-trained — served as court physicians to the caliphs, Jurjis's son Jibrīl (d. 828) attending Hārūn al-Rashīd and al-Maʾmūn. Around 800 the family's presence at court was the living proof of Wing I's thesis: Gundeshapur's Greek medicine had not been translated into Baghdad. It had moved there, in persons. c. 770s CE Translations at al-Manṣūr's court — the movement begins. Under al-Manṣūr (r. 754–775), translation into Arabic became a court activity rather than a private one: astronomical and medical works were rendered from Persian and, through Syriac, from Greek; Indian astronomy arrived with an embassy and was translated as the Sindhind ; Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ (d. c. 756) was already turning Persian statecraft into Arabic prose of the first order. The scale was still modest beside what followed under al-Maʾmūn. But the principle was set — the caliphate would buy Greek learning, at caliphal prices, and expect it in Arabic. 8th–9th century CE Balīnās and the Secret of Creation — the Emerald Tablet's Arabic home. The Kitāb sirr al-khalīqa ( Book of the Secret of Creation ), ascribed to Balīnās — Apollonius of Tyana in his Arabic afterlife — frames its cosmology of the elements and the generation of all things with a discovery story: a vault beneath a statue of Hermes, an enthroned elder, and a tablet of emerald bearing the text the Latin world would call the Tabula Smaragdina . No Greek or Latin manuscript of the Emerald Tablet survives from antiquity; this Arabic book, whose own date is debated within the 8th–9th centuries, is its earliest attested witness. The Tablet's text runs to thirteen sentences in the usual segmentation, fourteen in editions that divide the closing sentences — a small fact this archive states identically in every hub that touches it. 786–809 CE Hārūn al-Rashīd and the Barmakids — patronage at full stretch. Under Hārūn al-Rashīd (r. 786–809) and his Barmakid viziers — a Persian family from Balkh whose fall in 803 was as sudden as their rise — Baghdad's patronage of learning reached its famous pitch: physicians summoned, translators salaried, embassies sent to Charlemagne's Francia and, by report, books requested from Byzantium. The Barmakids' own interests ran to medicine and astronomy in particular. Patronage is a Wing I subject in its own right: the translation movement was not a spirit of the age but a budget line, and budgets have authors. c. 794 CE Paper comes to Baghdad — the movement's material basis. A paper mill was established at Baghdad around 794, in the Barmakid period, using a technology that had travelled west from China through Samarkand after the battle of Talas in 751 — the traditional account, whose details historians now qualify, but whose outcome is not in doubt. Within a generation, paper had undercut parchment and papyrus across the caliphate. The translation movement, and the book culture that preserved alchemy itself, ran on cheap writing material: a Wing I fact as material as any furnace in Wing II. c. 801–873 CE Al-Kindī — the first philosopher, and the chemistry of perfume. Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī (c. 801–873), "the philosopher of the Arabs," stood at the head of the Baghdad circle that commissioned and made translations, and wrote over two hundred treatises of his own. For this hub his bench book matters most: the Book of the Chemistry of Perfume and Distillations ( Kitāb kīmiyāʾ al-ʿiṭr wa-l-taṣʿīdāt ) gives over a hundred recipes for scented oils, waters and unguents, with the distillation apparatus to make them — the earliest surviving Arabic formulary of applied chemistry. Al-Kindī also wrote against the alchemists' central claim, in a treatise warning that men cannot make what nature makes in metals. The hub reports both books: the golden age argued with itself from the start. 813–833 CE Al-Maʾmūn — the translation movement institutionalised. Under al-Maʾmūn (r. 813–833), who had won the caliphate in a civil war against his brother and ruled an empire he was determined to make rational and centralised, translation from Greek became state policy on an unprecedented scale: manuscripts sought from Byzantium by embassy, translators paid — by the famous report — the weight of their books in gold, and the work organised around the Bayt al-Ḥikma, the "House of Wisdom." Modern scholarship, Gutas above all, cautions against picturing the Bayt al-Ḥikma as a grand academy on the modern model: it was a caliphal library and bureau whose importance grew in later retelling. The movement it housed needs no embellishment. In two generations it moved the Greek scientific corpus, whole, into Arabic. 809–873 CE Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq — the translators' translator. Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq (809–873), a Nestorian Christian from al-Ḥīra, learned Greek — by his own account, the hard way, in Byzantine territory — and became the central figure of the Baghdad movement. His method set its standard: collate Greek manuscripts, translate first into Syriac or directly into Arabic as the patron required, then revise against the Greek again. His Risāla , a letter-catalogue to a patron, lists 129 works of Galen and states, for each, whether he translated it, revised it, or could not find it — the single most informative document the pre-modern translation world produced about its own practice. His son Isḥāq ibn Ḥunayn (d. 910) and his nephew Ḥubaysh carried the workshop into the next generation; Aristotle and Plato reached Arabic substantially through this family's hands. 820–912 CE Qusṭā ibn Lūqā — the movement's second generation. Qusṭā ibn Lūqā (820–912), a Christian of Baalbek who worked in Baghdad, translated and revised Greek works on medicine, astronomy, mechanics and natural philosophy, and wrote original treatises — on the difference between spirit and soul, on contagion, on the celestial sphere — that Latin Europe would later translate in their turn, as Costa ben Luca . He stands here for the movement's maturity: a generation for whom Greek-to-Arabic translation was no longer an experiment but a profession with masters, methods and a market. 836–901 CE Thābit ibn Qurra of Harran — the Sabian bridge. Thābit ibn Qurra (836–901) was a Sabian of Harran — a member of that city's pagan, star-worshipping community, which had preserved Greek learning, and its astral religion, intact into the Islamic centuries. Recruited to Baghdad (the story says a patron found him working as a money-changer), he became a translator and reviser of Apollonius, Archimedes, Euclid and Ptolemy, and a mathematician and astronomer of the first rank in his own right. His family served Baghdad's learning for four generations. Harran's contribution to the movement was exactly Thābit: a city where Greek had never stopped being read, supplying the capital with readers. c. 850–950 CE The Jābirian corpus composed — a school under one name. The vast body of Arabic alchemical writing ascribed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān — the Books of the Balances , the Book of Seventy , the Book of Stones , some hundreds of treatises in the traditional lists — was composed, on Paul Kraus's dating in his monumental Jābir ibn Ḥayyān (1942–43), not by one eighth-century author but by a school working across roughly a century, c. 850–950, in Iraq, in circles Kraus connected with early Ismāʿīlī Shīʿism. The dating is Kraus's dating , stated as such wherever this hub relies on it: a historical Jābir of the late eighth century may stand somewhere behind the corpus, and some scholars have argued for a longer or earlier composition, but the school-corpus model remains the working account of the scholarship. Its doctrines — the balance ( mīzān ) as a quantified science of nature, the sulphur–mercury constitution of metals, the elixir ( iksīr ) as medicine for metals and bodies alike — are Wing II's first subject. 865–925 CE Al-Rāzī and the Secret of Secrets — the art as laboratory discipline. Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakariyyāʾ al-Rāzī (865–925) — Rhazes, to the Latin world — physician of Rayy and Baghdad and the most uncompromisingly practical of the Arabic alchemists, composed the Kitāb sirr al-asrār ( Book of the Secret of Secrets ), the tradition's bench manual: a classification of all substances the art uses — spirits, bodies, stones, vitriols, boraces, salts — an ordered catalogue of apparatus, and procedures for sublimation, calcination, solution and coagulation written so that another worker could repeat them. Al-Rāzī believed in transmutation and defended the art against al-Kindī's attack; he also insisted, in a famous professional credo the hub paraphrases rather than quotes, that the adept earns the name by work at the furnace, not by talk. His classification, not his theory, is what the later tradition — Arabic and Latin alike — actually inherited. c. 900 CE The Turba Philosophorum in its Arabic milieu. The Turba philosophorum — the "Assembly of the Philosophers," in which the sages of antiquity, Pythagoras presiding, debate the generation of metals and the one thing from which all things come — survives in Latin, but Julius Ruska argued in his 1931 edition that a lost Arabic original stands behind it, composed around the turn of the tenth century in the same Egyptian-Iraqi milieu that produced the Jābirian books. Ruska's thesis is stated here as a thesis : the Arabic original does not survive, and the argument rests on the Latin text's names, doctrines and Arabic-derived vocabulary. What is not in doubt is the Turba 's later authority — for the Latin Middle Ages it was the art's parliament, its debate the form in which generations of readers first met the sulphur– mercury doctrine. c. 900–930 CE Ibn Waḥshiyya and the Nabataean Agriculture . Ibn Waḥshiyya (fl. early 10th century), an Iraqi scholar of alchemical and occult interests, presented his Nabataean Agriculture as a translation from ancient "Chaldaean" sources — a claim modern scholarship treats as a literary frame for a genuine compilation of Mesopotamian agricultural and magical lore. Beside it stand works on poisons and on the decipherment of ancient scripts, the latter a real, if partial, anticipation of hieroglyphic studies. He belongs on this timeline because the Arabic art never separated the furnace from the field and the amulet as cleanly as modern categories do — and because his books show Wing II's literature absorbing the lore of the land it was written in. c. 872–950 CE Al-Fārābī classifies the sciences — and places the art. Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī (c. 872–950), the "Second Teacher" after Aristotle, included alchemy in his Enumeration of the Sciences ( Iḥṣāʾ al-ʿulūm ) among the natural sciences — and paired the listing with a short treatise on the necessity of the art, answering its critics. His treatment is measured where the Jābirian books are enthusiastic: the art is a legitimate science of what nature does in the earth, and its claims are to be judged by natural philosophy, not by enthusiasm or contempt. The Enumeration itself travelled — into Latin, as a map of all knowledge — carrying the art's classified place with it. fl. c. 900–960 CE Ibn Umayl in Egypt — the commentary of images. Muḥammad ibn Umayl al-Tamīmī (fl. c. 900–960), working in Egypt, composed the Book of the Silvery Water and the Starry Earth ( Kitāb al-māʾ al-waraqī wa-l-arḍ al-najmiyya ) — a commentary, in prose and verse, on the sayings and images of the ancients, above all on a picture Ibn Umayl describes seeing in an Egyptian temple: a sage holding a tablet on which the whole work is figured. Where the Jābirian school built systems and al-Rāzī built procedures, Ibn Umayl built the tradition's third register — exegesis: the ancients meant something by their birds, waters and kings, and the commentator's task is to say what. Latin readers would meet him, centuries later, as Senior Zadith . c. 950s CE The Rasāʾil of the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ — the Brethren's encyclopedia. In Basra, an anonymous fellowship — the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, the Brethren of Purity — composed the Rasāʾil , fifty-two epistles amounting to an encyclopedia of all knowledge, from arithmetic to magic, conventionally dated to the later tenth century, c. 950s and after. Their epistles on minerals and on the crafts give the art a cosmology to live in: metals generated in the earth from sulphur and mercury under celestial influence, crafts ranked as the soul's training in matter. The Brethren's Neoplatonism, their number-lore and their doctrine of the universal soul fed directly into the intellectual world of the Jābirian corpus's readers — and, on Kraus's argument, of its authors. c. 948–951 CE Dioscorides in Cordoba — transmission inside the Arabic world. The Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III of Cordoba received from the Byzantine emperor a splendid Greek manuscript of Dioscorides' De materia medica — and, because Cordoba had translators but few Greek readers, a monk, Nicholas, sent from Constantinople around 948 to teach them.
