Manuscripts and Modern Study: An Edition Still in Progress XVIII. Sources I. A Corpus, Not a Book: What the Name Jābir Names Every other article in this wing can begin with a person or a text. This one must begin with a caution, because its subject is neither securely a person nor a single text. “Jābir” — in full, Jābir ibn Ḥayyān , Latinised as Geber — is the name attached to the largest surviving body of alchemical writing in Arabic: a corpus of some two hundred extant treatises (the count is argued in Section V), organised by its own internal references into named collections, teaching a single interlocking system of matter, number, and operation, and presenting itself throughout as the work of one master dictating the teaching of his own master, the imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq. Modern scholarship, following Paul Kraus's demonstration of 1942–43, dates the corpus in the form we have it to c. 850–950 and reads it as the product of a school — a milieu of writers working under a single prestigious name across two or three generations — rather than of the eighth-century individual the tradition describes. That dating is this archive's canonical position, held consistently with the Egyptology hub's treatment (see Islamic Egyptology, §IX ). It is also, as Section IV sets out in full, a debated position: serious scholars have defended an earlier date and a historical Jābir, and the question remains open in a sense this article will define precisely rather than blur. The discipline of this article follows from that situation, and it is stated here once, at the head, so that its application everywhere below needs no repeating. Where authorship is at issue, this article does not write “Jābir wrote”. It writes “the corpus ascribed to Jābir”, “the Jābirian treatises”, “the corpus teaches”, “the corpus claims”. Where the traditional biography is being reported, it is reported as the tradition's account, in the tradition's own terms, and labelled as such. Where the corpus's doctrines are expounded — and they are expounded here in full, because they are among the most ambitious intellectual constructions of the medieval world — they are expounded as the corpus's doctrines, which they are whoever held the pen. The distinction costs a few words per paragraph. It buys the only thing this material cannot survive without: the reader always knows which kind of claim is being made. THE NAME Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, surnamed in the tradition al-Azdī, al-Ṣūfī, and al-Ṭarsūsī or al-Kūfī in different sources — the instability of the surnames is itself part of the evidence surveyed in Sections II–IV. Latin: Geber — a name that will acquire a second, unrelated corpus in Latin (Section XVI), and the two must never be merged. THE CORPUS Some 215 extant treatises by the count this archive uses, within a catalogue tradition that runs higher once lost and doubtful works are included (Section V). Organised into the Seventy Books, the Books of the Balances, the Five Hundred, and further collections, and bound together by an explicit system of cross-reference and deliberate dispersion (Sections V–VI). THE SYSTEM The science of the balance (ʿilm al-mīzān): every substance carries the four natures — hot, cold, wet, dry — in a determinate, computable proportion, in its outer and its inner constitution alike; the letters of a thing's Arabic name encode that proportion; and the canonical proportion of a perfected substance is 1:3:5:8. Expounded in Sections VII–IX. THE QUESTION One eighth-century author, or a ninth- and tenth-century school? The traditional biography, Kraus's redating, and the century of argument since are the spine of this article: Sections II–IV state the positions, name their holders, and specify what evidence would settle the matter and why it has not. A second caution concerns quotation. The Jābirian corpus is, in its great majority, untranslated. A handful of treatises exist in modern editions and translations — the works listed in the Sources are the working shelf — but most of the corpus can still be read only in Arabic, much of it only in manuscript. It follows that this article gives no direct quotation from the corpus at all . Everything the corpus is reported as saying is paraphrase, drawn from the modern scholarly literature named in the Sources — Kraus's analysis above all, with Haq's systematic exposition and Lory's studies — and paraphrases are written as paraphrases. Where a formula is the corpus's own technical shorthand — the proportion 1:3:5:8, the paired terms ẓāhir and bāṭin, the name ʿilm al-mīzān itself — it is given as terminology, not dressed as quotation. Readers who meet flowing English “quotations from Jābir” in popular books are almost always meeting a modern author's paraphrase, a Latin pseudo-Geber text in disguise, or an invention; the archive's rule is to make the join visible. // HOW TO READ THE DATES IN THIS ARTICLE // Three dates recur and must not be fused. c. 815 is the traditional death-date of the biographical Jābir. c. 850–950 is the dating of the corpus in its surviving form on Kraus's thesis, the dating this archive uses. c. 1310 is the outer limit for the Latin pseudo-Geber's Summa perfectionis , a different body of writing altogether (Section XVI). An account that slides between the first and the second, or attributes the third's contents to either, has lost the thread of the whole subject. What, then, is the corpus for ? Read on its own terms, it is nothing less than a complete science of nature built on a single instrument: the balance. Where Greek alchemy — the world of the Greco-Roman hub's Wing II — worked by recipe, sympathy, and apparatus, and left its theory largely implicit in its operations, the corpus ascribed to Jābir builds the theory first and derives the operations from it. Metals are constituted of sulphur and mercury in proportions the balance can state (Section X). The elixir is not a wonder-substance stumbled on by adepts but a composition whose nature- proportion can be computed before it is compounded (Section XI). Language itself is drawn into the system: the letters of a name are a quantitative signature of the thing named, so that analysis of a word and analysis of a substance are two entries to one table (Section VIII). And the ambition does not stop at the laboratory door: the same balance is applied to souls, to the heavens, and to the structure of religious knowledge itself (Section IX). No earlier alchemical literature attempts anything on this scale. Whether the attempt is science, arithmology, theology, or a fusion for which modern categories have no single word is a question the corpus forces on every reader; Sections VII–IX give the system in enough detail for the reader to feel the force of the question. The corpus also matters historically in the plainest way: it was read . Al-Rāzī worked in a world the Jābirian treatises had already furnished (see Al-Rāzī ); the later commentators — al-Ṭughrāʾī, Abū al-Qāsim al-ʿIrāqī, above all al-Jildakī — preserved, in their quotations, treatises otherwise lost (Section XV); one collection crossed into Latin in the twelfth century (Section XVI); and the sulphur–mercury constitution of metals, in the corpus's systematised form, remained the art's default matter-theory into the eighteenth century (see The Sulphur–Mercury Theory ). A corpus that founds a science's literature for eight hundred years is not a footnote to the history of alchemy but one of its main chapters, and this article treats it at that length. II. The Traditional Biography: Kufa, Jaʿfar, and the Caliph's Court The tradition's Jābir is a vivid figure, and the tradition tells his story with a completeness that is itself one of the problems. In the account preserved by the bibliographer Ibn al-Nadīm in the Fihrist (completed 987) and elaborated by later biographers, Jābir ibn Ḥayyān was a client or scion of the Azd tribe, associated with Kufa in Iraq and, in some reports, with Ṭūs in Khurasan, where his father Ḥayyān is said to have been a druggist or perfumer executed for supporting the ʿAbbāsid cause before its triumph. The son, formed in Kufa — in the tradition's telling, the great Shiʿi city of early Islam — became the disciple and intimate of the imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (d. 765), the sixth imam of the Shiʿa and a figure of immense religious authority, from whom, the corpus itself insists on nearly every page, all of its teaching derives. Drawn to Baghdad, the traditional Jābir found patrons in the Barmakid viziers and stood, in the story's fullest form, at the court of the caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd (r. 786–809); when the Barmakids fell in 803 he withdrew, and he died — the conventional date is c. 815 — in Kufa, in concealment or in retirement, leaving behind the ocean of books the tradition numbers in the thousands of treatises. Every element of that paragraph must carry its label: it is the tradition's account , assembled from sources written a century and more after the events they describe, and from the corpus's own presentation of itself. That is not a dismissal. Medieval biographical traditions often preserve real kernels, and Section IV gives the scholars who defend this one's kernel their full hearing. But three features of the account belong to the biography of a legend-forming name as much as to the life of a man, and the reader should see them plainly. First, the master: attachment to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq gives the corpus the highest religious warrant available in its milieu — the teaching is not the author's invention but the imam's disclosed knowledge — and that warrant functions identically whether or not any historical discipleship occurred. Second, the court: attachment to Hārūn's Baghdad places the art at the summit of the age's patronage, in the city and generation of the great translation movement (see The Translation Movement ), and again the placement is exactly the placement a later corpus would choose for its founder. Third, the productivity: a single lifetime's output of hundreds of systematic treatises, cross-referring to one another as parts of one design, is a literary fact about the corpus before it is a biographical fact about any writer, and it is the fact Kraus's thesis is built to explain. KUFA The tradition's home city and the corpus's recurring setting: a garrison city become a centre of Shiʿi learning, grammar, and speculation in the eighth and ninth centuries. Kufa's milieu — imam-centred teaching circles, disputation, esoteric exegesis — is the soil in which both the biographical Jābir and, on Kraus's reading, the school that wrote under his name are equally at home. JAʿFAR AL-ṢĀDIQ (d. 765) The corpus's named master, addressed in its pages with a devotion no other authority receives: the teaching is repeatedly presented, in paraphrase, as what Jaʿfar disclosed, permitted, or commanded to be written. Alchemical and occult works were ascribed to Jaʿfar himself in the same centuries — the imam's name anchors a whole literature, of which the Jābirian corpus is the largest part. THE BARMAKIDS AND HĀRŪN'S COURT The tradition's patronage setting: the Barmakid viziers, patrons of translation and of the sciences at Baghdad until their fall in 803. The association explains, within the story, both the corpus's Greek learning and its author's disappearance from public life — a narrative joint that does double duty, and is flagged here for doing so. THE FIHIRST'S EARLY DOUBT Decisive for the debate's shape: Ibn al-Nadīm, our earliest full witness (987), does not transmit the biography as uncontested fact. He reports, in paraphrase, that a party of scholars denied that Jābir had ever existed and held the books to be the work of others writing under his name, while the Shiʿa claimed him as one of their great ones and the philosophers claimed the books. The doubt is as old as the record. That last card deserves its paragraph, because it disciplines everything that follows. The question of this article is sometimes presented as a modern scepticism imposed on a trusting tradition. The Fihrist shows the opposite: by the late tenth century the existence of Jābir, the attribution of the corpus, and the sectarian ownership of both were already live disputes among scholars who stood far closer to the material than we do. Ibn al-Nadīm himself comes down, in paraphrase of his discussion, on the side of a real Jābir and real authorship — while faithfully preserving the denial he disagrees with, together with a catalogue of the works that is one of the foundations of all later counting (Section V). The debate of Sections III–IV is therefore not anachronistic. It is the continuation, with better tools, of an argument the Arabic tradition was already having about its own foundation corpus within a century of that corpus's completion on the dating this archive accepts. // THE BIOGRAPHY'S EVIDENTIARY STATUS, STATED ONCE // No contemporary document — no dated manuscript, no inscription, no citation by a securely dated eighth-century author — attests the biographical Jābir. The earliest witnesses are the corpus itself, whose testimony is the thing in question, and the tenth-century bibliographical tradition, which already reports the dispute. This does not prove the man did not live; eighth-century Iraq leaves many real scholars nearly as shadowy. It fixes the burden of the argument: the biography is a tradition to be assessed , not a datum to be assumed, and Sections III–IV assess it on the internal evidence of the books themselves, which is where Kraus located the decisive testimony. III. Kraus's Thesis: A School of the Later Ninth and Tenth Centuries The modern debate begins with one scholar and two volumes. Paul Kraus (1904–1944), a Prague-born orientalist working in Cairo, devoted the last years of a short life to the corpus ascribed to Jābir, and his Jābir ibn Ḥayyān: Contribution à l'histoire des idées scientifiques dans l'Islam — volume II, on Jābir and Greek science, in 1942; volume I, presenting the corpus and its catalogue, in 1943 — remains the foundation on which all subsequent study stands, including the work of his critics. He had prepared the ground with an edition of selected treatises, the Mukhtār rasāʾil Jābir ibn Ḥayyān (Cairo, 1935), and the Contribution brought to the corpus, for the first time, the full apparatus of source-criticism: a catalogue raisonné of the works, an analysis of their Greek sources, and a reconstruction of the system from the inside. Its conclusion about authorship was stated without equivocation and has never been displaced as the position to beat: in paraphrase of Kraus's argument, the corpus is not the work of an eighth-century author but the collective production of a school, composed and redacted in the later ninth and the tenth century — in the dating this archive adopts, c. 850–950 — within a Shiʿi, specifically Ismāʿīlī-linked, intellectual milieu. The Arguments: Anachronism, System, and Cross-Reference Kraus's case is cumulative, and its strands should be distinguished, because his critics answer them with unequal success. The first strand is doctrinal anachronism . The corpus's intellectual world — its Neoplatonic emanation schemes, its developed cosmology of intellect and soul, its handling of Aristotelian logic and categories, its religious vocabulary of outer and inner, its parallels with the encyclopaedia of the Brethren of Purity and with early Ismāʿīlī thought — belongs, on Kraus's analysis, to the Arabic philosophy of the ninth and tenth centuries, not to the eighth. A disciple of Jaʿfar who died about 815 would have had to anticipate, by two generations and more, systems that the dated record shows being built, piece by piece, by the translation movement and its successors across exactly the decades to which Kraus reassigns the books. The second strand is the corpus's Greek science , the subject of Kraus's second volume: the treatises know Greek medicine, physics, and alchemy in forms mediated by the Arabic translations, and their citations of Greek authorities run through the channels — and sometimes through the specific renderings — of the ninth-century translators, a dependence hard to square with an author who died before most of those translations existed. The third strand is literary : the corpus cross-refers to itself as a planned whole, distributes one teaching across hundreds of treatises by an avowed method (Section VI), and speaks, beneath the changes of genre and addressee, in a recognisably single doctrinal voice over an output no plausible biography can contain. A school, writing and revising across generations under one master-name, explains all three strands at once; a single eighth-century author explains none of them without strain. // WHAT KRAUS DID NOT CLAIM // Kraus's thesis is often vulgarised into “Jābir never existed”, and the vulgarisation should be refused. Kraus demonstrated, to his own satisfaction and largely to the field's, that the corpus as we have it is a school production of c. 850–950. That demonstration is compatible with several positions on the man: that no historical Jābir stood behind the name at all; that a real eighth-century alchemist's name and perhaps a small core of writings were taken up and vastly expanded by the school; or that the school's master-figure is a deliberate construction around Jaʿfar's authority. Section IV keeps these positions distinct, because the scholars who hold them do. The milieu Kraus proposed for the school gives the thesis its second, still-debated half. The corpus's religious architecture — its imam-centred authority, its hermeneutic of outer (ẓāhir) and inner (bāṭin) senses applied to nature as to scripture, its cyclical and hierarchical cosmology — struck Kraus as specifically Ismāʿīlī , and he connected the school's activity with the Ismāʿīlī missionary movement of Iraq and western Persia in its Qarmaṭian phase, the decades around 900 when that movement was building states and armies as well as doctrines. The connection, if it holds, would make the corpus a document of one of the most consequential religious movements of the medieval Islamic world, and its science an arm of that movement's teaching. Section XIV examines the claim at the length it deserves and with the caution later scholarship has counselled; here it is enough to register that Kraus advanced it as an inference from doctrinal parallels and historical fit, not as a documented affiliation — no colophon names a mission, no treatise preaches a rising — and that the inference has been received accordingly: as the most interesting unproven proposition in Jābirian studies. One further element of Kraus's work must be named here, because Sections V and XVII both rest on it: the catalogue — a numbered catalogue of 298 items , extant, lost, and doubtful together, each with its manuscripts and its place in the corpus's own collection-scheme. The number 298 is therefore a count of catalogued titles , not of surviving books; its relation to the archive's working figure of some 215 extant treatises is a matter of counting units, addressed head-on in Section V. Kraus died in Cairo in 1944, and the field he founded has spent eighty years inside the house he built — working from his catalogue, his collection-scheme, and his statement of the problem. IV. The Debate After Kraus: Sezgin, Haq, Lory, and an Open Question Kraus's thesis did not pass unchallenged, and the challenge came from the scholar best equipped to make it. Fuat Sezgin , in the fourth volume of his Geschichte des arabischen Schrifttums (1971), devoted to alchemy and the sciences, mounted the systematic defence of the traditional position: a historical Jābir, an eighth-century floruit, and a corpus whose core is genuinely his. Sezgin's method was bibliographical mass brought to bear on Kraus's anachronisms one by one. Where Kraus saw a doctrine that could not predate the ninth century, Sezgin argued, in case after case, for earlier channels: Greek material available in Syriac before the great Baghdad translations, ideas circulating in the eighth century that the surviving dated record happens to attest only later, citations that need not depend on the specific translations Kraus matched them to. The defence also pressed a methodological point with real force: arguments from the silence or lateness of surviving parallels are fragile in a field where most eighth- and ninth-century Arabic scientific writing is lost, and Kraus — Sezgin held — had converted that fragility into certainty. Sezgin's Jābir is the tradition's Jābir restored by erudition: the disciple of Jaʿfar, the contemporary of the first translations, the founder writing at the fountainhead rather than a school writing at the delta. Between the poles, the field's working positions have settled into a spectrum rather than a verdict, and the two names that mark its most influential middle positions are Haq and Lory. S. Nomanul Haq , in Names, Natures and Things (1994) — the fullest modern exposition of the balance system in English, and one of this article's principal guides to Sections VII–IX — accepts the essential shape of Kraus's redating while refusing to let the authorship question swallow the philosophy. Haq's corpus is layered: treatises of differing date and hand, gathered into a system whose coherence is a fact about the school's work of redaction as much as about any originating mind; and his book's energy goes not into the biography but into demonstrating that the system, so produced, is a serious and internally articulated philosophy of nature, to be analysed with the same care as any Greek or Latin system. Pierre Lory , in Alchimie et mystique en terre d'Islam (1989) and in a continuing body of editions and studies, reads the corpus from its religious side: a Shiʿi-inflected spiritual alchemy in which the laboratory work and the soul's transformation are one teaching in two registers, its Ismāʿīlī colouring real but to be handled — Lory is explicit — as resonance and milieu rather than as a membership card. Lory's editions of individual treatises have also done the unglamorous work on which all positions depend: putting reliable Arabic texts, with translation and commentary, into scholars' hands. 987 THE FIHIRST RECORDS THE DOUBT Ibn al-Nadīm catalogues the works ascribed to Jābir, reports the denial of his existence by a party of scholars, and himself accepts a historical Jābir. The debate is coeval with the bibliography. 1920s THE FIRST MODERN EDITORS Holmyard, Stapleton, and their contemporaries publish the first modern editions and studies of individual treatises, broadly within the traditional biographical frame; Ruska's critical work begins the source-analysis Kraus would complete. 1942–43 KRAUS: THE SCHOOL THESIS The Contribution redates the corpus to c. 850–950, catalogues 298 titles, and proposes the Ismāʿīlī-linked school. The position this archive adopts, with the debate kept open below. 1971 SEZGIN: THE DEFENCE Geschichte des arabischen Schrifttums IV defends a historical eighth-century Jābir and answers the anachronism arguments case by case. The strongest form of the traditional position in modern scholarship. 1989 LORY: THE RELIGIOUS READING Alchimie et mystique en terre d'Islam expounds the corpus's spiritual alchemy and counsels caution on the Ismāʿīlī affiliation — milieu and resonance, not proven membership. 1994 HAQ: THE SYSTEM EXPounded Names, Natures and Things accepts a layered, school-redacted corpus and reconstructs the balance as a philosophy of nature. The standard English exposition of ʿilm al-mīzān. An honest article must end this survey by saying what would settle the question and why nothing has. The question would be settled, or radically narrowed, by evidence of three kinds. A dated early witness — a manuscript of a Jābirian treatise copied in the eighth or very early ninth century, or a quotation of a distinctive Jābirian doctrine in a work securely dated to those decades — would vindicate the early dating at a stroke; none has appeared, and the surviving manuscripts are centuries later than either proposed date. A demonstrable dependence of a core treatise on a source itself securely dated after about 850 — a specific translation, a datable doctrine in its developed form — would close the case for Kraus treatise by treatise; Kraus offered many such dependencies, and Sezgin's rejoinders show that most can be individually contested even where their cumulative weight impresses. Finally, stylometric and redactional analysis across the whole corpus, of a kind the still-unedited state of most treatises makes impossible (Section XVII), could map the school's growth directly. The evidence has not settled the question because the corpus is vast, mostly unedited, preserved in late manuscripts, and internally layered — a body of evidence on which a cumulative case can be built for more than one conclusion. This archive's position — Kraus's dating, c. 850–950, a school behind the name — is adopted because the cumulative anachronism and cross-reference arguments remain, on balance, the strongest reading of the evidence available. It is adopted as a position , stated here with its holders and its opponents named, and nowhere in this hub is it allowed to harden, silently, into the pretence that the eighth-century Jābir has been disproved as a man rather than displaced as an author. // THE ARCHIVE'S RULE FOR CITING JĀBIR // Throughout this hub: doctrines are cited to “the corpus ascribed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān (c. 850–950)”; the biography is cited to “the tradition”; the Latin Summa perfectionis is cited to the pseudo-Geber and never to Jābir. A citation that follows the rule cannot mislead; one that breaks it — “Jābir wrote in 800 that” — smuggles a contested biography, a contested date, and sometimes a Latin forgery into a single clause. V. Counting the Corpus: Catalogues and the Great Collections How many works ascribed to Jābir are there? The literature offers numbers that differ by an order of magnitude — the tradition's thousands, Kraus's 298, this archive's working figure of about 215 — and the differences are not errors. They are counts of different things, and reconciling them honestly is a small model of how to handle every number in Jābirian studies. The tradition's thousands — the Fihrist already reports attributions running to thousands of treatises, and later biographers repeat and swell them — count attributions as rumoured : every short tract, excerpt, and recipe-scroll that ever carried the name, swollen by the medieval habit of crediting a famous master with a whole literature. Kraus's 298 counts catalogued titles : every distinct work his catalogue could identify from the corpus's own lists, the bibliographers, and the manuscripts — including works known only by title, works surviving in fragments or in other authors' quotations, and works whose attribution Kraus himself flagged as doubtful. The archive's c. 215 extant treatises , the figure used in the Egyptology hub's treatment and retained here, counts surviving treatises : works of which a text, complete or substantially complete, is preserved in at least one manuscript. Subtract the lost and the merely titular from 298 and the figures converge; the residue of difference is the genuinely uncertain margin — excerpts that may be chapters, chapters that may be treatises, double titles for single works — on which cataloguers of an unedited corpus will always differ by a handful. The honest sentence is the compound one: 298 titles catalogued by Kraus, of which some 215 treatises survive — and any source that gives a single bare number for “the works of Jābir”, without saying what it is counting, should be read accordingly. Count Source What it counts Thousands The medieval biographical tradition, reported already in the Fihrist Attributions as rumoured: every tract, excerpt, and scroll ever fathered on the name. A measure of fame, not of survival. 298 Kraus, Contribution , vol. I (1943), catalogue Distinct catalogued titles: extant, lost, fragmentary, and doubtful together, each with its manuscript evidence. c. 215 The working count used in this archive, following the Egyptology hub's treatment Extant treatises: works of which a substantially complete text survives in manuscript. 500 The corpus's own collection-title, the Five Hundred A collection's name, not a shelf-count: a round, programmatic figure for a late, large gathering of treatises (see below). The Great Collections The corpus does not present itself as a heap of tracts. It presents itself as a set of collections , each with a name, a place in the teaching, and — characteristically — a number for a title. Kraus's reconstruction of the collection-scheme, from the corpus's own lists and cross-references, distinguishes the following great gatherings. The 112 Books , the earliest stratum on Kraus's ordering, dedicated in the corpus's framing to the Barmakid patrons of the traditional biography. The Seventy Books ( Kitāb al-Sabʿīn ) — seventy treatises of doctrine and practice, and the one collection with a great Latin future (Section XVI). The Ten Books of Rectification , short works of correction and supplement. The Books of the Balances ( Kutub al-Mawāzīn ) — the theoretical heart of the whole corpus, the collection in which ʿilm al-mīzān is built, and the collection this article's subtitle honours. And the Five Hundred ( al-Kutub al-Khamsamiʾa ), the vast late gathering whose title, like the tradition's thousands, is a programme rather than an inventory: a claim that the teaching, fully dispersed, comprehends everything. Around and beneath these stand treatises the scheme does not capture — independent works, fragments, and the pseudepigrapha within the pseudepigraphon, later attributions to Jābir that even the medieval cataloguers doubted. THE SEVENTY BOOKS — KITĀB AL-SABʿĪN Seventy treatises moving between theory and workshop practice: the constitution of metals, the elixir, the operations. Translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona as the Liber de septuaginta , and thereby the corpus's principal ambassador to Europe (Section XVI). THE BOOKS OF THE BALANCES — KUTUB AL-MAWĀZĪN The corpus's theoretical summit: the treatises — among them the Greater and Lesser Books of the Balance — in which the science of the balance is stated as a universal method. Sections VII–IX are, in substance, an exposition of this collection's teaching. THE FIVE HUNDRED The great late collection, gathering treatises on every part of the art and its neighbouring sciences. Its scale is the school's monument: whatever the exact count of its contents in any recension, the Five Hundred is where the corpus's ambition to be a complete library under one name stands most fully realised. THE CROSS-REFERENCE SYSTEM The collections are bound by the corpus's own citations: treatise refers to treatise by title, doctrine is deferred to its proper book, and the reader is sent forward and back across the whole. The system is the school's signature — no heap of independent tracts cites itself into a curriculum — and a principal strand of Kraus's case (Section III). The cross-reference system deserves a final emphasis, because it changes what kind of object the corpus is. A recipe-scroll does not refer its reader to a theoretical treatise in another collection for the grounds of its procedure; a curriculum does. The treatises behave, persistently, like chapters of a dispersed encyclopaedia that knows its own table of contents: the practical books presuppose the Balances, the Balances remit applications to the practical books. That scattering has a name and a doctrine of its own, and it is the subject of the next section. VI. Tabdīd al-ʿIlm: Dispersion as the Corpus's Own Method The corpus explains itself, and its explanation is one of the most remarkable pieces of methodological self-consciousness in medieval literature. The teaching, it states in paraphrase across many prefaces and asides, has been deliberately dispersed : tabdīd al-ʿilm , the scattering of knowledge, is the corpus's own term for its own form. No single treatise contains the whole doctrine. A principle is stated in one book, its proof deferred to a second, its application exemplified in a third, and its key term defined — if anywhere — in a fourth; the reader who would possess the science must gather it, treatise by treatise, in the order the cross-references prescribe, and the gathering is itself the initiation. The corpus is explicit, again in paraphrase, about the reasons. Knowledge of this power must not fall entire into unfit hands: dispersion is a lock, and only the reader who has done the work of reassembly — under a teacher, within the discipline the books demand — holds the key. And dispersion is also a preservative: a teaching scattered across hundreds of books in many cities cannot be destroyed by the loss, suppression, or burning of any one of them. Modern readers divide over how to take the doctrine, and the division maps onto the authorship debate without coinciding with it. On one reading, tabdīd al-ʿilm is sincere pedagogy and sincere secrecy : the school's genuine method, of a piece with the esoteric hermeneutics of its milieu, in which truth is by nature bāṭin — inner, veiled — and a book that handed it over

What it did not do — on the surviving documentary record — is describe the strong mineral acids. This article gives the operations and reagents their full procedural due, grades every “sharp water” claim at its real strength, and puts the acids where the documents put them: in the Latin pseudo-Geber corpus, centuries later. The Claim and the Correction: What This Article Adjudicates Open almost any older popular history of chemistry, any school textbook written before about 1980, and a fair number of encyclopaedia entries still in circulation, and the same sentence is waiting. In paraphrase of its usual form: the Arab alchemist Geber — Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, eighth or ninth century — discovered or first described the great mineral acids: nitric acid (aqua fortis, “strong water”), sulphuric acid (oil of vitriol), hydrochloric acid (spirit of salt), and their mixture aqua regia (“royal water”), the one common solvent that attacks gold itself. The sentence is tidy, memorable, and — on the surviving documentary record — wrong . Not wrong in detail, in the way a date can be wrong by a decade. Wrong in its attribution, its language, and its century. The first clear, repeatable descriptions of the strong mineral acids occur in a Latin corpus, written in Latin, in the Latin West, in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries : the works ascribed to “Geber” that modern scholarship therefore calls the Latin pseudo-Geber corpus, whose centrepiece is the Summa perfectionis magisterii — the Summa perfectionis , the “Summa of Perfection”. Those works are not translations of the Arabic Jābir corpus. No Arabic original for them has ever been found, and their contents — the acids above all — have no counterpart in the Arabic texts that do survive. That distinction is this article's reason to exist, and every section of it serves the distinction. But the correction must not be allowed to do the opposite injustice. Stripping the acids from the Arabic record does not strip the Arabic workshop of its achievement; it restores the achievement to its real shape. What the Arabic texts of the ninth to fourteenth centuries demonstrably did — in the corpus ascribed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān (the Jābir corpus, dated by Paul Kraus and the scholarship following him to c. 850–950 , a dating stated throughout this hub as debated), and in the surviving works of Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakarīyā al-Rāzī (865–925) — is something arguably more consequential than any single reagent: they systematised the operations of the art into a canonical, teachable list; they classified the substances of the workshop — spirits, bodies, stones, salts, boraxes, vitriols — into a working taxonomy; they stocked, sourced, traded, and characterised a reagent shelf of salts, alums, vitriols, and fluxes that Latin chemistry would inherit entire; and they carried the Greek assay tradition — touchstone, cupellation, cementation — into the mints and markets of the Islamic world, where al-Bīrūnī raised one branch of it, hydrostatic weighing, to a precision Europe would not match for centuries. The acids, when they come, come on top of that system, in a Latin workshop culture that had learned its operations, its apparatus, and much of its shelf through Arabic transmission. Credit where the documents put it cuts both ways, and this hub's standing rule is to follow it in both directions. THE POPULAR CLAIM — MISATTRIBUTED “Geber (Jābir) discovered nitric, sulphuric, and hydrochloric acids and aqua regia.” No passage of the surviving Arabic Jābir corpus, and no passage of al-Rāzī, gives a preparation of any of the four that a reader could repeat at a bench. Graded misattributed throughout this article (Sections II, IX–XI, XIII). THE DOCUMENTARY POSITION — ATTESTED The first clear mineral-acid preparations — aqua fortis from vitriol, saltpetre, and alum; aqua regia by the addition of sal ammoniac; oil of vitriol from vitriol driven hard — are in the Latin Summa perfectionis tradition, late 13th–early 14th century. Graded attested , in Latin, at that date (Section XI). THE REAL ARABIC ACHIEVEMENT — ATTESTED The canonical operation-list, the substance taxonomy, the reagent shelf, and the assay practice of Sections IV–VII and XIV–XV: documented in the Jābir corpus, in al-Rāzī's Book of the Secret of Secrets ( Kitāb Sirr al-asrār ), and in the mint and market literature. This, not the acids, is the Arabic workshop's title to fame. THE MIDDLE GROUND — CLAIMED The Arabic texts do describe corrosive and solvent “waters” — distilled vinegar, sal ammoniac solutions, sulphur and arsenic waters — and some of them claim, in words, to dissolve metals including gold. A claim in words is not a recipe. Each is graded claimed and assessed at its real chemical strength in Sections VIII–X. A note on method, in the form this archive uses wherever a famous name invites invention. No direct quotation is given in this article. Every ancient and medieval text in it — Jābir corpus, al-Rāzī, pseudo-Geber, al-Rammāḥ, al-Bīrūnī — is rendered in paraphrase, labelled as paraphrase . The discipline is deliberate: the mineral-acid legend grew precisely by unlabelled paraphrase hardening into supposed quotation and then into supposed fact. Where scholarship disputes a point — the Jābir corpus's dating, the Summa 's author, a saltpetre term — the dispute is stated as a dispute. Procedures assembled from a text's hints plus the later workshop literature are labelled reconstruction . And every acid claim carries one of Section II's three grades — attested, claimed, misattributed — in so many words. // TWO GEBERS, ONE NAME // Jābir ibn Ḥayyān is the name on a large Arabic corpus, composed — on Kraus's dating, followed here with the debate flagged — in the later ninth and early tenth centuries, probably by a circle rather than one man. Geber is the Latin form of the name. Under it, Latin Europe read both genuine translations from the Arabic and original Latin works falsely ascribed to the Arabic master — the pseudo-Geber corpus included. Same name, two bodies of writing, four centuries apart. The article's route follows the bench, not the legend: the grading instrument (Section II) and the inherited apparatus (Section III); the eight canonical operations in full procedural weight (Sections IV–V) and the reagent shelf, reagent by reagent (Sections VI–VII); then the “sharp waters” the Arabic texts actually describe (Sections VIII–X), the Latin contrast case (Section XI), the saltpetre problem (Section XII), and the misattribution's history (Section XIII). The closing movement carries assay forward into Arabic mint practice and al-Bīrūnī's hydrostatics (Sections XIV–XV), ending where the stories join: the acids, in their true Latin century, becoming the new assay (Section XVI). Companion dossiers: The Jābir Corpus for the corpus and its dating debate, and Al-Rāzī for the Sirr al-asrār 's lists, presupposed here and not duplicated. II. How to Grade an Acid Claim: Attested, Claimed, Misattributed Before any text is opened, the instrument for reading it must be calibrated. Claims about early acids fail, almost without exception, in one of three ways: a text says a water dissolves a metal but gives no way to make the water; a text gives a way to make a water but the water it makes is not the acid later readers name; or a text that does give the acid is silently moved — in date, in language, in authorship — from the corpus where it stands to a more prestigious one where it does not. The three grades used throughout this article are built to catch exactly those three failures. ATTESTED A surviving text gives a preparation — named materials, in workable relation, subjected to a named operation — from which a competent reader can produce the substance in question, and whose described behaviour matches what that substance does. Attestation is a property of a text at a date , not of a name. CLAIMED A surviving text asserts the effect — a water “dissolves gold”, a solvent “opens all bodies” — without a repeatable preparation, or with a preparation whose product, on modern chemical assessment, cannot do what is asserted, though it may do something real and weaker. Claims are evidence of ambition and of vocabulary, not of possession. MISATTRIBUTED The preparation is attested — somewhere — but the credit is assigned to a text, author, language, or century where it does not occur. The mineral acids' assignment to the Arabic Jābir and to al-Rāzī is this article's type case: real recipes, wrong shelf, wrong century. The Four Tests a Recipe Must Pass First, the materials test. A mineral-acid recipe needs the acid's parents on the bench. Nitric acid, in every pre-modern preparation, is born from a nitrate — saltpetre — driven by heat with vitriol or alum. Sulphuric acid is born from a vitriol or from sulphur burned under conditions the Arabic texts do not describe. Aqua regia is not born at all until nitric acid exists to be married to a chloride. A text whose shelf contains no purified saltpetre cannot be making aqua fortis, whatever its waters are said to do — which is why Section VI's shelf and Section XII's saltpetre horizon are not background colour but part of the proof. Second, the operation test. The strong acids are distillation products. They are not made by soaking, steeping, or dissolving, however long or however hot. A “water” made by dissolving salts in vinegar is a salt solution in a weak organic acid: it can pickle, clean, corrode a surface, and feed a cement — real workshop powers, graded as such in Section VIII — and it is not, and cannot concentrate itself into, a mineral acid. When a claimed acid's stated operation is solution rather than distillation, the claim fails at the operation test before its ingredients are even examined. Third, the behaviour test. Each acid has a signature behaviour no other common water shares, and a genuine description betrays it. Aqua fortis dissolves silver eagerly and leaves gold untouched — the parting behaviour of Section XVI. Aqua regia does the one thing aqua fortis cannot: it dissolves gold. Oil of vitriol is oily, heavy, thirsty for water, and chars organic matter. A text that describes its water's behaviour in terms matching a signature — as the Summa perfectionis does, in paraphrase, for aqua fortis and silver — earns its identification. A text whose “gold-dissolving water” is never shown sparing silver, or whose “oil” is never shown doing anything oily, has given the reader a name without a behaviour, and names are the cheapest thing in alchemical writing. Fourth, the silence test — used with care. An argument from silence is weak where survival is patchy, and strong where the corpus is large, practical, and loquacious about exactly the relevant matters. The Arabic alchemical corpus is the second case. Al-Rāzī's Sirr al-asrār lists apparatus piece by piece, classifies substances group by group, and gives operation after operation in bench detail. The Jābir corpus runs to hundreds of treatises on the working of metals and the making of waters. That neither corpus, in all that procedural abundance, anywhere sets down the distillation of vitriol with saltpetre — while a Latin text of c. 1300 sets it down in a paragraph — is a silence with evidentiary weight. It is not proof that no Arabic practitioner ever saw a drop of nitric acid form in a retort; stray phenomena leave no texts, and this article claims nothing about unrecorded accidents. It is proof of what this archive grades: the described, repeatable preparation is Latin and late, and the Arabic attribution is a later construction. Section XIII shows the construction being built. // A WORD THAT HIDES THE WHOLE PROBLEM: “WATER” // Arabic māʾ (plural miyāh ), like Latin aqua , names any liquid preparation the workshop makes: a solution, a distillate, an infusion, a corrosive liquor. “Sharp water”, “divine water”, “water of sal ammoniac” — the phrases are everywhere in the Arabic texts, and every one has been Englished by an eager historian as if it named a mineral acid. It does not, until the four tests above are passed. This article keeps “water” in its period sense throughout. One more calibration, of the opposite kind. Grading the acid claims down is not grading the Arabic workshop down: a sal ammoniac solution that bites copper, a distilled vinegar that eats a pearl, a cement that strips silver out of gold at red heat are real chemical powers, described at full strength in Sections VIII–X. The discipline is symmetrical — no inflation of a claim into an acid, and no deflation of a genuine surface chemistry into nothing. III. The Apparatus Inheritance: From Maria to the Arabic Workshop The Arabic workshop did not invent its glassware. It inherited the apparatus tradition of Hellenistic Egypt — the tradition this archive's Greco-Roman division treats in Maria the Jewess and the Apparatus Tradition — preserved it, standardised its Arabic names, extended its sublimation furniture, and, most importantly for this article, wrote it down as lists : named inventories of vessels and furnaces against which any reader could equip a bench. Al-Rāzī's apparatus chapters in the Sirr al-asrār are the type case, and their full treatment is in this division's Al-Rāzī dossier. The present section states the inheritance at the strength the operations of Sections IV–V need, and no stronger: it treats what the vessels do in an operation, not their catalogued forms, which belong to the companion articles. The Three Heat Regimes Every Operation Chooses Among Arabic workshop writing is precise about heat in the way that matters at a bench: not in degrees — no pre-modern text has them — but in regimes , each with its apparatus, its fuel discipline, and its characteristic failures. The water bath — Maria's balneum , the bain-marie that still carries her name — holds a vessel in boiling water and so caps its charge at the gentlest sustained heat the workshop commands: the regime for distilling delicate aromatics without scorching, for digestions, and for the slow solution of salts. Its failure mode is its virtue inverted: it cannot drive a stubborn distillation, and a worker who asks it to will boil his bath dry and crack his vessel. The ash bath and sand bath interpose a bed of sifted ash or sand between fire and vessel: slower to heat, slower to cool, proof against the sudden flare that shatters glass, and the standard regime for sublimations and for distillations that must be held steady for hours. The open fire and the muffle furnace give the workshop its top heats — calcination, cupellation, the roasting of ores and vitriols — at the price of control: the charge is at the fuel's mercy, volatile products are lost to the flue unless the vessel is closed and luted, and the endpoint must be read from colour, because nothing else survives to be read. Every operation in Sections IV–V is specified against these three regimes, because the Arabic texts specify them so: the same nominal operation at the wrong regime is a different operation, with a different product. The Vessels the Operations Run In The still — cucurbit below, alembic head above, delivery tube to a receiver — is the distillation engine, treated in its perfume-workshop form in Al-Kindī and the Perfume Distillers , whose inventory this article does not duplicate. What matters here is the still's one decisive property: it separates by volatility, returning a condensed liquid that was never in the pot as a liquid. That property is why distillation, and only distillation, can concentrate an acid — and why the operation test of Section II is an apparatus test in disguise. The sublimation vessel — in al-Rāzī's lists the al-uthāl family, a lower pot and an upper vessel or cone on which the risen solid deposits — does the same separation for solids that rise as vapour and fall as flower: sal ammoniac, sulphur, the arsenic sulphides, mercury compounds. The crucible and the cupel serve the open-fire operations, calcination and cupellation (Sections IV and XIV). Luting — the clay seals usually Englished as “philosophers' clay” — is the unglamorous technology on which every closed operation depends: a failed lute is a failed sublimation, a lost distillate, and, with mercury in the vessel, a poisoned workshop. The texts' attention to luting recipes indexes how much closed-vessel work they actually did — which was a great deal. // READING AN OPERATION LIST AS EVIDENCE // An apparatus list is a claim about practice, and it can be graded like any other claim here. A list that names a vessel, its material, its lute, and its failure — as al-Rāzī's lists do — is the deposit of a working tradition: attested practice. The Arabic corpus passes this test for stills, sublimation vessels, crucibles, cupels, baths, and furnaces — the full furniture of Sections IV–V. Judged by the same standard, it offers no apparatus arrangement for making or handling a strong mineral acid: no specially luted still for a corrosive distillate, no receiver discipline for a fuming product. The furniture and the silence belong to the same record. The inheritance, then, in one sentence: Maria's Egypt gave the art the still, the water bath, and the reflux idea; the Arabic workshop received, named, and listed them, and built around them the most explicit operational literature the art had yet possessed. What it built is the subject of the next two sections. IV. The Operations Systematised I: Distillation, Sublimation, Calcination The canonical list varies in ordering and membership from text to text — the Jābir corpus and al-Rāzī do not file the art identically — but a stable core of eight operations recurs across the Arabic workshop literature and passes from it into the Latin lists: distillation, sublimation, calcination, solution, coagulation, filtration, ceration, and fixation . This section and the next give each operation as the texts organise it and as the bench requires it: purpose, apparatus, heat regime, endpoint, and failure modes. Procedural connective detail that the texts assume and the later workshop literature spells out is labelled reconstruction , per Section I's rule. Distillation (Taqṭīr): Separation by Rising and Falling Purpose. Distillation separates the volatile part of a charge from its fixed residue and delivers it, condensed, as a liquid — a “water” or an oil — cleaner than anything solution and filtration can produce. In the Arabic workshop its great documented employments are the perfume and drug waters of the al-Kindī tradition, the preparation of distilled vinegar (Section VIII), the winning of mercury from cinnabar in its retort form, and the concentration of liquids by repeated redistillation — cohabation, in the later Latin term, where the distillate is poured back on fresh or residual matter and driven over again. Apparatus and procedure (reconstruction of the standard sequence). The charge — liquid, or solid matter moistened or mixed with a liquid — goes into the cucurbit, filled no more than about two-thirds, so that boiling cannot throw crude matter into the head. The alembic head is set and every joint luted. Heat is raised slowly : the first regime is the water bath for delicate charges, the ash or sand bath for stubborn ones. The worker watches the head, not the fire: when vapour reaches the head and the first drops gather in the delivery tube, the heat is held, not increased — the still is now working, and the whole art of the operation is to keep it exactly there. Distillate is collected in fractions where the texts direct it: the first runnings, the heart, and the tail are different goods, and a perfume distiller or a vinegar maker who mixes them has wasted the operation. The run ends when the drops slow and change character — thinner, weaker in smell, or, in a dry charge, when the residue begins to scorch and the distillate takes a burnt note. The residue in the cucurbit, the caput mortuum of the later Latin lists, is not necessarily waste: calcined, dissolved, and filtered, it yields the fixed salt of the charge in the standard later work-up. Endpoints and failure modes. The endpoint is read in the receiver: volume against expectation, smell, taste where the texts permit it, and behaviour — a distilled vinegar that does not bite, a rose water that smells of the pot, are failed goods with named causes. The failures are four. Too fierce a fire : the charge boils over into the head, the distillate comes crude and coloured, and a sealed still can burst its lute — or its glass. Too weak a fire : nothing rises, the bath boils dry, the vessel cracks. A leaking lute : the volatile part — the very thing the operation exists to catch — escapes as invisible loss, and the worker blames his materials for his seal. Scorching : an organic charge heated dry past its water gives an empyreumatic, burnt-smelling oil that no redistillation fully cures. Every one of these failures is a failure the Arabic perfume literature knows by name and corrects — which is the practical background against which Section XI's point must be heard: this was a workshop culture fully capable of distilling a corrosive acid had the recipe been in its texts . The capability is attested. The recipe is not. Sublimation (Taṣʿīd): Separation by Rising and Settling Purpose. Sublimation is distillation's solid twin: a volatile solid is driven up as vapour by heat and caught, re-solidified, on a cooler upper surface, leaving fixed impurities below. It is the Arabic workshop's great purifying operation for the volatile “spirits” and their kin — above all sal ammoniac (nūshādir) , whose commercial purification is a sublimation (Section VI), and for sulphur, the arsenic sulphides, and mercury preparations. Repeated sublimation — three times, seven times, in the texts' characteristic counts — is the standard idiom for “purified to the working standard”. Apparatus and procedure. The ground charge goes into the lower vessel of the sublimation apparatus — the al-uthāl family of al-Rāzī's lists — often mixed with a fixed helper: common salt, alum, iron filings, or ash, which holds back impurities, prevents the charge from melting into an unworkable pool, and gives the vapour a cleaner road up (the helper varies by charge and text; the principle is constant). The upper vessel or cone is set and luted. The regime is the ash or sand bath, heat raised by degrees: too sudden a fire melts what should rise, or drives it past the cool zone and out of the lute. The sublimate gathers above as a crust, cake, or flower — sal ammoniac in dense white crusts, sulphur in pale flowers — and the operation is judged finished when no more rises at a heat that has been held steady, and the upper vessel, cooled before opening, shows its full harvest. The vessel is always cooled before opening: a hot sublimation vessel opened early exhales its product — and, with arsenic or mercury in the charge, its poison — into the worker's face. Endpoints and failure modes. The endpoint is the clean separation itself: white, light, friable sublimate above; dark, fixed residue below. Failures: fusion instead of sublimation (heat too fierce or too direct; the charge melts and seals its own vapour in); sooting (an organic or sulphurous charge chars and blackens the product — the fire was raised before the volatile part had risen clear); loss at the lute , the standing failure of every closed operation; and false completion , where a first thin crust persuades the worker to stop while half his charge still sits below. The texts' insistence on repetition is the correction for the last two: what one sublimation misses, the third catches. // SPIRITS AND BODIES // The operation-list presupposes the corpus's master classification, stated here at the strength this article needs and treated in full in The Jābir Corpus and Al-Rāzī . The spirits are the volatile substances — sulphur, mercury, sal ammoniac, and the arsenic sulphides in the usual lists — which fire drives off as vapour. The bodies are the fixed, fusible metals. Sublimation purifies spirits; calcination breaks bodies down; fixation (Section V) is the attempt to make a spirit behave like a body. The taxonomy is a bench taxonomy: a substance's class is what the fire does to it. Calcination (Taklīs): Breaking a Body Down to Its Calx Purpose. Calcination subjects a body to sustained strong heat, usually in open air, until it loses its metallic or stony character and becomes a powdery, earthy calx — in modern terms, usually its oxide, though the period texts know it only as the body's ash, its opened and mortified form. The calx is the workshop's intermediate of choice: a metal that will not dissolve as metal will often dissolve as calx; a stone that will not powder under the pestle will powder after the fire. Calcination is also the first stage of the vitriol work of Section VII: green vitriol calcined to red colcothar is a calcination with a colour endpoint every worker could read. Apparatus and procedure. The charge — metal in thin plates, filings, or small pieces, to maximise the surface the air can work on; mineral in lumps no larger than the heat can penetrate — goes into an open crucible or a shallow dish, in the muffle or the open furnace, at the workshop's top regime. The charge is stirred or turned where the texts direct, because a calcination crusts: the surface oxidises, seals, and protects the unburnt core beneath, and an unturned charge can roast for hours and emerge as a shell of calx around living metal. Time is the operation's real measure — hours, and for stubborn bodies repeated days of firing, cooling, grinding, and refiring, the grinding breaking the crust the fire made. Lead and tin calcine readily and their calces — the litharge family — feed cupellation (Section XIV). Iron calcines to a red scale. Copper blackens and reddens by stages the texts read as progress marks. Endpoints and failure modes. The endpoint is constancy: the calx no longer gains the character of burning, no longer shows metallic glints when ground, and — in the careful workshops — no longer changes weight between firings. Failures: incomplete calcination under a sealed crust (corrective: grind and refire); vitrification , where too fierce a heat or a fluxing impurity melts the calx into a glass that no solvent will open (the charge is lost as a calx and kept, if at all, as a coloured glass); volatilisation loss , where a body with a volatile component — a mercury or arsenic preparation mistaken for a fixed body — simply leaves by the flue; and contamination from the vessel , a clay crucible at top heat contributing its own substance to a charge that will later be weighed or assayed. The operation looks like the crudest on the list — put it in the fire and wait — and its literature is correspondingly full of the corrections experience teaches: thin charges, turning, grinding between firings, and patience as a specified ingredient. V. The Operations Systematised II: Solution, Coagulation, Filtration, Ceration, Fixation Solution (Ḥall): Opening a Body in a Water Purpose and procedure. Solution brings a solid into a liquid — a salt into water, a calx into vinegar, a metal into a sharp water — so that it can be filtered clean, mixed intimately with another dissolved body, or recovered pure by coagulation. The bench form is unglamorous and exactly specified in the working texts: the solid is ground fine first (surface is everything), added to the solvent in portions, worked in a mortar or a warmed vessel — the water bath's gentle regime speeds most solutions — and the mixture is left to digest, warm and covered, for the hours or days the recipe names. The endpoint is clarity: a solution that has stopped taking up solid and stands clear over its residue is saturated or complete, and the residue goes to filtration. Failure modes: passivation , where the first action coats the solid with an insoluble skin and the solution stops with the body barely touched (the pickle-maker's standing problem, Section VIII); false solution , a cloudy suspension mistaken for a dissolved body, which filtration exposes; and solvent exhaustion , charged to the material when the measure of solvent was simply too small. Solution is the operation on which every Arabic “sharp water” claim of Sections VIII–X is executed — which is why its limits matter: solution in a salt water is a real operation with real effects, and it is not distillation, and its product is not an acid concentrate. Coagulation (ʿAqd): Bringing the Dissolved Back to a Body Purpose and procedure. Coagulation is solution's reverse and partner: the dissolved or liquid body is made solid again — a salt recovered by evaporating its solution, a dissolved metal thrown down by a reagent or by a baser metal laid in the liquor, and, in the corpus's most ambitious idiom, mercury “coagulated” into a fixed, solid body. The bench forms are three. Evaporation : the solution is boiled down gently — water bath, then ash bath — until crystals form on cooling or the whole sets to a salt; the endpoint is the crystal habit the texts describe, and the failure is scorching a charge driven dry over direct fire. Cooling : a hot saturated solution deposits its salt as it cools, the standard purification rhythm — dissolve hot, filter hot, cool, collect — by which saltpetre itself would later be purified (Section XII). Precipitation and cementing-out : a body in solution is displaced by a stronger claimant — copper thrown down from its vitriol water by iron laid in it is the workshop's classic, known since antiquity and described across the Arabic literature — and the thrown-down body is filtered, washed, and dried. The failure modes are impurity carried down with the precipitate (corrective: wash, redissolve, repeat) and the coagulated product that redissolves in its own mother liquor when the worker is slow to separate them. Filtration (Tarshīḥ): The Workshop's Sieve of Cloth and Felt Purpose and procedure. Filtration separates the clear liquor from its sediment — the operation that turns a turbid solution into a workable water and a precipitate into a collectable solid. The Arabic bench filters through cloth — linen, in folds, laid in a funnel or strained across a vessel's mouth — through felt cones and sleeves for liquors that would eat or clog cloth, and by simple decantation and settling where the sediment is heavy and the liquor patient. Hot filtration, for solutions that crystallise on cooling, is done fast, with the funnel and receiver warmed. Endpoints are visual and absolute: the filtrate runs clear, drop by drop, and a second passing through fresh cloth changes nothing. Failures: blinding , where a fine precipitate seals the cloth at once (corrective: let it settle, decant the bulk, filter the dregs last); passage , where the precipitate is finer than the filter and the “clear” liquor is a suspension in disguise; and loss , the liquor a thirsty felt cone drinks and does not return. Filtration makes no one's reputation and ruins no one's legend, and it is in every serious recipe in the corpus — a reliable marker, again, of texts written from benches. Ceration (Tashmīʿ): Making a Body Flow Like Wax Purpose and procedure. Ceration is the list's most specialised operation: a hard, refractory powder — a calx, an earth, a fixed salt — is brought, by repeated imbibition with a liquid and gentle heating, to a soft, wax-like consistency in which it will fuse and flow at a heat it previously endured unchanged. The bench rhythm is cyclical: the powder is moistened with its directed water or oil, worked to a paste, dried gently, ground, and moistened again, cycle on cycle, until the mass softens on a warm plate like wax rather than sitting like sand. The endpoint is tactile and the texts name it so: the body cerates — it takes an impression, it flows at gentle heat, it has become workable. Its purpose in the system is preparatory: a cerated body fuses evenly with its partners instead of segregating in the melt, and several of the corpus's elixir procedures route their fixed ingredients through ceration before the final conjunction. Failure is under-cycling — a mass that looks waxen wet and reverts to powder dry — and over-wetting, where the imbibing liquid's own salts contaminate a charge whose purity was the point. Fixation (Tathbīt): Making the Volatile Stay Purpose and procedure. Fixation is the operation the whole system strains toward: a spirit — mercury above all, but also sulphur, sal ammoniac, the arsenics — which the fire naturally drives off is so treated that it stays : endures the furnace, enters a body, and does its work there instead of leaving by the flue. The bench strategies the corpus deploys are combinations of the operations already given: repeated sublimation of the spirit with a fixed body, so that each rising carries less of it away; prolonged digestion and coagulation with salts, calces, and oils; calcination of the spirit's compounds into their fixed calces — mercury to its red calx is the type case — and slow, sealed heating in which the spirit is given nowhere to go until it combines. The endpoint is a test, not an appearance: the fixed product is put to strong fire and weighed before and after — what loses nothing has been fixed; what smokes and lightens has not, whatever it looks like.
