The Theory Stated: Two Parents for Every Metal The sulphur–mercury theory is the central matter-theory of Arabic alchemy, and through Arabic alchemy of the Latin Middle Ages as well. Stated in its classic form — the form it receives in the Arabic corpus ascribed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, where its earliest full surviving exposition stands — it holds that all metals are composed, in their inner constitution, of two principles . The first is a sulphurous principle : in Arabic, the principle of kibrīt , sulphur — combustible, earthy, hot and dry in its quality signature, the agent in a metal of its colour, its hardness, and its liability to burn, rust, and calcine. The second is a mercurial principle : in Arabic, the principle of zaybaq , mercury or quicksilver — fusible, metallic, cold and moist in its quality signature, the agent in a metal of its lustre, its weight, its malleability, and its power to melt and run as one body. Neither principle is, in the theory's careful use, the bench substance of the same name; that distinction is important enough to get a section of its own (Section II). What matters for the statement is the claim of composition: a metal is not an elementary stuff, and it is not a heap. It is a true compound of these two, united in its substance, and everything a metal does — shining, ringing, bending, breaking, tarnishing, resisting the fire — is the behaviour of the two principles in the condition in which that metal holds them. From composition, the theory draws its second claim, and the second claim is the one that made it famous. The metals differ from one another only in accident, not in kind of stuff. They differ, in the theory's standard three terms, by the purity of their two principles — how clean or how fouled with earthy impurity the sulphur and the mercury are; by their proportion — how much of the one is united to how much of the other; and by their cooking — the degree of maturation, the concoction by subterranean heat over time, that the union has undergone. Lead, tin, iron, copper, silver, and gold are one family because they are one recipe taken to different degrees of success. Gold is the limiting case: its sulphur and its mercury are, in the theory's paraphrased formula, the purest obtainable, in the most exact balance, cooked to completion — which is why gold neither rusts nor burns away in the fire, why its colour is fixed and its lustre undimmed. A base metal is the same two principles in a worse condition: the sulphur impure, burning, and blackening; the mercury crude, fugitive, or present in the wrong measure; the union undercooked, so that the metal is soft where it should be hard, dull where it should shine, and mortal in the fire where gold is not. THE SULPHUROUS PRINCIPLE — KIBRĪT Hot and dry. Combustible and earthy. In a metal it gives colour, hardness, and fixity of form — and, when impure or in excess, blackening, brittleness, and loss in the fire. The father, in the corpus's frequent generative imagery; the active, determining partner of the pair. THE MERCURIAL PRINCIPLE — ZAYBAQ Cold and moist. Fusible and metallic. In a metal it gives lustre, weight, malleability, and coherence — the properly metallic character itself — and, when crude or in excess, softness, dullness, and flight before the fire. The mother, in the same imagery; the receptive, material partner. The third claim follows at once, and it is the claim that turned a piece of mineralogy into a programme. If metals differ only by the purity, proportion, and cooking of two shared principles, then the difference between a base metal and gold is, in principle, correctable. Purify the two principles further than nature, working blindly underground, has purified them in the base metal. Adjust the proportion toward the golden balance. Complete the cooking that the mine left unfinished. A practitioner who can do those three things has not performed a miracle and has not violated nature; he has repaired her work — and the product, if the theory is true, is not a gilded counterfeit but gold itself, gold in substance, because gold is nothing but the two principles in that condition. Transmutation, on this theory, is a correction of proportion and purity. That is the sentence on which a thousand years of laboratory work was staked, and it is why this article treats the theory not as a curiosity but as what it was for its holders: the reasoning that made alchemy a rational programme rather than a hope — a programme with a stated mechanism, a stated diagnosis of failure, and stated operations (Sections XII–XIII) deduced from the diagnosis. A note on method, in the form this hub uses wherever the sources invite invention. No direct quotation from an Arabic text is given in this article. The Jābir corpus, al-Rāzī, and Ibn Sīnā are paraphrased throughout, and the paraphrases are labelled as paraphrase where a specific doctrine is being reported. The one verbatim quotation in the article is from Aristotle's Meteorologica in E. W. Webster's Oxford translation, verified for the hub's companion article on Aristotle and matter theory, and it is flagged at the point of use with its translator named. Transliteration follows the hub's convention: long vowels are marked (kibrīt, zaybaq, iksīr, mīzān), and Arabic technical terms are given at first use and then carried in their transliterated form. Where scholars dispute a point — and on this theory they dispute the dating of its first statement, the route of its Greek ancestry, and the identity of its authors — the dispute is stated as a dispute, with the main positions and their holders named, rather than silently settled. One dispute shadows the whole article and is flagged here at the threshold: the genealogy that derives the two principles from Aristotle's two exhalations is a reconstruction by modern scholarship , argued from texts and dates. It is not a doctrine Aristotle states, and Sections IV–V present it under that label throughout, in exact consistency with the hub's Greco-Roman article on Aristotle and matter theory , whose Section XIII is this article's companion and control. // WHERE THIS ARTICLE STANDS IN THE HUB // This is a Wing II — The Art article: it treats a doctrine of the Arabic tradition in the form that tradition gave it. Its companions are the hub's article on the Jābir corpus , where the theory's home texts, their dating, and the science of the balance are treated in full; on al-Rāzī , the theory's great contemporary user and corrector; and on mineral acids and practice , where the bench world the theory governed is described. Its Greek foundations are treated across the division boundary, in the Greco-Roman hub's Four Elements and Aristotle and matter theory articles. The plan of the article follows the theory's own logic. First the words (Section II) and the qualities inside the principles (Section III): what “sulphur” and “mercury” mean when they are principles, and how each principle is itself compounded of the four natures of the older physics. Then the ancestry, honestly labelled (Sections IV–V): what Aristotle actually supplied, and what the road from his exhalations to the Arabic principles must have crossed — and how much of that road is conjecture. Then the Arabic systematisation itself (Sections VI–IX): the corpus that states the theory, the three variables that differentiate the metals, the underground ripening that produces them, and the balance by which the corpus proposed to weigh their constitutions. Then the pressures the theory met inside its own culture (Sections X–XI): al-Rāzī's bench-level use and modification of it, and Ibn Sīnā's principled refusal of its central promise. Then the theory at work (Sections XII–XIV): the elixir as its practical arm, the operations it licensed, and an unflinching account of what it could not do. A closing section (XV) follows its afterlife into Latin, into Paracelsus, and into its long displacement — briefly, and by pointer, since those are other hubs' stories. II. A Matter of Words: Principles, Not Bench Substances Every exposition of the sulphur–mercury theory must begin by disarming its own title, because the theory's two names are also the names of two substances on the workshop shelf, and the slide between the two senses — principle and substance — is the single most fertile source of misunderstanding in the whole literature, ancient and modern. The bench substances are familiar. Common sulphur — brimstone — is a yellow, brittle, non-metallic solid that melts at a gentle heat and burns with a blue flame and a choking fume; it was dug from the earth, known since antiquity as one of the products of the dry exhalation (Section IV), and used in fumigation, medicine, and the colouring of metals. Common mercury — quicksilver — is a liquid metal, dense and bright, that runs into globules, amalgamates with gold, silver, and most other metals, vanishes into vapour at a moderate heat, and poisons those who work with it unguarded. A theory that said, without qualification, that lead is made of these two would be refuted by the first assay: lead contains no brimstone a refiner can recover, and its quicksilver, if it held any, would flee the cupel long before the lead melted. The texts know this. The theory, in its developed form, does not make that claim. What it claims is subtler, and the subtlety must be stated exactly. The sulphur and mercury of the theory are principles — proximate constituents of the metals, defined by their quality signatures and their functional roles, of which the bench substances are the nearest visible approximations and the source of the names. Principle-Sulphur is that in a metal which is hot and dry, combustible, colour-giving, and form-fixing, whatever its material vehicle; principle-Mercury is that in a metal which is cold and moist, fusible, lustrous, weighty, and coherent. The bench substances earn the principles' names because each displays its principle's behaviour in an unusually pure and striking form: nothing in the workshop burns as sulphur burns, and nothing in the workshop is metallic while liquid as mercury is — mercury is, to pre-modern eyes, metal caught in the act of being metal, its metallic nature unconcealed by the solidity that in other metals hides the fluid constitution within. The names are therefore not arbitrary labels. They are arguments: the principles are like their namesakes in nature, and the likeness is the theory's bridge between the visible bench and the invisible constitution. // THE HUB'S CONVENTION, STATED ONCE AND USED THROUGHOUT // In this article, Sulphur and Mercury with initial capitals name the principles ; sulphur and mercury (or quicksilver) in lower case name the bench substances . Arabic kibrīt and zaybaq are used where the texts' own vocabulary is in view, with the same distinction carried by context and flagged where it matters. The convention is this hub's, adopted because the Arabic texts themselves slide between the senses — sometimes within a paragraph, and sometimes, as Section XIII shows, deliberately, because the operations are performed on the bench substances in the expectation that they act on the principles. A reader who keeps the two senses apart will find most of the theory's apparent contradictions dissolve into that slide; a reader who does not will find the theory absurd in places where it is only compressed. The slide, it must be said fairly, is not only a modern reader's problem. It is built into the theory's own history. The principles were abstracted from the substances — from sulphur's burning and colouring, from mercury's amalgamating and fleeing — and the texts never complete the abstraction: a Jabirian recipe may purify “the sulphur” and “the mercury” by operations performed on brimstone and quicksilver and then conjoin the products, moving between principle-language and substance-language as the operation requires. Modern scholarship has a term for the theoretical end of the spectrum: the Latin tradition will speak of sulphur philosophorum and mercurius philosophorum , the sulphur and mercury “of the philosophers”, expressly not the common kinds; the Arabic texts mark the same distinction less systematically, by qualification — the sulphur and mercury of the metals , their inner sulphur and mercury, the purified and prepared kinds — rather than by a fixed terminological pair. The honest summary is that the theory lives on a spectrum: at one end, two abstract quality-bearers; at the other, two shelf substances with striking properties; and every historical statement of the theory occupies some position on the spectrum, usually without announcing which. Expositions that fix the theory at either end misrepresent it. Fixed at the abstract end, it becomes a bloodless quality-algebra that no practitioner could have worked by; fixed at the bench end, it becomes the absurd claim that lead is a mixture of brimstone and quicksilver in the refiner's sense, which its authors were too good as observers to hold in that crude form. Why These Two Substances? The Workshop Logic of the Names The choice of namesakes was not inevitable, and seeing why these two were chosen is seeing the theory's empirical root. Consider what a pre-modern metalworker actually handles. Sulphur is the one common substance that attacks metals with colour and fire : it blackens silver, it is an ingredient in the surface-colouring recipes that descend from the Greek workshop tradition, it burns out of certain ores in roasting and leaves the metal changed, and ores that carry it are the refractory, difficult ones. Mercury is the one common substance that enters metals and leaves them : it wets gold and silver, swallows them into amalgam, and can be driven off again by heat, restoring the metal — a visible, repeatable cycle of union and separation between quicksilver and the precious metals that no other pair of workshop substances performs. And the two unite with each other: mercury and sulphur, worked together, produce a red substance — cinnabar, the artificial form of which is vermilion — and cinnabar, heated, gives its mercury back (Section XIII treats this cycle as the theory's bench emblem). A theory looking for two visible parents of the metals could hardly have chosen otherwise. One parent had to carry combustibility, colour, and earthiness; the other had to carry metallicity itself, in its fluid, fusible, shining form. The bench offered exactly two candidates, and the theory took them. Term Bench substance Principle (capitalised in this article) kibrīt Sulphur, brimstone: yellow, brittle, burns with a blue flame; a dug-up product of the earth. Sulphur : the hot-and-dry, combustible, colouring, hardening constituent present in every metal. zaybaq Mercury, quicksilver: liquid metal, amalgamates, volatilises; won chiefly from cinnabar. Mercury : the cold-and-moist, fusible, lustrous, weighty constituent that makes a body metallic at all. iksīr — no bench substance of this name — The elixir : the prepared agent that corrects a metal's two principles; Section XII. mīzān A balance, scales. The Balance : the corpus's science of weighing proportions of natures and letters; Section IX. One later development is flagged here, at the terminological threshold, so that it is never mistaken for part of the Arabic theory. In the sixteenth century, Paracelsus recast the two principles as three — the tria prima : sulphur, mercury, and salt , salt carrying the properties of solidity, fixity, and incombustible body that the two-principle scheme had lodged inside its Sulphur. The tria prima is a Latin, Renaissance development, a revision of the Arabic theory and not a restatement of it, and its story — what problem salt was added to solve, and what the addition cost the scheme's elegance — belongs to the Latin hub, with a pointer in Section XV of this article. Nothing in the Jābir corpus, in al-Rāzī, or in Ibn Sīnā is a three-principle theory, and expositions that read salt back into the Arabic texts are committing the same backdating error, in miniature, that Sections IV–V refuse for Aristotle. III. The Four Natures Inside the Two The two principles do not replace the older physics of the four elements and their qualities; they are built out of it. This is the first refinement the Arabic systematisation adds to the bare statement of Section I, and it is the refinement that connects the theory to everything else in this archive. In the Jābir corpus's analysis — paraphrased here from the modern scholarly accounts listed in the Sources, above all Paul Kraus's study of the corpus and S. Nomanul Haq's study of its Book of Stones — Sulphur and Mercury are not simple. Each principle is itself compounded of the four natures — the hot, the cold, the wet, and the dry, the primary qualities of the Aristotelian physics — combined in a characteristic predominance. Sulphur is the principle in which the hot and the dry predominate: it is, in the vocabulary of the quality square this hub states everywhere in its canonical form, the fire-like partner, Fire being hot and dry . Mercury is the principle in which the cold and the wet predominate: the water-like partner, Water being cold and wet . The full square, for reference, runs: Fire = hot + dry; Air = hot + wet; Water = cold + wet; Earth = cold + dry — Aristotle's couplings in On Generation and Corruption II.3, treated in full in the Greco-Roman hub's Four Elements article. The two principles take two opposite corners of that square. Sulphur stands where fire stands; Mercury stands where water stands; and a metal, on the theory, is what results when a fire-corner constitution and a water-corner constitution are united in one body and held there. The predominance language matters, and it is inherited directly from the Greek machinery of Section IV. To say the hot and dry predominate in Sulphur is not to say the cold and wet are absent from it; it is to say they are present in the lesser measure and mastered by their contraries. Every body in this physics is a resultant of all four natures in some ratio — that is the doctrine of mixture, mixis , that the Arabic authors received with Aristotle's texts — and the principles are distinguished not by possessing different ingredients but by holding the same four ingredients in opposed proportions. Two consequences follow, both of which the corpus exploits. First, the principles can themselves be analysed and adjusted : a Sulphur that is too fierce can in principle be tempered, a Mercury that is too crude can in principle be subtilised, because each is a mixture whose ratio can be worked on. The operations of Section XIII presuppose exactly this. Second, the analysis can be iterated: because a metal is a compound of two compounds of the four natures, its full constitution is a set of proportions within proportions, and a sufficiently determined theory could hope to specify a metal completely by numbers — the hope the science of the balance, Section IX, takes up. Principle Predominant natures Square position What it explains in a metal Sulphur (kibrīt) Hot + dry Fire's corner Colour; hardness; combustibility; calcination and rust; the metal's liability to be consumed or blackened by fire. Mercury (zaybaq) Cold + wet (moist) Water's corner Lustre; weight; malleability; fusibility; coherence — the metallic character itself. Read the table's last column as the theory's diagnostic chart, because that is how its holders used it. A metal that blackens and wastes in the fire is showing its Sulphur — impure, excessive, or insufficiently mastered by its Mercury. A metal that is dull, soft, and dead-looking is showing its Mercury — crude, watery, or present in a measure its Sulphur cannot fix into brilliance and strength. Iron's hardness and rust, lead's softness and grey, tin's cry and brittleness, copper's red colour and green corrosion, silver's whiteness and black tarnish, gold's immunity: each phenomenon files itself, in the theory's hands, under one principle or the other, or under the state of their union. That filing power — the ability to give every observed metallic behaviour a stated address inside a two-term constitution — is a large part of the theory's historical strength, and Section XIV will weigh it against the corresponding weakness: an address is not a prediction, and a scheme that can file everything after the fact may be explaining less than it appears to explain. // THE GREEK PHYSICS UNDERNEATH, IN ONE PARAGRAPH // The four natures are the Arabic reception of Aristotle's four primary qualities — hot, cold, wet, dry — of which the hot and the cold are the active powers and the wet and the dry the passive determinants, and from whose four possible couplings the four simple bodies are derived. The Arabic terms run parallel to the Galenic medicine the same culture practised: a body's mixture (mizāj, the counterpart of Greek krasis) is its position on the quality axes, in a metal as in a patient. The sulphur–mercury theory is therefore not a rival to the four-element physics but a second storey built on it: elements and natures below, two principles compounded of the natures in the middle, the metals compounded of the principles above. The full foundations are laid in the Greco-Roman hub's Aristotle and matter theory article, Sections VI–VIII, and this article presupposes them without re-arguing them. A refinement within the refinement deserves its own sentence before the article turns to ancestry, because later sections rely on it. The corpus does not only ask which natures predominate in a metal's two principles; it asks where they predominate — on the metal's exterior, in the constitution it presents to sense and to fire, or in its interior, the constitution it would present if it were opened, inverted, or fully matured. The doubling of the quality square into an exterior and an interior square — lead externally cold and dry but internally hot and moist, gold the reverse, in the corpus's standard example as the modern reference literature reports it — is treated in Section IX, where it belongs, with the balance. It is flagged here so that the simpler statement of the present section is not mistaken for the corpus's whole analysis: the two principles carry the four natures twice over, once for the surface a metal shows and once for the depth it hides, and the work of the art, in the corpus's boldest formulation, is to bring the interior out. IV. Greek Roots I: Aristotle's Two Exhalations — A Reconstruction, Labelled The sulphur–mercury theory has Greek roots. Stating what that sentence does and does not mean is the most delicate task in this article, and it is performed here under a standing label, repeated at every joint where it matters: the line from Aristotle to the two principles is a genealogy reconstructed by modern scholarship — Julius Ruska's generation first, and the historians who followed him — not a descent any ancient or Arabic text states in full, and not a doctrine of Aristotle's own. The hub's Greco-Roman article on Aristotle and matter theory states the same position in its Section XIII, under the title “A Genealogy, Honestly Stated”, and this section is written to be consistent with it in every particular. A reader who wants the Greek texts expounded at length should go there; what follows is the minimum, set out with the labels on. Aristotle's contribution is a mechanism, given in the Meteorologica , Books I–III — works whose authenticity has never been seriously doubted. The sun's heat, acting on the earth, draws up from it two exhalations — Greek anathymiaseis . From the earth's moisture rises a moist, vaporous exhalation : moist and cold in character, potentially water, the source above ground of rain and dew. From the dry earth itself rises a dry, smoky exhalation : hot and dry in character, potentially fire, the source of the winds and, ignited aloft, of shooting stars and comets. Neither exhalation occurs pure; each carries some of the other, and to name either is to name a predominance. Shut up inside the earth, in its cavities and in the body of its stones, the same two powers do underground work. The locus is Meteorologica III.6 (378a15–b6), quoted here in the one verbatim quotation this article permits itself, in E. W. Webster's translation in the Oxford Translation, verified for the hub's Aristotle article: “We maintain that there are two exhalations, one vaporous the other smoky, and there correspond two kinds of bodies that originate in the earth, ‘fossiles’ and metals.” — Aristotle, Meteorologica III.6, 378a, trans. E. W. Webster (Oxford Translation) The chapter's division of labour, in paraphrase of the same passage, is this. The dry exhalation makes the fossils — orykta , “things dug up”, the infusible stones and coloured earths: realgar, ochre, ruddle, cinnabar, and sulphur among them. The vaporous exhalation makes the metals : shut up especially in stones, compressed by the dryness around it, it congeals — as dew or hoar-frost congeals — before it can separate off into actual water. Metals are therefore, in Aristotle's deliberately paradoxical paraphrased formula, water in a sense and in a sense not: their matter is what might have become water, fixed before it could. Hence they are fusible and malleable. And because the two exhalations never occur pure, the metals still contain the dry exhalation shut up within them — which is why they are affected by fire, gold excepted: gold, in the passage's statement, is the limiting case, the metal in which the earthy, combustible admixture is at its least. The companion book, Meteorologica IV — transmitted under Aristotle's name, its authorship debated in modern scholarship and treated with its caveat in the hub's Aristotle article — adds the framework of the homogeneous bodies, of concoction as perfection by a body's proper heat, and of water and earth and their respective exhalations shut up in the compound bodies, metals included. WHAT ARISTOTLE SUPPLIES Metals generated inside the earth, over time, from an exhaled vapour congealed under compression; two exhalations in play, the moist predominating in metals, the dry present within them; the moist exhalation moist and cold, the dry hot and dry — the exact quality signatures the Arabic theory assigns to Mercury and Sulphur; fusibility explained by the moist constituent, combustibility by the dry; gold exempt from fire as the limit of purity; mixture as ratio and concoction as perfection by heat. WHAT ARISTOTLE DOES NOT SUPPLY No pair of metallic parents. Aristotle's metals have one material cause — the vaporous exhalation — with the dry present as admixture and contaminant, not as co-principle. No identification of the vaporous exhalation with quicksilver: mercury is never mentioned in III.6. And sulphur appears in his list as a product of the dry exhalation, among the fossils — not as a constituent of metals. No sulphur–mercury theory, in those terms, exists in his text. The kinship, then, is real but partial, and its exact shape can be stated in one sentence: Aristotle supplies the theory's grammar — subterranean generation, opposed exhalations bearing the right quality signatures, mixture as proportion, concoction as perfection, gold as the fire-proof limit — and the Arabic development converts that grammar into a doctrine he never states. The conversion, as modern scholarship reconstructs it, required three moves, none of them Aristotle's, and the hub's Aristotle article enumerates them in the form this article follows. First, hypostatisation : the two exhalations — processes, predominances of quality in rising vapour — hardened into two constituent substances, present in every metal as its ingredients. Second, identification : the hardened principles took the names and much of the behaviour of the two most theoretically suggestive substances in the workshop, sulphur and mercury (Section II gives the workshop logic). Third, systematisation : the doubled quality square and the quantitative science of the balance were built on the two principles — the Jabirian school's own creation, in a world Aristotle could not have imagined. John A. Norris's study of the mineral exhalation theory, listed in the Sources, documents the mechanism of the descent with a precision this article adopts: the exhalation theory was variously incorporated with the sulphur–mercury theory by medieval Arabic authors — incorporated with it, as a distinguishable doctrine combined with another, not simply renamed into it. // THE HONEST SENTENCE, FOR THIS HUB // Aristotle did not teach the sulphur–mercury theory. No passage of his states that metals are composed of sulphur and mercury, and the passage the theory descends from lists sulphur among the dry exhalation's products and never mentions mercury at all. What Aristotle taught is the framework inside which the theory became thinkable. The Arabic authors, reading him through the commentators and through their own laboratory experience of brimstone and quicksilver, built the doctrine; modern scholars — Ruska, Norris, and the historians of the Latin corpuscular tradition among them — reconstruct the building as a genealogy. A genealogy is a claim about descent with modification, argued from texts and dates. It is not a quotation, and neither this article nor its Greco-Roman companion presents it as one. The alchemical tradition itself, by contrast, routinely presented the finished theory as Aristotle's — an attribution the next section examines where it belongs, among the tradition's own acts of legitimation. V. Greek Roots II: The Missing Middle — Intermediaries, Appeals, and Conjecture Between Meteorologica III.6, written in the fourth century BCE, and the Jābir corpus, written in the ninth and tenth centuries CE, lie some twelve hundred years. The genealogy of Section IV crosses them. This section walks the crossing slowly and marks, stretch by stretch, what is document, what is inference, and what is conjecture — because the middle of the road is where honest labelling matters most, and where popular accounts are most tempted to pave over the gaps with a smooth story of “transmission”. What Is Documented: The Commentary Road The first stretch is solid ground. Aristotle's physical works were lectured on, in Greek, in late-antique Alexandria, by the commentator generation — the hub's Greco-Roman article on the commentators treats them in full — and Olympiodorus's commentary on the Meteorologica , carried into Arabic, became a principal channel by which the exhalation theory and the fourth book's physics of homogeneous bodies entered Islamic natural philosophy. Alongside the lecture hall ran the workshop tradition: the Greek alchemical corpus itself, from the pseudo-Democritean recipe stratum through Zosimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE) and the commentators who expounded him, which speaks constantly of bodies and spirits, of sulphurous and mercurial agents drawn out of bodies by fire, of the “divine water” that is also, in the texts' deliberate punning, sulphur water. That corpus gives the later theory its practical vocabulary and its bench experience — the sublimations, amalgams, and colourings in which sulphur and mercury were already the two most active reagents — without yet stating the two-principle doctrine as a theory of metallic constitution. The distinction is worth holding: using sulphur and mercury everywhere is not the same act as theorising all metals as composed of Sulphur and Mercury, and the surviving Greek texts, on the standard scholarly account, perform the first act voluminously and the second, at most, in germ. What Is Inference: The Syriac and Early Arabic Stretch The second stretch is inference from real but fragmentary evidence. Greek natural philosophy passed into Syriac in the schools and monasteries of the Sasanian and early Islamic centuries, and from Syriac and Greek together into Arabic in the great translation movement centred on Baghdad — Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq and his circle are its emblematic names — through the eighth to tenth centuries. That the Meteorologica and its commentary tradition travelled this road is documented. That somewhere along it the exhalations were progressively substantialised — spoken of less as risings of vapour and smoke, more as two stuffs shut up in the earth and in the metals — is a plausible reconstruction from the theory's finished Arabic form and from the habits of the intermediary literatures, but the intermediate texts that would show the hardening step by step survive, where they survive at all, in fragments, excerpts, and pseudepigrapha whose dating is itself contested. Ruska's foundational studies of the Arabic alchemical literature mapped this terrain and proposed much of the route still followed; Kraus's study of the Jābir corpus then redated the destination, with consequences the next section states. The responsible summary is the one the hub's Aristotle article gives: the steps of the line from exhalations to principles run through late-antique and Syriac and Arabic intermediaries, and those steps are partly conjectural . A genealogy with a conjectural middle is not thereby worthless — it remains the best explanation of the finished theory's structure, whose quality signatures match Aristotle's exhalations too exactly for coincidence — but it is a reconstruction, and this article never lets it wear the dress of a record. The Threshold Restated: 1144 From the Other Side Every hub in this archive has a door it stops at, and this hub’s door is the Greco-Roman hub’s exit. The Greco-Roman hub closes its alchemy wing with a long account of transmission — Byzantine commentators and codices, the narrow Syriac bridge, the Baghdad rebuilding — and ends it, deliberately, on a dated morning: 11 February 1144 , when Robert of Chester completed the Liber de compositione alchemiae , the first dated Latin translation of an Arabic alchemical book. That article, Transmission , tells the story from the Greek side and stops at the threshold, as its hub’s scope requires. This article is written from the other side of the same door. It belongs to the Arabic hub because what crossed in 1144 was not, in any simple sense, Greek alchemy arriving late. It was the Arabic tradition’s own book — Arabic in language, Arabic in its literary form, Arabic in the authorities it invoked — beginning a second transmission, into a second new language, four centuries after the first one. The door is the same door. The direction of travel, and the questions worth asking, are reversed. The reversal matters because it changes what counts as the story. From the Greek side, 1144 is an ending: the last link in a chain of survival. From the Arabic side, 1144 is a dispatch . The Arabic tradition did not end when its books began to be translated into Latin; it continued, in Arabic, for centuries afterwards, largely indifferent to its European afterlife. Nor was the Latin translation movement a single event with a single address. The traffic of the twelfth century ran through at least two great doors — Toledo in Castile, where the Arabic tradition itself was translated, and Sicily , where a Norman court translated Greek originals directly alongside Arabic ones — and through a scatter of smaller passages: individual translators working in Barcelona, Tarazona, Segovia, Béziers, and the Ebro valley, Jewish and Mozarabic intermediaries whose names survive only in prefaces, and books that crossed in baggage no catalogue records. This article follows the alchemical traffic specifically. Astronomy, medicine, and philosophy crossed in far greater volume, and the alchemical books cannot be understood apart from that flood; but the flood is the context, not the subject. The subject is a small shelf of books about the composition of the elixir, the secrets of salts and alums, and the sayings of the ancients — and the disproportionate future that shelf turned out to have. THE CLAIM, STATED NARROWLY Robert of Chester’s Liber de compositione alchemiae , completed 11 February 1144 by its colophon tradition, is the first dated Latin translation of an Arabic alchemical work, and the earliest such translation generally recognised. The narrowness is deliberate: undated recipe material had crossed earlier, and medicine had crossed a generation before. See Sections II and IX. THE SCOPE, STATED PLAINLY This article ends where this hub ends: at the Latin world’s first receipt of the art, and at the horizon of c. 1300 where a Latin author writing as Jābir closes the period of assimilation. The Latin art that follows — its summae, its controversies, its own golden age — belongs to a future Latin hub, and is outlined here only so the reader can see what the door opened onto. See Section XVI. Three disciplines of evidence govern what follows, and they are the same disciplines the Greco-Roman transmission article imposed on itself, carried across the door. First, no invented quotations. The famous sentences of this story — Robert’s preface above all — are given as labelled paraphrase throughout, and a reader who needs the Latin wording is directed to the named editions in the Sources. Second, legend is labelled as legend. The book that opened the door is itself a legend with a textual history: a dialogue in which a Byzantine hermit teaches an Umayyad prince of the seventh century, preserved in a Latin translation of the twelfth, from an Arabic original that has never been securely identified. Sections III to V give that legend a full movement of its own — its frame, its function, its career in two literatures — and assess, separately and honestly, the historical residue underneath it. Third, institutions are stated at their real evidentiary strength. The celebrated “School of Toledo”, the organising image of a hundred popular accounts, is partly a modern construction, and Section VIII says so with the correctives named. A transmission history that cannot distinguish a colophon from a charter myth has learned nothing from its own subject, which is, in large part, the study of how charter myths are made. // HOW THIS ARTICLE MEETS ITS COMPANIONS // The Baghdad movement that made the Arabic books is treated in this hub’s Translation Movement article; the corpus Gerard of Cremona would translate, in The Jābir Corpus ; the allegorical tradition behind the Turba , in Ibn Umayl and Allegory . The Greek side of the road is the Greco-Roman hub’s Transmission , whose Sections XIV to XVII this article presupposes and does not repeat: its Syriac and Baghdad sections in particular are not duplicated here. Where the two articles overlap — Robert, Gerard, the date itself — they are written to agree. One preliminary distinction will do work in every section that follows, and it is worth making before any names are named. Translation and transmission are not the same act. Translation is what a bilingual worker does to a text, at a desk, in a determinate place and year; it leaves colophons, prefaces, and glossed manuscripts, and it can be dated. Transmission is what a culture does to a literature over generations: selecting, copying, commenting, teaching, misunderstanding creatively, and finally writing in the received idiom as if it had always been one’s own. The Latin door is a translation event — several of them, in fact, each with a name and a city attached. The Latin reception of alchemy is a transmission process, and it took a century and a half to complete its first phase. This article keeps the two apart: Sections II to XIII are about translators and their books; Sections XIV to XVI are about what the receiving culture found in its hands once the translators had done their work, and what it began, tentatively, to make of it. II. The Book That Opened the Door: The Liber de compositione alchemiae The book itself is short, strange, and — for a founding text — unusually well framed. The Liber de compositione alchemiae , the Book on the Composition of Alchemy, presents itself as the record of a teaching: the hermit Morienus — Latin for Maryānus, in Arabic Maryānus al-rāhib, Morienus the monk — instructs the Umayyad prince Khālid ibn Yazīd in the composition of the elixir, in dialogue, at the prince’s persistent request. Around that dialogue the Latin book gathers its apparatus of authority: a preface transmitted under the translator’s name, in which the art is defined and its absence from the Latin world is announced as the translation’s justification; a genealogy of the art’s ancient masters, in which Hermes stands at the head; and, within the dialogue itself, the tradition’s characteristic furniture — the one thing from which the elixir is composed, the insistence that the composition is natural and not magical, the warnings against the unworthy and the greedy, and the promise that the work, rightly understood, is simpler than its seekers suppose. The book’s titles multiply in the manuscripts — Liber de compositione alchemiae , Testamentum Morieni (the Testament of Morienus), simply Morienus — and it circulated in manuscript for four centuries before its first printing at Paris in 1559. Lee Stavenhagen’s edition and English translation, A Testament of Alchemy (1974), remains the standard modern access to the Latin text, and it is the edition this article’s paraphrases follow. A precision about the title repays attention, because it measures the distance the receiving culture still had to travel. In 1144 the Latin word alchemia — borrowed, whole, from the Arabic al-kīmiyāʾ — did not yet securely name a discipline. In the book’s own usage, as the recent scholarship on the Morienus tradition has emphasised, it names in the first instance the mysterious substance itself: the composition the book teaches is the composition of the elixir , the transmuting agent, and the title is more exactly the Book on the Composition of the Elixir. The discipline took its name from its product, as disciplines borrowed across a language frontier often do. Robert’s Latin readers were not being offered a new science with a syllabus. They were being offered a substance, a secret, and a scene — an old man, a young prince, and a conversation in which the secret changes hands. The scene proved as transmissible as the substance. Latin alchemy would imagine its own pedagogy in dialogues of master and disciple for centuries, and the Morienus book is where that imagination was learned. The Preface, in Labelled Paraphrase The preface transmitted under Robert’s name contains the most quoted passage in the whole history of alchemical transmission, and this archive’s rule applies to it without exception: it is given here as paraphrase, labelled as paraphrase , and no part of it is presented as quotation. In paraphrase, then, the translator addresses his Latin reader directly and says, in substance: this book of yours is the composition of alchemy; and because the Latin world does not yet know what alchemy is, or what its composition is, he will explain it in the present work. He then offers the definition he attributes to Hermes and the line of sages after him, in substance: that alchemy is a material substance, taken from one thing and composed by one process, which joins precious substances to one another by affinity and natural effect, and transforms them by natural mixture into better substances. Two scholarly cautions attach to the passage, and both were recorded in the Greco-Roman hub’s account and are repeated here because they are part of the record. The attribution of the preface to Robert himself has been questioned in the recent literature, though the dating of the translation does not depend on that attribution. And the definition, whatever its authorship, is a translator’s artefact in its own right: a compressed, Latin, twelfth-century statement of what an Arabic book meant by its central term, offered to readers who had no other statement to compare it with. For generations of Latin readers, alchemy was what the preface said it was. That is what a first translation does. It does not introduce a literature; it defines a word. // THE FAMOUS SENTENCE, HANDLED HONESTLY // Popular accounts quote Robert’s preface in ringing English — usually to the effect that the Latin world “does not know what alchemy is” — and the sentence is genuinely there in substance. But the English wordings in circulation descend from a small number of modern translations, differ among themselves, and are routinely quoted without any edition named. This article therefore paraphrases, names its edition (Stavenhagen 1974), and flags the preface’s disputed attribution. The substance — a translator announcing a subject his readers lack, and defining it for them — is not in dispute. The wording is a matter for the edition, and the edition is where a reader who needs the wording should go. What, then, is the book’s own account of where it came from? It claims an Arabic exemplar, and behind the exemplar a seventh-century scene; and it is at exactly this point that the article must change register. The Latin book of 1144 is a documented artefact: manuscripts survive, a colophon dates it, a translator can be followed through other dated work. The Arabic book behind it is not documented in the same way at all. No Arabic manuscript has been identified that stands to Robert’s Latin as exemplar to copy in the straightforward sense; an Arabic dialogue tradition under Khālid’s and Maryānus’s names exists and is related, but the Latin and the surviving Arabic materials each contain matter the other lacks, and the precise exemplar Robert worked from is, in the standard scholarly formulation, lost or unidentified . Charles Burnett’s studies of the Morienus tradition — the indispensable modern work on the question — treat the Latin text as a witness to an Arabic transmission that was already plural and already old when Robert reached it. The door, in other words, opens onto a corridor, not a room. The next three sections walk the corridor: first the legend as the book itself tells it, then the work the legend did in the Arabic tradition that produced it, then the residue that survives when the legend is set, respectfully and completely, to one side. III. The Morienus Legend I: The Hermit, the Prince, and the Dialogue The story must first be told as its tellers told it, at full strength and in its own order, before it is assessed. Everything in this section is the tradition’s own account — the archive’s second tier of evidence, an ancient and medieval narrative precious as evidence for the cultures that told it, and unusable, without corroboration, as evidence for the events it narrates. The labelling is not a dismissal. It is the condition of taking the story seriously as a historical artefact in its own right. In the tradition’s account, then: Morienus — Maryānus — was a Christian of the Roman world, a monk and hermit who had withdrawn to the desert near Jerusalem after a life spent acquiring the art. His own master, in the fuller versions of the pedigree, was Stephanus of Alexandria , the professor who had lectured on the sacred art at Constantinople under the emperor Heraclius: the chain thus begins, pointedly, in the imperial Greek schoolroom of the Greco-Roman hub’s closing centuries. Morienus wrote, or dictated, a book of the art, and after his death the book was lost to view — until a seeker named, in the Latin versions, Adfar, a philosopher of Alexandria, recovered it and carried its teaching abroad. The prince enters from the other side of the world the conquests had made. Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya was a son of the caliph Yazīd I and grandson of Muʿāwiya, founder of the Umayyad dynasty: a prince of the ruling house who, in the tradition’s telling, had been passed over for the caliphate and had turned the energies of a disappointed succession to the pursuit of wisdom instead. He sought teachers, gathered scholars, and — hearing of the hermit’s learning — summoned Morienus, or sought him out, and prevailed on him, against the hermit’s reluctance to disclose the secret to the powerful, to teach him the composition of the elixir. The teaching takes the form the Latin book preserves: a dialogue of questions and answers . The prince asks; the hermit answers, corrects, warns, and at length discloses. The form is doing precise work, and a reader should notice it before noticing anything else in the book. A dialogue lets a text stage its own transmission: the secret is not merely stated, it is handed over , in speech, from an authorised holder to a worthy recipient, under conditions the dialogue itself enforces — persistence, humility, freedom from greed, willingness to be corrected. The prince’s questions are a beginner’s questions, and every Latin reader who afterwards took up the book was invited to occupy the prince’s place in the conversation and be taught as he was taught. The Arabic dialogue tradition behind the Latin — the Masāʾil Khālid li-Maryānus al-rāhib , Khālid’s Questions to the Monk Maryānus — belongs to the same pedagogical world as the question-and-answer literature of late-antique and early Islamic scholarship generally, in which a science is presented as the sediment of a conversation between a master and the disciple who asked well. Form, here, is not decoration on the transmission. Form is the transmission, imagined. MORIENUS (MARYĀNUS) As the tradition presents him: a Christian hermit of the Roman world, settled near Jerusalem; pupil, in the pedigree, of Stephanus of Alexandria; author of a book of the art; reluctant teacher of the prince. No independent documentary trace of him exists outside the alchemical tradition that celebrates him. See Section V. KHĀLID IBN YAZĪD (d. 704) As the tradition presents him: Umayyad prince, disappointed of the caliphate, who turned to wisdom, summoned the hermit, learned the art in dialogue, and ordered the books of the art translated — the founder, in Arabic memory, of Arabic alchemy itself. The prince was historical; the alchemy, on the modern assessment, is the tradition’s charter. See Sections IV–V. The dialogue’s doctrine, in paraphrase of the Latin text as Stavenhagen presents it, can be stated briefly — and its brevity is itself a datum. The elixir is composed from one thing : a single material, common, despised, and everywhere available, which the text circles with cover-names and refuses, in the tradition’s manner, to name plainly. The composition is a work of nature assisted by art, not of magic or of demonic aid — the book is emphatic, in the paraphrase, that the operation follows the order of natural generation, as a plant grows from a seed. The work requires the joining of what the tradition calls body and spirit, the purification of the material, its dissolution and its recoagulation, and a regimen of fire patiently governed. And the whole is wrapped in the moral frame the dialogue form supplies: the art is God’s gift, given to the worthy, ruined by haste and by avarice, and not to be sold. A Latin reader of 1144 who finished the book possessed, therefore, not a laboratory manual — the Morienus dialogue is famously short on weighable procedure — but a complete idea of the art: its object (the elixir), its matter (one thing), its method (nature imitated), its ethics (the worthy recipient), and its pedigree (Hermes, Stephanus, the hermit, the prince). Ideas travel lighter than manuals, and further. The shelf of practical books that followed, in Sections XI and XIV, would supply the procedure. The Morienus supplied the warrant. The Genealogy of Hermes One element of the Latin book’s frame deserves separate notice, because it shows the pseudepigraphic machinery of the Arabic tradition crossing the door intact — a theme Section XV takes up at length. The preface’s genealogy, in paraphrase, distinguishes three Hermeses : a first Hermes before the Flood, identified with the antediluvian sage of the Arabic Hermetic tradition; a second, Babylonian Hermes after the Flood; and a third, Egyptian Hermes, the philosopher of Egypt. The scheme is not a Latin invention. It is the Arabic tradition’s own solution to the embarrassment of Hermes’ ubiquity — the same multiplication of Hermeses that the Arabic bio-bibliographical literature performs, and behind it the late-antique habit of filing distinct literatures under one great name. Its presence at the head of the first Latin alchemical book means that Latin Europe received, along with the elixir, a ready-made ancient history of the art: antediluvian, Babylonian, Egyptian, Greek, and now — by the act of translation itself — Latin. The receiving culture did not have to invent a pedigree for its new science. The pedigree was in the parcel, with the names already in order. Section XV argues that this may have been the most consequential item in the whole consignment. IV. The Morienus Legend II: Pedigree, Patronage, and a Lost Original A legend that successful invites a functional question: what work was it for ? The Morienus–Khālid story served two literatures, in two languages, at two different moments, and it did different work in each. In the Arabic tradition that composed it, the story is a foundation charter . In the Latin tradition that received it in 1144, it became a scene of instruction — the template in which Latin alchemy imagined its own teaching. The two functions are distinct, and conflating them is the commonest error in popular accounts of the book. The Charter in Arabic: A Greek-Christian Pedigree and a Royal Pupil Consider what the story gives Arabic alchemy, item by item. It gives the art a pedigree that is Greek and Christian at its source : the teaching descends from Stephanus, professor in Christian Constantinople, through a Christian monk — so that the art enters Islam not as pagan magic or as a conquered people’s craft lore, but as a science with a school lineage , of exactly the kind Arabic scholarly culture honoured in medicine and philosophy, where the chain of masters (the isnād habit of mind, generalised beyond its hadith home) was the standard warrant of a teaching’s authenticity. It gives the art a royal pupil of the Prophet’s own century and of the ruling house : Khālid is not a marginal adept but a grandson of Muʿāwiya, and his discipleship places the art’s Arabic beginning inside the first Islamic century, under caliphal patronage, before the Abbasid translation movement that the documentary record actually shows. And it gives the art a founder for its translation movement : the same Khālid, in the tradition’s fuller telling, ordered Greek scholars in Egypt to translate the books of the art from Greek and Coptic into Arabic — pushing the birthday of Arabic translation itself back from Baghdad and the Abbasids to Damascus and the Umayyads. Each gift answers a need. A young literature, conscious of its Greek debts and exposed to religious suspicion of its aims, acquires antiquity, orthodoxy of lineage, and royal sponsorship in a single narrative. The story is, in the strict sense, too good: it supplies exactly the credentials the tradition required, in exactly the form its culture prized. That goodness is evidence — about the tellers, not about the seventh century. The charter’s career in Arabic can be followed in the bio-bibliographical record, which is where a historian can watch a legend being filed as fact. Its most consequential filing is in the Fihrist of Ibn al-Nadīm (completed 987), the great Baghdad catalogue of books and their authors, whose tenth discourse treats the alchemists. Ibn al-Nadīm reports, in paraphrase, that Khālid ibn Yazīd was the first in Islam to have books of the art translated from Greek and Coptic into Arabic, that he pursued the art after being disappointed of rule, and that works of the art circulated under his name — poems and treatises among them. The Fihrist is a catalogue, and it is used in this hub at catalogue strength: it proves that by the later tenth century the Khālid story was the Arabic tradition’s received account of its own beginning, told by its most careful bibliographer. It does not prove — and Ibn al-Nadīm, who flags marvels elsewhere in his book with a cataloguer’s scepticism, does not ask it to prove — that the events of the seventh century happened as the story says. Between the prince’s death in 704 and the catalogue of 987 stand nearly three centuries, and the story’s attestations thicken, on inspection, toward the later end of that interval. Section V states the modern assessment in full. // THE ARABIC DIALOGUE TRADITION // An Arabic dialogue of Khālid’s questions to Maryānus circulates in the manuscript tradition under titles of the Masāʾil Khālid li-Maryānus al-rāhib type, alongside a small shelf of poems and treatises ascribed to Khālid himself. The surviving Arabic materials and Robert’s Latin overlap without coinciding: each contains matter the other lacks, and no surviving Arabic codex has been shown to be the exemplar from which the Latin was made. The honest formulation — the one this article uses throughout — is that Robert translated an Arabic Morienus book, of a tradition that was already plural, and that the exemplar is lost or unidentified. The Scene in Latin: How a Secret Is Handed Over In Latin hands the story’s centre of gravity shifted. Latin readers of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries had no need of a charter for Arabic alchemy; what the dialogue gave them was a model of reception itself . The book dramatises the exact situation its readers were in: a seeker from a culture that lacks the art petitions a holder from a culture that possesses it, and is taught — slowly, conditionally, and only after his motives are examined. The Morienus dialogue thus became the Latin tradition’s favourite literary machine. The dialogue of master and disciple, the journey to the hermit, the reluctant disclosure, the prince or the monk or the personified art herself as teacher: the Latin alchemical literature of the following centuries is populated with scenes built on this plan, from the Turba Philosophorum ’s assembly of ancients (Section XIV) to the great dialogues of the later Middle Ages. Transmission, the Morienus taught its new readers, is not something that happens to books. It is something that happens between persons, under moral conditions, in speech. The Latin art believed its founding book on this point for five hundred years, and organised its pedagogy — real and literary — accordingly. There is a final function to record, quieter than charter or scene, and it belongs to the translators themselves. A book whose own story is about a translation — Greek learning, held by a Christian monk, rendered intelligible to an Arabic-speaking prince — is a book that authorises translation as the art’s native mode of travel . Robert of Chester, rendering that book from Arabic into Latin, was doing inside his own century exactly what his text depicted Morienus doing inside its fiction: carrying the secret across a frontier of language and confession, to a worthy recipient who had asked. Whether or not Robert chose the book for that reason — no evidence says he did — the fit between the first Latin alchemical translation and its subject is exact, and the tradition noticed. The Morienus was still being printed, prefaced, and argued over in the seventeenth century. Founding books that describe their own founding have a long half-life. V. Khālid ibn Yazīd: The Historical Residue, Assessed What remains when the legend is set aside? The question deserves a section of its own, conducted at the standard this hub applies to every foundation story: the documented residue first, the attributions second, the modern verdicts named and dated, and no harmonising synthesis offered where the evidence supports none. The documented residue is a prince, not an alchemist. Khālid ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya (c. 668–704; some sources give 709 for his death) is a historical figure of the Umayyad house: son of the caliph Yazīd I, brother of the caliph Muʿāwiya II, and himself a candidate in the succession struggles that followed Yazīd’s death, in which he was passed over in favour of Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam and the Marwānid line. The early Arabic historical and literary tradition remembers him as a man of learning and eloquence — a poet, a transmitter of hadith, a patron in the ordinary courtly senses — and that reputation for learning is itself documented early enough to be the seed from which larger reputations grow. Of alchemy, of translation projects, of a monkish teacher, the early record knows nothing. The alchemical Khālid — the poems and treatises under his name, the tutelage of Morienus, the sponsorship of the first translations — enters the record in the ninth and tenth centuries , in the literary circles of Abbasid Iraq, two hundred years and a change of dynasty after his death. // THE KHĀLID FILE, SUMMARISED // Documented: an Umayyad prince, c. 668–704, passed over for the caliphate; a reputation, attested early, for poetry, hadith, and learning in general. Attributed from the ninth century onward: alchemical treatises and poems under his name; instruction by the hermit Morienus; the first commissioning of Greek-to-Arabic translation. Not documented at any date: a historical Morienus; an Umayyad translation bureau; any alchemical activity by the historical Khālid. First caliphal sponsorship of translation on the standard account belongs to the Abbasid period, from the reign of al-Manṣūr (r. 754–775) — two generations after Khālid’s death. See this hub’s Translation Movement article for the documented movement. The modern verdicts, named as this hub names them everywhere, converge from different directions. Julius Ruska , in his studies of the Arabic alchemists (1924), first subjected the Khālid dossier to systematic source criticism and concluded that the alchemical writings under the prince’s name are pseudepigrapha of the Islamic centuries, not Umayyad survivals. Manfred Ullmann , in his work on the natural and secret sciences in Islam (1972) and his dedicated study of Khālid (1978), gave the legend its classic modern formulation: a construction of the ninth and tenth centuries, and he proposed a mechanism for it — in paraphrase of his argument, an early description of Khālid as the man who sought what he could not attain, spoken first of the caliphate he missed, was reread by later tradition as spoken of the unattainable art, and the rereading accreted a biography, a teacher, and a library. Pierre Lory has proposed a complementary social mechanism: writings from a humbler milieu fathered on an Umayyad prince of known learning to lend them nobility and protection. The mechanisms differ; the conclusion is shared, and it is the conclusion the Greco-Roman hub’s transmission article states and this article repeats without diluting: Khālid was real; his alchemical studies are attested only by the tradition that profits from them. The Morienus tutelage has no corroboration outside that tradition, and Morienus himself has no existence the record can verify at all. Two things do not follow from that verdict, and the article refuses both. It does not follow that the legend is worthless. As Sections III and IV have shown, the legend is a primary document of how the Arabic tradition understood authority, pedigree, and the ethics of disclosure — and it is the very book through which Latin Europe first met the art, so that its fictions had real effects on real readers for half a millennium. A charter myth is not a failed chronicle; it is a successful constitution, and it is filed in this archive accordingly, in the tier reserved for traditions about the past. Nor does it follow that Arabic alchemy’s real beginnings are obscure in the same way. They are not. The documented movement — Syriac intermediaries, Abbasid patronage, the Baghdad translation enterprise, the emergence of an Arabic technical literature in the ninth century — is recoverable in detail, and this hub’s Wing I has told it in its earlier articles: the bridge cities in Harran and Gundeshapur , the movement itself in The Baghdad Translation Movement , and the Egyptian side of the same centuries in the Egyptology division’s Islamic Egyptology . The legend’s function, seen against that record, is precise: it gives a documented ninth-century beginning a legendary seventh-century birthday. Traditions that value antiquity as this one did will always prefer the birthday. Historians are paid to keep both dates, labelled, on the same page — as this section has done. VI. Toledo After 1085: The City That Could Translate Translation movements happen in places, and the places are not interchangeable. The Arabic-to-Latin movement of the twelfth century happened, in its densest and most consequential form, in Toledo — and Toledo could do the work because of what the city had become in the half-century since its conquest. In 1085 Alfonso VI of León-Castile took Toledo from its Muslim rulers, and the city entered the Christian kingdoms as something no other city in Latin Europe was: a great Arabic-speaking capital, intact, inside a Latin-ruled frontier state. Its libraries had not been burned. Its population had not been expelled. What the conquest changed was sovereignty; what it preserved — for a crucial two generations, and in diminishing measure for two centuries — was a complete Arabic urban civilisation now living under Christian rule, in daily contact with Latin clergy, Castilian settlers, and the courts of the north. Every condition a translation movement needs was present in one walled city on the Tagus, and Section VII will show the movement exploiting each of them in turn. THE LIBRARIES Toledo had been a capital of learning under its Muslim rulers, and its collections — caliphal and private, in the cathedral’s orbit after the conquest and in the city’s Arabic book culture throughout — put Arabic codices of astronomy, medicine, philosophy, and the sciences within a translator’s walk. A translation movement begins with books to translate, in a place where a translator may sit down with them. THE MOZARABS Toledo’s Mozarabic Christians — Arabic-speaking Christians whose community predated the conquest by centuries — were the city’s living bridge: Latin in liturgy, Arabic in daily and learned life, Romance in the street. Their bilingualism was not an accomplishment but a birthright, and the translation teams of Section VII are unthinkable without it.
