How We Know: The Fihrist, the Risāla, and the Biographers XVII. Sources I. A Movement, Not a Whim: The Phenomenon Sometime around the middle of the eighth century CE, scholars working in and around Baghdad began, systematically and at someone else's expense, to translate Greek books into Arabic. They did not stop for roughly two hundred and fifty years. By the time the effort wound down, around the year 1000, the Arabic language possessed — in translation — the greater part of the Greek scientific and philosophical inheritance: Galen's medicine nearly entire, Hippocrates with his commentators, Aristotle nearly whole, Euclid, Ptolemy's Almagest , Archimedes and Apollonius in part, Dioscorides on drugs, Plato in part and often at one remove, and, travelling on the same roads and sometimes in the same baggage, the technical Hermetica and the Greek alchemical corpus. Nothing on this scale had been attempted before. The Roman world, which ruled Greek speakers for centuries, had translated remarkably little Greek science into Latin. The Syriac churches had translated a great deal, but for their own schools and within a theological frame. Baghdad's movement was different in kind: it was a sustained, funded, socially broad campaign to move an entire foreign literature of knowledge into a language that, at the campaign's opening, did not yet possess the vocabulary to receive it. The framing this article follows — and states at the front, because the older framing still dominates popular accounts — is Dimitri Gutas's, in Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998). On the older telling, the movement is a caliph's whim enlarged: al-Maʾmūn dreams of Aristotle, founds a House of Wisdom, and Greek wisdom pours into Arabic at his command. Gutas dismantled that picture piece by piece. The movement, he showed, was a social movement : it began before al-Maʾmūn, continued after him, was funded by caliphs but also by viziers, generals, court physicians, merchants, and scholars themselves, and it drew its energy from the ideology of the early Abbasid state — a new empire, ruling from a new capital, presenting itself as the heir and restorer of the sciences of the peoples it had succeeded, Persian and Greek alike, against its Byzantine rival, which possessed the Greek books and, in Baghdad's polemical view, was letting them rot. Translation was cultural policy, social ambition, professional strategy, and genuine intellectual hunger at once, distributed across hundreds of patrons and practitioners over ten generations. A movement of that shape cannot be switched on by one man's dream, and it was not switched off by one man's death. THE DATES c. 750–1000 CE. Isolated translation under the Umayyads and the first Abbasids; organised caliphal patronage from the reign of al-Manṣūr (r. 754–775); the great age of the Ḥunayn circle in the ninth century; translation continuing, in changed forms, through the tenth. THE SCALE Hundreds of works, by the catalogues' count: the medical corpus of Galen and Hippocrates, the Aristotelian school corpus, the mathematical and astronomical canon, and the technical and occult shelf beside them (Sections XII–XIII). THE DISCIPLINE Collation of Greek manuscripts, revision of earlier versions, team translation, and the deliberate creation of an Arabic technical vocabulary — a philology, not a copying exercise (Sections VII–IX). THE CONSEQUENCE Arabic becomes a language of original science. By c. 900 the heirs of the translators are no longer only translating Greek knowledge; they are extending, correcting, and superseding it (Section XV). A note on method, in the form this archive uses wherever the sources invite romance. No direct quotation is given in this article unless it is explicitly attributed to a named published translation that was consulted for it. In practice the article paraphrases throughout, and paraphrases are labelled as paraphrase in the text. Where scholars dispute a point — and on the Bayt al-Ḥikma they dispute the institution's very nature — the dispute is stated as a dispute, with the positions named, rather than silently settled. Anecdotes are flagged as anecdotes at the point where they appear. The movement's own documentary remains — above all Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq's Risāla and Ibn al-Nadīm's Fihrist — are treated in Section XVI at their real evidentiary strength, biases included. This article deepens, and does not replace, the Greco-Roman hub's account of the same corridor. Readers who want the movement as one link in the longer chain that carried Greek alchemy from Alexandria to Latin Europe should read Transmission in the Greco-Roman division, whose Section XI treats Baghdad from the Greek side. The present article stands inside Baghdad and looks at the machinery: the paper, the money, the institution, the translators, the method, the books — and the books that were pointedly not translated. // NAMES AND TRANSLITERATION // Arabic names are given in a scholarly transliteration with diacritics throughout: Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, Isḥāq ibn Ḥunayn, Bayt al-Ḥikma, Banū Mūsā, al-Maʾmūn. The article sign (al-) is not capitalised mid-name. Dates are CE unless a reign is being dated, in which case the caliph's regnal years are given as such. Greek titles are given in their familiar Latin forms — Almagest , Elements — where the tradition has fixed them. One framing caution, because it governs everything that follows. The translation movement was not a rescue operation mounted for posterity's benefit, and the translators were not librarians of a burning world. They were working scholars in a competitive court economy, translating the books their patrons wanted, for uses their patrons understood: medicine for the caliph's body and the court's prestige, astronomy and astrology for the calendar, the horoscope, and the empire's ideological astronomy, mathematics for administration, inheritance law, and the exact sciences' own sake, philosophy for the theological and intellectual contests of a capital arguing about reason and revelation. Alchemy travelled inside that economy — never at its centre, as the Greco-Roman Transmission article already established, but persistently at its working edge, carried by the same translators, the same patrons, and the same Syriac bridge as Galen and Ptolemy. To understand how the alchemical corpus reached Arabic, there is no shortcut around understanding how everything else did. That is the work of the sections that follow. II. Before Baghdad: The Syriac Bridge and the Roads In Baghdad did not invent Greek translation. It inherited a going concern, some three centuries old, staffed by the Syriac-speaking Christians of Mesopotamia and Syria — and the first precondition of the Arabic movement is that the concern existed. The archive's full treatment of that inheritance is the companion article Harran and Gundeshapur in this division, which follows the Syriac schools, the Harranian Sabians, and the medical tradition of Gundeshapur in detail. This section states the bridge at the strength the present article needs, and no stronger. Syriac — the literary Aramaic of the Christian East — had been receiving Greek texts since the fifth century: first theology, then, decisively, medicine, logic, and natural philosophy. The founding figure of the scientific line is Sergius of Reshaina (died 536), an Alexandria-trained physician-priest who rendered some thirty works of Galen into Syriac, translated Aristotle's Categories and Porphyry's Introduction , and wrote the first Aristotelian commentary in the language. After him the practice never lapsed. The West Syrian (Jacobite) and East Syrian (Nestorian) schools — Edessa, Nisibis, Reshaina, the monasteries of northern Mesopotamia — taught a curriculum in which Greek logic and Galenic medicine, in Syriac dress, were the higher studies; the translators of the seventh and eighth centuries, Athanasius of Balad and Jacob of Edessa among them, revised the older versions toward ever closer fidelity to the Greek. By the time the Abbasids founded Baghdad in 762, there existed, within a few days' journey of the new capital, a bilingual scholarly class that had been translating exactly the books Baghdad would want, into exactly the intermediate language Baghdad would start from, for two hundred years. Gundeshapur and Harran: Two Nodes of the Bridge Two places name the bridge's ends. Gundeshapur , in Khuzistan in south-western Persia, was a Sasanian royal foundation with a famous medical tradition: a hospital and teaching centre, staffed heavily by East Syrian Christians, where Greek medicine in Syriac transmission met Persian and Indian practice. Its great family, the Bakhtīshūʿ , supplied court physicians to the early Abbasid caliphs — Jibrīl ibn Bakhtīshūʿ was summoned to Baghdad by Hārūn al-Rashīd — and thereby carried the Syriac medical tradition physically into the caliphal palace, where it became one of the translation movement's engines: a court physician who reads his Galen in Syriac is a standing argument for Galen in Arabic. Harran , in the north, was the bridge's other kind of node: a pagan Hellenophone city — its Sabians, as the Arabic sources call them, kept a Greek astral religion and a Greek philosophical curriculum alive under Islamic rule — and the home of Thābit ibn Qurra (836–901), the movement's greatest mathematical translator, whose family carried the Harranian line into the tenth century (Section X). The companion article Harran and Gundeshapur gives both nodes their full dossiers, including the cautions: Gundeshapur's later legend of a full-blown university is, like the Bayt al-Ḥikma's, an inflation the sources do not support, and it is filed there at its real strength. // THE BRIDGE, STATED AT CATALOGUE STRENGTH // The Syriac bridge is documented for medicine, logic, and philosophy by surviving translations and by Ḥunayn's own catalogue of his Syriac predecessors. For alchemy specifically, the Syriac evidence is narrower — a documented body of Syriac alchemical treatises, Zosimos among them, in late manuscripts — and this archive states it at that strength in the Greco-Roman Transmission article (§X) and the Egyptology division's Zosimos dossier. Nothing in the present article requires the alchemical bridge to have been wider than the evidence shows. The movement's general machinery — Syriac first, Arabic second — is what alchemy demonstrably travelled on; the size of its own baggage is a separate question, answered elsewhere in the archive and not enlarged here. There were other roads in, and a complete account names them so that the Syriac bridge is not mistaken for the whole map. Persian material — astronomical tables, astrological doctrine, courtly and administrative literature — entered Arabic from Middle Persian, sometimes through the same court circles; the early Abbasid translation effort under al-Manṣūr drew heavily on Persian as well as Greek exemplars, and the caliph's astrologers, Nawbakht and Māshāʾallāh among them, worked in that Persianate tradition. Indian astronomy and medicine arrived too, famously in the Sindhind tradition of Brahmagupta's astronomy, rendered into Arabic in the 770s. And Greek books themselves were physically obtainable: the Abbasid world bordered Byzantium along a frontier that was crossed by embassies, ransomed prisoners, merchants, and — Section IV's subject — deliberate manuscript-buying missions. But for the Greek scientific corpus proper, the road that mattered ran through Syriac. It ran through Syriac because the men who could walk it were already there. d. 536 SERGIUS OF RESHAINA The Greek-to-Syriac scientific translation practice founded: Galen in bulk, Aristotle's Categories , Porphyry. The bridge's first pier. 7th–8th c. THE SYRIAC SCHOOLS REVISE Athanasius of Balad, Jacob of Edessa, and their circles revise the Syriac versions toward close fidelity — the philological standard Baghdad will inherit. 762 BAGHDAD FOUNDED Al-Manṣūr builds his round capital on the Tigris, within reach of the Syriac scholarly world of Mesopotamia and of Gundeshapur's physicians. 770s THE SINDHIND Indian astronomy rendered into Arabic at al-Manṣūr's court — proof, early in the reign, that the capital meant to import the sciences of every predecessor civilisation, not Greece alone. III. Paper: The Material Precondition A translation movement is, among other things, a manufacturing problem. Hundreds of long technical books had to be copied, collated, corrected, re-copied, and shelved — and the writing material of the eighth-century world was equal to that problem only in one place. Parchment, the Mediterranean standard, is prepared animal skin: a single large codex consumes a flock, and its cost sets a hard ceiling on how many books a society can afford to make. Papyrus, the Egyptian standard, is cheap but brittle, disliked for codices, and a regional monopoly. Paper — rag paper, made from macerated linen and hemp fibre, sized and burnished — broke the ceiling. It was cheap enough to copy on speculatively, durable enough for a working library, and manufacturable anywhere water and rags were available. The translation movement and the paper economy grew up together in Baghdad, and neither is fully intelligible without the other. The traditional account of paper's arrival runs through Central Asia. Papermaking was a Chinese technology, centuries old by the time it moved west; the Arabic sources connect its transmission to the Muslim victory at Talas in 751 , after which Chinese papermakers — prisoners, in the usual telling — are said to have established the craft at Samarkand , whose paper became a famous export. The modern caution belongs in the text, not the margin: paper was known in Central Asia before Talas, and the prisoner story has the shape of a foundation anecdote; what is not in dispute is the sequence that matters. Samarkand paper circulated in the eastern Islamic lands in the later eighth century, and in 794–95 a paper mill was established at Baghdad itself, an initiative the sources associate with the Barmakid vizier al-Faḍl ibn Yaḥyā. Within a generation the Abbasid administration was shifting its own paperwork onto paper; within two, Baghdad had a booksellers' and copyists' quarter — the market of the warrāqūn , the stationer-copyists — whose trade is the physical substrate of everything the Fihrist catalogues. WHAT PAPER MADE CHEAP Drafts and working copies. Collation — the movement's core method (Section VIII) — requires several copies of the same work open at once, corrected against each other and discarded or re-copied as the text improves. On parchment that workflow is a luxury. On paper it is a routine. WHAT PAPER MADE POSSIBLE A book market. Private patrons (Section IV) could commission translations because the finished product — a paper codex — cost a fraction of its parchment equivalent; scholars could own working libraries; a bookseller like Ibn al-Nadīm could spend a lifetime cataloguing a literature that physically existed in thousands of copies. The point deserves one more turn, because it is easy to file paper as background colour. It is not background; it is a load-bearing precondition, and the comparison proves it. Byzantium possessed the Greek books, the Greek language, and a continuous scholarly tradition — and produced, in these same centuries, a respectable but modest copying culture, parchment-bound and court-centred. Baghdad possessed fewer Greek books and no native Greek scholarship at all — and out-copied, out-translated, and within two centuries out-composed the empire that owned the originals. The difference was not talent. It was demand organised as patronage (Section IV) multiplied by a writing material cheap enough to meet the demand. When the Latin West's turn came in the twelfth century, it too would wait on its material base: the Toledo translations circulated first on parchment, in a thin stream, and flooded only as paper mills spread through Christian Spain and Italy. Translation movements run on paper the way armies run on roads. // A DATING CAUTION // The Baghdad mill's date is given as 794–95 in the standard literature, on the Arabic sources' association of the foundation with al-Faḍl ibn Yaḥyā's governorship and the Barmakid ascendancy. Like the Talas story, it is a reported date, not a document-dated one, and this article gives it as the tradition's date. The archaeology of early Islamic paper — surviving dated documents and codices — supports the broader claim beyond serious dispute: paper was in administrative and book use in Iraq by the early ninth century. Paper also changed what a translation was . A parchment culture copies monuments; a paper culture copies working texts, and expects to copy them again. The Arabic versions of Galen and Aristotle were not made once and frozen: they were made, revised, re-made by a second translator, epitomised, commented, and re-copied in each form — the version-history that Section XI traces for whole corpora. That restless textual economy, in which no version is final because another copy is always affordable, is the movement's native element. It is also, not incidentally, the economy in which the Arabic alchemical corpus would grow: the Jābir corpus's hundreds of treatises, endlessly re-collected and re-attributed, are a paper phenomenon as surely as the Galen translations are. IV. Patronage: Caliphs, Viziers, Physicians, and Private Money Translation is skilled labour, and skilled labour is paid. The second precondition of the movement — after the Syriac bridge and beside the paper — is a patronage market deep and various enough to employ translators for ten generations. Gutas's social-movement framing (Section I) is, in large part, a claim about this market: that it was never a single caliphal budget line, but a whole economy of buyers, each purchasing translation for their own reasons. This section walks the market's tiers. The Caliphs Caliphal patronage opens the story, on the standard account, under al-Manṣūr (r. 754–775), the capital's founder, whose court imported Persian and Indian astronomy and the astrologers to work it, and under whom the first state-sponsored renderings of Greek material — much of it arriving through Persian and Syriac channels — were made. Under Hārūn al-Rashīd (r. 786–809) the court's medical establishment, headed by the Bakhtīshūʿ physicians from Gundeshapur, deepened the demand for Galen. Under al-Maʾmūn (r. 813–833) caliphal patronage reached its celebrated height: translation was folded into the caliph's broader ideological programme — the promotion of rational inquiry, the contest with Byzantium for the Greek inheritance, embassies and missions after Greek manuscripts — and the Bayt al-Ḥikma of Section V belongs to his reign and his successors'. The famous story that al-Maʾmūn was set on this course by a dream in which Aristotle appeared to him and defined the good is preserved in the Arabic sources and repeated in the Fihrist ; it is filed here as what it is — the court's own foundation story for a policy, evidence for how the policy wished to be remembered, not for how it began. The policy itself predates the dreamer and outlasts him: al-Mutawakkil (r. 847–861), no one's candidate for a philosopher-caliph, was Ḥunayn's patron and employer, and translation continued under caliphs who cared for it and under caliphs who merely paid the court physicians who did. The Viziers: The Barmakids Between caliph and translator stood the administrators, and the first great ministerial patrons were the Barmakids , the Persian vizieral family who ran the empire under Hārūn al-Rashīd until their fall in 803. Yaḥyā ibn Khālid al-Barmakī and his sons al-Faḍl and Jaʿfar sponsored translation from Persian and Indian sources, patronised the court's physicians and astrologers, and are credited by the tradition with the Baghdad paper mill of Section III — a fitting emblem of their role: the Barmakids built infrastructure. Their patronage also set the pattern that outlived them. In a court where advancement ran through the vizier's salon, sponsoring a translation was a legible act of magnificence and ideological alignment; every subsequent ministerial household — the Ṭāhirids, the Banū al-Furāt, the Buyid-era viziers of the tenth century — inherited the expectation that a great man's court contained translators the way it contained poets. The Court Physicians The market's most reliable buyers were its doctors. Medicine was the one Greek science whose utility no patron needed explained, and the great medical households — the Bakhtīshūʿ above all, Nestorian Christians from Gundeshapur who served as caliphal physicians across seven generations — were patrons, translators, and commissioners of translation in one. A court physician's standing depended on his Galen; his Galen depended on the Syriac versions he inherited and the Arabic versions he caused to be made; his rivals at court were other physicians whose Galen might be better. The translation of medicine therefore had what no other field quite matched: a professional guild with money, court access, and a permanent competitive motive to fund better versions. Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq's career (Section VI) was made inside this economy — he was a physician first, the caliph al-Mutawakkil's doctor, and his translation enterprise was the medical profession's own infrastructure project. Private Patrons: The Banū Mūsā The market's most instructive buyers were private. The Banū Mūsā — the brothers Muḥammad, Aḥmad, and al-Ḥasan, sons of Mūsā ibn Shākir — were ninth-century Baghdad's model scholarly patrons: themselves accomplished mathematicians and engineers (their Book of Ingenious Devices is a landmark of Arabic mechanics), wealthy at court, and systematic purchasers of translation. The Fihrist reports — and the report is given here as a report, at the strength of a catalogue's testimony — that the brothers spent on the order of five hundred dinars a month on translation, maintained translators including Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, Ḥubaysh, and Thābit ibn Qurra on salary, and sent manuscript-buying missions into Byzantine territory to acquire Greek books their library lacked. Whether the figure is exact matters less than what its preservation shows: contemporaries understood translation as a salaried industry with running costs, foreign procurement, and competing employers, and they kept the accounts in round, boastful numbers because the spending itself was the prestige. Viziers The Barmakids (Yaḥyā, al-Faḍl, Jaʿfar); later vizieral households Persian and Indian translation; court science; infrastructure — the paper mill is the tradition's emblem of Barmakid patronage. Court physicians The Bakhtīshūʿ family; Ibn Māsawayh's circle Galen and Hippocrates, in Syriac and then in Arabic; the professional library of the caliphal medical establishment. Private patrons The Banū Mūsā brothers Mathematics, astronomy, mechanics; salaried translators; manuscript missions to Byzantium — translation as a private research institute. Scholars themselves Al-Kindī's circle; the translators' own commissions Philosophy above all: al-Kindī (d. c. 870), the first philosopher of the Arabs, maintained a translation circle whose versions served his own philosophical programme. Read the table as a market and the movement's resilience stops being mysterious. A single patron's death, disgrace, or change of taste — the Barmakids' fall in 803 is the type case — closed one purse and left the others open; translators moved between employers, taking their skills and their half-finished versions with them. The demand, moreover, was self-renewing: every translated book created readers who wanted the books it cited. Galen sends you to Hippocrates; Aristotle sends you to Plato and to his commentators; Ptolemy sends you to Euclid, and Euclid to Apollonius and Archimedes. The curriculum itself was a subscription that renewed by reading. What finally wound the movement down (Section XV) was not a failure of patronage but the demand's satisfaction — a different ending, with a different moral. V. The Bayt al-Ḥikma at Its Real Evidentiary Strength Every account of the translation movement must sooner or later walk through a famous door: the Bayt al-Ḥikma , the House of Wisdom at Baghdad. Popular accounts walk through it into a vast research institute — a university before universities, with departments, an observatory, a faculty of translators working in organised schools, and al-Maʾmūn presiding like a chancellor. This section walks through the same door at the speed the evidence permits. What stands on the other side is smaller, later-attested, and — stated plainly — more interesting: a caliphal library and translation bureau of a type the Islamic world inherited from Sasanian Persia, whose real history shows how the movement actually organised its centre, and whose modern inflation shows how easily a famous name becomes a container for everything a period is admired for. What Is Attested The attestations, assembled in Françoise Balty-Guesdon's study of the Bayt al-Ḥikma in the Arabic sources ( Arabica 39, 1992) — the corrective investigation on which modern caution rests — are these. An institution called the Bayt al-Ḥikma, or described as the caliph's khizāna (treasury, storehouse) of books of wisdom, existed at the Abbasid court. It functioned as a library : a place where books — Persian books first, on the earlier evidence, and the Greek scientific translations as the movement produced them — were kept, copied, and consulted. Translation work was associated with it: it served as a translation bureau in the modest, accurate sense that translators worked under its auspices and its holdings supplied their exemplars. And it had named heads. The sources name Salm — a Persian courtier of al-Maʾmūn's reign, associated with translation from Persian and with the library's direction — and after him Sahl ibn Hārūn (died 830), a Persian secretary and man of letters, as the institution's director under al-Maʾmūn. An institution with a library, a bureau's function, and a named director in the sources is a real institution. That much, the record carries. What Is Not Attested The record does not carry the rest of the popular picture, and the corrective scholarship — Balty-Guesdon's source-study, and Gutas's treatment in Greek Thought, Arabic Culture , which places the Bayt al-Ḥikma in its Sasanian institutional lineage — is plain about the gap. No source describes lecture halls, a curriculum, a student body, degrees, or departments. No source makes the Bayt al-Ḥikma the movement's headquarters in the sense that the great translators worked there as its staff: Ḥunayn's enterprise (Sections VI–VIII) was his own, funded by the patrons of Section IV, and its association with the House is a later tidiness, not a documented employment. The observatory sometimes attached to the institution belongs to al-Maʾmūn's separate astronomical programme — the observations at Baghdad's Shammāsiyya quarter and on Mount Qāsiyūn at Damascus — which the sources treat as its own undertaking. And the very phrase's grandeur misleads: a bayt al-ḥikma is a house of the books of wisdom — a royal library on the Sasanian model, where the Persian kings had kept their dynastic and scientific archives — before it is anything else. The early Abbasid institution was, on the evidence, substantially a Persian-style court library that the Greek translation movement grew around and through. // THE DISPUTE, STATED WITH POSITIONS NAMED // The maximal picture — House of Wisdom as research institute and proto-university, coordinating the movement — is the picture of older popular and some older scholarly literature, built by aggregating everything al-Maʾmūn's court did with books under the institution's one famous name. The corrective picture (Balty-Guesdon 1992; Gutas 1998): the sources attest a caliphal library with translation activity and named directors — Salm, then Sahl ibn Hārūn — modelled on the Sasanian royal book-store; the institute picture is an inflation not supported by the sources. This article's position follows the corrective, and states the institution at the corrective's strength throughout. The movement does not need the inflation: a translation economy distributed across the whole patronage market of Section IV is a larger and truer marvel than any single building. Why did the inflation happen? Three causes, each instructive. First, the name is magnificent, and magnificent names attract contents the way the name of Hermes attracted treatises. Second, later Arabic usage itself broadened the term — other courts and other centuries founded their own houses of wisdom, most famously the Fatimid Dār al-Ḥikma at Cairo (founded 1005), which did have something closer to a teaching function, and the Cairo institution's profile has been read back into Baghdad's. Third, modern admiration wanted an address. A social movement is hard to put on a postcard; a House can be drawn, modelled, and opened by a caliph in a single scene. The archive's rule applies to institutions as to texts: give the evidence at its real strength, and let the real thing be interesting enough. A palace library whose shelves filled, within two generations, with the translated science of three civilisations — Persian statecraft and astronomy, Indian mathematics, and the Greek corpus arriving volume by volume from the translators' workshops — whose director was a Persian man of letters and whose readers included the men remaking Arabic thought: that house needs no departments invented for it. // THE DIRECTORS, AS NAMED // Salm (fl. under al-Maʾmūn): courtier associated in the sources with the Bayt al-Ḥikma's direction and with translation from Persian; the Fihrist connects his name with versions of Aristotelian material as well. Sahl ibn Hārūn (died 830): Persian secretary, author of works on statecraft and the famous Book of the Tigress and the Fox , named as the House's director under al-Maʾmūn. The succession of two Persian secretaries at the head of the caliph's book-store is itself the Sasanian lineage made visible. One last precision. To deflate the Bayt al-Ḥikma is not to deflate al-Maʾmūn's court, whose patronage of astronomy, geography, and translation was real and lavish — the world map commissioned under him, the meridian measurements, the embassies after Greek books. It is to locate that patronage where the sources locate it: in the court as a whole, its library among its instruments, its translators mostly employed elsewhere. The movement's centre of gravity was never a building. It was a labour market and a library network, and its greatest single enterprise was not the caliph's at all. It was a Christian physician's from al-Ḥīra, and it is time to meet him. VI. Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq: The Man and the Circle Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq (809–873) is the translation movement's centre of gravity: the most productive translator of the age, the methodologist who described the work from inside, and the head of a family workshop whose versions of Galen and Aristotle set the standard every later translator measured himself against. The biographical tradition on Ḥunayn is rich — he is a hero of the Arabic biographical dictionaries — and correspondingly embroidered; this section gives the documented outline, flags the embroidery where it is famous, and reserves the method for Sections VII–VIII, where Ḥunayn's own document carries the weight. He was born in 809 at al-Ḥīra , the old Arab Christian city of southern Iraq, an East Syrian — Nestorian — Christian whose first languages were Arabic and Syriac and whose Greek had to be acquired as a deliberate professional act. The biographers tell the acquiring as a story: the young Ḥunayn, come to Baghdad to study medicine under the great physician Yūḥannā ibn Māsawayh , asks too many questions, is dismissed by his exasperated teacher — in the anecdote's sharpest form, with a contemptuous word about the money-changers' sons of al-Ḥīra — disappears for years, and returns with perfect Greek, reciting Homer to his astonished former master. The story is an anecdote, shaped like a parable of the translator's vocation, and it is filed here as one. What stands behind it is plausible and sufficient: Ḥunayn spent years acquiring Greek to a standard no contemporary matched — the biographical tradition sends him to the lands of the Byzantines, and his own Risāla shows him travelling in search of Greek manuscripts through Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt — and he built his career on the conjunction nobody else could offer: a physician's training, a Syriac schoolman's formation, and a Hellenist's Greek. The career that followed made him the age's indispensable man. He served as physician to the caliph al-Mutawakkil ; he survived the court intrigues that destroyed lesser favourites — the biographical dictionaries relish his refusal, at mortal risk, to compound a poison for the caliph, and his imprisonment and restoration — and he died in 873, by the tradition's account the most honoured translator of his century.
